China is entering the 15th Five-Year Plan (2026–2030) with a rare explicit number on consumption. In July, the State Council approved the Expansion of Consumption 15th Five-Year Plan, setting a quantitative target: social retail sales of consumer goods around RMB 60 trillion by 2030. For a country that has spent post-COVID years trying to reflate domestic demand, that kind of headline number matters. It reads like a clear, unambiguous priority.
So many investors are asking the same thing: Is this the window where Beijing finally puts serious stimulus behind domestic consumption? A numeric target in a five-year plan can feel like the setup for a beta trade — especially when consumer equities already look depressed.
1/4 China’s consumption names are cheap but still unloved
The consumer staples and discretionary sectors remain deeply discounted at a 25–27% five-year percentile after a mild rebound, standing in sharp contrast to the CSI 300’s elevated 92.7% percentile. This stark valuation divergence clearly reflects how capital markets are pricing a K-shaped economic reality—buoyed by strong momentum in the “new economy”, specifically AI and data centers, while domestic consumption remains sluggish.
In a past Baiguan Pro issue, we highlighted how computing infrastructure and new energy leaders have been replacing traditional enterprises within the CSI 300. Consequently, the index itself has transformed into a much more accurate proxy for China’s emerging 'new economy.'
2/4 Does the RMB 60 trillion target mean massive stimulus is coming?
From 2025’s RMB 50.1 trillion (+3.7% YoY), reaching ~RMB 60 trillion by 2030 requires only about 3.7% CAGR. That is almost exactly the 2021–2025 post-COVID trend (~3.3%). The current H1 2026 run-rate of +1.3% would miss the target badly.
The target in the plan just asks China to keep its post-COVID trend: some improvement from today’s soft goods print is implied — but nothing like a boom. Cheap ≠ buyable beta.
3/4 Households are still spending on services
Although consumption of goods and staples is likely to remain sluggish (not a broad beta rebound), China is not in a total spending freeze. Service retail has maintained a mid-5% YoY growth band for a year. (As of 2025, per capita services consumption made up 46.1% of China’s total consumption.)
4/4 “Services” is not one trade: where is organic growth inside services — and how to express it?
Organic growth in the services sector is heavily concentrated in experiences, led by tourism consulting and leasing (+11.3%), as well as culture, sports, and leisure (+10.4%). Conversely, catering (+2.8%) is actually dragging the overall average down.
By “experiences,” I refer to high-engagement, in-person activities. This momentum is vividly captured by the surge in live performances (+28.3%) and museum tours (+24.6%) [*]. Inbound tourism has also rebounded strongly, driven by an expansion of visa-free arrivals that catalyzed a 30.6% year-over-year growth in visitor trips.
Other categories, such as education, are notably absent from the highlights. Given China’s demographic headwind of a declining population, I personally think education is unlikely to drive significant organic growth going forward.
This means that secondary-market expressions need to be selective. Frankly speaking, exact equity proxies for China’s “experience economy” are still quite elusive. To bridge this gap, we are taking a first cut at constructing a basket that best captures this interest-driven, experiential growth. Our basket spans OTAs, live-experience ticketing platforms, hotels, and digital discretionary categories like gaming and entertainment. More on this in our Baiguan Pro tier.
Ending notes: possible 2H catalysts for consumer names
Apart from longer-term themes, HK internet and e-commerce giants could see several positive catalysts in H2 this year as delivery wars quiet down and profit margins improve. Specifically, the commercial landing of AI and agentic applications could provide strong catalysts for upside given current depressed valuations.
For instance, the expansion of cloud services, Kuaishou’s Kling, Tencent’s WorkBuddy (which the company claims is China’s most used productivity AI agent by DAU), and the launch of agents within the WeChat ecosystem could all serve as positive catalysts for H2.

Real estate: activity broadens after the Chinese Spring Festival
Property viewings and transaction volumes are both tracking materially above their 2025 levels following the Spring Festival. Specifically, the transaction volume of second-hand homes has surpassed the peak following the 2023 Spring Festival, when a surge was driven by pent-up demand from COVID.
The recovery of the second-hand home transaction also seems even across city tiers:
The inventory level also improved materially across all city tiers, albeit at different paces. “Charts of the Week” is Baiguan’s series that features key data points to help you quickly grasp the general state of affairs in China in just a few minutes. We handpick the highlights of the data charts from a variety of sources, analyzing and delivering insights trusted by 100+ top institutional and corporate clients worldwide at BigOne Lab. Don’t forget to subscribe before you continue reading!
China’s Jan & Feb prints were improving across the board
Inflation: In January–February 2026, China’s CPI rose 0.8% year-on-year, and Core CPI hit 1.3% — the strongest reading since January 2023. PPI also showed encouraging signs at the factory gate, with industrial producer prices rising for five consecutive months on a month-on-month basis.
Spring Festival spending held up well, with services standing out. We covered this in detail in a previous post.
The key question: Is this organic or policy-driven?
This is where the honest read gets more nuanced. Much of the consumption uplift to date has been policy-assisted — trade-in subsidies, vouchers, and a record-long nine-day holiday that pulled spending forward.
The 2026 Government Work Report set a GDP target of “4.5% - 5%”—realistic but unexciting. The report prioritizes technology and new productive forces. The report prioritizes technology and new productive forces. Among its measures, China plans to issue RMB 250 billion in ultra-long-term special government bonds to support trade-in subsidies for consumer goods and to establish RMB 100 billion in fiscal-financial coordinated funds to boost domestic demand. To put that in perspective, these measures amount to less than 0.2% of GDP — hardly a massive fiscal stimulus. There is also no large-scale direct transfer to households on the table.
The elephant in the room: Is the strong Jan & Feb spending organic, and will it continue?
To put this into perspective, in today’s Charts of the Week, we return to two key pillars of domestic consumption: the wealth effect (real estate) and income expectations (salary).
Our January–February proprietary data on both fronts points in a positive direction.
Real estate: Our tracking of China’s online real estate platforms shows the second-hand housing market stabilizing under policy support, with transaction volumes in 90+ cities up 15% YoY. Viewing activity also picked up, with week-on-week viewings across 80+ sample cities rising 15%, reflecting strong buyer interest and a recovering market.
Salary: Average salaries growth across online recruitment platforms are gradually recovering, rising from near-zero in 2024 to around 4–5% in early 2026. This steady wage growth supports household purchasing power, suggesting consumption could continue at a measured pace.
Importantly, the worst of the real estate bubble’s impact on the workforce appears to be behind us, as we covered earlier:
Additionally, in select discretionary categories, we are already seeing what looks like organic spending growth that isn’t purely subsidy-driven. That is the signal worth watching. For example, we wrote about the Sports & Health sector yesterday and will follow up with more examples in future posts.
One additional tailwind: China sits in a different risk bucket than the rest of Asia
The escalation of the Iran conflict has rattled Asian markets, but not all of Asia is equally exposed. China actually sits in a more defensive position, holding large strategic and commercial oil reserves that help cushion short-term disruptions. It has also spent years diversifying its supply toward Russia and Central Asia.
In contrast, Japan relies on the Middle East for roughly 90% of its crude oil imports. South Korea sources about 70% of its crude from the region and routes over 95% of that through the Strait of Hormuz.
Market reactions reflect this. Compared to other Asian markets, China has seen a comparatively modest decline since the conflict began.
A-shares also carry a structural cushion that most markets lack: the “national team” actively intervenes when needed, reducing correlation to external shocks in ways that are hard to replicate elsewhere in the region.
Therefore, I am more constructive on Chinese markets, especially the on-shore market at this particular time.
We will continue tracking real estate and job market data — crucial macro datapoints for our paid subscribers in future posts.

text:
Last year, around Spring Festival, DeepSeek R1 was launched and became the sole topic that the whole nation (and the whole world) fixated on for a while. As China draws close to the Spring Festival this year, the major AI players are all geared up for showtime once again. Under such a context, it’s no wonder that China’s AI industry has been filled with drama in the last few weeks.
First, Alibaba’s Qwen triggered a nationwide frenzy by offering “tea freedom” through a massive milk tea subsidy, sending its Qwen AI app to the top of the charts and creating messes at some milk tea shops as delivery people scrambled for orders.
Not to be outdone, Yuanbao, Tencent’s own AI chatbot, launched a billion-yuan red packet campaign, hoping to recreate the success of WeChat Pay. However, the plot twisted when WeChat, the centerpiece of the Tencent family of products, abruptly restricted the sharing of these promotional links to curb spam and “induced sharing.”
ByteDance’s Seedance 2.0, on the other hand, stunned the whole world by its mesmerizing audio-video co-generation technology, strong character consistency, and director-level scene transition, effectively giving every social media user their own Hollywood-quality production studio.
And Spring Festival has not even started!
At this point, I want to put down some preliminary observations here, if only to make a mental mark for the record amid these rapid, crazy changes that are unfolding at this very moment.
Observation 1: The market rewards the cutting edge, but penalizes the old playbook
If it were a decade ago, Tencent’s Yuanbao red packet campaign would have excited the market. After all, the whole red packet playbook was exactly what ushered WeChat Pay into success a decade ago. However, this time, the campaign has caused much more doubt than excitement. As a result, Tencent’s share price has already dropped more than 15% year-to-date at the time of writing this piece.
Nor is the market very excited about BABA’s milk tea giveaways either. Its stock price has traded sideways despite its Qwen app almost becoming the most actively used AI app in China within an extremely short period of time.
Contrast that with Zhipu AI, believed to be behind Pony Alpha, an open-source coding model that many developers compare to Claude Code in capability. Zhipu also announced its GLM-5 model just now, which sent its shares almost quadrupling only a month after its IPO.
The divergence is striking. In this decade, the old playbook no longer inspires. The market is clearly looking for genuine frontier capability, not user growth engineered by subsidies. Merely having more users, if those users are acquired through incentives rather than through technological excitement, is heavily discounted.
Observation 2: The real market leader is not tradable
It’s also a pity that the company that is arguably leading China’s AI race is not listed.
ByteDance, which has Doubao, currently has the most popular AI chatbot in China and arguably the highest user stickiness. Many users already treat Doubao as a daily companion, almost in the sense portrayed in the film Her. While Qwen may be close in daily active users, much of that still appears subsidy-driven. Doubao’s user base feels more organic and durable, at least at this stage.
At the same time, ByteDance’s Seedance 2.0 has become the global leader in video generation since its recent debut. ByteDance’s trial with AI-native smartphone also inspires imagination. (You can check out a product test of Doubao phone here made by Voice of Context, our partner newsletter.)
Yet ByteDance is not listed. Neither is Huawei, another important AI force.
As a result, even if one believes strongly in the long-term future of Chinese AI, the Hang Seng Tech Index may unfortunately not be the most direct way to express that view at this moment. Core constituents such as Alibaba and Tencent have been weak, and the index has traded sideways.
Observation 3: The great divergence of how AI would impact other industries
As much as there is a domestic divergence in how old and new forces tackle AI, internationally, a significant divergence is emerging in how markets interpret AI’s impact on other industries.
In the US, when Anthropic or Google launched a new model, software and business service stocks sold off sharply. Hundreds of billions in market value could be erased in days. The dominant narrative is that the old industries are at risk of decimation.
In China, sentiment looks different. When major breakthroughs in video generation like SeeDance appear, online literature, film-making, and content platform stocks rally. Even if China’s software sector has not been exceptionally strong, it has not collapsed in the same way as in the West either. And milk tea brands like Guming and Mixue are emerging as the biggest net beneficiaries of Alibaba’s generous subsidies.
Why?
One reason is industry maturity. China’s SaaS industry never truly developed into a large, standardized, high-margin sector comparable to the US. Much of the market remains project-based and customized. Ironically, that lack of maturity could prove resilient in an AI era. Companies built around implementation and consulting may still be needed, while benefiting from lower AI-driven costs.
As for the entertainment industry, China does not yet have a Hollywood-sized creative market to disrupt. When AI improves content creation, investors focus on new possibilities rather than on the elimination of entrenched incumbents.
There may also be a deeper cultural and political layer. In the current Chinese context, it is difficult to imagine technology wiping out an entire industry overnight without at least paying some price. The concept of common prosperity has shaped expectations around these things.
I do not claim to have a definitive explanation here. But this divergence itself is worth watching.
Observation 4: Trust first, commerce later?
The next major milestone in AI, after coding, may be agentic commerce: how AI changes how people transact and live.
Alibaba is positioning itself as the leading global experimenter in this space. As the operator of one of the largest e-commerce ecosystems in the world, it is pushing consumers to shop in an AI-native way earlier than anyone else.
The results so far are mixed, however.
When I tried shopping through Qwen’s agent, the experience proved that AI-mediated shopping is technically feasible. But beyond that proof of concept, it did not feel revolutionary. Which leads me to think that chatting back and forth with a bot to find something to buy may not be the final form of commerce.
By classic internet logic, this is not a problem. “Move fast and break things” has been the motto for the industry since its very beginning. Early user experience can be rough as long as feedback loops are strong and iteration speed is fast.
But it may be too premature to push agentic commerce too aggressively, which leads to a more fundamental question: what do people actually look for when they shop?
For purely utilitarian purchases, such as recurring household goods, automated agents make sense. But much of consumption is not utilitarian. For many high-value purchases, the experience itself is part of the product: walking through a store, browsing shelves, and discovering items serendipitously. I don’t believe these are inefficiencies to be eliminated. For many, shopping is not just a means, but an end in itself.
A better model, intuitively and logically, would be to build trust first.
If users see their AI agents as friends, advisors, or companions, they will naturally ask them for shopping recommendations. Commerce then becomes an extension of trust, not vice versa.
If this theory is true, then agentic commerce does become mainstream, ByteDance, again, may still capture the largest upside. Doubao already has user trust and stickiness. Combined with Douyin’s e-commerce ecosystem, all the essential pieces are in place.
Tencent may also be underestimated. Even if it currently lags in model leadership, it possesses vast behavioral data to eventually build a trustworthy AI virtual assistant as well as a deeply integrated WeChat mini-program commerce ecosystem within to build a complete e-commerce experience.
Alibaba has limited social advantages and does not control the most popular AI companion app right now. It is therefore logical that it plays to its core strength: commerce. Whether that will work is questionable, but it just does not have many alternative strategic choices.
Observation 5: 2026 as the year of mass adoption
The upcoming Spring Festival holiday is shaping up to be another holiday about AI. Chinese AI companies are clearly timing product releases around this period, when users are at home, traveling, and experimenting with new apps.
It is not yet clear who will ultimately win. What is increasingly clear, however, is that 2026 is shaping up to be a year of mass AI adoption in China.
This adoption will go far beyond chatbot novelty. By the end of 2026, it is highly likely that a majority of urban consumers will have completed at least one transaction through an AI agent. Coders will routinely use domestic Chinese coding agents. Video creators will rely on AI-native tools as a standard workflow.
This unprecedented mass experimentation and mass adoption of AI applications, with all of the potential impact and consequences, will provide meaningful lessons for the whole world to see.
This should be our last post before the Spring Festival commences.
Finally, to all our readers, thank you for staying with us through another turbulent year in markets. May the Year of the Horse bring you momentum, milestones, and more exciting breakthroughs in your work and in your life!

text:
When the U.S.-China trade war began in 2018, many people understood it mainly as a tariff war. The United States raised tariffs, China retaliated; the United States raised them again, and China responded again. News coverage revolved around a few numbers: 10 percent, 25 percent, 50 percent, and how many billions of dollars’ worth of goods had been placed on tariff lists. At the time, the basic unit of U.S.-China trade friction was the product, and the main weapon was the tariff. Eight years later, that understanding is no longer enough.
On August 31, 2026, the U.S. House of Representatives passed the Protecting American Industry and Labor from International Trade Crimes Act (《保护美国工业和劳工免受国际贸易犯罪侵害法》). On the surface, the bill does not look particularly dramatic. It does not announce a new round of tariffs on China, nor does it blacklist any particular Chinese company. Instead, it calls for a dedicated mechanism within the Criminal Division of the U.S. Department of Justice, with additional prosecutors and staff assigned to investigate tariff and duty evasion, import and export violations, smuggling, trade-based money laundering, and other trade-related crimes. The House passed the measure by voice vote, and its sponsors and supporters included both Republicans and Democrats.
But I think the importance of the bill lies precisely in the fact that it does not look dramatic. U.S. economic policy toward China is moving from a “trade war” toward an “enforcement war.”
By “enforcement war,” I do not mean that the tariff war is over. Quite the opposite. The tariffs remain, as do export controls, industrial subsidies, investment restrictions, and efforts to restructure supply chains. What has changed is that the United States is beginning to place behind these rules an increasingly complete system of police, prosecutors, courts, and evidence. In the past, the message to Chinese companies was mainly this: you cannot sell these goods, you cannot buy these technologies, and you must pay more tax if these products enter the United States. Increasingly, the questions are different: Did you find a way around the rules? If you did, was it a crime? Who was involved? Where did the money go? Through which third country did the goods pass? Who signed the documents? Who knew who the ultimate customer was? That is a very different game.
The trade war that began in 2018 was fundamentally about changing prices. During Donald Trump’s first term, his administration took action against China under Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974 (《1974年贸易法》), with the Office of the United States Trade Representative using tariffs as one of its main tools. The Joe Biden administration did not dismantle that framework. After the four-year review completed in 2024, it retained most of the Section 301 tariffs and raised rates further on strategic products such as electric vehicles, semiconductors, solar cells, and critical minerals. Tariffs on Chinese electric vehicles rose to 100 percent, while some semiconductor and solar products were raised to 50 percent. Presidents changed and the language of policy changed, but the underlying direction—reducing dependence on Chinese supply chains and protecting strategic industries—did not.
That points to an important change: a tougher economic policy toward China is no longer simply the policy of one particular president. It is increasingly becoming part of the American political system itself.
A tariff war has an inherent weakness. Whenever there is a large enough price difference between markets, people will look for ways around it. If Chinese goods face high tariffs when shipped directly to the United States, some may consider routing them first through Vietnam, Mexico, Malaysia, or somewhere else. If a product is subject to anti-dumping duties, someone may try to change its customs classification. If a certain technology cannot be exported directly to China, someone may try to move it through intermediary companies, buyers in third countries, and complicated logistics networks. Of course, this does not mean that all third-country trade amounts to laundering a product’s origin, nor can every Chinese company be presumed to be breaking the law. Global supply chains are cross-border by nature. But from the perspective of American policymakers, the more rules there are, the greater the incentive to evade them; and the more evasion there is, the less sufficient it becomes simply to write new rules. Policy therefore moves naturally into a second stage: from building barriers to tracking down those who are trying to get around them.
That is what makes the August 31 bill worth watching. Under its provisions, the Justice Department would establish a specialized trade-crime mechanism within its Criminal Division, strengthen coordination across jurisdictions, and work with agencies including U.S. Customs and Border Protection and Homeland Security Investigations. The legislation also calls for greater capacity to investigate and prosecute trade crimes while allowing civil enforcement to proceed alongside criminal cases. The attorney general would be required to report annually to Congress on case numbers, prosecutions, and the use of funds. In other words, this is not a one-off crackdown. It is the creation of an institution.
Political science offers a useful way to judge whether a policy is becoming permanent: do not look only at what a president says. Look at whether the policy has a budget, personnel, institutions, and reporting requirements. Once there are dedicated prosecutors, annual appropriations, annual reports, and interagency coordination, the bureaucracy begins to acquire a life of its own. Prosecutors need cases. Agencies need performance measures. Congress wants data. Enforcement bodies must demonstrate their value. Policy begins to move from political rhetoric into routine administration. That is why this bill may ultimately matter more to Chinese companies than another tariff increase.
There is another detail that is easy to miss. The text of the bill itself does not say that it applies only to Chinese companies. Its definition of “trade-related crimes” is, in principle, universal. What puts China in the spotlight are the lawmakers promoting the bill and the House Select Committee on the Strategic Competition Between the United States and the Chinese Communist Party (美中战略竞争特别委员会). In its August 31 press release, the committee explicitly identified Chinese companies as the main target and accused them of tariff evasion, transshipment, smuggling, and trade-based money laundering.
That distinction matters. The United States is unlikely to write a law saying that Chinese companies are subject to Criminal Code A while American companies are subject to Criminal Code B. A more effective approach is to create rules that are formally universal and then direct investigative resources toward the targets policymakers care about most. The law may be universal, but enforcement resources can still have a direction. That is one reason modern state power can be more formidable than simple sanctions.
More important still, this new trade-crime mechanism is not the first time the United States has brought its competition with China into the criminal justice system. In 2023, the Justice and Commerce Departments created the Disruptive Technology Strike Force (“颠覆性技术打击力量”), focusing on advanced technology, export controls, and sanctions evasion. By the end of 2024, the task force had already supported a number of criminal cases involving export-control violations and smuggling connected to China, Russia, and Iran. In 2025 and 2026, the Justice Department announced a succession of cases involving the alleged illegal transfer of advanced AI chips, including cases in which controlled GPUs were said to have been routed to China through third countries. In March 2026, the department announced another case accusing individuals of attempting to ship controlled AI chips to China through Thailand. These remain criminal allegations, of course, and the defendants are legally presumed innocent unless and until convicted.
Two lines are now becoming visible. One is national-security enforcement: semiconductors, artificial intelligence, dual-use technologies, and export controls. The other is an emerging system of economic and trade enforcement: tariffs, rules of origin, transshipment, smuggling, trade-based money laundering, and false declarations. The 2026 bill deliberately excludes laws such as the Arms Export Control Act (《武器出口控制法》), the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (《国际紧急经济权力法》), and the Export Control Reform Act (《出口管制改革法》) from the main body of statutes covered by the new mechanism. That is not because these areas are unimportant, but because they already belong to a separate national-security enforcement system. The new bill is filling another gap: bringing ordinary trade violations more systematically into the machinery of criminal enforcement.
At that point, the outlines of an “enforcement war” become much clearer. In the past, a Chinese company dealing with the United States mainly had to ask three questions: How high are the tariffs? Can the product be sold? Can the technology be bought? In the future, it may need to ask three more: Where exactly did the goods come from? Where exactly did the money pass through? And will every document still stand up if an American prosecutor examines it several years from now?
That will change corporate behavior. A tariff is a cost, and costs can be calculated. If the tariff is 25 percent, a company can decide whether to raise prices, accept lower margins, change suppliers, or move production. Criminal risk is different. Once a case involves false customs declarations, smuggling, money laundering, or deliberate evasion of restrictions, a company is no longer facing only lower profits. It may face investigation, searches, asset seizures, heavy penalties, criminal prosecution, and even personal liability for executives. In one 2025 case involving tariffs on Chinese tungsten products, a U.S. importer agreed to pay $54.4 million to resolve allegations under the False Claims Act (《虚假申报法》) that it had evaded duties on imports from China. At the very least, the case shows that trade enforcement has already gone well beyond simply paying back unpaid customs duties.
The result for companies is straightforward: compliance costs will rise. In the past, a company might ask a supplier, “How much?” In the future, it will increasingly ask, “How can you prove it?” Certificates of origin, end users, beneficial ownership, shipping routes, the degree of processing in third countries, and payment accounts will all become more important. Banks, logistics companies, customs brokers, trading firms, and even accountants and lawyers will be drawn into this network. This is the biggest difference between a tariff war and an enforcement war. A tariff war mainly targets goods. An enforcement war begins to follow people, companies, money, documents, and supply chains.
Still, the opposite point also has to be made. The growing criminalization of trade disputes does not mean that the United States will necessarily achieve its industrial goals. Enforcement can raise the cost of evasion, but it cannot create factories by itself. Prosecutors can catch people who evade duties, but they cannot build semiconductor plants. Customs officials can investigate rules of origin, but they cannot solve the shortage of skilled workers in American shipbuilding. In its 2024 Section 301 review, the Office of the United States Trade Representative itself acknowledged that the economic effects of tariffs are complicated. They have encouraged some diversion of imports and diversification of supply chains and have benefited certain American producers, but retaliatory tariffs have also imposed costs on the United States.
So an “enforcement war” is not a cure-all. It addresses a different problem: once the United States has built increasingly high trade barriers, how can it keep those barriers from being easily circumvented?
Seen from this angle, U.S.-China economic relations are moving into a third stage. During the era of globalization, the basic question was: How can more Chinese goods enter the American market? After 2018, the question became: How can Chinese goods be made more expensive when they enter the United States? Now a third question is emerging: If the United States no longer wants certain goods, technologies, or capital to move in the old way, how does it know whether someone has found a way around the rules?
That is no longer simply trade policy. It requires customs officers, databases, financial intelligence, supply-chain tracking, prosecutors, courts, and sometimes cooperation from allies. The weapon of a trade war is the tariff schedule. The weapon of an enforcement war is the chain of evidence.
What Chinese companies may need to worry about most, then, is not whether the next tariff increase will be another 10 or 25 percentage points. The larger change is that the United States is trying to embed competition with China in its administrative procedures, criminal law, and bureaucratic institutions. Presidents can change. Tariffs can be negotiated. Agreements can be rewritten. But once an enforcement system has its own prosecutors, budget, databases, annual reports, and interagency networks, it often lasts much longer than a tariff schedule.
That is the most important thing about the shift from a “trade war” to an “enforcement war”: the United States is trying to turn economic competition with China from a policy of the president into a capability of the state.
If this trend continues, the most consequential battlegrounds in U.S.-China trade may no longer be limited to negotiating tables in Washington or tariff schedules at the border. They will increasingly be found in corporate ledgers, shipping-container routes, bank records, and court files. For China, the difficult question is changing with them. In the past, the most important task was to study what rules the United States was preparing to introduce. In the future, it will be just as important to understand how the United States intends to enforce them.

Recently, a letter said to have been written by a Chinese mother to her son studying overseas began circulating widely on the Chinese internet. Its title was strikingly blunt: Don’t Come Back. Go Make Your Way in the World.
The reports carrying the letter did not identify the mother, nor did they provide an original source that could be independently verified. But that uncertainty may itself point to something important. We may not know who wrote the letter, but the anxiety it expresses is real.
For many years, Chinese parents sending their children abroad tended to say some version of the same thing: study hard, learn what you can, and come home when you are finished. Now, suddenly, here was a mother saying the opposite: don’t come back. Don’t think in terms of “fallen leaves returning to their roots”; think instead of taking root wherever you land. Live where life suits you best. You do not have to remain the wandering child of some ancestral village. You can become a citizen of the world. She even tells her son that she hopes he will not come home next year, or the year after.
Why did those words touch such a nerve?
Because they gave voice to a question that many Chinese families have been asking quietly for years: after spending tens or even hundreds of thousands of dollars to send a child to university or graduate school in the United States, Britain, Canada, Australia, or elsewhere, should that child come back at all?
This is no longer simply a question about studying abroad. It has become a question of how to allocate the assets of a life.
The choices facing Chinese students overseas have changed several times over the past few decades. In the 1980s and 1990s, the difficult part was getting out. Winning a scholarship, securing a visa, and gaining admission to an American university were themselves major hurdles. China went through what people then called the “study-abroad fever.”
Later, as the Chinese economy expanded rapidly, multinational companies poured in, and the internet, real estate, finance, and the broader new economy boomed, another phenomenon appeared: the “sea-turtle” wave of returnees. Foreign degrees were still relatively scarce. Someone who studied in New York or London and returned to Beijing or Shanghai could often enjoy several advantages at once: the premium attached to an overseas degree, fluent English, and international experience.
Those conditions have changed.
China is expected to produce 12.7 million university graduates in 2026, 480,000 more than the year before. In July 2026, the urban unemployment rate among people aged sixteen to twenty-four, excluding students, reached 17.9 percent. The figure is partly seasonal because July is graduation season, and it should not be exaggerated. But competition for young people entering the labor market is unquestionably intense.
An overseas degree is no longer an asset that automatically appreciates. The reason is simple: once something becomes common, scarcity alone no longer gives it value. Employers ultimately ask more basic questions. What can you actually do? What problems can you solve? Is your field one we need? Beyond English and a diploma from a foreign university, what do you bring?
So it is not surprising that some parents have begun saying, “Don’t come back.”
But this is where the real problem begins. To move from “competition in China is brutal” to “life abroad must therefore be better” is itself a serious leap in logic.
Take the United States. In the 2024–25 academic year, there were still 265,919 Chinese students enrolled in American colleges and universities, making China the second-largest source of international students after India, although the number was down 4 percent from the previous year. New international student enrollment in the United States declined again in the fall of 2025. At the same time, participation in Optional Practical Training, or OPT, had previously risen sharply.
Taken together, these numbers tell a more complicated story. The United States continues to exert enormous educational and professional attraction, and many international graduates still want to stay and work. But both getting in and staying on have become more difficult.
One distinction matters above all: studying abroad, working abroad, and immigrating are three different things.
Admission to an American university does not guarantee an American job. OPT does not guarantee long-term legal status. Finding a job does not mean you will be able to remain permanently. International students must navigate not only the labor market, but visas, immigration status, policy shifts, and geopolitical uncertainty.
“Don’t come back” sounds wonderfully carefree. In practice, there is nothing carefree about it. First you need to find a job. Then you need to keep it. Then you need to settle your immigration status. After that come housing, health care, taxes, marriage, aging parents, children, and eventually the question of where you intend to grow old.
By the age of thirty-five, many people discover that what looked like a geographical question at twenty-three has slowly turned into a career question, then a family question, then an identity question, and finally something even more fundamental: Who am I, and where do I belong?
That is also why one of the most moving lines in the circulating letter—“Wherever the soil nourishes you, grow into a tree there”—is also one of the lines that deserves the most scrutiny.
Human beings are not trees.
A tree moved from one place to another needs soil, sunlight, and water. A person needs much more: language, friendship, marriage, professional networks, cultural familiarity, legal status, and a sense of belonging. More difficult still, our needs change over time. At twenty-five, a young person may care most about career opportunities. At thirty-five, a spouse and children may matter more. By forty-five, parents are aging. By sixty, the question may once again become: where do I actually want to spend the rest of my life?
There is therefore no single kind of “good soil” that can be measured by one indicator.
A high salary is good soil. Fast career advancement is good soil too. So are freedom, security, convenience, friends, proximity to parents, and good schools for one’s children. Different people assign different weights to these things.
What young people may need most today, then, is to free themselves from one habit inherited from earlier generations: the belief that they must decide, once and for all, where they belong.
For the generation before them, life was often a single line. You were born in one place, worked in another—or perhaps the same one—registered your household there, formed a family there, and very often died there. “Going abroad” and “coming home” therefore looked like opposite doors. Walking through one appeared to mean closing the other.
That is increasingly no longer the case.
Someone can be born in Beijing, attend university in Shanghai, go to graduate school in New York, work in Silicon Valley for several years, move to Singapore, and return to Hangzhou to start a company at thirty-five. Someone else may return to China at twenty-five and go abroad again at thirty-two. Some people work remotely for foreign companies while living in China. Others work for Chinese companies while spending most of their lives overseas.
What has changed is not simply that airplanes have become faster. Life itself has moved from a single track to multiple tracks.
In such a world, the most important skill is no longer choosing correctly once. It is preserving the ability to choose again.
Economics has a useful concept for this: option value. When the future is highly uncertain, a choice is valuable not only because of the return it offers today, but because of whether it preserves the possibility of making another choice tomorrow.
Applied to an overseas graduate, the logic is straightforward. If a twenty-three-year-old has just graduated from a foreign university and has a good job offer, staying for several years may make perfect sense. What that person gains is not merely a salary, but professional experience, language fluency, social networks, and the chance to understand another society from the inside. Deciding whether to return after several years of real experience is likely to be wiser than deciding, on graduation day and largely on emotion, where one should live for the next fifty years.
The reverse is equally true. If someone cannot find suitable work abroad, faces increasing difficulty over immigration status, and has better opportunities, family resources, or professional prospects in China, it makes little sense to remain overseas merely to prove that one is “international.”
Staying abroad is not victory.
Returning home is not defeat.
The more useful question is: Where can you build the greatest amount of capability that truly belongs to you?
This may be the most neglected point in the entire debate.
A semiconductor engineer, an AI researcher, an art-history PhD, a financial analyst, and a dentist are not answering the same question when they ask, “China or America?” Even two people in the same profession may arrive at different answers because their family backgrounds, personalities, language abilities, and tolerance for risk differ.
National averages cannot make personal decisions.
A high youth unemployment rate in China does not mean you personally cannot find an excellent job there. A high average salary in the United States does not mean you personally will be able to stay. Macroeconomic statistics describe millions of people. A life is lived by one person.
Reality, moreover, has not moved neatly in the direction of “everyone wants to leave.”
According to China’s Ministry of Education, 535,600 people who had studied overseas returned to China in 2025, 40,600 more than in 2024 and 120,000 more than in 2023. Since the beginning of China’s reform era, millions of Chinese students who completed their studies abroad have ultimately returned.
In other words, while people online are saying, “Whatever you do, don’t come back,” hundreds of thousands of people continue to arrive at Chinese airports each year with their suitcases.
There is no contradiction here.
What may really be changing in Chinese society is not that “people no longer love their country,” or that “people suddenly love it again.” It is something more important: individuals are becoming more accustomed to treating their own lives as their own.
That is a significant change.
For too long, we have moralized the geographical choices of young people. At one time, leaving the country could be condemned as worshipping the West. Later, returning home was praised as serving the motherland. Then, when someone chose not to return, people began describing it as “voting with their feet.”
But a twenty-four-year-old looking for a job does not need to carry such a heavy historical narrative on his or her shoulders.
Maybe that company is simply a better fit.
That can be reason enough.
By the same token, someone who leaves New York for Chengdu does not necessarily do so because of some sudden surge of patriotic feeling. Perhaps Chengdu offers a better job. Housing is cheaper. The parents are nearby. Friends are there. The hot pot is better.
None of those reasons is inferior to “fulfilling one’s grand ambition.” Life is made of precisely these things.
I would go further. A genuinely confident country should not spend its time asking young people why they do not come back.
It should ask: What would make them want to come back?
The difference between those two questions is only a few words, but the thinking behind them is completely different.
The first places responsibility on the young person: the country educated you, your parents paid for your schooling—why are you not coming home?
The second places responsibility where it also belongs: on society itself. Are our universities, companies, research institutions, salaries, housing, professional environment, and ways of life attractive enough that a young person who has seen the wider world would still choose to return?
Talent tends to move toward opportunity. That is one of the simplest lessons in thousands of years of human migration.
The United States did not attract so many world-class scientists because it constantly told foreigners that they ought to love America. It did so because, for a long time, it offered universities, laboratories, capital, markets, and opportunities for professional advancement. If China can offer better opportunities, it too will attract people back—and may even attract people who were never Chinese to begin with.
That is what real competition for talent looks like.
So when I return to that viral letter telling a son not to come home, what interests me most is not the phrase “don’t come back.” It is the change hidden behind it: a mother beginning to acknowledge that her child’s life is not the property of his parents.
Chinese families have long had a heavy sentence of their own: we sacrificed so much to send you abroad, so one day you must come home and take care of us. The letter tries to cut that cord. If the education parents give a child ultimately becomes a bond on which the child must pay annual interest in filial duty, then something about that education remains unfinished.
And yet I would not tell a child, as this mother does, “Don’t come back.”
Because that, too, is still making the decision for him.
A truly mature parent might say something simpler: Go out and have a look. If you can stay, see whether life there genuinely suits you. If you want to come home, do not treat coming home as failure. The world is large, and China is large too. The decision made by your twenty-five-year-old self does not have to bind the person you will be at seventy-five.
Being able to leave is a form of freedom. Being able to stay is a form of freedom. And being able to come back when you want to is a form of freedom too.
So yes, to return or not to return is a question.
But it should not be a multiple-choice question with only two answers.
For this generation, what may matter most is not finding a single, permanent homeland once and for all. It is being capable of building a life wherever one stands; going far without becoming afraid to return; and returning, when one does, not because every other door has closed.
A good family should not summon its children home through guilt. A good country should not demand the return of talent through moral obligation.
A place that is truly attractive does not need to call people home. They will come back on their own.

Moxin （心魔）
There is a concept called the “Liangjiazi Red Line.” You may not have heard of it. That is hardly surprising. The term was coined by Chinese internet users to describe a recurring pattern.
Liangjiazi is, however, a genuine historical term. It goes back at least to the Han dynasty. In those days, military recruitment took family background seriously. Sons of physicians and merchants, for example, were often excluded from regular military service. The army preferred young men from respectable, law-abiding households.
The Records of the Grand Historian introduces the famous general Li Guang with the words that he “joined the army as a liangjiazi to fight the Xiongnu.” In that era, these men were the backbone of the military and a source of honor to their families.
Soldiers received little in the way of regular pay, and often had to provide their own armor and weapons. Yet they fought fiercely. Why? Because they had something to go home to. Their families owned land. Their lives had prospects.
And this principle extends far beyond the army. Any system—a government, a company, an institution, almost anything—ultimately depends on a group of people who are dependable, conscientious and willing to do more than the bare minimum.
These are the people who generate what might be called a moral surplus. The veteran employee who checks the lights and water before leaving the office, even though nobody asked him to. The old security guard who hears a strange noise in the middle of the night and gets out of bed to investigate, even though no one will record it in his performance review. No one pays them for these extra acts. They do them because they feel responsible.
In today’s language, they are “running the system on love.”
Every organization also contains people who calculate every advantage and exploit every loophole. A few of them do not matter. Large systems can absorb a certain amount of opportunism. But only if there are enough conscientious people underneath, carrying the load. Those people are the load-bearing walls.
So where is the red line?
The red line is crossed when the system begins treating its load-bearing walls as free consumables. It assumes they can absorb endless wear without maintenance, and then keeps hammering away at them. One day the decent, dutiful people finally understand what is happening and decide they are done.
That is when the line has been crossed.
Everything may still look normal from the outside. In reality, the countdown has already begun.
Take Rome.
The Roman Republic did not dominate the Mediterranean simply because it had superior battle formations. Its real foundation was millions of small landowning farmers. They cultivated their fields in peacetime and, when war came, bought their own equipment and went off to fight. They fought hard because they had property, families and a stake in the republic.
Then Rome became too successful.
As conquest expanded, senatorial elites discovered a more profitable business model. They seized land and built large estates worked by slaves captured overseas. Slaves required no wages, so grain could be produced cheaply.
Now imagine the returning soldier.
He had spent seven or eight years at the front and somehow survived. He came home to find his farm neglected, his grain unable to compete with slave-produced grain, and his debts mounting. Eventually he sold his land for next to nothing and moved with his family into the city as part of the urban poor.
The Gracchi brothers saw what was happening and tried to carry out land reform, redistributing land to displaced citizens and veterans. The senatorial elite, determined to defend their estates, responded with violence. Both brothers were eventually killed in political bloodshed in Rome.
Once citizen-farmers were ruined, who would still want to serve in the army?
Gaius Marius reformed military recruitment and removed the old property qualifications. The poor could now enlist. But this changed the character of the army. Soldiers increasingly depended on their generals for pay, rewards and land. Their loyalty shifted accordingly: they followed whoever could provide for them.
What followed is familiar history. Sulla marched on Rome. Caesar crossed the Rubicon. Civil war and military strongmen consumed the republic. Many of the aristocrats who had grown rich from slave estates were eventually purged, dispossessed or killed.
If you personally turn the citizens who once fought for you into landless dependents, you should not be surprised when mercenary-style armies eventually enter the city and put a sword to your throat.
Now consider the Tang dynasty.
Everyone learns about the An Lushan Rebellion, but the deeper institutional problem is often left unexplained. One of the foundations of the early Tang military order was the fubing militia system. In simplified terms, relatively prosperous farming households, especially in the northwest, received land and certain tax privileges. In return, their men trained during agricultural slack seasons, provided their own horses and weapons, and served when the state called.
Being selected for military service could be a source of family honor.
The system began to break down under Empress Wu and Emperor Xuanzong. Powerful families accumulated more and more land, while the equal-field system gradually became hollow. Many militia households could no longer secure enough land even to support themselves.
Worse, military commanders began using soldiers as unpaid labor. One day they might be sent to build a commander’s private residence; the next, to transport his personal goods. Military service went from a respectable calling to a humiliating burden.
The conscientious farmers of the northwest could no longer bear it. They began fleeing in large numbers.
Some young men reportedly injured their own hands or feet with stones in order to escape conscription. The bitter expression was that such injuries brought them “fortunate hands and fortunate feet.”
By the Kaiyuan and Tianbao eras, the old militia system still existed on paper, but much of its substance had disappeared. The court increasingly recruited professional soldiers on the frontier—migrants, impoverished men and non-Han troops—and concentrated military and political authority in the hands of regional commanders.
Then came An Lushan, a man whose troops were tied more directly to frontier power and personal command than to the old civic order. He rebelled with a massive border army, and the glittering Tang high point shattered almost overnight.
The Ming dynasty offers another example.
The Chongzhen Emperor was famously hardworking. He reportedly slept only a few hours a night, wore patched robes and constantly pressed his officials to find money for war. Yet until the end, he never solved the most basic fiscal question: Who should actually be paying for the state?
The Jiangnan region was wealthy, but powerful gentry families enjoyed extensive tax privileges and protected one another through political networks. Much of the wealth of the southeast remained difficult for the state to tax effectively.
Meanwhile, the extra military levies imposed to fund the campaigns in Liaodong, suppress rebellions and build new armies fell heavily on poor farming households in the northwest—people who were already struggling to feed themselves.
The people who obeyed most were squeezed hardest. Those with the greatest capacity to contribute often contributed the least, while standing on the sidelines lecturing everyone else.
Eventually, some of those northwestern farmers who had wanted nothing more than to live quietly were pushed to the wall. They burned what remained of their property and joined the rebel armies. Many became some of Li Zicheng’s toughest soldiers.
The same pattern appeared inside the state. Generals such as Lu Xiangsheng died fighting at Julu; Sun Chuanting died at Tong Pass. The officials who were willing to shoulder responsibility often lacked troops, money and support.
When Li Zicheng finally approached Beijing, Chongzhen begged his officials to donate money for the defense of the capital. Senior officials pleaded poverty. The emperor’s own father-in-law, Zhou Kui, was famously reluctant to contribute.
Later, after the rebels entered Beijing, enormous quantities of hidden wealth were extracted from officials and aristocrats through torture and confiscation.
The precise figures in later accounts vary, but the political lesson is clear enough: the people willing to carry the state had been exhausted or eliminated, while those who remained were often highly skilled at protecting their own interests.
Everyone could calculate his personal balance sheet.
Almost no one was still calculating how the Ming dynasty itself might survive.
Dynasties work this way. Companies can too.
Boeing is a modern example often cited in this context.
Why did Boeing dominate commercial aviation for so long? Partly because it once had an engineering culture in which engineers possessed enormous authority. Its institutional backbone consisted of people obsessed—sometimes almost pathologically—with safety. If someone on the production line found that a component was outside tolerance, he could stop the process.
After Boeing merged with McDonnell Douglas in 1997, critics argue that financial priorities steadily gained influence over engineering culture. To managers focused on quarterly performance, veteran engineers who demanded costly redundancy, testing and redesign could begin to look less like guardians of safety than obstacles to margins.
Research budgets were squeezed. Experienced engineers left or were pushed aside. More production was outsourced. People who raised safety concerns could find themselves marginalized, while executives skilled at cutting costs, improving financial metrics and supporting share buybacks gained influence.
That logic culminated in the two crashes of the 737 MAX, which killed 346 people.
The subsequent investigations caused worldwide outrage. Among the central controversies was Boeing’s effort to avoid expensive pilot retraining and additional certification requirements while introducing the MCAS flight-control system. The system depended heavily on input from a single angle-of-attack sensor, and pilots had not been fully informed about how it functioned.
Trust accumulated over generations of engineering work was badly damaged in the space of a few financial quarters.
Now return to the original question.
One employment model has become increasingly common in recent years: outsourcing and labor dispatch. In China, the underlying logic is not entirely new. Decades ago, a similar category was simply called “temporary workers”: people doing much the same work but receiving different pay, different status and often less protection—while somehow being expected to stand in the front line when problems occurred.
Many people wonder how such an arrangement can function efficiently for so long.
The answer may not be that the system itself is particularly ingenious. It may be that the people carrying it happened to belong to generations unusually willing to endure it.
They were taught to love the work they chose, to do their duty and to be honest and hardworking. Even when their employment status was inferior and their pay lower, professional pride often pushed them to do the job well. Many still believed that if they worked hard enough and made no mistakes, sooner or later they would be given a genuine opportunity to advance.
It was this inertia of responsibility that kept a harsh employment model functioning for so many years.
But every arrangement has a life cycle.
Once a younger generation calculates the incentives clearly—no matter how hard I work, the promotion ladder is closed; the blame belongs to me, while the credit and equity belong to somebody else—the game of one-sided sacrifice becomes difficult to sustain.
The younger employee’s logic is brutally simple:
For this much money, why exactly should I risk my neck?
That does not necessarily mean young people have become weaker.
It may mean the liangjiazi are leaving.
And what happens next?
The first sign is that everyone activates a self-protection mechanism.
Tasks that were once completed through professional judgment and voluntary responsibility now require layers of approval, signatures, written confirmation, cameras and monitoring simply to ensure that anything gets done.
You begin to see something absurd. People spend more time proving “I did my part,” “this was not my fault,” and “here is the paperwork showing I am not responsible” than they spend solving the actual problem.
The system slowly rusts from the inside.
Worse, its ability to withstand shocks collapses.
During normal times, attractive spreadsheets and polished reports can keep the appearance of competence alive. But when a genuine crisis arrives and somebody actually has to stand up and take responsibility, everyone looks for an exit at once.
The logic is not complicated.
In a system that treats sacrifice as stupidity, no one will sacrifice his own interests for a machine that may discard him as a disposable part at any moment.
From the abandoned farms of Rome, to the empty treasury of the late Ming, to Boeing aircraft falling from the sky, there is nothing entirely new under the sun.
That is why the phrase “Liangjiazi Red Line” is worth thinking about.
What happens after the line is crossed is already written all over the history books:
At first, no one is willing to do extra work.
Then no one is willing to do the real work.
And finally, when disaster comes, someone calls for help—and no one answers.

Er Ge （二哥）
A friend once told me about what he called the “Three Ba” theory. His teacher had taught it to him years ago: a man goes through life needing to keep three things under control — his zuiba （嘴巴）, his mouth; his weiba （尾巴）, his tail; and his jiba （鸡巴）, his dick. In Chinese, all three words end in ba, hence the joke. It is crude, the sort of thing that sounds at first like something invented over drinks. But the longer you think about it, the more sense it makes. The mouth is about what you say. The tail is about how you behave in front of people more powerful than you. The dick is about desire. How a person speaks, how he acts before authority and how he handles his most basic impulses reveal a great deal about who he is.
But if the Three Ba are understood only as a lesson in personal discipline, the idea does not go far enough. Put it against the long history of Chinese officialdom, and against the way power still operates today, and a larger question appears: If a person cannot always control his own mouth, tail or dick, why should we assume that once he acquires public power, he will somehow know how to control that? That is where the Three Ba become more than a joke.
A friend once told me a story from his youth. He had a beautiful female classmate whom he had wanted badly when they were students. Years later, she came to him for help. Her brother-in-law had been arrested for illegally cutting timber, and she had heard that my friend was close to the local chief prosecutor. He took her to the prosecutor’s office. Over dinner, he jokingly introduced her as his “secret little sister-in-law,” leading the prosecutor to assume they were lovers. That night, a room was arranged for the two of them.
My friend drank heavily, went back to the room, fell onto the bed and slept until morning. Nothing happened. He later said that the moment he decided to help her, the old sexual desire disappeared. He did not want to take advantage of someone who needed something from him. His conclusion was simple: the big head can control the little one.
On the question of sex, I agree with him. When a woman needs something from you and you happen to possess access to something she desperately wants, the relationship is already unequal. Even if sex were eventually consensual, it would be hard to separate desire completely from dependence. To recognize that imbalance and step back is not sainthood. It is a basic sense of limits.
But the story has another half, and that half interests me even more. Why did the woman come to him in the first place? Because she believed he “knew the chief prosecutor.” And why did she believe he could help? Because a criminal case involving an ordinary citizen could, at least in her mind, be carried into a private network of personal connections.
Keeping the “Big Head” in Charge Is Not Enough
This is also why I now read my friend’s story differently. He said the big head could defeat the little one. That night, it did. The woman was beautiful. He was young. He had been drinking. They were in the same room. Nothing happened. Given that she had come to him for help, his refusal to cross that line deserves respect.
But political ethics is more complicated than sexual ethics. A man can control his dick without necessarily controlling power. There is even a certain irony here: The bed can remain clean while the relationship is not. The woman may remain untouched while procedure is touched.
Again, we do not know whether private connections affected the nonprosecution decision in that case. Without evidence, we should not pretend to know. But imagine a society in which people broadly assume that if you know someone at the court, the police station, the hospital, the school or the approval office, things will become “a little easier.” At that point, the problem is no longer simply that someone took a bribe. The public system has developed two entrances. The front door is called rules. The side door is called connections. Ordinary people wait at the front. Those with relationships knock at the side.
That is the deeper problem of a society organized heavily around personal ties. My friend’s refusal to exploit a vulnerable woman was an act of personal dignity. But public ethics demands one more step. Helping a friend can mean finding a lawyer, explaining the law or helping prepare documents. It should not mean assuming that knowing the person handling the case gives one a legitimate route to a different outcome. That is harder than controlling sexual desire. When lust appears, people usually know it is lust. When connections appear, people often call them friendship.
The law permits prosecutors, under certain circumstances, not to prosecute relatively minor offenses. The more interesting question is different: Why, when an ordinary person encounters a legal problem, is the first instinct so often not to hire a lawyer and follow the procedure, but to find someone who knows the prosecutor? At that point, the Three Ba stop being a story about men and women and become a story about politics. The little head may have been brought under control. But what about the mouth and the tail?
The Mouth: What People Surrender First Is Often Not the Body, but the Truth
One of the oldest arts of official life in China has never been merely taking money. It has been knowing what to say. The emperor likes one thing, so the ministers praise it. A leader declares that everything is going well, and those below quickly learn that discovering bad news may not be good for their careers. A superior announces an ambitious target, and the safest answer is often not, “Can this actually be done?” but, “We will absolutely accomplish it.” The mouth is supposed to describe reality. In a highly hierarchical organization, it can easily become an instrument for detecting the direction of power. That is the first of the Three Ba.
People often imagine corruption as something that begins with money. In reality, an organization can begin to rot much earlier: truth first loses its value, and pleasing falsehood begins to earn a return. If telling the truth risks offending a superior, while telling the superior what he wants to hear may improve one’s prospects, even an official who has never accepted a bribe can gradually learn the art of selective reporting. Bad news gets softened. Difficulties are delayed. Responsibility moves downward. Achievements move upward. Eventually the world the leader sees and the world that actually exists begin to separate.
This is not necessarily because everyone suddenly became immoral. The incentives changed. Every functioning organization has to solve one difficult problem: How does bad news travel upward? The same is true in business. A chief executive who cannot tolerate bad news will eventually run a company that cannot understand its own problems. It is even more dangerous in the military. If officers are afraid to report casualties, equipment failures or changes on the battlefield, the commander receiving the most reports may eventually become the person who understands reality least. Politics is no different.
A mature system therefore cannot simply exhort people to “tell the truth.” It must reduce the cost of doing so. Are whistleblowers protected? Can the press uncover problems? Can professionals openly dissent? Can a subordinate tell a superior, “This policy may not work,” without first calculating the damage to his own career? None of this looks, at first glance, like anticorruption. In fact, it is one of its deepest forms. Once the mouth answers only to power, facts lose their own authority. A society is in danger not merely when everyone lies, but when everyone knows the truth and also knows which truths are unsafe to say.
The Tail: The Hardest Habit in Officialdom Is Looking Upward
The second ba is the tail. The metaphor is vivid. Dogs wag their tails before their masters. Human beings are not dogs, of course, but in highly hierarchical organizations they can develop an extraordinary sensitivity to what is happening above them. Is the boss in a good mood today? Whom does he like? Whom is he preparing to promote? What kind of language irritates him? None of this appears in formal regulations, yet such information can circulate faster than official documents.
The Chinese saying that “an official one rank higher can crush you” is more than a complaint. It describes a structure of power. If a person’s promotion, resources, position and sense of security depend heavily on the person directly above him, the first question he learns to ask may not be, “Is this right?” It may be, “What does the leader think?” From the individual’s point of view, that can even be rational. We may call it flattery or opportunism, but the person doing it may simply be calculating professional risk.
The tail, then, is not merely a personality problem. It can be produced by institutions. If a county leader can largely determine the careers of those beneath him, it sounds admirable to demand that every subordinate remain fearless and incorruptible. It is also unrealistic. A political system cannot safely depend on the hope that everyone will behave like Hai Rui, the famously upright Ming-dynasty official. Why has history produced so few Hai Ruis? Because being Hai Rui is expensive.
A modern political order should not be designed to mass-produce saints. It should make it possible for an ordinary civil servant, one with no heroic appetite for martyrdom, to follow rules without constantly fearing that displeasing a superior will destroy his future. One ideal of modern bureaucracy is precisely this: people should obey offices, rules and procedures rather than the personal moods of their superiors. Bureaucracy has plenty of problems of its own, but at least in principle it tries to separate the question “Who is this person?” from the question “What does the rule require?”
That is the opposite of tail politics. Tail politics asks: Who said it? The rule of law asks: On what authority? Only a few words separate the two questions. An entire philosophy of power lies between them.
The Dick: What Makes Desire Dangerous Is When Power Gives It a Price
The third ba is, naturally, the one that attracts the most attention: the dick. Male sexual desire is not a political problem. Women have desire, too. Without sexual desire, humanity’s story would have ended fairly early. There is therefore little sense in treating sexual abstinence as proof of public integrity. The political question is different: Can someone exchange public power for sex?
Once that happens, the nature of the matter changes completely. China’s current party disciplinary rules explicitly prohibit the exchange of power for sex and money for sex, and official disciplinary notices have repeatedly described cases in which officials used their positions for personal gain while also engaging in such exchanges. Whatever one thinks of the political system, this much is clear: power-for-sex transactions are not a literary invention. They are a category that the disciplinary system itself recognizes.
Why do power and sex meet so easily? Because power is a special kind of resource. Money can buy a house, a car and many services. Public authority can provide things that money does not always buy directly: jobs, approvals, contracts, judicial convenience, policy access, licenses, promotions and scarce opportunities. A person who controls such things therefore possesses resources other people need. When oversight is weak, those resources can be privatized. One person exchanges power for money, another for office, another for loyalty, another for sex. On the surface, these look like different forms of corruption. At bottom, they are one thing: the conversion of public authority into private property.
That is why what is truly corrupt about a power-for-sex arrangement is not the sex. It is the power. Two adults who desire each other are dealing with private life. A superior who uses promotion, contracts, approvals or institutional pressure to obtain sex has moved beyond private morality. The problem has become political. The same distinction applies to adultery. An official may have an affair and therefore face a serious family or moral problem without necessarily having committed public corruption. But if the lover receives contracts, promotions, money or special treatment because of the relationship, the case has entered a different realm.
The measure of a political figure therefore cannot be reduced to what happens below his belt. The more important question is: Did his desire make public power pay the bill? That is the line separating private morality from public ethics.
Behind the Three Ba, There Is Only One Handle
The mouth must be controlled, but not merely by telling people to speak honestly. A system has to make sure that telling the truth does not carry an unbearable cost. The tail must be controlled, but not simply by insulting people for lacking backbone. A person’s fate should not rest entirely in the hands of one superior. The dick must be controlled, too, but the deeper goal is not sexual abstinence. It is to prevent jobs, approvals, contracts and promotions from becoming currencies for private desire.
Seen this way, the Three Ba are no longer merely a teacher’s vulgar joke. They raise three serious questions: How does a person face truth? How does a person face power? How does a person face desire? Political philosophy adds a fourth: What happens when that person also holds public authority?
Once you look closely, the mouth, the tail and the dick have something in common. Behind all three stands the same force: power. The “Three Ba” appear to be three things, but ultimately there is one thing that is much harder to control: the handle of power.
An ordinary person who says something foolish may do limited damage. A powerful official who tells a lie can turn it into policy. An ordinary person who wags his tail may humiliate himself. A senior official who flatters those above him and bullies those below can deform an entire organization. An ordinary man who cannot control his sexual impulses may destroy a family. A man with public authority who cannot control them may turn other people’s jobs, money, dignity and bodies into objects of exchange.
Civilization therefore begins with people learning to control their own Three Ba. Political civilization has to go further. It must do something more difficult: It must keep a person’s private impulses from being plugged into a power grid with no circuit breaker.
That may be where the Three Ba theory truly leads. A person who can control himself has character. An organization that can restrain its leaders has governance. A society in which no one’s appetites can easily rise above the rules has institutions.
Governing the Three Ba Through Institutions
Why does the mouth change? Because power rewards certain kinds of speech. Why does the tail wag? Because power decides who rises and who falls. Why can sex become a currency? Because power can convert jobs, opportunities and resources into private gratification. If the Three Ba theory stops at personal self-discipline, it is little more than a colorful piece of masculine ethics. Once power enters the picture, it becomes political philosophy.
The mouth represents truth and falsehood. The tail represents independence and submission. The dick represents desire and limits. All three eventually converge on a larger question: Once someone has power, who controls him?
Personal restraint matters. I do not dismiss it. No institution can turn every bad person into a good one. Shame, boundaries and the ability to refrain from doing something even when no one is watching are among the moral resources on which civilization depends. But a political order cannot be built on self-restraint alone. We cannot assume that everyone who acquires power will eventually sit alone at night and tell himself, “No. I cannot take advantage of this person.” Still less can we assume that someone who successfully resists one temptation will resist all the others — not when the stakes involve multibillion-yuan projects, thousands of jobs, vast tracts of land and the lives of tens of thousands of people.
One of the most important insights of modern political institutions is brutally simple: Human beings are not saints. If people have desires, do not make it easy for desire to become public policy. If people lie, create competing sources of information. If people flatter their superiors, do not give one superior absolute control over their careers. If those who hold power may abuse it, make their decisions subject to review, challenge, reversal and punishment.
A good system therefore does not depend on producing ten thousand paragons of sexual restraint. It works even when a scoundrel arrives. The point is not to make every official a saint. The point is to make sure that even a Ximen Qing cannot walk around with the county government’s seal in his pocket and do whatever he wants.
That is what institutions are for.

Rethinking the Geological Risks of the Lower Yarlung Tsangpo Hydropower Project After Nepal’s Glacier Collapse
The recent disaster in Nepal (尼泊尔) has posed a difficult question for large hydropower projects, one that has rarely been taken seriously enough. A glacier and the bedrock beneath it suddenly became unstable and plunged down a snow-covered mountain at high speed. Ice, rock, mud, and water mixed together and rushed through a narrow valley, gathering more material along the way. What began as a slope collapse turned into a flood and debris flow extending for dozens of kilometers. Villages, roads, bridges, and hydropower stations all lay in its path. After the disaster, several hydropower facilities in Nepal were damaged, and hundreds of workers were at one point trapped in tunnel areas. This was not a flood in the conventional sense. It was a classic disaster chain: glacier collapse, rock avalanche, debris flow, river blockage, landslide-dammed lake, and finally an outburst flood.
The problem is that this same kind of disaster chain is not merely a theoretical possibility in the Yarlung Tsangpo Grand Canyon (雅鲁藏布江大峡谷). It has happened repeatedly.
