In October 2018, two major glacier collapses occurred in the Sedongpu Gully (色东普沟) near Nyingchi (林芝). Roughly 130 million cubic meters of ice and debris entered the Yarlung Tsangpo River (雅鲁藏布江), blocking the main channel and creating a landslide-dammed lake. Researchers later reconstructed the first dam-breach event and estimated that its peak discharge exceeded 30,000 cubic meters per second. In March 2021, another ice-rock avalanche of about 50 million cubic meters descended from an elevation of roughly 6,500 meters at Sedongpu and again temporarily blocked the river. Researchers have found that over little more than a decade, this single tributary basin has experienced several large mass movements capable of partly or completely damming the Yarlung Tsangpo.
This tells us something important. The greatest engineering challenge in the lower reaches of the Yarlung Tsangpo has never been simply whether a dam can be built strongly enough. The deeper problem is that the project is being built in a world that is still moving.
The great bend of the Yarlung Tsangpo lies near the eastern Himalayan syntaxis. On one side rise peaks of more than 7,000 meters, including Namcha Barwa (南迦巴瓦) and Gyala Peri (加拉白垒); on the other is a canyon thousands of meters deep. The Indian Plate is still colliding with the Eurasian Plate. The crust continues to deform and rise, while the Yarlung Tsangpo cuts rapidly into the mountains. Recent research has described this region as one of the places on Earth with the highest rates of rock uplift and erosion. Remote sensing studies have identified at least 2,390 landslides larger than 10,000 square meters across the Yarlung Tsangpo basin, with a combined estimated volume of tens of cubic kilometers.
Climate change adds another layer of difficulty. The glaciers of southeastern Tibet (西藏) are strongly influenced by the Indian monsoon and are more sensitive than many of the continental glaciers farther inside the Tibetan Plateau. As temperatures rise, permafrost and ice-bonded rock weaken. Retreating glaciers can remove support from steep slopes, while meltwater entering fractures can further reduce rock stability. Heavy rainfall, unusual heat, and earthquakes may not produce catastrophe on their own, but together they can push an already unstable slope past a critical threshold. A 2025 study of glacier hazards in southeastern Tibet concluded that the region has become a hotspot for glacier-collapse disasters on the Tibetan Plateau.
The real warning that the Nepal disaster offers the lower Yarlung Tsangpo project is therefore not, “Nepal collapsed, so the Yarlung Tsangpo will collapse too.” It is something more serious: the hydrological and geological record of the past hundred years may no longer be a reliable guide to the risks of the next fifty. This is one of the hardest problems facing all mega-projects in an era of climate change.
Traditional dam design depends heavily on what engineers call design baselines. What is the hundred-year flood? What is the thousand-year flood? What is the maximum credible earthquake? How much disturbance can a slope withstand? But once glaciers retreat, permafrost thaws, and patterns of extreme precipitation change, the underlying probability distribution itself may begin to shift. Engineers are no longer drawing repeatedly from the same stable box. The box itself is changing.
The Lower Yarlung Tsangpo Hydropower Project therefore faces at least five kinds of risk. The first is the obvious one: earthquakes and engineering geology. This is an active tectonic environment, and the canyon is exceptionally deep. The planned use of extensive tunneling means that construction will take place not only along the river but deep inside the mountains. Deep-buried tunnels can encounter faults, fractured rock zones, high crustal stress, sudden water inflows, and rockbursts. Chinese authorities have stated that years of geological investigation were carried out and that the project layout was designed to avoid areas of high risk from major geological hazards. That claim deserves to be taken seriously. But “avoiding known high-risk zones” is not the same as saying that the entire system is free of risk, especially in a landscape that is still changing rapidly.
The second risk is less obvious to the general public than earthquakes: a mountain can suddenly arrive from upstream. Dams are usually designed with floods in mind, but an ice-rock avalanche does not simply add water to a river. It can suddenly dump tens of millions, or even more than a hundred million, cubic meters of solid material into the channel. That material can block the river and create a natural dam. Hours or days later, the blockage may fail and release an enormous mass of water, sediment, and debris. The 2018 event on the Yarlung Tsangpo proved that this mechanism is entirely real.
If a huge hydropower system lies downstream, the questions become more complicated. Can the intakes withstand such an event? Could massive sediment loads block diversion tunnels? Can spillways handle an extraordinary flood carrying enormous amounts of debris? Can turbines withstand severe abrasion? If a natural landslide dam interacts with an artificial reservoir, how can engineers prevent the danger from cascading from one project to the next? These questions may be more realistic than the familiar question of whether an earthquake could simply “shake the dam apart.”
The third risk is sediment. The Yarlung Tsangpo is not a clear and stable pipeline. It is a vast sediment-transport system cutting through the Himalayas. Recent studies suggest that sediment transport along parts of the river is already changing rapidly under the combined effects of warming, rainfall, and freeze-thaw processes. For a hydropower station, heavy sediment loads can cause reservoir siltation, block intakes, and wear down turbines. Downstream, dams and reservoir operations can also change when and how much sediment is carried along the river.
There is an important and somewhat counterintuitive fact here. Water flowing from the upper Yarlung Tsangpo does not make up the majority of the Brahmaputra River’s (布拉马普特拉河) eventual discharge. Some studies estimate its contribution at only about 15 to 16 percent, because enormous monsoon rainfall across northeastern India adds large amounts of water farther downstream. But the contribution of sediment from Tibet and the eastern Himalayas may be far greater than their share of the water itself. Some studies estimate that the Yarlung Tsangpo may supply roughly half of the sediment reaching the lower Brahmaputra. That means India (印度) and Bangladesh (孟加拉国) need to ask more than whether “there will be less water.” They also need to ask: When will the water arrive? When will the sediment arrive? Will flood peaks change? Will dry-season flows change? What will happen to fish and riverbank ecosystems?
The fourth issue is transboundary hydrology. Chinese authorities have stressed that the project does not “consume” water, that it mainly uses the river’s natural drop to generate electricity, and that it will not harm downstream water resources or ecological interests. In physical terms, hydropower does indeed differ from irrigation: it does not consume large volumes of water in the same way. If the project is mainly run-of-river, its long-term effect on total water volume could be relatively limited. But “not consuming water” is not the same as “having no hydrological impact.”
One of the most important things a hydropower project does is rearrange the timing and location of water flows. When water is released during the day, how much a seasonal flood peak is reduced, whether dry-season flows can be increased, and where sediment is deposited all depend on reservoir capacity and operating rules. Basin-wide modeling has even suggested that well-coordinated reservoirs across several countries could reduce some flood risks and improve irrigation security. But the reverse is also true: if operating rules lack transparency, downstream uncertainty can grow.
This leads to the fifth risk, and perhaps the one most easily overlooked. It is not an engineering risk at all. It is a risk of trust. China sees the project as a clean-energy and disaster-management project. India worries about the growing ability of an upstream country to control flows. Each side has its own logic. In 2025, India formally conveyed its concerns about the project to China, while China repeatedly said that the development would not harm downstream interests. The problem is that trust over a transboundary river cannot be built on assurances alone.
The most effective way to reduce this risk is through data. Rainfall, river discharge, reservoir levels, glacier movement, major landslides, landslide-dammed lakes, and unusual water releases can all be incorporated into real-time information-sharing systems. On a river like the Yarlung Tsangpo, an upstream warning of an ice-rock avalanche may be a hundred times more useful than a diplomatic statement. After the 2018 Sedongpu disaster, Chinese researchers established automated monitoring and early-warning systems that successfully issued alerts for some subsequent hazards. Expanding such systems into a transboundary disaster-warning network may be one of the most valuable public goods this mega-project could produce.
Does this mean the Lower Yarlung Tsangpo Hydropower Project should not be built? China has one of the world’s strongest capacities for constructing large hydropower projects, and the enormous natural drop of the Yarlung Tsangpo does provide an extraordinary concentration of hydropower resources. If the planned capacity of 60 gigawatts and annual generation of nearly 300 billion kilowatt-hours can be achieved, the project could play a major role in a low-carbon energy system. Nor are dams inherently only sources of danger. With enough storage capacity, sound operations, and effective early warning, reservoirs can also reduce some flood peaks and help downstream areas cope with disasters.
What deserves real caution is a different way of thinking: because our engineering is strong, the natural risk has already been solved. The disaster in Nepal reminds us of the opposite. The greatest danger of the Himalayas is not simply that the mountains are high, but that they are geologically young. It is not simply that glaciers exist, but that they are changing. It is not simply that rivers run through the region, but that those rivers are continually reshaping valleys in one of the most tectonically and erosively active environments on Earth. To build here is not to build on a static geological map. It is to build inside a chapter of Earth history that is still being written.
That is why the right question about the Lower Yarlung Tsangpo Hydropower Project is not merely, “Is the dam strong enough?” It is not even simply, “Was an environmental assessment carried out?” The question has to be raised one level higher: Has the project been designed for a Himalaya that is warming, losing ice, still experiencing earthquakes, and still capable of producing mass movements involving hundreds of millions of tons of rock and ice?
Do the design standards treat ice-rock collapse, river blockage, landslide-dammed lakes, and outburst floods as a single connected disaster chain rather than as separate, unrelated hazards? Is there a kind of “circuit breaker” between the five cascade hydropower stations to stop one disaster from triggering the next? How will sediment be managed over the long term? Can reservoir levels be lowered quickly during extreme events? How will tunneling, roads, and construction spoil be managed so that construction itself does not create new slope hazards? If climate conditions change substantially in several decades, can the project’s design assumptions and operating rules be revised? And perhaps most important, can the environmental-impact assessments, geological-risk models, and emergency plans be opened to enough independent scientists for serious scrutiny?
The information available to the public is not yet sufficient to answer these questions. Nepal’s glacier collapse is not evidence that “something is about to go wrong” with the Yarlung Tsangpo project. But it is a timely warning. It reminds us that the greatest enemy of Himalayan hydropower may not be an earthquake of a magnitude we already know how to calculate. It may be a chain of hazards that has never been fully written into conventional engineering experience.
For a project costing more than a trillion yuan, the most important test is not simply whether it can be completed today. The real test is whether it can still operate safely fifty or eighty years from now, in a Himalaya that is warmer than today, with thinner glaciers, less permafrost, and possibly more extreme events.
That is the question the Lower Yarlung Tsangpo Hydropower Project should be forced to answer after the disaster in Nepal.

Er Ge (二哥)
A video by Li Long (李龙), who describes himself as the founder of the theory of “subject evolution” and the founder of Dongshan Business Essence (东山商业精华), has been circulating online. My friend Mr. Guo forwarded it to me, and I watched it carefully. On one basic point, I agree with Li: when we judge China’s reforms of the 1990s, we should not take what we know today and use it to mock the people who had to make decisions then. History is not an exam that we get to retake after the answer sheet has been handed out. By the late 1990s, China had indeed reached an extraordinarily difficult stage in its transition. What should be done with state-owned enterprises? With the banks, housing, public finance, and the tax system? Should China join the World Trade Organization? Every one of these questions involved enormous shifts in interests, and no one could know with certainty what the country would look like twenty years later. Understanding the circumstances in which policymakers made their choices is therefore a basic requirement of serious historical judgment.
But this is exactly where the problem begins. Understanding the difficulties facing policymakers does not release them from responsibility. Nor does acknowledging the achievements of reform mean that its costs can simply be written off as “historically inevitable.” The main problem with the video is not that it says reform under Zhu Rongji (朱镕基) was difficult. Of course it was. The problem is the quiet shift in logic that follows: because reform was difficult, the decision-makers deserve our reverence; because China later experienced rapid economic growth, history has essentially vindicated their choices; and because refusing to reform might have produced even worse consequences, the losses suffered by particular people become an unavoidable price that simply had to be paid.
That argument sounds complete, but it leaves out one of the most important questions in political economy: Who received the gains from reform, and who bore its costs? That question matters far more than whether Zhu Rongji was a “good man” or a “bad man.”
Judging Reform Means Asking More Than How Much the Country Ultimately Gained
Economics has long wrestled with a basic problem. Suppose a policy increases total social wealth by 10 billion yuan. One group gains 15 billion, while another loses 5 billion. Should the reform be called a success? Under a relatively permissive standard of economic efficiency, if the winners gain enough that they could, in theory, compensate the losers and still come out ahead, the change may be said to represent a potential improvement in overall welfare. This is what economists call a Kaldor–Hicks improvement.
The crucial word here is potential. The winners’ ability to compensate the losers is not the same thing as the losers actually being compensated. This is the account that narratives of reform most often leave unpaid. GDP may rise, firms may become more efficient, exports may increase, and the fiscal position may improve. All of that matters. But if the benefits of reform arrive many years later while unemployment, falling incomes, disrupted medical care, housing insecurity, and loss of social status descend on one group within a year, we cannot simply use GDP twenty years later to settle the bill for a family that lost its livelihood twenty years earlier.
The reform of state-owned enterprises in the late 1990s is a classic example. It did not come out of nowhere. A substantial number of state-owned enterprises were genuinely in serious trouble. Many carried redundant workers, suffered from low efficiency, and operated under what the Hungarian economist János Kornai (亚诺什·科尔奈) called a “soft budget constraint”: even after running losses, an enterprise could often continue to rely on bank lending, fiscal support, or administrative intervention to survive. Kornai developed the concept to explain exactly this kind of institutional behavior. If a firm expects that someone will always rescue it after it loses money, the way it responds to costs and market competition will inevitably change.
So the question of whether state-owned enterprises needed reform was never a false one. Later research on Chinese firms also found substantial improvements in productivity in the state sector after the late 1990s. Using firm-level data, Chang-Tai Hsieh (谢长泰) and Zheng Song (宋铮) estimated that the restructuring of the state sector between 1998 and 2007 made a substantial contribution to overall growth in total factor productivity.
If the story ended there, Li would have a strong case. But history has another half-page. According to figures later published by China’s National Bureau of Statistics, 20.23 million workers were laid off from state-owned enterprises between 1998 and 2002. Including those already laid off before 1998 brought the total to 27.15 million. The 2003 Government Work Report likewise referred to “more than 27 million” laid-off workers.
That is not a number that can be brushed aside. Twenty-seven million people were not simply a variable in an economic model. They were twenty-seven million individual lives, surrounded by families, elderly parents, and children. At the time, a job in a state-owned enterprise was also much more than a paycheck. It was often tied to housing, medical care, pensions, arrangements for children, and a person’s social identity. When the “iron rice bowl” broke, workers did not lose only that month’s salary. Later research in labor economics found that some workers displaced during state-sector restructuring continued to suffer long-term income losses even after finding new employment. Many moved into lower-paid jobs requiring fewer skills and offering less stable employment, and some of those losses persisted for years.
That is where the real difficulty of reform lies. The question is not simply whether reform was right or wrong. It is this: When greater efficiency requires the elimination of inefficient jobs, who should pay the price for that increase in efficiency?
The Real Question Is Not Whether to Reform, but Who Pays for It
This is where the difference between the video’s narrative and a political-economic analysis becomes clear. The video asks: what would have happened if China had not reformed? That is a legitimate question. But another question must follow: Why should the costs of reform fall mainly on those with the least bargaining power? That is a very different question.
Joseph Schumpeter (约瑟夫·熊彼特) described capitalist development as “creative destruction.” In 2025, the Nobel Prize in Economic Sciences was awarded to Joel Mokyr (乔尔·莫基尔), Philippe Aghion (菲利普·阿吉翁), and Peter Howitt (彼得·豪伊特). A major contribution of Aghion and Howitt was to place creative destruction at the center of modern growth theory: new technologies, new firms, and new forms of production emerge, while old firms, old jobs, and old interests disappear. In explaining this theory, the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences also emphasized that creative destruction creates conflicts of interest, and that these conflicts must be managed. Otherwise, society itself may begin to resist innovation.
That point matters because economic growth never consists only of “creation.” Destruction comes with it. The question is not whether destruction can be avoided, but what happens afterward. Closing an inefficient state-owned enterprise may be an issue of economic efficiency. But when a forty-five-year-old worker who has spent twenty years in that enterprise suddenly loses his job, whether he can find another one, what happens to his medical insurance and pension, whether he can keep his housing, and how his children will manage are questions of social policy. These are not the same issue.
China did not entirely neglect compensation. Re-employment service centers, basic living allowances, social insurance, and the so-called “three security lines” were being built. The 2003 Government Work Report stated that more than 90 percent of the more than 27 million workers laid off from state-owned enterprises since 1998 had entered re-employment service centers, and that more than 18 million had subsequently found employment through various channels. Those efforts deserve recognition. But having compensation measures is not the same thing as providing adequate compensation.
A large body of research on transition economies shows that the long-term political and social sustainability of market reform depends not only on whether reform eventually improves efficiency, but also on whether society builds a strong enough safety net to catch people who are displaced by structural change through no fault of their own. Research by the International Monetary Fund on transition economies has similarly stressed that reform cannot consist only of cutting, closing, and marketizing. Systems of unemployment insurance, pensions, health care, education, and social assistance also have to be rebuilt.
So the question I really want to ask about the state-owned enterprise reforms of the 1990s is not, “Why did Zhu Rongji reform?” It is this: if the macroeconomic gains from reform were ultimately shared by the country as a whole, why could the microeconomic losses not have been borne more broadly by society as a whole? This is a question of welfare economics, but it is also a question of political justice.
If a reform makes the country richer overall while concentrating especially heavy losses on people with the fewest alternatives, later generations cannot simply say, “Without their sacrifice, there would be no prosperity today.” The word “sacrifice” easily conceals the most important facts: Who decided that they would make the sacrifice? Did they have a choice? How much compensation did they receive? And after reform created new wealth, how much of it flowed back to the people who bore the original costs? GDP cannot answer these questions.
Joining the WTO Was Not a Permanent Pass from Scrutiny
Then there is China’s accession to the World Trade Organization. Here too, I do not agree with a simple story of “Zhu Rongji’s brilliant decision.” But neither do I accept the opposite extreme: that China entered the WTO from the beginning with the intention of exploiting loopholes, or that the later deterioration in China’s relations with the West can simply be traced back to the accession decision. The historical evidence does not support so neat a chain of causation.
China’s WTO accession came after fifteen years of negotiations. According to WTO records, the process involved thirty-eight meetings of the working party, forty-four bilateral market-access agreements, and eventually hundreds of pages of legal documents and detailed commitments. China agreed to lower tariffs, expand market access, amend domestic laws and regulations, and accept a number of accession conditions more demanding than those imposed on many developing countries.
Economically, WTO accession also transformed China. One firm-level study published in the American Economic Review found that tariff reductions after accession raised productivity among Chinese manufacturing firms and intensified market competition. Another influential study found that China’s accession, together with the United States granting China permanent normal trade relations, sharply reduced uncertainty over future U.S. trade policy toward China. That greater predictability itself accounted for an important part of the subsequent rise in Chinese exports.
This was in some ways more important than the precise amount by which tariffs fell. Why would a company build a factory that would not pay for itself for ten years? Why invest in a supply chain? Why would foreign firms move production into China? Because they were not judging only today’s prices. They were also asking whether the rules might suddenly change five or ten years later. This is what institutional economics calls a credible commitment.
In their work on political institutions, Douglass North (道格拉斯·诺斯) and Barry Weingast (巴里·温加斯特) posed an important question: how can a state persuade others that it will not arbitrarily overturn tomorrow the commitments it makes today? One important function of institutions is to constrain future power, making long-term investment and transactions among strangers possible. Seen this way, joining the WTO did more than give China access to foreign markets. It also locked part of China’s domestic reform into an international framework of rules.
But there is another side to this bargain: if a country enjoys the benefits that come from the credibility of rules, it must also bear the costs of following those rules. So there is no reason to avoid the criticisms China later faced from other WTO members over subsidy transparency, state-owned enterprises, intellectual property, market access, and the political use of economic measures. Many of these concerns were raised during the WTO’s trade policy reviews of China in 2021 and 2024. They deserve serious discussion.
Serious discussion, however, does not justify manufacturing evidence. The claim that China was “sued more than two thousand times by WTO members” after joining the organization cannot be sustained. WTO statistics show that from the organization’s creation in 1995 through the end of 2024, all members combined filed only 631 formal requests for consultations under its dispute-settlement system. China alone therefore could not possibly have faced two thousand formal WTO cases. China has certainly been one of the principal targets of trade-remedy investigations worldwide. There have been many antidumping, countervailing-duty, and safeguard cases. But a trade-remedy investigation is not the same thing as a WTO lawsuit, nor does it mean that the WTO has ruled that China violated its obligations. Mixing these categories turns a potentially valid criticism about institutional credibility into an argument that collapses as soon as someone checks the numbers.
Likewise, I have not found reliable primary evidence that Zhu Rongji privately said anything along the lines of “get into the WTO first, then we can ignore the rules later,” or “there are loopholes in the rules that we can exploit afterward.” Such stories therefore cannot serve as evidence in judging a major historical decision. We can criticize later disputes over compliance without taking later problems and projecting them backward as proof that someone twenty-five years ago must have entered the agreement with fraudulent intent. That is a basic rule of historical evidence.
Polanyi Should Not Be Turned into a Theory of Everything
There is another idea in the original commentary that I would keep: at its foundation, a market economy does depend on trust. Why do strangers sign ten-year contracts? Why does a bank lend money today to someone who will repay it five years from now? Why does a foreign investor build a factory under a legal system far from its own? Because markets are never only about prices. They also depend on property rights, contracts, courts, policy stability, and confidence in government.
But there is no need to construct a supposed “five-layer theory of trust” and attribute it to Michael Polanyi (迈克尔·波兰尼). Polanyi did develop the idea of “tacit knowledge,” and he wrote the famous essay “The Republic of Science” (《科学共和国》), emphasizing independent judgment, professional traditions, and mutual recognition within the scientific community. But the move from tacit knowledge through science, markets, constitutional government, religion, and finally a “clash of civilizations” is not a coherent theoretical system that can simply be attributed to Polanyi.
If we want to understand China’s experience after joining the WTO, North’s theory of credible commitment is more direct. If we want to understand the relationship between globalization and domestic social stability, the political scientist John Ruggie’s (约翰·鲁杰) idea of “embedded liberalism” is more useful. The postwar international economic order was able to sustain openness not simply because governments believed in free trade, but because open markets were combined with domestic employment, welfare, and social protection. International markets could open, but states also had to retain the capacity to protect people harmed by market shocks.
This brings the WTO and state-owned enterprise reform back into the same story. Openness creates wealth and competition raises efficiency. But if the losses generated by openness and competition repeatedly fall on the same groups while the gains flow elsewhere, even the most efficient reforms will eventually encounter political resistance. This is not because ordinary people “do not understand economics.” It is because they will ask a very simple question: Why am I always asked to understand the big picture, while the big picture is never asked to understand me?
That is the real difficulty at the heart of the political economy of reform.
How Much Responsibility Should Zhu Rongji Bear?
So in the end we have to return to Zhu Rongji himself. I do not agree with turning the reforms of the 1990s into the story of a lone hero saving the country. But neither do I agree with putting the layoffs of more than twenty million workers, the displacement caused by the Three Gorges project, and every later trade dispute China encountered into one man’s historical ledger. These two narratives appear politically opposite, but they make the same mistake: they turn institutional history into personal history.
China’s reforms of the 1990s were a vast institutional transition involving the Chinese Communist Party Central Committee, the State Council, local governments, state-owned enterprises, the financial system, and society as a whole. The direction of state-owned enterprise reform had already begun to take shape before Zhu became premier, while the negotiations over WTO membership extended across several governments. The Three Gorges Project was approved by the National People’s Congress in 1992, when Zhu was not yet premier. It is simply inaccurate to explain institutional changes spanning decades as the expression of one man’s will.
But the opposite conclusion does not follow. Saying that these were “collective decisions” should not dissolve individual responsibility altogether. Political power and political responsibility should correspond to each other. The greater a person’s power within the decision-making system, the more information he controls, and the more resources he can allocate, the greater the political responsibility he should bear for policy outcomes. This is a basic principal-agent problem in political science: one cannot emphasize leadership when claiming credit for decisions and then, when costs appear, suddenly insist that everything was collective.
A fairer judgment, then, would be this: Zhu Rongji was an extremely important policy driver of China’s market reforms and WTO accession in the late 1990s, and he deserves historical credit proportionate to the role he actually played. By the same principle, he should also bear policy responsibility proportionate to the power he actually exercised. The achievements cannot all be credited to him, and the costs cannot all be blamed on “the times.” That is what a mature historical judgment requires.
“Integrity,” Too, Cannot Be Proved or Disproved by Rumor
The People Who Deserve Our Respect Were Not Only Those Sitting Behind Desks in Zhongnanhai
Now return to the line in the video: when the person making decisions has more than a billion people before him, even God might sweat if asked to sit at that desk. It is an evocative line. And I agree that governing a country of more than a billion people in the middle of a vast institutional transition was extraordinarily difficult.
But I would move the camera a little. If we are asked to understand the pressure on the policymaker sitting behind that desk, should we not also try to understand the workers in Shenyang (沈阳), Anshan (鞍山), Fushun (抚顺), and Benxi (本溪) who suddenly lost their jobs? A worker did not know that twenty years later China would become the world’s largest manufacturing nation. He knew only that there would be no paycheck next month. A forty-five-year-old woman did not know how much China’s exports would grow after joining the WTO. She knew only that after more than twenty years in a state-owned factory, she now had to find another way to live.
That, too, is history. And it may be the part of history most easily forgotten by grand narratives. This is why I resist simply calling these people “the price that reform had to pay.” The word “price” has no subject. The moment we ask who paid the price, history looks different.
This is where I truly disagree with the video. I do not deny the necessity of much of the reform of the 1990s, nor do I deny Zhu Rongji’s important role in fiscal reform, taxation, finance, state-owned enterprise restructuring, and China’s WTO accession. The later rise in Chinese manufacturing productivity, the expansion of the private economy, the growth of trade, and China’s rapid integration into global supply chains were not imaginary achievements. Firm-level research on both state-enterprise reform and WTO accession provides substantial evidence for these conclusions.
But precisely because those achievements were real, they do not need a heroic myth to protect them. A mature view of history should be able to hold several apparently contradictory truths at once: reform may have been necessary, while the costs of reform were still distributed unfairly; a leader may have made important contributions, while policies he promoted still caused lasting harm to some groups; China’s accession to the WTO may have been a hugely important strategic choice, while China’s later problems concerning international rules and market institutions remain open to criticism.
These judgments do not cancel one another out. History is not a courtroom with only two buttons marked “guilty” and “not guilty.” It is more like a ledger. Growth occupies one column, efficiency another, employment another, inequality another, human dignity another, and institutional credibility yet another. A strong number in the GDP column does not give us permission to tear out all the others.
The Final Test of Reform: Do People Have More Choices?
What I really want to discuss, in the end, is not Zhu Rongji himself. It is how reform should be judged. Chinese history has never lacked projects of “enriching the state and strengthening the military.” Shang Yang’s reforms (商鞅变法) sought to strengthen Qin. Wang Anshi’s reforms (王安石变法) sought to enrich the state. Zhang Juzheng’s reforms (张居正改革) sought to restore fiscal order. The Self-Strengthening Movement (洋务运动) of the late Qing also pursued wealth and strength. State capacity, fiscal strength, and military power all matter.
But the real difference between modern politics and traditional statism cannot simply be that the state becomes more efficient. We also have to ask: Have ordinary people gained more freedom, more security, and more choices?
If a reform strengthens public finances and makes enterprises more efficient, but people who lose their jobs are left without basic protection, then the reform is not complete. If opening markets creates enormous trade wealth, but part of that wealth is not converted into education, health care, pensions, unemployment protection, and the capacity to find new work, then opening up is not complete either. If a country asks foreign investors to trust its rules while reserving the right to change those rules whenever it chooses, then market credibility cannot last.
Good reform, then, is never simply a matter of “having the courage to cut.” It also requires knowing whom the knife cuts, who is bleeding, how to stop the bleeding, and how, once reform succeeds, those who bore the original costs can share in the wealth later created. That is the real difference between modern political economy and the older tradition of reform in the name of national strength.
So if I were judging Zhu Rongji today, I would neither kneel in admiration nor stand up merely to curse him. I would ask four questions: Why did reform have to happen then? Were there less costly alternatives? Who bore most of the costs? And once reform succeeded, how were those people compensated?
Only when we can answer those four questions do we begin to understand the 1990s. And only then do we truly respect history. Because the deepest respect for history does not come from looking up at the person behind the desk. It comes from seeing both the desk and the homes where the numbers on that desk finally landed.

The real question behind China’s bride-price debate is not how much marriage should cost. It is how much uncertainty young people are being asked to bear.
I read Justin Sun’s open letter to Hu Xijin twice. If I were answering on Hu’s behalf, I would not begin with whether “a man should behave decently,” or whether 30 million yuan is really that much money for a billionaire. Those are side arguments. Sun is asking a harder question: when a young Chinese person decides to marry, what exactly is he committing himself to? What responsibilities will he assume, what costs will he bear, and what degree of certainty can he reasonably expect in return?
That is a real question. The problem is that Sun has placed several different questions into the same account. Before answering him, we need to separate them.
The first point is simple: Chinese men are under no legal obligation to pay caili, or bride price. Sun writes, “A bride price has to be paid one way or another.” That may accurately describe his experience of Chinese social custom. It does not accurately describe Chinese marriage law. The Civil Code establishes freedom of marriage and equality between men and women, and prohibits demanding property through marriage. The Supreme People’s Court’s 2024 judicial interpretation on disputes involving betrothal gifts did not establish a legally acceptable price for marriage. It was meant to resolve disputes over payments that had already been made. And the 2026 No. 1 Central Document again called for continued efforts to curb excessively high bride prices in rural China.
The direction of policy, in other words, is not to answer the question, “How much should a man pay?” It is to allow a custom to exist without allowing that custom to harden into an admission fee for marriage. So when Sun asks whether bride price should be a fixed amount or a percentage of a man’s wealth, the answer is: neither.
The law does not say that a man with 10 million yuan should pay 300,000, while a man worth one billion should pay 30 million. When courts decide whether a bride price is excessively high, they look at the circumstances: local income levels, the financial position of the payer’s family, local customs, how long the couple lived together, whether they had children, and how the money was actually used. A couple who lived together for years and raised a child is not legally in the same position as a couple who broke up shortly after becoming engaged. In cases published by the Supreme People’s Court, some payments have been ordered returned in full, some only in part, and some not at all after long-term cohabitation and the birth of children.
There is a reason the law works this way. Marriage is not a sale. If it were, things would actually be easier. A car has a price. A house has a closing date. A contract can specify delivery, default, and damages. Marriage cannot. Love, companionship, pregnancy, childbirth, childcare, care for aging parents, housework, career sacrifices, illness, loyalty and decades of shared life cannot all be priced on the wedding day. Economists call this an incomplete contract. Ordinary language says it better: two people cannot settle forty years of accounts before they have even begun to live together.
That brings us to Sun’s second question: How much should a man have to pay for childbirth? Again, there is no price.
Pregnancy and childbirth impose physical burdens on women that men do not bear. That is a biological fact. In practice, women also frequently absorb more of the costs that come afterward: childcare, career interruption, lost income and unpaid care work. Men, meanwhile, have obligations of their own—to support, raise, educate and care for their children. Chinese law treats the raising and protection of children as a shared parental responsibility. What it does not do is treat reproduction as a service purchased by men from women.
That distinction matters. A modern society should not respond to the unequal burdens of reproduction by inventing a private price for childbirth. It should distribute those burdens more broadly. Some are borne jointly by the couple, some by the extended family, and some should be borne socially, through childcare, education, health care, parental leave, housing policy and other public services.
If nearly all of those costs are pushed back onto the individual family, men and women will eventually sit across the table and start adding up their losses. The man counts the apartment, the bride price, the wedding and the expectation that he provide. The woman counts pregnancy, childbirth, career interruption, housework and years of caregiving. By the time the arithmetic is finished, both sides believe they are being asked to make the worse bargain. That may be one of the deepest problems in Chinese marriage today: love has become increasingly private, but marriage has begun to look increasingly like a major capital investment.
Sun’s third question deserves an equally clear answer: Must a man satisfy every demand a woman makes before or after marriage? Of course not.
The basic principle of a modern marriage is not that a man must satisfy a woman. Nor is it that a woman must obey a man. It is that two adults both have the right to say no. Whether to buy a home can be negotiated. Who manages the money can be negotiated. Whether to live with either set of parents can be negotiated. How many children to have can be negotiated. The division of housework should be negotiated too.
But bodily autonomy and personal dignity belong to a different category. Consent cannot be purchased. Marriage itself must be voluntary. A person who does not want to marry has the right not to marry. A person who does not want children has the right to refuse parenthood. A person who does not consent to a particular intimate act does not acquire an obligation to perform it merely because the other party spent money. Payment cannot convert another person’s body into a debt.
What happens, then, if the marriage never takes place? Now we are dealing with property law. If money was genuinely transferred as a betrothal gift in contemplation of marriage and the marriage did not occur, the payer may seek its return through the courts. Even after legal marriage, a court may order some money returned when the couple lived together only briefly and the payment was exceptionally large. The opposite is also true. If the couple lived together for years, had children, or used the money for their common life, a court is unlikely to apply a crude rule of “I paid you X, therefore you owe me X.”
So when Sun asks whether a man can go to court if the woman leaves, the answer is straightforward: of course he can. There is nothing indecent about filing a lawsuit. There is nothing indecent about asking a court to decide whether 30 million yuan constituted bride price, a gift, or some other form of property transfer.
According to a public statement released by Sun’s lawyer on August 27, 2026, the relevant property dispute has been accepted by a court. The amount at issue exceeds 30 million yuan. The defendant has challenged jurisdiction, and the case has not yet proceeded to a determination on the merits. There is no final judgment. That means outsiders are in no position to decide which payments legally qualify as bride price, whether any of them must be returned, or in what amount. That is the court’s job.
The harder question comes afterward. Sun asks: Do I have the right to tell the public my side of the story? I chose to speak. Was that wrong?
My answer is that he unquestionably has the right to speak. But the right to speak is not the right to publish every detail of another person’s private life. That distinction has been almost completely lost in this controversy.
“I gave her 30 million yuan, I want it back, and I believe I was treated unfairly” is a public claim. “I have filed suit, and I believe those payments should legally be treated as bride price” is also a public claim. But if one tries to prove that claim by publishing intimate conduct, private correspondence, bodily information, family details or other material the other person never agreed to make public, the dispute changes character. A court adjudicates property. The internet adjudicates character. And unlike a court, it often does so without rules of evidence, proportionality or appeal.
China’s Civil Code separately protects privacy, including private spaces, private activities and private information. Those rights do not disappear because two people once loved each other. They do not vanish because the relationship ended badly. And they do not automatically yield because one side believes he has been wronged.
So if I were answering Sun for Hu Xijin, I would put the point somewhat differently from “a man should be decent.” I would say: Take the money dispute to court. Do not turn the internet into a tribunal for the relationship itself.
This principle is not gendered. A man who believes he has lost money may sue, report wrongdoing, seek preservation of assets, produce evidence and publicly state his legal position. A woman has the same rights. But secrets entrusted to someone during an intimate relationship should not automatically become ammunition when the relationship collapses.
Otherwise, intimacy itself becomes dangerous. What you tell someone you love today may become material used against you tomorrow. A private photograph may become a public exhibit. A conversation held in confidence may become a viral screenshot. A bedroom shared by two people may become entertainment for millions. If people begin to believe that every private relationship carries that risk, they will behave accordingly: they will disclose less, trust less, commit later, and sometimes decide not to commit at all.
Sun ends his letter by connecting the bride-price dispute to China’s demographic decline. On this point, he raises a question worth taking seriously. China recorded only 7.92 million births in 2025. In 1990, the national birth rate was 21.06 per thousand, which, given the population at the time, meant more than 20 million births. In 2024, only 6.106 million couples registered marriages, a decline of 20.5 percent from the year before. These numbers describe a profound transformation in Chinese marriage and family formation.
But they do not prove that the “missing” millions of births were driven away by bride price. Demography does not work that way. People are marrying later, marrying less and having fewer children for many reasons at once: longer education, urbanization, expensive housing, insecure employment, high childcare costs, greater professional opportunities for women, changing expectations of marriage, rising ages at first marriage and, increasingly, the simple fact that there are fewer young adults available to marry. Bride price raises the barrier to marriage in some places and among some groups. But it is one part of a much larger story.
Still, Sun makes one observation that deserves more attention than it has received. People may not withdraw because the price is high, he writes. They may withdraw because they cannot see where the price ends. That is the most important sentence in his letter. The problem is uncertainty.
Must there be an apartment before marriage? How much bride price is expected? Who pays for the wedding? Whose surname will the child take? Who stops working when the baby arrives? Who cares for aging parents? Does one spouse turn over his or her salary? How much are the parents on either side expected to contribute? If the marriage ends, what happens to the house, the savings and the money transferred before the wedding?
Traditional society once supplied answers—often unfair answers—to many of these questions. Those answers have weakened, but a new consensus has not fully replaced them. Young Chinese people have acquired much greater freedom in choosing how to live. They have also acquired much greater responsibility for negotiating almost every term of intimate life themselves. Freedom has expanded. So has uncertainty.
And this creates a peculiar equilibrium. Men fear becoming the family’s payer of last resort. Women fear becoming its caregiver of last resort. Men worry about open-ended financial obligations. Women worry about open-ended reproductive and domestic obligations. Both sides fear investing first. Both fear that the other person retains an easier exit. Both fear becoming the one left holding the risk.
Once those expectations take hold, delay becomes rational. Wait another year. Save a little more. Watch what happens to other marriages. Do not have the child yet. Do not register the marriage yet. Perhaps do not marry at all. That, more than any hypothetical national bride-price schedule, is the real “two hundred million people” problem.
What young people are waiting for is not a government-issued price tag for marriage. They are waiting for clearer boundaries.
Those boundaries are not difficult to describe. Bride price is not an entrance fee to marriage, and an extravagant bride price is not a man’s legal duty. Large transfers before marriage should be documented clearly. Each spouse retains full bodily and personal autonomy. Money, housework and childcare are shared responsibilities, though the precise division will differ from family to family. When a relationship ends, property disputes belong in court; intimate secrets should remain private.
And society has responsibilities too. If a country wants more people to marry and raise children, it cannot place nearly all the financial and professional risks of family formation onto two young adults and then wonder why they hesitate. Housing, childcare, education, parental leave and career interruption are not merely private problems. They shape national demographic behavior.
The goal should not be to make marriage cheap. It should be to make its risks more legible and its responsibilities more bounded. Then marriage might once again look less like an exercise in counterparty risk and more like what it is supposed to be: a way of building a life with another person.
So, Mr. Sun, if thirty years from now a young man comes to you and asks, “How much does a man have to pay to get married?” I hope you do not tell him 30,000 yuan, 300,000, three million or 30 million. Tell him something else: you are not buying a wife. She is not selling you a family through childbirth. Marriage is a decision by two free adults to make themselves partly responsible for each other’s future.
Money should be traceable. Rights should be explicit. Responsibilities should be reciprocal. And some things should remain beyond price.
The question young people most need answered is not: How much does marriage cost? It is: If I enter this relationship, are there limits to what I can be asked to give? Are my rights protected? Will the other person bear responsibilities too? And if one day we can no longer live together, can we still separate as two adults rather than destroy one another?
If a society can provide credible answers to those questions, whether the bride price is 30,000 or 300,000 yuan begins to matter much less. And if China is genuinely worried that young people are retreating from marriage and parenthood, the worst possible response would be to teach men and women to calculate against each other more aggressively. The better response is to build a society in which neither side has to fear that love is an unlimited liability.
Appendix: Justin Sun’s Open Letter to Hu Xijin
Dear Mr. Hu,
You ended your second article by saying that people should try to be honest and decent. So I would like to ask you something honestly.
I was born in 1990. I am thirty-six years old, at the age when marriage and children become real questions. You are exactly thirty years older than I am. I was already reading your articles when I was studying at Peking University. That is why I want to ask you rather than someone else.
There are about two hundred million men in China between the ages of twenty and forty, and about two hundred million women. I am not in a position to speak about the costs women bear. I will speak only about our side. We do not know how to build relationships with women, how to form families or how to raise children. We have never walked this road before. No one taught us how. For outsiders, these questions are gossip. For two hundred million young men, they are part of everyday life.
I do not know whether a Chinese man is expected to pay a large bride price. If he is, should it be a fixed amount or a percentage of his wealth? I do not know what price a man is expected to pay for having children. I do not know whether a man is expected to satisfy every request made by a woman before and after marriage. If he does not, and she leaves, does he have the right to recover the bride price? If she refuses to return it, may he go to court?
Nor do I know whether, after a man has observed all the expected formalities, met the parents, been separated for a long time, failed to recover his money and can no longer find the other person, he has the right to tell the public what he thinks. I chose to speak. Was that wrong?
I do not have answers to these questions. The state has answered some of them. The No. 1 Central Document addresses the issue, and the Supreme People’s Court has issued judicial interpretations. I have read them, and I trust them. But government documents are written on paper. Bride prices are negotiated around dinner tables. Between the two lies social reality.
You are my elder, and I respect your answer as well, just as I will unconditionally respect the court’s final judgment in the bride-price case.
A bride price has to be paid one way or another. North or south, educated or uneducated, the difference is largely whether it is 30,000 yuan, 300,000, three million or 30 million. This is a cost two hundred million young Chinese men are expected to bear. We accept that.
When a person cannot calculate the limits of a bargain, the safest choice is not to enter it. In 1990, the year I was born, more than 23 million children were born in China. Last year, there were 7.92 million—the lowest number since the founding of the People’s Republic.
I do not believe this entire decline can be explained by one calculation. But among the two-thirds who are now missing, many did not withdraw because they did not want marriage or children. They withdrew because they did not know what this road would ask of them, how much they would have to give, or whether what they gave would ultimately count.
People do not necessarily walk away because the price is high. They walk away because they cannot see where the price ends. We do not know the rules governing that price.
Two hundred million people are waiting for an answer, because this is the first step toward forming families, and it will help determine who makes up this country over the next thirty years. I do not have the answer today. I hope that thirty years from now, when a young person asks me the same question, I will be able to give him one.
Justin Sun

Ma Siwei
In the age of AI, one comforting phrase is often heard: everyone is back on the same starting line. This sentence is half true, and half dangerous.
The true part is that AI has indeed lowered many thresholds. In the past, an ordinary person who wanted to write a decent business plan had to know the format, do research, organize the language, and revise it again and again. Now AI can produce a framework in a few minutes. In the past, someone who could not code had a hard time building even a small tool. Now he can ask AI to generate scripts, web pages, spreadsheets, and automated workflows. In the past, writing, design, translation, market analysis, PowerPoint presentations, and résumé revision all required long training. Now many surface-level tasks have been flattened by tools almost at once.
This is where the idea of “the same starting line” comes from. Tools have become cheaper. Entry has become easier. For the first time, ordinary people have access to forms of assistance that once belonged mainly to professionals. A small shop owner can use AI to write advertising copy. A freelancer can use AI to prepare a client proposal. A student can use AI to simulate an interview. An ordinary worker can use AI to study an equipment manual. A crack has indeed opened.
But the danger lies here as well. The starting line may look the same, but the resources behind it are not the same. Some people own models, computing power, equity, data, platforms, and distribution channels. Others merely have a chat window. Some use AI to expand their companies. Some use AI to keep their jobs. Some use AI to train teams. Some use AI to help their bosses make their own labor cheaper. The tools look similar on the surface, but the positions are not similar at all.
So ordinary people in the age of AI should not be over-comforted by the phrase “the same starting line.” The real question is not whether everyone has a tool. The real question is who can use the tool to tell a different story, find a problem others have not seen, and turn that story into a plan that can actually land.
Peter Thiel’s thinking is useful here. His most famous question is: What important truth do very few people agree with you on? This sounds like a question from an investor, but it is also a survival question for ordinary people in the AI age. AI is especially good at producing “what most people have already said.” Ask it where the next big opportunity is, and it will easily give you an average answer. Ask it to write an industry analysis, and it will mix public information, mainstream views, and common judgments into one smooth document. It will be fluent, complete, and plausible. But very often, it is only the statistical product of imitative desire.
This is AI’s narrative trap. Human beings are already prone to imitating one another. When others say short videos make money, everyone rushes into short videos. When others say livestream commerce is an opportunity, everyone rushes into livestreaming. When others say AI applications are the next wave, everyone rushes into AI applications. Now AI makes this imitation faster. A person who was merely following the crowd can now follow the crowd more elegantly with AI. A company that was merely copying its competitors can now use AI to produce, at greater speed, a strategy that sounds advanced.
So competition becomes more crowded. This is not because everyone has become more creative. It is because everyone can produce a passable narrative faster than before. In the past, storytelling still had some cost. You had to know how to write, how to package, and how to prepare a proposal. Now the cost of narrative is close to zero. In one night, a person can generate ten business plans, twenty brand stories, and thirty short-video scripts. But when everyone can tell a story, the truly valuable thing is no longer the ability to tell one. It is whether what you are telling is something others have not yet seen.
This is what Thiel calls a “secret.” A secret is not a mysterious conspiracy. Nor is it some piece of inside information hidden from the public. It is more like a real problem that has not yet been accepted by the mainstream narrative. The secret Airbnb saw in its early days was this: strangers might be willing to stay in strangers’ homes. The secret Uber saw early on was this: in many cities, the problem was not simply a lack of cars, but a foolish way of matching vehicles, drivers, and passengers. These secrets later became business models. But before they were proven, they sounded like strange, counterintuitive remarks.
In the AI age, ordinary people also need to look for their own “secrets.” This secret does not have to be the founding of a unicorn company. It can be small. A teacher discovers that students are not unable to write essays; they have simply never gone through the experience of asking real questions. A nurse discovers that patients fear not only the test result, but the fact that no one explains it in language they can understand. A factory technician discovers that machine vision can detect defects, but does not know which kind of defect will become a major problem in a later process. A community worker discovers that elderly people are not unable to use smartphones; they are afraid that if they press the wrong button, no one will help them. A small shop owner discovers that customers do not only want low prices; they also want to be remembered.
These secrets come from the scene itself. AI can summarize existing knowledge on the Internet, but it is hard for it to walk into the scene for you. It can generate a nursing workflow, but it cannot see a patient’s fingers clutching the bedsheet. It can write an education plan, but it cannot hear the sense of inferiority in a student’s silence. It can analyze a market, but it cannot tell you why, at four in the afternoon, no one suddenly passes the door of a small shop. The advantage of ordinary people is often hidden in these places. It is not grand, but it is real. It may not be beautiful, but it is useful.
So the first survival rule for ordinary people in the age of AI is anti-imitation. Do not immediately ask AI to help you make a similar version the moment you see what someone else is doing. The more easily something can be copied by everyone, the faster it will lose value. First ask: Is this a story that has already been told to death? Is this demand real? Has this problem appeared in the actual scene? Is there a detail that the mainstream narrative has always ignored?
The second survival rule is to turn the “secret” into a small, verifiable plan. Simply saying “AI will change education” is not a story. It is empty talk. Saying “AI will help us improve efficiency” is not a story either. It is waste language. A real story must be specific. For example, a community school can use AI to do three things: help teachers generate tiered exercises, help students understand mistakes, and help parents read learning reports. Each task must be testable. Do students understand better? Do teachers spend less time on repetitive labor? Are parents less anxious? If it cannot be verified, the story is only a slogan.
The third survival rule is definite optimism. Definite optimism does not mean shouting every day that “the future will be better.” That is too easy. Real definite optimism means believing that the future can become better, and then offering a concrete path. In the AI age, the most useless sentence is “AI is important.” That sentence contains no information anymore. A more useful sentence would be: in the next three months, AI can help a certain group of people reduce a certain kind of low-value labor; it can reduce a certain kind of error in a certain workflow; it can give one ordinary person a certain new ability. The future must land in specific things. Otherwise, it is only motivational noise.
The fourth survival rule is to protect one’s own main brain. AI can help draft, compare, search for materials, and generate counterexamples. But the final judgment cannot be handed over. A person who knows only how to ask AI questions, but not how to judge AI’s answers, has not become stronger. He has only become easier to lead by polished language. The smoother the answer AI generates, the more slowly a person should move. Where might it be wrong? Is there a source? Is there a counterexample? Who benefits? Who bears the cost? These questions are not complicated, but they can save a life.
The fifth survival rule is to accumulate materials that AI cannot easily touch. The most valuable person in the future may not be the one who writes the best prompts, but the one who has real experience, real observation, and real problems. A person who has spent ten years in nursing, a person who has delivered food for five years, a person who has long adjusted machines in a factory, a person who knows the needs of elderly people in a community, a teacher who truly understands the psychology of students—all of them have their own materials. The problem is that in the past, they often did not treat these materials as knowledge. In the AI age, they must learn to speak these experiences out, organize them, and turn them into plans, courses, products, services, and public discussion.
The sixth survival rule is to treat AI as an exoskeleton, not as a substitute. An exoskeleton helps a person go farther. A substitute slowly hollows a person out. Using AI to write a first draft does not mean letting AI think for you. Using AI to do analysis does not mean letting AI make judgments for you. Using AI to make a plan does not mean letting AI face the consequences for you. Ordinary people need to learn a new rhythm of work: first raise the question themselves, then let AI expand it; first decide the direction themselves, then let AI gather materials; first write a rough idea themselves, then let AI help refine it; and at the end, revise, verify, and take responsibility themselves.
The real gap in the AI age will not appear only in whether people know how to use the tool. The deeper gap will appear here: some people use AI to imitate others, while some use AI to enlarge themselves; some use AI to produce clichés, while some use AI to test secrets; some use AI to chase trends, while some use AI to build their own direction; some use AI to submit a prettier assignment, while some use AI to discover a question no one has seriously asked before.
This is the true survival method for ordinary people. Do not imagine that the starting line is really fair, but do not give up simply because resources are unfair. Ordinary people do not need to compete with giants in computing power. They do not need to compete with models in speed. What they can truly do is protect their own scene, train their own judgment, find a small but real problem, connect AI to it, and slowly deepen it.
AI will make mediocre narratives cheaper and cheaper. It will also make real experience more precious. It will make following the crowd easier, and make resisting the crowd more valuable. It will allow most people to say the same thing faster, and it will reward the few who can say something that truly belongs to them.
In this sense, the most important competition in the AI age is not a race between humans and machines. It is whether a person can avoid being carried away by machines and the crowd at the same time. Are you imitating someone else’s story, or are you telling your own? This is the first question ordinary people must answer as they stand before the AI tsunami.

BY：Du Hongwei （杜鸿威）
There is a popular “floor theory” of cognition. Some people, the idea goes, stand on the second floor and can see only the street in front of them; others stand on the eighth floor, where the view is broader and stretches much farther. Even when they are looking at the same world, they therefore reach very different judgments. The metaphor is vivid, and it does capture something real about life: differences in knowledge, experience, professional training, and sources of information can lead people to form very different pictures of the world. But the second-floor/eighth-floor metaphor also contains a danger. The moment someone says, “I’m on the eighth floor and you’re on the second,” a metaphor meant to explain cognitive differences quietly turns into a cognitive hierarchy. A harder question follows: Who decides which floor anyone is on? Could someone who is actually on the second floor be absolutely convinced that he is already on the eighth? If people assign their own floors, there is no reliable distinction between “I can see farther than you” and “I believe I can see farther than you.”
This is where the problem of cognition becomes genuinely interesting. People obviously differ in knowledge, experience, and ability. But what turns those differences into a gulf that is difficult to cross is often not how much a person knows today, but whether his cognitive system is still capable of revising itself. What matters most is not whether someone stands on the second floor or the eighth, but whether there is still a staircase between them.
Kant Never Issued Anyone an “Eighth-Floor License”
When people discuss cognitive differences, they often invoke Kant’s idea that “the human mind legislates for nature.” It is easy to take this to mean that people possess different cognitive capacities and therefore see different worlds—some more superficially, others more deeply. But that is not what Kant was really saying. Critique of Pure Reason asks a more fundamental question: How is human experience possible? How do space, time, and the basic categories of the understanding take part in our knowledge of the empirical world? Kant argues that what we can know are phenomena as they appear through the forms of human cognition; we cannot simply identify what we know with the “thing in itself.” More importantly, these forms of cognition are, in his account, common conditions that make human experience possible. They are not private cognitive operating systems, one installed in Zhang San and another in Li Si.
What Kant can genuinely contribute to the second-floor/eighth-floor debate, then, is not cognitive superiority but epistemic humility. Seeing the world is not the same as possessing the world as it is in itself. Knowing a great deal does not give anyone a God’s-eye view. Every judgment we make has already passed through perception, language, concepts, experience, and prior knowledge. The more clearly a person understands this, the less he should ask, “Why can’t other people see the view from my eighth floor?” and the more he should ask: How do I know that I am really on the eighth floor? One of the easiest mistakes for intellectuals to make is not ignorance, but turning their knowledge into a ruler with which to measure everyone else’s intelligence. The more one knows, and the more tools one has for explaining the world, the easier it can become to mistake one’s map for the world itself.
The old saying “You cannot speak of ice to a summer insect” is a beautiful metaphor. An insect that lives only through spring, summer, and autumn has never seen snow or ice, so it is hardly surprising if it does not believe in winter. The metaphor could lead us toward tolerance: human experience is always limited, and we should not immediately conclude that someone is stupid simply because he does not know what we know. Yet the metaphor can also slip almost imperceptibly in another direction. It begins with “everyone has limitations,” moves to “his limitations are greater than mine,” and ends with “I understand why he is wrong because I stand higher than he does.” What began as epistemic humility has become an epistemic hierarchy.
The deepest wisdom in “You cannot speak of ice to a summer insect” may not be that some people will never understand winter. What matters more today is another possibility: any of us may be that summer insect. Someone who sees political questions very clearly may become a summer insect when the subject turns to economics. An economics professor may be one in medicine. Even someone who has read Kant closely may become a summer insect when new facts appear, simply because he has become too attached to his theory.
True epistemic humility, then, does not mean standing on the eighth floor and feeling sorry for those on the second. That is still the arrogance of the eighth floor. Real humility means admitting that the view before us also has limits, that there may be a ninth or tenth floor we do not yet know exists, and even that what we once took to be the “eighth floor” may turn out to have been a mistaken mark on the map.
In the end, cognitive differences between people can be measured by two very different questions. One is: What floor are you on now? The other is: If new facts prove you wrong, are you willing to take the stairs? The first question easily produces a sense of superiority. The second determines how far a person, a science, an organization, or even a civilization can ultimately go. Genuine cognitive strength has never meant being right forever. It means preserving a capacity that is not very flattering, and can sometimes be painful: when you discover that you were wrong, you actually change.
The Greatest Danger Is Cognitive Self-Immunity
If someone says, “You disagree with me because your cognitive level is lower than mine,” meaningful discussion is already difficult. If he goes a step further and says, “The more you argue back, the more clearly it proves that your old programming has activated its defense mechanism,” the theory acquires a very dangerous property: it becomes almost impossible for it to fail. If you agree, that proves it is right. If you disagree, that also proves it is right. If you become angry, your programming has been triggered. If you calmly present facts, that can be interpreted as evidence that your programming is simply more sophisticated. Whatever happens can eventually be reinterpreted as proof that the theory itself was correct. A theory capable of explaining every possible outcome may look extraordinarily powerful, but in fact it violates Gödel’s incompleteness theorem and, more important, loses the one thing it most needs: it no longer knows what could prove it wrong.
Popper’s account of falsifiability has, of course, been revised and challenged in many ways, and science is far more complicated than the phrase “capable of being falsified.” Yet one simple epistemic principle remains useful: a claim about reality should at least allow for the possibility that some facts might conflict with it. Otherwise, what we have is no longer a judgment open to testing by reality, but a belief system designed to protect itself from reality.
This condition can be called cognitive self-immunity. The biological immune system identifies and rejects foreign substances; a cognitive system can develop a similar mechanism. Any information inconsistent with an established worldview is automatically recoded as “enemy propaganda,” “manipulation by vested interests,” “the other side has been brainwashed,” “their cognitive level is too low,” or simply “you don’t understand.” The result feels comfortable: one’s worldview can never lose. But the cost is enormous. A cognitive system that can never fail also loses the capacity to learn.
So there is a better question for judging someone’s cognitive level than “How much do you know?” It is this: What evidence, if it appeared, would make you change your mind? If the answer is “none,” it no longer matters very much whether the person is on the second floor, the eighth, or the eighteenth. The staircase has already been torn down.
What we really need to distinguish, therefore, is not “high-cognition people” from “low-cognition people,” but two different cognitive structures. One may be rich in knowledge yet closed. Such a person may have read widely, mastered a large vocabulary of concepts, possess strong logical skills, and be especially good at debate. Yet all that knowledge ultimately serves one purpose: proving that he was right all along. Another person may know less, but remain open. He habitually asks: Which parts are facts, and which are merely inferences? How strong a conclusion does this evidence actually support? Are there alternative explanations? If my prediction fails, how much should I revise my original model?
The first person may already stand high above the street, but have no staircase. The second may still be on the second floor, yet remain capable of climbing. Knowledge is therefore something like cognitive stock, while the capacity for correction is cognitive mobility. How much a person carries in his head certainly matters, but another question matters even more: Does he have a mechanism for discarding false knowledge, revising old models, and absorbing new evidence? This is why being “smart” is not the same as having strong cognition. Some intelligent people are exceptionally skilled at finding reasons for their own mistakes. The better their logic and the greater their knowledge, the more elaborate the fortress they may be able to build around their original conclusions.
The hardest cognitive skill is not proving that you are right. It is recognizing: This time, I may be wrong. A person can test himself with a few simple questions. Can I accurately state the strongest argument on the other side, instead of attacking only its weakest or most foolish version? Have I ever publicly revised a judgment because the facts changed? When a prediction fails, do I revise my model, or do I keep adding qualifications until I can once again conclude that “I was never really wrong”? These questions tell us more about the quality of a person’s cognition than how many books he has read or how many philosophers he can discuss.
The Core of Civilization: Can Errors Be Discovered, Transmitted, and Corrected?
Once the issue moves from individuals to institutions, something even more interesting appears. Three major institutions of modern civilization seem very different from one another: science, competitive markets, and democratic politics. They deal respectively with knowledge, resources, and power. Yet at a deeper level they share one premise: anyone can be wrong.
Scientists are not saints. They make errors of judgment, become attached to their own theories, and can be influenced by prestige, funding, academic schools, and personal interests. Science remains one of humanity’s most reliable systems for producing public knowledge not because scientists never make mistakes, but because science has developed mechanisms such as open methods, testing against evidence, peer criticism, replication, correction, and retraction. What makes science reliable is not that every paper is reliable, but that errors can, in principle, continue to be challenged.
Markets, under certain conditions, contain a similar logic.
