When Friedrich Hayek wrote about “the use of knowledge in society,” his most important point was not that entrepreneurs are smarter than government officials. It was that the knowledge required for a functioning society is dispersed among countless individuals and cannot be fully assembled in any single central mind. Where competition is able to operate, prices, profits, losses, and exit continually provide feedback. Entrepreneurs can certainly be wrong, but errors carry costs, while new participants remain free to propose another solution.
This does not mean that markets are always right. In Competition and Entrepreneurship, Israel Kirzner also makes clear that the permanent condition of real markets is not orderly equilibrium but ignorance, disequilibrium, and disorder. Sellers do not fully know buyers’ maximum demands; buyers do not know where lower prices may be found. Resources are misallocated, supply and demand become disconnected, and information barriers exist everywhere. These cognitive blind spots, shared by everyone in the market, are precisely where entrepreneurial profit arises. Every market participant sees only part of the picture and operates with incomplete information. Pure entrepreneurial profit, in this account, does not come from labor, capital, or technology as such, but from differences in perception.
This challenges the ordinary intuition that rewards simply follow labor or capital. Why do some people work from dawn to dusk all year and still remain close to subsistence? One answer is that they compete on tracks everyone can already see, exchanging time and physical effort for standardized compensation. Why do others appear to enter a field almost effortlessly and earn extraordinary returns? Because alertness allows them to notice cognitive blind spots others have missed and move into spaces where competition has not yet arrived.
For Kirzner, the essence of entrepreneurship is neither innovation nor risk-taking, but alertness. Schumpeter’s theory of innovation has been enormously influential, and generations have come to imagine the entrepreneur as a revolutionary who destroys an old order and creates something new, disrupting equilibrium through creative destruction. Kirzner supplied a different part of the picture. The two describe different commercial logics: Schumpeter’s entrepreneur disrupts equilibrium; Kirzner’s entrepreneur discovers and helps correct disequilibrium. Most ordinary people lack the power to reinvent an industry or the capital to reconstruct an entire market, but entrepreneurial alertness is not necessarily reserved for a tiny elite. Profit opportunities often do not have to be created from nothing. They may already exist, unnoticed.
None of this means that markets are omnipotent. Monopoly, externalities, asymmetric information, public goods, and badly designed incentives can all distort market feedback. The important question is therefore not whether “the market is always right,” but whether a system can expose errors and reallocate resources after failure.
Democratic politics follows a similar logic. The best defense of democracy has never been that “the majority is always right.” Majorities can make disastrous decisions. One of democracy’s more important virtues is that it can turn political mistakes into mistakes that are, in principle, correctable: policies can be criticized, information can enter the public sphere, those in power can face opposition, and governments that fail can be peacefully replaced through institutional procedures.
Seen from this perspective, science, competitive markets, and democracy belong to very different domains, but they share an important civilizational logic: they do not place their hopes in finding someone who will always be right. They try instead to prevent errors from becoming permanent. That may matter far more than deciding who is the smartest.
Return now to the second floor and the eighth. The problem looks different. Societies obviously contain real differences in expertise. Doctors generally know more about medicine than laypeople. Structural engineers know more about bridges than political commentators. Economists who have spent years studying monetary policy are usually better equipped than outsiders to understand inflation. Pretending that every opinion deserves equal professional weight is not epistemic humility; it is the abolition of expertise.
But expertise cannot automatically become an “eighth-floor license.” A brilliant economist may know almost nothing about viruses. A Nobel laureate may make terrible judgments once he leaves his own field. The more complex modern knowledge becomes, the less plausible it is that anyone can remain on the eighth floor of every subject.
So the real question is not whether different floors exist. It is whether there is still a staircase. Can new information enter? Can criticism be voiced? Can counterexamples be preserved? Can mistakes be made public? Can a theory be revised when its predictions fail? Can a policy be changed when it fails? Can those in power be replaced when they fail? The true cognitive capacity of a civilization is ultimately determined not by the brilliance of its smartest few, but by whether errors can be discovered, transmitted, and corrected within the system.
This leads to a very different conclusion from the conventional second-floor/eighth-floor metaphor: the greatest danger to a society is not that too many people are on the second floor. It is that the people on the eighth floor close the staircase and announce to everyone below: There is no need to come up. I have already seen the whole view.
Many of history’s greatest disasters did not occur because ordinary people knew nothing. They occurred because people with immense power and resources became convinced that they already knew enough—and then removed other people’s ability to correct them.
That is the most dangerous form of cognitive self-immunity: the moment it moves from an individual mind into an institution. When one person refuses correction, he may ruin an investment, a relationship, or a judgment. When a powerful institution refuses correction, its errors can be reproduced across an entire society.

In January 2025, a notice appeared at the matchmaking corner in Chengdu’s People’s Park: “Registration for women is full and temporarily suspended.” A photograph of the sign quickly spread online and became the basis for a striking story. China has more men than women, so why does a matchmaking corner seem to be full of women looking for husbands? Soon an even more compelling explanation emerged: men have stopped coming. They have done the math. A home, bride price, wedding, and children all cost money, while marriage also carries the risk of divorce. So some men simply opt out and spend their money on travel, gaming, fishing, skincare, and themselves. Men once earned money in order to support a family; now, the argument goes, they are learning to spend it on their own lives.
The notice at People’s Park was real. On January 14, 2025, the park did temporarily suspend new registrations from women because the available spaces for their profiles had filled up. But park staff later told the media that the profiles actually displayed on the wall were still divided roughly fifty-fifty between men and women, and that there had also been occasions when the spaces for men had filled up first. A real notice was gradually enlarged into a national conclusion that the evidence did not support: the old saying that “a grown man should marry” had supposedly become “grown men no longer want to marry,” while the ranks of “leftover men” had somehow vanished, leaving only women unable to find husbands.
A 2023 special survey by the Center for Population and Development Studies at Renmin University of China, which examined people delaying or rejecting marriage and childbearing, found that only about one-fifth of unmarried or late-marrying respondents said they did not intend to marry in the future. In other words, most people who had not married had not rejected marriage altogether. Some 38.16 percent said they simply did not have enough time to date or get married. That finding matters because it brings the issue back from the realm of values and attitudes to the realities of daily life.
A young person may remain unmarried because he or she does not believe in marriage. But the reason may also be long working hours, unstable income, the lack of affordable housing, failure to meet a suitable partner, or the feeling that starting a family is simply beyond one’s current means. “Not marrying” includes both active refusal and involuntary delay. Chinese public discussion often blurs the two. If a man remains single, people say he has “given up.” If a woman remains single, they say her standards are too high. It is a convenient explanation because it puts responsibility back on the individual and makes the social structure disappear.
What is actually happening to marriage in China is far more complicated—and more consequential—than the claim that “men no longer want to marry.”
Why Do Women Still Feel That Men Are Hard to Find?
Start with the figure most easily misunderstood. China’s 2020 population census recorded 723.34 million men and 688.44 million women, a difference of roughly 34.9 million. The number is real. But those 34.9 million are not 34.9 million single men waiting for wives. They include children, elderly people, married men, widowers, and people living in different regions and belonging to different age groups. An excess of seventy-year-old men means almost nothing to a thirty-year-old woman looking for a partner. What matters in a marriage market is not the total number of men and women, but the number who can realistically match in age, place, education, income, and marital status.
The overall gender gap is also narrowing. According to the National Bureau of Statistics’ 2025 one-percent population sample survey, China had about 717.22 million men and 688.23 million women, reducing the gap to roughly 29 million and bringing the overall sex ratio down to 104.21 men for every 100 women. The more serious imbalance lies among people of marriageable age. One study based largely on 2020 census data estimated the sex ratio in China’s marriageable population at roughly 110 men for every 100 women. It also found 17.33 million never-married men aged thirty-five or older, around 8.82 million of them in rural areas. Rural men faced a substantially higher risk of remaining unmarried for life than urban men.
China, then, does not suffer from a nationwide “surplus of women.” In aggregate demographic terms, the opposite remains true. Men still outnumber women, and the burden of that imbalance falls disproportionately on men with lower incomes, less education, and fewer opportunities in regions losing population. This is the first marriage problem China faces: many men have difficulty finding wives.
And yet many urban women also genuinely feel that there are few suitable men around them. How can both things be true? Because a marriage market is not a stadium into which ten million men and ten million women can simply be poured and paired off one by one. Marriage is a matching process. Equal numbers do not guarantee compatible matches.
Over the past four decades, China has undergone three enormous social changes: mass migration from the countryside to the cities, a dramatic rise in women’s educational attainment, and major changes in household income and occupational structure. Marriage expectations, however, have not changed at exactly the same speed.
Traditional Chinese mate selection has long shown a broad tendency for men to marry women who are similar to them, somewhat younger, or somewhat lower in educational and economic status, while women have tended to prefer men whose age, education, occupation, and economic position are at least equal to their own. In the past, this system could operate relatively smoothly because men on average had more education and greater economic resources than women. The educational revolution has changed that structure. As more women attend university and enter professional careers, the old marriage hierarchy begins to malfunction. If women’s education and occupational status rise while the expectation that “the man should not rank below the woman” remains largely intact, a peculiar pattern emerges: more men accumulate at the lower end of the marriage market, while more women accumulate at the upper end. Both groups feel that suitable partners are disappearing.
A 2025 economic study of China’s marriage market found that educational expansion over the past two decades has itself contributed substantially to falling match rates. Changes in educational structure have affected both men and women, in part because highly educated women and less-educated men increasingly occupy opposite sides of a structural mismatch. The study found little evidence that highly educated women had begun marrying substantially less-educated men in large numbers. Earlier national research had already identified a similar pattern: men with low levels of education and women with high levels of education were among the groups less likely to enter marriage.
This produces one of the most revealing—and most misunderstood—scenes in contemporary China. Rural men say there are no women. Urban women say there are no men. Both may be describing their own reality accurately. The rural man means: there are too few women who are willing to stay here and marry someone like me. The urban woman means: there are too few men whose education, career, lifestyle, and views of family fit what I am looking for.
Tens of millions of statistically “extra” men do not automatically solve the marriage problem of a thirty-five-year-old female doctor, lawyer, or engineer in Beijing, Shanghai, or Chengdu. Nor will a low-income forty-five-year-old bachelor in a western county automatically marry a thirty-five-year-old highly educated single woman in Shanghai simply because both happen to be unmarried. They live in the same country, but not necessarily in the same marriage market. The so-called “leftover men” and “leftover women” are often the two ends left behind by the same structural mismatch.
Marriage Is Becoming Less a Life Stage Than a High-Cost Decision
Economics offers one of the most important keys to understanding marriage in China today. In the 2023 Renmin University survey, some respondents looking back on their wedding expenses reported an average cost of 330,400 yuan—more than eight times China’s per capita disposable income of 39,200 yuan that year. The figure must be used carefully. It came from a specific survey and should not simply be presented as “the average cost of getting married in China.” Nor does it mean that men alone pay all 330,400 yuan. In reality, marriage expenses may be divided among the groom’s family, the bride’s family, and the couple themselves, with enormous differences between regions.
Still, the number captures a real shift: the price of entering marriage has risen sharply. Housing, wedding ceremonies, bride price, renovation, and cars may only be the beginning. After marriage come mortgages, childbirth, childcare, education, and the care of aging parents. According to a 2024 estimate by the YuWa Population Research Institute based on official statistics, the average direct cost of raising a child from birth to age seventeen was around 538,000 yuan, rising to roughly 680,000 yuan through completion of an undergraduate degree. These are not official national standards, and individual families may spend much less or much more. But they illustrate the scale of the long-term financial burden facing young households.
Marriage has therefore undergone a profound change. For many people in the past, the main question was simple: I have reached the right age, so I should marry. Increasingly, young people now ask a different set of questions. Can I afford to marry? Will my life become better after marriage? Do I want children? Who will care for them? Who will pay the mortgage? Who will do the housework? Who will take care of both sets of aging parents? If there are no satisfactory answers, postponing marriage—or even declining it altogether—becomes understandable.
This does not mean that men suddenly became selfish or that women suddenly became demanding. Marriage is gradually changing from an almost compulsory stage of life into a long-term contract whose costs and benefits people feel entitled to examine.
The financial pressures on men are easy to see. The costs borne by women are often less visible. For many professional women, the greatest cost of marriage may not be the wedding itself, but what happens to their time afterward. Who becomes pregnant? Who gives birth? Who takes time off when a child is sick? Who attends school meetings? When an elderly parent needs care, whose working day gets cut short?
If a society expects women to have careers while continuing to assume that women will perform most family care, then the more education and occupational opportunities women gain, the greater the opportunity cost of marriage may become. This helps explain why rising female economic independence does not automatically produce higher marriage rates. On the contrary, economic independence gives women more power to reject poor marriages. In the past, an unmarried woman might face severe economic and social risks. Today she can work, rent or buy a home, travel, and maintain a social world of her own. Marriage changes from something she “must have” to something worth entering only if it improves her life.
Men are undergoing a related shift. For generations, the expected male life course was clear: earn money, buy a home, marry, have children, support the household. Some men now ask a different question: if my income barely supports my own life, why must I take on decades of housing costs and family obligations? It is misleading to call this a “retreat from responsibility.” A more accurate description is that family responsibility is shifting from a social command toward an individual choice.
The change affects both sexes, though not in exactly the same way. Men tend to be more sensitive to the financial threshold for entering marriage; women tend to be more sensitive to marriage quality, division of domestic labor, and the career costs of childbirth. Both sides are raising the conditions under which they are willing to marry. The market consequently becomes narrower.
Marriage and Childbearing: A Problem Chinese Society Cannot Avoid
China recorded only 7.92 million births in 2025. Marriage and childbearing remain closely linked in Chinese society, so a sustained decline in marriage will eventually affect births, household size, housing demand, schools, the pension system, and local government finances. Marriage may begin as a private matter between two people, but its consequences eventually spread through the entire society.
If policymakers understand the problem only as “young people do not want to marry,” they are likely to prescribe the wrong medicine. More matchmaking events will not solve unstable employment among rural men. Telling women to lower their standards will not address professional women’s concerns about the division of household labor. Criticizing men for “lying flat” will not make housing and childcare cheaper. Restricting excessive bride prices may reduce marriage costs in some regions, but it cannot eliminate a long-standing numerical imbalance between men and women. A few hundred yuan in marriage subsidies cannot offset the cost of a home, twenty years of child-rearing, and decades of family responsibility.
Effective marriage policy therefore eventually becomes social policy: reduce housing pressure on young adults, improve employment prospects, expand affordable childcare, reduce excessive educational competition, lower the cost of raising children, bring fathers more fully into childcare and eldercare, reduce the career penalty women face for having children, and build stronger pension and social-support systems for the large number of rural men who may remain unmarried throughout their lives.
At a deeper level, society has to accept a simple fact. The state can lower the barriers to marriage, but it cannot order one person to love another. Once a modern society gives people the ability to leave or reject low-quality marriages, it cannot fully return to an era when reaching a certain age automatically meant getting married. That is not necessarily a bad thing. The difficulty is that marriage itself has changed rapidly in China, while housing, employment, gender roles, eldercare, childcare, and expectations about suitable partners have not all changed at the same pace.
That is why China now presents such an apparently contradictory picture. There are still tens of millions more men than women, yet women in major cities often say that suitable men are difficult to find. Some matchmaking corners fill up with female applicants, while large parts of rural China still contain substantial numbers of middle-aged men who cannot find wives.
The title of this essay—Men Struggle to Marry, Women Struggle to Find Husbands—seems at first to describe two separate stories. Look more closely, and they are really one. China does not lack men, nor does it lack women. What China increasingly lacks are matches in which two people can accept one another and have the material conditions to build a life together.
In the past, marriage mainly answered the question of whether one had a spouse at all. Society defined the proper age, families supplied resources, and individuals largely followed an established life course. Today the question is increasingly whether marriage is worth entering. Men calculate income, housing, and family obligations. Women calculate careers, housework, and the costs of childbirth. Both have more freedom than previous generations to walk away, and both face a higher price for walking in.
What is changing in Chinese marriage, then, is not that men have suddenly “woken up,” or that women have suddenly become too choosy. An ancient institution is confronting, on a mass scale, a modern individual’s question: If being together does not make life better for both of us, why must we marry? And if a couple’s income cannot support the cost of raising a child, why must they have one?
That is the question behind the figures—6.10 million marriages, 6.76 million marriages, or 3.27 million marriages in half a year—that Chinese society can no longer avoid.

The Ministry of Agriculture and Farmers Welfare convened a high-level virtual meeting on June 23 to prepare for an uncertain Kharif season, owing to the El Nino effect.
The World Meteorological Organisation had, as early as in March 2026, warned that an El Nino event was likely this year, while the India Meteorological Department’s long-range forecast issued in April placed seasonal rainfall at 92% of the long-period average.
Despite these early indications of a weak monsoon for a country where almost 64% of the population is dependent on agriculture, preparedness gathered pace only after the El Nino effect became increasingly evident. During June, rainfall deficiency was recorded at about 40%, and area coverage under Kharif crops declined 54% over the previous year.
While July rains are promising, we find ourselves in such a crisis situation each monsoon season, El Nino or not, raising concerns regarding a robust long-term strategy to monsoon-proof the economy, and efficiently manage water resources.
Agricultural output rests on a multitude of complex factors including fertilisers, seeds, mechanisation and tools, skills, R&D and so on. Timely access and adequate water remain the most critical enablers for the success of policy strategies for other inputs and vectors. India is heavily reliant on the southwest monsoon, and the country receives close to three-quarters of its annual rainfall during June to September.
Between 2019 and 2025, seasonal rain has performed well, with normal / excess rainfall occurring in over 75% districts in five of the seven years, and a reasonably good annual average GVA growth rate of 3.3% for agriculture and allied sectors in the last three years. The challenge is to effectively deploy this water abundance and build long-term resilience through irrigation facilities that will minimise the vagaries of the monsoon. This will not only support farmers, but also improve food management, inflation control, consumer demand and overall income growth.
India’s irrigation experience over the years has been modest.
First, India’s net irrigated area increased from 57 million hectares in 2003-04 to 82.4 million hectares in 2023-24. Gross irrigated area – the area irrigated for more than one crop during the year – rose from 41% of gross cropped area to 60%. Yet, the pace of expansion has not picked up in recent years, even as the monsoons have become increasingly erratic.
Two, wide regional disparities exist in irrigation access across the country. For example, in Punjab and Haryana, gross irrigation stands at over 90%, while some states have irrigation coverage below 25%, as per the Land Use Survey 2025.
Three, crop coverage of irrigation is largely concentrated in a few foodgrains. Rice and wheat benefit from better irrigation facilities, compared with other important crops such as pulses and oilseeds, distorting farmer incomes. While India has emerged as the top rice producer and exporter, the lack of adequate water for other major crops constrains consumption and raises imports in rainfall deficient years.
Four, the share of canals is giving way to the rising share of tanks and tubewells, affecting groundwater supplies. The government is rightly shifting from large irrigation projects to improving the efficiency of irrigation. The Pradhan Mantri Krishi Sinchayee Yojana, underway since 2015, aims to take water management to the farm level. The Accelerated Irrigation Benefit Programme, Modernisation of Command Area Development and Water Management, watershed development, Har Khet Ko Pani and Per Drop More Crop schemes collectively help enhance water productivity through renovation of existing facilities, groundwater management, and boosting micro-irrigation facilities.
However, it appears that the proposed budget outlay for these programmes has been reduced over the last few years. The transfers to states and UTs under the Har Khet Ko Pani programme stood at Rs 8.93 billion in 2025-26, and has been budgeted at just Rs 7.0 billion for 2026-27. The total PMKSY outlay for 2026-27 at Rs 71.37 billion is barely higher than the expenditure for the previous year of Rs 69.21 billion.
The Economic Survey 2026 cites limited access to water as one of the hurdles to Indian agricultural productivity, and calls for boosting access to assured water supply through micro-irrigation and revival of water bodies. As El Nino and other weather events increase in frequency and intensity, India’s irrigation strategy requires focused long-term attention from central and state governments. Else, the Indian economy will continue to remain hostage to the monsoon performance year after year.

A series of curbs on critical global economic flows, including trade, investment and technology, over the last year underscored the heightened vulnerability of international economic relations. At the current juncture of ‘turbulent times’ and ‘extraordinary changes’ that the international economy is experiencing at an accelerated pace, the developing world is forced to confront a highly unstable economic environment, eyeing the announcements and counter-announcements from the two dominant economies much like spectators at a tennis match.
For India, the future of the international economic environment and its bilateral commercial engagements represents an existential conundrum, with the potential to negatively impact its path to development and its aspirations for emerging as an economic powerhouse. As the tides of global economic uncertainties wax and wane in years ahead as they must, India must develop a toolkit of strategy options that will de-risk its growth strategy and clearly guide its responses to evolving external situations
Such a foreign economic policy, or national economic security doctrine, can be developed through a dedicated and institutionalised council that would draft strategies for conducting bilateral, plurilateral and multilateral economic engagement based on evidence and data.
This would greatly help businesses leverage external opportunities. Businesses currently operate in a vacuum where risks are magnified due to uncertainties in national policy response.
Several economic security documents have been released…
In recent months, several countries and groupings have presented national or economic security strategies to guide their policies within a rapidly-evolving global economic architecture.
The recent US National Security Strategy document elicited high global interest for its pivot towards the Western hemisphere and stated that ‘cultivating American industrial strength must become the highest priority of national economic policy’.
On December 2, the European Commission introduced a Joint Communication on Strengthening Economic Security, building on its 2023 Economic Security Strategy and focusing on addressing high-risk situations.
China released a white paper on the country’s national security in the new era in May 2025, ‘reinforcing security in development and pursuing development in security’ among other stated aims.
The OECD issued a report ‘Economic Security in a Changing World’ in September 2025, which focuses on risks due to vulnerabilities in international supply chains, energy security, international investment security, and cybersecurity, and outlines policy approaches for their mitigation.
As one of the largest economies in the world, India must bring out its own economic security aims and principles in alignment with its overall national security strategy.
Clarity needed on India’s economic engagement strategy…
An economic security document for India would need to deliberate on several key problem statements.
o How does diplomatic multi-alignment converge with economic development objectives given the often-opposing political and commercial forces at play?
o How can India strengthen its external influence deploying economic tools?
o How can it work towards building resilience in its future trade and investment flows and protect its sources of capital from external risks?
o What should be the areas of external cooperation based on its growing economic strengths that would optimize its outward impact and build its overall national security?
o With which countries should it work for developing resource security for its growth?
o What should be the key regions and countries that India should strategically incorporate into its economic engagement approaches keeping in mind that resources are limited?
o With any specific country, and especially with the major economies, what areas of cooperation now and in the future can yield the best outcomes for its progress?
o What domestic economic strengths must it fortify to address future vulnerabilities and potential shocks, including in advanced technologies, emerging sectors, and critical raw materials?
Analytical deliberations on such questions and more can guide future external economic policies, and could be derived from simulation and scenario-planning exercises akin to military policy exercises.
In general, a comprehensive and in-depth analysis of India’s economic security in a disruptive global economic environment is a visible gap that must be bridged quickly.
A set of guiding frameworks for economic relations can encourage businesses to align their strategies to national priorities.
To what extent should political relations impact economic relations?
A starting point for an Indian economic security doctrine should focus on the interplay of political and economic developments.
For instance, the India-China relationship faces the dichotomies of border management on the one hand and ‘business as usual’ economic interactions on the other. At the meeting with Prime Minister Narendra Modi in August 2025, President Xi Jinping reportedly said that India should not let border issues define their relationship. The two countries have commenced direct flights and calls for relaxing foreign direct investments (FDI) from China under Press Note 3 have increasingly arisen in Indian circles as the two sides dial down the freeze in relations.
The India-Canada economic engagement was also impacted due to political issues, prompting businesses of both sides to put on hold plans for expanding commercial ties.
The question is whether political and economic relations with any country need to be considered together or kept separate, the policy response to which would help guide businesses on their future course of action.
While political relations will invariably affect business sentiments and constrain economic ties, policy directions could provide the signals for the extent of the response. Most of the adverse bilateral developments that could arise from time to time would need to be examined on a case by case basis; however, a national economic security doctrine can offer some parameters on which decisions on India’s response can be based such as the partner country’s existing trade and investments, presence of diaspora, size of GDP and geographical proximity.
How can inward and outward supply chains be de-risked?
India’s inward and outward supply chains are threatened by overdependence on a single source as well as overdependence on key large markets for its goods and services.
Derisking India’s supply chains hinges on a dual strategy of diversification of import sources and export destinations.
A detailed mapping of its value chains, both inward and outward, and alternate markets and sources would help to identify key gaps as well as emerging and potential weaknesses.
Some long-term measures are currently being instituted to build resilience in these value chains including in sectors such as APIs, electronic parts, wafers, semiconductors, etc. through global agreements, domestic manufacturing and free trade treaties. An ongoing scenario-building exercise leveraging AI for data analysis could further support such de-risking measures.
Equally, the range of bilateral relations with specific partner countries could be better defined through an assessment of its trade strengths and areas of interest to India. As an example, the trade potential with a partner economy may depend on the size of its GDP, the size of its population as a future market, its level of global trade integration, and other factors.
India can strategically develop a matrix combining such parameters to identify certain economies for enhanced trade efforts and undertake dedicated measures such as high level interactions, free trade agreements and market building exercises in these countries.
Determining investment sources and destinations…
Investments sought from a country could potentially be based on its outward FDI as a proportion of its GDP, the spread of its multinational companies, its financial system, and its natural resources.
By examining such indicators, India could prioritise its outreach to the companies of identified partner economies, given that brand-building resources are limited and focused attention is required for select countries.
Equally, attracting FDI will need to be mapped with opportunities in India and support provided accordingly.
Certain other indicators could be noted to restrict inward FDI if required by political considerations through measures such as investment scrutiny, ownership limits and other instruments, based on pre-defined criteria for investment risk assessments.
India could also better target its own outward investments to seek markets, acquire technology, build infrastructure, or access natural resources based on partner country strengths, given limited fund availability.
Targeting identified partner countries for inward and outward investments will deliver impactful outcomes as per development priorities.
Indicators can guide relations in different sectors…
Data-based assessments would help in guiding partnerships in sectors beyond trade and investment. Key economic indicators could suggest the optimal mix of partnerships to be promoted.
Access to technology is a central determinant for India’s future economic trajectory and should be prioritized in any economic security strategy. Both directions of technology flows would need to be assessed to determine where India can best source which technologies, and likewise where it can share technologies safely to widen its sphere of economic influence.
External partnerships are proving to be vital in India’s technology quest in areas such as semiconductors, electronics, artificial intelligence, drug development and talent development, and expansion of such technology sharing would help build India’s R&D and innovation for a tech-led world.
In terms of renewable energy and climate change partnerships, guiding indicators could be solar irradiation, wind power potential, technology levels, progress towards international commitments and so on. India has entered into sustainability agreements with many countries and regional organisations.
With some countries, it seeks partnerships for its own climate action initiatives through project funding, relevant technologies and capacity building, among others. With others, it aims to bolster sustainability efforts through funding, information-sharing and joint projects.
A study of specific indicators would help shape a better matrix of cooperation for businesses.
Such exercises can also be carried out for cooperation in other areas.
India must consider the increasingly adverse mobility regimes that could impact its services exports and inward remittances, and attempt to protect its growing diaspora. Here, the list of potential factors feeding into policy formulation could include size of diaspora, visa arrangements in place, potential for future mobility, language facility, and an analysis of current political sentiments on migration in destination countries.
In the digital economy, nature of the relationship would vary depending on the digital prowess of a country across different sectors, skill levels, the threats to cyber security, and transparency.
For development cooperation, India could look at education and health parameters, as it has done in the e-Vidya Bharati and e-Arogya Bharati initiatives with Africa.
Indicators would also help select projects for development cooperation based on potential gains for India, such as small business development initiatives, skilling and capacity building, or large infrastructure projects.
Designing domestic capabilities to mitigate external economic risks…
India must analyze its domestic capabilities to respond to arising situations, identify economic vulnerabilities due to global conditions and institute targeted measures to bridge these gaps. The Production Linked Incentive Scheme and the Critical Minerals Mission represent good examples of domestic initiatives to counter global threats.
Finally, an overarching economic security statement would need to include mechanisms for future-gazing to identify emerging threats and opportunities, time-bound implementation of announced plans and projects overseas, monitoring of progress of the goals and advances in India’s global economic presence, and course correction as and when required.
Within a rapidly shifting global economic environment, ongoing modifications and innovative solutions can be baked into a dynamic strategy document at the outset.
Concluding thoughts…
In an ideal comprehensive economic security strategy, each partner country would be mapped to India’s diplomatic and economic goals with a proposed set of cooperation areas and roadmaps to implement them over the medium term.
This would be helpful to stakeholders in India’s economic domain such as large, medium and small businesses, job seekers, overseas investors and traders.
A progressive, future-oriented, and in-depth strategy document could set the foundation for other countries to better define their policies towards India and encourage them to seek new areas of partnership as well.
With India on a definitive high-growth pathway that will bring positive gains for global growth, the country must set its sights on emerging as an economic alternative of choice for other nations, both advanced and developing, and nurture trends that will position it as a reliable and credible partner economy.
An economic security doctrine could help shape its future external economic engagement optimally and go a long way towards this objective.

I can’t say my life so far, though unusual as a diplomatic spouse, has been full of important achievements. But I count learning Chinese as a great achievement for me. Here’s why.
First off, learning Mandarin is both easy and hard. Living in Beijing in the early 1980s, I found the spoken language fairly comfortable, but the written was super tough.
It was quick for managing daily tasks and getting around (because there was no alternative if you were based in China), but challenging to follow movies and read books and just impossible to read the newspapers.
In those days, given the small numbers, the Indian government permitted a spouse to take language classes, and the Chinese government was only too happy to send a tutor from the Diplomatic Personnel Service Bureau. Like all other DPSB personnel, the tutor presumably attended the weekly debriefing sessions!
And so, Yu Laoshi, a diminutive lady with curly hair, not young, not old, trotted over to my small apartment in the Qi Jia Yuan diplomatic complex three times a week. She was always dressed in the regulation dark blue trousers and jacket or white shirt. With her, she carried text books especially devised for foreigners.
I still have the books somewhere, Chinese characters in the first line, followed by the pinyin with tonal markings on top of vowels and then the English translation – a 3-layered text with the usual sentences on getting to know people and buying stuff.
The thing about Yu Laoshi was that she was a stickler for proper pronunciation. It took me a couple of lessons just to learn how to say her name – Yu, in third tone, starting at the right pitch, going down, then coming up again, without saying ‘y’ in the way it is done in English, but ‘u’ as in German umlaut.
Her voice was like a tinkling bell, clear and sharp, and she contorted her full face to get the tones just right for me to follow. She made me repeat syllables multiple times and wasn’t happy until I too made strange faces and got the tone reasonably okay.
It was worse when it came to the right ways of saying consonants like ‘j’, ‘q’, ‘zh’, ‘ch’, ‘sh’, ‘x’, etc where the English letters are merely symbols of the actual pronunciation. Here, I had to follow the contortions of her tongue and how she handled her breath to figure out the nuances.
Then came the writing part. She asked if I wanted to learn how to read and write Chinese characters, of which one needs to memorise over 3000 to be able to read well. I asked her how many of her diplomatic students did characters. None, she replied, but you can’t really learn Mandarin without learning characters.
So I said yes and she brought me loads of copybooks lined with checked boxes and taught me the shape of the strokes, the order in which they were to be pencilled, and the beginner characters.
You’d think that writing ‘yi’ for 1 would be a simple straight horizontal line. It wasn’t. There were subtle undulations, the length needed to be exact and the pressure of the pencil must be just so. Yu Laoshi often accepted my written homework with a heavy sigh and no comments.
Meanwhile, my daily vocabulary count was increasing due to having to communicate with the assigned DPSB staff. In a couple of months, I was actually able to give instructions, accompanied by a lot of gesticulation and pointing, and the staff was happily gossiping to me in Chinese about shocking emerging social behaviors.
The Indian government shortly withdrew the facility for Chinese tutors, and I cut down to two hours a week, continuing with Yu Laoshi on my own.
By the end of 16 months, when the China posting came to an end, Yu Laoshi had paced me through about 1200 characters, taking me to the more advanced textbooks and making me fairly comfortable in talking to local people.
And then we left Beijing and didn’t return for 29 years. I wrote Yu Laoshi a couple of letters but then caught up with daily life in Delhi, and that was the end of this chapter of my Chinese learning journey.
Posted in Hong Kong 15 years later, I tried Mandarin a few times, but people used Cantonese for speaking and writing and anyways understood some English. In Malaysia a few years later, I found the local Chinese population preferred Mandarin to English although my contact was limited to a couple of workers doing construction work in the residence.
Fast forward to the second posting in Beijing.
Getting out of the airport, I found myself conversing easily with Yue Shifu, the driver. In a couple of days, I was picking up the phone and shouting at spam callers. I tried speaking to gardeners and shopkeepers, managing quite well, and when the luggage arrived and I chanced upon one of my copybooks of thirty years ago, I could read most of my writing and understand it.
This was a revelation to me, that a language imbibed informally over just 16 months and not spoken for 29 years resided in the recesses of my brain, ready to jump out when I needed to use it again!
I did not go back to classes again, but once when I asked my husband’s occasional tutor what my language level was, she replied that I was probably between HSK 3 and HSK 4. HSK 4 was at the time the level that the Indian Foreign Service officer trainees were required to pass after a year of intensive college courses.
Coming close to the end of the Beijing posting, I thought I might as well go about getting the formal certificate and asked the embassy interpreter Han Lin to procure books for the HSK 4 exam. Apparently, there was a designated list of characters to be learned.
One day, attending an ambassadorial spouses lunch, I happened to be seated next to a young lady, the daughter of the Arabian hostess. While making polite conversation, she mentioned she had downloaded apps for the list of characters.
And scrolling through the character lists on apps became my training for the HSK 4 exam.
Fortunately, by this time, we didn’t have to actually write characters. It was possible to type out the pinyin on a computer, then select the exact characters from a drop down list of similar sounding words. This was easy enough.
The exam centre hosted a trial run before the actual exam to get students accustomed to the format. I was the oldest person in the hall, the only Indian in a room full of young anxious Japanese and Korean students and the odd Caucasian.
At the end of the trial exam, when my marks came in the 90s, the Chinese invigilator told me that with this level, I should be doing HSK 5.
Problem was, we were leaving Beijing and I would only have a month to study for HSK 5, double the number of characters from level 4. I waited practically till the last day, then thought Why not?, filled in the application form and downloaded the HSK 5 list of characters.
Meanwhile, I managed to track down Yu Laoshi and invited her for lunch along with Han Lin (in case I needed interpretation). Yu Laoshi looked very different and I would not have recognized her. It was, after all, over 30 years since I had last met her.
She carried with her the letters I had sent her those decades ago!
My handwriting, my words, my experiences! I was totally gob smacked.
We had a nice conversation (in Chinese) during which she was more forthcoming about her life than she had ever been in those 16 months. I learnt that she had written several books in English and had a daughter now in the US.
As for HSK 5, the exam results were satisfying, despite no formal classes ever. But that didn’t mean that I was fluent in speaking, could follow the TV serials, or even read. It just meant that I had gone through the app and textbooks well.
At that time, the highest test level was HSK 6. (A few years ago, Hanban added levels 7-9, taken in a single test.)
My Chinese learning was a decade ago. I still fondly dwell on passing these two exams, happily thinking of it as my grand success.
All thanks to the amazing Yu Laoshi!

Australia is one of only three countries with which India has an annual summit process. This means that prime ministers of the two countries meet – well, annually.
Image: @narendramodi on X
One would have thought that such summits would accelerate economic ties and projects. The list of outcomes from the just-concluded Modi-Albanese meeting includes mostly good-to-have, not game-changing, documents:
· Setting up sports centres and experience sharing in sports
· Indian military instructor in Australian Defence College
· Centre for development of academic excellence in mining
· Letter of intent for Flinders college campus and for vocational training regulatory alignment
· Bringing back 3 Indian antiquities
· Rooftop solar training academy
And various other MoUs.
The rest of the trip had many feel-good moments and passionate comments.
The rousing diaspora meeting was heartwarming for the two leaders and about 30,000 enthusiastic diaspora people present.
The documents on security, defense, maritime cooperation and energy security basically reprised earlier agreements, adding a few more details. The words used in the list of outcomes include ‘renews’, ‘enhances’, ‘operationalises’, ‘reaffirms’, and ‘builds upon’.
Education has been a key success story, with several Australian educational institutes setting up in India, while Indians are among the top largest international student cohorts in Australia.
It is good to take forward existing areas of cooperation. And these strengthen the framework for economic cooperation.
But those expecting concrete economic outcomes would be somewhat mystified by the hype.
There were no announcements on specific projects, investments or trade issues. Talks on the comprehensive economic cooperation agreement – to progress on the Economic Cooperation and Trade Agreement concluded as a first step in 2022 – are still on.
At the CEOs forum, PM Modi spoke about ‘strategic convergence’ and focused on sectors of potential in India, which was par for the course.
It seems as if previous summits have included all the possible sectors of cooperation and the two sides sat down to discuss ‘Now what?’
Meanwhile under ECTA, India’s exports to Australia dropped over 15% from US$ 8.6 billion in 2024-25 to US$ 7.3 billion in 2025-26, mainly owing to lower fuel exports.
In other 10 export items over US$ 100 million, exports of machinery increased by about US$ 300 million and exports of 5 items contracted.
The share of India’s exports going to Australia declined as well.
In some key categories like machinery, electronics and gems and jewellery, India does not export much of the items where Australia increased its imports.
India’s imports from Australia too contracted by over 11%, with Australia’s share in total imports coming down from 2.2% to 1.8%. Mineral fuels and gems and jewelry were the chief culprits.
Much depends on fuel and commodity prices. A basket of stable, higher value-added products is missing in the traded goods.
Australia’s cumulative FDI into India is US$ 1.7 billion from January 2000 to March 2026, ranking 26th as per DPIIT. However, the Australian High Commission in New Delhi places total investment into India at $17.6 billion, while India’s FDI to Australia is recorded at $34.5 billion (probably AU$, not US$).
The Australia India Critical Minerals Investment Partnership signed in 2022 has seen an agreement on exploration of 2 lithium and 3 cobalt projects in 2023. Not much is in the public domain on this after that.
A lot more areas of cooperation were identified by the India Economic Strategy brought out by Australia in 2018 and the Australia Economic Strategy by CII-KPMG in 2020.
The friendship between the two countries is obviously strong, close and deep. It is a strategic and important partnership in the global context.
For some reason, this does not translate into robust and dynamic economic and industry ties. Intensified and accelerated efforts are required, consistently and beyond annual summit meetings.

The good news is that the average Indian can look forward to an annual income of close to $ 4,500 by 2031.
While this would be 65% higher than the 2025 per capita GDP in current US dollar of $ 2,675.322, it would still be well below that of countries like South Africa, Indonesia and Vietnam. It would also be less than one-fourth of China’s per capita GDP.
The International Monetary Fund World Economic Outlook for April 2026, a much anticipated dataset following years of geoeconomic churn, brings out several interesting features of India’s growth trajectory in the coming five years to 2031.
First, as was widely believed prior to the revision of GDP figures, India is not the world’s fourth largest economy. In the last nine years from 2017, it largely remained the sixth largest economy, briefly overtaking the UK in 2022-24 to attain rank 5. This it again ceded to the UK in 2025, since it was not able to cross the milestone of $4 trillion, as per IMF WEO April 2026.
The WEO of April 2025 had pegged India’s GDP at $4.2 trillion for 2025, barely surpassing Japan by a billion dollars, giving rise to jubilation in India at becoming the fourth largest economy. However, this year’s WEO is based on India’s revised GDP numbers following updation of base year and considerable depreciation of the rupee. India’s downward revisions are welcome, pointing to better capture of data to avoid overestimation of the previous years.
By 2031, as per the IMF’s present growth projections, India would have overtaken Germany, the UK and Japan to reach the third position with a GDP size of $6.8 trillion.
Two, although other large emerging economies (Argentina, Malaysia, Vietnam, South Africa) enjoy much higher per capita income, these are not expected to become trillion-dollar economies even in the next five years.
Advanced economies like Canada, Italy, Australia and South Korea will likely have GDP about half to one-third that of India’s, placing the Indian economy in a strong position among global economies.
Three, the gap between India and China, the second largest economy, is narrowing slightly. As of 2025, India’s GDP was about 20% the size of the Chinese economy, but by 2031, this could enlarge to almost 25%. While the gap would remain quite substantial, there is some catching up possible over the next five years. Of course, given the size of China’s economy, it would be adding more than $1 trillion to its GDP every year from 2028 onwards.
Similarly, India’s GDP size was just 12.7% of the US GDP in 2025, which will go up to over 17% by 2031.
Four, in terms of per capita GDP in rupees, India came in at Rs 2.37 lakhs in 2025, and by 2031, this will increase to Rs 4.17 lakhs by IMF calculations. This is likely to further dent the poverty rate in India and create better income opportunities for the general population. However, India will need to guard against rising inequality by income class and region as well as among different sections of society to ensure that this growth reaches out to all in a balanced manner.
Five, India enjoys a high weight in contribution to global GDP, forecast to add 17% to the world growth rate. Therefore, its growth policies and trajectory matter significantly for the world and this needs to be factored in by other economies.
Six, in terms of the GDP growth rate, India remains the fastest growing large economy in the world up to 2031. Among the 21 trillion-dollar-plus economies as of 2025, India’s pace is expected to be by far the highest at an average of 6.66% (2025-2031). Next in line is the $1.4 trillion Indonesian economy which would achieve 5.13%.
The Chinese economy at 5% for 2025 is expected to drop to below 4% in the latter half of this period, falling to a bare 3.3% in 2031. Other developing economies like Brazil and Mexico are likely to remain subdued. Even the racing Vietnamese economy, just $460 billion in size in 2025, may stay at an average of 6.3%, below the robust Indian pace.
The IMF’s outlook comes with several caveats, chief among them being the state of the conflict in West Asia. As it gets prolonged, the world’s future becomes increasingly threatened. The strangulation of the Strait of Hormuz places at risk the entire developing world, impacting growth, employment and macroeconomic stability.
India’s projected trajectory is also subject to multiple domestic challenges, majorly the success of policies on employment creation, manufacturing and exports. The IMF forecasts are encouraging, but India would do well to hunker down, strengthen its resilience to global vicissitudes, build its economy for the future, and stay away from self-congratulatory messaging.

As investors watched the stock market slide inexorably in front of their eyes on 11 May, a question arose in their minds – why did the Prime Minister gratuitously exhort his fellow citizens to abjure so many items, from gold to fertilizers, from travel to petrol and live responsibly?
Actually, the PM was merely the vehicle for this wide-ranging assault on multiple industry sectors. The idea in fact arose from a committee of officials who for days have been appearing on national television to assure fellow citizens that, despite the trauma of the West Asia war, there are no shortages of critical items anywhere in the country and everything is under control. After 70 days of war, they simply got tired of looking confident and reassuring, and thought they should look less grim.
Here is how the conversation went.
Official 1: I have run out of saris to wear for the TV cameras. They won’t even allow me to use makeup, lest I appear frivolous in such a serious situation. We must do something about this endless press interaction.
Official 2: I agree. I’ve been wearing the same black bandi for the last 2 months. The war may continue for several more months. We can’t keep doing meetings and briefings for that long. I’m hardly able to work in my office and so much is pending.
Official 3: I spoke to the PMO and told them that we are looking a little ridiculous saying the same things ad infinitum. Even my mother has stopped watching the daily press briefing. But they said we must continue with it until Trump comes to some agreement with Iran.
Official 4 from MEA: We have ceased to even discuss where the war and the Hormuz blockage is heading. It will happen when it happens. Meanwhile, we are scouting for more Indian citizens to be evacuated, but they don’t want to be airlifted out of the war zone anymore.
Official 1: But look at our fellow citizens! They insist on buying gold only. Can’t they find some other asset to buy, like silver or diamonds or SIPs? These imports are killing our foreign exchange reserves.
Official 2: And how can they keep planning destination weddings? Entire families and their aunties and uncles and distant friends are going abroad to do weddings! If they are going to dance to Bollywood, they might as well do it in India. It’s upsetting the entire economy.
Official 3: We have been telling people for so long to buy electric vehicles and transport cargo on trains. Don’t understand what is the fascination for petrol nowadays. We have charging stations all over the place now, except in some areas outside the metro cities. And for that matter, why can’t they use the metro? We’ve got metros in 21 cities.
Official 4 from MEA: Don’t forget the urea imports. We have been in touch with all counterparts, begging to continue the supply lines for fertilisers. This is a good opportunity to promote organic farming. Anyway, with El Nino coming, there will be drought so the farmers can’t produce the usual crops.
Official 1: But the urea imports will be very important during drought, isn’t it? Do we have any data on use of fertilisers during droughts going up or down?
Official 2: Related to this is the issue of edible oil. First, we don’t produce our own edible oil. Second, our people should not be consuming the trans-fats that are being imported. They will be much healthier if they don’t have access to these partially hydrogenated edible oils. I read about it recently. We should take more olive oil.
Official 3: So we are agreed then. We must apprise the PMO about all these unhealthy habits that our fellow citizens are getting into. We must ask for a halt to foreign weddings, buying of gold, consumption of edible oil, fertilizer usage, petroleum vehicles, travel and airlines, and while we are at it, why not stop them from going to office as well? We did that during Covid and it hardly affected our work. It’s too hot to go out.
Official 4 from MEA: Quite correct. Our country has become too rich too soon with all these poor health practices which must be curtailed. It will help the workers and farmers too, otherwise the pressure on the rupee, rising current account deficit and fiscal gaps will lead to higher inflation. Not to mention that the big oil companies are suffering badly.
And so an appropriate speech was drafted in an attractive style. The PM merely delivered it. It is time for the citizens to once more come together, beat thalis and tighten the belt, even those hundreds of millions who are not going abroad or don’t have gas cylinders to cook edible oil.
This is an imaginary conversation in lighter vein.

By any measure, 2025 was a harrowing year for Indian exporters, yet it was also one in which they demonstrated an extraordinary capacity to surmount challenges. While several key policies were announced, prompt and effective government support remained a missing component of the operating environment. As 2026 dawns, much will continue to be demanded of these intrepid entrepreneurs and the vast workforce that depends on India’s external markets.
This was a year in which the very principles of competitiveness and globalisation were undermined, and the rules of global trade were cast aside, even as India struggled to leverage exports as a driver of growth. Unilateral tariffs of unprecedented scale and export controls on critical inputs strained supply chains, as manufacturers and exporters scrambled to diversify import sources and explore new markets. Domestically, India’s stable macroeconomic fundamentals, declining interest rates, and a depreciating rupee helped sustain export momentum.
Early in the year, India announced an Export Promotion Mission in the 2025-26 Budget, with details released in December. The package included Niryat Protsahan to improve access to export credit and Niryat Disha to support competitiveness, market promotion, and quality and compliance measures. The proposed outlay is ₹250.6 billion over six years, along with credit guarantee support of ₹200 billion.
Separately, the Reserve Bank of India undertook several measures to relax loan repayment terms, extend export credit tenures, introduce flexibility in working capital management, and lengthen the permitted time for export realisation. Its calibrated approach to rupee depreciation also provided limited support to exporters. However, as many of these measures were implemented late in the year, they offered only modest relief. MSMEs in several key industrial hubs faced closures and layoffs, particularly in textiles and apparel, leather, gems and jewellery, and metal products.
The year also saw rapid progress in India’s free trade agreements (FTAs), which have been positioned as a key strategy for export resilience. The highlight was the finalisation of the India-UK Comprehensive Economic and Trade Agreement, which expands opportunities in the large UK market. FTAs were also signed with Oman and New Zealand, both relatively small export destinations, while India opens up its much larger domestic market to these partners. Gains from the mobility agreement with Oman and the pledge of $20 billion in investments from New Zealand remain uncertain. Negotiations with the European Union are believed to be nearing a conclusion and could significantly support exports, although India is unlikely to be exempt from the EU’s onerous carbon border adjustment mechanism (CBAM) regime. Progress has also been made on other FTAs, which, once implemented, would help diversify export markets.
Reflecting the underlying resilience of the export sector, India’s merchandise exports declined by just over 1% in the ten months to October compared with the same period last year, remaining at around $369 billion. The contraction was particularly sharp in February and October, but was largely offset by strong growth in July and moderate increases in the following two months. The connection to US tariffs is obvious, as the initial reciprocal tariffs were slated to be implemented in April, and the 50% rates imposed on India took effect from August 27.
Despite the tariff onslaught, the US emerged as a stronger destination for Indian exports, with shipments growing 15% in the year to October, driven primarily by smartphone exports, which doubled during this period. Other major export categories also recorded strong healthy growth, including pharmaceuticals, machinery, and articles of iron and steel, even as exports of gems and jewellery and petroleum products declined. Uncertainties persist, however, as monthly export figures weakened between August and October.
Moreover, an India-US trade deal remains elusive, as broader geopolitical considerations continue to delay its conclusion.
Among other key destinations, exports to the UAE were flat despite the FTA, although the export mix shifted away from fuel towards gems and jewellery, electronics, machinery, and automobilestives. Fuel exports to the Netherlands declined sharply, while overall exports to Germany increased significantly. Export growth to China was also robust, reaching $14 billion over the ten months of 2025.
However, imports from China exceeded $102 billion, indicating a further deterioration in the adverse trade balance.
Petroleum products remained India’s top export item despite low prices and 26% contraction over ten months, followed by electronic products, which surged by over 36%. Machinery, pharmaceuticals, and automotives also recorded notable growth, while gems and jewellery exports continued to decline.
Looking ahead to 2026, US tariffs on other countries appear to have stabilised, but disproportionately high rates continue to constrain Indian exports. The export trajectory in the coming year will be primarily shaped by prospects for an India-US trade agreement, amid ongoing trade uncertainty driven by geopolitical conflicts such as the Russia-Ukraine war and US-China trade tensions. Domestically, the export promotion package will need to be substantially expanded in the short term. Support measures for informal workers affected by export volatility should be implemented promptly, in line with the labour codes.
While newly concluded FTAs will take time to yield tangible gains, it would be unrealistic to expect global supply chains to shift decisively to India in the near term. Labour-intensive sectors, therefore, will remain under considerable pressure. The year ahead will continue to test India’s export resilience, underscoring the need for sustained and targeted policy support.
