An urgent meeting was convened last month among senior Indian Government officials as the Middle East war raged on, critical supply routes were choked and energy shortages loomed over the economy. The question being studied was how to protect jobs and ensure that exports remained insulated from global vagaries.
Senior official 1 from Department of Commerce: Thank you for joining this very important meeting. We have to consolidate our views and ensure a whole-of-government approach to protecting and boosting our exports where mostly MSME exporters are affected and by extension, jobs are impacted. My colleague will provide an overview of the current state of play in exports.
Colleague 1: Sir, we have data up to February of this financial year. In April-February 2025-26, merchandise exports reached $403 billion and services exports came in at $388 billion. Total exports were $791 billion which is a very reasonable growth of almost 6%, Sir. The goods exports increased by a respectable 1.8% despite all the tariffs fluctuations conducted by our largest destination. Sir, our services exports increased by over 10%.
Senior official 2 from line ministry: This is extremely positive! I am delighted that our policies over the year such as new FTAs signed and soon to be implemented, the last-moment decision to continue RoDTEP benefits, QCO rollbacks, and some relief provided just when the 50% tariffs imposed by the US came into effect helped our exporting community so much. Our efforts have truly raised the confidence of exporters and they must be so grateful for the support provided by the government.
Colleague 2: Sir, let me highlight some of the sectors that performed well during April-January of the fiscal year. I am happy to mention that while we lost momentum on oil exports due to the fall in global oil prices, our electronic exports more than compensated with an increase of $10 billion. Sir, the PLI scheme is instrumental in this success. Many other sectors such as machinery, automotives, iron & steel, marine products, meat products, inorganic chemicals, etc. witnessed robust double-digit growth. There was a bit of slow growth for our textiles and apparel exports but that is because Bangladesh had lower US tariffs, not our fault, Sir.
Seniormost official at the meeting, representing finance ministry: This is very encouraging. It shows the great success of government efforts under the leadership of our prime minister. I would like to point out in this instance that government finances remain under pressure. The oil price rise is expected to impact tax collections. Is there any way that fiscal outgo for exports can be compressed, given that under challenging circumstances exports continue to do remarkably well? That would help meet our fiscal deficit targets for the year and ensure macroeconomic stability.
Senior official 1: Sir, we have shifted much of the support to credit guarantees and bank credit already. The remission of duties and taxes for export products scheme helps to compensate for the embedded central and state taxes that cannot be easily refunded.
Seniormost official: Yes, I know what RoDTEP is. My suggestion is to halve the RoDTEP incentive rates across all sectors. It is much more important to protect the overall jobs scenario through enhanced spending on infrastructure and social benefits. Why should exporters get an incentive when they are doing well?
Senior official 2: I definitely agree with you, Sir. We need to spend more funds on PLI incentives which will create jobs at home rather than RoDTEP. Our Ministry has been very successful in smartphone exports. All that needs to be done is to import kits and assemble them here for export, and automatically, the value of total exports goes up. This is the model we should follow for more items. This is how China and Vietnam have done it, Sir. We can always import from China and no export incentive will be needed.
Senior official 1: But… but… Sir, RoDTEP is not an incentive….
Seniormost official: Okay, so we have a consensus view here to reduce the RoDTEP rates by half. Let’s go ahead and issue the notification.
(A few days later)
Seniormost official to his finance ministry colleague: I have received some representations that the global war situation has further impacted our exports. Apparently, the reduction in RoDTEP incentives has got a lot of negative comments. I would like to send a message to the Department of Commerce to restore the RoDTEP incentives.
Colleague 3: Sir, we had spoken to them earlier to request exporters not to make the representations. They said that the RoDTEP scheme in any case is due to expire this week on 31 March.
Seniormost official: In that case, we can even extend it on 31 March. That will bring a lot of comfort to exporters and they can stop this whining and complaining about the global situation. How can we do anything about the global situation?! They must understand.
On March 31, the RoDTEP scheme was renewed for another 6 months when hopefully the global environment will be more beneficial for Indian exports. Other tweaks were made to other policies. Exporters are truly grateful, according to feedback received by senior officials.
(The data in this article is factual. All conversation is imagined in a lighter vein with due apologies to learned senior officials.)

Store-bought bread is a diabetic no-no, advised the nutritionist, and so I trawled through many whole-wheat bread recipes and videos online and baked a loaf of bread at home.
Biting into a warm, fresh slice dripping with butter, I started thinking about what it took me to prepare the loaf. It struck me that bread was the basis of economies, many of which went on to become rich cultures and civilisations.
All compliments are due to our innovative forepersons who first discovered that a grain growing wild was actually edible. This must have required a large number of hits-and-misses and many would have poisoned themselves in identifying plants that could be safely consumed. I do wonder though, if there is a natural de-selection process that evolution has bred into humans, but possibly not, going by the many unhealthy foods that we consume today.
From identifying the most suitable grain to grinding it into powder of the right consistency, mixing it with water to make a dough, shaping the bread, and putting it on a fire to cook without burning, was probably a series of steps that took hundreds of years. So many ‘eureka!’ moments might have gone into it, so much knowledge-building and knowledge transmission between populations across generations and geographies would have taken place.
The ancient civilisations realized that fermented dough would do better in terms of taste and texture, and so they started adding yeast to the mixture. Yeast itself is a remarkable organism that humans learnt to cultivate to make beer.
It is not a surprise actually that it was probably bread, along with rice, that led to the settling of populations, agricultural revolutions, urbanization and the foundation for economic activity beyond hunting and gathering. To make bread (and things to eat with it), people required tools, pots, ovens, and a whole paraphernalia for farming which eventually fed into segregation of occupations and economic stratification. The fields had to be protected from marauding neighbors as well, while a natural artistic tendency and desire for luxury items contributed to the rest of what makes up an economy.
At some point of time, bread emerged as a commercial activity, complete with a supply chain that became longer as time passed. People came up with different kinds of bread, many of which remain in use till today. For example, the humble chapati was probably among the first breads that became a staple and is today the easiest home-cooked bread, ubiquitous in Indian households in wheat-growing areas.
Bread today comes in wide variety, from flat-breads, puris and parathas to rolls, baguettes, croissants, doughnuts and pastries, and baos, and probably a lot more that I am not familiar with in different parts of the world. Most of these are not for the faint-hearted cook and come from specialised bakeries.
With Indians focusing on flat-breads made at home, other bread types are not as readily available in stores and therefore, coming back to my personal bread story, I remain dependent on a few unpalatable, mass-consumption brands of sliced bread for breakfasts and sandwiches.
Like all other products that are taken for granted in our daily lives, the bread economic history is replete with blue-ocean thinking, constant innovation, specialized-to-mass production, and a value chain that stretches from farms to stores with hundreds of sub-chains feeding into it.
My home-baked loaf of bread did not come out too well, but slathered with butter, it was still a huge improvement on the sawdust slices available in stores. Try it and think about the bread journey of yore!
More on the bread value chain in a later post.

A few days ago, I posted on LinkedIn that I should change my headline to ‘Dissenting economic policy commentator at large.’
There was hardly any response as most of my network probably thought this was a touch of humor on my usually sceptical feed. Not really.
But then I thought, what would make me stop dissenting and why am I always a pessimist when it comes to the economic policies of my country?
Well, here it is.
First, it would be good to learn of any strategy the government may have for its slogan of Viksit Bharat 2047.
Long term strategies or even documents of intent or goals help an economy progress. The government’s concept of a developed nation needs to be explicitly drafted and put out.
Planning didn’t work for sure. But there should be a midway between rigorous planning and complete absence of synergies in policy making.
Two, a major focus on education and skills would be good. We can’t have a situation where, decades after the Right to Education, I am teaching long division to a student supposedly studying algebra in secondary school.
Schools in rural areas don’t seem to have improved in infrastructure. And where I live in a city, there are no government primary or secondary schools for miles around where a poor student can hope to get admission.
In fact, I am surrounded by a huge knowledge park full of high-end private universities where the fees are exorbitant. And a college degree is now 4 years, an extra year of high fees.
Then there is skills and apprenticeship where policies must finally deliver real outcomes, pride in achievements, and actual well paid employment.
Three, the education foundation rests a lot on good nutrition and healthcare so that our kids are not stunted and wasted. To be sure, huge progress has been made in institutional deliveries, maternal mortality and gender ratio at birth. Ayushman Bharat is helping tremendously. Where are the gaps in public health now and how can they be rapidly addressed?
Four, so many policies and incentives have come for encouraging employment, first time jobs, formalisation, social security, but young people are still loitering at tea stalls, making videos on streets and gathering at street corners hoping to be picked up for day jobs.
The link between skills and employment is broken and migrant workers face horrendous situations in destinations.
Work seems to be a challenge without workable solutions.
Five, welfare benefits are unevenly distributed. Migrants seem to have no access once away from villages. Many don’t know how to get them in their villages. We need to fix this somehow.
Six, once the human angles are on track, the sectors deserve attention. Agriculture, manufacturing, exports, services, infrastructure, energy, investment climate, financial sectors, each one has issues to be defined and addressed.
Seven, our limited funds must be used optimally. Our budgets include small outlays here and there and large outlays where the narrative is sound but the outcomes underperform.
The major outlay heads sit on the balance sheet like unmoving leviathans, bloating unilaterally.
And the forms and procedures! I just spent hours trying to get an FD closed that was not linked to an account.
Another bank condescended to do my KYC only because I’d worked there 30 years ago
I don’t know how to get enrolled on the voter list on my new address. It was quite a task changing the address too. Ask anyone if interface with government is smooth!
We know the issues. We may even know the matrix of solutions. We just don’t know how to take them up.
Or if we do, it’s years before we acknowledge that they are not working.
My dissent is a lone call in the vast ocean of our economy. But I strive on, knowing that 2047 is far off and I can only mumble to myself on the sidelines.
Things may change. We may seize the moment. But what has not changed over decades is now far too entrenched. Hence my dissent, hoping to shift towards more informed and synergized policy making.
Over to the next generation.

There is little evidence that China would help build India’s footprint in global supply chains. In fact, China has taken steps that hinder India’s manufacturing growth such as curbs on export of critical minerals and rare earths over 2023-2025, informal delays in exports of electronics and solar manufacturing equipment, pressure on companies to avoid sending personnel to India, and so on.
March 28, 2026 at 1:36 PM IST
In 2017, Shanghai Fosun Pharmaceutical Group struck a deal to buy a majority stake in India’s Gland Pharma, the biggest buy of a Chinese firm in India. By 2019, 17 of India’s 24 startup unicorns were backed by Chinese investors, with the value of investments multiplying 12 times in 4 years across sectors such as fintech, edtech and retail. In early 2020, red flags were raised as the People’s Bank of China appeared in the list of investors holding more than 1% stake in India’s storied HDFC Bank. As Covid restrictions started impacting Indian corporates, anxieties arose on possible hostile Chinese takeovers of leading Indian companies, including data-rich tech enterprises.
This sequence of events serves as the backdrop to the introduction of Press Note 3 of 2020 on April 17, 2020, which brought foreign direct investments in Indian companies by land-bordering countries under the prior government approval route. PN3 aimed to curb ‘opportunistic takeovers’ by foreign firms which were ‘beneficially owned’ by citizens of or entities present in land-bordering countries.
In June 2020, a serious border clash took place between Indian and Chinese troops along the Line of Actual Control in the Galwan Valley, resulting in 20 valiant Indian soldiers being killed while an unacknowledged number of Chinese troops suffered casualties. This was the first such instance along the LAC in 45 years and automatically led to near-complete halt of approvals under PN3, along with many other Indian restrictions on overall bilateral relations. Chinese FDI was simply not welcome in an India shocked by repeated border incursions and Covid sufferings.
Murmurs regarding the relaxation of PN3 commenced shortly after Covid restrictions began to be scaled down. Indian industry cited the need for Chinese inputs, funds and technicians for its growth. Analysts made the case for attracting FDI from China as it is one of the world’s top three outward investing countries and could contribute to India’s goals of raising manufacturing value, technology acquisition and supply chain integration. Yet the government remained adamant on close scrutiny of Chinese FDI proposals.
This stance appeared to shift somewhat when the Economic Survey 2023-24 of July 2024 questioned India’s rationale of permitting rising imports from China while restricting FDI. “India faces two choices to benefit from China plus one strategy: it can integrate into China’s supply chain or promote FDI from China. Among these choices, focusing on FDI from China seems more promising for boosting India’s exports to the US, similar to how East Asian economies did in the past,” said the Survey.
In March 2026, the government announced relaxation of PN3 and introduced Press Note 2 of 2026. PN2 clarifies that foreign investors with non-controlling beneficial ownership — with a ceiling of 10% holding from land-bordering countries — can invest under the automatic route. Two, investment proposals for specific manufacturing sectors such as electronic capital goods, polysilicon and ingot-wafers would be considered within 60 days. PN2 marks a beginning towards attracting investments from Chinese (or other land-bordering country) investor entities under the automatic route, adding to ease of doing business.
At the same time, careful scrutiny of Chinese investments continues to be warranted. China’s total overseas direct investment was around $175 billion in 2025. However, its cumulative investments in India between April 2000 and December 2025 stood at just $ 2.5 billion, as per official data. This reflects its lack of interest in India as an investment destination, particularly since India has stayed away from its Belt and Road Initiative.
Further, there is little evidence that China would help build India’s footprint in global supply chains. In fact, China has taken steps that hinder India’s manufacturing growth such as curbs on export of critical minerals and rare earths over 2023-2025, informal delays in exports of electronics and solar manufacturing equipment, pressure on companies to avoid sending personnel to India, and so on.
The experience of rising Chinese FDI in ASEAN countries also reveals weak linkage on the trade balance dimension. Higher Chinese capital inflows contributed to a larger trade deficit and did not support enhanced productivity or technology transfers in ASEAN nations. India’s huge trade deficit with China of $ 116 billion in 2025 may further suffer if enhanced Chinese FDI leads to Chinese overcapacity being offloaded into the Indian manufacturing sector.
China is expected continue to dominate global manufacturing value addition with its share rising from 27% to 40% in the next few years, and given its excess manufacturing capacity, its exports would continue to grow, displacing India’s manufacturing and jobs.
India’s previous experience with Chinese companies operating in India has had its share of issues as well. The presence of Chinese shell companies, possible financial crimes, GST evasion, cyber fraud schemes, and other fraudulent activities in pre-Covid times call for vigilance in permitting Chinese investments. Such investments in startups and technology companies also bear the risk of Indian data transfer to China as well as control of user access.
The cautious approach outlined in PN2 is likely to benefit India in two key ways: first, by encouraging overseas investors with minor Chinese stakes to invest in India; and second, by accelerating foreign investments into Indian companies in strategically important sectors. However, it would be naïve to expect the new policy to attract significant Chinese FDI into Indian manufacturing, catalyse technology transfers from China, or help integrate India into China-led global supply chains. Given the persistent geopolitical tensions in India-China relations, a prudent and calibrated approach to permitting Chinese FDI remains the right strategy for India.

In the post-pandemic period, government investment has taken centre stage in supporting India’s economic growth. Capital expenditurehas risen more than fourfold between 2017-18 and 2025-26. In contrast, private capital expenditure, measured by private gross fixed capital formation, has remained subdued. Its share in GDP declined to 22% in 2023-24 from over 26% in 2012-13, and its contribution to overall investment has weakened in most years since 2015-16. While analysts have periodically pointed to “green shoots”, such signs of revival have repeatedly failed to sustain momentum.
A pickup in private capex in the first half of 2025-26 has nonetheless rekindled expectations that sustained public investment could finally crowd in corporate spending. The government’s infrastructure push over four consecutive years, however, has yet to translate into broad-based expansion of private capacity. In the Budget for 2026-27, capital expenditure growth has been pegged at 11.2% year-on-year, signalling continued public-sector support.
Capacity utilisation trends, however, suggest limited urgency for fresh private investment. The Reserve Bank of India’s Order Books, Inventories and Capacity Utilisation Survey for the second quarter of 2025-26 showed manufacturing capacity utilisationhovering around 75%, reflecting a range-bound pattern observed for much of the past decade. Historically, sustained readings above 80% have been considered necessary to trigger large-scale capacity additions.
That said, several factors could support revival in private capital expenditure over the coming year.
First, the post-pandemic public investment drive has materially strengthened infrastructure and logistics, lowering transaction costs and improving competitiveness. Personal income tax reductions and GST rationalisation last year, alongside relatively benign inflation, may bolster consumer demand. This is reflected in resilient vehicle sales, often viewed as a bellwether for consumer sentiment, and robust growth in consumer durables and non-durables, as indicated by recent Index of Industrial Production data.
Second, recent trade agreements with major markets such as the European Union and the United States have helped ease corporate concerns stemming from global trade uncertainty. While implementation will take time, improved clarity on trade policy may support business sentiment and lend impetus to export-oriented investment. At the same time, signs of stabilisation in India-China relations point to a less volatile external environment. Although the global backdrop remains fragile, it appears to be moving towards greater stability.
Third, corporate balance sheets are considerably stronger than in the previous investment cycle. Leverage has declined, profitability has improved, and cash balances remain comfortable, enhancing firms’ capacity to undertake new investments.
Fourth, access to credit has improved. The gross non-performing assets ratio of banks has declined to a decadal low of 2.1%, according to RBI data, strengthening the banking system’s lending capacity. Moreover, cumulative policy rate cuts totalling 125 basis points during 2025 have eased financing conditions and could further support capital formation.
Finally, structural reforms, including Production Linked Incentive schemes, improvements in the ease of doing business, financial-sector reforms, new labour codes, and the liberalisation of foreign direct investment norms, have created a more supportive policy environment for private investment.
Even so, the impact of these measures has yet to fully translate into a sustained capex cycle. The RBIIndustrial Outlook Survey for October-December indicates that business sentiment in manufacturing remains guarded, reflecting weak global demand and lingering cost pressures. Although expectations for the next financial year are more optimistic, recent data suggest that fresh private-sector announcements moderated in the second and third quarters. Investment activity over the financial year has been concentrated in select sectors.
Capital expenditure has been skewed towards new-age industries such as renewable energy, electric vehicles, and data centres, as well as pharmaceuticals, electronics, and defence manufacturing. A broad-based revival across traditional sectors remains elusive.
Ultimately, a durable recovery in private capex will hinge on stronger domestic demand and improved export prospects. While inflation has moderated, wage growth has been uneven, constraining the pace of consumption recovery. Government transfers and subsidies may provide short-term support, but they are unlikely to substitute for sustained income growth in driving private investment decisions.
A broad-based investment revival will depend on effective implementation of reforms, improved consumer confidence, and sustained demand-led increases in capacity utilisation. Until utilisation rates rise meaningfully above critical thresholds, government expenditure is likely to remain the primary engine of growth.

The one term that really defines Budget 2026-27 is ‘shoe uppers’. Any major economic statement from the government should surely not go into such micro details on taxes and procedures, and the selective picking of industries and items rather than a holistic boost for private industry in the Budget is emblematic of the continuing control mindset of policymakers.
The Budget stretches a line between such specific product tweaks, including parts for microwaves and walnuts, to a visionary but nebulous future marked by high-speed rail lines, rare earth independence, and data centre dominance. Arbitrary targets are outlined for cities, tourism centres, healthcare workers and girls’ hostels without significant outlay enhancement. Given the long-term initiatives proposed, it is likely that the Budget was truly underpinned by a yuva-shakti thinking of future imperatives rather than the present woes of job-seekers, small enterprises, investors and exporters.
With barely a passing nod to global economic turbulence, the Budget does well to maintain a high degree of stability and prudent macroeconomic steering which aims to insulate industry from the vagaries of external powers. Staying on the fiscal deficit pathway and not resorting to populist measures for upcoming elections may be the highlight of this pedestrian Budget that seeks to avoid excitement but misses an opportunity for announcing impactful reform policies.
Looking at the Budget’s manufacturing highlights, eleven areas have been prioritised. Of these, the vaunted India Semiconductor Mission 2.0 receives an outlay of ₹10 billion for 2026-27. The scheme to revive 200 legacy industrial clusters is not specifically mentioned in the scheme outlay document and the National Industrial Corridor Development and Implementation Trust is allocated ₹30 billion, unchanged from the revised estimates of the previous year.
While three dedicated chemical parks are announced, it is worth remembering that the earlier petrochemical and chemical parks did not really take off as expected. The stress on container manufacturing is welcome since China has a stranglehold on this critical product, but questions arise on whether India can be a credible alternative. The plan is to produce 1 million TEUs over the next decade by leveraging ₹100 billion in the next five years, reducing imports of 2 million imported empty containers.
The Electronics Component Manufacturing Scheme, notified in April 2025, garnered much higher investments than envisaged and its enhancement to ₹400 billion builds on the new proposals approved under the third tranche. It is puzzling that the expenditure planned for the year stands at just ₹10 billion, and possibly much of the incentives outgo will come on line over the next few years. The textile sector has been imparted a boost through various schemes such as National Fibre Scheme, skill development under Samarth 2.0 and support to handlooms. This is timely and will help to prepare for the opening of the large EU market once the India-EU free trade agreement is inked.
The rare earth corridors build upon the National Critical Mineral Mission and the Rare Earth Permanent Magnet scheme to incorporate processing into the value chain. This requires the development of a number of ancillary industries as well as skills but it is a good beginning to lower India’s reliance on imports over the long term. It is also interesting to note the Scheme for Enhancement of Construction and Infrastructure Equipment, which includes tunnel-boring machines. China had discouraged exports of these machines to India at a time of heightened strain in the bilateral relationship, and a proposal to build domestic capacities in such equipment is a nose-thumb at China, even though it may take years to develop the supply chain.
The policies announced for strengthening MSME competitiveness are rather vague and limited in scope, apart from the credit guarantee for discounted invoices on the trade receivables platform. Announcements on funds and industrial clusters have regularly been made in the past without transformational impact for MSMEs, and are at best a measure to fill growing policy and funding gaps rather than offer impetus.
It is questionable how much of a thrust the proposals on exemption of basic customs duty on specified parts for microwave ovens, aircrafs and parts, shoe uppers and specific inputs for processed seafood products for export will impart to overall manufacturing. These tweaks do not represent a support system for exporters and their workers, besieged by falling orders and rising tariffs in the key US market. The steps for Authorised Economic Operators and risk management system are also unlikely to sufficiently reduce cost of exporting to offset other costs in an uncertain world.
As for most government announcements, the success of many of these initiatives will rest upon effective implementation, spotty at best.
In larger macroeconomic terms, apart from enhanced public capex, the Budget offers little for driving consumption, boosting private capex, creating jobs, and stabilising exports for a new world. It is not a Budget addressing global volatility or domestic growth drivers, but focuses on a business-as-usual approach, earnestly hoping that negative geopolitical forces and domestic developments will resolve themselves over the coming year.

So a few days ago, I checked my ecom apps for sugar and found that all the sugar in the market was diverted to ethanol production and the price had shot up.
The question that immediately cropped up was how I would make my coconut barfi now! Just two weeks ago, I had volunteered to make coconut barfi for the monthly ladies’ pot-luck kitty party.
Now it was clear why all the sensible ladies had offered to make kaddu, bhindi, and potato dishes – and they were not even economists!
Image: Grok
It was actually not my fault. I was only going by the sensible government decision to increase the ethanol in petrol.
I applauded this decision. I actually agreed with the government that the Gulf War had wreaked havoc on crude oil prices and this was affecting foreign exchange rates, current account deficit, fiscal deficit and the entire economy.
It was an economic crisis situation that could only be solved through sugar! We have no control on the mad US-Iran peace / war process. But we grow our own sugar. It’s ours, when all else fails.
Besides, other things need to be considered for the benefit of the people. Since the ancient days, embedded in the Indian Knowledge System, Indians know that the only way to ease pain is to eat sweets. Not just one or two.
We must add sugar in our morning cup of chai. And what is breakfast without a few jalebis? Kheer for lunch, halwa for afternoon snacks and a couple of nice plump, golden-brown gulabjamun for dinner, supported by a few more sugar spoonfuls for the mid-morning tea and the staff coffee break and the before-snack tea and the post-dinner coffee.
And this intake of sugar is damaging our citizens’ health! Non-communicable, lifestyle diseases are going up. The sages did not spend hours on computers or scrolling Instagram, so they unfortunately could not anticipate this health crisis. Something had to be done immediately.
Since the beginning of time in 2014, as much as 31 million metric tons of crude oil were substituted by ethanol! Rs 1.9 trillion had been saved in foreign exchange!
The government had to also think about climate change and global emissions. Increasing ethanol in petrol avoided 93 million metric tons carbon dioxide emissions in 12 years!
It was good for half the population dependent on agriculture too! Farmers earned Rs 1.6 trillion, enabling them to become rich enough to eat more sweets.
It was time to scale this glorious policy up and save Indians by adding more of their sugar in ethanol. Not only would this make India resilient to oil price fluctuations, it would also make Indians healthier – nothing could be more win-win!
And for those worried about water use in sugar and rice cultivation, let us remind them that as many as 4 states have achieved 100% coverage of taps for drinking water, and the water is even flowing sometimes. Only a few populous states still have less than half the population without tap water, but they do have wells and hand-pumps, right?
While the government, like a responsible entity, tried to instill sense among the car-owners about the benefits of higher ethanol blending, several unfortunate things happened.
Oil prices unexpectedly dropped. No one could have predicted this. The war is still on, right!
Red Rot and Top Borer diseases hit sugarcane, coming from nowhere!
The expected drought turned into unexpected excess rainfall, causing waterlogging!
Consumer demand went up in anticipation of the festive season, a couple of weeks early!
Traders started hoarding!
None of this can be placed at the door of the government. These things happen.
Quick action has again been taken by a responsive and caring government to protect the citizens’ festivities.
The government has graciously given permission to import 1 million tons of sugar. Citizens are heaving sighs of relief.
Of course, since sugar has not been imported for ten years, the port facilities still need to be resuscitated. I gather this is being worked upon urgently.
In the meanwhile, I learnt a valuable lesson. The housewives and hoarders are better informed and prepared than the government, economists or industry.
I better get the lottery in the kitty party. Now for making that coconut barfi!

My article in BasisPoint Insight explores the recent reports on India’s skill development outcomes.
The Prime Minister, in his Independence Day speech, announced a target to formally train 10 million youth in Artificial Intelligence skills this coming year. The target is an ambitious one and will need a well-coordinated skill system across the country to be successful. Unfortunately, that is where India faces an obvious lacuna.
India’s Artificial Intelligence talent pool holds about 600,000 AIprofessionals, and nine of ten employees in enterprises use GenAI tools, according to the India Skills Report 2026. Demand for AI talent is on the rise across sectors such as manufacturing and BFSI, and the need for AI skills enhancement is definitely the need of the hour.
However, the workforce is lacking when it comes to skills in general, and that is a well recognised fact; only about 5% of those in the age group of 15 to 29 years have received formal vocational or technical training, as per the annual Periodic Labour Force Survey for 2025.
Why is that the case is the obvious next question. For, over the years, the government has not only accorded high priority to skilling but also instituted multiple missions and schemes starting with setting up a dedicated Ministry for Skill Development and Entrepreneurship (MSDE) and its Skill India Mission in 2015.
The National Skill Development Corporation, Sector Skills Councils, PM-SETU for Industrial Training Institutes (ITI) and Jan Shikshan Sansthans form the institutional architecture, along with regulatory bodies. These are supported by programmes such as the Pradhan Mantri Kaushal Vikas Yojana (PMKVY), PM Vishwakarma scheme, Skill India Digital Hubs (SIDH) and others. The Ministry of Education also runs the National Apprenticeship Training Scheme (NATS) while the MSDE operates the National Apprenticeship Promotion Scheme (NAPS).
An online programme of Skilling for AI Readiness (SOAR) hosted on the SIDH is underway for teacher and student training, covering 50 AI and AI-application courses. YUVA AI for All, another free online programme for AI basics, was introduced in November 2025. At the secondary school level, the National Education Policy 2020 has introduced AI from class III in CBSE schools, which is expected to reach about 21 million students by 2027.
In this potpourri of different programmes and schemes, it is challenging to quantify the collective outcomes.
A December 2025 report by the Comptroller and Auditor General of India (CAG) points out gaps in Pradhan Mantri Kaushal Vikas Yojana’s short term courses, stating that while the scheme achieved over 80% of its skilling target between 2015 and 2022, there appeared to be no strategy to its operations. Moreover, skills delivered were not really aligned to job requirements, and hence, only 40% of the trainees could be placed.
PMKVY 4.0, announced in the Union Budget 2023-24, offers over 600 new age courses, including AI. The programme has thus enhanced employment and self-employment, and contributed to higher incomes.
NITI Aayog’s report on skills states that 77 million persons have been trained in the last 12 years, but the outcomes are uneven. Another paper points out inadequacies in the apprenticeship scheme.
The India Skills Report, which captures hiring intent from over 1,000 organisations, has found only 46% of students from ITI and 33% from polytechnic courses are employable, and flagged AI literacy as a key factor in sustaining the growth of a multidimensional workforce including gig, AI-assisted and entrepreneurial options.
What ails the skilling sector
Structural issues such as inadequate fund allocations, poor skilling infrastructure, gaps in trainer capacities, and low alignment with industry requirements make the skill ecosystem far from the robust system that it was envisioned to be.
When it comes to AI, the skill development promise is more difficult to fulfill as this is a new and evolving sector, characterised by rapid changes. Computers, a basic requirement, are available in 70% of schools, but one in three schools does not have access to the internet.
Also, unless the government is contemplating more online AI courses, which are already heavily promoted by various private players, the target of 10 million beneficiaries might be a stretch.
With a youth population estimated at 345 million by 2036, India’s skill ecosystem requires consolidation and coordination among stakeholders, rather than a proliferation of new programmes.
There is need for localised skill mapping and skill courses, which would include opportunities for upskilling, reskilling and lifelong learning across districts. AI training can be integral to many of these courses. The focus should be on the metrics of outcomes in terms of placements, not inputs in terms of certifications granted.
Most importantly, the budget for skill development must be enhanced and work to ensure that the right infrastructure and quality trainers are in place.
It may be appealing to announce an ambitious target for AI skilling in the light of current issues being raised by Gen Z, but a real push for job-linked skill development will matter to the youth of the country much more.

There was a time when the advanced economies, spooked by China’s growing dominance of global markets and its tendency to weaponize its trade, were attempting to deleverage their China presence, find alternative centres for production and derisk their investments.
Or so we thought. For the last few years, we in India were talking up our manufacturing sector and export prowess to foreign investors to leverage the concept of China+1 and attract FDI into our economy, hoping that some of the declining FDI destined for China would come our way. Unfortunately, the fond hopes have now been dashed with the hotter relations between China and the US, cemented by President Trump’s recent call on President Xi in Beijing.
President Xi spent a lot of time in showing President Trump the circular premises of the Temple of Heaven and the serene environs of Zhongnanhai - the exclusive leadership complex - and in hosting multiple banquets and teas.
But the nub of the visit was the traveling contingent of the ‘top’ 30 CEOs of the US, collectively representing not just the hundreds of billions of their respective companies, but also the end of the dreams of Indian policymakers avidly following from the sidelines.
The economic part of the visit was the centrepiece for the US side. The Chinese side made their usual statements on Taiwan and got the US to back their formulation on a constructive relationship of strategic stability, according to the White House Fact Sheet of 17 May (but whether it will be fair and reciprocal in the future remains to be seen).
After a few perfunctory hat-tips to global issues like Iran and North Korea, the next part of the fact sheet puts the establishment of the US-China Boards of Trade and Investment as the ‘cornerstone’ of the historic visit.
These will manage the relationship, which probably means that any reciprocal tariffs, weaponizing of exports or trade and investment restrictions that either country may contemplate for the other are to be addressed amicably instead of leading to all-out trade wars as in the past. It also means that both sides will continue to be major markets and investment destinations for each other.
The following paragraphs on various Chinese pledges to purchase US aircraft and agricultural products, while short in content, do point to a clear rapprochement on bilateral economic relations. President Trump, after imposing 145% tariffs on Chinese goods and being forced to face rare earth restrictions, blinked first and backed down.
Which means that China is no more as much of a risk for US investors as it was over the past five-ten years.
Which means that US companies will again shift their priorities to China’s large markets and cheaper goods.
Which means that investors of other countries are heaving a sigh of relief and putting China back on their strategy tables.
Which means that China+1 is effectively buried.
According to the Chinese Ministry of Commerce, China received 9.5% less FDI in 2025 than the previous year, although over 70,000 new foreign invested enterprises were established in the country. In the first quarter of 2026, new foreign enterprises rose by 11%, while actual inflows continued to fall by 7.3% year-on-year.
According to the RBI, gross inflows recorded US$ 94.5 billion in 2025-26, but US$ 53.6 billion was repatriated by foreign companies, leaving a direct investment into India of US$ 40.9 billion. This is quite a bit higher than the figure last year of US$ 29.1 billion.
The bottomline is that India has to redouble its efforts to attract overseas investments and improve ease of doing business. As always….

At the 11th Governing Council meeting of NITI Aayog, Prime Minister Narendra Modi urged state chief ministers to undertake estimation of gross domestic product at the district level and track their progress. Such district domestic product (DDP) is expected to help uncover lagging districts across India’s approximately 800 such administrative units, and encourage better policy formulation to overcome developmental gaps.
Sub-regional calculation of GDP – the calculation of the value of goods and services produced in a small defined area over a specific period – is conducted by various countries and groupings, including the US at the country level, the EU under its NUTS 3 (Nomenclature of Territorial Units for Statistics, level 3) geocode standard, and the UK for local authority districts. Among large developing countries, China, Brazil and Mexico calculate GDP for certain municipalities but the data quality is uneven. India’s venture to develop the methodology for DDP is thus an ambitious and inclusive project, rightly prioritised by the Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation (MOSPI).
MOSPI brought out draft uniform guidelines for compiling gross state value addition and DDP on April 7, 2026. This was part of the exercise to update the base year of national accounts to 2022-23, and was followed by the issue of final guidelines on June 3, just ahead of the Governing Council meeting. Earlier, 26 states and UTs practiced the top-down approach for estimating DDP, wherein state GDP estimations were distributed across districts based on selected indicators such as population. However, this was not comparable across states and sectors, providing only a rough estimation that often masked intra-state deficiencies.
The new bottom-up framework aims at harmonisation and consistency in data tracking across the country. In its guidelines, MOSPI recommends states to use improved data sources to estimate the primary, secondary and tertiary sector production value through administrative and survey processes or, when not possible, through top-down measures. Updated sources such as the Annual Survey of Industries (ASI), Annual Survey of Unincorporated Sector Enterprises (ASUSE), Periodic Labour Force Survey (PLFS), Goods and Services Tax and other existing and upgraded databases are to be deployed by states to compile the data at the district level.
The concept of backward districts for targeted developmental activities is not new. It has been considered an apt measure for fostering equitable growth right from the beginning of the five-year plans process. Various area-based programmes have been launched over the years, including for drought-prone, hilly, tribal, border and other regions. The Rashtriya Sam Vikas Yojana of 2003-04 identified almost 150 districts as backward, and requiring special attention. Subsuming this programme, the Backward Regions Grant Fund came about in 2007 to support delivery of schemes and promote planning at the panchayat level in over 250 districts.
With the end of the Planning Commission and the launch of NITI Aayog, backward districts assumed a new nomenclature under the Aspirational Districts Programme (ADP) in 2018, covering 112 districts for special measures. NITI Aayog tracks these districts monthly for their progress on 49 key performance indicators relating to healthcare, education, agriculture, financial inclusion and infrastructure. Significant progress has been noted in these indicators in underdeveloped districts, especially in the health and agriculture sectors.
The experience of backward districts or aspirational districts over the years implies that much more needs to be done towards equitable growth, rather than merely identifying districts and datapoints.
States track their district data through directorates of economics and statistics. As per the Economic Survey 2024-25, Rangareddy district in Telangana enjoys the highest GDP per capita, followed by Gurugram (Haryana), Bengaluru Urban (Karnataka), Gautam Budh Nagar (Uttar Pradesh), Solan (Himachal Pradesh), and districts in Goa, Sikkim, Maharashtra and Gujarat. The differential between the richest and poorest districts within a state often skews its overall position in state rankings. For example, Gautam Budh Nagar hosts major global companies, and has emerged among the top districts for exports and FDI, thus pulling up the rank for Uttar Pradesh as a whole.
The MOSPI guideline, when implemented across states, would greatly improve the estimation of DDP and thereby contribute to evidence-based policymaking. It would provide granular information on key macro indicators that can be expected to yield standardised and reliable estimates of economic output to feed into decentralised planning.
It would also contribute to improve coverage of India’s vast informal sector and identify district-level economic hurdles and shocks, such as closure of factories or area-based excessive rains and droughts. Financial allocations can also be made in an informed manner. Another advantage would be to evaluate and monitor districts’ progress in development initiatives.
Several challenges would need to be addressed for the all-round success of the DDP initiative. Implementation would rest on resolving data gaps persistent at the district level, capacity of the state government statistics departments to maintain a high-level of granular data, and correctly assessing self-employment and the informal sector where employment is often flexible across sectors. For example, a farmer on a small plot may shift between agricultural work and retail activities in a single year.
The uniform guidelines for DDP mark a significant step towards better data on the economy, and, if executed well, could support evidence-based, decentralised policymaking and targeted interventions. The central and state governments must continue to collaborate strongly and invest in data collection systems and facilities, but with the understanding that building a geographically equitable India will require much more than just data.

One of the most encouraging data points in the recently-released economic statistics for the first quarter of the current financial year was seen in gross fixed capital formation, or GFCF — a proxy for investment — as a ratio of GDP at current prices at 34.3%. This was a significant jump from 31.4% in the same quarter of 2025-26. The real GFCF growth rate surged from 5.8% in April-June 2025 last year to as high as 11.9%.
Why this was considered a big boost is because the investment rate has remained somewhat subdued for years. Each time analysts and policymakers talk about ‘green shoots’ in the economy, the next round of data disappoints yet again.
India needs a sustained GDP growth rate of around 8% each year to reach high-income status by 2047. With investments historically contributing about half of India’s growth since 1991, a higher investment ratio can spur GDP growth rate to desired levels over the next two decades.
Historically, the GFCF ratio remained below 30% till 2004-05, after which it rose rapidly to reach almost 36% in 2007-08. This fast rise propelled the GDP growth rate to a new trajectory at the time, but it has not been repeated since then.
Losing steam following the Global Financial Crisis and the Taper Tantrum years, the investment rate once again dropped below 30% in 2015-16 and stayed here for the next six years. This kept GDP pace at around an average annual of 6.6% for the pre-Covid decade.
In the new GDP series at 2022-23 prices, the annual GFCF to GDP ratio stubbornly refused to cross the 32% mark for the three years of 2023-24 to 2025-26.
The last three financial years reveal that the GFCF ratio remains robust in the first half-year, while dissipating in the final two quarters. A peak was hit in the second quarter of 2025-26 at 34.5%, and the just-released data for April-June at 34.3% raises hopes that the desired investment trajectory is within reach.
The government has undertaken various initiatives to prop up the investment rate through its own capital expenditure as well as measures to boost private sector investments such as Production Linked Incentive Scheme, easier regulatory and business environment, and tax cuts.
New project announcements by private companies almost doubled in the first quarter of this year compared to the same time last year, according to CMIE. Investment growth is led by new projects in power generation and services sectors. This comes despite the West Asia conflict situation, high and volatile oil prices, and restricted transport chokepoints.
Similarly, the continued acceleration in the pace of bank credit to industry supports the recent uptrend in private sector investments. RBI data on performance of the private corporate business sector during the first quarter of 2026-27 displayed a peak of 19.4% in sales growth, the highest in the last two years. Growth of operating profits too stepped up for both manufacturing and services sectors. Sectors such as vehicles, petroleum and electrical machinery on the manufacturing side and, on the services side, IT sector and wholesale and retail trade are performing well.
On the other hand, the Reserve Bank of India capacity utilisation survey for manufacturing firms for the January-March 2025-26 quarter refuses to break away from the 75% post-Covid level, indicating that a surge in fresh investments by the private sector may prove to be challenging in the manufacturing sector.
So far, the government has been undertaking the heavy lifting in capital expenditure. But with the private sector contributing the bulk of share in the GFCF, its investment activity is key to driving prospective GDP growth. Rising investments in emerging sectors such as semiconductors, data centres and AI need to be replicated in labour-intensive sectors for broad-based income growth.
While early signs in the first quarter indicate an investment uptick, past experience shows that the second half of the year sees a decline in the GFCF ratio. Reaching the peak investment ratio of 36% as in the past will require a benign global business environment and facilitative policies at home. Slower growth in the agricultural sector too might impact consumer demand.
Much will hinge on central bank measures in the coming months, including the US Federal Reserve September action. In essence, it must be concluded that it is not yet time to get excited about the higher investment ratio in the first quarter of the current financial year and to be confident that private sector investment activity is in fact set for an inflection point.

Economic commentators have expressed unhappiness about India’s net FDI, which led me to explore the overall trends in global and Indian FDI.
In my latest paper published by the Vivekananda International Foundation, I examine how India can better attract FDI in an increasingly fragmented and uncertain global environment.
Grateful to VIF for bringing it out. You can read the full paper here with a brief summary below.
Global trends
Foreign Direct Investment remains one of the most powerful drivers of capital, technology, exports, employment, and global value chain integration for developing economies. Yet the world has changed. Geopolitical tensions, friend-shoring, supply chain relocations, tariff volatility, and rising policy uncertainty have altered capital flows.
Global FDI has never fully recovered its pre-2008 momentum and remains range-bound. Overall flows rose in 2025, but flows to developing countries contracted a bit. (The UNCTAD World Investment Report for 2026 came out just a day before this paper was published!)
Inward FDI trends show that recovery to 2013 levels is still a way off.
India’s performance
India has shown remarkable resilience, with trends often diverging from global flows especially during stress periods. Gross inflows have grown, reaching roughly US$94.5 billion in 2025-26. But net FDI as a percentage of GDP has fallen sharply to around 0.7%, regional and sectoral imbalances persist, repatriations have risen, and we continue to rely heavily on conduit routes.
Key observations include:
- Sectoral patterns: Services sectors continue to dominate inward FDI, while labour-intensive manufacturing sectors lag.
- Source countries: Singapore and Mauritius account for a very large share (often as conduits), while inflows from major economies like the US, Japan, and others are under-represented.
- Regional inequities: 31% of FDI in 2018-2025 went to Maharashtra, while Bihar received less than US$ 200 million.
The paper has special sections relating to India’s experience with offshore financial centres, the key FDI players of US and Singapore, the tricky question of FDI from China, and what India can do in the China +1 strategy.
A Strategic Framework for the Future
The core of the paper is a practical strategic framework built around three pillars:
1. Strategic Anticipation
India can institute better systems to track geopolitical risks, trade policy shifts, competitor actions, and developments in key source countries. The paper suggests creating an Indian FDI Risk Monitor to help policymakers stay ahead of volatility.
2. Strategic Integration
FDI policy should be closely integrated with industrial policy and trade policy (as often suggested by CII). Tariffs, incentives (like PLI), FTAs, and infrastructure development should come together to attract investment in priority sectors and deepen GVC participation.
3. Strategic Marketing
Attracting FDI requires proactive, targeted outreach, focusing on specific countries and companies in key sectors Strengthening Invest India’s capabilities and embassy-level engagement will be critical.
Key Recommendations
The paper outlines several key actions, including:
- Improving the domestic investment environment and ease of doing business.
- Introducing an investor-friendly Bilateral Investment Treaty (BIT) regime.
- Fast-tracking industrial infrastructure development.
- Building stronger technology partnerships.
- Implementing state-level business climate reforms.
A holistic strategy that combines forward-looking risk monitoring, policy coherence, and proactive promotion is essential to better leverage India’s advantages in the current global context.

India’s international space cooperation now features prominently in most of its bilateral relationship documents. Recent agreements with Norway, Italy and Sweden in May, France and Seychelles in June, and Australia and Indonesia in July, reflect India’s rising confidence in its space achievements - and its ambition to emerge as a major global space industry player. However, its overseas space success will rest on greater participation from the private sector, a crucial link between its space services exports and international cooperation.
As India approaches its fourth National Space Day on August 23, it can take justified pride in Skyroot Aerospace’s successful July 18 launch of Vikram-1, the country’s first privately developed orbital rocket. This consequential milestone makes India only the third country with private space entities capable of orbital launches. Backed by the Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO), its commercial arm NewSpace India Ltd (NSIL), and Indian National Space Promotion and Authorisation Centre (IN-SPACe), the private sector has the potential to emerge as a partner in India’s global space leadership aspirations.
The country’s space industry stands at about $8 billion-$9 billion, less than 3% of the global pie. It is targeted at $44 billion in 2033, and aims to capture 8% share as per the ‘Decadal Vision and Strategic for the Development of the Indian Space Economy’ brought out by IN-SPACe in 2023. India opened up the space sector to private industry in 2020 and followed that up by the Indian Space Policy 2023 and liberalisation of FDI in the sector. ISRO nurtures the private sector through a discounted pricing policy in accessing its facilities, and provides technical expertise and mentorship.
Today, there are more than 400 space startups in the country. In 2026, to date, $113 million investments have flowed into the sector, and cumulative private investments have now reached$871 million, increasingly moving from seed capital to growth-stage rounds. This falls woefully short of the funding in other countries, estimated at over $12 billion in 2025 alone.
IN-SPACe and SIDBI Venture Capitalaim to fill the gap with a ₹10 billion fund. The fund aims to offer startups capital for commercial activities including launch technologies, payload systems, in-space services and downstream applications. Again, the proposed amount appears insufficient to make a significant impact on private sector participation in space.
IN-SPACe stands as an approving body and grants authorisations to non-government entities for establishment and operation of satellites and payloads and space transport systems, among others. Just over a hundred have been granted so far, and a more facilitative and faster system needs to be instituted.
India’s space sector exports between 2015 and 2024 reached $433 million including the commercial launch of about 400 satellites for 34 countries, led by government entities. Indian startups in space technology and manufacturing have also begun to reach out to other countries. For example, Pixxel has been awarded a contract by the US National Reconnaissance Office to deploy its Firefly constellation for advanced hyperspectral imagery. Ananth Technologies is partnering with the Australian Space Agency, ISRO and a consortium of Australian companies for an orbital servicing vehicle, named Optimus, under the India-Australia Space MAITRI programme.
As more space startups enter operational activities, India’s diplomatic outreach will be vital to open demand for new opportunities. Recognising this, the country is strengthening cooperation with space leaders for technology and global supply chain integration. At the same time, it is reaching out to emerging markets to boost exports and offer satellite and geospatial services.
India has inked more than 300 space cooperation agreements with 61 countries and 5 multilateral organisations, and has launched more than 400 foreign satellites. It has long engaged with Russia’s ROSCOSMOS, US’s NASA, France’s CNES, the European Space Agency, and Japan’s JAXA, among others, for space research, training and capacity building, deep space exploration, resource assessment, earth observation and several other critical areas. India is a signatory to five UN space treaties and has also signed the Artemis Accord for governance of civil exploration and use of outer space.
However, incomplete alignment between diplomatic efforts and domestic capabilities means the country may have ceded the growing space export market to other countries. To narrow the gap, the country needs to focus on sustained investment, active launch cadence and manufacturing capacity at scale.
India’s advantages in space services exports include low-cost space infrastructure, highly skilled engineers and technicians, upcoming manufacturing clusters near launch facilities, and a rapidly emerging ecosystem of space component manufacturers. With the global space economy projected to reach $1.8 trillion by 2035, up from $630 billion in 2023, India must move fast in space services exports, including downstream activities.
R&D commercialisation and greater corporate participation in technology development will come from better tax options, faster government approvals, and demand creation through procurement. ISRO’s Space Technology Cells in leading educational institutions could help both in research and skill development. Facilitative transfer of proven technology, as envisaged in the 2023 space policy, can scale commercialisation.
Companies should also explore working intensively in space applications such as earth observation, in-orbit servicing, and space situational awareness. Space diplomacy in the development sector, including resource mapping, agriculture, and disaster management, can bring mutual gains to India and the Global South.
The next stage of space services exports would also require adequate space-related infrastructure in India, including more launch-pad slots, testing facilities and credit access. These should be routed through defined protocols, rather than as informal access to government-owned facilities. The new space port in Kulasekarapattinam, Tamil Nadu, will support small satellite launch vehicles starting 2026-27, with a third launch pad coming up in Sriharikota.
The delays in the proposed Space Activities Bill, under consideration since 2017, means that the private sector lacks necessary statutory backing in liability, insurance, intellectual property and dispute resolution. Trade finance, export credit guarantees, and export promotion policies are other areas to be addressed to boost exports.
A notable beginning has been made since the space sector was opened up to private industry six years ago. The government is working to converge diplomatic and scientific efforts through ISRO and other organisations for global space cooperation. With the right infrastructure, regulatory clarity and sustained policy support, India’s private sector is well positioned to convert its current momentum into lasting leadership in this high-technology domain.

The issues of China Shock 2.0 and devaluation of the RMB are capturing a lot of space these days in the X accounts I follow. The debate is rather vociferous - economists and analysts politely but firmly rebutting each other’s arguments through long, convoluted threads that include detailed charts and complex theories on China’s economic and trade policies.
Meanwhile, the recent G20 finance ministers and central bank governors meeting where all - except China - agreed to ‘eliminate non-market policies and practices that exacerbate imbalances’ attests to pervasive global views on China’s aggressive industrial and export policies.
Grok image
The accounts that crop up on my X feed belong to Brad Setser, Michael Pettis, Adam Tooze, Gita Gopinath, Christopher Balding, Arnaud Bertrand, Arvind Subramanian, and Greg Ip with a few others weighing in. Their points involve economic terms and explanations that mostly go above my head, and also, all of the discussion is probably not showing up in my feed.
So I asked my AI tool to summarize the arguments.
Gopinath, Gourinchas and Rey brought out a piece in The Economist in July arguing that asking for RMB revaluation is an incorrect diagnosis, and no cure for persistent imbalances. The exchange rate is an outcome, and not the cause, of excessive exports and cannot be the primary lever for rebalancing.
China’s suppressed household consumption, continued manufacturing support and, on the US side, large fiscal deficits and low savings are structural domestic savings-investment gaps that revaluation alone cannot resolve.
Setser (@Brad_Setser) has been talking about China Shock 2.0 for some time and his piece on CFR urges for a stronger renminbi. With China’s current account surplus at 4% of GDP, RMB undervaluation may not be 20% as calculated by the IMF, but as high as 30-35%. The Chinese government exercises strict control over its currency within a narrow band, and since mid-2025, the RMB is undergoing a slow revaluation.
Stronger domestic demand will not fix the surplus arising from China’s industrial and import substitution policies, and therefore a stronger yuan is essential to rebalancing its economy.
Ip (@greg_ip) in Wall Street Journal added a new angle by calling for a new Plaza Accord to revalue the yuan, contending that China refuses to pivot from exports to consumption. An Accord and a threat of tariffs could force it to do so to address its massive current account surplus. He places a chart from Goldman Sachs which shows China’s prices lower by 20-60% than that of the rest of the world across products from solar panels to industrial robots.
Pettis (@michaelxpettis and Substack) says the surplus comes from a domestic growth model that suppresses the household income share and produces excess savings which translates into higher exports. RMB revaluation will help income rebalancing and shift purchasing power from producers to households.
Balding (@BaldingsWorld) is strongly critical of the Gopinath approach as Beijing is not likely to revalue, restructure towards consumption or rebalance.
Subramanian (@arvindsubraman) and Chatterjee posit that China’s mercantilist strategy – prioritizing production and investment over consumption and welfare – harms other developing countries by continuing to occupy the low-skilled export space (termed as ‘China Squeeze’).
These distortions are sustained by exchange rate undervaluation. However, yuan undervaluation is just one of the factors weighing on trade surplus along with increase in Chinese productivity.
Tooze (@adam_tooze) is also less focused on yuan levels and more on macro imbalances. However, he took on Subramanian on the China Squeeze, saying that countries like India have not built industrial capacities due to their domestic failures.
Others like Arnaud Bertrand (@RnaudBertrand, who recently posted in real time his family’s 5-week Xinjiang camper tour on X, finding a whole lot of positives) and Jostein Hauge (@haugejostein) defend China’s industrial productivity, sophistication, ecosystem and technological progress, which is why it is outcompeting the West. Calls to control its savings, exports and imports do not align with the US’s increasingly distortionary policies. These are non-US views on the ongoing developments.
Of course, official discourse in China rejects charges on both the currency manipulation and deliberate undervaluation for competitiveness. The PBOC says it has no need to gain trade competitiveness through currency depreciation, and reiterates that all countries should pursue structural reforms.
Two other terms are of interest in the context of China’s imbalances. ‘Involution’ is a term coined by China on hyper competition among domestic firms leading to price wars, business losses and aggressive exports. An anti-involution campaign was launched, with little effect so far on overcapacity or excess exports.
‘Dual circulation’ is a policy to prioritise domestic circulation - boosting internal demand and consumption - supported by international circulation through exports and foreign investments. This too does not seem to have been effective in curbing China’s export juggernaut.
Whatever be the merits of this intense X discussion by foreign experts on the Chinese economy, there is no denying the power of the Chinese industrial ecosystem or equally the state support that makes it possible.
Ashok has written in detail about the China Shock 2.0 and its impact on India before and during this X debate. His comprehensive work calls for a ‘dual but differentiated derisking’ strategy from India – ‘not a reflexive protectionism but a disciplined industrial strategy that aligns finance, procurement, standards, and diplomacy around targeted and credible mid industrial stream objectives’.
My shopping expeditions in Beijing malls a decade ago found a cut-throat and innovative Chinese entrepreneurship class which determinedly took full advantage of industrial policies and did business aggressively. Visits to Shenzhen and industrial towns showed dense networks and spanking new infrastructure.
But there were also reports of migrants living in congested basement corridors, issues of ‘left-behind’ children, and lack of social security and healthcare.
So while the yuan is definitely undervalued (little rate change since my time in China ten years ago), economists are hardly likely to agree on the remedies.
Personally, I think that China needs to focus its substantial energies much more on its domestic demand, which will help lower its overcapacity and reliance on exports. And the rest of us should build our industrial competitiveness and reduce dependence on cheap imports from China.

Over three decades, India has built a wide and impactful network of Strategic Partnerships with advanced and developing countries. These build trust and signal special cooperation levels. Do these translate into robust economic outcomes?
My paper examines the economic dimension of India’s Strategic Partnerships, focusing on trade, investment, resources, technology, and skills and mobility.
Drawing on merchandise trade data (2011–2025), FDI and ODI stocks, and institutional mapping of nine long-standing partners—South Africa, France, Germany, Japan, Brazil, Malaysia, the UAE, Australia and the United States—it finds that the relationship between SPs and bilateral trade performance is tenuous.
Investment flows show a somewhat stronger association, particularly where dense institutional mechanisms and sustained political attention exist.
Sectoral cooperation in critical minerals, green transitions, digital public infrastructure and labour mobility has delivered more tangible results when supported by regular high-level reviews and private-sector engagement.
Partnerships with advanced economies generally display deeper institutional architecture, while several relationships with developing-country partners remain under-utilised.
The paper argues that SPs create valuable political trust but do not automatically generate stronger economic outcomes. It recommends clearer economic targets, more regular institutional calendars, focused sectoral agendas, greater private-sector and state-government involvement, systematic monitoring through the development of an index, and consideration of distinct Strategic Economic Partnerships to strengthen India’s bilateral economic engagements.
