I have watched Chinese firms climb the value chain for years now, but this one still made me sit up. Sony, the company that invented the Trinitron and turned the premium living room into a Japanese idea, has handed control of its televisions to a Chinese manufacturer.
For a cheque of roughly $473mn, TCL is buying 51% of Sony's entire home entertainment business.1 2 Fifty-one percent. A controlling stake. And Sony is the one who asked for the deal.
Let that sit for a second. The brand that Indian buyers pay a fat premium for, precisely because it is not Chinese, will from April 2027 be a consolidated subsidiary of a Shenzhen-listed company.2 The logo stays Japanese. The controlling shareholder becomes Chinese.
This is the clearest signal yet of where the television business is heading, and India sits right in the blast radius.
What Sony actually signed away
The definitive agreements were signed in March 2026, and the new company, Bravia, Inc., starts operating in April 2027.1 2 The shape of it matters, so here are the mechanics.
- The whole business is valued at about ¥102.8bn, roughly $650mn.2 3
- TCL pays about $473mn for 51% and gets operational control.1 2
- Sony keeps 49% and books it as an equity affiliate, which quietly lifts the low-margin hardware off Sony's own accounts.2
- Bravia, Inc. becomes a consolidated subsidiary of TCL Electronics.2
What moves across is not just the Bravia TV line. It is the entire home entertainment stack: product development, design, manufacturing, sales, logistics, service, the B2B display and projector businesses, and the home audio range of soundbars and receivers.1 TCL also takes full ownership of Sony's Malaysian manufacturing arm.2
Sony did not walk away naked, though. It keeps three of the five board seats, installs veteran executive Kazuo Kii as chief executive of Bravia, Inc., runs US sales out of San Diego, and crucially holds on to the XR Processor, the picture-processing brain that is the actual reason a Sony looks like a Sony.2 13
So read the division of labour plainly. TCL owns the equity, the factories, the panels and the supply chain. Sony owns the brand, the tuning and the software. China gets the body, Japan keeps the soul, and both pretend the soul is what sells televisions.
Why Sony wanted out of its own living room
To understand why Sony would do this, look at what Sony has quietly become.
For the year to March 2026, Sony posted record sales of about ¥12.5tn and record operating income of about ¥1.45tn, and almost none of that came from hardware.3 4 The money is in intellectual property now.
- Game and Network Services (the PlayStation ecosystem) threw off about ¥463bn in operating income.3
- Music delivered about ¥447bn.3
- Imaging and sensing, the chips inside the world's phone cameras, added about ¥357bn.3
- Together, games, music and pictures are now roughly two-thirds of Sony's revenue.3
And the television business? It lives inside the Entertainment, Technology and Services segment, Sony's lowest-growth unit, where operating income actually fell by about ¥32bn over the year even as the IP divisions soared.3 Industry-wide, TV hardware margins sit in the thin 5 to 10% band, squeezed by panel costs and by exactly the Chinese and Korean rivals Sony is now joining.
This licence-not-sale design, where Sony keeps the profitable IP and lets someone else carry the factories, is precisely the kind of quiet corporate mechanism I love pulling apart, and it is the sort of thread we chase most mornings in the Decoding the Dragon WhatsApp community, where I share a smaller China deep-dive like this with thousands of readers every day (t.ly/t7uhs).
The logic is cold and correct. Owning 49% of an efficient, scale-driven venture that TCL runs beats owning 100% of a business that bleeds capital in a price war Sony cannot win. Sony stops fighting on cost, keeps its face in your living room, and pours its money into PlayStation, anime and music catalogues instead.
The new pecking order in televisions
The deal lands on a market that was already turning Chinese, fast.
In December 2025, Counterpoint Research reported that TCL had overtaken Samsung in global TV shipments for the first time, taking about 16% of the market against Samsung's 13%.5 Samsung still holds the full-year crown it has worn for two decades, but the trend line is not on its side.
- TCL's December shipments grew about 10% year on year, Samsung's about 8%.5
- In the first half of 2025, TCL shipped about 13.5mn TVs, up around 8%, and its Mini-LED shipments jumped a staggering 176%.7
- TCL is already the world's number one in Mini-LED, the technology the premium tier is moving to.7
Now bolt Sony on top. Sony ships only about 4mn TVs a year, roughly a tenth of Samsung's volume.6 Small on its own. But grafted onto TCL's scale, it hands the Chinese firm the one thing money could not buy quickly: an ultra-premium halo.
Samsung is publicly unbothered. Its visual display chief Yong Seok-woo shrugged that "a simple merger alone will not be enough," and pointed to Samsung's 54.3% share of the premium tier and 29.1% of TV revenue.6 He may be right that a merger is not enough. He may also be describing the last comfortable year before a two-front war, because the Bravia venture can undercut Samsung at the top with a trusted brand and out-scale it at the bottom with Chinese cost.
The collateral damage is quieter and lands on a Korean neighbour.
- Sony has long bought its OLED panels from LG Display, because Sony never made its own.14
- TCL does not make WOLED panels; it makes Mini-LED and, increasingly, printed OLED through its panel arm CSOT.7 9
- With TCL running procurement, the incentive to keep buying panels from a direct rival like LG collapses.14
Losing Sony as a captive premium buyer is a real blow to LG Display, and mid-tier brands like Hisense and Vizio get squeezed from both ends at once.
The display shift hiding inside the deal
Here is the part that will actually change what you buy. Sony's newest flagships have quietly abandoned OLED.
The Bravia 9 II, which reached India in August 2026, drops OLED for a Mini-LED system Sony calls "True RGB," driven by independently controlled red, green and blue LEDs and its XR processor.8 Sony claims peak brightness of up to around 4,000 nits, far past what OLED manages, which neutralises OLED's old contrast edge in a bright Indian living room.15
- The 115-inch model carries a twelve-speaker audio system and runs Google TV.8
- It launched in India at about ₹29 lakh for the 115-inch, with the 75-inch at roughly ₹5.4 lakh.8
- The panels behind this push come from TCL's CSOT, the world's Mini-LED leader.7
The longer game is printed OLED. Traditional OLED is made with vacuum evaporation and fine metal masks, expensive and wasteful and hard to scale. CSOT has spent over a decade on inkjet-printed OLED, which sprays the organic material on like a giant printer, wasting far less and cutting cost.9
- CSOT's newest 8.6-generation printed-OLED line in Guangzhou topped out ahead of schedule in May 2026, with mass production targeted for 2027.9
- Printed OLED is meant to run roughly 20% cheaper than LG's WOLED.9
So Sony's escape hatch back into premium OLED, one day, runs through a Chinese factory, not a Korean one.
The Trojan Horse, and the Lenovo playbook
Strip away the finance and there is a geopolitical move underneath. Chinese hardware faces tariffs, security reviews and buyer suspicion across the West and in India. A visibly Chinese brand carries a tax that a Japanese one does not.
Buy control of a beloved Japanese label, though, and you can build Chinese hardware, sell it worldwide, and skip the friction entirely. The buyer in 2028 thinks "Japanese quality." The chassis, the panel and the operational control are Chinese.
We have seen this film before.
- In 2004, IBM sold its PC business, ThinkPad included, to Lenovo for $1.75bn.
- Sceptics said a Chinese firm could not hold IBM's engineering standard.
- Lenovo kept the management and the engineering centres, phased the brand slowly, and by the mid-2010s was the world's largest PC maker, ThinkPad intact.
TCL's structure is arguably a sharper version. Unlike IBM, Sony keeps its core IP and only licenses the brand into the venture, which is a stronger guardrail against quality slipping. If TCL shows Lenovo's restraint and lets Sony's engineers police quality, Bravia, Inc. captures premium share that TCL could never win under its own name.
What it means for India
India is where this gets personal, because Sony sees India eventually overtaking the US as its biggest TV market.
The prize is real and growing.
- India's television market was worth about $13.7bn in 2025 and is projected to reach about $37.8bn by 2034, growing near 12% a year.10
- Growth is all about premiumisation, as buyers jump from small screens to 55-inch, 65-inch and larger 4K and Mini-LED sets.
- Sony India booked about ₹7.9k crore of revenue in FY25, respectable but well behind the volume leaders like Xiaomi, Samsung and LG.11
For years, Indians paid a "Sony tax," a hefty premium for that XR picture and the badge. TCL's supply chain is about to compress it. Put Sony's tuning on CSOT's cheap panels and the premium narrows, which is good news for the upper-middle-class buyer and accelerates the whole market's shift upmarket.
It also fits India's manufacturing push. TCL is already deep inside "Make in India," with a CSOT panel plant in Tirupati, and here is the irony that should not be missed: that plant already supplies TV panels to Samsung India.12 India's biggest TV names, Japanese and Korean alike, increasingly sit on Chinese glass.
This dependence is exactly the kind of quiet leverage I keep flagging, and it is what we argue over daily in the Decoding the Dragon community, where a few thousand of us pull these China-India threads apart every morning (t.ly/t7uhs).
But there is a sharp edge for India too.
- Many Indian buyers pay up for "Japanese" precisely to avoid Chinese electronics, for reasons that are as much about the border as about the badge. Under Bravia, Inc., they will be buying a product a Chinese majority owner builds and controls.
- Modern smart TVs are data nodes, tracking what you watch and how your network behaves. As hardware, firmware and operations shift to a Chinese-controlled entity, the same questions India already asks of Chinese phones and telecom gear will, sooner or later, get asked of the television.
I do not doom-monger here. The XR brain and the tuning stay Sony, and Lenovo showed this can be managed for a decade. But origin is now an illusion, and Indian buyers deserve to know whose machine is really in the room.
What to watch
- Whether Sony's 2027 and 2028 India lineup quietly drops LG OLED panels in favour of CSOT's Mini-LED and printed OLED.
- Whether the "Sony tax" visibly falls on the next India Bravia launches, the real test of the cost synergy.
- Whether CSOT's Guangzhou printed-OLED line hits mass production on schedule in 2027, which decides how fast Sony re-enters cheap premium OLED.
- Whether any Indian procurement or security scrutiny lands on the Chinese-controlled Bravia entity the way it has on other Chinese hardware.
The one line
The television in your living room may still say Sony, but from 2027 its body, its factory and its controlling owner will be Chinese, and that is the whole story of how China climbs a value chain: not by beating the premium brand, but by quietly buying the right to wear it.

Here is a number that should not really be possible. Singapore, a city of about 6mn people on 734 sq km of reclaimed land, is sitting on a stock of inward foreign direct investment worth roughly 4.2 times its own GDP.1
Let that sink in for a second. The foreign money parked inside this one small island is worth more than four years of everything the island produces. At the end of 2024 that stock stood at about S$3.1tn, or roughly $2.3tn, up 9.5% in a single year.1
No normal economy looks like this. And the more I dig into who is actually parking that capital and why, the clearer it becomes that Singapore is not really Asia's Switzerland, a quiet vault for the nervous rich. It is something far more deliberate.
My view, after going through the filings, the tax schemes and the sectoral data, is simple. China does not globalise by shipping its factories abroad. Those go to Vietnam, Thailand and increasingly Johor. China globalises by sending its brain, its headquarters, its patents and its wealth, to Singapore. And that has a direct bearing on India.
Start with what that S$3.1tn actually is, because the composition is the whole story.
- Finance and insurance alone holds about 65.5% of Singapore's entire inward FDI stock, roughly S$2tn.1
- Most of that is not money building factories or hiring workers. It sits inside holding companies, corporate shells whose only job is to own things elsewhere.1
- Singapore's own outward direct investment stock is about S$1.7tn.2 Capital comes in, picks up a Singapore passport, and flows straight back out into the region.
This is what a capital re-exporter looks like. Singapore is not the final home for most of this money. It is the interchange.
And it has built itself for the job on purpose. Manufacturing, which was over 27% of GDP back in 2004, is down to around 16% today.3 Singapore has quietly walked away from making things.
In its place it sells what I would call soft infrastructure, and it is worth being precise about what that means:
- English common law and courts that enforce contracts predictably, so a Chinese firm can settle a cross-border dispute far from Beijing's reach.
- No capital gains tax, and one of the world's widest networks of double-taxation treaties.
- Deep private banking, fund administration and capital markets.
- A workforce where about 74% of people are of working age, the highest share in ASEAN, and comfortable in both English and Mandarin.4
GDP per capita is around $94,000, the highest in the region by a distance.5 You cannot compete on land or cheap labour at that price. So Singapore competes on trust.
China-washing: moving the brain, not the factory
The sharpest use of that trust is what gets called China-washing, and it is not a slur, it is a genuine corporate strategy. As Washington tightens tariffs, export controls and entity lists, Chinese firms shift their headquarters, holding structures and top executives to Singapore to soften their geopolitical profile while keeping full access to Western customers.
The case studies are hiding in plain sight:
- ByteDance runs TikTok's international operations out of dual hubs in Los Angeles and Singapore, with a Singaporean, Shou Zi Chew, as chief executive.6 He is a Singaporean and former Xiaomi finance chief, the non-Chinese face Western regulators wanted to see.
- That structure has just paid off in the most literal way. In January 2026 ByteDance closed a deal spinning TikTok's US business into a new joint venture majority-owned by American investors including Oracle, Silver Lake and MGX, with ByteDance keeping under 20%.7 The Singapore-centred design was the scaffolding that made a deal like that sellable.
- Shein, founded in Nanjing in 2008, moved its global holding company to Singapore in 2022 as Roadget Business Pte Ltd.8 Its supply chain, roughly 5,800 contract manufacturers, stays overwhelmingly in Guangdong.9
- Trip.com set up its international headquarters in Singapore back in 2020.10
Here is where it gets interesting, though. The West has noticed, and the cover is getting thinner:
- In 2025 the US scrapped the de minimis rule that had let parcels under $800 enter duty-free, the exact loophole Shein and Temu were built on. It went first for China in May, then for the whole world by the end of August.11
- And in June 2026 the US Trade Representative hit Singapore itself with an extra 12.5% tariff under a Section 301 forced-labour finding, effective 24 July 2026. It touches close to a third of Singapore's domestic exports to America, and Singapore's own trade ministry has formally objected.12
So the Singapore address buys less cover than it did a year ago. But it still buys a lot, and the migration has not slowed.
This licence-versus-ban, address-versus-origin game is exactly the kind of quiet mechanism I love pulling apart, and it is the sort of thread we chase most mornings in the Decoding the Dragon WhatsApp community, where I share a smaller China deep-dive like this with thousands of readers every day (t.ly/t7uhs).
The higher-value migration: research and patents
Corporate letterheads are the easy part. The more consequential shift is that Singapore is pulling in the actual brain, the research, the patents, the high-end manufacturing.
The clearest example is WuXi Biologics, one of China's biggest contract drug developers:
- In 2022 it committed about $1.4bn over ten years to an R&D and manufacturing site in Singapore's Tuas Biomedical Park, with 1,500-plus staff and 120,000 litres of new capacity.13
- That site topped out in June 2026 and is expected to be operational in 2027.14
Why move the crown jewels out of China? Because of the BIOSECURE Act, which the US finally signed into law in December 2025 as part of its annual defence bill.15 The law creates a mechanism to bar federal agencies and their contractors from dealing with Chinese biotech firms of concern.
A nuance most coverage misses: the enacted law does not actually name WuXi.15 It orders the US budget office to publish a list of concern within a year, and WuXi is not on it yet. But the threat alone is enough. By anchoring a $1.4bn hub in Singapore, WuXi can tell its Western clients that their data and their molecules now sit on neutral, trusted ground. The same logic is quietly pulling slices of semiconductor R&D onto the island too.
And then the money itself
The third migration is private wealth, and this is the one with the cleanest numbers.
- Single family offices, the private structures the ultra-rich use to run their money, numbered about 400 in Singapore in 2020.16
- By the end of 2024 there were around 2,000, roughly a fivefold jump in four years, driven predominantly by money leaving Hong Kong and mainland China.16
- Alongside them, Singapore's Variable Capital Company, a flexible fund vehicle launched in 2020, has already crossed about 1,200 incorporations holding nearly 2,700 sub-funds.17
This did not happen by accident. Singapore offers tax schemes, the 13O and 13U exemptions, that can take the tax on a fund's global investment gains to zero.18
But watch what Singapore did next, because it is the smartest part of the whole design. From January 2025 it tightened the rules:
- Higher minimum assets, with the old grace periods stripped away.18
- A required number of Singapore-resident investment professionals, at least one of them a non-family member for the larger scheme.18
- Tiered local spending, so a fund must actually pay Singapore lawyers, accountants and staff every year to keep its exemption.18
In other words, Singapore refuses to be a dormant parking lot. It forces the incoming wealth to hire locals and spend locally. It converts capital flight into domestic jobs.
I find this kind of policy design genuinely fascinating to study, the way a single rule can turn a passive inflow into a working economy, and it is the sort of thing I unpack in more detail with the Decoding the Dragon community every morning if you want to go deeper (t.ly/t7uhs).
The twin engine: renting Malaysia's land
Singapore has one hard limit. It has no spare land and no cheap labour. So it did the obvious thing and borrowed its neighbour's.
In January 2025, Singapore and Malaysia signed the Johor-Singapore Special Economic Zone, spanning about 3,571 sq km across Johor, more than four times Singapore's size.19 The design is openly modelled on Hong Kong and Shenzhen:
- Singapore plays the Hong Kong role: capital, law, R&D, headquarters.
- Johor plays the Shenzhen role: land, power for data centres, and labour at a fraction of Singapore's cost.
- A new cross-border rail link, cutting the Johor Bahru to Singapore hop to about five minutes, is due to open by the end of 2026.20
For a Chinese firm the arbitrage is now seamless. Domicile the holding company and the intellectual property in Singapore, build the factory and the data centre six minutes away in Johor, and the finished product ships as Malaysian, sidestepping tariffs aimed at Chinese-origin goods.
Why this was always going to happen
Step back and this fits China's whole de-risking playbook. As the US-China split hardened, Chinese capital needed a way to stay global without staying visibly Chinese. Singapore offered exactly that: a trusted, sovereign, common-law platform an hour's flight from the mainland.
ASEAN is the backdrop here. Foreign investment into the bloc hit a record of about $225bn in 2024.21 Vietnam, Indonesia and the rest are taking the factories. Singapore, growing at a modest 2% or so, is not chasing them.22 It is taking the layer above the factories, the ownership and the profit, which is worth far more than the assembly line.
That is the real lesson. In a fragmented world, the money is not in making the thing. It is in owning the structure that owns the thing.
What this means for India
India should read this closely, because it sits on both sides of the trade.
On one side, India is a factory winner, a China+1 destination like Vietnam. On the other, India keeps losing the brain stem, and Singapore is the main beneficiary:
- Singapore has been India's single largest source of FDI for seven years running.23 Much of that is not Singaporean money at all, it is global and Chinese capital domiciled there and routed onward into India.
- For years India's best startups did the very same thing, flipping their holding companies to Singapore or Delaware for cleaner capital and cleaner courts.
The encouraging shift is that India has finally started to fight back:
- A wave of startups is reverse-flipping home, from PhonePe to Razorpay, which completed its move ahead of its IPO in 2025.24
- GIFT City, India's own international finance hub, is building the Singapore playbook, a fund regime and, from 2026, a family-office and family-investment-fund framework of its own.25
But let me be honest about the gap. Singapore took two decades to build the trust, the law and the talent that make firms want to domicile there. GIFT City is a promising start, not a finished product. India can win the factories with sheer scale. Winning the brain stem is a much slower, harder game, and it happens to be the more valuable one.
What to watch
Four things I am tracking:
- Whether the US budget office names any WuXi entity when it publishes its BIOSECURE list of concern, due by the end of 2026.15
- Whether more Chinese firms route fresh Johor investment through Singapore holding companies once the JS-SEZ incentives are fully live.19
- Whether the new 12.5% US tariff on Singapore pushes any China-linked firms to rethink the Singapore address.12
- Whether GIFT City can register its first serious cluster of family offices and funds, and start pulling Indian wealth back from Singapore.25
China does not export its factories to go global, it exports its brain, and Singapore has spent twenty years becoming the skull it sits in.

On 1 August, China's State Council sat down and approved 8 new nuclear reactors in one go, a build worth roughly $24bn.1 Not a plan, not a consultation, not a "study". Eight actual reactors, greenlit in a single meeting, and the story barely made a ripple outside the trade press.
That is the part that stopped me. Not the number, the ease. China now approves reactors the way most countries approve highway stretches, and it has been doing it for years.
Here is the fact I keep coming back to: nearly half of all the nuclear reactors under construction anywhere on Earth right now are Chinese.2 Not a quarter. Nearly half. One country.
And India, which needs baseload power more desperately than almost anyone, has 8.78 GW of nuclear capacity across 24 reactors.3 China has 62.5 GW across 63.4 Let that gap sit for a second, because the rest of this edition is about how it got that wide, and what we can actually do about it.
The cadence is the story
The scale is stunning, but the cadence is what tells you this is deliberate.
Look at the approvals China has handed out, year by year:
- 2019: 6 reactors
- 2020: 4 reactors
- 2021: 5 reactors
- 2022 to 2025: 10 reactors, every single year5
- 2026 so far: 8 more, cleared on 1 August1
That is not a country reacting to events. That is a country running a production line and setting the annual output in advance. Six identical reactors get slotted onto one coastal site, then the next six on the next site.
The result:
- 63 reactors operating today, about 62.5 GW.4
- 38 more under construction, another ~40 GW.4
- 118 GW of prospective capacity across announced, pre-construction and building phases, more than the next seven countries put together.2
Sometime in mid-2026, China's operating nuclear fleet quietly slipped past France's to become the world's second largest, behind only the United States.4 The 15th Five-Year Plan, approved in March, sets a target of 110 GW of operating capacity by 2030.5 On current pace China will pass the US before the decade is out and become the largest nuclear power generator on the planet.
This licence-and-repeat rhythm is exactly the kind of quiet machine I find myself pulling apart most mornings, and it is what we go back and forth on in the Decoding the Dragon WhatsApp group, where I share a smaller China deep-dive like this with thousands of readers every day (t.ly/t7uhs).
The thing the West cannot copy: cost
Now here is where it gets genuinely uncomfortable for everyone else.
The West has not forgotten how to build reactors. It has forgotten how to build them at a price anyone can afford. The two cautionary tales everyone cites are Plant Vogtle in Georgia and Flamanville in France, both years late and multiples over budget.
The numbers are brutal:
- Vogtle's two AP1000 reactors landed at roughly $8,000/kW on an overnight basis, and closer to $16,000/kW once you count financing and delay.6
- China's 8 new units were cleared for about $24bn, roughly $3bn a reactor, which works out near $2,600/kW.1
Read that again. China is building the same class of large reactor for something like a third of the American overnight cost, and a fraction of the all-in cost. This is the single most important number in the whole story, more important than any target, because cost is what decides whether nuclear scales or stalls.
How does China do it? Four interlocking things, and none of them are magic:
- Localised supply chain. For the newer designs, over 90% of components are made in China.4 No waiting on a foreign forging that arrives 18 months late.
- Serial construction. Co-locating up to six identical reactors on one site shares infrastructure and cascades labour savings, cutting cost per kW meaningfully versus a one-off build.2
- A workforce that never stops. Because the pipeline never breaks, the same welders, foremen and project managers walk from a finished reactor straight to the next foundation. Western projects lose this muscle memory between builds, and pay for it.
- New money in the mix. The Jinqimen plant in Zhejiang is now taking private capital alongside state firms, a first for a sector that was wholly state-owned.7
The West calls the opposite of this the "nuclear cost curse", where idle specialists and missing parts inflate every project. China simply never let the curse take hold, because it never stopped building.
From copycat to frontier
For years the lazy take on Chinese nuclear was that it was borrowed technology. That take is now wrong.
The workhorse is the Hualong One, a home-grown 1,100 MW reactor built by CNNC and CGN, and on 1 August the State Council cleared its upgraded Version 2.0 for the Jinqimen and Taipingling sites.7 It is the reactor China now sells to the world.
But the more interesting action is at the frontier, where China has quietly moved ahead:
- Gen IV is already commercial. The HTR-PM pebble-bed reactor at Shidaowan began commercial operation in December 2023, the world's first fourth-generation plant. It can cool itself down with no human intervention, the holy grail of "walk-away" safety.8
- Small modular reactors. The Linglong One is the first SMR anywhere to clear an IAEA safety review, aimed at heating, desalination and remote grids.4
- Thorium and salt. An experimental thorium molten-salt reactor is running in the Gobi, a design that needs almost no water and suits China's dry interior.4
- Fusion. China's EAST tokamak held a plasma for a record 1,066 seconds in January 2025, and a successor machine, BEST, is being built to push towards actual electricity.9
You do not have to believe every timeline to see the direction. China is no longer importing the future of nuclear. It is increasingly writing it.
The export machine, and its dark twin
All of this feeds a foreign-policy engine.
The Hualong One is the designated export product, precisely because it is free of Western intellectual property and therefore free of Western export controls.7 China has floated an ambition to build as many as 30 reactors in Belt and Road countries by 2030, and it already has Hualong units running in Pakistan at Karachi.2 When you can offer a country a turnkey reactor at a third of the Western price, with the financing attached, you are not selling electricity. You are selling a 60-year relationship.
Then there is the part that keeps Western security officials awake.
- China is running the CFR-600, a fast breeder reactor on Changbiao Island, with Russian help on the fuel.10
- Fast breeders produce very pure, weapons-usable plutonium as a by-product.10
- The Pentagon reckons China already holds more than 600 nuclear warheads and could reach around 1,500 by 2035.11
- And since 2017, Beijing has stopped filing its voluntary civilian plutonium declarations to the IAEA, so the world is largely guessing.10
This is the uncomfortable duality of the whole programme. The same closed fuel cycle that makes China's civilian nuclear so efficient also blurs the line between the power plant and the arsenal. It is genuinely hard to build the first without creating the option of the second, and China has chosen opacity over reassurance.
The wider machine
None of this is really about electricity, or not only.
Nuclear sits at the intersection of three things Beijing cares about most: energy security in a country that still burns a mountain of imported coal and gas, technological self-reliance in an era of export controls, and industrial policy that keeps thousands of state and private firms fed with predictable order books. The Hualong programme alone is said to touch nearly 6,000 supplier companies.4
Approving 10 reactors a year is not an energy decision. It is a way of keeping an entire high-end manufacturing base warm, the same logic China applied to high-speed rail, then solar, then EVs, then batteries. Nuclear is simply the latest sector to get the treatment.13
The West has noticed. The United States passed the ADVANCE Act in July 2024 to speed up its own reactor licensing and cut regulatory cost.12 It is a sensible law. Whether a lighter regulator alone can close a five-times cost gap against a state that has been building without pause for 20 years is a very open question.
What this means for India
Here is where I want to be honest, in both directions.
The gap is real and it is large. China has 62.5 GW of nuclear and is heading for 110 GW by 2030. India has 8.78 GW and is aiming for 100 GW by 2047.3 5 Read those two timelines together and the uncomfortable truth is that India's 2047 goal is roughly China's 2030 goal, a 17-year lag on the destination, before you even count who is more likely to hit it.
I share these India cuts, alongside the daily China ones, in the same Decoding the Dragon community, and this is exactly the sort of comparison we chew on there (t.ly/t7uhs).
But the lesson from China is not "spend more". It is "build repeatedly". The reason Chinese reactors are cheap is boring and completely copyable: standard design, same site cluster, same crew, no gaps. India has historically done the opposite, building in ones and twos with long pauses, which is precisely the recipe for the Western cost curse.
The encouraging part is that India has just started moving in the right direction:
- A roadmap to 100 GW by 2047, with indigenous small modular reactors (the Bharat Small Reactor) as a centrepiece.14
- A push to open the sector to private capital and amend the old liability and atomic-energy laws that scared investors off.14
- Around 7 to 8 GW already under construction, including the Russian-built Kudankulam units.3
The negatives India has to stare at honestly:
- India cannot simply buy China's cheap reactors. The dual-use, opacity and border realities make that a non-starter, so India has to build the cost curve itself.
- India's uranium position is weak, and China has spent a decade locking up mines from Namibia to Kazakhstan.2 That is the supply-chain lesson underneath the reactor lesson.
- Pace is a mindset. China's advantage is not a secret technology. It is the discipline of never stopping, and that is the hardest thing of all to import.
What to watch
Concrete markers over the coming months:
- The first concrete pour on the Hualong One 2.0 units at Jinqimen and Taipingling, the real test of whether Version 2.0 cuts build time as promised.7
- India's SMR tenders and the promised amendments to the Atomic Energy Act and the nuclear liability law. If private money actually flows, the 100 GW target stops being a slide.14
- The second CFR-600 unit reaching full operation, and whether the IAEA gets any new transparency in return.10
- Whether the US, under the ADVANCE Act, can bring a single follow-on AP1000 in near MIT's hoped-for $4,300/kW. That number is the West's referendum on itself.6
The one line
China's real nuclear breakthrough is not a reactor, it is a production line, and the country that learns to copy the boring discipline of building the same thing over and over will own the next century of clean baseload.

I have been staring at one number all week, and it quietly rewrites how I think about the whole tea-and-coffee business: 97.6%.
That is the share of Mixue's money that has almost nothing to do with the tea in your cup.1
Mixue is now the largest food and beverage chain on earth by store count. Nearly 60,000 outlets at the end of 2025, ahead of McDonald's at roughly 44,000 and comfortably past Starbucks.1 2 And yet the cheerful Snow King mascot is a decoy.
Mixue barely sells drinks to you and me. It sells sugar, tea leaf, cups, syrup and ice-cream machines to the tens of thousands of franchisees who then sell the drinks. In 2025, 97.6% of its revenue came from supplying its own franchisees, and just 2.4% from the franchise fees you would assume a franchise lives on.3
Now let that sit for a second. The world's biggest F&B chain is, at its core, a business-to-business wholesaler wearing a consumer brand's costume. And the same model has already landed in India, not through Mixue, but through chai brands you have probably walked past.
The numbers behind the teacup
Let me put the current figures on the table, because they are genuinely staggering.
- Revenue of about $4.7bn in 2025, up 35.2% on the year.1
- Net profit of about $830mn.1
- More than 13,000 net new stores added in 2025, roughly 37 a day, every single day.1
- Around 55,356 stores in mainland China and 4,467 abroad across 14 countries.1
Now hold that against the drinks themselves. An ice-cream cone sells for the equivalent of about $0.30, and most beverages sit between $0.55 and $1.40. This is the cheapest menu at scale anywhere in the world, and it is deliberate.
Founded in 1997 as a single shaved-ice stall in Zhengzhou, Mixue took nearly three decades to become an overnight sensation. When it finally listed in Hong Kong in March 2025, retail investors bid a record ~$206bn for the stock, oversubscribing the retail tranche more than 5,000 times.13 The market had worked out what the mascot was hiding.
Here is the tell. Of that ~$4.7bn in revenue, roughly $4.6bn came from selling goods and equipment to franchisees, and only about $110mn from franchise and related fees.3
So Mixue does not really care how much tea any single store sells. It cares that every store keeps buying supplies. The franchisee takes the rent, the staff and the location risk. Mixue takes a wholesale margin, multiplied across ~60,000 shops. That is the entire trick.
To feel how strange the scale is, look at 2024, the last year with a clean side-by-side: Mixue's roughly 45,000 stores generated only about $6.5bn in system sales, while McDonald's made around $131bn from a similar number of outlets.4 More stores than anyone, a fraction of the till. The money was never meant to be at the counter.
The machine that makes it work
None of this works without an obsessive, vertically integrated supply chain. Mixue makes its core ingredients itself rather than buying from middlemen.
- It runs its own lemon farms in Sichuan and Chongqing, signing guaranteed purchase deals with growers to crush the cost of its bestselling lemonade input.4
- It keeps the menu to roughly 30 items, so its central factories can mass-produce a handful of core ingredients at brutal efficiency.3
- It runs its own cold-chain and warehousing so it can push standardised stock to every node cheaply.1
The margins tell you where the value sits. In 2025, Mixue's margin on goods and equipment was 29.9%, slipping from 31.2% a year earlier as the price war bit, while its margin on franchise services was a fat 82.6%.3 The retail cup is thin; the wholesale pipe is thick.
And here is the quietly devastating part. While rivals were shutting stores by the hundred, Mixue's own supply margin fell barely more than a point. The lowest-cost supplier in the market hardly felt the war it was busy winning, because it sits one layer above the fight, selling inputs to the very franchisees bleeding at street level.
This is the quiet mechanism I find myself pulling apart most mornings, the difference between a brand and the supply chain hiding behind it. It is exactly the kind of thread we chase in the Decoding the Dragon WhatsApp group, where I share a smaller China deep-dive like this with thousands of readers every day (t.ly/t7uhs).
A red ocean, and why the pipe is the moat
Do not mistake Mixue's success for a rising tide. China's new-style tea market is now worth about $54bn a year across more than 400,000 shops, but growth has collapsed to 6.4% in 2025 from north of 20% for most of two decades.5
The shakeout has been savage.
- In the year to November 2024, roughly 197,000 milk-tea shops shut across China.6 Surviving beyond 18 months now counts as longevity.
- A brutal price war has dragged the whole market down towards Mixue's sub-$1.40 pricing, squeezing everyone who built a costlier model.5
Watch how differently the rivals have fared, and it is always about the supply chain, not the flavour.
- Chagee, the premium, pure-milk-tea player, raised $411mn in a Nasdaq IPO in April 2025 at $28 a share.7 Since then its stock has fallen roughly 75%, and its same-store sales dropped about 28% in the third quarter of 2025 as the shine came off.8
- Nayuki and Heytea, the two brands that invented premium bubble tea in China, have had to cut their average ticket by around $1.50 over three years just to stay in the fight, and Nayuki alone shut 89 company-owned stores in a single quarter.6 The premium pioneers are being dragged down to Mixue's price floor.
- Guming went the other way and built a heavy, self-owned cold chain. It now runs more than 10,000 stores with 2025 revenue of about $1.8bn, delivers fresh ingredients to 97% of its stores every 48 hours, and keeps logistics below 1% of system sales.9 10 That density is its shield: when the price war hit, its franchisees did not have to switch to inferior local fruit to survive.
The pattern is impossible to miss. In a market this crowded, the recipe is copyable in an afternoon. The logistics network that lands cheap, consistent inputs at 60,000 doors is not.
Exporting the pipe, not the drink
Mixue is now taking the same playbook abroad. It has 4,467 stores outside China across 14 countries, opened its first US outlet in Los Angeles in December 2025, and is building export and warehousing hubs, including a base in Hainan, to feed Southeast Asia cheaply.1 4
The insight it has internalised is that you cannot export a bubble-tea brand on air-freighted fruit and hope the maths works. You export the supply chain first, localise the inputs, and let the brand ride on top. The drink is the last thing to travel.
The wider picture: a deflation-era champion
Step back and Mixue looks less like a fluke and more like the perfect company for the China of right now.
As growth slows and prices soften, the Chinese consumer has turned relentlessly value-seeking, and demand has shifted to lower-tier cities and towns rather than the glossy Tier-1 megacities. Mixue was built for exactly that customer: no-frills, grab-and-go, absurdly cheap, planted where rents are low and footfall is high.
This is what "involution" looks like in practice, the Chinese shorthand for competition so intense it eats its own profits. Mixue does not fight involution. It is the last one standing because it made itself the lowest-cost supplier in the room, then sold shovels to everyone digging.
What this means for India
Here is the part that should interest every Indian founder and investor, because the Mixue model is already in India. It just did not arrive wearing a Chinese label.
Mixue itself is not here. Its overseas map runs through Southeast Asia, Kazakhstan and now the US, not India.4 The playbook, though, has been imported wholesale by homegrown chai chains built on the very same logic.
- Tea Time, founded in 2016, now runs somewhere between 3,000 and 4,000 outlets, serves around 100,000 customers a day across 20-plus states, and lets a franchisee in for as little as ₹5-6 lakh.11
- Chai Sutta Bar, also founded in 2016, has crossed 550 outlets in more than 320 cities and pushed into Dubai and Oman.12
Both run the Mixue trick in spirit: ultra-low entry cost, a relentless focus on Tier-2 and Tier-3 India, and tight rules forcing franchisees to buy core inputs from the parent. The money, again, is upstream.
But India cannot copy the whole thing, and this is the interesting bit. The fresh-fruit-tea model rests on a cold chain India does not have. We still lose an estimated 30-40% of fresh produce after harvest for want of refrigerated storage and transport. So Guming's daily-fresh-fruit model is structurally unviable in an Indian small town.
India's answer is smarter than it looks: skip the cold chain entirely and run on shelf-stable premixes. Masala, ginger and cardamom tea powders that need only hot water give the Indian chains consistency, near-zero wastage and simple logistics that reach deep into rural India, exactly where the growth is. That is a genuinely different supply chain solving a genuinely different constraint, and it is a big part of why these chains have scaled so fast (t.ly/t7uhs, where I keep digging into how these India-China business parallels play out).
The honest read for India cuts both ways. The upside is real: a huge, under-organised chai market, formalising fast, creating tens of thousands of small-owner jobs. The catch is baked into the model. In a supply-first franchise, the person taking the location risk is not the person capturing the margin, and if the parent ever squeezes input prices, the franchisee has nowhere to go.
What to watch
- Whether Mixue finally files to enter India. It has skipped us so far, and the day it does not is the day the domestic chains get a real test.
- Mixue's goods margin, which slipped to 29.9% in 2025. If the price war keeps compressing it, the whole flywheel slows.5
- Whether anyone builds a Guming-style cold chain in India, which would unlock the fresh-fruit category we currently cannot serve.
- Consolidation among India's chai franchises, where hundreds of look-alike brands are now chasing the same Tier-2 high street.
The next great consumer empires will not be won at the counter. They will be won in the warehouse.

The West tried to kill the dollar's rival by weaponising the dollar
Here is a fact that should make every policymaker in Washington stop and think.
When the United States and Europe froze half of Russia's central bank reserves and cut its banks out of SWIFT in 2022, the stated goal was to isolate Moscow. Four years on, roughly 99% of all trade between Russia and China is now settled in rubles and the Chinese yuan, with the dollar and euro almost entirely squeezed out.2
The sanctions worked, just not in the way anyone intended. They did sever Russia from the West. They also handed Beijing the one thing it had chased for two decades and could not buy: a captive, resource-rich, trillion-dollar economy on which to stress-test its own currency as a real alternative to the dollar.
This is the thread I keep pulling on. Not the discounted oil, not the flood of Chinese cars. The financial plumbing underneath both, and what it means for a country like India that is now quietly wired into the same system.
The trade boom has hit a ceiling
Start with the headline number, because it is not the one you would expect.
In 2025, trade between China and Russia actually fell. It dropped 6.9% to about $228bn, the first annual decline in five years, according to Chinese customs data.1
- Russian exports to China, overwhelmingly oil, gas and coal, came to roughly $125bn.1
- Chinese exports to Russia, mostly cars, machinery and electronics, fell harder, to about $103bn.1
- China is now the source of well over half of everything Russia imports. Russia is worth less than 3% of China's total trade.
So this is not a partnership of equals. It is one giant leaning on another, and the giant sets the terms. The easy, emergency-driven growth of 2022 and 2023, when Chinese firms rushed in to fill the space vacated by fleeing Western brands, is over. What is left is a structural plateau, and the reasons for it tell you exactly how much leverage Beijing holds.
The yuan takeover was an accident, and it is nearly complete
The most consequential shift here is not physical at all. It is monetary.
Go back to 2021. The yuan accounted for less than 2% of Russia's international trade settlements.2 Russian companies wanted dollars and euros, because that is what the world accepts and what stays liquid. "De-dollarisation" between the two neighbours was a political slogan, nothing more.
Then 2022 removed the choice. With dollar and euro access gone, Russia had a binary option: total financial isolation, or the yuan. The rupee was too illiquid, the dirham too small. So the transition happened at a speed the world has rarely seen:
- By early 2024, the yuan was already handling close to 40% of Russia's trade settlements.2
- In June 2024, fresh US sanctions forced the Moscow Exchange to halt dollar and euro trading altogether. The yuan promptly became the most-traded foreign currency on Russia's own bourse.3
- By 2025, the ruble had overtaken the dollar in Russia's export payments, and national currencies were settling almost the entire China trade.4
The plumbing followed the money. Russian giants like Rosneft, RUSAL and Norilsk Nickel began issuing yuan-denominated bonds to match their new yuan revenues, and by late 2025 yuan bond issuance out of Russia was accelerating rather than slowing.5 Russia's sovereign wealth fund shifted its liquid reserves into gold and yuan. Russian banks plugged into CIPS, China's home-grown alternative to SWIFT, to move money entirely outside Washington's line of sight.
This is the sort of quiet, structural rewiring I find myself picking apart most mornings, and it is exactly the kind of thread we pull further in the Decoding the Dragon WhatsApp community, where I share a smaller China deep-dive like this with thousands of readers every day (t.ly/t7uhs).
But the yuan is a lifeline with a leash
Here is where the "no-limits" partnership shows its limits, and it is the most important part of the story for anyone betting on the yuan replacing the dollar.
Settling trade in yuan is one thing. Doing anything useful with the yuan you earn is quite another.
- Trapped capital. China runs strict capital controls. Russian exporters pile up yuan they cannot easily convert, move abroad, or invest, because Beijing will not let that money leave freely. The yuan is a regional currency wearing a global costume.
- Secondary sanctions. This is the killer. Washington has aggressively threatened any bank, anywhere, that helps Russia's war machine. It even sanctioned the Shanghai arm of Russia's VTB, which had been the main artery for cross-border payments.
- The chilling effect. Once that happened, China's big state banks got cold feet. Terrified of losing their own access to the dollar system, they slowed or stopped Russian settlements. Payments started queuing for months.
As one payments analyst put it bluntly, no one in China is willing to fall under secondary sanctions and lose the global market just for Russia. That single sentence is the whole relationship. Beijing will happily provide the currency and the pipes to keep Russia afloat. It will not sacrifice its own access to the dollar world to do it.
Energy is the backbone, and China holds the whip
Underneath the finance sits the physical trade, and here too the pattern is the same: Russia needs the sale far more than China needs the purchase.
Oil is the bulk of it. As Western buyers vanished, Russia had to offer China steep discounts to move its crude, and Beijing has pocketed the difference:
- China saved nearly $12bn on discounted Russian oil across 2022 to 2025, according to a study of the trade.6
- In 2025, Russian crude shipments to China fell about 8% to 91.4mn tonnes, and the revenue Russia earned from them dropped a fifth to $45.9bn as prices softened.6
Then look at gas, where China's leverage is naked. Russia desperately wants the Power of Siberia 2 pipeline, a 50bcm-a-year link to replace the European market it lost. It is going nowhere.
- Ahead of Putin's May 2026 visit, Beijing reportedly told Moscow to stop raising the subject altogether.7
- China is offering to pay roughly its own regulated domestic rate, around $50 per thousand cubic metres. Russia wants closer to $250.7
- With domestic output, Central Asian pipelines and even resumed US LNG to fall back on, China simply does not need the gas. It is a buyer's market, and Beijing knows it.7
The clearest signal came in January 2026, when China quietly switched off its electricity imports from the Russian Far East. Russian export prices had crept above China's controlled domestic power price, so Beijing stopped buying and covered the gap from its own grid, which is about a hundred times larger.8 No drama, no announcement. Just a reminder of who sets the price.
The car story is a warning about vassalage
Nowhere was Chinese market capture more dramatic, or the Russian pushback more revealing, than in cars.
When Volkswagen, Toyota and Renault fled in 2022, Chinese brands like Chery, Geely and Great Wall stormed in. Their share of Russia's market rocketed from single digits to well over half, and Russia became China's single biggest car export destination.
Then Moscow got nervous about becoming a pure consumer colony, and it fought back with policy, not tanks:
- In late 2024 it jacked up the vehicle "recycling fee", a tax dressed as an environmental charge, by 70% to 85%. It now adds around $8,700 to a standard imported car.10
- The effect was brutal. Chinese vehicle exports to Russia fell about 38% in 2025, and Chinese brands' overall market share slipped below 50% for the first time in years.10
- More than 600 Chinese-brand dealerships shut across Russia in 2025 as the retail bubble deflated.9
Exports did bounce back sharply in early 2026, nearly doubling year on year, but that is largely a trick of a collapsed 2025 base, not a genuine recovery.10 The deeper message stands: Moscow used the recycling fee to force China to build factories on Russian soil rather than just ship finished cars in. Chinese firms, wary of secondary sanctions and a volatile ruble, have mostly refused. Even inside the "no-limits" partnership, both sides guard their own interests hard.
What this means for India: the yuan trap we walked into
Now to the part that matters most for us, because India ran a strangely parallel experiment and ended up in Beijing's currency by a completely different road.
Like China, India feasted on cheap Russian oil after 2022. From under 2% of our crude imports before the war, Russia surged to become India's top supplier, at times a third of everything we buy.16 The savings ran to roughly $17bn over three years.
But India could not pay the way China does. China exports over $100bn of goods to Russia a year, so rubles and yuan recirculate. India sells Russia almost nothing. We buy well over $60bn of Russian energy a year and export barely $5bn back.15 The rupee-ruble scheme collapsed because Russian sellers ended up with piles of rupees stuck in Mumbai that they could not spend or repatriate.
So when Russian traders demanded a convertible currency, Indian state refiners did something remarkable. They started paying for Russian oil in Chinese yuan.11
Sit with that irony for a second. In trying to financially isolate Russia, Washington pushed its closest Indo-Pacific partner into settling trade in the currency of India's single biggest strategic rival. New Delhi is deeply uncomfortable with it and has moved to discourage yuan settlement,17 but commercial necessity keeps dragging it back. This is the kind of second-order consequence I think we underrate, and it is exactly what we chew over daily in the Decoding the Dragon community (t.ly/t7uhs).
The tariff storm, and the quiet recovery
The India-Russia oil story got far messier before it settled, and the resolution is very recent.
- In August 2025, the US hit India with tariffs that eventually reached 50%, explicitly punishing it for buying Russian crude.
- Then in October 2025, Washington sanctioned Rosneft and Lukoil, which together supplied most of India's Russian barrels. Imports briefly plunged.
- On 2 February 2026, a US-India trade deal cut the tariff from 50% to 18%, with India nominally agreeing to wind down Russian oil purchases and buy US energy instead.12
And yet. By June 2026, India's Russian crude imports had climbed back to a record, running near 2mn barrels a day, still around a third of the total.13 Despite the expired waiver and the paper commitments, the discounted barrels never really left.14 India, unlike Russia, has options and uses them, playing Washington, Moscow and the discount off against each other. That is the luxury of leverage Russia lost the day the sanctions hit.
The wider picture
Step back and this is really one story about currency power in a fracturing world.
Beijing has spent 20 years trying to internationalise the yuan through offshore hubs, swap lines and CIPS, with modest results. Western sanctions on Russia did more for that project in four years than Beijing managed in twenty. The yuan is now the default settlement currency for anyone operating on the wrong side of Washington, and increasingly for those merely trying to dodge the friction, like Indian refiners.
But the same episode also exposes the yuan's hard ceiling. Capital controls, non-convertibility and China's own fear of secondary sanctions mean the yuan can be a workaround, not yet a true reserve currency. It is the dollar's most functional alternative and, at the same time, nowhere close to the dollar's replacement. Both things are true.
What to watch
- Power of Siberia 2. Watch whether any real pricing agreement emerges after the next Putin-Xi meeting, or whether Beijing keeps it frozen. The gap between $50 and $250 is the whole game.
- Secondary sanctions on Chinese banks. Any fresh US action against a major Chinese lender for Russia dealings would test how far the "no-limits" pact really goes.
- India's yuan stance. Watch whether New Delhi formally restricts yuan settlement for oil, or quietly lets it continue. Its choice signals how it reads the China relationship.
- The US-India deal's fine print. Watch the actual Russian import volumes, not the press release. So far the barrels are winning.
Sanctions built to cage one economy ended up training the cage's lock to open for everyone else.

The most improbable comeback in retail
I have been watching China’s coffee market for years, and I still find this hard to believe. Starbucks spent 26 years turning China into its second home. This year it effectively gave up and sold control of the whole thing.1
The company that pushed it out does not sell an experience. It sells a cup of coffee for about $1.403, ordered on an app, handed to you from a kiosk smaller than your living room.
And here is the bit that should make every Indian founder sit up. That exact model, app-only, deep discount, tiny store, is now being cloned on the ground in Mumbai and Bengaluru.
So this is not really a story about coffee. It is a story about what happens when a “premium Western experience” runs into an algorithm that has stripped every last cent of fat out of the same product. The algorithm won, and it won comfortably.
The numbers are genuinely startling
Let me set the scene, because the scale is hard to overstate.
- Luckin Coffee, the chain that was caught fabricating over $300mn of sales in 20202 and thrown off Nasdaq, is not dead. It is the biggest coffee chain in China by a distance.
- In the first quarter of 2026 it crossed 33,596 stores and grew revenue about 35% to roughly $1.8bn, in a single quarter.4
- For the full year 2025 it did about $7bn in revenue, up 43%.5 Starbucks China, for comparison, did about $3.1bn.6
- So Luckin now sells more than twice as much coffee as Starbucks does in China. From a company left for dead six years ago.
Now let that sink in for a second. A business that committed one of the largest accounting frauds in modern markets did not just survive. It became the market.
The resurrection nobody priced in
When the fraud broke, the consensus was simple: the discounting was a con, demand was fake, and the whole thing would collapse. The consensus was wrong, and understanding why is the whole point.
The fraud was in the accounting, not in the store. Management had faked the scale of profitability. But the underlying small-format, delivery-led shop was quietly starting to work.
So instead of liquidating, an early backer, the private-equity firm Centurium Capital, recapitalised it, ring-fenced the retail operations from the corporate mess, forced out the founders, and made the company restate and clean up its books.2 Freed of the debt crisis, Luckin did the boring thing: it shut loss-making stores, stopped burning cash on vanity marketing, and obsessed over the economics of a single cup.
This licence-to-operate-cleanly turnaround is exactly the sort of thing I end up picking apart most mornings, and it is the kind of thread we pull further in the Decoding the Dragon WhatsApp community, where I share a smaller China deep-dive like this with thousands of readers every day (t.ly/t7uhs).
The $1.40 cup, taken apart
Here is the interesting bit. Western analysts assumed a coffee sold at about $1.403 had to be a loss leader. At scale, the maths actually holds.
- The promotional cup sells for about $1.40. Strip it down and the raw cost sits close to that: a few cents of beans, more on the milk and the cup than on the coffee itself, a sliver of rent, a sliver of labour.
- On that discounted cup the margin is razor-thin, sometimes negative. That is not where the money is.
- The trick is the blend. The average Luckin order is closer to $2.10, because the coconut lattes, cheese-topped drinks and fruit coffees carry fat margins.
Two structural choices make this possible, and both are the opposite of the Starbucks playbook.
- The store is tiny. A Luckin pick-up point is often 20 to 50 square metres with no seating, no cashier, and almost no front-of-house. Nearly every order goes through the app. That lets Luckin drop a high-volume node into an office lobby where a 200-square-metre café could never fit or pay rent.
- The product is re-engineered for local taste. Luckin bet, correctly, that the average Chinese consumer never wanted a bitter Americano. It built “beverage coffee”: sweet, milky, closer to bubble tea than espresso. That widened the market far beyond what Starbucks’ rigid global menu could reach.
This is the real moat. Not the brand, but a data-driven machine that treats coffee like e-commerce: app-only ordering, real-time inventory, and constant testing of new flavours priced to move.
Then the founders came back for revenge
If the model has one weakness, it is that the barriers to copying it are low. And the people who copied it best were the ones Luckin threw out.
- Cotti Coffee was founded in late 2022 by Lu Zhengyao and Qian Zhiya, the very founders ousted from Luckin in the fraud scandal.7
- Armed with the exact blueprint, they went scorched-earth: a fee-waiving franchise model, cups at $1.40, then $1.20, then one-off promotions dropping to a few cents, and a sprint that has now taken Cotti past 15,000 stores.7
For two years this forced a brutal price war, and by 2026 the strain is showing on both sides.
- Cotti itself is now pulling back, “lowering the heat”, because franchisees simply cannot make money selling milk drinks below cost.8
- Even the winner is bleeding margin. In Q1 2026 Luckin’s same-store sales actually turned negative, a fall from strong growth a year earlier, its operating margin slipped, and it announced its first-ever share buyback of $300mn to steady the stock.4
That is the honest footnote to this whole story. The app-and-discount model is structurally superior to the café, but it is so easy to copy that it collapses into a margin war the moment a rival with the same playbook shows up.
Starbucks stopped fighting
Caught in that crossfire, and wedded to a large-format “third place” it could not cheaply shrink, Starbucks China simply ran out of room.
- It cut prices and leaned into afternoon tea-based drinks to chase the value consumer.6
- It did not work fast enough. So in a historic retreat, Starbucks agreed to sell up to 60% of its China business to the local private-equity firm Boyu Capital.1
- The deal hands Starbucks about $4bn in cash and values the China retail business at more than $13bn including a decade of licensing. Starbucks keeps 40% and the brand.1
Read that as what it is: the company that invented premium coffee in China has effectively admitted it cannot run premium coffee in China alone any more. It has handed the keys to a local operator who understands the price-first market it never wanted to fight.
The wider picture: Guochao and the death of the “third place”
Step back and this is not a coffee anomaly. It is the coffee chapter of a much bigger Chinese story.
For two decades, foreign brands sold status. A Starbucks cup signalled you had arrived. That era is over. Under a slower economy and a wave of national confidence often called “Guochao”, or national wave, young Chinese consumers no longer treat Western brands as automatically superior. They want value and local relevance, and they are happy to get it from a domestic name.
Luckin is Guochao in a cup. It did not out-premium Starbucks. It refused to play the premium game at all, priced the product for daily habit instead of occasional treat, and let the physical “experience” go. In a price-sensitive, mobile-first market, that was the correct read of where the puck was going.
What this means for India
Now to the part I care about most, because India is about to run the same experiment.
The setup is almost identical to early China. Indians drink barely 30 cups of coffee a year against a global average nearer 200.9 The habit is tiny, urban, and wide open.
And the first wave here made the same bet Starbucks did.
- Premium, experiential chains raised big money to build large cafés. Blue Tokai took roughly ₹290 crore led by Verlinvest, plus a further ₹210 crore bridge round.10
- Tata Starbucks, the closest analogue, is feeling the exact squeeze its parent felt in China: FY25 losses widened to about ₹136 crore even as revenue rose only 5% to roughly ₹1.3k crore.11
Here is the tell that the pivot has already begun.
- Third Wave Coffee, one of the best-funded premium players, spent a brutal year killing loss-making cafés. It got more than 95% of its outlets to unit-level profit and narrowed FY25 losses to about ₹94 crore on ₹285 crore of revenue.12
- Crucially, it is now piloting small-format “Third Wave Zip” kiosks.12 The premium poster child is quietly copying the Luckin store.
And then there is the pure clone. abCoffee is building the Indian Luckin almost line for line.
- App-first kiosks of 120 to 250 square feet, more than 90 of them across Mumbai, Delhi-NCR and Bengaluru.13
- A cappuccino at about ₹97, against nearly ₹300 at Starbucks.13
- It just raised ₹61 crore led by Kliff Ventures, with revenue doubling and store-level EBITDA up 193% in a year, plus a subscription base that drives half its app orders.13
This is the thread I keep coming back to in the Decoding the Dragon community, because the India replay is happening in real time and the Chinese script tells you what comes next (t.ly/t7uhs).
The lesson India’s coffee founders should take is double-edged. The kiosk model works, and it works fast. But the Chinese ending is a warning too: once one player proves the model, the barriers are so low that a Cotti-style rival can turn the whole category into a margin war overnight.
What to watch
- Whether Luckin’s same-store sales climb back into positive territory, or the price war keeps grinding its margins through 2026.
- Whether Cotti’s pullback holds, or a fresh discount sprint reignites the war.
- Whether abCoffee’s ₹61 crore buys the dense store network it needs before a deeper-pocketed rival, possibly even a Chinese one, enters India.
- Whether Tata Starbucks and Blue Tokai formally shrink their formats, the way Third Wave just has.
The winning cup of this decade is not the one you sit down with. It is the one an app hands you on the way out, priced so low the premium café cannot follow.

Here is a number that stopped me cold.
In the first three months of 2026, Yatsen, the company behind Perfect Diary and the original poster child of China's homegrown beauty boom, spent 72% of its revenue on sales and marketing.1
Let that sink in for a second. For every $100 the company took in, roughly $72 went straight back out to rent the next customer's attention. Its gross margin, meanwhile, is a gorgeous 80%.1 Almost all of that lovely margin is incinerated before it ever reaches the bottom line.
This is not some struggling minnow. This is the brand that taught China how to sell makeup on the internet. And to me it is the cleanest proof yet of a simple idea: you cannot blitzscale a lipstick.
First, the rise was real
Let me set the scene, because the collapse only lands if you feel how big the win was.
C-beauty is shorthand for the wave of domestic Chinese cosmetics brands that, over the past decade, tore the shelf away from the century-old Western houses that used to own it. The fuel was "Guochao", the national-pride trend where young Chinese consumers started treating "made in China" as a badge rather than a compromise.
And it worked, spectacularly:
- Domestic brands took 57.4% of China's cosmetics market in 2025, their fourth straight year ahead of foreign rivals, in a market worth roughly $159bn.2
- Online is where they win outright: domestic products made up 65.4% of all online beauty sales in China last year.2
- In the 2025 Double 11 festival, Proya topped Tmall skincare with more than ~$560mn in sales, beating L'Oréal, Lancôme and Estée Lauder outright, while Kans led Douyin with over ~$1.1bn.23
- And the retreat on the other side is just as telling: around 27 foreign brands cut back or quit China across 2024 and 2025.2
So the headline story, the one you have probably read, is a triumph. Plucky local brands, armed with cultural storytelling and Douyin wizardry, humbling the global giants.
The problem is that the headline story is only the top line. The engine underneath it is where the trouble lives.
The blitzscaling illusion
Blitzscaling is a Silicon Valley idea: chase market share and revenue at breakneck speed, burn venture money, and worry about profit later. It works for software because the extra cost of one more user is close to zero and network effects lock people in.
Yatsen took that playbook and pointed it at physical makeup.
The weapon was "private domain traffic", a very Chinese idea worth explaining. Instead of renting attention from ad platforms every single time, Perfect Diary built its own closed garden inside WeChat: brand groups, tutorials, discounts, and a friendly virtual assistant persona called "Xiao Wan Zi" who felt like a real beauty adviser. At its peak the company was managing direct relationships with an estimated 8 to 10mn members this way.
For a while, it looked like magic. Revenue peaked near ~$900mn in 2021.1 Then physics arrived.
- Makeup is a physical good. It has real cost of goods, inventory, shipping and, crucially, zero switching cost. The moment a shinier brand appears on your feed, you are gone.
- As rivals piled onto Douyin, the price of traffic kept climbing, and the private-domain moat turned out to be a puddle.
- Revenue roughly halved to about ~$480mn by 2023, and the company has posted net losses year after year.1
This licence-to-print-revenue-until-it-suddenly-stops pattern is exactly the kind of mechanism I find myself pulling apart most mornings, and it is what we go back and forth on in the Decoding the Dragon WhatsApp group, where I share a smaller China deep-dive like this with thousands of readers every day (t.ly/t7uhs).
Now look at the most recent quarter, and you see the trap fully sprung:
- Q1 2026 revenue was $148mn, up a healthy 22.5% year on year.1
- But sales and marketing ate $107mn of it, or 72.2% of revenue, up sharply from 66.4% a year earlier.1
- Result: a net loss of ~$9mn, wider than the year before, on an 80% gross margin.1
- Management blamed, in its own words, "higher traffic acquisition costs on the Douyin platform".4
Read that again. The company has to keep buying its own revenue from the algorithm. It manufactured scale. It never manufactured loyalty.
Yatsen knows it. Its escape plan is to pivot into skincare, which enjoys higher loyalty and fatter margins than trend-driven colour cosmetics. It bought heritage names like France's Galénic and Britain's Eve Lom to skip the decades of R&D.
- Skincare is now 56.2% of revenue, up from 43.5% a year earlier, growing 58.5%.1
- Legacy colour cosmetics shrank 5%.1
The mix is improving. But better-quality revenue still has to be dragged to market by the same brutally expensive traffic. The disease is the cost of acquisition, and a nicer product does not cure it.
The scramble for a moat
If Yatsen is the cautionary tale, Proya is the brand that got furthest, and its recent stumble is the more unsettling signal.
Proya did almost everything right. It built a disciplined "hero product" strategy around a few high-margin serums, layered on sub-brands, and in 2024 became the first domestic beauty group to cross ~$1.5bn in annual revenue, dethroning L'Oréal on Tmall.5 For years it looked like the one C-beauty champion with real staying power.
Then 2025 happened:
- Proya posted its first-ever simultaneous fall in both revenue and net profit, with revenue down 1.7% to about ~$1.47bn and net profit off 3.5%.56
- This happened while the wider Chinese cosmetics market was still growing, so Proya was losing ground, not just riding a slow tide.6
- The flagship Proya brand itself fell 10.4%, and Q1 2026 stayed weak.67
The tell is what it did next. In May 2026 Proya took a 51% controlling stake in the quirky colour-cosmetics label Flower Knows for about ~$115mn, buying differentiation and an overseas footprint rather than building them.8 It is, in a gentler form, the same move Yatsen made.
And underneath sits the real gap. Proya's skincare leans on common, unpatented actives like peptides and niacinamide, while L'Oréal and Estée Lauder defend their premiums with proprietary molecules and decades of clinical science. Proya's R&D spend is under 2% of revenue, roughly ~$29mn.6 That is a marketing company with a lab attached, not the other way round. Without patents it cannot charge true luxury prices, and with its marketing bill it is too costly to fight at the bottom. That is the middle-market squeeze, and it is closing.
Florasis shows the third dead end: premium purely through beauty. Its scroll-and-jade packaging is stunning, and it commands the highest prices in C-beauty. But in September 2023, top host Li Jiaqi snapped at a viewer who called a 79-yuan (~$11) eyebrow pencil expensive, telling her to work harder. The clip drew over 1bn views and became a lightning rod for a country worried about stagnant wages.4 Aesthetic pride, it turns out, is thin armour when the economy wobbles.
The regulator just removed the cheat codes
Here is the part that makes all of this urgent rather than merely interesting. The Chinese state is dismantling the very conditions that let C-beauty grow this way.
Two moves matter.
First, the protective wall is coming down. For years, mandatory animal testing kept many Western clean-beauty and indie brands out of China, handing the space to locals. The 2021 CSAR rules cracked that open, and in late 2025 the NMPA's sweeping "24 measures" went much further: broader animal-testing waivers, a push for the "silver economy", and a "first-launch" pathway that lets foreign brands debut in China without selling abroad first.910 The floodgates for sophisticated foreign competition are opening on home turf.
Second, the cheap-traffic era is being legislated out of existence. From 1 February 2026, China's Order No. 117 brought livestream selling under the full weight of the Advertising Law.1112
- Livestream endorsements by influencers now count as formal advertising, with strict liability for dodgy claims.11
- Even clips, highlights and reposts carry the same legal weight as a TV commercial.11
- AI-generated hosts must be labelled continuously, and platforms must archive every stream for three years.11
- Regulators have also moved to curb heavy beauty filters, so hosts can no longer fake flawless skin to sell it.13
For a business model built entirely on fast, loose, cheap algorithmic selling, this is compliance overhead layered onto an already unaffordable customer-acquisition cost. The arbitrage is being taxed out.
The bigger picture: from traffic to trust
Step back and this is really a story about the maturing of an entire market. China's beauty sector is graduating from a wild, subsidy-and-hype phase into an institutionalised one, where the winners will look a lot more like the incumbents they set out to disrupt.
The lesson generalises far beyond makeup. Software blitzscaling assumes near-zero marginal cost and lock-in. Consumer packaged goods have neither. Every jar has a real cost, and every customer can leave for free. Pour venture money into that and you do not build a moat, you build a very expensive habit of renting revenue. The brands that survive are the ones that make the painful, unglamorous switch from traffic to trust: real distribution, real products, real repeat buyers who come back without being paid to.
What this means for India
And this is where it stops being a China story, because India is running the identical experiment in real time.
Look at the two outcomes side by side.
Honasa, the parent of Mamaearth, was India's Perfect Diary: digital-first, influencer-led, dozens of SKUs, huge ad bills. It hit a wall in FY25 when growth stalled. But it pivoted hard, and FY26 shows what surviving looks like:
- Revenue of ₹2,476 crore, up 15.4%, with profit after tax nearly tripling to ₹200 crore and a maiden dividend declared.14
- Advertising eased to about a third of revenue, ~₹180 crore in a single quarter, down from the ~₹661 crore-a-year intensity of FY24.1516
- The fix was omnichannel: pushing into 188,000-plus physical outlets and building a house of brands like The Derma Co and Aqualogica on the same backend.14
SUGAR Cosmetics is the other ending. It scaled fast, stayed almost purely digital, and never fixed its unit economics:
- FY25 revenue actually fell 17.8% to ₹415 crore, with EBITDA at minus ₹108 crore, a margin of around minus 26%.17
- After 13 years, it is still deeply loss-making, and in May 2026 it was seeking ₹100 to ₹150 crore of rescue funding at a steep down-round.18
Same playbook, two endings, and the difference is exactly the China lesson: whoever converts traffic into durable, physical, profitable demand lives, and whoever keeps buying revenue from an ad platform eventually runs out of road. That divide between the Honasas and the SUGARs is one I keep tracking, and it is the sort of thing the Decoding the Dragon community digs into daily (t.ly/t7uhs).
For Indian founders and the VCs funding them, the read is blunt: gross margin is not a moat, a patent or a shelf is. For Indian policymakers, China's regulatory turn is a preview of the compliance world our own creator-commerce boom is heading towards.
What to watch
- Whether Yatsen's marketing-to-revenue ratio falls back below ~65% in its next couple of quarters, or stays stuck above 70%.
- Proya's H1 2026 numbers, and whether the Flower Knows deal arrests the flagship brand's slide.
- How quickly foreign clean-beauty brands file through China's new "first-launch" pathway now the animal-testing wall is down.
- Whether SUGAR's rescue round actually closes, and at what valuation.
The future of beauty will not be won by whoever games the Douyin algorithm best. It will be won by whoever can survive the unforgiving arithmetic of the physical world.
