I want to start with a number that quietly redrew a map. In the year 2000, China bought less than 2% of everything Latin America sold to the world.1 Last year, China and Latin America traded a record $549bn.1
Now sit with that for a second. In a single generation, China went from a rounding error in the Americas to South America's largest trading partner. And it did not stop at buying soybeans and copper. It started building the ports the soybeans leave from, the grids the mines run on, and the railways that will carry it all to the Pacific.
This is the part that fascinates me. Latin America is meant to be America's backyard. The United States has treated it as its own sphere since 1823. Yet the biggest builder in that backyard today is Beijing. And in 2026 the pushback has finally turned kinetic. So let us decode what China actually built, why Washington is suddenly panicking, and where a very late India fits in.
From buyer to builder
For twenty years the China-Latin America story was boring and one-way. South America dug things up, soybeans, iron ore, crude, lithium, and shipped them east. China sent back phones, machines and cars. Pure commodities-for-manufactures.
What changed is that China stopped being a customer and became the landlord. It is now the financier, builder and operator of the continent's core infrastructure.
- More than 20 Latin American and Caribbean countries have signed on to China's Belt and Road Initiative.
- Colombia, long the most pro-Washington economy in the region, formally joined in May 2025 as the 22nd, signing up from the Great Wall itself.2
- Chinese firms now run the container terminals, the transmission lines and the salt flats, not just the export contracts.
The flagship of this shift sits about 60km north of Lima. And in the last few months it has become the single clearest test of who really controls the Americas.
Chancay: the port that broke Peru's courts
The Port of Chancay opened in late 2024 and it is a genuine marvel. It is a deep-water mega-port built to send South American cargo straight across the Pacific, skipping the ports of the United States, Mexico, and the drought-hit Panama Canal entirely.
- It is run by a joint venture that is 60% owned by China's state shipping giant COSCO, with Peru's Volcan holding 40%.3
- The first phase cost about $3.5bn and handles up to 1mn containers a year.3
- It cuts shipping time to Asia by up to 20 days.3
Here is where it got strange. COSCO argued that because Chancay was built with private money and had no state concession, Peru's transport regulator Ositran had no business overseeing it. In January 2026 a Lima court agreed, and ordered the regulator to stop supervising the port entirely.4 For a few months, a foreign state-owned company effectively ran a sovereign enclave on Peruvian soil.
And then, this month, it flipped. In early July 2026, Lima's Second Constitutional Chamber threw the exemption out.5 The court's logic was elegant: what triggers state oversight is public use, not who owns the asset. Chancay serves the public, so Peru's regulator gets to regulate it, private money or not.5
This reversal matters more than it looks. It is the first real crack in the model. And it is the closest thing Washington has to a win.
The US had gone in hard. The State Department warned bluntly that "cheap Chinese money costs sovereignty".6 Its ambassador to Peru made headlines saying that with the Chinese "looting your sea", Peruvians would have to make "hamburger ceviche".6 Beijing hit back that the US was spreading disinformation about a commercial port.6 This kind of quiet institutional tug-of-war, a court ruling that decides who controls a continent's trade gate, is exactly the sort of thread I end up pulling apart most mornings in the Decoding the Dragon WhatsApp group, where I share a smaller China deep-dive like this with thousands of readers every day (t.ly/t7uhs).
The railway that wants to erase the Panama Canal
Chancay only pays off fully if China can feed it from deep inside the continent. So the next move is a railway of almost absurd ambition.
In July 2025, Brazil and China signed a memorandum to study a transcontinental line, the Bi-Oceanic Railway.7 The plan is to run track roughly 4,500km from the port of Ilhéus on Brazil's Atlantic coast, across the Amazon and over the Andes, straight to Chancay on the Pacific.7
- The estimated cost is upward of $70bn.7
- Backers say it would cut Asia-South America shipping times by another 10 to 12 days versus the Panama Canal.7
- Moving goods across the interior by truck today is at least ten times costlier than bulk shipping, so the economic logic is real.7
It is still only a five-year feasibility study, and the engineering, the Amazon rainforest, the indigenous territories, and the sheer money make it a long shot.7 But the intent is the point. China is trying to build a closed loop that carries South America's commodities to Asia without ever touching a US-controlled chokepoint.
Soybeans, seeds and the quiet food play
While the ports and railways grab headlines, the deeper play is food. Brazil now supplies roughly a third of all of China's agricultural imports, and Beijing has moved to own the whole chain, not just buy the crop.
- China's COFCO is finishing a giant new terminal at the Port of Santos, its STS-11, designed to move 14.5mn tonnes of grain and sugar a year at full tilt in 2026, its largest export facility anywhere in the world.8
- Through past deals in seeds and trading houses, Chinese state-linked firms sit across Brazilian corn and soy genetics, not just the commodity flow.
For the United States, this is a slow-motion decoupling from its own farmers. Every extra tonne of Brazilian soy locked into a Chinese-owned terminal is a tonne American growers do not sell. China is deliberately turning the US farmer from an indispensable supplier into a backup one.
Electrifying the continent
Then there is power, and this is where the lock-in is deepest, because grids last for generations.
China's State Grid has become the dominant force in Brazil's electricity system. Its signature technology is ultra-high-voltage direct current, the only practical way to move huge volumes of power across Brazil's vast distances, from the hydro and wind of the north to the cities of the south.
- Its Belo Monte lines already run at 800 kilovolts across more than 2,500km, an "electricity expressway" serving over 20mn Brazilians.
- In mid-2025 it broke ground on its biggest yet, the Graça Aranha to Silvânia link: about 1,468km of UHVDC line, due to power more than 12mn people from 2029.9
- The investment is around R$23bn, roughly $4.3bn, the largest transmission project in Brazil's history.9
Here is the clever bit. The financing runs through the BRICS-backed New Development Bank, in a mix that lets China fund Western Hemisphere infrastructure while sidestepping the US dollar.9 Standardise a country's grid on your engineering, your hardware, your maintenance, and you tie its largest economy to you for decades.
The lithium triangle, where China finally hit friction
If food and power are about securing supply, lithium is about owning the future. China controls roughly 70% of the world's lithium refining and over three-quarters of global battery-cell output, so it needs the raw metal, and most of the world's best brine sits in the "lithium triangle" of Argentina, Bolivia and Chile.10
For years China simply hoovered it up. But 2026 is the year resource nationalism bit back.
- Argentina stays wide open, and China is winning there. Zijin Mining fired up its Tres Quebradas brine project in September 2025 at 20,000 tonnes of lithium carbonate a year, after sinking about $600mn into it.11
- Chile went the other way. The state is taking majority control of its lithium through Codelco, and China's Tianqi, which paid $4.1bn for its SQM stake, lost its final appeal against the takeover at Chile's Supreme Court in January 2026.12
- Bolivia, holder of the world's largest reserves, has stalled. A local court suspended its $1bn deal with a CATL-led Chinese consortium, freezing the plants that were meant to finally industrialise the Salar de Uyuni.13
So the picture is not a clean Chinese sweep. It is dominance in the free-market state, a bloody nose in the nationalist one, and paralysis in the biggest prize of all. That gap is precisely where a latecomer might squeeze in.
Where India actually stands
This is the thread I care about most, because India is exposed twice over. We import almost all our copper concentrate, and even when we secure raw minerals, we mostly have to send them to China to be refined.14 That is a double dependency on the one country we least want to depend on.
India's answer is a small, state-backed vehicle called KABIL, and in April 2026 it hit a genuine milestone.
- KABIL won environmental clearance from Argentina to start deep exploration at its Cortaderas blocks in Catamarca, right inside the lithium triangle.14
- The plan is 11 boreholes across about 15,700 hectares, to prove up the brine.14
- The committed spend so far is around ₹200 crore, about $24mn.14
Now hold that $24mn next to the numbers we just walked through. Zijin alone put $600mn into one Argentine project. China's Bolivia deal was $1bn. State Grid is spending $4.3bn on a single power line. India is showing up to a game where the table stakes are 20 to 200 times what it has put on the table.
That is not a reason to sneer at KABIL, it is the opposite. India is a decade late and orders of magnitude smaller, and it is still right to be in the room, because the alternative is total dependence. India's edge is not capital, it is timing and diplomacy: negotiating trade pacts with an explicit minerals mandate, and offering Bolivia and Argentina a partner that is not Beijing at exactly the moment they are wary of Beijing. This is the kind of India-versus-China gap I keep coming back to, and it is what the Decoding the Dragon community digs into most days if you want to follow the thread (t.ly/t7uhs).
Washington's answer: coercion, not capital
The US has finally noticed, and its response has a name. In November 2025 the White House published a National Security Strategy built around a "Trump corollary" to the Monroe Doctrine.15 The core line is stark: the US "will deny non-Hemispheric competitors the ability to... own or control strategically vital assets" in the hemisphere.15
And unlike past doctrines, this one has teeth.
- In January 2026 US forces launched Operation Absolute Resolve, capturing Venezuela's Nicolás Maduro and flying him to New York for trial.16
- Washington leaned on Argentina's Javier Milei to suspend a Chinese radio telescope in San Juan, reportedly tying $20bn of economic support to cutting strategic ties with Beijing.17
- It backed a BlackRock consortium's $22.8bn move to buy the Panama Canal-adjacent ports of Hong Kong's CK Hutchison, though that deal is now a mess, with China's COSCO demanding a controlling stake and Panama voiding the underlying concessions.18
Here is the structural flaw, and it is a big one. The US strategy is almost entirely stick and no carrot. It sanctions, it deploys warships, it warns about "debt traps". But it offers no capital at China's scale to replace what China is building. And when a Latin American leader is told to reject Chinese money, the obvious reply is: fine, what are you offering instead?
What this all adds up to
Step back and the shape is clear. China is not in Latin America for quick profit. It is buying long-life assets, ports, grids, railways, refineries and mines, that quietly reorient an entire continent toward Asia and away from the US.
The Chancay reversal shows the model is not unbreakable. Courts can push back, resource nationalism can bite, and the US can win the odd round. But winning rounds is not the same as offering an alternative. As long as Washington's plan is denial and Beijing's plan is construction, construction tends to win.
For India, the lesson is uncomfortable and useful. The countries that will define the battery century are being locked up now, at a scale we cannot match. Our only realistic path is to be the credible third option, fast, diplomatic and honest, in exactly the places where China has overreached and the US has nothing to build with.
What to watch
- Whether Peru's government and courts hold the line on Chancay oversight, or COSCO wins it back on further appeal.
- Whether the Brazil-Peru railway feasibility study produces a fundable route, or quietly dies in the Amazon.
- Whether Bolivia's suspended lithium deals are revived, re-tendered, or reopened to non-Chinese partners like India.
- Whether KABIL's Cortaderas boreholes actually hit commercial-grade brine, turning India's $24mn from a gesture into a foothold.
China spent twenty years learning that in the Americas, whoever pours the concrete writes the rules, and the US is only now realising it forgot how to pour.

Here is a number that stopped me cold this week.
In the stretch of high seas just west of India, out past the exclusive economic zones of Oman, Pakistan and India, there is a squid fishery. And 97.3% of the industrial fishing effort in it is Chinese.1
Not a plurality. Not "the largest single share". Almost all of it. By 2025, over 184 Chinese light seiners were working that patch of ocean, and the number comes from the Indian Ocean Tuna Commission's own May 2026 briefing, not from an activist pamphlet.1
The thing that unnerves me is not that China fishes far from home. Everyone knew that. It is where this one is, and how it is being done. This is not the South China Sea. This is the Arabian Sea, a few days' sail from Kochi and Karachi, and the fleet sitting there is doing something far more deliberate than chasing squid.
A fishery that legally does not exist
The reason China is there is almost elegant in its cynicism.
The Indian Ocean's high seas are policed by two bodies. The Indian Ocean Tuna Commission (IOTC) covers tuna and billfish. The Southern Indian Ocean Fisheries Agreement (SIOFA) covers everything else, but only in the southern Indian Ocean.
- The target species here is the purpleback flying squid.1 Squid is not tuna, so IOTC has no say over it.
- The fishing ground is in the northwest, so SIOFA's map does not reach it.
- Result: a large industrial fishery in a governance hole. No quotas. No conservation limits. No inspections. No one with the legal right to say stop.1
China did not stumble into this gap. It found the one square of the ocean that no rulebook covers and moved a fleet into it. And the "squid" framing is doing a lot of work, because IOTC's own briefing notes these light seiners routinely haul up tuna and other species too.1 A squid licence, in practice, becomes a licence to strip the whole column of water, right next to waters India considers its own strategic backyard.
This is a machine, not a fishing trip
To understand why one fishery matters, you have to see the size of the thing it belongs to.
China runs the largest distant-water fishing fleet the world has ever seen. An Oceana analysis released in 2025 found that between 2022 and 2024, Chinese-flagged vessels accounted for 44% of all visible fishing effort on Earth, roughly 57,000 industrial vessels logging over 110mn hours at sea, appearing in the waters of more than 90 countries.2 And that is only the ships transmitting their location. Once you add militia-linked and foreign-flagged boats, estimates of the true fleet run from 2,000 to as many as 16,000 vessels.2
Now, no honest fishing business operates at this scale in depleted and contested waters. It loses money. Which brings us to the engine.
The fleet runs on subsidies, not fish. Oceana's work on Chinese fisheries subsidies lands on a single damning ratio:
- China's distant-water fleet brings in about 22% of the national catch but soaks up roughly 42% of total fisheries subsidies.3
- The harmful subsidies flowing to the distant-water industry alone are estimated at around $1.75bn a year, the kind of money that keeps a boat fishing long after the fish, and the economics, are gone.3
Then comes the disguise.
- Flags of convenience. China now runs a large slice of its fleet under other countries' flags. In West Africa the takeover is near-total: roughly 90% of Ghana's industrial trawl fleet is Chinese-owned through local front companies, dodging bans on foreign ownership.4
- The bill lands on the poor. West Africa loses an estimated $9.4bn a year to illegal fishing, most of it tied to Chinese-controlled ships, hollowing out the protein supply of some of the world's most food-insecure coastlines.4
This licence-and-flag design, a fleet that is legally local and beneficially Chinese, is exactly the kind of quiet mechanism I keep pulling apart, and it is the sort of thread we go back and forth on most mornings in the Decoding the Dragon WhatsApp group, where I share a smaller China deep-dive like this one with thousands of readers every day (t.ly/t7uhs).
When a fishing boat is not a fishing boat
Here is where it stops being an environmental story and becomes a security one.
A large part of China's fleet is not really commercial. It is the People's Armed Forces Maritime Militia, civilian-looking boats that are subsidised, trained and tasked by the state to hold contested water. The doctrine is "decentralised ownership, centralised tasking": privately owned on paper, directed by the navy and coast guard in practice.
The tactic is called swarming, and it works because of an asymmetry no navy has solved.
- In June 2025, the Philippine Coast Guard logged over 50 Chinese militia vessels swarming Rozul Reef, deep inside the Philippine EEZ, sitting scattered and clustered, crews invisible, not really fishing at all.5
- A warship cannot open fire on a fishing boat without starting an international incident. So the "fishermen" hold the water, and the grey hulls wait just over the horizon.
That is the genius of it. China gets the effect of a naval deployment while keeping the deniability of a fishing cooperative.
And increasingly, the fleet does its work in the dark. Vessels switch off their AIS transponders, the beacons that are supposed to keep ships trackable and safe, and simply vanish. Peruvian fishermen call the squid armada El Gran Muro de Luz, the Great Wall of Lights, because at night you can see the floodlights of hundreds of boats that otherwise appear on no screen at all. The same instinct that hides an illegal catch also hides a survey run, an intelligence sweep, or a slow grid-pattern crawl along a rival's coast.
Why this was always coming
None of this is improvised. It is policy.
Beijing's stated goal is to become a "Great Maritime Power", and the fishing fleet is one of its cheapest instruments for getting there. The clever bit is how the money is hidden. Under an earlier five-year plan, distant-water fishing was reclassified as "strategic infrastructure", and the overseas ports, cold stores and bases that service the fleet were rebranded as Belt and Road investments. The World Trade Organization can cap fishing subsidies. It cannot cap "infrastructure". So vast capacity-building support simply walked out of treaty jurisdiction through a change of label.
The fleet, the subsidies, the militia, the dark shipping and the overseas bases are not separate problems. They are one system, pointed outward, and it has now reached the top of the Arabian Sea.
What it means for India
For India this is a direct challenge, and the honest reading is that New Delhi is behind, but finally moving.
The exposure is real. Chinese vessels pushed into India's own EEZ off Maharashtra back in 2019, and China's presence across the Indian Ocean has climbed steadily since 2022. India has long called itself the region's net security provider, yet an entire foreign fishery has set up next door in a legal blind spot.
India's answer is coming on three fronts.
- Surveillance. The Information Fusion Centre, Indian Ocean Region, launched near Delhi in December 2018 and now hosting liaison officers and 76 data linkages across 28 countries, is India's eye on exactly this kind of dark activity.6 It has been reinforced by the Quad's new Indo-Pacific Maritime Surveillance Collaboration (IPMSC), signed at the Quad foreign ministers' meeting in New Delhi on 26 May 2026, an India-proposed framework that fuses the four members' satellite and radio-frequency tracking into one near-real-time picture, initially focused on the Indian Ocean.7 Its whole point is to strip away the cloak: a ship can turn off its AIS, but it cannot easily hide the radio emissions from its own radar.7 This builds on the Quad's 2022 IPMDA initiative.7
- Diplomacy. India is reframing illegal fishing from an environmental nuisance into a core security issue, and using its Indian Ocean Rim Association platform to lead on it.
- Capacity. This is the one that matters most at home, and it is where the China story loops back into an Indian one.
The Palk Bay knot, and the deep-sea off-ramp
India's own fishing fleet is stuck in the shallows. Around 90% of the national catch is pulled from within 50 metres of the surface, which has wrecked the near-shore stocks and produced a chronic, ugly dispute with Sri Lanka.
In the narrow Palk Bay, Tamil Nadu trawlers, having exhausted their own side of the maritime boundary, cross into Sri Lankan waters and drag the seabed bare with bottom trawls. Sri Lanka arrests them. As of early 2026, 116 Tamil Nadu fishermen and 259 of their boats were in Sri Lankan custody, an issue now running straight up to Chief Minister Stalin and External Affairs Minister Jaishankar.8
The fix for both problems, the empty Indian deep water offshore and the overcrowded shallows inshore, is the same: move the fleet outward. That is the design of the Pradhan Mantri Matsya Sampada Yojana (PMMSY), a ₹20,050 crore programme running 2020 to 2025 and now extended to FY26.9
- It funds deep-sea vessels, unit cost around ₹1.2 crore, with a 40% subsidy for general beneficiaries and 60% for SC, ST and women.9
- Under the earlier Blue Revolution scheme, 918 deep-sea vessels were already sanctioned for traditional fishers.9
- Push the Palk Bay trawlers off the seabed and into the deep Bay of Bengal and wider Indian Ocean, and India relieves the pressure on Sri Lanka and plants its own flag in the waters China is now crowding.
This is the sort of second-order link I find quietly satisfying: an antidote to a bilateral irritant with Colombo turns out to be the same policy that answers a Chinese fleet in the Arabian Sea. It is the kind of connection we chase in the Decoding the Dragon community every day, where a few thousand of us pull these threads apart together (t.ly/t7uhs).
What to watch
- Whether the next IOTC session finally brings the northwest squid fishery under any conservation measure, or whether China again stalls scrutiny of its own fleet.
- Whether IPMSC produces a real shared operating picture of the Indian Ocean within the year, or stays a signed statement.
- The PMMSY deep-sea vessel numbers actually delivered to Tamil Nadu and Andhra Pradesh fishers, not just sanctioned on paper.
- The custody count in Sri Lankan jails, the fastest live gauge of whether any of this is working.
The one line to carry out of this: China has learned to turn a fishing licence into a foreign policy, and the cheapest way for India to answer it is to send its own fishermen further out to sea.

I used to think sea power was about warships. The more I read about how China actually operates, the more I think that framing is a decade out of date.
You do not need a bigger navy if you own the docks the other navies refuel at. You do not need to sink a rival's ships if you can see every container they load, in real time, on a platform you control. This is the quiet insight behind China's port strategy, and it is far more clever, and far more unnerving, than another aircraft carrier.
Here is the number that stopped me. Between 2000 and 2025, Chinese state money has flowed into roughly $24bn of port financing across 168 harbours in 90 countries.1 That is not trade. That is a map of control. And a big part of that map sits right on India's doorstep.
What China actually built
Start with the corporate machinery, because the scale is easy to miss.
Two state-owned giants run this network. China Merchants Port (CMPort) is now the world's second-largest container terminal operator, and COSCO Shipping Ports sits third, behind only Singapore's PSA.2 COSCO alone operates or manages 371 berths worldwide.1 These are not ordinary companies chasing quarterly profit. They are instruments of the state, and they behave like it.
The playbook is consistent everywhere it lands:
- Buy or build the deep-water terminal, ideally on a strategic chokepoint.
- Favour Chinese shipping lines, which favour Chinese construction firms for every upgrade.
- Keep capital, data and jobs inside a closed, state-aligned loop.
- Modernise the host country's port, and quietly move the long-term control, and the profit, back to Beijing.
The trophy assets tell the story. COSCO owns 100% of Piraeus in Greece, the "dragon's head" that funnels Chinese goods into Europe by rail.1 It holds 90% of a terminal in Abu Dhabi, 85% of Zeebrugge, and minority-but-influential stakes in Rotterdam, Valencia and even Seattle.1 AidData, the research lab that has tracked this for years, found that around 35% of these Chinese-financed ports involve some Chinese ownership or operational control, and a fifth have both a Chinese owner and a Chinese operator.1 Ownership was never the whole point. Operational control was.
The software layer nobody sees
The terminals are the hardware. The genuinely worrying bit is the software.
It is called LOGINK, a logistics data platform run by China's Ministry of Transport and handed out to ports and freight firms around the world for free.3 Free is the weapon. Western logistics software costs millions to license, so LOGINK simply undercuts everyone and buys market share with subsidy.
And the reach is staggering:
- LOGINK is active in at least 14 of the world's 20 largest ports.3
- It touches data on as much as half of all global shipping capacity.3
- It pulls in feeds from around 5mn trucks and 200-plus warehouses worldwide.3
And it is not just ship positions. The platform ingests the granular, sensitive stuff:
- Customs clearance papers and cargo valuations, so Beijing can see what everything is worth.
- Regulatory declarations, including on hazardous materials and munitions.
- Real-time GPS and RFID geolocation off individual trucks and shipments.
Now sit with what that means. Whoever runs LOGINK can see what is moving, where, for whom, and at what price, across a huge slice of world trade. Western militaries move a lot of their kit on commercial freight, so this is also a window into how rivals resupply. The US Department of Defense was worried enough to ban the Pentagon from using it.3
This licence-it-out-for-free design is exactly the kind of quiet mechanism I love pulling apart, and it is the sort of thread we chase most mornings in my Decoding the Dragon WhatsApp group, where I share a smaller China deep-dive like this with thousands of readers every day (t.ly/t7uhs).
The reason "voluntary data sharing" is a fiction here is China's own law. Under the 2017 National Intelligence Law, every Chinese organisation is legally obliged to "support, assist and cooperate" with state intelligence work.3 So the comforting corporate line, that LOGINK only sees what users choose to share, collapses the moment Beijing asks. A commercial logistics tool is, by statute, an intelligence tool.
Dual-use is not a theory, it is the doctrine
Here is where it gets strange. China has largely skipped the old imperial habit of building visible military bases, which invite friction and become targets. Instead it uses commercial ports that can flip military when needed.
This is codified. China's National Defense Transportation Law, in force since 2017, requires civilian transport infrastructure, including port terminals, to build in national defence needs by design, so these assets can be commandeered for the military.1 A Chinese-run port abroad is therefore a latent naval node, whether or not a warship is ever parked there.
The evidence is already visible:
- China's only openly acknowledged overseas base is in Djibouti, built for about $590mn, sitting right next to a Chinese-run commercial terminal where the navy has an exclusive berth.4
- AidData's earlier study of 78 harbours flagged eight, from Hambantota in Sri Lanka to Gwadar in Pakistan and Ream in Cambodia, as the likeliest candidates to become full naval facilities.5
The point is not that every port is a base. The point is that the line between "commercial" and "military" has been deliberately erased, and the West spent a decade pretending the line still held.
Even the great powers are pushing back
China's expansion is finally hitting resistance, and 2026 has been brutal for Beijing in two theatres.
In Panama, the Hong Kong conglomerate CK Hutchison agreed in March 2025 to sell 43 ports globally, including terminals at both ends of the Panama Canal, to a BlackRock-led group for about $23bn.6 Beijing killed it. China's market regulator launched an antitrust review, COSCO demanded a majority stake, and in February 2026 Panama's Supreme Court ruled the original concession unconstitutional and voided it altogether.6 A rare case of the leverage cutting the other way.
In Australia, the Port of Darwin, leased for 99 years to China's Landbridge in 2015, has become a national-security embarrassment sitting next to Australia's northern military hub. Canberra is now moving to force the port back into Australian hands, China's ambassador has openly warned of consequences, and Landbridge has hauled Australia into international arbitration.7 The "it is just commercial" defence died the moment Beijing started making threats.
The bigger machine this belongs to
None of this is improvised. It is the Maritime Silk Road, the sea leg of Xi Jinping's Belt and Road Initiative launched in 2013.
The logic threads together neatly. Control the terminals, and you control the flow of goods. Control the data platform, and you see the flow. Write the defence law, and you can seize the flow in a crisis. Ports are simply the physical anchor for a much larger ambition: to make the world's supply chains run through, and depend on, China.
The best live proof is Chancay in Peru, inaugurated by Xi in November 2024. COSCO owns 60% and holds 60-year exclusive rights over this $1.3bn deep-water megaport, the first Chinese-controlled hub on South America's Pacific coast.8 It handled around 336,000 containers in its first full year and is built to move ~1mn.8 Its real purpose is a direct China-to-South-America shipping lane that cuts out the United States entirely and pulls the continent's minerals straight to Chinese factories.
What this means for India
For India, this is not a distant story. It is the map of its own encirclement, the old "String of Pearls" made concrete, and 2026 has tightened the noose.
Look at the neighbourhood:
- Sri Lanka: CMPort holds an 85% stake and a 99-year lease on Hambantota, bought for $1.12bn in 2017, a deep-water port a short hop from India's shipping lanes.9
- Pakistan: Gwadar, the flagship of the China-Pakistan corridor, remains a top candidate for a future Chinese naval facility.5
- Bangladesh: the fresh wound. In mid-2026, Dhaka handed the Mongla port economic zone, a project long earmarked for India, to a Chinese state firm, CCECC, with around $650mn in proposed investment, after years of Indian delay.10 China now has a foothold on India's eastern flank, less than 200km from Kolkata.
And India's own counter-moves are struggling. Chabahar, India's answer to Gwadar on Iran's coast, has stalled badly. The US sanctions waiver that let India operate it expired on 26 April 2026 and was not renewed, this year's budget put almost nothing into it, and a US-Israel-Iran war has scrambled the whole region.11 The western workaround is on life support just as the eastern flank gives way.
So where is the good news? It is at home, and it is real:
- India's major ports handled a record ~915mn tonnes of cargo in FY26, and average ship turnaround has roughly halved since 2014, from 96 hours to under 50.12
- Under the Sagarmala programme, 315 projects worth about ₹1.6 lakh crore are already done, with a new mega-port at Vadhavan in the pipeline.12
- On the data war, India's Information Fusion Centre for the Indian Ocean now hosts resident officers from 17 navies and links up with 28 partner countries, a direct counter to the visibility LOGINK hands Beijing.13
This tension, between a China that delivers infrastructure with ruthless speed and an India that keeps losing projects to its own bureaucracy, is the exact thread I keep tugging at, and it is what we argue about most in the Decoding the Dragon community every day (t.ly/t7uhs).
The honest read is mixed. India is finally building serious port capacity and maritime awareness at home. But abroad, it is being out-executed, out-financed and out-manoeuvred, one terminal at a time.
And the gap is mostly self-inflicted. Mongla was India's to build for years, lost to indecision, not to a better Chinese bid. Chabahar sat under-funded through the very window it needed momentum. China's state firms show up with cheap capital, a single chain of command and a bias for speed, while India's projects wander through clearances, consultants and cost revisions. Beijing treats a port as strategy. India too often treats it as a file to be processed. Until that changes, the map keeps tilting the wrong way.
What to watch
- Whether India can convert the US-Israel-Iran turmoil into a fresh Chabahar waiver, or whether it writes the project off for good.
- Whether COSCO ends up with a stake in the Panama ports after all, or the BlackRock consortium walks.
- Whether Canberra completes the forced sale of Darwin, and how far Beijing escalates in response.
- Whether any of AidData's eight candidate ports, especially Ream in Cambodia, openly turns into a Chinese naval facility.
The one line
China did not out-build the world's navies. It quietly bought the docks they all depend on, and India is discovering that the most dangerous ports on its map fly no flag at all.

Five days ago, KKR agreed to buy Medicover's Indian hospital business for €1.2bn, about ₹13.2k crore.1 Twenty-four hospitals, roughly 4,800 beds, spread across the south and west.
Here is the number that did not make the headlines. In the twelve months to June 2026, that business generated EBITDA of €26.1mn, roughly ₹280 crore, on revenue of about ₹2.4k crore.1
Do the division. That is an enterprise value of close to 46 times operating earnings, on a margin of 11.8%.
I have read a lot of Indian deal notes. Nobody pays 46 times for a business they intend to run exactly as it is. You pay 46 times because you have a very specific plan for that 11.8%.
So this edition is not about whether private capital belongs in Indian healthcare. It already is Indian healthcare. It is about a narrower and much more uncomfortable question: what has to change inside those 24 hospitals for ₹13.2k crore to look cheap in 2031, and who pays for that change.
The setup: how India got here
Start from the baseline, because the trajectory is the story.
For most of independent India, a hospital was a doctor's asset. A surgeon built a nursing home, ran it for thirty years, and handed it to a partner or a child. Charitable trusts did the rest. Capital was scarce, ambition was local, and nobody talked about multiples.
That world is essentially gone. The numbers today:
- Private equity has put roughly $6bn a year into Indian healthcare over the past five years, across about 120 transactions annually.2
- Healthcare exits hit $6.2bn in FY25 and another $5.6bn in FY26, making healthcare about a fifth of India's high-value PE exits in 2025.2
- Announced healthcare deal value crossed ₹10k crore in a single quarter (Q2 FY26) across hospitals, diagnostics and specialty care.3
- The BSE Healthcare index trades at roughly 44x earnings, against about 21x for the Sensex.2
The consolidation is now visible in the league table. Aster DM and Blackstone-backed Quality Care merged into a network of 38 hospitals and over 10,150 beds, with Blackstone holding 30.7% of the combined entity.4 Manipal, backed by Temasek, has built out to roughly 49 hospitals and about 12,000 beds and filed for a $1bn-plus IPO in March 2026, which would be the sector's largest.5
And the single-specialty roll-up has quietly become the most profitable corner of the market. Single-specialty formats took about 30% of India's private healthcare market in 2024 and are projected to reach 40% by 2028, a market of around ₹2.6 lakh crore.6 Mature IVF centres report returns on capital employed approaching 100%.6
This is real capacity in a country that needs it. India has roughly 1.6 hospital beds per 1,000 people.7 Somebody has to build the rest.
The mechanism: what 46 times actually demands
Here is where it gets interesting, and where most coverage stops short.
A 46x entry multiple is not a bet on India's demographics. It is a bet on arithmetic. If KKR takes Medicover India's EBITDA margin from 11.8% to the 20% to 25% range that listed Indian chains already run at, and grows revenue in line with the sector, the effective entry multiple collapses to something in the high teens. That is the trade.
So the question becomes mechanical: where does an Indian hospital find 10 percentage points of margin?
There are only four places, and every one of them lands on a person.
- Case mix. Shift the beds towards oncology, cardiac, neuro and complex orthopaedics. Aster's cardiology revenue grew 25% and oncology 23% in FY26.8 High-acuity work carries a far higher revenue per bed than a routine admission.
- Price per bed-day. ARPOB, the average revenue per occupied bed, has been climbing 10% to 16% a year across the large chains.3 That outpaces general inflation by a wide margin.
- Throughput. Robotic and minimally invasive procedures shorten the length of stay, so the same bed turns over faster. Occupancy at the big chains already runs at 62% to 76%.8 Every point of occupancy on a higher-ARPOB case mix is pure margin.
- Cost. Nursing ratios, consultant compensation structures, procurement, and the pharmacy margin.
None of these are illegitimate on their own. A hospital that does more cardiac surgery is a hospital doing more cardiac surgery. The problem is that the financial model does not ask for one of them. It asks for all four, simultaneously, on a five to seven year clock.
This is exactly the kind of second-order mechanism I end up pulling apart most days, and it is what we argue about in the BharatNama WhatsApp group, where I share a smaller India deep-dive like this with thousands of readers every morning (t.ly/h2jq1).
The thing that changed six weeks ago
Now the part almost nobody has connected to the deal flow.
On 13 February 2026, the Reserve Bank of India issued amendment directions permitting banks to finance acquisitions. They took effect on 1 July 2026.9 The terms:
- Banks may fund up to 75% of an acquisition's value, with the acquirer putting in the remaining 25%.9
- Post-acquisition consolidated debt-to-equity may not exceed 3:1, on a continuous basis.9
- Acquisition finance is capped at 20% of a bank's eligible capital, inside an overall 40% capital-market exposure ceiling.9
- Acquirers need a net worth above ₹500 crore and three years of profits.9
India has just built the plumbing for the leveraged buyout. That is a genuine reform, and for most of the economy it is overdue. Indian M&A has been starved of debt for decades, which is precisely why Indian buyouts have been so equity-heavy and so conservative.
But apply it to hospitals and the picture changes. A hospital's cash flow is unusually rigid. Clinical capacity is fixed, nursing is chronically short, and a large slice of revenue arrives late from government schemes.10 Layering bank debt onto that cash flow transfers risk in a specific direction: if the plan works, the returns are private; if it does not, the ward that closes is one the public was relying on.10
The timing is not a coincidence. The framework went live on 1 July. The largest hospital buyout in Indian history was announced on 6 August.
Where India stands, against the world
India is not running this experiment first. The United States ran it, and the results are in.
The most recent evidence is a September 2025 study in the Annals of Internal Medicine, covering 49 private-equity-acquired hospitals against 293 controls, spanning more than 1mn emergency visits and 121,000 ICU admissions.11 After acquisition:
- Emergency department salary spend fell about 18%.11
- Full-time staffing fell nearly 12% hospital-wide.11
- Mortality in those emergency departments rose about 13%, roughly seven additional deaths per 10,000 visits.12
- Transfers out to other acute hospitals rose, with ICU transfers up close to 11%.12
That builds on the 2023 JAMA study of 51 PE-acquired hospitals, which found hospital-acquired conditions up 25%, falls up 27%, and central-line infections up 38% even though those hospitals were placing 16% fewer central lines.13
I want to be careful here, because the lazy version of this argument is wrong. American hospitals are paid differently, staffed differently, and sued differently. India will not reproduce those numbers.
But the causal chain the studies identify is not American. It is arithmetical. A fixed-horizon return target plus a leveraged balance sheet produces pressure on the largest controllable line item, which in a hospital is people. That chain works the same in Hyderabad as in Houston.
The other side of the comparison is Japan, and it is the more useful one. Japan's hospital sector is more privatised than India's popular imagination allows: about 70% of hospitals are owned by private medical corporations, running 56% of beds.14 Yet out-of-pocket spending is just 12.2% of health expenditure (2023), against India's 43.4%.14
Same private ownership. Utterly different household outcome. The difference is not ownership. It is who sets the price.
Where India stands, against itself
Now break the national number open, because this is where the real story lives.
India's National Sample Survey ran its 80th round through calendar 2025, and the results published in April 2026 are the most current picture we have.15
- Average out-of-pocket spend per hospitalisation: ₹34,064.16
- In a government hospital: ₹6,631. In a private hospital: ₹50,508.16
- That is roughly 7.6 times, and for the same illness the gap runs five to ten times.17
- Yet 57.9% of rural and 64.6% of urban hospitalisations happen in private facilities.15 People are not choosing the expensive option. They are choosing the available one.
- Insurance coverage has genuinely transformed, from 14.1% of rural India in 2017-18 to 47.4% in 2025, and 19.1% to 44.3% in urban India.15 Coverage is not the same as protection.
The state spread is starker still. Average hospitalisation cost runs about ₹55k in Telangana and ₹52k in Tamil Nadu, against roughly ₹22k in Odisha and ₹8k in Ladakh.17
And the public side mirrors it. Per capita government health spending in 2022-23 ranged from ₹10,675 in Puducherry down to ₹1,419 in Uttar Pradesh, a spread of more than seven times.18 Karnataka and Maharashtra now spend under 1% of their state output on health.18
That is the disparity that decides where the next 20 private hospitals get built, and it is exactly the kind of state-versus-state thread we keep pulling in the BharatNama community (t.ly/h2jq1).
The state stepped back at exactly the wrong moment
Here is the fact that reframes everything above, and it is very recent.
The National Health Accounts estimates for 2022-23 show that out-of-pocket expenditure rose back to 43.4% of total health spending, from 39.4% the year before.19 That reverses a decade of steady decline from 64.2% in 2013-14.20
Total health expenditure also fell to 3.3% of GDP, from 3.8%.20 Government health spending sits at 1.48% of GDP, still well short of the National Health Policy's 2.5% target.19 The Union's share of public health spending has slipped from 41.8% to 36.3%, so states now carry roughly two-thirds of the bill.20
Some of that is a pandemic base effect, and it should be read as such. But the direction of travel is the point. Households started paying more again in precisely the years private capital was scaling fastest.
The public payer is also losing its grip on the private sector it depends on. PM-JAY, as of 30 June 2026, has authorised 12.69 crore cashless admissions worth ₹1.92 lakh crore across 37,413 empanelled hospitals.21 Private hospitals carry the majority of that load.
And yet:
- New hospital empanelment collapsed from an average of 316 a month in 2024 to 111 a month in 2025, a fall of about 65%.22
- 609 private hospitals have voluntarily withdrawn from the scheme since 2018, citing package rates and delayed payments.22
- The government did move. CGHS rates were revised in October 2025 across nearly 2,000 procedures, the first major revamp since 2014, with a tier structure by accreditation, city and ward.23
Meanwhile the insurers are squeezed from the other side. In FY25, public sector general insurers ran a combined incurred claims ratio of 99.84%, meaning almost every rupee of premium went straight back out as claims.24 Standalone health insurers held at 68.06%.24 Somebody has to absorb rising hospital bills, and it ends up being the policyholder through co-pays, room-rent caps and proportionate deductions.
What India can actually learn from Japan
Japan is the right teacher here, and not for the reason people assume.
Japan did not nationalise its hospitals. It kept them private, mostly small, mostly physician-founded, exactly the ecosystem India is currently consolidating away. What Japan did instead was take pricing off the table entirely.
- The Ministry of Health sets a single national fee schedule covering essentially every procedure, revised on a fixed cycle.14
- The June 2026 revision raised base fees by 3.09%, the first significant positive revision in twelve years, with extra points for hospitals adopting shared electronic records and continuity planning.25
- Because the price is fixed, competition happens on quality, volume and efficiency, not on billing.
The consequence is that a Japanese hospital can be privately owned and profit-seeking without the patient's bill being the variable that flexes.
India is groping towards this and keeps stopping short. The Clinical Establishments Act has had a rate-range provision on the books since 2010 and it has never been enforced nationally. Where states have tried, they get litigated: in December 2025 the Supreme Court granted interim protection to private hospitals challenging Kerala's Clinical Establishments Act, including its requirement that every establishment display its fee and package rates.26
What transfers to India, honestly:
- A published national rate band is portable. The CGHS revision proves the state can do the technical work of costing 2,000 procedures with tier adjustments. Extending that logic as a ceiling, not a scheme rate, is a policy choice, not a capability gap.
- A single claims rail is portable, and India is closer than most. The National Health Claims Exchange, built on the ABDM stack, is designed to standardise claims into a common format so insurers can auto-adjudicate rather than argue line by line.27
- Japan's fiscal base is not portable. Japan spends 10.7% of GDP on health.14 India spends 3.3%.20 You cannot fix a financing gap with a fee schedule.
That last point matters. Price caps without public money do not create access. They just move the shortage.
What to watch
Four specific things over the next few quarters.
- Whether the KKR-Medicover deal closes on schedule in Q4 2026, and how it is financed. A bank-funded structure under the new RBI framework would be the first real test case of leveraged healthcare buyouts in India.
- Medicover India's EBITDA margin in the first full year post-close. Watch whether the move from 11.8% comes from case mix and occupancy, or from staffing and procurement. The composition tells you everything.
- The monthly PM-JAY empanelment run rate. If it stays near 111 a month against 316 in 2024, the scheme's private capacity is quietly shrinking even as its card count grows.
- The Supreme Court's handling of the Kerala Clinical Establishments Act challenge, and whether the Centre finally notifies a rate range under Rule 9 rather than leaving it to states and litigation.
The one line
India has just legalised the financial machinery that made American hospitals fragile, and the first ₹13,000 crore cheque arrived before the ink was dry.

Here is something that should not really be able to happen.
In the same six months that India's competition regulator opened a formal abuse-of-dominance investigation into IndiGo, the airline went and posted the highest domestic market share any Indian carrier has ever recorded.
In June 2026, IndiGo carried 66.3% of every domestic flyer in the country.1 Not the low-sixties it had held for two years. A record. Its highest print ever, landed while the Competition Commission of India was sitting on complaints about exactly this power.
Now let that settle for a second. A dominant firm under antitrust scrutiny usually treads carefully. IndiGo grew.
The thing is, this is not a story about one airline having a good quarter. It is a story about what happens to a market when a single player gets big enough that the rules meant to check it start bending around it instead. And it is a story about a specific tactic, capacity dumping, that sits in the grey zone between aggressive competition and predation, and that India has never once penalised.
Two airlines, ninety percent of the sky
India runs one of the fastest-growing aviation markets on earth, and also one of the most concentrated. Strip out the noise and two groups own the sky:
- IndiGo: 66.3% of domestic passengers in June 2026, a record.1
- The Tata-owned Air India group (Air India plus Air India Express): 23.9%, and shrinking.1
- Everyone else fights over the crumbs. Akasa Air, the four-year-old challenger, hit its own record of 6.4%. SpiceJet, once a serious number two, is down to 1.9%, the smallest of the scheduled carriers.1
Together, IndiGo and the Air India group now carry more than nine of every ten domestic passengers. Across the first half of 2026 their combined share sat above 90%, on a base of roughly 8.6 crore passengers.2
For most of the last decade this concentration was sold to us as efficiency, and for a while it genuinely was. IndiGo built a fleet of around 420 aircraft on a ruthless low-cost model: a single family of Airbus narrow-bodies, point-to-point flying, unbundled fares, and heavy use of operating leases that kept the balance sheet light.3 While Kingfisher, Jet Airways and GoFirst loaded up on debt and died, IndiGo survived every downcycle and hoovered up their share.
That is the baseline India came from: a graveyard of collapsed carriers, and one survivor that got very good at surviving. The question BharatNama cares about is what happens next, once the survivor is this big.
Why capacity dumping is the tactic nobody can prosecute
The antitrust worry here is not simple price-fixing. It is subtler, and it is specific to airlines.
Classic predatory pricing means selling below cost to kill a rival, then jacking prices up once they are gone. The standard legal test, the Areeda-Turner rule, asks whether a price sits below the seller's marginal cost. In most industries that works. In aviation it falls apart.
The reason is that the marginal cost of one more passenger on a flight that is already departing is close to zero. A bit of extra fuel for the weight, a boarding pass, a snack. Almost every real cost of the flight, the lease, the crew, the landing charges, the base fuel burn, is fixed the moment the aircraft is scheduled. So a dominant airline can crash fares to punishing levels and still, technically, stay above the marginal cost of a single seat. The price-based test cannot catch it.
Which is why regulators in mature markets shifted their gaze from price to capacity. The tactic is called capacity dumping, or predatory capacity, and it works like this:
- A small challenger opens a route with one or two daily frequencies.
- The incumbent, sitting on a huge fleet reserve, floods that exact route at that exact time, sandwiching the new flight with departures just before and just after.
- Fares on the route collapse. The challenger, with no wider network to cross-subsidise the losses, bleeds cash.
- Once the challenger folds, the incumbent quietly pulls the extra capacity back and lifts fares to recover.
The honest legal question is the "profit sacrifice" test: does the incumbent's move make business sense only because it kills a rival? Moving an aircraft off a profitable monopoly route onto a contested one, purely to drown a smaller competitor, is exactly the conduct antitrust law is meant to stop. This was the heart of the US Department of Justice's case against American Airlines two decades ago, over its treatment of the challenger Vanguard.
In India, it has never been tested. Until, arguably, now.
The December crisis that gave the regulator a way in
The abstract debate turned concrete in the winter of 2025.
In the first week of December, IndiGo's operation broke down spectacularly. Around 4,500 flights were cancelled between 2 and 9 December, peaking at roughly 1,600 cancellations on a single day.4 More than 10 lakh passengers were stranded. The airline later spent over ₹24 crore on compensation.4
The stated cause was a crew shortage triggered by revised Flight Duty Time Limitation norms, the rules that cap how long pilots can fly, which cut permitted night landings from six to two a week. But the deeper cause was that IndiGo had under-hired for years, adding just 1,247 pilots for 91 new aircraft between 2022 and 2024.5 It grew the fleet faster than it grew the people to fly it.
Then came the part that drew the regulator in. As IndiGo cancelled at scale, passengers alleged its algorithm repriced the scarce remaining seats sharply upward. One complaint, filed by a flyer named Karthikeya Rawal over a Delhi-Goa-Bengaluru booking, alleged a cancelled ticket was effectively replaced by one costing more than twice as much.6
The CCI took the bait. On 4 February 2026 it ordered a formal investigation, forming a prima facie view that IndiGo, using its dominance, had imposed unfair conditions and withheld capacity, in potential breach of Sections 4(2)(a)(i) and 4(2)(b)(i) of the Competition Act.6 Crucially, in its assessment the CCI noted that IndiGo is the sole carrier on more than 330 domestic routes and controls close to 60% of all available seat kilometres.6 On those routes, a stranded passenger has no substitute. That is the definition of locked-in.
This route-by-route monopoly, hidden inside the national average, is exactly the kind of thread I keep pulling at in the BharatNama WhatsApp community, where I share a smaller India deep-dive like this with thousands of readers every morning (t.ly/h2jq1). The national share tells you IndiGo is big; the 330 sole-carrier routes tell you where it is untouchable.
The regulator that can watch but cannot act
Here is where India's structure fails the challenger.
Domestic fares were fully deregulated back in 1994, and airlines price through revenue-management software that splits each cabin into invisible fare "buckets" that open and close by the minute. On a contested route, a dominant carrier can simply keep the cheapest buckets open indefinitely, starving a rival of yield. There is nothing illegal about it.
The DGCA runs a Tariff Monitoring Unit, but it is a passive observer. It watches a sample of routes each month to check airlines do not exceed their own filed fares. It has no power to cap fares dynamically or to halt a predatory price drop in real time. Even the Supreme Court has questioned why a passenger pays wildly different amounts for the same seat on the same day.
And the new law does not obviously fix this. The Bhartiya Vayuyan Adhiniyam, 2024, the statute that replaced the colonial-era Aircraft Act of 1934, gave the DGCA fresh authority. IndiGo has argued this specialised law ousts the CCI's jurisdiction over aviation pricing altogether. The CCI rejected that, leaning on the Supreme Court's Bharti Airtel precedent that sectoral regulators and the competition watchdog occupy complementary, not conflicting, spheres. But the very fact that jurisdiction is being fought over tells you how thin the enforcement is.
Two structural features make it worse, and both quietly protect the incumbent:
- Airport slots. At Delhi, Mumbai, Bengaluru and Hyderabad, peak-hour demand far exceeds runway capacity, so these are "Level 3" slot-controlled airports. Under the global "grandfather" rule, an airline that uses a slot 80% of the time keeps it forever. The prime 7am-to-9am metro slots are permanently locked up by the incumbents, and airlines have been known to run near-empty "ghost flights" just to hit the 80% threshold and keep a slot off the market.7
- The Route Dispersal Guidelines. To ensure remote regions get connectivity, any airline flying lucrative trunk routes must also fly loss-making ones: 10% of its Category I capacity on the north-east and islands, plus a mandated share on other underserved routes.8 A giant like IndiGo absorbs this easily by cross-subsidising from its huge profitable network. A small challenger must divert a painful chunk of its tiny fleet to loss-making routes just to comply, which accelerates its ruin if its trunk routes are being dumped on.
Where India stands: against the world, and against itself
Set India beside the one country that has just lived through this exact movie, and against itself.
India versus the world. Australia is the cautionary tale, and the numbers are almost a mirror:
- Qantas and Virgin Australia together control about 94% of the Australian domestic market.9
- Two challengers tried to break in. Bonza collapsed in 2024; Rex fell into administration that July.
- After they exited, the ACCC confirmed domestic airfares surged, rising around 40% on affected routes, with the best-discount fare on the Melbourne to Gold Coast route up about 70% in the months after the challenger was gone.10
That is the recoupment phase made visible. Cheap fares during the turf war, then a hard snap-back to monopoly pricing once the challenger is dead. India's concentration is now worse than Australia's was, with a single carrier at 66% where Australia's leader sits around 60%.
India versus itself. The national average hides the real story:
- Nationally, IndiGo is at 66%. On its 330-plus sole-carrier routes, it is at 100%.6
- IndiGo flies around 420 aircraft; Akasa, the only credible new entrant, flies a fraction of that.3 The fleet gap is the whole barrier: a challenger simply cannot match capacity on a route it is being swamped on.
- The concentration is not evenly felt. A flyer on a busy Delhi-Mumbai trunk has real choice. A flyer to a smaller city, served by one carrier, has none, and pays accordingly.
What India can learn
The lesson from abroad is not "break up IndiGo". It is that watching is not enough, and India already knows this.
- The United States did not rely on price tests. It went after predatory capacity directly, arguing that shifting aircraft onto a challenger's route to run it out of business was itself the violation. India's Competition Act already contains the tools; what is missing is a single completed case that draws the line between healthy matching and predatory dumping.
- The European Union treats prime slots as a competition asset, forcing airlines to give up slots as a remedy when dominance threatens competition. India's grandfathered slots do the opposite, cementing the incumbent.
What transfers is the principle, not the copy-paste. India cannot simply mimic US litigation timelines or EU slot divestitures given its state capacity and federal structure. But it can do three portable things: give the DGCA's tariff unit real teeth under the new BVA framework, reform slot allocation so peak-hour capacity actually reaches new entrants, and let the CCI finish at least one capacity case so the threat becomes credible.
The live test of intent is Adani. In late July 2026, the Adani group, which controls Mumbai's airport and the new Navi Mumbai one, publicly denied plans to launch its own airline, even as a leaked letter showed it lobbying to relax the rules that stop an airport owner from also owning a carrier.11 If that firewall falls, the capacity war moves from the skies to the tarmac, where the entity allocating slots also flies planes. This is precisely the kind of structural fault line I dig into in the BharatNama community every day (t.ly/h2jq1), because the concentration that matters most is often the one being negotiated quietly, before anyone takes off.
What to watch
- The CCI's decision on IndiGo's commitments. IndiGo has offered a Section 48B settlement without admitting guilt: a Crisis Management Group activated within an hour of a large disruption, automatic refunds, rebooking within 48 to 72 hours, and a pledge not to charge above its last filed fares during a crisis. The CCI opened public comments on 23 July 2026, with submissions due by 13 August.12 Watch whether it accepts these or pushes for structural remedies.
- The Adani ownership question. Track whether the government relaxes the airport-airline ownership firewall.11
- Akasa's share. It just hit a record 6.4%.1 Watch whether it can hold and climb, or whether it plateaus, the tell-tale sign of a challenger hitting the capacity ceiling.
- IndiGo's move upmarket. With its A350 business class and premium "Stretch" cabin, IndiGo is now chasing the high-yield flyer too.13 The low-cost disruptor is becoming the full-service incumbent.
The uncomfortable truth is simple: India built a brilliant airline, and then let it get big enough that the market now depends on the good behaviour of a single company. A 66% share reached during an antitrust probe is not a sign the system is working. It is a sign the system has no brake.

Here is a fact that stopped me cold. India, the country whose desert postcard is a camel against a Jaisalmer sunset, now owns roughly 0.6% of the world's camels.
India has about 2.5 lakh camels, and the number is falling off a cliff.1 The world has about 42mn, and the number is climbing.2
That gap is not an accident of geography. It is the direct result of a law that was written, in good faith, to save the animal.
In 2014 Rajasthan made the camel its State Animal. In 2015 it passed a law banning camel slaughter and choking off the trade that moved camels out of the state. The intent was pure. The outcome was a textbook case of a policy making the exact problem it was built to solve much, much worse.
This is the cleanest example I have seen in years of a simple, brutal rule: you cannot protect an animal while quietly killing the only economy that makes people want to keep it.
The setup
Start with the baseline, because the trajectory is the whole story.
- India's camel herd peaked at over 1mn in the early 1990s, and was higher still in the 1970s.3
- By the 2012 Livestock Census it was down to roughly 4 lakh.1
- By the 2019 Census, the latest we have, it had crashed to 2.5 lakh, a 37% fall in a single seven-year window.1
That single window is the one that matters, because it straddles the law.
In 2015 the Rajasthan Assembly passed the Rajasthan Camel (Prohibition of Slaughter and Regulation of Temporary Migration or Export) Act.4 It did three big things:
- It banned the slaughter of any camel in Rajasthan, at any age or health.4
- It banned the possession, sale, or transport of camel meat.4
- It banned moving camels out of the state if slaughter was the likely intent, and buried any lawful movement under a District Collector permit regime.4
Breaking the law carried one to five years in jail, and it turned anyone transporting camels into a potential criminal abettor.4 On paper, a shield for the "Ship of the Desert". In practice, an anchor tied to its neck.
The Cobra Effect, in slow motion
The phrase "Cobra Effect" comes from colonial Delhi, where a bounty on dead cobras led people to breed cobras for the reward. The British scrapped the bounty, the breeders released their now worthless snakes, and the city ended up with more cobras than before. A well meant intervention that produces the opposite of its goal. Rajasthan's camel law is the same effect in slow motion.
To see why, you have to understand how the camel economy actually worked. It never ran on meat. The Raika, the pastoral community who have herded these animals for centuries, hold a strict taboo against eating camel.3 Their income came from one thing:
- Female camels stayed in the herd, breeding and giving milk.
- Young male camels were sold, mostly to buyers in Punjab, Haryana, Gujarat and Uttar Pradesh, for farm work, carting and desert transport.
- The sale of a few males each year, largely at the Pushkar fair, once the world's largest livestock market with tens of thousands of camels changing hands, paid for the fodder, water and vet care that kept the whole breeding herd alive.
Sever the sale of the males, and the entire financial logic inverts. That is exactly what the export ban did.
- Out of state buyers stopped coming, because moving a camel across the border now looked like suspected smuggling for slaughter.4
- Demand collapsed inward to a Rajasthan market already drowning in camels and mechanising fast.
- A healthy adult male that once fetched over ₹40,000 crashed after the Act, and calves fell to as little as ₹2,000 to ₹3,000. Even now, a decade on, an adult fetches only about ₹20,000.4
Sit with that calf number. The state animal became cheaper than a baby goat.
A camel still drinks and eats whether or not it earns. Once the male could not be sold, it stopped being an asset and became a liability that walks. So breeders did the rational thing: they stopped breeding, and thousands of unsellable males were simply abandoned to the desert, where feral herds began raiding the very farms that once bought them.
This kind of second order collapse, where a rule aimed at one bad use kills all the good uses, is exactly the thread I keep tugging at, and it is the sort of thing we argue over in the BharatNama WhatsApp community, where I put out a smaller India deep dive like this one every single morning (t.ly/h2jq1).
The chokepoint no one talks about
There is a second, quieter mechanism, and it is about trucks, not camels.
The Act and its sister livestock laws let officials seize any vehicle suspected of moving camels illegally, and handed custody of the vehicle to the District Collector rather than a regular court.4 The idea was administrative speed against smugglers. The effect was a deep freeze.
- A trucker carrying camels, even for a legitimate in state farm buyer, could have the vehicle confiscated on a mere allegation of intent to slaughter.
- Getting the truck back meant slow, opaque proceedings and often a bank guarantee worth far more than the freight.
- So commercial transporters simply refused to carry camels at all.
The law meant to catch smugglers ended up quarantining the animal inside a few districts and cutting the Raika off from every market beyond them. The logistics network died, and the camel died with it.
And none of this happened in a vacuum. The camel was already under strain before 2015:
- Tractors and pickup trucks had made the male draught camel largely obsolete since the 1990s.
- Grazing land was vanishing as the Indira Gandhi Canal turned rangeland into farmland.
- The sacred Oran groves that were traditional grazing commons were increasingly handed to solar parks for India's renewable push.
The law did not start the decline. It took an animal that was already wobbling and kicked the last leg out.
Where India stands: against the world, and against itself
This is where benchmarking makes the story land, because India's collapse is uniquely India's.
India against the world. While India's herd fell, the global camel population nearly doubled, from around 18mn in the late 1990s to about 42mn now.2 It rose because the rest of the camel world monetises the animal instead of freezing it.
- Chad: ~10.7mn camels, the most on earth.2
- Somalia: ~7.5mn.2
- Sudan: ~4.8mn.2
- India: ~2.5 lakh, roughly 0.6% of the world total, and shrinking.2
In East Africa the camel is farmed for milk and meat at commercial scale, and in the Gulf it is bred for racing and dairy worth serious money, so keeping camels pays, so herds grow. India banned the paying use and the herd emptied out. Same animal, opposite policy, opposite result.
India against itself. The national number hides an even sharper story inside our borders.
- Rajasthan alone holds about 85% of India's camels, roughly 2.12 lakh.3
- Gujarat is a distant second at about 28,000.3
- The rest of the country barely registers, even as states like Haryana and Uttar Pradesh once bought the bulk of Rajasthan's male camels.
And the collapse is uneven even across breeds. The racing Jaisalmeri of the western desert has thinned sharply, while the milch Mewari of the Aravalli hills is now considered critically endangered, with only a few thousand left, and the coastal Kachchhi of Gujarat is squeezed as its mangrove grazing shrinks. Four distinct desert cultures, each unravelling at its own speed.
So this is not one national crisis. It is a Rajasthan crisis that is really a Raika crisis, concentrated in a handful of desert districts, inside a country that thinks of itself as a camel nation but is statistically almost camel free.
What India can learn
The good news is that the fix is already visible, and it is not more protection. It is the opposite: give the camel a job that pays.
The rest of the camel world runs on milk and meat. India's taboo rules out meat, but camel milk is a genuine opportunity. It is lower in lactose than cow milk, rich in insulin like proteins, and sells globally as a functional food for diabetics and the lactose intolerant.
For years this went nowhere because the FSSAI did not even recognise camel milk as a food. After sustained lobbying by the National Research Centre on Camel in Bikaner, the regulator finally set standards for non bovine milk, and the market opened up.9
The early results are the most hopeful numbers in this whole story:
- Sarhad Dairy in Kutch, an Amul cooperative and India's first camel milk plant, procured about 4,754 litres a day in 2024-25 and paid over ₹8.5 crore to more than 350 pastoral families.7
- Private brands like Aadvik Foods have scaled camel milk into powders, chocolates and skincare sold nationwide.
- Even so, India makes only about 7,000 tonnes of camel milk a year, under 0.2% of global output, so the runway is enormous.3
The lesson from abroad is not "copy Chad". It is structural: herds survive where the animal earns, and they vanish where it is only revered. India revered the camel into near extinction. The transferable move is to build the paying market, not to police the animal into a museum piece.
This shift from banning a use to building a use is the exact debate I keep coming back to, and it is one of the running threads in the BharatNama community, where thousands of us pull apart India's policy choices every day (t.ly/h2jq1).
Encouragingly, the state has finally started to reverse course:
- On 3 October 2025, Rajasthan notified new rules lifting the 11 year export ban, allowing male camels to move interstate for farming or dairy with a permit and a health certificate.5
- The per calf breeding incentive under the state's camel scheme was doubled from ₹10,000 to ₹20,000.6
- In 2024 the central National Livestock Mission was expanded to cover camels, offering a 50% capital subsidy for organised breeding and dairy units, routed through SIDBI.8
What to watch
- Pushkar's numbers. The 2025 fair was the first after the ban lifted. Watch whether out of state buyers actually return and whether prices climb back toward that ₹40,000 mark, or whether the permit friction the herders fear keeps them away.5
- The 21st Livestock Census. Enumeration began in late 2024. Its camel print will be the first hard read on whether the slide has slowed. If it shows another double digit fall, the reversal came too late.1
- NLM uptake. Track how many camel breeding and dairy units are actually sanctioned under the 50% subsidy, versus how much stays on paper.8
- Milk scale. Watch whether Sarhad's model spreads into Rajasthan, where 85% of the animals are, rather than staying a Kutch success story.7
The one line
India passed a law to stop people killing its camel, and in doing so it killed the reason anyone wanted to keep one alive.
