Walk onto the floor of a modern solar gigafactory in Gujarat or Telangana today and you will see the same robotic stringer doing two jobs at once.
On one side, it lays up modules stamped DCR, bound for government-subsidised rooftops and farm pumps, sold at a heavy premium. On the other, the identical machine turns imported cells into non-DCR panels for private developers and exports, fighting a brutal price war.
Same steel, same workers, two completely different economies. And the reason is a number that should stop you: India can now assemble around 210 GW of solar modules a year, but it can make barely ~27 GW of the solar cells that go inside them.1
That is nearly an eight-fold gap between what India can bolt together and what it can actually manufacture. The whole strange, split market flows from that single hole in the supply chain.
How India ended up assembling more than it makes
Start with the module number, because it is genuinely a triumph. India added a staggering 119 GW of module capacity in 2025 alone, taking the total past 210 GW and making the country, on paper, the second-largest solar module manufacturer on earth after China.1 2
Now set the cell number beside it. India added just over 9 GW of cell capacity in the same year.1 Cells are the hard part: capital-heavy, chemically complex, power-hungry, and slow to build. Modules are the easy part: you can stand up an assembly line for a fraction of the cost.
So the country did the easy part at scale and left the hard part thin. As of mid-2026, cell capacity enrolled on the government's approved list stands at around 26 to 30 GW.3 Go one step further upstream to ingots and wafers and the number is close to zero. Polysilicon, the raw material, India makes essentially none of.
Here is the setup you need to hold in your head:
- Modules (assembly): ~210 GW capacity, ~119 GW added in 2025.1
- Cells (the semiconductor bit): ~27 GW capacity, ~9 GW added in 2025.1 3
- Ingots and wafers: under 5 GW, over 90% imported.
- Polysilicon: near zero, effectively 100% imported.
That is not a supply chain. That is a very long assembly shop with a Chinese spine. And it is exactly the imbalance the government's policy machine is now trying to squeeze shut.
The policy engine: a WTO defeat, redesigned
India's whole approach was forged in a loss. In its early solar push, India told developers they had to use Indian-made cells and modules to win government power contracts. The United States dragged India to the WTO, and in September 2016 the Appellate Body ruled decisively against India.4
New Delhi lost the argument but kept the ambition. It simply re-engineered the policy to fit inside the rules. Today the Domestic Content Requirement, or DCR, the mandate to use Indian cells, is ring-fenced to programmes where the government is the direct financier or buyer:
- PM Surya Ghar Muft Bijli Yojana, the residential rooftop scheme, which has crossed ~40 lakh installations and 14 GW, with a subsidy of up to ₹78,000 per home and a near-term target of 75 lakh homes by December 2026.5 6
- PM-KUSUM, the farm-pump solarisation programme.
- CPSU projects built by state-owned firms like NTPC.
For everyone else, private utility-scale developers and the commercial market, India could not legally mandate DCR. So it built a wall instead.
The wall has two layers. The first is tariffs. India put a Basic Customs Duty on imports, and after the 2025 Budget it sits at 20% on both imported cells and modules, down from the old 40% on modules and 25% on cells but still a serious tax on Chinese kit.7
The second layer is the clever one: the Approved List of Models and Manufacturers, or ALMM. Think of it as a government whitelist. If your project touches the grid, a subsidy, or open access, you can only use kit made by an approved Indian manufacturer. It is a non-tariff barrier a WTO panel cannot easily touch.
And ALMM is climbing the supply chain deliberately, one rung at a time:
- List-I (modules): live since April 2024. Only approved Indian modules qualify.
- List-II (cells): in force from 1 June 2026. The cells inside those modules must now come from an approved Indian cell line too.4
- List-III (wafers): in draft, targeted for 2028.
List-II is the earthquake. It closes the loophole where you assembled a module in India but stuffed it with cheap Chinese cells. And the moment it landed, reality bit: there simply are not enough domestic cells to go around. In July 2026 the government blinked, extending the List-II exemption for net-metering and open-access projects to 31 December 2026, while holding the line for utility tenders and PM Surya Ghar.8
This is the kind of policy-versus-plumbing story I keep pulling apart, and it is the sort of thread we chew over in the BharatNama WhatsApp community, where I share a smaller India deep-dive like this with thousands of readers every morning (t.ly/h2jq1).
The maths behind the two prices
Now the dual market makes sense. The scarce ~27 GW of domestic cells is legally required for every subsidised project, so it commands a fat premium. The abundant imported cell is cheap but locked out of the subsidised market.
So the same panel sells at two prices depending on which cell is inside it:
- DCR TOPCon modules: around $0.29 a watt, because domestic cells are scarce and mandated.9
- Non-DCR modules: around $0.16 a watt, using imported cells in a hyper-competitive market.9
That is nearly double for a physically identical panel. For a manufacturer that owns its own cell line, routing captive cells into its own DCR modules is close to free money. It is why the integrated players are printing margins while pure-play assemblers get squeezed.
There is a genuine cost to this, and it lands on the taxpayer. A homeowner on PM Surya Ghar must use the pricier DCR panel to claim the subsidy. So public money is partly absorbing a premium that exists only because the state mandated scarce hardware in the first place. The subsidy is real, but some of it is paying for an inefficiency the policy itself created.
The technology twist: the subsidised market runs a slower panel
Here is the bit almost no one flags. The two markets are not just two prices, they are two different technologies.
- The export and private market has moved to N-type TOPCon cells, with module efficiencies above 22.5% and better heat performance, and the frontier players are pushing into heterojunction (HJT) at 26%-plus.
- The domestic DCR market has historically leaned on older PERC technology, because retooling a cell line from PERC to TOPCon costs roughly $30mn per GW against ~$22mn for PERC, and while domestic cells sold at a premium regardless, there was little reason to spend.
So for a while the subsidised Indian rooftop was getting a technically older panel than the one India shipped to Texas. That gap is now closing fast as new capacity comes on N-type by default, but it tells you something uncomfortable: protection can slow down the very modernisation it is meant to fund.
Where India stands: against the world, and against itself
Set India beside the one country that matters here, and the picture is sobering. This is BharatNama's whole point, so let us be honest about both sides of it.
India vs the world:
- China controls over 80% of global manufacturing capacity at every stage of the solar chain, from polysilicon to modules, and closer to 95% at the wafer stage.10
- India is the clear number two in modules, on track to be the world's second-largest module maker, but that ranking flatters us, because it measures the easy step.2
- On polysilicon and wafers, the parts that are hard and strategic, India is a rounding error and China is almost the entire market.
India has won the assembly race and barely entered the one that counts. A module ranking without a wafer base is a house with a grand facade and no foundation.
India vs India:
- Integrated players (Waaree, Adani, Premier) that own cells capture the DCR premium end to end. Pure-play assemblers with no cell line are crushed, forced to buy expensive domestic cells for DCR orders while fighting imports on non-DCR.
- Geographically the base is clustered. Gujarat, Tamil Nadu, Telangana and Rajasthan hold the bulk of the gigafactories, while most states are pure consumers of this hardware, not makers of it.
- Even the demand splits: the DCR world is rooftops and farms across the whole country, the non-DCR world is large private utility plants and exports.
The titans who mastered the split
The smartest firms do not choose between the two markets. They run both lines and arbitrage between them.
- Waaree Energies, India's largest, has enrolled ~5.3 GW of cell capacity on ALMM List-II and about 23.7 GW of total enlisted capacity, is building a 10 GW ingot-wafer plant in Maharashtra, and posted Q1 FY26 revenue of ₹4.6k crore, all while feeding a growing US export order book.11 12
- Premier Energies is the merchant-cell kingmaker. It is scaling cell capacity from 3.6 GW toward 10.6 GW by September 2026, and its EBITDA margin hit 32.1% in FY26 on an order book of around ₹14k crore, much of it selling scarce domestic cells to desperate rivals.13 14
- Reliance is leapfrogging the lot, skipping PERC entirely and commissioning HJT lines at Jamnagar, with the first 200 MW out and a path to 10 GW and then 20 GW.15
- Tata Power has brought India's largest single-location cell-and-module plant, 4.3 GW at Tirunelveli, into production.16
This integrated-versus-pure-play divide is exactly the sort of split I love picking apart, and it is the kind of thing readers and I trade notes on daily in the BharatNama community (t.ly/h2jq1), where a smaller India deep-dive like this goes out every morning.
What India can learn
The country that solved this is the one India is walled off against: China. And the lesson is not "copy China", because India cannot and should not replicate that model. The transferable lesson is about sequencing.
China did not start at modules and work backwards. It built polysilicon, wafers and cells first, subsidised power and scale relentlessly, and let module assembly follow. India did the reverse, and is now trying to reach back up the chain under a WTO ceiling, with far less fiscal room and a federal structure that slows land and power decisions.
Two things genuinely transfer:
- Reward depth, not assembly. India's own PLI scheme already points this way. Its second tranche allocated 39,600 MW of integrated capacity to 11 firms with a ₹19,500 crore outlay, and crucially it pays out on domestic value addition, not on modules bolted together. That is the right instinct: pay for the cell and the wafer, not the screwdriver.17
- Use the export pull, not just the import wall. The US Inflation Reduction Act hands generous per-watt credits to modules assembled on American soil, which is why Indian firms are racing to build US lines and win US orders. India can ride that decoupling, but only if it climbs to wafers, or it will forever be assembling other people's cells.
The honest read is that ALMM List-II is India finally forcing the hard step it skipped. It is painful, it is causing genuine shortages, and the December 2026 exemption shows the plumbing is not ready. But the direction is right. You cannot benchmark your way to a supply chain by assembling faster. At some point you have to make the cell.
What to watch
- Whether the ALMM List-II exemption for net-metering and open access is extended again past 31 December 2026, or allowed to expire. An extension signals the cell shortage is still acute.8
- Whether Premier, Waaree and Adani hit their FY26-27 cell and wafer commissioning targets, which is what actually closes the deficit.12 14
- The trajectory of the DCR premium. As domestic cell supply catches up, the gap between the $0.29 and $0.16 panel should compress. Watch it narrow.9
- Whether ALMM List-III (wafers) stays on track for 2028, which would wall off the chain one step further upstream.
The one line
India built the world's second-largest solar assembly line and then discovered it forgot to make the cell, and the two-price market is the sound of a country paying to fix that mistake in public.

The Delhi Metro is the best mass-transit system India has ever built. In 2025 it carried a record 235.8 crore passenger journeys, more than any other Indian network.1 And it still runs at roughly 47% of the ridership its own planners once forecast.2
Let that sink in. The crown jewel, the one every minister points to, is missing nearly half the riders it was promised to carry. And Delhi is the success story.
Go down the list and it gets worse fast. The newer networks are not running a little below plan. They are running at a small fraction of it.
This is not a story about bad trains. India builds excellent metros. It is a story about how these projects were costed, forecast and financed before a single pillar went up. The engineering is world-class. The economics were broken at the drawing board.
The scale, and the shortfall
Start with the scale, because it is genuinely enormous.
- India crossed 1,000 km of operational metro in 2025 and is now the world's third-largest network, behind only China and the United States, spread across more than 20 cities.3
- Since 2014 the Centre has sanctioned around ₹3.44 lakh crore across 38 metro projects covering more than 1,050 km of line.4
- The network has quadrupled from about 248 km in 2014 to over 1,000 km today.3
That is a real achievement, and worth saying plainly. India went from a couple of metro cities to a continental network in a single decade.
Now set the ridership beside it.
- Most Indian metros run at just 25% to 30% of their projected ridership.2
- Delhi, the best, sits near 47%.2
- Kochi is at about 14.5%, Hyderabad 15.2%, Lucknow 8.6%, Jaipur 7.6%.5
- Kanpur, at one point, was carrying as little as 2% of its DPR estimate.6
When the flagship misses by half and the followers miss by ninety per cent, the problem is not the city. It is the forecast.
To be fair, ridership is climbing in absolute terms. Delhi's 235.8 crore journeys in 2025 were a record, and Bengaluru's Namma Metro keeps setting fresh daily highs.1 10 The trouble is that the forecasts always sprinted further ahead than the riders ever could. The growth is real. It is the promise that was fantasy.
The appraisal illusion
So how do projects that will carry a seventh of their forecast riders keep getting cleared? The answer sits in a single number: 14%.
The Metro Rail Policy 2017 requires every new metro to clear a 14% Economic Internal Rate of Return, the EIRR, which is a measure of a project's wider payoff to society, counting things like fuel saved, time saved and pollution avoided.7 Clear 14% and central funding is unlocked. Miss it and the project stalls.
Here is the perverse bit. A metro is a prestige project for any state government, a visible symbol of arrival. So the incentive is not to test whether that 14% is real. It is to produce a Detailed Project Report, the DPR, whose numbers clear 14% by construction.
- The ridership forecast is the lever. Push projected riders up, the benefits stream rises, and the EIRR clears the bar.
- The tool used to push it is the decades-old "four-step" transport model, built for car-based Western cities and a poor fit for dense, mixed-use, informal Indian ones.
- These models routinely assume population and jobs will bloom along the corridor, that last-mile connectivity will be seamless, and that commuters priced out by fares will somehow ride anyway.
The result is a forecast that was never going to hold, dressed up as a hurdle cleared.
This gap between the number on the DPR and the number on the platform is exactly the kind of thread I keep pulling at, and it is the sort of thing we go back and forth on in the BharatNama WhatsApp community, where I share a smaller India deep-dive like this with thousands of readers every morning (t.ly/h2jq1).
India's commute does not fit the metro
There is a deeper mismatch underneath the bad maths, and it may be the most important fact in this whole story.
Metros are built for long, high-capacity, arterial journeys. Indian cities do not travel that way.
- IIT-Delhi's work on urban travel found that in megacities like Delhi and Mumbai, nearly 35% of residents commute less than 5 km a day.8
- Across large, dense Indian cities, only about 17% of trips are longer than 10 km.8
- For a 5 km hop, a two-wheeler, an auto or a brisk walk beats a metro on time, cost and convenience every time.
Then there is affordability. The metro is simply too dear for the people who lean on public transport most.
- IIT-Delhi estimated that a household earning ₹12,000 a month can afford only about ₹26 per person a day on travel, while a metro trip can cost ₹40 or more.8
- On that maths, only a tenth to a fifth of an average city's population can actually afford to use the metro daily.8
This is why the humble bus quietly out-carries the metro in city after city, despite decades of underinvestment. In Bengaluru the metro handles a low single-digit share of daily trips while buses carry many times more. India built a Ferrari for a city that mostly needs bicycles and buses.
The farebox trap
Now the money. Indian metros were financed almost entirely on the assumption that ticket sales would carry them. When the riders do not show, the whole model buckles.
- Passenger fares make up the overwhelming share of revenue: roughly 89% in Mumbai, 79% in Bengaluru, and around 42% to 48% in Delhi and Chennai.5
- Construction costs, meanwhile, have roughly doubled: from about ₹180 crore per km in Delhi's early phases to ₹250 to ₹400 crore per km now, with Mumbai's elevated line near ₹389 crore and Bengaluru around ₹327 crore.4 9
- Underground stretches cost far more again.
Put a collapsing revenue line beside a soaring cost line and you get permanent deficits.
- Even Bengaluru's Namma Metro, whose revenue has now crossed ₹1,000 crore, is watching its losses widen, not shrink.10
- Once debt servicing and interest are added, the big networks post net losses year after year.
A metro that carries a third of its forecast riders cannot cover its costs from fares. That is not an operational hiccup to be patched with better feeder buses. It is arithmetic.
And notice what this does to the private sector's appetite. If the state, with its patient capital and cheap debt, cannot make the farebox work, no private operator will step in to take the demand risk. That single fact quietly kills the idea that metros can be financed on ticket sales at all.
India against the world, and against itself
Here is the benchmark that reframes everything. The most profitable metro on earth barely lives off fares at all.
Hong Kong's MTR is the model. It takes no government operating subsidy, runs at 99.9% on-time, carries about 5.5mn journeys a day, keeps fares low, and still turns a healthy profit.11
- In 2025 the MTR posted a net profit of about $1.9bn.12
- Of that, roughly $1.4bn, about three-quarters, came not from trains but from property development.12
- Its fares cover more than 100% of operating costs, but the real money is in the "Rail plus Property" model: build the line, capture the land-value uplift it creates, and plough it back.13
The MTR is, in effect, a property developer that happens to run trains. India's metros are trains that happen to lose money.
And India set against itself is just as stark.
- Delhi at ~47% of forecast, the national best.2
- Kochi ~14.5%, Hyderabad ~15.2%, Lucknow ~8.6%, Jaipur ~7.6%.5
- Kanpur as low as ~2% at one point.6
The same DPR methodology and the same 14% hurdle produced a roughly 20x spread between the best network and the worst. That spread is the tell: these were never demand forecasts, they were approval documents.
Sell the land, not just the ticket
The lesson from Hong Kong is not "run trains better". It is "capture the value the train creates". When a metro opens, the land around every station jumps in value. In Hong Kong the state grants that land to the MTR at pre-rail prices, the MTR develops it with private partners, and the uplift funds the railway.13 In India, that windfall goes to whoever already owns the plot next to the station.
India has tried to import this, through Transit-Oriented Development and Value Capture Finance written into the 2017 policy. It has mostly failed in execution, for reasons that are structural, not accidental.16
- Land in India is privately owned and fragmented, so no agency can quietly bank land at pre-rail prices the way Hong Kong's state does.
- Floor Space Index, the cap on how much can be built on a plot, is kept low: roughly 1.2 to 4 in Delhi and 1.5 to 3.25 in Bengaluru, against transit-node norms above 10 globally.16
- Governance is split three ways between the metro corporation, the municipal body and the development authority, so no single agency can rezone, densify and monetise.
Hyderabad is the cautionary tale, and it just got sharper. The L&T Hyderabad Metro was built as the world's largest metro PPP, with real estate meant to carry about half of revenue.14 Ridership came in near 15% of forecast, the fare pillar collapsed, and by late 2025 L&T was exiting the project entirely, with the Telangana government stepping in to take it over.15 Even a well-run private developer could not make the farebox maths work.
So what is portable? The principle, above all: legislate land-value capture before the line is sanctioned, not after. Acquire station-area land at pre-rail prices, give metro agencies real authority over that land, lift FSI sharply around stations, and put one Unified Metropolitan Transport Authority in charge so buses feed the metro instead of competing with it. What is not portable is Hong Kong's all-powerful state landlord. India has to engineer the same outcome through law and coordination, not ownership.
This shift, from thinking of a metro as a train set to thinking of it as a real-estate engine, is the argument I find myself making again and again, and it is one of the threads I dig into with readers in the BharatNama WhatsApp community every day (t.ly/h2jq1).
What to watch
- Whether the Telangana government's takeover of Hyderabad Metro leans harder on TOD land monetisation, or simply absorbs the losses into the state budget.
- Whether any state legislates pre-rail land acquisition and higher station-area FSI as a funding tool, rather than a planning afterthought.
- Whether the next wave of DPRs is stress-tested on realistic ridership, or keeps clearing 14% on paper.
- Whether cities finally fund the humble bus and feeder network that actually carries the short trips, instead of starving it to build rail.
India has learned to build metros. It has not yet learned that a metro is a real-estate business that happens to move people.

I keep coming back to one number, and it unsettles me every time.
For every hundred units of electricity India pushes into its distribution grid, it collects money for only about eighty-five. The rest, nearly one in seven units, vanishes before a single rupee is billed against it.1
Now here is the part that should stop you. China, running a grid larger than India's across a country every bit as vast, loses barely one unit in twenty-three.3
That is not a rounding error. It is a chasm. And I have become convinced the reason it exists is not the reason most people assume. This is not fundamentally a story about old wires and weak transformers. It is a story about who the state chooses to bill, and who it quietly chooses not to.
What the number actually measures
The metric here is called AT&C loss, aggregate technical and commercial loss. It is the single cleanest gauge of how well a power distribution company, a DISCOM, actually runs. It bundles two very different things into one figure:
- Technical loss. The electricity that genuinely disappears as heat in wires and transformers over long distances. This is physics, and every grid on earth pays this tax.
- Commercial loss. The electricity that is delivered but never billed, or billed and never collected. This is theft, unmetered supply, and collection failure. This is not physics. This is governance.
India's national AT&C loss came in at 15.04% in FY25, down from 15.97% a year earlier.1 That is real, and it is the best reading India has posted in over a decade, down from nearly 25% around FY13 and 21.9% as recently as FY21.5
There is even a genuine milestone buried in the FY25 data. For the first time ever, India's DISCOMs as a whole turned a profit after tax at the all-India level.5 After decades of red ink, that deserves to be said plainly.
But hold the celebration next to the benchmark. China's State Grid, the largest utility on the planet, runs a comprehensive line loss of just 4.4%.3 India, even at its best-ever number, loses more than three times as much of its power. The gap is the whole point of knowing where you stand.
The physics is not the problem
Here is the thing. If India's losses were mostly technical, this would be an engineering bill: heavier conductors, better transformers, high-voltage lines closer to homes. Expensive, but solvable with capital.
They are not mostly technical.
When a well-run grid pays its physics tax, technical losses land somewhere between 3% and 6%. India's pure transmission and distribution loss sits closer to 19%,4 and its AT&C loss at 15% is dominated by the commercial layer sitting on top of the physics: power that is stolen, hooked, unmetered, or simply never collected.
That distinction matters enormously, because the two halves of the number ask for completely different fixes:
- The technical half wants money and steel.
- The commercial half wants meters, audits, and the political will to disconnect a non-paying consumer.
China's 4.4% is essentially all physics. India's 15% is physics plus a vast, off-the-books subsidy that nobody will admit is a subsidy. That is why I keep saying this is an administrative choice, not an infrastructure sentence.
The agricultural alibi
So why does the commercial leak persist, year after year, when it would bankrupt any private business inside a quarter?
The honest answer sits in the fields. After the Green Revolution, states raced to electrify rural India and win the farm vote. Rather than hand farmers transparent cash support, they gave them free or flat-rate, unmetered electricity for irrigation pumps. It was popular, it protected vulnerable growers, and it quietly destroyed the grid's accounting.
Once a large slice of the grid is legally unmetered, a convenient blind spot opens up:
- A substation can measure exactly how much power flows out onto a rural feeder.
- But if the farm connections downstream are unmetered, nobody can reconcile what was actually consumed against what was billed.
- So theft by residential, commercial, and industrial users on that same feeder gets quietly booked as "agricultural consumption".
In other words, unmetered farm supply is not just a subsidy. It is the ledger where a lot of ordinary theft goes to hide. Field research has long found power theft is most intense precisely in India's most agricultural districts, which is exactly what you would expect if the farm category is doing double duty as a cover story.
This state-versus-state, feeder-versus-feeder detective work is the kind of thread I love pulling apart, and it is the sort of thing I go back and forth on with readers every morning in my BharatNama WhatsApp community, where I share a smaller India deep-dive like this daily (t.ly/h2jq1).
What the leak costs the exchequer
None of this is free. A DISCOM that cannot recover the cost of the power it buys eventually defaults on the generators and lenders it owes, and the hole lands on the state's books.
The balance sheets are still brutal, even after every bailout:
- Accumulated losses of India's distribution utilities stood at ₹6.92 lakh crore as of March 2024.2
- Their combined net worth was negative, at around ₹1.73 lakh crore.2
- Total borrowings climbed to ₹7.52 lakh crore, up from ₹6.84 lakh crore a year earlier.2
- Outstanding loans to the distribution sector had reached about ₹5 lakh crore by December 2025, nearly 40% of the entire loan books of state-backed lenders PFC and REC.6
The recent good news is real but fragile. The gap between what power costs to supply and what utilities earn, the ACS-ARR gap, has narrowed to just 6 paise a unit in FY25 from 89 paise in FY21.6 The trouble is that much of that improvement came from the centre forcing states to clear subsidy backlogs and pay up, not from organic efficiency. The liabilities did not vanish; they moved from the generators to the state-backed banks.
And it drags on sovereign finances directly. Power purchase costs eat roughly three-fourths of a typical state's cost of supply, and interest alone consumes more than 10% of it in states like Rajasthan, Tamil Nadu, Andhra Pradesh, and Jharkhand.6
The Chinese playbook: total visibility
Now to the country on the other side of the gap, because the lesson is instructive even where it is not portable.
China's State Grid faced 5% to 15% losses across many regions in the early 2000s, not unlike India today. It has since driven overall grid losses down from 6.8% in 2015 to 4.4% in 2024,3 and it did so less by laying copper than by building an architecture of total measurement.
The core moves, all from State Grid's own reporting:
- It wired the grid with over 650mn smart meters, from ultra-high-voltage lines down to individual homes, into a single cloud ledger it calls the "One Data Chain", collecting readings at 15-minute intervals across hundreds of millions of end-users.3
- On top of that data it runs an AI "loss engine" that continuously reconciles power dispatched against power billed, flags anomalies that signal theft or tampering, and pushes recovery orders straight to field crews without waiting for managerial sign-off.3
- Crucially, it ties the pay and promotion of some 13,000 county-level managers directly to line-loss targets, ranked publicly every month. A manager cannot blame "technical constraints" when the algorithm can see the leak.3
The payoff has been enormous: State Grid says it cut its high-loss lines from 44% of the network to under 1%, saving roughly 236 TWh of electricity, an efficiency gain worth close to $12bn over 2016 to 2024.3
Where India stands, against the world and against itself
Set the numbers side by side and the picture is stark, but the more revealing comparison is India against India.
Against the world:
- China (State Grid): 4.4% grid loss.3
- Global average, per the World Bank, sits at roughly 8% of output.4
- India: 15.04% AT&C, and about 19% on pure T&D.1 4
Against itself, and this is the part that proves the loss is a choice:
- Gujarat's DGVCL posted AT&C losses of just 1.31%, among the most efficient utilities anywhere on earth.11
- Delhi's private DISCOM Tata Power-DDL ran 5.54% in FY25, down from 53% when it took over the network in 2002.7
- The national average is 15%.1
- Punjab, meanwhile, was still bleeding around 19% in FY25, having installed zero of its 9mn sanctioned smart meters.5
A single country contains both a 1.3% utility and a 19% one. That roughly fifteen-fold spread is not explained by geography or weather, because these utilities serve the same kind of consumers under the same union rules. It is explained by governance.
The private turnaround India already has
This is why I find the "India is just structurally leaky" argument so unconvincing. India has already solved this, at home, more than once.
Delhi is the textbook case. In 2002 the state-owned Delhi Vidyut Board was collapsing, billing barely 57% of the power it distributed, with aggregate losses of 45% to 60%. The distribution business was unbundled and handed to private joint ventures, Tata Power-DDL and the two BSES DISCOMs, under a hard contractual mandate to slash losses.
The results speak for themselves:
- Tata Power-DDL: from 53% AT&C in 2002 to 5.54% in FY25.7
- The BSES DISCOMs settled into the mid-6% range on the same trajectory.
- Odisha, which privatised four DISCOMs, saw AT&C losses fall by 11 to 16 percentage points between FY20 and FY25.12
Across India, where public and private utilities operate side by side, the private ones run AT&C losses about 8 percentage points lower.6 SBICAPS has estimated that privatising DISCOMs in 11 viable states, including Uttar Pradesh, Punjab, Haryana and Bihar, could cut their combined fiscal deficit from about 3.5% to 3.0% of state GDP, with individual states gaining anywhere from 25 to 281 basis points of headroom.6 That aligns almost perfectly with the fiscal consolidation the 16th Finance Commission is pushing for.
The mechanism is not magic. Private capital demands cost recovery, cost recovery demands metering, and metering demands that theft finally be treated as theft.
Can India copy the playbook?
So what actually transfers, and what does not?
The technology is the easy part, and India is buying it. The Revamped Distribution Sector Scheme (RDSS), a ₹3.04 lakh crore programme running to FY26, is built on exactly China's logic: meter the feeder, the transformer, and the consumer, then let automated energy audits pinpoint the leak. It mandates about 23 crore prepaid smart meters, of which roughly ₹1.31 lakh crore is earmarked for metering alone.8
The catch is that a meter is only as good as the will to act on what it sees:
- As of early 2026, only about 5.83 crore smart meters were installed, just 25% of the target, and the deadline has already been pushed back two years.8
- The rollout is patchy, strong in reform-minded states, stalled where it matters most.
- Where consumers or politicians resist, as in Gujarat's billing backlash or Punjab's total non-start, the capital spent on meters earns nothing.
This is the honest limit of the China lesson. State Grid's closed-loop accountability works because a county manager cannot claim a political exemption. India's linemen get assaulted attempting disconnections, and local leaders still demand illegal connections stay live to keep a vote bank happy. The hardware is importable. The political will to disconnect a defaulter is not, and that is the real frontier.
This is the tension I keep circling in these deep-dives, and if you want the daily version, the running thread on India's political economy, do come join the BharatNama WhatsApp community (t.ly/h2jq1).
What to watch
A few concrete markers over the coming quarters:
- The RDSS meter count. Whether installations move meaningfully past 25% before the extended deadline, and whether laggards like Punjab and Tamil Nadu start metering agricultural feeders at all.
- Fresh privatisation moves. Watch UP, which has floated plans to privatise its worst DISCOMs, as the next big test of the Delhi-Odisha template.
- Whether the FY25 profit holds. The first-ever all-India DISCOM profit5 is fragile; if subsidy payments slip again, the ACS-ARR gap will reopen.
- The demand backdrop. India just met a record peak of about 256 GW in April 2026,9 and crossed 500 GW of installed capacity with more than half from non-fossil sources.10 A leaky, insolvent distribution grid is the weakest link under all of it.
The one line
India's grid does not leak because it lacks wires; it leaks because, for decades, it has been cheaper for the state to look away than to send the bill.

Here is a number that has stayed with me all week. In 2024, India lost roughly 247bn potential hours of work to extreme heat.1
That is not a projection for some distant, air-conditioned future. That is last year.
Put a price on those hours and it comes to about $194bn of income that simply never got earned.1 To give that scale, it is larger than the annual budget of almost any Indian state, evaporated into the afternoon air.
And the part that unsettles me most is this: almost none of it shows up in our official numbers.
What we are actually talking about
Let me set the scene, because the structure matters more than any single figure.
About 75% of India's workforce, roughly 380mn people, works in heat-exposed jobs: farming, construction, brick kilns, salt pans, street vending, delivery riding.2 This is not a fringe. This is the real economy.
- Heat-exposed work produces about half of India's GDP.2
- It drives about 30% of India's GDP growth.2
So when a farmer in May slows to half pace, or a rider shelters in the shade for twenty minutes every hour, that is not a human-interest story. That is the supply side of the economy quietly shrinking.
The baseline tells you the direction of travel. India's heat-driven labour losses in 2024 were 124% higher than the average across the 1990s.1 We have more than doubled the damage in a single generation.
On average, each Indian lost about 419 hours of safe working capacity to heat last year.1 Think of it as five working weeks, gone, per person, unbooked anywhere.
The drag is now structural, not seasonal
For years, heat was treated as an event. A bad fortnight in May, some headlines, then the monsoon arrives and everyone moves on. That framing is now simply wrong.
The economists have started saying so plainly. Without serious adaptation, heat is projected to shave 0.5 to 1 percentage point off India's potential annual GDP growth, on a recurring basis.3 For an economy straining to grow at 7 to 8%, quietly surrendering up to a full point to weather you can forecast but not yet manage is enormous.
And the forward projections are worse than the present:
- McKinsey estimates 2.5% to 4.5% of India's GDP will be at risk by 2030 from lost labour hours, worth $150-250bn.2
- The World Bank lands in the same band, up to 4.5% of GDP.3
- The ILO projects India will account for 34mn of the world's 80mn heat-related job losses by 2030.4
Sit with that last one for a second. India has about 18% of the world's people, yet is projected to absorb roughly 43% of the world's heat-related job losses.4 That is the benchmark I would pin to a wall in every ministry.
The losses are concentrated, not spread evenly:
- Agriculture took 66% of India's heat-related labour-hour losses in 2024.1
- Construction took another 20%.1
Agriculture also shows how the damage compounds. In the 2022 heatwave, wheat yields fell 10 to 15%, cutting the crop from about 110mn to 99mn tonnes and pushing the government into an export ban.5 Lower labour capacity, lower yields, higher food inflation, and then the real wages of the very workers who lost the hours fall further still. It is a loop, not a straight line.
This kind of feedback loop, where a labour number, a food-inflation number and a real-wage number turn out to be the same story wearing three hats, is exactly the sort of thread I keep pulling apart in the BharatNama WhatsApp community, where I share a smaller India deep-dive like this one with thousands of readers every morning (t.ly/h2jq1).

The frontline, where the body gives out first
The averages hide brutal margins. Between 80 and 90% of Indian workers are informal, with no paid breaks, no cooling, no health cover, no financial buffer for a lost day.6
Study the extreme trades and you see how thin the survivability line has become. In India's salt pans and brick kilns, researchers record wet-bulb globe temperatures that sit above the internationally accepted safe threshold for the workload, day after day, with many workers surviving a full shift on barely a litre of water.6 At that point the heart is spending its energy cooling the body rather than doing the job, so output falls even when the worker is standing right there.
The gendered version of this is worse, and more current than most people realise. A 2026 assessment found extreme heat now costs women informal workers about $57bn a year globally, with Indian cities among the hardest hit.7 Women make up a fifth of urban heat deaths in the cities studied, while carrying both outdoor paid work and indoor unpaid work over a stove.7 Roughly 81% of India's working women are in informal jobs, so they sit at the sharp end of every number above.8
And this is spilling into the new economy, not just the old one. India logged more than 40,000 suspected heatstroke cases in 2024, and a growing share of the exposed are gig and platform workers, the delivery riders and cab drivers we now treat as invisible infrastructure.9
The blind spot, a brand-new GDP series that still cannot see heat
Here is the part I find genuinely remarkable, and it is the heart of today's edition.
On 27 February 2026, India rolled out a brand-new GDP series, shifting the base year to 2022-23 and finally adopting "double deflation", which strips price effects out of inputs and outputs separately for a cleaner read on real growth.10 It is a real, overdue upgrade.
Yet even this rebuilt machine cannot see heat. And the reason is subtle.
The output of the informal half of the economy is estimated by leaning on the Periodic Labour Force Survey, the PLFS, which is the government's main employment survey. The PLFS captures "hours actually worked" in a reference week.
But "hours worked" is a measure of presence and duration. It says nothing about intensity or pace.
- A construction worker on site for nine hours, taking undocumented micro-breaks in the shade to avoid collapse, still reports a full day.
- A field labourer working at 30% slower pace in 44-degree heat still logs the same hours.
The national accounts then multiply those intact-looking hours by a baseline productivity weight to build value added. So the model quietly assumes optimal output was produced. Heat rarely destroys the job outright, which is what a survey would catch as unemployment. It destroys the productivity inside the job, which the survey cannot catch at all.
The result is a kind of phantom GDP: an economy that records a full day of work while the worker doing it produced markedly less. We have upgraded the ruler, but it still cannot measure the thing that is shrinking.
The law just got weaker, not stronger
While the statistics miss the problem, the regulation is actively retreating from it. This is the twist that should worry a policymaker most.
On 21 November 2025, India brought its four new labour codes into force, consolidating a sprawl of older laws.11 The Occupational Safety, Health and Working Conditions Code is now the governing law for workplace safety.
- Under the old Factories Act of 1948, states like Maharashtra, Tamil Nadu and Gujarat had notified hard wet-bulb limits, often 30°C, beyond which a factory was legally unsafe.9
- The new OSH Code specifies no temperature, humidity or ventilation threshold at all, even for formal factories, and centralises the power to set such standards.12
- Gig and platform workers, the group most exposed to outdoor heat, are left out of the OSH Code entirely and parked under the Social Security Code, which carries no occupational-hazard mandate.9
In plain terms, we replaced enforceable, inspectable numbers with a vague duty to keep conditions "adequate", and handed heat safety back to employer discretion just as the heat got worse.12 Unions from the app-based transport and warehouse workforce are now demanding what the law removed: paid cooling breaks of 20 minutes every two hours on heatwave days, a heat-welfare fund, and protection from being penalised by an algorithm for stopping in the sun.9
Where India stands, against the world and against itself
Benchmark it, because the gaps are the whole point.
India versus the world:
- India's 247bn labour hours lost in 2024 make it one of the most heat-exposed large economies on earth, and its 419 hours lost per person is far above the level in temperate advanced economies.1
- Half of India's GDP comes from heat-exposed work; in a rich economy that share is a fraction of it, which is why the same heatwave is a macro event here and a nuisance there.2
- India is set to carry 43% of the world's heat-linked job losses with 18% of its people.4
India versus India, which is the sharper mirror:
- Kerala has used its own Minimum Wages Act to mandate a rest ban for outdoor workers through the 12pm to 3pm window on hot days, and has issued guidance covering delivery riders.9
- At the other end, a 2024 assessment of nine high-risk cities found several, including Gwalior and Ludhiana, running heat response with weak or absent long-term plans, while Haryana maps industrial hubs like Gurugram and Faridabad into its highest heat-risk zone.13
- The nine cities studied, home to just over 11% of urban India, almost all did the cheap emergency things, water and shade and hospital readiness, and almost none did the structural things: cooling for workers, greening, heat insurance.13
The gap between what Kerala mandates and what Gwalior does not is exactly the state-versus-state spread we go back and forth on in the BharatNama group, where a quieter India deep-dive lands every single day (t.ly/h2jq1).

What India can learn
The good news is that a cheap, working model already exists inside India. After a 2010 heatwave killed an estimated 1,344 people in a single week, Ahmedabad built South Asia's first Heat Action Plan in 2013: early warning, public outreach, trained hospitals, water and cooling points. It is credited with avoiding roughly 1,100 deaths a year.14
But Ahmedabad saves lives; it does not protect output, and it does not fix the law. For that, look abroad at the one thing India just deleted: enforceable thresholds.
- Spain, after workers died in the fields, amended its safety law in 2023 so that authorities can prohibit outdoor work outright when the weather agency issues a red or orange heat alert.15
- The United States has proposed a federal heat rule covering about 36mn workers, tying mandatory water, shade and paid rest breaks to a defined heat-index trigger.16
The transferable lesson is not "copy Spain". India's federal structure, informal labour and thin state capacity make a blanket ban hard. The portable idea is narrower and cheaper: a clear, humidity-aware temperature trigger that automatically switches on paid rest, water and shade, written into the OSH Code rules and extended to gig workers. India already knows how to run the warning system. It has simply chosen, for now, not to make the protection binding.
What to watch
- Whether the Central Government notifies actual wet-bulb or heat-index thresholds in the OSH Code rules, or leaves "adequate" as the standard.
- Whether MoSPI or the NSO builds any heat or productivity-intensity adjustment into the new GVA method, rather than trusting hours-worked alone.
- Whether more states follow Kerala with legally binding rest-hour orders before the 2026 summer.
- The next Lancet Countdown print, to see whether the 247bn-hour loss was a peak or a new floor.
Heat is no longer a weather story for India. It is a labour-supply story, an inflation story and a measurement story, all at once, and right now we are managing the one part of it that is easiest to count.

Here is a number that should bother anyone who believes in the "Make in India, sell to the world" story. India sells roughly $5bn of goods online to the rest of the planet each year1. China sells close to $300bn2. That is a gap of nearly sixty to one, between two countries that both call themselves factories to the world.
This is quite unnerving for me. We have the sellers, the products, and the ambition. What we have not had is the machine that moves a handmade lamp from Moradabad to a doorstep in Munich without the maker drowning in shipping forms.
On 23 July 2026, India tried to buy that machine off the shelf. It changed a rule it had guarded for almost a decade3.
What actually changed
The government issued Press Note 3 (2026 Series), and it does one surgical thing. It allows 100% foreign direct investment in the inventory-based model of e-commerce, but exclusively for exporting goods made in India3.
To see why that is a big deal, you need the one distinction that has governed Indian e-commerce since 2016.
- The marketplace model. The platform is a matchmaker. It connects an independent seller to a buyer, takes a commission, and never owns the goods. Foreign money has been allowed here, up to 100%, for years4.
- The inventory model. The platform buys the goods itself, owns them on its balance sheet, and sells them directly. For any company with foreign equity, this was banned4.
That ban was not an accident. It was a wall built to protect millions of kirana stores from well-funded foreign giants buying stock in bulk and undercutting everyone on price4. Press Note 3 of 2016 drew that wall, and it held.
Press Note 3 of 2026 cuts a single door into it. Foreign platforms can now own inventory, on one condition: the goods must be exported, not sold to an Indian consumer3. The compliance is tied to the Foreign Trade Policy 2023 and FEMA rules, so it sits inside the existing export plumbing rather than beside it3.
How the new machine is meant to work
Strip away the jargon and the mechanism is elegant.
A foreign platform can now set up a separate, ring-fenced Indian export company. That company behaves like a principal buyer, not a middleman.
- It buys textiles, handicrafts, auto parts or wellness products outright, in rupees, from an Indian factory or an artisan cluster.
- The maker gets paid on delivery inside India, so the crushing wait for cross-border payments and the currency risk simply vanish for them.
- The platform then swallows all the friction: freight, customs, foreign warehousing, marketing abroad, and returns from a customer in Ohio or Abu Dhabi.
This is the interesting bit. The policy quietly separates where the sale happens from who owns the stock. The Indian maker gets a domestic transaction. The platform gets a global one. That is the whole trick.
And the timing is not random. The government wants total exports to hit $2 trillion by 2030-315, with e-commerce exports alone climbing from ~$5bn today to a $200bn target, which it frames as roughly a tenth of the projected global online-export market1. You do not get from $5bn to $200bn by asking small sellers to fill out more shipping labels. You get there by handing the job to whoever already runs a planet-sized logistics network.
Why India is copying China, on purpose
The honest way to read this policy is as India studying its rival's homework.
China did not build the world's largest cross-border trade engine through millions of tiny sellers each battling customs alone. It did it through the inventory model. Platforms like Shein and Temu buy stock outright from dense manufacturing clusters, predict demand with data, pool freight, and ship at a scale that collapses the per-unit cost.
The results are not close.
- China's cross-border e-commerce trade was worth ~$375bn in its latest full year, with the export half alone at ~$300bn, growing nearly 17% a year2.
- India's online exports sit at ~$5bn1.
This state-versus-rival gap is exactly the kind of thing I keep pulling apart, and it is the sort of thread we go back and forth on in the BharatNama WhatsApp community, where I share a smaller India deep-dive like this with thousands of readers every morning (t.ly/h2jq1).
There is a second reason the timing works in India's favour. As global brands hunt for a "China plus one" supplier to de-risk their supply chains, India suddenly has both the factories and, now, the legal permission for a foreign platform to buy from them at scale. The door is open exactly when buyers are looking for a second room.
The giants have already put numbers on it
You can measure how much foreign platforms wanted this by how fast they moved once it landed.
- Amazon runs its Global Selling programme since 2015. It has onboarded over 200,000 Indian exporters across 28 states and 200-plus cities, and it crossed $20bn in cumulative exports from India, hitting its 2025 goal early. Its new target is $80bn in cumulative exports by 20306.
- Small towns are already in the data. Karur in Tamil Nadu, a home-textiles cluster, did about $147mn of exports through the platform in a single year6.
- Walmart, which owns Flipkart, has committed to sourcing $10bn of Indian goods every year by 20277. It has already sourced around $30bn from India over two decades7.
The knock-on effect is showing up in warehouses before the goods even move. India's industrial and warehousing demand jumped 22% year on year in the first quarter of 2026, a four-year high, with about 11mn sq ft leased across the top eight cities8.
- Delhi NCR took the largest share at 28%, followed by Chennai at 21%8.
- E-commerce and automobile firms together drove 32% of the leasing, and third-party logistics players nearly a third of it, with their activity running 1.8 times the level of a year earlier8.
Investor certainty is the quiet win here. As one tax adviser at EY put it, the note "removed uncertainty" and gave foreign investors policy predictability, because the old rules were silent on whether inventory-led exports were even allowed9.
Where India stands: against the world, and against itself
BharatNama's job is to place India next to something. Two comparisons matter here.
India against the world (online exports, latest available):
- China: ~$300bn, export cross-border e-commerce2
- India: ~$5bn1
- The gap: ~60 times, which is the single number this whole policy exists to shrink
India against itself:
- The build-out is clustering, not spreading. Delhi NCR (28%) and Chennai (21%) alone soaked up nearly half of Q1 warehousing demand8, while the tier-two and tier-three makers the policy is meant to lift sit far from those hubs.
- India's overall FDI held up well through this, with inflows of about $59bn in FY26, up 18%10, so the country is not short of foreign capital. It has been short of the kind of foreign operation that owns stock and moves it out.
The story India tells itself is of a lamp-maker in Moradabad reaching Munich. The infrastructure, for now, is being poured in Gurugram and Sriperumbudur. Both things are true at once, and BharatNama exists to hold them together rather than pick one.
What India can actually learn from China
The temptation is to say "India should just copy China". The reality is more careful.
What China actually did was sequence three things:
- It set up over 165 cross-border e-commerce pilot zones with simplified customs and tax rebates.
- It built dense bonded warehousing so stock could sit near ports, cleared for export.
- It let platforms own inventory and integrate logistics end to end, from factory to foreign doorstep.
Press Note 3 of 2026 is India reaching for the third lever. The first two are the harder, less glamorous ones, and they are where the real work sits.
- What transfers: the inventory-led export model, bonded warehousing near ports, and a single foreign platform absorbing logistics risk for a scattered supplier base. This policy makes all three legal.
- What does not transfer easily: China's manufacturing density and logistics velocity took two decades and enormous state spending to build. India cannot legislate that into existence. A rule change opens the lane; it does not lay the road.
The lesson is that the FDI note is necessary but nowhere near sufficient. Without cheaper freight, faster customs and export incentives that match China's, India gets the permission slip without the performance.
The risk nobody at DPIIT can fully price
Now let me be honest about the other side, because a BharatNama edition that only cheers is not doing its job.
The sharpest critique comes from the Global Trade Research Initiative. Its founder, Ajay Srivastava, makes two arguments worth sitting with11.
- India gave away a negotiating chip for free. Access to India's vast digital and retail market is one of the biggest cards India holds in trade talks, especially with the United States. Srivastava argues this concession should have been traded inside a deal for lower US tariffs on Indian goods, not handed over unilaterally in advance11.
- The inventory model hands the platform the whip. Once a platform owns the goods rather than just listing them, it has every incentive to push its own stock, read the data on which Indian products sell best, and either source those directly or launch cheaper own-label versions. Independent sellers and traditional export houses get squeezed out of the middle11.
Then there is the fear on the ground. Traders' bodies, led by figures like CAIT's Praveen Khandelwal, call this a Trojan horse12. Their worry is simple: once foreign giants are allowed to own inventory locally "for exports", how do you stop that stock leaking into the domestic market, and how long before the lobbying to sell it to Indians too becomes irresistible12?
- CAIT has flagged that the current rules do not even mandate physical audits to check that export inventory stays separate from domestic stock12.
- Some in the trade body have gone further and demanded an outright rollback, arguing the change favours foreign platforms over Indian retailers and small exporters2.
This is where I keep landing, and it is the sort of policy trade-off we argue out in the BharatNama community rather than pretend is settled (t.ly/h2jq1). The enforcement problem is real: keeping one identical product legal-for-export and another legal-for-domestic, inside the same fungible supply chain, is an administrative nightmare. It works only if the customs-bonded, physically segregated, digitally tracked firewall actually holds. On paper it can. In a system this large, holding it is the whole game.
What to watch
- The fine print from DGFT. Watch for the operational directive on physical segregation, customs-bonded warehousing and GST refunds. That document decides whether the firewall is real or rhetorical.
- The first inventory-led export hubs. Track whether Amazon and Flipkart actually break ground on dedicated export warehouses near ports, and where.
- Any leakage case. The first proven instance of "export" stock turning up in the domestic market will be the political flashpoint that decides the policy's future.
- The US trade talks. Watch whether India extracts anything in return, or whether GTRI's "gave it away for free" warning proves right.
The one line
India has handed the world's biggest platforms the keys to its export engine, and the only thing standing between a genuine trade breakthrough and a backdoor into the kirana store is a firewall that has never been tested at this scale.

I think India just made one of the most quietly revealing decisions of the decade, and almost nobody is talking about why.
We are going to build a giant urea plant. A 2mn-tonne one. But not in India. In Russia.1
In December 2025, three Indian fertiliser firms, the state-owned RCF and NFL and the cooperative-sector Indian Potash, signed a memorandum with Russia's Uralchem to build a roughly $2bn urea complex at Tolyatti, in the Samara region.1 2 The ammonia will come from Togliattiazot next door, and the urea is meant to sail almost entirely to Indian farms.3
Here is what stopped me. India is the largest urea importer on earth. We are also, this very year, spending public money to become self-sufficient in urea at home.4 And yet the single biggest new bet we have placed is a plant on another country's soil.
That is not a contradiction. Once you see why, it tells you something uncomfortable about where India actually stands.
Let me set the scene with the numbers, because they are the whole story.
- India consumes about 40mn tonnes of urea a year.4
- We produce roughly 30mn tonnes at home, from 33-odd plants.4
- The remaining ~10mn tonnes, about a quarter of what we use, is imported.4
Urea matters more here than anywhere else. Over 76% of all the fertiliser India made in 2024-25 was urea.5 It is the cheap nitrogen that keeps the wheat and rice coming. It is also politically radioactive, which is why a 45-kg bag has been frozen at ₹242 for the farmer for years.4
The catch sits under all of it. Urea is, in plain terms, solidified natural gas. You make ammonia from gas, then turn ammonia into urea, and gas is both the raw material and the fuel. It works out to 60-80% of the cost of every tonne.4 6
So the real question behind fertiliser security is not "where do we build the factory". It is "where is the gas".
And that is exactly where India is exposed.
We do not have enough gas of our own. Our fertiliser plants lean heavily on imported LNG, which has run as high as 63% of the sector's gas use.6 Imported gas is dear and violently unstable.
- In early 2022, spot LNG spiked to around $36 per unit.6
- Even in calmer times, delivered gas to Indian urea plants sits near $10-15 per unit.6
- India imports roughly half of the LNG it burns, much of it through the Strait of Hormuz.4
Russia is the mirror image. It sits on the largest gas reserves on the planet, its regulated gas costs low single digits, and since Europe stopped buying, a lot of that gas has nowhere to go. Stranded gas is cheap gas.
Now the Tolyatti choice makes sense. Togliattiazot is one of the world's biggest ammonia makers, and for decades it exported through a pipeline to the Black Sea that ran via Ukraine. That pipeline has been shut since the war began. So Russia is sitting on world-scale, low-cost ammonia with no easy buyer, and India walks in as exactly that buyer.
Read plainly, the deal is this. India is not really importing urea. India is importing Russia's cheap gas, in a solid form our farmers can spread on a field.
This shift in who feeds India is the kind of thread I keep pulling at in the BharatNama WhatsApp group, where I share a smaller India deep-dive like this with thousands of readers every morning (t.ly/h2jq1).
To feel how far we have travelled, rewind the tape.
At Independence, India barely made any nitrogen fertiliser and imported almost all of it. The Green Revolution of the late 1960s was built on subsidised urea, and India spent the next fifty years building a domestic industry that now makes ~30mn tonnes a year. That is a genuine achievement, and it is why the import share is a quarter, not three-quarters.
But the arc is now bending the wrong way. Because gas is the binding constraint, and India's gas problem has not been solved, our import dependence for fertilisers overall is projected to climb past 41% in 2025-26.5
The map of who supplies us has also flipped in just a few years, and this is the part that should make policymakers sit up:
- The Gulf, once two-thirds of our urea, has fallen from about 75% of sourcing to 38%.5
- Russia and China together now account for nearly 40% of India's urea.5
- China's slice alone jumped from 1.5% in 2024-25 to about 20% in 2025-26.5
And this is not new for Russia. Its share of India's overall fertiliser imports has climbed from under 8% in 2017-18 to around 27% by 2023-24, one of the fastest supplier shifts in the trade.11
We have quietly swapped dependence on the Gulf for dependence on two countries with whom the strategic weather can change fast. China, remember, curbs its own urea exports whenever domestic prices threaten to rise, precisely to shield its farmers.7 A supplier that shuts the tap to protect its own is not a supplier you can build food security on. Which is exactly why a plant India part-owns starts to look less strange.
Now set India against the country that actually solved this. China.
China is largely self-sufficient in urea. It will make about 77mn tonnes in 2026 against demand near 66mn, and it exports the surplus.7 More importantly, it makes its urea a completely different way. About 78% of Chinese urea is made from coal, not gas.7
That one choice changes everything, because China has cheap domestic coal and does not have to import expensive gas. The result, in the same world market where India pays through the nose:
- Chinese urea sold at roughly $260 a tonne in early 2026.7
- The global benchmark at the same moment was around $740 a tonne.7
- That is close to a 3x cost advantage, sitting inside China's borders.7
So the benchmark is stark. China insulated its farmers by building self-sufficiency on a feedstock it owns. India cannot copy that, because we have neither China's coal-to-chemicals base nor cheap gas of our own. Our version of the same idea is to go and rent someone else's cheap feedstock. That is what Tolyatti is.
There is a second gap, and this one is inside India, not across a border.
Look at who pays for a bag of urea. The farmer pays ₹242. The government pays the rest, and the rest is enormous: the true cost of a bag runs ₹2,200 to ₹4,000, so the state absorbs the difference through subsidy.4 For 2025-26, the fertiliser subsidy is budgeted at ₹1.71 lakh crore.4
That gap does something quietly destructive. Because urea is kept artificially cheap while phosphorus and potassium are not, farmers pour on nitrogen. India's N:P:K use ratio has skewed to about 9.8:3:1, against a recommended 4:2:1.4 We are subsidising soil degradation.
And here is the sting for the Russia plant. Cheaper imported urea eases the subsidy bill in the short run, which is a real fiscal win. But it does nothing about the underlying distortion that makes us over-consume urea in the first place. We are treating the symptom, expensive gas, and leaving the disease, mispriced fertiliser, untouched.
So what can India actually learn here, given we cannot become China?
The honest answer is that self-sufficiency in the factory is not the same as self-sufficiency in energy, and India keeps conflating the two. In July 2026 the Cabinet cleared a new urea policy, NIPU-2026, to build 8 to 9 new plants at home and add about 10mn tonnes of capacity, on a 12-16% return-on-equity band.4 8 It is sensible industrial policy. But every one of those domestic plants will still run on gas India mostly has to import.4
That is the deeper lesson from both China and Russia. The country that wins fertiliser security is the one that owns its feedstock. China owns coal. Russia owns gas. India owns neither at the scale it needs. So India is doing two rational things at once:
- Building at home for physical resilience, so a blockade or a sanction cannot cut the supply entirely.
- Building in Russia for cheap economics, renting the feedstock advantage it cannot manufacture domestically.
There is even a name being floated for the second idea, "Making in Russia for India".9 It flips Make in India on its head: put the energy-hungry step where the energy is cheap, and ship the finished product home. For a product that is 80% embodied gas, that is not heresy. It might be the only honest arithmetic.
The precedent, worth remembering, is Oman. For two decades the OMIFCO plant, part-owned by IFFCO and Kribhco, has shipped its urea to India under a buy-back deal.10 Tolyatti is that model again, just bigger, and inside a sanctioned economy. This is exactly the sort of state-versus-state and country-versus-country contrast I dig into daily with the BharatNama community (t.ly/h2jq1), because the numbers rarely say what the headline says.
What I would watch over the next few quarters:
- Whether Tolyatti clears its final investment decision. As of now it is still a memorandum, and financing plus sourcing equipment inside a sanctioned Russia is genuinely hard. "Being built" is, for now, "agreed to be built".1 2
- The sanctions exposure. Uralchem's ownership has faced Western sanctions, and state-owned RCF and NFL taking equity carries real secondary-sanctions risk.1
- How the payment is settled. Watch for a rupee or rouble mechanism that quietly uses the rupee balances Russia has struggled to spend from our discounted-oil trade.
- Whether NIPU-2026 plants actually break ground, or whether cheap imported urea makes domestic capacity look unattractive all over again.4 8
India's fertiliser problem was never really about factories. It was always about gas, and we are answering a gas problem by borrowing someone else's cheapest molecule and calling it food security.

The state that reached India's future first
I keep coming back to one number, and it unsettles me a little every time. In 2026, 18.7% of Kerala's people are over the age of 60.1 For the country as a whole, that figure is roughly 11%.2
So Kerala is not a slightly older version of India. It is a different demographic country altogether, living a future the rest of us have only read about in reports.
And this year, Kerala did something no Indian state has ever done. It stopped treating old age as a corner of the social justice department and built an entire machinery around it: a dedicated Department of Senior Citizens' Welfare, a statutory Elderly Commission, and a separate, tracked Elderly Budget worth ₹46,236 crore, about 19.07% of the entire state budget.3
That is the number in the title, and it is the one I want to sit with you today. A state has just decided to route nearly a fifth of everything it spends towards its old. Not by accident. On purpose, in a printed budget document, the first of its kind in India.
What Kerala actually built
The pieces landed fast, and in a specific order. The Left government presented the Elderly Budget in January 2026.4 Then Kerala voted, the Congress-led UDF swept in with 102 of 140 seats, and the new government moved quickly on the institutions.5
Three things now exist that did not a year ago:
- A Department of Senior Citizens' Welfare, created on 20 May 2026 via Government Order 63/2026/GAD, the first dedicated department for the elderly set up by any state government in India.6 It is the nodal agency, meant to pull eldercare out of the silos it was scattered across (health, housing, local bodies) and run it as one.7
- The Kerala State Elderly Commission, set up under the Kerala State Elderly Commission Act, 2025 (Act 5 of 2025), a statutory, quasi-judicial body with the teeth to intervene on neglect, eviction, and economic abuse of the old.8
- The Elderly Budget itself, a document that forces every department to show exactly how much of its money reaches seniors, separating what the state chooses to spend from what it is legally bound to.4
Here is why this matters beyond Kerala. The traditional Indian safety net for old age was never the state. It was the family. Kerala is the first place in India where that contract has visibly frayed enough that the government has had to step in and formalise it. This is the demographic future of Tamil Nadu, of Punjab, of Himachal, arriving early in one corner of the country.
How Kerala got old so fast
The speed is the part that gets lost. This was not gradual.
- In 1961, just 5.1% of Kerala was over 60, slightly below the national average of the time.1
- By 2001, it was 10.5%, already well ahead of India.
- By 2021 it hit 16.5%, and by 2026 it is 18.7%.1
- The state's own projections put it at 22.8% by 2036, when Kerala will have around 8.4mn people over 60.9
The engine was Kerala's own success. Early public health, near-total female literacy, low fertility and rising life expectancy are exactly the things development is supposed to deliver. Kerala delivered them decades before anyone else, and the demographic bill for that head start is now arriving.
The dependency maths is where it bites. The old-age dependency ratio, the number of elderly per 100 working-age people, is climbing towards 34.3% in Kerala over the coming years, against a national ratio less than half that.9 In plain terms, Kerala is heading towards a world where one in three working-age adults is effectively supporting an elderly dependent.
This state-versus-state gap is exactly the kind of thread I love pulling apart, and it is the sort of thing we go back and forth on every morning in the BharatNama WhatsApp community, where I share a smaller India deep-dive like this with thousands of readers (t.ly/h2jq1).
Where Kerala stands: against India, and against itself
Two comparisons make this real. Both matter, because a single number for Kerala tells you almost nothing until you set it beside something.
Kerala against the rest of India. On the 2021 official state shares of the 60-plus population, the spread inside one country is enormous:10
- Kerala: 16.5% (the oldest, and now 18.7% in 2026)
- Tamil Nadu: 13.6%
- Himachal Pradesh: 13.1%
- Punjab: 12.6%
- Andhra Pradesh: 12.4%
- Bihar: 7.7% (the youngest large state)
So Kerala's elderly share is more than double Bihar's. India is not ageing as one country. It is a young north and centre carrying an old, prosperous south and a greying Punjab, and the national average of ~11% hides that split entirely.
Kerala against the world. Put Kerala on the global map and it stops looking like an Indian state and starts looking like East Asia:
- India (60+): ~11%2
- Kerala (60+): 18.7%1
- China (60+): 22.0%, around 310mn people at end-202411
- Japan (65+): a record 29.4%, the oldest society on earth12
Kerala today sits closer to China than to India, and it is walking the same road Japan walked a generation ago. The difference, and this is the uncomfortable bit, is that Japan grew rich before it grew old. Kerala is growing old on a middle-income budget, with borrowing limits set in Delhi.
The empty houses behind the numbers
Ageing in Kerala does not look like ageing in Japan, and the reason is migration.
Kerala exports its young. The Kerala Migration Survey 2023 counted 2.2mn emigrants, most of them working-age, alongside 1.8mn return migrants and remittances of about ₹2.17 lakh crore flowing home in a single year.13 Student emigration has doubled, with young people now leaving as early as 17.14
The money is a lifeline. The social cost falls on the people left behind:
- The share of older adults living alone or only with a spouse has climbed sharply, the "empty nest" now a mass phenomenon.
- Ageing here is heavily feminised. Women outlive men by years, and a large majority of Kerala's elderly women are widows, often with no service pension, few property rights and thin savings.
- Loneliness and psychological distress rise where the adult children have gone, precisely because the informal caregiver, the family, is on a plane to the Gulf or Canada.
Why the budget is mostly a trap
Now to the number in the title, and why 19% of a budget going to the elderly is less generous than it sounds.
The Elderly Budget is split into two very different things. There is Plan spending, the developmental money that builds new services, day-care centres, mobile clinics, the "silver economy". And there is Non-Plan spending, the statutory money the state is legally bound to pay whether it likes it or not.
The split is brutal:4
- Total Elderly Budget: ₹46,236 crore.
- Of which Non-Plan (mostly pensions): about ₹44,895 crore, roughly 97% of the whole thing.
- Leaving the State Plan for elderly welfare at only around ₹1,342 crore.
Read that again. For every ₹100 Kerala routes to the old, roughly ₹97 is locked in pension cheques it cannot legally stop paying, and barely ₹3 is left to actually build anything new. Service pensions for retired staff alone run to tens of thousands of crores.
This is the crowding-out problem in one state, ahead of schedule. Committing a fifth of the budget to the elderly, almost all of it non-negotiable, is a fifth that cannot go to schools, jobs, or the young. And the pressure is only rising: the discontinuation of the revenue-deficit grant and a tighter 16th Finance Commission settlement are squeezing Kerala's fiscal room just as these bills come due.
The new government has still promised more. Its flagship Oommen Chandy Free Health Insurance Scheme offers cover of up to ₹25 lakh per family, with an initial ₹10 crore to get it going.15 The intent is right, because out-of-pocket costs are the real killer here. But funding rich health cover for an ageing population, on a shrinking tax base, is the exact squeeze the whole edition is about.
The health bill nobody budgeted for
Ageing does not just mean more pensioners. It means a different, far more expensive kind of patient.
- Over 70% of Kerala's elderly live with at least one chronic disease.
- Multimorbidity, two or more chronic conditions at once, affects 52.2% of older adults in Kerala, against a national average of 23.3%.16 That is more than double the country's rate.
- Kerala spends more on health than any Indian state, yet a large majority of health spending is still out-of-pocket, and private hospitals dominate the specialised care the old need most.
So you get a cruel combination: the sickest elderly population in India, the highest treatment intensity, and a payment system that still lands much of the bill on the family. This is why the health-insurance promise is politically irresistible and fiscally terrifying at the same time.
What India can actually learn
The good news is that other societies have been here, and Kerala is openly studying them. The honest question is not "should India copy Japan", it is "what actually transfers".
- Japan built universal Long-Term Care Insurance in 2000 and shifted the whole model to community-based care, deliberately keeping the old out of expensive hospital beds.12 Kerala's day-care centres (Pakalveedu) and mobile Vayomithram clinics are the same instinct, done on a fraction of the money.
- South Korea threw technology at the problem: AI companions, monitoring devices and telecare for elders living alone. For a state defined by empty nests and absent children, subsidised remote monitoring is arguably a better fit for Kerala than for anyone.
- Scandinavia offers the ethic, not the model. Its high-tax, fully state-funded institutional care is out of reach for a middle-income state with Kerala's debt. What is portable is the standard: dignity, regulation, and a statutory body to enforce it, which is precisely what the new Elderly Commission is for.
What does not transfer is the money. Japan, Korea and the Nordics all had the fiscal depth to fund this. Kerala's real innovation is being forced to design an ageing-society welfare state on a budget none of those countries had to work with. If it cracks that, it writes the manual for the rest of India.
That tension between a serious long-term vision and a genuinely tight balance sheet is the thread I find most interesting, and it is the kind of thing I dig into every day with the readers in the BharatNama community (t.ly/h2jq1).
What to watch
A few concrete things over the next few quarters:
- The Oommen Chandy scheme's real cost. Watch whether the ₹25 lakh cover survives contact with the actuaries, or gets quietly trimmed to critical illness only once the premium bill is totted up.
- Whether the Department gets teeth or stays a letterhead. Its first real test is auditing and consolidating the patchwork of existing schemes, not just existing on paper.
- The Elderly Commission's first interventions. Does it actually act on property disputes and elder abuse, or become another advisory body?
- The other southern states. Tamil Nadu and Andhra are a decade behind Kerala on this curve. Watch whether they start copying the institutional triad before their own bills arrive.
The one line
Kerala has become the first Indian state rich enough to grow old and too stretched to fully afford it, which is exactly the paradox the rest of India is walking towards.
