Here is a fact that should stop any Indian defence planner cold. Right now, on the tarmac at Hindustan Aeronautics Limited in Bengaluru, sit around 30 fully built Tejas Mk1A fighters. Airframes complete. Avionics fitted. Radar installed. Test-flown, in some cases. And not one of them can be handed to the Indian Air Force.1
The reason is absurdly simple. They have no engines.
India can design a modern fighter jet. It can build the wings, the fly-by-wire, the indigenous Uttam radar, the whole complex machine. What it cannot build, after 37 years of trying, is the one part that actually makes a jet a jet: the engine.2 That single gap is the most expensive sentence in India's defence story, and in 2026 it finally forced a reckoning.
The anatomy of a captive
The engine India is waiting on is the GE F404, made by General Electric in the United States. In 2021, HAL signed a ₹5.4k crore (~$716mn) deal for 99 of them to power the Tejas Mk1A.3
Then the deliveries did not come.
- GE had shut its F404 line around 2016 after an earlier order, and restarting a cold production line proved brutally slow.4
- As of July 2026, GE has handed over just seven engines against a schedule that was meant to deliver 24 to 26 a year.5
- HAL has publicly slapped GE with liquidated-damages penalties, but a penalty does not build a fighter squadron.5
Now sit with the strategic meaning of that. India's frontline light-fighter programme, the backbone meant to replace the retiring MiG-21s and Jaguars, can be paused by a supplier 12,000 km away missing a delivery slip. This is what dependency actually looks like when the bill comes due.
It is worth being precise about the arithmetic, because it is stark. HAL has built the airframes faster than GE can supply the engines to put in them. So the bottleneck is not Indian factories or Indian engineers. It is a single imported component that India is not allowed to make, and cannot yet make itself. Even the maintenance depot for the F404 is only now being set up on Indian soil, years into the programme.4
And the bill is coming due at the worst possible moment. The IAF is down to roughly 29 to 30 fighter squadrons against a sanctioned strength of 42, its thinnest in decades.6 Every grounded Tejas is a hole in that number.
This is exactly the kind of structural vulnerability I keep coming back to in the BharatNama WhatsApp community, where I share a smaller India deep-dive like this with thousands of readers every morning (t.ly/h2jq1). A country that cannot power its own weapons does not fully own them.
The 37-year shadow
To understand why India is here, you have to go back to 1989, when the Cabinet cleared the Kaveri engine programme, meant to power the Tejas by 1996.2
It never happened. And the reasons are a masterclass in how not to fund hard technology.
- The programme was sanctioned with roughly ₹383 crore. A serious military turbofan needs multiples of that, spent on destructive testing, exotic metallurgy, and high-altitude rigs.
- The often-cited illustration of the gap: where GE reportedly tested dozens of alloy formulations to perfect the F404's turbine, India's materials budget stretched to a mere handful.2 So Kaveri's turbine blades kept failing at combat temperatures.
- India had no high-altitude test facility of its own, so prototypes were shipped to Russia for validation, at great cost and delay.2
- After US sanctions following the 1998 Pokhran tests cut off collaboration, GTRE was left reinventing several complex domains at once, alone.
By 2008, the engine was overweight and underpowered, topping out near 73 kN of wet thrust against the 80-plus a Tejas needs.2 The government blinked. It formally delinked Kaveri from the Tejas in September 2008 and bought GE engines instead.2 Kaveri became a technology demonstrator: a museum piece with a pulse.
The lesson is painful and it is the whole point. India spent decades starving the programme to save money, then spent far more importing engines to cover the gap. Short-term thrift, long-term capture.
The thing that changed in 2026
Which is what makes this year genuinely different. On 16 February 2026, with Defence Minister Rajnath Singh watching, GTRE ran a full afterburner test of an upgraded Kaveri and finally crossed the line it had missed for a generation: 81 to 83 kN of wet thrust.7
Let that land. That is broadly the same league as the GE F404 (~84 kN) that India has been importing all along.7 The number India could not reach in 37 years, it reached this year.
How? Partly by finally spending, and partly by borrowing brains from an unlikely place: BrahMos Aerospace, the supersonic-cruise-missile joint venture, whose engineers helped redesign the afterburner's flame holders and combustion.7 India had the propulsion talent all along. It just kept it in different silos.
- The upgraded engine leans on modern single-crystal superalloy blades and digital engine control, the exact metallurgy the 1990s programme could never afford.7
- Even quieter, and arguably more important, is the "Dry Kaveri", a 49 to 51 kN non-afterburning variant now closing on certification, targeted for the end of 2026.8
- That dry engine is the one meant to power the DRDO Ghatak, India's stealthy flying-wing strike drone, and a whole planned family of unmanned combat aircraft.8
And this is where the payoff gets interesting. The Ghatak is built for a doctrine called manned-unmanned teaming: a piloted Tejas Mk2 acting as the quarterback, directing a pack of stealthy Ghatak drones ahead of it as "loyal wingmen" to scout, jam and take the first hits.8 The IAF wants well over 100 such drones. Crucially, none of that fleet flies unless the engine is Indian, because no one exports you an engine for a drone meant to penetrate a rival's air defences.
None of this means the Kaveri flies on a fighter tomorrow. Certification, endurance testing and flying testbeds will take years. But for the first time, the core physics is no longer the obstacle.
Where India stands: against the world, and against itself
Here is where the benchmarking gets uncomfortable, because it always does. The club of countries that can independently design and build a fighter jet engine has maybe five members: the United States, Russia, the United Kingdom, France, and now China.9 India wants to be the sixth. Look at the gap to the newest entrant:
- China. Went from importing Russian AL-31 engines to fielding its own WS-15 in serial production, powering 300-plus J-20 stealth fighters flying on fully domestic engines.10 Its indigenous turbofan sits in the ~140-160 kN class.
- India. After 37 years, has just touched 83 kN on a test bed, and has never flown an indigenous engine on a fighter.2
That is the real scoreboard. China and India both started their serious engine journeys as importers. One now flies hundreds of stealth jets on home-built engines; the other is celebrating a bench test. The gap is not talent. It is decades of sustained funding and institutional patience that India chose not to give itself.
Now turn the lens on India against itself, because the more revealing comparison is India-then versus India-now:
- The old model: a single state lab, GTRE, starved of cash, working in isolation, shipping prototypes abroad to test.
- The new model: a funded push with the private sector inside the tent. Godrej Aerospace and Larsen & Toubro are building engine modules and the Ghatak airframe; BrahMos is fixing the afterburner; and in July 2026 Hyderabad's Azad Engineering handed over India's first indigenous expendable turbojet, a 350 kg-thrust-class engine built in 24 months under a public-private model.11
The same country, two entirely different theories of how to build hard technology. The second one is finally the one being funded.
The price of the trap, and the French escape hatch
The 2026 crisis was not only about the F404. It was about leverage. When India went to buy the heavier GE F414 for the Tejas Mk2 and the fifth-generation AMCA, GE knew India's airframes were frozen around that exact engine, and priced accordingly.
- The F414 quote reportedly jumped to around ₹210-240 crore (~$24mn) a unit, roughly three times the earlier ₹70-80 crore (~$9mn) projection.12
- Swapping the engine out was near impossible: the AMCA's stealth shaping and intakes were built around the F414's geometry, and changing it would reset years of flight testing.12
So New Delhi did the one thing that actually breaks a monopoly. It went shopping for the technology itself, not the product. France's Safran is now close to a landmark pact to co-develop a clean-sheet 120 kN engine for the AMCA Mk2, with what is described as 100% technology transfer, full intellectual-property rights, and no export strings, a roughly $7bn programme targeting 400-plus engines.13 Britain's Rolls-Royce has pitched a rival 110-130 kN engine on the same 100%-transfer terms.14
This is the part worth sitting with in the BharatNama community too (t.ly/h2jq1): the difference between buying an engine and buying the ability to build engines. One keeps you a customer. The other, eventually, ends the dependency for good.
What India can learn
The lesson is not abroad this time. It is in the mirror, and in China.
China's engine programme succeeded because it was funded relentlessly for two decades through repeated, humiliating failures, without the state losing its nerve or delinking the engine to save face. India delinked Kaveri in 2008 the moment it got hard. That single instinct, cut the losing programme, is exactly what kept India a captive customer.
What transfers:
- Fund through the failures. Engine development is destructive testing at industrial scale. There is no cheap version. The 2026 re-funding of Kaveri and the NAETC national engine-test complex being built at Ramanagara so prototypes never ship abroad again are, finally, an acceptance of that.15
- Keep the private sector inside. The Azad, Godrej, L&T and BrahMos involvement is the structural change that matters more than any single test.11
- Own the IP, not just the assembly. The Safran and Rolls-Royce offers are valuable only because they hand over the metallurgy and the design authority, the exact things a licence-build never gives you.
What does not transfer is the shortcut. There isn't one. A jet engine is the one technology money and patience buy, and nothing else does.
What to watch
- Whether the Dry Kaveri clears final certification by the end of 2026, the trigger for the CCS to fund full-scale Ghatak drone prototypes.8
- Whether the Safran co-development pact actually reaches CCS approval, or stalls like so many before it.13
- Whether GE's F404 deliveries finally hit the promised 24-a-year run rate and let those 30 grounded Tejas reach the IAF.5
- Whether the 130 kN twin-engine test bed and the NAETC break ground on schedule, the infrastructure that decides whether any of this is repeatable.15
The one line
India spent 37 years learning that you cannot import your way to air power, and 2026 is the year it finally started paying the real price of building it at home.

The nine points that go missing
Here is a number that should bother anyone who cares about how India is run. The Finance Commission says India's states are entitled to 41% of the Centre's tax pool. The states actually get about 32%.10
That nine-point gap is not an accounting slip. It is the single most important fact about Indian fiscal federalism today, and almost nobody frames it this way.
The trick is elegant. The Constitution lets the Centre keep two kinds of tax entirely to itself. One is a cess, a tax levied for a stated purpose, say education or clean energy. The other is a surcharge, a tax on a tax. Neither is shared with the states.5
So the Centre has a lever. Raise money through ordinary income tax or GST, and 41 paise of every rupee flows to the states. Raise the same money through a cess instead, and the states get nothing.
Guess which one a revenue-hungry Centre reaches for. The headline devolution rate has never looked more generous. The effective one has rarely looked worse. That is the whole story.
How the pool actually works
Start with the plumbing, because the plumbing is the point.
India's Constitution hands the Centre the big, buoyant taxes: corporate tax, income tax, GST, customs. It hands the states the big spending jobs: hospitals, schools, police, roads, agriculture. That mismatch between who collects and who spends has a name, vertical fiscal imbalance, and every large federation lives with some of it.
To bridge it, the Constitution orders a Finance Commission every five years to decide what share of the Centre's taxes the states get. That shared portion is called the divisible pool.
- The 14th Finance Commission raised the states' recommended share from 32% to a landmark 41-42%.1
- The 15th kept it at 41%.1
- The 16th, whose report covers 2026 to 2031 and was accepted in the 2026-27 Budget, kept it at 41% again, resisting demands from 18 states to push it to 50%.1 2
On paper, then, nearly half the Centre's taxes go to the states. In practice, far less does. The reason sits in one line of the Constitution.
The loophole was written in the year 2000
Before 2000, the sharing arrangement was narrower and messier. The 80th Amendment fixed that by pooling all central taxes together and giving states a single share of the lot.5
It was sold as a win for the states, and in one way it was. But tucked inside the same amendment was a carve-out. Cesses raised for a specific purpose, and surcharges under Article 271, were placed outside the divisible pool.5
The original logic was reasonable. A cess is money collected for a named job, so the argument went that it should not be handed to states as untied cash to spend on anything. The Fourth Finance Commission said as much back in 1965.
Here is where it gets strange. That logic only holds if the money actually reaches the job it was collected for. Increasingly, it does not.
The share of cesses and surcharges in the Centre's gross tax revenue tells the story of a loophole growing into a pillar:
- Around 10.4% in 2011-12.3
- A peak of 20.2% in 2020-21, roughly double.3
- Still 14.5% in 2023-24, well down from the peak but far above where it started.3
Every rupee inside that rising share is a rupee the 41% formula never touches. The pool shrinks before the split even happens.
The auditor's inconvenient numbers
The one defence of keeping cesses out of the pool is that they are ring-fenced for their stated purpose. India's own auditor has demolished that defence.
The Comptroller and Auditor General, in its Report No. 16 of 2025, found that ₹3.69 lakh crore of cess money had simply never been moved to the reserve funds it was earmarked for, as of March 2024.4 It was collected in the name of highways, health, education and the rest, and then left sitting in the Centre's general account.
The detail is worse than the headline:
- The oil industry cess raised about ₹2.9 lakh crore since 1974-75. Just ₹902 crore, or 0.3%, reached the fund it was meant for.4
- Health and education cesses worth ₹37,537 crore collected between 2018-19 and 2023-24 never reached their dedicated funds.4
This is not new. An earlier CAG audit found that in 2018-19 alone, 35 different cesses raised about ₹2.75 lakh crore, of which only ₹1.64 lakh crore went to the funds they were levied for.12
So the sequence is this. The Centre taxes citizens in the name of a specific cause. It keeps the states out of that money by calling it a cess. Then it often does not spend it on the cause either. The earmark is a label, not a ring-fence.
This is exactly the kind of thread I keep pulling on, and it is the sort of thing we go back and forth over in the BharatNama WhatsApp community, where I share a smaller India deep-dive like this with thousands of readers every morning (t.ly/h2jq1).
December 2025: the loophole gets a new lease
If you think this is a story about old habits, watch what just happened.
The GST compensation cess was a special levy, brought in when GST launched to make good the revenue states lost in the switch. Its proceeds flowed back to the states. It was always meant to be temporary, and its statutory life runs out on 31 March 2026.6
Instead of letting that revenue fold into ordinary, shareable GST, Parliament acted in December 2025. It passed the Central Excise (Amendment) Bill and moved the Health Security to National Security Cess Bill, both aimed at tobacco and pan masala.6
- The excise duties rise to offset the ending compensation cess.6
- A new production-based cess targets pan masala and gutkha machines.6
- Demerit goods like tobacco sit at the 40% GST slab, but the top-up now comes through excise and a cess, not a shared tax.6
Read the manoeuvre plainly. A levy that used to flow to the states is expiring. It is being replaced by levies that stay entirely with the Centre, wrapped in the language of public health and national security. A state-friendly tax dies, and a Centre-only tax is born in its place.
Where India stands, against itself
Now break the national number open, because the pain is not shared evenly.
Cesses fall heaviest on consumption, and consumption is highest in India's richer, more industrialised states. So the states that generate the most tax are the ones that lose the most when revenue is routed through a cess rather than the pool. The loophole quietly punishes the states doing the economic heavy lifting.
The 16th Finance Commission tried to answer this on the distribution side, and this is where its real changes sit. It left the 41% share alone but rewired the formula that splits the pool between states:2
- A new "contribution to GDP" criterion, weighted 10%, rewards high-output states for the first time.2
- The old "tax and fiscal effort" weight was scrapped.2
- Income distance, the equity measure, was trimmed from 45% to 42.5%; population nudged up to 17.5%; area cut from 15% to 10%.2 1
The result is a tilt towards the productive south and west:
- Karnataka rises from 3.65% to 4.13%, the single biggest gainer.8
- Maharashtra edges from 6.32% to 6.44%.8
- All five southern states gain share under the new formula.8
But notice what this really is. Rewarding rich states with a bigger slice partly offsets the fact that those same states lose the most to cesses. It treats the symptom, the division of the pool, while leaving the disease, the shrinking of the pool, untouched.
And the 16th FC went further in a way that stings the weakest states. For the first time, it discontinued the Article 275 revenue deficit grants that used to plug the gap for states like Himachal Pradesh and Punjab, betting that state finances will run surpluses.9 It did expand local body grants sharply, to about ₹7.9 lakh crore.9 But that shifts money from untied constitutional entitlements towards conditional, Delhi-designed grants. That is centralisation dressed as cooperative federalism.
What India can learn from Australia
India is not alone in facing a wide gap between who taxes and who spends. Australia's federal government collects roughly 80% of public revenue and lets its states carry a huge share of the actual services. The imbalance is as steep as India's. The difference is entirely in the machinery.
Australia's answer is a ring-fenced pool. The entire GST take is dedicated to the states and territories, and Canberra cannot invent a "national security cess" to siphon money out before the split. There is no loophole to grow.11
The sharing is run by the Commonwealth Grants Commission, an independent body that does something India's system does not. It measures each state's real capacity to raise revenue and its real cost of delivering services, then tops up the weaker states so every state can offer a comparable standard.11
Two features are worth India's attention:
- A "no worse off" guarantee, legislated to 2026-27 and extended by agreement to 2029-30, protects every state during reform. Crucially, Canberra funds these top-ups from its own money, not by raiding the shared pool.11
- A relativity floor, now 0.75, ensures no state's per-person GST share collapses below a set level.11
The lesson is not "copy Australia". India's scale, its federal politics and its fiscal room are all different. The transferable idea is narrower and sharper. A federation can run a huge vertical imbalance without wrecking trust, but only if the shared pool is broad, ring-fenced, and immune to unilateral carve-outs. India has the independent body in the Finance Commission. What it lacks is the sealed pool.
The state-versus-state spread and the Centre-versus-state tug are the kind of tension I unpack most days for the BharatNama community, and if this edition is your sort of thing, that is where the daily version of it lives (t.ly/h2jq1).
What to watch
- Whether the 2026-27 Budget's numbers hold: fiscal deficit is targeted at 4.3% of GDP, down from 4.4%, and tax devolution to states is pegged at ₹15.3 lakh crore.7 A tight deficit target is exactly the pressure that pushes the Centre towards cesses.
- The rollout of the Health Security to National Security Cess from April 2026, and how much tobacco and pan masala revenue it locks away from the pool.6
- Whether the discontinued revenue deficit grants force hill and special-category states into fresh borrowing.9
- Any move, however unlikely, to bring cesses and surcharges back inside the divisible pool. Without that, the 41% will keep meaning 32%.
The one line
India's states were promised 41% and handed 32%, and the missing nine points are not lost to arithmetic but to a loophole the Centre has every incentive to keep widening.

Here is a number that should stop you. India runs one of the fastest-growing large economies on earth, with a deposit base that has nearly tripled in a decade, and yet its banks lend barely 55% of GDP to the private sector.1
China lends 194%.2 Vietnam, which started poorer and reformed later than India, lends about 145%.3 South Korea sits near 170%.4
So the obvious story writes itself: India is under-banked, Indians do not save, financial inclusion has failed. Except every part of that story is wrong.
The more I dig into this, the more I think India's credit problem has almost nothing to do with mobilising money, and almost everything to do with who gets first claim on it. And that changes what the fix has to be.
The banking system that quietly doubled
Start with the thing everyone gets wrong. India is not short of deposits.
- Total bank deposits crossed ₹254 lakh crore by end-December 2025, up from about ₹225 lakh crore a year earlier and roughly ₹88 lakh crore a decade ago.5
- Non-food bank credit reached ₹208 lakh crore over the same period, growing 14.5% year-on-year by December 2025.6
- Total assets of India's formal lending system more than doubled as a share of GDP, from 58.8% in 1997 to 118.2% by 2022.7
Let that sink in. The pool doubled. The plumbing that carries that pool into the hands of factories, exporters and entrepreneurs did not. That is the whole puzzle in one sentence.
If deposits have tripled and the system has doubled, but private credit is stuck near 55% of GDP, the leak is not on the funding side. It is on the asset side, in how a bank is allowed to use the money once it has it.
How a ₹100 deposit gets carved up
This is where financial repression stops being a textbook phrase and becomes a set of very specific rules. Follow a single ₹100 deposit as it enters an Indian bank.
- ₹3 goes to the RBI as the Cash Reserve Ratio (CRR), earning nothing. The RBI cut CRR in phases through late 2025, from 4.5% down to 3%, which freed some cash, but the principle stands: a slice is locked before any lending happens.8
- Around ₹18 to ₹22 goes into government bonds to meet the Statutory Liquidity Ratio (SLR), the rule that forces banks to park a fixed share of deposits in central and state government securities. The statutory floor is 18% today, down from a peak of 38.5% decades ago, but banks routinely hold well above it.9
- Of whatever is left, 40% is ring-fenced for Priority Sector Lending (PSL), the mandate that directs credit to agriculture, micro enterprises and weaker sections rather than to whoever the market would price best.10
Add it up and less than half of every ₹100 is left for unconstrained commercial lending to industry, infrastructure and high-value services. The sovereign and a set of social mandates get first call on the nation's savings. Private enterprise gets the residue.
None of this is an accident. It is a deliberate, decades-old architecture, and each piece was built for a reason. SLR gives the government a captive buyer for its debt. PSL pushes credit to farmers and small firms the market would ignore. The intent is defensible. The macroeconomic side-effect is that industrial credit in India is made artificially scarce, and therefore artificially expensive.
Because their mandated holdings earn less than a market-priced loan would, banks recover the difference by charging fatter margins on the shrinking pool of commercial credit they are free to give. The unconstrained borrower, the factory or the exporter, ends up subsidising the repressed rest of the balance sheet. That is why Indian industry borrows dear even though Indian banks are unusually safe.
The banks are healthy. That is part of the problem.
Here is the twist. India's banks have rarely been in better shape, and that has made them more cautious, not less.
- Gross non-performing assets (GNPA) have fallen to a multi-decade low of about 2.2% as of September 2025, with net NPAs at just 0.5%.11
- That is down from a peak near 11.5% in 2018, when a wave of bad infrastructure and corporate loans nearly broke the public sector banks.11
After that trauma, and the brutal clean-up that followed, bank managements learned a lesson: government bonds carry zero risk weight and never turn into a non-performing loan, while a corporate loan can. So even beyond the statutory minimum, banks lean into sovereign debt as a defensive crouch. Safety and repression point the same way, and the private borrower loses twice.
This tension, between a banking system that is finally sound and an industrial sector that still cannot get cheap capital, is exactly the kind of contradiction I keep pulling apart in the BharatNama WhatsApp community, where I share a smaller India deep-dive like this with thousands of readers every morning (t.ly/h2jq1).
Where India stands: against the world
Now put India on the same chart as the countries it wants to compete with. Using the World Bank's private-credit-to-GDP measure:
- India: ~55% of GDP. Barely half the average for emerging markets, which sits around 135%.1
- Vietnam: ~145%. A country that liberalised after India and from a lower base.3
- South Korea: ~170%. A high-income economy that used deep credit to industrialise, and now wrestles with household debt near 89% of GDP.4
- China: ~194%. Decades of state-directed credit, now tipping into overcapacity and hidden defaults.2
The lesson is not "more credit is always better". China is the cautionary tale at the top end: credit poured into loss-making local government vehicles and a property bubble, and its true bad-loan pile is far larger than the official numbers admit. Korea shows the mid-life risk, where deep credit curdles into household leverage.
But India is nowhere near those problems. India is on the opposite failure: too little productive credit, not too much. It is starving, not bingeing. And a country cannot build a manufacturing base on the residue of its own savings.
Where India stands: against itself
Now break the national number open, because the average hides the real story.
- Bank credit-to-GDP in India's richer, industrialised states runs up to three times higher than in its poorer, agrarian ones.
- Bihar and Uttar Pradesh, home to roughly a quarter of all Indians, show credit-to-GDP ratios of just 25% to 30%, dragging the national average down.
- The industrial and metro clusters of Maharashtra, Tamil Nadu, Karnataka and Delhi soak up a hugely disproportionate share of formal credit.
So the system is not just shallow, it is uneven. It mobilises deposits from the whole country and then re-deploys them into a handful of commercial hubs. A saver in Patna funds a factory in Pune. That is fine as far as it goes, but it means the credit gap is really a set of gaps, and the states that most need investment get the least of it.
The shadow-banking bypass
When banks will not or cannot lend, someone else does. India's answer has been the explosive rise of Non-Banking Financial Companies (NBFCs), the shadow banks.
- NBFC assets grew from 2.6% of GDP in 1997 to 16.3% by 2022, one of the fastest expansions in the system.7
- Their credit book roughly doubled from ₹24 lakh crore in 2021 to about ₹48 lakh crore by March 2025, and NBFCs now supply around a fifth of all systemic credit.12
But the bypass has a fatal flaw. NBFCs cannot take cheap retail deposits, so they fund long-term loans with short-term market borrowing. When confidence cracks, as it did when IL&FS collapsed in 2018 and DHFL in 2019, the funding freezes and the whole sector seizes. Their stressed-asset ratio had climbed back to 5.9% by March 2025, a reminder that the shadow system trades one problem for another.13
So NBFCs solved the availability of credit for some borrowers, but never the cost. Money routed through wholesale markets is dearer than money routed through a savings account, and that premium lands on the same industrial borrower again.
What India can learn from Vietnam
If you want the transferable lesson, do not look at China's firehose or Korea's mature markets. Look at Vietnam.
- In 1995, Vietnam's bank-credit-to-GDP ratio was just 19%. By 2025 it had reached about 145%.3
- It did this by actively steering mobilised deposits into the real economy, into export zones, infrastructure and private manufacturing, rather than parking them in government paper.
- That deep domestic credit, paired with open trade, made Vietnam the prime winner of supply chains shifting out of China.
The honest caveat is that Vietnam is now managing the hangover, with credit concentrated in property and thin bank capital buffers, and its central bank is tightening. So the lesson is not "flood the system". It is narrower and sharper: a developing country that wants to industrialise has to let its banking system finance industry, not the fiscal deficit.
What is portable for India is the direction of travel: deepen the sovereign bond market so pension funds, insurers and foreign investors buy government debt instead of banks, then phase down SLR as they step in. Shift the burden of priority lending onto transparent fiscal subsidies rather than a hidden tax on bank balance sheets. Give well-run NBFCs cheaper, more stable funding. None of it is easy in a federal country with a large deficit, but none of it is impossible either.
This is the sort of structural question, why the plumbing matters more than the pump, that the BharatNama community goes back and forth on every day, and I would love for you to be part of that conversation (t.ly/h2jq1).
What to watch
- Whether the RBI signals any further move on SLR or the CRR path in upcoming policy reviews, the clearest sign that repression is easing.
- Whether foreign portfolio limits in Indian government bonds keep rising, which would let banks step back as the residual buyer of the deficit.
- Whether the new PSL Master Directions, effective from April 2025, change how much genuine industrial credit gets crowded out.
- Whether NBFC stress at 5.9% stabilises or forces another round of RBI intervention.
India has the savings, the demographics and, for the first time in a decade, a genuinely healthy banking system. The money required for its manufacturing push is not missing. It is sitting in the vault, spoken for.
The one line: India's credit problem is not that it cannot raise the money, it is that it has already promised most of it to someone else.

The landlords of the Himalaya
I have come to believe India's Himalayan states no longer see themselves as hosts to the national grid. They see themselves as landlords. And the rent is going up.
On 2 July 2026, Himachal Pradesh did something that tells you exactly where India's hydropower story has gone. Chief Minister Sukhvinder Singh Sukhu directed his officials to start taking back three working dams from SJVN, a central public sector company that spent years and thousands of crores building them.1
The three projects, Sunni (382 MW), Luhri Stage-I (210 MW) and Dhaulasidh (66 MW), add up to 658 MW.1 The state's argument is blunt: hydropower is the backbone of its economy, and it wants its rightful share of its own rivers.
The instrument the hill states use is a single line of policy. And once you understand it, you understand the whole shift.
The 13%, and how it actually works
Every hydro project in India must hand the host state 12% of its power, free, for the life of the dam, plus another 1% as cash for a local development fund.2 Thirteen per cent, off the top, forever.
The detail is the whole story, so start with the mechanism. From the day a plant synchronises with the grid, its output is sliced up before the developer sells a single unit:
- 12% of everything generated goes to the host state, free of cost. The developer carries all the capital and running costs, the state carries none, and takes an eighth of the output as pure revenue.2
- 1% more is converted to cash and paid into a Local Area Development Fund (LADF), the pot meant for the villages the dam displaces.2
- The state is asked to match that 1% from its own free-power share, and developers must give each project-affected family 100 free units of electricity a month for ten years.2
This was not designed as leverage. It grew out of an older, decent instinct: share a resource windfall with the region that bears the ecological cost. Dams submerge ancestral land, move communities and re-plumb rivers, so the state that loses the valley should share the gains.
Now the scale, because it explains the power shift. India has about 50 GW of large hydro installed, and just over 55 GW including small hydro, around a tenth of the total power mix as of October 2025.3 Against an assessed potential of roughly 133 GW, only a little over 40% is built.3
Almost all of what remains sits in the Himalaya and the Northeast. Whoever owns those valleys owns India's last big block of dispatchable clean power. And they have worked out what it is worth.
From compensation to a cash register
The clearest sign of the shift is what Himachal did with its free power over the past year.
For decades the state simply fed its 12% into its own board, the HPSEB, at a soft rate, and used it to keep local and farm tariffs low. Free power was a domestic subsidy.
At the end of 2025 the state cabinet tore that up. On 30 December 2025 it stripped the HPSEB of 438 MW of free power from the big Sutlej projects, Nathpa Jhakri and Rampur, and handed it to a new Energy Management Centre inside the Directorate of Energy, whose only job is to sell that power on the open exchanges.4
The logic is cold, and honestly hard to argue with as pure finance:
- In summer evenings, when solar collapses at dusk and demand peaks, dispatchable hydro fetches premium spot prices.
- Selling to the exchange puts unencumbered cash straight into the treasury.
- Feeding it to your own board at a soft rate leaves money on the table.
But the state utility and its customers foot the bill. Himachal also ended its old "banking" arrangement, where it lent summer surplus to Punjab, Haryana and Delhi and drew it back in the lean winter.4 Punjab alone reckons the switch could cost it around ₹400 crore in a single paddy season.5 And the HPSEB now has to buy expensive winter power on the market, which lands back on Himachali consumers as fresh surcharges.
The treasury wins. The board loses. This is the kind of thread I keep pulling on, how a welfare rule mutates into a trading desk, and it is exactly what we go back and forth on in the BharatNama WhatsApp community, where I share a smaller India deep-dive like this with thousands of readers every morning (t.ly/h2jq1).
Someone always pays for "free"
The word "free" hides who actually pays.
When a developer loses 13% of its saleable power up front, it still has to recover its full cost from the remaining 87%. The Central Electricity Regulatory Commission bakes this in: a hydro plant's annual fixed cost is split, and the free-power share is subtracted from the saleable energy in the tariff formula.6 Shrink the base you can sell over, and the per-unit price for everyone else rises.
So the arithmetic is blunt. A Haryana or a Delhi consumer, buying their slice of a Himalayan dam, pays a slightly higher tariff to fund the free power gifted to Himachal or Arunachal. The host state's windfall is a surcharge on the plains.
And the plains have started to push back. Himalayan hydro is front-loaded and dear in its first 10 to 15 years, while the developer services construction debt, exactly when cheap solar is flooding the exchanges:
- Haryana's distribution companies are already carrying a mountain of deferred fuel-and-power surcharge, and in early 2026 their own firms asked the regulator to let them push the recovery even further out.7
- The Haryana regulator has been refusing power deals it judges unaffordable, knocking back a solar PPA in April 2026 on precisely that logic.8
- Meanwhile NHPC is signing 40-year hydro deals elsewhere, like the 3,576 MW Sawalkot and Kamala block it tied up with Gujarat's GUVNL.9
The tension is real. States that host the dams want maximum rent. Developers want firm 40-year buyers. And the states that must actually buy the power increasingly say the price is too high.
Why the Centre keeps subsidising it anyway
You would think this friction would stall the sector. It has not, because Delhi cannot let it.
India crossed 505 GW of total installed capacity by the end of 2025, with non-fossil sources past half the base for the first time, and is chasing 500 GW of non-fossil capacity by 2030.10 The grid is filling with intermittent solar and wind. When the sun drops at 7pm, something has to ramp up in seconds, and only hydro and pumped storage can do it at scale.
So the Centre pays to keep the peace:
- It makes buyers take hydro whether they like it or not, carving a Hydro Purchase Obligation into the renewable purchase mandate, the broader trajectory climbing towards 43% of power procurement by 2029-30.11
- It waives inter-state transmission charges for hydro and pumped storage for years after commissioning, quietly suppressing the delivered price so regulators like Haryana's will swallow it.6
Both are subsidies that hide the cost of the host state's 12%. The free power is never free. It is smeared across obligations and waivers so that no single bill ever shows it.
Where India stands, against the world
Set India's model beside the country that has done this longest, and the gaps are instructive.
Norway, on hydropower rent:
- Host municipalities can buy up to 10% of a plant's output at a regulated cost price, close in spirit to India's 12%, but they pay for it rather than getting it free, and the difference funds local budgets transparently.12
- Developers pay a resource-rent tax of 45% on top of the 22% corporate tax, a combined marginal rate of about 67%, so the national exchequer, not just the local one, captures the windfall.13
- Municipalities and the state together collected roughly $90mn in licence fees in a single year.12
Then Bhutan, which turned the same resource into a nation's balance sheet. Hydropower is about a fifth of its economy and 63% of its exports, and India is the buyer.14 In Thimphu, hydro rent built a country. In Shimla, it is starting to build a treasury.
And where India stands, against itself
The domestic spread is the real story, because the same 12% rule is being played three completely different ways:
- Himachal Pradesh, the aggressive extractor. It is monetising free power, formally asking the Centre in June 2026 to raise the royalty beyond 12% and to clear ₹7,784 crore in BBMB arrears,15 insisting dams revert to the state free of cost after 40 years, and moving to seize working projects.1 It even tried a water cess on generation, until its own High Court struck it down as unconstitutional, since electricity is a central subject.16
- Jammu & Kashmir, the accommodator. Its 2025 hydro policy eases terms to attract developers rather than squeeze them,17 because in a high-risk, high-cost basin a smaller share of a built dam beats a full share of a stalled one.
- Arunachal Pradesh, the sleeping giant. Holding roughly a third of India's potential, in 2023 it handed 11,517 MW across 12 projects to central companies in one stroke,18 and expects to earn upwards of ₹4,500 crore a year from free power by 2035.19
Same rule, three different games. That state-versus-state spread is the sort of India-versus-India comparison I find most revealing, and it is what the BharatNama WhatsApp group, where thousands of us dig into a smaller India story each morning, exists for (t.ly/h2jq1).
What India could take from Norway, and where it cannot
Norway cracked the exact problem India is fumbling: how to share hydro rent fairly without wrecking the sector or the consumer.
What travels:
- Charge for the local share, do not gift it. A priced entitlement, like Norway's concession power at cost, still enriches the host region but shows up honestly in a budget line, instead of being smeared across every other state's tariff.12
- Ring-fence and audit the local fund. Norway's fees flow to local bodies on a transparent formula. India's 1% LADF too often never reaches the valley, with compensation money for displaced families dogged by governance gaps.
- Tax the rent nationally, so the windfall is shared beyond the one lucky border district.13
What does not travel so easily:
- India is a federation of 28 states, not one national utility, so a single state can genuinely hold a central developer hostage in a way a Norwegian municipality cannot.
- India's dams sit in far more fragile geology. In October 2023 a glacial lake burst in Sikkim and wiped out the 1,200 MW Teesta-III dam,20 a reminder that no revenue formula compensates for a project built in the wrong place.
The lesson is not "copy Norway". It is that India has built an elaborate machine to move hydro rent around, and forgotten to make it transparent, fair to the consumer, or safe for the people living below the wall.
What to watch
- Whether Himachal actually completes its takeover of the 658 MW of SJVN projects, or settles for a higher royalty. It is the test case for how far a state can push.1
- Whether the Centre concedes any rise above the 12% baseline. Himachal is formally asking, and a yes would reset the economics of every future project.15
- Whether more plains regulators follow Haryana and refuse long-dated hydro contracts on cost grounds, which would force the Centre to sweeten terms even further.8
- Whether a single rupee of the extra spot-market money Himachal is now earning ever reaches the HPSEB's stranded consumers, or stays in the treasury.
The one line
India's hill states have realised their rivers are not just scenery, or even electricity. They are a sovereign wealth fund, and the meter is running.

For a decade, the smart money was certain the classroom was dead. Software would eat it, the way it ate retail, taxis and travel.
They were wrong. And the correction has been brutal, and instructive.
In July 2026, a European buyout firm, Vitruvian Partners, paid ₹1,159 crore for roughly 16% of K12 Techno Services, the company behind the Orchids chain of schools.1 That values a business with ₹523 crore of revenue and a net loss of about ₹25 crore at around ₹7,200 crore.2
Call it 15 to 16 times sales. For a school operator that does not yet turn a profit.2
Now let that sit for a second. The same class of investor that spent 2021 funding apps to make schools obsolete is now paying software-style multiples to own the schools themselves.
The disruption that got disrupted
This is a rotation, not a one-off. To see why, rewind to the boom that just collapsed.
Indian EdTech raised money at a pace that looked unstoppable:
- ~$1.88bn in 2020, then a peak of ~$4.73bn in 2021.3
- Then the fall: ~$2.6bn in 2022, and just ~$297mn in 2023.3
- Roughly 4,500 startups were fighting for the same shrinking market, and over 14,000 people were laid off in 2022 alone. Lido and Udayy shut entirely; Byju's, once the poster child, imploded.3
The moment physical schools reopened, the demand for a screen substitute evaporated. Without a building to enforce attendance, without the peer group, without the childcare a school quietly provides, the churn was savage. The survivors, Byju's and PhysicsWallah, ended up spending heavily to buy physical coaching centres.3
Here is the interesting bit. Investors did not conclude that education was a bad business. They concluded the opposite. The physical school was never the weakness in the model. It was the moat.
Why a school beats a SaaS app
Apply the two numbers every investor lives by, and you see what they saw.
- Customer acquisition cost (CAC): what it costs to win one customer.
- Lifetime value (LTV): the total profit that customer throws off before they leave.
In software, an LTV to CAC ratio of 3 to 1 is considered healthy. A premium school makes that ratio look almost embarrassing, for three reasons.
- Near-zero churn. Once a family clears the admissions gauntlet and enrols a child, the odds of that child switching schools before Class 12 are tiny. One acquisition buys 12 to 15 years of recurring fees. A SaaS company would kill for that retention.
- Inelastic, K-shaped demand. In a downturn, a family cancels the holiday, delays the car and eats out less, long before it touches the child's school. And the segment PE is chasing, the aspirational top, is the one whose incomes have risen fastest.
- Brutal barriers to entry. Prime urban land, a maze of approvals, good teachers and, above all, decades of trust. You cannot spin up a credible school in a funding round. That scarcity is pricing power.
This kind of buried unit economics, the thing that quietly turns a school into a 15-year annuity, is exactly what I keep pulling apart in the BharatNama WhatsApp community, where I share a smaller India deep-dive like this one with thousands of readers every morning (t.ly/h2jq1).
The legal fiction that makes it investable
There is one problem. In India, you are not legally allowed to run a school for profit.
For generations, the law has insisted that schooling be charitable. Schools must sit inside not-for-profit trusts or societies. They cannot pay dividends. Any surplus must be ploughed back. To a buyout fund, whose entire job is to return capital, that is uninvestable.
So the industry engineered a workaround, the same one it built for private hospitals. The school is split into two entities:
- The not-for-profit Trust. It holds the licence and the board affiliation, employs the teachers, and technically enrols the students. It collects the fees. It cannot distribute profit.
- The for-profit Operating Company, or OpCo. This is where the PE money goes. It owns or leases the land, the technology, the brand and the curriculum, and sells all of it back to the Trust through long-term management and service agreements.
The surplus the school generates is then drained out of the charitable Trust and lands on the OpCo's books as revenue, amplified by the high-margin extras: uniforms, transport, digital subscriptions, catering. The distinction between a philanthropic school and a profit machine becomes, in practice, a legal fiction.
K12 Techno is the OpCo done at scale. It does not own the school trusts. It sells them a full stack, curriculum, software, hiring, admin, marketing, across more than 113 institutes in 17 cities.2 That is the business Vitruvian just paid ₹7,200 crore to buy a slice of.1
And the re-rating is the tell. K12 Techno was worth about ₹4,721 crore in its previous round; the July step-up to ₹7,200 crore let an early backer, Peak XV, the old Sequoia India, book close to a 12-fold return on its original bet.2 When an asset class starts minting returns like that, the rest of the capital follows fast.
Where India stands, against the world
Zoom out, and India is early to a game the world has already matured into.
- In October 2024, a consortium led by Neuberger Berman with EQT and Canada's CPP Investments agreed to buy Nord Anglia Education for an enterprise value of $14.5bn, one of the largest education deals ever. It closed in March 2025.4 5
- Nord Anglia runs 80-plus schools across 33 countries for more than 85,000 students, with tie-ups to MIT, Juilliard and UNICEF. EQT first invested back in 2008 and has compounded the asset ever since, bringing in CPP in 2017.4
- Its mirror image, Inspired Education, backed by TA Associates, Warburg Pincus, Stonepeak and Singapore's GIC, now runs more than 125 schools across five continents.6
Against that, India's chains are small. K12 Techno at ₹7,200 crore is roughly $850mn, a fraction of a single Nord Anglia. And that gap is precisely the pitch: the runway is enormous, and the roll-up has barely begun.
Where India stands, against itself
Now break the national number open, because this is where the real story sits.
The UDISE+ 2025-26 data, the government's own school census, is stark:
- Government schools have shed enrolment from ~128mn to ~119mn, losing roughly 8.6mn students in two years.7
- Private unaided schools have gone the other way, from ~90mn to ~99mn, adding roughly 8.8mn students.7
- Private unaided schools now hold close to 40% of all enrolment.7
So the migration is real and it is large. But the slice PE actually wants is tiny. Of India's ~248mn school students, only about 7.9mn sit in schools charging ₹1 lakh a year or more, drawn from perhaps 28.2mn households that can afford it.1 That is the sliver the capital is racing for.
This split, 8.6mn children walking out of one system while 8.8mn walk into another, is the sort of India-versus-India thread we chew on daily in the BharatNama WhatsApp group (t.ly/h2jq1), where a version of this deep-dive lands every morning.
The other big consolidator shows how far this goes. KKR-backed Lighthouse Learning, the old EuroKids, now runs 1,850-plus preschools and 60 K-12 schools for more than 190,000 students, under EuroSchool, Kangaroo Kids and Billabong High.8 KKR bought EuroKids in 2019 for about ₹1,400 crore9, brought in Canada's PSP Investments in a fresh round in late 20258, and is now buying the ultra-premium Pathways School in Gurgaon for around ₹1,500 crore.1 A trophy IB asset, at the very top of the market.
What India can learn
Here is the uncomfortable part, and it is why this matters beyond the deal pages.
The rich world has already run this experiment, in higher education, and the results are on record. A landmark study by Eaton, Howell and Yannelis found that when private equity bought colleges, enrolment and profits went up, but educational inputs fell, tuition and student debt rose, graduation rates dropped and graduates earned less.10 The firms were very good at capturing subsidies. They were not good at teaching.
The mechanism to watch is the teacher. Salaries are the biggest cost line in any school, so the incentive is to trim them, raise class sizes and lean on younger staff. But the evidence says that is exactly where the damage lands. Ronfeldt, Loeb and Wyckoff, studying over 600,000 student records in New York, showed that higher teacher turnover measurably lowers achievement in maths and English, and not only by losing good teachers, but by tearing the school's social fabric.11
And the consumer squeeze is already visible in India as "eduflation". Fees at a school like Delhi Public School, Vasant Kunj roughly doubled from ₹90,000 in 2019-20 to ₹1.7 lakh by 2024-25, and many urban families now spend 20% to 30% of household income on their child's education.12 When a handful of well-capitalised chains set the regional benchmark, that pricing power only hardens.
And underneath all of it sits a mismatch that no amount of financial engineering resolves. A buyout fund needs its exit in three to seven years; a school's reputation compounds over decades. The pressure to inflate value before the exit window is precisely the pressure that pushes against patient, expensive, unglamorous good teaching. That is the unresolved variable in this entire thesis.
So what is portable, and what is not?
- Portable: transparency and fee discipline. India already has the tools, state fee-fixation committees and disclosure laws in Delhi, Rajasthan and Chhattisgarh. The gap is enforcement, not statute.
- Not portable: a simple "cap the fees" answer. The Supreme Court, in TMA Pai and PA Inamdar, protected private schools' autonomy while barring profiteering. India has to hold both at once, capital that funds good schools, without letting the classroom become pure extraction.
What to watch
- Whether K12 Techno or Lighthouse files for an IPO. The exit is the whole point of a buyout, and a listing would price the entire sector.
- Whether states tighten scrutiny of the Trust-OpCo structure and ancillary charges, or keep looking the other way.
- Whether the Pathways deal actually closes at ₹1,500 crore, and what multiple it sets for trophy schools.
- The court cases and protests, from the Orchids affiliation row in Bengaluru to the fee-hike agitations in Gurgaon and Delhi, and whether any regulator's order is actually enforced.
The one line
Private equity did not disrupt the Indian classroom; it discovered that the classroom was the safest annuity in the country, and quietly bought the annuity.

India is the largest mango producer on earth. We grow roughly 26mn tonnes a year, about 43% of the entire global crop.1 And we export less than 1% of it.1
Let that sit for a second. The country that basically defines the fruit sells almost none of it to the world.
That one number tells you most of what you need to know about where Indian agriculture actually stands in 2026. We have never been better at growing food, and we have never negotiated harder to sell it. Farm exports hit $53.1bn in 2025-26, a whisker below the all-time record and up 2.3% in a year when overall merchandise exports barely moved.2
And yet, at inspection counter after inspection counter, our produce keeps getting turned away.
We win the negotiation, then lose the container
Here is the thing. India has quietly become very good at one half of trade, and stayed fragile at the other.
The first half is market access, the diplomacy of tariffs. On that, New Delhi has been on a tear:
- New Zealand signed a free trade deal on 27 April 2026 giving India duty-free access across all 8,284 of its tariff lines, plus a $20bn investment pledge over 15 years.3
- The India-UK CETA came into force on 15 July 2026, scrapping duties on about 99% of Indian goods and targeting a doubling of two-way trade to $56bn by 2030.4
The second half is compliance: the world of sanitary and phytosanitary rules, or SPS, the residue limits, fumigation certificates and heat-treatment protocols that decide whether a container actually clears the border. On that, we are bleeding shipments every week.
- Australia has just suspended 44 Indian fumigation agencies.5
- The EU ranked India first in the world for pesticide alerts last year.6
- Japan halted our mangoes for the first time in 20 years.7
- And banned antibiotics drove 43% of our shrimp rejections.8
This is the compliance paradox. We have optimised the art of the trade deal, and our fragmented supply chain still cannot meet the zero-tolerance rulebooks on the other side. This split, brilliant at the table and shaky at the counter, is exactly the tension I keep pulling apart, and it is the sort of thread we chew on every morning in my BharatNama WhatsApp community, where I share a smaller India deep-dive like this one with thousands of readers (t.ly/h2jq1).
The new trade diplomacy: take a lot, give a little
India's trade posture has flipped. For decades we were the reluctant partner who walked out of RCEP. Now we are signing, and fast.
But read the fine print and one pattern jumps out. We take almost everything, and give back carefully. Call it asymmetric liberalisation.
New Zealand:
- Wellington opens 100% of its 8,284 lines to us, immediately.3
- India liberalises 70.03% of its lines, and only 30% of those go to zero on day one; the rest phase in over three to ten years.3
- Crucially, India walls off 29.97% of its tariff lines completely: dairy, onions, chickpeas, corn, sugar and edible oils.3
UK CETA:
- Britain drops duties on about 99% of Indian goods.4
- India opens roughly 89.5% of its lines, but only 24.5% of UK exports get duty-free access immediately.4
- Scotch whisky, for instance, only falls from 150% to 100% now, reaching 40% after a decade.4
- Dairy, cereals, millets, pulses and apples stay excluded.4
The logic is defensible. About 89% of India's agricultural households farm under two hectares.14 You cannot expose that base to New Zealand milk powder or Australian chickpeas overnight.
But here is the quiet cost. By winning duty-free access abroad and shielding the farm gate at home, the government has handed the entire burden of execution to the exporter. Tariffs are gone. Non-tariff barriers are not. And non-tariff barriers are technical, unforgiving, and exactly where India's supply chain breaks.
Look at the UK prize. Britain imports about $37.5bn of agriculture a year and takes just $811mn of it from India, around 2.2%.9 The headroom is enormous. Shrimp, tuna and fishmeal that carried 4.2% to 8.5% UK tariffs are now duty-free.9 Tea, spices and basmati walk in free.9 On paper, a windfall. In practice, only if the container clears inspection.
SPS: the barrier that replaced the tariff
When tariffs fall, the friction does not disappear. It just moves to SPS and to technical barriers to trade, or TBT: the standards, certifications and residue limits a country is allowed to set under WTO rules, as long as they rest on science and are not disguised protectionism.
As tariffs vanished worldwide, SPS notifications surged. They have quietly become the modern weapon of trade friction, and they fall hardest on developing exporters who cannot pivot the moment a rule changes.
India's problem is rarely the intrinsic quality of the food. It is the chain of proof. In global trade the absence of contamination is not enough; you need an unbroken chain of accredited paperwork and residue compliance. When that chain snaps, or when a foreign regulator moves faster than our farms can adapt, the shipment dies. Four live crises show exactly how.
1. Australia: the cost of a broken certificate
Australia runs one of the strictest biosecurity regimes on earth. It does not test every container; it trusts accredited Indian fumigators to treat rice with methyl bromide or aluminium phosphide before it sails.
On 13 July 2026, its agriculture department suspended 44 Indian fumigation agencies, roughly 60% of the ones it accredits, most clustered in the basmati belts of Haryana and Punjab.5 Audits had found certificates that did not add up, including consignments recorded as packed before they were fumigated.5
The fallout is brutal:
- More than 100 containers of basmati, worth about ₹200 crore, are stuck in regulatory limbo.5
- Each now faces mandatory re-fumigation on arrival, at $700 to $1,200 a container.5
The rice itself may be spotless. But the paperwork lost its validity, so the shipment became a liability. That is the paradox in a single container.
2. The EU: a chemical chasm
India and the EU farm by different rulebooks. Our food regulator sets residue limits for a hot, humid, pest-heavy country; Brussels pushes maximum residue limits toward near-zero for anything it has banned. Chemicals our farmers lean on are simply illegal in Europe.
The collision shows up in the EU's rapid alert system. In 2025, India ranked first in the world for pesticide alerts, with 124 of them, ahead of Turkey at 105, Egypt at 88, China at 48 and Brazil at 34.6 Being number one in that particular league is not a badge anyone wants.
The repeat offenders are familiar: ethylene oxide, a banned fumigant, turning up in sesame; tricyclazole, a rice-blast fungicide, in basmati; chlorpyrifos in rice. Indian sesame now carries a 20% EU border-check rate for ethylene oxide, and cumin a 30% rate for other residues.10 Every alert triggers destroyed consignments, higher insurance and slower clearance for everyone shipping behind you.
3. Japan and Nepal: blocked by a protocol
For 20 years India shipped premium Alphonso and Kesar mangoes to Japan using vapour heat treatment, a chemical-free process that cooks out fruit-fly larvae. Then, on 29 May 2026, Japan suspended imports carrying certificates issued after 25 March, after inspectors flagged lapses at a treatment facility in Rehmanpur, Uttar Pradesh.7
Japan is tiny for us, about $1.54mn a year, mostly Gujarat's Kesar.7 But it was our first Japanese restriction in two decades, and the reputational hit travels.7
Nepal added to the noise. Reports of a Nepali "ban" flew around, but both governments have since clarified there is no formal ban; Nepal has instead introduced new phytosanitary conditions, including hot water treatment, and India is contesting the measures through the WTO and bilateral channels.11 Notice the pattern across all three: the block is never about the fruit. It is about a protocol.
4. Shrimp: zero tolerance on antibiotics
Our marine sector faces the hardest wall of all. Western regulators permit no trace of antibiotics like chloramphenicol or nitrofurans, because of links to antimicrobial resistance.
Per India's own drug regulator, banned residues drove 43% of shrimp rejections in 2025 across the EU, the US and Japan.8 The US FDA alone logged 93 antibiotic-linked shrimp refusals that year, its sixth-highest count in 24 years.8
Where India stands, against itself
Now BharatNama's favourite question. Where inside India does the problem actually live? Because the national number hides a very lopsided map.
When our marine authority traced the farms behind the 2026 antibiotic detections, the concentration was staggering:
- Andhra Pradesh accounted for 74% of the implicated farms.8
- Odisha made up 13%, West Bengal 8.7% and Gujarat 4.3%.8
One state drives three-quarters of a national reputational risk. The basmati story is just as concentrated: the suspended fumigators sit overwhelmingly in Haryana and Punjab.5 These are not "India" problems in the abstract. They are problems of a handful of clusters, which is the bad news, concentration of risk, and the good news, because a handful of nodes is exactly what you can fix. This kind of state-versus-state spread is the sort of number I find genuinely fascinating, and if unpacking them is your thing too, come join the daily India deep-dives in the BharatNama WhatsApp group (t.ly/h2jq1).
Where India stands, against the world
Set India beside the countries it actually competes with, on current numbers, and the picture sharpens.
- On EU pesticide alerts, India leads the whole table: 124 against China's 48 and Brazil's 34.6 Yes, we ship more, so we trip more, but the gap is not only about volume.
- In seafood, Vietnam out-earns us outright. It exported about $11.3bn of seafood in 2025, shrimp alone at roughly $4.65bn, growing 13% in a year.16 India's marine exports were about $7.45bn in 2024-25.17
Vietnam is the tell. It faced the same Western zero-tolerance wall we do. It responded by wiring tighter traceability, cold chains and compliance into the supply chain, and then climbed the value ladder.16 We are the bigger farm; they are the better exporter.
What India can learn
The countries that cracked this all did one thing we have not. They pushed compliance upstream, to the farm, instead of trying to inject it at the port.
- Vietnam built traceability and third-party certification into its seafood chain, and is now an $11.3bn exporter.16
- Kenya and Peru turned smallholder horticulture into EU-grade exports by clustering farmers under GlobalGAP certification, so a single verified block, not a lone farmer, carries the audit.18
What actually transfers to India, and what does not, matters here, because I have no time for lazy "India should just copy them" takes.
Portable:
- Farm-level traceability, geo-tagged plots, residue testing before harvest, and clustering small farmers into certified blocks. We have started: our marine authority runs pre-harvest ELISA testing across a network of 12 labs and a Shaphari antibiotic-free certification scheme, and APEDA is building farm-to-port traceability for crops.12,13
Not portable wholesale:
- We cannot simply adopt EU residue limits. India's roughly 89% smallholder base farms in humid, pest-heavy conditions and depends on affordable agrochemicals to feed 1.4bn people.14 A blanket ban on tricyclazole would help exporters and hurt domestic yields. The realistic path is phased harmonisation inside designated export zones, not a national copy-paste.
Credibility begins at home
There is a home-front dimension foreign regulators watch closely. In July 2026, our food safety authority suspended the licence of Westend Agro Products, maker of the "Organic Shastra" brand, after finding machinery altering batch numbers and expiry dates, and packaging that falsely claimed the goods were "organic".15
When your own regulator keeps uncovering date-tampering and fake-organic claims, foreign border agencies quietly mark up your risk profile. The enhanced checks abroad and the adulteration raids at home are two ends of the same credibility problem.
And underneath it all sits the real question: who actually owns export quality? On paper, everyone. In practice, no one. State governments run primary agriculture, the food authority sets domestic safety, APEDA promotes crop exports, the marine authority governs seafood, Plant Quarantine issues phytosanitary certificates, Customs signs the exit. Every silo does its slice; none owns the outcome. The exporter, aggregating produce from hundreds of untraceable micro-farms, ends up a collector of paperwork rather than an architect of quality. When Brussels tightens a residue limit, the signal has to crawl back through that maze to a village pesticide dealer, and by then the container is already destroyed.
What to watch
- Whether India wins a one-time Australian exemption for the ₹200 crore of basmati already in transit, using the consultation framework in the India-Australia trade agreement.5
- Whether Japan restores mango access once the Rehmanpur treatment facility is re-audited.7
- Whether pre-harvest testing actually pulls Andhra Pradesh's antibiotic rejection share down over the next two shrimp cycles.8,12
- Whether APEDA's farm-to-port traceability moves from pilot to scale before UK CETA volumes ramp up.4
India has learned to open the world's doors. It has not yet learned to walk its containers through them.
