I have been staring at two numbers all week and I cannot get them to sit comfortably together.
In October 2018, India launched SATAT, the Sustainable Alternative Towards Affordable Transportation programme, and promised 5,000 compressed biogas plants producing 15 MMT of gas a year by 2023-24.1
As of 6 August 2026, two years past that deadline, India has 217 commissioned plants producing 0.4 MMSCMD.2
That is about 4% of the plant target. On volume it is under 1%.
And on that exact same day, the Union Cabinet approved GOBARdhan, the National Circular Bioenergy Scheme, with ₹23,731 crore behind it over ten years.3
So the question I keep coming back to is not whether biogas matters for India. It obviously does. The question is why the last promise did not land, and whether ₹23,731 crore actually fixes the thing that broke.
What was actually approved
Compressed biogas, or CBG, is simple in principle. You put cattle dung, paddy straw, sugar mill press mud or wet municipal waste into a sealed digester, let bacteria eat it, and you get a gas that is 55% to 65% methane. Scrub out the carbon dioxide and the hydrogen sulphide, push methane purity past 95%, and you have a fuel chemically identical to CNG that runs in the same engines and the same pipelines.
The residue left behind, Fermented Organic Manure or FOM, is a fertiliser.
GOBARdhan does not invent any of this. What it does is collapse five separate programmes into one. SATAT, the Market Development Assistance for organic manure, the Biomass Aggregation Machinery scheme, the Development of Pipeline Infrastructure scheme, and the older capital assistance window now sit under a single roof at the Ministry of Petroleum and Natural Gas.4
The mechanics that matter:
- A legally enforceable blending mandate. City gas distribution companies must blend 3% CBG into CNG for transport and PNG for homes in FY2026-27, 4% in FY2027-28, and 5% from FY2028-29 onward.3
- A fixed administered price of ₹2,110 per MMBTU, roughly ₹105 per kg, locked for a minimum of ten years.5 That is a jump of about 43% on the ₹1,478 per MMBTU (₹77.4 per kg) that producers were getting in mid-2025.6
- Capital assistance of up to ₹2 crore per tonne per day of installed capacity for greenfield plants.3
- ₹1,500 per tonne of Market Development Assistance on Fermented Organic Manure.5
- An 85% credit guarantee on loans to MSME-scale CBG projects.2
The government's own projection over the decade: ₹40,000 crore of import substitution, 1.5 lakh jobs, ₹75,000 crore added to GDP, 250 MMT of organic fertiliser and a 40 MT cut in carbon dioxide.2
Read that list and it looks like the sector's every complaint has been answered at once. Which is exactly why it is worth asking what went wrong the first time.
Why 3,694 letters of intent became 217 plants
Here is the interesting bit. The bottleneck was never demand for the gas, and it was never enthusiasm from entrepreneurs.
By October 2022 the oil marketing companies had already handed out 3,694 letters of intent.1 Today 1,908 plants are formally registered. Only 217 are commissioned. Another 339 are under construction. And 1,352 have simply not started.2
The failure happened after the paperwork, at the plant gate. Four things killed it:
- Feedstock is not a commodity, it is a logistics problem. Wet organic waste has low bulk density and high moisture, so hauling it beyond about 25 to 30 km destroys the plant's margins. Every CBG plant is therefore trapped inside a tiny catchment, and must aggregate from thousands of scattered smallholders. Press mud is available roughly six months a year. Dung prices in one surveyed plant rose 40%.7
- So plants ran half empty. Indian CBG facilities operate at 20% to 60% of designed capacity. European plants routinely clear 80%.8
- The gas had nowhere to go. Only about 15% of functional Indian plants are connected to a city gas distribution network.8 The rest truck compressed gas in steel cascades on diesel lorries, which is expensive and quietly undercuts the whole carbon argument.
- The manure was a liability, not a revenue line. Every 10 tonnes of gas leaves behind roughly 25 tonnes of solid digestate and 80 tonnes of liquid.8 Without a market for it, plants physically clog.
Add to that a developer having to walk eight government departments that rarely coordinate, and officials rotating out every two years, and you get 1,352 registered projects that never broke ground.8
This is the pattern I keep running into across Indian infrastructure, where the announcement is federal and the failure is local, and it is the kind of thread we pull apart most mornings in the BharatNama WhatsApp group, where I share a smaller India deep-dive like this with thousands of readers every day (t.ly/h2jq1).
The cattle problem hiding inside the energy problem
There is a second story buried in this scheme, and it is the one I find genuinely elegant.
India's last published livestock count, the 20th Livestock Census of 2019, put the bovine population at about 303mn animals, of which roughly 5mn were stray.9 The 21st Census was enumerated through 2024 and 2025 and its results are still not out, so 2019 remains the newest official number we have.
The cause is not sentiment, it is mechanisation. Tractors made bullocks commercially useless. Slaughter restrictions mean a farmer cannot sell a non-productive animal. Fodder still costs money. So the animal gets released onto the road, where it eats standing crops and plastic and causes accidents.
CBG changes the arithmetic of owning that animal. India generates roughly 3mn tonnes of cattle dung a day, enough in theory for about 180mn m³ of biogas daily.7 A gaushala that can sell dung to a digester stops being a charity line item and starts being a feedstock supplier.
That is the part legislation alone has never managed to solve, and a fuel-blending mandate might.
Where India actually stands
Now the comparison that matters, and it is not flattering.
India consumed 197 MMSCMD of natural gas in June 2026, with 56% of that imported as LNG and domestic output flat at 87 MMSCMD.10 CBG contributes 0.4 MMSCMD. That is about 0.2% of India's gas.
Set that beside the countries that took biomethane seriously:
- Denmark: biomethane is about 40% of total gas consumption, up from roughly 10% in 2019, with a target of a fully green gas grid by 2030. It does this with just 173 biogas plants, about 55 to 60 of which upgrade to grid quality.11
- United States: the world's largest biomethane producer at roughly 136 PJ, having grown 2.2 times since 2020.12
- Germany: the largest combined biogas and biomethane market on earth at 329 PJ in 2024, though output has been broadly flat since 2017.12
- India: the IEA expects combined Indian biogas and biomethane output to grow just 21% between 2024 and 2030.12
And the theoretical Indian potential? About 62 MMT of CBG a year. Current output is below 1% of it.13
Now break India open against itself, because the national number hides the real story. Of the 217 commissioned plants:
- Uttar Pradesh: 40
- Gujarat: 25
- Maharashtra: 2414
Three states hold roughly 40% of India's CBG fleet. Until recently only four states, Uttar Pradesh, Haryana, Bihar and Gujarat, had any bioenergy policy supporting CBG at all.15 Maharashtra only notified its own CBG policy on 5 May 2026, with viability gap funding of up to ₹75 lakh per tonne of capacity, capped at ₹15 crore a project, and ₹500 crore allocated for FY2026-27.14
So the binding constraint is not central money. It is that most Indian states have no CBG policy, no land norms, no single-window clearance and no feedstock aggregation machinery. A central price guarantee does not build a district-level dung supply chain.
What India can learn from Denmark
Denmark is the right teacher here, and not for the reason people usually assume. It is not that the Danes are greener. It is that they solved precisely India's feedstock problem.
About 75% of Danish biogas feedstock is livestock manure and slurry.11 Denmark then did four specific things:
- It mandated the manure. A national target that 50% of livestock manure be processed for biogas by 2025 turned a waste-disposal obligation into guaranteed plant feedstock.11
- It guaranteed grid access. A right to inject gives biomethane producers a standardised, non-negotiable connection to the gas grid.11 Compare that with India's 15% CGD connection rate.
- It gave 20-year contracts. Since 2024, competitive tenders award two-decade production contracts to the lowest bidder, which is what banks actually lend against.11
- It capped energy crops at 4% of feedstock from 2025, deliberately keeping the industry on waste rather than on farmland.11
India has now copied the price certainty and the offtake mandate. It has not copied the manure mandate or the right to inject, and those are the two that solve the exact problems that killed SATAT.
What does not transfer is scale. Denmark runs 173 plants for 6mn people in a compact country with an existing gas grid. India needs thousands of plants across a subcontinent where the gas grid does not reach most of the catchments that have the feedstock. That is why the Development of Pipeline Infrastructure component, at ₹994.5 crore, may matter more per rupee than the headline capital subsidy.5
The money has already moved
The corporates are not waiting to find out.
- Reliance has put in ₹6,500 crore, has 55 CBG plants in execution of which 41 are operational, and reckons it accounts for about a quarter of India's CBG ecosystem. Its stated long-term target is 500 plants.16 It broke ground on the first of a planned 500 plants in Andhra Pradesh in April 2025 under a ₹65,000 crore state commitment.17
- Adani Total Gas is building a 500 TPD bio-CNG plant on Ahmedabad's Pirana dumpsite for the municipal corporation, on a 20-year PPP at about ₹130 crore.18
- GAIL acquired a 49% stake in Leafiniti Bioenergy, TruAlt's CBG subsidiary, in March 2026.19
Two regulatory changes quietly de-risked all of this. In March 2025 the Fertiliser Control Order was amended to create a whole new category, Organic Carbon Enhancer, formally recognising FOM and its liquid form as fertilisers.20 And in April 2025 the CPCB created a Blue Category for industries providing essential environmental services, which lets qualifying waste-to-energy and CBG plants run on a two-year extended consent instead of re-applying constantly.21
The fertiliser angle is the one that should interest the finance ministry most. India budgeted ₹1.71 lakh crore for fertiliser subsidy in FY2026-27, and the Department of Fertilisers has said the bill could exceed ₹3 lakh crore if West Asian supply disruption persists, against about ₹2 lakh crore in FY2025-26.22 India imported over 100 lakh tonnes of urea last fiscal year. Every tonne of quality FOM that displaces imported urea is a rupee the exchequer does not spend.
This is the sort of second-order link I think gets badly under-covered in Indian business writing, and it is the kind of thing I unpack daily in the BharatNama community (t.ly/h2jq1).
Why CBG and not hydrogen
One last piece of context, because the obvious objection is that India should be building for hydrogen instead.
Green hydrogen in India currently clears competitive tenders at about ₹397 per kg for supply to Indian Oil's refineries and ₹387 per kg for BPCL and HPCL, including GST. Against a 2030 target of 5 MMT a year, commissioned capacity stands at 8,000 tonnes, which is 0.16% of the target.23
CBG sells at roughly ₹105 per kg, needs no new engine, no new pipeline standard and no new refuelling network. For heavy trucking and intercity buses over the next decade, that is not a compromise, it is the only thing that actually works today.
What to watch
- Whether the CBO is enforced or quietly relaxed. The 3% obligation bites in FY2026-27. Watch whether city gas distributors are penalised for missing it, or granted a waiver on grounds of unavailable supply.
- The conversion rate of the 1,352 not-started projects. That number, not the announcement, is the real scoreboard. Track it against the 339 currently under construction.
- Whether more states follow Maharashtra. Watch for CBG policies with viability gap funding from Karnataka, Tamil Nadu, Punjab and Andhra Pradesh over the next two quarters.
- Whether FOM actually sells. The ₹1,500 per tonne MDA only works if the Organic Carbon Enhancer category generates real farm demand. Watch FOM offtake volumes, not production.
- The 21st Livestock Census release. It will tell us whether the stray cattle population has grown since 2019, and therefore how big the dung feedstock base really is.
India did not fail at biogas because it lacked cattle, straw or ambition. It failed because it wrote a target in Delhi and then asked a district to build the supply chain for free.

Here is a number that should not really be possible for an Indian state. The money Keralites working abroad sent home in 2023 came to ₹2.17 lakh crore, which is 23.2% of the state's income.1
Now put that beside a country instead of a state, and it lands. Nepal, the textbook remittance economy, runs at about 26% of GDP.2 Kerala is sitting right next to it. India as a whole is at just 3.5%.2
So on this one metric Kerala does not really behave like a part of India. It behaves like a small nation that exports its people and lives on what they wire back. That model has worked beautifully for half a century. This year, a war is quietly asking whether it still works.
A state that runs on other people's wages
The mechanics are worth stating plainly, because they are unusual.
Kerala does not earn its keep by making things. It manufactures very little, imports most of what it eats, wears and builds, and pays for those imports with foreign wages. Roughly 2.2mn Keralites work overseas,1 about one in every fifteen people in the state, and their money has quietly underwritten the hospitals, the schools and the property market that the "Kerala model" is celebrated for.
Two features make this fragile.
- It is dangerously concentrated. 80.5% of Kerala's emigrants are in the six Gulf states, and 38.6% are in the UAE alone.1 There is almost no geographic hedge.
- It is exposed to precisely one thing going wrong: instability in the Gulf.
That is the thing now going wrong. The 2026 war between Israel, the United States and Iran has flared through this year, with a fragile ceasefire that keeps breaking down into fresh strikes across the region.3 For most of India this is an oil-price story. For Kerala it is an income story, and a far more direct one.
The people who track this closely, led by the migration economist S. Irudaya Rajan, expect remittances into Kerala to fall by around a fifth this financial year if the war drags on.4 The state's new Chief Minister has put the same number on record. V.D. Satheesan, who took charge in May 2026 after the Congress-led UDF ended the Left's ten-year run,5 told an interviewer in July that he expects a 20% dip in remittances this year, called them "the backbone of the state economy", and confirmed he has gone to Delhi asking for special assistance to ride it out.6
A 20% fall does not sound apocalyptic until you remember what those remittances actually do.
How far Kerala has travelled, in the wrong direction
The instinct is to assume Kerala has been slowly weaning itself off the Gulf. The data says the opposite. The dependence has deepened.
- Remittances into Kerala went from ₹85 thousand crore in 2018 to ₹2.17 lakh crore in 2023, a rise of about 155% in five years.1
- As a share of the state's income, they climbed from 13.5% to 23.2% over the same period.1
In other words, in the years when everyone assumed Kerala was diversifying, the state actually became more hooked on foreign wages, not less. The Gulf money flowed in, went first into repaying the debt that funded the migration, and then into land, houses and gold, inflating an asset base that has very little to do with what Keralites at home actually earn.
This is exactly the kind of thread I keep pulling at, and it is the sort of thing we go back and forth on in the BharatNama WhatsApp group, where I share a smaller India deep-dive like this most mornings (t.ly/h2jq1).
The composition of who leaves has shifted underneath all this, and that shift is the real story of the next decade.
- Student emigration from Kerala doubled, from about 130 thousand in 2018 to 250 thousand in 2023, and students are now 11.3% of all emigrants.1
- Among women who leave, 51.6% go as nurses, and 40.5% of them now prefer Europe and the West over the Gulf.1
The young and the highly qualified are increasingly skipping the Gulf entirely for Canada, the UK, Australia and Germany, where there is a path to residency and a life, not just a contract. That is good for those families. It is quietly terrible for the remittance model, because a nurse who settles in Toronto with her family stops wiring the bulk of her salary back to Kochi in a way a construction supervisor in Dubai never did.
Where India stands: against the world, and against itself
Two comparisons make the position clear, and both are built on current, like-for-like data.
India against the world. On remittance dependence, Kerala is an outlier not just within India but globally:
- Tajikistan: about 48% of GDP.2
- Nepal: about 26%.2
- Kerala: 23.2% of state income.1
- Philippines: about 9%.2
- India as a whole: 3.5%.2
Kerala belongs on the list of economies that survive on their diaspora, sitting beside Nepal, far above the Philippines, while the country it is part of barely registers. That is a genuinely strange place for one of India's richest, most literate states to be.
India against itself. Here is the sharper contrast. India's remittance base has already pivoted away from the Gulf. Kerala has not.
- For India as a whole, the United States is now the single largest source of remittances at 27.7%, having overtaken the UAE at 19.2%, according to the RBI's latest survey.7
- Advanced economies, the US, UK, Singapore, Canada and Australia together, now send more than half of all money remitted to India, while the Gulf's share has slipped to 38%.7
- Kerala, meanwhile, is still 80.5% dependent on those same Gulf states.1
So the rest of India has, almost accidentally, diversified its way to safety through white-collar migration to the West. Kerala is still carrying the blue-collar Gulf model that India as a whole is walking away from. When a war hits the Gulf, the country shrugs and Kerala shakes.
The fiscal scissor closing on the state
None of this would matter so much if Kerala had room in its budget to absorb a shock. It does not. It is caught in what economists call a scissor effect: revenue is being squeezed from one side while spending obligations are fixed on the other.
Start with the spending blade. Kerala's 2026-27 budget shows a state with almost no financial flexibility left:
- Committed expenditure, the money it has no choice but to spend, is 72% of revenue receipts, split across salaries (31%), pensions (21%) and interest payments (20%).8
- Interest alone eats one in every five rupees the state earns.8
- Capital spending, the money that actually builds the future, is stuck near 1.2% of GSDP, among the lowest in India.8
- The revenue deficit is 2.2% of GSDP and outstanding debt is 34% of GSDP.8
Now the revenue blade, and this is the fresh cut. When a state consumes less, its tax take falls, because Kerala's revenue is overwhelmingly consumption-based (it makes little to tax at the factory gate). A 20% drop in remittances feeds straight through into weaker spending on cars, gold and construction, and therefore into weaker GST. The income that funds the state and the income that gets taxed are the same Gulf income.
That is the trap. The shock that cuts Kerala's revenue is the same shock that would force it to spend more, on returning, jobless migrants who need rehabilitating.
The federal squeeze, and a case that could redraw the map
Faced with a revenue hole, any government would normally borrow. Kerala's problem is that it cannot, and the reason has become a landmark constitutional fight.
Two things happened at once. First, the Sixteenth Finance Commission, whose award runs from 2026, raised Kerala's share of central taxes slightly, from 1.925% to 2.382%, but scrapped the revenue deficit grants that had cushioned the state.9 Kerala had drawn ₹37,814 crore in such grants over the previous five-year cycle; the new figure is zero.9 The Chief Minister called it "a huge shock to the state exchequer".6 Kerala gains on paper and loses in cash.
Second, the Centre tightened the borrowing rules. States can normally borrow up to 3% of GSDP under the fiscal-responsibility framework. But the Union began counting the off-budget borrowings of state entities, most importantly the Kerala Infrastructure Investment Fund Board (KIIFB), against that same ceiling, shrinking the room Kerala actually has to raise money.
Kerala's response was extraordinary. In December 2023 it sued the Union of India in the Supreme Court, arguing that borrowing is a state subject and that Delhi was strangling its fiscal autonomy. In April 2024 the court refused Kerala interim relief of ₹26,226 crore in borrowing space, but it also referred the deeper questions to a five-judge Constitution Bench, because Article 293, which governs how states borrow, has never been properly interpreted in the country's history.10 That reference is still pending, and whenever it is decided it will settle, for every Indian state, exactly how much fiscal freedom the Constitution actually grants.
This is the part I find genuinely gripping, and it is the kind of structural, second-order story we dig into daily in the BharatNama community rather than just the headline (t.ly/h2jq1).
What India can learn: the Philippines figured this out
India does not have to invent an answer here. The Philippines, the other great labour-exporting economy, faced the same dependence decades ago and built its way out of the worst of it.
- It diversified geography relentlessly. Filipino workers are spread across more than a hundred countries, so no single war or oil crash can take down the whole flow. Kerala's 80.5% concentration in one region is the opposite of this.
- It built institutions around migration, culminating in a full Department of Migrant Workers, with mandatory pre-departure training, contract vetting and reintegration support for returnees.
- It kept remittances at a manageable share of GDP, about 9%,2 precisely because the domestic economy, especially business-process outsourcing, grew fast enough to give people an option at home.
The transferable lesson for Kerala and for India is not "copy the Philippines". It is narrower and harder: diversify the destinations, formalise and protect the skilled migration that is already happening (the ILO and Kerala's own NORKA agency began exactly this work on nurses and care workers in 2026), and above all build enough of a domestic economy that a returning migrant has somewhere to land. Kerala has the human capital; what it has never built is the local job.
What to watch
- Whether the 2026 Gulf ceasefire holds, and whether Gulf construction and hiring restart. This is the single biggest swing factor for Kerala's FY27.
- Kerala's own remittance and bank-deposit data through the year, to see if the projected 20% fall actually shows up.
- Whether the Centre grants Chief Minister Satheesan the special assistance he has asked for, and on what conditions.
- Whether the Supreme Court's Constitution Bench finally takes up the Article 293 reference, the outcome of which binds every state.
Kerala spent fifty years proving that you can build a rich, healthy, literate society without building an economy. The bill for that shortcut is now arriving in the same envelope as a war.

Here is a number that should stop any celebration of India's rise cold. After three decades of world-beating growth, roughly 9 in 10 Indians who work still do so informally.1 No written contract. No paid leave. No provident fund. Nothing between them and a bad month.
I keep coming back to this because it quietly breaks the story we tell ourselves. We have the GDP. We have the unicorns. We have UPI rails clearing more digital payments than any system on earth. And yet the typical Indian worker is about as exposed today as their parent was a generation ago.
The thing is, this is not an accident of bad luck. It is the direct result of the particular road India took to get richer. We grew fast, but we skipped the one phase that usually turns growth into secure work.
First, what "informal" actually means
Two ideas get muddled here, so let me separate them cleanly.
- The informal (or unorganised) sector is about the enterprise: tiny, unregistered firms that sit outside the tax, legal, and regulatory net. About 82% of India's workforce sits in it.1
- Informal employment is about the worker: no written contract, no social security, no paid leave, whoever the employer is. Nearly 90% of Indians are informally employed.1
That second gap is the important one, because informal employment exists even inside formal, registered companies. The contract cleaner in a gleaming IT park and the delivery rider working for a listed, deep-pocketed platform are both informally employed, working for very formal firms.
And this is not a fringe of the economy. The unorganised sector still produces close to 45% of India's GDP.2 This is the water most Indians swim in, not a puddle at the edge.
Look at the shape of who works and how, from the latest Periodic Labour Force Survey, the government's official employment survey:
- Self-employed: 56.2% of all workers in 2025, the largest slice by far.1
- Regular wage or salaried: 23.6%.1
- Casual labour: 20.2%.1
Even that "regular" fifth is misleading. Most of them still have no contract and no benefits. Genuine formal, protected jobs are a rounding error, not the norm.
We took the services lift and skipped the factory floor
To see why we are stuck, go back to the baseline. Around 1991, agriculture employed close to 60% of Indians. By 2025 that is down to 43%.1 Vast numbers left the farm. The question is where they went.
The textbook path, the one every East Asian success story followed, runs farm to factory to formal. Surplus farm labour moves into labour-intensive manufacturing, and the factory itself does the formalising: it needs payrolls, contracts, shift rosters, and eventually provident funds and unions.
India did something unusual. It jumped straight from farms to services, largely bypassing the factory phase. Economists call it "premature de-industrialisation", ageing out of manufacturing before ever fully industrialising.
The tell is in one stubborn number. Manufacturing's share of employment has barely moved in a decade, sitting at just 12.1% in 2025.1 It simply never became the sponge that soaked up the people leaving agriculture.
Services grew instead, and grew spectacularly. But modern services, IT, finance, professional work, are capital-heavy and skill-heavy. They cannot absorb the enormous numbers of workers with modest schooling. So the labour leaving farms did not walk into air-conditioned offices. It walked into the low-productivity end of services: petty retail, security, domestic work, construction, and now app-based delivery.
This is the thread I find myself pulling on again and again, and it is exactly the kind of structural puzzle we chew over in the BharatNama WhatsApp community, where I share a smaller India deep-dive like this with thousands of readers every morning (t.ly/h2jq1).
The missing middle, and why firms refuse to grow up
If services could not absorb low-skill labour, why did manufacturing not step up? Because the incentives actively punish scale.
India's factory landscape is barbell-shaped. A vast ocean of tiny firms at one end, a handful of giants at the other, and almost nothing in the middle. Roughly three-quarters of enterprises employ fewer than ten people. These micro-firms run on thin margins and have neither the money nor the reason to put workers on formal payrolls.
Why stay small on purpose? Because growing up is expensive and frightening:
- A growing enterprise can face over 1,450 compliance obligations a year, costing around ₹13 lakh annually, with a chunk carrying the risk of jail for procedural slips.3
- Formal credit is scarce. Only about 14% of MSMEs can access formal, institutional credit at all.4
- The sector's credit gap is roughly ₹25 lakh crore, so the rest borrow from moneylenders at punishing rates or stay stunted.4
Faced with that, thousands of firms make a rational choice: stay below the radar. Stay informal. Which means their workers stay informal too.
When even the formal sector goes informal
Here is where it gets genuinely uncomfortable. Even when the organised sector does grow, it increasingly refuses to create secure jobs. It hires contract workers instead of permanent ones.
The number is striking, and it is current. Contract workers are now 42% of the organised manufacturing workforce, the highest share since 1997-98.5 Go back to 1999-2000 and it was around 20%. It has doubled.5
The usual explanation is that rigid labour laws make it hard to fire permanent staff, so firms hire contract labour to stay flexible. But deeper plant-level work by economists Radhicka Kapoor and P.P. Krishnapriya finds a sharper motive: contract labour is used to dilute the bargaining power of permanent workers and keep overall wages in check.6
Tellingly, contractualisation kept rising even as the wage gap between contract and permanent workers narrowed. If it were only about cheap labour, that should have slowed it. It did not. This is about control, not just cost. The formal sector has learned to reproduce informal conditions inside its own gates.
And you can see the result in pay. The real monthly wage of a regular salaried worker actually fell to about ₹10,925 in 2022, from ₹12,100 in 2012.7 A decade of headline growth, and the typical salaried Indian was earning less in real terms at the end of it.
Where India stands, against the world and against itself
This is the part that matters most to me, because a number for India alone is just a fact. Set beside others, it becomes an insight.
India versus the world, on the metric that drives formalisation, factory jobs:
- India: manufacturing employs ~12% of workers.1
- Vietnam: closer to a fifth, around 21%, and rising every year.8
- South Korea, at its industrial peak, took manufacturing to about 25% of employment while farm work collapsed from 50% to under 20%.9
Same starting point, roughly. Poor, agrarian, labour-rich. Wildly different destinations. Vietnam and Korea pulled their farm workers onto factory floors that formalised them by design. India did not build enough of those floors.
India versus India is just as revealing, and here the disparities and the commonalities both bite:
- Even in the richest western and southern states, three in four workers still sit outside the formal sector.10 Formality is thin everywhere, not just in poor states.
- Unemployment ranges from 0.9% in Gujarat to 8.3% in Goa.1 One national average, many different countries inside it.
- Earnings vary most in self-employment across states, far more than in regular salaried work.10 The people with the least protection also face the widest spread in what they take home.
What India can learn from the ones who cracked it
I am wary of lazy "India should just copy X" takes, so let me be specific about what actually transfers and what does not.
Vietnam is the closest parallel. It was agrarian and poor in the 1980s. Then, from the 1986 Doi Moi reforms, it slashed tariffs on manufactured goods from about 16.6% to 1.1%, threw the doors open to foreign investment, and became a factory to the world. South Korea alone has poured in over $92bn and is now Vietnam's largest foreign investor.8 Those big, compliance-bound multinationals hire on formal contracts by default.
Then Vietnam went further and legislated. Its new Social Insurance Law took effect on 1 July 2025, pulling part-time workers, unsalaried managers, and long-contract foreigners into compulsory social insurance, and reclassifying deliberate non-payment as "evasion" that can trigger criminal proceedings.11
South Korea did it a generation earlier, with the 1973 Heavy and Chemical Industry drive, channelling capital into large industrial groups that scaled fast and formalised as they grew.9
What is portable for India: the sequence of scale first, enforcement second. Build firms big enough to formalise, then legislate to lock it in. India has laid the groundwork with e-Shram, its registry of unorganised workers, now carrying over 30.9 crore registrations, 53.68% of them women.12 Registration is real progress. But a name in a database is not a provident fund. The next step is portable social security that a migrant carries across state lines and between gig apps without losing cover.
What does not transfer neatly: India's federal structure, its tighter fiscal room, and a state that is brilliant at big-bang digital rollouts but patchy at the daily grind of enforcing labour law across a sea of tiny firms. This is exactly the gap between formalising the economy and formalising the worker, and it is the thread I most enjoy arguing out with readers in the BharatNama community every day (t.ly/h2jq1).
What to watch
- Whether the four new labour codes are actually implemented, not just notified, and whether they widen social security or simply ease hiring and firing.
- Whether e-Shram registrations convert into real, portable benefits, or stay a database.
- The manufacturing employment share in the next PLFS. If it does not break clearly above 12%, the structural problem is unchanged.
- The contract-labour share in the next Annual Survey of Industries. A move past 42% means the formal sector is informalising further, not less.
The puzzle of India is not that it failed to grow. It is that it grew rich in output while staying poor in the one thing that makes growth felt in a household: a secure job.

I want to start with a number that should not be possible. Mumbai generates roughly a third of India's income tax and around 40% of its foreign trade1, and yet about 41% of the city lives in slums.2 That is close to eight million people, in the richest city in the country, packed into settlements with no proper roads, no sanitation, and barely any light.
The easy explanation is poverty, or migration, or corruption. I believed some version of that for years. But the deeper I go into how Indian cities are actually zoned, the more I think we did this to ourselves, deliberately, with a single number written into a rulebook.
That number is the Floor Space Index. And the whole tragedy of Indian urbanism sits inside one misunderstanding of it: capping floor space does not cap people. It only caps housing.
What a single number controls
The Floor Space Index (FSI), known globally as the Floor Area Ratio, is simply the ratio of the total built-up floor area you are allowed to construct to the size of the plot.
- An FSI of 1 on a 1,000 sq m plot means 1,000 sq m of floor, full stop. One tall tower on a small footprint, or one flat building sprawled across the whole plot, but never more total floor than that.
- Mumbai wrote FSI into its very first development plan in 1964, and for decades held the base at 1.33 for the island city and 1.0 for the suburbs.3
- The logic was Malthusian: cap the floor, and you cap how many people and firms can crowd onto the existing water pipes, drains, and streets.
Here is the flaw, and it is fatal. People do not move to Mumbai because floor space is available. They move because the jobs, the capital, and the opportunity are there. The migration is driven by wages, not by building rules.
So when you cap the legal floor, the people arrive anyway. The demand does not vanish. It simply gets pushed out of the formal, legal market, because in any market where you freeze supply, the rich outbid everyone else for the little that exists. The clerk, the delivery rider, the nurse, the construction worker: none of them can win that auction. So they build their own housing, informally, off the books, where no FSI rule can reach them.
That is what a slum is. Not a failure of the poor. A workaround for a supply cap.
A city that fought its own geography
Mumbai is the sharpest case in the world because geography already dealt it a terrible hand, and then policy made it worse.
Within a 25 km radius of the old city centre, roughly 66% of the surface is water. For Jakarta that figure is 22%, for Seoul just 5%.4 Mumbai has less than half the developable land of a normal coastal megacity before a single rule is applied.
Every other land-starved city on earth responded to that constraint by building up.
- Manhattan zones its prime districts for a floor-area ratio as high as 15.5
- Central Tokyo permits ratios up to 13 in its densest commercial core around Marunouchi.6
- Singapore, an island as cramped as Mumbai, allows floor ratios climbing into the 20s in its central nodes, and still ends up with more greenery, because taller towers on smaller footprints free the ground.7
Mumbai, facing the worst land shortage of the lot, did the opposite. It held its base FSI at 1.33. A city that should have been the densest vertical metropolis in Asia was legally required to sprawl.
The human cost shows up in one brutal statistic. The urbanist Alain Bertaud calculated that the average Mumbaikar consumed about 4.5 sq m of residential floor space, a level you would expect from a city in wartime rationing, not the financial capital of a $4trn economy.4 Meanwhile the slums, which escape FSI entirely by being informal, cover nearly all their ground and leave no room for a road, let alone a park.
This is exactly the kind of thread I keep pulling at, and it is the sort of thing we go back and forth on in the BharatNama WhatsApp community, where I share a smaller India deep-dive like this with thousands of readers every morning (t.ly/h2jq1).
The metros we build, then starve
The second cost of capping floor is sprawl, and sprawl quietly sabotages the most expensive thing Indian cities are building right now: mass transit.
When a city cannot grow up, it grows out. The edge pushes further from the centre, commutes lengthen, and everyone is forced onto two-wheelers and cars. To fight the resulting gridlock, India has gone on a metro-building spree that is genuinely world class.
- India now runs over 1,000 km of operational metro, across 29 cities, the third-largest network on the planet after China and the US.8
- Delhi alone operates nearly 400 km; Bengaluru and Mumbai are expanding fast.8
But a metro only pays for itself if enough people live and work within walking distance of its stations. That is the entire logic of Transit-Oriented Development (TOD): concentrate dense, mixed-use towers around the station so the train is the natural choice and the fares actually cover the cost.
And here is where the old FSI mindset defeats the new infrastructure. Bengaluru is the cautionary tale.
- The state allowed extra building rights only in a thin 150 m band around metro stations, shrinking the prize before anyone could claim it.
- Even inside that band, developers often could not use the higher floor allowance, because the old setback and ground-coverage rules still applied to the small, fragmented plots typical of the inner city.
- To build dense you had to merge plots, but the state offered no incentive to do so, so the amalgamation rarely happened.9
The result was a multi-billion-rupee metro running past land the rules would not let anyone develop. The transit got built; the density to feed it did not.
Where India stands, against the world and against itself
Set India beside the leaders and the gap is stark. But the more useful comparison, as always, is India against itself, because within the same country one city has quietly cracked the problem.
India versus the world, on the floor cap:
- Mumbai base FSI: 1.33.3
- Manhattan: up to 15.5
- Central Tokyo: up to 13.6
- Singapore: into the 20s.7
India versus the world, on what happens next. Tokyo is the control experiment. Its permissive, supply-first system means the city has held more homes than households for three decades, with vacancy near 11% and housing stock growing about twice as fast as its population.10 The pay-off: even after recent rises in its central wards, Tokyo rent remains a fraction of London's or New York's for a comparable flat.10 Shanghai makes the same point from the other direction: it lifted average floor space per person from 3.6 sq m in 1984 to 34 sq m by 2010, simply by raising FSI and letting redevelopment rip.11
India versus India. This is the part that should give planners pause.
- Mumbai clings to a base FSI of 1.33 and a 41% slum share.2
- Ahmedabad, using its Town Planning Schemes, pools and re-plots land, funds its own trunk infrastructure, and sells premium FSI along its transit corridors. Revenue from that premium FSI grew from about 10% of the city's land-based finance in 2009 to roughly 60% by 2016.12
Same country, same constitution, opposite philosophy. One city treats density as a threat to be rationed. The other treats it as the asset that pays for the city.
What India can learn from Japan
The deepest lesson is not really about numbers. It is about who gets to say no.
In India, and much of the West, zoning is local and discretionary. A local body can delay, dilute, or block a dense project, and wealthy neighbourhoods use that veto to keep apartments out. Supply stays frozen because the people who benefit from scarcity hold the pen.
Japan took the pen away from them. Under the City Planning Law of 1968, zoning is national. The whole country runs on just 12 standardised land-use zones, applied uniformly, with local plans needing central sign-off.13 Three features make it work:
- Nuisance-based, not exclusionary. Even the strictest residential zone allows a clinic, a small shop, a home office. Mixed use is the default, which is what makes walkable, transit-friendly neighbourhoods form on their own.13
- By-right approval. If your design meets the objective national rules on height and light, the permit must be issued. No discretionary gauntlet, no room for the quiet extraction that plagues Indian approvals.13
- Continuous deregulation. After its 1990s crash, Japan kept loosening the codes to pump out supply, and prices obeyed.
Not all of it transfers. India is a federation, land is a state subject, and state capacity varies wildly. But the portable idea is precise: standardise the rules, make density a right rather than a favour, and take the veto away from whoever profits from scarcity.
Delhi is inching this way. Its freshly notified TOD policy opens roughly 207 sq km along metro and rapid-rail corridors, allows a floor-area ratio up to 500 (that is, 5.0) on payment of charges, and reserves at least 65% of that floor for smaller homes.14 Whether it works will depend entirely on whether the old setback and coverage rules are relaxed to let that bulk actually get built. Bengaluru already showed what happens when they are not.
That distinction, between a rule that looks generous on paper and one that a developer can actually use, is exactly the sort of thing worth chewing over, and it is the kind of thread we keep pulling in the BharatNama community (t.ly/h2jq1).
What to watch
- Whether Delhi's TOD notification is followed by matching relief on setbacks, ground coverage, and parking minimums, or stalls the way Bengaluru's did.
- Mumbai's DCPR 2034 in practice: how much of the higher transit-corridor FSI (up to 5, and up to 7 near some metro stations) is genuinely usable versus trapped behind narrow roads.3
- Whether any large state copies Ahmedabad's Town Planning Scheme and premium-FSI model to self-fund infrastructure, rather than waiting on central grants.
- The next PLFS and urban housing data for signs that formal supply is finally outpacing household formation in the big metros. It has not, yet.
The one line
India's cities did not run out of land. They ran out of permission to build on it.

Here is a number the government is proud of, and it deserves a second look. India's forest and tree cover now stands at ~8.3 lakh sq km, or 25.17% of the country's land, the highest it has ever been recorded.1
That is the headline of the India State of Forest Report 2023, the biennial audit that is still the country's latest word on its own forests.1 It is a good news story. Forest and tree cover rose by 1,445 sq km in two years. India's forests hold a carbon stock of 30.43bn tonnes of CO2 equivalent, and have already added 2.29bn tonnes of the 2.5 to 3.0bn-tonne sink India promised the world by 2030.2
Now here is the number nobody puts on a press release. Over the decade to 2021, roughly 93,000 sq km of India's forests, an area larger than Andhra Pradesh, structurally degraded: dense forest thinning to open, forest and scrub collapsing into bare land.34
Both numbers are true at once. That is the paradox this edition is about.
The definition doing all the work
Start with what "forest cover" actually means in India, because the definition is doing almost all the work.
The Forest Survey of India counts as forest any patch of at least one hectare with a tree canopy of 10% or more.1 That is it. Not who owns it, not whether it is a legal forest, and crucially, not what is growing there. As the FSI's own methodology says, the count includes commercial orchards, bamboo, and palm and rubber plantations.4
So the picture is stitched together from satellite imagery, mostly the indigenous LISS-III sensor at 23.5-metre resolution.4 A satellite is superb at seeing green. It cannot tell an ancient, multi-layered rainforest from a monoculture rubber estate. Both read as "forest".
Layer on the classification the FSI uses within that green:
- Very Dense Forest (VDF): canopy above 70%.
- Moderately Dense Forest (MDF): canopy 40 to 70%.
- Open Forest (OF): canopy 10 to 40%.
- Below 10%, land is scrub or non-forest.
The trouble is that a number can climb even as the thing it measures falls apart. A rubber plantation crossing 10% canopy adds to the tally exactly as a thinning old-growth forest slips down through the classes. The aggregate goes up. The ecology goes down. This is a story I keep coming back to in the BharatNama WhatsApp group, where I share a smaller India deep-dive like this with thousands of readers every morning, and forest data is a near-perfect case of a metric that flatters the thing it is meant to police (t.ly/h2jq1).
The mechanics of a comforting number
Look under the aggregate and the direction of travel reverses.
Between 2011 and 2021, inside recorded forest areas, the degradation ran in a clear downward staircase:34
- 40,709 sq km of Very Dense and Moderately Dense Forest, India's richest carbon and biodiversity stores, thinned into Open Forest.
- 5,573 sq km of forest slipped further, into scrub.
- 46,707 sq km of forest and scrub lost their canopy entirely and became non-forest.
That is close to 93,000 sq km of structural loss. The FSI itself concedes that restoring this degraded land to its former density would lock up an additional ~637mn tonnes of carbon.3 That is the sequestration the current trajectory is bleeding away.
So how does a report built on that reality announce a net gain? Through a step that has spatial ecologists genuinely puzzled. A straight comparison of the 2021 and 2023 raw data suggests nearly 1,93,000 sq km of dense and open forest was lost or altered.4 The published report applies an unexplained "normalisation factor" that turns that gross loss into a net increase of just 297 sq km for those categories.4 The method is opaque to independent researchers, which is a polite way of saying nobody outside the FSI can reproduce it.
Here is the tell that makes the whole thing click. Organised plantation activity in India is estimated at nearly 18,000 sq km every year.4 Yet total forest and tree cover rose by only 1,445 sq km over two years.1 Either vast tracts of natural forest are being cut at a pace that almost cancels all that planting, or most of those plantations are simply dying. Neither reading supports the triumphant headline.
Not aesthetics, chemistry
The instinct is to shrug: a tree is a tree, green is green. The soil says otherwise.
Most of a forest's durable carbon is not in the trunks and leaves you can see. It sits underground, as soil organic carbon, held there by the tangle of diverse roots, continuous leaf litter, and stable microbes that only a natural forest builds up over centuries.
A study by the Kerala Forest Research Institute and collaborators in the southern Western Ghats put paired plots side by side: pristine natural forest and adjacent teak plantations of 40 to 50 years.5 Over the top 50 cm of soil, the natural forest held roughly 225 tonnes of organic carbon per hectare. The teak plantation held about 195.5
That gap is the buried cost of every "offset" plantation. When a complex forest is cleared for a monoculture, the plantation may hit the 10% canopy bar within a few years and register as recovered cover, but the soil carbon, the acidity, the buffering capacity, all degrade over successive harvest rotations. On the satellite it looks like a win. In the ground it is a slow, uncounted haemorrhage.
Where India stands: against the world, and against itself
Strip away canopy area and measure forests the way foresters actually do, by "growing stock", the volume of living wood per hectare, and India's position is far more sobering.
Growing stock captures height, girth, age and density. It is the honest proxy for how much forest is really there. On this measure:
- India: roughly 56 m³ of wood per hectare.6
- World average: around 110 m³ per hectare.6
- OECD average: about 131 m³ per hectare.7
- South Korea: 165 m³ per hectare, as of 2020.7
India's forests, in other words, hold barely half the wood per hectare of an average forest anywhere, and roughly a third of South Korea's. India's total growing stock is nudging up in aggregate, to ~6.4bn cubic metres, but that is being propped up by trees outside forests, orchards and farm trees, even as the dense natural forests that carry the real volume thin out.1
The picture from abroad is not all grim, and honesty cuts both ways. The FAO's Global Forest Resources Assessment 2025 ranks India 9th in the world by total forest area, at 72.7mn hectares, up a place, and 3rd globally in annual forest gain.8 India's forests remove ~150mn tonnes of CO2 a year, the 5th-largest forest carbon sink on earth.8 India is planting furiously. The question is what it is planting, and what it is losing to plant it.
Now turn the lens inward, because the national average of ~56 m³ per hectare hides a striking spread:6
- Kerala: ~139 m³ per hectare, more than twice the national figure.
- Uttarakhand: ~106 m³ per hectare.
- Goa: ~101 m³ per hectare.
And the loss is concentrated in exactly the places India can least afford to lose. Between 2021 and 2023, almost every northeastern state, the country's richest biodiversity belt, lost forest inside its recorded areas: Tripura shed 116 sq km, Assam 86, Manipur 47, Arunachal Pradesh 45, with Mizoram the lone exception.9 In the Western Ghats, forest cover outside protected areas fell by 58 sq km against 2013 levels.3 Mangroves, India's coastal shield, slipped to 4,991 sq km, a net loss of 7.43 sq km, with Gujarat alone down 36 sq km.3
Even fire tells a local story the national average erases. Overall fire hotspots fell, yet Uttarakhand's incidents exploded from 5,351 in 2022-23 to 21,033 in 2023-24, and Himachal Pradesh's rose more than 1,300%.1011 A single dry season in the hills can undo years of slow canopy gain.
What India can learn: the South Korea playbook
If one country has earned the right to lecture on forests, it is South Korea, and its lesson is precisely about the metric.
By 1953, war and colonial extraction had stripped Korea's forests to roughly 10 m³ of growing stock per hectare, near-total devastation.7 Seoul launched a national rehabilitation drive in 1973, wove it into the Saemaul Undong village movement, and planted billions of trees. So far, so familiar; India plants at scale too.
The difference was what Korea chose to measure. Not hectares of canopy, but growing stock, the three-dimensional volume of the forest. And it climbed relentlessly: to 50 m³ per hectare by 1990, and to 165 by 2020.7 Korea did not get there by watching saplings grow. It actively thinned overcrowded stands, paid landowners to convert commercial plantations back to natural forest, and stretched timber rotation ages by decades.7
This is the thread worth pulling, and it is exactly the kind of "what actually works abroad" comparison we chew over in the BharatNama community every day (t.ly/h2jq1). The portable lesson is not "plant more". India already does. It is to change the yardstick: reward volume, soil carbon and biodiversity, not the bare fact of green. What does not transfer easily is Korea's state capacity and its smaller, more uniform geography. India's federal, forest-dwelling, wildly diverse landscape makes the accounting harder, which is all the more reason to get the accounting honest.
The money that never moves
None of this is accident. It is incentive.
When forest is diverted for a mine or a highway, the user agency pays into CAMPA, the compensatory afforestation fund, which states are meant to spend replanting an equivalent area. In practice the money sits still. Between 2019-20 and 2023-24, National CAMPA approved ~₹3.85 lakh crore for state plans, of which only ~₹2.6 lakh crore, about 68%, was actually spent.12
Andhra Pradesh is the parable. It holds a CAMPA corpus of ~₹2,257 crore, yet spent just ₹658 crore between 2019-20 and November 2025, leaving ₹1,947 crore idle in government accounts.13 Planting is seasonal and monsoon-bound; when funds arrive months late, the window is missed and saplings die. National assessments put the survival rate of compensatory saplings at ~33.5%, roughly half the 60 to 65% the Forest Research Institute considers viable.13
Then there is the newer instrument, the Green Credit Programme, launched in October 2023, which lets companies buy credits by funding plantations on "degraded" land.14 Two problems have surfaced fast:
- There is no firm definition of "degraded", so naturally open ecosystems, savannas, grasslands, scrub that support unique species and pastoralist livelihoods, get swept in. Roughly 13,240 hectares selected under the scheme overlap with likely open natural ecosystems.14
- The human cost is real. In Assam's Goalpara, reporting found five sites covering 214 hectares cleared of homes, farmland and even schools in the name of restoration.14 Plantation survival on these sites runs between 6 and 30%.14
And in August 2025 the government widened the programme so those credits can now count towards compensatory afforestation itself, letting industry, as one former forest officer put it, buy an easy route out of land it would otherwise have to replace.15 The scheme now faces a Supreme Court challenge.14
What to watch
- The Supreme Court and the definition of "forest". In interim orders on 3 February and 4 March 2025, the Court told every state to keep applying the wide 1996 Godavarman definition of forest, and barred any reduction of forest land without compensatory land first, effectively freezing the dilution in the Forest (Conservation) Amendment Act 2023.1617 Watch for the final ruling.
- ISFR 2025. The next State of Forest Report is due. Watch whether the FSI finally separates natural forest from plantations, or repeats the normalisation.
- CAMPA drawdown. Track whether idle state balances, Andhra's ₹1,947 crore above all, actually get spent on the ground before the next planting season.
- Green Credit rules. Watch the litigation and whether the "degraded land" definition is tightened to protect open natural ecosystems.
India's forest map is greening on a satellite screen while its natural forests thin out underneath, and until the country measures wood, soil and biodiversity instead of bare canopy, it will keep mistaking a plantation for a forest.

Right now, until 13 July, the government has the National Food Security Act open on its desk for amendment.1 Public comments are being invited on a draft bill. And here is what it proposes to change: the fixed 35kg monthly grain quota for the very poorest households would become 7kg per person, capped at 35kg per family.1
That is the reform on the table. A tweak to how grams are split inside a household.
What the draft does not touch is the hole that actually matters. India's food law is legally supposed to cover two-thirds of the country. It currently rations that coverage using population figures from the 2011 Census.2 More than a decade later, that single design choice has quietly locked out somewhere between 10 and 14 crore of the poorest Indians.3 4
This is not corruption. It is not a leaky ration shop or a stolen sack of wheat. It is an exclusion written into the arithmetic of the law itself. And that, to me, is the more unnerving kind of failure, because you cannot fix it by catching a thief.
What the law actually promises, and how it counts
The NFSA, passed in 2013, was a genuine landmark. It turned subsidised food from a discretionary scheme into a legal right, and it made the eldest woman of the household the ration-card holder by law.2 It entitles up to 75% of rural India and 50% of urban India to cheap grain, which works out to roughly two-thirds of the population.2
The catch sits in Section 9. The Act says the number of people to be covered "shall be calculated on the basis of the population estimates as per the census of which the relevant figures have been published."2
In plain terms: the size of the safety net is pinned to the last published census.
- In 2013, the last published census was 2011, when India had ~1.21bn people.2
- Apply 75% rural and 50% urban to that, and you get a national ceiling of 81.35 crore beneficiaries.2
- That ceiling has not moved since.
Every state gets a slice of that 81.35 crore and cannot legally exceed it. As of July 2025, states had filled 80.56 crore of those slots, leaving room for just 0.79 crore more names nationwide before the cap is breached.2 A country of 1.46bn people has legal headroom to add fewer than 80 lakh ration cards.
The frozen headcount versus the growing country
Here is the interesting bit. The census froze. The population did not.
India crossed China to become the world's most populous nation, and the UN now puts the count at ~1.46bn for 2025.5 The denominator kept climbing. The numerator stayed bolted to 2011.
- Economists Jean Drèze, Reetika Khera and Meghana Mungikar did the arithmetic that made this concrete. On 2020 population projections of ~1.37bn, the two-thirds mandate should have covered ~922mn people. Actual coverage was ~809mn. The gap was already ~113mn.3
- By late 2024, reporting using the government's own projections put the shortfall at ~13 crore.4
- Run the same sum on today's 1.46bn and the number only grows. Two-thirds of 1.46bn is close to 98 crore. India covers ~80.6 crore. On paper, the law owes food to millions it has never counted.
Now let that sink in for a second. These are not people who failed a means test. They are people the state has simply refused to see, because seeing them would mean admitting the 2011 baseline is dead.
And here is where it gets strange. The system is perfectly capable of subtracting names. It just cannot legally add them.
- In the past few months alone, states weeded out ~2.25 crore beneficiaries flagged as ineligible, and 2.49 crore cards have been cancelled since 2020 for death, duplication or migration.14
- That machinery works because removing a name never breaches the cap. Adding one does.
- So the pool churns furiously at the edges while its total stays frozen. A poor family can only get in if another family drops out, regardless of how many genuinely need it.
The result is a welfare net that is energetically policed for who should leave and legally blind to who should enter. That asymmetry is the whole tragedy in miniature.
This kind of buried, structural number is exactly what I keep pulling apart, and it is the sort of thread we chase most mornings in the BharatNama WhatsApp community, where I share a smaller India deep-dive like this with thousands of readers every day (t.ly/h2jq1).
The court could see them, even when the government would not
The proof that these people exist did not come from the census. It came from a different government database.
After the 2020 lockdown exodus, the Supreme Court took up the plight of migrant workers and pushed the Centre to build the e-Shram portal, a register of unorganised-sector workers. It has now crossed 30.9 crore registrations.6 When the court cross-checked it against ration records, the gap was stark: of the workers registered, around 8 crore had no ration card at all.7
So in March 2024, the court did something remarkable. It ordered every state to issue ration cards to those 8 crore workers, and to do it irrespective of the Section 9 quotas, later setting a final deadline of 19 November 2024.7 It effectively told the executive to bypass its own frozen formula because, in its words, the hungry cannot wait.
The executive did not agree. And this is where the story stops being administrative and becomes a genuine clash of worldviews:
- The judiciary reads the right to food as flowing from Article 21, the right to life, and treats the 2011 freeze as a violation to be overridden.7
- The executive, backed by NITI Aayog, reads Section 9 literally: coverage cannot change until a new census is published, full stop.8
And NITI Aayog wants to go the other way entirely. Rather than expand, it has floated cutting coverage from 75/50 down to 60/40, which would drop the covered pool to ~71.62 crore and save the exchequer roughly ₹47k crore a year.8 One arm of the state wants to add 8 crore names. Another wants to remove nearly 10 crore. The poor sit in the middle of that argument.
Where India stands: the world updates, India waits
This is the part that should sting, because the fix is not a mystery. Other countries stopped tying welfare to a decadal snapshot a long time ago.
The cleanest benchmark is Brazil's Cadastro Único, the single social registry behind Bolsa Família and dozens of other schemes.9
- It is continuous, not decadal. A family that falls into poverty can walk into a municipal centre and register any day of the year, and benefits follow.9
- It is huge and live: over 40mn families sit in the registry, with ~19.9mn families drawing Bolsa Família today.9
- Because everyone vulnerable is already pre-registered, Brazil could switch on emergency cash to millions within weeks during COVID, simply by activating dormant records.9
The gap is really a gap in clocks. Brazil's headcount updates the day a family's circumstances change. India's updates once a census, which has now meant once every 16 years and counting.5 One system is designed to notice poverty as it happens. The other is designed to wait.
India, by contrast, waits for a census. When COVID hit and the Centre gave free grain over and above the NFSA quota, every one of those extra kilos went only to people who already held a card. The 10-crore-plus excluded got nothing, because to the system they did not exist.
The lesson from Brazil is not "copy Bolsa Família." It is narrower and sharper: delink the count from the census, and let a live registry do the counting.
Where India stands: against itself
Now break the national number open, because the intra-India picture is where the real inequity lives.
With the Centre frozen, richer states have quietly built their own parallel safety nets out of their own budgets:2
- NEEM cards (entitlements equal to or better than NFSA) cover ~90mn people, funded by states, not Delhi.10
- LEAN cards (lesser entitlements) cover ~51mn more.10
- In the southern states, NEEM cardholders make up 31% to 45% of everyone the PDS reaches. Tamil Nadu runs a universal system and gives rice free to all.10 11
Combine these and states are feeding ~14 crore people the Centre refuses to count. That is a quiet act of federal generosity, but it is also a scandal.
What India can learn, and already knows
Here is the honest bit: India does not need Brazil to prove this works. It has already built the pieces at home.
- Haryana's Parivar Pehchan Patra gives each family an 8-digit ID and pushes pensions and certificates to people automatically, no re-application needed.12
- Karnataka's Kutumba and Rajasthan's Jan Aadhaar do the same, and Uttar Pradesh has copied the model.12 When Karnataka linked scholarships to its family registry, uptake nearly doubled overnight because the system found eligible students instead of waiting for them to apply.12
- And the e-Shram database already holds 30.9 crore unorganised workers, live and Aadhaar-linked.6
So the technology, the data and the state capacity all exist. What is missing is the legal will to let a dynamic registry override a dead census. That requires Parliament to amend Section 9, which is precisely the sort of change the draft bill on the table this week could have made, and did not.1
There is a real prize here too, not just a fix. A live family registry lets the state track intergenerational poverty, target nutrition, and respond to shocks in weeks instead of a decade. That is the opportunity India keeps leaving on the table.
What to watch
- The amendment bill. Comments close on 13 July.1 Watch whether the final draft touches the coverage cap at all, or stays limited to the 7kg-per-person tweak.
- Census 2027. House-listing began in April 2026, enumeration is set for February 2027, and the Centre has put ₹6k crore behind it.13 5 But results will not land until ~2028, so the freeze holds for at least two more years.
- The 8-crore compliance. Track whether states actually issue the e-Shram ration cards the court ordered, and whether the Centre supplies the extra grain to back them.7
- State fiscal strain. Watch how long poorer states can keep funding NEEM and LEAN cards without central tide-over grain.10
The one line
India has built a food-security net wide enough to be the envy of the world, then chosen to measure it with a ruler that stopped growing in 2011.

Here is a number that stopped me cold. India's own accounting says air pollution costs the economy 1.36% of GDP. An equally credible method says the real figure is 9.5%.12
Same country. Same toxic air. Same year, near enough. The two numbers are seven times apart.
That is not a rounding error. It is a fault line running straight through how the Indian state decides what to spend on clean air, and which side of that line you sit on quietly decides whether pollution control looks like a cost or the highest-return investment India could make.
The health story is well told by now. In 2022, fine particulate matter (PM2.5) was linked to about 1.72mn premature deaths in India, roughly a third of all such deaths on the planet.1 What almost nobody talks about is the accounting. And the accounting is where the money, and the policy paralysis, actually lives.
The two numbers, and why they diverge
Both numbers are real. They just answer different questions.
The World Bank used what economists call the human capital, or lost-output, approach. It asks a narrow question: if a person dies early or falls sick, how much economic production is lost? Add up forgone wages and medical bills, discount to today, and you get a figure.
- The result: air pollution cost India about $36.8bn in 2019, or 1.36% of GDP.2
- Of that, ~$28.8bn was lost output from premature death, and ~$8bn was the direct cost of illness.2
The Lancet Countdown, the health-and-climate assessment run with the WHO, used a completely different lens: the Value of a Statistical Life (VSL). It does not price a named person. It measures how much a whole society is collectively willing to pay to shave down the risk of dying early, and multiplies that across the deaths.
- The result: the monetised cost of premature mortality from outdoor air pollution in India in 2022 was $339.4bn, or 9.5% of GDP.1
- That is nearly ₹30 lakh crore, a sum that dwarfs India's entire annual health budget.1
Now, the honest caveat first, because BharatNama does not paper over these. The World Bank figure is 2019 data and the Lancet figure is 2022 data. But the three-year gap explains almost none of the divergence. India's GDP did not grow seven-fold in between. The gap is about method, not timing.
The lost-output approach has a brutal blind spot: it values you only for your wages.
- A retiree who dies from pollution-triggered heart failure has zero forgone earnings, so the model records almost nothing.
- A child, an unpaid homemaker, an elderly parent: all near-invisible on the ledger, precisely the people most likely to die from bad air.
- It captures the pay cheque you lose, and nothing of the life.
The VSL method captures the welfare loss the lost-output method throws away. Neither is "wrong". But when a finance ministry runs a cost-benefit test on a clean-air investment using the lost-output number, it is comparing the full cost of scrubbers and grid upgrades against a benefit figure that has been deflated by a factor of roughly seven. Cleaning the air looks like a luxury India cannot afford. That is the fiction the accounting builds.
The bill that never reaches the health ministry
Mortality is only the headline. The quieter drain is what pollution does to people who are very much alive and at work.
The landmark study here, by Dalberg with the Clean Air Fund and the Confederation of Indian Industry (CII), put the cost to Indian business at about $95bn a year, close to 3% of GDP.3 Break it open and it stops being abstract:
- Presenteeism, ~$24bn. Employees show up but underperform, because ultrafine particles trigger inflammation that dulls stamina and cognition. This is the single biggest line, and it is roughly the size of India's entire pharma output.3
- Consumer pull-back, ~$22bn. On filthy-air days people stay home, and offline, footfall-dependent businesses (restaurants, apparel retail) eat the loss.3
- Absenteeism, ~$6bn. India loses about 1.3bn working days a year to pollution-related sick days and caring for sick dependents.3
Sit with the presenteeism number for a second. It is the most invisible of all, because attendance looks fine on the register. The person is at the desk. They are just thinking a little slower, all day, every high-pollution day. In a services economy that sells cognition (software, analytics, finance) that is the worst possible tax to levy, and it lands hardest on exactly the sectors India is betting its future on.
This is the sort of buried, second-order number I keep pulling on, and it is the kind of thread we go back and forth on in the BharatNama WhatsApp community, where I share a smaller India deep-dive like this with thousands of readers every morning (t.ly/h2jq1).
Where India stands: against the world, and against itself
Air pollution is not evenly spread, and this is where BharatNama's two comparisons earn their keep.
India vs the world. India carries a share of the global air-pollution death toll wildly out of proportion to its share of people.
- India accounted for roughly a third of all global PM2.5 deaths in 2022, on about 18% of the world's population.1
- The Indo-Gangetic Plain, stretching across India's north, is one of the single most polluted large regions on Earth. Counting it with the Himalayan foothills, close to ~1bn people breathe hazardous air there, with exposure often more than twenty times the WHO safe limit.8
- China, once the poster child for the "airpocalypse", cut its national PM2.5 from 72 to 29 µg/m³ between 2013 and 2022.6 India has not managed anything close to that pace.
India vs India. The national average hides a spread that is itself the story. On the World Bank's own state numbers, the economic drag is heavily concentrated in the north and east:
- Uttar Pradesh: 2.15% of state GDP. Bihar: 1.95%. Madhya Pradesh and Rajasthan: 1.70% each. Chhattisgarh: 1.55%.2
- These are multiples of what cleaner southern states lose. A single national figure of 1.36% flattens a landscape where the worst-hit states bleed nearly twice as much.
That north-heavy pattern is not a coincidence, and it points straight at why India's whole approach is built on the wrong map.
The governance gap: a city-sized answer to a regional problem
India's flagship response is the National Clean Air Programme (NCAP), launched in 2019. Its target has since been sharpened: up to a 40% cut in particulate concentration by 2025-26, against a 2019-20 baseline, across 131 "non-attainment" cities, up from the original 20-30% goal.4 Progress is tracked on a dashboard called PRANA.
The intent is right. The architecture is where it breaks, on two counts.
First, it is city-shaped, and pollution is not. NCAP hands each of 131 cities a local action plan for road dust, local traffic, and waste burning. But PM2.5 does not respect a municipal boundary.
- The north's winter smog is a regional airshed problem: stubble burning in Punjab and Haryana, industrial clusters in the hinterland, weather inversions that trap it all.
- A single city has no legal power to regulate an upwind farm or a power plant a hundred kilometres away. Isolating the fix to the city guarantees the fix falls short. The World Bank is now pushing India toward exactly this: its first regional airshed plan for the Indo-Gangetic Plain, spanning seven states.8
Second, the targets are advisory, and the enforcement void is glaring. Nowhere is this clearer than coal power, which is a major source of the sulphates and nitrates that become PM2.5.
- Emission norms mandating Flue Gas Desulphurisation (FGD) to capture sulphur dioxide were first set in 2015, with a 2017 deadline. Deadlines were then extended, and extended again, for a decade.
- Then in July 2025, the environment ministry did not just delay, it retreated. A new notification fully exempted the roughly 78% of coal units categorised "Category C" from installing FGD at all. Only ~11% ("Category A", near Delhi and big cities) must comply, by December 2027; another ~11% ("Category B") by 2028, subject to review.5
- The stated reason: FGD costs about ₹1.2 crore per MW, and the ministry argued sulphur dioxide's role in PM2.5 was limited. Ten years after the first mandate, the primary source of baseload pollution got a pass.5
When regulatory deadlines are this soft, no heavy industry has any reason to internalise the cost of the air it fouls. The externality just stays external, and the 9.5% keeps compounding.
This state-versus-state, city-versus-airshed mismatch is the kind of structural knot I dig into daily, and it is one of the threads readers and I keep chasing in the BharatNama community (t.ly/h2jq1).
What India can learn from China
China faced a worse "airpocalypse" than India has and pulled out of it fast. The lesson is not "copy China", because much of it does not transfer. But two parts genuinely might.
What China actually did in its $270bn 2013 action plan:6
- It set legally binding, region-specific targets, not city ones. Whole airsheds (Beijing-Tianjin-Hebei, the Yangtze and Pearl River Deltas) got hard numerical mandates. Beijing was told to cut PM2.5 34% from 2013 levels, full stop.6
- It rewired the incentives of officials. Environmental performance was written into the "cadre evaluation" system that decides promotions. Suddenly a mayor's career depended on clean air, not just local GDP. That single move converted paper targets into aggressive local enforcement, and Beijing-Tianjin-Hebei saw particulate exposure fall by more than half.6
The result was one of the fastest air-quality turnarounds in modern history. What is portable to India: the shift from city plans to binding airshed authorities, and hard targets with real consequences. What is not portable: China's top-down control over promotions has no clean analogue in India's federal, multi-party democracy, where states guard their turf and coal towns vote.
And here is the caveat India must not miss. In 2023, China's national PM2.5 rose for the first time in a decade, up about 3.6%, with 80% of provincial capitals worsening.7 The moment Beijing pivoted back to post-Covid growth, industry roared and the gains reversed.
The lesson inside the lesson: end-of-pipe fixes and temporary bans do not hold. Only a structural move off fossil fuels does. If political pressure swings back to pure GDP maximisation, dirty air comes straight back.
What to watch
- Whether the Indo-Gangetic Plain airshed plan actually gets statutory teeth, or stays advisory like NCAP.
- Whether any Category A coal units genuinely hit the December 2027 FGD deadline, or win yet another extension.
- Whether NITI Aayog or the finance ministry start using VSL-based valuation in cost-benefit tests. That single accounting change would reprice every clean-air investment overnight.
- The next Lancet Countdown, for whether India's mortality and cost figures move at all from the 2022 baseline.
The one line
India is not failing to fix its air because it cannot afford to; it is failing because its own books value the damage at a seventh of what it costs, and you do not fund a fight you have decided is cheap.
