Conclusion: Breeder Blankets and Smart HTS Magnets
Breeder blankets are just one area where fusion can be helped significantly by quantum computing. Improving inertial fusion energy beam and target geometries, magnetic fusion energy field geometries, stellarator magnet configurations, and program magnetic fields are just a few areas where quantum computing could be helpful. While artificial intelligence is helpful in spotting patterns that would otherwise stay obscure, it is less helpful in areas where changing the properties of a fusion machine requires changing the physical geometry of the machine, which generally involves both time, money, and lost opportunity costs; these are problems where quantum computing can help significantly. And it is just the kind of application where smart magnets can work best.

The Fusion Report has covered the efforts of numerous companies to achieve commercial fusion energy; in most cases the engineering and scientific approaches are the same, even if the fusion technologies utilized differ. Typically, companies build test systems using a subset of the technologies they are trying to verify, run the experiment, and then see if the results are what they expected. If they are, they build the next step of the experiment and try to run it; if not they change their approach slightly and try to re-verify the new approach. Regardless of the fusion technology being perfected, the approach is the same, as is the goal: finding out how to commercialize fusion energy.
The other thing that is the same, at least for fusion, is the need for capital. Even for companies like Commonwealth Fusion Systems (CFS), which has raised nearly $3B in funds, you can never have too much money given that the expected cost for a working prototype fusion energy power plant is in the range of $3B to $10B, not counting non-recurring engineering (NRE) charges for prototyping, or the cost of any missteps.
That’s why this step from Barclays to get involved in funding is so important: it puts real cash behind commercial fusion energy deployment. With total assets of £1.54T and net income of £7.2B, Barclays consistently ranks as one of the top five banks in Europe. Additionally, today we bring to you the fusion energy commercialization roadmap for Inertia, one of the leading Inertial fusion energy (IFE) companies. While Inertia is new to the game, the founders of the company were some of the chief innovators at the Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory (LLNL) National Ignition Facility (NIF), the only facility so far that has achieved Q>1. Inertia’s Roadmap To Commercialize Inertial Fusion Energy
While Inertia is one of the newer companies in the commercial fusion industry (they were publicly launched less than a year ago in August of 2025), they have certainly been busy. We have covered them several times, including an interview with their CTO and co-founder Mike Dunne roughly four months ago, where he laid out their priorities to commercialize fusion energy. While we will not go over the specific details of their Phase 1 Commercial Roadmap (the link to their roadmap is here), we will include their “Top 10 List” to accomplish during Phase 1 (Component Development) of their four-phase program (BTW, Phase 2- Subsystem Integration; Phase 3 – End-to-End Integration; Phase 4 – Deployment):
1) Increase yield to >25x. The hardest part of Laser Indirect Drive fusion is done: proving it’s possible to achieve ignition. This milestone took the US government 60+ years and more than $30B.1 Currently, the target used at NIF generates over 8 MJ of energy per shot. That’s an impressive 4x yield against the 2 MJ that goes in. But for commercial scale, we need to generate enough heat energy from each target shot to power the laser and put a meaningful amount on the grid, all after lossy conversion from heat to electricity. Despite that, our plant’s initial operation requires only 25x target yield to generate 250MW of grid electricity.2 We will demonstrate that we can scale up our target to generate an initial >25x gain for a total of >250 MJ of energy per shot. We will demonstrate this by executing a “Virtual NIF Shot” (referencing the same ICF design codes that LLNL uses to achieve ignition), and demonstrate at the highest possible fidelity that our design, including mass-manufactured targets, preserves the proven physics while scaling to commercially relevant gain.
2) Make laser diodes cheap. The laser at the NIF is impressively large (both in energy and in physical size), but it is very inefficient. It loses ~99.5% of the electricity it draws from the grid, emitting only ~0.5% of that energy as laser light onto the target. Without higher efficiency, generating commercial energy is impossible. While the NIF laser is an engineering marvel, it surprises most people to learn that it is literally powered by gas-filled vacuum tubes (called flash lamps). The key to making a laser that is more powerful, more energetic, more efficient, and more compact is the same transition that’s made every major technology smaller, more powerful, and more efficient: moving from vacuum tubes to semiconductors. Laser diodes are the answer, but as of today, they’re considered cost-prohibitive. That’s because the market for our particular variety of high-power, frequency-tuned laser diodes is currently tiny. But we’re going to change that; the demand for just one of our commercial power plants will need 500 years’ worth of today’s global supply! That means we need to scale up production to meet our anticipated demand. We will (with our industry partners) demonstrate that we can scale up high power laser diode production by several orders of magnitude, and bring the cost down by about 50x from today’s prices. 3
3) Make an efficient and high repetition-rate laser amplifier. The NIF laser is operable for roughly one shot per day, and requires substantial maintenance and cool-down time between shots. For commercial energy, our diode-pumped laser must operate continuously at 10 Hz. Migrating from flash lamps to laser diodes helps enable high repetition rates, but there are many design tradeoffs needed to make the amplifier performant and efficient. We are building a ¼ scale amplifier test stand, demonstrating high-efficiency coupling of diode laser light to the gain medium, while cooling it for continuous operation at 10 shots per second.
4) Make laser optics durable. At Inertia, we will build a laser that is the world’s most energetic (most energy per shot) and the world’s highest average power (100 MW continuous operation). One of the challenges in high-power lasers is finding the sweet spot between making optics large enough to handle all that energy, but small enough to manufacture and handle at scale. The NIF (which was built with optics that were state-of-the-art at the time) intentionally operates above its damage threshold. It was a conscious tradeoff in costs versus longevity—one that won’t work for continuous commercial operation. We will work with industry partners at our in-house optics lab to demonstrate that state-of-the-art optics are durable and economical enough to operate at plant scale.
5) Industrialize carbon shell manufacturing. The fuel targets used by the NIF are made of four main parts: (1) an outer canister (called a hohlraum), (2) a high-density carbon (HDC) shell, (3) frozen deuterium-tritium (DT) fuel inside the shell, and (4) several thin-film tents that hold the shell in place in the hohlraum and seal the hohlraum. In the process of commercialization, we are using this proven design—changing as little as possible—as we cost-effectively scale up manufacturing. Currently at the NIF, these HDC shells take several months to grow and polish in small batches via Chemical Vapor Deposition (CVD). This is a well-known process in manufacturing (widely used in the semiconductor industry), but more typically applied on flat surfaces instead of the round sphere of our target. We are demonstrating that we can scale up fabrication and reduce the cost of these shells through larger batches and shorter cycle times—all while maintaining the required tolerances calibrated on NIF data. We will demonstrate that a scalable CVD process can be applied to meet these properties.
6) Track and hit the targets. At the NIF, the fuel targets are shot one at a time, stationary in the chamber, inserted and aligned using a precision robotic positioning system with detailed manual alignment by a team of technicians. For commercialization, we won’t shoot a single target at a time; we’ll be shooting targets at roughly 10 Hz (10 times per second). This means injecting the target into the chamber at a high velocity and hitting it on the fly with laser beams. (This is similar to how ASML’s EUV lithography system hits injected tin droplets with a laser at 50 kHz.) While this may sound hard, photons are actually very fast compared to matter! But this is a control system that needs to be developed. We will demonstrate that we can track and engage a target moving at the required speed of injection and with the required precision to achieve ignition.
7) Make durable, cheap thin film tents. The carbon shell of a fusion target is held in place by thin films. At the NIF, these films are very thin to ensure they don’t interfere with the fuel implosion. But unlike NIF’s stationary targets, we’ll be injecting the targets at 10 Hz at a high velocity into the chamber. The thin films must be stronger to survive this injection and to endure the high temperature of the fusion chamber. We will demonstrate that economical films exist that are both thin enough to enable ignition and gain, and also strong enough to survive the thermo-mechanical insults 4 of injection.
8) Make target assembly scalable. As mentioned, the NIF targets consist of just four parts. But they must be assembled into a fusion target, including the step of fueling the target with DT fuel. At the NIF, where only a handful of ignition-quality targets are assembled and shot per year, they can be fueled and sealed manually. To achieve commercial scale, we must automate the target assembly. We will demonstrate that a scalable, batch assembly process exists to fill and seal the fusion targets.
9) Fuel targets quickly. At the NIF, fueling the targets is a slow process. It often takes days—and sometimes more than a week—to grow a single pristine DT crystal on the inside of the HDC shell. For commercialization, we need to fuel more quickly and in large batches. That is for efficiency, and also ensures that the amount of tritium in our fueling stage at any one point in time is kept to an acceptable regulatory level. We will demonstrate that a method exists to quickly fuel targets with high-enough ice quality to produce high fusion energy in large batches while keeping low tritium inventory.
10) Integrate everything for a working fusion power plant. The point of commercialization is to eventually produce economical energy (process heat and/or electricity). One of the hard problems in designing a fusion plant is long-term survival of the walls that form the fusion chamber. Inertia’s baseline design uses a simple gas-armored first wall to absorb the bulk of the insult, coupled with low-cost, easily replaced solid walls. This approach doesn’t require a breakthrough in materials science, and crucially, enables low fusion gain, relaxing the requirements on the physics performance. But tradeoffs remain; the larger the chamber, the longer the walls last but the more expensive it is to build. With more beamlines, plant operations become easier, but the plant will breed less tritium. We need to find the optimal solution within the set of tradeoffs. We will demonstrate a self-consistent plant design that utilizes demonstrated physics and incorporates our laser design decisions, target survival decisions, and fuel needs of a sustainable plant.
Conclusion: Why These Stories Are Important for Fusion Energy
The biggest problem in fusion is something that fusion companies don’t control: raising capital to fund a pipeline of commercial fusion energy power plants, starting with the first-of-a-kind (FOAK) plant to prove the concept. Fusion energy could provide a significant amount of energy without the baggage of fossil fuel or nuclear fission energy sources. As Group Chief Executive C.S. Venkatakrishnan puts it, “Fusion has the potential to become an important part of a secure, resilient and low-carbon energy system. Barclays is pleased to support the UK Infinity Fusion Consortium as part of their efforts to advance sustainable innovation.” To say that a reliable source of capital is valuable in this effort is an understatement, and it is great that Barclays is one of the first banks to put their money behind their mouth.
The second biggest problem in fusion is picking the right direction. Fortunately, in that approach we get to stand on the shoulders of our predecessors, who have shown us a lot of what works and what doesn’t, and what likely needs to be done to finish the job. This is especially true for IFE, which LLNL NIF has blazed a trail on how to exceed Q>1 (multiple times!). While LID IFE is not the only approach possible to commercialize fusion energy, it is one of the simpler ones – it is in a way a “brute force” method. In a way, it is a true engineering problem (or problems), rather than a physics problem, which is good for Inertia. In some ways, they have done a better job than anyone else in laying out exactly what their priorities are going forward, which certainly helps. Now as they say, it’s simply a small matter of execution…

The Fusion Report has covered the architecture of Pacific Fusion’s pulser-based inertial fusion system, which utilizes an array of impedance-matched Marx generators (IMGs) to produce a high-current, high-voltage beam directed towards the fusion target. A full power system will utilize 156 pulsars, each one three times the length of the one shown above. But prior to building a full-scale system, Lawrence Livermore National Laboratories (LLNL) and Pacific Fusion decided to build a one-third scale pulser module and test its output capabilities. This article is about the test of the 1/3rd scale pulser, and the results of those tests.
Pacific Fusion and LLNL’s Pulser Concept
For those of you who are not familiar with Pacific Fusion’s pulser concept, it is a quintessential inertial fusion approach, but one that does not use lasers. Like the Sandia Z-Machine, it utilizes massive electrical currents to generate extreme pressures on a fuel target, resulting in fusion. The currents are produced by cascading arrays of Impedance-matched Marx Generators (IMGs), with the arrays forming 156 “pulsers”.
Each pulser consists of 32 circular stages, with each stage having 10 “bricks”; a brick consists of two matched capacitors and a high-speed gas discharge switch. The stages produce a travelling electromagnetic wave in the electromagnetic media in the center of the stages that make up each pulser. The pulsers are configured on three rings by 52 rows around the fusion chamber, where the 156 beams converge to implode the target.
Like all inertial fusion energy (IFE) system, Pacific Fusion’s machine is pulsed rather than continuous in operation. Like most IFE systems, it has a nominal pulse repetition rate of roughly 1 Hz (one pulse per second), which means that the life of each “brick” is measured by the number of “shots” that it can sustain before being replaced. With a nominal shot rate of 1 Hz, that means that a capacitor array with a lifetime of one year would have to sustain roughly 31.5 million shots before failure. Testing whether a scaled-down pulser could operate for 3,000 consecutive shots (equivalent to 1 hour of continuous operation) was the purpose of this test.
The Press Release: Lawrence Livermore-Pacific Fusion collaboration breaks new record to advance America’s high-gain fusion capability
LLNL pulsed-power prototype surpasses 3,000 shots through collaboration with Pacific Fusion, demonstrating the maturity of a key U.S. capability and the value of government-industry partnership.
FREMONT, Calif. (July 16th) — Pacific Fusion today announced that a pulsed-power prototype designed and built at Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory has surpassed 3,000 shots under a Cooperative Research and Development Agreement with Pacific Fusion, marking a key milestone in the development of high-gain fusion and a practical example of government-industry partnership at work.
The prototype, called Sirius, is an impedance-matched Marx generator (IMG), which is a new pulsed-power architecture designed to deliver short, powerful electrical pulses efficiently and repeatedly. It is the same core technology Pacific Fusion is now scaling for its own fusion system. The 3,000-shot campaign shows how technology first developed at a national laboratory can be validated through repeated testing and scaled quickly by industry to support national needs.
That matters because the United States urgently needs new sources of affordable, reliable electricity to power surging demand for AI and electrification, as well as new high-yield experimental capabilities for stockpile stewardship. Pacific Fusion is building rapidly to support both, developing a modular pulser platform to produce abundant, affordable energy and advance the high-energy-density science essential to national security.
“This is a concrete example of what government-industry collaboration can deliver when both sides are committed,” said Keith LeChien, Co-founder and Chief Technology Officer of Pacific Fusion. “We are taking innovation from the lab and moving quickly to build and scale systems that serve America’s needs. The result is a credible shot at high-yield, high-gain fusion this decade — and a path to turning U.S. scientific leadership into a critical capability that will keep the U.S. ahead of China.”
Pulsed power works by taking electricity from the wall plug, storing it briefly, and releasing it in an enormous burst — like a lightning bolt — in about 100 nanoseconds. For fusion energy, that burst can create the extreme conditions needed to compress fuel and release energy. The same pulser technology can also create extreme states of matter for high-energy-density science experiments, with applications ranging from materials testing, radioisotope production and national security.
The IMG was co-invented by LeChien and LLNL researcher Bill Stygar as a more direct way to deliver a fast, efficient electrical pulse. Conventional pulsed-power machines, called Marx generators, stack voltages. By contrast, the IMG stacks waves using a pulser by charging capacitors in parallel and then discharging them in a single step, through carefully timed stages on a common transmission line. The pulse is then transmitted directly to the target. In the Sirius campaign, each pulse of the four-stage prototype delivered 60 gigawatts to a resistive load in a 100-nanosecond pulse, with 95% energy efficiency.
Researchers at LLNL say the appeal of the IMG approach is its relative simplicity. “Conventional pulsed-power machines often require several stages of pulse compression, which can add complexity, maintenance demands and safety considerations,” said Kumar Raman, LLNL project manager in a LLNL blog.
The 3000-shot campaign supported through the Pacific Fusion CRADA focused on component lifetime and reliability – real experimental data that’s proven invaluable to understanding how components behave over many repeated shots.
It’s data that Pacific Fusion has used to design, build and scale its own pulsed-power technology at extraordinary speed. In June, the company announced the completion and validation of a pulsed-power prototype that expanded the Sirius platform by roughly 11x – delivering ~440 GW of peak output power and ~1.1 MV peak voltage in 80 nanoseconds – the highest-power, single-step pulsed-power driver ever demonstrated. Pacific Fusion is now working to demonstrate a system that’s roughly 40x the size of Sirius.
Pacific Fusion has raised more than $1 billion in private capital and is working to achieve net facility gain by 2030. Later this summer, Pacific Fusion will break ground on the world’s largest high-gain, high-yield facility called the Demonstration System in Albuquerque, New Mexico. The system is designed to produce fusion bursts exceeding 100 megajoules – or more energy output than the total stored energy used to drive the reaction, making it the first and only net facility gain fusion facility in the world.
“China is moving aggressively to build the next generation of fusion infrastructure, pouring billions into new facilities,” LeChien said. “The U.S. invented many of the breakthroughs that made this moment possible here and abroad, but to win we have to build. The government needs a significant coordinated investment in energy and national security fusion infrastructure, and months matter. The stakes could not be higher.”
Conclusion: A Great Demonstration, But Still a First Step
This was clearly an important first step towards a working production system. However, a production pulser would need to be able to operate for at least a year (~31.5M shots), roughly 10,000 times the number demonstrated here. Additionally, Pacific Fusion’s targets consists of frozen deuterium and tritium (D-T) fuel, and while D-T fusion is energetically favorable (it requires the lowest temperature of any Earth-bound fusion reaction), it has several drawbacks, including the need to be able to sustain continuous high-energy neutron damage, and to breed tritium. Many believe that these challenges are surmountable given time (all IFE systems have these challenges); now the real question is how much time is needed to do so…

LLNL and Pacific Fusion Partnership Drives the Sirius Pulsed Power Prototype Past 3,000 Shots and a Peak Power Record
Pacific Fusion and Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory announced that Sirius, an LLNL pulsed power prototype built on the impedance-matched Marx generator (IMG) architecture co-invented by Pacific Fusion CTO Keith LeChien during his time at the lab, has surpassed 3,000 shots, demonstrating the reliability and maturity of a new architecture designed to deliver short, powerful electrical pulses efficiently and repeatedly. Backed by more than $1 billion in private capital, Pacific Fusion has already scaled the same core technology into a prototype roughly 11 times larger, delivering the highest peak power ever demonstrated by a single-step pulsed power driver and offering a working example of how national lab breakthroughs can move rapidly into commercial infrastructure for high-gain fusion energy.
Inertia Unveils Its New Livermore Headquarters, Home to the World’s First Fusion Fuel Target Factory
Inertia Enterprises announced the opening of its new headquarters in Livermore, California, a 50,000 square foot facility that will house the world’s first fusion fuel target factory and the world’s most advanced high-energy laser system. The company, co-founded by CEO Jeff Lawson, CTO Mike Dunne, and Chief Scientist Annie Kritcher, has already built a fuel target manufacturing lab and a high precision metrology facility in six months, and has recruited manufacturing and supply chain leaders from Apple, Corning, Halliburton, Kairos, Edmund Optics, and Waymo. Oak Ridge, Cleveland Clinic, and IBM Complete the First Known Quantum Computations of Fusion Fuel Materials
Oak Ridge National Laboratory, Cleveland Clinic, and IBM announced that they have calculated nine molecular configurations of FLiBe, the fluorine, lithium, and beryllium molten salt that is a leading candidate material for breeding tritium in fusion reactors, in the first known computations of fusion materials on a quantum computer. Published on arXiv, the work used quantum-centric supercomputing, pairing quantum processors with classical machines, to model how strongly different FLiBe configurations bind tritium at the molecular level, calculations that are difficult for classical computers to scale on their own. The team calls it a fundamental step toward optimizing tritium production, one of the hardest bottlenecks standing between fusion and abundant clean energy and a key objective of the Department of Energy’s Genesis Mission.

Among other things in the commercial fusion industry, The Fusion Report tracks closely is the success at which the industry raises new venture capital (VC) funding rounds in the past 12 months. For the commercial fusion energy industry’s lifecycle, lifetime funding is the most illustrative of the health of the industry, and that of the individual companies that make up the industry. While the most important measures for fusion will change over the next few years as commercial fusion energy becomes more focused on deploying commercial power plants, at this moment lifetime funding is probably the most important given the incredible expense of developing fusion power plants.
Our approach is focused on private VC and/or equity-based fundraising, utilizing publicly-reported numbers through press releases and/or third party sources. We also only report on the fundraising of companies that are focused on the goal of building complete fusion energy systems, and not on companies that only build fusion system components. While these supply chain companies are incredibly important, including their numbers simply inflates the reported numbers for the fusion energy industry, and doesn’t accurately reflect its health; in most cases these companies also manufacture systems and components for customers outside the fusion industry as well (we will soon publish a supply chain report which focuses on the fundraising and revenues of those companies). We also do not include companies whose primary focus is to utilize fusion for purposes such as medical isotopes or nuclear testing/hardening technology, and not on commercial fusion energy. Finally (for today), we are not including private funding for Chinese fusion energy companies, since that market is somewhat opaque, as are the lines between private and public funding in China.
How is The Fusion Industry Doing Raising VC Investments?
As of June 30th 2026, the total lifetime private funding raised across the commercial fusion energy industry was $11.52B, up roughly $2.4B in total lifetime funding from the year before (June 2025). Today, there are four (4) companies with over $1B in total lifetime private funding (up from three this time last year.):
- Commonwealth Fusion Systems (CFS), with $2.923B in total private funding;
- Helion Energy, with $1.502B in total private funding;
- TAE, with $1.321 billion in total private funding; and
- Shine Fusion, a newcomer to the list with $1.040B in total private funding.
There are also eleven (11) companies with over $250M in total lifetime private funding, up from eight (8) in June 2025; the new entrants include Inertia, Marvel Fusion, and Focused Energy. However, the top three companies in fusion (Commonwealth Fusion Systems at $2.923B, Helion Energy at $1.502B, and TAE at $1.321B) still have roughly half of all of the lifetime commercial private funding, roughly the same situation as one year ago. Finally (as of June 30, 2026), two companies are on the road to becoming public companies (TAE and General Fusion), though both are going public through special purpose acquisition companies (SPACs) rather than through Initial Public Offerings (IPOs). While these companies often focus on their total share value (i.e., market capitalization) in public statements, we will include only the value of the shares when they were sold on the market (or later equity sales), since those reflect money the company has received from the public and which it has to fund its business.
New Commercial Funding Between July 2025 and June 2026
There are several private funding deals that occurred between July 2025 and June 2026 which merit mentioning:
- CFS raised $863M in a Series B2 round that closed in August 2025. This was the largest round raised in commercial fusion since CFS’s original Series B round of $1.8B in 2021.
- Helion Energy raised $465M in their Series G funding round that closed in June 2026. This represented their second largest funding round ever (after their November 2021 round of $500M).
- Newcomer Inertia raised $450M in their February 2026 Series A funding for their laser inertial fusion system approach.
- Shine Fusion raised $240M in February 2026, to become the fourth private fusion company to go over the $1B lifetime funding mark.
- Focused Energy raised $240 million in May 2026, well over doubling its total cash raise to date to $415 million.
- Thea Energy raised $100 million Series B funding round in May 2026, breaking the $100 million boundary with $130 million in total lifetime funding For its software-defined approach to a fusion stellarator.
Additional and lesser funding, primarily raised by companies with under $100 million in total lifetime funding, amounts to roughly $31 million during this time period.
Commercial Fusion Funding vs Nuclear Fission, Other Investments
One way to tell how well a sector is doing is to look at investments in the sector versus investments in competing sectors. For commercial fusion, the most similar investment is new private investments in commercial nuclear fission energy startups. While this sector is not an exact competitor for fusion energy since several large players already exist in nuclear fission, from an investment standpoint it is a good match, especially in the small modular reactor (SMR) space.
In the same period (July 2025-June 2026), several nuclear fission/SMR companies achieved roughly $2B in fundraising, comparable to that raised by commercial fusion energy companies. Highlights include X-Energy (a $470M Series D round in November 2025, followed by a $1B IPO in April 2026), TerraPower ($650M round in June 2025), and AALO Atomics ($100M Series B in August 2025).
While this may sound like a lot, it is important to remember that global venture capital (VC) funding reached $510B in the first half of 2026. From that perspective, the funding invested in nuclear fission and fusion energy together is well less than 1% of the total VC funding in that period. Unsurprisingly, private investments in artificial intelligence (AI) funding massively dominate the current venture capital space; the AI space captured 70% of global VC funding in Q2 2026 alone. Anthropic and OpenAI together raised $217B in the first half of 2026, nearly 43% of all global VC funding; roughly 100X the funds raised for fusion energy and nuclear fission combined in the same time frame.
The Outlook for Fusion Energy is Good, But Could be Better
While the purpose of this article is not to complain about the money going into AI versus fusion energy, it is hard to escape the conclusion that fusion space should be able to do better than it currently has. One of the obvious issues is that Q>1 has not yet been demonstrated in any of the commercial fusion systems being built, and probably won’t be for at least two and one-half years. Assuming Helion’s aggressive schedule holds AND the investments in AI don’t fall apart and crash the VC marketplace, perhaps 2029 will see a significant improvement in the funding levels for fusion energy. We can only hold our breath and hope for the best…
Postscript: Proxima Fusion Raises $468M in New Funds, While General Fusion Goes Public (July 2026)
As a postscript to our article, Proxima Fusion announced on July 7th that they have raised €411M ($468M US) in new funding, for a total lifetime funding of $668M. While this fund raise is outside the first half of the year funding raises, it’s still obviously very important because this places Proxima Fusion as the most highly-funded European commercial fusion company. The round was led by XTX Ventures and East X Ventures, supported by RWE and Google as strategic investors. This also makes Proxima Fusion the sixth highest company in terms of total funding in commercial fusion industry. And roughly a week later on July 13th, General Fusion went public on the NASDAQ Stock Exchange, creating roughly $150M in new liquidity for the company. Between the two transactions, this raised the number of companies at $250M or above in total funding to twelve (12), and raises the total funding in commercial fusion energy to $12.18B.

The Fusion Report has covered the expansion of the commercial fusion energy industry numerous times over the past 12 months as it opens up new locations and new facilities. These expansions represent significant investments in the areas that they are being built in, whether in Denver, Mexico, New Jersey or other locations. Realta Fusion, who is building their next generation magnetic mirror project called HAMMiR, has chosen to build their new headquarters and Research and Development Facility in their hometown of Madison, Wisconsin. As a spin-out of the University of Wisconsin-Madison’s (UW-M) Wisconsin HTS Axis Symmetric Mirror (WHAM), the choice makes perfect sense. Below is the press release describing their plans for their new facility.
Realta Fusion Selects Wisconsin For Fusion Energy R&D Facility
Wisconsin Commits Up to $55 Million to Secure Realta’s Selection of Former Oscar Mayer Plant in Madison as Location for “The Realta Forge”
Madison, Wis. – July 15th, 2026 – Realta Fusion, the world’s leading magnetic mirror fusion energy company, today announced a commitment from the state of Wisconsin and the city of Madison for up to $55 million to develop its corporate headquarters and fusion research facility at OM Station, the site of the iconic former Oscar Mayer plant. Realta expects to create over 600 jobs at this facility, including both technical and non-technical roles.
Wisconsin’s financial incentive package combines an estimated $37.5 million in state sales and use tax exemptions, up to $15 million in performance-based enterprise zone (EZ) tax credits from the Wisconsin Economic Development Corporation (WEDC), and $2.8 million in tax increment financing (TIF) for job creation at OM Station from the City of Madison.
“We spent the better part of the past two years searching across the country to find the most favorable business environment and the most attractive site to build our R&D facility, and we found it in our own backyard,” said Realta CEO Kieran Furlong. “The state of Wisconsin and the city of Madison have made it clear they understand the promise of fusion energy and share our vision for the future, and now they’ve thrown their lot in together to make that vision a reality.”
Realta expects to break ground on “The Realta Forge”, its dedicated R&D facility where it will begin building the prototype magnetic mirror fusion machine it calls Hammir, before the end of the year.
“In terms of cash today, avoided costs tomorrow, and accelerating progress, this is the most impactful state-supported fusion deal ever done in the United States,” said Realta VP of Technical Development Dominick Bindl, who led the company’s site selection effort. “Wisconsin has taken unprecedented steps toward becoming the most credible regional hub for fusion activity in the country.”
Wisconsin Governor Tony Evers and WEDC secretary and CEO John W. Miller were instrumental in ensuring a strong foundation for commercial fusion activities in the state. In April, Governor Evers signed into law Wisconsin Act 165, the first standalone piece of state legislation in American history to exempt capital expenditures on fusion energy projects from state sales tax. Miller extended a performance-based offer to Realta for EZ tax credits in the largest such commitment to a startup in Wisconsin’s history.
“Fusion energy is not only good for our planet and our power grid, but it plays to all of our strengths as a state with our world-class research universities, research laboratories, and an incredible manufacturing and supply chain network supported by our dedicated and highly skilled workforce,” said Gov. Evers. “Thanks in large part due to our efforts, we are getting closer every day to making fusion power part of our energy infrastructure and a commercially viable source of energy, and this new partnership will only strengthen that work. We are thrilled to help Realta grow its science and engineering expertise, build up its technology, and bring the economic benefits of fusion home to Wisconsin.”
“Fusion energy is an emerging global industry where Wisconsin and the Great Lakes Region are uniquely positioned to lead,” said WEDC Secretary and CEO John W. Miller. “WEDC welcomes Realta’s decision to stay in Wisconsin and continue its game-changing work where it all began.”
Madison Mayor Satya Rhodes-Conway and District 12 Alder Julia Matthews championed the jobs TIF at the city level, the final element of the package which unlocked Realta’s decision to choose OM Station for The Realta Forge. This is the first time in 10 years that Madison has issued TIF to a private company for job creation.
“Madison does not take the decision to provide tax increment financing lightly, but this was the right kind of project for the city to support,” said Mayor Rhodes-Conway. “This is an opportunity to bring hundreds of high-paying jobs in the sustainable energy sector to our community and revitalize a largely vacant property that means so much to Madisonians.”
Before selecting Wisconsin, Realta considered comparable sites in Illinois, New Jersey, New Mexico, Tennessee, and beyond.
2025 Wisconsin Act 165 codified language authored by Representative Benjamin Franklin and Senator Dan Feyen in 2025 Assembly Bill 657 and 2025 Senate Bill 636 respectively.
Conclusion: Why Realta Selecting Madison, Wisconsin is Important
Much in the same way as selecting Princeton, New Jersey for Thea Energy’s new facility, Madison WI makes perfect sense for Realta Fusion’s new facility. Their design is now a growth of the UW-M’s WHAM facility, which revitalized the idea of dual fusion mirrors. To date, Realta has raised $54M in total venture capital funding, with the last raise of $9.5M occurring in February of this year. I suspect we will also see in the near term a funding announcement for Realta as well; after all, that building a new facility is not cheap. My (uneducated) guess is that we’ll see our summary of something in the order of $100M by the end of the year, which would put the company roughly $150M in total lifetime funding, a good amount to push to the next technical milestone, with the eventual goal of success building a prototype fusion energy power plant. As of all fundraising for Fusion Energy, keep your fingers crossed for positive results.

As part of the transaction, Audax will retain a minority equity stake in FCH, continuing to back the company alongside Blackstone and management.
The rollover keeps the seller exposed to further upside in a segment where demand is accelerating.
Based in Cincinnati, Ohio, FCH supplies coolant distribution units, in-row manifolds, and secondary fluid networks to original equipment manufacturers and hyperscalers. As the latest generations of AI hardware run hotter, liquid cooling has become critical to managing energy use and chip efficiency, offering data centre operators a more efficient alternative to air cooling that also lowers emissions and improves power usage.
Blackstone is drawing on two of its strategies for the deal, combining funds from Blackstone Capital Partners and Blackstone Energy Transition Partners, the latter its vehicle for control-oriented energy investments.
“We believe that FCH has enormous tailwinds for continued growth as the latest generations of high-performance AI infrastructure increasingly rely on liquid cooling technology for significantly improved energy and chip efficiency,” said Bilal Khan, senior managing director, and Mark Zhu, managing director at Blackstone. They said the plan was to invest in the company’s capacity expansion and “support unprecedented liquid cooling demand,” describing the AI infrastructure buildout as “one of Blackstone’s highest-conviction investment themes.”
Audax backed FCH through 10 acquisitions and investments in new production and distribution capacity over its hold. “We view the FCH investment as a text-book example of Audax’s ability to build strategic assets through disciplined execution of the Audax Value Agenda and Buy & Build approach,” said Don Bramley, a partner at Audax, who called the sale “a tremendous outcome” for the company’s team and investors.
For context on scale, Blackstone manages over $1.3tn in assets across real estate, private equity, credit, infrastructure, and other strategies, while its Energy Transition Partners platform has committed roughly $30bn of equity globally. Audax, focused on the North American middle market, managed around $20bn as of July 2026 and has invested in more than 180 platforms and over 1,500 add-on acquisitions since its founding in 1999.

The deal hands the two incoming backers control of a fast-growing healthcare business, and delivers an exit for HGGC and Snapdragon after a five-year hold.
Founded in 2011, Fullscript runs an integrated platform that gives practitioners access to data, diagnostic resources, and clinical tools, spanning supplement recommendations and fulfilment, laboratory management, wearable health data integration, and patient adherence features. More than 135,000 practitioners now use the platform to support care for 10 million patients a year across North America.
“The convergence of conventional and functional medicine is happening at a rapid pace,” said Marc Magliacano, managing partner at L Catterton. He said that a growing numbers of Americans are seeking trusted education and treatment to manage chronic conditions and prevent disease, and that the firm looked forward to helping build “the most trusted and independent brand in all of whole-health care.”
Rajan Shah, a partner at L Catterton, added that the firm would put its network and operating resources behind the business to “deepen practitioner support, and help more patients take a proactive approach to extending their healthspan.”
HGGC and Snapdragon are exiting after backing Fullscript through a period of rapid expansion. HGGC said its ownership had supported the company’s evolution into a leading platform for practitioners, including investments in clinical support, technology, and growth initiatives, and expressed confidence that the incoming owners were well placed to support the next phase.
Fullscript’s 2024 acquisition of Rupa Health added advanced laboratory ordering and management tools, while a January 2026 tie-up with Oura brought wearable biometric data into clinical workflows. In April 2026 the company launched Fullscript Journeys, a more consumer-facing health experience, and University Hospitals recently became the latest major health system to integrate the platform into its Epic electronic health record workflow.
“Altas and L Catterton share our conviction in where healthcare is headed, and their investment and experience will help us accelerate that vision,” said Chief executive and co-founder Kyle Braatz, while thanking HGGC and Snapdragon for their support over the past five years.

ADIA lifted its long-term strategy allocation range for private equity to between 15% and 20%, up from 12% to 17%.
It also widened its range for financial alternatives, the category that houses hedge funds and managed futures, to between 7% and 12%, from 5% to 10%. To make room, the fund trimmed its real estate range to between 2% and 7%, from 5% to 10%, though it stressed that absolute exposure to property held steady and that the reduction reflected the relative growth of other asset classes rather than a retreat from real estate.
The reallocation caps a multi-year repositioning at the fund, which manages capital on behalf of the Government of Abu Dhabi and ranks among the largest sovereign investors globally.
In his letter accompanying the review, managing director Hamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan highlighted a more systematic and higher-velocity approach to deploying capital. “The defining theme of global markets in 2025 was a return to breadth and balance, in which the technology-driven gains of recent years evolved into a broader rally across asset classes,” he wrote, adding that supportive conditions had given private market teams the opening to recycle capital out of mature holdings and into new opportunities.
For ADIA’s Private Equities Department, 2025 was a year of active portfolio churn on both sides of the ledger. The team, which operates across buyouts, growth equity, private credit, and venture capital, leaned heavily into take-private transactions alongside its core general partners. Technology was the priority, with the department backing the take-private of Dayforce, a US human resources software platform, and investing in IFS, a European cloud software company focused on industrial artificial intelligence applications.
Healthcare and industrials featured prominently too. ADIA joined a consortium to take US-headquartered Hologic private, gaining exposure to a leader in mammography and molecular diagnostics, and backed the French diagnostics group Sebia. Industrial commitments spanned Alvest, a Paris-based maker of airport ground support equipment, SK Specialty, a South Korean supplier of high-purity gases for semiconductor manufacturing, and Clarience Technologies, a US commercial vehicle safety business. In consumer, the fund invested in European Camping Group and expanded its stake in the ice cream manufacturer Froneri through a GP-led liquidity process.
For a fund now leaning further into the asset class, ADIA also demonstrated an ability to get money back out. The department agreed the sale of its stake in Pension Insurance Corporation, a UK specialist insurer, and offloaded its holding in the packaging group IFCO. Its longest-held win came from Medline, the healthcare supplies distributor it had owned since 2018, which reached the public markets in what ranked as the largest initial public offering globally in 2025.
The timing aligns with a broader recovery in private equity activity. Global buyout deal value rose 23% year on year to $2.2tn in 2025, while exit volumes topped $1tn for the first time since 2021. Fundraising, by contrast, remained subdued, falling 22% as limited partners concentrated commitments on their closest relationships. The industry is still working through a backlog of more than $3.7tn in assets held for over five years, which has pushed sponsors towards continuation vehicles and other liquidity workarounds.
On the hedge fund side, ADIA’s Alternative Investments Department reported strong absolute returns with minimal correlation to equity markets, and continued to expand its use of a managed account platform. The department signalled it would keep pursuing top-tier managers and talent through 2026.
Looking ahead, bin Zayed Al Nahyan struck a cautious note on an increasingly fragmented global backdrop and the concentration of returns in a narrow band of large companies. In a market being reshaped by quantitative tools, he argued, the edge still lies in blending technology with human judgement. “Competitive advantage will continue to be found at the intersection of machines and people,” he wrote.

The vehicle is targeting €200m, with a hard cap of €250m, which would take it comfortably beyond the €154m gathered by Fund II.
The two development finance institutions account for a substantial share of the first close between them. The EBRD is committing up to €40m, while the EIF has committed a total of €40m, part of the latter channelled through Romania’s National Recovery and Resilience Plan framework. Crucially for the firm, the bulk of its existing limited partners returned, with new commitments arriving from family offices and institutional investors.
The EBRD views its participation as a way to develop private equity markets across its regions and to provide an alternative source of long-term financing for growing businesses. By mobilising institutional capital behind local enterprises, the fund is expected to help deepen the region’s financial markets, an agenda the bank has pursued across its economies for more than three decades.
“The first close of Fund III is a strong signal of continued investor confidence in Emerging Europe and in CEECAT’s strategy,” said Anthony Stalker, a partner at the firm. “Most of our existing LPs have re-upped on the back of Fund II’s performance and exit record, and they have been joined by new institutional investors and family offices.”
Fund III will focus primarily on companies in Bulgaria, Croatia, Romania, Serbia, Slovenia, and Türkiye, backing businesses with strong growth potential and helping them expand operations, sharpen competitiveness, and pursue cross-border deals.
The approach carries over from the strategy CEECAT has pursued since Fund II launched in 2021. The firm backs established local businesses in fragmented sectors and builds them into regional platforms through cross-border consolidation. As Stalker put it, “capital should follow companies with a credible path to scale, not simply exposure to a single country,” a strategy he tied to gathering EU accession momentum in the Western Balkans and the convergence of the region’s economies with Western Europe.
The mechanics of deployment will mirror the prior fund. Around 65% of Fund III’s investments are expected to be majority transactions, with equity tickets of €15m to €20m at final close, spread across a disciplined five-year investment period. Alongside business expansion, the fund will promote higher standards of corporate governance and responsible business conduct, seek out green investment opportunities, and apply a gender-inclusive approach aimed at broadening economic participation.
With Fund III, CEECAT is also layering a sector dimension onto its regional coverage. Didem Ilgaz Anil continues to lead the firm’s healthcare focus, while Yilmaz Karakas will drive its artificial intelligence and technology agenda, both in sourcing tech-enabled targets and in accelerating digital and AI adoption across the portfolio. The firm is widening its geographic reach too, adding Poland, the region’s largest economy, as a new investment market where fragmented mid-market sectors offer scope for the cross-border consolidation at the heart of its model.
The fundraise also builds on momentum from the prior vintage. Fund II, which closed in 2022, has backed nine companies across technology, financial services, manufacturing, business services, and retail. In early 2026, it completed its first exit, selling La Cocos to companies of the Schwarz Group, with two further exits said to be at an advanced stage and expected to complete in the coming months.
Operating from five offices in London, Luxembourg, Bucharest, Belgrade, and Istanbul, CEECAT plans additional hires and expects to open a further regional office as it builds out the team behind Fund III. A longstanding EBRD partner, the firm has invested in small and mid-market companies across the region and Türkiye since 2005.

The raise pulls in a mix of new backers and returning investors, and lands as capital continues to flow into AI applications built for specific professional workflows.
Diffusion and Lightspeed both come in as new investors, joined by fellow newcomers Sapphire Ventures and Whale Rock. They sit alongside an existing roster that returned for the round, including Sequoia, Kleiner Perkins, a16z, Coatue, Conviction, Elad Gil, Evantic, GIC, Goldman Sachs Alternatives, Verified Capital, and WNDR.
The proceeds are earmarked for product development and hiring, as Harvey looks to help law firms, in-house legal teams, and professional services firms build and manage their own AI capabilities at scale.
The round follows the company’s release of its first post-trained open-weight model and the launch of Harvey LAB, its legal agent benchmark.
“The opportunity for companies to accelerate their competitive advantage with AI has never been higher,” said co-founders Winston Weinberg and Gabe Pereyra. “Harvey wants to be the global partner legal teams turn to for this work, and we plan to hire and develop the best team in the space to support our clients through the next wave of AI transformation.”
The investor interest is underpinned by Harvey’s traction among large legal buyers. The company said 80% of Am Law 100 firms now use its platform, alongside leading in-house legal teams that include five of the Fortune 10.

The deal hands the firm one of the more recognisable names in the category and marks the fifth brand to join the platform in under two years.
Belle Brands was built on the thesis that “exceptional beauty brands can be advantaged by scale while not undermining the distinction and authenticity of their brand or connection with their community,” according to William Sweedler, chairman of Belle Brands and chief executive and managing partner of Windsong. He described Vegamour as “a natural fit.”
Alongside his role at Windsong, he is co-founder and managing partner of Tengram Capital Partners, where he helped build HRB Brands, a stable of mass-market personal care names including Alberto VO5 and Brut.
Belle Brands applies a similar playbook to a more premium, community-led corner of the market. It was formed in 2024 after Windsong acquired JVN Hair and Pipette out of the bankruptcy of their former parent, Amyris, reportedly for $1.25m and $1.75m respectively. KVD Beauty followed in late 2025, bought from LVMH-owned incubator Kendo - the first time the group had ever sold a brand. Versed, the clean skincare and colour line founded by Katherine Power, joined in July 2026. Vegamour now extends the portfolio into hair longevity, a segment none of the existing brands directly occupies.
Vegamour’s appeal rests on a combination of standout products, an engaged community, and accessibility. Founded in 2016 by Daniel Hodgdon, a plant-sourcing veteran, the brand helped define the “hair wellness” category with plant-based serums, supplements, and scalp treatments sold direct-to-consumer and, increasingly, through prestige retail. It secured an $80m minority growth investment from General Atlantic in 2021, cementing its position as a category leader during a period of rapid direct-to-consumer expansion.
Its exclusive distribution through Sephora was a central draw. According to Teresa Lo, global president of Belle Brands, Vegamour ticked every box the firm looks for. “Brands with a clinically-backed approach to product development, a deeply passionate community, and a focus on accessibility are the kind of brands Belle Brands looks for when it comes to building out our portfolio; Vegamour has all of those attributes and more,” she said, pointing to its role in bringing hair health “front and center to countless consumers.” Lo, who spent time in marketing at Sephora earlier in her career, added that the firm was focused on “maximizing its potential” rather than overhauling what works.
The strategic emphasis on the retail relationship was echoed by Michael Dill, a partner at Windsong and a Belle Brands board member. He said the platform was intent on “invigorating our relationship with Sephora” and investing in new products to defend Vegamour’s position in the category.
For Windsong, founded in 2006 and focused squarely on the branded consumer sector, Vegamour deepens a long track record in beauty and wellness that spans past and present holdings such as Algenist, This Works, and Tone It Up. The firm and its predecessor funds have completed 60 transactions totalling more than $10bn in enterprise value.
With five brands now under one roof spanning hair, skin, colour, baby care, and hair wellness, Belle Brands is fast becoming one of the more acquisitive independent beauty platforms in the market, and Vegamour is unlikely to be its last purchase.

The sale delivers an exit from a platform the two private equity firms built together, and ranks among the larger aerospace transactions of the year.
Warburg Pincus has invested across the aerospace and defence sector through holdings such as TransDigm, TRIUMPH, and Wencor Group. “We are incredibly proud of the platform we have built in partnership with Berkshire Partners and CPP’s talented management team,” said Dan Zamlong, managing director at Warburg Pincus. He added that the company had been “transformed into a leading precision casting company in the industry, with significant investments in its operations, technology, quality systems and talent”.
Berkshire Partners, an employee-owned investor currently deploying its roughly $7.8bn Fund XI, echoed the sentiment. “Berkshire Partners is grateful to have partnered with CPP’s management team and Warburg Pincus during a critical chapter of the company’s growth,” said Blake Gottesman, managing director at the firm. He said the two owners had “strengthened CPP’s leadership in the castings industry”.
GE Aerospace is paying around 18 times CPP’s expected 2027 EBITDA including anticipated net synergies, or roughly 26 times without them. The buyer intends to fund the purchase with $7bn in cash and the balance in new debt, and expects the acquisition to add to adjusted earnings per share and free cash flow in the first year. GE Aerospace said the transaction would not alter its existing capital allocation plans. “Investing in mission-critical casting capacity is needed to support the strong simultaneous demand across commercial engines, aftermarket and defense,” said H. Lawrence Culp, Jr., chairman and chief executive of GE Aerospace.
Founded in 1991 and headquartered in Cleveland, Ohio, CPP produces investment and precision sand castings in super alloy, titanium, aluminium, magnesium, and steel for commercial and military aircraft, weapon systems, helicopters, and industrial gas turbines. The business employs roughly 6,600 people across more than 20 facilities and has supplied GE Aerospace for over 15 years.
The transaction is expected to close in the second half of 2027, subject to regulatory approvals and customary closing conditions.

The transaction marks the first time Tanda has taken on external capital since it was founded in 2012.
Thoma Bravo said its capital would support Tanda’s product development, its artificial intelligence roadmap and its push into new markets. Crucially for continuity, Tanda’s co-founders will remain significant shareholders and continue to run the business, with Jake Phillpot staying on as chief executive.
Founded in Brisbane and operating internationally as Workforce.com, Tanda supplies rostering, time and attendance, compliance, payroll and HR tools to around 8,000 businesses across hospitality, retail, quick-service restaurants, healthcare, and other frontline industries. Its customer base reaches across Australia, North America, the UK, and Southeast Asia. The company built its product suite on a single codebase, an approach Thoma Bravo views as well suited to complex, heavily regulated markets.
According to Carl Press, a partner at Thoma Bravo, accurate pay remains a stubborn challenge for frontline operators, who he said are frustrated by “a patchwork of legacy systems that cannot address their complex needs and expose them to operational and legal risks”. He added that Tanda’s founders had “laid the groundwork to become the definitive AI-native workforce management solution in the shift-based economy”.
Having grown without outside capital for 14 years, Tanda framed the deal as a deliberate step towards scale rather than a change of direction. “Thoma Bravo was the obvious choice as our financial partner,” said Phillpot. “They understand software at an extraordinary level, have spent decades helping companies like ours scale and share our ambition for what Tanda can become.”

The pair will take over when Rob Lucas, who has led the firm since 2021, steps back from the top job.
Sisitsky’s arrival is a notable crossing of lines between two of the industry’s biggest names. He joins after more than 23 years at TPG, most recently as president and co-chair of its management committee, and previously as a board and executive committee member.
He built his career as a healthcare investor and as a leader of the firm’s flagship fund, TPG Capital, before his remit widened to oversee many of TPG’s private equity strategies and to help drive its organic and acquisitive growth. At CVC, he will also chair the partner board.
A managing partner and CVC’s president, Rutland has spent 19 years at the firm and oversees its credit and insurance, secondaries, and infrastructure strategies, having long led its global financial services team. His appointment signals continuity across the diversified platform CVC has built beyond its private equity roots.
The succession structure is designed to avoid disruption. Lucas, who steered CVC through its April 2024 initial public offering on Euronext Amsterdam, will remain closely involved after handing over, continuing on key investment committees and serving as a named “key man” for the Europe/Americas Fund X. Soren Vestergaard-Poulsen, meanwhile, stays on as chief investment officer for private equity and chair of several investment committees.
By splitting the top role between a dealmaker recruited from a major US rival and a long-serving leader of its credit, secondaries, and infrastructure businesses, CVC is signalling that performance, growth, and diversification will define the post-Lucas era.

The mandate will be run by Brookfield’s Investment Solutions Group, a unit the firm has been building to package its capabilities into bespoke multi-asset portfolios for institutional, wealth, and family-office clients.
The NLF is handing Brookfield a discretionary mandate to deploy capital across the firm’s full range of strategies, spanning infrastructure, energy, private equity, real estate, and private credit, through a mix of funds, direct investments, and co-investments.
“NLF has an exceptionally long investment horizon, and that creates an opportunity to invest differently,” said Alper Daglioglu, Head of Brookfield’s Investment Solutions Group. “Our partnership is built on a shared belief in long-term thinking, disciplined capital allocation and the power of compounding over decades. We will draw on the breadth of Brookfield capabilities to customize a portfolio around NLF’s specific objectives and continue to evolve that portfolio as opportunities and needs change over time.”
The Nuclear Liabilities Fund exists to ensure that money is available to cover the future cost of decommissioning eight of the UK’s nuclear power stations, and it selected Brookfield after a competitive process. Chief executive Melissa Hope said the firm stood out for its depth of global investment capability, long-term perspective, and disciplined approach to portfolio construction and governance.
Brookfield reported record second-quarter results in August, raising $77bn in the quarter, and completed its acquisition of the credit manager Oaktree the same month, deepening its private credit capabilities. It is also a substantial player in nuclear itself, through its majority ownership of Westinghouse alongside Cameco, though that sits on the asset side of its business rather than within this investment mandate.

Bennani will drive the expansion of the firm’s private markets activities, spanning private equity, infrastructure debt, and real estate.
She joins from Mirova, where she was chief executive of its US business, and brings more than 20 years of asset-management experience.
Rather than filling an existing seat, the Geneva-based group has carved out a dedicated strategic-development mandate for its unlisted business. This mirrors a wider industry trend, as traditional asset managers build out private equity, private credit, and real assets to capture the fee margins and long-duration capital that public-market strategies increasingly struggle to deliver.
Bennani’s brief covers the three pillars where the firm sees the most runway. Private equity and real estate are long-established Edmond de Rothschild franchises, while infrastructure debt has become one of the fastest-growing corners of private credit, backed by the financing needs of the energy transition and digital infrastructure.
Her task will be to sharpen and expand the strategy across all three as the firm competes for institutional and wealth capital flowing into private assets.

The round, struck at a post-money valuation of more than €21bn, was led by Samsung Electronics, with the Scaleup Europe Fund managed by EQT and existing investor PSG Equity as co-leads. It lands just three years after Mistral’s launch.
The Scaleup Europe Fund, managed by EQT, co-led the round, and the broader syndicate is thick with private capital names, including new investor Advent and funds managed by BlackRock, alongside existing backers such as Eurazeo, General Catalyst, Index Ventures, Lightspeed, and a16z.
Samsung’s lead role, following a Series C led by ASML, also gives Mistral strategic backing from the front rank of advanced manufacturing and industrial technology.
New backers also include the Grand Duchy of Luxembourg.
Mistral said the round will significantly expand its frontier research, fund the compute capacity needed to train more powerful models, and accelerate its commercial and international growth. The company now operates across 20 countries and supports more than 125 large enterprises, including Airbus, ASML, and HSBC, in their AI adoption.
Mistral is pitching itself as the provider of “sovereign” AI, a full-stack offering that spans open-weight models, the infrastructure and compute to run them, and the products to deploy them, designed so that customers and governments retain control over their data, models, and systems rather than depend on a single vendor. As enterprises and states weigh the long-term dependencies that come with AI, the company argues, demand for that combination of performance and control is growing.
The scale and composition of the round mark a notable moment for European technology. It brings together strategic and financial investors across Europe, Asia, and North America. In particular, its size, at a valuation above €21bn, signals growing conviction among global investors, including major private equity and growth funds, that a European company can compete at the frontier of AI.

The new vehicle, Crescenta S.A. Sicav ELTIF, Private Equity Access I, replicates the strategy of the firm’s existing funds and targets a size of €35m.
It seeks a net annual internal rate of return of 15% and a 2x investment multiple over an expected 10-year life, with capital called and returned gradually.
Spanish private equity funds are typically available only from a €10,000 minimum, and to investors with net worth above €100,000. The ELTIF structure removes that floor, and while Crescenta has chosen to keep a €5,000 minimum, it has paired it with a lighter eligibility test, open to investors with at least €50,000 in gross annual income, a threshold the firm frames as consistent with responsible access rather than a free-for-all.
“We arrived in the market with the goal of democratizing investment in Private Equity and now, barely three years later, we are taking another step in that direction,” said Chief executive and co-founder Ramiro Iglesias. The launch is designed to serve everyone from retail savers to high-net-worth individuals, as well as institutional clients such as financial advisers and family offices. “With Private Equity Access I, we open investment to the wide diversity of profiles we have observed in the market and in response to the demand we have identified beyond Spain,” Iglesias added.
Notably, the firm has resisted using the wrapper to dilute the underlying product. President and co-founder Eduardo Navarro argued that the fund keeps the traditional shape of private equity intact. “Using the ELTIF structure has great advantages, but we wanted it to be with an underlying investment that respected the traditional structure of Private Equity: closed-end funds, with capital calls and distributions,” he said. “We believe that technology and innovation do not exist to simplify the product, but to bring the best offering closer to more people.”
On strategy, the fund will hold a concentrated portfolio of five to seven funds from managers with decades of experience, blending private equity buyouts, growth equity, and secondaries. It offers global exposure across the lower-mid, middle, and, to a lesser extent, large-cap segments, spanning sectors including healthcare, technology, and industrials.
The launch lands amid a broader industry race to open private markets to individual investors, in which the ELTIF, the EU’s retail-focused long-term investment fund wrapper, has become a favoured tool.
Crescenta, founded in 2023 by Navarro and Iglesias and supervised by Spain’s CNMV, has built its model around that shift, pairing digital access with an investor-education platform.

The fund, known as SF2, comes in about 75% larger than its predecessor, the Strategic Financials Fund, drawing strong re-ups from existing investors alongside a number of new commitments.
SF2 will pursue that sector while extending into business services and technology, media, and telecoms, targeting what Cinven sees as an attractive incremental opportunity set. The dedicated team will chase control positions in high-growth, asset-light businesses across Europe.
Cinven frames its edge as a “Sector-Regional matrix” that pairs the specialist knowledge of its sector teams with the local networks of its regional teams, supported by portfolio, capital markets, and North America functions that help European businesses expand into the Americas. The approach is designed to generate proprietary deal angles and, by connecting the mid-market fund with the wider platform, to create two-way benefits through deeper thematic investing and knowledge-sharing across the Cinven funds.
“We are grateful for the strong support for the SF2 from both longstanding and new investors globally, that we believe is testament to our unrivalled European focus; sole focus on PE buyouts; decades-long track record of successfully investing through cycles; and full alignment with our investors,” said Co-Managing Partners Bruno Schick and Jorge Quemada. “The significant step-up in fund size from the SFF allows us to capitalise on the large and attractive opportunity set we have identified in the European mid-market through our differentiated Sector-Regional matrix approach.”
The fund is co-led by Cinven partners Luigi Sbrozzi and Michael Weber, who between them bring more than 40 years of private equity experience, supported by a growing team of 16 dedicated professionals spanning financial services, business services, and TMT.
The fund is already at work, having signed four investments that Cinven says are performing on or ahead of plan. They are Objectway, a digital platform for wealth managers, banks, and asset managers; Flint Global, a professional services firm advising on regulatory, policy, and economic matters; Ongoing Warehouse, a cloud-native warehouse management system provider; and Optio Group, a specialty insurance managing general agent platform. All four were founder or employee-owned businesses.

The buyers, grouped in a new vehicle called Tulip UK Bidco, comprise Toscafund Asset Management, the UK private equity firm Three Hills, and US investment manager Ares.
Their recommended cash offer of 250p per share values Spire’s equity at about £1,026.5m and implies an enterprise value of roughly £2.31bn including debt. It represents a 66.2% premium to Spire’s closing price on 13 May, the last trading day before the approach became public.
Debbie White, Spire’s chair-designate, said the board was satisfied the deal was the best available outcome. “The cash offer of 250 pence per share was higher than all other formal proposals received during this process, and provides certain value in cash today for Spire shareholders,” she said. Private ownership, the company argued, would give it better access to capital for growth and acquisitions.
Toscafund was already one of Spire’s largest shareholders, and its founder Martin Hughes framed the take-private as a chance to back a healthcare business for the long term. Alongside Toscafund’s stake and Three Hills’ and Ares’ equity, the specialist investor Song Capital is providing about £500m of debt financing to support the deal.
Spire launched a strategic review in September 2025, and earlier suitors circled without success. Private equity firms Bridgepoint and Triton were in talks but walked away in March 2026 after failing to firm up an offer, leaving Toscafund to assemble the winning consortium months later. In July 2026, Spire sold a portfolio of 12 acute-care hospitals to funds managed by Blue Owl Capital for about £1.3bn ($1.75bn), separating a large slice of its freehold property from its operations.
Chief executive Justin Ash will retire after nine years, with non-executive director and vice-chair Sir David Sloman stepping in as interim chief executive, while Ian Cheshire leaves as chair and is succeeded on an interim basis by White. Sloman brings extensive NHS experience, having run several NHS trusts and served as chief operating officer at NHS England.
Spire operates 38 private hospitals and more than 55 clinics across England, Wales, and Scotland, and treated about 1.36m patients in 2025, making it the UK’s largest independent integrated healthcare network, serving both private patients and the NHS.

An agreement may be reached soon, the sources said.
Launched in Hamburg in 2017, Hyrox stages mass-participation fitness races in which competitors alternate between runs and workout stations, and it has become one of the fastest-growing participation sports in the world. Its momentum is increasingly global. Hong Kong will host the 2027 World Championships, the first time the event has been held outside Europe or North America.
L Catterton’s consumer portfolio already spans Equinox fitness clubs and Hydrow, the connected rowing-machine maker, and last year it invested in L.A.B. Golf, a maker of high-tech putters.
Hyrox is owned by the Swiss sports-marketing group Infront Sports & Media, which counts China’s Dalian Wanda Group among its backers. Bloomberg reported in October that a consortium led by Boyu Capital was in talks to acquire Infront. A representative for Dalian Wanda declined to comment, while Hyrox and Infront did not respond to Bloomberg’s requests.
Sky News reported in June that L Catterton was in talks to buy a stake in Hyrox. The latest reporting suggests those discussions are now approaching a conclusion.
