For a few minutes on Wednesday, Hunter Biden’s meme coin looked like one of the most valuable things in crypto. Then it almost disappeared.
$LAPTOP launched on Base and immediately went vertical. Depending on which price feed you were watching, the token traded into the hundreds of dollars, with CoinMarketCap recording prints above $400. Less than a day later, it was trading around 80 cents. Even by the standards of meme coins, where occasionally losing 99% of your money before lunch is apparently considered a feature, this was impressive.
But the price itself does not adequately capture how ridiculous this became. Blockchain analytics firm Arkham showed $LAPTOP reaching a fully diluted valuation of roughly $144 billion just two minutes after launch. For context, that would have made Hunter Biden’s laptop token theoretically worth more than Starbucks, Nike or Coinbase and placed it among the largest crypto assets in the world. It would also have put it well above the peak fully diluted valuation of Donald Trump’s $TRUMP token.
There was one small problem. The liquidity pool supporting that $144 billion theoretical valuation contained roughly $48,000.
Yes, you read that correctly. For a brief moment, a token backed by enough available liquidity to buy a nice car was being valued on paper at roughly $144 billion.
This is already one of the funniest sentences I have ever had to write about crypto, and somehow the story gets better.
The token was supposed to be a political statement. Hunter Biden has spent the past year publicly reclaiming the laptop that became synonymous with years of scandal, media coverage, congressional investigations and partisan warfare. He described $LAPTOP as a symbol of “resilience, redemption, and recovery,” turning the object that had been used against him politically into something he could own culturally and, apparently, financially. Naturally, the logical conclusion in America in 2026 was to put it on a blockchain and let strangers gamble on it.
The market was happy to oblige. Bots and snipers piled into the launch, the price exploded almost instantaneously, and people chasing the move began buying at valuations that had lost any connection to reality. Within minutes, the entire thing reversed. $LAPTOP crashed by roughly 99% from its highest prints, individual losses began circulating across X, and one trader reportedly lost nearly $200,000 after buying close to the top.
Normally that would be enough for a spectacular crypto cautionary tale. But $LAPTOP had another feature that takes the whole episode from merely stupid to almost perfect satire: Hunter Biden launched it partly as a response to Donald Trump’s meme coin.
Before the launch, Hunter had repeatedly criticized $TRUMP as a grift and pointed to the billions of dollars that retail investors had lost trading it. The $LAPTOP tokenomics even reserved a portion of the supply for people who had lost money on $TRUMP. The idea was literally to give tokens from a new political meme coin to people who had been destroyed buying the previous political meme coin.
You almost have to admire the efficiency.
One first family launches a political meme coin, retail gets crushed and the token falls more than 95% from its peak. A member of the other first family looks at the carnage, calls it a grift and launches his own political meme coin. That token proceeds to create an even more absurd paper valuation before collapsing roughly 99% almost immediately.
There are not many truly bipartisan institutions left in America, but apparently monetizing political fandom through meme coins remains one of them.
Hunter pushed back hard on the characterization that the launch was a failure. In a post after the collapse, he said that “the available liquidity simply couldn’t sustain the strong level of interest at launch,” blamed predatory snipers for the initial spike and emphasized that the team allocation remained locked. He said nobody on his side had sold and that he personally had not made a dollar. He also pointed to the token’s remaining billion-dollar fully diluted valuation as evidence that the project remained valuable and argued that the media was misrepresenting what happened.
I am willing to take seriously the distinction between a disastrous launch and an intentional rug pull. There is no evidence that Hunter personally dumped his tokens into the frenzy, and the founder allocation was subject to lockups. Market makers and project-linked wallets moving tokens around launch also does not automatically prove wrongdoing. Meme coins are perfectly capable of destroying retail investors without anyone committing fraud.
But Hunter’s explanation that liquidity could not sustain demand is not really a defense of what happened. It is an almost perfect description of the problem.
If $48,000 of liquidity can temporarily support a $144 billion theoretical valuation, then the valuation is fiction. It exists mathematically, but not economically. Nobody could have sold $144 billion worth of $LAPTOP. Nobody could have sold $14 billion. Nobody could have sold remotely close to the number being displayed on the screen without annihilating the price.
This is where meme coins routinely break people’s brains. A token can have a billion units of supply, but only a tiny fraction of those tokens actually need to trade to establish a price. If a few frantic trades push that price to $144, multiplying $144 by one billion tokens produces a $144 billion FDV. It looks enormous. It gets screenshotted. People start calculating how rich holders have become. But the money was never actually there.
Price tells you where the last trade happened. Liquidity tells you whether you can get out.
Those are very different things, particularly in a market like this. The $144 billion number was not evidence that investors had poured $144 billion into Hunter Biden’s meme coin. It was evidence that an extraordinarily thin market had briefly produced an extraordinarily stupid price.
The political element makes this more interesting than a normal meme coin collapse because political tokens turn an already emotional trade into something even less rational. People are not just purchasing an asset. They can feel like they are buying membership in a tribe, supporting a person, trolling the opposing side or participating in a cultural moment. That gives the token something most bad investments would kill for – millions of potential buyers who already have an emotional relationship with the product before it exists.
$TRUMP demonstrated exactly how powerful that can be. Now $LAPTOP has demonstrated that the phenomenon is not confined to one political family or one side of the political spectrum. The names change, the politics change and the marketing changes, but the economic proposition to retail looks remarkably similar: turn fame and tribal loyalty into a tradeable object, create an enormous burst of attention and hope you are not the person buying after everyone else has arrived.
There is an uncomfortable irony here for crypto because all of this is happening while the industry is becoming more legitimate than it has ever been. Banks are experimenting with stablecoins. Tokenized assets are moving into mainstream finance. Bitcoin sits in ETFs and corporate treasuries. Wall Street is adopting market structures that crypto pioneered. We are finally seeing serious financial applications emerge from technology that spent years on the fringe, while simultaneously watching Hunter Biden’s laptop become a $144 billion asset for a few minutes because somebody put a ticker on it.
Both things can be true. The technology can mature while human behavior remains completely unchanged.
And that is ultimately what I take from $LAPTOP. Hunter says the project is playing the long game, and maybe it is. The token could recover from 80 cents, disappear entirely or somehow become the greatest comeback story in meme coin history. None of those outcomes changes what happened at launch. People bought a token for hundreds of dollars in a market that could not remotely support those prices because the chart was vertical, the name was famous and everyone believed someone else would arrive behind them willing to pay even more.
Less than a day later, a token that briefly generated a $144 billion theoretical valuation was trading for less than a dollar. No complicated valuation model is necessary to extract the lesson from that. Political fame can manufacture attention, and attention can manufacture a price, but neither manufactures liquidity or value. If there is one thing both American political families have now managed to prove, it is that putting a famous name on a meme coin does not change who ultimately pays when the music stops.
Retail does.

The Stock Market Is Quietly Losing Breadth
The percentage of S&P 500 stocks trading above their 50-day moving average has fallen sharply even as the headline index remains relatively close to its highs. That divergence matters because a cap-weighted index can continue looking healthy while fewer and fewer individual companies participate underneath the surface. Narrowing breadth does not automatically mean the market is about to fall apart, but it does mean more of the index’s performance is being carried by a smaller group of stocks at exactly the moment oil, yields and broader macro pressure are becoming less friendly.
Why it matters: strong markets usually broaden as more companies participate. When the index stays near the highs while participation deteriorates, the rally becomes more dependent on a smaller group of winners. That makes the market more fragile if one of those leaders finally stumbles.
U.S. Bank completed a live cross-border payment using USBDC, its proprietary dollar-backed stablecoin, on Stellar. The transaction moved between bank entities in North America and Europe while remaining connected to the bank’s existing compliance, risk and operations infrastructure. This is exactly what real crypto adoption may eventually look like – not millions of consumers suddenly learning about wallets and gas fees, but traditional financial institutions quietly using blockchain rails underneath products their customers already understand.
Germany’s Finance Ministry has proposed eliminating the rule that currently allows private investors to sell Bitcoin and other crypto tax-free after holding for more than a year. Under the draft, newly acquired crypto would instead fall under the country’s normal capital-gains regime regardless of how long investors hold it, while existing positions would be grandfathered. Ironically, short-term traders could actually benefit because they currently face much higher personal income-tax rates, while patient long-term holders would lose one of the most attractive crypto tax treatments in Europe.
Consensys is splitting into two independent companies, with the existing entity becoming MetaMask while a new Consensys houses Linea and the institutional Ethereum infrastructure businesses. The separation is interesting because MetaMask has evolved from a browser extension into one of crypto’s most important direct relationships with consumers. After years of crypto conglomerates bundling wallets, infrastructure, chains and enterprise software together, MetaMask may now be valuable enough as a standalone consumer platform to justify becoming the entire company.
Before You Go
Political meme coins may be the cleanest example of what happens when identity replaces analysis. The ticker becomes a team jersey, the chart becomes the thesis and suddenly nobody cares whether the market underneath it can support the price. That usually works beautifully until the exact moment everyone wants to sell.

Bitcoin treasury companies have trained investors to focus on one number: Bitcoin per share. The logic is straightforward. A company issues stock, debt or some other security, uses the proceeds to buy Bitcoin, and tries to structure the transaction so that the amount of Bitcoin attributable to each existing shareholder increases. If management can repeatedly pull that off, dilution is not necessarily a bad thing. Strategy built an entire corporate-finance machine around this idea, and dozens of companies have spent the past two years trying to reproduce some version of it.
Metaplanet became one of the most aggressive examples. The Japanese company transformed itself from a relatively obscure public company into one of the largest corporate holders of Bitcoin in the world, accumulating 43,000 BTC while repeatedly tapping the capital markets to fund purchases. Investors accepted enormous increases in the share count because the pitch was never simply that Metaplanet was issuing more stock. The pitch was that management could use that stock to acquire Bitcoin in a way that increased the economic value attributable to existing shareholders.
That is the part of the Bitcoin treasury model everyone understands. The current Metaplanet controversy is about the part that is considerably easier to miss.
Before Metaplanet became a Bitcoin treasury company, it created an executive option program known as the Series 10 Stock Acquisition Rights. Executive options themselves are hardly unusual. The important detail was how this particular pool worked. The number of shares potentially available through the program was tied to Metaplanet’s fully diluted share count rather than being permanently fixed.
Then the company discovered Bitcoin.
As Metaplanet issued huge quantities of new shares to raise money and accumulate BTC, the fully diluted share count grew. Because the executive option pool was tied to that number, the potential option pool grew alongside it. An incentive structure designed for a much smaller company operating under a completely different strategy suddenly became attached to one of the most aggressive equity-issuance machines in public markets.
The numbers became enormous. The potential shares attached to the Series 10 rights expanded from roughly 46 million to about 319 million. In August, Metaplanet eliminated the floating adjustment mechanism, capped the pool at roughly 319.5 million potential shares and imposed a five-year lockup on shares acquired through exercising the rights. Importantly, the company itself acknowledged that the previous structure amplified the dilution borne by existing shareholders.
That is the sentence investors should pay attention to, because it exposes an important weakness in how Bitcoin treasury companies are often analyzed.
Imagine a company owns 10,000 Bitcoin and has 100 million shares outstanding. On a simplistic basis, every share represents an economic claim on 0.0001 BTC. Management then issues another 20 million shares and uses the proceeds to buy enough Bitcoin that Bitcoin per share actually increases. Great. That is the accretion treasury investors are looking for.
But now imagine that sitting around those common shares are hundreds of millions of options, warrants, convertible securities, preferred shares and other potential claims on the company. Some may eventually become common shares themselves. Others may dilute the common shareholder economically. Some may sit ahead of common equity altogether.
Suddenly the calculation becomes a lot less clean.
A company can truthfully say that its Bitcoin holdings increased. It might even truthfully say that Bitcoin per currently outstanding share increased. Neither statement necessarily tells you how much of the Bitcoin ultimately belongs to you.
The denominator matters every bit as much as the numerator.
Metaplanet provided a particularly vivid example when CEO Simon Gerovich exercised 92,000 Series 10 rights in late August and received roughly 64 million common shares, subject to the five-year transfer restriction. The lockup matters because those shares cannot simply hit the market tomorrow, but a lockup does not make dilution disappear. For someone trying to understand long-term ownership economics, those shares still matter. Investors clearly noticed. Metaplanet fell roughly 17% across Monday and Tuesday even as Bitcoin itself was comparatively stable.
I do not think the useful conclusion is that Metaplanet secretly engineered some sinister scheme or that the entire Bitcoin treasury model is broken. The Series 10 structure predates the Bitcoin strategy, the options were disclosed, management has now frozen the expansion mechanism and added a long lockup. Equity incentives are also completely normal in public companies.
The interesting lesson is what happened when an old compensation structure collided with an entirely new corporate strategy.
Bitcoin treasury companies are unusual businesses because capital formation is effectively part of the product. A normal company sells software, cars or insurance and occasionally raises capital to finance the business. A Bitcoin treasury company can raise capital precisely because investors believe management will recycle that capital into Bitcoin at attractive economics. When the stock trades at a premium to the underlying value of its Bitcoin, issuing equity can become reflexive: sell expensive shares, buy Bitcoin, potentially increase Bitcoin per share, support the premium and repeat.
We have discussed that machine before. The Metaplanet episode shows why investors also need to understand who else has a claim on the machine.
Bitcoin per share is only useful if you are using the right share count. Basic shares outstanding may be the easiest number to find, but fully diluted ownership can tell a very different story. Investors need to understand options, warrants, convertible debt, preferred securities, employee compensation and any other instrument that can eventually alter their economic claim.
And price matters too. An option to buy stock close to the current market price is very different from an option that gives someone the right to acquire shares for a tiny fraction of that price. Metaplanet’s Series 10 exercise price was just ¥10 per share, which is why the economics became so consequential once the company’s stock and capital structure exploded in size.
This gets to something deeper about the entire treasury trade. Investors are not simply buying Bitcoin sitting on a corporate balance sheet. If that were the only goal, they could buy Bitcoin directly or use an ETF. They are paying management for the ability to operate a capital machine that can hopefully turn access to equity and credit markets into increasing Bitcoin exposure over time.
That makes governance part of the investment thesis.
A Bitcoin treasury company is effectively asking shareholders to trust management with two scarce assets at once: the Bitcoin and the equity. Everyone watches the Bitcoin because it is visible, easy to count and makes for a great headline every time another purchase is announced. The equity can be considerably messier, buried across filings, option agreements, warrants, convertibles and compensation plans.
Metaplanet is a reminder to watch both.
The next time a treasury company announces an enormous Bitcoin purchase, do not stop at asking how many coins it bought. Ask what it issued to buy them. Ask what the fully diluted share count looks like afterward. Ask who else received claims on the company along the way. Ask what securities sit ahead of you, how management gets paid and whether the transaction increased your economic claim on the Bitcoin rather than merely increasing the company’s headline BTC balance.
Because there is a huge difference between a company owning more Bitcoin and you owning more Bitcoin.
For anyone investing in the treasury trade, figuring out that difference may be one of the most important calculations they can make.
Hyperliquid open interest climbed to a record $14.3 billion Tuesday as HYPE reached an all-time high. The bigger story is that a crypto-native perpetuals exchange is reaching a scale that would have sounded absurd for an onchain venue only a few years ago. We have spent years debating whether decentralized markets could ever compete with centralized exchanges on liquidity and user experience. Hyperliquid is increasingly forcing investors to take that question seriously rather than treating DeFi as an interesting experiment.
Visa says stablecoin settlement across its network has reached an annualized run rate above $20 billion, more than 15 times where it stood a year ago. This is exactly the kind of crypto adoption that matters because most consumers may never know it is happening. Stablecoins do not need everyone to become crypto traders. They need to become better plumbing for dollars moving between banks, payment companies and businesses. When the technology becomes invisible, adoption is probably working.
The House has shortened its September schedule, leaving lawmakers only a handful of working days before the midterm elections and making passage of the CLARITY Act considerably harder. The Senate is still expected to move on market-structure legislation, but bipartisan negotiations remain stuck over several issues, including restrictions connected to political officials’ crypto activities. Crypto spent much of this year assuming comprehensive market-structure legislation was increasingly inevitable. The calendar is becoming a very real opponent.

Most people think about crypto security in terms of keys. Lose your private key, lose your money. Let someone steal your seed phrase, lose your money. Leave assets on an exchange with terrible operational controls and, well, maybe lose your money. We have spent more than a decade teaching people some version of the same lesson: protect the keys and you protect the asset. The Liquid Network incident over the weekend is a very good reminder that this is not always true.
Roughly 4,000 BTC, worth about $320 million at the time, was withdrawn from Liquid’s federation wallet on Sunday, representing roughly 95% of the Bitcoin reserves backing Liquid Bitcoin, or L-BTC, on the network. Liquid paused activity, exchanges suspended L-BTC deposits and withdrawals, and for a few hours it looked like another enormous crypto hack. Then it got considerably weirder. The people responsible identified themselves as white hats and began communicating with Blockstream through messages embedded in Bitcoin transactions, telling Blockstream to fix the bug first. Blockstream later said its bridge nodes had been patched, and shortly afterward 3,400 BTC was returned. The attackers still control roughly 598.5 BTC, worth around $47 million, which is a fairly aggressive interpretation of a bug bounty, but the majority of the Bitcoin is back.
The fascinating part is how the Bitcoin left in the first place. According to the current explanation from the parties involved, the Peg-out Authorization Key used in the transaction was not compromised. The attackers apparently did not steal the private keys protecting the federation wallet. Instead, the L-BTC involved in the withdrawal had been created because of a bug in Elements, the software underlying Liquid. In simple terms, someone found a way to create Bitcoin on Liquid that was not actually backed by Bitcoin, and then the system redeemed that fake claim for real Bitcoin.
That distinction matters enormously.
Liquid is a Bitcoin sidechain. When someone moves Bitcoin onto Liquid, real BTC is locked in a federation-controlled multisig wallet and an equivalent amount of L-BTC becomes available on the network. The accounting relationship is supposed to be extremely simple: one Bitcoin goes in, one L-BTC exists. If that L-BTC is later destroyed through an authorized peg-out, one actual Bitcoin can come back out. The entire system depends on maintaining that relationship perfectly because L-BTC is only useful if everyone can trust that every unit represents Bitcoin sitting somewhere behind it.
Think of a coat-check counter. You hand over a very expensive coat and receive ticket number 417. At the end of the night, you give the attendant ticket 417 and get your coat back. The security problem everyone naturally worries about is someone stealing your ticket, because whoever holds the legitimate claim can potentially take the coat. But imagine instead that somebody discovers a flaw that lets them print a second ticket 417 that the coat-check system believes is authentic. Nobody stole the key to the coat room. Nobody broke into the building. Nobody cracked the safe. The system simply accepted a claim that should never have existed and handed over the real asset.
That is what makes the Liquid incident so interesting. Bitcoin itself worked exactly as designed. Bitcoin’s monetary policy was not compromised, nobody created 4,000 new BTC on the Bitcoin network, and there is no indication that Bitcoin’s cryptography failed. The problem appeared in the layer sitting above Bitcoin – the infrastructure responsible for maintaining the relationship between a digital representation of Bitcoin and the actual Bitcoin backing it. The base asset remained intact while the accounting system wrapped around it briefly lost track of what was real.
And this is where the story gets much bigger than Liquid.
We spent a lot of time last week talking about tokenization. Banks are building stablecoins, brokerages are experimenting with tokenized stocks, private companies are putting assets onchain, and Securitize and Socios are even trying to create regulated structures that could let fans own actual minority interests in professional sports teams. The investment case is compelling because almost anything can theoretically become a digital claim – a Treasury bond, a share of Apple, a dollar, a building, a private company, a sports franchise or Bitcoin itself. But the moment you tokenize an asset that exists somewhere else, you introduce a deceptively simple question that may end up being one of the most important questions in finance: what makes the token equal to the thing?
That sounds trivial until trillions of dollars depend on the answer. A tokenized Treasury is only valuable if there is actually a Treasury behind it. A stablecoin is only worth a dollar if the issuer can honor the claim. A tokenized stock needs to correspond to real economic ownership of the underlying shares. A tokenized piece of real estate has to map to enforceable ownership rights in the actual property. Wrapped Bitcoin is only Bitcoin-equivalent if every digital claim is backed by the Bitcoin it says exists. The blockchain can prove perfectly that you own the token, but it cannot, by itself, guarantee that the token represents what everyone thinks it represents.
That is the uncomfortable part of the tokenization story that often gets skipped. Crypto is extremely good at verifying digital ownership. It becomes much less magical when the digital asset is a claim on something outside the system. At that point you need custodians, issuers, legal agreements, software, redemption mechanisms, auditors, oracles, bridges and other pieces of infrastructure connecting the token to reality. Every one of those connections becomes part of the security model, and every one creates another place where the representation and the underlying asset can potentially become detached.
Liquid is an unusually clean example because even the underlying asset is digital. There was no courthouse, transfer agent, shipping warehouse or gold vault involved. Yet simply representing Bitcoin on another network was enough to create an additional accounting layer where something could go wrong. Now imagine doing this with everything Wall Street wants to tokenize over the next decade. The larger the market gets, the more valuable these claims become and the more important the systems that guarantee the connection between token and asset will be.
None of this means tokenization is a bad idea. Quite the opposite. I continue to think moving financial assets onto better rails is one of the clearest long-term applications of blockchain technology. Faster settlement, fractional ownership, programmable assets, global distribution and markets that operate with fewer artificial restrictions are all compelling. But the next generation of crypto security may look very different from the last one. We spent the first era teaching everyone to protect the keys. The next era may be about protecting the claims.
If trillions of dollars of real-world assets eventually live onchain, the critical question will not simply be whether someone can steal the token. It will be whether the token can ever become detached from the asset it supposedly represents, whether through a software bug, an accounting failure, a legal mismatch, a dishonest issuer or something nobody has thought of yet. That is a harder problem because the blockchain can only verify what happens inside its own rules. It cannot magically guarantee that reality outside the chain continues to match the ledger.
In Liquid’s case, the damage may ultimately be relatively contained. Most of the Bitcoin has already been returned, the vulnerable bridge infrastructure was patched, and the people responsible appear to have been trying to force a fix rather than disappear with the entire $320 million. But the lesson is bigger than the outcome. The attackers apparently did not break Bitcoin and did not need to steal the keys protecting the Bitcoin. They found a way to create a valid-looking claim on Bitcoin that did not actually exist, and the infrastructure did exactly what it had been programmed to do – it paid them.
As more of finance moves onchain, that distinction is going to matter a lot. Creating a token is easy. Making absolutely certain that the thing behind it is real, remains real and can always be redeemed as promised is considerably harder.
Bitcoin ETF Buyers Are Back
U.S. spot Bitcoin ETFs took in $730.8 million on Thursday and another $174.6 million Friday, bringing the two-day total to just over $905 million. Thursday was the strongest single inflow day since January, with BlackRock’s IBIT alone taking in $454 million. That matters because the recent Bitcoin recovery has increasingly been accompanied by real spot demand rather than simply leverage and short covering.
Why it matters: We’ve been looking for confirmation that the move off the lows is being supported by actual buyers. After the ugly outflow on September 1, ETF demand snapped back hard. One big day can be noise, but consecutive positive sessions after the reversal are a much healthier signal than price ripping solely because shorts are getting squeezed.
Robinhood Chain has generated roughly $39 million in fees since launching in July, according to Bernstein, with daily fees recently running around $2–4 million. Even more remarkably, the network generated about $33 million over the past 15 days – more than Solana or BNB Chain – and Robinhood reportedly keeps roughly 90% of the economics. The chain also has around $1.5 billion in TVL and $140 million of tokenized stocks. We spent Friday discussing Wall Street adopting crypto-native infrastructure. Apparently Robinhood decided to provide a live demonstration over the weekend.
The Ethereum Foundation has set December 2029 as its target for making Ethereum’s execution, consensus and data layers fully resistant to quantum attacks. The timeline assumes that sufficiently powerful quantum computers could arrive as early as 2030, even though most estimates put that moment considerably further away. This is the right way to think about existential security risks – you do not wait until someone invents the machine capable of breaking your cryptography before beginning the upgrade. Ethereum is effectively trying to replace parts of the airplane while it is still flying.
Harmony, once pitched as an Ethereum competitor, has proposed voluntarily shutting down its Layer 1, moving ONE balances onto Ethereum and redirecting future token emissions toward an AI-video business. The seven-year-old chain suffered a $100 million bridge exploit in 2022 and another major incident last month, and its developers now say defending the network against increasingly sophisticated attackers is becoming too difficult. There is something beautifully crypto about spending years building an Ethereum killer only to eventually move the token onto Ethereum and pivot to AI.

For most of crypto’s history, the argument went something like this: eventually crypto will grow up, become regulated, behave more like traditional finance and get absorbed into Wall Street.
That may have been backwards.
Yesterday, Coinbase disclosed that it has filed registration documents with the SEC as it seeks a path to offer equity perpetual futures in the United States. Perpetuals are one of crypto’s signature financial products – derivatives that track the price of an asset but, unlike traditional futures contracts, never expire. Coinbase already offers them internationally on stocks including Apple, Microsoft, Nvidia and Amazon. Now it wants to bring that structure home.
The filing is only the beginning. Coinbase still needs regulatory approval, including from the CFTC, and there is no guarantee that U.S. stock perpetuals will ultimately look exactly like their offshore crypto cousins. But I think focusing narrowly on whether Coinbase gets this particular product approved misses the much bigger story.
Traditional markets are starting to look increasingly like crypto markets.
Think about what made crypto trading feel so foreign a decade ago. Markets never closed. You could trade Bitcoin at 3:17 on Sunday morning because apparently humans occasionally need that option. Assets moved globally without waiting for a bank to open Monday. Perpetual futures gave traders leveraged exposure without monthly or quarterly expirations. Stablecoins moved dollars around the world around the clock. Settlement increasingly happened in minutes or seconds instead of days. Markets existed for assets and outcomes that traditional exchanges had never bothered to list.
For years, much of Wall Street looked at that infrastructure as either a curiosity or a casino.
Now Wall Street is rebuilding pieces of it.
The SEC is holding a roundtable later this month specifically about preparations for 24-hour U.S. equity trading. The agenda includes Nasdaq, Citadel Securities, Jane Street, Schwab, Interactive Brokers, DTCC, State Street, Citi and a long list of other firms discussing overnight liquidity, settlement, cybersecurity and what eventually moving toward 24/7 markets would require.
That is not a crypto conference.
It is the U.S. securities regulator and some of the largest institutions in finance discussing how to make the stock market behave more like the market crypto traders have used for years.
Tokenized equities are moving in the same direction. Coinbase announced this summer that it intends to offer tokenized U.S. stocks backed one-for-one by underlying shares. Kraken has been pushing tokenized equities internationally. Robinhood has built its own tokenized-stock infrastructure in Europe. Yesterday we discussed Securitize and Socios trying to bring actual fractional ownership of professional sports teams onchain.
Stablecoins are becoming payment infrastructure. Banks are building them. Fintech companies are building them. Asset managers want exposure to the economics behind them. This week we talked about 21 major financial institutions preparing a dollar stablecoin venture after the original consortium began with 10.
Prediction markets have pushed the boundary from traditional gambling into federally regulated financial contracts. And now Coinbase wants Americans to trade perpetual contracts on stocks.
These are not isolated crypto products sneaking into traditional finance.
They are pieces of a new market architecture.
Here’s where I think the distinction matters. There has been a tendency in crypto to assume that mass adoption means everyone eventually leaves their brokerage account, opens a wallet, buys tokens and starts interacting directly with decentralized applications.
That may happen at the margins. I doubt it happens for most people.

The more likely outcome is that people keep using financial products that look familiar while the machinery underneath them becomes increasingly crypto-native.
Your brokerage account may still look like a brokerage account. But it may operate almost continuously. The asset you buy might be represented onchain. Dollars may move through stablecoins behind the scenes. Settlement could happen nearly instantly. Derivatives created in crypto may become standard products. Assets that were previously private, illiquid or inaccessible may become fractional and globally tradable.
The customer may never even know that any of this has anything to do with crypto.
That is probably a feature, not a bug.
The internet won because people stopped talking about “using the internet.” Nobody describes ordering dinner as conducting an internet transaction. The technology disappeared into the product.
Crypto may ultimately follow the same path.
Bitcoin is somewhat different because its value proposition is not merely better financial plumbing. Bitcoin is the asset itself – scarce, bearer-native money with a monetary policy that no bank, company or government can modify. But almost everything surrounding Bitcoin is part of a much broader experiment in how markets should operate.
And traditional finance has been watching that experiment play out in public for more than a decade.
Some of it failed spectacularly. Crypto produced plenty of leverage, fraud, worthless tokens and market structures that should probably never be exported anywhere. There is no reason to romanticize all of it.
But it also gave markets a laboratory with very few legacy constraints.
What happens if markets never close?
What happens if dollars settle instantly?
What happens if anyone can issue an asset?
What happens if derivatives never expire?
What happens if ownership becomes programmable?
What happens if markets can be created around almost anything?
Crypto tested all of those questions at enormous scale, often painfully, and Wall Street got to watch the results without paying the entire tuition bill.
Now the parts that worked are being pulled into the regulated financial system.
That is why I think Coinbase’s equity-perpetual filing is more important than another product announcement. Coinbase is effectively asking regulators whether one of the most successful pieces of crypto market structure can be applied to American stocks.
Maybe regulators say no. Maybe they approve a heavily modified version. Maybe someone else gets there first.
The direction of travel is still difficult to miss.
Wall Street spent years waiting for crypto to become more like Wall Street.
Instead, stocks are moving toward 24-hour trading. Dollars are becoming tokens. Private assets are moving onchain. Prediction markets are competing with sportsbooks and financial exchanges. Perpetual futures are trying to escape crypto entirely.
Crypto is certainly becoming more institutional.
But at the same time, institutions are quietly becoming more crypto.
And that may ultimately be the far more important form of adoption.
The Fed Trade Just Flipped Again
Gold jumped roughly 2% yesterday while Treasury yields and the dollar fell after Fed Governor Christopher Waller said he could support leaving rates unchanged this month if inflation continues to cool. Markets went from pricing roughly a 70% probability of another September hike earlier in the week to something close to a coin flip ahead of this morning’s jobs report.
Why it matters: A market that was becoming increasingly convinced the Fed would hike again suddenly became much less certain in a matter of hours. Today’s payroll report can move that probability dramatically in either direction. Gold around $4,470 is the useful visual here – not because gold itself is the trade, but because it is showing how violently expectations around rates, the dollar and real yields are moving.
U.S. spot Bitcoin ETFs took in $730.8 million yesterday, according to Farside – a sharp reversal after $236.5 million of outflows Tuesday and only $101.1 million of inflows Wednesday. BlackRock’s IBIT accounted for $454 million of the total, with Fidelity, Bitwise, Ark/21Shares and several others also positive. This matters because the latest Bitcoin move is increasingly being accompanied by actual spot demand rather than simply leverage and short covering. That is exactly what I want to see if the broader bottoming thesis is going to keep gaining credibility.
The OCC has conditionally approved Revolut’s application to create Revolut Bank US, another step in the increasingly blurry line between fintech, crypto and traditional banking. Revolut still needs FDIC, Federal Reserve and final OCC approvals before opening, so this is not a completed bank charter. But the proposed bank is targeting a 2027 launch with checking accounts, credit cards, loans, foreign exchange and eventually a stablecoin. Yesterday Coinbase wanted to make stocks behave like crypto. Now a crypto-friendly fintech wants to become a federally regulated bank. Apparently convergence works both ways.
New Jersey has asked the Supreme Court to settle the increasingly important question of whether sports event contracts offered by federally regulated prediction markets are financial derivatives or gambling products subject to state law. Lower courts have begun reaching conflicting conclusions, which makes Supreme Court review more plausible. The stakes are enormous for Kalshi and eventually Polymarket because sports markets have become a massive part of the business. At some point the legal system is going to have to answer the question we keep coming back to: when does a bet become a trade simply because you put it on an exchange?
Before You Go
The most interesting thing happening in crypto right now may not be another token or another blockchain.
It may be watching ideas that looked completely insane when crypto introduced them slowly become normal financial infrastructure.
Markets that never close. Dollars that move instantly. Assets represented onchain. Perpetual derivatives. Fractional ownership of things most people could never previously buy.
Crypto spent a decade stress-testing the future of finance in public. Wall Street appears to have been taking notes.
If you know someone who still thinks “crypto adoption” simply means more people buying coins, send them today’s Wolf Den.

Crypto has spent years trying to convince sports fans that they owned something.
Teams launched fan tokens that let supporters vote on jerseys, unlock experiences, access special content and occasionally decide which song should play after a goal. Some of those products found real audiences and created interesting new ways for teams to engage with fans. But there was always a fairly obvious limitation.
You didn’t actually own any of the team.
That may be about to change.
Yesterday, Securitize and Socios announced a partnership to develop regulated tokenized equity offerings representing minority ownership interests in professional sports teams. Socios already has relationships with more than 70 major sports organizations, while Securitize has built much of the regulated infrastructure now being used to bring traditional assets onchain. The idea is to combine those two worlds and eventually allow eligible investors to buy digital tokens that represent real financial interests in a team.
Not access. Not governance over the pregame playlist. Equity.
There are plenty of caveats before anyone starts budgeting for a piece of the Yankees. No teams have actually announced offerings, league and club approvals would still be required, securities laws apply, investor eligibility may vary by jurisdiction and we don’t yet know what the first offering will look like. Securitize and Socios are building the infrastructure and working with teams and owners – they are not announcing that every fan can buy a fraction of any franchise tomorrow morning.
But I think the direction is considerably more interesting than another tokenized Treasury fund.
For years, tokenization has been presented as one of crypto’s largest potential use cases. Larry Fink talks about it constantly. Banks are experimenting with it. Treasury funds, private credit, money-market products and even public stocks are increasingly moving onchain. The value of tokenized real-world assets has climbed dramatically, and I have little doubt that number becomes much larger over time.
The problem is that much of what we’ve tokenized so far was already fairly easy to own.
Putting a Treasury bill on a blockchain can improve settlement, collateral mobility and market efficiency, but it doesn’t fundamentally change my access to Treasury bills. I could already buy them through a brokerage account or own them through an ETF with a few clicks.
Professional sports teams are different.
Securitize and Socios estimate the global professional sports-franchise market at roughly $500 billion, yet ownership remains overwhelmingly private, concentrated and difficult to access. These are among the most recognizable assets in the world, with incredibly passionate customers and genuine scarcity – there is only one Real Madrid, one Dallas Cowboys and one Ferrari Formula 1 team – but unless you happen to have a few billion dollars and the phone number of an existing owner, participation has generally been off the table.
This is where tokenization starts becoming much more interesting to me. The most powerful version of the technology may not be putting assets we can already buy onto a better database. It may be taking assets that have historically been inaccessible, illiquid or cumbersome to divide and creating infrastructure through which ownership can be distributed much more broadly.
Tokenization is most interesting when it changes access, not merely the database.
Imagine an existing owner of a professional team wants to sell a 5% minority stake without giving up control. Today, that can involve finding a wealthy individual or private-equity fund, negotiating a bespoke transaction, satisfying league ownership rules and potentially waiting years for another buyer if that investor eventually wants to exit. Tokenization doesn’t eliminate those restrictions, but it can theoretically divide that minority interest into much smaller pieces, automate ownership records and transfer restrictions, and make distribution to a larger pool of eligible investors considerably easier.
That doesn’t magically create liquidity either. Putting an illiquid asset on a blockchain does not summon buyers from the heavens, just as putting a terrible company on Nasdaq doesn’t make it a good investment. There still needs to be demand, reasonable pricing, regulatory compliance and some mechanism through which investors can eventually sell.
Sports might be unusually well suited to solving part of that problem because the demand is already there.
People don’t need to be educated about why they care about Barcelona or the Lakers. They already spend enormous amounts of money on tickets, merchandise, subscriptions and travel because their relationship with the team is emotional in a way that their relationship with a private-credit fund will never be. Socios says its own recent survey across five countries found that 72% of respondents were interested in buying a digital asset that represented minority ownership in their club. Take any survey commissioned by the company selling the product with the appropriate grain of salt, but the underlying idea isn’t difficult to understand.
Fans have always wanted to say, “that’s my team.” Some of them may actually want that sentence to become financially true.
There is also a useful lesson here in how crypto products evolve.
Fan tokens were an early attempt to merge blockchain technology with enormous existing sports communities. They proved that teams could issue digital assets directly to fans, but the economic proposition was always somewhat awkward because enthusiasm for the underlying team did not necessarily translate into value for the token. The new equity product being contemplated is explicitly different. One is an engagement asset. The other would represent a regulated financial interest.
That distinction is enormous, particularly after our discussion earlier this week about what crypto tokens are actually worth. An equity token doesn’t require us to invent “utility” to justify its existence. If I own a genuine minority interest in a sports franchise, I can analyze the value of the underlying business, its revenue, profitability, media rights, sponsorships, franchise appreciation and whatever economic rights accompany the security. The blockchain changes how the ownership is issued and administered. It doesn’t have to manufacture the reason the asset has value.
That may ultimately be one of the healthiest directions crypto can take.
We spent the first era creating digitally native assets and asking the world to discover why they mattered. The next era may increasingly involve taking things the world already knows are valuable and using crypto rails to make ownership, settlement and transfer more efficient.
Sports teams are a particularly compelling example, but they are hardly the endpoint. Private companies, real estate, infrastructure, collectibles and other scarce assets all suffer from some combination of high minimum investments, limited distribution and illiquidity. Not every one of them should trade 24/7 on a blockchain, and fractionalization can just as easily make a bad investment available to more people. Access and quality are not the same thing.
Still, this is the version of tokenization that I think normal people can immediately understand.
Don’t tell someone that blockchain will revolutionize transfer-agent infrastructure and watch their eyes glaze over. Tell a lifelong fan that they might eventually be able to own an actual economic piece of the team they have supported since childhood, and suddenly the technology becomes considerably less abstract.
We are not there yet. Securitize and Socios still need teams willing to participate, leagues willing to approve the structures and regulators comfortable with how the securities are distributed and traded. The first offerings may be small, restricted or nothing like the frictionless global marketplace crypto people imagine.
But the direction matters. Crypto spent years selling fans digital tokens that represented their relationship with sports teams. The more interesting future may be using the same technology to sell them something that doesn’t need a complicated explanation at all – a piece of the team.
Tokenized Stocks Are Quietly Exploding
The number of wallets holding tokenized equities has surged this year, while onchain transfer volume reached roughly $29.5 billion over a recent 30-day period – up more than 400%. Solana alone settled $8.8 billion of tokenized-equity volume in the second quarter, more than four times its first-quarter total.
Why it matters: Today’s sports-team announcement isn’t happening in a vacuum. Investors are already demonstrating real demand for equities that can move onchain, and a significant portion of tokenized-stock trading is happening outside normal market hours. Sports franchises would take the same infrastructure into an asset class that most investors have never been able to access at all.
The CFTC has asked a federal court to dismiss CME’s lawsuit challenging Kalshi’s Bitcoin perpetual futures, arguing that CME cannot claim competitive harm when it is free to list similar products itself. The regulator’s filing was unusually blunt – essentially telling the world’s largest derivatives exchange that if customers want perpetuals, CME can build them too. Crypto-native market structure keeps forcing traditional exchanges to decide whether to fight new products or copy them. Increasingly, regulators seem comfortable with the second option.
The SEC has finalized the agenda for its September 17 roundtable on extending U.S. equity trading toward 24 hours, with participants from Nasdaq, Schwab, Jane Street, Citadel Securities, State Street, DTCC and others. The discussion will cover everything from overnight liquidity to settlement and eventually 24/7 markets. Crypto has trained an entire generation of investors to expect markets that never close. Now one of the defining features of crypto market structure is steadily migrating into traditional finance.
U.S. spot Bitcoin ETFs took in roughly $101 million yesterday, reversing the previous session’s $236.5 million outflow. BlackRock’s IBIT brought in about $115 million on its own, while GBTC lost roughly $56 million. One day of flows doesn’t tell us much, but the quick reversal is worth watching with Bitcoin still absorbing a difficult macro backdrop. Institutional demand hasn’t disappeared because rates, oil and geopolitics became uncomfortable – it just continues to arrive in increasingly uneven bursts.
Before You Go
Tokenization has spent years sounding much more complicated than it needs to.
The technology becomes easier to understand when the pitch changes from “putting financial assets on a blockchain” to something much simpler: giving more people access to things they previously couldn’t own.
We don’t know whether sports-team equity becomes the killer use case, and the first products will almost certainly come with more restrictions than crypto purists would like. But if the next generation of tokenization gives ordinary investors genuine ownership in scarce assets rather than another token loosely connected to them, that’s progress worth watching.
If you know someone who has spent their life saying “we” when talking about a team they don’t actually own, send them today’s Wolf Den. Maybe eventually they’ll finally be right.
See you tomorrow.
– Scott

For most of crypto’s history, traditional banks treated stablecoins somewhere between a nuisance and an existential threat. They warned about deposits leaving the banking system, fought over whether stablecoin companies should be allowed to pay rewards and generally seemed determined to prevent crypto companies from building a better version of the dollar.
Apparently they also took notes.
A stablecoin project that started with 10 major banks last fall has now expanded to 21 global financial institutions – including Bank of America, Citi, Goldman Sachs, Wells Fargo, Deutsche Bank, UBS, Santander and Fidelity. The group plans to form a new company and is targeting a U.S. dollar stablecoin launch in the first half of 2027, with a euro version expected to follow.
That matters because this is no longer just an exploratory conversation among a handful of banks. The group is moving toward commercial execution.
It also isn’t happening in isolation. Earlier this summer, more than 140 companies including Visa, Mastercard, Coinbase, Stripe and BlackRock backed OpenUSD, a separate project designed around a shared stablecoin model that returns much of the reserve income to the businesses actually distributing the token.
Everyone suddenly wants a stablecoin.
That shouldn’t be surprising. Stablecoins have become one of the best businesses in finance. Customers give you dollars, you issue digital representations of those dollars, much of the reserve sits in short-term government securities, and you earn the interest. At enough scale, the economics become absurdly good.
Nobody has demonstrated that better than Tether.
I had Paolo Ardoino, Tether’s CEO and a friend of mine, on the podcast Sunday, ostensibly to talk about the company’s first full KPMG audit. We did that, but I came away considerably more interested in what Tether is actually becoming. Calling it a stablecoin company increasingly feels like calling Amazon an online bookstore.
USDT now serves more than 650 million users, with much of that adoption coming from emerging markets where access to dollars is either difficult or extraordinarily valuable. Paolo reminded me that Tether didn’t initially win by competing for JPMorgan’s customers. It went after people JPMorgan and PayPal couldn’t or wouldn’t serve – people living with unstable currencies, weak banking systems and limited access to the global financial system.
I think of it as a hyperdollar network.
Hundreds of millions of people around the world want dollars, Tether gives them a digital version they can hold and move almost anywhere, and the reserves backing that network end up heavily invested in U.S. Treasuries. Paolo believes Tether could eventually become one of the five largest buyers of U.S. government debt.
There is already something wonderfully strange about that arrangement. A person escaping currency debasement in Argentina or Turkey buys USDT, indirectly creating demand for U.S. government debt. Instead of a foreign central bank making one enormous decision about whether to own Treasuries, hundreds of millions of individuals collectively become part of the buyer base simply because they want access to dollars.

But the really interesting part happens after Tether gets paid.
Tether earns enormous income from the assets backing USDT, particularly Treasuries. The reserves backing customer tokens remain there to support USDT, but the company has also accumulated substantial excess capital and profits. And instead of simply keeping all of that wealth tied to the same monetary system that generates it, Tether has increasingly used its own corporate capital to buy things like Bitcoin, gold and farmland.
That was one of my favorite parts of the conversation with Paolo because the apparent contradiction is remarkable.
Tether is spreading the dollar while simultaneously hedging against the dollar.
Paolo described Tether as a “stable company,” meaning the goal is not merely to keep USDT worth one dollar tomorrow morning. He wants the company itself to survive extreme scenarios over decades. That is why Tether owns Bitcoin. It is why it owns substantial amounts of physical gold. It is why the company has invested in land and agricultural businesses. The largest stablecoin issuer in the world is effectively using the profits from global demand for dollars to accumulate assets whose supply cannot be expanded as easily as dollars can.
Think about that flywheel for a moment. People around the world want dollars, so Tether issues USDT. The reserves generate income, much of it from U.S. government debt. Tether earns profits from operating that enormous dollar network and then invests portions of its own capital into Bitcoin, gold, land and other businesses.
Wall Street can absolutely copy the first part.
The question is whether that is where the moat actually lives.
Circle has built USDC around regulatory credibility, institutional integrations and enormous distribution across crypto. OpenUSD is attacking the economics from another direction by sharing reserve income with the companies that distribute it. The new bank consortium arrives with advantages neither Tether nor Circle can easily replicate – massive existing customer bases, banking relationships, regulatory infrastructure and direct connections to the traditional financial system.
This is why I don’t think the right question is whether the banks are coming for Circle or Tether. They’re coming for the stablecoin business because they have finally realized how valuable it can be.
But stablecoins themselves may eventually become much more commoditized. If Citi, Goldman, Coinbase, Stripe, Circle, Tether and a dozen other credible institutions can all issue a regulated digital dollar that settles on public blockchains, the token itself becomes less differentiated. The real competition shifts toward distribution, liquidity, trust, integrations and who gets to keep the economics generated by the reserves.
That is where Tether’s position becomes particularly interesting.
A consortium of American banks can potentially dominate institutional settlement without making much of a dent in the person in Nigeria who wants digital dollars on their phone. USDT’s deepest moat may not be the technology or even the reserve portfolio – it may be the enormous global network of people who already use it as money because they actually need dollars. Recreating that distribution is considerably harder than deploying another token contract.
And Tether is already using the profits from that network to become something else entirely.
There is a broader investing lesson here that applies well beyond stablecoins. When a new technology wins, the company that invented or popularized it doesn’t necessarily own the economics forever. Regulatory clarity around stablecoins is overwhelmingly positive for the category, but it also lowers the barrier for enormous incumbents to compete. The GENIUS Act can simultaneously make stablecoins more important and make being a stablecoin issuer less special.
The next phase therefore isn’t about proving that stablecoins work. That argument is basically over. Twenty-one of the world’s largest financial institutions don’t double the size of a stablecoin consortium and move toward launching a product because they are still wondering whether blockchain-based dollars have a future.
The fight now is over who owns the rails, who controls distribution and who captures the profits.
Circle wants to be the regulated digital dollar. OpenUSD wants to share the economics with distributors. The banks want to bring stablecoins inside the existing financial system. Tether, meanwhile, has spent more than a decade building a global dollar network and is increasingly converting the profits from that network into Bitcoin, gold and hard assets.
Wall Street may have finally discovered Tether’s money machine.
The interesting part is that Tether may already be building the next one.
CHART OF THE DAY: Tether Owns The Digital-Dollar Market
DefiLlama currently shows total stablecoin supply at roughly $304 billion. USDT alone is $183.3 billion, giving Tether about 60.3% market share. USDC is a distant second at $73.7 billion – roughly 24%.
That makes today’s bank-consortium story much easier to understand visually: Wall Street isn’t entering an empty market. It’s coming after a business where Tether alone already has nearly $183 billion of digital dollars in circulation.
G20 finance ministers and central bank governors committed overnight to creating “clear pathways” for responsible digital-asset innovation, explicitly acknowledging that crypto and digital finance can contribute to economic growth. They also called for continued work on global stablecoins and longer operating hours for large-value payment systems. The language matters. A few years ago, global policymakers were debating whether crypto should be contained. Increasingly, the conversation is about how to integrate it into the existing financial system.
The SEC is holding a roundtable on what it would take to move U.S. securities markets toward round-the-clock trading while separately proposing changes to transfer-agent rules with direct implications for blockchain-based securities. Crypto has operated 24/7 from day one, while traditional markets still largely shut down at night and on weekends. Tokenization increasingly makes that distinction look arbitrary. The more securities move onto programmable rails, the harder it becomes to explain why investors should have to wait until Monday morning to trade them.
Bitcoin is holding up relatively well despite an ugly macro backdrop that includes oil above $90, sharply rising global bond yields and a stronger dollar. Higher-beta crypto assets have taken considerably more damage, while even gold has struggled. None of that guarantees Bitcoin will continue to hold, especially with the dollar creating another headwind, but markets often reveal their character through how they react to bad news. For now, Bitcoin is absorbing conditions that would normally be expected to hurt it considerably more.
BEFORE YOU GO
The stablecoin story has moved remarkably fast. We spent years debating whether banks would ever embrace crypto dollars, and now the more interesting question is whether they can compete with companies like Tether that already have hundreds of millions of users and an enormous head start.
If today’s Wolf Den gave you a different way to think about that fight, forward it to one person who still thinks stablecoins are just crypto casino chips. They’re increasingly becoming part of the plumbing of the global financial system – and the battle over who owns that plumbing is just getting started.
See you tomorrow.
– Scott

For most of crypto’s history, asking what a token was actually worth was a surprisingly difficult question.
Bitcoin was relatively easy. It was scarce digital money with a fixed supply and a clear monetary thesis. Ethereum became more complicated but eventually developed its own economic model through staking and the burning of transaction fees. Once you moved farther down the market, however, things got considerably fuzzier. A protocol could generate hundreds of millions of dollars in fees while the token supposedly associated with it gave you little more than the privilege of voting on governance proposals that almost nobody read.
We called this “utility.”
Public-market investors would probably call it a terrible business model.
That may finally be changing. According to the Financial Times, crypto projects have spent a record $640 million buying back their own tokens in 2026, already surpassing the $545 million spent during all of last year. Hyperliquid and Pump.fun account for nearly 90% of those purchases, and several other major protocols are experimenting with buybacks, burns or mechanisms that redirect revenue toward token holders.
I think this is considerably more important than whether $640 million of mechanical buying temporarily pushes a few token prices higher. Crypto is finally beginning to confront the question that investors in every other asset class eventually ask:
How does owning this thing actually make me money?
That question sounds embarrassingly basic, but it provides a useful framework for separating some of the more interesting tokens in the market from everything else.
HYPE Sets The Bar
Hyperliquid is currently the cleanest example.
The decentralized derivatives platform generates real revenue from people actually using the product, and according to the FT, roughly 99% of that revenue has been directed toward repurchasing HYPE. The mechanics are not identical to a public-company buyback, but economically the concept is familiar. The underlying business generates cash flow, some of that economic output creates demand for the token, and the supply available to everyone else is reduced.
That gives us something we can actually analyze.
If Hyperliquid grows trading volume and revenue, the amount available for HYPE purchases can increase. If activity falls, buybacks should fall with it. Suddenly we are discussing revenue growth, margins, market share and valuation rather than simply hoping enough people become excited about the logo.
That does not automatically make HYPE cheap. A great business can have an absurdly expensive asset attached to it. But at least we can begin asking the right questions, which is a meaningful improvement over the old model of “the protocol is growing, therefore surely the token will figure out how to capture that value someday.”
Pump.fun provides an interesting comparison. The platform spent months directing essentially all of its revenue toward PUMP purchases and ultimately burned tokens representing roughly 36% of circulating supply. Earlier this year, however, it changed the model. Going forward, 50% of net revenue is directed toward automated buybacks and burns, while the other half stays available to actually run and grow the business.
I actually prefer that model conceptually. Returning every dollar to token holders sounds fantastic until you remember that healthy businesses also need employees, product development, marketing and capital for acquisitions. A buyback that slowly kills the company generating the cash is not particularly useful.
This is where the analysis gets more interesting than simply ranking projects by how many tokens they buy.
Not All Revenue Belongs To You
Uniswap may be the best example of how much this market has evolved.
For years, UNI was almost the perfect symbol of crypto’s value-accrual problem. Uniswap processed enormous trading volume and became critical DeFi infrastructure, but UNI holders had no meaningful economic claim on that activity. The protocol could succeed spectacularly while the connection between that success and the token remained frustratingly vague.
That changed in December when Uniswap governance finally activated protocol fees and a mechanism that uses those fees to burn UNI. Protocol fees are now active across v2 and v3 pools on multiple chains, with collected fees ultimately exchanged for UNI that is permanently removed from supply.
For the first time, increased economic activity on Uniswap has a much clearer path toward affecting UNI itself.
AAVE tells us why even that isn’t enough to blindly buy the token. Aave launched a substantial buyback program in 2025 and acquired more than 205,000 AAVE, about 1.3% of supply. But protocol revenue subsequently weakened, the planned annual buyback budget was reduced from roughly $50 million to $30 million, and purchases were ultimately paused after the rsETH exploit created a reason for the DAO to preserve its balance sheet.
That’s not necessarily bearish. I would argue that it is what responsible capital allocation looks like. Buybacks should be what you do with excess capital after protecting the business, not a religious commitment maintained regardless of circumstances. But it demonstrates why “this token has buybacks” is nowhere near enough information to make an investment decision.
The source of the money matters.
Sky offers yet another model. Its latest structure directs roughly 55% of designated surplus toward SKY buybacks while 45% goes to staking rewards. That’s much closer to a traditional capital-return policy – some value reduces supply while another portion rewards holders willing to stake.
Then there is ARB, which may be the most useful warning in the entire exercise.
Robinhood Chain is built using Arbitrum’s technology and returns 10% of its net protocol revenue to the Arbitrum ecosystem, with 8% flowing to the ArbitrumDAO treasury and 2% to the developer guild. That sounds fantastic for ARB until you ask the question that should now become automatic:
Does that money actually accrue to ARB holders?
Not necessarily.
Revenue flowing into an ecosystem treasury is not the same thing as revenue flowing to the token. ARB could eventually develop stronger mechanisms connecting ecosystem economics to token holders, but today those are two different things. A successful protocol, chain or company does not automatically create a valuable token any more than a successful restaurant automatically makes the gift cards in its drawer equity in the business.
That distinction is going to matter more and more.
The New Crypto Fundamentals
I think investors can now start evaluating at least some crypto assets with a surprisingly traditional checklist. Does the protocol generate real revenue? Is that revenue recurring? How much reaches the token through buybacks, burns or staking rewards? How much new supply is simultaneously being issued? Does the project have enough capital to keep growing after returning value? And finally – perhaps most importantly – what price am I paying for those economics?
That last question is where I suspect there may actually be alpha.
Crypto investors have become remarkably sophisticated at analyzing token unlocks, wallet flows, funding rates and onchain activity, yet we still spend comparatively little time discussing something equity investors obsess over every day: valuation. If two protocols generate similar revenue but one trades at five times the implied economic value and another at fifty times, that should probably matter.
Bitcoin remains different by design. It doesn’t generate cash flow and isn’t supposed to. Its value comes from scarcity, network effects and its monetary properties rather than a claim on a business. ETH sits somewhere in between – network activity burns ETH through EIP-1559 while proof-of-stake rewards holders who provide security, creating an economic relationship between usage and the asset without turning Ethereum into a company.
But for the enormous universe of tokens that have spent years selling themselves as investments, the standard should be getting considerably higher.
“Governance” isn’t enough. “Utility” isn’t enough. A protocol making money isn’t even enough if none of that value ever reaches the asset you actually own.
The interesting shift in 2026 is that some projects are finally building that bridge. HYPE is probably the cleanest example today. UNI has fundamentally improved its economics. SKY is explicitly splitting value between buybacks and stakers. AAVE shows why capital return has to remain subordinate to balance-sheet health. PUMP shows that aggressive buybacks can be real while still forcing questions about the durability of the business underneath them. ARB demonstrates why ecosystem revenue and token-holder value should never be confused.
For years, crypto asked investors to value tokens largely on narratives about what their networks might someday become. Increasingly, we can ask a much less romantic question: what does this network earn, and how much of it ultimately benefits me?
That won’t make crypto as easy to value as a stock – far from it. But it may finally give us a way to distinguish tokens backed by genuine economic machines from tokens whose primary cash flow remains the money coming from the next buyer.
And in a market that has spent years pricing almost everything on narrative, simply knowing the difference could be an edge.
