I. Another Ghost Appears
The Ghost of Software Future appeared in February on the heels of the doomsday predictions about the future of software in the age of AI. He pointed his bony finger toward Silicon Valley, reigniting the first SaaSpocalypse since, well, 2022. His appearance led to indiscriminate selling that drained about a trillion dollars from public software company market caps.
Lately, his less dramatic friend, the Ghost of Software Present, has been paying me nightly visits. No black robe. No smoke machine. Just a rusty scabbard without a sword. He wakes me up, opens a door, lets me look for a minute, closes it, then disappears. The next night there’s another door, another glimpse inside an enterprise software company boardroom. We run it all back again, and I’m half expecting I Got You Babe to jolt me awake on the clock radio the next morning.
At the end of March, I published The Ghost of Software Future, an essay that helped me make sense of the latest in a long line of platform shifts. My argument then was that the gloomy narrative, and then the many investors, had skipped a few steps in the journey. SaaS was being priced as though AI had already replaced it, when most of us knew the likely path would be messier, just like other major technology (r)evolutions. My hunch was that AI would quickly get absorbed into the tech stack, Systems of Record would keep handling the boring, critical work companies must do, and many incumbents would harness AI’s intelligence rather than get run over by it. Of course, many software companies would either ignore the Ghost’s premonition or fail to execute. My position then was that enterprise software would domesticate AI. And for much of the spring I looked wrong.
By mid-April the software index had given back 30% on the year. SMB darling HubSpot cut net-new customer guidance nearly in half after retention slipped. Enterprise stalwart IBM pre-announced weak Q2 results, and the stock dropped 25% in a day. Then in August, Airtable (once valued by investors at $11 billion) sold to Bending Spoons for just $1.3 billion. It’s so over.
But most SaaS companies’ operating results kept refusing to line up neatly with the narrative. Figma, left for dead the morning Claude Design shipped, grew 48% in Q2. SaaSpocalypse poster child Atlassian printed one of its best quarters ever in June, and, in August, Silver Lake started circling Workday, in what could become one of the biggest software buyouts ever. To cap off the summer, Salesforce reported one of its best quarters in years and the stock jumped 23% in a day. We’re so back!
Pick a week of headlines since March, and you could find enough evidence to confirm your priors.
In his story, Dickens gave the Ghost of Christmas Present only one night. “My life upon this globe is very brief,” it tells Scrooge. Most SaaSpocalypse narratives have lasted about as long, leaving Evan Osheroff at Jefferies to sum up the mood: “This is the weirdest, hardest, most challenging time I’ve seen in software.”
All this drama in 2026 and the IGV Tech-Software Sector ETF is up about 7% as of the end of August.
Same disclosure as always: I have a trade on here. My funds own a dozen enterprise software companies, and we’re trying to buy more. I’m talking my book here, but I have also been investing through these cycles for thirty years. One thing you eventually learn in this business: noise and signal run on different timelines. Markets move in seconds. Customers decide in quarters. Platforms shift over years. And private equity funds have ten-year lives.
So, let’s get deeper than the headlines: why the model war matters less to software investors than it seems; why the old Record layer-versus-Engagement layer debate has become a race to own the Action layer; what the operating data says about whether software fundamentals actually broke; and how we separate the winners and losers through all this chaos.
And we’re sharing what we know by publicly releasing ParkerGale’s AI Resilience Scorecard and our companion Claude Skill that turns it into an interactive underwriting tool. We built both for ourselves first. Now you can use them, argue with them, make them better, and share what you know with us.
II. The War You Don’t Have to Win, to Win
When I wrote the first Ghost piece, the conventional bear case for software was that AI models would commoditize it, if not fully replace it. Six months later, the more interesting story is that foundation models might just be the things getting commoditized.
I’m not throwing shade. Commodities are important. Oil is a commodity and still supports trillions of dollars of economic activity. The important point for software investors is that intelligence increasingly looks like an input: several good suppliers, falling prices, and interchangeable depending on the task. Stripe’s recent announcement about acquiring OpenRouter for more than $7 billion should drive the point home. OpenRouter routes work across 400+ models based on price, performance, and availability. CEO Alex Atallah said: “We believe intelligence will be multi-model: no single model will be optimal for every task.” You don’t care how Stripe routes your credit card, and soon you won’t care how it routes your prompts and agents. And a year from now, we likely won’t even be talking about model routers because they’ll disappear into applications like all middleware eventually does.
That doesn’t mean every model is the same. The point is that price, performance, speed, and availability vary enough (and change fast enough) that being able to switch is more valuable than being loyal. When the government shut down Anthropic’s Mythos for nineteen days earlier this summer, it drove the point home for every software investor on the planet. Model dependency is a real business risk. Suddenly “model agnostic” isn’t just a bullet in the Architecture section of the tech due diligence report. It’s now the first item in the Risks section of the IC memo.
OpenAI’s August expansion of Zero Data Retention is a tell. Enterprise customers want frontier-model capability without handing the model provider the prompts, responses, and proprietary context that make the model useful. During the same week in July, Palantir’s Alex Karp and Microsoft’s Satya Nadella made loud public warnings about these risks. The labs themselves are also signaling how difficult enterprise deployment really is. OpenAI, Anthropic, and Microsoft have each launched heavily staffed services businesses to help customers embed AI into messy corporate systems and workflows. Silicon Valley calls them forward-deployed engineers, but they’re just consultants in hoodies.
This is just the hard reality of making software for large, messy enterprise customers. The model arrives knowing an astonishing amount about the world and almost nothing about how your company works. Somebody must still connect the data, permissions, exceptions, and workflows, and, oh right, navigate the politics. That gap between what the model knows and what actions the enterprise needs to take is where a lot of the future value lives for the software companies. And that leads to one of the more useful conclusions I’ve reached since March: we don’t have to win the model war.
Enterprise software sits downstream from the labs. Better closed models help you. Better open models help you. More competition helps you most of all because it means better intelligence at lower prices. Chinese models can benefit you even if they never deploy one because they pressure the price and performance of the models we do use. I lived through VHS versus Betamax (and LaserDisc!) in the ‘80s, so I learned early not to bet on who wins the next format war.
Now, that argument only works if the model layer doesn’t swallow the application layer. The labs are trying with forays into coding, design, support, finance, and sales. But entering a category is not the same thing as displacing the systems already running it. Six months into the panic, four years after ChatGPT and hundreds of billions of dollars of investment later, I can point to credible encroachment at the edges, but I still can’t point to a foundation-model company that has meaningfully displaced an enterprise system it was supposed to make obsolete. If you know of ones I’m missing, hit me up in the comments.
None of this makes the models unimportant. Quite the opposite: they may be the most powerful new tools software companies have ever been handed. But if intelligence keeps getting cheaper, the more interesting question becomes who can turn that intelligence into trusted action inside the enterprise. And the battle is happening on two fronts, which takes us back to a debate that started more than a decade before ChatGPT arrived.
III. Record, Engagement, Action
If you’ve read my other stuff, you know I’m going to start with a history lesson because this debate isn’t new. In 2011, Geoffrey Moore (the Crossing the Chasm GOAT) wrote a piece for AIIM called Systems of Engagement and The Future of Enterprise IT reflecting on the consumerization of IT following the release of the iPhone. In the white paper, he predicted that enterprise software would split between Systems of Record and Systems of Engagement. Systems of Record are the command-and-control layer: transaction-oriented, provisioned by IT, built to be the authoritative account of what happened. Systems of Engagement are user-centric, collaborative, and built around how people actually work.
Moore was right, as usual, and for the next dozen years investors poured money into the Engagement layer (productivity, collaboration, design, business intelligence) while Systems of Record companies poured money into modernizing user experience. The debate between the dumb database and the pretty wrapper might sound familiar because it’s the same one we’re having today, and Moore wrote about this fifteen years ago.
Then generative AI arrived and made engagement cheap.
This is what freaked out Silicon Valley, so they piled into AI and (mostly) abandoned SaaS. The two things an entire generation of VCs and startups had relied on as differentiators (10x engineers and pretty software) were now the cheapest things to reproduce. Not easy, but cheap. Now we all have armies of agentic engineers through Copilot, Cursor, and Codex, plus design tools like Figma, Framer, and v0 that turn ideas into polished interfaces on demand.
So, the value moves again, with the next prize the System of Action: the layer that executes the work for you.
Booking.com is a useful analogy, though outside enterprise software. AI is great at planning your next vacation, and for many of us, it was our first cool chatbot experience. But Booking.com still completes the transactions, settles payments, handles cancellations, and deals with the mess when something goes wrong. Discovery is Engagement. Completing the transaction is Action.
Record layers have relied on nearly impenetrable moats that are now vulnerable. Theory Ventures General Partner Tomasz Tunguz argues that the strategic asset is the harness, the software wrapped around the model that decides what context comes in, what gets logged, what actions are available, and how the model is used. If employees live inside the harness long enough, it can learn how the company actually works. The old Systems of Record underneath risk becoming invisible databases that are eventually replaced.
Here’s what I think the argument misses. The race isn’t static. It is being fought from two directions. The Engagement layer is climbing down toward the Records. They have intelligence, speed, and user experience on their side. The Record layer is climbing up toward Engagement. They usually move more slowly, and their interfaces are uglier, but they start with something hard to recreate: authority. That distinction between intelligence and authority is probably where I have tightened my thinking since March.
Intelligence is exciting, but it’s just a vessel to be filled up. Authority is boring but has all the context. And despite what AI maximalists are saying, intelligence and authority are not interchangeable. You can be mostly right about how far along a prospect is in the pipeline. You must be perfect with payroll.
The Wells Fargo research team agrees: “lower cost of intelligence increases value of incumbent data.” If intelligence becomes abundant, the scarce asset may increasingly be proprietary context (e.g. domain expertise) and the authority required to make it useful. Probabilistic systems are useful in CRM, forecasting, search, design, content, and coding. They’re a much more awkward fit when the answer must be exact: payroll, ERP, trading, regulatory. This doesn’t make probabilistic tools useless in critical enterprise systems. It just means the intelligence there can move more easily, and so can the value. Mission-critical enterprise software was never valuable because it was intelligent. It was valuable because it was always on and always right. It knows what is true right now. It knows who has permission to act. It knows what happens next. It knows the exceptions. And the exceptions to the exceptions. And it keeps the record. So, six months (or six years) from now, an auditor, a regulator, or a lawyer can see who approved a transaction, under which policy, using what information, and if that person had authority to do so on that day.
State. Permission. Process. Audit.
Boring stuff.
Even OpenAI’s new Presence product tacitly acknowledges this: once an agent moves from answering questions to taking actions, the requirements are permissions, policies, guardrails, monitoring, and human escalation. Intelligence gets you to the door. Authority is what lets you through it. But be careful. I saw the movie WarGames enough times in the ‘80s to know you don’t connect your company’s computer to NORAD!
That doesn’t mean the Engagement layer can’t acquire authority. It can. But authority gets earned one customer, permission, exception, and integration at a time. The incumbent starts with authority and must acquire intelligence and a better user experience. The challenger starts with intelligence and must acquire authority.
Systems of Action belong to whoever closes that gap first.
Given how quickly intelligence is getting cheaper and easier to deploy, I’d rather start with authority. That’s why I called AI a gift to lower-middle-market software investors in March. Enterprise software companies have been handed the tools to modernize themselves before AI runs them over. The challenge is whether they will use them fast enough. The next question is what recent financial results can tell us about what’s real versus what was predicted.
IV. Fundamentals Before Valuations
If the models were consuming the application layer as quickly as the bear case predicted, retention should be where the bodies start showing up.
As we all saw play out over the last few years, Net Revenue Retention (NRR) started declining in 2022, as the post-COVID seat glut was slowly rightsized by newly empowered CFOs tightening their belts. In Jamin Ball’s Clouded Judgement, he shows median net retention peaking around 120% during the pandemic and hitting 108% by the end of January 2026. Land-and-expand can also contract, apparently. Then AI was supposed to kick the chair out from under the remaining seats. But by late July, Ball’s median was back up to 110%, and the SaaSpocalypse narrative started to fray. The claim was that agents were already replacing seats and the software stock carnage was simply the market reflecting the damage before it showed up in the financial statements. Six months later, lots of funeral announcements. Still very few bodies.
Snowflake accelerated growth while net retention climbed back to 126%. Salesforce, whose core CRM franchise was supposed to be squarely in the blast zone, reported growing seat counts and the lowest attrition in its history. Those are not the numbers you would expect if enterprise customers were rapidly replacing software seats with agents. That doesn’t mean everyone was spared. ZoomInfo reported NRR fell to 90%, and plenty of slow-growing software companies are struggling with retention, pricing, or relevance. The point isn’t that software is healthy everywhere. The point is that there are individual winners and losers in this race, not category wipeouts.
This is playing out in our own portfolio. We are not seeing a meaningful AI-driven deterioration in retention. We are seeing some larger enterprise sales cycles stretch out, and bookings get choppy quarter to quarter as customers take longer to make big commitments in a noisy environment. That is a different problem from customers ripping out third-party software they no longer need.
So, the risk I worry about isn’t replacement. It’s erosion.
Guggenheim’s July survey of 150 large enterprises makes that distinction pretty clearly. Across CRM, ERP, HCM, payroll, ITSM, and contact-center software, only 5% to 8% expected full replacement by AI-native products over the next one to three years. But about one-third expect significant reductions in functionality. That’s a much sneakier, though less dramatic, bear case. A few seats here. A module there. The customer keeps the System of Record but moves the Engagement and Action layers elsewhere. The logo stays. The invoice gets smaller at renewal.
Erosion doesn’t necessarily show up as churn. It can also show up in the product’s economics. Companies like Figma are already monetizing AI credits, but most customers also expect their software vendors to keep improving the product with the latest technology without increasing price. AI can protect retention, improve the product, and still fail to create a new revenue line. That combination (perceived disruption risk without automatic growth acceleration) might help explain why the market has been so jumpy.
Weird. Challenging. And hard.
But stock market gyrations don’t impact fundamentals, and as companies kept delivering results, it looked like the Ghost of Software Future I wrote about in March knew what he was talking about.
Last August, the median public software company traded at 5.1x forward revenue. It dropped to 4.1x in January, bottomed at 3.2x in April, and finished at 4.4x at the end of August. A haircut, not a beheading. The middle-tier companies, the 15% to 20% growers, went from 7.1x forward a year ago to 7.6x today. Slow growers (less than 15%) fell from 4.0x to 3.9x. High-growth software (>20%) took the biggest hit. They traded at 30.5x last August and sit at 17.3x today. But this group was already down to 12.4x forward in January before the panic even got going, which, as I’ve written about previously, was just the market recognizing growth had slowed, NRR had slipped, and valuations needed a reset. AI showed up late and took all the credit.
If you can believe it, the last SaaSpocalypse was worse. By late 2022, mid-growth software was trading around 5x revenue, slow growth around 2x, and even high growth only around 7x. 2026 has felt far more existential because AI gave the selloff a much scarier story, but the actual valuation damage has been surprisingly milder.
After a quiet spring, private equity is getting back in the game. In June, Thoma Bravo agreed to buy life-sciences software company Kneat for about 8x revenue in a competitive process that attracted at least a dozen bidders. And Silver Lake is reportedly discussing a take-private of Workday at roughly 5x to 6x revenue. Two great examples of software companies, one vertical growing 20%+ and one horizontal growing low-teens, getting valued about where you’d expect pre-panic. Tech buyout funds are all breathing sighs of relief with a couple decent comps for next quarter’s marks.
Public market investors eventually sort hundreds of software companies into broad piles, and you can buy the index. In private equity, we don’t get to underwrite a bucket. We must choose one company at a time and live with it. “AI winner or loser” isn’t a useful underwriting guide, so we built something more useful.
V. Picking Winners and Losers
In the spring, we built Version 1.0 of ParkerGale’s AI Resilience Scorecard. We scored our existing portfolio, shared it with our management teams and LPs, and started testing it on new investments. The goal wasn’t to predict what AI would do to software as a category. It was to force ourselves to decide what AI could do to one company we might own for the next five years. We kept using it through the spring and summer, which turned out to be the best way to find the holes. Version 2.0 reflects what we’ve learned from our own history of underwriting software companies, recent public company performance, model-company encroachment, our recent portfolio company execution, and the new investments we’ve evaluated since the spring.
The Scorecard tries to help us answer three questions:
- How could AI hurt this company while we own it?
- How can we use AI to make the company better before we sell it?
- Does AI make the market this company serves bigger or smaller?
The first two were in Version 1.0. We added the third after realizing that, in the middle of the SaaSpocalypse, we had become so focused on what AI might damage that we weren’t asking what it might enhance.
To answer these three questions, we evaluate five categories.
Category 1 :: Source of Truth
Is this where the customer’s authoritative record actually lives, or does the product mostly read data from somewhere else and make it prettier?
Give it the 72-hour test. If the product goes dark for three days, do customers stop operating, lose revenue, or are they damaged in some other measurable way? When CDK’s dealer-management system went down in 2024, thousands of auto dealers were using pens, paper, and calculators to sell cars. That’s a source of truth. If the answer is “people would be annoyed,” you probably have something else.
Exact matters, too. A general ledger reconciles to the penny; a CRM field may be somebody’s best guess after a sales call. And an authoritative record trapped in an inaccessible old schema isn’t automatically safe anymore. The moat only matters if the company can make the data usable by the new tools.
Category 2 :: Workflow Depth
Is the product the actual workflow, or a tool somebody opens while doing the workflow?
Beware of fake workflow. If a customer can churn by changing a login and spending an afternoon training on another tool, that is not workflow. Real workflow is integrations, configuration, approvals, handoffs, exception paths, retraining, and a stretch where the old and new systems run side by side because everybody is too scared to shut off the old one. One crude test is implementation time. Days means it’s a tool. Months starts to look like workflow. Ask management to describe a typical implementation; the more exhausted everyone looks, the higher the score.
Category 3 :: Uniqueness
When code and intelligence are cheap, what does the company own that a competitor cannot easily replicate?
The good answers tend to live outside the code: proprietary data that improves with scale, hardware or sensors in the field, a network or marketplace, regulatory certifications, or taking liability when something goes wrong. If the answer is “our team really knows the domain” or “we have a great UI,” keep digging. Those may be real advantages. They are also becoming less durable.
This category has already changed the way we look at deals. We’ve looked at several investments where the Scorecard surfaced a Source-of-Truth or Uniqueness problem almost immediately. The product looked sticky, the metrics looked fine, but when we dug into what the company actually owned that another well-funded competitor couldn’t recreate, our confidence got squishy.
Category 4 :: Pricing
If AI reduces the number of humans using this product, what happens to revenue?
Pure seat-based pricing is exposed if ten people can suddenly do the work of fifteen. Pricing by transaction, asset, claim, payment, machine, location, or value created might be better. If AI can reduce the number of humans while increasing the amount of work the software processes, you want to be paid for the latter, not the former.
Watch out for traps. NRR can look healthy while seats contract underneath expansion revenue, so we want to look at gross retention and seat behavior by cohort. Flat pricing against heavy inference usage can turn product success into a gross-margin problem. Figma’s Q2 gave us both sides at once: terrific growth and retention, real AI adoption, and higher cost to serve all that usage.
Back in February, seat-based pricing was in the SaaSpocalypse bullseye. Not so much today as results have come in, but this category is still worth close examination.
Category 5 :: AI Stance
How far is this company from using AI offensively during our hold period, and what will it cost to close the gap?
As people get more sophisticated with AI, we can see what “offensively” means. One of our portfolio finance teams has gone from spending a few weeks closing the books to doing it in about a day using AI-enhanced tooling. At another company, agents now write the first pass of new production code end to end and, more importantly, then test it automatically. Those aren’t AI features we sell to customers. They’re meaningful changes in the economics of running a lower-middle-market enterprise software company.
We’ve also built plenty of things that didn’t stick. We built custom AI agents around our CRM and talent network that were useful (for a time). Then we swapped out our CRM and got the same functionality (plus a lot more) natively, with much less maintenance. That has happened enough over the past six months that we’ve stopped getting emotionally attached to whatever AI thing our portfolio companies or we just built. A feature can have a six-month half-life because the next model is better, your next build is better, or the enterprise software underneath absorbs the capability. AI debt is still tech debt. It’s just that now everyone in your company is making it, not just the engineers.
Category 5 is also where model portability belongs. You want your customers’ switching costs to be expensive, and your switching costs away from an AI model provider to be cheap. If the architecture depends on one model staying best, cheap, and available for your holding period, that is not innovation. It is a hostage situation.
The Scorecard document goes way deeper on each category, so check it out at the bottom of this post.
The average score matters less to me than the shape of it. Our favorite profile is “Defensible but Sleepy”: high scores on Source of Truth, Workflow and Uniqueness, with lower Pricing and AI Stance scores. These companies own valuable positions but haven’t exploited them yet. We know how to work with that at ParkerGale. “Building on Sand” is the opposite: great AI execution and a modern product sitting on someone else’s data, shallow workflow, and a moat made mostly of code. The demo looks great, and the team is smart, but the competitive advantage might be too hard to predict.
Scoring is the easy part. The management still has to do the work. Rewire the workflow. Instrument the data. Modernize processes. Retrain the team. Convince customers. And keep grinding after the novelty wears off. Quantifying the risk (or opportunity) is easier than executing the plan. I can make a great case that capable incumbents now have the weapons to fight their way up the Action layer. I just have to hope the management team picks up those weapons before a more determined competitor does.
The Scorecard is a helpful framework, but we also built a Claude Skill that turns it into an interactive underwriting tool. Give it as little as a website and teaser, and it will produce a rough assessment. Give it the investment memo and your diligence files, and it will analyze your work, identify what you missed, create follow-up questions for management, and generate a high-confidence score. Think of the Skill as a mildly annoying IC member who keeps asking the obvious question you accidentally missed.
We are releasing Version 2.0 (PDF below) and the Claude Skill (link below) publicly for you to use, change, and (hopefully) tell us how we can improve it. This is partly because sharing what we know is one of our core values here at ParkerGale. But it’s also a fun, efficient way to collectively build an improved Version 3.0.
VI. The Empty Scabbard
Six months after the first Ghost appeared, I’m less interested in whether SaaS is dead or back. That question was always too naïve and broad to be useful. Despite some isolated carnage, software fundamentals have mostly held. Public markets are starting to separate strong companies from weak ones again. The current fight is over who owns the System of Action, or maybe more accurately, who gets there first.
Which brings me back to my Ghost friend and his empty scabbard, which is too delicious a narrative device for a humanities major like me not to leave unexamined.
I’ve had the metaphor backward until now. For decades, Systems of Record have accumulated the boring stuff: the data, the workflow, the permissions, the exceptions, and the audit trail. That’s the scabbard. It is built over years, handmade, custom-fitted. But most legacy software companies have let it rust on the belt, and they have no sword to put in it. Then intelligence got abundant and cheap, and suddenly they all have a shiny, sharp, deadly new toy. They just need to learn how to swing it.
The AI-natives, coming down from the Engagement layer, have the opposite problem: they were practically born with the sword in their hands, and they know how to use it. But they have no place to put it. They still must earn the authority to act inside the enterprise, one integration, permission, exception, and liability clause at a time.
The Ghost wasn’t warning us all those nights. He was showing us the choice.
In Dickens’ story, Scrooge asks the last Ghost, “Are these the shadows of the things that will be, or are they shadows of things that may be, only?” The Ghost doesn’t answer. He just points at the headstone. Scrooge works out the rest himself. That’s the point for him, and for this essay. The grave isn’t destiny. It’s just one possible outcome of not picking up the sword.
AI will not destroy enterprise software. It will destroy a great many enterprise software companies that fail to exploit the position they’re in. The winners will be companies that learn how to swing the sword before someone takes their place.
Which ones those will be is still up for grabs, and more in your control than you might think.

The leveraged buyout was invented to buy companies that owned things. Steel mills. Shipping. Businesses where the value sat on a loading dock or was bolted to a concrete floor. A bank could send someone to count it. Software companies don’t really own anything a banker could count, nothing a repo man could snatch, and nothing that would stop the software developers from walking out the door to a competitor across the street.
When Kohlberg Kravis Roberts took over RJR Nabisco in 1989 for $31 billion (the deal that inspired Barbarians at the Gate and scripted a generation’s worth of cocktail-party shorthand about greedy financiers), the banks didn’t lend on faith. Assets led the charge: processing plants, trucks, conveyor belts, warehouses stocked with Camel cigarettes and Oreo cookies. If a deal went sideways, the banks could repossess stuff. Physical, retrievable, sellable stuff. Software companies have none of that. IP, sure. But assets? No.
Asset-based lending, rooted in ancient civilizations, is built on a formula called the borrowing base. Under the modern model, lenders advance 70% to 85% against accounts receivable, 50% to 80% against inventory, and a fraction determined by the lender against equipment and real estate. Field auditors show up periodically to count things, confirm they exist, and ensure no one is inflating the numbers. The whole system was predicated on a business with a physical footprint worth seizing if the borrower stopped paying.
Now let’s go back to 1995 and examine a typical software company. What’s on the balance sheet? Computers that depreciate faster than a new car. Maybe some furniture. And some accounts receivable from customers that paid up front for perpetual licenses. The actual product (the code that makes the company valuable) lives on a server that will be obsolete in a few years. The most important assets are the employees, and they go home every night. Maybe they return. Maybe they go across the street and join a competitor.
In my early days in the industry, when a software company needed money, venture capital was the answer. If an investor needed a loan for a software buyout, they might tap a venture debt provider, because a traditional bank wasn’t in the cards. No collateral, no deal. While there were occasional tech buyouts in the 1990s, most of these had hardware products backing the loan. True software buyouts, like the one crafted by private equity firm Welsh, Carson, Anderson & Stowe for Servantis Systems, and Prime Computer’s $1.3 billion sale to J.H. Whitney, were still almost a decade away.
No Collateral, No Deal
To understand why software was largely off-limits for buyouts, you have to understand how deals were structured back then. In the 1980s, debt-to-equity ratios in leveraged buyouts regularly exceeded 9:1. That math demanded a predictable business with reliable cash flow, and software wasn’t what we think of today. Michael Milken’s junk bond machine at Drexel Burnham Lambert changed the game, growing the high-yield market from $10 billion in 1979 to $189 billion by 1989, enabling deals of unimaginable scale. The template was elegant in its brutality: buy a company with mostly borrowed money, use the company’s own cash flows to pay down debt, improve operations or sell assets, and keep what’s left. If the company had hard assets and predictable cash flows, the model worked perfectly. If it didn’t, the deal was off.
Software companies had neither. Revenue from perpetual software licenses was lumpy and unpredictable. A company might book a $5 million enterprise deal in Q1 and $500,000 in Q2, entirely dependent on customer timing. Other than a small maintenance contract, there was no recurring revenue to model against, no annuity to lever. The cash flow was real but jagged, and jagged cash flows are a banker’s nightmare when debt service is a fixed monthly obligation. You can’t service a constant payment from an irregular income stream without eventually running short.
As lenders were becoming more comfortable with technology companies at the time, the market fell apart and dashed hopes. Drexel collapsed in 1990 after a Department of Justice fraud investigation. The junk bond market imploded. A wave of highly leveraged deals from the late ‘80s defaulted, including several spectacular ones, and the entire LBO industry went through what you might politely call a period of reflection. Debt-to-equity ratios settled closer to 50/50 through the ‘90s, a seismic shift from the 90/10 days. Lenders became more conservative about collateral. For any software company hoping the credit markets might eventually loosen up enough to support a leveraged transaction, the post-Drexel hangover was as punishing as the aftermath of a weekend bender at your class reunion — and much longer.
As the 90s progressed, software was everywhere. From the cover of The Economist, labeling Marc Andreessen the “New Digital Messiah,” to the screen of the laptop you customized with a customer service rep at Dell. As VC investments bled into private equity (remember that in 1996 Hellman & Friedman led a $200 million growth round in DoubleClick) and lenders distanced themselves from the junk-bond debacle while software turned mainstream, the dot-com crash jolted everything. The Nasdaq fell nearly 80% between 2000 and 2002. Hundreds of technology companies imploded. The ones that survived often traded for years at a fraction of their peak valuations. For the private equity investors and the bankers who lent to them and were on the fence about technology, the dot-com bust was a confirmation. Still too risky for private equity.
Four Amigos, the Engineer, and the Tennis Player
At the absolute peak of the dot.com bubble in 1999, four people with complementary backgrounds started a firm called Silver Lake. Jim Davidson had run technology investment banking at Hambrecht & Quist. Glenn Hutchins came from Blackstone and had advised Bill Clinton on economic policy. Roger McNamee was a venture capitalist who loved the Grateful Dead. Dave Roux was a former executive at Oracle and Lotus. They called themselves “the four amigos.”
There’s a joke in there somewhere. A banker, a buyout guy, a VC, and an operator walk into a bar...
Their thesis was simple and contrarian at the time: acquire mature technology companies (established businesses with real products and real customers) and apply the same operational playbook PE firms used on industrial companies. Venture capitalists didn’t want these businesses because they were old, boring, and didn’t grow fast enough. Growth equity guys didn’t want them because they don’t buy control. Silver Lake would become the suitor companies everyone else was ignoring.
The pitch was perfect. Silver Lake raised $2.3 billion for its debut fund in 1999. The LP list read like a technology hall of fame: Bill Gates, Larry Ellison, Michael Dell, CalPERS. People who understood technology and believed the traditional PE model could adapt to fit it.
Their first major deal in 2000 was a $2 billion leveraged buyout of hard-drive maker Seagate Technology. Seagate had physical assets. Even so, the numbers required a complicated spinoff and merger with Veritas Software to work. It was, as one observer put it, “a new page in the dog-eared annals of leveraged buyouts.” Today, Silver Lake manages over $110 billion — and the four amigos have all moved on to other things.
A year later, Robert Smith started Vista Equity Partners on a similar hunch. After an engineering stint at Kraft and an MBA from Columbia, Smith joined Goldman Sachs in San Francisco, where he became the first person in Goldman’s West Coast office to focus solely on technology mergers and acquisitions. At Goldman, Smith evaluated hundreds of software companies and kept seeing the same mistakes. Because the enterprise software industry was still young, and most CEOs were engineers and product people, there was no established playbook for running a software business efficiently. Smith found one company (Universal Computer Systems, which would ultimately become Reynolds & Reynolds) that had standard operating procedures, leading him to strategize about scaling those processes.
The mechanism behind Vista’s approach became legendary in private equity: a 110-point operating playbook applied to every portfolio company. As one longtime Vista investor described it: “Their process is like a factory. A deal comes in, gets compartmentalized, and they assign experts to each compartment. After it goes off the assembly line, the margins are higher.”
Smith’s first two funds had Robert Brockman (the owner of Universal Computer) as their sole LP. And despite his focus on enterprise software, his first deal was SourceNet Solutions, an accounts payable outsourcing business. More BPO than ERP.
Smith’s most important innovation, though, wasn’t operational. It was financial. He helped convince an entire lending market to view software subscription revenue as a reliable annuity worth lending against. His argument was blunt:
“Software contracts are better than first-lien debt. A company will not pay the interest on its first lien until after they pay their software maintenance or subscription fee. We get paid our money first. Who has the better credit? You’ll skip your bank payment before you skip the payment on your ERP or CRM system, because you need it to operate.”
This might be the single most important statement uttered to get underwriting committees on board to lend to software companies. Smith argued that payment priority made recurring software revenue more predictable than almost any other form of corporate cash flow. And if it’s more predictable, you can lend against it.
Gregg Lemkau, then co-leader of Goldman’s investment banking division, put it this way: “Robert, over time, convinced an entire market to see this cash-flow stream of software revenue as a reliable annuity that could be financed with debt.” Today Vista manages over $100 billion. Smith’s argument was greatly aided by the early-2000s migration from perpetual licenses to subscription pricing, pioneered by Salesforce.com. Without that shift, Smith’s thesis likely doesn’t hold.
And then there’s Thoma Bravo, which might be the best story of the three because it involves a tennis player and a hundred cold calls.
The firm’s roots go back to 1980, when Carl Thoma and Stanley Golder started Golder Thoma in Chicago, one of the first private equity firms in the country. Thoma essentially invented the “buy and build” strategy: acquire one company, use it as a platform, and bolt on acquisitions to drive growth. By the late 1990s, the firm was known as GTCR and headed for a divorce. In 1998, the partners split: Golder and Bruce Rauner (later governor of Illinois) kept the GTCR name and went after bigger deals, while Thoma and Bryan Cressey formed a smaller firm to focus on the middle market.
Then Orlando Bravo arrived. Born in Puerto Rico in 1970, Bravo moved to the U.S. as a teenager to attend Nick Bollettieri’s Tennis Academy in Florida, the same program that produced Andre Agassi and Maria Sharapova. When he graduated from Stanford in 1998 with a JD/MBA, he wanted a job in private equity but couldn’t get hired. He made over a hundred cold calls before Carl Thoma picked up the phone and gave him a shot.
But Bravo’s first deals almost sank him. He backed two dot.com startups (NerveWire and Eclipse Networks) just as the bubble burst, losing most of the money invested. For most 28-year-olds, losing that much of their firm’s money would be a career-ending event. But Bravo saw something in the wreckage and adjusted. The veteran investor was patient enough to avoid pulling the plug and realized that for the same money he’d lost on speculative startups, he could have bought established companies selling niche software to loyal customers. Businesses with real revenue, real margins, and real room for operational improvement. His first move in that direction was the acquisition of Prophet 21, a distribution ERP company, in 2002, with a small amount of leverage. The thesis was right, but the financing wasn’t there yet.
With Thoma’s blessing, Bravo led a pivot. The “buy boring software businesses” strategy started working immediately. He made partner in 2001 at age 30. By 2005, he recruited Scott Crabill, Holden Spaht, and Seth Boro to focus on software applications, cybersecurity, and web infrastructure. When Bryan Cressey left to start his own firm in 2008, the firm was renamed Thoma Bravo, and the pivot to software-only was complete.
The firm’s growth from there is extraordinary. From $450 million in AUM in 1998 to $24.3 billion for a single flagship fund in 2022 – the largest tech-focused buyout fund ever raised by an independent firm. In 2023, they closed $34.4 billion across three funds, oversubscribed to the hard cap. The firm now manages $183 billion and has completed over 565 software transactions. By any measure, they are the largest technology-focused buyout firm in the world.
The software buyout market matured in 2004. After four years of buying companies with equity, Robert Smith in 2004 talked lenders into financing Applied Systems. That same year, Bain, Silver Lake and Warburg carved UGS out of EDS. In November 2004, Hellman & Friedman and JMI bought Vertafore. That’s not a coincidence. That’s the credit market changing its mind, and every sponsor who had been standing outside the door now saw a crack to open it. Money was cheap back then; the term loan B market had matured; the CLO machine was warming up; and the post-dot.com survivors were delivering real earnings. After that, the floodgates opened: SunGard and DoubleClick in 2005, followed by Serena, Intergraph and Activant in 2006. Kronos in 2007. By then, software was something you could borrow against. And most borrowers did.
But look at that first cohort: insurance agency management, property and casualty claims processing, distribution ERP, product lifecycle management, workforce management. Vertical, mission-critical, maintenance-heavy systems of record. Software that can’t be turned off without shutting down the entire business. That was the bargain the lenders made in this first wave, and it was a good one. They weren’t lending against software. They were lending against the fact that a car dealer can’t sell a car without the DMS, and an insurance agency can’t write a policy without the agency management system. The recurring revenue was real because the alternative to paying it was going out of business. Robert Smith’s point exactly.
That distinction is the differentiator. Subscription revenue looked a lot like those early maintenance contracts, at least on a spreadsheet. What got lost in translation was the underlying question: Is this software something the customer genuinely cannot function without, or is it just something they’re paying for right now? The answer to that question was paramount.
Subscriptions Change Everything
The pioneers proved you could buy software companies and make money. But what turned software from a niche PE strategy into the dominant play was how software itself was sold.
For most of the enterprise software era, the business model was perpetual licensing. A company buys your product for a large upfront fee (maybe $50,000, maybe $5 million) and then pays an annual maintenance fee of 15% to 20% for ongoing support and updates. Good in years when you closed big deals, terrible when you didn’t. From a lender’s perspective, it made revenue forecasting an exercise in optimistic fiction.
Then Salesforce went public in 2004 and showed the world what subscription software looked like at scale. Instead of selling a product for a lump sum, you sold access to it as a service, a fixed monthly or annual fee billed automatically with automated renewals. The customer didn’t own the software; they rented it. This model had three traits that made PE investors and their lenders very happy.
First, the revenue was predictable. If you had a thousand customers each paying $5,000 a month, you could see next month’s revenue with remarkable clarity. Second, the revenue was sticky. Because subscription software typically wove itself into a customer’s daily operations – their accounting, CRM, or supply chain – switching costs were enormous. Net revenue retention rates north of 110% were common, meaning existing customers were buying more each year, not less. Third, the margins could get hefty. Subscription software gross margins in the 70% to 80% range were standard; operating costs were lower than the licensed model as DevOps matured; and the predictability of revenue meant you could plan and deliver consistency rather than swing with the volatility inherent in the license model.
Predictable revenue. High retention. High margins. SaaS companies started to look less like technology companies and more like toll booths.
The cloud eased delivery at scale. When Amazon launched AWS in 2006, it created the infrastructure that allowed every software company to deliver its product over the internet instead of shipping CDs or sending engineers to install servers on-site. Recurring revenue made technology palatable for PE and debt investors; the cloud made it operational.
This new model ushered in a new kind of lending. Traditional LBO debt was sized as a multiple of EBITDA – earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation, and amortization. But many fast-growing SaaS companies had low or negative EBITDA because they were reinvesting everything into growth. So investors and lenders invented the ARR loan: debt sized as a multiple of annual recurring revenue instead of earnings. A company with $100 million in recurring revenue and negative EBITDA could borrow $200 million under this framework, with the loan converting from ARR-based covenants to traditional EBITDA covenants after two to three years – by which point the company would have achieved profitability, at least in theory.
This financial innovation unlocked the entire software buyout market. ARR-based lending was the structural execution of Robert Smith’s argument. Private credit funds provided most of the ARR debt at first, accepting higher interest rates in exchange for lending against a revenue stream. The loans started flowing between 2015 and 2018. Once the traditional banks got involved, the dam broke.
The Gold Rush
By the late 2010s, the case for software buyouts wasn’t contrarian anymore. It was the consensus. And with cheap, abundant debt now available for software companies, tech buyouts went from a niche corner of the industry to mainstream Monday meeting discussions.
The numbers tell the story. In 2000, information technology accounted for about 21% of the U.S. private equity market value, according to Cambridge Associates. By 2021, that number had grown to 38% – the largest share of any sector, by far. The total market itself had grown roughly tenfold, from $97 billion to $1.1 trillion. Technology’s slice grew even faster than the pie. Bain & Co. reported that PE investors closed $284 billion in tech deals in 2021, accounting for 25% of total buyout value and 31% of deal count. Software accounted for 90% of that – $256 billion. More than $105 billion was invested in taking public software companies private.
In 2011, venture capitalist Marc Andreessen published his famous Wall Street Journal op-ed: “Why Software Is Eating the World.” He argued that software companies were poised to take over large swaths of the global economy – retail, finance, media, transportation, basically everything. He was right. What he didn’t predict was who would show up at the table with the biggest appetite.
Private equity firms were reading that day. And then private equity ate software.
The firms that pioneered tech buyouts were now managing staggering amounts of capital. Thoma Bravo went from a mid-market player to a firm with almost $200 billion in AUM. Vista grew to over $100 billion. Silver Lake went from $2.3 billion to over $110 billion. These weren’t niche strategies. They were among the largest PE firms in the world.
And the generalists got in on the game. Blackstone launched a dedicated growth equity fund and closed $4.5 billion in 2021. KKR, Carlyle and Apollo all built tech-focused teams. If you were running a PE firm in 2020 without a software strategy, you were a gold miner skipping California during the rush.
Performance data justified the frenzy. A Bain analysis of tech deals over the prior decade showed that software investments were more likely to outperform deals in other sectors and less likely to lose money. More than half of software buyouts returned 2.5x or greater on invested capital. The returns appeared to be driven primarily by revenue growth (rather than financial engineering and multiple expansion), which made the narrative more appealing. These weren’t strip-and-flip operations. These were businesses that grew under PE ownership.
The definition of a “tech deal” kept expanding, too. Is a payment processor a financial services company or a tech company? What about a healthcare analytics platform? A digital logistics provider? Technology had embedded itself so deeply into every industry that the lines dissolved. Bain suggested that if you counted all deals where technology was a key part of the investment thesis, well over half of all PE deal activity revolved around tech in some way. Every deal was becoming a tech deal, which meant every PE professional needed to become a tech investor – whether they were capable or not.
By 2021, at the peak, you could be forgiven for thinking the software buyout machine would run forever. Interest rates were near zero. SaaS growth rates were defying gravity. Multiples were high but seemingly justified by the growth. ARR-based lending was flowing freely from lenders happy to earn premium yield for what felt like low-risk exposure to recurring revenue. Everyone was Chuck Prince, the former CEO of Citigroup who told the Financial Times in July of 2007, “When the music stops... things will be complicated. But as long as the music is playing, you’ve got to get up and dance. We’re still dancing.”
After The Gold Rush
In the early 1990s, private equity couldn’t put leverage on a software company. The assets were intangible, the revenues were unpredictable, and the lenders weren’t interested. Three decades later, the industry solved all of those problems. Recurring revenue made the cash flows predictable. ARR-based lending made financing possible. Operational playbooks made value creation repeatable. It was a genuine triumph of the capitalist machine.
Then, someone turned off the music.
Consider Pluralsight, an educational technology company that taught software developers new skills through online video courses. Vista Equity Partners took it private in late 2020 for $3.5 billion, paying a 25% premium on its 30-day trading average – despite the fact that Pluralsight had never been profitable. The deal was financed in part with a $1.2 billion recurring-revenue term loan at LIBOR plus 800 basis points, premised on two assumptions: rates would stay low, and subscription revenue would keep growing while Vista’s playbook extracted massive profits.
Neither held. Interest rates spiked, making debt service crushing. Competition mounted. AI began automating some of the developer skills Pluralsight was teaching, undermining the growth thesis. Multiple rounds of layoffs followed. By May 2024, Vista had written off the entire equity value of its investment, $3.5 billion, down to zero in three years. Co-investors, including AustralianSuper and Saudi Arabia’s Public Investment Fund, were wiped out too.
Pluralsight isn’t a one-off. Earlier this year, Thoma Bravo handed customer experience software company Medallia to its lenders after writing off the entire $5 billion it had invested, the second-largest private equity loss in history. Orlando Bravo was candid at the recent Sohn Conference: “It was a big mistake. We were moving really fast during that time. We underwrote really fast growth, and in hindsight we paid too much because that growth didn’t materialize.” Vista and Elliott’s $16.5 billion takeover of Citrix in 2022 saddled the company with roughly $15 billion in debt that banks couldn’t syndicate without eating $1.3 billion in losses. Clearlake’s software portfolio is underwater across multiple holdings, with its Quest Software debt trading around 25 cents on the dollar and Cornerstone OnDemand loans marked down sharply. And those are just the names that made the papers.
According to PitchBook LCD, a record $25 billion in software loans in the Morningstar LSTA US Leveraged Loan Index were trading below the distress threshold of 80 cents on the dollar as of January 2026 — representing 31 percent of all distressed loans in the index, despite software accounting for just 13 percent of the market. By late June, the average bid on performing software loans had slipped to 86 cents, nine points below the broader market, a gap that widened fivefold since the start of the year. Software’s share of new PE-backed loan issuance collapsed from 24 percent at its 2020 peak to just 8 percent in 2026. As PGIM’s Engin Okaya told PitchBook: “This is a market of haves and have-nots, and software is among the have-nots.”
The math that made software buyouts work in the 2010s no longer worked. According to Bain’s 2026 Global Private Equity Report, during PE’s “golden decade” of the 2010s, a typical PE investment required only 5% annual EBITDA growth to generate a target 2.5x multiple on invested capital over average five-year holding periods. In today’s environment, with borrowing costs in the 8% to 9% range, leverage ratios of 30% to 40%, and purchase multiples in record territory, typical deals now require around 10% to 12% average annual EBITDA growth to generate the same benchmark 2.5x return over five years. 12 is the new 5, which is a very different bar, and not many PE-owned software companies are clearing it.
Bain’s own analysis confirms the problem: 94% of software buyout models projected significant margin improvement over five-year hold periods, but actual margin growth “badly trailed these models.” Revenue growth and multiple expansion – not operational improvement – powered virtually all of the value creation in software deals over the past decade. Revenue growth contributed 53%. Multiple expansion contributed 43%. Margin improvement contributed 4%. Looking back, the software buyout playbook often amounted to buying high-multiple companies, hoping they’d keep growing, and planning to sell them at even higher multiples to the next buyer.
The private credit dimension makes this more interesting and potentially more dangerous. Much of the debt financing for software buyouts is now held by private credit funds, some of which are managed by the same PE firms that own the equity. This creates a peculiar circularity: PE firms raising private credit funds to lend money to other PE firms, buying software companies with subscription revenue that justifies the lending in the first place. When software was growing 20% to 30% a year, the loop worked. The BIS documented how thoroughly it worked: outstanding loans to SaaS firms grew from roughly $8 billion in 2015 to over $500 billion by the end of 2025, reaching 19% of total direct lending. When growth slows — and it has slowed across the SaaS industry, with declining growth rates and declining net revenue retention — the leverage that was supposed to amplify returns starts amplifying losses instead.
In April 2026, the Center for Economic and Policy Research published a piece noting that the triggering event for a wave of private credit redemptions at the end of 2025 was “a fear that many software companies that have borrowed from PE-owned private credit funds are vulnerable to AI and may not be able to repay the loans they took out.” PitchBook’s analysis from February 2026 showed that PE’s exposure to software jumped to 18% of total U.S. deal value in 2025 — up from a decade average of 14% — just as public software valuations were being reset downward by more than one standard deviation due to AI disruption concerns. Morgan Stanley’s research desk projected that direct-lending defaults could reach 8% in 2026, approaching the peak default rate seen during the pandemic.
MSCI estimates that U.S. private equity funds returned 5.8% annually from mid-2022 to the third quarter of 2025, compared to 11.6% for the S&P 500. That’s a period in which PE’s largest sector bet — software — faced rising rates, slowing growth, and an AI-driven valuation reset all at once. The underperformance isn’t entirely attributable to software, but software is the biggest category in the portfolio. When your biggest bet stumbles, the whole asset class feels it. Bain’s 2026 mid-year analysis put it plainly: “If software investing has delivered anything to private equity investors so far in 2026, it is the disquieting certainty that the world has changed — probably forever.” PitchBook’s 2026 mid-year private equity review showed software deal value dropped 66% in Q2.
And AI is not to blame. Not yet at least. Competition from vibe-coded apps and AI-native competitors hasn’t hit company performance. In fact, I think that over the next few years, enterprise software companies will see more benefits than threats from AI. I wrote about it in my piece called The Ghost of Software Future. The threat of AI has hurt the multiples, but that doesn’t explain the defaults and distress across PE-owned software companies. The simple explanation is an old one — too much optimism combined with too much leverage is dangerous, no matter what your company makes or what industry you sell into.
Patterns Ignored
The irony is obvious.
The private equity industry spent thirty years solving the software problem. They built tech-specialist firms. They invented operational playbooks. They convinced lenders that recurring revenue was as safe as hard assets. They created an entirely new debt category that let you finance a company on its subscription revenue even if it had no earnings at all. It was a genuine accomplishment.
And then they solved the problem so well that they created a new one. Today, the pain in software private equity isn’t that you can’t put leverage on these companies. It’s that too many people did – at too-high prices, with too-optimistic assumptions about never-ending growth. The industry spent thirty years figuring out how to finance software buyouts and overshot so badly that leverage became the vulnerability instead of the barrier.
And now LPs are staring at portfolios of software companies their GPs bought at 12x revenue with debt they can’t refinance, wondering if growth will return to bail them out or if the math is just mathing, as the kids like to say.
Howard Marks, co-founder of Oaktree Capital and one of the most reliable voices in credit markets, was asked directly about private credit’s exposure to software earlier this year. His answer was measured but not reassuring: even if a first-lien lender loses half its money on a quarter of its investments because the whole software sector deteriorates, the portfolio loses 12.5%. With one-to-one leverage, you’re down 25% of your capital. “These things are bad,” he said, “but they’re not... losing a quarter of your capital because the whole software industry lost five-sixths of its value is not abysmal. It’s just bad.” That’s the optimistic case from a measured voice. His partner at Oaktree put it more plainly: “Direct lending is going to be okay. But it might take a cycle to get there.”
In 1989, the barbarians used borrowed money to buy Camels and Oreos. In 2021, the nerds used it to buy ones and zeros. The collateral changed. The confidence didn’t. Private equity’s greatest innovation over the past thirty years was convincing itself, and everyone who lent it money, that this time the leverage was safe because the business model was better. And the business model was better. Recurring revenue is a genuinely superior asset to a warehouse full of cookies. But no business model, however elegant, survives the weight of debt that assumes growth that never slows and rates that never rise. Every era of private equity produces the same three-act story: someone figures out how to finance a new kind of company, everyone copies the playbook, and then the leverage that enabled the strategy becomes the thing that endangers it. Oil, banks, real estate, retail, media — each took its turn. Software was never going to be the exception. It was always going to be the next chapter. The only surprise is that an industry built on pattern recognition didn’t see the pattern until it was too late.
