The View from Upstate
I just returned from an Irish wake where my uncle received the sendoff he rightly deserved. Lines around the block for four straight hours. Everyone came with a story of a simple kindness, an off-color joke, or words of encouragement in a time of doubt. Around town, he was known as the Human Jukebox, always ready with a tune. He had range. Classics from the old sod to modern pop. But he really loved Neil Diamond. The following day at church, his son had the whole place (even the local bishop) singing Sweet Caroline at the top of their lungs. It was a eulogy for the ages, on the kind of cold, sunny upstate New York afternoon that reminds you how a life should be measured. And gets you wondering if you’ll earn the same treatment when your day comes.
At the reception, my aunt approached me, looking concerned. I was ready to cheer her up with stories about summers playing shuffleboard at Williams Lake. But she wasn’t sad about the day’s events; she was worried about me. “This private equity industry you’re in,” she said, “it’s rough, huh? Are you ok?”
I left upstate New York thirty-three years ago to get a PhD in Sociology. With an Art History degree from SUNY Binghamton, my family’s “Are you ok?” really meant, “How are you going to find a job?” I’ll share that long story over a beer about how I went from aspiring professor to PE guy for another time, but after a few years in equity research and then a career in private equity, I went from “is he gonna make it” to “get a load of this guy” at most family gatherings.
Not this time, though. Was it as bad as the headlines? Was my business in trouble? My aunt brought receipts: her local hospital was acquired, and friends were laid off. My uncle’s PE-owned financial advisor was pitching something about credit this and uncorrelated that. He couldn’t remember the exact details, but it sounded fishy. He wanted my advice.
No more Sweet Caroline for me on this day. I heard Love on the Rocks instead.
Small Cracks
My family is right. The headlines are brutal. The PE industry has a well-deserved PR problem. But what I tried to explain, between the corned beef and Jameson chasers, was that the industry they were reading about was not the same as what I do. Yes, it’s all private equity, but the worlds are miles apart. The big funds they read about are like the PGA, where you can make millions while missing the cut, and I’m hacking away down at my muni, paying my own greens fees.
I run a lower middle-market private equity firm in Chicago called ParkerGale. We buy small, profitable, founder-owned software companies. Small, like for less than $100 million. I’ve been running the same plays since I started in private equity in 1995. I have a dog in this fight, so take my arguments here with a healthy dose of humility.
I am not going to apologize for the industry. I’m going to explain the difference between the big guys and the small guys. And I am going to make the case (with a lot of data and maybe a little humor) that what I do is the real private equity. The private equity that built the industry’s reputation for solid returns and economic growth. The one that attracted curious, ambitious builders who admired entrepreneurs. We’re the OGs, the original recipe. The big guys? They’re the outliers, but they get all the press. Small buyouts are the engine that worked before PE got supersized, financialized, and attracted deal guys enamored with spreadsheets, operating playbooks, and value-creation initiatives.
Big Problems
Let’s start with the problems and what prompted my aunt’s worries at the reception.
There is no easy way to say it. The private equity industry is backed up. Funds are sitting on 32,000 unsold companies worth $3.8 trillion, according to Bain. Nearly 40% of these companies have been held for more than five years. The average holding period at exit has drifted to seven years, up from just over five a decade ago. Hugh MacArthur, Bain’s head of global PE, predicted it will take another five years for this to shake out. Even for great companies, IRRs tend to stagnate around year seven and then decline. Time is the enemy, and LPs are forced to wait.
The primary reason for the logjam is lofty entry valuations. PitchBook data show that the median EV/EBITDA multiple for buyouts over $1 billion reached 15.5x in 2024, a 40% increase over the past decade and on par with the S&P 500’s trading multiple. Large funds have been paying public company prices for private companies, despite private company liquidity constraints.
Since 2018, capital calls have exceeded distributions by roughly $1.5 trillion, according to Morgan Stanley. Distributions to LPs have been below 15% of net asset value for four consecutive years, a first for the industry. LP cash flows have been negative for five of the last six years. MSCI estimates that between 2022 and Q3 2025, U.S. PE funds returned an annualized 5.8%, or less than half the S&P 500’s 11.6% over the same period. McKinsey’s 2026 report found that top-quartile global buyout funds averaged 8% returns in 2025.
And the credit side of the equation is cracking simultaneously. Fitch recorded a 9.2% default rate among U.S. private credit borrowers in 2025, the highest ever measured. Private credit funds either halted quarterly redemptions or raised the caps to handle a surge in withdrawal requests. The asset managers who spent years telling wealth advisors – and, more recently, my uncle – that private credit was smooth and uncorrelated now face angry clients and a potentially slowing stream of new allocations.
U.S. buyout fundraising fell 41% year-over-year in total dollars and 57% in fund count, but the money that did flow went overwhelmingly to the top. Yet LP money keeps flowing into the biggest funds with the biggest exposure. In 2025, the top 10 PE funds captured 46% of all U.S. PE fundraising, the largest share in over a decade. Funds under $1 billion captured just 14.7% of capital raised, the lowest level in at least a decade.
Small Beginnings
Most folks don’t realize a key tenet in the history of private equity: the industry’s best returns didn’t originate from the big deals that made the headlines. They were generated from much smaller deals that will never grace the pages of the Wall Street Journal or the Financial Times.
Private equity started as a cottage industry. A handful of firms in the 1970s and early 1980s, like KKR and Forstmann Little, would buy a company, often from a founder or from a carve-out of a conglomerate, at a reasonable price. They’d use some debt, recruit better leaders, improve operations, sell to a strategic buyer a few years later, and return cash to their investors. Fund sizes were in the hundreds of millions. Deal teams were small. The model was simple, bespoke, but repeatable.
Then came the excess, the supersize model. In the late 1980s, Michael Milken’s junk bond machine at Drexel Burnham Lambert turned the debt volume up to eleven. Deals, like RJR Nabisco and Federated Department Stores, loaded companies with debt-to-capital ratios above 90%, with equity slices as thin as 4% of the purchase price.
No surprise, many of these deals went bankrupt. Congress held hearings. The press had a field day. The junk bond market collapsed, Drexel went bankrupt, and the mega-deal machine sputtered. Sound familiar? Jerome Kohlberg – the “K” in KKR, the guy who helped invent the leveraged buyout – exited his own firm because he wanted to go back to basics.
What followed was the most productive period in the history of private equity.
With access to cheap leverage gone, PE firms in the early 1990s had no choice but to buy smaller companies at reasonable prices, use moderate debt, improve operations, and sell to strategic buyers. Funds raised between 1989 and 1994 (often buying at 5x to 7x EBITDA, leveraging at 3x to 4x, holding for 3 to 5 years) generated median net IRRs of 20% and net MOICs above 2x. Cambridge Associates’ data shows the 1993 vintage delivered a pooled net IRR of 25.3%. Chicago Booth School of Business professor Steven Kaplan, using Burgiss data on over 1,400 funds, found that the average buyout fund during this era earned investors excess returns of 20% to 27% over the S&P 500.
These results set the PE allocation machine in motion and validated Yale’s famous Swensen model. The golden age. The way it used to be.
But in some parts of the PE market, this approach remains the North Star. The deal characteristics of that era, when entry multiples were low, leverage was prudent, fund sizes were moderate, businesses improved over time, and exits were often to strategic buyers, are still alive and well. It’s what lower-middle-market PE firms still do every day. The golden age never ended. It just moved down market.
Big Luck
History repeated itself. When cheap credit returned in the 2000s, the industry scaled right back up. The first $10 billion PE fund closed in 2006. The following year, Blackstone went public. KKR followed in 2010; Apollo in 2011; Carlyle in 2012. Once PE firms had public shareholders, they began emphasizing the steady fees from new financial products rather than the lumpy profits from traditional PE deal-making. While they’re all lumped together as private equity firms, the original buyout strategies that got them public now account for a declining share of their diversified operations. They make most of their money from credit, infrastructure, insurance, and real estate. What gets called “private equity” isn’t really traditional private equity anymore. These funds made it to the PGA tour after dominating the public courses and never looked back.
Ironically, Apollo Global, one of the largest financial supermarkets, published a report called “Private Equity Returns to Its Roots” in January 2026. This, from a firm managing over $1 trillion in assets! But let’s take a closer look. The thesis is simple: the firms that will outperform in the future will do so by “reclaiming the practices that defined private equity’s foundational decades: buy well, control the controllable, make fundamental improvements to a business and look to return capital early and often.” These fundamentals, Apollo wrote, “were central to PE’s earliest successes but were lost sight of during periods of excess.” They are the same principles that historically drove returns, “except for the 2010–2022 period” they said. Purchase price is “once again the dominant driver of returns” they remind us. Apollo’s own data from 2010 to 2022 showed roughly 66% of value creation came from leverage and multiple expansion. That’s what people in the biz call beta, folks, not alpha.
We have an entire generation or two of professionals who learned the business during this period — the luckiest in PE history, driven by one of the longest ever bull runs without a recession. And many of my colleagues have confused luck with skill. The period many consider normal operating procedure was a once-in-a-lifetime exception. And with every quarter that slips by without an exit, as they watch their IRR decline and their carry disappear, they would be wise to apply the old rules to succeed in the future. But how can they when they never played by those rules?
Lower-middle-market PE has always taken the path Apollo now prescribes as the new road for private equity. Why? Because constraints drive creativity. Because our deals can’t attract as much leverage as the big ones. Because we must grow and execute our way to a return. And unlike large funds with dozens of portfolio companies across multiple products, small buyout fund portfolios aren’t well-suited for CVs, NAVs, and manufactured liquidity. Small firms never lost their roots. We are the roots. Apollo and many others are calling it a strategic pivot. We call it another day at the office.
Meanwhile, fundraising data shows the industry moving in the opposite direction. Fund closes fell from 1,089 in 2022 to 327 in 2025, a 70% decline. But the money didn’t disappear; it consolidated. As I mentioned above, almost half of the money raised by US PE firms in 2025 went to 10 funds.
Small Targets, Big Edge
The case for small buyouts is simple arithmetic that even Art History majors like me can track.
Start with the opportunity set. According to JPMorgan, there are roughly 147,000 small and mid-sized companies in the United States. That’s companies with $10 million to $300 million in revenue. That’s 96% of all privately held companies. The addressable universe for mega-buyout funds? About 6,000. That’s a 25-to-1 difference in opportunity set. And how would anyone know this? Small buyouts don’t make the front page of the Wall Street Journal. Andrew Ross Sorkin isn’t featuring them on a CNBC segment. All the oxygen gets consumed by the brand-name deals the big funds are chasing. And when you recall there are only about 4,000 public companies, the fact that we have several television networks dedicated to their daily movements seems a little out of balance.
Now, let’s review what you have to pay to get in. PitchBook data show the median entry multiple for buyouts over $1 billion reached 15.5x EV/EBITDA in 2024. GF Data, which tracks the core middle market ($10 million to $500 million in enterprise value), reports an average of 7.2x, with the smallest deals at about 6.4x. That’s a 30% to 60% discount at entry. When you’re buying at 6x, and the public market comparable is trading at 15x, you don’t need much to go right to generate a decent return. You just need a few things to keep from going wrong. Remember, Apollo now argues that “purchase price is once again the dominant driver of returns.”
So how much can you borrow? Average leverage for large buyouts is around 6x Debt/EBITDA, according to LSEG. Some large tech buyouts even reached 10x. Middle-market and small buyouts are below 4.5x. Cambridge Associates data backs this up: it’s 3.2x for small buyouts versus 5.9x for mega-deals. StepStone also agrees, and its data show that this leverage gap has been consistent for over 20 years. PineBridge reports that 98% of lower-middle-market loans carry maintenance covenants (meaning the lender has built-in trip wires if the business deteriorates), compared to the large deal market, which has increasingly gone (and remained) cov-lite. This is what happens when the private credit market expands so quickly. Underwriting deteriorates, large borrowers borrow more, and when things crack, they crack big.
Value creation is different, too. The typical small buyout acquisition target is a founder-owned business with $5 million to $25 million in EBITDA, informal management, underdeveloped technology, and no real marketing function. The playbook is not financial, it’s operational: professionalize management, upgrade systems, build out sales and marketing, and close some add-on acquisitions. The tools to do this, as we have discussed on the PE FunCast for the last 12 years, have never been better, cheaper, or more readily available. And when this model is put to work at small companies, results materialize pretty fast. If you deliver multiple expansion at exit, that comes from helping the business operate like a larger, more sophisticated company as it grows. That’s when buyers pay premium multiples. Mega buyouts, by contrast, have a much narrower toolkit. The businesses they buy are already professionalized. So, the game is leveraging, cost-cutting, and hoping the exit multiple holds up. Apollo’s own report conceded that two-thirds of recent returns were macro market conditions, not micro business building. The rising tide carried them, while the fish just jumped into the boat. But, hey, they can still call themselves fishermen.
And credit data shows the difference as well. Proskauer’s Private Credit Default Index breaks down defaults by company size. In Q4 2025, borrowers with EBITDA under $25 million (the small buyout sweet spot) defaulted at a rate of 1.7%. Borrowers with EBITDA over $50 million saw their default rate double in a single quarter last year, from 1.2% to 2.4%. The mid-tier ($25 million to $50 million) jumped from 2.6% to 3.6%. The stress isn’t evenly distributed across the market. It’s concentrated on the high and higher end. So far, it appears that the smallest borrowers have been the most stable credit cohort throughout the entire cycle. Why? Because they likely have the lowest leverage, and the GPs who own them have the most to lose if things go badly.
Now, let’s compare exits. Over 90% of lower-middle-market exits go to strategic buyers or other financial sponsors, not IPOs. When IPO activity cratered by 80% in 2023, mega-funds watched their distribution rates collapse, while small buyout funds kept selling to strategics and larger sponsors that needed platforms and add-ons. Mountains of dry powder at the large funds need to be deployed, and well-run companies owned by smaller funds are exactly what they’re shopping for. StepStone’s 2024 research predicted that mega-fund dry powder would become an exit tailwind for small buyout managers. They are correct. Our last nine exits at ParkerGale have been sales to larger buyout funds. And when it comes to returning capital, PGIM’s data show small buyout funds have outperformed on DPI across all vintage cohorts from 2003 through 2021. I haven’t found data more recent than this, but my bet is the trend has continued, given the constipation at the high end of the market.
Add the demographic wave in favor of small buyouts to the mix. There are 12 million boomer-owned businesses, 10,000 owners turning 65 every day, 58% with no succession plan. I like to say the four horsemen of small buyout deal flow are Death, Disease, Divorce, and Depression. I’m only kinda joking. Life events lead owners to look for the exits, and younger generations today often don’t want to take over their parents’ business. They want to work in private equity! Most of these companies are too small and too messy for the big funds, so they are natural targets for small buyout managers who can professionalize, grow, and eventually sell them to upstream buyers.
And then there’s the part that has nothing to do with returns and really makes me sound like I work for the private equity PR department. Small PE-backed companies grew employment 9% in the 12 months ending July 2025, according to the National Center for the Middle Market, while the overall economy grew jobs at 1.2%. During the Global Financial Crisis (GFC), the same segment added 2.2 million jobs while larger companies were mostly shedding headcount. An NBER study of 3,200 PE-backed firms found that net job losses attributable to PE ownership were under 1% and concentrated almost entirely in large public-to-private deals. Remember, my aunt’s hospital got bought by PE, and her friends were laid off. That’s the supersized private equity playbook. Downstream? We’re hiring.
Let’s take stock of all that. More targets. Less competition. Lower prices. Less debt. Better tools. Lower defaults. Multiple exit paths. Higher DPI. Built-in deal flow. More job creation. And LPs are aggressively moving upmarket into just a handful of big funds? Got it.
Small Funds, Big Alpha
Bain’s 2026 report shows that over five- and 10-year periods, aggregate U.S. buyout returns (14% and 15% net, respectively) have trailed the S&P 500’s public-market equivalent returns of 17% and 16%, respectively. MSCI estimates annualized U.S. PE returns of 5.8% net from 2022 through Q3 2025 versus 11.6% for the S&P. This isn’t what you paid 2-and-20 for.
Now, let’s carve out small buyout funds from these aggregate numbers.
RCP Advisors’ Small Buyout Index, comprising 253 funds under $1 billion formed between 1999 and 2024 with deal-level data on 9,310 fully realized transactions, shows 5-year net returns of 19.9%, 10-year returns of 20.7%, and 20-year returns of 16.8%. Compared to the S&P 500’s 14.5%, 13.1%, and 10.3%. Now that’s what you paid 2 and 20 for!
Cambridge Associates, using 30 years of data, found a clean inverse relationship between fund size and returns. Andrea Auerbach, Cambridge’s Global Head of Private Investments, has noted that mega-funds returned essentially the same as the Russell 3000 PME, with correlation to public markets nearly twice that of smaller funds. So, if you believe Andrea (and you should), you’re basically paying to invest in a leveraged index fund with a ten-year lockup. Maybe check out the Vanguard Total Stock Market Index Fund (VTASX) instead?
At the deal level, small companies can shine too. RCP’s data on 9,310 realized transactions show that among deals with enterprise values under $100 million, 19% achieved a 5x gross or better return on invested capital. Among deals over $250 million, only 10% hit that mark. The median MOIC for small deals was 2.5x gross versus 1.5x gross for large deals, while the small-deal loss rate was only three percentage points higher. Modestly more downside risk for massively more upside opportunity.
And in a crisis? During the GFC, small buyouts lost 7.3% net cumulatively. Large buyouts lost 32.6% net. The S&P 500 lost 45.8%. StepStone found that small buyouts captured only 30% of the downside in falling markets but 94% of the upside in rising ones across three separate crash-and-recovery cycles: the dotcom bust, the GFC, and COVID. And, consistent with RCP’s findings, StepStone also found that of the 387 realized North American private equity investments that generated 10x gross MOIC or more, 77% were small buyouts.
The Small Print
None of this should be digested as “small buyouts are easy” or “any small fund will outperform.” The same dispersion that creates the opportunity also creates the risk of being wrong.
Bottom-quartile small buyout returns are historically lower than bottom-quartile large buyout returns. The worst small funds are consistently worse than the worst big funds. Apollo’s report noted that the dispersion between top- and bottom-quartile PE funds now exceeds 25 percentage points. GEM, using Burgiss data over 20 years, found a 14.3-percentage-point spread between top- and bottom-quartile managers in the small buyout segment. You could fit a Costco parking lot between those results, so be careful. Manager selection is the name of the game. An allocator coming down market without a broad network and rigorous diligence can get hurt.
This is part of the reason LP money tends to concentrate at the top. Mega-funds offer narrower dispersion. They have more data points to diligence. There is a herding effect. Less chance of a disaster, but also less chance of a home run. That flight to quality we keep hearing about is really just a flight from variability. And that’s a rational emotional choice. It just isn’t a rational economic one, because data show that narrower dispersion comes with compressed returns that barely exceed those of liquid public-market alternatives.
And LPs aren’t the only ones to blame. GPs love bigger funds too! The high-performing small funds are often the same ones that graduate into the next size bracket, then the next, until they become the mega-funds they once derided. More than 80% of the funds that closed in 2024 were bigger than their predecessor. The pull to get bigger is almost universal because AUM scales nicely, and small deals are just as hard (if not harder) than the big ones. My biggest surprise since founding ParkerGale over a decade ago is that our competitors back then are no longer our competitors today. They all graduated and moved out of town, while I’m still sitting on the same stool at the same bar. Every few years, I compete with a whole new crop of emerging managers, while my old peers, like the Jeffersons before them, are “Movin’ on Up!” But that’s a story for another essay.
Small is the New Big
To my friends who still rock the small buyouts, I salute you. Queue up the AC/DC. The next time someone tells you that private equity is a mess, that the returns stink and the fees are too high, that it can’t return capital to LPs, that the leverage is a systemic risk to the economy, just nod along. They’re not wrong. They’re just talking about that other private equity industry. The supersized, financialized, 3XL version.
The private equity I work in (the original version, the one that buys small companies from founders, uses a little debt, attracts good leaders, returns cash through actual exits, and has outperformed public markets through cycles over 26 years) is doing just fine.
Despite all this, LP allocations keep moving upmarket to larger funds faster than ever. The small guys are getting squeezed, so now is the time for small funds to speak up. We need to get loud and tell the stories ourselves. We must make the case for money flowing back into the small end of the market. We still have some of the institutions on our side. And we have the data to prove it.
But if the current trend of money consolidating upmarket continues and the funeral for small buyouts is coming, can you please queue up Sweet Caroline one last time for me?
Where it began
I can’t begin to know when
But then I know it’s growin’ strong

Salespeople are especially hard to interview because they’re good at the part of the interview that (a) makes you like them but (b) doesn’t actually predict how they’ll perform on the job.
Here’s what I mean. Working in sales teaches you a few things. It teaches you how to create rapport and connection. It teaches you how to read people’s energy and mirror it back. It teaches you how to take a completely mediocre idea and package it into something that just sounds good. And it teaches you how to influence, persuade, and use conversational jiu-jitsu on people to get them to do what you want them to do.
The ability to sell is a powerful dark art. And without the right techniques to neutralize that dark art, you as the hiring manager puts yourself at risk of a completely-unqualified candidate charming your pants right off and wasting one to two valuable years as they explain away how they manage to spend all their time “building pipeline” but never close a damn thing.
Look, these soft skills we’re talking about (charm, energy, and polished communication) matter when you’re selling. I’m not saying they don’t. You don’t want to hire someone who can’t connect with people and who doesn’t know how to make customers and prospects feel good about working with you. That’s important. People buy from people they like. You want to hire people who know how to make other people like them.
But those skills (and the feelings they create) are absolutely not what separates the rep who closes millions of dollars of business a year from everyone else.
The things that make great sales reps great are more subtle, more important, and (thankfully) not that difficult to test for.
You just have to know what to ask.
That’s what our latest PE FunCast episode is all about:
- Why hiring salespeople is so important to any investment thesis
- What makes it so hard (and the tricks salespeople will try to pull on you during the interview)
- And exactly what you should ask them to improve the odds that your next quota-carrying hire is a great one
Why Hiring Salespeople Is Hard
Good salespeople are professionally trained to get you to like them. You walk out of that interview room feeling like you’d like to spend more time together. That feeling feels good.
But remember what liking someone in an interview tells you. It tells you this person is good at building rapport. It does not tell you how effectively they’ll work a territory, follow up on leads, tell the story you need them to tell about the product, or handle the part of your growth plan you’re thinking about handing them responsibly.
Here’s our take on how to avoid the rapport trap and what to test for instead.
The First Thing You Should Ask About
Most sales interviews measure the wrong thing. You spend 45 minutes on backstory, deal anecdotes, and hypotheticals, and you walk out with a strong impression… but no data.
There’s a simpler test. Ask what their number was. Ask how they performed against it for the last few years. And don’t move on until you get a specific answer for both.
You’ll be amazed at how many candidates can’t answer the question. (Or won’t.) You’ll see all sorts of squirming when you ask this question. People who can’t remember their number, people who start explaining why the quota changed halfway through the year, and people who try to bamboozle you with a footnote about how the definition of new versus upsell mix shifted on them instead of just answering the question. (Hint: The good ones answer the question first, then offer to explain why things went down the way they did.)
Asking about results doesn’t just give you an honest read on how this person has performed historically. It also gives you a natural jumping off point for all the contextual stories you definitely can and should get to in an effective interview. You can ask what drove their performance. You can ask whether the motion that produced those results looks anything like what you’re hiring them to do. You can figure out whether their best year happened in a situation that just doesn’t apply to yours.
All of that is easy to ask after you learn how they performed against their quota. But ask about that performance first.
It won’t tell you everything. But it sure tells you a lot.
The ParkerGale-Approved Guide to Interviewing Salespeople
Here are the qualities we believe drive high-performance for B2B sellers. They’re also the qualities you should find a way to test for every time you interview a seller or sales leader for your team.
- Customer focus: Can they simplify your product and connect it to real customer problems, or are they just a brochure with legs rattling off technical specs?
- Structure: Do they have a disciplined process for moving deals forward, or do they just wing it and hope for the best?
- Accountability: Can they connect what they did to the outcomes they got, or do they just blame their territory and the market when things don’t go their way?
- Problem-solving: Can they handle complex deals that require creativity and persistence, or do they only know how to work layups?
- Drive: Do they know what they need to work on to get better and actively work on it, or are they just going through the motions?
1. Customer Focus
What you’re testing for:
Can they explain the product in a way that connects with customers?
What to ask:
“Explain your product to me like I’m a potential customer. What questions do you ask them to uncover problems you can help to solve, and what are you listening for when you ask those questions?”
Follow-up Questions:
- “What problems or pain-points tell you that this person has a high need for your product vs. a lower need?”
- “How do those pain-points vary by the personas that you encounter?”
- “What is a hidden gem of your product? Something valuable that not enough customers know about or take advantage of yet?”
- “What is a feature of your product customers think they need at the beginning of sales process that they don’t use or value as much once they become customers?”
What to listen for:
- Can they simplify? Do they lead with customer-centric, “day-in-the-life” pain points or jargon-heavy product features?
- Do they pattern-match to real customer situations or just recite back what’s on the website/product specs?
- Can they adjust their pitch and positioning based on different types of buyers and buyer contexts?
- The “brochure-with-legs” candidates will rattle off specs and capabilities and leave you feeling unclear re: what the value of the product is and why someone would buy it.
- The customer-focused candidates will show you that they can connect a customer pain-point or problem to something the product can help with - and that they’ve done the work to understand their customer and the job they’re trying to get done.
2. Structure
What you’re testing for:
Do they have a real sales process? Or are they just winging it?
What to ask:
“Walk me through your sales process—what does a good first meeting look like, what does a good second meeting look like, and what is important to get right when you get to the later stages?”
Follow-up Questions:
- “What’s the thing that tends to kill deals later in your sales process? How do you identify those obstacles in advance early in your process?”
-“How do you know when you’ve had a good first meeting vs. a bad one?”
- “What needs to happen in the second meeting (or demo) for you to feel confident the deal is going to close?”
- “Walk me through how you identify and engage the economic buyer and navigate the buying process—at what stage does that typically happen?”
- “When you share a proposal or quote, how do you do that?”
What to listen for:
- Specific answers with actual mechanics (vs. vague platitudes) indicate that they’re doing things on purpose and not just winging it.
- Do they have strong opinions about what a good first meeting looks like versus a good second meeting?
- Do they proactively look for the thing that’s going to lose them the deal later later (e.g., the economic buyer who’s not engaged, the paper process they didn’t know about, etc.) or do they get surprised?
3. Accountability
What you’re testing for:
Can they connect what they did to the results they got?
What to ask:
“Walk me through the last two years—what was your number each year and how did you perform against that number?”
Follow-up Questions:
- “What’s the one thing you focused on in your process or how you approached your day that made the biggest difference in your results?”
- “When you missed your number (or a quarter), what was the reason? What did you change as a result?”
-“What’s something you tried that didn’t work? How did you figure out it wasn’t working and what did you do differently?”
-“If I asked your manager what made you successful and what you need to work on, what would they say? Do you agree with that assessment?”
What to listen for:
- Watch for squirming and hedging — can they cite actual numbers and performance without hesitation?
- Can they name the specific thing they did that drove performance?
- Good answers show tight awareness of performance vs. goal, self-awareness about what drives their performance, and honest reflection about what they still need to work on
- Bad answers are generic: “I worked hard,” “I built relationships,” “I was persistent”
- Great people tend to know exactly how they performed and tend to have a track record of overperforming their quotas in good times and bad - this doesn’t have to be complicated!
4. Problem-Solving
What to ask:
“Tell me about a gnarly deal that took lots of extra effort and problem solving to get over the line—how did you do that?”
Follow-up Questions:
- “What’s the one thing you focused on in your process or how you approached your day that made the biggest difference in your results?”
- “When you missed your number (or a quarter), what was the reason? What did you change as a result?”
-“What’s something you tried that didn’t work? How did you figure out it wasn’t working and what did you do differently?”
-“If I asked your manager what made you successful and what you need to work on, what would they say? Do you agree with that assessment?”
What to listen for:
- Level of detail about what made it hard
- The specific steps they took to wrestle it to the ground
- Do they talk about the customer’s world or just their own activity?
- This reveals how much they actually know about their customers
- Shows whether they can adjust and think creatively when forced to
- Vague answers = they’ve never done it or they only work layup deals
5. Drive
What to ask: First: “On a scale of one to ten, how would you rank your sales ability?” Then follow up with: “What’s the thing you need to work on that would move you up by one point on that scale?”
Follow-up Questions:
- “Who has given you feedback on that growth opportunity? What have you done with that feedback?”
- “How have you worked on it to date?”
-“If I were to help you develop that quality, how would you want to be coached on it? What do you need to be most effective in your role?
What to listen for:
- The first question is a bit of a trick. Nobody says ten. They all say eight or nine. That gives you the opening you need to ask the second question (the real question).
- Great sales reps know exactly what they need to work on and could talk for 20 minutes about how it shows up and how they’re working on it. You might actually have to cut them off.
- The bad ones either don’t know or give extremely generic answers like “time management.”
- Great reps will also be able to share a story or two about how the quality from question two has held them back in specific deals - don’t be afraid to ask lots of follow-ups here.
Final Thoughts
The goal when you’re interviewing salespeople isn’t to figure out who you like. It’s to develop conviction around who can learn your product, connect what it does to something a customer actually cares about, and independently own and drive a meaningful portion of the growth your company’s future value depends on.
The reps who can do that can talk you through exactly how they’ve done it before, and how they’ll do it for you.
Ask the right questions, and they’ll tell you.
The ones who can’t answer these questions are telling you something too.
Believe them.

Every PE firm out there talks about their value creation playbook. And the way they talk about it makes it sounds like an immutable, repeatable process. The same moves, in the same sequence, for every company.
That sure sounds good. It’s comforting to believe your investors can just buy a company, plug in their fancy value creation machine, and let that machine (and the repeatable process it runs on) do its thing.
Unfortunately, this isn’t how it actually works.
Real-world value creation requires an “it depends” approach.
Every company has different strengths, gaps, challenges, and opportunities. And experienced PE ops teams spend a lot of time assessing “what they’ve got” during diligence, building a simple, short-term plan to address the key improvement levers in the business, and then making lots of little adjustments to that plan once the deal closes (and after they learn a lot more about how things really work inside the business, its market, and its customer base).
Real-world value creation is also about building backwards from the exit you’re trying to create. Who is likely to buy this company a few years from now? What data will they ask for? What evidence of progress and opportunity will they want to see? What questions will we need to answer for them to get them excited about the next 5-10 years for this business? The longer it takes you to answer those questions, the more of an unpleasant surprise selling the company is going to be - especially if someone surprises you with a potential offer a few years into the hold.
In this episode, Operating Partners Paul and Jim walk through what value creation actually looks like once you own the company: Why the work is different every time, what parts of the playbook stay consistent underneath all that variation, and how you can start thinking about exit-readiness before you even close the deal.
Some of the key questions we cover:
- What does “don’t buy a company you don’t know how to sell” mean? This is about brainstorming what your potential future buyer will care about on day one and working backwards from the questions you know they’ll ask you.
- What does value creation actually look like company by company? Our operating team focuses on the same few areas in every business (e.g., sales and marketing, product, finance and M&A, and people) but the specific plays we run (and how we sequence them) are different every single time. Jim and Paul talk about why, and what goes into both the art and science of building a value creation plan.
- What are the few things you can do in year one of an investment that set you up to be exit-ready? These don’t always feel like they’re making a difference while you’re doing them. But if you finish them, you’re ahead of the vast majority of companies when it’s time to sell.
Time for the highlights.
Start Thinking About the Exit Right Away
If you’re doing it right, the day after you close a deal, you should already be thinking about what the business needs to look like for the next buyer. You don’t control the end market. You don’t control when offers show up. If six months into a hold the market gets hot and offers start coming in, you want to be in a position to respond — not scrambling to get the business ready for a conversation you weren’t expecting to have yet.
Here’s Paul and Jim on why exit readiness isn’t a year-four project, it’s a day-one mindset.
Look For Growth In The Customer Base
Most of the software companies we buy have more than one product. And if you go talk to an average customer and ask them what else the company could be doing for them, they have no idea. Nobody ever told them what else was on the menu.
So one of the first things we do with almost every business is fix that. Go to the existing customer base with what Paul calls “the apologist pitch”:
“Hey, I’m actually calling with a small apology. We had a meeting as a leadership team and realized we’ve done a really poor job of communicating everything we can do for you. I’m not assuming you’re going to buy something today. I just want to make sure you know (a) what’s on the menu and (b) when to call us when these things come up. Can we book a short meeting to take you through that?”
When you do this, two things happen:
- Customers tell you, “I had no idea you guys did this other stuff.”
- Some of them have a problem you can help them with (Pipeline! Nice!)
This is value creation at its simplest. No new product, no new market, no new customers. Just telling the people who already trust you what else you can do for them.
Here’s Paul and Jim on why the easiest growth in a portfolio company is usually found inside the customer base.
Exit Readiness Starts With Clean Customer Data
When a buyer starts looking at a software company, the first thing they ask for is the customer data. Who are your customers, what have they bought, how long have they been with you, what do they pay.
And the moment they ask, the clock starts. How long does it take you to respond? Can you pull it together in a day, or does it take two weeks of stitching together spreadsheets and reconciling against financial statements? The speed of that response sends a signal about the operational state of the business that’s hard to fake. Companies that can’t produce clean customer data quickly don’t just slow down the process — they create doubt before the real diligence even starts. Even PE firms that own portfolio companies without a good customer database will ding the next company they look at for the same problem. Everyone knows it matters. Not everyone does the work.
Here’s Paul and Jim on why clean customer data is the single most important thing you can have ready before a process starts.

(This article accompanies a podcast episode that you can find here and will be linked below, but it can stand alone if reading the summary on Substack instead of watching/listening to an hour long podcast episode is more your scene.)
In 1995, almost nobody in private equity had dedicated operating people on staff. Deals got done by deal people. Management teams ran the business. If you needed something, you hired a consultant or swapped out the management team. That was the whole model.
By 2011, a Lancor study estimated that about 500 people were working in PE Ops roles across the entire industry. Today, that number is around 20,000(!)1
That’s not slow growth. That’s a function that went from nonexistent to everywhere in roughly one career arc. This week, we’re trying to break down how we got from there to here.
The “I Got a Guy” Era (1990-2010)
Before there was PE Ops, there were operating partners who were really just expensive Rolodexes. Their value wasn't operational execution as we'd think of it today. It was sourcing and connections. Useful, but not what we'd call "PE Ops" now.
The expectation in this era for a PE firm was simple: PE is in the deal selection and talent selection business. Management teams run companies. That worked fine …until the global financial crisis (“GFC” for those unfamiliar with the abbreviated term - ahem, Cass).
Why did that model make sense at the time? Through the 1980s and into the early 2000s, financial engineering (leverage plus multiple expansion) accounted for more than 50% of PE returns. Operational improvements contributed only around 18%. When debt is cheap and multiples are expanding, you don't need operators. You need deal people who can find the right assets and finance them correctly. The management team was the operating model.2
A handful of firms were starting to experiment with something different. KKR stood up KKR Capstone in 2000 (essentially a captive McKinsey that worked only for KKR portfolio companies). TPG and Vista created operating consulting arms around the same time. But as Devin puts it, "Capstone didn't even fall on my radar until several years later. When it was like, oh, this is a thing." The broader industry wasn't paying attention yet.3
A few years after these captive consulting firms popped up, there was increased regulatory scrutiny of PE operating models, adding guardrails for other firms testing out these models to follow.
The Professionalization Era (2010-2020)
In the 2010s, middle-market firms started getting religion about PE Ops and testing their own versions of it.
Three distinct models emerged, and which one a firm chose said a lot about its philosophy.
The "Capstone model" is a separate legal entity, billed to portfolio companies, operating like a captive consulting firm. This worked for the largest funds that could afford the infrastructure. Most middle-market GPs couldn't, so they went looking for a Swiss Army knife instead: a generalist ops partner, usually an ex-strategy consultant or former C-suite executive who could work across situations. A third model was simpler still: a senior advisor network of former CEOs who sat on boards, worked their networks, and lent credibility. Easy to stand up, cheap to maintain, limited in execution depth.
By the mid-2010s, the data was starting to back up the thesis. Since 2010, operational improvements have accounted for roughly 47% of value creation in buyouts - up from 18% in the 1980s - while financial engineering’s contribution fell from over 50% to around 25%. The decade of zero interest rates made this hard to prove cleanly (cheap debt lifted all boats), but firms that had built real operations capability were starting to separate from those that had just checked the LP box.4
There’s a talent dynamic from this era that rarely gets discussed: the Ops Partner hiring process was almost entirely focused on hard skills: functional expertise, operating track record, and prior P&L ownership. But research from Egon Zehnder found that the existing population of operating partners showed relatively small variation in hard skills. What actually differentiated effective Ops Partners from ineffective ones was soft skills - the ability to influence without authority, earn trust from a CEO who was already suspicious of you, and serve two clients with opposing anxieties at the same time: the deal partner who needed conviction, and the portfolio CEO who needed autonomy.5
By 2018 and 2019, not having an ops story wasn’t just unusual; it was a real liability in a fundraise. As Devin describes it in the episode: “That’s a pretty big slide that’s missing from your deck.” LPs weren’t prescribing which model to use. But they expected a philosophy, and they expected a firm to own it and defend it. The funds that couldn’t were being asked increasingly uncomfortable questions about how they actually created value in the companies they owned.
The Proliferation Era (2020 - today)
As alluded to at the end of the “Professionalization Era,” by 2020, showing up to a fundraising meeting without an ops story was a real problem.
Part of what drove that urgency was COVID, which functioned as an unplanned controlled experiment. A McKinsey study released in 2020 found that PE firms with dedicated operating teams outperformed peers by roughly five percentage points of annual IRR during the crisis years: 23% versus 18% for firms without them. Maybe a bit of a self-fulfilling prophecy, but those same firms grew fund sizes 53% in the post-crisis period, while firms without Ops teams saw fund sizes decline 15%. For the first time, there was clean data separating the firms that had actually built something from the firms that had put a name on a website.6
Specialization moved fast after that. Cass tells a story in the episode that captures the shift at ground level: when she moved into a finance-focused ops role in 2020, she and a colleague tried to find others doing the same thing — PE Ops professionals focused specifically on CFO-facing finance work, not generalists, not ex-consultants doing everything. In Chicago, they guessed there might be 10 of them. They found 15 to 18. Today, that list in Chicago alone is around 60.
By function, across go-to-market, talent, and technology, the same explosion was happening simultaneously. Heidrick & Struggles data tells the same story at the industry level: in 2021, roughly 7% of people inside PE firms identified as operators on the Ops team. Two years later, that figure was 21%.7
But somewhere in there, the logic got stretched. If one PE Ops hire is good, a PE Ops hire in every functional area is better. If a generalist helps, a specialist helps more. And if you’re charging fees to the portfolio, why not staff up?
ParkerGale went through this. Devin is candid about it: "I feel like we over-rotated too fast before we knew how to manage it." CEOs were getting calls from different people at the private equity firm with different mandates. The "to-do list" got confusing and overcomplicated. And sometimes, well-meaning operating partners were filling in gaps to hide cracks in the system.
This is a question worth sitting with if you (or your firm) run a portfolio ops team: are we helping, or are we propping up?
Here’s Devin on how to tell the difference, and why the incentive structure in captive consulting models can make propping up feel like value creation.
Where It Goes From Here (the next 5 years)
The predictions in this episode are worth hearing because all three people on this recording have skin in the game and are coming from three different perspectives.
Devin thinks we’re headed toward a skinnier operating model. Not necessarily fewer operators, but fewer of the wrong kind, deployed in the wrong places, doing work that masks problems rather than solves them. The correction is coming as more management teams run through multiple PE cycles and get loud about what they actually want.
Cass sees the generalist-to-specialist arc that hit investing firms playing out next in ops teams. The ROI needs to be demonstrable, project-level, and function-specific. Vague operational influence won’t survive a tighter fundraising environment en masse (although some will continue to do it well, as we’ve also seen for some generalist investors).
And then there’s AI, which Paul points out is doing to PE Ops right now exactly what PE Ops did to deal teams in 2010. Everyone knows they probably need it. Nobody quite knows how to deploy it. The firms that figure it out first will look like geniuses. The rest will have hired an AI specialist with a broad mandate who is spread too thin.
Here’s Paul on where ParkerGale landed on the size and function focus of their operations team.
If you’re newer to the space, this is the origin story nobody wrote down. If you’ve been in it for a while, you’ll recognize most of it, and we welcome your thoughts (or corrections!) and predictions in the comments.

September 2016. We closed ParkerGale Fund I.
With our aluminum anniversary approaching, Jim and I sat down to record the ten things we’ve learned over the past ten years. It was supposed to be a nostalgia lap in between meetings. By the time we were done, it was clear we were in an introspective mood and ready to air out the laundry. Here are five highlights covering portfolio operations, doing too much, deal sourcing, inorganic growth, and what GPs tell LPs when first starting out.
Too Many Daves
Just like Mrs. McCave in the Dr. Seuss story, when a PE-backed CEO calls out “Yoo-Hoo!” all twenty-three Daves come running. That’s what it feels like now for most PE-backed CEOs navigating the mountains of operating partners thrown their way to solve all their problems. In 2022, a Heidrick & Struggles survey found 7% of PE professionals calling themselves operating partners. By 2024, it was 21%1. The Daves tripled while the operating challenges stayed about the same.
How did that happen? Post GFC, GPs at the large funds wanted to show their LPs that they weren’t just a bunch of deal guys overpaying and overleveraging late in the cycle. PE wasn’t just about financial engineering; it could drive results by improving how businesses operate. So, they built out large operating teams to support portfolio company management to execute their value-creating initiatives. Post-pandemic, this trickled down to even the smallest funds and has pretty much become an expected part of the PE playbook.
For our size, we were early to load up on Ops. When we founded ParkerGale, I wanted a “Jim in every pot.” See, at our prior firm, Jim was the only operator, and I watched him move the needle in a big way for our engineering and product teams. When we launched ParkerGale a decade ago, I wanted Jims in every function – Talent, Systems, Sales, Marketing, Product, Finance – and we went out and recruited our Daves. We taught them our playbooks, and we unleashed them on the portfolio.
During the pandemic, I had a revelation. Grounded for the first time in thirty years, I had time to reflect. On a call with one of our CEOs, as he walked me through a new initiative one of our Daves had launched, it hit me. We were WAY over-operating the portfolio. Our management teams were getting pulled in too many directions. While each individual initiative had value, we were giving our companies too much medicine all at once. Good people, all trying to help. No coordination. Competing agendas. So, we scaled it back, going in the opposite direction of many of our peers and raising questions from our LPs.
This is no knock on operating partners. We think we are the poster child for how to integrate the investing and operating sides of the house — Jim and I are equal partners, same comp, same carry, same GP ownership, and we don’t charge our companies for our operating team. But ask most CEOs how much value they’re getting from the operating resources at their PE overlords, and, if they’re being honest, most will say “not much.” Ask most operating partners, and they’ll say “a lot.” And every survey on the topic backs this up. We have pared things back to the essentials, and that leads us to the next thing we’ve learned.
Little’s Law
John Little was a professor at MIT who proved that (in manufacturing) the more things you push through at once, the less comes out the other end. We find the same is true with our portfolio companies.
Lower-middle-market companies don’t struggle with a lack of ideas. They often struggle because they have too many. Our longtime friend and now-retired portfolio CEO, Rick Noble, liked to say that every company he walked into had either no plan or too many plans; neither is good, but the latter is way worse.
It’s what we regularly see in diligence. Founders at small companies come back from a customer meeting excited about a new feature, greenlight it, then move on to something else. Some poor employees work on it for a year and never finish before moving on to the next thing. We met a developer at a prospective investment who spent twelve months building a feature the customer later said they never even asked for.
Now, introduce four operating partners across four functions on top of a company like that, each one armed with their to-do list from the Value Creation Plan. And you can’t blame them. That’s what they were hired for, and many of them are charging their time back to the portfolio company, so they have an incentive to be busy billing companies. It’s usually work that needs to get done. But does it need to be done right now, given the other projects underway and the team’s bandwidth? When this happens, you don’t get more done. You get less. I know, because we were making these mistakes, too.
And one of two things happens. You are either confusing the management team by loading up competing initiatives and slowing things down. Or you are propping up a management team incapable of tackling these projects themselves. The former is forgivable and fixable; the latter is potentially catastrophic for your returns. In private equity, we love to say that we “back great management teams.” If they’re so great, why do they need so much help?
What is our approach after years of trying to fly at the right altitude? We try to provide the exact right solution at the exact right time and then get out of the way. Sixty to ninety days. Pick a thing. Finish it. Move on. We want to be an effective extension of the team, a simplifier, or a force multiplier. If we find ourselves doing things that the management team should be capable of doing themselves, then we have the wrong team, and we should make a change. One of my sayings is that “we are in the management selection business, not the management rehabilitation business.” Most portfolio ops people I know love to rehabilitate people. It feels like coaching and mentorship, but it’s actually propping up people who shouldn’t need that much help. By doing less, or at least only the essentials, you quickly find out whether you have the right management team.
I Don’t Care About Your Pipeline
Technology hit 33% of global buyout deal value in 20242. When Jim and I started almost thirty years ago, it was maybe single digits. Tech has become the dominant sector exposure for LPs over the past twenty years, and to keep that machine running, every tech-focused fund has built an army of deal sourcers. And unlike back in the day when you could build a differentiated sourcing machine, today everyone uses the same tools – DealCloud, Affinity, Salesforce, PitchBook, Grata, Apollo, LinkedIn, and now with AI, custom agents to research and scrape data from the Internet. Oh, and don’t forget the Inc. 5000 list, which is the new Yellow Pages for biz dev teams.
This arms race needs inventory. And lately, that inventory is at smaller PE funds like ParkerGale. I get it. Big funds have a job to do, and that job requires constantly building a funnel of new investment opportunities. And when they show up on Monday morning to report on that funnel to their boss, they are going to make damn sure that funnel is full. What gets measured gets done they say. Well, guess who is on the other side of that funnel report? Me. We get dozens of emails every week about the dozen companies we own. And guys, you all sound the same. And you all have the same request. My time! To set aside some of it to tell you about the companies we own, how they are doing, and when we plan to sell them to you.
Very few offer me anything in return.
Here’s the thing. I’ve gotta source, too. But I believe differentiated sourcing is more of a “give” business than a “get” business. Offer something valuable before you ask for anything in return. You get pulled into a conversation because you have access, insight, or a unique skill from which someone can benefit. You meet a founder (or me) through someone they already trust, after reading something you wrote, after hearing you on a podcast. That’s a funnel that converts. It is the long game. And it doesn’t show up on the Monday pipeline report, which is why most of the industry is still doing it the same way. You should try the new way. Trust me. It works.
Add-Ons: From Strategy to Crutch
Add-ons were about half of all private equity deals in 2014, according to PitchBook. They hit 80% in the last few years.3 For healthcare services rollups, fine — you buy another dentist office in the next town over until you have saturated a geography — that’s the whole strategy. For software companies, it’s a lot harder. In the last ten years, we have seen the buy-and-build playbook applied to tech. But what usually happens is someone buys a half-dozen companies on a half-dozen stacks with four roadmaps, calls it a platform, and reports pro forma EBITDA to show their LPs it’s compounding. That worked in a short window post-pandemic when debt was free, diligence was quick, and hold times compressed. Integration was the upside for the next buyer. That game is over. Now, with organic growth rates coming down across software, funds roll out the roll-up strategy to create value. Be careful.
We are purists, so we’ve done acquisitions in only about half of our companies. With a co-founder like Jim and a partner like Paul, who have votes at the IC, I don’t get to buy a tuck-in unless we can integrate its products into the business’s core tech stack and run them through our existing go-to-market channels. Add-ons that work are the ones that were integrated to the studs — one codebase, one go-to-market motion, and integrated, simplified reporting. And as AI becomes the dominant conversation when underwriting new deals and acquisitions, not only your codebase, but how you produce and test the code, will become even more critical to your exit value. Buying stuff for scale and profit works outside of software, but poorly executed consolidation can slow growth and innovation and become an albatross for tech funds when it comes time to sell.
Nobody Actually Stays Small
Every emerging manager starts their pitch with the same speech: we like the small end of the market, where 85% of the companies live, and only 15% of the capital chases them. We’re gonna stay small! That is until the next fundraise. When the fund doubles. And then doubles again. I get it. AUM scales nicely, and the fees are great. And some funds have proven that bigger is better for their strategy.
But that is more the exception than the rule. As StepStone found, funds that more than doubled in size posted a 6-percentage-point decline in IRR versus the prior fund.4 Why? Fewer deals, more competition for each one, higher entry prices, and a narrower set of buyers on the way out. It’s just math.
We have chosen the path that the math supports. More companies to chase, fewer funds to compete with, funds sized to keep deployment steady, and potential upside where a single great outcome can move the needle for the whole fund. Finding companies and recruiting experienced management teams down here at the small end of the market is more challenging, but, for us, it’s also so much more rewarding. Like Dolly Parton says, “figure out who you are and then do it on purpose.” We figured it out a decade ago, and it feels like we’re just getting good at this, so why go up-market and learn new ways of operating?
The Next Ten Years
The through-line of the last ten years, at least the way we lived it, was this: don’t be afraid to change your mind; do less, but do it better; build community, not pipelines; create enduring businesses, don’t just deploy capital; and be content with who you are and what you’re good at.
We won’t wait this long to check in again. Or maybe Ryan and Nori will have wrestled the mic and keyboard out of our hands by then, and they’ll share what they’ve learned ten years after putting up with Jim and me. I wonder which of these lessons will look obvious in hindsight, which will look dumb, and which ones stand the test of time.
