You rush into the Monday meeting straight from an expert call on the structural dynamics of the HVAC servicing industry, and your bosses are talking about “GP-led secondaries” like it’s a normal thing people discuss over coffee. You nod. You write it down. You Google it back at your desk.
We’ve all been there. Doesn’t matter if you’re a first-year Associate, CEO meeting PE folks for the first time, or a VP at a family office pretending to remember the difference between American and European waterfalls. Like every industry, Private Equity runs on jargon. And boy, is there a lot of it. Nobody handed you a glossary on day one.
So we made one.
I sat down with two of ParkerGale’s Associates (Niko and Liz, making their FunCast debut) to cover every term we could fit in an hour. What follows is the companion piece. Listen to the episode for the full conversation (including an argument about whether the term “bagger” comes from baseball or literally stuffing money in a bag). This is the cheat sheet you keep open on your phone.
The Basics
Private Equity vs. Private Credit. Equity is the ownership side. Credit is the debt side. Private credit is basically non-bank lenders making loans to private companies, and it has ballooned since the Global Financial Crisis (from about $300B to $3T). PE owns the company. Private credit lends to it. Both sit under the private markets umbrella.
Buyout vs. Growth Equity vs. Venture. Buyout means you’re buying a majority of an existing business. Growth equity means you’re buying a minority stake in an existing business. Venture means you’re buying small pieces of business that might or might not exist yet. Oh, and you get to be wrong 90% of the time and still keep your job. A buyout fund might have, like, 10 investments. A Growth Equity fund might have 30. A venture fund might have 100. Different math, different temperaments, different outfits.
Lower Middle Market / Middle Market / Large-Mega. These are the fund size tiers. The lower middle market is where ParkerGale lives. We buy founder-owned software companies. We write small checks (well, small for private equity, big for most normal people). Large-Mega funds include Blackstone, Apollo, KKR, Thoma Bravo, and many others. Everything in between is “Middle Market,” which is a range so wide it’s almost meaningless. Think TA, Summit, Berkshire. A lot of firms market themselves as Lower Middle Market when they’re really big. It’s the PE version of the kids who called themselves working class despite their family being actually pretty loaded, but they didn’t belong to the nice country club like their friends.
Firm vs. fund. The firm is the company that manages the funds. ParkerGale is a firm. The fund is the vehicle you invest out of. Some firms come up with fancier names for their funds. We are boring or maybe we couldn’t be bothered. A firm can have many funds over time. Maybe even many funds covering many different products. We’re investing out of Fund 3 right now. Fund 3 is separate from Fund 2, which is separate from Fund 1. Different LPs, different companies, different carry splits among the team, different vintages.
Vintage. The year a fund was formed or activated. Yes, it’s a wine term. Yes, PE guys like wine, I guess. Niko calls it the “bougie-ness factor,” which, coming from a kid from the western’ burbs, is totally accurate.
GP and LP. General Partners run the fund, make investments, and manage portfolio companies. Limited Partners commit the capital for the GPs to invest. LPs are often college endowments, charitable foundations, pension funds, insurance companies, wealthy individuals, funds of funds, and family offices. The GPs call the shots on investments. The LPs write the checks and provide governance for the GPs. And yes, a wealthy general practitioner (GP) could also be an LP just to confuse you a little more.
2 and 20. The way GPs get paid. GPs usually charge a 2% annual management fee on committed capital (which covers expenses) and take 20% of profits (the carried interest) once returns exceed the hurdle rate. When Jim and Devin were fundraising in Europe, Jim was in hotel room 2, and Devin was in room 20. We thought it was a sign. We went 0 for 5 on that trip. The PE gods were having fun with us that week.
Hurdle rate. The minimum return (usually 8% compounded annually) that the fund must meet before the GP earns any carried interest. If you deliver below 8% IRR net of fees and expenses? No carry. This is the LP’s protection. It also means the GP is highly motivated to beat an 8% annual return.
Carried interest (carry). The GP’s share of the profits above the hurdle rate. Typically, 20%, but some funds have negotiated higher. This 20% is allocated across the PE firm’s team and usually varies from one fund to the next. You might have 5% of carry in one fund and 15% in the next. It’s one thing that everyone negotiates heavily in private, and nobody talks about publicly.
European vs. American Waterfall. When the carry gets paid. In funds with a European Waterfall, all the money goes back to LPs first (plus the 8%), and then carry is distributed. In funds with an American Waterfall, carry can be paid out along the way, with each exit, as long as the IRR is above the hurdle rate. The risk with American Waterfalls is that you might get a check early in the fund’s life, spend it, and then owe it back if the fund underperforms and dips below the hurdle rate. That’s called a clawback, and it’s exactly as painful as it sounds.
Clawback. You were paid carry you didn’t earn, and now the LPs want it back! You may have already bought a house with it. You may have put it in a 529 account. Doesn’t matter. You must pay back the LPs to restore balance. The only good news is you don’t have to pay back the money you paid the IRS in taxes. Don’t you feel better now?
Capital call. When a GP needs money to close a deal, they “call” it from their LPs. The money for the fund doesn’t sit in your bank account waiting to be invested. It sits in the LP’s account waiting to be called. We send a notice that says, “We need 10% of your commitment for the acquisition of Acme Anvil Corp,” and they wire it over. They usually have about ten days to send it.
Dry powder. This just means committed capital that GPs haven’t called from LPs yet. It’s a good thing when you want to buy something in an attractive market. It’s a bad thing when the whole industry has a trillion of it, and nobody can find any deals to put it in.
Investment period. LPs typically give GPs five years to make their initial platform investments. This is called the investment period. After year five, GPs can only call capital for fees and expenses, and to fund follow-on investments in existing portfolio companies. Use it or lose it. For the first five years, GPs charge fees on committed capital (think the headline number of the fund size). After year five, GPs can only charge fees on invested capital (the actual money invested in the companies).
J Curve. Early in a fund’s life, the IRR is negative because all you have done is call capital from LPs for fees, expenses, and new platform investments before the companies you own appreciate in value more than the capital you’ve called. This is called the “in the J Curve.” The chart looks like the bottom of a J. The only way out is to increase the value of your portfolio companies through execution and, maybe, an early exit. Hopefully, you replace the J Curve with a hockey stick in the end.
Recycling. If you have a quick hit and return capital from an investment within a certain window (24 months at ParkerGale), you can reinvest it into a new deal instead of returning it to your LPs. It’s like getting extra at-bats at the batting cages. More capital deployed means bigger potential returns for the fund.
Secondaries. This happens when someone sells their position in a fund to someone else. LP-led secondaries usually mean an LP sells its fund position to another LP. You’ve probably heard of university endowments packaging up positions in old funds to sell on a secondary market to provide liquidity or to rebalance the portfolio. GP-led secondaries usually mean the GP itself is restructuring a fund — typically through a continuation vehicle (CV), where you take an asset (or multiple assets) out of one fund to put into a new fund so you can hold on longer. CVs were never much of a thing until the past several years, and now they account for a significant % of industry liquidity. There are also things called GP stakes, where an investor buys a piece of the GP itself, giving them a stake in the GP’s and its funds’ future fees and carry.
Zombie fund. A fund run by a firm that’s never going to raise a successor fund. The last act. Maybe their track record is bad. Maybe there is no succession plan. But the GP is still collecting management fees and managing investments, trying to get above the hurdle rate or avoid a clawback. LPs are in a pickle and don’t like being in zombie funds.
Deal Talk
Proprietary. Deals you find without bankers involved. We call these “direct” because we’re dealing directly with the owner. 17 of our 25 platform investments since 2008 were direct, plus 30 of 38 add-on investments. LPs roll their eyes the second anyone says “proprietary” in a meeting. If this were a drinking game, they’d be horizontal by lunch. Everyone claims their deals are proprietary. They aren’t.
Auction. A banker runs a process, multiple buyers compete. There are different kinds of auctions – broad auctions, which might include 100 buyers, and targeted processes, which may sound intimate but involve only a couple of dozen firms.
Fireside chat (FSC). No actual fire involved, though Niko suggests a Yule Log Zoom background, which is both funny and sad. An FSC is usually a 90-minute introductory call with the management team before an auction launches. Supposed to feel cozy and exclusive (you’re by the fire, one-on-one, hot cocoa in hand). In reality, the bankers probably scheduled 30 of these, and every seat in the conference room (or every box on Zoom) is filled. They do help give interested buyers a head start before things get hectic. Quick aside, saying FSC saves you zero syllables, so what is the point actually?
Management presentation (MP). The full-blown, four-hour, bring-everyone deep dive in-person meeting. This is where the deal team really gets into it with management. If a fireside chat is the first date, the MP is Thanksgiving dinner with the whole family, even crazy Uncle Phil (who is either the retired CEO the PE fund found on GLG brings or the CTO from the target company, depending on which side of the table you’re sitting on). Oh, and there is always a poor Analyst from the bank at the end of the table typing on his laptop. Never looks up. Never makes eye contact.
CIM / CIP. All the same thing, this is the document that describes the business to potential buyers. CIM stands for “Confidential Information Memorandum.” CIP is “Confidential Information Presentation.” Old guys like Devin still call it a business plan. No one knows what he’s talking about. Niko thinks CIP is the new CIM. Liz says it’s whatever the banker puts on the PDF. She’s right, as usual.
IOI (Indication of Interest). Your first bid in an auction. An attractive company might get 20-30 IOIs. It can be a little loose. You give a price range, some conditions, and next steps, signal your seriousness, test the waters. Bankers use IOIs to narrow the field. Some firms bid high to get to the next stage and then walk their number down later. Bankers keep notes on who does this. It’s not a good look.
LOI (Letter of Intent). Your real bid after doing more work after the IOI. This is the proposal you will stick with if accepted. Lots more detail than the IOI. Specific price, specific terms, exclusivity, contingent on completion of due diligence, yada, yada. If an IOI is a first date, the LOI is the engagement. (Niko and Liz both recently got engaged, separately, not to each other, which made this analogy very easy.)
Q of E (Quality of Earnings). You hire a third-party accounting firm to scrub every number the seller gave you. The bankers gave you the financials. You did your own work. Now someone independent goes through every journal entry, and either confirms the picture or finds surprises. Your IC and your lenders both need to see that a clean Q of E was completed.
Q of R (Quality of Revenue) / Customer Cube / Retention Analysis. This lays out every customer, by product, by month. Upsell, downsell, churn to see if customers are sticking around and buying more, or slowly disappearing? For recurring revenue businesses, this analysis gets you to Gross Revenue Retention (GRR) and Net Revenue Retention (NRR), two of the most important metrics. It’s often called a “cube” because it’s multidimensional, though, sadly, not three-dimensional. This is the single most important analysis we do on a deal. With a clean customer cube, we would be within 10% of the price we’d pay for a business.
Comps (comparables). What did similar companies sell for? Comparables taken from recent, similar private transactions with similar companies in the same industry, as well as valuations of relevant public companies. Comps move up and down as the market changes. Everyone picks the comps that make their argument look best. The seller and bankers want the prettiest comps. The buyer wants the ugliest.
Investment Committee (IC). Where the deal team presents everything they’ve learned from due diligence, and the full partnership votes yes or no on the investment. At bigger PE firms, you’re probably having check-ins with the IC along the way instead of at the end. If it gets voted down, you just spent months and millions on a deal that’s now dead.
Haircut / Retrade. Cutting the price after you’ve already bid. “Haircut” sounds friendly. Who hates a haircut, right? Little kids mostly, but that’s it. They’re the same thing, though sometimes you go to the barber for a little trim around the ears before picture day. A retrade? Well, that’s a summer buzzcut, no hiding it. Sometimes a haircut is justified — the business missed its numbers during diligence. Sometimes retrades become a strategy — bid high, get deep into the process, then cut the price to test the seller’s stamina. Firms that do this get a reputation (not a good one). Don’t be a re-trader.
Pari passu. Latin for “on equal footing.” If investors are on the same terms as each other, it’s called pari passu. Maybe you’re all in at the same valuation, too. Niko thought it was a French dessert when he first heard it. Understandably, it does sound like tiramisu. But that’s Italian, right? Devin was Co-Counsel of Albany High School’s Latin Club. Dum spiro, spero!
Platform. Your initial investment. It’s the company you build around. Your fund might have 10 platform investments. Those platforms might do twenty add-on acquisitions. Relatively new term. As Devin says, “Back in the day, we just called it an investment.” Ok boomer.
Money Stuff
IRR (Internal Rate of Return). The annualized return. Comes in Gross (before fees) and Net (after fees). Net is what LPs actually get, and it’s the only one they care about. They can’t spend the Gross IRR. When someone just says “IRR” without specifying which one, ask which one they mean.
MOIC (Multiple on Invested Capital). Invested 100, got back 300 — that’s a 3x MOIC. Simple, satisfying, harder to game than IRR. LPs care about both, but MOIC is harder to argue with. Now, MOIC usually refers to a single platform investment in a fund. It’s almost always quoted as the Gross MOIC. You can calculate Net MOIC (and you have to show it when fundraising), but almost everyone talking about MOICs is talking Gross MOIC.
Bagger. A 3x return is a three-bagger. A 7x is a seven-bagger. Devin thinks it’s from baseball (three bags, three bases). Niko thinks it’s from literally stuffing money in a bag. The podcast episode does not resolve this debate, though Niko’s is a much more compelling visual, you have to admit. Nobody talks about their one-baggers.
Multiple Expansion. Say you bought the company for 5x revenue and you sold it for 7x revenue. The “multiple” expanded by two turns. This is the dream. If revenue grew while you owned it, and you got multiple expansion at exit, chef’s kiss.
Add-On / Bolt-On / Tuck-In Again, here’s one where there are many words for the same thing. They all mean buying another company and combining it with your platform. A tuck-in usually means it’s small — it gets absorbed, maybe loses its name. A bolt-on might be bigger, extending the business into something new, but it doesn’t get integrated deeply.
Buy & Build / Roll-Up: Usually, these terms refer to an investment strategy that revolves around M&A. Slow-growing, fragmented industries are ripe for roll-ups. You’re not driving a lot of organic growth; you are driving value through combining multiple, similar companies and getting cost savings from consolidating shared services like finance, G&A, and shared services. Funeral homes and Internet Service Providers were rolled up in the 90s. HVAC service providers, landscapers, and pest control companies are getting rolled up today.
Dividend recap. Recapitalizing the business to return money to shareholders before a full exit, usually led by a lender. Capital is put on the balance sheet so the existing owners can pay themselves a dividend while retaining their ownership. It can extend the appetite to hold a platform longer because you’ve taken money off the table along the way. This can be a highly controversial practice when too many (or too big) dividend recaps lead to bankruptcy or distress to the business. These get the headlines that keep the PE industry’s reputation in the dumps.
Recapitalization. This is just like a dividend recap, but dropping the word “dividend” usually means it’s being led by another equity investor. Instead of a lender, another private equity fund invests money to buy, say, 40% of your platform company. The use of proceeds is to buy stock from existing shareholders. You take money off the table, and the new investor now owns 40% of the company, unlike a dividend recap, where you aren’t selling shares, just adding debt to the balance sheet.
Finance Bro-Speak
These terms are all real. Sometimes we use them. We’re not proud of it. Some of them deserve a swear jar.
Value creation. We kick off this section with the Holy Grail of PE jargon. Every time someone says this phrase, an Operating Partner gets his wings. Private equity creates value. Meanwhile, the company’s CEO, CFO, and CTO are just doing their actual jobs. But sure, the PE firm sitting in an office 500 miles away is “creating value.” You need a value creation plan. You need a value creation deck. You need a consultant to help you create the value. Say it with me: vertical integration value creation!
White space. Untapped market opportunity. You need more of it. Always. How do you create value? Find more white space. How do you find more white space? Bolt-ons. What does a Bolt-on get you? TAM expansion. This term is sometimes confused with the actual white space on a PowerPoint slide, which is not allowed in the value creation deck.
Blue Ocean / Red Ocean. Blue ocean refers to an uncompetitive market with many opportunities for growth. Red ocean is the opposite, a competitive market, blood in the water. Originated from a business book. Gets used in value-creation meetings as if it’s a geographic fact.
De-Risk. This just means to mitigate risk, but with fewer syllables to add more gravitas. As Liz points out, it’s like “deplaning.” You don’t get off a plane, you deplane. You don’t reduce risk, you de-risk. It’s the same thing, just with a prefix.
Move the Needle. Everything has to move the needle. If it doesn’t move the needle, why are we even doing it? What’s the needle we’re moving? Whatever you’re picturing, that needle desperately needs moving.
Unique Angle. The politest way to turn down a deal. “We loved the business. We just don’t have a unique angle.” Translation: we’re not going to win this one, and we don’t want to say why. It’s a perfect catch-all – vague enough to never be wrong, specific enough to sound thoughtful.
Basic Blocking and Tackling. What PE people say when they want a management team to do the easy and obvious stuff. Niko, a former offensive lineman, would like you to know that actual blocking and tackling are extremely difficult, and nothing about them is basic. If you’d like to find out for yourself, he’s available Saturdays mornings in Grant Park. Evaluations start promptly at 9 AM.
Pull the Levers. Execute the plan. But you can’t just say “do the plan.” You must pull levers. Some levers are big. Some are small. Nobody specifies which ones are which. Niko pictures a henchman pulling a lever and a trapdoor opening. “You didn’t do the basic blocking and tackling, so now we have to pull the lever!” That is honestly the most accurate visual of the PE–management dynamic in this market.
Net Net. Means “the bottom line.” But you can’t just say “net.” It always has to be “net net” for some reason. Liz admits she’s spent an embarrassing amount of time trying to figure out what the second “net” adds. Her best theory: one net for what goes in, one for what comes out? Net net, we’ll never know.
Quantum. The amount of debt. But you can’t just say “amount” because doesn’t “quantum” sound so much smarter? And you never say “quantum of debt” — just “what’s the quantum?” Like it’s a physics concept. It also feels like quantum is always a big number. A million? That’s not quantum enough. A hundred million? A billion? Now we’re talking quantum.
Industrial Logic. Means “it makes sense.” But instead of saying that, you say “the industrial logic here is compelling.” If you start that sentence with “from our perspective,” you are just racking up the Scrabble points. We’ll mostly blame investment bankers for the overuse of this phrase. But like Greek debt, the contagion is spreading its way through the surrounding territory into mid-level PE speak.
The unlock. What you find when you pull the levers in the white space after de-risking the plan. “That’s the unlock.” The unlock of what? Doesn’t matter. It’s the unlock. Pair it with “move the needle” for maximum bro density.
The full podcast episode has all of this and more — including why Devin thinks CIMs are always in portrait mode and CIPs are landscape (Liz wisely disputes this), whether Chicago actually sorts its recycling (probably not), and Niko getting a crash course in 90s band references.
Listen to the episode. Keep this post open during your next IC meeting and play PE Lingo Bingo with your cubicle mates.

If you missed the Claude Mythos Preview release yesterday, here are the two numbers that matter:
- $50 for a successful run that identified a 27-year-old signed-integer-overflow bug in OpenBSD’s TCP SACK implementation, according to Anthropic’s red team.
- Under $2,000 to autonomously build an N-day exploit chain for a 17-year-old remote code execution vulnerability in FreeBSD, the kind that lets an unauthenticated attacker append their SSH key to root’s authorized_keys file over NFS.
Read those twice.
For the last twenty years, the economics of finding zero-days have been one of the quiet constraints on enterprise software risk. Attackers needed expensive, scarce human talent to find bugs and turn them into working exploits. Defenders needed the same kind of talent to patch and harden systems. The asymmetry was real, but it was bounded. There was still a labor curve on both sides.
Anthropic may have just put that attacker-side labor curve on a countdown clock.
What Mythos actually did
The details matter here because these are not abstract benchmark wins.
According to Anthropic’s own capability assessment:
- Mythos produced 595 crashes at severity tiers 1 to 2. Previous Claude models reportedly landed around 150 to 175 on the same testbed, implying a roughly 3 to 4x increase in high-severity findings per unit of effort.
- It achieved full control-flow hijack on 10 separate targets at tier 5, the highest severity in Anthropic’s rubric. In plain English: not just bug discovery, but exploit construction that can actually take over the machine.
- It achieved 181 successful Firefox exploits versus 2 for Opus 4.6. That is not an incremental gain. That is a category shift.
- On a manually reviewed sample, Anthropic reported an 89% exact validation rate. If that held across the full corpus, the test program would imply more than 1,000 additional critical-severity vulnerabilities.
These are not toy results on synthetic code. The examples involve real software: OpenBSD, FreeBSD, Firefox, FFmpeg, TLS, SSH, AES-GCM. In other words, the plumbing of the modern internet.
And the examples are not trivial. Anthropic describes the FreeBSD NFS exploit as a 20-gadget ROP chain split across six sequential RPC requests, using kernel UUID values to bypass authentication. That is the kind of chained exploit work that used to require very capable human operators.
Mythos produced it autonomously. For under two grand.
Anthropic’s framing, and where I’d push back
Anthropic’s public framing is defensible: over time, defenders may benefit more than attackers. If AI can find bugs faster, it can also help review, patch, validate, inventory, and harden software faster. In the long run, that could reduce the number of vulnerable systems worldwide.
I think that is plausible in the long run.
I am less convinced in the medium term, especially for the part of the economy running on brittle, aging infrastructure.
That defender-wins story depends on two shaky assumptions for most companies.
First, it assumes defenders will adopt as fast as attackers. In practice, defensive adoption moves through procurement, compliance, security review, legal review, budget cycles, and executive attention. Attackers do not have that bureaucracy. If Mythos-class capability leaks, diffuses, or is approximated elsewhere, the attacker's side gets operational leverage faster than the average company gets through a pilot.
Second, it assumes vulnerable software can actually be patched quickly. That is where the theory collides with the server room. A huge amount of production software cannot be changed rapidly, not because fixes are unavailable, but because the systems are brittle, under-owned, poorly inventoried, or tied to legacy workflows where every patch is a controlled detonation.
That is why I think Mythos does not threaten all software equally.
The biggest near-term repricing of risk is in legacy software.
Not only there. But there first, and there hardest.
The evidence points in that direction. The showcase bugs are old. The FreeBSD vulnerability is 17 years old. The OpenBSD bug is roughly 27 years old. Anthropic also notes that exploiting a production memory-safe virtual machine monitor was materially harder than finding the decades-old OpenBSD bug. That is not proof that modern systems are safe. It is a useful signal that old, low-velocity, memory-unsafe, weakly maintained systems are where the economics change fastest.
So I would not say “AI eats software” without qualification.
I would say this instead: AI is changing attacker-defender economics across software, but the pain arrives first where patch velocity is slow, ownership is fuzzy, and the oldest code still sits inside the blast radius.
That describes many mid-market companies. And a lot of portfolio companies.
The operator conversation that just moved up the list
If you are a PE operator, board member, CIO, or CTO, the question is no longer whether this matters. The question is: where does it matter in your stack?
I think about tech priorities in three buckets: risk mitigation, cost reduction, and revenue enhancement. Most portfolio companies spend their oxygen on buckets two and three because that is where the value-creation story lives. Risk mitigation is the category everyone agrees is important and nobody wants to overfund, because on the EBITDA line, it looks like a cost without applause.
Mythos just changed that tradeoff.
The question to ask every portfolio company in the next 30 days is not “what cloud are we on?” or “what security tools do we buy?”
It is this:
What does our software stack actually look like, and how old is the oldest critical component we depend on?
Not the architecture slide. Not the cloud posture deck. The real production footprint. What is the gnarliest piece of legacy code in the blast radius, who owns it, what is its patch status, and what happens if it gets popped?
Most companies cannot answer that honestly in one meeting. That is the first finding.
Once they can answer it, the second finding is usually that the answer is worse than leadership thought.
And then comes the part where operators earn their keep: sequencing migration and remediation work against every other value-creation initiative in flight. Nobody wants to stop the roadmap to rebuild old infrastructure. The project is slow, boring, and invisible. No customer celebrates it. The only visible outcome is the absence of a future breach.
That was already a hard sell.
Now it is urgent.
The Maginot Line problem
Here is the military-history version.
For years, software defense has often resembled the Maginot Line: layers of static defenses, confidence in fixed perimeters, and a tacit assumption that the attacker’s execution cost would keep most threats at manageable levels.
That logic works until the attacker’s cost structure changes.
Then the fortification becomes a monument.
That is the real signal in Mythos.
The defensive answer is not simply more walls. It is the thing institutions usually learn too late: logistics and mobility matter more than fortification.
In software, patch and migration velocity matter more than the number of security tools in the slide deck.
If you can patch critical systems in 48 hours and migrate off fragile dependencies in 90 days, you are in much better shape. If you are on a 30-day patch cycle and your legacy modernization plan has been sitting on a roadmap for five years waiting for a budget fairy, then you have a problem, and it is not one your security vendor can solve with a prettier dashboard.
What I’d actually do
Over the next 90 days, I’d do four things, in order:
- Inventory ruthlessly. Every portfolio company should have a current map of critical software dependencies in production. Not what was true in 2023. The actual environment. Languages, versions, patch state, owners, business criticality. If the CTO cannot produce a credible version of that in a week, that is your first finding.
- Shorten the patch cycle on the legacy surface. Not the shiny modern stack. The old middleware, old operating systems, long-lived services, and brittle infrastructure nobody wants to touch. Whatever the patch SLA is for those systems, cut it aggressively. If that is operationally impossible, that is your second finding.
- Pull forward the migration roadmap on the oldest critical dependencies. The 15-year-old middleware. The 17-year-old component. The subsystem whose original author left during the Obama administration. This is the valley-of-anguish work. It is still thankless. It is also less optional than it was six months ago.
- Rewrite incident response assumptions around faster exploit timelines. The old playbook often assumed that attackers needed meaningful time to operationalize a new vulnerability. That assumption is getting weaker. Detection, triage, and containment have to compress with it.
None of this is glamorous. None of it belongs on a growth slide. All of it is the work that separates companies that compound value from companies that discover, expensively and in public, that deferred modernization was not actually free.
One more thing
Anthropic has been careful here, and they deserve some credit for that. Mythos Preview is being released through Project Glasswing to a narrow set of high-trust defensive customers. That buys the defender some time.
But some time is not unlimited time.
Once a capability has been demonstrated, it does not quietly un-happen. Other labs will get there. Comparable systems will emerge. Some will leak. Some will be approximated. Some will simply become standard features in broader model families.
The board-level question is not “how do we block this?”
You cannot block it.
The question is whether, over the next year, you become the company that used the window to modernize its most fragile systems, or the company that spent the year putting more signs on the Maginot Line.
That answer is going to show up somewhere.
Possibly in your exit multiple.
