I. The Panic
It is Monday, February 23, 2026, and by 9:30 in the morning, my group chat is on fire.
The iShares Expanded Tech-Software Sector ETF (IGV) is down nearly five percent before lunch. Year-to-date, it’s off about 30%. ServiceNow, Salesforce, and Adobe have each shed about a third of their value since January. One trillion dollars in market value vanished in seven days. Short interest in IGV sat near 19%, close to an all-time high. January 2026 was already the worst January in IGV’s history: down 15%, worse than the dot-com crash, worse than the GFC, worse than March 2020. Hedge funds had already made $24 billion shorting software stocks in 2026 alone.
The trigger for the February 23 sell-off was a 4,000-word thought exercise published by Citrini Research on Substack over the weekend, titled The 2028 Global Intelligence Crisis. The piece described a hypothetical future in which AI agents mature, white-collar layoffs accelerate, private credit defaults pile up, and unemployment hits 10%. It went viral when Michael Burry (you know, Christian Bale from The Big Short) amplified it to his millions of X followers with the comment, “And you think I’m bearish.” Boom goes the dynamite.
What wasn’t clear at first was that the report was quietly co-authored by Alap Shah, Chief Investment Officer of Lotus Technology Management, a hedge fund that had a trade on. DoorDash, Asana, Monday.com, ServiceNow, credit card companies, and some large public PE funds were in his sights. On Bloomberg Television the following day, Shah confessed that Lotus held “a set of shorts against businesses that we think are going to be disrupted by AI.” A hot dog truck crashed through a storefront. The guy in the hot dog costume said it wasn’t him.
Don’t get me wrong. Short sellers do useful work. They are often the ones in the room telling the truth. Legendary short seller Jim Chanos makes deeply rational arguments against fraud, excess, and exuberance. He called Boston Market in the 1990s, Enron in the early 2000s, and he’s been after Tesla’s accounting shenanigans for years. But Jim is transparent about his book. The Citrini scenario describes real risks for real companies, but let’s be honest, the guy had a trade on, and social media helped it go parabolic.
This piece came on the heels of another essay that had already found its way into everyone’s inbox earlier in February. Matt Shumer, CEO and co-founder of OthersideAI, published Something Big Is Happening on LinkedIn. He described the moment he realized he could describe software he wanted built, walk away from his computer for a few hours, and come back to perfectly executed code. The piece reached approximately 50 million readers, about a dozen of whom forwarded it to me asking what it meant for their kids.
And if investors needed real-world validation that AI was coming for their jobs, Jack Dorsey announced on February 27 that he was cutting 40% of Block’s headcount due to AI-driven “efficiencies.” For the shortest month of the year, February had some real bangers for jittery software investors.
Ethan Mollick, the Wharton professor and author of Co-Intelligence: Living and Working with AI, examined these events and concluded that these “were not what they first appeared to be.” The Citrini report was a “fictional scenario” from a little-known firm that happened to strike a nerve. And the Block layoffs, he argued, likely used AI as cover for cuts necessary after years of mismanagement and COVID-era bloat, a move that coined the term “AI-washing” to blame AI for operational cleanup.
Software stocks fell 60% to 80% during the dot-com crash. They fell 40% in summer 2022 after interest rates started rising. Each time, the obituaries were written. Each time, most patients recovered, and many thrived. From what we see inside our dozen portfolio companies every day, nothing fundamental has changed yet. Employees are still humans, sales still have cycles, and competitors still say whatever it takes to win the deal. Some tools we employ to professionalize our companies just got a lot cooler, creating a huge opportunity to move faster, build what our customers want, and make our most ambitious employees more effective at work.
One note of caution before we dive deeper. I have a trade on here, too. I am long enterprise software, across three funds. I’m talking my book. But I have also been investing in small, scrappy enterprise software companies for 30 years. I started my career covering public software companies at William Blair before moving into private equity. I have a good sense of public market investor dynamics. This longevity gives me some perspective, and I want to share what I think as someone who’s lived and invested through a few freakouts.
II. The Pattern
The science fiction writer William Gibson said in the late 1990s, “The future is already here, it’s just not very evenly distributed.” I’d add a corollary: the past is also unevenly distributed, which is why investors and market followers keep treating repeating cycles as novel ones. Every major computing platform shift of the last fifty years arrived with a credible argument that the incumbents were finished.
In the 1980s, the shift from mainframes to personal computers was supposed to end centralized enterprise computing. IBM mainframe software, repeatedly a dead man walking, became one of the most profitable software businesses in the world. While IBM has seen better days, it still generates $68 billion in revenue and $15 billion in free cash flow today.
In the 1990s, client-server architecture was supposed to kill on-premise software, and with it, the on-prem poster child SAP. What happened? SAP grew from roughly $500 million in revenue in 1992 to over $32 billion today. My best friend since I was four has been working on the same SAP implementation for over twenty years. Not because it doesn’t work. Because it works so well, the project keeps expanding to new departments and geographies.
The open web arrived in August 1995, when Netscape went public and traded up to $2.9 billion on its first day. Marc Andreessen declared that Netscape would reduce Microsoft to “a poorly debugged set of device drivers.” His argument as a 24-year-old superstar at the time: the browser would become the new platform, making packaged software obsolete. Andreessen was on the cover of Time, and The Economist anointed him “The New Electronic Messiah.” By 1999, Microsoft’s Internet Explorer browser had secured 99% market share. Netscape was sold to AOL and abandoned. Windows still runs on a billion devices. Marc ended up ok. Most University of Illinois grads do.
The iPhone arrived in 2007 and was supposed to make enterprise software irrelevant. Gartner labeled consumerization “the most significant trend affecting IT in the next 10 years.” The thesis was that consumer app experiences (Evernote, Dropbox, Yammer) would displace clunky enterprise software from the bottom up. What actually happened? Enterprise software co-opted consumer hardware. Apple ended up partnering with IBM, SAP, and Cisco rather than displacing them. SAP’s own CIO bought 40,000 iPads.
The cloud transition is the richest and most recent example. By 2012, the conventional narrative was that Amazon had won the cloud war, Google was playing catch-up, and Microsoft had missed the wave. Microsoft's stock had gone nowhere for almost two decades despite quadrupling its revenue during that period. Satya Nadella took over as CEO in 2014 with revenue of $86 billion and a market cap of roughly $300 billion. His first email announced a mobile-first, cloud-first strategy that explicitly deprioritized Windows, the product that had made Microsoft, well, Microsoft. A decade later, revenue exceeds $230 billion. Azure grew from essentially zero to over $75 billion annually. The market cap hit $2.5 trillion. The stock appreciated nearly tenfold. The investors who wrote Microsoft off in 2012 missed the train. The cloud hadn’t passed Microsoft by. Instead, Microsoft’s transition to the cloud made it the powerhouse it is today. The company just needed someone with more vision and better dance moves than Steve Ballmer.
Not every company pulled it off. Siebel Systems dominated CRM in the early 2000s with roughly half the global market. It treated the cloud transition as a threat to its licensing model. Salesforce ate it alive, and Oracle acquired the carcass in 2006. Plenty of enterprise software players also got left behind. But there are many more cases of incumbents figuring it out than going the way of Siebel.
Every major technology platform shift is a visit from the Ghost of Software Future. The vision shown is stark. A world where your product is irrelevant, your customers have moved on to your competitors, and the market has reorganized around you. Siebel met the ghost and went back to sleep. Nadella met it and called an all-hands meeting. Across the software industry, the ghost appears about every ten years, and the companies that navigate the transition are those who treat the visit as a briefing, not a haunting. They see it as a premonition, not just a bad night’s sleep. And for those that don’t survive, the cause of death is often not competition, but self-inflicted wounds like fear, complacency, or hubris.
Steven Sinofsky, the former head of Microsoft Office and Windows, published a piece last month titled, not subtly, “Death of Software. Nah.” His conclusion: “AI changes what we build and who builds it, but not how much needs to be built. We need vastly more software, not less.” That line should be pinned above every Bloomberg terminal. While this line confirms my priors, it aligns well with my experience investing in enterprise software since the early 1990s. There is plenty of opportunity ahead for incumbents and startups to thrive.
III. The Bear Case
But let’s not dismiss the bears too quickly. I’ve been called a perma-bear throughout my career for my cautious approach to entry valuations. And I have infamously called five of the last two recessions, so take my opinions here with a healthy dose of humility.
I see four core arguments for the bear case, each of which is just true enough to instill fear in those looking to be scared. 1) AI-induced private credit stress at the large end of the software market will not stay contained; 2) Seat-based pricing models are vulnerable if AI agents replace humans and/or if AI decimates white-collar workers; 3) Vibe coding lowers barriers to software creation and will compress competitive moats that enterprise software companies have historically enjoyed; 4) In direct contrast to the first three, AI is a bubble ready to pop, and the subsequent collapse in capex from hyperscalers and data center buildouts will do lethal damage to an already vulnerable economy, whether the technology is valuable or not.
Private Credit
The private credit stress in software is real, it is not new, and it has been building for longer than the February sell-off would suggest. Pluralsight defaulted in 2024. Finastra, with more than $5 billion in debt (one of the largest private credit loans in history), spent months trying to refinance until Vista worked out a $1 billion NAV loan to help right-size the capital structure. Solera, ConvergeOne, and Ivanti have all shown varying degrees of stress. Debt at Medallia, the Thoma Bravo-backed customer experience software company, is now marked at about 78 cents on the dollar by Apollo and Blackstone (levels that technically qualify as distressed) while other lenders in the same loan hold it above 90 cents. One loan, several different marks. This is not a software vs AI story. It is a capital structure story with a transparency problem baked in.
The growth of private credit has been eye-popping. Private credit AUM has grown from roughly $300 billion in 2010 to over $3 trillion today, with high-net-worth retail investors accounting for nearly a quarter of that, according to S&P Global. Pressure to deploy that capital at attractive yields meant lending standards had to stretch somewhere. Recurring revenue loans (structures premised on software companies valued as a multiple of revenue rather than EBITDA) became the engine of the unitranche market. The math worked beautifully when rates were near zero, and software multiples were near their highs. It stopped working as rates rose and growth decelerated post-COVID. Companies financed under lower-for-longer assumptions found themselves short on free cash flow and in uncomfortable conversations with their lenders.
And recent headlines have not helped calm the market. New Mountain sold about half a billion dollars of credit assets at 94 cents on the dollar in late February, signaling to the market that even solid lenders were managing exposure. Blackstone and Blue Owl halted redemptions on private credit funds (what the industry calls “putting up the gates”), which was exactly the wrong headline at exactly the wrong moment. Now add the Cliffwater Corporate Lending Fund to the list. The $33 billion vehicle saw redemption requests nearly triple in a single quarter, jumping from 5.3% to nearly 14% in Q1 2026. Then John Zito, Co-President of Apollo’s asset management division, found himself above the fold on the front page of the Wall Street Journal on March 16, caught on tape at a UBS client meeting, saying, “I literally think all the marks are wrong” about private equity software valuations. He then predicted that lenders to generic mid-size leveraged software companies could recover only 20 to 40 cents on the dollar. Apollo’s PR team walked back the comments and assured analysts that software accounts for less than 2% of its assets under management, which tells you a lot about how seriously they took their assessment. When the people selling the fear are simultaneously distancing themselves from the exposure, you’re watching a market in the early stages of a narrative getting ahead of reality.
Here is the important distinction. If you believe AI will truly decimate enterprise software (eliminate the moats, vaporize the revenue, and make the underlying businesses worthless), then yes, private credit has a serious problem given its exposure to software assets. But that’s an argument you must win first. For Pluralsight, Medallia, and the others, it was leverage, not AI, that bit them. Too much debt, financed at the wrong rates, in businesses that didn’t perform. How is this different than any of the past cycles across industries? And if AI actually does eliminate white-collar jobs at the scale some are predicting, I am confident that private credit losses on software loans will be the least of our economic worries.
In the lower-middle market, the lending environment is structurally different. Recurring revenue loans are closer to 0.5x revenue and 3x to 4x EBITDA. Most loans have liquidity covenants that build in a cushion to fix things before they get too bad. Debt is just one of the tools we can use to drive acceptable risk-adjusted returns. In many larger deals, debt is the primary tool to drive them.
One thing worth noting before we leave this topic. The problems in private credit, real as they are, are largely landing in institutional portfolios rather than bank deposits. That is structurally better than where these risks have historically accumulated. Pension funds, sovereign wealth funds, and sophisticated family offices can absorb markdowns in ways that depositors cannot. The duration mismatch between retail investors wanting liquidity now and private credit funds holding long-term paper is worth watching, and when the gates go up, the run-on-the-bank narrative tends to spiral. But the likely outcome here in a scenario where AI doesn’t hasten the collapse of the US economy is that patient institutional capital takes the assets off twitchy retail hands at a discount, the underlying businesses keep operating, and everyone learns the same lesson about selling in a panic all over again. The cockroaches Jamie Dimon warned us about last fall are real. They are not, however, a sign of the coming apocalypse.
Seat Licenses
Before we get too worked up about seat licenses, it’s worth remembering that the software industry has been trying to move past them for years. Consumption-based pricing was supposed to be the answer. The logic was that customers would pay only for what they use, better aligning with the value delivered. Snowflake, Twilio, Datadog, and Confluent built some of the fastest-growing software businesses in history on the model. Then 2022 arrived, interest rates rose, the economy softened, and CFOs started optimizing their cloud bills. Stocks of the consumption-pricing companies got hit the hardest. Twilio’s CEO lost his job, while Salesforce’s did not. The pricing debate has been live for a decade. AI is just the latest reason to have it.
The seat-license pressure is real, though. The irony that ChatGPT and Claude are both built on monthly seat-license models is worth a chuckle, but it doesn’t resolve the actual concern. A CFO watching AI reduce the headcount required to run a workflow isn’t going to pay the same amount for fewer people doing more. They’re going to pay less. That’s how CFOs work, and any pricing argument that ignores it is fooling itself.
In a world of agents, it’s no longer about the seats or consumption. It’s about who controls the workflow that the agent needs to function. Jason Fried, co-founder of 37Signals (maker of Basecamp, a horizontal project management software company with 85,000 users), described the mechanics on his ReWork podcast earlier this year: “People are going to end up bringing their own agents to our products and just have them be normal users. We’ve already seen this. We already have agents in our Basecamp account.” Gartner projects that 40% of enterprise applications will have embedded AI agents by the end of 2026, up from 5% today. An agent that works around the clock doing data hygiene, report-running, and pipeline cleanup is a new kind of user. The question is what it costs to let that user in, and who sets the price.
The answer depends on what the software does in that transaction. An API that merely exposes customer data is a tollgate, and tollgates get arbitraged. Smart players will find alternatives. But an API that reads transformed, context-rich data and writes back into live workflows isn’t a tollgate anymore. It’s a participant. And participants pay differently than pass-throughs. DealerBuilt, our auto dealer management software business, generates meaningful revenue from third-party vendor API access. Those vendors aren’t paying for raw data. They’re paying for access to a system their products can’t function without. One that has years of dealer-specific workflow logic, compliance history, and customer context baked in. That’s the leverage. Not the data itself, but the workflow the data powers and the context that only the incumbent has accumulated.
PitchBook ran the math on the potential upside: the $1,200 annual human seat becomes a $10,000 automated workflow when the addressable market shifts from IT budgets to labor budgets. Sequoia estimates that outsourced services budgets are roughly six times larger than software budgets. I’m not saying software companies will capture that shift, as many of the VCs are saying. But the ones that own mission-critical workflows in industries where AI agents are urgently needed (banking, aerospace, healthcare, supply chain, energy) are sitting on the right side of that negotiation. Those agents don’t enter as blank slates. They enter through the software that already runs those industries. The software is not threatened by the agent. The software is how the agent gets to work. I think incumbents who can harness AI themselves have the leverage when the CFO shows up at renewal time.
Vibe Coding
On to vibe coding, which is far more fun to talk about than the others. The technical barriers to writing code have not been the primary drivers of software moats for some time. As our own Jim Milbery likes to say, “AI replaces typing the code, not making it.” And Jim makes little typing movements with his fingers when he says it, just to drive home the point. Determining what to build next, how to architect it, and how it should function within a broader system is fundamentally more important and more challenging than simply coding it. That requires domain expertise, a deep understanding of the problems being solved, and years of accumulated institutional knowledge about how specific industries operate, not to mention how to architect a system from the ground up to solve problems and scale solutions.
Most customers won’t vibe-code mission-critical systems when competitive off-the-shelf alternatives already exist. Operational risk, security, maintenance burden, and competitive disadvantage of diverting internal engineering resources from your core business are so costly that most companies won’t even attempt it, especially on bleeding-edge AI platforms still unproven deeply in most enterprises. Enterprises hire large software companies for functionality, but they are hiring them for safety, too. Vibe-coded applications (whether developed internally or by new entrants) won’t have the same hardened cybersecurity defenses as products from large incumbents. That alone will slow AI first replacements. Ask any Fortune 500 CEO how confident they are in their internal IT teams’ ability to build and maintain secure, custom software. Especially in highly regulated industries, where failure to comply threatens a business’s livelihood and reputation, which is why RegTech investments have been among the most successful private equity deals over the last two decades.
We have been here before with similar coding tools at least twice. In 1991, Microsoft launched Visual Basic (VB) with an explicit promise to democratize software development. VB offered drag-and-drop tools that let anyone build Windows applications without writing professional code. By the time Visual Basic 6.0 shipped in 1998, nearly 3.5 million developers were building in it, more than ten times the number of C++ programmers, and two-thirds of all business application programming on Windows ran through it. Today, Visual Basic accounts for 4% of developer usage, according to Stack Overflow’s 2025 survey, almost entirely for maintenance work on software applications built decades ago. Nobody chooses it for new enterprise applications anymore. Then came the low-code and no-code wave. By 2021, Gartner was predicting that 70% of new enterprise applications would be built on low-code platforms by 2025, up from less than 25% in 2020. Microsoft predicted that 450 million applications would be built on no-code tools. It didn’t happen. In both cases, the technical barrier to writing software fell dramatically. All the while, incumbents kept growing, new enterprise software companies formed and flourished with and without these tools. The complexity of mission-critical enterprise systems didn’t get simpler because the tools got easier. It never does. Writing the code has never been the part that makes you special.
AI Bubble
The fourth bear case might be the doozy. What if AI isn’t as powerful as they tell us and we’re in a massive bubble? Last summer, Project NANDA, out of MIT, produced a report that spooked readers for the exact opposite reason that vibe coding does. The results from interviews and surveys with enterprise AI users found that 95% of AI projects fail to move beyond the initial pilot phase. The three main reasons projects fail were 1) lack of domain-specific data, 2) poor workflow integration, and 3) insufficient vendor trust. The things that cause agentic AI to fail at large companies are precisely the things that most vertical software applications already solve. We had issues with how the research was conducted, primarily due to its limited scope. And, let’s be honest, NANDA had a trade on, at least metaphorically. They are competing to be the foundational system for how the Agent Web interacts and collaborates across platforms, in a way that is competitive with MCP’s evolution to solve similar issues.
Last summer was dog years ago in terms of AI maturity. I think we are past the “does it work?” phase for many important use cases (though not all the ones people claim), but technology projects often fail, and mostly because humans are human, and change management is really hard. Many more AI projects will fail, just as many enterprise software projects will. It’s usually not the software’s fault. Have you ever tried switching CRMs? Or accounting systems? We’ve done it twenty-five times in the last twenty years at our portfolio companies, and it’s hard to get right. AI projects will be no different.
I don’t think we are in an AI technology bubble. If AI only ever works to revolutionize software development (and I believe it does), the positive impact on the world will be enormous. I am far more worried about hyperscaler capex bust and the broader economic damage that would follow than I am about private credit defaults, seat-based pricing, and vibe coding (though, let’s be honest, the hyperscaler and private credit risks might be deeply intertwined). We have seen this movie before with the telecom buildout in the late 90s and early 2000s, when everyone became an expert on dark fiber overnight. Buyout funds morphed into VCs, and robots were employed to pull fiber optic cables through city sewer systems (true story). This story ended in tears when the dotcom crashed, investors bailed, and companies slashed capex budgets. Like the CLECs before them, hyperscalers and data centers will eventually have to deliver returns to investors. If it goes bust, the pain will travel downstream, and it won’t be just software investors climbing out of a ditch if not a major recession, given all the other pressure on the global economy right now.
The software bears are making real points about real problems, but right now, they are conflating a terminal-value debate with a fundamental crisis. There is a worthwhile debate about the value of software companies in the age of AI. Just like there have been during other platform shifts. Massively discounting the terminal values of software companies based on thought experiments and misunderstandings of generative AI’s capabilities ultimately leads to multiple compression and panic selling. For people on the inside of these companies, building products and meeting customers, we are more optimistic about how we can use AI to stay competitive and grow than we are about the economic disruptions it may cause.
IV. The Mispricing
I understood the February sell-off by separating the trigger from the cause. The trigger was the Citrini report. The cause ran deeper: after a long, successful run in software stocks at historically high valuations, investors were looking for an off-ramp. This had been bubbling on the surface for a while. Entrepreneur and opinionated early-stage investor Jason Lemkin claimed that a meaningful portion of the sell-off was overdue repricing in response to growth deceleration that began in 2021, not an AI panic. Many of these companies grew explosively during COVID and never re-earned those multiples as growth normalized. Investors bought every dip along the way. Companies led investors to believe that AI would reaccelerate revenue growth, which never materialized. AI gave the sell-off its villain, but the culprit was always the frothy valuations.
In 2023, we published a research report called What is a Software Company Worth? to make sense of the 2022 SaaSacre, the last time this happened. We tracked two cohorts over two decades of public software company data. A growth-equity bucket (fast-growing, little or no profit) and a lower-middle-market buyout bucket (moderate growth, high EBITDA margins). As you would expect, the growth cohort peaked at over 25x trailing revenue in 2020; today, those same names trade at about 7x trailing revenue. The lower-middle-market cohort peaked at around 9x revenue and averaged around 5x over the entire period, which is about where they sit today.
The 2022 pullback was largely a reaction to rising interest rates as investors fell back in love with value after an unprecedented run in speculative growth from 2017 to 2021. With the S&P index down about 20% that year, the growth index fell 30% in 2022, while the value index fell only 7%. But how do software stocks perform during technology platform shifts like this one? William Blair recently analyzed the 2010 to 2015 transition from license to subscription models, a period highly relevant to today. The average public software company’s valuation troughed at a 15% discount to the S&P 500 during that transition. Today’s cohort of AI-stressed software incumbents is trading at an 11% discount. To be clear, I am not calling a bottom. But the math says we’re getting close to where the prior transition found its floor, and, because we are still so early in the AI transition, and predictions of its impact vary so widely at the moment, the market is mostly guessing right now about how this one will go.
It is helpful to examine what happened to vulnerable incumbents during the cloud transition. Microsoft, Adobe, Oracle, and SAP all hit their lows in 2011 or 2012. Microsoft, which traded around $25 at its June 2011 low, is now over $400. Adobe went from approximately $23 at its October 2011 low to over $270. Oracle rose from roughly $26 to over $160. SAP never traded at a discount through the transition and has roughly tripled since. Collectively, those four companies are worth over $3.5 trillion today. If you sold any of them at their trough because you were convinced the transition to the cloud would pass them by, you have watched from the sidelines as your mistake has compounded over the last fifteen years. And we’ve seen some of this mispricing so far in the AI transition. Recall that a year ago, Google was written off as late to the AI game, and the stock sank as low as $142. Today, the stock is above $300. Pendulums gotta swing.
The incumbents that don’t adapt rarely blow up; like old soldiers, they just fade away. CA Technologies spent the 2010 to 2015 period essentially flat on revenue. $4.4 billion in 2012 and $4.5 billion when Broadcom acquired it in 2018 for $18.9 billion. Six years of treading water, and CA still got a 4x revenue multiple.
Living and investing through market-sentiment shifts and platform transitions informs our approach to entry valuations at ParkerGale. Since 2008, we have acquired 25 platforms and closed 38 add-on acquisitions. Nine of our last 10 platforms were unbanked, increasing our tally to 17 of the 25. Add to that 30 of the 38 add-ons acquired directly from founders, and we have a pretty good track record of unique access to deal flow.
On average, we are paying a few turns below the long-term historical mean for public software companies. Our rationale is simple: buy companies below the mean, improve them alongside new management, and then expect to sell them at the mean. Don’t rely on elevated valuation sentiment at exit to generate our returns. We’ll take it when we can get it; in the summer of 2021, we made a series of exits while the market was hot. We try to control what we can, which is: 1) what we pay upfront, and 2) what we do with the company after we own it.
We sold when the market was hot, but how did we buy when things were frothy? During the 2020 to 2021 valuation peak, we bought four companies at entry multiples below market peaks. Three of the four were unbanked. In each case, we partnered with new CEOs to improve the businesses. In the fall of 2022, we recapitalized one with a larger PE fund, and in the winter of 2023, we sold one to a strategic buyer. We bought well during the peak, executed the operating plan with management, and sold into markets when DPI was scarce, generating liquidity at exit multiples in line with the historical mean rather than at peak bubble levels.
So where are things headed? At the risk of predicting future stock prices, I’ll take a stab at where I think public software company valuations settle out in the coming quarters. In February, investors chose to sell first and ask questions later with little discernment among winners and losers. Investors appear to be coming home in March, but it’s hard to know whether they are returning to the safety of the Mag 7 in response to a potential global oil shock or doing the fundamental work on individual companies to see through the noise. I think, as 2026 rolls on, many enterprise software companies will post solid results, and as it becomes increasingly apparent that AI is a software enhancer rather than a software replacement, more AI-enhanced products will be shipped. I don’t believe we will see a significant reacceleration of growth. Instead, we’ll see companies hit their projections, retain customers at high levels, and deliver operating leverage as AI initiatives bring efficiency. I believe valuations will move back toward the historical mean for companies that hit estimates. This will make it hard to drive outsized returns from private equity-owned software companies acquired at high multiples over the last six years, because, as we have written about before, no amount of value creation can outrun this much multiple compression. Entry price has always mattered, even though many investors convinced themselves that the mean had permanently moved up a few turns. It hasn’t.
V. The Argument
I won’t bury the lede, so here is my position on who wins the fight: AI will not replace enterprise software. Enterprise software will domesticate AI.
The software-is-dead argument rests on the premise that AI will replace the core functions that enterprise software currently serves. It can’t. Not because AI isn’t powerful (it is, increasingly so) but because AI is solving a different problem than enterprise software does.
Stephen Bersey at HSBC recently drew a distinction: AI is a “thinking machine,” while software is an “execution machine.” Enterprise software requires determinism. The same input must produce the same output every time, reliably, with an audit trail. Foundation models are non-deterministic by design. That is not a flaw. It is how they generate novel outputs. But enterprises can’t abide novel outputs on mission-critical systems. When a hospital’s drug-interaction software catches a dosage error, “pretty confident” is not an acceptable risk for a patient. Back-office mission-critical functions require accuracy thresholds often exceeding 99%. Front-office tasks typically run 90% to 95%. The gap between those numbers is where enterprise liability lives.
NVIDIA CEO Jensen Huang made this point plainly at Cisco’s AI Summit last month: “There’s this notion that the tool in the software industry is in decline, and will be replaced by AI . . . It is the most illogical thing in the world, and time will prove itself.” If the king of the AI revolution is making this point so clearly in the middle of the panic, then it tells you a lot about the psyche of a market whipsawing over a couple of Substacks from short sellers and vibe coders.
Another clear statement from the front lines came from Peter McCrory, Anthropic’s Head of Economics, speaking at the company’s Enterprise Agents event in late February. Transforming knowledge work, McCrory said, is “not just about the fundamental capabilities of the model,” it’s about “the broader data ecosystem and infrastructure required to deliver the right data at the right time.” Please read that again. Anthropic’s economist, speaking to its enterprise customers last month, explained that the constraint on AI-driven transformation of knowledge work is not the model. It is the data infrastructure surrounding the model. That infrastructure, in most companies, is called enterprise software.
William Blair summarized Anthropic’s event this way. Claude is positioned as the “thinking engine” that makes existing software more capable, not as a replacement for it. “The future is not a decision between either the AI labs or software vendors,” both play “important and complementary roles as critical infrastructure.”
The bears who argue that AI makes software replaceable are looking at only one layer of what makes a software business valuable. Data feeds workflows, and workflows feed automation. The companies with the deepest customer and industry data and the deepest embedded workflows are best positioned to build the automation layer on top, because automation is only as good as the data and process knowledge beneath it. A foundation model can generate code. It cannot generate twenty years of accumulated knowledge about how a specific insurance carrier processes claims, or how a particular fleet operator tracks maintenance cycles. That knowledge lives in the software and, even more so, in people’s heads and in the unstructured data of emails, file systems, Slack conversations, CRM fields, Post-It notes, etc.
It is worth noting that the framing of software as encoded judgment rather than stored code has never been much of a debate, which suggests it is less a contrarian view than a convergent one. For many software investors and operators, this was never something we thought about that hard. It just was. But nothing like a trillion-dollar correction to get us all on our typewriters to combat the narrative that software is just code.
George Sivulka, CEO of legal vertical software company Hebbia, is one voice who summarizes where the startup CEOs and early-stage investors are converging. On a16z’s blog last month, he wrote, “Software is a stored process. It’s not a neutral tool: it’s an opinion for how a group of people should collaborate, encoded in a durable system. Software is a social contract.” I share his view that better foundation models don’t thin the application layer, they thicken it. When OpenAI released its o-series models, the prediction was that legal vertical software players would be crushed because the underlying model had gotten so good. But the opposite is happening. The orchestration layer is becoming more valuable, not less. With the number of people turning to Claude and ChatGPT for legal advice, you would think software players in the legal vertical are in the perfect storm for LLM replacement. So far, that’s not happening. We expect the same dynamic to play out across most domains with vertical software depth. Systems of record will endure, while the interface, automation, and extension layer built on top of them becomes the new software frontier. And incumbents now have the tools not only to stay relevant but to thrive.
There is one more dynamic the bears are missing, and it may be the most important one. Traditional software switching costs came from data migration friction and retraining pain, which is real, but finite. AI agents create an entirely new kind of switching cost that compounds over time. The longer an agent is deployed inside a specific workflow, the more context it accumulates: the preferences, exceptions, edge cases, and institutional quirks of a particular customer. A competitor starting fresh starts at zero. A capable and nimble incumbent keeps getting better. For lower-middle-market vertical software companies with years of proprietary customer data and deeply embedded workflows, this is not just a defense against disruption. It is a new source of compounding advantage that accelerates the longer you hold the asset.
Not every software company has the same moat, however, and the distinction matters more right now than it ever has. Data alone is usually not enough because integrations are becoming easier to reproduce, and workflow advantages may matter less as AI agents move across systems. This maps cleanly onto the pattern we have already described. In the public markets, investors have punished everyone so far, particularly the companies that compete largely on interface design, integration breadth, and data access. Categories where the barrier to replication is falling. Over the long term, valuations will improve for companies that own the workflow itself: the compliance logic, the exception handling, the institutional rules about how a specific industry operates. That distinction between those two groups is the most important underwriting question in software right now. The market is not yet pricing it precisely, which is causing confusion and concern right now, but this is exactly the kind of dislocation that creates opportunity for investors who know the difference.
My friend Dave Kellogg read an earlier version of this piece and pushed me to think harder about my argument here. He asked, “If you are right, and software domesticates AI, then where does the value accrue and who gets paid?” I believe we can again look to the past for the answer because value has migrated between layers before. Databases were once the defensible layer. Then the cloud redistributed the economics. The question of whether software survives AI is genuinely different from the question of where value accrues within the stack as AI matures. We are watching the second question be answered in real time, so my confidence here draws heavily on past transitions. My current thinking draws on an idea that Andrej Karpathy, formerly of Tesla and OpenAI, articulated a few years ago and called Software 2.0. The traditional model, where humans write code and software executes it, is giving way to a model in which you train systems on data, and behavior emerges. Code and data start to look interchangeable. If that framing is right, then the defensibility question shifts. Writing code is no longer an advantage, as we have already discussed here. Knowing what to write is everything. And knowing what to write requires an understanding of edge cases, compliance requirements, workflow exceptions, and what breaks in production. My confidence that vertical software survives is that it is best positioned to define the prompts, constraints, and validation for AI systems in ways that current general-purpose AI models cannot. Karpathy likely agrees with Sivulka that if Software 2.0 is the future, then application layers don’t think. They thicken. My answer to Dave’s question about “who captures that value” will play out in the coming years, but today, I say the applications will likely become an even more valuable resource in an abundant world of agents in need of scarce context.
While it is still too early to call a winner, we can look at what’s happening already. Roper Technologies, one of the most active acquirers of vertical software businesses, disclosed in its fiscal 2025 results that the indirect revenue impact from AI readiness exceeded its direct AI revenue, and investors pummeled them for it (with the stock down 20% so far this year) because they are looking for acceleration from a new line item called AI. It’s in there, but it’s just embedded in the existing line items being empowered by AI. It shows up as better retention, faster implementation, higher willingness to pay, less stress on customer service, and improved margins.
VI. The Evidence
The pattern we are seeing across our dozen portfolio companies is consistent with what Roper found. At the moment, AI readiness is currently driving more commercial value and operational efficiency than standalone AI revenue, and it is showing up in existing line items on the income statements of our portfolio companies.
A quick aside for those who are not familiar with ParkerGale’s investment strategy, we buy founder-owned B2B software companies (meaning niche, profitable, bootstrapped, with no prior professional investor ownership). They are generally at least ten years old and have between $10 million and $30 million in revenue. The summaries below are anonymized examples of what is actually happening in the current portfolio. And you should evaluate them through a lower-middle-market private equity buyout lens, not a VC, Growth Equity, or mega Buyout lens (meaning we are not playing a go-big-or-go-home strategy in winner-take-all markets).
Research & Development
At one of our companies, engineering output is already 95% AI-generated, which is astonishing for a business that was assembled through four acquisitions of legacy software companies. But the engineers will tell you that what’s more important than having the AI generate the code is that 100% of that code is now automatically reviewed by AI. When we acquire a company, we are excited to see 30% of software testing automated. Most of it is manual (at best) because small companies struggle to attract and keep good QA people. Low test coverage means that new product releases are infrequent, and, because 70% of the production code isn’t tested in a consistent way (or at all), customer support queues fill up with bug reports. We’re ok stepping into this in most cases because with new tools, we can quickly get close to 100% (without adding headcount). The result is that the entire product release cadence accelerates, driving more frequent deployments, cleaner code, and fewer inbound support tickets. What does that mean in business speak? More revenue faster, higher customer retention, lower customer support headcount (or, more likely in our case, adding fewer people as you grow). And, more importantly, happier customers and, in turn, happier employees because winning is fun. Since our initial investment, this company has used automation to meaningfully expand gross margins, reduce headcount by 30%, all while growing revenue in the low teens.
Over at another, the team will accelerate new product releases and plans to grow revenue by over 20% this year. This company grew by only 9% the year we acquired it. To pull this off, they have budgeted zero headcount growth. Not zero growth in engineering. Zero across the whole company. How? Because just like at other companies we own, the CTO has automated 95% of code development and 100% of test coverage. Nothing like some healthy competition across portfolio companies. This team also built a proof of concept in under a week using existing customer data. It is already generating customer interest and may even become a standalone product we hadn’t anticipated. At another early adopter of AI automation in product development, our CTO’s initiatives have driven meaningful improvement in both gross margins and customer retention. Not because the product got cheaper, but because it got stickier.
Lower-middle-market CTOs are generally cautious people. Stuff can break easily. One of ours was genuinely skeptical heading into 2025. He also didn’t have time to experiment because we had just closed the deal, re-built the entire engineering team, and were staring at a long list of platform upgrades. A year ago, AI coding tools were significantly better at writing new code than updating old code. The tools would hallucinate too much. So instead of spinning wheels and distracting his team, we doubled engineering spending to update the tech foundation the old-fashioned way. Every quarter, spurred on by his CEO and Jim Milbery, our CTO would check back in on the progress the AI tools were making.
And other experienced technology leaders outside the portfolio were cautious, too. David Heinemeier Hansson (DHH), creator of the Ruby on Rails open-source application framework and co-founder of 37Signals, described a threshold crossing late last year that aligns with what we experienced as well. In early 2025, AI-generated code was not worth keeping in most cases. By late 2025, DHH was keeping roughly 80% of what the agents produced. That is not a gradual improvement. That is a step change. Then came another step change in February 2026 with the latest release of Claude Code, which allowed those who cautiously waited to practically catch up overnight. David’s co-founder, Jason Fried, was explicit about the wisdom of waiting: “I’m not sure the world was ready in 2025. I’m not sure we were ready. I think we made the right call to wait.”
And, just like David and Jason, our skeptical CTO changed his mind in February, too. He booked an Airbnb and took his top engineers to architect a new major platform release. We sent care packages to keep them well-fed and hydrated. Sometimes the best argument for a technology is that a thoughtful skeptic changed his mind.
One inside-baseball note on how we build versus how we deploy, and at the risk of getting too deep in the weeds, I think this is a good example of how in the AI weeds we are with our companies. By now, we’ve all played around with Gemini, ChatGPT, and Claude. And for $20/month, an individual can do incredible things. So incredible, sometimes it feels like magic. And it’s so cheap! But scale that up from individual use to embedding these models deeply within enterprise applications with thousands of users across the installed base, and the costs can eat you alive.
To avoid this, we build products using the frontier models but deploy them via hosted endpoints on AWS Bedrock and Azure. The build environment is experimental and model-agnostic. We can switch models when we think a better one is available. The production environment, however, is governed, cost-controlled, and tied to specific infrastructure. One of our companies cut its OpenAI costs by 80% by switching to cheaper hosted alternatives and implementing smart caching. This is more of a governance story than a technology story, because when you build things with future costs in mind, every dollar spent on AI must prove its worth.
One more area where AI is changing how we build — and where Jim Milbery has been ahead of the curve. The best software development model has always been paired engineering: a senior engineer working alongside a junior one, moving faster because the senior can see the whole field, while the junior learns by doing. The problem is that paired engineering is expensive. You are paying two people to do the work of one accelerated one. With AI coding tools, that equation has flipped. The junior engineer in the pair is now an agent — or increasingly, several agents running autonomously across multiple workstreams at once. Your most experienced engineers are now force multipliers, orchestrating work rather than executing it line by line. The result is faster, higher-output work from the people who already know what they’re building and why. I get that this is bad news for recent computer science majors, but they never wanted to work at our boring software companies, anyway.
This shift also reinforces who we hire as our CTOs. The technical leader who could grind out the most code was always a limited model for lower-middle-market software companies. What these businesses need instead is someone who can develop great people, build repeatable processes, and lead through change. That was true before AI. It is even more true now. The CTO who thrives in this environment is the one who can manage a team of senior engineers, each leading their own team of agents, while coordinating with the product management team, who also use agents to craft product requirements documents and application wireframes. Curious, collaborative leaders with strong EQs matter more than ever. We have always believed that. Now the technology requires it.
Sales & Marketing
AI is dramatically changing how our portfolio companies sell, and we are using it extensively and seeing promising results that we can replicate across the portfolio. At a company we bought less than a year ago, it took just one week to launch a complete demand-generation campaign for a new product, including video product walkthroughs, landing pages, and automated email sequences. A short recording session to capture the core message, AI to synthesize the positioning and draft the creative, a few rounds of AI-assisted editing, and we were live. It might have cost a few hundred dollars. The same project previously would have taken months and tens of thousands of dollars with a creative agency. We have replicated this playbook at other companies with similarly good results. At another company, reports that used to sit unused by sales are now synthesized into customized prospect outreach across the entire pipeline in under an hour. The company just closed its largest deal ever, and the customer signed for three-years.
Our most exciting go-to-market saw the marketing team at a portfolio company build an AI agent to convert proprietary data for every prospect in the country (almost 20,000 of them) into a self-refreshing pipeline. The system identifies which target accounts are experiencing the biggest changes in the signals that predict receptivity to our products, then automatically generates personalized prospecting content for each account — turning a data asset that effectively covers our entire market into a continuous outbound motion. AI works at every layer of the process: prioritizing which accounts to focus on, validating contact data for the right personas at those accounts, writing personalized outreach fueled by real-time market signals, and syncing everything to HubSpot to build institutional knowledge and create accountability. By the time a business development rep (BDR) picks up the phone, the AI has already done the work. Even in early testing, the system has meaningfully expanded the number of accounts our BDRs can actively work, and a full team rollout is underway. Before this system, our best BDR could make 100 calls per month. We believe that using the new system, we could reach 500. We aren’t looking to cut heads; we plan to grow without adding any, driving up profit margins along the way.
Every company in our portfolio uses customer and prospect calls as a core data asset. This conversational data has become the most important raw ingredient for content marketing, voice-of-customer research, personalized prospecting, and proposal templates. We also use AI tools to build simulation-based sales certification programs with scenario assessments drawn from real customer calls, for companies that would never have the budget or headcount for dedicated sales enablement assistance like this.
General & Administration
Finance is where AI has the least dramatic story so far, and we’re ok with that for now. Our portfolio companies run lean finance teams with just a handful of people. At that scale, we are not cutting heads, but even small reductions in friction have a big impact. Our companies are saving time closing the books, reducing administrative tasks, analyzing large data sets, and pulling together board materials. This gives them more time to focus on strategic projects with the CEO and leading cross-functional initiatives. One CFO describes the pattern well: provide structure and requirements, then let AI generate the first draft of model templates, variance analysis, board decks, and then validate, iterate, and finalize. The hard analytical judgment stays human, but the scaffolding gets built in minutes instead of hours.
At another company, the CFO automated transaction data crunching that previously took days of building Excel pivot tables and gut instinct, and now surfaces patterns and tests hypotheses in minutes. The result isn’t just speed. It’s rigor. One of our teams is automating board variance analysis and commentary for the board package. Another team led a project that drove 90% efficiency gains in document and email processing, providing a nice boost to gross margins.
Outside of engineering, AI is more of a skill than a technology. It makes our people better and more dangerous inside the applications they already use. We aren’t cutting heads in the accounting department. We are helping our teams spend more time on the important stuff. We are not replacing sales teams. We are making them capable of things they would never have taken the time to do before. Are the people more productive? I don’t know. Are they more effective? Hell, yes! Based on what we have seen over the past few years of first experimenting and now deploying AI across the portfolio, I think we are ready to make a call. With the current capabilities, AI tools are more of a “ceiling raiser” than a “floor raiser.” By that I mean, it is making our best employees (the ones with the most experience, expertise, and ambition) significantly more effective. For employees with fewer miles on the road and less context, it’s a helpful tool that makes them a little better, maybe a little faster, but it is not a game-changer. The game-changer at our size companies isn’t that we are doing things faster or better. We are now doing things we wouldn’t have done before because we didn’t have the time or budget. We can punch above our weight and compete on par with larger competitors across the organization.
VII. The Opportunity
The Ghost of Software Future has appeared again. We called an all-hands meeting.
Our core investment thesis is that we can acquire good software companies at below-market values and improve them by quickly upgrading talent, technology, sales effectiveness, and financial rigor. Our “the future is already here” mantra that I mentioned earlier. So far, this AI transition feels a lot like the other transitions we have invested through, but I have noticed one big difference. I have never seen a time when the gap between people who know how to use a new piece of technology and people who don’t is this wide and this consequential. The gap between investors’ understanding of the situation is just as wide. Somehow, the era that will see the fastest proliferation of software in history has become the moment when the investing world decided software is over. Sinofsky points to what has happened at every prior transition: “There will be more software than ever before,” not because of AI coding agents, but because “we are nowhere near meeting the demand for what software can do.” In each prior case, the thing that was supposed to die ended up vastly larger.
AI is a gift to ParkerGale and our portfolio. Our biggest challenge over the last twenty years, buying founder-owned software companies, has always been the speed at which we can modernize product development, accelerate growth, and harden financial reporting. We were patient and determined to grind it out alongside management until the flywheel was built. Sometimes it took a year. Sometimes two. But these new tools are different. In the right hands, they are a force multiplier. We are upgrading infrastructure faster than ever; we are rapidly building new applications to drive innovation and growth; we know more about our customers sooner; and we have more time to experiment, iterate, and test new initiatives with confidence and at low cost. I believe this will lead to faster operating improvements and better investment outcomes.
There is an asymmetry worth noting. Large software companies will use AI primarily to take costs out, reducing headcount to expand margins. For portfolio companies, the story is different. We are deploying AI to gain capabilities we simply could not afford before. 100% automated test coverage, demand generation without agency fees, sales certification programs on par with the best, and lean finance teams closing the books quickly. We are not replacing people with AI. Our people are moving faster because of AI. We are fielding teams that punch above their weight. The big guys get leaner. We get better.
A recent piece from a16z aimed at public software CEOs framed the choice starkly: add 10 more points of growth through new AI-native products or deliver 40% operating margins. No middle lane allowed. The comfortable middle, they argued, is already dead. The companies trapped in no-man’s land are the public growth equity cohort we described in our 2023 research report, as well as those we have all seen across the private equity industry over the past several years. Good companies at bad valuations. A lot of public and private software companies will soon know what it feels like to be Microsoft from 2000 to 2017, when even quadrupling revenue couldn’t fix multiple compression.
The companies we like were never in that lane. Founder-built, leanly staffed, profitable, acquired at disciplined valuations. These businesses can pursue growth and margin expansion simultaneously thanks to the new tools and our old skills. While others face a binary choice between two difficult paths. We get a third option, and we get it now. Are these the exciting software companies that make headlines? No. Can they deliver attractive, risk-adjusted returns? I believe they can.
Go back to that Monday morning in February. The alarm went off. The chat lit up. And somewhere in our portfolio, a CTO was renting an Airbnb to build a product a year ahead of schedule, a developer was managing five autonomous agents, a sales rep was nailing a pitch that upsized the deal, and a CFO was getting ten more days a month to think about what’s coming next instead of reporting on what just happened. The future is already here. It just needs ParkerGale to distribute it more evenly.
Thank you for reading. I hope it helps frame the debate and offers some insight into how we approach times like these. We would love to hear what you think, and we are available anytime to talk with you and your teams about what we are seeing in the market and how we are using AI within our firm and across the portfolio. Reuters reported in March that OpenAI has been offering private-equity firms a guaranteed minimum return of 17.5% in an enterprise-focused joint venture, while Anthropic has been pursuing its own conversations with PE firms as both companies look for capital and, more importantly, distribution.[1] The logic is obvious enough: if you can get a large buyout firm on your side, you are not just getting money. You are getting access to hundreds of portfolio companies, each a potential customer, each a candidate for standardization, each another node in the revenue machine.
Reuters separately reported that OpenAI was in advanced talks with TPG, Bain Capital, Advent International, and Brookfield Asset Management to raise roughly $4 billion for that vehicle at about a $10 billion pre-money valuation.[2] That number applied to the OpenAI structure, not to some combined OpenAI-plus-Anthropic total. Once these stories hit the market, numbers have a way of breeding like rabbits in a power outage.
As someone who actually has to deploy this stuff across portfolio companies, this is the most interesting part of the current AI market. Not the benchmark knife fights. Not the weekly parade of “our model now beats their model on a test nobody outside Palo Alto has ever heard of.” The interesting question is whether any of this makes sense for the people who actually have to deploy technology across real businesses with real budgets, real workflows, and real consequences.
Right now, I think the answer is: not in the way the AI giants want it to.
Scale Is Not The Same Thing As Durability
Global venture funding reached $189 billion in February 2026, according to Crunchbase, and 83% of that capital went to just three companies: OpenAI, Anthropic, and Waymo.[3] That is not a healthy market. That is a capital structure with all the subtlety of a Vegas sportsbook.
Enterprise buying patterns are already shifting quickly. Menlo Ventures estimates that Anthropic now earns 40% of enterprise LLM spend, while OpenAI has fallen to 27%, down from roughly 50% in 2023.[4] Read that sentence again and imagine you are a PE firm considering a multibillion-dollar relationship intended to shape purchasing across your portfolio. Market share in this space disappears like the drummer in Spinal Tap — you look up one day and it has just mysteriously vanished. If the score changes this fast now, what exactly are you locking in? A moat, or a moment?
That is the part that should make any serious investor squint.
OpenAI’s revenue run rate is already enormous, but the business still raises obvious questions for anyone used to underwriting software companies with some expectation of eventual operating discipline. Sacra has estimated OpenAI at roughly $25 billion in annualized revenue and about 33% gross margins.[5] Public reporting also points to spending and cash requirements in the many-billions range, with infrastructure commitments stretching years into the future.[6] You do not need the exact decimal points to see the shape of the thing. The beast has to feed itself, and this particular beast eats compute like it is going out of style. However you slice it, this is not a business profile that drops neatly into a classic private-equity template.
That does not mean it is doomed. It does mean you should be careful about confusing scale with durability.
Skepticism about the long-term economics is no longer confined to the usual suspects in the cheap seats. Benedict Evans has argued that OpenAI lacks unique technology, strong network effects, and meaningful product stickiness.[7] Sequoia has made a related point at the market level: AI end-market revenue is still measured in tens of billions of dollars annually, while the infrastructure and energy commitments being made around the sector are measured in trillions over the next five years.[8] The mismatch is not subtle. It is the kind of mismatch that usually ends with somebody giving an “important strategic update” on an earnings call (which is corporate for “we lit a pile of money on fire and would prefer not to discuss it further”).
There Are Two AI Markets
And yet, for people working inside portfolio companies, the economics of AI look nothing like the economics of the frontier-model arms race.
That is the distinction that gets lost CONSTANTLY.
There are really two AI markets right now. The first is the frontier market, where companies spend staggering sums on training runs, compute clusters, model labs, and enough electrical demand to make a utility executive blink twice. Epoch AI estimates GPT-4’s training cost at roughly $78 million and argues that the largest frontier training runs could exceed $1 billion by 2027.[9] Lewis Black used to have a bit about cable executives wasting a billion dollars: “What were they trying to do — build their own space program?” The joke landed because a billion dollars was supposed to be an absurd exaggeration. Turns out you probably could have built a space program for a billion — if the Muskrat hadn’t sunk $5 billion and counting into a Starship design that every serious YouTuber with a physics degree saw coming apart at the seams years ago. But that is a rant for another day. The point is: the AI labs are burning through money at the same rate, on training runs alone — not over twenty years, in twenty months — and nobody has even figured out the unit economics yet. At least when a rocket fails, it has the decency to explode on the pad so everybody knows where they stand. That is one game.
The second is the application-layer market, which is where operators actually live. In that market, the cost curve is falling down an elevator shaft. Stanford HAI reports that the cost to query a model with GPT-3.5-equivalent benchmark performance fell from $20 per million tokens in November 2022 to $0.07 by October 2024, a drop of more than 280-fold in about 18 months.[10] Yesterday’s miracle becomes tomorrow’s utility with unnerving speed.
That is why the PE angle here feels backward to me. The giant labs want PE firms to think like strategic distributors of frontier-model capacity. PE firms should be thinking like buyers of outcomes.
For most portfolio companies, especially the $10 million to $50 million revenue software businesses that occupy so much of the middle market, AI does not need to be magical. It needs to be useful. It needs to shorten a workflow, accelerate a decision, reduce dependency on tribal knowledge, help a support team answer questions faster, help an engineering team ship faster, help a finance team close faster, or help a sales team stop playing telephone with product specialists.
That is not a billion-dollar-training-run problem. That is an implementation problem.
And the good news, if you are an operator, is that the implementation economics are often shockingly reasonable. Anthropic says Claude Haiku 4.5 starts at $1 per million input tokens and $5 per million output tokens.[11] OpenAI lists GPT-5.4 nano at $0.20 per million input tokens and $1.25 per million output tokens.[12] That means a huge share of practical enterprise workloads can run on models whose economics already look more like software than science fiction.
This is especially true in software development, which remains one of the highest-value AI use cases inside the kinds of companies private equity actually owns. Most engineering teams do not need the best frontier model on Earth for every task. They need something fast, reliable, and cheap enough to use constantly. Code generation, refactoring, test creation, documentation, bug triage, codebase search. The workhorse models are good enough for a remarkable amount of that work, which is exactly why the real action in the application layer feels so detached from the theatrical financing rounds at the top of the stack.
Implementation Is the Moat
Here’s the thing that should really matter to PE firms: implementation, not model allegiance, is where value gets created.
McKinsey reports that 88% of organizations now use AI in at least one business function, but only 39% report EBIT impact at the enterprise level.[13] BCG says only about 5% of companies are generating substantial value from AI at scale.[14] That is an EXTRAORDINARY gap. If you have ever been through a large ERP implementation or a platform migration, you recognize this shape immediately — it is the Valley of Anguish, that brutal middle stretch where everybody has the tools and nobody has the results yet. The problem is no longer access. The problem is embedding those tools into processes that actually matter.
This is exactly what operators should expect. The graveyard of enterprise technology is full of products that were bought enthusiastically, demoed beautifully, and then sat in the corner like an expensive Peloton wearing a blazer.
That is why Orlando Bravo’s skepticism about these JV structures matters. Bain reports that, at Vista, most portfolio companies are already using AI-based code-generation tools, scaled adopters have seen up to 30% coding-productivity gains, and 80% of those companies are also deploying generative AI internally or building products with it.[15] None of that required a multibillion-dollar joint venture. It required focus, discipline, and people willing to identify workflows worth fixing.
That is how this usually works in the real world. Not with some grand portfolio-wide decree from Olympus saying, “Henceforth, all subsidiaries shall use Vendor X.” Look, I have spent enough time around portfolio companies — and failed at enough standardization efforts, if we are being honest — to know that getting ten management teams to standardize on anything is like trying to choreograph a knife fight. Half of them are already using something else. A few are convinced their use case is special. One is still running the technological equivalent of a Civil War field telegraph and insisting it is mission-critical (I wish I were exaggerating).
Now imagine trying to impose one AI vendor across that landscape because the fund signed a giant JV.
Good luck with that.
Even if you could force it, there is a timing problem. AI pricing and performance are moving so quickly that any multiyear commitment signed at today’s terms risks looking visibly unattractive long before the ink is dry. The labs are pitching scarcity. The actual application-layer market is moving toward abundance.
Anthropic itself has made this point, albeit indirectly. For smaller knowledge bases, the company says the full corpus can simply be placed into the prompt, with no need for elaborate RAG architecture, especially when combined with prompt caching.[16] That is a useful reminder that a surprising amount of AI value is not waiting at the end of a $2 million transformation initiative. Sometimes it is waiting on the other side of a practical engineering decision and a willingness to stop overcomplicating things.
That, to me, is the real lesson.
The frontier-model race is fascinating. It may even prove historically important. But for PE firms and portfolio-company operators, it is mostly someone else’s capex problem. The real game is LOWER in the stack. It is about cost reduction, throughput, resilience, and execution. It is about whether a management team can take a capability that is suddenly cheap and abundant and wedge it into the operating gears of the business in a way that produces measurable value.
If you are a PE firm, that should be the investment thesis. Not whether you can secure a preferred relationship with this quarter’s model champion. Not whether a guaranteed minimum return makes the structure look less speculative than it really is. And definitely not whether one of the labs promises to sprinkle your portfolio with AI fairy dust in exchange for a few billion dollars and a strategic press release.
The models will keep changing. The benchmarks will keep changing. The pricing will keep changing.
What will matter is whether your companies can use the tools better than their competitors can.
That is not a frontier-lab problem.
That is an operating problem.
And operators will use the tools that work — not the ones we negotiated a JV to distribute.

Buying a company is a controllable process. You decide what to look for, when to move, and how hard to push.
Selling a company is different. Someone else has to make a market, and the variables you can’t control tend to pile up right when you most want them not to.
What you can control is how prepared you are when it comes time to sell, and how well you and your team are set up to move fast and not get surprised. Most of the things that go wrong in a sale process are knowable in advance. Most of them are also preventable.
Devin and Ryan have been through this many times, on both sides of the table. In this episode, they walk through the full arc: when to sell, whether to hire a banker and how to pick one, how to get the business ready for a process, what buyers are going to probe hardest (including the #1 thing that’s killing deals right now), how to protect your management team, and what the deal stages actually look like from launch to close.
If you’re a PE investor, a CEO heading into a process, or just trying to understand how a sale actually gets done — this is the episode for you.
Some of the key questions we cover:
- What’s the one document that tells a buyer almost everything they need to price the deal? Ryan and Devin walk through what it is and why it matters — and explain why not being able to produce it in PE-grade format is itself a red flag.
- What’s killing deals at the investment committee level right now? It’s the same dynamic cyber created a few years ago, just with a different acronym. Devin explains what buyers are going to probe and how to show up ready.
- What happens when you spring management’s rollover situation on them the week before close? We have a story about how to do it right — and another story about what happens when you don’t.
- What’s the one reason to hire a banker? Not the obvious answer. Devin’s test is specific enough that you can use it to evaluate every banker you meet.
- How does a sale process actually flow from launch to close? Ryan walks through the stages (fireside chats, IOIs, management presentations, LOI, exclusivity) and explains why pace at each stage matters as much as price.
Time for the highlights!
The Customer Cube
If you’re selling a software business, there’s one document that determines how the first week of a process goes. It’s the customer cube — every customer, how long they’ve been a customer, what products they own, what they pay, whether they’ve upsold or down-sold, when ex-customers churned and why.
A clean customer cube, produced in an organized, PE-grade format, tells a sophisticated buyer almost everything they need to price the deal and assess the risk. If you can hand it to them on day one, you’re compressing weeks of back-and-forth into days, and sending an important signal about the saleability and operational state of the business.
AI Is the New Cyber
A few years ago, Jim Milbery used to joke that cyber diligence was the easiest way to kill a deal. Not because the business was bad — because investment committee members who weren’t close to the deal would see a red-flagged cyber report and pull the plug before the deal team could argue otherwise.
AI is doing the same thing now. Buyers are going to want to know: Is this company using AI in the product? In product development? Is the tech stack modern enough to build on, or is it going to get eaten? And the IC members asking those questions may not be technical — which means a vague or defensive answer is going to read as exposure, whether or not it actually is.
Devin’s advice is to show up with AI readiness, AI defensibility, and a clear story about how AI is being used before anyone asks. The companies that get ahead of this clean up the question early. The ones that don’t are going to find it costs them either the deal or the price.
Here’s Devin on what buyers are looking for — and how to prepare for it.
Have the Tough Conversations Early
One of the most predictable ways a sale process gets complicated is also one of the most avoidable: management’s equity situation doesn’t get discussed until the deal is already in motion.
Rollover expectations, succession plans, restrictive covenants — these aren’t surprises if you’ve had the conversations early. They become surprises only when you haven’t. And by the time you’re three weeks from close with a buyer’s money ready to wire, nobody’s in a position to negotiate calmly.
Devin shares a story here: a CEO who said upfront he wasn’t rolling over and wasn’t staying after the transition. They planned for it, communicated it to buyers, and the process went smoothly because none of it was a last-minute revelation. The calls Devin gets from management teams at other people’s companies (48 hours to decide on a non-compete they’ve never seen) are the wrong version.
Here’s how Devin and Ryan think about getting management ready before a process starts.
How to Know Which Banker To Hire
There are plenty of reasons to hire a banker to sell a business — organization, project management, market intel, credibility signaling. But Devin has distilled it down to one test he gives CEOs who ask how to choose between firms that all seem good. And it’s all about how to manufacture conviction in the final stages of a process.
Breaking Down The Sale Process
Most people who haven’t run a sale process have a rough sense of the stages but not the logic connecting them. Why does pace matter so much? What’s actually happening between IOI and LOI? When do buyers do their work, and what are you trying to accomplish at each gate?
Ryan walks through the whole sequence — fireside chats to warm up serious buyers before launch, IOIs to put everyone on the same page on price and cull the herd, management presentations to give committed buyers enough to firm up their bid, LOI to get to exclusivity, and then the confirmatory diligence sprint to close. Each stage has a job. Letting any of them drag is how you lose momentum and give buyers time to get cold feet.
Here’s Ryan’s take on how a well-run sale process flows from launch to close (including what matters most at each stage).
