You close the deal. The wire clears. Congratulations.
You own a business now!
You’ve done months of diligence. You have a value creation plan. You think you know what to do with what you bought.
But here’s what Paul and Jim from the ParkerGale team will tell you: your take on the challenges and opportunities inside that shiny new business of yours is (most likely) at least a little bit wrong.
Not completely wrong. Just wrong enough that if you walk in treating the diligence deck as your immutable plan for the next few years, you’ll miss a few things.
See, during diligence, you’re looking at the business from the outside. But it isn’t until after you close that you start to find out how the business actually works.
- Which problems are structural and which ones are just distractions.
- Where the real opportunities are hiding.
- Who in the company already knows what needs to happen and just hasn’t been able to get anyone to listen.
Paul Stansik runs commercial value creation at ParkerGale — sales, marketing, and go-to-market. Jim Milbery runs product and engineering. Between them, they’ve been through this handoff across every kind of situation: inside CEOs, outside CEOs, companies with half a C-suite, and companies where the founder is still in the building.
In this episode, they walk through what the first six months actually looks like inside a new investment, and how you square up the plan you had during diligence with everything you learn once you actually own the business.
If you’re a deal partner, an operating partner, or a CEO who just got acquired and is trying to figure out what comes next, we think you’ll enjoy this one.
Some of the key questions we cover:
- Is your value creation plan from diligence still relevant after you close? Paul’s answer is direct: if you haven’t changed your mind on the most important thing in the first six months, you haven’t gotten deep enough yet.
- How do you know you’ve actually built trust with a new CEO? There’s a specific signal our team looks for — even if it usually comes in at an inconvenient time, from an inconvenient place.
- Why is hiring one of the best places to focus on early in the hold? Not because it’s the most strategic lever, but because of what it lets you do alongside the CEO while you’re doing it.
- What are the two things worth focusing on above everything else in the first six months? This framework almost sounds too simple — but it explains most of the sequencing decisions you’ll face, and it’s the key to building a value-creation plan that actually sticks.
Here are the highlights.
The 8:45pm Phone Call
There’s a signal Paul looks for in the first six months of an investment that has nothing to do with financial performance. It’s a phone call.
Not a scheduled call. Not a board prep call. The call that comes in at 8:45pm when the CEO steps away from their kid’s baseball game because they had an idea they wanted to run by you before they lost it. Half-formed, not ready for a slide deck, just — hey, I was thinking about something.
That call is evidence of two things at once: that the CEO sees you as someone worth interrupting their evening for, and that they feel safe enough to share something that isn’t fully baked. Both of those take time to build. And if that call hasn’t happened by month six, Paul says it’s a signal you haven’t gotten close enough yet.
Here’s how he thinks about what it takes to get there.
Why Hiring Is the Easiest Early Win
Most operating partners come into a new deal looking for the strategic move — the insight from diligence, the initiative that’s going to change the trajectory of the business. Paul’s first move is usually more practical: find the open seat on the management team and help fill it.
Hiring is one of those things that CEOs almost universally accept help with, because running a good hiring process is genuinely time-intensive and most of our portfolio companies aren’t doing it every week. We are. We’ve got performance profiles, interview guides, homework assignments, panel interview experience. We can do 80% of the work and just need the CEO’s eye on what we’re testing for.
But the reason it’s valuable isn’t just the efficiency. It’s what you learn while you’re doing it. You find out what the CEO values in their team, what they want the new person to accomplish in the first six months, and where the real friction points are. And you build trust by doing something together that’s both hard that’s satisfying to finish.
Curiosity and Connection
Paul’s two central ideas for “where to focus in the first six months with a new investment” can be summed up in two words: curiosity and connection.
Curiosity means asking a lot of questions, staying genuinely interested in how the business makes money, and resisting the urge to declare what the answer is before you develop a fingertip feel for what’s actually going on. Connection means building the kind of trust inside the company that lets you do the actual work — because anything that’s going to move the needle in a PE investment is too big a job to do by yourself. You need co-conspirators inside the company. People who’ll help you interpret the data, do the work, and make the inevitable changes actually stick.
Here’s how he explains it.

Most people get into private equity because they like the idea of doing a deal: Finding, evaluating, and then finally owning a real business.
What nobody really documents is everything that has to go right (and everything that can go wrong) in the space between “we think we want to buy this company” and “we’re officially closed.”
For example: How do you find a business that isn’t officially for sale? How do you build credibility with a banker who’s never heard of you? What does it actually mean to win over a founder, and how do you know when you have? What’s an LOI really communicating beyond the price? And what does closing day feel like when it finally happens?
Devin and Ryan have been doing this for decades, almost entirely focused on the founder-owned lower middle market. In this episode, they walk through the entire deal-making arc: sourcing, thesis-building, working with bankers and brokers, navigating the IOI-to-LOI dance, bringing in lenders, surviving diligence, and what it’s actually like to stand in a room full of employees who just found out their company was sold.
If you’ve ever been curious about what goes into actually buying a company, this is the episode for you.
Some of the key questions we cover:
- Who should actually be doing outreach to founders? Why the standard model (junior deal team members with a CRM and a generic call/email cadence) is backwards, and what “scaling intimacy” with a partner-led sourcing model looks like instead.
- What’s a thesis actually for? Sure, it’s a research document. But it’s also an important fuel additive for your sourcing engine. Devin’s “heating up molecules” framework explains why the firms that wait for the phone to ring will always be behind those willing to put their thinking on paper and share it.
- What role does the LOI play? The price is the obvious part. The phrases buried in the document — the exclusivity language, the working capital placeholder, the diligence carve-outs — are where the real negotiation lives. Ryan breaks down what to put in and why.
- Why does closing day feel so anticlimactic? Signing off and officially closing the deal is a big deal, but closing day itself can actually feel… a little boring? Devin and Ryan explain why, what goes on during a typical closing day, some of the last-minute issues buyers and sellers can run into, and even share one of their favorite “announcing the deal” stories involving an emotional town hall address, a champagne saber, and a pizza receipt.
Here are the highlights.
Partner-Led Sourcing and Scaling Intimacy
Most PE firms have made the same structural mistake in how they approach sourcing: they’ve handed the most important job in the firm to the person with the least authority to do it.
The logic seems fine on paper. You hire analysts and associates, give them a CRM and an email cadence, and point them at a list of founder-owned businesses. Volume goes up. Activity metrics look good in the Monday meeting.
The problem is that reaching out to a founder you want to buy isn’t a volume activity — it’s a trust activity. And trust doesn’t travel well through a 23-year-old with a templated email sequence and no authority to have a real conversation. Founders know when they’re being plugged into a pipeline. They can feel it in the first thirty seconds.
Devin calls the alternative “scaling intimacy” — the idea that you want a founder to feel like they’re getting a one-to-one call from someone who matters, even when you’re doing it at scale.
What’s a Thesis Actually For?
Most people think of an investment thesis as a research document — a way to get specific about what you’re looking for so you don’t waste time on deals that don’t fit. That’s true, but it’s the smaller part of the value.
The bigger reason to have a thesis running is what Devin calls “heating up molecules.” When you’re actively working a space (talking to executives, getting a sense of the competitive landscape, meeting founders who may or may not be ready to sell) you become a person everyone in that ecosystem people want to chat with. The inbound starts. The warm intros multiply. And opportunities start presenting themselves.
Here’s how Devin and Ryan think about building an effective thesis, and why the executive relationships you form while doing it often matter more than the thesis itself.
Working Capital: Get Clear Early
Working capital is one of those deal terms where it pays to get as clear as possible as early as possible. If you haven’t defined the methodology by the time everyone’s deep in diligence, both sides can game it — there are fifteen legitimate definitions of the same term, and whoever defines it last tends to win.
Ryan’s advice: write the methodology into the LOI. Not a placeholder — the actual formula. The 12-month peg, which items are in and out, how deferred revenue gets treated. You fill in the numbers once the QofE is done. This way, the framework is agreed on ahead of time, saving you both friction and cycles later in the deal process.

Most people who think about starting a PE firm spend their time thinking about the investing part. Finding companies, doing deals, building something. The fundraising part (the part that has to happen first) gets a lot less airtime.
What nobody really talks about (at least in any detail) is the gap between the day you decide to go out on your own and the day the final close is inked. For example: Before you talk to a single LP, what do you actually need to have ready? How do you figure out if your story is going to work — before you’ve wasted six months finding out the hard way? What happens in the first five minutes of an LP meeting that most GPs completely miss? And when does a fundraise finally tip over from grinding to closing?
Devin and Jim have been through this. ParkerGale’s first fund took over 150 meetings to get 15 institutional LPs to say yes, and they raised more money in the last six weeks than in the first sixteen months.
In this episode, they walk through the whole arc: getting ready to get ready, building your target LP list, running the roadshow, conducting a successful LP meeting, and the joy and stress of reaching the finish line.
If you’ve ever thought about starting your own firm, or wondered what the fundraising process actually looks like from the inside, or been through it yourself, you’ll love this episode.
Some of the key questions we cover:
- What actually helps when you're trying to raise a first-time fund? Devin walks through the three things that move the needle (and why having even one of them can change the dynamic with LPs).
- Should you use a placement agent? They can make or break your process. But boy are they expensive. Even if you’re going DIY, there’s a specific reason to take those meetings anyway (and it has nothing to do with hiring them).
- What do you do in the first five minutes of an LP meeting? Most GPs go straight into the pitch. Devin’s approach is different, and it only takes about five minutes to completely change how you conduct the rest of the meeting.
- What does it actually feel like to be in the middle of a fundraise? Twenty-five meetings in three cities in five days (oh, and twenty-four of those were “no’s.” A narcoleptic LP. Getting kicked out into the rain in Connecticut. A meeting where Jim got held up with security, so Devin had to fly solo. Devin and Jim share all the stories and lessons from their first fundraise - good, bad, and just plain weird.
Here are the highlights.
Why You Should Meet With Placement Agents (Even If You’re Not Going to Hire One)
Going DIY on a fundraise is a legitimate choice, especially at the smaller end of the market. But there’s a specific reason to take placement agent meetings anyway, even if you’ve already decided you might not be hiring one.
Placement agents will tell you things LPs won’t. See, LPs are (mostly) nice. They’ll sit through your pitch, nod politely, and then that’ll be the end of the conversation. Placement agents will tell you the truth: Why this is going to be a hard raise, what’s wrong with your story, and what the rest of the market is saying about funds just like yours.
Basically, it’s free feedback in a live environment with real stakes, before you’ve burned any of your actual LP relationships on a pitch that isn’t ready for primetime yet.
Those who won’t take you on will still likely still take the meeting. And that feedback is worth a lot.
How to Run the First Five Minutes of an LP Meeting
Most GPs walk into an LP meeting and start pitching. The LP sits back, flips through the deck, maybe asks a question or two. Forty-five minutes later, it ends in a polite standoff, and everyone goes home.
There’s a different way to run it. Before you say anything about the fund, ask them three questions: How much do you typically invest per fund? How many funds do you invest in per year? How many slots are already committed? And here’s a bonus question: What do you love when GPs cover in a meeting and what do you hate when they skip? In five minutes, they’ve told you exactly how hard it’s going to be to get a check, whether this is a real opportunity or a relationship-building conversation, and how to prioritize the rest of the meeting.
They’ve also told you whether to go straight to the part of the deck they care about, or whether to run the standard sequence.
Almost nobody does this. Most GPs are too eager to get into the pitch to ask the questions upfront that would make the whole pitch land better.
Here’s how Devin thinks about it.
The Tip Over Point
ParkerGale raised more money in the last six weeks of their first fund than in the first 16 months. Devin’s explanation for why is one of the more useful things in this episode for anyone who’s grinding through a fundraise and wondering if it’s ever going to turn.
The short version: momentum in fundraising compounds in ways that aren’t visible until they suddenly are. The people who said no 16 months ago have been watching. Their allocations shift. And when there’s not much room left, the urgency that was impossible to manufacture at the start shows up on its own.
Here’s how Devin describes the tip over point — and what it takes to stay in the game long enough to reach it.

It All Started at the Macaroni Grill
ParkerGale’s origin story starts in the same place as every other great investor’s origin story: In a suburban Charlotte strip mall.
It was 2014. Devin and Jim were on the road fundraising for their prior firm, staying at a Residence Inn. After a long week on the road, they could only motivate to walk across the parking lot to the nearest dinner option — Macaroni Grill. They sat at the bar, began to order a couple of glasses of wine, and their bartender (a man who truly understood value for money) pointed something out: the bottle of entry-level cabernet was actually cheaper than the two glasses they’d just already ordered. Might they want to go that route instead?
As value investors themselves, they did, in fact. And over that $12 bottle of value Cabernet, they made a decision:
It was time to go do this PE thing on their own.
In this episode of the PE FunCast, Devin and Jim rewind the clock to the moment they decided to start their own firm and explore the questions, decisions, and trade-offs that go into building a private equity firm from scratch.
If you’ve ever thought, “I think I might want to start my own firm someday”
(or if you’ve asked “how do you even decide to start your own PE firm?”) then this episode is for you.
Some of the key questions we cover in this edition of the FunCast:
- What’s your actual edge? Why knowing the reason a sophisticated investor would wire you money before you’ve bought a single company.
- What kind of firm should you even be building? A traditional fund, a fundless sponsor, a holdco? — They’re not just different structures; they’re different games with different rules, different pressures, and very different ways to win or lose.
- How long can you fund the burn? The gap between “we’ve decided to do this” and “we can pay the bills” is longer, lonelier, and more expensive than almost anyone expects.
- And maybe most importantly: who are you splitting that $12 bottle of wine with at your firm? The person sitting across from you when you make this decision will shape everything that comes after.
Here are the highlights from Jim and Devin’s conversation - and a bit more color on why we think they’re helpful for anyone thinking about (or reflecting on) the journey of starting their own fund.
What We Learned Building ParkerGale
The Name Makes It Real
There’s a moment in every new venture when it stops being a plan and starts being a thing. For ParkerGale, that moment came from a URL and a Frank Lloyd Wright story.
Devin and Jim had some rules for naming the firm: no Greek gods, no bodies of water, no street names, no trees, no personal names, and you had to be able to buy the .com. No [link] for us!
“ParkerGale” came from an unlikely place. Frank Lloyd Wright designed seven houses in Oak Park while secretly moonlighting for private clients — which got him fired — before launching his own legendary career. Devin and Jim had made seven investments at their prior firm. Two of Wright’s houses were built for the “Parker” and “Gale” families in Oak Park. And they just happened to live next door to each other. Both houses are still standing today, 130 years later.
The URL was available. And the moment they had the name, something shifted. It wasn’t just a plan anymore. As Devin puts it: “Oh, this is real, and it’s really going to happen.”
No Plan B
Most people who think about starting a firm also think about what they’ll do if it doesn’t work. Devin and Jim made a different choice. Their working title for the firm (before they ever had a fund, an investor, or an office) was “No Plan B Capital Partners.” It wasn’t a slogan. It was what they’d call the firm in the early days.
The boats were burned. The decision was made. The only direction was forward.
This sounds like bravado, but there’s real intention underneath it. A backup plan is also a kind of hedge on entrepreneurial courage. Raising a first fund is a long, grinding, uncertain process. If there’s an exit ramp, some part of your brain will always be looking for it.
What Makes You So Special?
This is the question every aspiring fund manager needs to answer before they answer anything else. Not for their pitch deck. For themselves. What’s your edge? Why should someone give you money in the first place?
This all comes back to what’s unique about you — and in Devin’s opinion, there are basically five reasons an investor might actually wire you money before you’ve bought a single company.
- Operator. You’ve run companies. You’ve been a CEO. You know what to do with a business after you own it. You just need someone to help you find and buy it.
- Sourcer. You have a network that opens doors no one else can. If you can find the asset, the capital will follow.
- Track record. You’ve already done the thing. This is the Steve Martin joke. “How do you become a millionaire? Step one: get a million dollars.” The easiest path in, and also the least accessible.
- Relationships. You’re so deeply embedded in a sector that deals come to you. Sourcing means you’re hunting. Relationships mean you’re being hunted.
- Market insight. You see things other people don’t. People take your calls because they want to know what you think. If that’s you, you may not need a track record — you just need to prove you can execute and operate a deal.
The key here is being honest with yourself about which of the five you actually are. Not only because your potential investors will ask you, but because of how this clarifies your strategy (and how you build out your team as you raise a fund).
What Do You Mean By “Pressure To Deploy”?
Most people sitting in their own version of the Macaroni Grill, deciding to go do this on their own, are thinking about the exciting parts. Finding companies. Making deals. Building something. What they’re almost never thinking about is the pressure that starts the moment a traditional fund closes — and doesn’t let up until every dollar is deployed.
In a traditional fund, you have five years to put your investors’ money to work. Whether you’re finding the deals you love in those five years or not, you’re taking a fee that entire time — with the expectation that you’re deploying that capital against the strategy you promised. That kind of pressure can cause investors to go off strategy. Not because the manager made a conscious choice to stop believing in their thesis, but because the deployment clock kept getting louder and louder until it drowned out everything else.
Other models don’t carry that same weight. The independent sponsor only moves when they have a deal. The holdco buys on its own timeline, using cash flow from the companies it already owns. Neither has a clock ticking in the background.
This isn’t about whether you’re cut out for the pressure. It’s about knowing it’s coming so it doesn’t catch you off guard — and making sure the model you choose aligns with how you actually want to operate.

Here at ParkerGale, we like to challenge ourselves by making yearly predictions and then looking back to see how we did. This year is no different, and PG partners and PE Funcast hosts Jim Milbery and Devin Mathews came ready with the crystal ball. Part 1 of ParkerGale’s 2026 predictions covered Jim’s predictions in the tech and software spaces.
Here, we dive into Devin’s predictions for the private equity market and software companies in general. Read on to find out who we think will be the big winners of the year, the trends that will drive investing, and how a certain horse in a hospital will have a big impact on the market in the back half of 2026.
1) Liquidity Improves (But With Help From The Secondary Market)
This will be another year of returning capital through nontraditional means. Liquidity in the market will improve from the chokehold it was in last year, but a lot of that liquidity will come from the secondary market, i.e., continuation vehicles and all the flavors that have derived from them that aren’t “authentic exits,” as Andrea Auerbach of Cambridge Associates suggested last November.
We’ll still see PE firms buying directly from other PE firms, but the bid-ask spread will persist. It will be especially notable in the software sector, where GPs think they own solid, defensible, and possibly even unique assets, whereas the buyers will use AI and the recent pullback in public markets to hammer valuations down to earth.
People talking about OpenAI, Anthropic, and SpaceX IPOs help get clicks, but those are isolated outcomes that have little to do with generating liquidity for the typical institutional private equity LP. Investors in those companies will likely be very happy with the outcomes, but that won’t drive liquidity through the PE market. Instead, it will be driven by secondary funds that have raised massive amounts of money in recent years and are looking to put it to work just like any private equity fund.
2) Fundraising Will Stay Brutal & Get Even More Bifurcated (Sorry, Everyone)
Those hoping that the constipated fundraising climate will soften this year are likely in for disappointment. All indicators point to the barbell effect remaining in place at least through 2026. The big private equity firms will get bigger, the smaller funds will get nichier, and mid-sized firms will be left scrambling.
In recent years, the biggest PE firms–think Blackstone, KKR, and Apollo–have only continued to grow and add more products. They’ve added services like wealth management to their offerings, making them one-stop shops for both large institutions and mom-and-pop investors seeking access to their products. As such, the trend of money moving in that direction isn’t about to reverse course; the flow of money moving upmarket will continue.
At the other end of the barbell, smaller funds that have a defined niche in less-crowded markets should also find fertile ground this year. As we’ve seen over the past few years, owning a specialized space and having a unique edge are how smaller firms like ours try to stay competitive and even thrive.
The challenge with smaller firms is that they will scour the globe to pick up nickels, dimes, and quarters on their way to a final close. Big institutions just can’t write small checks, and many traditional investors in smaller funds (endowments, family offices, foundations) need liquidity to pick up for them to keep investing in private equity, so the usual suspects might still be out of money this year. Even so, the opportunities will still be there.
On the flip side of things, the middle of the barbell will struggle in 2026. There is a harsh joke going around the industry that many firms have raised their last funds, they just don’t know it yet. With big firms gobbling up ever-larger market shares and smaller firms staking claims in less-competitive spaces, mid-sized firms (think $2-$4 billion) with investments across multiple industries will find the months ahead challenging, unless they have delivered significant, recent liquidity and outsized returns.
The keys to differentiation for firms stuck in the middle will be more “what have you done for me lately,” so you'd better have a repeatable recent track record of sourcing, winning, and exiting to generate DPI. Otherwise, you’ll likely find yourselves stuck spinning your wheels this year as the pool of money continues to flow upmarket to the big guys or downmarket to the boutique firms.
3) The Lower End Of The Market Will Still Have Lots Of Activity
In 2026, most of the dollars will still flow upward (the top 10 PE funds raised almost half of all the money in 2025). But most of the action will unfold at the lower end of the market, where founders still drive sales opportunities and small firms can get creative to close deals outside of traditional sales processes.
Why will it still be business as usual downmarket? Simple: No one is getting any younger, and founders still want to sell. The four Ds of the lower middle market aren’t going anywhere. Death, divorce, disease, and depression will still be drivers of founders deciding to sell this year. The other constant is, of course, that aging founders want to retire, but their kids have no interest in taking over the family business.
We think AI will only make the decision to sell clearer this year. Owners who have managed their companies through the major events of the past 20 years–booms, busts, wars, recessions, pandemics, horses in hospitals–might just see this AI wave coming and decide to throw in the towel rather than navigate one more wave.
4) Exits This Year Will Be Frontloaded (But Pick Up Again After November)
Timing is everything, however, and exits will be frontloaded in 2026; we’ll see most of this movement happening in the first half of the year. Founders and investors will inevitably start asking, “Should I try to get out ahead of the midterms and sell before everything changes?”
Despite the recent rotation out of public software companies, the pump is primed for exits after a slow 2025. But as we get closer to the midterm elections in November, the volume will likely slow down like in other years. And this year, which appears to be one of the more closely watched and predicted midterms, things should be no different. Get out between now and June, sit tight over the summer, see how things go into November, and then launch with the hopes of a close by year-end.
The market loves gridlock, and if we get it, 2027 could be a strong year for liquidity after a few years of disappointment.
5) Cybersecurity Becomes #1 In Due Diligence Processes
In truth, this entry is technically Jim’s prediction and could have fit into Part 1 of our 2026 predictions, but it has as much to do with private equity and investing as it does with software and technology.
2026 is the year companies will start getting tighter with cybersecurity, not because it’s important (though it is), but because it’s the first place third parties and potential buyers always look to knock down the price of a purchase. It’s the easiest area for a potential buyer to do diligence, as it’s the easiest place to find problems–and the area a partner in a private equity firm is least likely to understand.
That’s why it’s always where third parties start, as they can use any perceived risks to negotiate down the sale price while doing the rest of their due diligence. Software companies are catching on to this tactic, though. If they’re smart, they’ll prioritize shoring up cybersecurity infrastructure to ensure it’s no longer a perceived weak point in negotiations.
6) Software Is A Mature Market, So Start Investing Like It Is
Software is still being invested in as if it were an emerging industry capable of sustaining amazing compounded growth rates in perpetuity. But the reality is that the world is over-softwared and has been for a long time. Software has cooled off, no matter how much the market wants to pretend it’s still the hot, new thing. It’s easy to buy, it’s easy to make, and in the past decade, so many new companies going after the same problems have sprung up, while big companies are also focused on fixing those same problems. While it’s still better than most industries (in my humble opinion) and there are always pockets that outperform, B2B enterprise software is hardly a booming growth industry in 2026.
It’s worth remembering that the COVID-19 pandemic created a false positive, a time when companies were suddenly gobbling up new software to deal with the sudden shift to a workforce handling business remotely. Now, some of that software bought during the pandemic is a lot like the Pelotons we all bought then, too–metaphorical laundry hangers and not much else. The only difference is that it’s easier to cancel your SaaS subscription than move the Peloton out of the basement.
This year is when investors will start looking at software companies and seriously question whether their growth rate is worth the valuation. Now that we’re past the pandemic bump, B2B software is a slog for market share. You cannot invest in it as a class anymore; you either have to become a better stock picker (in the public markets) or know how to build a company (if you’re a private investor). The world wants more predictability right now than opportunity, so we’re back to three yards and a cloud of dust investing. It’s back to basics, everyone: Not just a great Billy Bragg album, but my proposed mantra for the industry.

Predictions are always a popular game to play in Q1 of any given year, from people placing their bets on potential Oscar winners to how events might unfold in a particular industry. But prognostication is a tricky business, one that can make even a seasoned soothsayer look foolish depending on how the year evolves. Unforeseen variables always risk upending a nice, neat prediction, particularly in business.
It’s fair to wonder, then: Why even bother making yearly predictions at all? Despite the risk, there are still benefits to making Q1 predictions based on our experience. Having an idea of what’s to come can help any company or industry navigate rough waters, prepare for change, and take advantage of opportunities rather than be left behind.
On the PE Funcast, we put together our own ParkerGale list of predictions for 2026 across private equity and tech. The main themes for the year ahead? AI is here to stay, so take advantage now – but don’t get caught up in the hype. And, sorry everyone, fundraising will remain challenging, but there are opportunities.
Here are our predictions in the realm of software and technology for 2026, so you can better prepare yourself and your business. Tomorrow comes Part 2, where we dive into our crystal ball to predict what’s ahead for private equity.
1) We’re Still At Least 5-10 Years Away From AGI
Most people not intimately involved in the tech world are still barely getting their heads around the concept of AI, but already, the big, buzzy new hype is that we’ll soon achieve AGI, artificial general intelligence. Think fully autonomous AI programs: self-driving cars like Waymos and Teslas, Data from Star Trek – you get the gist.
Yet, Tesla’s Optimus robots can’t even walk without falling over, let alone drive. And those “self-driving” Waymos, as it turns out, are still being remotely controlled by workers in the Philippines. Less self-driving, more self-driving…mostly. Eventually.
The truth is that, regardless of the noise coming out of certain parts of Silicon Valley, we’re still at least half a decade away from AGI becoming a reality. Right now, all the money is being poured into LLMs like ChatGPT. Despite the influx of cash, they haven’t improved much. Reaching true AGI will require marrying LLMs with more tightly controlled, established forms of AI, such as fraud detection and other closed algorithms. And merging those will require both to be far more advanced than they are now.
We’re simply not there yet. Give it another 5-10 years, and then we’ll talk.
2) Bigger Public LLM Models Such As ChatGPT Will Fall Out Of Favor
Right now, public, generative LLM models are sucking up all the AI oxygen. It’s no surprise: their adoption rate has been astronomical. If you can use social media, you can use ChatGPT. If you have a credit card, you can get started. That ease of uptake has been great for companies looking to test out AI and determine whether it will benefit their business. The answer for most software and smaller companies is that it can – but it has to change.
If 2025 was the proof-of-concept testing phase, then 2026 will be the execution phase, and this year, software companies and portfolios will discover that ChatGPT isn’t always the right fit. Instead, they’ll turn to more tightly controlled programs specific to their domain, ones they can build in-house and customize to their needs. That level of specificity and customization is something that large, public LLMs simply can’t achieve.
2026 will see more and more software companies crunching the numbers and realizing it’s actually more cost-effective to build their own open-source programs than burn millions of dollars on OpenAI tokens and other similar public models. Look to open-source companies like Mistral, Hugging Face, and Llama as the big winners this year in embedded AI.
3) The AI Gold Rush Starts To Slow Down
It seemed like everyone and their mother was launching an AI company or app in 2025; the .ai domain was ubiquitous. As with any new tech that catalyzes a battle for first-to-market dominance, however, the smoke is thinning around AI, and it’s clear who the victors are. Unsurprisingly, the winners of the AI gold rush are the giants with the capital to spend: Microsoft, OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google.
Smaller niche companies have carved out a foothold by filling specific voids that the giants haven’t yet focused on. Rest assured that the eye of Sauron – or, in this case, the Big 4 – will turn that way, though. Sooner rather than later, the giants will focus on building out the smaller features they’d previously deprioritized and incorporating them into their own products.
When that happens, the AI apps and boutique companies built to fill these gaps will need to differentiate themselves or risk their one-off products becoming obsolete under the AI behemoths’ one-stop-shop models. Just look at how many AI image generators were around a year ago that disappeared once OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google built their own right into proprietary models.
All indications are that this year is poised to be a bloodbath in the AI space, akin to the first internet meltdown of the early aughts. Given this inevitability, private equity firms should be wary of their portfolio companies investing in one-trick technologies. The harsh truth is that betting on small companies in the AI space is a bad gamble these days, as few of them will still be around in the next year or two.
4) Software Jobs Aren’t Going To Disappear; AI Will Just Change How They’re Done
There are still two general camps of thought surrounding AI: “It’s completely useless” or “It’s the greatest thing ever.” The reality is that it’s somewhere in between, and arguably leans toward the former if you don’t know how to properly use it – and too many companies, and their execs, still don’t.
Right now, people are worried that AI will replace their jobs, particularly entry-level roles in fields such as software engineering. After all, we’ve seen numerous C-suite execs openly brag about how many human employees they’ve laid off and replaced with AI. Less well-publicized, however, has been their sheepish about-faces as they’ve quietly rehired people after realizing that AI doesn’t stack up to human expertise and knowledge.
AI just can’t compete with humans yet, and in many industries, it never will. The current reality of LLMs is that they simply can’t do what the Sam Altmans and Elon Musks of the world promise. ChatGPT can spit out a correct answer, but it hallucinates just as often. When an entire company is plugged into an AI system without actual humans, you run the risk of things going very badly on a massive scale.
The bottom line is that AI needs humans more than humans need AI. No matter how much tone-deaf CEOs want to crow about all the people they’re cutting out of jobs, their dreams of the human-free workplace are just that: dreams.
5) Automation Will Not Eat Private Equity Admin Work
It’s not just in software that AI still needs humans; private equity does, too. Robert Smith of Vista was one of those aforementioned CEOs cutting a swath of employees and replacing them with AI to handle all the firm’s lower-level and administrative work.
Beyond being a demoralizing message for any junior team to hear, it’s simply not a smart business decision. There are some interesting developments in the AI for PE space, but, as we’ve seen with virtually every other LLM, none of them are game-changers. Again, private equity still needs humans – it still needs those associates, because they can do what AI can’t.
If AI is asked to analyze potential deals, for example, it will default to showing the most obvious ones. But that’s not helpful – every competitor also knows these are the most interesting deals, which means you’ll either be massively overpaying to beat the competition, or you have to come at it from an utterly unique angle.
If the machine can be trained to look deeper for that unique angle based on your perspective, your network, and your experience, then it gets interesting. But current AI can’t do that, and certainly not on its own. Again, it requires a human to be involved in the process, a human who actually understands the business. In other words, it requires an associate.
6) The Next Phase Of AI Development Will Be Logging Companies
Even if AI isn’t permanently replacing jobs on a massive scale any time soon, it’s here to stay. 2026 is the year AI will become like plumbing in software companies’ larger infrastructure. Already, it’s being adopted and integrated into operations like any other long-established tool, from the Google search engine to Microsoft Office.
Even great plumbing needs a plumber from time to time, and that’s why logging companies will become the next major player in AI development. As more companies adopt AI, whether their own proprietary open-source models or models borrowed from the big guys, it’s inevitable that the technology will, at some point, break. And when it breaks, it will be more important than ever to have an exact log of what went wrong and how.
Companies like Datadog, Observify (recently acquired by Snowflake), and others will certainly expand into AI model management to address the rapidly increasing need for logging. It will be especially crucial for smaller companies incorporating AI into their business, as their plumbing often tends to be a house of cards to begin with. Staying on top of it when it breaks, both so it can be quickly fixed and to ensure it doesn’t happen again, will be a requirement for any software business that wants to stay in the game.
7) AI Will Become Invisible Infrastructure Within The Product
Similar to AI becoming plumbing within the broader infrastructure of software companies, it will also become invisible infrastructure within products themselves. If you’re a software or tech-related company just now piloting AI in 2025, you’re already behind the ball. 2025 was the year companies put the relatively nascent tech through its paces; 2026 will be about figuring out how to seamlessly integrate it into products and services.
The barrier to entry for AI is low, and it’s been easy for engineers and developers to put it to the test. The best now know exactly where it can help, where it can’t, and how to take the next step of making it an unobtrusive, key component of their products to better serve their customers.
Ironically, this is where smaller software companies have an advantage over bigger, more sprawling companies. Their more streamlined operations mean they can be quicker to adopt and adapt AI technology than big companies, where the gap between what the CEO thinks AI can do and what it can actually do remains a huge hurdle. The opportunity presented by AI will be huge for companies that know how to properly grasp it.
8) Cloud Costs Get Sober
Before AI, it was the cloud. Everything was in the cloud. Your data? The cloud. Your operations? The cloud. Your servers? The cloud. Your grandmother’s pictures from 1983? The cloud. For years, the cloud was treated like a magical Mary Poppins bag, where you could put everything and anything and retrieve it whenever you wanted.
The problem is that, unlike Mary Poppins’ magical carpetbag, cloud computing costs money, and lots of it. Constantly escalating cloud costs are likely to have software companies rethinking whether everything needs to go to the cloud in 2026. Does it need to be in a public cloud? A private one? Is it local to them? Companies will be pondering the right way to go.
Chicago-based Basecamp, for example, famously ditched all its AWS servers a few years ago and built its own. While that may not be feasible for all companies from a cost and management perspective, we’ll inevitably see the hybrid cloud computing model become the norm as individual companies determine the best option for their businesses. The pressure will be on the Microsofts, Amazons, and Googles of the world as workloads potentially start to come down in 2026.

Much of my job consists of reading about companies our fund might want to buy. I usually read about them long before I meet the people who started them. I have a soft spot for entrepreneurs, as you might already know, so I am easily inspired by all the different ideas people have turned into thriving businesses. However, when you do something a few hundred times a year for a couple of decades, you can get pretty surgical about what you look for in a new investment. Often, this means the stories behind the businesses (and the people who built them) get lost in the routine because when you are working through a stack of investment opportunities, you don’t make time for nuance. I’m sure our limited partners feel the same way; they spend all day reading about fund prospects, their “value-added, proprietary strategies,” and their “top-quartile” returns. Even trying to avoid cynicism, it’s easy to get a little jaded over time as you look for the uniqueness. As a result, we develop heuristics to speed up the process.
For anyone who has read Daniel Kahneman’s book Thinking Fast and Slow (here’s a review, so you don’t actually have to slog through it), you know these heuristics are just our brain’s way of avoiding the hard work of thinking through complexity, an automatic response our brains use to find shortcuts to the straightforward, comfortable answers.
A recent paper by a team at Georgia State University drew on research on heuristics by Kahneman and others and applied it to how private equity (PE) firms screen for new investments. For the most part, the paper is pretty “inside baseball” stuff. Still, if you’ve ever worked in the industry, the quotes from the PE partners they interviewed for the project could easily have come directly from the Monday deal meetings at any fund in the country.
Even if you’re not into behavioral economics books or academic papers on PE, if you spend any time around people in the PE or venture capital industry, you will hear the term “pattern recognition“ all the time. “This is a pattern recognition business” is definitely in the top ten PE clichés, just behind “value add” and “proprietary deal flow.” This term is generally shorthand for “I’ve been in the business for a while; I have a lot of experience; I’ve seen it all; nothing gets past me.”
Some of the typical “patterns” in PE are no husband-and-wife teams, no first-time CEOs, never get involved in a land war in Asia. These simple statements are written in stone at most firms, as the Georgia State authors found out, and pretty much every partner at every firm has a few extra handy for every investment their fund considers. Most PE execs would argue that having pattern recognition gives you a leg up on rookies who haven’t put in the required time to acquire this “mystical power” themselves. “You aren’t given this power from a unicorn, son; you only acquire the right to be intellectually lazy after years of hard work! Now print me out that board deck so I can read it on the early train to Greenwich!”
In this industry, your pattern recognition skills are a badge of honor. Much of your conviction for or against a deal is built on the patterns you’ve seen fail or succeed in the past. But what is meant to be code for rigor, experience and wisdom are actually just Daniel Kahneman’s pesky “System 1“ thinking fooling you with false confidence. In reality, the patterns private equity folks see around them aren’t patterns at all; they’re just mirages of simple thinking which your lazy brain defaults into so it can avoid taxing itself with complexity.
Here’s my simple case against these pattern seers: say you’ve been in the business for twenty years (which is pretty long for a relatively young industry like private equity) and say you have closed one new investment each year during that time (and that would be a hall of fame pace – I’m not joking there is actually a PE Hall of Fame). This would give you twenty data points across twenty different companies. But these companies operated during different economic cycles, were led by other management teams, and competed in markets with various macro and micro forces driving them over the years. Each company also experienced varied growth, regulatory, competitive, and other critical dynamics during the investment period. Because of all this variability, I don’t believe that you can really develop any reliable patterns.
Even if you include all the investments made by everyone at your firm during that same period, had a few others from friends’ firms, a handful of stories you heard where investments didn’t go so well for one reason or another; I’d still argue there isn’t enough data to discern anything close to a pattern – there are just too many competing variables to solve for in such a small data set. At best, you might have some metadata; but that’s a topic for another post.
Instead, what you have is Kahneman’s and Amos Tversky’s (a longtime collaborator of Kahneman) Availability Heuristic. This is a mental shortcut people use to estimate the probability of something because it’s easy to think of examples, combined with a heavy dose of Substitution (using a simple question to answer a difficult one). Everyone who has ever sat through a Monday deal meeting at a PE firm knows what I’m talking about. Invariably, someone will bring up a recent personal experience to make a point about a potential investment and expect that to count as reliable evidence. In the Georgia State paper, the authors found similar behavior across a couple of dozen firms using Paul Slovic’s (and others’) Affect Heuristic – the reliance on feelings when making decisions, especially when judging risks.
Calling it pattern recognition makes it sound like there are data and math behind the argument (the pattern part), wrapped up in the wisdom of a long career (the recognition part). It’s one of those things that is taken prima facie, without rebuttal. A skill younger practitioners in our business aspire to over their careers as a familiar knock on someone’s investment judgment is that they haven’t yet developed enough pattern recognition. But the idea of pattern recognition in private equity investing is classic “System 1” thinking; it’s dominated by emotions, not logic.
According to Kahneman’s research, “System 1” thinking uses the automatic, subconscious part of the brain, and it’s where this thing called pattern recognition in PE thrives. Your brain spends most of its time using “System 1” to keep things simple, but there is plenty of scientific research proving how flawed “System 1” is when assessing risk and seeing reliable patterns. The insidious part about “System 1” thinking is this: because it is automatic, it feels like it comes from wisdom and experience (your gut!) when it actually comes from laziness. Folks who study how the brain works recognize this for what it is.
By creating these heuristics, our brains don’t have to fire up “System 2” to sort things out the hard way, with slow, effortful, and deliberate consideration. This means the pattern recognition you summon isn’t the result of thinking deep thoughts and experiencing the hard knocks of a long investing career; it is really just your brain sitting in front of the TV with a beer in your hand, Cheetos dust on your stomach, watching Night Court reruns.
To practice what I preach, I’ll put my heuristics on the table in the list below. Like a much more eloquent Irishman than I once sang, I’ll wear it proudly. With my “System 1” thinking in full force, these are the biases I run through as I think about new investment opportunities:
- Maniacal focus on the customer: Is the management team obsessed with the customer experience? Have they built a product that is the result of in-depth customer insight? By this, I don’t mean that they “know their customer,” I mean, do they do the things the great product companies do? See Scott Cook and the constant re-imagining that goes on at Intuit for a reference point. Have they kept this discipline as the company grew, or does it need a refresh?
- Subscription or transaction-based revenue model: Key points here are customer and revenue retention from year-to-year. A simple test to track momentum for subscription models is to look at growth in the Deferred Revenue line on the balance sheet. And in case you were wondering, repeat customers don’t count as recurring revenue!
- Mission-critical product: Is this something that the end-user can’t operate her business without? Is it painful to switch? What are the available substitutes? That doesn’t necessarily mean that the product is a big piece of enterprise software. Just look at how payment gateways have become a critical component of the SaaS and mobile app market – pretty simple software, but you can’t get paid without it.
- Short sales cycles: I prefer companies that can close a new customer in less than forty-five days (from the first interaction to collecting the cash) and, in some cases, close a customer on the first interaction. Call this a “one-call close.” Short sales cycles also generate lots of data, so you can quickly adjust your approach and get immediate feedback. My goal with every company in which I invest is to build the talent and the tools to know if we had a good day or a bad day every day.
- Decision-maker contact: I like companies that can talk to the decision-maker in the sales process (reinforces my one-call close above). I stay away from companies that sell to buyers with layers of decision-making or sell products that require layers of approval. This drives my interest in companies that sell into the small-to-mid-sized businesses (SMB) and companies with discreet products that don’t need lengthy evaluations.
- Many targets: Maybe one of the more obvious ones on the list, but the market should have lots of end-customers to target. Even in small markets, you can build successful companies if there are many customer segments. The key in a small market is to develop a company that can win 50% or more market share.
- Cross-sell/up-sell: It’s always great to sell more products to your existing customers. Not all companies have this opportunity, but when they do, it can really drive predictable growth when combined with highly tuned organic sales efforts. Some call this “land and expand,” and it can really work well in technology companies if you have a wedge application that gets you in the door and then builds off the excellent customer experience you deliver.
- Cash flow: Subscription and transaction revenue models often lead to strong cash flow because customers pay up front or because revenue is highly predictable. At the stage our firm invests, we are well beyond the cash-burn days of startups; the companies we pursue often have handsome cash flow margins. We’ll save the debate about what’s more critical, cash flow or earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation, and amortization (EBITDA) for another time (but let me give you a hint, it’s cash flow!).
- Non-linear upside: Are there elements about the market dynamic or the business model that could drive exponential growth? Like when you not only grow by adding new customers, but you also grow when your customers grow (see the payments industry). Are there scenarios in which a strategic acquirer would pay an outlier multiple of revenue or profits to acquire the business? Having these characteristics isn’t always necessary for success, but they sure are nice to have.
- Downside protection: This is the opposite of the point above but even more critical in my view. I like investment opportunities where, even if things don’t go as planned, I can still achieve a return through a good structure, an attractive valuation, or a resilient business model. Private equity (unlike venture capital) is a business where your bad investments still need to return capital if you expect to generate decent returns for your investors. Losses are fund killers. As an investor in the rapidly changing technology sector, this means risk mitigation is my primary consideration.
As you can see from the list above, many of my biases revolve around the product, revenue model, and sales cycle. When it comes to analyzing these components for new investments, call me old-school, but I rely on primary research rather than pattern recognition to drive my decisions. Pattern recognition is the mental algorithm to avoid the hard work of fighting your biases to uncover great investment opportunities – you build it, it gets smart, and then you just let it run. The difference in approach is like the difference between the algo/flash traders on Wall Street and the buy-and-hold guys from a generation ago.
While no company checks every box above, I look for varying degrees of emphasis across these components to quickly gauge whether I want to dig deeper. Laying out my biases with my team helps expose where we might be missing something essential or worrying too much about something unimportant to the likely outcome. I ask my team to throw theirs on the table along with mine to make the exercise transparent. This is where careful consideration comes in and when the real analysis begins, absent any claims of pattern recognition.

Somewhere along the bootstrapping journey, the worries that consume successful company founders start to change. Back in the early days, just making payroll was enough to stress anyone out. You didn’t have time to worry about the consequences; you just found a way to get through. But once the business is stable enough, allowing you to pause and catch your breath, you often find yourself starting to worry about more distant threats:
- Does my team care about our customers as much as I do?
- Are my salespeople hungry enough for that next big deal?
- Do we really need to make the investments that my engineers keep stressing about?
Congratulations. Worrying over these things means your business is stable enough to worry about the future. But with most of your net worth wrapped up in the company, you should be worried. So much for diversification. That’s having all your eggs in one very fragile, very personal basket. But beware, this is often the stage in which the company loses its Chief Executive Officer and gains a Chief Worry Officer. You can try to hide your new role, but your team can see it on your face and hear it in your voice, and you can bet they talk about it when you aren’t in the office.
This new role usually takes shape after a company has achieved some success, when founders worry less about losing everything and more about just keeping what they’ve got. I stole this title from a founder I acquired a business from fifteen years ago. After getting to know each other, I asked him why he was selling his business. He said, “I’m no longer the CEO, I’m the CWO.”
He explained that for the last couple of years, he just started saying “no” to everything. With several million in cash flow and a nice, stable business, as he told me that day, he had stopped “playing to win” and had started “playing not to lose.” It takes a self-aware CEO to be that reflective. While he wanted to see his team succeed in the business, he didn’t want to take the personal risks required to reach the next level of success, given all the hard work it took to get to his current, comfortable position. If you grew up watching football, you know this move. A team builds a lead, shifts to the prevent defense, and then watches helplessly as the other team marches right down the field. In football, they say, the only thing it prevents is winning. Same for companies.
This isn’t rare, either. The Exit Planning Institute found that only 20 to 30 percent of businesses that go to market actually sell. Many who failed to sell got stuck in CWO mode for too long, letting the business plateau until it lost its appeal to buyers altogether.
How can entrepreneurs break out of the CWO funk and get back in the CEO seat? What can they do to get back to playing to win again? Over my career, acquiring companies from founders, I’ve discovered that you need to revisit four things if you find yourself in this common slump. Let’s call them the “Four Ts” so we can all remember them.
Tone
This is an easy one. A key factor in any company’s success is the tone established from the top; if you’ve slipped into the CWO role, refreshing your tone is more important than ever. I’m not suggesting that you get a personality transplant. Just that your team has to feel the renewed passion, see the willingness to take (calculated) risks, have the approval to spend a little money testing a few new ideas, and feel confident in your ability to handle some failures along the way.
There’s research to back this up. Gallup has found that about 70% of the variance in team engagement can be traced directly to the person leading the team. If you’re radiating anxiety and caution from the corner office, it’s trickling down to every conference room and Slack channel in the building. And disengaged teams are expensive. Gallup’s 2025 global workplace report estimated that low engagement costs the global economy $438 billion in lost productivity. You don’t need to become a motivational speaker. Even small, visible shifts in tone can unlock energy your team forgot they had. Think less Stuart Smalley, more Ted Lasso. Show them you believe winning is still possible, and soon enough, they’ll start believing it too.
Touch
This is a fun one. When was the last time you visited customers in their office? When was the last time you manned the booth at a trade show? How about meeting with your competitors’ CEOs? You need to get out there and touch the market again.
McKinsey’s research on B2B customer experience found that companies committing to real customer experience transformations saw revenue growth of 10 to 15 percent and cost-to-serve reductions of 10 to 20 percent. That’s not from a new product launch or an acquisition. That’s from listening and responding to the people who actually pay your bills. One CEO McKinsey profiled cut customer churn by 75% and nearly doubled revenue over three years. His summary of the strategy? “It’s amazing the things you can do when you shut up and listen to your customers.”
If you haven’t read George Day’s The Market-Driven Organization, go out and get a copy. If you haven’t sat onsite with customers and quietly observed how they use your product, do that a dozen times. Call the CEOs of your competitors and ask them to dinner. You’ll be surprised how much they worry about all the same things as you do.
And one final exercise: find a few companies you admire, call their CEOs, tell them what you are worried about, and ask if you can spend a day at their company learning about how they run their business. This is the business equivalent of what the main character does in Nick Hornby’s High Fidelity, going back to talk to all his exes to figure out what went wrong. Except in this version, you’re calling people you admire to figure out what’s going right. I guarantee they will say yes, and I know you will come back with some great ideas for your team to implement.
Team
This is the hard one. After you change your tone and after you get back out in the market, you need to take stock at headquarters. Is the team that got you where you are today the same team that can get you where you need to go? The answer is probably “yes and no.” Or maybe even “I don’t know.” For this exercise, I suggest that you do two things:
Get Some Help: Find an outside consultant or advisor who conducts executive assessments, team dynamics, and leadership development services (make sure you get references because you need someone you can really trust). We love the teams at Wind + Sail and The Table Group. Starting with yourself, assess the skills you have on the team to determine what gaps exist that will stop you from reaching the next company milestone. Be ready to fill the gaps by taking on new roles or adding missing skills. Then sort out how your team works together and where personalities might get in the way of collaboration. Be prepared not only to give more responsibility to those who are ready, but also to remove the cynics and to change reporting structures to get conflict out of the system. It is really hard to remove loyal team members who have been with you for the ride, but it’s unfair to them and the others to keep people in a role they are no longer qualified for or motivated to do.
Give Some Help: Now you need to invest in developing your people so their skills align with the goals. For all their hard work and for the value they’ve created for you, your team deserves the investment in their development. And the data says you’ll get it back. A study from The Fossicker Group found that companies see an average return of $7 for every $1 invested in leadership development, driven by increased revenue, higher retention, and lower recruiting costs. Forty-two percent of companies in the study reported direct revenue and sales increases. You’ll see your team take on responsibility and fill leadership roles in ways that surprise you. What’s the old story? A CEO asks his head of HR, “What if we spend all this money training our people and they leave for our competitor?” And the head of HR says, “What if we don’t train them and they stay?”
Unfortunately, not everyone on the team is going to fill the roles you need, so you’ll have to make hard choices. This process will likely reveal critical gaps, so you might need to look outside the organization to find the necessary skills. In my experience, when you combine raising expectations with team development, people accept change more easily because they see you believe in them and want the best for the business. It’s like the line from The Breakfast Club: people want to know that someone sees them for more than what they appear to be on the surface. Invest in your people, and most of them will run through walls for you.
Tech
This is an expensive one. There is no end to the number of IT projects that could improve your business. Many founders delay the big ones over the years because things seem “good enough” from where they sit. But the technology bill comes due sooner or later when an event disrupts operations, or when you start losing ground to competitors who slowly catch up and pass you.
And that bill has gotten bigger. Deloitte’s research shows that average technology spending across businesses rose from about 4.25% of revenue in 2020 to roughly 5.5% in 2022. For small companies with revenue under $50 million, Gartner pegs it at closer to 6.9%. AI investments will likely increase that number. If you’ve been pinching pennies on technology for years, you’re likely falling further behind than you realize.
There are only two kinds of IT projects: hard and difficult. The hard, but obvious, projects require spending money on new products or features. With these projects, it’s easy to imagine the revenue that will flow in once they’re complete and the team is out in the market selling. Every company has a few obvious product investments that will quickly make customers happy, so start with those.
Difficult projects lack obvious potential payback and require the most change in how the business operates. These projects involve harnessing technology to run the business better: customer relationship management, marketing automation, data analytics, and AI. Nobody throws a parade when you implement a new CRM, but the companies that get these enterprise systems right tend to be the ones still standing and growing five years from now.
Don’t know where to start? I suggest this as a topic of conversation when you spend a day inside the companies you admire. They can help by showing you the technology they use to help run their businesses. Plenty of technologies can deliver a significant impact with relatively small investments for businesses that commit resources and time. You need to identify the best ones for your company and commit to getting them done.
If you find yourself becoming the Chief Worry Officer for your company, take a hard look at the Four Ts above. Change your Tone, get back in Touch with your market, invest in your Team, and stop deferring your Tech decisions.
The CWO role feels comfortable, but comfort is just a slow way of falling behind. Good luck, and let me know how it goes.
