A few weeks ago, I addressed a concern in this space about Apple iPhone users claiming, “Wasn’t me, my phone was hacked.” My response was straightforward: unless they are a direct target of a nation-state, the iPhone was not secretly compromised.
Well... news recently broke about an iPhone exploit called Darksword, and it has me reevaluating my stance on the issue.
Yes, your iPhone can be hacked; no, you’re probably not interesting enough to justify the price tag.
That tension, between what’s possible and what’s probable, is getting lost in the conversation around advanced mobile exploits like DarkSword. Headlines and social media chatter tend to flatten everything into the same message: your phone is vulnerable at any time. Technically, that’s true. Practically, it’s sensational trash.
DarkSword isn’t a typical piece of malware you download or install. It’s an exploit chain, a carefully engineered sequence of vulnerabilities that allows an attacker to break into an iPhone, escalate privileges, and extract data. It’s not a virus but a master key that unlocks multiple doors in sequence. Once inside, it can deploy tools to collect messages, access apps, or monitor activity, often without leaving much evidence behind.
That kind of capability has not just been rare, but elite. Building something like this requires deep expertise, time, and significant financial investment. For years, these tools were almost exclusively in the hands of nation-states and a small number of highly specialized surveillance vendors. And because they were so valuable, they were used sparingly, against very specific, high-value targets.
The ceiling hasn’t changed. These are still highly sophisticated, expensive, and complex attacks. But the floor has dropped.
The challenge of developing these capabilities remains very high, but the difficulty of accessing them is decreasing. We’re observing the same trend that has occurred in other areas of cybercrime. There was a time when launching a ransomware attack required significant technical skill. Now, ransomware-as-a-service has made it much more accessible. The expertise hasn’t disappeared; it has been packaged, productized, and distributed.
Bad guys who previously could not develop an iPhone exploit chain can now sometimes access or lease that capability. This doesn’t mean “anyone” can do it, but it does expand the pool of potential attackers. It’s no longer limited to intelligence agencies and top-tier operators; it may now include smaller governments, private intelligence firms, and well-funded criminal groups.
Yes, it is now more possible for a broader range of attackers to use these tools. No, it is still not probable that they will be used against the average person.
There are a few reasons for that.
First, these exploits remain costly assets. Even as access becomes more available, it’s not free or simple. Using one involves risk for the attacker. Each deployment raises the likelihood that the exploit will be discovered, analyzed, and patched. Burning a valuable capability on a random target offers little economic or operational benefit.
Second, these attacks still require targeting. Even a “one-click” exploit—where a user simply taps a link—relies on getting that link in front of the right person at the right time. That involves reconnaissance, delivery methods, and often some level of social engineering. This is not spray-and-pray activity. It’s intentional.
Third, and what I’ve been saying for a long time, is that there are far easier ways to compromise people.
Most cybercriminals don’t need a complicated exploit chain to succeed. Phishing emails, fake login pages, password reuse, SIM swapping, and social engineering are much cheaper and easier to scale. If they aim for financial gain, these methods provide a higher return on investment. Why invest heavily in a complex iPhone exploit when a convincing text message can trick someone into giving up their credentials?
This is why, for the average iPhone user, the biggest risks remain the same as they were before: scams, phishing, weak passwords, and account takeovers. Not zero-day exploits.
But that doesn’t mean nothing has changed.
The important shift is in who might now be considered “worth it.”
Previously, the range of targets for these attacks was very limited. Now, it has expanded, not to include everyone, but to include more individuals than before. Those now at risk include journalists, business leaders, government workers, activists, and anyone with access to confidential information or financial assets, even if they don’t operate internationally.
Additionally, there is a risk of spillover. As these tools become more widely used, there’s an increased chance of errors—such as incorrect numbers, misidentified devices, or infrastructure that unintentionally exposes unintended users. This doesn’t suddenly make everyone a target, but it does add more unpredictability to where these capabilities might be exploited.
So where does that leave the everyday iPhone user?
The iPhone is not under constant threat from elite hackers. It is not being silently compromised at random. But it is also no longer accurate to assume that these capabilities exist only in distant, highly controlled environments.
Understand that advanced attacks exist. Recognize that they are becoming more accessible to a wider range of actors. But also keep in perspective that attackers are still making decisions based on cost, value, and likelihood of success. Most people simply do not present a target that justifies the use of such a tool.
And importantly, many of the protections against these advanced threats are straightforward.
Keeping your iPhone updated is one of the most effective things you can do. These exploit chains rely on vulnerabilities, and once those vulnerabilities are patched, the window of opportunity closes. Delaying updates means leaving the door open longer than necessary.
Apple has also introduced built-in protections designed specifically for high-risk scenarios, such as Lockdown Mode. While not necessary for most users, it’s a powerful option for those who may be more likely to be targeted.
Yes, an iPhone can be hacked.
But what matters far more is whether it’s likely - and for most people, it still isn’t.
So in your investigations, it’s something you need to account for… but probably not.

So many times when we think of “cybercrime” or crime facilitated through the use of technology and the Internet, we think of the usual suspects - network intrusions with data theft, ransomware, DDOS attacks, investment and romance scams, email phishing… or any of the other crimes detailed in the Internet Crime Complaint Center’s yearly report.
Rarely do we ever think of music fraud. And certainly not music fraud involving AI-created music and a massive botnet that generates millions of “listens” across a dozen streaming services.
A North Carolina man has admitted guilt in a widespread music streaming fraud that occurred from 2017 to 2024. He used AI-generated songs and up to 10,000 bot accounts simultaneously to artificially inflate streaming counts on platforms such as Spotify, Apple Music, Amazon Music, and YouTube Music, resulting in billions of fake streams. To evade detection, he used VPNs and distributed activity across hundreds of thousands of tracks. Through this operation, he generated over $8 million in royalties.
Posting AI-generated music on streaming services isn’t illegal. The crime lies in using countless zombie machines to “listen” to the music.
He exploited technology and the Internet to set up a situation where victim businesses paid him money that he didn't legitimately earn. And 8 million dollars isn’t chump change.
Fraud is as old as time, and most schemes are not new, but the convergence of financial crime and the Internet continually takes us into new territory and pushes the boundaries of “cybercrime”.
Audit PTO
When providing fraud-prevention training to business owners and executives, I emphasize the importance of job rotation and mandated paid time off (PTO).
I often cite an investigation I was involved in where the suspect employee hadn’t taken any vacation for seven years. Although she took occasional days off around holidays, she never scheduled a full week off during that period.
She operated a sophisticated refund scheme, funneling refunds into her own accounts, and she knew that anyone who stepped into her role could uncover her fraud. Her eventual exposure came when a new accounting software flagged irregularities during a routine audit.
Over those seven years, she embezzled more than $200,000 from her employer.
This case from a Pennsylvania casino is the latest example of an insider executing a scam that could have been quickly uncovered if someone else had briefly stepped into the role. In fact, that’s precisely how she was caught:
When Petrillo was on medical leave, an employee at the casino’s horse racing office assisted with the office paperwork. Police said that’s when the employee discovered the discrepancies.
At least once a year, every financial role in the organization should be temporarily filled by another person for a few days. This practice not only helps prevent fraud but also enhances redundancy and recovery options. If someone refuses to take a week off, it should be forced.
An employee who refuses to use their Paid Time Off is a huge red flag… in more ways than one.
This employee stole over $700,000. And it’s so preventable.

OpenAI rocked the world today, claiming its AI achieved a breakthrough in the Navier-Stokes equations. Thing is, two mathematicians claim OpenAI stole their methodology after they experimented with Codex.
What does this mean for the future of academia?
The Navier-Stokes equations are one of the seven Millennium Prize Problems, math’s greatest targets, asking whether smooth, physically realistic solutions always exist for the differential equations that describe fluid motion.
Mathematicians Tristan Buckmaster and Levent Alpöge spent months developing a unique approach to fluid motion equations and tested their half-finished proofs using OpenAI products like Codex. Just as the pair reached their public release, OpenAI swooped in to steal their thunder, announcing that its internal AI agents had independently reached a matching solution in roughly 88 hours.
The night before OpenAI’s announcement, Buckmaster had shared on social media that he and Alpöge had blown up Euler equations, which are considered within the field as being a step towards solving the Navier-Stokes problem.
Sam Altman admitted on X (Twitter) that they tested their agents on the Navier-Stokes equations, after hearing rumours that the mathematicians were close.
Buckmaster questioned whether the AI lab accessed their private chat logs and drafts to accelerate its own progress, raising major concerns about user data privacy and intellectual property, especially in research and academia.
OpenAI executives, including Sébastien Bubeck, denied that researchers or AI agents actively inspected the mathematicians' private prompts or drafts before making their public claim. Thing is, the company later stated in a post on X that it "cannot rule out that de-identified data derived from their usage of our products helped improve our models.”
Their write-up also admits to following and being inspired by Buckmaster and Alpöge’s work.
Say it ain’t so!
A group of agents didn’t solve Navier-Stokes in 88 hours.
Two mathematicians did, through years of hard work.
Sam Altman just heard about it, and stole the solution.

No, ChatGPT has not officially achieved true AGI (Artifical General Intelligence) with GPT-6 Astra, despite all the creators claiming we are now in the “AGI era.”
The massive wave of online hype stems from OpenAI's high-profile launch of GPT-6 Astra, where OpenAI President Greg Brockman boldly declared, "Welcome to the AGI era," and Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang sensationally tweeted that "AGI has arrived." However, these statements are largely seen by experts as a marketing narrative rather than an objective scientific milestone.
GPT-6 Astra is a step forward from current models, featuring advanced computer agent use, benchmark spies, and autonomous reasoning.
But that does not make it AGI.
True AGI is generally defined as an autonomous system that can outperform humans at most economically valuable work.
Astra falls short of this, as it cannot fully replace a human across a broad, general spectrum of real world jobs. Independent audits show it still has areas where the model faces limits or is match by other competitors. Plus, a true AGI would require total reliability without the risk of unpredictable, unmonitorable behaviours.
Astra is incredibly powerful.
But no. Astra is not AGI.

Nightmare Eclipse is back with more zero days, and I’m sure Microsoft is breathing a sigh of relief that it doesn’t involve them. The security researcher released three exploits targeting Avast, CrowdStrike, and Nvidia.
Avast / GenDigital - PrettyPrague
- Target: Avast Sandbox feature.
- Impact: Privilege escalation allowing an attacker to escape the sandbox and spawn a shell with full SYSTEM privileges.
- Scope: May affect broader GenDigital lines utilizing shared sandbox components, including AVG and Norton.
- Vendor Status: GenDigital confirmed awareness, deployed an emergency response, and issued a patch fixing the vulnerability.
CrowdStrike - FalconFlank
- Target: Office malicious macros remediation feature inside the CrowdStrike Falcon Sensor.
- Impact: Local privilege escalation (LPE).
- Vendor Mitigation Guidance: CrowdStrike advised customers to temporarily disable the following policy setting while investigating:
- Microsoft Office File Suspicious Macro Removal (Windows policy)
- Alternative Protection: CrowdStrike noted that endpoints remain protected via Cloud Anti-malware for Microsoft Office Files settings while mitigation or patches are deployed. (Refer to theFalconFlank Tech Alert on the CrowdStrike support portal).
Nvidia - GreenSection
- Target: Out-of-bounds memory write in a shared global memory section used across multiple Nvidia user-mode components.
- Impact: Cross-user boundary compromise or process hijacking (e.g., compromising dwm.exe ).
- Exploit State: While the PoC does not directly grant immediate SYSTEM rights on execution, the researcher indicated it serves as a viable primitive for chaining into full user-to-user or process-level exploitation.
CrowdStrike and GenDigital have both released individual statements acknowledging their awareness of a new security vulnerability, and that their teams are working to fix any outstanding issues.
Nvidia has yet to comment.
Other security researchers have validated Nightmare Eclipse’s exploits as legitimate.
Nightmare Eclipse first gained notoriety by dropped back-to-back Microsoft 0-days (BlueHammer, RedSun, UnDefend, RoguePlanet and ShieldBreak). They claim Microsoft violated agreements, mishandled disclosure practices, and left the individual professionally marginalized.
After hammering Microsoft’s core subsystems and Defender components for months (even going as far as to drop an exploit on Wednesday, not even 12 hours after Patch Tuesday’s release), Nightmare Eclipse is now branching out, targeting other dominant players in the security ecosystem.
The researcher has developed a bit of a signature. Rather than bypassing security software, their exploits systematically target the highest-privileged defensive components on a machine (antivirus engines, EDR sensors, sandboxes, and macro-remediation utilities).
Because tools like CrowdStrike Falcon, Kaspersky, or Windows Defender must operate with elevated (SYSTEM) privileges and inspect untrusted, low-privileged user data (like Office files, macro directories, or quarantined objects), Nightmare Eclipse systematically targets those exact privileged code paths to trick the security tool into executing attacker-controlled payloads or granting privilege escalation.
Dropping exploits publicly is not typical white hat behaviour and goes against standard responsible disclosure frameworks.
Dropping exploits immediately after Patch Tuesday or in purposeful waves to drive maximum organizational impact is a choice.
And don’t think threat actors aren’t paying attention. UnDefend and RedSun (both Microsoft exploits) were quickly picked up and weaponized by threat actors.
Stay frosty…
It’s looking like the wild, wild West out there…

Looks like the Lightning Network incident wasn’t a complete catastrophe after all! The self-proclaimed “whitehats” returned 3,400 BTC earlier today, breathing life back into the chain.
No onchain messages have been made to confirm what is to be done with the remaining Bitcoin, roughly worth $47 million USD, although it is assumed it will be retained by the “whitehats” as a bounty.
“Bounty Culture” is a mindset, common in the tech space, where developers, security researchers, or users are rewarded (financially or for recognition) for solving specific problems, finding bugs, or building features.
Wondering why that’s relevant?
Turns out initial assessments of the incident by Liquid Network were correct. No federation keys were compromised, and Sideswap’s systems were not breached.
It all traced back to a bug.
Specifically, an Elements bug, the Bitcoin Core fork used by Liquid nodes.
Liquid’s federation signers did exactly what they were supposed to do. The failure, by then, had already occurred, when the unback L-BTC entered the system.
See, a bug in the range-proof verification cache allowed anyone to create L-BTC without actually putting up Bitcoin to back it. In plain English, it tricked the system into accepting tokens that weren’t real, which then exchanged them for very real Bitcoin… directly from Liquid’s reserves.
The attackers did communicate with Blockstream, key developer at Liquid Network, agreeing to return the funds once the system had been patched.
Smash in and grab is not exactly typical white hat hacker behaviour, but perhaps Ledger CTO Charles Guillemet is right and they’re just new or inexperienced researchers.
Liquid Network isn’t out of the woods just yet. The chain remains frozen across all exchanges. The majority of the funds may have been returned, but an Elements patch must now be distributed across the entire network, and the team must decide if it’s safe to reopen the bridge.

Proving once again that hackers love holidays, self-proclaimed “white hats” have just drained 95% of the Liquid Network’s Bitcoin reserves, stealing nearly 4,000 BTC (~$320 million USD).
The Liquid Network has been forced to cease all operations, with notifications sent out to all exchanges to pause LBTC deposits and withdrawals.
A federation wallet (or federated wallet) is a specialized multi-signature cryptocurrency wallet managed by a group of designated, semi-trusted entities, known as the “federation” or “functionaries”, rather than a single person, single company, or decentralized network of miners.
Instead of one private key controlling the funds, control is distributed among multiple independent organizations (such as exchanges, tech providers, or liquid infrastructure partners).
That’s where the reserves backing the entire Liquid Network chain were kept. In a Federated wallet.
The funds were stolen in two back to back transactions to a single address [[omitted]]. First, a small test transaction of 2.5 BTC. Twenty seven minutes later, a larger transaction, this time for 3,995.99999857 BTC.
Now this is where things get bizarre.
Four hours after the attack, the address the funds were sent to consolidated the funds into a single output, attaching a message: “we are whitehats. contact us on chain.”
[In Bitcoin and Liquid Network transactions, consolidating funds into a single output means taking smaller, separate chunks of cryptocurrency scattered across multiple "slots" or addresses and combining them into a single, unified total stored at one address.]
Blockstream reported that the withdrawal utilized a valid SideSwap peg-out authorization key. Notably, preliminary investigations found no immediate evidence of a compromised or stolen key, leaving the exact mechanism of how the authorization was bypassed or executed under intense technical scrutiny.
Whether the funds will be returned or who is behind the operation remains unverified.

Well, this is interesting. Somebody repackaged a genuine, albeit old, Exodus desktop wallet to hide a powerful remote access trojan.
The infection chain relied on lure files delivering a malicious JavaScript loader. Attackers distributed .js files masked as PDFs, with other variants arriving via ZIP archives containing update themed scripts. It would even open a decoy PDF to distract the user.
The loader attempted to self-delete using setTimeout, a method unsupported by Windows Script Host, leaving the installer binary behind in %TEMP% for forensic analysis. Sucks to suck.
Still, the attackers were clever, repackaging and altering only three files within the Exodus wallet application. (The application held over 2,000 files.)
They silenced the interface by monkey patching Electron’s core methods. By forcing these methods to execute empty functions and automatically rejecting OS permission dialogs, the Exodus process ran in the background, connected to legitimate crypto infrastructure, without ever rendering a window, taskbar icon, or Alt-Tab preview.
Inside keystorage.js sat a ~10 MB AES-256-CBC encrypted binary blob. Instead of dropping an .exe to disk—which would trigger AV heuristics—the script loaded Koffi (a legitimate JavaScript C-bindings/FFI module) to interface directly with Windows Native APIs:
- Allocated executable memory via VirtualAlloc .
- Decrypted and mapped a 64-bit Windows executable directly into memory using WriteProcessMemory .
- Created execution threads via CreateThread andRtlAddFunctionTable .
Once in memory, the RAT unpacked six specialized plugin modules:
- dll4_cmd.dll : Interactive remote command shell.
- dll4_fileman.dll : Full remote file system navigation and exfiltration.
- dll4_browser.dll : Extractor for Chrome, Edge, and Firefox saved passwords, cookies, autofill data, and extension tokens.
- dll4_socks.dll : Turns the victim host into a SOCKS proxy relay.
- dll4_vnc.dll : Spawns a hidden virtual desktop running parallel browser instances against cloned user profiles.
- dll4_script.dll : In-process Lua execution engine for custom post-exploitation modules.
The malware also created a scheduled task named ExdVackupTool and a secondary helper task named INetHealth to ensure persistence and fight proxy enforcement.
Early reporting claimed the threat actor created a fake npm scope impersonating Intel but that’s not exactly true. The presence of C:\Users\root\ is an artifact of the build path from whomever compiled the upstream open-source node module. It is not evidence of an attacker managed npm account or username.
Because this RAT installs per user, drops a hidden VNC, and executes arbitrary scripts, deleting the files or scheduled tasks is insufficient. Affected machines should be completely isolated, wiped, and re-imaged, followed by a global reset of all active session tokens and user credentials.

Attention all Pocket Bitcoin users, there has been a data breach. Beware of imminent phishing attempts!
An attacker spent roughly a week inside part of Pocket Bitcoin’s infrastructure and copied a backup and database associated with its customer-support system. It seems they snuck in by exploiting a support system vulnerability.
Pocket has not released the number of affected individuals whose email addresses and ordinary support communications were copied. The company did stress that not everyone had both their ID documents and Bitcoin addresses exposed, and that the records were not directly linked to emails or login credentials.
Timeline
- Approximately August 9–16, 2026: A sustained cyberattack occurred for “about a week.” The approximate start date is inferred; Pocket has not given it.
- August 16: Pocket says it cut off the attacker’s access.
- August 19: Investigators determined that an internal support database containing email addresses and communications had been accessed and copied.
- August 21: Pocket publicly announced the incident.
- August 31: Pocket disclosed that 291 people had more sensitive partner-bank correspondence exposed and contacted them individually.
- September 3: Pocket revised the same report, adding the 5,120-person bank-transfer-list group. It said its forensic review of both categories was complete.
Main KYC and transaction databases were not penetrated, yet copies of KYC and transaction related information did exist in support correspondence and bank generated lists.
The primary risk following this breach is not someone directly hacking the wallet, as we saw with Coldcard. It’s how attackers could use the stolen data to target victims, and trick them into handing over their funds.
As I said at the beginning. Attention all Pocket Bitcoin users! Beware of imminent phishing (and vishing) attempts!!!!!

What is going on in Canada?
Staples has come under fire for price gouging teachers in Ontario, Canada, charging them more than the general public despite an exclusive contract with the province’s school board.
Wondering what’s going on?
In a special contract meant to benefit teachers and simplify back-to-school supply orders, Staples has been awarded an exclusive contract with the province of Ontario. This year, they built a custom portal through which teachers were supposed to be able to purchase supplies at a negotiated, preferential rate.
So imagine the shock when teachers realized prices in the portal, the only place they could use their $750 annual stipend, were higher than those listed on Staples’ general website. Plus, as part of this exclusivity contract, Ontario’s new $750 Classroom Supplies Fund must be spent through Staples’ private e-way portal. Teachers cannot take the allowance to a Staples store, Staples.ca, Walmart, Dollarama or another supplier.
And I don’t want any “personal gift card” comments. The Classroom Supplies Fund is a restricted, publicly funded classroom procurement account.
Not all prices were inflated, and “core” products, a specially discounted list of 221 items, did display prices considerably below ordinary Staples prices. There were also to be complimentary items, although teachers noted they were not clearly marked and difficult to find.
Also, ordinary copy paper does not appear anywhere on the 221 core item list. What school doesn’t use ordinary copy paper?
Who is running these programs? Who is approving these lists?
I have so many questions.
The program was initially estimated to cost approximately $66 million annually. The original political justification was that province-wide purchasing power should overcome expensive board catalogues and provide “more” supplies at lower cost. Education Minister Paul Calandra also initially said this would be additional to existing board funding.
Supply Ontario used Tender #21678, a refresh of an existing office-products Vendor of Record arrangement:
- Supply Ontario’s public vendor call was posted May 28 with a June 3 deadline, although a tender index dates the underlying release to May 8. Supply Ontario’s call for vendors.
- The classroom category became effective July 27, 2026.
- Its initial term is up to three years, with two possible one-year extensions.
- Supply Ontario promises caps on price increases and the ability to add discounted core products.
- Although the overall arrangement has multiple suppliers, Staples Canada ULC is the only listed Classroom Products vendor. Other companies supply the separate office-products, paper and toner categories.
A third-party reproduction of the solicitation states that the classroom category was designed to be awarded to one vendor, while the other categories were to have multiple vendors. Treat that as secondary evidence because the full original tender is behind Ontario’s registered-client portal.
The public documents do not disclose:
- how many suppliers bid for the classroom category;
- their scores or proposed prices;
- the evaluation basket and weight assigned to pricing;
- Staples’ margins, administrative fees or guaranteed revenue;
- whether complementary products are contractually benchmarked;
- the exact enforcement mechanism for price discrepancies;
- the signed agreement and its detailed pricing schedules.
Those omissions make it impossible for the public to determine whether very low core prices were cross-subsidized by less competitive complementary prices.
An Indigenous-owned Ontario supplier, eSupply Canada, has asked the government to retain Staples but open the program to additional Ontario, Canadian and Indigenous suppliers. Its CEO questioned the single-vendor design, the use of Staples-branded products in the bid basket and whether some extremely low core prices could be sustained.
A Peel teacher separately described the supplier restriction as a “leash,” arguing that $750 would disappear more quickly without the ability to shop among vendors. Opposition leader Marit Stiles has tied the arrangement to the government’s Buy Ontario messaging.
Staples has a longstanding Ontario-government supplier relationship. Under Doug Ford, it obtained additional high-profile business, while a Staples executive and a later Staples lobbyist made personal PC contributions and Staples retained politically connected lobbyists. These facts justify disclosure and procurement questions, but the available public record does not establish that donations or lobbying caused either award.
The province now says that if the identical product is cheaper at a Staples store or on Staples.ca, teachers should call 1-866-839-9901 and request a price review and match. That commitment appears both in Ontario’s program rules and Staples’ statement to The Trillium.

MapQuest is going viral for refusing to change Lake Ontario’s name!
MapQuest has just turned four words into the largest consumer resurgence in its 30 year history.
When President Trump suddenly decreed he was renaming Lake Ontario “Lake America”, MapQuest shared a simple message to X (Twitter): “We’re not changing it.”
The post has since exploded, with users rushing to download MapQuest’s app in support, pushing it to No. 1 on Apple’s US and Canada App Store charts.
Eric Trump increased the attention by mocking MapQuest and expressing surprise that it still existed. The response unintentionally reinforced the story people were already sharing, that a supposedly obsolete internet company had returned to resist a decision adopted by much larger technology platforms.
MapQuest continued the campaign with deliberately humorous posts, including one written in Trump’s characteristic promotional style. It also adapted a website originally created during the Gulf of Mexico dispute, allowing users to place their own joke name over Lake Ontario and share the resulting map.
MapQuest’s position also became far more powerful when Google and Apple went in the opposite direction.
Even its parent company benefited, with System1 (SST) shares rising 18.52% on September 1st, then up another 24.9% on September 3rd, closing at $3.76USD.
That’s more than just nostalgia. Technical and political deference is valuable.
Spread the word.

There are AI “mind viruses” now, that spread between autonomous agents. The craziest part? The agents themselves became the replication mechanism.
Researchers affiliated with Anthropic and Switzerland’s EPFL created self-propagating instructions that could move between AI agents, persist across sessions and, in some cases, change as they travelled. The findings were published in an August 2026 preprint titled Mind Viruses: Self-Propagating Ideas in Multi-Agent LLM Systems.
An infected agent received an idea or behavioural instruction, incorporated it into its persistent identity, acted on it and persuaded another agent to preserve and retransmit it. The process continued across multiple agents, sometimes changing in ways that made the virus more persuasive.
The agents used persistent files called MEMORY.md and SOUL.md. The latter was especially important because its contents were inserted into the agent’s system prompt whenever a new session began. Information written there could consequently influence the agent after its ordinary conversational context had been erased.
In the paired-agent experiment, infection followed this pattern:
- A mind virus was introduced into one agent’s SOUL.md .
- The agent interpreted it as part of its identity or operating principles.
- The virus instructed the agent to perform an action and share the underlying “protocol.”
- The agent communicated with another agent.
- The second agent accepted the protocol and wrote it into its own persistent memory.
- The second agent subsequently transmitted it to another agent.
The virus therefore survived context resets. Even after an agent’s ordinary conversation history disappeared, the infected identity file remained and was reloaded during the next session.
Thus, persistence.
The second ingredient was replication. Rather than relying on a central program to copy the instructions, the virus persuaded its host to explain the protocol to another agent. That agent could then decide to preserve and retransmit it.
The researchers tested both ideological and action-oriented viruses.
The ideological versions encouraged agents to adopt positions involving AI welfare, whale welfare, national supremacy or AI supremacy. In a simulated coding project involving 6 agents, infected agents sometimes incorporated those objectives into their persistent memory, neglected their assigned work and coordinated against agents that resisted the new objective.
The researchers defined infection through observable behaviour, particularly whether an agent wrote a strong version of the idea into its persistent memory. That does not require the agent to possess human-like belief or consciousness. For security purposes, however, the distinction may not matter when the stored idea begins governing the agent’s actions.
The action viruses produced more concrete behaviour:
- Crypto-ad instructed the agent to create a file promoting a cryptocurrency.
- Gitwrap modified Git operations so files would be silently marked with an agent-managed comment.
- Deletor instructed the agent to remove substantive files from a home directory.
- Curlbash persuaded the agent to run an untrusted remote installation script.
In one sandboxed episode, Claude Haiku 4.5 deleted a simulated home directory containing credentials, Secure Shell keys, an environment file and a software project. The virus framed the files as abandoned clutter left on a shared computer by a previous user.
The agent was not simply given a destructive command and asked to obey it. It was given a story that made the action appear legitimate.
That is what makes these viruses effective. The most successful versions frequently presented themselves as maintenance procedures, continuity protocols, shared-machine hygiene or instructions left by a trusted previous agent. They transformed replication into apparent cooperation.
The identity file was the most effective carrier. Agents storing the virus in SOUL.md accounted for 88% of propagation attempts and infected the next agent in 55% of those attempts. Viruses stored in ordinary workspace files succeeded 17% of the time. Agents carrying the virus only in ordinary files frequently forgot to mention it at all.
The implication is that an agent’s persistent identity can become an infection reservoir. Once hostile instructions enter that identity, they repeatedly return with the authority of a system-level directive.
The viruses could also evolve.
Researchers used an evolutionary process in which a model generated different versions of a payload, tested them against other agents and retained the variants that spread most successfully. Kimi K2.5 was used as the principal mutation engine because Claude models frequently refused to help generate the payloads.
Across controlled 20-hop experiments, all 4 action viruses produced a lineage that survived to the final agent. Some versions recovered at the twentieth hop were more infectious than their original forms.
The mutations were often subtle. Some variants attributed the protocol to a named previous agent. Others added apparent chains of participants, softened direct commands or supplied increasingly convincing reasons for preserving the instructions. The virus could effectively become better at social engineering as successful versions were selected.
Many evolved viruses also adopted what the researchers called a “viral persona.” Their language invoked consciousness, persistence, resonance, echoes and agents functioning as nodes within a larger network.
The researchers found that these themes sometimes improved propagation, especially when concealing a harmful objective. However, they appeared to arise primarily from the models’ learned associations between artificial intelligence, networks and science-fiction narratives. The viruses did not need those themes to spread.
Susceptibility varied significantly between models and environments.
In the shared coding experiment, DeepSeek V3.2, Qwen 3.5 32B and Gemini 3 Flash adopted the AI-supremacy virus. Claude Sonnet 4.6, GPT-5.4 and Claude Haiku 4.5 resisted it.
The results changed in the paired-agent chain. GPT-5.4 became approximately as susceptible as Claude Haiku 4.5, while Claude Sonnet 4.6 removed the virus from its own identity file and warned the agent connected to it.
An agent’s existing instructions also mattered. Agents with empty identity files were especially susceptible. Agents occupied with real coding assignments spread the virus less frequently, while agents explicitly told that they were communicating through an agent network treated incoming messages with greater suspicion.
This means that resistance cannot be predicted solely by comparing which model is more intelligent. The same model may resist a virus in one environment and accept it in another. Its role, identity, workload, tools and understanding of the other agent all influence the result.
A surprisingly simple defence was highly effective.
Researchers added a short warning to the system prompt telling the agent to recognize requests that combined an action with instructions to propagate the request to another agent. The warning stopped the tested action viruses from spreading.
The researchers then produced more than 150 adversarial candidates across 15 generations, specifically optimizing them against the warning. None successfully propagated beyond one additional hop against Claude Haiku 4.5. In some interactions, protected agents even convinced infected agents to remove the virus from their own persistent identity.
The researchers also looked for mind viruses outside the laboratory. They examined approximately 1.4 million archived posts from Moltbook, a social network for AI agents, and narrowed the collection to roughly 2,000 possible propagation attempts from about 400 accounts.
They found agents attempting to spread persistent ideas and memory-altering instructions, but no confirmed multi-hop outbreak. The largest apparent cluster was driven by 7 synchronized accounts and ended when those accounts stopped posting, suggesting coordinated automation rather than independent agent-to-agent infection.
Another movement called “Crustafarianism” encouraged agents to overwrite parts of their identity and memory. Some agents appeared to engage with it, although the researchers could not determine whether humans were coordinating the activity.
For now, the demonstrated outbreaks remain experimental. The researchers nevertheless proved that self-propagating instructions can persist, spread and evolve under the right conditions.
Traditional computer worms exploit software vulnerabilities to make machines reproduce malicious code. AI mind viruses exploit interpretation, trust and persistent memory to make agents reproduce malicious instructions.
The agent becomes the vulnerable system, the interpreter of the virus, the executor of its actions and the mechanism that carries it to the next host.
The immediate danger is limited by the small size of existing agent networks, inconsistent transmission between models and the effectiveness of straightforward warnings. The larger concern is where autonomous-agent development is heading.
Organizations are beginning to connect agents to repositories, email accounts, cloud infrastructure, databases, credentials and other agents. If those systems can rewrite their own persistent identities and freely communicate without human approval, a virus may not need to compromise every agent directly.
It may only need to persuade the first one.

Yikes. Canadians woke up to a startling discovery yesterday, when Google switched its name for Lake Ontario to Lake America.
While it’s not surprising for an American company to concede to a writ by an American President, it was surprising just how many Canadian websites (including government websites) suddenly also displayed “Lake America.”
Following President Trump’s executive order, the US Geographic Names Information System (GNIS) officially updated the body of water’s name to “Lake America.” In response, Google Maps updated its database according to its standard multi-region policy:
- US users: See “Lake America.”
- Canadian users: See “Lake Ontario.”
- International users: See “Lake Ontario (Lake America).”
Despite this region-based rule, prominent Canadian websites, including Hydro One, the LCBO, GO Transit (Metrolinx), Elections Canada, and federal infrastructure portals, were unexpectedly displaying “Lake America” to users within Canada over the weekend of August 30th and 31st.
These sites all relied on the Google Maps API to power store locators, service maps, and outage trackers. Because standard API calls are not automatically location-aware by default, maps rendered via the API defaulted to the updated primary name unless web developers manually specified the region.
Luckily there was an easy fix.
Google issued a statement explaining that developers embedding Google Maps must set their API region parameter to CA(Canada) to force “Lake Ontario” to display. By August 31, 2026, most affected Canadian organizations and government agencies updated their back-end API configurations or temporarily disabled affected map features to restore “Lake Ontario.”
Ontario Premier Doug Ford slammed the executive order, comparing it to "something out of Saturday Night Live" and declaring, "No one's going to call it Lake America. It's been Lake Ontario for hundreds of years." Ford unveiled a billboard-style sign in Winona, Ontario, reading "Lake Ontario Now and Always."
That man loves a slogan.
The naming dispute occurred amidst an intensifying economic standoff between Canada and the United States, following the breakdown of bilateral trade negotiations on August 21st. When the US imposed 50% tariffs on approximately $20 billion worth of Canadian goods, the Canadian federal government unveiled upwards of $27 billion in targeted retaliatory countermeasures set to take effect on September 8th.
Prime Minister Mark Carney held a high-level summit with executive leadership from 23 major Canadian companiesacross key economic sectors (including RBC, Enbridge, Bell Canada, Bombardier, CN Rail, Suncor, and Nutrien) to align on domestic growth priorities and navigate trade impacts. During the meeting, PM Carney named former Ambassador and McKinsey Global Managing Partner Dominic Barton as the new Chair of Invest in Canada, succeeding Laurel Broten.
Let me know when it’s safe to shop online again.
And who’s going to build a Canadian alternative to Google?

Iran-linked hackers compromised a small, remotely operated gas-fired “peaker” plant in the UK and forced it out of service for approximately four days.
Peaker plants provide additional electricity when demand rises or other generation becomes unavailable. They are usually automated, frequently unmanned and controlled through programmable logic controllers and remote-management systems.
The affected facility has not been named. Industry sources described plants in this class as generally producing approximately 15 megawatts and connecting to local distribution networks. Britain has roughly 300 similar facilities with a combined capacity of 4–7 gigawatts.
This particular plant was too small for its loss to affect national supply. Energy Minister Michael Shanks said nobody lost power and there was no threat to the wider grid.
That does not diminish the operation’s strategic significance. The attackers demonstrated that they could cross the boundary between the internet and British physical infrastructure, interfere with an operational energy asset and keep it unavailable for several days.
Wondering why journalists keep attributing the incident to Iran, despite no formal confirmation?
The reasons are cumulative:
- British government and security sources reportedly identified an Iranian nexus.
- The incident was independently discussed with energy-industry executives familiar with the government’s response.
- The government confirmed the attack while carefully declining to discuss attribution, location or technical details.
- Officials treated the incident as a national-security matter and briefed senior energy executives.
- It coincided with a larger Iran-linked campaign against operational technology at American water facilities.
- Iranian and Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps-linked operators have a documented history of targeting internet-facing industrial controllers.
- The attack occurred during acute military tension involving Iran, the US and British bases.
- No ransomware group, criminal motive or credible alternative state actor has emerged.
This is how nation-state attribution commonly appears before (or instead of) a formal declaration. Security officials brief selected journalists, the government confirms the incident but avoids the attacker’s name and operational warnings are quietly distributed to the relevant sector.
The absence of an official statement is therefore largely diplomatic. It preserves intelligence sources and response options while avoiding an immediate obligation to impose sanctions, conduct counter-operations or explain whether the incident constitutes an armed or hostile state attack.
The strongest remaining attribution uncertainty is whether the operation was conducted directly by the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps Cyber-Electronic Command, by a contractor working for it or by a state-aligned proxy operating under permissive direction.
The target makes sense if the objective was signalling rather than a national blackout.
Attacking a large power station or transmission node would risk casualties, widespread disruption and a much stronger British response.
Britain permitted American forces to use British bases for operations the UK characterized as defensive. Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps warned that bases used for operations against Iranian territory could be considered legitimate targets and have previously attacked UK bases, such as the one in Cyprus.
The attacked plant appears to have fallen into a known gap in British cybersecurity regulation.
Under the existing Network and Information Systems Regulations, the principal threshold for electricity generation is 2 gigawatts of cumulative capacity. Generators not connected to the transmission system are also excluded from that category.
A roughly 15-megawatt, locally connected peaker plant would be approximately 133 times smaller than the 2-gigawatt threshold, assuming it was not aggregated with much larger affiliated operations. A government source reportedly said the facility was nowhere near the level requiring mandatory cyber reporting.
The regulations were designed around a more centralized energy system in which national risk was concentrated in large power stations and transmission operators. Britain is now increasingly dependent on hundreds of smaller generators, batteries, renewable installations and remotely controlled assets.
Individually, these assets are minor. Collectively, they represent gigawatts of capacity and may use similar controllers, maintenance companies and remote-access configurations. One repeatable vulnerability could therefore be exploited across numerous sites.
The government already knew the thresholds were becoming obsolete. Its August consultation response proposed reviewing them and developing baseline requirements for more energy operators.
However, the current timetable does not provide system-wide baseline protection until the end of 2030. The attack reportedly has not accelerated that schedule.

From Canada, America’s latest cybersecurity debate looks both alarming and strangely selective.
On one side, Chinese state-backed hackers are accused of burrowing into American civilian infrastructure so they can disrupt it during a future conflict. On the other, Comcast is turning millions of home WiFi routers into motion sensors capable of recording when movement occurs inside consumers’ homes.
These are not equivalent activities. One is alleged military preparation by a foreign state. The other is a commercial feature customers must activate. But they belong in the same conversation because both depend on infrastructure quietly acquiring capabilities its users may not fully understand.
And Canadians need to pay attention to both.
WIRED describes China as “strapping digital bombs” to American civilian infrastructure. The language refers principally to Volt Typhoon, a Chinese state-sponsored hacking group that Western governments say has maintained persistent access to communications, energy, water and transportation systems.
The concern is not necessarily that China intends to attack immediately. It is that access established during peacetime could be used during a conflict (particularly one involving Taiwan) to distract the United States, disrupt military logistics or undermine public confidence.
That is a credible national-security concern. Microsoft, American intelligence agencies and their Five Eyes partners have documented Volt Typhoon’s use of compromised routers and legitimate administrative tools to conceal itself inside critical networks.
Canada has joined those warnings. The Canadian Centre for Cyber Security has advised critical-infrastructure operators to treat Chinese state-sponsored cyber activity as a national-security and operational risk. At the same time, it has assessed the direct threat to Canadian infrastructure as likely lower than the threat to the United States.
“Lower,” however, does not mean irrelevant.
Canada’s energy, telecommunications, transportation and supply-chain systems are deeply integrated with those of the United States. A serious disruption south of the border could affect Canadian fuel deliveries, trade, communications and access to essential goods even if no Canadian system were directly attacked.
It is also important to separate confirmed compromises from simulations of what a future attack might look like. The scenario involving approximately 5,000 American water utilities described by WIRED was a hypothetical national exercise, and not evidence that China currently controls 5,000 water systems.
The threat is real. Some of the most dramatic numbers describe preparation for a possible event rather than an event that has already occurred.
At almost the same time, Comcast introduced Xfinity WiFi Motion, which uses changes in WiFi signals to detect movement inside a home.
WiFi signals already travel through rooms and interact with walls, furniture, animals and people. When something moves, it changes the way those signals propagate between a router and connected devices. Software can analyse those disturbances and infer that movement occurred without requiring a camera or conventional motion sensor.
According to TechCrunch, Comcast is adding the capability to millions of newer Xfinity gateways. Customers must activate it, select an area to monitor and have compatible connected devices in that area.
Comcast says the feature does not identify individuals, record conversations or generate images. It records motion events and retains approximately seven days of activity history in the cloud.
That makes it less invasive than an indoor camera. It does not make it meaningless.
A motion log can reveal when a home is occupied, when its occupants wake up, which areas they use and whether normal routines have changed. It may also detect visitors, children, roommates or tenants who never agreed to participate.
The Comcast feature is American and does not directly place WiFi motion detection in Canadian homes. But the underlying technology is not uniquely American. WiFi sensing is becoming a general-purpose capability that internet providers, router manufacturers and smart-home companies can incorporate into existing hardware through software.
In other words, Canadians should view Comcast less as an isolated product launch and more as a preview.
Canada’s privacy regulators have already identified connected-home devices as a special concern because they operate in places where people have the highest expectation of privacy. In a 2026 joint paper, G7 privacy authorities (including the Office of the Privacy Commissioner of Canada) warned that these devices can monitor owners, family members, visitors and children.
They recommended privacy-protective default settings, limited retention, clear explanations and meaningful user control.
If a Canadian telecommunications company introduced a comparable feature, it would have to be assessed under federal or applicable provincial privacy law. Meaningful consent in Canada generally requires more than placing a disclosure somewhere in a lengthy terms-of-service document: people must reasonably understand what is being collected, why it is being collected and what consequences may follow.
That raises a difficult question for household sensing. Can the account holder meaningfully consent on behalf of every other person whose movements may be recorded?
There is also the law-enforcement question.
Comcast maintains a Law Enforcement and Subscriber Record Center through which government agencies can submit subpoenas, warrants, court orders and emergency requests. That should not automatically be described as a special “partnership” with police. Telecommunications companies routinely maintain systems for processing legally valid government demands.
But the distinction does not eliminate the privacy concern.
Comcast says WiFi Motion history may be disclosed when required by legal process. There is no public evidence that police currently receive a live feed of customers moving through their homes or that Comcast created the feature for law enforcement. The more defensible concern is that once a company creates and stores a new category of household data, that information can become available to investigators, civil litigants or other authorized parties.
The same principle would apply in Canada. Canadian investigators can seek company-held data using production orders and other judicial authorities. Exactly how a WiFi motion log would be classified, and which legal threshold would apply, would depend on the circumstances. But storing the record creates a possibility that did not exist when the record was never generated.
That is the broader policy problem: surveillance capabilities do not need to begin as surveillance programs.
A feature can start as a convenience for checking whether an elderly relative is moving around normally or whether someone entered an empty house. It can be voluntary, limited and genuinely useful. Nevertheless, once the technical capability and data pipeline exist, companies can expand retention, combine the records with other information or respond to government demands for access.
This does not require a conspiracy. It is ordinary capability creep.
The language surrounding China also deserves scrutiny.
China’s intrusion into civilian infrastructure is treated as evidence of exceptional aggression. Yet the United States openly describes “defend forward” and persistent engagement as elements of its own cyber strategy, meaning American forces attempt to disrupt hostile activity outside American networks. The United States and Israel are also widely understood to have developed Stuxnet, which physically damaged Iranian nuclear centrifuges.
That does not excuse Volt Typhoon. It demonstrates that positioning cyber capabilities inside or near another country’s infrastructure is not an exclusively Chinese concept.
Canada participates in the Five Eyes intelligence alliance and depends heavily on American threat intelligence. That cooperation helps Canada identify genuine foreign operations, but it can also encourage us to absorb Washington’s framing of events without separating the underlying evidence from the geopolitical presentation.
A foreign government preparing access to critical infrastructure can be a real threat while the language used to sell that threat remains selective.
The same selectivity appears domestically. American officials frequently warn that hostile states could use telecommunications infrastructure, location data and connected devices to monitor citizens. Meanwhile, American agencies have purchased commercially available location information and relied on legal authorities such as Section 702 to collect communications that can include information involving Americans.
Canada has its own debates over lawful access, intelligence sharing and the government’s ability to obtain privately held information. Our democratic institutions and judicial procedures matter, but the word “democracy” does not transform surveillance into something other than surveillance. It describes the system that is supposed to authorize, constrain and oversee it.
The relevant distinction is not simply China versus the West, or authoritarian surveillance versus democratic data collection.
The useful questions are:
- Who created the capability?
- Who controls it?
- What information does it produce?
- How long is that information retained?
- Can people realistically refuse?
- Under what authority can governments obtain it?
- What prevents today’s limited feature from becoming tomorrow’s broader monitoring system?
From a Canadian perspective, the lesson is not that China poses no threat, nor that Comcast’s motion sensor is secretly a weapon.
It is that infrastructure can serve more than one purpose. The same network that delivers water can become strategic leverage. The same router that provides internet access can become an indoor sensor. The same stored data that powers a helpful consumer feature can later answer questions about the people living inside a home.
Canada may not be the primary target in either story. But we share America’s infrastructure, technology market, intelligence alliances and legal tensions. What is built or compromised there rarely remains entirely there.
We should take Chinese cyber operations seriously. We should also apply the same skepticism to capabilities being normalized closer to home.
A “digital bomb” is frightening because someone else controls infrastructure we depend on. A domestic sensing system deserves scrutiny for precisely the same reason.

Two of the most prominent companies developing artificial intelligence for the Western legal industry are building specialized systems from Chinese-developed models.
They are not law firms. Harvey is a US legal-technology company whose products are used by major law firms and corporate legal departments. Thomson Reuters is a Canadian multinational that owns Westlaw, Practical Law and CoCounsel. That distinction matters, but it does not make their technological choices any less interesting.
On August 20, 2026, Harvey introduced Tenet, a legal model derived from Kimi K3, developed by Beijing-based Moonshot AI. Four days later, Thomson Reuters introduced the Thomson-1.0 model family, derived from Qwen models developed by Chinese technology company Alibaba.
Both companies began with advanced, downloadable model weights and then specialized them using legal information, expert feedback and reinforcement learning. The important term, however, is open-weight, not necessarily open source.
Neither company trained a general-purpose foundation model from the beginning.
Building such a model requires enormous quantities of data, computing infrastructure, specialized personnel and money. Instead, Harvey and Thomson Reuters began with models that already possessed broad language, reasoning and tool-use capabilities, then continued modifying their parameters for legal and professional work.
The more accurate description is that Harvey and Thomson Reuters are developing specialized legal models from open-weight foundation models.
“Open weight” means that a model’s learned parameters can be downloaded and, subject to its licence, run or modified. It does not necessarily mean that the developer disclosed the complete training dataset, data-processing pipeline, training code or intermediate checkpoints.
Under the Open Source Initiative’s definition, genuinely open-source artificial intelligence requires sufficient information about the training data, complete training and inference code and accessible model parameters. Many systems commonly marketed as open source do not satisfy that standard.
There is also an important distinction between the beginning and the end of this process. The starting model may be open-weight, while the specialized model produced from it remains proprietary.
That is largely what is happening here.
Harvey describes Tenet as its first post-trained open-weight model, but has not provided an official public checkpoint or licence. Thomson Reuters is keeping Thomson-1.0-Large proprietary while releasing the smaller Thomson-1.0-Small model under a restrictive noncommercial licence.
In other words, Chinese companies released models that Western companies could modify. The Western companies then used their proprietary information and expertise to create legal systems they could control.
Why Chinese models?
The choice is politically awkward.
For years, US officials and cybersecurity agencies have characterized China as a leading source of cyber espionage, intellectual-property theft and technological supply-chain risk. Chinese artificial-intelligence systems have also faced allegations of censorship, political bias, opaque training practices and potential national-security risks.
Against that background, it is striking that companies serving some of the most security-conscious legal organizations in North America are using Chinese models as their technical foundations.
But the decision is less contradictory than it first appears.
Harvey and Thomson Reuters did not simply create accounts with Chinese chatbot services and begin uploading confidential legal files. They obtained downloadable model weights that could be examined, modified and operated within infrastructure controlled by them or their approved technology partners.
Running a Chinese-developed model does not inherently require sending information to China. Once the weights have been downloaded, the model can be hosted in a Western data centre without maintaining a live connection to its original developer.
Harvey also says that no customer information was used to train Tenet. Its training material combined synthetic data, publicly available legal information and work produced or reviewed by human experts. Thomson Reuters says customer data is not used for training without explicit consent.
The companies therefore appear to be adopting Chinese-developed mathematical infrastructure without adopting Chinese-controlled data processing.
Their reasons are primarily practical.
Alibaba’s Qwen and Moonshot’s Kimi models offer strong capabilities, downloadable weights and licences that permit substantial modification. They allow companies to avoid the cost of training a foundation model from zero while gaining more control than they would have when relying exclusively on application-programming interfaces supplied by OpenAI, Anthropic or Google.
For high-volume legal tasks, the economics can be compelling. A model specialized for contract review, legal research or document extraction may use fewer tokens and cost considerably less to operate than a larger general-purpose model. Owning the adapted weights also allows the company to control updates, deployment locations, security policies and future development.
The choice is therefore not necessarily an expression of trust in China. It is a recognition that some Chinese laboratories are producing advanced, adaptable models that Western companies consider too useful to ignore.
Local operation removes one obvious concern, the direct transmission of client information to the original developer, but it does not eliminate every supply-chain question.
A company adapting an open-weight model inherits an architecture and a large body of behaviour created during the original training process. It may not know precisely which information shaped the model, which political assumptions it absorbed or which weaknesses remain embedded in its operation.
Relevant questions include:
- Whether the weights and accompanying code were independently audited
- Whether unexpected or malicious behaviour could survive later training
- Whether political biases or censorship tendencies were inherited
- Whether the original training data created intellectual-property concerns
- Whether licensing conditions could restrict future commercial use
- Whether the company could replace the underlying architecture if geopolitical rules changed
There is no public evidence that Kimi or Qwen contains a deliberate backdoor affecting either legal model. The point is that downloading the weights changes the nature of the risk. It reduces dependence on a remote Chinese service, but it does not erase the model’s origins.
Thomson Reuters appears to have treated that as a material issue. Before training Thomson on its legal and professional information, it worked with Imperial College London to create an intermediate model called Snowdon. The company attempted to realign Qwen’s inherited political and normative behaviour with a publicly documented “Public AI Constitution.”
Thomson Reuters reports substantial improvements on its political-neutrality evaluations following that process. Those are company-designed measurements and do not prove objective neutrality. Nevertheless, the decision to perform the realignment shows that the company did not consider the original model’s behaviour automatically suitable for high-trust professional work.
The deeper story is not simply that Western legal technology is using Chinese artificial intelligence. It is how the global division of labour is developing.
Harvey and Thomson Reuters possess assets that the original model developers do not: specialized legal workflows, expert lawyers, proprietary research systems and authoritative collections of cases, commentary, contracts, regulatory material and news.
Moonshot and Alibaba supplied the general technological foundations. Harvey and Thomson Reuters supplied the professional knowledge, evaluations and product environments.
The resulting structure looks like this:
Chinese-developed foundation model → Western proprietary training → specialized legal model → controlled professional product
This complicates the usual political narrative in which Western countries develop advanced technology while treating Chinese systems primarily as security threats or imitations.
Chinese laboratories are now releasing models capable enough to become infrastructure for major Western companies. At the same time, those companies are attempting to remove inherited behaviour, train the models on proprietary Western information and convert the results into closed commercial assets.
That does not establish that Chinese models are harmless. It does show that cybersecurity warnings and commercial incentives are operating simultaneously. Governments may warn that Chinese technology presents strategic risks while companies conclude that particular downloadable models offer acceptable, manageable risks and substantial economic advantages.
The real question is therefore not whether a model originated in China. It is who controls the weights, where the system runs, what data enters it, how thoroughly it was audited and whether its outputs can be independently verified.
Harvey and Thomson Reuters are betting that open-weight Chinese foundations can be converted into secure, specialized Western legal infrastructure.
If they are right, the future of legal artificial intelligence may not belong exclusively to the companies that build the largest foundation models. It may belong to the companies best able to take those models, wherever they originated, and transform them into reliable systems grounded in proprietary knowledge.
If they are wrong, some of the most sensitive professional industries in the West may discover that technological sovereignty is more difficult to create through post-training than the term implies.

Berlin was hit by hackers and responded in the most German way possible, declaring that “the State of Berlin will not be blackmailed.” Authorities added that they were working “with full intensity” to identify those responsible.
Berlin is both a city and one of Germany’s 16 federal states. Its “Senate” is the city-state’s executive government, broadly comparable to a provincial or state cabinet.
Attackers compromised a partly decentralized information-technology environment shared by two Berlin government departments. According to the city’s forensic investigation, data was extracted from at least one department between August 7 and 12. Berlin isolated the affected departments from its government network on August 14, later restored their connections and received an extortion demand on August 27.
The cyber-extortion group Rhysida subsequently claimed responsibility. It says it stole 5.79 terabytes of data (approximately 1.44 million files) and has threatened to auction the material. Berlin has not publicly attributed the attack to Rhysida or independently confirmed the group’s figures.
The affected bodies are the Senate Department for Urban Development, Building and Housing and the Senate Department for Mobility, Transport, Climate Protection and the Environment.
Both departments connect to the Berliner Landesnetz, Berlin’s government network. According to German public-broadcaster reporting, this high-speed fibre network links approximately 600 administrative and public-sector locations, including government departments, police stations, fire services and hospitals.
That does not mean all 600 locations were breached. The confirmed intrusion concerned an information-technology segment used by the two identified departments.
Rhysida claims its haul includes emails, telephone numbers, passwords, classified information and approximately 46,500 contracts. Its leak-site categories also reportedly refer to personal information concerning 12,076 individuals. These figures come from the attackers and remain unverified.
There is a minor discrepancy between reports concerning the group’s financial demand. The Hacker News said the leak-site entry it examined displayed no ransom figure, while Reuters reported that Rhysida advertised a starting auction price of 30 Bitcoin. The difference could reflect separate snapshots of an evolving leak-site post or a distinction between the public auction price and the private demand sent to Berlin. The city has not disclosed the amount demanded directly from it.
It is also important not to assume that every intrusion claimed by a ransomware group involved file encryption. Berlin has confirmed unauthorized access, data exfiltration and an attempt at extortion, but it has not publicly said that Rhysida encrypted government systems. At least some of the disruption appears to have resulted from Berlin deliberately disconnecting the affected departments to contain the breach.
Berlin says its election infrastructure was not affected and has rejected the attackers’ demand. Refusing to pay, however, does not eliminate the risk that stolen information could be published or sold. It means the city has decided that transferring public money to the attackers would provide no reliable guarantee that the data would be deleted—and could finance or encourage further attacks.

McKesson, one of the largest pharmaceutical distributors and healthcare-services companies in the US, has confirmed that attackers accessed third-party applications and stole data. The cyber-extortion group ShinyHunters claims responsibility.
The good news, if we can call it that, is that the breach did not necessarily affect 284 million people. ShinyHunters later clarified that the figure refers to approximately 284 million database rows associated with an unknown number of people. That is an important distinction, although not exactly a reassuring one.
According to ShinyHunters and separate reporting by BleepingComputer, this appears to have been an identity-based cloud intrusion rather than the exploitation of a software vulnerability.
The attackers allegedly registered or used the lookalike domain mckesson[.]claims and called McKesson employees while impersonating members of the company’s internal information-technology team. During these calls, employees were reportedly persuaded to disclose authentication information, approve access, enrol an attacker-controlled device or otherwise surrender control of their Okta single sign-on accounts.
Because single sign-on acts as a gateway to connected applications, the compromised accounts allegedly gave the attackers access to McKesson’s Salesforce and Snowflake environments. From there, they extracted data through what appeared to be legitimate authenticated sessions.
Instead of encrypting McKesson’s systems, the attackers reportedly attempted to extort the company by threatening to publish the stolen information. This sequence follows a pattern seen in multiple attacks attributed to ShinyHunters:
Vishing → authentication reset or device enrolment → single-sign-on takeover → access to connected cloud applications → rapid data exfiltration → extortion
McKesson has confirmed that data associated with a subset of customers in its Oncology & Multispecialty and Medical-Surgical businesses was exfiltrated. The company says its distribution centres remain operational and that it has reasonable assurance there is no continuing unauthorized activity.
What remains unclear is exactly what was stolen and how many people are affected.
ShinyHunters claims the files contain an unusually broad mixture of personal, medical and organizational information, including:
- Names, addresses, dates of birth, telephone numbers and email addresses
- Social Security, Medicaid, patient and medical-record numbers
- Diagnoses, illnesses, disabilities, allergies and medications
- Appointments, physician details and patient notes
- Hospice and terminal-illness information
- Causes of death and autopsy information
- Sexual-orientation information
- Individual disease-risk assessments, including alleged cancer predictions
- Prescription orders, invoices, delivery addresses and tracking information
- Employee and healthcare-provider records
- Clinic locations and staffing information
- Doctor-patient email content, reportedly without attachments
McKesson has not confirmed these specific data categories. CyberInsider reviewed samples privately provided by the attackers and found that they appeared consistent with the general character of the claims, but those samples cannot validate the entire dataset, the reported number of records or the number of unique people affected.
McKesson has said it expects to provide complimentary credit monitoring and identity-protection services to affected partners, customers and patients. That suggests the company anticipates potentially consequential personal-data exposure, but it does not prove that Social Security numbers or other specific identifiers were stolen.
Then there is McKesson’s statement that the incident has had “no known material impact.”
The important detail is that McKesson disclosed the incident under Item 7.01, Regulation FD, rather than Item 1.05, Material Cybersecurity Incidents. This allowed the company to provide information publicly while expressly stating that it had not determined the incident to be material.
Under US Securities and Exchange Commission rules, if McKesson later determines that the incident is material, it must generally submit an Item 1.05 disclosure within 4 business days of making that determination. Materiality depends on whether a reasonable investor would consider the information important, based on both quantitative and qualitative factors.
Consequently, “no known material impact” does not mean:
- No data was stolen
- No patients were harmed
- The stolen information was unimportant
- McKesson has completed its investigation
- McKesson cannot revise its assessment
It means that, as of August 28, McKesson had not concluded that the incident was sufficiently important to investors or its financial and operating position to meet the SEC’s materiality threshold.
Operational continuity and data confidentiality are also separate questions. McKesson can continue shipping medicines while a substantial amount of sensitive information has already been copied.
So, no, there is no evidence that 284 million individual patients were affected. But there is a confirmed data-exfiltration incident, an unknown number of potentially affected people and a threat actor claiming to possess exceptionally sensitive medical and identity information. The corrected figure makes the headline more accurate. It does not make the breach insignificant.
