AliExpress has just been caught fingerprinting users, and you’ll never believe how.
A security researcher, Matthew Callaghan, was browsing on AliExpress when he noticed a problem with his Bluetooth headphones. They would cut out… but only when he was in the AliExpress tab. If he closed it, they worked fine.
No matter what he tried, each time he loaded AliExpress, the audio stopped.
Key Technical Concepts: How the Exploit Works
- Web Audio API: A browser feature that allows websites to generate, process, and synthesize audio dynamically.
- Why Audio Fingerprinting Works: When a browser renders an audio signal (e.g., a sawtooth wave), tiny floating-point arithmetic differences occur based on the operating system, CPU architecture, audio drivers, and audio hardware. Measuring the numerical output of these rendering operations yields a stable, unique signature for that specific machine.
- The “Zero-Volume” Trick: To hide what it was doing, AliExpress set the volume ( GainNode ) to zero so no physical sound played. However, because the script still routed the signal to the browser’s audio destination (AudioContext.destination ), the browser treated it as an active stream, forcing the host OS to keep the hardware audio pipeline engaged.
The scripts—primarily collina.js and fireyejs.js—were hosted on an Alibaba AWSC directory on an Alibaba media domain. They form part of Alibaba's proprietary security, risk management, and anti-abuse telemetry framework to detect bots and fraudulent orders without relying on cookies.
Beyond audio rendering metrics, the scripts were extracting canvas rendering data, WebGL shader precision, screen resolutions, hardware concurrency (CPU cores), system memory, installed plugins, WebRTC endpoints, network details, and tracking mouse/touch interaction patterns.
Privacy experts emphasize that while fingerprinting is often justified as fraud prevention, doing so silently via hardware triggering audio graphs violates basic consumer expectations and privacy norms.
Security researchers note that audio fingerprinting is generally considered an outdated, brittle technique in 2026 compared to Canvas or WebGL fingerprinting, making its intrusive deployment puzzling.
Brave, a web browser, announced that its built-in shields actively block the Alibaba security scripts responsible for the audio fingerprinting. Meanwhile, a Firefox engineer publicly clarified that Firefox neutralized WebAudio fingerprinting by default back in 2023 (by introducing subtle random noise into WebAudio output for ~99.24% of users), rendering the tracking metric useless while calling out the script for unnecessarily holding the audio subsystem open.
Security analysts did point out that Chrome remains far more susceptible to WebAudio and multi-signal hardware fingerprinting techniques due to weaker built-in anti-fingerprinting defences.

Sony and Nintendo are racing each other to piss off the most customers, although, from a business perspective, I do sort of understand Sony’s hands might be tied.
Sony has started removing paid digital content from users’ libraries due to expired license agreements. Meanwhile, Nintendo’s arguing in court that consumers are “not entitled” to rebates from tariff refunds… despite the consumers being the ones who paid the tariffs.
Sony announced that 551 StudioCanal titles (including films like Terminator 2, Apocalypse Now, and Paddington) will be permanently deleted from PlayStation Store digital libraries in Europe and the UK. Customers who bought these movies are receiving no refunds or compensation. This mirrors a December 2023 incident where Sony notified users it was wiping over 1,200 Discovery TV shows from user accounts due to expired licenses (though a last-minute deal with Warner Bros. Discovery temporarily preserved access).
It discontinued new movie and TV show sales on the PlayStation Store back in 2021. Because Sony no longer operates an active video storefront, it generates no new revenue from digital video sales to cover the cost of renewing expensive licensing rights with third-party distributors like StudioCanal.
Legally, digital storefront End-User License Agreements (EULAs) classify purchases as revocable, non-exclusive access licenses rather than permanent property ownership.
As for Nintendo, this bad press is entirely of their own making. After the U.S. Supreme Court ruled that certain U.S. import tariffs were illegal (freeing up approximately $166 billion in refunds for importing corporations) Nintendo sued the US government to collect its share.
Two consumers filed a class-action lawsuit in the US District Court (Western District of Washington), alleging Nintendo would be "double-dipping" if it kept the refunds. In 2025, Nintendo had raised retail prices on original Switch consoles (by $30–$50) and accessories (by $5–$10) to offset tariff costs. The lawsuit contends that because consumers paid those higher price tags, they are owed a portion of Nintendo's government payout.
In a motion to dismiss, Nintendo countered that consumers "received exactly what they bargained and paid for" when purchasing products at the advertised retail price. Nintendo argued that buyers are "not entitled to a rebate simply because of intervening legal developments related to tariffs", adding that price adjustments were driven by multiple macroeconomic factors (such as RAM and shipping costs) and that Nintendo chose to absorb tariff costs on other hardware, like the Switch 2.
Lawyers representing Nintendo went as far as to say that "[i]f a consumer did not want to pay the advertised price, they were free to abstain from purchasing the product or seek out competing products".

Every so often the fix for a wildly sophisticated cyberattack is not a patch, not a threat-hunting platform, not a $2 million appliance… It’s four people, a car and some scissors.
Could practically be a Scooby Doo episode.
New Bloomberg reporting revealed how, in November 2024, T-Mobile’s cybersecurity staff identified and expelled Chinese hackers from its network during a spate of industry-wide intrusions, and their decisive move was to physically cut the cable to a compromised system. Four T-Mobile security staffers drove to a data center in Bellevue, Washington, located the compromised box, and cut its cable — a call made by the company’s security head, Jeff Simon, at the height of the attack.
The hackers were Salt Typhoon, and the campaign they were part of is enormous. The Chinese government-backed group compromised hundreds of phone companies, internet giants, and data center providers with the goal of collecting phone records and information about senior US government officials, including then-presidential candidates. The FBI says Salt Typhoon has now breached at least 200 companies across 80 countries, a scale far larger than initially disclosed. The victim list is a who’s-who of American telecom (AT&T, Verizon, satellite network Viasat, and infrastructure giants Charter and Windstream), with attackers obtaining phone data belonging to millions of Americans and targeting figures including President Donald Trump, Vice President JD Vance, and members of Kamala Harris’s 2024 campaign.
Here’s the part that makes the scissors more than a gimmick. T-Mobile spent months hunting for suspected intruders without success. Then they caught a break. Unusual activity on one system that appeared to originate from a router belonging to another telecom company. In other words, the threat was riding in through a trusted interconnection with another carrier, the kind of relationship you can’t just firewall away without breaking the phone network. Rather than flipping the router off remotely, the team chose to physically sever the cable connecting the compromised hardware to the network.
Why go full analog? Because when you don’t know how deep an intruder is or how long they’ve been there, remote commands can be logged, intercepted, or simply not trusted. Cutting the cable was the fastest, surest way to isolate the attack once the infected hardware was found. No software middleman, no chance the hackers see it coming, just an air gap created with hand tools.
And the genuinely important lesson, buried under the very funny headline: T-Mobile came out of this far better than its peers, and not because of the scissors. It avoided a large-scale breach for one specific reason. It caught the activity early, before intruders reached customer data or core systems. The dramatic snip only worked because the detection did. Speed is the actual story.
Speaking of which, T-Mobile is not letting this one go. The snipped cable now sits framed at the company’s headquarters as a “trophy.” Which, honestly, fair. When your incident response plan out-performs half the telecom industry and doubles as office décor, you’ve earned the flex.
Hilarious.

On Friday, August 13, 2026, a lot of people picked up their iPhones to a genuinely unnerving message. Apple alerted users targeted in 110 countries that they’d been hit by mercenary spyware, and says it has now notified customers in over 150 countries since the program began in late 2021.
The notification itself is admirably blunt: “Apple detected a mercenary spyware attack targeted at your iPhone. There are actions you can take now to protect your data and device.”
What’s new this time isn’t just the scale. It’s that the warning got a lot harder to ignore. The alerts now appear directly on the iPhone Lock Screen and in Settings, putting them in front of targeted users before they even reach their inbox. That’s a meaningful shift, and not a purely comforting one. As one analysis pointed out, a Lock Screen banner is visible to anyone standing near the phone (a border officer, a colleague, a relative in a household where being flagged as a target is itself dangerous).
For context on what this software actually is: mercenary spyware is the top-shelf stuff, typically used by governments to target a small number of specific individuals, most commonly tech firms, journalists, activists, politicians, and diplomats. Apple’s own description doesn’t undersell it.
“The extreme cost, sophistication, and worldwide nature of mercenary spyware attacks make them some of the most advanced digital threats in existence today.”
The people who study this for a living think the latest wave is a big deal. An unprecedented number of Apple customers reported receiving the notifications, and John Scott-Railton of The Citizen Lab put it plainly.
“The scale and geographic diversity of public posts about receiving notifications are pretty unprecedented. For every public notification like this, you can imagine there’s a huge notification iceberg that the public will never learn about. This is a clear indication that something bigger is going on.”
Access Now, which runs a helpline for at-risk users, reported a record number of people contacting them after this batch went out. Among the recipients is a Ukrainian Armed Forces soldier who said he was surprised by the warning and didn’t think he was important enough to be targeted, and noted other soldiers got it too.
Apple, as ever, is saying who it isn’t naming. It has not connected the August 2026 campaign to Pegasus, NSO Group, or any named vendor, and says it doesn’t attribute notifications to particular attackers, governments, or regions. The NSO backdrop is hard to ignore, though: a federal court found NSO liable for violating anti-hacking laws in the WhatsApp case, a jury awarded roughly $167 million in May 2025, a permanent injunction took effect January 28, 2026, and Meta filed a contempt motion in June 2026 alleging NSO ran new campaigns against WhatsApp users within days of that injunction.
A few practical notes, because this is the rare threat where the advice actually matters. An alert signals suspected targeting, not confirmed compromise. Apple issues them when it has high-confidence intelligence that someone was singled out. Verify it’s real by typing account.apple.com into a browser yourself; a genuine notification appears at the top of the page, and Apple will never ask you to open an attachment, install a profile, follow a link, or hand over your password or a verification code. That warning is not paranoia: researchers have already documented campaigns that stuff scam text into Apple Account name fields so the message ships inside a real, SPF/DKIM/DMARC-passing Apple email, and a fake spyware alert is an obvious next move. If you’re at risk, Access Now advises not to erase the device, because wiping it destroys forensic evidence.
And the one genuinely reassuring data point: Apple has confirmed that no device running Lockdown Mode has been successfully compromised by mercenary spyware since the feature launched in 2022, a finding Amnesty International’s Security Lab has independently corroborated. The most advanced digital threat in existence, defeated by a toggle most people have never opened.

Turns out “expired” is more of a suggestion than a rule.
When it comes to credit cards, at least.
Researchers at the University of Massachusetts Amherst (Raja Hasnain Anwar, Gerard DeCunha, and Muhammad Taqi Raza) presented an attack at USENIX Security 2026 that revives expired Visa contactless cards and lets them complete real in-store purchases, in a paper titled, with appropriate theatrics, “Zombie Cards Back Online.”
The trick works because of a genuinely dumb gap in how expiry gets checked. Card expiration in EMV contactless payments is enforced as a policy check performed by the terminal, not as a cryptographic fact baked into the card itself. The chip’s private keys never expire, and the certificates that authenticate the card often stay valid well past the printed date to smooth over reissuance. That leaves the actual expiry decision resting on one plaintext field the terminal reads and, crucially, Visa’s EMV implementation (Kernel 3) doesn’t adequately bind that expiration field to cryptographically authenticated transaction data.
So the attack is almost insultingly simple. The team built a relay from two ordinary NFC-enabled smartphones: one phone activates the expired card and pulls its payment data, a second phone rewrites the expiration date to any future value and passes it to the terminal and to an outside observer, the whole thing looks exactly like someone paying with a digital wallet. The attacker doesn’t even need to know the card’s real replacement date, since almost any future date works.
The good news, such as it is, is that this isn’t universal.
Only Visa cards fell for it (Mastercard, American Express, and Discover rejected the tampered transactions, because their kernels actually notice when you fiddle with the expiry). Visa’s approach instead kicks the authentication decision down the road to the bank, so the attack’s success depended on how each bank handled it. One bank approved zombie transactions for amounts up to $500 because it only validated the account and cryptogram rather than the specific card; another consistently declined and told the terminal to use the replacement card. Delightfully, even a non-expired card that had already been replaced kept working on the same account.
There are meaningful caveats before you panic. The attack requires physical possession of the expired card or sustained NFC proximity to it, plus a man-in-the-middle relay, and it only works while the account stays open under the same account number, which is standard when a bank sends a replacement. In other words, it’s not someone skimming your live card from across a café. It’s someone doing something with the dead one you tossed in a drawer or the trash.
Which is rather the point the researchers were making. The work was motivated by documented patterns of improper expired-card handling: issuers tell you to destroy expired cards, but people underestimate the risk precisely because expired cards are assumed to be inactive.
As for the vendor doing something about it: the authors notified Visa in May 2025 and again in December 2025, and neither Visa nor the notified banks have confirmed they’ve fixed the expiration issue. Visa didn’t respond to press requests for comment either. So for now, the mitigation remains the one your bank already told you and you ignored. Put the scissors through the old card.
The Register put it best.
Let the dumpster dive for discarded cards begin.

The following comes from my new paper for the Great British Business Council, Unconditional Surrender! The paper covers all areas of the UK EU Reset, but I’ll focus on the energy section here.
There are two parts to the Energy Reset: the first involves the UK joining the EU’s Internal Electricity Market (IEM) and obeying all of the requirements for membership, such as the EU’s renewable energy targets, while the second part requires the UK to join the EU’s Emissions Trading System (ETS) and abandon its own cheaper ETS, as well as joining the EU’s Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM), which covers 350 individual products and components used to make cement, fertiliser, iron and steel products, aluminium products, as well as hydrogen and electricity. Thus, joining the EU’s ETS will not only increase manufacturing costs in the UK, but also increase the cost of imported materials used by UK manufacturers. These costs will be passed on to customers when possible; however, for goods sold internationally, such as cars, they must remain competitive in global markets, so they may not be able to pass on higher EU ETS and CBAM costs.
The Cost of joining the EU’s Internal Electricity Market
Let’s start at the beginning: The UK already has the highest industrial electricity costs in the developed world, for small, medium, large, and very large electricity users. The graph below is from the UK’s Department for Energy Security and Net Zero (DESNZ) and shows electricity costs, including taxes, for the UK and the 14 most industrial EU Member States:
The problem isn’t just UK taxes, although they are a problem, as shown in the chart below, which shows wholesale prices and environmental taxes and policy costs for various EU member states. You may also see the tiny savings in pink at the bottom of the UK column. That is how much UK electricity companies would save in transmission costs if the UK paid to join the EU’s IEM. The government strangely believes that joining the IEM would make it easier to sell electricity to the EU, but the graph below also clearly shows that the UK’s wholesale electricity prices are much higher than any other country. The only time the UK exports electricity to the EU is when the wind is blowing so much in the North Sea that the UK has wind electricity to spare, but this is ‘sold’ at a minimal price or actually given away, as usually other North Sea EU countries such as Denmark also have excess electricity from their wind farms. Exporting electricity to the EU at almost no cost reduces the need to ask wind farms to turn off their turbines, reducing the need to pay compensation, known as curtailment fees. The electricity still costs the UK the same amount, as this is determined by the Contract price agreed when the Wind Farm was built. Giving the electricity to the EU for nothing does not change this.
If you are wondering why I chose these particular countries, it is because some of the UK’s major manufacturing companies have factories or are building factories there, as shown below. So they are our major EU competitors for manufacturing jobs, while France is our main competition if we want to sell electricity to the EU’s IEM. French electricity is so much cheaper than the UK’s that they already supply us with 8.5% of our electricity each year. This would be higher if electricity imports weren’t constrained by the number of grid connections. This constraint is being addressed, with several new connections planned or under construction. So we should expect to be able to buy even more electricity from France, and possibly give away more ‘free’ electricity to EU members, although not Free for us; we will still have to pay wind farm owners their contracted price.
From the graph above, it is easy to see why the UK is a major net importer of electricity from the EU, as shown in the table below.
But joining the EU’s IEM would also create other problems, most importantly the need to meet the EU’s Target for renewable energy as a proportion of total gross final consumption. The EU target is for its members to collectively reach 42.5% renewable energy by 2030, just four years away. The key point is that this is an ENERGY target, not an electricity target, and the EU’s target is collective, so countries with high renewable shares can offset countries with very little renewable energy. The UK would not have this benefit and would have to meet the target on its own. The UK has also committed to a nuclear electricity program, but the EU does not recognise Nuclear as ‘renewable’. The EU would prefer that we burn high-CO2-producing wood rather than rely on no-CO2-producing nuclear electricity to provide baseload electricity.
In 2025, the UK’s overall renewable energy share was just 16.8%; reaching 42.5% by 2030 would be impossible, and probably impossible over any time period. It would require transport to move from 6% renewable to over 40% renewable and Heating to move from 10% to over 40%. Neither is likely: the UK doesn’t have enough electricity, electric vehicles, or charging points; nor enough heat pumps; nor enough heating engineers to install electric heat pumps, along with the necessary insulation.
The Cost of Joining the EU’s Emission Trading System and its Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism
When the UK left the EU, it also left the EU’s Emission Trading System and established its own market. However, despite the UK’s more zealous restrictions on emission allowances, or perhaps because of this, the UK’s ETS price quickly dropped below the EU’s. This is probably because fewer industrial manufacturers in the UK needed to buy emission allowances, as the Cameron/Clegg government also introduced an additional carbon tax in 2013 called the Carbon Price Support (CPS) levy, which drove more and more manufacturers out of the UK or out of business entirely. The UK still has the CPS, and the Government has promised to abolish it in the 2028 tax year. However, if the UK joins the EU’s ETS before then, the UK’s fewer remaining manufacturers will have to pay both the EU’s higher ETS and the UK’s additional CPS. This will surely drive them out of the UK. And it won’t just harm UK manufacturers – the EU’s ETS system also covers shipping, so it will increase the cost of importing and exporting. While this might make sense for the continental EU Customs Union, it makes no sense for an island nation that relies on sea transport.
The EU’s ETS auction price was about 18% higher than the UK’s ETS auction price at the end of July, but the variation between the two markets has moved from about 40% higher at the end of May 2026 to just 10% higher at the end of January 2026. As shown in the Graph below:
The closure of many industrial businesses in the UK will have other consequences for UK manufacturers if the UK join the EU’s ETS, as the EU has insisted that joining the EU’s Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM) would be a necessary condition. They claim this will create a ‘level playing field’. Except it won’t. Primarily because the UK has stopped making many of the goods that are covered by the EU’s CBAM and instead relies on imported goods as inputs into the UK’s upstream manufacturers. Many of the goods the EU adds to its CBAM are goods the UK no longer makes and has to import. And these imports don’t come exclusively from the EU; many also come from outside the EU.
A CBAM is like a tariff, but it is charged on the weight of the imported good and the emissions associated with its production. It is not dependent on the value of the good. Thus, CBAM adds a large proportion to the import price of heavier, low-value goods with high carbon emissions, such as cement, but adds an insignificant amount to the import price of high-value goods and lighter finished or semi-finished parts.
The most ridiculous example of the UK applying the EU’s CBAM is in Anhydrous ammonia. Anhydrous ammonia is an essential ingredient in fertiliser production. The UK no longer makes Ammonia, although it used to both make it and export it as recently as 2022. Now the UK imports about 350,000 tonnes of ammonia, almost exclusively from countries with cheap gas, as ammonia is made from methane (natural gas). In 2025, the US supplied about a third of the UK’s ammonia imports, as it was the UK’s cheapest supplier. Joining the EU’s CBAM would have increased the import price of US Ammonia by about a third in 2026 and pushed up the price of the UK’s more expensive suppliers by between 10% and 14%. This is insane. The UK needs fertiliser; fertiliser needs ammonia; ammonia is made from gas; the EU doesn’t have much gas; both the UK and the EU have to import ammonia to make fertiliser, but both are increasing the cost of importing something neither makes. Why does anyone think this is a good idea?
But while NOT joining the EU’s CBAM will make fertiliser production cheaper in the UK, NOT joining the EU’s ETS system will also, strangely, make UK steel products more competitive in the EU market. The EU has assigned relatively low default values to UK steel products, at least low relative to India and China, two of the world’s largest steel producers. IN 2025, UK-made hot-rolled bars and rods in irregular coils in the EU market were about 40% more expensive than Indian hot-rolled bars and rods in irregular coils, but in 2026, with each country’s default emissions value applied to calculate the CBAM charge, the price differential between Indian and British steel coils drops to just 5%. Joining the EU’s ETS while continuing to pay the UK’s CPS would have increased the UK’s production costs, so the differential between Indian and British prices would be greater.
This is before the EU has granted any Article 9 reductions in the CBAM charge for payments made in its domestic ETS market. The UK is one of only 3 countries, along with South Korea and South Africa, to have the requisite Carbon market to receive CBAM discounts from the EU.
For a non-EU or EEA country to be eligible for a reduction in CBAM charge under Article 9 of the CBAM regulations (EU) 2023/956, its domestic carbon prices must be: defined in law; be a monetary amount paid as a tax, levy, or fee for emission allowances; it must have been paid, not a free allowance, a credited allowance, or an accessed allowance; the scheme must be legally binding, not voluntary; the exporter must have detailed proof of payment; and the allowance must be attributed to a specific good. The UK’s ETS system already meets all of these requirements, meaning there is no need to join the EU’s ETS.
The worst is yet to come
But the extra costs imposed on UK manufacturers and their imported materials are one thing, but the EU has also tied membership of the EU’s Internal Electricity Market to paying into the EU’s Cohesion Fund – A fund to level up poorer areas of the EU. But poorer areas of the UK would not be able to benefit from these payments. UK taxpayers would already be required to pay towards the cost of running the EU’s internal electricity market and towards the EU’s ETS and CBAM ‘policy costs’ if the UK continues with the Reset. While UK businesses will have to pay more for their emission allowances under the EU’s ETS, and importers will have to pay CBAM charges on many imported materials, while ports and shipping companies will have to buy carbon allowances. Finally, British households will need to buy electric vehicles and heat pumps to meet the EU’s renewable energy targets, while also paying more for both domestically produced and imported goods. In total, joining the EU’s IEM, ETS, and CBAM would cost the UK economy about £3.5 billion in 2027, rising to about £6.3 billion by 2030, when the RED III target should be achieved, and CBAM charges will be applied at about 50%. This will increase further as the EU’s CBAM will be fully applied to imported goods by 2034.
The UK has no upside to paying to comply with EU energy regulations or to joining its IEM, ETS and CBAM. The UK is already just 0.8% of global emissions, and paying the EU’s ETS and CBAM charges will not lower global emissions; it will simply drive more manufacturers out of the UK or out of business, and increase the cost of living for UK consumers, who will find that higher emissions charges are passed on to them either as more expensive imports or as more expensive domestic goods.
For more information about the EU Reset, please read the Great British Business Council’s new paper: Unconditional Surrender!, which you can download at gbbc.uk.

The Great British Business Council has just published a paper on the UK’s Reset with the EU. It is one of the most one-sided agreements I have ever read. There is no upside for the UK; the few benefits are negated by the massive cost and regulatory straitjacket the UK will find itself bound by. I have reproduced the Executive Summary below, and the full paper is on the GBBC Website; you can find it here: [link]
Executive Summary
1. In every single part of the Reset, the UK would be giving up its sovereignty and agreeing to blindly follow EU regulations.
2. The UK would become a rule-taker with an obligation to adopt EU laws immediately and exactly. Even when the rules do not suit the UK economy, do not apply to it, or lower UK standards.
3. Dynamic alignment means identical rules, on the EU’s timetable and on their agenda, with no British involvement or right of veto.
4. All future UK laws in the areas covered by the EU Reset will be EU laws and, therefore, under the exclusive jurisdiction of the European Court of Justice. The UK’s government and courts will have no ability to alter them.
5. Britain would pay for the privilege of obeying. The Reset will cost British taxpayers, businesses, and universities an estimated £17.6 billion in 2027, rising to £20.5 billion per annum by the 2030s, with an additional £12 billion in one-off compliance costs. This does not include other potential costs, such as the loss of the UK’s Agtech industry if the government cannot secure a regulatory carve-out.
6. In addition, the UK is committing to a PERMANENT contribution to the EU Cohesion Fund, which levels up poorer parts of the EU. The UK will not be eligible to receive funds from the Cohesion Fund. The UK would be borrowing more to send money to the EU.
7. The UK would also be expected to subsidise EU youths up to the age of 30 to freely move to the UK and benefit from subsidised university fees, free NHS access, and the ability to apply to bring their family members with them.
8. The cost would be£2.7 billion in lost fee income for UK universities, lost Immigration Health Surcharge payments, and lost opportunities for UK youth.
9. British 18- to 24-year-olds — already facing 16% unemployment with a million NEETs for the first time ever - would have to compete with nearly 3 million unemployed EU youths for jobs and with 19 million EU students for university places.
10. Erasmus+ is sold as a bargain. It is not. The UK would pay £570 million from 1 January 2027, rising to £810 million from 2028. On pre-Brexit outgoing numbers, that is £42,100 per UK participant -almost three times the £14,850 it cost before we left the EU!
11. The supposed benefits were made up: the Reset will not let UK nationals to use the EU passport lanes in EU airports because this is a national competency and out of the hands of the European Commission.
12. Despite UK Government claims and European Commission assurances, the Reset will not stop illegal immigrant crossings, as again this is controlled by the French and Belgian governments.
13. Providing accommodation and sustenance to illegal immigrants cost the UK £4.36 billion in 2025/6, but in France immigrants are left to live on the streets despite the European Court of Human Rights finding that France has breached asylum seekers’ rights under the European Convention on Human Rights. The Reset wouldn’t change this.
14. The Reset will not increase UK agrifood exports either. The UK doesn’t export much food now, and it didn’t before Brexit. In fact, UK exports of Food and live animals to the EU make up just 1.3% of total UK exports. The UK is a food importer. The Reset will just push some export companies’ costs onto UK taxpayers and make it harder to import food from non-EU countries.
15. Every UK farm and food business will have to comply with EU regulations (regardless of whether they trade with the EU), even if this means incurring massive costs to change their internal processes and existing supply chains.
16. Packaging changes alone are a multi-billion pound cost. By mid-2027, manufacturers must meet EU recycling, labelling and nutrition rules, ban PFAS and oxo-degradable plastics in food contact packaging, and tether bottle lids. Estimated cost: £2–3 billion once, then £400–700 million a year by 2030.
17. Farmers take a direct hit. A mid-2027 cliff-edge alignment with EU maximum residue limits would cut horticultural profits by £500–800 million and Total Income from Farming by 7–11%, hitting potatoes, apples, brassicas, carrots, onions and sugar beet.
18. Certificate-free borders are not a free lunch. They will not magically increase farm exports. They can, however, walk Foot and Mouth, African Swine Fever, Lumpy Skin Disease, and Peste des Petits Ruminants, as well as several plant diseases, onto British farms. The EU has these diseases now. Britain does not.
19. Agtech is the industry the Reset would damage the most. It only took off after Brexit and is already worth £28 billion — more than double the UK’s £12 billion of food and live-animal exports to the EU in 2025. Dynamic alignment with EU GMO rules would put that growth back under the precautionary principle.
20. Cheaper electricity transfer costs are a rounding error. Joining the EU’s internal market trims a sliver off of import-trading cost. It does nothing about the taxes, levies and policy charges that actually make British power the most expensive in the World.
21. Joining the EU’s ETS system will push up emission taxes by about 20% for the few manufacturing industries still operating in Britain. The government is keeping the Carbon Price Support tax until 2028, so UK industry will be even less competitive than EU manufacturers, who only pay the ETS.
22. Jining the EU’s CBAM will not help UK exporters, as the EU’s CBAM default values for the UK are generally low for the high value products that the UK exports, such as aluminium gas cylinders, while for low value homogenous products, UK goods will be more competitive in EU markets than their Chinese and Indian competitors whose EU CBAM default values are considerably higher than the UK’s (Yes, seriously — read the chapter explaining this).
23. CBAM will push up prices for UK imports from non-EU countries. These imports are often key materials used to make more valuable finished goods, such as cars and aircraft parts.
24. Adding CBAM to ammonia, the key ingredient in fertilisers, is insane. The UK no longer makes ammonia, and the EU doesn’t either. The US is the UK’s main supplier, but the EU’s CBAM would increase US ammonia prices by 34% in 2027, rising to 60% in 2034.
25. Joining the EU’s defence schemes will help EU manufacturers, as 65% of all spending must take place in the EU, EEA, or Ukraine. UK defence companies would be forced to enter into a partnership with an EU company and cede their intellectual property to the EU partner. The UK should spend the money on UK-made equipment for the UK Armed Forces.
26. Signing the EU’s £90 billion Ukraine Support Loan (USL) ties the UK to an EU process of financial obligation and obliges the UK to pay interest on EU managed funding from the international market, with no end date. The UK is legally responsible for interest payments, and possibly 16% (€14 billion) of the €90 billion loan, as Ukraine relies on reparations from Russia if it loses the war. No public documentation of this scheme exists.
27. Leaving the Hague Convention was a major benefit of Brexit; under the Hague 2019, UK courts will have to recognise foreign judgments, even from smaller, unreliable EU Member State courts.

Shortly after being elected, the Starmer Government proposed that the UK should dynamically align with the EU’s food and agricultural regulations. This wasn’t in their manifesto, but they decided to do it anyway, claiming it would boost UK exports in food and agriculture: an area of the economy constrained by the UK’s small landmass, cold climate, and relatively large population. But, hey ho.
Starmer has now gone, and so has his European Union Relations Minister, Nick Thomas Symonds, the man behind the idiotically badly thought-through UK Reset with the EU. But what of the Reset itself?
At the moment, it is not clear whether the new Burnham Government intends to continue with the Reset. Although government publications about the Reset now have a stamp proclaiming that:
These notices usually appear after a change of government to one with a new plan, so hopefully this is also true of the Reset. However, in case Burnham does intend to continue with it, the article below is a list of some of the things that are wrong with the agrifood section of the Reset, which covers:
animal and plant health,
live animal welfare,
animal transport regulations,
food safety,
food production regulations,
distribution and consumption of agri-food products,
pesticide regulations,
consumer protection rules regarding food,
food contact materials,
organic production rules and labelling, as well as
marketing standards applicable to agri-food products.[1]
This is not an exhaustive list; DEFRA believes 75 agri-food sectors will be covered by the Reset. Each sector contains multiple new EU regulations introduced after the UK left the EU. So while the UK has not altered many of the regulations it followed as an EU member, the EU has introduced thousands of new regulations and altered many of the old ones that we continue to use. Under the Reset, the EU’s regulations will apply to all UK agri-food businesses, not just those that trade with the EU. So all farmers and food manufacturers will need to alter their products and processes to comply. This will be a very expensive process for most of them, although not for the government ministers who came up with the plan.
The aim of the agri-food section of the Reset is, according to the European Commission, so that ‘the vast majority of movements of animals, animal products, plants, and plant products between Great Britain and the Union being undertaken without the certificates or controls that are currently required or expected.’[2] However, I suspect the real aim is to reverse the increase in British food imports from non-EU countries, up by 27% since 2019 according to the ONS, using CVM to account for inflation.[3]
However, dynamic alignment with the EU’s SPS area is unnecessary and will not increase UK food exports; it will just be another burden on UK taxpayers, and potentially very dangerous for the UK’s plant and livestock farming for the following reasons:
- Background and context of the UK proposal to align dynamically with EU food and agriculture legislation.
SPS alignment is unnecessary because the UK’s entire Food and live animal exports to the EU were only £12 billion in 2025.[4] This was just 0.4% of the UK’s GDP of £3,037 billion in 2025[5] and only 1.3% of total UK exports.
Most UK food production is consumed domestically, and an additional 35% of the food consumed in the UK has to be imported.[6] The UK does not even fully supply the foods that can be grown in the UK climate. Imports of ‘indigenous foods’ vary from 20% to 25% depending on domestic yields. Consequently, the UK does not have much surplus food to export to the EU; cutting red tape won’t change this.
The UK is a major importer of food, and the EU is one of its major suppliers. This has continued since Brexit without the need for regulatory alignment. Consequently, the supposed benefits of the Reset will be very small. The UK does not have the capacity to increase its food production in order to reap any benefits that certificate-free trade could produce.
All that regulatory alignment would achieve is to shift the private costs of exporters onto the public purse while forcing all non-exporting agri-food businesses to change their production methods, processes and packaging to meet EU regulations.
2. Limited potential savings from dynamic alignment
The UK’s Reset negotiator, Nick Thomas Symonds MP, has claimed that UK agrifood exporters to the EU have spent just £210 million on something he called a ‘paperwork tax’ over the three years from 2023 to 2025. This is only £70 million annually and a tiny fraction, just 0.6%, of the UK’s annual agrifood exports, which are in turn a tiny fraction of the UK’s total exports, as mentioned earlier. Dynamic alignment with the EU’s SPS regulations will only reduce exporters’ ‘paperwork tax’ by a small amount.[7] But UK taxpayers will be asked to pay 10 times this amount for access to the EU SPS area.
Not that SPS health certificates are the only cost of exporting food to the EU: UK exporters will still have to complete: customs declarations; rules of origin compliance to qualify for zero tariffs under the Trade and Cooperation Agreement; VAT obligations and potentially register for EU VAT and file EU VAT returns on Business to Consumer sales; comply with EU safety, labelling, and packaging rules including EU waste rules; complete EU Economic Operations Registration and identification (EORI) forms; EU Safety and Security declarations, packing lists and transport documents; and submit to EU customs risk checks, anti-fraud checks, security screening and weight/volume inspections as well as pay the usual haulage costs, insurance and cold chain energy costs. All those other costs will still exist, even under the proposed EU SPS Reset.
The primary difference will be that the small savings will benefit private companies trading with the EU while the high costs will be paid by UK taxpayers who do not profit from trading with the EU.
3. Paying for EU dynamic alignment
Dynamic alignment will not be free. The UK will be asked to contribute to the EU’s Cohesion Fund as the EEA and EFTA countries do in return for access to the EU market.
During the 2021-2028 EU budget period, Norway will contribute €3.17 billion to the EU’s Cohesion Fund for access to the EU SPS area. This is equivalent to approximately €453 million (£385 million) per year. Norway also contributes between €400 million and €500 million annually to other EU programs. Its total annual contribution to the EU is between €850 million and €950 million. Norway exports approximately €7.4 billion in agri-food goods to the EU, predominantly seafood, and imports agri-food worth around €6 billion from the EU, which accounts for about 64% of Norway’s total agricultural imports. Norway does not pay to access the EU’s ETS and CBAM, as it has been a full participant in the EU ETS scheme since 2008.
However, the UK could be asked to pay much more than Norway for SPS access, as the UK exports more to the EU: in 2024, UK SITC 0 Food and Live Animal exports to the EU, measured in current prices, were £11.35 billion, equivalent to about €12.84 billion and 74% more than Norwegian agri-food exports. Therefore, the EU would likely require an annual payment of £690 million to access its SPS system. Dwarfing the £70 million potential gains. [8]
4. Potential gains for EU companies not UK farmers
In total, the UK only exported food and live animals worth £12.1 billion to the EU in 2025.[9] Removing SPS checks is unlikely to increase UK food exports at all, let alone boost GDP by ‘up to’ £5 billion a year as some vested interest groups have apparently claimed.[10]
The UK doesn’t have the capacity to increase its agri-food production by this amount and didn’t export anywhere near that amount of food when it was a full EU member with ‘certificate-free’ trade. In 2020, the last year of the UK EU Transition Agreement, UK food and live animal exports to the EU were only £10.8 billion, in 2020 prices, despite full EU access, and only £12.9 billion in CVM-adjusted prices.
At least Dunbia, the meat processor extoling the Reset in government publications, is honest enough to explain that the Reset ‘should result in potential cost savings for our businesses’. But the publication doesn’t mention that UK taxpayers will be subsidising their cost savings by paying 10 times this amount to the EU’s Cohesion funds. Nor do Government publications mention that Dunbia is a Northern Ireland meat processor, fully owned by the Irish meat processor Dawn Meats. Ireland supplies about 70% of British meat imports. So the Reset, purporting to help British agricultural EXPORTERS, is actually helping EU companies export to Britain.
It is also worth noting that the Irish meat lobby group, Meat Industry Ireland, is upset that its share of UK meat imports has fallen from 80% before Brexit to just 67% in 2025.[11] They blame this on the post-Brexit UK trade deals with Australia and New Zealand. But the chart below from Ireland’s Bord Bia makes it obvious that the increase in the price of meat imports from Ireland has nothing to do with the cost of red tape or veterinary checks. And the Reset will not fix this. But the Reset could force the UK to buy more expensive Irish meat rather than import cheaper meat from Australia, New Zealand, Canada, Mexico or Chile. The EU would just need to change its (precautionary principle-based) food standards to achieve this.
5. The UK’s booming Agtech sector could disappear under EU regulations
By being outside the EU and its regulations, the UK has developed a growing agricultural technology industry. There are almost 2,500 companies employing over 56,000 people in the UK Agtech sector. The sector is worth roughly £28.4 billion, which is more than double the UK’s total Food and live animal exports to the EU. The Agtech sector covers farming efficiency, precision breeding, sustainability and biotechnology.
The UK’s Agtech industry has pioneered innovations in: climate-resilient crops; fungal-based biopesticides to suppress aphids; UK-climate-tolerant rubber plants; plants containing Omega-3 fatty acids; root-mist nutrient delivery systems; robotic harvesting of soft fruits; and pollinator-tracking sensors.[13]
The UK has the potential to develop new crops and export them around the world, but if we adopt dynamic alignment with the EU, we may find that UK farmers are prevented from benefiting from these developments. The CJEU found in July 2018 that genetically edited plants and animals should be treated as GMOs.[12] Defra agrees that GMOs will be in scope of the Reset’s SPS alignment.
6. No influence in EU decisions
The European Commission, Council Decision, Register of Commission Documents - COM(2025)408, main document, Section 5.1 paragraph 2, clearly states that the Reset will not give the UK the right to participate in the EU’s decision-making, while paragraph 3 states that the agreement provides an obligation for the UK to dynamically align to EU legislation and that regulation should be applied simultaneously with the EU.
We have seen that even as a member of the EU, the UK had little influence in the Union’s agricultural decision-making. For example, the EU restricted UK beef exports for about 10 years after the BSE crisis, even though the UK was a member of the EU; it had no ability to influence EU SPS regulations.[14]
Dynamic alignment means all UK Food and Agriculture regulations will be EU law, and therefore all of them will fall under the ECJ’s jurisdiction. This is clearly explained in the EU’s Council Decisions, Register of Commission Documents - COM(2025)408, main Document, Section 5.1, paragraph 5:
‘the Court of Justice of the European Union is the ultimate authority for all questions of European Union law, with possibilities for appropriate measures to protect the [European] Union interests in case of non-compliance with the agreements.’
The Reset requires all UK agri-food companies to follow the EU’s regulations immediately, whether or not they export to the EU. The EU has made this clear in Section 5.1, paragraphs 3 and 4, which are reproduced below;
‘3. Both agreements should provide for an obligation for the United Kingdom to dynamically align to the relevant [European] Union legislation. The principle of dynamic alignment should ensure that identical rules within the scope of the agreement are simultaneously applied.’ [my emphasis]
‘4. Both agreements should ensure uniform interpretation and application of [European] Union law on the basis of the case-law of the Court of Justice of the European Union; in particular, the interpretation given to the applicable rules within the Union should also apply in the context of the relations between the Parties.’ [15] [my emphasis]
7. Dynamic Alignment means identical rules applied simultaneously
It is impossible to misunderstand what the EU means by dynamic alignment, yet UK politicians are trying to convince themselves that they will be able to influence EU decision-making, pick and choose the agri-food regulation they want to follow and ignore those that don’t suit the UK climate, UK agriculture, or UK food manufacturing.
The Starmer Government also overlooked the most important detail – most UK food and agricultural companies are domestically focused. Their primary customers are British citizens, not EU ones, but they will still have to follow EU laws. This also applies to companies exporting agri-foods to the US, China, the Middle East or any other country that does not follow EU regulations. Consequently, the Reset could reduce the UK’s growing exports to non-EU markets rather than increase UK exports to the EU. UK exports of Food and Live Animals to non-EU countries increased by 34% between 2019 and 2025, while exports to the EU increased by only 12%, both measured in current prices.
So I reiterate, Dynamic alignment means that the UK follows EU laws identically and immediately. The Reset will force changes to everything from pesticide production and use, to food colouring, packaging materials and nutritional information; all based on the EU’s precautionary principle rather than risk-based scientific methods. The Reset will even alter UK animal welfare regulations and live animal transport rules.
8. The disease risks associated with a common SPS Area are real
If the Reset continues and achieves its aims of removing health certificates, border controls, and creating a common SPS area between Great Britain and the continental EU, it would be extremely dangerous for UK animal-based agriculture.
The EU does not have an exemplary record of limiting animal and plant diseases from crossing its borders. For example: In January 2025, a Foot and Mouth Disease outbreak started in Germany, by February it was in Hungary and by March it was in Slovakia – despite EU regulations this disease easily spread across EU borders affecting more animals as it spread: the first outbreak in Brandenburg, Germany, affected 14 animals; the next outbreak in Kisbajcs, Hungary, affected 1,400 dairy cattle; a second outbreak in Hungary, affected 3000 animals; then Gyor-Sopron, Hungary, another 1000 cattle; a second outbreak in Gyor-Sopron, Hungary, affected 2,500 animals; Slovakia’s multiple outbreaks involved approximately 10,000 animals on farms in Bratislavsky, Trnavsky, and Nitriansky.[16] Foot and Mouth Disease reached Cyprus in February 2026 and reached Greece in March 2026.[17] Why would we want this in the UK?
The UK has a climate where Foot and Mouth Disease thrives in the type of animals most commonly kept on UK farms. The last outbreak of Foot and Mouth Disease in the UK was in 2007, almost 20 years ago. It infected 60 animals and was over within 3 months. The best way to avoid new FMD outbreaks is to prevent trade with countries that have or could have FMD. This is why DEFRA’s restrictions on meat and dairy imports from Germany, Hungary and Slovakia in 2025, which all had outbreaks, also applied to Austria, which did not have FMD but has ‘certificate-free’ borders with the other three countries. Similarly, Defra’s ban on non-commercial imports extends to EFTA countries, Greenland, and the Faroe Islands because they have free trade with the EU.
The UK does not have similar restrictions on its non-EU agricultural trading partners, which Defra does not list as having FMD.[2] Both Australia and New Zealand, which export meat and dairy products to the UK, are FMD-Free. North America, Central America and the Caribbean are officially recognised as FMD-free by the World Organisation for Animal Health (WOAH). There have been no cases of FMD in the Mercosur countries since 2013, when Venezuela had an outbreak. As of 2020, 98.6% of South America’s cattle population was officially recognised as FMD-free by the WOAH due to a vaccination program. The region is working towards full eradication. The only CPTPP country to have had a recent FMD outbreak is Malaysia, but the UK has never imported any dairy products or any beef, pork or sheep meat from Malaysia. Nor are we proposing to drop our border controls with them.
The EU’s disease problems are not limited to foot and mouth disease. It also has current and ongoing cases of African Swine Fever in pigs, Lumpy Skin Disease in cattle and Peste des Petits Ruminants in sheep.
The UK has never had an outbreak of African Swine Fever (ASF). However, ASF outbreaks have been ongoing in the EU since 2017, when they first appeared in domestic pigs in Romania. Romania has had 72 outbreaks so far this year in domestic pigs, following 478 outbreaks in 2025, 213 in 2024, and 533 in 2023. Other EU countries with ASF outbreaks in domestic pigs since 2023 include Bulgaria, Croatia, Estonia, Germany, Greece, Italy, Latvia, and Poland. EU countries with outbreaks in their Wild boar populations are Bulgaria, Croatia, the Czech Republic, Estonia, Germany, Hungary, Italy, Latvia, Lithuania, Poland, Romania, Spain and Sweden.
The WOAH and Defra in the UK have been monitoring the EU’s outbreak of African Swine Fever.[18] The WOAH records the number of outbreaks but not the number of animals infected. The UK’s National Pig Association reports that an outbreak in Estonia in 2025 occurred on the country’s largest pig farm and resulted in the culling of 28,500 pigs. According to WOAH, there have been no months without outbreaks in either domestic pigs or wild boar in Europe between January 2023 and April 2026.
Only 2 CPTPP countries have had cases of ASF during the last 5 years. Malaysia experienced an outbreak in 2021, which it controlled through quarantine, culling, and tighter biosecurity measures. Vietnam is the only CPTPP country to have had an ASF outbreak during the last 5 years that was anywhere close to those in the EU.
Fears of diseased meat entering the UK food supply are not exaggerated. In February 2025, the BBC reported that Dover Port Health Authority had confiscated 100 tonnes of diseased meat in 868 separate consignments.[19] This was during a period when the UK required any meat, dairy, fish or eggs from the EU to have full third-country SPS paperwork: Export Health Certificates; Customs Declarations; Pre-notification on the UK’s Import of Products, Animals, Food and Feed Systems (IPAFFS); and routine SPS border checks by Port Health Authorities of documents, identity and physical checks. Had the UK had dynamic alignment and certificate-free trade with the EU, much of this meat would have entered the UK. Without the current level of checks, this diseased meat would have entered the UK food chain.
Adopting the EU’s SPS regulations and removing our border controls could lead to our non-EU trading partners imposing similar precautionary restrictions on UK agricultural products. Canada currently restricts imports of dairy and beef products from France, Italy and Switzerland to prevent Lumpy Skin Disease getting into Canadian dairy cattle, even though Switzerland has not had an outbreak of LSD. It shares borders with France and Italy.
9. UK and EU regulatory divergence in agri-food
Since leaving the EU, Great Britain has predominantly changed animal welfare rules, such as the transport of live animals for slaughter and fattening, and it has banned the dredging for sand eels in English waters. The EU has also changed its agricultural rules but with an emphasis on crop production rather than animal welfare. For example: The EU has lowered its Maximum Residue Limits for pesticides for both domestic production and imported produce.
The Reset will force British farmers to align with EU rules on: active substances authorisation, pesticide residue levels, and the sale and marketing of pesticides. This will have implications for farmers and growers, agrochemical manufacturers, distributors, food retailers and other businesses using pesticides. This will prevent the UK from importing crops and cereals from many other countries that have pesticide regulations based on risk-based scientific assessment. The EU’s pesticide regulations are based on the hazard-based precautionary principle rather than the risk-based scientific assessment used by the majority of the developed world, including Great Britain.
The Reset will require the UK to change its pesticide regulations immediately whenever the EU does. So far in 2026, the EU has made 20 changes to its Plant Protection List.[20] In 2025, the EU made 38 changes to its plant protection product lists, while in 2024 it made 78 changes.[21] Since leaving the EU, Great Britain has not followed the EU’s many MRL changes but has instead aligned 764 MRLs with international standards known as Codex Alimentarius.
Since leaving the EU, Britain has also dropped the EU’s “3 crop rule”, crop diversification requirement under Regulation (EU) No 1307/2013, which applied to farms with more than 30 hectares of arable land and required at least three crops, with a 75% limit on the share of the main crop. This rule prevented Britain’s large farms from maximising their returns by preventing them from using all of their land to grow the most profitable crops. The Reset would force the UK to follow the EU’s rules again. The EU has retained this requirement but made it slightly more flexible by including crop rotation and mixed planting.
10. Food contact material means packaging
Defra’s publication on the UK regulations to be impacted by the Reset clearly states that any materials that come into contact with agri-food products must comply with EU requirements for packaging materials.[22] The EU has recently banned or limited the use of several types of PFAS plastics commonly used to package takeaway food in the UK. The EU also has different food standards and food marketing requirements. The Reset will force UK food producers and manufacturers to change their packaging for wholesale and retail agri-foods and may require some food manufacturers to change their utensils.
In the DEFRA publication, UK-EU SPS Agreement - Legislation in scope - GOV.UK, packaging is covered in three sections:
a. Food Contact materials, which means both wholesale and retail packaging, as well as vessels used in food processing and manufacturing. Defra explains this in the description: ‘Alignment with EU rules on plastics, ceramics and other food contact materials will affect packaging manufacturers, food processors, laboratories, retailers and the NHS.’
b. Packaging will also be affected under the section: General Food Law and Consumer Information. This will affect the required information on retail packaging.
c. Food composition and labelling standards on retail packaging will be affected under the section: Marketing Standards for Specific Foods.
British food and drink manufacturers have recently had to change their packaging to conform with UK recycling regulations and to add ‘Not for EU’ labels. Forcing them to change again to conform with EU regulations will be a very expensive exercise, especially for small and medium-sized manufacturers who are less likely to export goods to the EU.
Conclusion
In a recent interview with the BBC, Andy Burnham said he would always put UK interests first; well, I have a list for him of how he can do this, but close to the top of the list would be to abandon the Reset. UK agricultural trade is doing fine without it, and UK taxpayers can’t afford to subsidise private company costs.
