Our latest piece comes from Emily Ritchey at T&E, and illustrates how industrial strategy often suffers from the chicken-and-egg dilemma. In this case, Europe is exporting a key material that could be better used at home, but at the same time, the home market has not reached the capacity necessary to process it.
Ritchey outlines the challenges Europe has been facing in its recycling market, waste management, and regulatory structure — and offers ways for policymakers to begin making sense of this crucial issue.
By Emily Ritchey, Policy Manager, Supply Chains, T&E
Valuable battery waste is currently leaving Europe on ships headed halfway across the world. And little is being done to stop them.
Whilst Europe manages to collect old batteries and shred them into so-called black mass, this valuable dust is sent to South East Asia to be refined, and for all the valuable raw materials to be extracted.
According to the latest T&E analysis, at least 60% of Europe’s black mass is leaving the EU, equal to around €150 million worth of material a year. This is likely only the tip of the iceberg, with lots more black mass leaving the EU, hidden in different customs codes, and unable to be traced. Scrap aluminum tells a similar story: $2.4 billion worth was exported from the EU in 2024, material that could otherwise support European manufacturing.
According to the analysis, the majority of this black mass, as well as waste batteries, are being shipped to South Korea and Southeast Asia. On top of this, China currently leads material recovery capacity globally, holding 94% of total capacity.
This dominance is often attributed to subsidies and lower financing costs, but the explanation is likely incomplete. China regulated its battery recycling sector early and built a large domestic processing and midstream industry, thereby creating captive demand for its own recovered material well before Europe began to address the issue. That combination of early regulation and guaranteed domestic demand, more than cost alone, is likely what allowed Chinese recyclers to achieve the process efficiencies and accumulated scale that now make them so competitive.
If nothing is done to limit black mass leakage, and Europe continues to export at least 60% of its black mass, this number will only grow. Based on current estimates of future black mass production in Europe, we could expect at least 200kt of black mass to leave the EU in 2030, the recoverable battery material from roughly 1.7 million cars. Using today’s black mass prices, this could be the equivalent of €1.1 billion of material.
Europe’s inability to close this loophole and keep these critical raw materials on the continent means it is missing out on a golden opportunity to reduce its dependencies on other countries. The US government has just restricted exports of black mass, recognizing its strategic importance. Why can’t the EU do the same?
The comparison is instructive, but only if we are clear about what allows the US to be more effective. The US has a growing domestic industry ready to turn recycled material into value. Europe’s midstream capacity, the cathode active material and precursor production that would absorb recycled content, is smaller. Restricting exports will be key. However, this must come hand in hand with measures to drive capacity and demand in Europe. The lesson from the US is that restricting exports will be most effective if it is accompanied by efforts to build the capacity to use black mass at home, and to restrict exports to protect that investment.
In building domestic recycling capacity, Europe can lean on several advantages — proximity to feedstock, regulatory leverage over waste flows, and closeness to the automakers who will need recycled content.
Currently, the EU is heavily dependent on imports for many critical minerals. There is, however, huge potential in Europe to recover these raw materials from waste batteries. By scaling recycling capacity in Europe, we can avoid importing over 80kt of lithium by 2035, enough to power around 2.5 million EVs. In the long term, recycling is therefore one of Europe’s tools to reduce dependencies, and secure its energy security.
It should therefore be a no brainer to scale recycling capacity in Europe. However, it’s not quite that simple. Over half of Europe’s battery recycling capacity is currently at risk. Despite the huge potential, Europe is not yet ready to capture this opportunity.
Recyclers in Europe are facing a number of challenges. Firstly, as explained, there is a lack of feedstock as almost all our valuable scrap is leaving Europe to be processed and create value elsewhere.
Perhaps more importantly, without a battery value chain in Europe, there will be little demand for recycled materials in Europe. To effectively scale its recycling industry, Europe will need to onshore the entire battery value chain, whilst building integrated value chains with strategic partners globally. In particular the midstream industry, including cathode active materials and their precursors (pCAM), will be a key offtaker for EU recyclers. This points to a key issue behind Europe’s black mass exports: it is not simply that valuable material is leaving, but that there is currently no sufficient, competitive domestic buyer for it. Without a midstream industry to absorb recycled output, EU recyclers are competing for feedstock without a market to justify scaling up. Any policy response needs to address both the demand-side gap and the export challenge.
T&E analysis shows there is potential to onshore the battery value chain in Europe. However, strong local content rules for CAM and pCAM under the Industrial Accelerator Act, currently being negotiated, can help Europe’s nascent midstream industry to scale. These rules should be expanded to cover precursor cathode active material (pCAM) as well as anode active material (AAM) and critical raw materials more broadly, with incentives for these added as a third phase starting in 2032 — giving Europe’s midstream industry a clear, time-bound signal to invest against.
Finally, European recyclers struggle to compete globally, facing higher energy costs and extended project timelines. Companies recycling in Europe need targeted financial, de-risking, and industrial support to compete on the global scene.
Such support needs to help EU recyclers compete with lower-cost Asian processors, and cushion existing black-mass producers through the transition as export options narrow.
Fundamentally, we need to see the economic opportunity in our waste, instead of the environmental burden. The upcoming Circular Economy Act must set out the right policy measures to help scale recycling facilities in Europe and secure access to all important raw materials.
Taken together, these are four distinct constraints: insufficient domestic demand for recycled material, an unresolved cost and scale gap with Asian processors, fragmented internal EU rules that raise the cost of building capacity domestically, and a leakage problem.
This is a familiar chicken-and-egg industrial strategy challenge: supply-side action and demand-side action each depend on the other happening first. Restricting exports creates value when there’s a domestic buyer ready to use what’s retained. Supporting that buyer only makes sense if there’s confidence the feedstock will actually stay in Europe. Neither side wants to move first. China avoided this trap by moving both sides together — regulating recycling and building domestic demand for recovered material at the same time. The recommendations below try to do the same: export restrictions, demand-side mandates, and a phased local content timeline need to happen in coordination to move supply and demand on the same clock.
Firstly, Europe needs to ensure its valuable waste, including end-of-life batteries and black mass, as well as scrap steel and aluminum, stays in Europe. Europe lacks extensive primary reserves of raw materials, and therefore its waste serves as a key source of much needed CRMs. Nevertheless, this waste is leaving the EU. This means Europe’s recyclers lack the much-needed feedstock and are often unable to compete with Asian recyclers who can pay much higher prices for black mass.
Despite the European Commission having taken some steps, notably by classifying black mass as hazardous, thereby limiting its exports to OECD countries, circumvention persists. Black mass should therefore only be exported outside of the EU if it is to be treated by EU facilities abroad or shown to benefit the EU battery value chain.
Restrictions on exports must move in step with growing EU midstream capacity, and create a trade-off for Europe’s existing black-mass producers, who currently rely in part on higher prices available abroad. Managing that transition, through financial support, phased timelines, or guaranteed EU offtake, will be key.
Secondly, Europe needs a truly European single market for waste. Currently, the process for shipping waste between EU member states is complex and burdensome. Different countries apply different requirements, even coming down to the color of the pen needed for filling out forms. This makes the process of moving waste costly and time consuming. As a result, the European Commission should commit to amend the Waste Shipment Regulation (WSR) and apply the simplified green-listing procedure to waste streams containing critical raw materials destined for approved EU-based facilities. This should — and actually can — be done without increasing safety risks.
Related to this, the Circular Economy Act should harmonize end-of-waste criteria for CRM-containing waste, with clear implementing guidance for member states; without a consistent EU-wide definition of when recycled material stops being classified as waste, cross-border recycling investment remains harder to plan around.
Finally, to send a strong demand signal, the Circular Economy Act should amend the EU Batteries Regulation’s recycled content targets to ensure that only materials recycled in Europe count. This will be key to incentivizing recycling and refining capacity within Europe. This is the demand-side counterpart to restricting exports: guaranteed EU demand gives producers a reason to prioritize the domestic market even before restrictions fully take effect, and gives midstream investment the market certainty it needs to scale.
There is a strong pipeline of recycling projects in Europe. Recent T&E analysis tracked a total of 93 projects, of which 39 are already operational. However, over half of this recycling capacity is currently at risk. Strong local content rules under the EU Batteries Regulation will help to secure and expand Europe’s secondary materials base over the coming decade.
The rationale for recycling has never been clearer. Now is the time to seize the opportunity and scale European recycling champions.

Whether driven by energy, national security, or economic concerns, industrial strategy is rapidly becoming a central part of government policymaking in the United States and across the world. As these approaches become more widespread, questions about their political durability are becoming more pressing, especially in democracies where governments and strategic direction can shift quickly. This is playing out already in energy policy, where the push to meet America’s booming electricity needs has spilled over into a political debate over how to do it, where to do it, and who benefits.
At the New Energy Industrial Strategy Center, we’re convinced that investing in and supporting new energy technologies now will help the industries of the future thrive — and provide energy security to boot. But getting those projects off the ground means designing an energy industrial strategy that is politically resilient. With so much divisiveness in politics already, can we build that future? Is there a coalition or coalitions that could support the kinds of policies that bring projects over the line?
To discuss these questions and others, in June we convened an expert roundtable to explore how some of our partners are dealing with this challenge. The discussion brought together practitioners working with stakeholders across the political spectrum, including in industrial policy, labor, civil society, business, philanthropy, and political strategy. The conversation was held under Chatham House rules, so the observations below are presented without attribution.
Much of the discussion focused on the relationship between policy design and the constituencies that ultimately determine whether a strategy can be implemented and sustained. Participants didn’t always agree. In fact, they differed on several important questions, including how much industrial policy should try to accomplish at once, when domestic production should take precedence over lower-cost deployment, and how political considerations should enter the policy development process.
These difficult conversations, and the disagreements they surface, are integral to the NEIS Center’s mission. In order to move with the necessary speed to address our energy, industrial, and geopolitical needs, we need to surface and resolve tensions confronting energy industrial policy implementation quickly and effectively.
Five themes emerged from the conversation.
1. Build political durability into industrial strategy
Industrial strategy operates on a difficult timeline. Building supply chains, manufacturing capacity, infrastructure, and workforce capabilities can take a decade or more. Elections occur every few years, creating repeated opportunities for governments to change direction.
Experience with industrial policy in democracies points to several sources of continuity. Some countries have maintained a degree of cross-party agreement around core economic objectives. In others, demand from businesses, communities, or other constituencies has made particular industries difficult for successive governments to ignore. Institutions with some independence from political leadership can also provide continuity.
These mechanisms matter because even a well-designed policy may struggle to produce results if it is repeatedly reversed. In highly polarized systems, however, cross-party consensus may be difficult to achieve. Participants discussed the need to understand constituencies that do not fit neatly into conventional political categories, including emerging factions on the right with interests in domestic production, security, and a stronger role for the state in economic development. There was also a warning against concentrating so heavily on engagement with the right that changes underway on the left receive too little attention.
Political durability can therefore take several forms. Formal bipartisan agreement is one. A sufficiently strong constituency for continued investment is another. In practice, governments may be able to change the instruments or emphasis of a strategy while leaving much of the underlying industrial activity intact.
For policy design, this raises questions about who will have an interest in maintaining a strategy several years after its adoption and which institutions or economic relationships could provide continuity when political leadership changes.
2. Build coalitions around concrete interests
Different constituencies come to industrial strategy with different priorities. Manufacturers may want stable demand and access to financing. Labor organizations may focus on wages, training, and job quality. Communities may be interested in investment and greater influence over local economic development. Defense institutions may be concerned about strategic dependence and supply-chain resilience. Regional governments want investment and employment, while consumers may be more concerned with prices.
Several examples from the discussion showed how those interests can overlap without requiring agreement on a common political rationale.
- European battery manufacturing is relevant to decarbonization, defense applications, automotive competitiveness, supply-chain security, and regional development. A coalition involving battery companies, defense users, automakers, and regional policymakers consequently looks quite different from one assembled primarily around climate objectives. The policy may be similar, but the reasons for supporting it vary across the coalition.
- Critical minerals create another set of possible alignments. In some countries, mineral development intersects with security, crime prevention, local development, environmental protection, and national sovereignty. Those connections can bring institutions and constituencies into industrial policy discussions that have historically had little involvement in climate or clean energy policy.
This approach has practical limits. Industrial policy distributes costs and benefits unevenly, and some interests will remain in conflict. Participants returned several times to the difficulty of compromise when constituencies expect policies to deliver across a long list of objectives. A workable coalition may therefore depend on choosing a relatively specific economic objective and identifying the groups whose interests align sufficiently around it.
The same consideration applies to messengers. Manufacturers, defense officials, workers, and local governments have different kinds of credibility with different audiences. Their participation can broaden the political base for a strategy, particularly where industrial policy instruments have become closely associated with one political or policy agenda. Historically, efforts to engage a diverse stakeholder community on an ongoing basis have been inconsistent, which can make leveraging a diverse set of messengers appear opportunistic rather than genuine.
3. Use participation to improve policy and build constituencies
There was considerable interest in involving workers, communities, and other affected groups earlier in policy development. Participants described two reasons for doing so.
The first concerns policy quality. National policy experts often have limited knowledge of how a proposal will interact with local labor markets, permitting processes, political institutions, or community organizations. Earlier engagement can expose implementation problems and identify priorities that are difficult to see from the national level.
The second concerns political support. Organizations involved in developing a policy have more reason to invest in its passage and implementation. Examples discussed during the roundtable suggest that policy development can help build relationships among constituencies that later become important to legislative or political campaigns.
Community benefits agreements illustrate the potential alignment. Developers want to reduce project delays and community opposition. Labor organizations want good jobs and accessible training pathways. Community organizations want locally defined economic benefits and influence over development decisions. Under the right conditions, an agreement can address parts of all three agendas.
Participants also acknowledged the familiar problems with participatory policymaking. Poorly structured processes can take too long, produce diffuse demands, or give disproportionate influence to the people with the time and resources to participate. More successful approaches tend to define the policy objective in advance, identify the constituencies relevant to that objective, secure a commitment from policymakers to act on the outcome, and combine stakeholder knowledge with technical expertise.
There was some difference in emphasis over how early political considerations should shape the process. One approach centered on iterative work among experts, policymakers, workers, and communities. Another gave greater weight to political and communications expertise at the outset, arguing that public salability should influence which policies are developed in the first place. Both approaches treat political viability as relevant to policy design, though they assign it different weight relative to technical analysis.
Participation also leaves some decisions unresolved. Stakeholders may identify genuine conflicts that no design process can reconcile. Governments still have to decide how to weigh competing objectives when that occurs.
4. Specify what industrial policy is intended to achieve
The most substantive disagreement in the discussion concerned prioritization. One view held that clean energy industrial policy should continue to link deployment with good jobs, affordability, and community benefits. Recent experience was cited as evidence that these outcomes can reinforce one another when policies are deliberately designed to connect them. From this perspective, problems with recent policy warrant adjustment rather than retreat from the broader approach.
Another view placed greater weight on deployment and economic activity. Participants advancing this argument questioned tariffs, domestic-content requirements, and other measures that can increase costs or slow the adoption of clean technologies. They also raised the possibility that governments should stop trying to maintain domestic manufacturing in sectors where technologies have become highly commoditized. Solar was the clearest example discussed, with EVs and batteries raised as areas where similar questions could eventually arise.
The appropriate balance depends heavily on the objective assigned to a particular intervention. Rapid deployment can favor access to low-cost imports. Supply-chain resilience may justify higher costs for domestic or diversified production. Regional development can support investments that would not be selected on cost alone. Labor standards and community requirements can generate wider economic benefits while also affecting project economics and implementation.
Affordability generated a related discussion. Participants generally recognized its political importance, particularly in the current economic environment. Some wanted to connect clean energy policy more directly to household costs and other pocketbook concerns. Others worried that affordability could become so dominant that industrial capacity, innovation, security, and climate objectives receive less attention.
These disagreements also sharpened the discussion of the “everything bagel” approach to industrial policy. The strongest defense of a multi-objective approach was relatively selective: policies can combine objectives that work well together, but that does not justify attaching every desirable outcome to every intervention. Community benefits agreements, for example, may combine developer interest in project speed with labor interest in job quality and community interest in local benefits. Other combinations may create much harder trade-offs.
Clearer priorities would make those decisions easier to evaluate. A sectoral strategy could identify a primary objective, a smaller number of secondary objectives, and the trade-offs government is prepared to accept. That would also make it easier to assess whether the policy is working.
5. Build credibility through implementation and adjustment
Concern about government competence ran through much of the conversation. Constituencies may have very different economic priorities, but skepticism about whether governments can execute their plans appears to cut across many of them.
Industrial strategies can reinforce that skepticism when projects are repeatedly delayed, costs exceed expectations, factories fail to materialize, or promised benefits remain difficult to see. Long lists of objectives can compound the problem by creating multiple standards against which a policy can appear to fall short.
Participants offered somewhat different approaches to building credibility. Some placed considerable emphasis on political communication, including the need for trusted messengers and arguments that connect industrial policy with the priorities of particular audiences. Others gave more weight to visible economic activity. On this view, additional deployment and investment can create their own constituencies as households, businesses, workers, and communities develop a direct interest in the industries involved.
The difference has implications for how organizations allocate resources between persuasion and implementation, although the two approaches can work together. Projects that produce tangible benefits give credible messengers something concrete to discuss, while political support can make additional projects easier to build.
Subnational experimentation can also help. States, regions, and cities offer opportunities to test financing models, workforce policies, community benefit requirements, and approaches to project development before applying them more widely. Several U.S. examples discussed during the roundtable followed this model: develop a policy where a viable coalition already exists, observe how it performs, refine the design, and preserve the option to scale it during a future federal policy window.
Industrial policy also requires room for failure and adjustment. Some firms will fail, technologies will develop differently than expected, and policy instruments will produce unintended effects. Governments need mechanisms for distinguishing between failures that justify ending an intervention and those that call for modifying it.
A more disciplined approach to implementation could also improve political durability. Clear objectives make outcomes easier to measure, and a demonstrated willingness to adjust can help address concerns that industrial strategy amounts to maintaining programs regardless of their performance.
Questions for the next phase of industrial strategy
The discussion highlighted a set of issues that sit alongside the familiar technical questions about sectors, financing instruments, trade policy, and government support. Political durability depends partly on which constituencies develop an interest in a strategy and whether that interest survives changes in government. Coalition-building requires understanding where interests genuinely overlap and where compromises will be necessary. Participation can improve both policy design and political support when the process is sufficiently focused. Clear priorities become particularly important when deployment, domestic production, affordability, job quality, and community benefits pull policy in different directions.
The disagreements in the roundtable were concentrated in these choices rather than in the basic case for considering politics and constituencies more carefully. Participants assigned different weights to deployment and domestic production, to affordability and longer-term industrial objectives, and to communications and visible delivery. Those differences are likely to vary by sector and geography rather than yield a single general formula.
For practitioners, several questions were clearly useful to ask and design policy processes around at the outset of devising new industrial strategy approaches: Which constituencies have a durable interest in the strategy? Where do their priorities overlap? Which objectives can be pursued together without undermining the central goal? What trade-offs are acceptable when those objectives conflict? And what evidence should lead policymakers to adjust course?
Working through those questions early may help industrial strategies remain coherent as they encounter the political, economic, and implementation pressures that inevitably emerge over time.

This week, we’re sharing the NEIS News Roundup, a monthly recap of major international developments in new energy industrial strategies and advanced energy systems. This roundup is designed to give readers a clear overview of the global trends shaping industrial strategy and competitiveness by highlighting shifts in investment, policy, trade, and technology.
Here are five major stories we’re following this month:
#1: United States bans new foreign-made inverters on cybersecurity grounds
In late July, the US Federal Communications Commission (FCC) announced an immediate ban on imports of new, foreign-made power inverters on national security grounds. The ban does not apply to inverter models already approved by the FCC and available on the market today.
Inverters convert direct current (DC) electricity produced or used by solar, battery, and wind power systems, as well as EV chargers and heat pumps, into alternating current (AC) that can be transmitted on power grids. Most modern inverters are connected to the internet to receive control instructions and software upgrades from manufacturers. This creates a vulnerability: foreign manufacturers could interfere with or shut off equipment that supplies a large share of US energy.
The US announcement follows Europe’s move in May to ban public funding for projects with Chinese-made solar inverters, citing cybersecurity concerns, which Reuters estimated would affect 14 GW of planned solar capacity, or around 20% of Europe’s annual solar capacity installations. Earlier bans on Huawei equipment in 5G telecom networks across many NATO countries followed similar national security logic. (Reuters, Reuters)
Views are mixed on the near-term impact of the FCC’s move on US renewable energy projects. PV Magazine warned the ban will cause a “massive equipment shortage that will delay upcoming commercial and utility projects”. Canary Media, however, reports that utility-scale clean energy and battery projects can mostly ride this out for now, since the restriction only applies to new models — meaning sales of previously-approved models remain unaffected. Canary noted that expanding the ban to cover all foreign-manufactured inverters would have a far more dramatic effect, and that even the current ban will bite harder over the next year or more, as older models become obsolete and manufacturers release new models — whether for technical improvements or to meet new federal requirements — that will need fresh approvals.
Chinese firms lead the inverter market share globally, with Sungrow and Chint Power supplying most power inverters for utility-scale projects in the United States, while domestic manufacturers account for just 7% of the US solar inverter market. (Canary Media, PV Magazine) That said, non-Chinese firms are better positioned here than in other technologies, such as batteries. US-based Enphase Energy, German SMA, Austrian Fronius, and Israeli firm SolarEdge all rank among the top ten global solar inverter manufacturers. (Wood Mackenzie) In response to the earlier European bans, Fronius said it could scale up production to fulfill European demand within a year, suggesting inverter manufacturers can respond relatively quickly to shifts in demand. (Reuters) For energy storage systems, US-based EPC Power and Tesla have significant domestic manufacturing capacity, while Spanish firm Power Electronics is considering scaling up its US operations. (Canary Media)
Notably, the US ban covers all foreign-made inverters, including those manufactured in Europe — an approach that may be designed to limit Chinese retaliation against being singled out. In practice, where the FCC has imposed foreign-made bans before (e.g., on internet routers), it has readily granted conditional approvals to individual manufacturers that satisfy security requirements, creating a de facto pathway for European manufacturers while restricting Chinese firms. (Electrek, PV Magazine) How the FCC’s new inverter restrictions play out remains to be seen.
#2: Europe throws a lifeline to local battery manufacturers — while another one folds
The European Commission has opened its €1.5 billion Battery Booster Facility (BBF) for applications. The facility provides interest-free loans to support commercial first-of-a-kind battery cell manufacturing facilities through their crucial ramp-up phase — where European firms, including Northvolt and Morrow, have stalled and failed in recent years. (European Commission, The Battery Chronicle) The BBF is part of a larger €1.8 billion Battery Booster Strategy first announced in December 2025 as part of the Automotive Action Plan, with the remaining €300 million earmarked for critical raw materials projects. (Energy Storage Europe)
Europe views sovereign battery manufacturing capacity as critical for economic security, with battery technology now underpinning the future of energy, transport, and defense. China’s dominance of the battery supply chain — it controls over 80% of cell capacity and 60-90% of refined materials — leaves Europe and other regions vulnerable to export restrictions, supply disruptions, and price manipulation. (Carnegie)
But the same dominance undermines the commercial viability of other firms. Battery cell manufacturing faces an oversupply of roughly twice demand by 2030, with China’s capacity alone projected to significantly exceed global demand. This has depressed forecast prices and driven a wave of European projects to be delayed, downsized, or canceled. (Carnegie Endowment, CWIEME) In late July, it also contributed to the collapse of German battery manufacturer Varta, which filed for self-administered insolvency after losing its contract to supply batteries for Apple’s headphones to a Chinese competitor. (PV Magazine)
Beyond overcapacity, achieving high yields in battery cell manufacturing is notoriously difficult, especially for new firms lacking cell manufacturing experience and know-how. The many intricate steps in the production process — coating, dying, calendering, formation, and inspection — are prone to yield loss at each stage, and scrap often runs 15%-30% in early years, making it hard to hit revenue targets and fulfill customer contracts. (Battery Chronicle)
The BBF specifically targets this failure point, offering interest-free loans to support companies during the ramp-up phase between “C-Sample” — when cells are ready for customer qualification — and full commercial operation. (CWIEME)
The BBF comes with tight parameters. Eligible factories must have a minimum nameplate capacity of 10 GWh, be intended for electric vehicle applications, and be a first commercial facility owned by a local firm (ruling out, for example, European facilities owned by Korean firms or JVs with established global capacity). The facility must also be in the targeted ramp-up phase during the six-week window during which the call for applications is open. In short, this is a lifeline for established companies, not an incentive for new ventures. Funding per facility is also capped at €500 million or 60% of the facility’s total cost. (European Commission, ESS News)
While commentators agree that European policymakers are targeting the right issue, and have generally welcomed the package, several critiques have emerged. NEIS partner Milo McBride at the Carnegie Endowment argues that Europe should be investing in strategic partnerships with Korean and Japanese firms (second and third behind China on production capacity), which have the technical know-how to skip extended periods of validation and yield improvement. Carnegie also flags the need for Europe to invest in active materials — a supply chain step between critical raw materials and cell manufacturing — where European capacity lags.
In the Battery Chronicle, Christopher Chico argues the BBF’s 10 GWh minimum scale requirement replicates the “scale-first” failure mode that undid Northvolt, and suggests that incentivizing firms to fine-tune a 1-2 GWh line before replicating it would be a more capital-efficient approach. He also notes the short application window and stringent conditions seemingly limit eligibility to three facilities: PowerCo’s 20 GWh cell facility in Salzgitter, Germany; the Automotive Cells Company facility in France; and Verkor’s 16 GWh facility in Dunkirk, France—all still in early-stage operations. Finally, Chico points out that €1.5 billion is a modest sum against the overall capital investment needed to build a European battery supply chain, underscoring a gap between Europe’s ambition and the resources behind it.
#3: Korea’s ‘Three Megaprojects’ get boost from production incentives and permitting reform
In South Korea, two separate policy packages announced in August will help crowd in private investment to support strategic industries, including the ‘Three Megaprojects’ — Korea’s massive investment initiatives in semiconductors, AI data centers, and physical AI — which were unveiled at the end of June. (Reuters)
On August 3, the Korean government announced 10-year production tax credits for six sectors, including semiconductors, solar and wind generation facilities, recycled batteries, core materials, and AI robots. Producers must demonstrate both “domestic production” and “domestic sales” to qualify, while production outside the capital region can attract 50% higher incentives. Korea also extended its 15-30% investment tax credit for hydrogen facilities to “next generation energy,” a category which now includes nuclear micro and small modular reactors. (Chosun)
On August 13, the Korean government announced it would ease zoning and permitting regulations and tax settings for industrial complexes to help unlock $3 billion of private investment in sectors including semiconductors, batteries and biotechnology. (Korea JoongAng Daily, UPI)
Deputy Prime Minister and Finance Minister Koo Yun-cheol said the government would prioritize projects that have demonstrated demand but faced delays due to administrative processes or regulatory barriers. At the country’s Yongin semiconductor cluster, for example, current building regulations require projects to operate under a single construction permit, forcing an expanding facility to repeatedly reopen and revise its original permit. The reform will allow additional structures to receive separate permits—a change that officials expect could accelerate roughly $1.8 billion in pent-up investment. Other reforms target higher density and greater sector diversity in industrial complexes, easier pathways to designating industrial zoning, tax exemptions for test facilities, and faster processes for establishing and certifying safety measures. (Korea JoongAng Daily, UPI)
Together, the domestic production incentives and regulatory and permitting reforms represent a substantial boost for private investment in Korea’s industrial development, complementing major public spending commitments in recent months.
#4: Sony, TSMC bet on image sensors as Japan’s next chip niche
Japan’s Sony Group and Taiwan’s TSMC have agreed to invest close to 1 trillion yen ($6.3 billion) in a next-generation fab producing chips for image sensors — vital components for the robotic and automotive applications underpinning “physical AI.” (Sony Group, Reuters)
Sony will take a 60% stake in the facility, to be built within its existing image sensor site in Kumamoto Prefecture, an emerging semiconductor cluster in southern Japan. The companies have moved forward with the announcement on the expectation that the facility will also be supported by Japanese government funding, and are targeting production by 2029. (Bloomberg, Quartz, Reuters)
This is Sony and TSMC’s second joint venture in Japan, following the 2021 launch of Japan Advanced Semiconductor Manufacturing (JASM), in which TSMC holds the controlling stake. The partnership reflects Sony’s evolution towards a “fab-light” strategy after decades of vertical integration. Reducing the capital burden of building new fabs allows Sony to free up resources to focus on its other businesses, including music distribution, film, and video games. (Bloomberg, Quartz)
The move also fits a broader pattern in Japanese industrial strategy: aiming for globally-significant leadership while recognizing that Japan’s strength may lie less in high-volume, low-cost competition than in high-value, specialized niches that play to its precision engineering and design expertise. (Think China)
#5: Indonesia’s pursuit of a nickel-based battery industry may be out of sync with shifting demand
Indonesia’s Energy and Mineral Resources Minister Bahlil Lahadalia has indicated the government is considering incentives for nickel-manganese-cobalt (NMC) batteries as part of a strategy to accelerate domestic battery and EV production and vertically integrate the country’s nickel resources. His comments, made on August 3rd, build on earlier hints from government ministers of an EV incentive program—first floated in the wake of the Hormuz crisis. Details remain vague, but NMC incentives could be a risky bet, given how rapidly the global EV market has shifted toward lower-cost lithium iron phosphate (LFP) batteries. Bahlil explicitly deprioritized LFP batteries, noting Indonesia lacks the raw materials to manufacture them. (Antara, Jakarta Post, Vietnam Plus)
The incentives would sit alongside the broader package flagged by Finance Minister Purbaya Yudhi Sadewa in May, targeting 100,000 electric cars and 100,000 electric motorcycles this year via VAT relief and per-unit motorcycle subsidies, with the exact benefit tied to whether the vehicle uses a nickel-based or non-nickel battery. (Vietnam Plus)
The nickel-centric roadmap builds on Indonesia’s 2019-2020 nickel-ore export ban, which pushed the country from raw-ore exporter to a key global processor of nickel products, and on ministry ambitions to translate that position into a US$121 billion pipeline of EV battery ecosystem investment—part of a longer-term downstream push the government says could eventually draw US$618 billion in total investment. (Antara, Jakarta Post)
But the bet cuts against where the global market is heading. While nickel-based batteries held roughly 60% of the global EV battery market in 2022, LFP batteries have climbed rapidly from under 10% market share in 2020 to about half of the global market by 2025 on the back of prices more than 40% lower, largely thanks to Chinese-dominated LFP manufacturing (although the battery market for EVs is also observed to be segmenting in ways that may preserve some market share for NMC batteries). (Jakarta Post) Indonesia’s own EV market reflects the same shift—over 90% of EVs sold domestically in 2025 used LFP rather than nickel-based batteries, with nickel-based models priced out of reach for most local buyers. Analyst Asido Nabadan, writing in the Jakarta Post, argues Indonesia would be better served diversifying into higher-purity refined nickel for broader industrial uses (stainless steel remains nickel’s largest demand source) rather than betting narrowly on battery-grade intermediates whose market may be a shrinking slice of the pie.
Other stories we’re following…
- Japan has joined Horizon Europe, the EU’s €93.5 billion research and innovation program, allowing Japanese organizations to tap European research and project funding. (EU-Japan Centre for Industrial Cooperation)
- China’s State Council has approved eight new nuclear reactors, which will cost around $25 billion, and all use one of two standardized domestic reactor designs. This roughly matches the cadence of 10 reactor approvals per year that we’ve seen in China in recent years. (Bloomberg, Power Magazine)
- President Trump ordered the rebuilding of America’s shipbuilding industrial base — expecting that the United States would be able to leverage investment commitments made during trade deal negotiations, particularly by South Korea, into new shipbuilding capacity. (White House)
- The European Commission released revisions to the Industrial Accelerator Act’s ‘Made in Europe’ requirements, aiming to iron out some of the confusing rules in the first draft. (Politico)
