By Lachlan Carey, Director of Strategic Analysis, NEIS Center
In early July, a NEIS Center delegation traveled to Tokyo, Seoul, and New Delhi. We went to understand how the region’s leading industrial economies were adjusting their energy and industrial strategies to a more fractured geopolitical environment. Over two weeks, we met with government officials, industry executives, financiers, and researchers in each capital.
We expected three different conversations about the energy transition. We found three countries with different strengths, different development needs, different relationships to Washington and Beijing, yet all working on the same five shocks and revealing the same constraint: none of them can solve their problems or achieve their goals alone.
Hormuz exposed dependence on distant fuels and vulnerable sea lanes. “China Shock 2.0” is bringing both technologically advanced products and supply-chain vulnerability. The AI boom is creating vast new demands for generation, grids, batteries, and semiconductors. Trade and geopolitical fragmentation are forcing governments to ask what they must produce at home, where they need partners, and whom they can trust. And the end of the 2019–23 cleantech investment boom has disciplined corporate balance sheets and budgets.
Each country meets these shocks from a different position. Japan is a precision-manufacturing and energy-security expert. South Korea is an export and outward-investment champion — the indispensable “silver medalist” across much of the electro-industrial stack. India combines seemingly limitless demand with vast development needs, and offers perhaps the only route to manufacturing scale outside China.
Those differences are the point. The same shocks are hitting the three countries asymmetrically, repeatedly exposing capability gaps another may be better placed to fill. Japan has patient capital, sophisticated institutions, and advanced components but struggles to scale. Korea has manufacturing scale and execution capability but depends on foreign resources and export markets. India has demand and engineering talent but lacks important upstream equipment and process know-how. As capital becomes scarcer, the question shifts from how much each country can localize to what it must retain, what it can safely import, and which partners can provide the rest.
The Hormuz Shock: Energy Policy Is Now Security Policy (Again)
When we arrived in Asia, the region was still absorbing one of the largest energy-security shocks in modern history. Before the crisis, around 80 percent of the oil and nearly 90 percent of the liquefied natural gas transiting Hormuz was destined for Asian markets,. Japan, Korea, and India were among the economies most exposed to an oil price shock, before accounting for strategic reserves (Exhibit 1, below). We found the energy transition was no longer discussed primarily as a climate project, but as both a source of new vulnerabilities and a potential solution to an enduring security problem.
Exhibit 1
Nowhere was this clearer than in Japan. Before the crisis, roughly 95 percent of Japanese oil imports passed through Hormuz, yet extensive fuel stockpiles largely cushioned the blow. Through its POWERR Asia initiative, Japan is now offering fuel-procurement finance, stockpiling expertise, and supply diversification across the region, an example of Japan turning its energy-security institutions into regional statecraft, albeit one still focused narrowly on fuel resilience.
Japan’s experience since China restricted rare-earth exports in 2010 has also forced it to look beyond fuels to the industrial inputs that underpin its economy. For example, the Institute of Energy Economics, Japan (IEEJ), has modeled that a 75 percent disruption to the country’s rare-earth supply would reduce economic activity by 2.4 percent, cut electronic-component production by a quarter, and cost nearly one million jobs.
Japan’s response is institutional rather than episodic. METI, JOGMEC, and JBIC give the government permanent capacity to map vulnerabilities, coordinate with companies, finance alternatives, and sustain projects when markets alone will not. Some grant and stockpiling programs require firms to disclose supply-chain information through multiyear plans, giving officials visibility into deeper tiers of dependence.
Support for Lynas Rare Earths shows the model at work. Beginning in 2011, Sojitz and JOGMEC put $250 million behind Australian mining and Malaysian processing capacity, securing up to 9,000 tonnes a year — then roughly 30 percent of Japanese consumption. In 2026, they reinforced that relationship, committing to buy 5,000 tonnes of NdPr annually through 2038, with a $110-per-kilogram floor. The result was not independence from China, but a promising alternative, built with patient capital, assured demand, and diplomacy.
Hormuz reinforced a shift already underway in India’s security debate. What was once primarily about securing energy supplies is increasingly about economic security across the mineral and technology supply chains that underpin the energy transition. It now encompasses semiconductors, manufacturing equipment, trusted technology partnerships, and the physical resilience of the energy system itself.
India frames its domestic response through atmanirbharta, or self-reliance, paired with affordability and development. Its mission-driven initiatives span deep-water oil and gas exploration, nuclear power, coal, and solar manufacturing. Abroad, it has diversified fuel suppliers, technologies, and strategic relationships. Yet the transition is also creating new dependencies of its own — especially in the solar supply chain.
One Indian official organized the strategy around four pillars: raw materials, industrial architecture, technology, and partnerships. India is combining overseas mineral acquisition and domestic production incentives with an ambition to shift from “Make in India” toward “Design in India”, while using foreign partnerships to access fuels, minerals, finance, and technologies India cannot efficiently develop alone.
Korea approaches these same pressures from a different position. Conversations in Seoul focused more on competitiveness and climate than resilience. The government is trying to build globally competitive industries at home while using exports and outward investment to sustain the scale those industries require. Whereas climate ambition is being tempered elsewhere, the Lee government is moving in the opposite direction, pairing a major renewables push with stronger emissions targets and a new climate-and-energy ministry. Tensions described between Korea’s climate and industry ministries reflect a broader divide between environmental ambition and industrial delivery.
The shared lesson was not that every country should reproduce Japan’s stockpiles, or India’s self-reliance agenda, but that energy security, and success in the energy transition more broadly, increasingly depends on access to capabilities beyond national borders. Or in other words, countries need diversified partners almost as much as diversified energy sources.
The China Shock: Striking a Balance
China was the second thread running through every conversation — not only the concentration and coercion potential of new energy supply chains, but Beijing’s widening technological lead across advanced manufacturing.
In this second China shock, Chinese firms have entered sectors once dominated by Japan and Korea, contributing to a manufacturing surplus exceeding two percent of global GDP — the largest external imbalance in modern history. China now directly competes with countries in advanced manufacturing industries once considered well out of its reach (see Exhibit 2). Weak domestic demand may be pushing China toward exports (see Exhibit 3), but subsidies alone do not explain its strength in vehicles, batteries, robotics, machine tools, and solar equipment. Chinese firms combine extraordinary scale, dense supply chains, fierce competition, and growing technological sophistication.
Exhibit 2
Exhibit 3
For Korea, the pressure is most immediate in batteries. Korean producers lost 20 percentage points of European market share between 2023 and 2025, almost entirely to Chinese competitors. Their position in the United States was protected by tariffs, local-content rules, production subsidies, and restrictions on Chinese suppliers. Korea’s bet on premium nickel-manganese-cobalt (NMC) chemistry has been undermined by China’s cost advantage in lithium-iron-phosphate (LFP) batteries, now roughly half the global lithium-ion market, and by China’s lead in sodium-ion. Chinese cells sold in Europe are estimated to be 10–27 percent cheaper in NMC and 24–50 percent cheaper in LFP.
Korean firms nonetheless remain indispensable to diversification. LG Energy Solution, SK On, and Samsung SDI are among the world’s ten largest cell producers, and Korea leads all countries with 27 overseas battery-cell facilities. But idle lines, weak EV demand, thin margins, and Chinese price competition are forcing Korean firms to choose between competing in LFP, pursuing advanced chemistries, or redirecting capacity towards markets such as stationary storage, drones, robots, and AI data centers.
Japan faces a different version of the same problem. Japanese companies repeatedly developed world-leading solar, battery, and fuel-cell technologies only to lose ground when they failed to scale them. Today, just one Japanese company remains among the world’s ten largest battery-cell manufacturers, accounting for just 4.5 percent of global production.
Japanese interlocutors were less exercised by head-to-head competition than Beijing’s leverage over concentrated supply chains, increasingly reading the 2010 rare-earth restriction as the start of a pattern. Japan’s initial response also revealed the danger of poorly designed diversification when some magnet manufacturers moved to China to preserve raw-material access, transferring capabilities China later used to dominate the downstream supply chain.
The objective is not full decoupling, which Japanese officials regard as unrealistic. It is to build enough diversified capacity and prearranged cooperation to reduce the vulnerability of any one country or input that could disrupt an entire industrial system.
India’s concern is more fundamental to its development model. Rather than competing with China for technological supremacy, Indian stakeholders worry that China is “pulling away the ladder” behind it. By controlling critical materials, production equipment, and process technologies — and deploying overcapacity before competitors can reach scale — China can block other countries from following the manufacturing- and export-led development path it used itself.
India has made remarkable progress in renewable deployment and downstream solar manufacturing. But polysilicon, ingots, wafers, machinery, specialty chemicals, and much of the surrounding capital goods ecosystem remain Chinese. In India’s solar factories, the modules leaving the line are Indian, but the machines that make them, the software running those machines, the technicians who service them, and the process knowledge behind all of it are not. There are concerns not only that some of these machines can be controlled remotely, but that they are a generation behind what runs in Chinese plants — preserving a large and growing productivity gap.
Taken together, our conversations showed how China’s scale and technological depth are creating different pressures across the industrial system, but with a shared implication that meaningful diversification will be difficult for any country to achieve alone. These pressures would be concerning enough in a world of steady energy demand. It becomes more consequential when electricity, computing, batteries, and grids are all needed at once.
The AI Shock: The Race for Electricity
Conversations returned repeatedly to rising demand from AI, data centers, semiconductor manufacturing, and electrification. As in the United States, AI is collapsing the distinction between energy policy, digital policy, and industrial strategy. Reliable and affordable electricity is becoming a prerequisite for attracting the industries that governments view as central to growth and security. This has been reflected in explosive stock market growth (see Exhibit 4).
Exhibit 4
Korea is especially exposed to both the promise and volatility of AI. For example, its government has announced three semiconductor, physical-AI, and data center “mega projects” with Samsung Electronics and SK Group, representing more than $880 billion in public and private investment. They imply roughly 40 gigawatts of additional electricity demand — around a quarter of Korea’s existing grid — with no planned generation source for the majority of it.
The result is a reconsideration of nearly every part of Korean energy policy: nuclear, gas, renewables, storage, transmission, and the proposed “energy highway” linking generation regions to industrial loads. Among other changes, the government is shifting from a renewable portfolio standard toward auctions for long-term power-purchase agreements that can include storage. But the existing framework still gives data centers no direct route to contract for the round-the-clock, clean power many seek. The challenge is sharpened by the government’s commitment to phase down and ultimately retire coal-fired generation even as electricity demand accelerates.
Japan entered the AI era from the opposite starting point. Electricity consumption had been expected to decline, giving utilities little reason to expand transmission. Now grid access is becoming a central constraint on new data centers. Japan’s topography, regional divisions, and poorly connected grids make expansion especially difficult. Transmission projects can take a decade or more, and much of the equipment needed to build them has long lead times.
Japan manufactures world-leading transformers, switchgear, cables, cooling systems, and power electronics. Yet much of it is bespoke, tailored to individual utilities, and companies hesitate to add capacity without confidence that demand will persist. The caution is understandable after repeated market disappointments, but it creates a collective action problem where every company waits for certainty while scarce capacity makes the grid slower and costlier to build.
India’s electricity challenge is larger still. The Viksit Bharat vision of a developed economy by 2047 requires a power system roughly four times its current size. Per-capita electricity consumption is intended to double by 2030, and double again by 2047. All while India works toward net-zero by 2070.
Across all three countries, grids remain under-prioritized as an area of strategic focus, investment, and coordination despite being the physical foundation of the AI boom. Here, the complementarities are apparent: Japan and Korea possess critical equipment capabilities, while India and other fast-growing power systems provide the multi-decade demand that could justify additional manufacturing capacity. The missing piece is a mechanism to aggregate that demand across borders.
The Trade Shock: The Middle-Power Moment
The “rupture” in the rules-based order is visible throughout the region in the increasingly transactional and bilateral character of trade, investment, and diplomacy -— fragmenting long-standing relationships while beginning to lay the foundations for a more complementary Indo-Pacific industrial base.
Japan, Korea, and India are responding to this middle-power moment in different but ambitious ways. Each is large enough to shape parts of the international system but too small to resolve its vulnerabilities alone. Exhibit 5 visualizes the relevant partnerships signed in 2026 alone.
Exhibit 5
Source: ChatGPT Image Generator from NEIS Partnership Database
Prime Minister Takaichi has given Japan a more assertive posture, recasting the “Free and Open Indo-Pacific” of her predecessor around economic security. Her government is willing to challenge China, fill gaps in regional leadership, and strengthen US and Korean relationships while pursuing economic renewal. Officials emphasized Japan’s stability and ability to add weight to its partnerships through patient finance, institutional capacity, and project delivery.
Korea occupies the most precarious position between its largest trading partner and its security guarantor. Chinese retaliation has made Seoul cautious, while US volatility has made dependence on Washington costly. President Lee’s “pragmatic diplomacy centered on national interests” treats industrial champions as instruments of foreign policy. With Washington, the relationship increasingly rests on trading Korean capacity in shipbuilding, semiconductors, energy, and critical minerals for tariff relief, security commitments, and technology cooperation. That same uncertainty has made Japan more valuable as a hedge, subordinating historical disputes to practical coordination on critical minerals, supply chains, deterrence, fuel swaps, and stockpiling.
India combines self-reliance with diversified partnerships, concluding both that the country cannot catch up with China alone and that dependence cannot be negotiated away through diplomacy. The near-term goal is not to replace China across entire value chains, but to become the credible alternative in selected segments through joint ventures, shared know-how, and targeted cooperation with Japan, Korea, Europe, Australia, and others. Prime Minister Modi’s recent visits to Indonesia, Australia, and New Zealand exemplify this approach. Rather than join a fixed bloc, India is positioning itself as an autonomous pole, assembling bilateral bargains that link partners’ minerals, capital, and manufacturing to Indian demand, technology, and growth. The constraint is that India’s demand can become leverage only when partnerships move beyond declarations into offtake, investment, and technology transfer. That requires predictable policy, suitable capital, stronger domestic absorptive capacity, and a clearer internal hierarchy among strategic autonomy, employment, and global competitiveness — objectives that cannot all be maximized at once.
Three middle powers, three theories of how to become indispensable: Japan through reliability and finance, Korea through capability it can trade, India through the scale of its market. Each depends on the others to make its own theory work — Japanese finance needs somewhere to go, Korean capacity needs buyers, Indian demand needs equipment and know-how. And all three now run into the same constraint: ambitions that cannot all be funded at once.
The Capital Shock: From Green Bubble to Hard Choices
The first four shocks have forced countries to be more resilient, but it is the fifth that is forcing them to admit they can’t go it alone. The cleantech manufacturing boom of 2019–23 was built on cheap capital, rising demand forecasts, generous public support, and investor enthusiasm. That era is over (see Exhibit 6). Scarcer capital is not merely slowing investment; it is forcing governments and firms to distinguish between technologies they would like to support and those they are prepared to finance, scale, and defend.
Exhibit 6
Counterintuitively, this has pushed all three countries to double down — but along narrower fronts, and from different starting conditions. Korea was hit hardest because its industrial push relied heavily on American and European policy support and consumer demand. India has been buffered by its domestic market, but remains exposed in its export markets. In Japan, inflation has helped end a three-decade deflationary slump, even as corporate risk aversion persists.
From 2019 through the IRA years, Korean industrial strategy leaned heavily outward, as firms built strategic manufacturing capacity in the United States and other major markets with diplomatic and financial backing from Seoul. That model is now being rebalanced as fiercer Chinese competition, higher financing costs, and reduced US policy support are forcing Korean firms to scrutinize overseas expansion more carefully. Policymakers described this to us as “co-movement investment”: pairing international production with renewed domestic investment so that advanced manufacturing capacity, knowledge, and strategic supply lines remain anchored at home.
Batteries illustrate the pressures Korea is under. EV and battery companies face overcapacity, weak utilization, and balance-sheet stress, forcing them to triage: cutting marginal expansion, redirecting capacity toward stationary storage, and preserving capital for markets with durable demand. The result is not the abandonment of Korean industrial ambition, but its narrowing around products, markets, and facilities that can demonstrate credible demand.
Nuclear and grid manufacturers have fared better because they can increasingly point to identifiable customers and projects. In nuclear, prospective US reactor deployment has drawn Korean manufacturers such as Doosan into partnerships with developers including NuScale, TerraPower, and X-energy, whose designs depend on manufacturing capabilities that are difficult to reproduce quickly at home. The divergence is instructive: in a higher-rate environment, capital flows toward firm orders, durable policy support, and defensible capability — not toward capacity built on optimistic forecasts.
Japan’s problem is almost the reverse. Inflation and renewed industrial ambition have created an opening after decades of deflation. The Takaichi administration has announced a $2.26 trillion public and private investment roadmap spanning 17 sectors over 15 years, including critical minerals, next-generation solar, and nuclear fusion, helping spur a wave of foreign investment associated with the “Takaichi trade.” Yet recent pressure on the yen and in bond markets suggests capital markets will impose their own prioritization.
Offshore wind offers an early illustration of this new discipline. Rising costs and deteriorating project economics have led developers to withdraw from projects that were recently expected to anchor Japan’s renewable buildout, forcing policymakers to reconsider auction design and the allocation of market risk.
Companies, meanwhile, remain reluctant to invest beyond core capabilities or against speculative demand. For this reason, METI is revising the Corporate Governance Code to address insufficient “growth investment, which it estimates accounts for only 17.7 percent of Japanese companies’, compared with 29.4 percent in the United States and 27.2 percent in Europe. One industry representative said at least five years of predictable public finance would be needed to justify new capacity, reflecting this broader caution.
In India, domestic demand continues to grow, but the country has reached its first serious utilization and bankability test. Production-linked incentives and domestic-content rules have rapidly expanded solar-module and cell capacity while leaving major gaps in upstream materials, equipment, and process capabilities. Scarce capital is forcing hard choices about what India must build itself, what it should develop with partners, and what it can safely continue to import.
Everywhere we went, the capital shock was turning industrial strategy from an accumulation of ambitions into a hierarchy of choices. In other words, scarcity is forcing countries to specialize. The prospect of collectively developing scale among like-minded countries in the region was so enticing because it potentially allows governments to preserve strategically sufficient capacity without having to finance the entire stack.
Specialize and Conquer: Baby Steps Towards a Joint Industrial Base
The five shocks are pushing Japan, Korea, and India toward the conclusion that neither national self-sufficiency nor a return to frictionless globalization is plausible. The more realistic objective is managed interdependence — countries specializing, trading, and investing together without letting any single dependency become an instrument of coercion. Success will require identifying which capabilities are strategically consequential, where reliance on partners is acceptable, and what demand, finance, and policy certainty complementary industries need to reach scale.
Their strengths are complementary to a joint industrial base. Japan brings finance, stockpiling expertise, advanced components, and institutional capacity. Korea brings speed, manufacturing depth, clustering, and project execution. India brings demand, workers, entrepreneurship, and the volume needed to make diversified supply chains viable.
Coordination does not require dividing the world into rigid blocs or removing China from every supply chain. Some Chinese inputs will remain commercially necessary and relatively low risk. The harder task is deciding what must be produced domestically, what can be safely imported, and where trusted countries should build shared capacity. That middle ground surfaced in several proposals.
One Indian participant floated an Airbus-style solar consortium, pooling capital, technology, research support, and assured demand to build a solar supply chain no country could create alone. A related “silver medalist” strategy would pair India with leading non-Chinese producers: Korea in batteries, Japan in grid technologies, and European firms in magnets and selected equipment. A Japanese interlocutor proposed an “Article 5 for Economic Security,” where members would respond collectively when interdependence was weaponized against one of them — not to protect every company, but to deter coercion.
The common view was that critical-minerals agreements, energy-security memoranda, and competitiveness initiatives have to move beyond rhetoric and must yield projects: mines, processing plants, battery factories, transmission corridors, shared nuclear supply chains, equipment partnerships, and assured procurement. Governments must share risk, companies must share knowledge, and countries must accept that resilience carries a premium.
Whether that premium gets paid is the thing to watch. The Airbus consortium and the economic Article 5 are, for now, ideas floated in conference rooms. The test of this middle-power moment will be whether any of them acquires a budget line.

While price support mechanisms linked to government-backed offtakes are emerging, only an ex-China market underpinned by an ex-China price index that addresses China’s price retaliation risk would truly support resilient ex-China critical-minerals supply chains. The challenge this piece addresses is a general one: how do governments build resilient supply chains in sectors where a dominant supplier controls price discovery? The answer developed here — moving from price floors to contracts-for-difference to independent price formation — is a sequencing logic that applies wherever Chinese pricing makes diversification non-bankable. It can be thought of alongside other commentaries we’ve published focused on critical mineral market formation.
By Bryan Bille, Benchmark Mineral Intelligence
China not only dominates several critical mineral supply chains, such as rare earths, cobalt, and graphite, but it can also influence prices, bankrupt rivals through supply gluts, and restrict supply to squeeze downstream OEMs, as with its April 2025 export controls on seven rare earths and permanent magnets. Since these controls, a bifurcated rare earths market has emerged, with heavy rare earths such as dysprosium and terbium trading several times higher outside China. Chinese prices sit below the level at which many non-Chinese projects can be financed, and downstream buyers, especially European OEMs, remain wary of paying a resilience premium without government intervention. The resilience premium — the gap between the true cost of diversified supply and what markets will pay without coordination — is not unique to critical minerals. It appears wherever a dominant low-cost supplier sets the reference price and downstream buyers cannot justify paying more unilaterally. Closing it requires collective action, not just project-level subsidies.
Price floors and contracts-for-difference (CfDs) linked to government-backed offtakes, along with public and corporate equity finance, have emerged as tools to de-risk ex-China projects and build resilient supply chains. Public-private partnerships and the equity-for-offtake model have been deployed among G7 members to decrease China’s dominance across mine-to-anode and mine-to-magnet supply chains: General Motors and Panasonic Energy have each taken equity stakes in Nouveau Monde Graphite and signed active anode material (AAM) offtake agreements, while the Canadian government has signed a graphite offtake with rights to store and resell. In France, Japan’s JOGMEC and Iwatani have provided €110 million in debt and equity finance to Carester’s Caremag plant, a rare-earth recycling and refining facility, in exchange for a heavy rare-earth oxide offtake. At the same time, Stellantis has secured a ten-year offtake for light- and heavy rare earth oxides.
What we can learn from Japan and Australia
Japan has been the frontrunner and guide. After China’s 2010 rare earth export restrictions, JOGMEC and Sojitz, through their special purpose vehicle, Japan Australia Rare Earths (JARE), backed Lynas with a US$250 million funding package consisting of loans and equity in exchange for long-term supply. Lynas is now the largest rare earths producer outside China, Japan’s biggest ex-China supplier, and the only scaled producer outside China of separated heavy rare earths, producing dysprosium, terbium and samarium, all of which are crucial for magnets in EVs, wind turbines, and drones.
In March 2026 the Lynas–JARE partnership was extended to 2038 on terms that amount to a government-backed offtake with an embedded CfD: a US$110/kg NdPr floor, an offtake of 5,000 tonnes a year (up to 7,200 available to Japan), 75% of heavy rare earth oxides made available to Japan, and 30% of realised prices above US$150/kg (capped at US$10 million a year) returned to JARE. Lynas has made a similar arrangement with the US Department of War: US$96 million over four years at the same floor, ahead of NDAA rules barring Chinese-refined magnets from US defence systems from January 1, 2027.
Australia adds the strategic reserve model, blending government-backed offtake, CfD and stockpiling. Its A$1.2 billion Critical Minerals Strategic Reserve splits into A$1 billion for offtake and price-support transactions and A$185 million for targeted stockpiling of rare earths, gallium and antimony. Its price-support leg is a collared CfD, with the government acting as offtaker of last resort, securing output at an agreed floor and on-selling it. Its first deployment already counts: a 500-tonne-a-year NdPr offtake in May 2026 tipped Arafura’s Nolans project past its board’s 80%-contracted FID threshold.
Yet none of this neutralizes the risk of Chinese price retaliation: prices have crashed before due to Chinese market interventions, making supply diversification harder for its competitors. The endgame must therefore be the development of ex-China markets anchored in ex-China price indices, with a sequenced strategy, keeping government intervention transitional, temporary, and targeted.
The sequencing spine: from price floors to an ex-China market
The sequencing logic laid out here applies beyond critical minerals. Government intervention in concentrated markets should move through three phases: first, subsidizing activity (price floors) to keep viable projects alive; then anchoring markets (CfDs) to attract private capital without permanent fiscal exposure; then building institutions (independent price indices, futures markets) that make the market self-sustaining. The goal at each stage is to do enough to reach the next one, then step back.
Price floors are the first step. However, if a government underwrites a floor to derisk a critical mineral project, the fiscal risk remains with the state, price discovery is distorted and nothing is hedgeable or scalable across the supply chain or among allies. Furthermore, price floors are initially best reserved for materials with little or no liquid market.
CfDs are the better middle step and the workhorse of the transition. The mechanism is proven: for over a decade, the UK has used two-way CfDs to build a large offshore wind fleet, a model the EU is now incorporating into its electricity rules. Its first real use in critical minerals is the MP Materials–Pentagon deal, which has been coined as a “US$110/kg price floor”, but which is really a CfD, with MP selling its NdPr at market price while the US Pentagon pays any shortfall to US$110/kg and takes 30% of the upside. Under this scenario, the downstream buyer continues to pay the market price, so the gap closes at the source without inflating downstream costs. Bundled with smart project finance, such as equity and concessional loans, along with tax credits to address higher ex-China operating costs, ex-China projects could achieve bankability.
But the destination is a resilient ex-China market. Supply resilience requires an independent, ex-China price that producers, financials and downstream companies can hedge and finance against, which is the missing piece of sovereign price formation policymakers often overlook. The underlying problem is structural. When one supplier controls the reference price, physical diversification alone does not produce financial resilience — contracts, hedges, and project finance all still anchor to that price, leaving producers exposed to the same retaliation risk the diversification was meant to avoid. Market formation, not just supply diversification, is therefore the correct policy objective.
The logic runs as follows: an independent ex-China price, reflecting supply and demand outside China, enables the trading and settlement of futures contracts, which in turn enable hedging and allow producers, financial institutions, and downstream companies to lock in future prices, protecting them against Chinese price swings. Because price risk is hedgeable, lenders and investors can underwrite projects with confidence, unlocking private capital. Lithium and cobalt futures already trade on the Intercontinental Exchange (ICE) and the first NdPr contract is in development. The binding constraint, though, is ex-China liquidity, especially for rare earths such as NdPr, which is why pooling volumes across allies matters. A market also lets this support scale across the chain and among allies with thin fiscal room, especially the EU, which cannot fund US-style floors and instead leans mainly on tools like demand aggregation. Floors and CfDs are the bridge, while the ex-China market is the endgame.
In parallel, a coordinated allied stockpile can buffer price shocks and guarantee access to niche materials such as heavy rare earths and tungsten. Stockpiling should be market-transparent, targeted, and focused on small- and niche-market minerals, potentially with governments acting as offtakers of last resort, as Australia’s reserve shows.
What this means for the G7+ members and FORGE
Governments that limit themselves to subsidizing individual projects leave price formation in the hands of the dominant supplier. Industrial strategy in concentrated markets succeeds when it builds the market institutions — benchmarks, futures, coordinated offtake — that allow rival producers to survive without permanent public support.
Besides a broad toolkit, combining targeted, time-limited CfDs and government-backed offtakes to anchor demand, smart project finance (equity, concessional loans, untied loan guarantees) to de-risk projects and tax credits to address high operating costs, developing ex-China markets supported by robust, independent ex-China price indices should be a G7+ priority and part of FORGE. In addition, the G7+ and FORGE members should become the anchor users of an ex-China benchmark. This means settling price floors, CfDs, and reserve purchases against an ex-China reference price rather than Chinese quotations, as well as conditioning project finance on the use of that reference price. Together, this pools thin volumes into liquid ones and turns a patchwork of national price support schemes into one financeable market.

By Jonas Nahm, Research Director, NEIS Center
Almost a year ago, this Substack laid out a framework for a new energy industrial strategy — one that moves beyond emissions-only logic to harness clean energy in service of competitive economies and national security. A subsequent piece posed the questions policymakers need to answer to make that strategy work in practice: when does competition between nations drive innovation versus waste resources, what makes policies survive political transitions, what capacities do governments actually need, and how do we know what works?
A year of research and observation has produced advances on many of these questions. The empirical picture of where investment is actually going has improved: new tracking tools and datasets now make it possible to follow clean energy capital flows across countries and sectors. A central lesson from the analysis of how industrial strategy performs in practice is that design is fundamentally a matching problem. The right instrument depends on where a technology is in its development cycle, the right accountability structure depends on the institutional context and the policy objective, and more intervention is not always better. Detailed performance requirements and administrative conditions to prevent capture can deter participation, favor actors with administrative sophistication over those with industrial merit, and generate workarounds that hollow out the policy’s intent. We also learned that the bottleneck is no longer just financing or political will, but extends to governance capacity, site and grid readiness, workforce pipelines, and the demand-side mechanisms that make projects bankable. Getting the instrument right matters little if the delivery infrastructure isn’t there to translate it into capacity on the ground.
At the same time, the past year has shown that some of the assumptions underlying the original questions have shifted in ways that matter for how industrial strategy should be practiced.
Multiple objectives
Green industrial strategy has always served multiple objectives simultaneously. Climate, competitiveness, and energy security were never fully separable — the premise of green industrial strategy was at least in part that pursuing clean energy could serve all three at once. What is changing is the hierarchy among them. For most of the past two decades, climate was the primary rationale for clean energy industrial policy, with security and competitiveness as supporting arguments that helped make the case politically. Several things have shifted that balance: the volatility of energy markets exposed by Russia’s invasion of Ukraine and, more recently, the Hormuz crisis, supply chain vulnerabilities laid bare by the pandemic, intensifying geopolitical rivalry with China, and the arrival of clean technologies at costs that have made them genuinely competitive across many applications. Energy independence, supply chain security, and competitive positioning in strategic industries are now motivations in their own right.
That means that the coalition behind clean energy investment is broader than it has been. Defense establishments, semiconductor manufacturers, data center operators, and a broad swath of energy-intensive industry now have independent reasons to care about the same investments — reasons that exist regardless of where climate politics happens to be.
But it also makes for more complex policy design, because these objectives don’t all point in the same direction. Deploying clean energy — building domestic generating capacity, regardless of who manufactured the equipment — delivers energy security and cheaper power. Building the industry delivers domestic industrial capacity and the strategic and economic advantages that come with it, but requires manufacturing at home at considerably greater cost and effort, and is only worth attempting where competitive advantage is achievable. The parts of the energy transition that deliver security and competitiveness benefits are increasingly self-sustaining politically. The parts that don’t — the decarbonization of steel, cement, and industrial heat, where clean options still cost more (in most cases), and the benefit remains a global public good — risk being left behind precisely because the new political logic doesn’t reach them. Being explicit about which objective a given policy is primarily serving, and designing instruments and measurement frameworks accordingly, matters more than it did when climate was a more central motivation for clean energy industrial strategy.
The nature of manufacturing
The original questions were organized around a theory of how industrial strategy works politically: factories generate employment, employment generates constituencies, constituencies sustain policy across political cycles. It is the logic that implicitly structured most thinking about the IRA and equivalent programs elsewhere.
What the past year has made clearer is that this theory of change is under pressure — not because the policies were badly designed, but because advanced manufacturing is changing in ways that disrupt the employment logic at its core. Advanced manufacturing facilities are increasingly capital-intensive and energy-intensive relative to their employment footprint. A battery gigafactory that employs two thousand people and draws several hundred megawatts of power serves a community very differently than the labor-intensive plants that anchored the original industrial strategy playbook — closer in some ways to a data center than a traditional factory, generating concentrated economic value while producing thinner local employment and weaker community identity than the political theory assumed.
If the employment density that historically justified public support and created political coalitions can no longer be relied upon, industrial strategy needs to find different foundations for political durability. The growing salience of competitiveness, energy security, and national security arguments may be doing some of that work — factories that don’t generate many jobs may still generate political support if they are understood as essential infrastructure for strategic industries or energy independence. Which arguments can carry the political weight that employment once did, and under what conditions, is one of the more important open questions we now face.
When (and where) not to intervene
The original questions we posed were organized almost entirely around how to do industrial strategy: how to design better policies, how to build state capacity, how to measure success, how to coordinate internationally. What the past year has revealed is that the how question rests on a prior question that deserves equal attention — when and where not to intervene.
Not every sector is worth supporting. In some cases, the strategically rational choice may be to accept dependence on lower-cost foreign suppliers in sectors where catching up is unlikely and where the costs of attempting to do so outweigh the benefits. The energy transition requires enormous volumes of solar panels, batteries, and other equipment. Buying some of that from wherever it is produced most efficiently, while concentrating industrial policy investment in sectors where competitive advantage is achievable, may be a more defensible strategy than trying to do everything at once.
The political challenge is that making this distinction clearly and credibly is difficult. Industrial policy constituencies form around sectors that receive support, and withholding or withdrawing that support is politically costly even when the economic case for doing so is clear. The default, when fiscal space allows, is to intervene broadly — which is how industrial strategy ends up covering too many technology categories and too many policy objectives simultaneously, diluting its effectiveness across all of them. What we need are shared analytical frameworks for making sector selection decisions that are rigorous enough to guide policy and robust enough to withstand political pressure. What criteria justify intervention? Is it strategic importance, technological uncertainty, security exposure, the availability of domestic capabilities? Different answers lead to very different sector selection decisions, and without clearer frameworks for making these judgments, the temptation to intervene everywhere will remain stronger than the case for selective restraint.
A different challenge for the developing world
The original questions assumed that the analytical challenges of industrial strategy were broadly shared — that policymakers in advanced and developing economies alike were grappling with the same questions of design, capacity, and coordination, even if with different resources. Subsidy data now makes clear that assumption has not held up.
The industrial strategy race of the past several years has been a highly concentrated phenomenon. China, the United States, the European Union, Japan, and Korea have deployed the largest volumes of support, crowding many developing countries out of manufacturing industries and supply chains they might otherwise have entered, while simultaneously constraining their policy space through trade and supply chain policies that favor domestic investments over diversification. But the problem runs deeper than crowding out alone. The manufacturing-led development path that allowed earlier generations of developing economies to climb the value chain worked because low labor costs provided a foothold in labor-intensive industries. That entry point is increasingly unavailable in the sectors now being contested in the industrial strategy race, which are highly automated and where low labor costs provide little competitive advantage. For many developing economies, the manufacturing escalator may be structurally less accessible than it once was.
This changes the question of what industrial strategy should be for in the developing world. Development finance institutions have long supported clean energy deployment in developing economies, and that work remains valuable. More recently, attempts have been made to extend manufacturing finance there too, partly to build supply chain alternatives that reduce advanced economy dependence on China. Whether that serves EMDE development interests as well as it serves advanced economy strategic ones is a question worth investigating. Manufacturing in highly automated sectors may generate less employment and fewer spillovers than the development rationale assumes, and services-led development — where most employment in these economies actually is — has received far less analytical attention than the potential scale of the opportunity warrants. The right theory of industrial strategy for the developing world may look quite different from what either the historical manufacturing escalator model or the current supply chain diversification push suggests.
What this means for the questions ahead
The questions posed a year ago were the right ones to start with, and a year of serious work has yielded much progress on each. We understand instrument design better, we can track investment flows more precisely, and we have a clearer picture of where the design and implementation constraints actually lie. But good research programs also reveal new questions, in addition to answering existing ones. The past year has made clear that industrial strategy is more context-dependent than a single playbook can capture. The right approach depends on which objective is primary, which sectors are still in play, and where in the world policies are being applied. That’s not a reason for discouragement, but a sign of progress, as we move from debating whether to do industrial strategy to grappling seriously with how, where, and for whom.

This week, we’re sharing the NEIS News Roundup, a monthly recap of major international developments in new energy industrial strategies and advanced energy systems. These selections capture global trends shaping industrial strategy and competitiveness, with a focus on investment, policy, trade, and technology.
Here are the five major stories we’re following:
#1: China makes technical and diplomatic advances on AI
China had a banner month in artificial intelligence. The most prominent was the release of Kimi K3, a frontier AI model from Chinese startup Moonshot AI. On certain tests and benchmarks, Kimi K3 outperforms many global models — including Anthropic’s Claude Opus 4.8 and OpenAI’s GPT 5.5 — while trailing slightly behind the leading-edge Claude Fable 5 and GPT 5.6. (CNBC) The news upended conventional wisdom about America’s lead in frontier models, echoing the shockwave from DeepSeek R1’s release in January 2025. Commentators now estimate the US lead has narrowed to three to six months. (CNN)
Though US frontier models still hold a performance edge, Kimi K3 differs from them in two important respects: it is cheaper, and it is “open weight” — its trained parameters are released publicly and can be downloaded, used, and fine-tuned by anyone. This contrasts with closed-weight models like those from Anthropic and OpenAI, whose parameters are proprietary and accessible only through software interfaces or web services. That makes Kimi K3 especially attractive to users who are price-sensitive or concerned about data control and privacy, since open-weight models can run cheaply on a user’s own servers.
The release has triggered debate over whether American firms should adopt a similar open-weight strategy. The case for: open-weight models are more likely to become the foundational architecture companies build on and stay loyal to. The case against: releasing weights erodes whatever time and performance advantage the US still holds over China. (New York Times)
From the opposite angle, Chinese authorities are reportedly considering tighter export controls of their own on AI models, to restrict foreign users from downloading open-weight systems, and on semiconductors, to prevent chipmakers like TSMC and Qualcomm from producing advanced semiconductors designed by Chinese companies such as Huawei and Alibaba. The latter move would push demand toward domestic Chinese chipmakers. (Reuters, Reuters)
Secondly, at the World AI conference in Shanghai, Chinese President Xi Jinping launched the World Artificial Intelligence Cooperation Organization (WAICO), announcing 29 founding members. In his remarks, Xi said “AI development should not be a solo performance by a single country, but a symphony of international cooperation.” (Bloomberg)
WAICO was quickly compared to the US-led Pax Silica, a 24-member initiative focused on securing AI’s physical foundations, from critical minerals to semiconductors. The comparison isn’t one-for-one, however: China’s stated aim for WAICO is to promote safe, inclusive, and fair global AI development – while positioning itself in the center of multi-lateral conversations around AI safety, standards, and use. (Bloomberg, Jakarta Globe)
Finally, Chinese memory chipmaker ChangXin Memory Technology (CXMT) debuted on China’s stock market, with shares soaring 466% on their trading debut, lifting the company’s market capitalization from $85.5 billion at IPO to $488 billion and making it China’s most valuable listed company. (Reuters)
The funds raised will finance a major capacity expansion of CXMT’s wafer fabrication and upgrade of its DRAM (memory chip) technology. Memory chips — a crucial part of the computing and AI hardware stack currently facing global shortages and rising prices — are dominated by Korea’s Samsung and SK Hynix and America’s Micron, which together hold over 90% market share for standard DRAM and high-bandwidth memory. CXMT’s expansion signals its intent to build a domestic supply chain of comparable scale to these market leaders, though it currently produces only standard DRAM, not the high-bandwidth memory chips essential for AI applications.
#2: Takaichi sets out an ambitious industrial investment plan for Japan
Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi has laid out her government’s plan to invest 370 trillion yen ($2.3 trillion USD) across seventeen strategic industrial sectors by 2041, including defense, digital technologies and cybersecurity, quantum technology, resource and energy security, and shipbuilding. (Nomura) The largest share by far will go to artificial intelligence: roughly one-quarter of the total — 102 trillion yen, or $630 billion — is earmarked for AI and chips, including state-backed chip venture Rapidus. (Japan Times) Where other countries have concentrated industrial policy on a handful of top sectors, Japan’s broad-based approach stands out for its ambition, while raising questions about the country’s fiscal capacity and whether spreading attention this widely comes at the cost of strategic focus.
The plan, known as Honebuto no Hoshin (“big-boned policy”), marks a striking departure from the relatively more restrained public investment schemes of Takaichi’s predecessors, who were constrained by Japan’s high debt levels and hampered by sluggish growth and tax revenues.
Details on how the funding will be mobilized remain light, though Takaichi has said that she expects the $2.3 trillion will come from a mix of public and private capital. The proposal has advanced through Japan’s Cabinet process, and will now be fleshed out further. (Japan Times, Asahi Shimbun).
Reaction has been mixed. Some commentators have welcomed the ambition behind the industrial revitalization push; others have sounded the alarm about fiscal profligacy and its knock-on risks to national debt. Critics have also questioned how this spending will be accommodated alongside a proposed cut to the consumption tax on groceries, as well as likely increases to the defense budget. The Nikkei has fallen since the proposals were released in June, the yen has continued its slide against the dollar, and yields on Japanese government bonds have risen to multi-decade highs on Takaichi’s watch. (The Guardian, Japan Times)
What we’re watching next: further detail on how public investment will be rolled out; and ongoing market reaction as the proposal progresses through Japan’s legislative process.
#3: Korea doubles down on AI and semiconductors with fresh investment
In contrast to Japan’s broad-based sector bets, Korea continues to double down on AI and semiconductors as its engines of economic and industrial strength. On June 29, President Lee Jae-myung’s government unveiled a 1,350 trillion won ($880 billion USD) initiative labeled “Three Mega Projects for Korea’s Great Leap Forward,” centered on:
- Semiconductors: Samsung and SK Hynix will each build two semiconductor fabs, with 800 trillion won ($550 billion USD) in government investment supporting a total of 4,755 trillion won (3.3 trillion USD) into a semiconductor cluster in Korea’s southwest. Korea aims to double its memory production capacity within five years and pull its manufacturing capabilities far ahead of potential competitors - including China’s CXMT, whose IPO to fund its own memory expansion followed shortly on the heels of Lee’s announcement.
- AI data centers: The government has allocated 550 trillion won ($380 billion USD) to build an 8.4 GW AI data center — with possible expansion to 18.4 GW in future — in cooperation with SK Group, GS Group, and Naver.
- Physical AI: Lee has set a goal for South Korea to become the global leader in physical AI by 2030, investing 20 trillion won ($13.7 billion USD) in manufacturing AI to commercialize AI-powered robots across 10 major industries.
(Seoul Economic Daily, Reuters, Bloomberg)
Korea’s government has historically been heavily involved in directing its strategic industrial sectors, and these mega-projects continue that trend. The Three Mega Projects build on a raft of related government-backed initiatives: a sovereign wealth fund investing in AI and semiconductor startups (Maeil Business News Korea), a state-backed Public Growth Fund targeting AI, semiconductors, and biotech (Korea Times), the public-private M.AX Alliance driving AI-led manufacturing transformation (Chosun Daily), and government funding for AI factory transformations (Korea JoongAng Daily). Following the Mega Projects announcement, the government signaled plans for a further fund drawn from windfall tax revenue on Korea’s memory chip boom. The fund would support the three mega projects alongside housing, startups, and other economic priorities. (Bloomberg)
#4: Potential layoffs at Volkswagen highlight China Shock 2.0’s impact on European industry
Major European automaker Volkswagen is considering up to 100,000 layoffs — about 15% of its workforce, up from a previously announced figure of 50,000 — in response to competitive pressures from low-cost Chinese vehicles entering European and global markets. (CNBC) Other strategic recalibration includes plans to cut production capacity from 12 to 9 million vehicles per year and halve its model lineup. (CNBC)
Labor looks like a logical place to cut costs: Volkswagen produces 13.6 vehicles per employee per year, less than half that of Toyota at 28.9. (Axios) But making workforce changes in Germany is not easy. Government and union pushback to Volkswagen’s announcement was immediate, with IG Metall, Germany’s largest labor union, vowing to fight the cuts. Volkswagen’s ownership structure also complicates workforce restructuring. The German state of Lower Saxony, where Volkswagen is headquartered and operates six facilities, holds a 20% voting share in the company, and therefore a critical say over any major operational change. (Euronews)
The pressure from China’s automakers is real: Chinese brands are expected to capture 17% of the European market by 2031, up from negligible levels a few years ago. (Axios) This sits within a broader picture of Europe’s trade relationship with China, where the EU’s trade deficit with China has nearly doubled in five years. As Adam Tooze notes in Chartbook, the shock has landed disproportionately on the auto sector in Germany, with vehicles driving 60 percent of the €27 billion swing in Germany’s trade balance with China between 2021 and 2025.
Tooze and others trace this back to China’s broader industrial strategy and economic situation: enormous investment in production capacity, paired with weak domestic consumption, has left China reliant on exports — often priced below the cost of production due to overcapacity — to sustain growth. With the US market largely closed off, Chinese goods have been flooding other export markets instead, from Australia to Southeast Asia to Europe. (Chartbook, Foreign Affairs)
Tooze argues elsewhere that automakers themselves share some blame, having been slow to innovate and launch affordable EVs. (Chartbook) Still, ‘China Shock 2.0’ is forcing hard policy choices across Europe. Trade restrictions could level the playing field and buy time for automakers to adapt, but would likely raise consumer prices at a moment when cost-of-living pressures are already biting, and would dull the competitive pressure to innovate. They also risk Chinese retaliation — most plausibly export controls on the critical raw materials that feed industrial supply chains, including automotives and defense. Yet doing nothing risks hollowing out one of Europe’s most important industries, in terms of economic contribution, industrial capability, and the energy transition.
That there’s no straightforward answer shows in the differing postures of European nations. Spain and Hungary have welcomed joint ventures and other investments from Chinese firms, while countries like France, Germany, and Italy lean toward tighter import and investment controls.
#5: Critical minerals remain at the forefront of global industrial rivalry
Critical minerals remain a key focal point for industrial policy, with China’s control of upstream supply chains providing leverage to challenge countries’ efforts to build independent supply chains and shield domestic industries from low-cost Chinese competition.
Recent developments in critical minerals policy include:
- G7 Leaders issued a declaration on critical minerals cooperation in June 2026, setting a target to reduce dependency “on a single supplier outside the G-7 and partner countries for rare earths and permanent magnets to under 60 percent by 2030.” The declaration outlined seven areas for cooperation: industrial cooperation, financing, market structuration, transparency and traceability, stockpiling, recycling, and the Critical Minerals Resilience and Production Alliance. Arnab Datta, writing for the NEIS Center, calls this a step in the right direction but argues the G7 should focus more on building market infrastructure - “the exchanges, intermediaries, and other entities that encourage transparent price discovery and liquidity” - that would make proposed policies like stockpiles and price floors less costly and more durable, accelerating investment and transactions between G7 and partner countries.
- China flexed its muscles on export controls. In response to the G7 framework announcement, China defended its critical minerals export controls as “in line with international practices”. (Reuters) Days later, China added ten US firms - including MP Materials and USA Rare Earth - to its export control list, effectively banning sales of dual-use military and commercial export items to them. Both firms sit in the mine-to-magnet supply chain and have received substantial US government investment under the Trump administration. (Reuters) China also announced a public reporting mechanism encouraging citizens to report smuggling of restricted minerals, part of a wider effort to tighten enforcement. (Reuters)
- Europe is reportedly close to releasing more details on its Critical Raw Materials Center, proposed in December 2025 as part of the European Commission’s ReSourceEU Action Plan to monitor, jointly purchase, and stockpile minerals vital to EU industrial sovereignty. The Commission’s public consultation concludes at the end of July. (Clean Energy Wire)
As strategic and trade tensions play out across industries, critical minerals will remain a hotspot in industrial policy, given their role as a critical upstream input for so many industrial products - and China’s continued chokehold on many of the key materials.
