By Oleksiy Tatarenko, RMI
When describing Ukraine’s drone innovation system, most Western articles focus on production capacity, battlefield improvisation, and the novelty of drones. These stories echo the old parable of the blind men and the elephant. One man touches the trunk and says it is a snake. Another touches the leg and says it is a tree, and so on. While all of them are right, none of them is describing the whole thing. That is exactly how the media talks about drone industry innovation in Ukraine. One story is about production capacity growth, another is about UAV operators on the front line, and another is about how medium-range drones paralyze Russian logistic lines. Most of these stories are accurate. At the same time, they describe products and technologies and miss the elephant — the Ukrainian industrial innovation ecosystem.
The elephant is the system that made all drone innovation, scale-up, and deployment possible. Ukraine did not simply industrialize drone production. It developed a complex innovation system that connected institutions, demand, data, procurement, deployment speed, partnerships, and learning at war speed. This is not a story of production scale-up or a single type of weapon innovation. That is why the CEO of German defense giant Rheinmetall, Armin Papperger, completely missed the point when asked about Ukraine’s drone development after his visit earlier this year. Papperger compared major drone Ukrainian manufacturers to “housewives,” saying that “They have 3-D printers in the kitchen, and they produce parts for drones”, adding: “This is not innovation.”
While the decentralized nature of production is important in Ukrainian war realities to protect the industry from daily Russian missile attacks, it wasn’t the main innovation. And Papperger is not alone, as industrial innovation is often mistaken for technological innovation. However, even a breakthrough technology, such as UAVs without manufacturing capacity, procurement, financing, a business model, data, and feedback loops, remains a laboratory product. So, what exactly is the Ukrainian secret sauce for industrial innovation? It is worth unpacking this multi-dimensional success story as its lessons can be valuable for anyone who works on industrial policy and innovation.
Institutions: characters and backgrounds matter
One of the central figures of the Ukrainian institutional backbone is Mykhailo Fedorov, who came to the civil service with a strong business and digital background and a track record of building complex, innovative systems. Fedorov became Ukraine’s Minister of Defense in January 2026, after serving as the Minister of Digital Transformation since 2019 and implementing multiple civil digital service platforms in the country. Once the full-scale invasion began, Fedorov focused on building a wartime innovation operating system, Brave1, which the Ministry of Digital Transformation describes as a coordination platform for the defense technology sector. This background is very unusual for Ukrainian defense ministers, who were traditionally bureaucrats whose job was to supply the army by funding projects and holding tenders.
The Brave1 system was created in 2023 by key defense institutions to provide organizational, informational, and financial support to innovators. Its stated mission is to accelerate technologies that can change the course of the war. In Fedorov’s own words, back in 2023, Ukraine’s task was to create the best conditions in the world for the development of Ukrainian UAVs. So, the Brave1 mission was focused on system design from its very inception and underpinned by clear objectives stating the need to scale drone production so that every brigade and unit would have a stable drone supply. These objectives focus on outcomes and start with the frontline, describing the change that should occur there.
Fedorov is not a conventional defense minister, but a system builder focused on continuous innovation and deployment. Under his leadership, the Ministry of Defense moved beyond the classic model of collecting inputs, allocating budgets, and then executing procurements, and became the platform for coordinating innovation, international partnerships, and the scale-up of the most promising technologies.
System-level change: on sea, in the air, and on the ground
Elina Ribakova and Lucas Risinger, writing recently in Foreign Affairs, have described Ukraine as Europe’s foremost practitioner of drone interception, layered air defense, electronic warfare, and unmanned systems deployed cheaply and at scale, and Ukraine has indeed built a layered ecosystem for unmanned warfare. However, the far bigger story is that Ukraine has managed to build an industrial and institutional machine that keeps improving its systems and the way they interact with one another.
The Black Sea campaign was the first place this became visible. In early phases of the war, Ukrainian drone and missile operations helped push Russia’s fleet back to its naval bases from the Black Sea. This was the first instance in which naval drones played a central role in a military campaign that denied Russia sea control. What was important was that Ukraine had basically developed the entire class of weapons from scratch, as it had never had naval drone capabilities before. This first innovation cycle inspired Ukraine to learn in one domain and then transfer the lessons across the system to other domains, transferring know-how from the naval drone industry to the air and ground drone innovation.
Ukraine has also managed to create a unique system that integrates all parts of the value chain into a virtuous circle of innovation, production, deployment, data collection, AI, and back to innovation. This system starts with challenges and tasks to be solved on the battlefield or through deep strikes, and returns to the teams that lead innovation with a solution-based mindset, where everything is possible and within reach.
Demand and feedback loop
In April 2025, the Ministry of Digital Transformation launched the Brave1 marketplace for military units. The marketplace architecture is simple yet revolutionary: units earn combat points for verified battlefield results. Those points can then be exchanged for drones and other equipment. The Brave1 system drastically reduced the time to supply the battlefield from several days to real time by making demand visible in real time. It also created a feedback loop that shows which systems are in the highest demand. By June 2026, hundreds of combat units had ordered more than 500,000 drones and other systems worth nearly $ 1 billion, according to the ministry.
People who describe Ukraine’s drone warfare as a production story miss the point. While the country makes drones, the important thing is that Ukraine has moved from supply-led production to demand-driven iteration. The military no longer waits for a top-down procurement cycle to deliver. Combat units signal what they need in real time, and producers respond. The state clears the market by managing the digital platform, which also helps it cut red tape and traditional corruption in the defense sector. Ukraine has essentially created a wartime version of the Amazon marketplace that delivers solutions at scale from both domestic and foreign producers.
The numbers illustrate the scale of the transformation delivered by Brave1, which has registered more than 3,600 technological solutions from more than 1,500 companies. In 2026, the Ministry of Defense of Ukraine is planning to produce more than 7 million drones. By comparison, the Pentagon has only recently launched initiatives to place orders for around one million low-cost drones over the next several years.
When it comes to industrial innovation, scale-up demand determines everything. The solar industry didn’t scale because panels magically became cheaper, but because governments created a predictable demand that then created competition and brought the costs of solar panels down. In contrast, hydrogen technologies are struggling to scale today largely because demand remains uncertain. The same logic applies to defense innovation: demand is the engine of scale and technology deployment. Ukrainian industrial base and supply chains underwritten by the Brave1 market platform became a central pillar of Ukraine’s industrial strategy and war economy.
Partnerships and collaborative business models
Ukraine realized early that it doesn’t need to own all production. During the first years of the invasion, Mavic drones were purchased by volunteers at electronics stores and sent to Ukraine. Later, as needs grew larger and more diverse, Ukraine realized it needed its own production capacity, recognizing gaps and vast opportunities to reduce costs by localizing production. However, Ukraine has also concluded early on that it does need many producers — domestic and foreign — to compete, improve, and scale rather than try to invent and produce everything within the country. Security considerations of having production lines outside of Ukraine also played a role in the decision-making process.
The open innovation approach became another central piece of the ecosystem. Ukraine has built a unique ecosystem that brings in American software, European manufacturing, Japanese capital and technologies, and battlefield-proven local companies. Many companies now building a so-called “army of drones” did not even exist at the start of the full-scale invasion. Essentially, instead of trying to devise some master plan for producing the best set of technologies, Ukraine has created a competitive environment and an open innovation ecosystem where private companies — both domestic and foreign — took center stage. Here are three examples of international collaborations that hold lots of potential for Ukraine and its allies:
“Designed in Ukraine, Made in Germany” production model. In late 2025, Quantum Systems and Frontline Robotics launched Quantum Frontline Industries, a German-Ukrainian joint venture to produce the Linza drone. This joint venture is the first industrial-scale foreign-based production of Ukrainian drones in Europe. President Zelenskyy and Boris Pistorius visited the facility, which has a production capacity of up to 10,000 drones per annum. This collaboration sets a blueprint for industrial-scale win-win partnerships in the defense sector between Ukraine and the European Union. Ukraine gets secure production in Europe, while Europe gains access to combat-tested designs and learnings.
“Designed in Ukraine, Made in Ukraine, Co-Owned with Japan” joint venture model. In April 2026, Russia summoned Japan’s ambassador in Moscow after Terra Drone, a Tokyo-based firm, invested in Ukrainian interceptor-drone producer Amazing Drones. It was a politically significant milestone because it marked the first investment by a Japanese company in Ukraine’s defense sector. The Terra A1 drone flies at a maximum speed of 300 km/h and is intentionally designed to intercept Shahed strike drones (standard speed is 200 km/h) used by Russia and Iran easily. The production cost of Terra 1 is $1,000-2,000, while Shahed costs around $70,000-100,000. The Japanese investment recognized that Ukrainian battlefield innovation has become commercially valuable and will scale up globally.
“Ukrainian Data. American Software. AI-based Global Innovation.” Yet, probably the most interesting and least understood partnership that Ukraine has established is with the US AI technology company Palantir, which entered Ukraine shortly after the full-scale invasion. Initially, Palantir provided software that enabled Ukraine to integrate vast amounts of information into a single operational picture, particularly to defend against Shahed drone attacks. Later, Ukraine began leveraging Palantir to plan its own long-range strikes. And recently, this partnership has moved to the next stage, helping Ukraine build an ecosystem where domestic companies can develop AI-enabled defense technologies. This brings us to the broader point of AI and data-driven innovation.
Data-driven innovation
In January this year, the Ukrainian Ministry of Defense, in partnership with Palantir, launched the Brave1 Dataroom, a secure environment for training military AI solutions. The project is a collaboration involving Brave1, the Ministry of Defense, the Armed Forces, military intelligence agencies, and Palantir. This project aims to help Ukrainian companies accelerate the development and deployment of autonomous AI solutions. Essentially, the platform will be open access for Ukrainian defense solution developers and should enable them to train, test, and validate their own AI models using relevant combat data.
Ukraine can now leverage its industrial-scale datasets to improve its production capabilities by reducing the time between battlefield experience and design changes. In return, there will be indirect technology transfer to Ukrainian allies. Even if Palantir never shares a single Ukrainian image or intelligence record with other countries’ defense sector players, the experience and solutions gained while supporting Ukraine’s Brave1 Dataroom will be used to train Palantir’s AI models for use outside Ukraine. Current Western procurement systems are slow and inefficient, as it takes years to organize and execute procurement processes. Ukraine’s procurement and innovation iteration cycles are currently measured in weeks and months. Hence, the potential for improving the procurement and innovation practices of all NATO allies is enormous.
Focus on economics
As Ukraine had scarce support from the West and faced a far larger foe with greater resources, it had to focus sharply on economics. And Ukraine has become very good at finding cheaper solutions, such as interceptor drones, long-range strike drones, and other unmanned systems designed around the logic of asymmetry. After the summer of 2023, it became clear that the conflict was a war of attrition. Ukrainian military strategy increasingly relied on industrial innovation, with UAV technologies becoming the backbone of Ukraine’s asymmetric defense. The central point of this strategy was to inflict heavy damage, increase costs for Russian operations, and make them expensive, time-consuming, and harder to sustain. If a low-cost interceptor costing $1,000 can destroy a high-cost incoming threat costing $100,000, the economics favor the defender.
In 2026, after scaling its production capabilities for long-range drones and missiles, Ukraine has applied the same logic to offensive operations, hitting high-value legitimate military targets such as refineries, chemical plants (that produce explosives), missile production facilities that are often located 1,000km–1,500 km deep within Russian territory. Using Palantir’s AI systems for planning effective attacks enables Ukraine to execute attacks in waves and overwhelm Russian air defense systems. Normally, they start with cheap drones and, once the defense systems are identified and overwhelmed, end with long-range missiles that strike strategic targets with precision. The damage inflicted during such attacks far exceeds the costs Ukraine has incurred.
Lessons for European and global energy industrial strategy
Of course, Ukraine’s drone industrial revolution experience cannot be transferred automatically to other contexts, as wartime realities dictate conditions that no country can replicate. The existential pressure created a sense of urgency, political focus, and tolerance for experimentation in Ukraine that are fundamentally different from the conditions countries face in peacetime.
Yet this difference doesn’t diminish the value of fundamental lessons such as the role of institutions in creating an industrial innovation system capable of learning, adapting, and scaling continuously. By the way, another untold story that emerged in response to continued attacks on the Ukrainian energy sector is the ongoing transformation of the country’s energy system toward a more decentralized, renewables-based system. While at the beginning of the war, BESS solutions were mostly used by households (often in combination with solar panels on the balconies of multi-story buildings), they are now a widespread solution for autonomous critical infrastructure such as hospitals, banks, telecoms, etc.
The lessons from Ukraine’s hard-earned experience extend well beyond the defense sector, and for Europe, perhaps, the most important lesson is that industrial strategy should become less about supporting individual sectors or technologies and more about building innovation systems and institutional muscles that continuously generate, commercialize, deploy, and improve new technologies:
- An effective industrial innovation system is a complex network of institutions and organizations enabled by data and AI that collectively create, improve, commercialize, deploy, and scale new technologies. Supporting manufacturing capacity alone is not enough. Innovation and deployment, procurement and financing, and digital and market infrastructure should function as one integrated system, with feedback loops that facilitate quick iterations and innovation. Ukraine has demonstrated the value of institutions led by system builders with acquired civil servant skills rather than bureaucrats. Industrial strategy increasingly requires leaders capable of connecting government, innovators, investors, manufacturers, digital service providers, and end users into one continuously improving ecosystem. Integrative leadership is the most important skill set (and mindset) for making such systems work, and it is not necessarily career civil servants who are best positioned to create such ecosystems.
This is a major unresolved pain point for Europe, where there is a tendency to over-index on support for R&D programs while markets are fragmented and institutions are siloed, with weak connections to the private sector. Therefore, Europe’s greatest challenge is institutional rather than technological. Europe has world-class research institutions, engineering capabilities, and innovative companies. However, promising technologies move too slowly from laboratories to commercial deployment because permitting, procurement, regulations, public financing, and decision-making remain fragmented across institutions and national markets. Building a genuine single market for clean technologies, reducing administrative complexity, digitizing government processes, and accelerating permitting is just as important as increasing public investment to unlock private capital.
- Demand is the engine of industrial scale-up. Of course, Ukraine has leveraged battlefield demand during wartime. However, was this demand “immediate” and created by the “invisible hand” of the market? I would argue that, while volunteers and innovators have experimented and demonstrated what drones could do during the first year, it was the state institutions that created a virtuous demand-supply cycle through platforms such as Brave1 and state procurements. This lesson holds for energy technologies where governments need to create predictable long-term demand through market design, procurement, infrastructure planning, standards, and stable policy frameworks that give companies confidence to invest and compete. The history of solar industry scale-up, driven by Germany, Japan, the USA, and a few other countries, demonstrates how predictable demand can drive cost reductions through competition. At the same time, hydrogen illustrates the difficulties of scaling technologies when demand remains uncertain.
- An effective open innovation ecosystem should be rooted in competition and partnerships. Ukraine deliberately combined domestic innovation with international capital, software, and manufacturing partnerships, both inside and outside Ukraine, rather than relying on the model of growing domestic champions. New energy industrial strategies should focus on building competitive ecosystems that combine domestic industrial capabilities and trusted international partnerships, rather than pursuing technological nationalism or relying on centralized planning (as in the Russian approach to drone-industry scale-up). That is why debates around the “Made in Europe” strategy and its implementation principles (e.g., how to strike the right balance between supporting local players and remaining open to partnerships) matter so much.
- Industrial policy should stimulate shortening learning cycles. This builds on the previous lesson about the importance of partnerships and competition. Ukraine has managed to compress research, development, procurement, deployment, operational feedback, redesign, and production cycles to months. Obviously, energy technologies operate on longer investment cycles, and this lesson will be difficult to apply to traditional sectors such as nuclear. However, the same principle would still apply to most clean technologies: reducing the time between R&D and deployment becomes a source of competitive advantage. While a few years ago European innovators and OEMs were ahead globally in the hydrogen family of technologies, today they are falling behind Chinese manufacturers on costs and the pace of innovation because the R&D-to-deployment cycle has been slowed by lagging demand and a lack of focus from policymakers.
- Real-time data and AI will increasingly determine the effectiveness of industrial innovation systems. Data is no longer simply an input into innovation. With the arrival of AI on the scene, data became critical infrastructure that connects research, manufacturing, deployment, operations, and continuous product improvement. Countries that build these learning systems most quickly and gain access to real-time data will increasingly set the pace of industrial innovation. This may become an increasingly problematic area for European energy industrial strategy, as Europe lacks strong AI champions and relies on American counterparts. Europe will have to either grow its own AI champions and/or find effective ways to partner up with American tech companies.
- Industrial policy is now an integral part of economic and national security. For decades, industrial policy has largely been defined in terms of competitiveness, productivity, and economic growth. The geopolitical shocks and energy crises of the past 5 years disrupted supply chains and heightened strategic competition, underscoring that industrial capabilities determine resilience and long-term energy and economic security. Europe’s challenge is therefore not only to deliver on the promise of the energy and industrial transition, but also to ensure that the industries underpinning this transition are competitive and resilient to external shocks.
The lessons listed above extend beyond Europe; the underlying challenges and strategic guiding principles will be similar across countries pursuing effective energy and industrial strategies. The main lesson Ukraine should have given policymakers around the world is that effective innovation, energy, and industrial policies require institutions and systems (including data- and AI-enabled ones) that enable all actors in the ecosystem to collaborate and learn from one another continuously and at speed. The countries that learn from the lessons outlined above first can build stronger defense industries grounded in systems and institutions that learn faster than their adversaries.
For several decades, industrial policy has largely been defined in terms of competitiveness, productivity, and economic growth. Ukraine demonstrated to us how central industrial policy is to national security. The tragic war in Ukraine not only redefined what modern warfare looks like but has also shown what successful industrial policy looks like under extreme conditions. If European, American, and Asian allies take this lesson seriously, they will not just learn modern warfare, but also how democracies can innovate and build their industrial capabilities when the stakes are highest. Hopefully, when this war ends, Ukraine and its allies will emerge in a more peaceful future with a better industrial model underpinning it.

Earlier this week, we shared part one of my conversation with Timur Gül, the chief energy technology officer at the International Energy Agency, and the lead author of my favorite IEA report: Energy Technology Perspectives.
Today, we’re bringing you part two, where we discuss topics explored in this year’s report, including trade, emerging economies, and the importance of manufacturing efficiency.
—Sarah Ladislaw, founding director, the NEIS Center

This conversation, recorded on June 12, has been edited and condensed for clarity.
Sarah Ladislaw, NEIS Center: Another area I wanted to ask about is trade. Trade regimes around the world are changing for a whole range of reasons, and there is a rise in trade policies. You documented something like 600 restrictive clean-energy trade policies in 2015, rising to more than 3,000 by 2024.
That is part of the broader question of how countries protect clean energy supply chains and domestic manufacturing in markets where they are not fundamentally competitive, often by using trade as a tool. At the same time, you note that the value of clean energy trade and clean energy supply chains has grown and is projected to keep growing. So trade is essential, but the environment is becoming more protectionist.
What were you thinking about when talking to governments about the role of trade in relation to their industrial strategies and clean energy investments?
Timur Gül, IEA: When we started working on this trade work, we built a manufacturing and trade model, the MAT model, for the 2024 edition of ETP. It is a sophisticated, bottom-up, and fascinating modeling architecture. When we first started building it, we spoke with a lot of trade experts, and I was comforted by the idea that trade policy does not change that much over time. That is how it was presented to me, at least. Maybe that was just their perspective.
But we are now living in what I would describe as a very dynamic period for trade policy, from tariffs to non-tariff measures, anti-dumping duties, export controls, and more. The IEA has documented that well in recent work. Clean energy technologies are obviously not immune to that.
Still, as you said, trade in clean energy technologies continued to rise last year. Despite the tariff discussions, only around 15 percent of global clean energy technology imports last year came from countries that imposed substantially higher tariffs. That helps explain why the trade flows kept going.
We are also seeing this in the context of the energy crisis. Every few days, you see another article or post about rising exports of solar PV and electric cars, often linked to the global energy crisis, but also connected to increasing exports from China to Southeast Asia in particular.
The main point we make to governments is that trade policy is not the final policy. Trade follows other policy objectives, whether those are energy security, climate, or industrial policy. Trade is a facilitator somewhere in between, and there are trade-offs between these goals.
This matters because importing clean energy technologies can be a bonus for energy security, since it reduces exposure to fuel imports and shifts some of the security issues to the domestic level, such as grid integration. But if you are pursuing industrial policy, importing those technologies may not be the outcome you want, because you want your own stake in the manufacturing base. So we are asking governments to be clear-eyed about the trade-offs and about the role trade plays in balancing these policy objectives.
Sarah Ladislaw, NEIS Center: One assumption you run into a lot is that only advanced industrialized economies can do this kind of diversification in clean energy manufacturing. But your report also emphasizes the role emerging economies can play in these supply chains.
You give examples showing that many emerging economies could produce clean energy technologies at competitive cost relative to China. So how should we think about the role of emerging economies in the clean energy manufacturing base?
Are they going to be the clean energy powerhouses of the future, as some have suggested? Or is this still mainly about incremental capacity-building and gradually playing a larger role in emerging supply chains over time?
Timur Gül, IEA: One thing that stands out when presenting ETP findings in advanced economies is the frustration caused by heavy geographical concentration. Then, when we show how much cheaper it is to produce these technologies in China compared with Europe, the reaction is even stronger.
Our analysis finds that every single technology and component can be produced between 30 and 65 percent cheaper in China than in Europe. That is a huge hurdle. But the cost advantages are not uniform, and they differ by technology.
There is a common narrative that China’s competitiveness mainly comes from low labor costs or subsidies, and those factors do matter. But each technology has specific reasons for why China is cheaper.
For solar PV, the biggest factor is energy cost, because steps like polysilicon and wafers are energy-intensive. For wind, labor costs matter most, because the production of components is labor-intensive and requires skilled labor. For batteries, manufacturing efficiency and automation weigh most heavily.
That is where emerging economies can find opportunities. Technology supply chains are not fuels; they are made up of individual components, each of which is a manufactured good. Emerging economies can leverage their own competitive advantages. In solar PV, for example, regions with cheap energy, such as the Middle East and North Africa, can compete in certain components. India already has a wind industry and can produce some components competitively, even if not yet at China’s exact cost.
So there are real opportunities for countries to step in. I would not say that automatically makes them clean energy powerhouses, but it does mean they can move up the value chain. The same is true in other materials, like steel. If countries understand their competitive advantages and focus on where they are strong, they can build durable positions in parts of the clean energy manufacturing universe.
Sarah Ladislaw, NEIS Center: I agree. One of the key lessons for policymakers and companies over the last few years is that diversification of clean energy markets is incremental. It takes time. It does not require thinking about becoming a clean energy powerhouse in some grand sense. It requires asking what you can do, what you can do well, and how you stay with it long enough for it to become a durable investment that can be integrated into global supply chains.
I want to turn to a couple of technology stories in the report, because I know you are a technologist at heart even though you spend a lot of time on the policy side too. One is battery manufacturing and what you call manufacturing efficiency.
Your report says European battery manufacturers are about 50 percent more expensive than battery producers in China, but that 80 percent of that cost gap could be explained by manufacturing efficiency. This concept seems to come up a lot in supply chain conversations, both in energy and in other sectors.
How do you define manufacturing efficiency, and why do you think more countries are or are not focusing on it as a key element of their comparative advantage?
Timur Gül, IEA: That is a good question, and the battery story is a good example of how China has advanced in this space and become such a dominant player. Manufacturing efficiency is really about what goes in and what comes out. There are two main components behind China’s cost advantage.
The first is tightly integrated supply chains, very high process efficiency, and access to low-cost components at scale. That is all part of an industrial strategy where a company has access from critical minerals all the way through components to the final product.
The second is automation. China has become a real leader here. The only other manufacturers that come close in terms of automation are in Japan and Korea. They do not produce at the same scale, but they can in theory reach very high levels of automation. In China, fewer than one in ten batteries in a factory fail the quality test. In Europe, that number can be two to three times higher.
There is a lot to learn from that. But it is not something you can do simply by deciding to build highly automated plants tomorrow. It takes time, supply-chain learning, and manufacturing experience. That is also why I am skeptical when people say they may not be good at lithium-ion or LFP batteries, but they will jump straight to the next generation, like sodium-ion. You will not lead the next generation if you are not efficient at producing today’s batteries.
China’s industry learned over the last eight or nine years by integrating supply chains and automating production. That is not immediately reproducible. It requires learning and experience.
One interesting example comes from the global car industry. If you look back to 2018, the United States and China had produced roughly the same amount of batteries and were producing at about the same cost. Europe was already a bit behind. At the time, Chinese producers were small and not necessarily at the technology frontier. The frontier was the Tesla-Panasonic Gigafactory.
What happened next is that China produced eight times more batteries cumulatively since then than the United States, let alone Europe. By 2024, the Shanghai region alone had more battery manufacturing capacity installed than all of Europe.
Sarah Ladislaw, NEIS Center: One layer deeper, I think what we do not appreciate enough in the US, Europe, and other places trying to stand up manufacturing capacity is how much trial and error China deployed over that period.
It is not just learning and steadily improving. It is like practicing anything: you have to fail, try something else, fail again, and keep going. Our systems of government are not always well suited to that kind of experience, but it is part of what it takes to become good at these industries.
Timur Gül, IEA: Many companies do not exist anymore. That is what happened in China. Exactly.
Sarah Ladislaw, NEIS Center: Right. And as a sports analogy for young people watching the World Cup and hoping to play for their team someday, the only way you get there is practice. It is the same thing.
Timur Gül, IEA: Very much so. I did not practice enough, clearly (laughs).
Sarah Ladislaw, NEIS Center: One more question, because there is another interesting observation in the report. You point out that electrolyzer deployment curves are sitting roughly where solar PV deployment curves historically were. We have been through several hype cycles around hydrogen and then seen the cycle come back down again.
What are you thinking about the future of electrolyzers? Are we headed for another cycle where hydrogen produced by electrolyzers follows the same trajectory as solar PV? Is that what you were suggesting?
Timur Gül, IEA: I do not think that is what we were trying to suggest. In fact, we have our Global Hydrogen Review, and we have been tracking project announcements very closely over the last seven years since we released The Future of Hydrogen.
The reason we drew the analogy is that attention to technology moves in waves. Hydrogen is just one example, though there are others. This is at least the third hype cycle around hydrogen over the last 30 or 40 years.
At the beginning of this decade, everyone thought hydrogen was the next big thing, and there were many project announcements, many of which are now being rolled back or are no longer being talked about. Those announcements suggested something around the corner that was really an overstatement at the time. The project pipeline was never as real as people thought.
A few years ago, I was presenting our Global Hydrogen Review and we had more than 400 gigawatts of electrolyzer capacity announced for 2030, while only about 1 gigawatt was actually installed. That was an enormous gap between expectations and reality.
We always try to distinguish between phases: what has reached final investment decision, what is under operation, what is under construction, and what is just a plan or an announcement. But what has happened over the last year is the opposite: people now look at hydrogen and electrolyzers as if nothing is happening, or as if it is a complete failure, which does not reflect the actual progress.
The point is not that hydrogen will be the next solar PV. We are not saying that at all. But if you look at the expectation to 2030, the pattern is similar to what solar PV experienced between 2010 and 2020, and electrolyzers may be following a similar arc between 2020 and 2030. That does not mean the same outcome, but it does mean the progress should not be underestimated.
Sarah Ladislaw, NEIS Center: Well, I just want to say this is an excellent report, as it is every time you put it out, but particularly this year because we are seeing the energy security crisis, affordability concerns, and the way countries approach policies, trade, incentives, and regulation.
Everything you are talking about in this report is critical to countries and companies contributing to energy security and affordability objectives. If we get it wrong, we go in the wrong direction. If we think carefully and stay disciplined over time, we can make progress.
I have said recently that this is one of the most tumultuous periods we have been through in energy in a very long time, but it is also one where we are well positioned to emerge a decade from now with the best energy system we have ever had. That will help us build competitive economies, more diversified supply chains, and the industries we want to create.
There is a lot to get right right now, and I want to thank you and your colleagues for helping point the way.

Of all the excellent reports the International Energy Agency puts out each year, I think the Energy Technology Perspectives report is my favorite.
It’s a wonderful read for those of us at the New Energy Industrial Strategy Center because it looks not just at how we deploy clean energy and advanced energy technologies around the world, but also at how countries shape those industries through manufacturing, trade arrangements, and supply chain diversification.

That is right at the core of what the International Energy Agency has always done, and it tracks what I consider as the cutting edge of policymaking and international security on energy and climate.

So I was delighted to sit down via Zoom in June to talk with the report’s lead author and the IEA’s chief energy technology officer, Timur Gül, to dive into some of the nuances of the report and to get his take on the global energy crisis that is likely to make next year’s report even more of a must-read.

Read on for part one, with part two coming later this week.

—Sarah Ladislaw, founding director, the NEIS Center

This conversation, recorded on June 12, has been edited and condensed for clarity.

Sarah Ladislaw, NEIS Center: I wanted to start with a question. You worked on these Energy Technology Perspectives reports over a long period of time, and you finished this report before the current energy crisis, something Fatih Birol has rightly called the largest energy security crisis in history. It is still ongoing, and it has already gone beyond what many of us thought would be the breaking point for a serious about-face in energy policy.
So how has the current energy crisis, and the broader supply-demand imbalance in oil and gas, changed the way you think about some of the major trends in the Energy Technology Perspectives report?
Timur Gül, IEA: Thanks, Sarah. It’s really great to be here with you.
As you said, we prepared the report before the crisis. Much of the modeling started in 2025, and the analysis that underpinned the report came before the launch in March this year. But there are a couple of developments that matter even more in the context of the energy security crisis.
The first is that clean energy technologies are no longer a niche market or just a climate story. They are a major industry, especially the technologies that underpin what we call the age of electricity. If you multiply price by volume of sales, you get to a market worth well over 1 trillion US dollars a year. There are other markets too, of course, but they are smaller.
The second point is that all the policies that had already been enacted, and all the policies that had been announced at the time of writing, point to continued growth in these markets. In our exploratory scenarios, we look at the implications of policy over the long term, and what we find is that in the next 10 years the market either doubles or triples compared with today’s levels.
Then comes the global energy crisis. Our executive director has described it as the largest in history, more severe than the crises of the 1970s and 2022 in Europe taken together. We have responded on multiple fronts, but those responses are necessarily focused on the near term. So now we are looking at the consequences that may follow.
It is difficult to speculate, but if you look at past crises and what they did to the energy sector, especially in the 1970s, you see lasting effects on technology. Nuclear power was ramped up in the late 1970s and early 1980s. Solar PV commercialized in the early 1980s. Research into lithium-ion batteries, which today are a multi-billion-dollar market, began in earnest in the early 1980s, and the first patent was actually released in the United Kingdom in 1981.
So there have been many lasting effects on what is now a major market for clean energy technologies. Given the scale of the current crisis, and what we are already seeing in energy markets, I think there is much more to come.
Sarah Ladislaw, NEIS Center: One of the things you pointed out in the report is that investment on the clean energy manufacturing side seems to have peaked in 2023 at around 220 billion US dollars, and that this manufacturing piece of the investment picture is not projected to grow very much between now and 2035 in a stated-policy scenario.
For countries that see manufacturing as an anchor for growth and for solving a range of other problems, what does that picture look like to you now, especially given what you just said about how people may think about reinvesting in energy after the crisis?
Timur Gül, IEA: You’re right that manufacturing investment, or investment in manufacturing capacity, has peaked. We now have hundreds of facilities in nearly 60 countries operating around the world, so a lot of capacity has already been built. The peak was roughly 220 billion US dollars in 2023, followed by a gradual decline.
But it is important to understand why this is happening. The main reason is that we have a massive surplus of existing manufacturing capacity relative to current demand, especially in solar PV and batteries. We could supply the world with solar PV and batteries multiple times over relative to current demand. So the energy crisis does not fundamentally change the calculus for investing in manufacturing at that top-line level.
Where the real story is happening is in the composition of investment. Even under existing or stated policies, we have seen diversification efforts and investment driven by the EU and the United States, and we expect that to continue. There are weaknesses in supply chains that many countries will want to invest in over time.
So even if the headline number does not tell a dramatic investment story, there is still a story of more manufacturing value and more investment in certain areas to come. That is not a bad story. It is simply a consequence of the fact that we have already invested a great deal, and much more than current demand requires.
Sarah Ladislaw, NEIS Center: One thing I have seen in conversations with countries and companies is growing appreciation for the amount of capacity China holds across clean energy supply chains. In some cases it is 60 to 85 percent, and in some nodes it is as high as 95 percent.
That has led to a serious discussion about how much of a problem that really is. Since you have now produced this report for several years, and this point is much more widely recognized than when you started, how do you think about Chinese concentration in supply chains?
How concerned should people be about it? And what can countries do to increase their own manufacturing share or diversify those supply chains?
Timur Gül, IEA: That is a good question. When we started looking into this a couple of years ago, I was struck by the sheer level of geographical concentration. It was not something the agency had tracked systematically before, and I am not aware that anyone else had tracked it in that way either. Across all the clean energy technologies we observe, the concentration is very stark.
There are really two sides to this equation. First, we have to recognize what this has done for the deployment of these technologies. Solar PV, wind, batteries, heat pumps, and similar technologies have benefited enormously. Mass manufacturing in China has reduced costs and made these technologies increasingly competitive in many more markets around the world. From a clean energy transition perspective, that has been a major success story.
But now we are also in a situation of significant dependence. Many countries are grappling with the fact that so much of the manufacturing base is in China. It would be less of a problem if countries could satisfy their own demand through domestic manufacturing, but that is not the case.
In this year’s Energy Technology Perspectives, we carried out a so-called N minus one analysis, something you might know from the power sector or fossil fuel markets. We asked what happens if you remove the largest supplier from the market, which in clean energy technologies is obviously China. We did this across the full technology spectrum and across each step of the supply chain to identify the weakest links.
What we found is that in many supply chains there is enough capacity outside China to produce the final product. For electric cars and batteries, there is sufficient manufacturing capacity in the rest of the world to make the end product. But in each supply chain we found at least one manufacturing step for one component where less than 25 percent of global demand without China could be supplied.
And of course, what is the point of having an electric car factory or a battery factory if you do not have the input you need? In batteries, the weak link is cathode precursors. In solar PV, it is wafers. In heat pumps, it is rotary compressors. The pattern is the same: you always find at least one critical step where the rest of the world cannot fully produce the final product without China.
That changes the conversation. The concentration was initially daunting because it looked like everyone was dependent on China. But when you think about the specific component steps where diversification is needed, it becomes more manageable and more pragmatic.
There has been some progress. There has been investment in solar PV and battery manufacturing in several countries. But much more will need to be done. One lesson from China is that demand certainty is critical for investment. The goal is not to compete with China head-on at scale. That is very difficult. The goal is to focus on each country’s own strengths and opportunities.
The conversation continues in part two, coming to inboxes later this week.

For much of the past decade, batteries have been viewed primarily through the lens of the energy transition. Today, they have become something much larger: a defining technology of economic competitiveness, national security, and geopolitical influence. From electric vehicles and renewable energy storage to artificial intelligence infrastructure and advanced defense systems, the countries that develop and manufacture batteries will shape the industries — and strategic alliances — of the decades ahead.
That reality has exposed a difficult challenge for governments and industry alike. China has established a commanding lead across much of the battery value chain, from mineral processing and manufacturing to commercialization of next-generation technologies. As policymakers seek to reduce strategic dependencies without slowing the clean energy transition, the debate has often been framed as a stark choice between accepting Chinese dominance or attempting to recreate entire supply chains at enormous cost.
But as our NEIS partner Milo McBride of the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace uncovers in his latest report, Battery Geopolitics: Balancing Industrial Power in the Race to Store Energy, that choice is not so binary. Rather than treating battery competition as a zero-sum contest, the report outlines a pragmatic framework for cooperation among partner economies to build more resilient, diversified supply chains while accelerating innovation. In a conversation with NEIS Founding Director Sarah Ladislaw, McBride discusses the changing geopolitics of batteries, where the greatest opportunities lie, and what governments and industry should do next.
Sarah Ladislaw: Milo, thank you so much for joining us. It’s a real pleasure to talk about the geopolitics of batteries report you’re putting out as part of the NEIS Center’s work on innovation.
This report is part of a broader series on competitiveness and innovation across a range of technologies. We’re pleased to have you leading this effort, looking across different technologies to understand how countries approach both innovation and manufacturing.
The report is especially timely. We’ve recently spoken with our partners at the Rhodium Group, who have cataloged the investment taking place across the sector, and with Timur Gül from the IEA, who has been talking about supply chain diversification in his own work.
To start, how do you characterize China’s lead and dominant role in this space? How do you think about it in the context of competition? And a question that doesn’t always get asked, but is on the minds of many policymakers: How essential is it to compete with China? Why is that fundamentally important?
Milo McBride: Thanks, Sarah. It’s a pleasure to be putting out this report as part of the NEIS Center.
At a high level, the enormity of Chinese dominance across supply chains and innovation cannot be understated. We can talk about the details of why that is and where it’s heading, but the framing we offer is that batteries are essential strategic technologies of the 21st century.
They are central to the frontiers of artificial intelligence and warfare. They are also the essential lifeblood of the modern automobile industry and key drivers of demand for critical minerals. For those reasons, we might place them in a different category than solar photovoltaics.
The Chinese lead is gargantuan. Today, at least at the cell level, about 55 percent of global battery cells are produced by two Chinese companies. Further down the rankings, there are Korean companies and one Japanese firm in the top 10. What becomes more concerning is what happens upstream, particularly in the materials used to produce lithium iron phosphate, or LFP, batteries. That is essentially a unilateral Chinese supply chain.
Looking ahead, Chinese battery cell capacity could meet or surpass global demand by 2030. This is not just a battery issue. It’s a broader question of Chinese political economy, involution, and overcapacity, and it will make competition incredibly challenging.
It’s also important to recognize that OECD economies, no matter how well they collaborate and cooperate—which they should—are highly unlikely to ever outcompete China.
The goal, and the North Star of all this, is to diversify and produce high-quality battery cells as economically and efficiently as possible with a range of actors. Some may be Chinese, while others may be Korean, Japanese, European, and so forth. It’s not the easiest political goal to offer policymakers, but I think it’s a sound strategy and one at the core of the NEIS Center’s philosophy: building durable industrial ties in these important niches.
Sarah Ladislaw: You mentioned in the report that OECD economies do have a foothold. There’s clearly significant Chinese dominance across a range of factors, but OECD economies still have strengths. Where do you see those footholds?
You also mentioned opportunities for collaboration. Are there ways you advocate in the report that countries should be working together?
Milo McBride: If we look at the U.S. and European markets, these are the largest battery markets outside China. By 2030, each could see about one terawatt-hour of battery demand.
The good news is that battery belts in both regions are already being built. By 2030, I think we’ll see a majority of the battery cells purchased in those markets actually being produced domestically. The industrial base is brewing, and that’s a good start.
The Koreans are also an important legacy silver medalist in all of this. Ten years ago, they were in a better position than they are today, but they still produce high-quality battery cells. They’ve largely been locked into the incumbent nickel-cobalt, or NMC, battery value chain.
One idea we offer in the report is that the U.S. and Europe should use their remaining market access strategically. That could include bringing Korean companies into joint ventures with startups, which are going to struggle to scale on their own. It could mean attracting Chinese investment in certain parts of the value chain where there are no viable alternatives. And it could mean building industrial clusters around emerging battery ecosystems and filling out supply chains in the process.
There are opportunities. It will require cooperation and collaboration, but the challenge may not be as overwhelming as some of the headline numbers suggest.
Sarah Ladislaw: Those strategies around partnerships, industrial clusters, and comparative strengths are central to the work we’re doing in the United States, Europe, and increasingly across Asia.
The report also spends considerable time examining battery chemistries, end-use markets, and the role of startups versus incumbents. You discuss how countries and companies should think about long-term battery innovation strategies, whether that’s a portfolio of chemistries or a portfolio of end uses.
At the same time, you point out that many next-generation battery startups in the United States are moving to markets where demand is stronger, particularly for EV batteries.
How should policymakers think about this innovation landscape? And why does the United States continue to struggle to turn its innovation advantage into large-scale manufacturing?
Milo McBride: It’s a huge question. Part of our analysis looked at high-integrity patents across different battery chemistries. One conclusion was that, in some next-generation chemistries, U.S. patent activity was actually at parity with Chinese patent activity. We also looked at startups and timelines to market and found similar patterns. The gap was not as wide as many would assume.
That said, scaling a startup with innovative technology in today’s environment is challenging. We’ve already locked in a great deal of incumbent battery cell capacity, so there’s limited room for newcomers to gain market share.
The second issue is that I think many of us in the policy community underestimated the complexity of battery manufacturing. This isn’t simply a matter of building a bigger factory. In many respects, it resembles semiconductor manufacturing. The machinery required to produce battery electrodes is extraordinarily sophisticated.
That doesn’t mean startups will fail. Some are making progress. An American start-up, for example, IPO’d recently. But I think a winning strategy is finding ways for startups to work with incumbents that already know how to build gigafactories at scale.
That creates political challenges. Does the incumbent absorb the intellectual property? How do you structure those partnerships? Those are difficult questions, but we want to create pathways that allow innovative companies to reach the market.
The most interesting takeaway from our work is that sodium-ion batteries are here. They are going to be commercial, and we should take them seriously. They’re compelling on cost, they can be produced in existing battery infrastructure, and their critical mineral requirements are negligible.
For those reasons, I think a portfolio approach is the right strategy. Sodium-ion batteries were widely dismissed only a few years ago, yet we now see more than a dozen commercial-scale facilities emerging in China.
If this technology can be scaled in the West, it could help reduce China’s mineral leverage simply because it requires fewer minerals. We conducted a modeling exercise that shows just how significant that reduction could be.
Sarah Ladislaw: It’s a fantastic report because it provides baseline information on different battery chemistries, offers guidance on portfolio strategies, analyzes where countries stand today, and models how markets may evolve over time.
At the NEIS Center, and through our partnerships with organizations like Carnegie, we spend a great deal of time talking with policymakers and companies trying to navigate this landscape.
What are the key dos and don’ts when developing a battery strategy? We’ve seen highly capable countries invest heavily in battery companies and facilities that ultimately failed. Clearly, this is an area where many are still struggling.
Milo McBride: The biggest takeaway is that we need to adjust our expectations about what a successful battery strategy looks like.
As you mentioned, a number of companies in Europe are declaring bankruptcy despite being major hopes for policymakers.
We need to accept that scaling these technologies is often easier with incumbents. We also shouldn’t reject Chinese foreign direct investment outright. Instead, we should think pragmatically, strategically, and surgically about where Chinese investment is most important.
For example, there’s a lot of discussion in Washington about bringing Chinese firms in to manufacture LFP cells. But Korean companies are already making LFP cells and adapting their production lines.
Where the United States has a much bigger gap is in anodes and spherical graphite. That’s where Chinese investment may have greater value. I also sense some discussion of this emerging in Europe.
The point is not to reject participation simply because China dominates a particular segment. It’s to think carefully about where investment would have the greatest impact.
Finally, we should recognize that success may come at a smaller scale. It may not always mean building massive gigafactories. Securing industrial clusters and building durable industrial capabilities can be an effective de-risking strategy, and we should think seriously about how to prioritize those efforts.
Sarah Ladislaw: Absolutely. Part of this is relearning how to do something well so that we can continue improving over time.
One point that comes through clearly in your work is that battery strategy and critical mineral strategy are related, but they are not the same thing. Policymakers don’t necessarily have to solve both challenges simultaneously, but they do need to think about them together. That’s an important distinction.
Milo McBride: Exactly. Our modeling shows how different battery chemistries can reduce mineral demand, but that doesn’t eliminate the near- and medium-term challenge of bringing new mines and processing facilities online. That work remains essential.
At the same time, when thinking about a long-term battery and minerals strategy—much as we think about recycling—we need to consider how evolving chemistries could affect future demand. That’s going to be an important part of the broader picture.
Sarah Ladislaw: Excellent. Milo, we encourage everyone to read the report and reach out with questions. We also encourage readers to watch for the next installment this fall, which will include country-specific deep dives.
This is incredibly rich work. Thank you for doing it, and it’s always a pleasure to collaborate with you on these topics.
Milo McBride: It’s a pleasure. Thanks for having me, Sarah.
Read the full report.

This week, we’re sharing the NEIS News Roundup, a monthly recap of major international developments in new energy industrial strategies and advanced energy systems. These selections capture global trends shaping industrial strategy and competitiveness, with a focus on investment, policy, trade, and technology.
Here are five major stories we’re following:
#1 India Races to Lock In Trade Deals – But Structural Barriers Remain
India is in the middle of a major free trade agreement push — nine agreements signed over the past three years are set to come into force within the next ten months, with more in the pipeline covering the US, UK, Canada, and South Korea. Earlier this month, Commerce Minister Piyush Goyal announced he is aiming to execute these over the next year. (Business Standard)
India’s goals are to cement its position as a global manufacturing hub by attracting foreign investment and growing exports, and to diversify its trade relationships – particularly energy supplies — amid ongoing geopolitical disruption. For example, the comprehensive economic partnership agreement (CEPA) under negotiation with Canada could help India diversify its supplies of fertilizers and energy products (of which it currently imports $605 million from Canada), and expand civil nuclear cooperation. In exchange, Indian businesses anticipate expanded opportunities to export pharmaceutical products, iron and steel, chemicals, and electrical equipment. (Business Standard)
Meanwhile, talks to upgrade a previous CEPA negotiated with South Korea involve negotiation sub-groups covering digital trade, supply chain cooperation, and strategic industrial cooperation. (Business Standard) During Korean President Lee Jae-myung’s visit to India in April — accompanied by the Chairs of Samsung, SK, Hyundai Motor Company, and LG — the countries emphasized opportunities to cooperate in areas including semiconductors, shipbuilding, and steel. (Korea Herald, Korea Times, Korea Times) Indeed, South Korea could become a key partner in India’s aspiration to become a semiconductor manufacturing hub. (Business Standard)
But critics of India’s frenetic trade push point to several structural problems. First, past agreements haven’t always delivered for Indian exporters – its CEPA signed with South Korea in 2009, for example, saw India’s trade deficit nearly double within five years of implementation, as imports surged while exports lagged. (Economic Times)
Second, India’s inverted duty structure means tariffs on raw materials and components are often higher than on finished goods. This undercuts domestic manufacturing competitiveness and limits how much exporters can benefit from new market access. For example, steel and aluminum can attract import duties of 7.5-10%, while industrial equipment made from these materials enters India duty-free under several FTAs – meaning Indian manufacturers pay higher input costs while competing against cheaper imported machinery. In addition, certification and documentation burdens mean only 20–30% of India’s eligible exports actually utilize FTA benefits. (Economic Times)
The implicit tension is that India is signing deals at pace to signal openness to investment and lock in market access, while the underlying conditions to make the most of those agreements – and protect against adverse trade outcomes – remain unresolved.
#2 Europe’s Industrial Ambition – and the Rules That Could Make or Break It
Europe’s Industrial Accelerator Act, proposed by the European Commission in March 2026, is the EU’s most ambitious attempt yet to use public money, regulations, and procurement rules to shore up domestic manufacturing and reduce strategic dependence on imports. It sits at the center of a sharp debate about how far Europe should go in decoupling from Chinese technology – a debate with no easy answers, since the choices involve real trade-offs between cost, security, decarbonization speed, and geopolitical risk.
The pressures on European industrial competitiveness are intensifying. In the first quarter of 2026, Europe’s trade deficit with China reached record levels as imports rose sharply – from a base of $418 billion in 2025 – driven, in part, by Chinese carmakers’ push into Europe. The import surge is threatening European manufacturers and causing “a sense of imminent collapse of industry, of imminent danger” in Brussels, according to Bruegel director Jeromin Zettelmeyer. (New York Times)
The IAA responds with four core policy pillars: mandatory “Made in EU” and low-carbon requirements for public procurement and government support schemes; conditions on foreign direct investment above €100 million in sectors where a single third country controls more than 40% of global production capacity; faster permitting for industrial projects; and the designation of industrial acceleration areas. The headline target is for manufacturing to reach 20% of EU GDP by 2035, up from 14% today. (Bruegel)
The “Made in EU” provisions are contentious. For EV subsidies, 100% of support must flow to EU-origin production. For other covered clean-tech sectors, governments must allocate 45% of support budgets to EU-made goods. European automakers Volkswagen, Stellantis, and Renault – representing about 60% of EU vehicle output – support the principle but are pushing for a simpler “70/70” rule (70% of vehicles sold under public procurement or subsidy schemes should contain 70% local content) and a more realistic battery localization timeline. Non-European carmakers, including Toyota, Honda, and Jaguar Land Rover, have warned that the geographic scope would raise costs and exclude components from strategic partners, including the UK, Turkey, and Japan. (Financial Times)
Bruegel endorses the IAA’s intent but is pointed in its critique. The authors dismiss the 20% GDP manufacturing target as nostalgia; all developed economies have seen manufacturing shares decline as services expand. The origin-based content rules risk delaying decarbonization, raising costs, and inviting retaliation, including World Trade Organization (WTO) challenges. The Commission’s own impact assessment estimates that excluding Chinese solar cells from incentive schemes would more than double the price governments pay for solar panels, while supply chains would still depend on Chinese polysilicon. And since Chinese firms are responsible for more than two-thirds of battery cell capacity currently under construction in the EU, blocking Chinese FDI could slow rather than accelerate Europe’s clean-tech build-out. Bruegel recommends replacing blunt content rules with sustainability and resilience criteria already developed under the Net-Zero Industry Act, which could achieve similar localization incentives without the legal exposure. (Bruegel)
Economist Noah Smith takes a harder line, arguing that Europe’s dependence on Chinese-made components means it cannot manufacture key military equipment, including drones, without Chinese supply chains. Smith represents the view that this is less a trade policy debate than a defense and sovereignty question. (Noahpinion)
China has already threatened retaliation against the IAA’s proposed measures. And with export restrictions and corporate inspection powers already deployed in recent years, it need not wait on a WTO ruling to apply pressure.
Negotiations among European lawmakers are expected to run into 2027.
#3 Nvidia Is All In on South Korea
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s six-day visit to Seoul in early June 2026 – his second in seven months – saw Nvidia announce a series of deepening partnerships with South Korea’s major industrial conglomerates. The visit reflects Nvidia’s view that Korea occupies a unique position in the emerging “physical AI” economy: the application of AI to real-world physical systems like robots, autonomous vehicles, smart factories, and digital twins. (Korea Herald)
Korea’s decades of precision manufacturing in automobiles, electronics, and robotics make it a natural home for physical AI. For Nvidia, which is building a full-stack physical AI platform spanning humanoid robot models, simulation environments, and the Isaac robotics platform, partnerships with Korean industry offer the opportunity to take those technologies off the drawing board and into real factory deployment. (Korea Herald)
The most significant deal announced was with SK Group. SK Group and Nvidia announced a “long-term” partnership covering co-development of chips for AI accelerators, AI infrastructure, including semiconductor fabs and data centers, and joint AI R&D road mapping, which will see SK hynix’s role evolve from a memory chip supplier to a co-designer of next-generation memory from the planning stage of Nvidia’s AI platforms. SK Telecom will separately build gigawatt-level AI infrastructure across Asia, with the first AI data center set to begin operations in Korea in 2027, powered by Nvidia’s Blackwell GPUs. (Korea Times) Naver and Doosan also signed up for AI data center deployments using Nvidia technology. (Manufacturing Digital)
Hyundai Motor Group’s partnership with Nvidia, formalized at APEC last year, is set to deepen around Boston Dynamics’ humanoid robot Atlas, which Hyundai is advancing as a mobility solution in AI factory and industrial settings. Under the partnership, Hyundai will also benefit from Nvidia’s Alpamayo autonomous driving system, which could help close its gap with Tesla and Chinese rivals in self-driving. Meanwhile, Nvidia and LG discussed collaboration on motor technology, mechanical systems, and AI for humanoid robots, with LG’s CLOiD home robot already using Nvidia’s chips and platforms. (Manufacturing Digital, Korea Times, Korea Herald)
Notably, the trip didn’t just consist of corporate meetings. Huang appeared on one of South Korea’s most popular talk shows and threw the first pitch at a Doosan Bears baseball game – a deliberate charm offensive that echoed the media buzz generated during his October 2025 visit, when a dinner with Samsung and Hyundai chiefs at a fried chicken restaurant went viral locally. The cultural outreach underlines how seriously Nvidia is courting Korea as a long-term strategic partner, not just a supplier. (Asahi Shimbun)
Huang summarized Korea’s position by ranking it third globally in AI capability behind the US and China, citing its combination of semiconductor manufacturing, heavy industry, and software expertise as a “perfect environment” to capitalize on the AI revolution. (Korea Times)
#4 Bipartisan Pushback Threatens to Put the Brakes on America’s Data Center Build-Out
A wave of community opposition, state legislation, and regulatory action is emerging across the United States that threatens to constrain the pace of data center development — with significant implications for the AI industry’s infrastructure ambitions.
In certain regions, electricity demand growth is staggering. Texas’s grid operator reports that more than 480 proposed data centers have requested grid connections by 2032, representing over 418 GW of capacity – nearly five times the state’s all-time power demand record. (Houston Chronicle) A UN report projects that by 2030, global data center electricity demand could be equivalent to that of the world’s sixth-largest power-consuming country. (Axios)
Concern over cost pressures is crystallizing into concrete regulatory battles. For example, in North Carolina, Duke Energy proposed an 18% household rate hike to prepare the grid for new load growth. As an alternative, consumer groups are advocating the creation of a new “large load” class that would pay to support new infrastructure. (Canary Media) In parallel, North Carolina lawmakers have advanced legislation aimed at mitigating consumer cost impacts by putting guardrails on data center development while preventing fossil plants from retiring until the state can replace them with nuclear generation. (WUNC)
Elsewhere, Virginia has introduced a new energy consumption tax of $0.011 per kilowatt hour on data center electricity use, capped at $600 million annually. (Politico) In parallel, a long-planned 100-mile transmission line in PJM territory, intended to primarily serve data center loads in Virginia, is causing controversy over cost allocation. (Latitude Media) In the US southwest, where concerns over water scarcity are top-of-mind, Arizona has paused certain data center tax incentives for three years, with regulators wrestling with both the pace of grid build-out and the tradeoffs between water and electricity use in cooling technologies. (Axios)
At the federal level, the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC) has unveiled what one former chairman described as potentially “the most significant FERC action in decades” – a policy to speed data center grid connections while putting costs onto developers rather than existing customers. (Bloomberg, Axios)
Despite hyperscalers’ pledges to ensure their demand growth is cost-neutral for consumers (Politico, Utility Dive), community resistance is hardening rapidly across the political spectrum. A new survey shows opposition to local data centers has more than doubled since September. (Heatmap) Monterey Park, California, is on track to become the first US city to permanently ban data centers. (The Guardian) Seattle and New York have enacted one-year moratoriums, while Ohio and Texas governors have paused or called for eliminating data center tax incentives. (AP, Axios, Seattle Times, Politico, News10)
Environmental and public health concerns are also mounting alongside the cost debate. Virginia’s data centers are connected to 10,500 diesel backup generators, which may pose public health risks even when used sparingly, while residents near xAI’s Memphis facility have filed a class-action lawsuit over noise and nuisance from mobile gas turbines. (Washington Post, Mississippi Today)
That said, the narrative that data centers are simply raising electricity bills is contested. Analysis from Columbia University’s Center on Global Energy Policy and the Electric Power Research Institute both suggest that, to date, data centers have not been a principal driver of price increases, with EPRI’s modeling estimating they actually lowered average residential rates by around 6% between 2019 and 2024 by spreading fixed grid costs across a larger customer base. Both reports caution that forward-looking conclusions are premature given the scale of development still in the pipeline and the risk that ratepayers could be left holding the cost of grid upgrades if data center demand disappoints. (Columbia, EPRI)
For countries where data center development is ramping up, the US experience offers an early read on the policy challenges ahead. The pattern suggests communities and governments tend to reach a tipping point – often triggered by electricity bill impacts or a single high-profile project – at which goodwill toward tech investment converts quickly into organized opposition. Australia, a hotspot for data center growth in the Asia Pacific, is already seeing divergent regulatory approaches emerge: South Australia is moving proactively to legislate a streamlined development pathway for data centers that bring new, firm supply with explicit guarantees of no negative impact on consumer bills. Yet at the federal level, the Greens have called for a moratorium on data center approvals ahead of a Senate inquiry. (InDaily)
The US experience suggests the policy design choices made now – on cost allocation, energy sourcing, and community engagement – will determine how Australia and other fast-followers navigate this transition.
