By Sarah Ladislaw, NEIS Center Founding Director, and Jonas Nahm, NEIS Center Research Director
Given the headwinds of war in Iran and the ensuing energy crisis, expectations for last week’s US-China summit were low — and they were met.
The United States and China arrived without a shared sense of purpose — uncertain, at a fundamental level, about what they want from each other. But with the stakes so high for the global economy, and with much of the rest of the world actively trying to derisk from both superpowers simultaneously, that uncertainty is no longer acceptable.
There are consequential things that only the United States and China can do together. And if this summit was a missed opportunity, the three more leader-level meetings reportedly planned for later this year offer another chance for real movement on topics given passing interest at the summit, like artificial intelligence and trade, and others that were largely untouched: industrial overcapacity, investment, and energy supply chains. The pace of China’s industrialization and expansion into international markets means these conversations cannot wait.
Our mission at the NEIS Center is to advance new energy industrial strategy around the world, and no two countries hold the fate of that progress in the balance more than the United States and China. Here we outline three areas where greater dialogue could lead to better outcomes, and help the rest of the world by providing a more stable system of cooperation.
AI Governance
The United States and China are, by a wide margin, the world’s two dominant AI powers in terms of total investment and models produced. In 2024, the two countries made modest but real progress: a government-to-government AI dialogue, an extension of their science and technology cooperation agreement (which does not include AI but does cover and allow for science and technology cooperation), and a shared commitment that decisions to use nuclear weapons should remain under human control. These were meaningful steps. They were also nowhere near sufficient.
AI governance cooperation between Washington and Beijing remains dangerously immature relative to the technology’s pace and stakes. What was needed — and absent — from this summit was movement on shared protocols, common evaluation methods, and verification tools; progress toward safety frameworks, however contested the underlying concepts remain; coordination on testing standards; and a structured, regular channel for managing cross-border AI risk. The recent emergence of Anthropic’s Mythos model offered a concrete and timely impetus for accelerating exactly these conversations, which have long been stalled by the arms-race logic that dominates the broader bilateral relationship. That opening was under-exploited.
Foreign Direct Investment and the EV Question
The decline in bilateral foreign direct investment is one of the clearest measures of economic decoupling. Chinese investment in the United States has fallen 90 percent from its 2014–2017 peak — a steeper drop than from any other major economy. The cumulative US investment position in China stood at roughly $127 billion in 2023, but new flows have slowed sharply, and in 2021 and 2023 net US direct investment flows to China turned negative — meaning divestment exceeded new investment.
Nowhere is this more consequential — or more complicated — than in electric vehicles. Ford’s decision to license battery technology from CATL for its Michigan plant, structured to avoid Chinese equity ownership, and GM’s parallel apparent retreat from aggressive EV targets, illustrate how deeply American automakers are already entangled with Chinese technology even as they struggle to maintain competitive distance.
Chinese automakers and battery manufacturers have built structural advantages in cost, scale, and vertical integration that Western firms cannot quickly replicate. China accounted for more than 70% of global EV production in 2024, with Chinese OEMs making up more than 80% of domestic Chinese production, up from roughly two-thirds in 2021. The question is no longer whether China will dominate the global EV market. It already does. The question is whether the United States will have any meaningful role in shaping how that dominance unfolds and preserving a pathway for non-Chinese auto firms to exist going forward.
The American policy debate has largely been binary: block Chinese EVs and investment on national security grounds or accept that the economics of the energy transition (and future for their auto industry) require engagement with Chinese capital and technology. Both positions capture something real; neither is sufficient on its own. Countries that have relied on tariffs alone have succeeded mainly in raising consumer prices and slowing their own energy transitions — without building the domestic industrial capacity those sacrifices were supposed to produce. A more carefully constructed pathway exists: one that takes seriously the genuine security risks embedded in specific connected-vehicle technologies while creating structured conditions under which Chinese manufacturing investment could strengthen, rather than displace, American industrial capacity.
What that looks like in practice is investment conditioned on technology transfer to American suppliers, joint venture requirements that build domestic capability in the United States rather than simply adding Chinese capacity, and differentiation between technologies by actual security risk profile rather than blanket restriction — roughly the conditions Western firms accepted to access the Chinese market for decades, and that Europe is now beginning to apply in reverse.
This is not naivety about Chinese industrial strategy. It is a recognition that the alternative — a decade of escalating restriction that leaves American automakers weaker, American consumers paying more, and Chinese firms dominating every other major market unopposed — serves neither American security nor American prosperity.
Managing Overcapacity
China’s industrial overcapacity is not a cyclical problem, and its drivers are more complex than a story of deliberate state policy alone. Beijing has consciously directed subsidies, policy credit, and state capital into strategic manufacturing sectors — EVs, solar, batteries, and advanced semiconductors. But much of what is flooding global markets has a different origin. Local governments, facing GDP targets and the collapse of land revenue after the real estate crisis, have kept loss-making manufacturers alive through cheap credit and subsidized inputs, competing with each other to retain factory jobs regardless of viability.
At the firm level, intensifying domestic competition has driven margins toward zero across sector after sector — what Chinese observers call involution — leaving export markets as the only route to survival for producers who cannot cover costs at home. The interaction of central industrial strategy, local government competition, and firm-level involution is what makes overcapacity so difficult to negotiate away: there is no single lever Beijing can pull, and in many cases, no political will to pull it even where one exists.
The global effects are severe. Cheap Chinese exports are eroding the market share of advanced manufacturing nations across Europe and export-dependent Asia. Because the United States has erected high tariff barriers, much of this flow is deflected elsewhere — undercutting foreign competitors not just in their home markets but across the Global South. The IMF estimates China spends roughly 4 percent of GDP on industrial subsidies, nearly three times the EU rate. China’s global trade surplus reached a record $1.1 trillion in 2024, even as direct US-China trade fell.
Chinese manufacturers have reorganized around third-country assembly, supplying the intermediate inputs that flow into Vietnamese, Mexican, and Thai factories before reaching Western markets. Supply chains are diversifying, not decoupling. The distinction matters, because Chinese industrial capacity continues to shape what American consumers buy and what manufacturers in the rest of the world compete against, regardless of what the bilateral trade statistics show. China is the largest exporter in nearly 60% of all product categories in 2024, and accounted for more than 20% of global export flows for industrial goods — up from just 5% in 2001.
There are no clean solutions here, and the summit was not expected to produce them. But it could have opened a serious, structured conversation about managing this imbalance in ways that don’t accelerate a slide toward 1930s-style protectionism. It did not. Western governments cannot compel Beijing to rebalance its economy toward domestic consumption — China’s leadership views industrial dominance as a matter of national security. Nor can they fully decouple from Chinese supply chains without dramatically raising the cost of the clean energy transition. What they can do, and what the United States and China could have begun doing together, is build the kind of bilateral and multilateral frameworks that turn an escalating confrontation into something more like managed competition. The summit passed without that work beginning.
Europe, facing the same pressure with considerably less leverage, has at least begun building a structural response. The proposed Industrial Accelerator Act treats overcapacity not as a bilateral irritant but as a feature of China’s economic model — and responds with local content requirements, conditioned procurement, and investment rules designed to prevent redirected Chinese exports from simply filling the space that US tariffs closed off. It has real limitations, and Beijing has already threatened countermeasures, but it is asking the right question. The United States, with more leverage and more at stake, has not yet done the same.
The EU comparison points to a broader failure of ambition, but there is also a subtler cost to the summit’s outcome. Both leaders have now personally endorsed a framework of ‘constructive strategic stability’ — and any future US action on overcapacity, investment conditions, or export controls can be characterized by Beijing as a departure from that commitment. That is not an argument against engagement. It is an argument for ensuring that the next three summits build specific agreements rather than extend a general truce.
The window for ambition is not permanently closed. But it is narrowing. The United States and China, as the two largest economies and most technologically capable countries in the world, have a responsibility to do better than staying out of each other’s way. There are core issues to be resolved — or at least actively managed — that are in the shared interests of both countries. Tackling these issues would not only give the relationship more purpose, it would provide a stabilizing effect for countries around the world.

It takes a range of perspectives to drive the policy behind building the advanced energy systems of the future. So far, we’ve looked at how the United States can better secure its critical mineral supply chain through analysis of its current critical minerals strategy, as well as exploring the wisdom of stockpiles in safeguarding these materials.
Today, we’re sharing a piece by Julia Poliscanova, a supply chain expert at NEIS partner T&E, that looks at the stakes for critical minerals policy in Europe. We hope you find it insightful and look forward to your feedback.
By Julia Poliscanova, Senior Director, Vehicles & Emobility Supply Chains, T&E
The energy crisis highlights the need to avoid new dependencies for critical raw materials. Stepping up the EU’s ‘minerals diplomacy’ can offer a way forward – if coupled with financial firepower.
Every oil crisis exposes how vulnerable Europe is to fossil fuel imports.
Switching to renewables and electric vehicles will change that, but how do we avoid a similar dependency on the critical minerals needed?
First of all, unlike oil these minerals are highly recoverable, so once imported they can remain in the system. Secondly, the metals are numerous and can be found in many places around the world, so securing a sustainable and diverse supply is key. That’s why critical minerals diplomacy with like-minded partners has been on the agenda for years.
The results have been mixed.
The European Commission has taken a number of global initiatives. These include the Critical Raw Materials Act, Global Gateway funding and numerous agreements with third countries, recently upgraded into Clean Trade and Investment Partnerships, or CTIPs.
But the concentration of critical minerals supplies has only worsened.
China controls processing for 19 out of 20 critical minerals, and export controls on raw materials continue to proliferate. And while 15 EU strategic partnerships with the likes of Chile and Zambia have been signed, these have not yet brought new supply to the market.
The problem is not the lack of regulatory frameworks or political support. The need to work with like-minded partners is repeated by senior politicians at every occasion. And no Omnibus ‘deregulation package’ for minerals will solve the problem.
The issue is the disconnect between good intentions in political declarations and having the actual tools to make progress on the ground.
So, how do we go from handshakes to shovels in the ground?
A major reset of Europe’s global minerals policy is needed.
First, the EU needs to make its partnerships and CTIPs deliver concrete projects on the ground. As we explained earlier, this means choosing partners strategically and bringing domestic companies to the table that can provide the investment, know-how and offtake that resource-rich countries are looking for.
The CTIP with South Africa is particularly interesting. The country has abundant resources of manganese, a mineral that is central to western-led battery chemistries’ (NMC) ability to compete with China-led lithium-iron ones (LFP). Replacing some of the nickel in those batteries with manganese would cut costs without undermining the performance.
Given that China today refines almost all battery grade manganese, helping South Africa set up facilities should be a no brainer. This means bringing funding support and companies – for example, Umicore – to help the country ramp up the technology and provide offtake.
Second, the EU needs the right tools to deliver on its minerals partnerships and diplomacy. This means having the ability to invest in projects directly.
Australia, Canada, Japan and the US are all doing this already. Canada has moved quickly to secure the supply of scandium directly from Rio Tinto, while the US has taken a direct stake in rare earths processor MP Materials.
Taking equity directly or providing some sort of price support would increase the investability of those projects.
The EU has so far relied on the disjointed actions of national export credit agencies (ECAs) who have the cash but no strategy. The newly announced Critical Raw Materials (CRM) Centre should change this.
The centre should go a lot further than mere coordination and stockpiling. Just like Japan’s JOGMEC, it should have sufficient budget – from both the resilience pillar of the new MFF and the Global Gateway – to support domestic and global projects financially. Ultimately, it should have an independent mandate and bring together miners, refiners, investors and offtakers.
Finally, this does not mean going back on sustainability or social standards. Supporting projects directly also means shaping how their water treatment, tailings disposal or community engagement are done.
When it comes to standards, where the EU should better leverage its soft power is in the G7 Minerals Alliance. Rather than selecting endless lists of projects, the one effective thing this forum should do is finally agree on the market access standard talked about for years. In other words, whose supply is in and whose is out.
Such a framework, based on a targeted set of few environmental and social criteria to begin with, can then be taken up by like-minded partners in their various initiatives. This includes the new FORGE pushed by President Trump.
The EU needs to equip its minerals diplomacy with financial firepower and bring business to the table to move from handshakes to shovels in the ground.

By Luuk Schmitz, Max Planck Institute for the Study of Societies (MPIfG)
Almost every discussion of industrial policy conditionality treats it as a story about too little. Without strings attached, the worry goes, public money flows to politically connected incumbents, subsidies become corporate welfare, and the state ends up captive to the industries it was meant to steer. That concern is real, well-documented, and historically grounded. But it is only half the picture, and without thinking about the other end of the rope, these strings may yet undo the industrial policies they are meant to keep on track. Put differently, conditionality is not simply a safeguard against waste. It is also a design choice that affects whether firms participate, whether projects move quickly enough to matter, and whether public support builds real industrial capability. The challenge is not whether industrial policy should come with strings attached. It is which strings to attach, when to attach them, and how to ensure they discipline firms without deterring the investments policymakers are trying to mobilize.
Applying conditionalities in real-world settings can be costly. The procedures, performance benchmarks, and eligibility tests that align private behavior with public goals consume time, administrative capacity, and firm attention. They shape who participates and who doesn’t. They produce workarounds. And they mandate certainty in fundamentally uncertain processes.
Drawing from my own collaborative work on the European Union, which applies stringent conditionalities in its Important Projects of Common European Interest (IPCEIs), these trade-offs come into view. IPCEIs are one of the European Union’s main tools for allowing member states to support strategic industrial projects that would otherwise fall afoul of EU state aid rules. They are meant to enable large-scale, cross-border projects in areas such as batteries, hydrogen, microelectronics, and cloud infrastructure where private investment alone may be insufficient. But because they operate as an exception to the EU’s normal restrictions on subsidies, firms and governments must show that public support is necessary, proportionate, and directed toward an important common European objective. First deployed in 2018, IPCEIs allocate over €37 billion in public funding across ten initiatives in microelectronics, batteries, hydrogen, cloud, and health. But fourteen out of twenty-seven member states have never participated in one. Approval timelines routinely run four to five years. And policymakers who have overseen the process describe participants, not entirely in jest, as ‘damaged for life.’
IPCEIs are shaped by the EU’s unusual governance structure: member states provide much of the money, but Brussels sets the rules under which that support can be approved. That makes the instrument distinctively European. Still, the lessons travel. Every government pursuing industrial policy faces the same basic problem: how to attach conditions that prevent waste and capture without making strategically important projects too slow, too costly, or too difficult to pursue. Getting conditionality right means taking its costs as seriously as its benefits.
Conditionality is more than a dial
Public debate treats conditionality as a single dial to be turned up or down to impose stricter discipline on private actors. That framing obscures the choices that actually matter. Conditionality is a set of decisions about what to demand of firms, when to demand it, and whose interests to prioritize.
Industrial policy conditionalities can cover very different goals, each with its own failure mode. Directional conditions steer firms toward higher-value activities, novel technologies, or the commercialization of public R&D. They can help push firms beyond business-as-usual investment, but they risk locking in the wrong technological bet if policymakers demand too much certainty too early. Localization conditions require domestic production, local content, or job creation. They can build domestic capacity and political support, but they can also create sheltered industries that never become competitive. Social conditions secure worker protections, environmental standards, or affordable access to subsidized products. They can broaden the public value of industrial policy, but if designed poorly, they may make participation too burdensome. Geopolitical conditions restrict who can participate, where production can expand, and how intellectual property can travel. They can protect strategic capabilities, but they may also alienate allies or fragment supply chains.
A further problem in the public debate is that we underappreciate how these categories interact with technological uncertainty. Our comparative historical cases for good industrial policy and, by extension, good conditionality, all stem from East Asia in the 1980s-90s. But the conditionalities suited to late-developer catch-up — strict performance targets, output benchmarks, export quotas — were designed for a world in which the technology was known and the task was to climb a familiar ladder.
Frontier industrial policies targeting strategic sectors such as microelectronics, batteries, hydrogen, or advanced manufacturing face a different problem. When the technology path is uncertain, the supply chain is still forming, and the relevant capabilities are still being discovered, it is unrealistic to impose detailed ex-ante expectations of success. Market actors still need discipline, but that discipline should often come through milestones, learning requirements, repayable advances, and ex-post evaluation rather than rigid upfront tests. Here, Europe’s IPCEIs serve as a cautionary tale.
The IPCEI Experience
The way a state uses conditionalities in industrial policy involves more than technical design. Conditionalities inherit the institutional habits, legal traditions, and political assumptions of the system that produces them. Here, the European Union has layered a fifth logic on top of the four categories above.
State aid — public support that gives a selective advantage to a private firm — is restricted by default under the EU treaties. The purpose is to prevent subsidy races among member states and protect fair competition inside the single market. IPCEIs rest on an exception to that logic. They allow public support when projects address a major market failure, contribute to a common European objective, and would not happen in the same form without state aid. This is a coherent framework for limiting waste and preventing subsidy races. But it is a less natural framework for building strategic industries, where speed, scale, uncertainty, and capability-building often matter as much as proving that a narrow market failure exists. Much of the European tension comes from trying to reverse-engineer industrial policy through competition law.
That mismatch produces three costs, each visible in IPCEI projects. The result is not simply “too much conditionality.” It is a particular kind of conditionality, one optimized for legal defensibility and market-discipline tests, rather than for the practical needs of frontier industrial development.
The first cost is perverse outcomes: conditions that defeat the policy’s own purpose. To justify state aid, IPCEI projects must often demonstrate innovation “beyond the global state of the art.” The goal is understandable. Public money should support additional innovation, not subsidize routine investment. But in frontier sectors, the requirement can backfire. For a firm like TSMC, a European facility that exceeded the technological frontier of its Taiwanese operations would raise obvious strategic concerns, including the risk of weakening Taiwan’s “silicon shield.” A condition designed to push the innovation frontier can therefore exclude precisely the firms most capable of delivering strategic capacity.
The second cost is adverse selection. Much of the IPCEI approval process requires firms to provide detailed information about funding gaps, expected returns, project design, and why public support is needed. This can reduce unnecessary state aid, but it also creates delay and administrative burden. Approval timelines have often run four to five years. The result is that IPCEI participation tends to favor member states and firms with the bureaucratic infrastructure to manage the process. Conditionality becomes a filter for administrative capacity rather than strategic value.
The third cost is workarounds. When procedures become too burdensome, firms and governments adapt in ways that preserve the appearance of conditionality while weakening its substance. Germany’s Economy Ministry, for example, developed an “Early Start Mechanism” that allows firms to begin investment at their own risk before Commission approval. But this creates a paradox: if a firm can credibly start without aid, it becomes harder to prove that aid was necessary in the first place. Firms have also begun structuring projects to stay just below the €50 million threshold that would trigger future subsidy clawback rules. In each case, conditionality does not disappear; it is rerouted.
These outcomes are not simply implementation failures, but reflect a deeper design problem: conditionality that is calibrated to prevent distortion can become poorly calibrated for building industrial capacity under uncertainty.
Conditionality for a Second-Best World
The way conditionalities come about, what they demand from private actors, and how they are implemented reflect a fundamentally political process. There is no universal formula for conditionality. A condition that works well for a mature industry may fail in a frontier sector. A rule that is politically durable may be administratively difficult to enforce. A requirement that protects public value may also slow investment. Conditionality design is therefore a second-best problem: policymakers must choose among trade-offs rather than optimize in the abstract. Optimal design becomes a question of matching the rules to the political environment in which industrial policy actually operates.
Three design principles follow.
Match conditionality to uncertainty. The more uncertain the technology, market, or supply chain, the less conditionality should rely on rigid upfront specifications of success. Directional conditions in frontier sectors — steering firms toward new technologies, novel value chains, or capabilities still being discovered — should be milestone-based, iterative, and open to ex-post adjustment. By contrast, low-uncertainty conditions, where the relevant parameters are stable and measurable, can carry clearer upfront targets. The current EU regime often gets this calibration backwards: heavy ex-ante review of innovation criteria sits alongside relatively weak ex-post discipline.
The US Inflation Reduction Act tilted the other way, trading ex-ante directional rigour for performance-based and security-driven content rules. Even after the 2025 One Big Beautiful Bill Act repealed much of the IRA’s clean-energy machinery, the design philosophy that survived: escalating threshold percentages, material-assistance cost ratios, and milestone-based phase-ins more closely track what frontier industrial policy needs.
The IRA had its own weaknesses, but its conditionality was often easier for firms to understand and act on: meet a content threshold, locate in a qualifying community, satisfy labor standards, or produce an eligible good. That kind of rule may be cruder than the EU’s project-by-project assessment, but it can be more usable in fast-moving industrial sectors.
Sequence by political robustness. Some conditionalities are easier to sustain politically than others. In the current environment, geopolitical conditions — rules about who can participate, where production can expand, and how technology can travel — often enjoy broader support than more contested social or localization requirements. That makes them a durable starting point. But governments should not stop there. Directional, social, and localization conditions may be equally important for building public value, but they require greater enforcement capacity and more careful design. Sequencing conditionalities can therefore be a way to build state capacity over time rather than loading every objective into the first version of a program.
Tolerate bounded failure. The goal should not be to minimize the chances that mistakes will occur, but to minimize the costs of mistakes when they do. That insight matters especially for frontier industrial policy. If the state is supporting technologies, value chains, or capabilities that do not yet fully exist, some failure is inevitable. Conditionality should make failure informative and bounded, not impossible. A regime that produces zero failures is either not trying hard enough or is paying its costs invisibly, through firms that decline to participate at all.
The IPCEI experience is a particularly clear case, but the underlying problem is general. Every government now pursuing industrial policy faces the same calibration challenge. Too little conditionality risks waste, capture, and corporate welfare. Too much, or the wrong kind, can deter participation, slow investment, and select for bureaucratic sophistication rather than industrial capability. Conditionality is not a single dial. It is a series of choices about uncertainty, capacity, time, and political opportunity.

Today we’re sharing the NEIS News Roundup, a monthly recap of major international developments in new energy industrial strategies and advanced energy systems. These selections capture global trends shaping industrial strategy and competitiveness, with a focus on investment, policy, trade, and technology.
Here are five major stories we’re following:
#1. Hormuz shock drives clean technology demand surge, exposing divergent industrial strategies.
The fossil energy supply shock triggered by the near closure of the Strait of Hormuz has triggered a sharp uptick in demand for clean energy technologies across multiple markets.
Electric vehicles are seeing sales accelerate globally:
- EU registrations surged 51% in March, per E-Mobility Europe
- US sales jumped 12% in Q1 2026, with Hyundai reporting a 40% increase between February and March (Financial Times, Semafor)
- In the UK, inquiries to Octopus Electric Vehicles rose 36% in March (Bloomberg)
- In Pakistan, electric rickshaws are selling out (Bloomberg)
Policymakers — particularly in Southeast Asia, where fuel import dependence is creating scarcity concerns — have moved swiftly to accelerate EV adoption (Argus Media):
- Indonesia announced a goal to convert all motorcycles to electric and scale solar from 11 GW to 100 GW within two years.
- Laos cut EV charges by 30% while raising charges for fuel vehicles by the same amount.
- Vietnam called for 50% of city public transport to switch to EVs.
China is best positioned to meet surging demand. Bloomberg reports that solar cell, EVs and battery exports rose 80%, 53%, and 34% year-on-year respectively, per China’s General Administration of Customs on Saturday. Ember puts the combined increase across these categories at 70% for the year and 38% from February to March alone.
Countries were already pursuing divergent industrial strategies vis-à-vis China’s supply chain dominance, and the clean technology demand surge is likely to accentuate these differences:
- Those with negligible domestic supply chains — including Australia and the Philippines — are opening the door to low-cost Chinese imports, a move that also suits Chinese automakers already seeking export markets to absorb domestic overcapacity.
- Others — including Spain, Hungary, Canada and Brazil — are welcoming Chinese investment in local manufacturing. In April, SAIC Motor announced plans for an EV factory in Spain to reduce EU tariff exposure, while Chinese wind turbine maker Ming Yang is also considering Spain after the UK blocked its proposed Scottish facility (Bloomberg, Financial Times).
- A third group — including the United States, much of Europe, and India — views reliance on Chinese supply chains as a national and economic security risk, and is pursuing sovereign manufacturing capability.
For this last group, the demand surge presents a potential opening for domestic suppliers under pressure. Rhodium Group reports that US and EU clean energy manufacturing slowed in 2025, partly due to fierce competition from China’s enormous overcapacity, which has depressed global prices. However, China is not the only country with potential excess capacity. Looking ahead, Rhodium predicts that US battery production capacity will be 2.8 to 5.8 times domestic demand by 2030, as policy shifts have weakened the demand outlook for EVs and grid storage – threatening to strand significant battery manufacturing investments.
This retrenchment is already playing out in corporate decisions: GM has idled a Detroit EV plant and shifted production back to ICE and hybrid models (Reuters, Crain’s Detroit), while Volkswagen has announced it will cease production of EVs at its Tennessee facility (New York Times).
The crisis-driven surge in consumer EV interest may, however, represent exactly the demand signal US and European factories need to stabilize their investment cases — particularly in the US, where federal EV and storage incentives were wound back early.
#2. Clean energy deployment hit a record in 2025, but pace has faded.
Several recent reports highlight that the global energy transition is moving in the right direction – with warning signs that momentum is slowing:
- Global generation from renewables drew equal to coal, with the IEA reporting in its Global Energy Review 2026 that coal and renewables each contributed 34% to electricity generation in 2025. Think tank Ember reached a similar conclusion, putting renewables a touch ahead.
- According to the IEA, solar contributed over 70% to the global growth in electricity generation and over 25% to the growth in primary energy — the first time that solar has contributed the largest share. Gas, oil, and coal grew at slower rates than previous years.
- Electricity generation increased 3%, more than double the increase in primary energy of 1.3%, signaling that electrification is increasing electricity’s share of total energy demand. Electric vehicle adoption drove 38% of electricity demand growth, followed by data centers at 17%.
- Rhodium Group reported that total clean energy investment hit a record $1.96 trillion across the manufacturing and deployment of clean energy technologies in 2025. While this represents a tripling of investment from only 7 years ago, 2025 saw growth slow to 7% year-on-year vs. a peak of 28% in 2023. (Rhodium analysts shared their insights on this data in the NEIS Center newsletter in late March – find it here).
- CTVC also reported record-level clean energy investment but slowing growth. CTVC tracked $92 billion in new capital raised, while deployment outpaced fundraising, with the amount of unspent capital or “dry powder” dropping from $112 billion to $92 billion over the year.
- CTVC also highlighted a trend toward consolidation, with 75% of all new capital raised concentrated in just 58 mega-funds, including Brookfield, CIP and EQT.
- The 2026 editions of the IEA’s State of Energy Policy and Energy Technology Perspectives, as well as its new 2026 Energy Crisis Policy Response Tracker, provide additional snapshots on the state of the energy transition.
#3. Brussels wants electrification; EU nations opt to cut fuel taxes.
The European Commission’s AccelerateEU plan, published on 22 April, is a response to the energy shock caused by the near-closure of the Strait of Hormuz. The Commission frames the Iran crisis as a catalyst for structural change — pushing the EU to accelerate electrification and reduce its long-standing dependence on volatile imported fossil fuels.
A central tension in the Commission’s position, however, is that most levers for short-term consumer relief sit with national governments, not Brussels. Per Bruegel’s summary, AccelerateEU therefore focuses on coordination efforts in three main areas:
- Organizing efficient gas storage refilling ahead of winter
- Promoting joint oil and gas purchasing, and
- Establishing a “fuel observatory” to map European refining capacity and resolve contradictions in publicly available supply data.
These are meaningful contributions, but they are inherently second-order compared to the direct financial interventions that national governments can deploy.
Where the EU does hold genuine influence is in setting the medium- and long-term policy architecture. To that end, AccelerateEU calls for:
- Quick adoption of rules to enhance grid resilience
- Progress on planned proposals on energy taxation and electrification, and
- Acceleration of clean energy investments funded by emissions trading scheme revenues and EU finances.
Bruegel‘s assessment is that if Europe exits this crisis having built a credible electrification strategy — with electricity’s share of final energy consumption finally moving beyond its decade-long stagnation at around 20% — that would represent a major policy achievement.
However, the gap between EU ambition and national action is illustrated sharply by how member states have actually responded to rising prices.
- Spain rolled out a package of 80 emergency measures worth €5 billion, with a headline reduction in VAT on fuel from 21% to 10% (Idealista).
- Germany’s coalition agreed to cut the mineral oil tax on petrol and diesel by 17 cents per liter for two months (Euronews) — a politically expedient response to public frustration, but one that runs directly counter to the Commission’s preferred approach.
The EU has consistently argued that where governments do intervene, relief should be targeted at vulnerable households through direct income transfers or clean-technology support schemes — not broad-based fuel tax cuts that entrench fossil fuel consumption and are fiscally costly.
Germany’s own economy minister, Katherine Reiche, noted the awkward dynamic: higher energy prices are diverting government attention away from overdue structural reforms toward short-term support, which is widely regarded as a poor long-term strategy (CNBC). The Commission’s preference — supporting fossil demand reduction and electrification through measures like social leasing schemes for heat pumps and electric vehicles — requires more political patience than a headline fuel tax cut, but is far more aligned with the EU’s broader energy security and decarbonization goals.
#4. From assembly to integration: India’s clean energy manufacturing push and its remaining challenges.
India has made significant strides in building integrated value chains across critical energy technologies, but faces strategic constraints that could slow momentum if left unaddressed.
Since 2021, India’s Make in India 2.0 policies have pushed its manufacturing sector beyond final assembly toward higher-value upstream production — with notable results:
- In electronics, India has shifted from a final assembly destination to an exporter of critical components — including printed circuit board assemblies and specialized modules — back to China. Exports grew from negligible levels two years ago to $920 million in FY2025, and are on track for $3.5 billion in FY2026 (Economic Times).
- This shift has been driven by successive policy layers:
- From 2021, the production-linked incentive (PLI) scheme attracted major manufacturers, including Apple, Foxconn, and Tata Electronics, scaling assembly capacity while most components were still imported.
- In 2025, the Electronic Component Manufacturing Scheme (ECMS) targeted domestic production of materials and components — with early signs of traction visible in growing component exports to China.
- The India Semiconductor Mission (ISM 2.0, launched February 2026) extends this logic further upstream, targeting chip design and fabrication — with fabs still in development but positioned to benefit from downstream demand as the value chain matures.
- In solar, India again used a PLI approach, making awards in two tranches (2021 and 2023) to encourage gradual build-out of an integrated solar supply chain, from polysilicon to modules (IEEFA). With module oversupply a growing concern, the Ministry of New and Renewable Energy issued a December 2025 directive to lenders to prioritize financing for integrated facilities that include upstream cell, ingot, and wafer production (Reuters, Business Standard). Major announcements have followed, including ReNew Energy’s recent announcement of a 6.5 GW ingot and wafer facility in Andhra Pradesh (Economic Times).
- In EVs and batteries, recent developments signal progress up the battery value chain:
- Ola Electric launched an in-house-developed LFP cell, with product integration planned for next month (Economic Times).
- Andhra Pradesh approved a $290 million investment by NSPSL Specialty Chemicals to manufacture cathode materials (Economic Times).
- A high-level Korean delegation visit yielded a joint development agreement between Hyundai and TVS Motor for an electric three-wheeler designed for India’s last-mile mobility market (Business Standard).
Three strategic bottlenecks, however, require urgent attention:
- First, grid and storage investment has badly lagged renewables deployment — India’s cumulative installed battery capacity of 1 GWh represents less than 0.5% of the 236 GWh the Central Electricity Authority projects will be needed by 2031-32 (Renewables Now, IEEFA), while the New York Times reports that only a quarter of power from new sources is actually reaching consumers.
- Second, capacity additions remain below overall targets and uneven across different parts of the value chain. For example, only 56% of solar module and 14% of polysilicon capacity was achieved as of June 2025 (IEEFA). Industry groups have warned that domestic sourcing rules — designed to support localization — may begin to constrain supply, as India’s upstream manufacturing capacity in ingots, wafers and cells cannot yet meet deployment demand (DigiTimes).
- Third, and most structurally difficult, China remains an indispensable supplier of key components and continues to ring-fence its technological know-how. Bloomberg reports on Reliance Industries’ experience: after importing $1.1 billion of Chinese equipment for a battery plant, it was told by its Chinese partners that additional Chinese technology would be required to operate it. India’s ambition to build end-to-end supply chains and serve as an alternative manufacturing hub runs directly into a dependency on the very country it is trying to diversify from.
#5. US Power Sector: Nuclear and Geothermal Deals Multiply as Data Centers Face Community and Grid Constraints.
Surging US electricity demand continues to bolster clean-firm power procurement, with a flurry of US deals and announcements in nuclear and geothermal. However, affordability concerns are creating a backlash against data centers, a swift-moving headwind for the hyperscalers driving advances in AI.
Nuclear received support from state policymakers and federal regulators:
- Six New England states agreed to explore advanced nuclear facilities (Maine Morning Star)
- New Jersey lifted its ban on new reactor construction (Canary Media)
- New York signaled it will select a new nuclear plant site this year (Bloomberg)
- Texas launched a $350 million program to help build nuclear reactors (E&E News)
- Idaho, Nebraska, Tennessee, and Utah told the federal government they’re interested in hosting nuclear energy projects, including waste storage facilities (Axios)
- The federal Nuclear Regulatory Commission renewed the license for California’s Diablo Canyon nuclear plant (Los Angeles Times), and moved closer toward the release of an updated draft rule on how the National Environmental Protection Act will affect nuclear licensing (Axios).
- However, grid operator PJM told Three Mile Island that it may not be able to connect to the grid until 2031 – owner Constellation has appealed to the federal regulator for assistance to ensure it can restart by the end of 2027 (Reuters).
And private sector announcements show tangible momentum:
- Holtec completes another critical step to reopen Palisades nuclear plant in Michigan (Power Engineering)
- Valar Atomics raises $450m in debt and equity (Bloomberg).
- Blue Energy raised $380 million to help fund its first project (Axios).
- X-energy raised $1 billion in its initial public offering (IPO) (Quartz).
- TerraPower broke ground on Wyoming project for advanced nuclear (WyoFile), which was funded under a 50/50 cost-share arrangement with DOE (TerraPower).
- Kairos Power breaks ground on its first commercial-scale advanced reactor (World Nuclear News).
Geothermal is also attracting significant investment to scale up:
- Zanskar project debt deal for geothermal (Axios)
- Mazama Energy raises $100 million (Axios)
- XGS Energy strikes 115 MW supply deal with California community choice aggregators (Business Wire)
- Fervo files for IPO (Canary Media)
Clean firm power sources are still lagging behind gas as the main power source for new data centers, with Microsoft looking to build or contract 3.9 GW gas-fired power across Texas and West Virginia (Bloomberg, Latitude Media), and Google pursuing gas power for its Texas data center (The Guardian).
Meanwhile, Lawrence Berkeley National Lab and the Brattle Group report that residential electricity prices rose 33% nationwide from 2019 to 2025, with higher increases in California, the Northeast and parts of the mid-Atlantic (Utility Dive). With rapid growth of data centers the latest and most visible factor contributing to rising power prices in some areas, they are attracting a building wave of local opposition. In April, we saw:
- Residents of Port Washington, Wisconsin vote to restrict future data centers (Politico) and Maine lawmakers pass a bill that would block development of data centers larger than 20 MW until November 2027 (Maine Morning Star).
- Analysis from Heatmap that found 270 data centers have faced opposition across the US — compared to 258 onshore and offshore wind projects, a stat that highlights the “intensity of angst over big tech infrastructure”.
Community opposition creating siting challenges is just one bottleneck on data center growth, another is the shortage of electrical equipment such as transformers, switchgear, and batteries to build the supporting electrical infrastructure and grid. Both these factors mean that almost half of the US data center capacity additions planned for this year are likely to be delayed or canceled, according to Bloomberg — an outcome that poses a potential challenge as the United States competes for leadership in the AI race.
Other stories we’re following:
Private sector announcements and deals:
- USA Rare Earths will acquire Serra Verde Group, which owns a rare earth mine in Brazil, in a $2.8 billion cash and stock deal (WSJ).
- Sweden’s Stegra secured $2.3 billion in finance needed to bring its first-of-a-kind green steel plant to completion (Canary Media).
- Suniva plans to build a 4.5 GW solar cell factory in South Carolina (PV Magazine)
- Korea’s Hanwha Group signed an MOU with the Government of Alberta in Canada spanning energy infrastructure to defense procurement. The agreement arrives amid Hanwha Ocean’s bid for the Royal Canadian Navy’s lucrative submarine contract (Korea Times)
Government activities:
- The US government announces creation of high-tech manufacturing zone in the Philippines under Pax Silica to forge supply chains circumventing China (WSJ, US State Department)
- President Trump invokes the Defense Production Act to try to bolster domestic production of fuels and electricity (Axios)
- India invites bids for its first 220 MW small modular reactor (Economic Times)
- India’s government announces new ‘Fund of Funds’ with $1 billion investment to support India’s startups (Economic Times)
- Korean President Lee Jae Myung visited Vietnam and India, accompanied by chiefs of South Korea’s four largest conglomerates, Samsung, SK, Hyundai Motor and LG – leading to a series of joint investment and cooperation announcements (Korea Herald, Korea Times, Korea Herald, Korea Herald, Korea Times, Business Standard, Korea Times)

By Joss Garman, Executive Director, Loom Strategy Centre
Europe’s response to the oil and gas supply crisis in the Strait of Hormuz is likely to quietly entrench another structural energy dependency: this time on Chinese clean energy technologies.
The fastest, cheapest route to deploying clean energy at scale — solar panels, battery storage, grid technologies, heat pumps — currently runs overwhelmingly through China. Beijing’s dominance across these supply chains is the product of decades of deliberate industrial strategy.
At the end of last year the energy think tank Ember published a landmark analysis suggesting “Chinese industrialists have made climate scenarios look attainable” and that China can now “deliver the bulk of the goods needed for the global energy transition at prices affordable in most markets.”
Researchers at John Hopkins found Chinese firms have pledged at least $227 billion across green manufacturing projects, surpassing the $200 billion invested by the US over four years of the Marshall Plan.
China’s dominance in these technologies means we could see one European chokepoint replaced by another, no less real for being completely different in nature than fossil fuel dependencies (where the threat is more to sudden disruptions to supply and price volatility), and less visible on an energy bill.
Li Shuo, director of the China Climate Hub at the Asia Policy Institute, argues China’s lead in low carbon technologies is now “virtually unassailable.” “If you want to surpass China, you had to get your act together 25 years ago.”
In the climate community, this is increasingly accepted conventional wisdom. It’s the basis on which some advocate Europe making common cause with Beijing, and regard any attempt to catch up in any of these technologies as futile.
In 2024, China supplied 98% of Europe’s solar panels. Its share of lithium-ion battery imports stood at 88%. Six in ten inverters — the devices that make solar and wind power usable — came from China. These aren’t marginal shares. They are near-total dominance of the infrastructure on which Europe’s energy transition depends.
There is a discomfort about this topic in climate circles out of a fear that even raising the issue hands ammunition to those who would delay or derail the transition altogether. That fear is understandable. It’s a real problem that the old climate consensus has never adequately addressed.
Jason Bordoff, the director of the Center on Global Energy Policy at Columbia University’s School of International and Public Affairs, told the NYT’s Ezra Klein just this month, “If it (dependency on China for low carbon technologies) is perceived as an unacceptable risk, that’s a large amount of sand in the gears of the clean energy transition.”
The unmanaged risk
But inconvenient arguments tend to surface because the underlying problems are real.
Ignoring a dependency risk doesn’t dissolve it. It simply means someone else is managing it, on their terms, not yours.
Just over a year ago the former head of Britain’s security services issued a warning on the front page of The Times that security risks from Net Zero policies are arising and that existing policies are handing too much power to Beijing.
Earlier this month the UK blocked a Chinese wind firm, Ming Yang, from building a £1.5 billion turbine factory in Scotland, reportedly on national security grounds.
This followed reports the German government would likely block China’s entry into their wind energy market too, also on security grounds.
In December Italy launched an auction for new solar projects requiring modules to be ‘non Chinese.’
A shifting calculus
The latest fossil fuel shocks may push European governments to increasingly opt to overlook these risks — treating dependency on Beijing as a necessary evil or even a good thing.
It’s clear many Europeans welcome the influx of affordable Chinese clean technologies as a positive development — offering cost savings, a hedge against fossil fuel volatility, and a means to meet climate goals and diversify away from Russia, the US, and the Middle East.
Recent polling in Politico suggests that majorities in historical US ally nations in Europe and Canada are now beginning to see working with China as the lesser risk.
Trade-focused visits to Beijing by Starmer, Carney, Macron, Merz and Sanchez since the start of the year may signal leaders in these nations could be starting to feel the same way.
For now there are confusing mixed signals coming from different parts of different European governments as well as from the EU. Policy silos in Brussels and national capitals prevent coordinated action, compounded by differences in priorities and risk tolerance among different European nations.
The fundamental issue is a complete absence of a holistic approach.
This is precisely the failure at the heart of the old consensus: the assumption that energy and security policy could be managed in separate silos, by technocratic processes insulated from geopolitical realities. The China dependency problem is what happens when that assumption meets a world of great-power competition. The framework has to change before the dependencies do.
Continuing to prioritise cost and carbon targets while overlooking risks to the future of Europe’s industrial base, national sovereignty, and implications for Europe’s defence, could prove counterproductive for the transition too. If it leads to job losses and vulnerabilities in our military defences rather than more security and economic renewal, and right at the moment when economic and security issues are topping the agenda, public support for climate policies will erode — perhaps terminally.
Eight risks, hiding in plain sight
That’s why Loom is publishing new research that brings an independent assessment of the national security risks of China’s role in Europe’s energy transition.
Our findings — based on twenty interviews with European national security insiders and the expertise of authors who are respected authorities in this field — identify eight distinct security risks arising from Europe’s growing dependence on Chinese clean energy technologies. Some of these have been discussed before, in fragments. What this research does is connect them and look at them in the round, which is important - especially as they could all materialise at once. What emerges when you do that is unsettling.
The economic damage is already underway
China decimated Europe’s solar industry. Automotive and wind manufacturing could be next.
If the energy transition leads to job losses instead of economic renewal, public support for decarbonisation will erode. Over the long-term, Europe’s trade deficit with China will widen and Chinese leverage will strengthen, including through an outsized influence over prices. Europe’s AI ecosystem, a strategic priority, risks becoming dependent on Chinese batteries. If China restricted battery exports, AI development here would slow.
The authors are careful not to overstate the threat. Contrary to sensationalised press reports, large-scale Chinese cyberattacks designed to shut down European energy systems are rated “very unlikely.” But several risks — including the economic ones — are rated “very likely.”
Rearmament runs through Beijing too
Rearmament and decarbonisation draw on the same supply chains. Rare earth magnets and batteries, both dominated by China, are critical inputs for modern warfare. Without new energy industrial strategies, Europe’s defence sector will very likely become more dependent on China too.
Washington’s ultimatum
The most underappreciated risk identified in the research doesn’t originate in Beijing. It comes from Washington DC.
The US could sanction Chinese suppliers or components, and demand European nations remove them from their energy systems, or face tariffs or other sanctions such as the withdrawal of the US from European security architecture.
The Trump administration’s hostility to Europe’s clean energy direction is barely concealed. The US National Security Strategy published in December criticises European climate and energy policies as a challenge to US fossil fuel exports — something to be corrected. The scenario European governments need to plan for is this: Washington demands that Europe reduce or remove Chinese clean energy technology — or faces tariffs, sanctions, or reduced security commitments.
When Trump threatened 100% tariffs on Canada if Ottawa “makes a deal” with Beijing, it gave a sense of the register.
This has happened before. European governments spent years insisting that Chinese digital infrastructure was manageable. Then the US threatened to cut intelligence sharing over Huawei, and the technology was shuttered in the UK immediately.
The energy stakes are higher. The dependencies are deeper. The technology is woven through the entire infrastructure of Europe’s energy transition. Unwinding it under duress, on American terms rather than European ones, would be vastly more disruptive and costly — and would set back the energy transition itself, not just Europe’s industrial position.
The energy transition in Europe can still deliver what Loom has argued should be the organising principles of the continent’s new energy strategies: economic strength, sovereignty, affordability, resilience, and national security. But China overdependency cuts across all five simultaneously. It undermines economic strength by offshoring industrial value. It erodes sovereignty by recreating the single-source dependency Europe is trying to escape, which could also affect prices. It threatens resilience by concentrating chokepoints. And — as this research makes clear — it creates national security risks that European governments have barely begun to map.
Few argue for full decoupling — but in select key industries like auto, batteries and wind, the window to build sovereign, competitive alternatives is still open. It won’t stay open.
Structuring Europe’s energy future entirely around Chinese supply chains while calling it diversification isn’t a strategy and isn’t a hedge. It’s a blindspot.
