By Tom Moerenhout, Columbia Center on Global Energy Policy
Over the past decade, OECD governments have deployed public finance at unprecedented scale to support clean energy technologies and attempt to regain competitiveness vis-à-vis Chinese producers. The Biden administration alone committed close to $1 trillion to clean energy, industrial supply chains, and strategic manufacturing across the Bipartisan Infrastructure Law, CHIPS and Science Act, and Inflation Reduction Act.
Yet even with massive resources, progress across OECD countries appears slow. We argue that this is not always because there was too little support, but often because the wrong kind of support was deployed at the wrong moment. In practice, advanced economies have struggled less with how much to spend than with how to sequence instruments over time. The instrument mismatch problem is one of the least discussed but most consequential design challenges in industrial policy.
To dig into this, the NEIS Center and the Center on Global Energy Policy (CGEP) at Columbia University convened two closed-door roundtables, one in Palo Alto focused on early-stage technologies, and one in New York focused on commercial scale-up.
These roundtables included participants spanning technology developers, venture and infrastructure investors, project finance lenders, and former senior government officials across DOE, Treasury, and national security agencies.
This Substack draws on their input to lay out a practical framework of how public finance instruments should evolve as technologies move from early research through first-of-a-kind (FOAK) demonstration into commercial deployment, and to highlight where industrial strategy often breaks down in execution.
The Framework: TRLs as a Financing Map
The concept of Technology Readiness Levels (TRLs) was originally designed to track technical maturity. But it can equally be used as a map of risk profiles, and ask the question of what public financing instruments are most appropriate to help cover risk at each stage. While this logic is widely understood in theory, it is often misapplied in practice, leading to gaps in financing at critical transition points.
The risk logic is straightforward. At early stages (TRL 1–3), the dominant uncertainty is scientific, and the question is whether the technology will even work at all. At the middle stages (TRL 4–7), the question shifts to demonstration and execution, focusing on whether the tech can be scaled up and operated outside the lab. At later stages (TRL 8–9), the challenge is commercial, and the risk lies in securing finance and competing in the market.
Each stage calls for different policy responses. Getting this sequencing wrong, for example, by offering a loan guarantee to a technology that still needs a research grant, or funding a first-of-a-kind (FOAK)project with a pure grant when cost-sharing would enforce commercial discipline, is a major source of avoidable policy failure. In practice, this often shows up as governments offering concessional finance to technologies that still require technical validation, or relying on grants where some form of commercial discipline is already needed.
Early Stage (TRL 1–3): Tolerance for Failure Is a Feature, Not a Bug
At early stages, the central challenge is not mobilizing large volumes of capital but ensuring that sufficient risk-tolerant funding exists for iterative experimentation. That includes the many pathways that will not succeed. Learning by doing is learning by failing.
Roundtable participants were unequivocal in their assertion that public R&D grants are the right instrument here, and their design matters as much as their size. Flexibility to pivot research directions in response to early results was described as essential. Small, agile grants with clear but adaptable technical objectives were often viewed as more valuable than larger, rigid packages.
One participant offered a striking data point: In the United States, the average time from grant application to disbursement is around 12 months. In China, the equivalent process runs about 3 months. That 9-month gap, in the context of a startup race, can be decisive. More broadly, administrative speed is a determinant of technological competitiveness.
The policy implication for the US and OECD countries more broadly is crystal clear: Over-bureaucratized programs undermine the very risk-taking they are intended to support.
And critically, failure should be normalized as an expected outcome of a functioning innovation program, not treated as a policy shortcoming.
A few examples illustrate what this looks like in practice:
• ARPA-E has been the gold standard for high-risk, high-reward energy R&D. The program foresees in small grants with significant flexibility that are distributed across a portfolio of competing technical pathways. The DOE’s Nuclear Energy University Program (NEUP) follows a similar portfolio logic.
• A good example of execution is Sila Nanotechnologies, which developed a silicon-based anode as a complement to graphite. Sila received its first public financing through a $3.2 million ARPA-E grant and a $500,000 NSF grant between 2010 and 2012. Those early grants enabled the technical milestones needed to attract private capital, and the company went on to complete its first commercial manufacturing facility at Moses Lake in 2025.
The key design principles at this stage are: (1) Fund portfolios, not just projects; (2) protect programs from short-term political pressure through multi-year authorization; (3) resist the temptation to introduce financial optimization incentives too early, which can distort technical decision-making.
Middle Stage (TRL 4–7): Bridging the Valley of Death
Technologies at TRL 4–7 have validated their core science but face what is generally known as the “valley of death” because while they are scientifically feasible, they are not yet commercially bankable. The binding constraint shifts from technical uncertainty to demonstration risk, construction execution, and early commercial viability.
Private capital starts engaging at this stage. Venture capital, strategic corporate investors, and occasionally structured institutional capital toward the upper end of the range start coming in, but overall capital allocation remains constrained. The gap between what private investors will fund and what it actually costs to demonstrate a technology at scale is often where promising projects stall.
Participants broadly agreed that cost-sharing agreements outperform pure grants at this stage. By requiring the recipient to commit significant private capital alongside public funding, cost-sharing enforces commercial discipline while still absorbing risks that private capital alone cannot bear. A sliding-scale structure makes this more precise. For example, a project at TRL 4 might warrant a 50/50 public-private split, while one at TRL 7 (i.e., closer to bankability) might only require 30% public support.
A critical finding from both roundtables was the value of technical validation by public agencies acting as a quasi-financing instrument in its own right. Public validation can serve as a bridge between technical feasibility and financial credibility. When a government agency certifies a technology’s performance against clear milestones, it fills an information gap that many private investors lack the expertise to close themselves. That certification can unlock capital for current and future funding rounds far beyond the dollar value of the government commitment.
Examples that illustrate this stage:
• TerraPower’s Natrium reactor in Wyoming received a 50/50 cost-sharing agreement under DOE’s Advanced Reactor Demonstration Program with the government matching up to $2 billion of TerraPower’s investment dollar-for-dollar. The sodium-cooled fast reactor concept had strong theoretical foundations but required a financing structure that no private investor could absorb alone, given both the FOAK risk and the absolute size of the capital requirement.
• Ascend Elements received $480 million in DOE grants (with a 50/50 cost-share requirement) for its battery recycling facility in Kentucky, which is the first commercial-scale build-out of a technology previously proven only at pilot scale. The partial cancellation of that grant in 2025 due to “changing market conditions” shows that political durability of multi-year programs is especially critical at this stage, when projects operate on long development timelines.
• EnergySource Minerals’ ATLiS project (a commercial-scale lithium hydroxide facility in California’s Salton Sea region using direct lithium extraction from geothermal brines) received a conditional DOE loan commitment of up to $1.36 billion. With the DLE technology validated at pilot scale but not yet at commercial operation, the project straddled TRL stages. As a result, the loan structure was calibrated to that specific layer of residual risk, rather than to the project’s overall commercial maturity.
Later Stage (TRL 8–9): Revenue Certainty Unlocks the Capital Stack
At TRL 8–9, the technology works. At this stage, the central constraint is not access to capital per se, but the lack of predictable revenue streams that meet project finance requirements. The question is whether the project can secure financing at commercial scale. Here the constraint is not technical feasibility but the gap between the revenue certainty that project finance lenders require and the market realities that new clean energy or critical minerals projects face. Both are, of course, deeply impacted by existing surplus capacity in China.
Here, participants emphasized that project finance needs to be understood as a rigid instrument. Lenders set strict parameters around price certainty and volume certainty. Even where expected returns are adequate, the range of possible returns (driven by commodity price volatility, demand uncertainty, or regulatory risk) can push a project outside the acceptable envelope for senior debt.
Revenue stabilization instruments are the primary lever at this stage. Contracts-for-difference, price floors, and long-term government offtake arrangements reduce exposure to market price volatility, which enables the cashflow predictability that project finance requires. Government price floors for rare earth producers offer the clearest recent examples of this working in practice. Examples include the US Department of Defense’s 2025 partnership with MP Materials that established a 10-year price floor for rare earth oxides, or two similar deals by Lynas with the US government and Japan’s state-backed Japan-Australia Rare Earths JV.
Tax incentives, particularly production tax credits, play an important complementary role. The IRA’s 45X Advanced Manufacturing Production Credit has been one of the most powerful instruments for clean manufacturing at this stage and has proven to be standardized, project-agnostic, and highly scalable across a broad range of technologies. Its design features (technology-specific credit levels, phaseout timelines, transferability) reward actual production and can be layered alongside project finance.
Concessional loans and loan guarantees remain appropriate for capital-intensive projects with national security dimensions or where end-markets don’t yet offer bankable offtake contracts. DOE’s $996 million loan to Ioneer’s Rhyolite Ridge lithium project in Nevada is a recent example of how concessional loans can support a strategically important asset using largely conventional mining techniques, but facing a volatile lithium market.
One underutilized instrument flagged repeatedly are contingent facilities such as credit lines or insurance drawn on only if specific risks materialize. These can include construction cost overruns, regulatory disruptions, supply chain failures, and so forth. These allow projects to satisfy lender reserve requirements without tying up capital unnecessarily, and can be structured to cover risks that are largely outside the project developer’s control but are difficult to hedge through the insurance market.
Last but about as least as possible, the consistent theme across the TRL 8–9 discussion is of course permitting and regulatory uncertainty, which should be in their own right considered as financing constraints, not just development ones. Participants noted cases where a project with strong expected returns was nonetheless unattractive to lenders because of multi-year permitting timelines and regulatory/litigation unpredictability. Streamlining permitting is, in this sense, as much a financing policy as a regulatory one.
Instruments That Warrant Further Development
Across the roundtable discussions, participants surfaced a number of instrument ideas that go beyond the established toolkit. These potential policy options reflect gaps where existing instruments do not adequately align with the risk profiles observed in practice, particularly in the transition from demonstration to commercialization. It is crucial to note that these are not off-the-shelf solutions, and most raise open design, legal, or fiscal questions that need further work. But they point to where the next generation of industrial policy tools may need to go. We present a selection organized by technology cluster.
Mineral extraction and processing
• Early-stage critical mineral processing faces deep uncertainty about what the offtake market will look like by the time a technology reaches commercial scale. At TRL 1–3, highly specific refinement and purity specifications are being developed without clear visibility into future demand. Advance market commitments or non-binding demand commitments tied to achieving defined technical performance milestones could help provide that line of sight and pull R&D toward bankable specifications without subsidizing deployment prematurely.
• For DLE and other processing technologies transitioning from FOAK to commercial scale, ramp-up periods create acute bankability problems and even technically sound projects may fall short of volume targets in early operations. A government-backed debt service reserve account that is contingent on the project meeting agreed product-quality thresholds could backstop lenders during this initial production period, targeting volume uncertainty rather than processing risk.
• Many mineral processing facilities are highly equipment-intensive, with assets that retain value and can be redeployed if a project fails. Asset-backed equipment finance in the form of publicly supported collateralized loans against this recoverable equipment could limit public downside while still closing a financing gap that conventional lenders are unwilling to fill.
• For strategically important mineral smelters facing international competition, backstop floor price contracts on treatment and refining charges could protect project economics against the kind of aggressive pricing that are driving non-Chinese smelters out of the market.
Battery manufacturing
• Battery technology developers at TRL 1–3 face similar market uncertainty to minerals processors, i.e., highly specific chemistries that are being developed without a clear line of sight to commercial demand. Advance market commitments tied to predefined cell performance metrics (cycle life, safety, fast-charge rate) could help orient R&D toward commercially viable specifications without committing deployment subsidies.
• FOAK battery facilities often face extended qualification and testing periods before offtakers begin purchasing at volume. These ramp-up periods extend interest-during-construction phases, putting pressure on total financing size. Publicly subsidized interest-during-construction reserve accounts could reduce this financing burden. Alongside this, public co-funding of qualification engineers (which is a human capital bottleneck that extends timelines) could directly compress the qualification period.
• Even after passing qualification, FOAK battery facilities face residual performance risk in the initial operating period. Time-limited performance insurance (publicly supported coverage compensating lenders if contractual specifications are not met during early operations) could bridge this gap without requiring ongoing subsidy.
Wind and solar
• FOAK floating offshore wind projects face insurance markets that are either unavailable or prohibitively expensive, because private insurers lack sufficient historical loss data to price technology-specific risks. A time-limited public reinsurance facility backstopping defined tail risks for FOAK projects would not replace private insurers but would allow them to underwrite lower premiums.
• Conventional wind and solar projects increasingly face multi-year interconnection queues, as utilities upgrade transmission infrastructure. Providing standardized terms for provisional interconnection with a mandatory curtailment regime paired with a public curtailment insurance guarantee could allow projects to begin generating revenue earlier while protecting cash flow during the provisional period.
Geothermal
• Geothermal and mineral deposit developers incur high upfront exploration and drilling costs but have low or no immediate taxable income, meaning conventional tax deductions cannot be monetized by project developers themselves. A flow-through style exploration tax credit that allows developers to transfer deductions for drilling and subsurface validation expenses to investors could crowd in early risk capital for a phase of development where financing is particularly scarce. Canada’s flow-through share mechanism for mining offers a working precedent.
• Early-stage geothermal innovation is constrained not only by financing but by access to suitable high-enthalpy sites and shared subsurface data. Public geothermal testbeds that provide low- or no-cost access to land and shared infrastructure for universities and firms trialing novel drilling and reservoir approaches could accelerate technical validation by concentrating experimentation in well-characterized environments and openly sharing non-proprietary geological data.
Cross-Cutting Lessons
The rebalancing now underway in global clean technology manufacturing (excellently documented in Rhodium Group’s recent analysis of 2025 investment trends) makes instrument design more consequential, not less. As capital becomes more selective and policy support more uncertain, the sequencing and credibility of public tools becomes a central determinant of investment outcomes. Global manufacturing investment declined 42% from its 2023 peak, driven by Chinese overcapacity and US policy reversals. The question of which public tools can sustain momentum through market volatility and political cycles has never been more pressing. Four overarching lessons should be emphasized in a bipartisan way to develop an industrial policy that allows the United States to compete on next-generation clean energy technologies:
1. Instrument mismatch is a cause of policy failure. In practice, we repeatedly observe that instruments effective at one stage become counterproductive when applied at another. Recalibration of public support as technologies mature should be explicit and active, not assumed. Sila Nanotechnologies’ trajectory from ARPA-E grants to DOE technical assistance to a cost-sharing agreement as it approached commercial scale illustrates what deliberate sequencing looks like, and the results it can unlock.
2. Administrative effectiveness is a strategic variable. Slow approvals, fragmented program landscapes, and inadequate government technical capacity directly undermine the competitiveness of public financing programs. A single, accessible register of available public support across federal, state, and local levels would materially improve uptake, particularly for smaller developers.
3. Political durability requires deliberate institutional design. Arms-length lending agencies, credible public narratives about acceptable failure rates, and multi-year authorization all affect whether industrial policy programs survive election cycles. The partial cancellation of the Ascend Elements grant is a reminder of how exposure to political risk can materialize even after commitments are made.
4. Conditionality can build or break programs. Embedding local content requirements, labor standards, community benefits plans, and foreign entity restrictions into financing tools can align programs with broader industrial policy goals and build political legitimacy. But excessive or poorly designed conditionality can make tools unusable. The IRA’s “bonus adder” structure for domestic content is one model for threading this needle.
Getting the sequencing and design right is the difference between public investment that builds durable industrial capacity and taxpayer dollars that are wasted, or worse, crowds out the private capital it was meant to catalyze all along. Ultimately, the challenge is less about policy ambition than about execution, which depends on timing, sequencing, and long-term credibility.
The full white paper, with detailed policy maker considerations, technology cluster case studies, and instrument family mapping across TRL stages, will be available on the CGEP website.

By Sarah Ladislaw, Founding Director, NEIS Center
At the NEIS Center, we focus on measures to ensure countries have advanced energy systems that support competitive economies and industries of the future. This means we care about how countries shape their domestic energy policy and shore up supply chain security in partnership with other countries. We tend to focus on newer energy technologies where deployment is ramping quickly, and where supply chain security and economic chokepoints are newly emergent and not yet adequately addressed. However, globally traded oil and natural gas have long been susceptible to concerns about supply chain security and are vitally important parts of the global economy.
As I’ll comment on toward the end of this piece, yes, supply and demand-side measures are huge parts of how to guarantee energy security and economic resilience. But transit of goods is a third and critically important element of the equation. Energy security challenges differ across systems: fossil fuels are particularly vulnerable at the point of transit, while many clean energy technologies are more acutely vulnerable at the point of production and supply chain concentration.
Supply chain security gets more and more complicated for complex, technology-based supply chains, but are critically important in oil and gas markets given that it’s the transit of the fuels themselves that is at risk, not just the equipment used to produce energy in the case of solar, wind, or even batteries. In the case of the Strait of Hormuz, it is a vital transit chokepoint — responsible for 20 percent of global oil and oil-related produce supply and 25 percent of liquified natural gas supplies, not to mention a host of other important chemicals and commodities serving agriculture and high-tech needs around the world.

At the webinar, we will hear from expert speakers on the latest findings from the Rhodium Group’s Global Clean Investment Monitor (CIM), including the landscape of clean technology investment in the United States, China, Europe, India, and Middle Powers. As I wrote in our multi-perspective response post last week, even if the conflict stopped tomorrow, the economic impact of the closure will have a long tail with ramifications for the rest of this year and possibly next. However, the prospect of the Strait not re-opening — or re-opening under a diminished capacity — has implications that span well beyond the next year and would be transformative and potentially destabilizing for the region and the world. For that reason, I want to write about some of the options on the table to shore up oil and gas transit security going forward, why all three may be necessary, and why they will likely increase costs for resources leaving the region. The three options I’ll explore are: expanded stockpiles, alternative evacuation routes, and a new multilateral security arrangement. These responses do not increase supply in the traditional sense — they restructure risk, redistribute costs, and embed a security premium into energy systems.
(1) Expand strategic and commercial stockpiles.
Countries and companies keep both regular and emergency inventories of various grades of crude oil, oil products, and natural gas. The International Energy Agency (IEA) manages the strategic petroleum stockpile system that coordinates across countries and advises on natural gas stockpiles. Governments currently have 1.2 billion barrels of stockpiled oil, with 600 million barrels more in company possession but obligated to government stockpile programs.
In the wake of the current energy crisis, IEA member countries agreed to release 400 million barrels of oil onto the market. In recent years, several countries have expanded their strategic stockpiles (most notably China and India) while others have explored options to do so. The United States has gone back and forth on the issue, with some members of Congress seeking to sell off the stockpile for revenue, and successive administrations seeking to refill the existing reserve after a record drawdown during the Russian energy crisis of 2022. Europe has raised the level of natural gas storage required for winter coverage in response to the 2022 events as well, and coordinates with countries in Asia to ensure a more aggressive build-up in gas storage levels does not lead to price volatility and excessive cost increases.
Middle Eastern producers have also forward-deployed commercial stocks at strategically positioned refineries outside the region. The question now is whether and how to most effectively expand those stockpiles and commercial storage to further hedge against security or transit issues in the Strait of Hormuz or wider Middle East region.
Storage and stockpile expansion can happen organically (individual countries and companies making decisions) or it can be more coordinated. Regardless of whether it’s coordinated or not, there’s a lot of analysis that can and should go into those decisions. The risk of not coordinating is that you drive up prices if everyone builds at the same time. It’s also costly to both build or hold more storage, whether in expanded infrastructure costs, maintenance costs, fuel purchasing costs, and the market implications of additional storage (which can depress regional prices on the margins). All of these costs should also deliver some sort of savings against what is a higher security premium (either real or perceived) by relying on regular and uninterrupted transit through the Strait.
(2) Create alternative ways to get oil and gas out of the region
Amos Hochstein has a good article on this topic in The Atlantic, where he argues that a massive and internationally coordinated effort to build infrastructure that will bypass the Strait of Hormuz entirely is now clearly necessary. Right now, there are only two pipelines that move oil out of the region and avoid passage through the Strait: Saudi Arabia’s Petroline (also called the East-West Pipeline), which takes crude oil across the peninsula to the Red Sea ,and UAE’s Abu Dhabi Crude Oil Pipeline (ADCOP), which evacuates crude oil to the Gulf of Oman. These two pipelines have been critically important during the current energy crisis — taking what would have been a 20 million barrel a day oil shortfall and making it closer to 13 million barrels per day by allowing alternative avenues to market.
There are four deficiencies related to regional infrastructure. First, there is no alternative transit line for essential crude oil products like diesel, gasoline, and jet fuel. Second, there is no alternative export option for natural gas coming from the region, which is volumetrically less significant to global natural gas consumption, but still vitally important to many countries, particularly in Asia. Third, the existing crude oil export alternative route capacity is inadequate relative to the volumes typically exported from the region. The first and the third of these problems are likely to be solved more easily as oil-related infrastructure is easier to build than gas liquefaction infrastructure. The fourth deficiency is that neither Kuwait nor Iraq has access to any of the alternative export infrastructure. To address this issue, Hochstein recommends constructing “a modern, high-capacity pipeline corridor of oil and natural gas and products from southern Iraq and Kuwait to northward through Iraqi Kurdistan to the Ceyhan export terminal on Turkey’s Mediterranean coast.”
A number of Gulf countries are reviewing multiple options to expand or complement existing pipeline routes and export facility expansions in the Red Sea or Mediterranean. All of these options are extremely expensive and time consuming to deliver and protect. While some have called for the United States to rally countries to develop this infrastructure, the current administration has already signaled that it regards oil and gas coming from the Gulf as important for the rest of the world but not the US economy. The expense and coordination to manage a massive new network of pipeline infrastructure to match the volumes of the Strait of Hormuz is likely untenable, but given the importance of oil and gas exports to the regional economy and the way the current alternative infrastructure has provided a lifeline to those producers and global consumers, it is likely that interest to expand these networks in some way will be successfully revived.
(3) Finally, a new security arrangement will need to come to pass for ships passing through the Strait of Hormuz.
Before the current conflict, an average of 138 ships passed through the Strait each day using a narrow passage in the territorial waters near Oman. Security in the Persian Gulf relied on a layered and multinational configuration of forces that included permanent US basing, international naval coalitions, and regional partnerships to maintain freedom of navigation and deter Iranian aggression as well as other transnational crimes.
The post-conflict status quo is anything but clear. So far, the Iranian government has declared control of passage in the Strait, says it will charge a fee to transit the Strait (and has reportedly been collecting $2 million per ship thus far), and has suggested a new transit route close to Iranian shorelines. Upon an unsuccessful first round of negotiations on the first weekend of the ceasefire (the time of writing this post), the United States intends to erect a blockade of the Strait, saying it intends to stop any ship coming or going from an Iranian port.
It is particularly unclear how this standoff to re-establish control of the Strait will pan out. Earlier statements by the US president indicate that the United States expects to see more countries contributing to Gulf Security arrangements. The UK is expected to hold an initial set of talks on the topic this week and reportedly 40 countries have agreed to provide support for Strait security once the conflict subsides. Several countries like France, the UK, and others, have sent additional assets to the region. It seems like the likely outcome is more, not fewer military assets in the region from a larger array of countries, with, potentially a smaller role for the US military if indeed the Trump administration’s view holds that it is time for other countries to provide security in the Strait. However, it is still unclear whether there is any way to wrest control of the Strait back from Iran without significant re-escalation (though the blockade and negotiations are ostensibly meant to achieve this goal). It is not entirely clear what type of security arrangement would be necessary in a world where control of the Strait remains contested.
A few points about these strategies. First, it is more expensive to have a Strait that requires tolls, alternative evacuation routes, and a greater regional security presence. As I said in a LinkedIn post when the ceasefire was announced, all these options incur more cost than the pre-conflict status quo. Those costs on their own don’t determine how much more or less expensive oil and natural gas prices will be over the long run, because those prices are determined by a wide variety of factors, but the costs of moving oil and gas in and around the region will be higher.
The costs may also be distributed differently. Regional oil and gas producers will need to invest in pipeline infrastructure, consuming countries and oil and gas companies will bear the cost for strategic stocks, other countries will foot the bill for greater security presence (it is not clear whether the United States will have a larger or smaller presence at this point), and Iran could make a great deal of money from charging for passage. Second, it isn’t at all clear that any one of these supply-side options will be sufficient on their own. New regional pipeline infrastructure is still vulnerable to attack, and the same thing goes for Strait passage — even under multilateral military protection, and strategic stocks are likely prohibitively expensive to replace supply sources that, oh by the way, you need to somehow ship from Middle East producers.
Finally, by now, many of you are standing on your chairs screaming “Yes but what about developing additional supply or reducing demand!” Of course, additional supply from places like the United States, Canada, Brazil, and other countries is important, but will take time to develop and is not large enough to replace the resources produced in the Middle East. So, greater supply will help, but it will take time and is not sufficient in and of itself. As we will write more about in the following weeks, reducing demand for oil and natural gas is another important way to take pressure off prices and insulate your economy from many of the impacts of supply disruption-related price volatility.
There are lots of policy options for trying to reduce demand across the electricity, industry, and transportation sectors, and the most achievable options will depend on the country. For example, countries like the Philippines, Thailand, Vietnam, and Korea still rely a great deal on oil and natural gas for heating and are exploring options to replace that with renewables and a grid more capable of handling intermittency. Countries across South East Asia, India, and Africa that mostly rely on oil for transportation fuel are increasingly deploying electric 2- and 3-wheel vehicles to insulate consumers from high diesel prices. All of these demand and supply side measures matter and, in fact, past measures to increase efficiency, as well as expand and diversify the sources of oil and gas on which we rely and the types of energy that fuel our economies, are the main reason why the current historic supply disruption has not led to widespread and immediate economic catastrophe.
So, both supply and demand side measures are important, but none of those measures will immediately eradicate the need for oil and gas to flow out of the Middle East, and no single solution exists to make those flows more secure and reliable, given the unsettled geopolitical environment in the region.

Week 35: 08/24–08/30/2026
This week, four institutional moves, three policy developments and two institutional reports were tracked across tokenized securities, digital bank money and next-generation settlement infrastructure.
The Signal:
This week’s signal was the convergence of tokenized assets with the money and infrastructure needed to settle them.
Institutions are moving beyond issuing digital representations of assets and beginning to connect ownership, distribution and settlement inside financial workflows.
1. Key Takeaways
- Tokenized securities and tokenized bank money were used together at meaningful scale. CIMB settled RM1.38 billion of tokenized sukuk using tokenized deposits for 12 institutional investors.
- Distribution and network ownership are becoming strategic. Coinbase placed direct claims on U.S. equities on Base, Standard Chartered became the first bank distributor of Hong Kong’s HKDAP stablecoin, and 39 U.S. banking associations organized to build a bank-owned blockchain network.
- Governments are beginning to redesign financial-market infrastructure around tokenization. The United Kingdom proposed adding payment innovation to the Bank of England’s mandate, while Japan and India advanced plans connecting blockchain-based securities with central-bank money.
2. The Weekly Breakdown
2.1 Institutional Moves
- CIMB settles RM1.38 billion of tokenized sukuk using tokenized deposits CIMB Islamic Bank completed a pilot in Bank Negara Malaysia’s Digital Asset Innovation Hub that used tokenized deposits to settle tokenized sukuk. Of the RM1.68 billion issuance, RM1.38 billion was tokenized and subscribed by 12 institutional investors, while RM300 million was issued conventionally. The controlled pilot connected a tokenized security directly with commercial-bank money without changing the sukuk’s economic or Shariah structure.
- Coinbase-issued tokenized U.S. stocks go live on Base Tokenized Apple, Nvidia, Meta and Alphabet shares launched on Base for eligible users outside the United States. Institutional market makers acquire the underlying securities, which Alpaca holds in a bankruptcy-remote structure supervised under Abu Dhabi Global Market regulation. Holders receive direct claims on the underlying shares rather than synthetic price exposure.
- Thirty-nine state banking associations establish the BankChain Alliance State banking associations from 39 states formed the BankChain Alliance to develop an industry-owned and industry-governed blockchain network. The planned infrastructure would let banks offer tokenized deposits, bank-issued stablecoins, programmable payments and automated settlement. A technology partner is still being selected, with launch targeted for 2027.
- Standard Chartered becomes the first bank distributor of HKDAP Standard Chartered Bank Hong Kong became the first bank authorized to distribute Anchorpoint’s regulated Hong Kong-dollar stablecoin to eligible institutional clients. The bank is preparing applications covering tokenized money-market-fund settlement, intragroup treasury transfers and cross-border payments. The fund-settlement workflow is targeted for the fourth quarter and is not yet live.
2.2 Regulation and Policy
- United Kingdom — government proposes a payments-innovation objective for the Bank of England The UK government intends to give the Bank of England a statutory secondary objective to support innovation in payment systems and digital money, including stablecoins. The mandate would remain subordinate to financial stability and require the Bank to report annually to Parliament. Implementation requires amendments to the Financial Services and Markets Bill.
- Japan — authorities plan blockchain-based real-time settlement for stocks and government bonds Japan’s Financial Services Agency, Ministry of Finance, Bank of Japan and financial institutions are preparing a study group for blockchain-based securities settlement. The proposed infrastructure would connect stocks and Japanese government bonds with digital central-bank money, potentially replacing the current T+2 and T+1 settlement cycles with near-real-time settlement. A development plan is expected around early 2027.
- India — RBI and SEBI prepare the country’s first tokenized corporate-bond pilot India’s central bank and securities regulator prepared a pilot in which state-owned REC would issue up to ₹5 billion of tokenized corporate bonds. Participants would use DEMAT 2.0 securities wallets and wholesale digital-rupee wallets, allowing the securities and cash legs to settle through compatible digital infrastructure. The August development was disclosure of the plan; issuance was scheduled for September.
2.3 Reports
- BIS Financial Stability Institute examines who may issue stablecoins and what activities issuers may conduct The 17-page report compares stablecoin frameworks across jurisdictions, focusing on eligible issuers and activities such as lending, staking and custody. It finds that banks are generally permitted broader activities because consolidated prudential supervision already addresses the resulting risks, while bespoke nonbank regimes impose tighter limits. The report warns that entity-level restrictions can be circumvented through affiliates unless oversight extends across the issuer’s wider corporate group.
- Federal Reserve Bank of Dallas assesses how tokenized deposits could affect bank liquidity and maturity transformation Dallas Fed researchers examined how programmable deposits, continuous transfers and automated rate-shopping could make bank funding more sensitive to interest rates. Their scenario suggests that a 10% increase in deposit-rate sensitivity could reduce the banking system’s capacity to carry approximately $700 billion of ten-year-equivalent duration risk. The figure is a modeled reduction in maturity-transformation capacity—not a forecast of deposit outflows or an equivalent decline in lending.
3. Closing
This week showed different layers of tokenized finance developing simultaneously. CIMB connected tokenized securities with tokenized commercial-bank money in an institutional transaction. Coinbase placed direct claims on publicly traded equities onto a permissionless blockchain. BankChain and Standard Chartered addressed the network and distribution channels through which regulated digital money could reach financial institutions and their clients.
Policy is moving in parallel. The United Kingdom is considering an explicit innovation mandate for payment-system supervision, while Japan and India are examining how tokenized securities can settle using central-bank money. Meanwhile, the BIS and Dallas Fed are focusing attention on the institutional boundaries and banking risks that will emerge if these systems scale.
The next measure of progress is execution beyond controlled pilots and initial distribution: recurring transactions, interoperable settlement and evidence that tokenized assets and digital money can move together across institutions rather than inside isolated networks.

Week 34: 08/17–08/23/2026
This week, five institutional moves and six policy updates were tracked across interbank tokenized deposits, digitally native debt issuance, DLT settlement in central-bank money, institutional stablecoin lending and agentic payments.
The Signal:
This week's signal was the movement of tokenized settlement from inside individual institutions to between them.
Separate bank systems are beginning to connect, and the infrastructure intended to settle them in central-bank money now has named operators and a launch date.
1. Key Takeaways
- Tokenized deposits moved between institutions rather than within one. Swift’s ledger exchanged payment messages and matched and netted obligations across HSBC’s and Standard Chartered’s separately built tokenized-deposit systems. The connection matters more than the transaction, which settled over existing payment infrastructure and disclosed no value.
- Digital market infrastructure is acquiring named operators and firm dates. Standard Chartered became the first G-SIB to fund itself through Euroclear’s digital platform, and Pontes identified four registered operators ahead of a September 21 production launch, subject to readiness and certification.
- Regulators moved in parallel across four jurisdictions in five days. 5. Conclusion and Thinking
April made one thing clearer: onchain finance is no longer only a product category. It is becoming a competition over market structure.
Stablecoins are becoming the cash and settlement layer for payments, treasury, and tokenized assets. Banks are responding with tokenized deposits and bank-controlled digital money networks. Asset managers, custodians, exchanges, and transfer agents are building the operational infrastructure around tokenized securities. Regulators are moving from broad policy statements into implementation-level rules.
The next stage of institutional onchain finance will likely be shaped by three questions:
- Will the dominant digital cash leg be stablecoins, tokenized deposits, central bank money, or a mix of all three?
- Will tokenized assets gain real liquidity, or will the market first spend several more years building custody, servicing, collateral, and legal infrastructure?
- Will crypto-native infrastructure mature fast enough to meet institutional standards for verification, risk controls, recovery, compliance, and governance?
April’s answer was not final, but the direction was strong: the winners in onchain finance will not only be the firms that issue tokens. They will be the firms that control the trusted operating layers behind digital money and tokenized markets.

The State Bank of Pakistan issued a circular allowing regulated banks to provide accounts and services to licensed virtual-asset service providers after the creation of Pakistan’s virtual-assets authority. 3. Closing
Onchain finance is turning into a market-structure battle.
Banks are shaping the money layer. Exchanges, custodians, and post-trade firms are shaping the asset layer. Regulators are shaping the operating perimeter.
The core issue for institutions is simple: who will own the trusted rails behind tokenized markets?

Stablecoins have become one of the clearest venture categories in onchain finance. This study tracks 111 venture financings in stablecoin-centered companies from 2013 to Q1 2026, covering 82 companies, 411 disclosed investors, and about $4.0B in disclosed funding.
The purpose is to interpret how the market formed, where capital has gone, who has been most active, and what that may mean for the next phase of onchain finance.
The study covers
- Market development: how stablecoins evolved from crypto-native liquidity tools into a broader payments, treasury, and enterprise category
- Financing history: how venture activity changed from 2013 to Q1 2026
- Company landscape: which companies and business models attracted the most capital
- Investor landscape: which investors have been most active and persistent
- Broader implications: Why stablecoins continue to attract investment, and what financing patterns suggest about the next phase of on-chain finance

Join our upcoming April 15 live roundtable on LinkedIn
Founders on Chain — Onchain Finance in 2026: Where Is the Opportunity?
- Front-line insight from founders closest to the market
- Signal on what is real now — and what is coming next
Section 1. Stablecoin development
Stablecoins represent one of the earliest and clearest venture entry points into onchain finance. Their development is relevant not only as a product category, but also as an indicator of how financial activity is moving onchain. Fundraising in stablecoin-centered companies accelerated meaningfully in 2025 and remained strong through the first quarter of 2026. Alongside prediction markets, stablecoins have emerged as one of the two most prominent themes in the broader Web3 market.
At the most basic level, stablecoins are blockchain-based instruments designed to maintain relatively stable value, most commonly against fiat currencies such as the U.S. dollar. Their importance comes from a simple but powerful function: they make cash programmable. Stablecoins are not all structured in the same way. Their underlying models differ in terms of collateral, design, and risk profile, which has shaped both market development and investor interest.
The category has evolved through four broad eras. In the genesis phase, stablecoins solved crypto-native liquidity problems. In the next phase, regulated issuers and new models tested how stable-value assets could scale. Since 2023, stablecoins have expanded into a broader payments, treasury, and enterprise story. By 2025, regulation had also become a defining force. MiCA in Europe, the GENIUS Act in the United States, and Hong Kong’s stablecoin licensing regime all helped move the category from a regulatory grey zone toward regulated infrastructure. From 2026 onward, the investable question is increasingly not whether digital cash works, but who controls the workflows around it.
The market-cap trend helps explain why stablecoins have become an important venture theme. Stablecoin supply rose from roughly $27.0B in 2020 to about $310 billion at year-end 2025, and to about $316.0B by the end of the first quarter of 2026. This expansion helps explain why venture capital has increasingly funded not only issuers, but also the broader set of businesses supporting stablecoin-based activity.
Section 2. Venture Deals
The purpose of the study is to assess how venture capital has funded the stablecoin category over time. This study examines 111 accepted financings in stablecoin-centered companies over 2013 to Q1 2026, representing $4.0 billion of disclosed funding. The dataset covers 82 company entries in the accepted deal list and 411 disclosed investors named across those financings. Unless otherwise noted, 2026 figures are year-to-date through March 31, 2026.
The screening method focuses on disclosed venture or equity financings in companies whose core business centers on stablecoin issuance, protocols, or stablecoin-specific infrastructure. It excludes token sales, undisclosed financings, and companies where stablecoins are only peripheral. The year-by-year table shows how the category moved from a small historical base into a real financing market.
Several signals matter. First, 2025 was the category’s breakout year with 43 deals and $1.4B of disclosed funding. Second, Q1 2026 alone already exceeded full-year 2024 disclosed funding. Third, funding concentration has fallen as the market broadened: in 2021–2022, a few large rounds dominated the category, while in 2025 the top five deals accounted for 55.5% of annual disclosed funding rather than nearly all of it.
In terms of stages, seed was the largest stage by deal count with 45 deals, followed by Series A / Early Growth with 30 deals. Together with 6 Pre-Seed deals, these early-stage rounds accounted for 81 of 111 deals. This suggests that the category is no longer driven only by a small number of scaled issuers.
Capital, however, remained concentrated in larger rounds. Series B+ accounted for 13 deals but $1.3B of funding, slightly above the $1.25B raised across 30 Series A / Early Growth deals. Other financing added another $1.0B across 17 deals. ‘Other financing’ captures disclosed rounds that were reported without a standard venture stage label or that fit alternative structures such as strategic.
The chart below shows that this broadening shift became more visible after 2023. The earlier cycle was more episodic and issuer-led, while 2024–2026 saw the development of a broader pre-seed, seed, and Series A pipeline. This suggests that stablecoins have evolved into a broader venture category spanning issuance, payments, treasury, settlement, and related infrastructure.
Section 3. Company Landscape
The company landscape shows a clear shift in what the market values. Earlier funding was concentrated in a small number of foundational issuers, especially Circle and Paxos. More recently, capital has expanded into the businesses built around stablecoin usage, including payments, treasury, settlement, and distribution.
The company base is global but still concentrated in a few hubs. The United States leads with 33 companies, followed by the United Kingdom with 9, Singapore with 8, Hong Kong with 6, and Switzerland with 4. Canada has 3, while Australia, Italy, the United Arab Emirates, Argentina, and Mexico each have 2.
All-history funding is still led by the earliest category leaders. Circle ranks first, followed by Paxos. This reflects the earlier stage of the market, when venture funding focused on proving that stablecoins could become credible financial products.
The newer leaders look different. Tempo, Rain, RedotPay, OpenFX, M^0, BVNK, KAST, and Agora point to a market that is now backing broader stablecoin workflows, not just issuers. That includes cross-border access, treasury tools, payments, and infrastructure.
Since 2023, repeat fundraising has increasingly clustered around companies tied to distribution, treasury, settlement, cross-border access, and infrastructure. Recent repeat-financed names such as Rain, RedotPay, OpenFX, and others suggest that investors see durable value not only in launching stablecoins but also in building the operating layers around them.
Section 4. Investor Landscape
The accepted deal list includes 411 disclosed investors. The investor base is led by the United States (255), followed by the United Kingdom (25), China (23), Hong Kong (16), and Singapore (13). This shows that stablecoin venture funding is global but still centered in a small number of financial and crypto-native capital hubs.
The investor landscape already has a visible center of gravity. Coinbase Ventures is the clear category leader, with 17 backed deals across 7 active years. On persistence, Coinbase Ventures stands out as well.
Repeat backing is especially informative because it shows where investors believe durable control points are emerging. These patterns suggest that investors are not only seeking exposure to stablecoins as a theme but also doubling down on specific workflow winners.
For founders, the early-stage investor set is often more useful than the overall ranking. Early stage refers to pre-seed, seed, and hybrid seed-plus rounds.
The stablecoin market now has a recognizable investor core. A small group of firms is showing repeated activity, multi-year persistence, and follow-on conviction. For audiences trying to understand where real category ownership is forming, that group matters much more than the long tail of one-off participants.
Section 5. Notable Findings
1. Stablecoins are now a real venture market
The dataset contains 111 studied financings and 4.0B of disclosed funding spanning 2013 to 2026. It shows that stablecoins have developed into a distinct capital-formation market with their own stage mix, investor base, and repeat winners.
2. Stablecoins are still early-stage by count
More than seven in ten financings are still Pre-Seed through Series A / Early Growth, which means new company formation remains open even as the market matures.
3. 2025 was a breakout in breadth
The year delivered 43 deals, $1.4B of disclosed funding, and 33 first financings. The top five deals accounted for 55.5% of annual funding, well below the near-total concentration seen in earlier peak years. Even excluding Tempo’s $500.0M round, 2025 still outperformed 2024. Q1 2026 alone already exceeded full-year 2024 disclosed funding.
4. The center of value capture has moved downstream
All-history funding is still led by Circle and Paxos, but the newer leaders—Tempo, Rain, RedotPay, OpenFX, M^0, BVNK, KAST, and Agora—are concentrated in access, distribution, payments, treasury, settlement, and issuer tooling. The investable surface has moved outward from the coin itself to the workflows built around the coin.
5. The early-stage funnel broadened after 2023
Pre-Seed, Seed, and Series A / Early Growth account for 81 of 111 deals, showing a real company-formation pipeline. But Series B+ and other financing account for only 30 deals and $2.3B of funding. This is what a maturing venture market looks like: breadth for new entrants, concentration around scaled winners.
6. Repeat financing is a stronger signal than one-off headline rounds
One-off headline rounds can distort the picture. Repeat-backed companies show where investors believe compounding advantage is real. That is where durable workflow control points are most likely forming.
Section 6. Why Stablecoins Continue to Attract Capital
For institutional VCs and strategic investors, stablecoins stand out from most crypto sectors for five reasons: real usage, clear economics, institutional validation, and improving regulation.
1. Growth is increasingly driven by real use cases
Stablecoin growth is no longer only a trading story. It is increasingly tied to payments, cross-border settlement, and treasury workflows. Stripe has highlighted stablecoins as a way to reduce the time and cost of cross-border money movement. BVNK reported $30.0B in annualized stablecoin payment volume in 2025, up 2.3x year over year, with about $10.0B from the U.S. market. Visa-linked stablecoin card spend reached a $3.5B annualized run rate in Q4 FY2025, up about 460% year over year. Together, these data points suggest that stablecoin activity has moved beyond crypto-native use and into real financial flows.
2. The business model is clearer than in most crypto categories
For issuers, the model is straightforward: reserve-backed stablecoins generate income from cash and short-duration government assets. Tether reported that year-to-date net profit had surpassed $10.0B by the end of Q3 2025. Circle’s IPO at about $6.9B at pricing provided a public-market benchmark for the category. For infrastructure companies, monetization comes from transaction fees, network fees, and SaaS revenue tied directly to payment and treasury volume.
3. Institutional adoption has reduced risk
Large payment networks are no longer only watching the category; they are buying and integrating it. Mastercard agreed to acquire BVNK for up to $1.8B. Stripe completed its acquisition of Bridge, a deal widely reported at about $1.1B. Visa selected BVNK to power stablecoin payments for Visa Direct pilot programs. These actions matter because they validate stablecoin infrastructure as part of mainstream payment and settlement rails, not just a crypto-side experiment.
4. Regulation is becoming a market enabler
A clearer regulatory framework has improved the investability of the sector. The study already notes that MiCA, the GENIUS Act, and Hong Kong’s stablecoin regime helped move stablecoins from a regulatory grey zone toward regulated infrastructure. That does not fully explain the funding cycle, but it reduces one of the biggest barriers to institutional capital: legal uncertainty.
Notes on data and limitations
This study is based on publicly disclosed venture and equity financings in stablecoin-centered companies. It excludes undisclosed rounds, token sales, and transactions where stablecoins were only peripheral. The dataset should therefore be read as a view of the disclosed market, not a complete record of all stablecoin-related investment activity. Actual sector investment is likely higher than reflected here, as some deals may not have been publicly reported or may not have disclosed sufficient detail for inclusion.

The bigger takeaway is that bank-based stablecoin and digital-asset functionality is being packaged as an enterprise banking and treasury product, not just as a crypto feature.

- Treasury said on April 1 that this NPRM is the first regulation it has proposed to implement the GENIUS Act. The proposal focuses on how Treasury should determine whether state-level regulatory regimes for smaller payment stablecoin issuers are “substantially similar” to the federal framework. 3. Closing

Twenty-one financial institutions are forming a company to issue stablecoins pegged to G7 currencies. A dollar token first, a euro token after, targeted at the first half of 2027. Bank of America, Citigroup, Goldman Sachs and Mitsubishi UFJ are named. The other seventeen are not, at least not yet.
Five weeks ago we told you Goldman was a holdout. It is now a founder.
That is the part worth your time. Not the announcement. The reversal.
What We Told You in June, and Why It Was Only Half Right
On June 7, writing about JPMorgan, Bank of America, Citi and Wells Fargo building a shared network through The Clearing House, we made a structural argument. Banks were choosing tokenized deposits instead of stablecoins, and the reason was capital efficiency. A tokenized deposit stays on the issuing bank’s balance sheet and can be lent against under fractional reserve rules. A stablecoin’s reserves sit in cash and short-term Treasuries and cannot be lent at all. Banks keep the spread. Regulators keep money creation inside the perimeter.
On August 2, those same four consolidated their separate blockchain projects onto shared rails. We told you then to watch two names: Goldman Sachs and State Street, the large institutions that had not signed on.
Then on August 15 we moved. Writing about Wells Fargo, we argued the banks meant to own both forms of programmable money and would use whichever one fit the flow. That was the right call. This week retires the June framing for good.
Deposits versus stablecoins was never the question. It was always deposits and stablecoins, divided by how far the dollar has to travel.
Why a Bank Needs Two Kinds of Digital Dollar
Here is the thing a tokenized deposit cannot do easily. It cannot simply leave the banking perimeter.
A Citi deposit token is a claim on Citi. It settles beautifully against a Bank of America deposit token, so long as both sit inside a shared utility with a common rulebook. A Federal Reserve account sits at the end of that chain. That is exactly what The Clearing House is building, and it solves the domestic interbank problem. Interoperability beyond it is a design choice rather than an impossibility, but every hop needs a legal and settlement arrangement negotiated in advance. Move outside that perimeter, to a counterparty in Singapore with no correspondent relationship, and the claim has nowhere to land.
A stablecoin behaves more like a bearer instrument. It travels to whoever holds it, with no relationship negotiated first. That is its advantage, and it is the reason Tether found its market in places where dollar bank access is thin rather than in Manhattan.
So the banks are running two tracks. Tokenized deposits for domestic institutional settlement, where the counterparties are each other. A stablecoin for cross-border and cross-currency flow, where they are not. The G7 scope in this announcement is the tell. A euro token is not a domestic American product. Neither is a joint venture with Japan’s largest bank in it.
Which brings us back to Goldman. Goldman does not have a $2 trillion retail deposit base to protect. For Bank of America and Citi, a bank-issued stablecoin cannibalizes their own funding, which is why they spent a year building the version that does not. Goldman has almost nothing to cannibalize and a great deal of cross-border institutional flow to win. A holdout on the deposit project becomes a founder on the stablecoin one. I read the holdout as reluctance. It was specialization.
So who loses? Not the technology, and not stablecoins as a form. The loser is the independent issuer’s privileged position between tokenized markets and the banking system, where it currently charges for the passage. Run the chain the banks are assembling: deposit franchise, tokenized deposit, bank-sponsored stablecoin, tokenized securities settlement, cross-border flow. They are not trying to kill the instrument, they are trying to own both ends of it.
What This Means for Your Dollars
Three things change, and one does not.
Issuer economics get harder. Circle earns the overwhelming majority of its revenue from interest on reserves, the same spread banks have collected for decades, and it currently keeps nearly all of it. Twenty-one banks arriving with their own funding costs and their own distribution put that arrangement under pressure. It could give way through lower fees, reserve-sharing, institutional pricing, or simple loss of share. Where regulators allow it, some may reach holders. What looks hard to sustain is an issuer keeping essentially all of the reserve income while bank-sponsored alternatives compete for the same balances.
Tokenized securities get a native settlement asset. Today they mostly settle against USDC, which means a bank-issued bond token settles against a non-bank liability. A bank consortium stablecoin removes that mismatch, which could help make tokenized collateral usable in size. The settlement asset is one input among several, not the whole problem.
Access tightens rather than widens. This will be permissioned. KYC’d corporates, qualified purchasers, institutional counterparties. If you are waiting for a permissionless alternative to Tether with a Wall Street balance sheet behind it, this is not that, and it was never going to be.
What does not change is your position this year. Nothing here ships before 2027. Announcements are not products, and the banks have announced a great deal since 2019 that never reached a customer.
What to Watch Next
Two signals, and they are more specific than usual.
First, the legal structure. Shared equity stakes and co-equal board seats mean a company. Nonbinding memoranda and a working group mean another Project Guardian, another Canton, another decade of white papers. The difference will be visible in the incorporation documents, not the press release.
Second, watch whether this venture and The Clearing House project ever mention each other. If the overlapping banks describe them publicly as one strategy with two instruments, the two-track reading is right and both survive. If each pretends the other does not exist, it is a turf fight between the transaction bank and the markets side, and one of them quietly dies in 2027. I have watched that specific fight happen inside three institutions. It usually ends with the side that controls the client relationship winning.
And a smaller thing: the full list of twenty-one has not been published. Watch whether JPMorgan and Wells Fargo, the two loudest voices on tokenized deposits, are on it. If they are, the strategy is coordinated. If they are not, the industry has just split into two camps, and the camp with Goldman in it is the one selling to everybody else.
