On Monday morning, Coinbase (Nasdaq: COIN) put Nvidia, Apple, Meta, and Alphabet on Base.
Four stocks, four new tickers, NVDAc, METAc, AAPLc, and GOOGLc, now live on Base and trading around the clock.
Each token is a claim on a real share sitting with Alpaca, a regulated custodian, under Abu Dhabi Global Market rules.[1]
Jesse Pollak, who runs Base, says the target over time is ‘thousands.’[2]
Now, you may have noticed the regulated under Abu Dhabi rules above.
That’s because from the U.S. you can’t touch them yet. Ugh, don’t you just hate slow regulation…
Coinbase has fenced them off to eligible jurisdictions outside America, which is another reminder that for all the chest thumping the U.S. government is doing around crypto, it’s still glacial in putting anything into actual law.
But for all the interest in Coinbase tokenizing stocks, the real story is about their pricing.
You see Coinbase picked Chainlink (LINK) as the official price oracle for every one of those tokens.[3]
Now as ‘boring’ as a price oracle might be, Chainlink continues to show that it sits at the epicenter of a multi-trillion-dollar opportunity.
Everyone Needs a Price
A tokenized stock on its own is a relatively useless thing. You can hold it, send it, and swap it. That’s about it.
To do anything with it, like lend against it on Aave, or build anything cleverer than a swap, a protocol needs to know what the token is worth.
And it needs to trust that number.
That’s the job Chainlink does. Its data feeds take the underlying share price and multiply it by a number Coinbase publishes onchain.[4]
Pay a dividend and Coinbase doesn’t post you cash, it bumps the multiplier so one token is now redeemable for 1.02 shares.
Ten-for-one split? Coinbase pauses the feed, the multiplier jumps to 10, and the token price never moves.
That’s clever, it adds value within the token, which makes the token itself more productive.
And it’s what makes more about Chainlink that about Coinbase tokenized stocks.
Coinbase is now the third tokenized stock issuer to hand its pricing to Chainlink.
Ondo, which I wrote about in January when it pushed 200 stocks onto Solana, does it all through Chainlink.
Robinhood Chain, which I wrote to you about yesterday, went live on 1 July. Chainlink is also its official data and cross-chain oracle.[5]
Coinbase, Robinhood, and Ondo are effectively battling it out with each other. They disagree on which chain, which custodian and which token standard.
But they all agree on Chainlink.
Chainlink is connective infrastructure. And that makes it invaluable to a future of tokenized stocks.
What Could Go Wrong?
The scale of what could come is astonishing.
Token Terminal puts the current tokenized stock market at around $2.8 billion.
The growth has been explosive already.
But in comparison to the rough value of all U.S. listed companies at $76.9 trillion,[6] it’s clear we’re barely an inch over the start line here.
But that differential is the opportunity.
So far, it doesn’t matter who’s listing the tokenized stocks, it’s still Chainlink at the center of it all.
Now, admittedly LINK has been a frustrating hold for years, its price is no different to what it was six years ago.
But when you look at what’s happening, and the explosive growth of tokenized equities, perhaps LINK was just too far ahead of its time, until now.
It we end up in a world where all equities are tokenized, which I expect we will, and Chainlink is at the centre of a $77 trillion market. It’s fair to say a price at $11.80 (which is what it is now) probably looks like a bargain.
Trust in crypto,
Adam Atlantic

I love it when a bull market fires up.
And you want to know, how I know, that this bull market is now underway?
Because the hottest investment in July and August has been a cat meme.
CASHCAT, a memecoin, touched a $200 million market cap in mid-July, fell to around $35 million early August, and has now bounced back to around $150 million.
From $0.
This kind of memecoin explosion reminds me of the Solana ecosystem in 2021.
But have a guess what chain Cash Cat lives on…
Ethereum? Nope.
Solana? Nope.
Base? Nope.
It’s all happening over on Robinhood Chain
That chain is Robinhood Chain, an Ethereum layer-2 the broker launched on 1 July. I’ve written to you all year about the tokenization arc, from the NYSE building its tokenized platform in January to Ondo pushing 200 tokenized stocks onto Solana two days later.
Robinhood Chain is the next step in that same story, except this one comes with about 28 million funded customers attached.
And the growth since launch has been silly.
By 13 July, the chain held about $312 million[1] in total value locked (TVL) and was clearing 3.6 million transactions a day. Within three weeks, it passed Base for daily active users.
Today, it’s nearly at $1 billion TVL[2].
The growth is explosive, and now the memecoin and degens have arrived. Welcome to Robinhood Season.
The Cat Came First
Tenev clearly wants Robinhood to be the epicenter of retail traders. And he’s smart, he knows that’s stocks, crypto, prediction markets… everything a degen could possibly want.
And we’re all here for it!
Tokenized stocks are going to be a massive driver of activity on Robinhood, but so will a bull market memecoin season.
It’s uncanny the similarities that I’m seeing here with Solana in 2021.
Solana kind of went through it in reverse though. It was held up as a casino for years, with the dog coins, the NFT mints, the pump-and-dumps, the lot.
Then the liquidity stuck, the builders followed the liquidity, and now Ondo settles tokenized Apple shares on it. Solana has had to reshape its identity of late, a good move, but even so, it’s still managed to find a market cap over $54 billion.
Robinhood, on the other hand, is already established as a trusted player. Its reputation as a disruptor is already there. There’s no identity crisis, it’s just Robinhood.
On 18 August Tenev said[3],
‘It is becoming increasingly clear that we are in the early innings of a global tokenization supercycle. Last year, I called it a freight train that cannot be stopped—and one that will eat the entire financial system.’
This is the layer he presents to the ‘suits’ that Robinhood Chain is ‘purpose-built for real-world assets’ but he also knows what drives success is the volume that retail traders pump through crypto in a bull market.
So How Do You Play It?
I do think Robinhood Chain is going to be one of the factors that drives the bull market. Along with Bitcoin resuming its pumpenomics, the AI x crypto convergence trade and tokenized equities.
But you can’t buy Robinhood Chain the way you could have bought SOL at $2.
There is no token for it, for now at least.
Instead, your exposure comes three ways instead, through the memecoins you can trade now on it, the ecosystem projects building on it, or Robinhood (Nasdaq: HOOD) stock.
The memecoins are wild. Fun. But wild. You can lose the shirt off your back real quick.

In 1946, the U.S. Supreme Court looked at a Florida orange grove and created a test that still decides what is and isn’t a security in America.
W. J. Howey was selling rows of his citrus groves to hotel guests, with a contract attached for his company to farm the land and post them the profits.
The SEC said that package was a security.
The court agreed and gave us the Howey test.
The test requires four elements to be satisfied:[1]
- There must be an investment of money by the investor,
- The investment must be made in a common enterprise where the fortunes of the investor are tied to others,
- There must be a reasonable expectation of profits, and
- Those profits must be derived primarily from the efforts of others, such as the promoter or a third party.
Eighty years on, that orange grove logic has been hanging over every crypto portfolio, every token in it like, well, like a bag of rotten oranges.
Bitcoin skates through the test by the way.
There is no team, no promises, no one’s ‘efforts’ to rely on. But nearly everything else in crypto has a founding team, a foundation, a roadmap.
And the old SEC’s working position was horrendous.
Their argument was once a security, always a security. A token sold under an investment contract in 2018 is still that in 2024, no matter how decentralized the network had actually become. There was no exit once they’d made up their mind.
On Wednesday, I took you through how the ICO was back, and then we got a little derailed by Trump pumping crypto at the White House.
But here, something bigger and more important than all of that…
Safe Harbor
Buried in the SECs new crypto regulation proposal is what’s called a conditional safe harbor.
A crypto asset would be deemed to no longer be subject to an investment contract once the issuer has ‘completed or permanently ceased all essential managerial efforts’[2] it promised investors.
That line, that innocuous tiny line means that decentralzsation actually means a whole host of crypto moves from the edge of prosecution to freedom!
Build the network you sold people, hand over control, and the token that might once have got you sued through Operation Chokepoint now sets you free.
Raise under the fundraising exemption, disclose along the way, ship the thing, decentralize... and come out the other side holding an asset that trades free of the 80-year-old oranges rule.
That pathway has never existed.
Probably doesn’t make those that got sued sleep any better, but hey, better late than never.
Hester Peirce wants to take it even further. Her statement openly asked the public how crypto assets could be allowed to function more like equity,[3] with token holders sharing in the growth of the enterprise itself.
The SEC is asking how tokens can carry equity-like upside. It just further reinforces my long-standing point that soon enough, crypto, equities, it won’t matter, it’ll be all onchain, all tokenized, tradable anywhere, anytime.
A whole new world of capital markets is emerging.
Gaming the System
Of course, there will be abuses of this if it becomes law, which I do expect it will.
You can bet projects and their team will declare their managerial efforts are complete, meanwhile, a background foundation multisig runs the whole show.
So, the SEC will still have its work cut out for it.
But really, for a decade, the question hanging over this entire market was is it a security? And for a decade, we’ve said the Howey test does not, should not, apply to crypto.
Finally, it looks like we’ve got the answer and the pathway to a sensible, reasonable, common-sense outcome.
Who’d have thought this was coming two years ago!
Trust in crypto,
Adam Atlantic

The crypto markets have a habit of surprising you out of nowhere.
I even messaged a colleague yesterday saying the market was a bit ‘s***house’ at the moment.
And truthfully, it has been.
Bitcoin just plodding along in the low $60K range for weeks, months on end.
Meanwhile, the wider market, also just plodding along looking for that one little spark to get things going…
And then, like the flip of a light switch, the market turned on again.
Now, I had envisaged delivering you part two of my ‘ICOs are back’ essay, continuing on from yesterday. But that can wait another day before I dive into the safe harbor of when a token stops being a security.
I’m bumping that by a day because overnight President Trump said America is ready to BUY, BUY, BUY Bitcoin!
A Tease Again or the Real Deal?
The President stood at the dais in the Roosevelt Room, flanked by the SEC chair, the CFTC chair and Jeffrey Sprecher, boss of Intercontinental Exchange (NYSE: ICE), owner of the New York Stock Exchange.[1]
Also in the room… Coinbase, Ripple, Robinhood, Kraken, Gemini, Nasdaq, and Chainlink.
The topic of the day? Bitcoin and crypto.
The heaviest hitters in crypto, in the White House, there for Trump to proclaim America again as the crypto capital of the world.
Trump told the room,
‘We ended the war on crypto once and for all.’[2]
Then a reporter asked whether the government could acquire ‘sizable amounts’ of Bitcoin, and this was the answer…[3]
‘Well, it’s been talked about. I think I’d probably rely on Paul and the whole group for that. He’ll make a decision. You guys will make a decision and you’ll let me know.’
Paul being Paul Atkins, the SEC chair, who as we wrote about yesterday, proposed the SEC’s new ‘Regulation Crypto Assets’ rules for token fundraising.
Trump also said crypto has ‘taken a lot of pressure off the dollar.’
And that if Atkins came in with ‘some recommendations,’ then Trump would ‘certainly listen.’[4]
So, the man in charge of the world’s reserve currency says a government Bitcoin buy is under discussion, and that crypto is good for the dollar...
Five years ago, that sentence would have got you laughed out of the building.
Words that Moved Markets
The room didn’t just talk Bitcoin either.
Trump said CFTC chair Mike Selig is ‘working to bring Hyperliquid into the United States in a fully compliant and legal fashion.’
Hyperliquid is the big onchain perpetual futures exchange that Americans officially can’t use, and its HYPE token jumped 17% on that one line.[5]
He also named prediction markets among the technologies America must lead in.[6]
Back in February, I asked whether Polymarket and Kalshi were flying too close to the sun.
Well, the sun is now inviting them over for dinner, so a regulatory shutdown looks a lot less likely.
Bitcoin and the entire crypto market loved all this.
Bitcoin is back nearly to $70,000. Ethereum jumped 18% to trade over $2,200, and Hyperliquid pumped a handy 20% off the positive news.
Two weeks ago, the fear index was pinned at extreme lows, and fear was the name of the day.
That’s not so much the case now. There is just a sprinkling of hopium back in the market.
Not the End Game Yet, But on the Way
Keep your head, though, because ‘listen to recommendations’ is not the same as ‘hell yeah we’re going to buy one million Bitcoin… to the moon!’
And Trump is a dab hand at pumping up the hopes of the crypto market and then doing a big chunk of nothing for months on end.
Remember, at the first White House crypto summit in March 2025, the strategic Bitcoin reserve turned out to hold only seized coins, and Bitcoin fell about 3% on the day.[7]
There’s no plan here, no timeline and no budget line, just words.
But again, we do need to give some perspective here. Everything in a day is never the outcome. But the fact that Brian Armstrong, Vlad Tenev, the Winklevoss twins are all at the White House shoulder to shoulder with Trump and the market regulators talking up the big American crypto dream is something that was utterly unfathomable only just a couple of years ago.
We aren’t at the end game by any stretch of the imagination, but this sure does at least prove we’re very much heading in the right direction long term.

Last week, I wrote to you about the impending resurgence of the initial coin offering (ICO) that perhaps we were on the brink of the ICO being BACK!
But this time around, in a more refined and responsible way.
That would be a good thing because while 2017 and 2018 was fun, it was utterly and insanely wild.
Big money made, big money lost, big frauds, and a heck of a lot of investor risk.
So, a more refined and sophisticated ICO summer would be much welcomed from this veteran campaigner!
Good news is that yesterday, we got a step closer to that reality.
The SEC held a vote on ‘Regulation Crypto Assets,’ and it passed.
The ICO is back.
Officially, formally, on SEC letterhead, press release 2026-76 if you want the paper trail.[1]
Everything I took you through last week made the cut.
- The startup exemption of roughly $5 million over four years.
- The fundraising exemption of up to $75 million in any 12 months, with financials filed at the Commission.
- And the safe harbor that ends the investment contract once the team delivers the work it promised.
I’ll come back to that last one, because I’ve now read the details and I think it’s the sleeper of the whole proposal. Such is the significance of this, I’m going to write more about it tomorrow.
Actually, this all may end up as a far bigger deal than the CLARITY Act ends up. Dare I say, screw CLARITY, we’ve now got the platform for 2027 to be the ICO boom a decade after the first time around.
Take it Federal!
What I like about what the SEC has done here is they’ve looked ahead and not behind.
The proposal overrides state securities registration and qualification requirements for these ICO offerings, and for certain secondary market trades too.
If you’ve never had the pleasure, U.S. securities offerings don’t just answer to the SEC.
They answer to ‘blue sky’ laws in all 50 states. Fifty regulators, 50 filing regimes, 50 chances for someone to stuff up everything.
Can you imagine the stress and strain this would have on a tiny start-up crypto project that just wants to launch into the market. The American spirit of entrepreneurship hammered down by state regs and red tape.
Well, the SEC has said, stuff that up your sweater and bin it.
For new token offerings under this regime, the states are out. Just one rulebook, the federal, done and done.
That’s the kind of practical common sense that decides whether founders actually use these rules or keep incorporating in the Caymans or Malta like they have for the past decade.
‘Subpoenas and Litigation Rather than Answers’
The second thing is what the SEC has actually said.
I’d go as far as saying the SEC has never sounded this, well, this reasonable in its 92-year history.
Commissioner Uyeda described the old approach as handing good-faith builders ‘a bureaucratic runaround,’ with ‘subpoenas and litigation rather than answers.’[2]
Hester Peirce, who has carried this fight longer than anyone else has, ‘Rules should be written so that well-intentioned people can follow them without having to abandon legitimate pursuits.’[3]
And Atkins summed it up better than any regulator has previously, ‘minimum effective dose, maximum freedom to build, and durable clarity.’[4]
See… we’ve got clarity without CLARITY.
Five years ago, the SEC was a junk pile of litigation against crypto.
Now the Chairman is talking about freedom to build.
I’m the first to hate on a regulator, but this is genuinely useful.
Ok, reality check. What passed on Tuesday is a proposal, and once it lands in the Federal Register, a 60-day public comment window opens.
Then redrafts, then another vote on a final rule.
Months at best, but still also with CLARITY meandering through Congress in the background. But I think, regardless of if the CLARITY Act gets passed, these ICO frameworks are good to go. I don’t see objection coming here.
Also worth noting, the ICO exemptions might not even be the biggest prize of the last 24 hours.
That would be the safe harbor, a vital piece of the crypto puzzle that challenges the most antiquated rule of securities that’s ever existed and answers the question when does a token stop being a security?
Tomorrow, I’ll step you through the answer the SEC has proposed, and why it changes how you should think about every token you own.
Trust in crypto,
Adam Atlantic

This is the definition of ‘yield’ (in the financial sense) straight from the pages of the Merriam-Webster dictionary,
‘To produce as return from an expenditure or investment: furnish as profit or interest.’[1]
A farmer’s field yields a crop. Your cash in the bank yields interest. A rental property yields rent returns. A dividend stock yields a slice of the profits.
In these examples, there is an asset, the crop, the cash, the property, the stock that produces the yield.
But not all assets produce yield.
Let me give you an example.
Bitcoin.
Bitcoin does not produce a yield. It is by nature a non-yield-bearing asset. Baked into its code from its genesis block all the way back in January 2009 is the fact it does not generate yield.
But the boffins at TradFi’s biggest investment institutions don’t like taking no for an answer.
So, they’ve waved their financial wizardry wands and manufactured complex, convoluted ways you can ‘earn yield’ from Bitcoin.
My question, is this an improvement to Bitcoin, or a gigantic house of cards under construction, inevitably meant to come crashing down?
Where Does the Yield Come From?
Bitcoin is perhaps the most basic asset on Earth. Just 21 million units, a public blockchain, open-source code and an open network that anyone anywhere can join. Its beauty is in the fact it’s so simple.
There is no cash flow inside Bitcoin at all, and it is not like its crypto-cousins like Ethereum, where proof-of-stake allow for inbuilt yield potential.
That means when extracting ‘yield’ from Bitcoin it has to be manufactured.
Big instos like BlackRock and Goldman understand this, but they are also the kings of manufactured products.
On 12 August, Goldman Sachs (NYSE: GS) agreed to pay up to $2.25 billion[2] for NEOS Investments, an ETF provider whose crown jewel is BTCI, a Bitcoin ‘high income’ ETF distributing around 27%.
That comes hot on the heels of BlackRock (NYSE: BLK) launching BITA on 16 June, the iShares Bitcoin Premium Income ETF,[3] selling call options on up to 35% of its Bitcoin for a 15% to 25% target yield.
Again, to reiterate the entire opening to today’s essay, none of that yield is produced by Bitcoin. It is manufactured from Bitcoin’s volatility through the wizardry of TradFi.
But there’s a catch.
BTCI pays that oh-so tantalizing 27%... but it fell 42.55% over the past year.[4] Added to this, its prospectus freely discloses that distributions may partly be your capital getting handed back to you.[5]
Then there’s Michael Saylor, who I wrote to you about this week with his ‘Digital Finance Stack,’ with Bitcoin as Digital Capital, Strategy’s (Nasdaq: MSTR) STRC preferred stock as Digital Credit, the SR-strcUSX token as Digital Money, and USDT as Digital Currency.
The allure of STRC is that chunky 12% dividend, but to keep paying it and to try and get the par value back to $100, Strategy has been selling off Bitcoin and selling MSTR stock to fill the cash coffers.
What this all points to is that Bitcoin is being rinsed for all of these layers of complexity to try and extract yield from an asset that inherently does not deliver yield. And I think there’s a bit to worry about here.
Remember the Good Old Yield Days?
Remember the ‘yield wars’ of 2021? When platforms like Anchor Protocol, Celsius Network, and BlockFi were all promising eye-watering yield returns on crypto?
Remember how they all failed in 2022?
Yes, FTX was central to a large portion of that failure, but if the whole house of cards was sustainable anyway, then it wouldn’t have collapsed now, would it?
I can’t help but think funds that are claiming 20%+ yields on Bitcoin are destined for the same ending, or at the very least rinsing out all the capital of the fund to end up on the junk heap.
The fact they’re tied to Bitcoin too, isn’t a great look, but when you drill down into it all, the good news is that even if these Bitcoin yield products do end up in the crypto-products rogues gallery, only remembered as giant failures, Bitcoin would still remain untouched.
Complex products manufactured and overlayed onto the world’s most simple asset is TradFi down to a tee.
My take is that as more of these silly things get launched into the market, that you edge further and further away from them.
Bitcoin is what it is, don’t pretend it’s something else that TradFi can abuse.
Just own the asset, stack sats, hold your keys, and let volatility fade away with a long-term hodling strategy rather than trying to extract more from it that simply isn’t there.
If you disagree with me and want a slice of these funds, fine, but know exactly what you’re buying into, and that some of the yield may be your own money coming full circle, and that none of it is actually generated by Bitcoin itself.
Bitcoin yields nothing, and anyone pretending otherwise is kidding themselves.

Adam Atlantic

Strategy (Nasdaq: MSTR) sold 1,690 Bitcoin last week[1] at an average of $64,262 a coin, well under the $75,385 cost basis on those coins.
Every dollar of it went into buying back STRC.
That’s the fourth sale of 2026, and 6,948 coins gone this year.
From the first 32 coins in May through to the 3,588 in July, Michael Sellor really did just throw away the OG playbook, didn’t he?
Considering he turned ‘never sell’ into a religion, I guess it’s fair to ask, has he lost the plot?
And then he went on a tweet storm to post about the ‘monetary spectrum’ overnight, complete with AI-generated imagery (as we all know he loves a bit of AI to help him run the company…)
Crude Oil and Jet Fuel
I’ll share with you some of the posts. Bear in mind, they may initially resemble the workings of a madman, but stick with me and I’ll decipher them for you into plain English (or I’ll at least attempt to).
Saylor posted what he calls a monetary spectrum[2], with four assets arranged left to right.
Bitcoin is Digital Capital. It’s volatile and high-powered, but the basis of the modern iteration of sound money. It’s like modern gold.
STRC is Digital Credit. That’s Strategy’s variable rate preferred stock, semi-stable, paying a 12% cash dividend twice a month. It’s like a traditional bond.
SR-strcUSX is Digital Money, and that one is new.
So, take a breath…
Solstice Finance launched it on Solana[3] on 10 August. You get in by depositing their USX token into a vault holding STRC exposure.
If Bitcoin is digital gold, this is a claim on the income from gold that somebody else is holding…
Starlink brings about $1.6T mobile shakeup
SpaceX told investors it plans to launch a Starlink mobile service for U.S. consumers.
That’s a direct shot at Big Telecom and would put SpaceX head-to-head with Verizon, AT&T, and T-Mobile in a $1.6T market.
For most investors, that sounds like a telecom shakeup.
For Mode Mobile, it could be much bigger.
Mode built a platform that rewards users for everyday smartphone activity like browsing, listening, using apps, and charging.
If Starlink brings internet access to places cell towers can’t reach, it could significantly expand Mode’s addressable market.
More connected phones.
More active users.
More ways for people to earn from the device already in their pocket.
Mode has already reached 490M+ users, helped users earn and save over $1B, and generated $115M+ in cumulative revenue.
But the bigger story is what happens next.
If global connectivity keeps expanding, that model could reach more people, in more markets, with fewer barriers than ever before.
That’s why 60,000+ shareholders are already watching Mode ahead of a potential IPO.
With their Nasdaq ticker secured and more than $90M invested, Mode’s pre-IPO shares are still available at $0.52, but only until August 14.*
Strategy owns the gold, and STRC is the paper it issued against that gold, paying 12%. The vault buys the paper and cuts the income in two.
It’s a mortgage tranche, but with Bitcoin, not houses.
Then USDT is Digital Currency, stable and transactional and the thing you actually spend.
Saylor tried explaining a bit of it,
‘You can live on Bitcoin. You can also build on it. Crude oil is valuable, but civilization gets more utility by refining it into gasoline, jet fuel, plastics, lubricants, and asphalt. Bitcoin is Digital Capital. Innovation turns capital into credit, money, and currency[4].’
So, the Bitcoin sales aren’t a loss of faith, he’s now just trying to run a Bitcoin refinery.
Hal Finney Got There in 2010
None of this is new thinking. And it might sound like Saylor is some kind of Bitcoin financialization savant, but the real OG of forward Bitcoin thinking was Hal Finney.
On 30 December 2010, on the Bitcointalk forum, Hal Finney wrote that there was good reason for ‘Bitcoin-backed banks to exist, issuing their own digital cash currency[5].’
‘Actually, there is a very good reason for Bitcoin-backed banks to exist, issuing their own digital cash currency, redeemable for Bitcoins. Bitcoin itself cannot scale to have every single financial transaction in the world be broadcast to everyone and included in the block chain. There needs to be a secondary level of payment systems which is lighter weight and more efficient.
Bitcoin backed banks will solve these problems. They can work like banks did before nationalization of currency. Different banks can have different policies, some more aggressive, some more conservative.’
And he concluded,
‘I believe this will be the ultimate fate of Bitcoin, to be the “high-powered money” that serves as a reserve currency for banks that issue their own digital cash. Most Bitcoin transactions will occur between banks, to settle net transfers. Bitcoin transactions by private individuals will be as rare as... well, as Bitcoin based purchases are today.’
Maybe Finney ends up right, and where we are now is that mid-point to getting there.
Also, if Finney is right, I expect that greatly increases the underlying value of Bitcoin.
So yes, Saylor may appear a bit unhinged with what he’s doing now. But maybe he’s the critical link that gets us to Hal Finney’s long-standing prediction?

2027 and 2028 may become the year of the pivoting pivoters.
Every time I hear that word, ‘pivot,’ I can’t help but think of that hilarious Friends episode of Ross moving the sofa up the stair well.
The pivot though today is not from a 90s and 2000s era sitcom. But from a 2010s and 2020s group of Bitcoin miners.
Back in April, I told you the big miners were walking away from Bitcoin. They were pivoting to a more lucrative industry, AI compute, or HPC (high performance computing).
I also said that was good news for the rest of us. It meant cheaper machines and an easier network for anyone still willing to mine solo.
Well, overnight we just got an even bigger indication of the speed that’s moving in and how good it might be for solo miners in 2027, at least for a short while.
Riot Platforms (Nasdaq: RIOT) has signed a 20-year lease on 191 megawatts of compute at its Rockdale campus in Texas, worth $9.1 billion[1], and two extension options could take it to $16.1 billion by 2048.
The filing named the tenant only as a leading frontier AI lab. Bloomberg says it is Anthropic, the lab behind Claude[2].
Chief executive Jason Les called the deal
‘a defining moment in our evolution into a leading developer of large-scale data centers.’
He is right, and that is exactly the problem.
To fund the build, Riot has been selling Bitcoin. Its treasury fell from 15,680 Bitcoin to 11,380 in a single quarter[3].
Not only that, you look at the value of their Bitcoin. On 31 December 2025, it was $1.2 billion. Now, just $340 million.
A mining company selling Bitcoin so it can stop mining Bitcoin…
And Riot is late to this. Public miners have now announced over $70 billion in AI and high-performance computing contracts[4], and CoinShares reckons AI could be 70% of listed miner revenue by December, up from about 30%.
The Gaping Hole for You and Me
This all comes as network difficulty has fallen roughly 19% from its November peak near 156[5] trillion and now sits around 127 trillion.
That is only the second year-on-year fall in Bitcoin’s 17-year history. The first was China banning mining back in 2021.
Network hashrate has gone from about 1,108 EH/s down to roughly 890 EH/s.
Meanwhile, the gear is being dumped. Bitmain has quoted $3 to $4 per terahash on older hydro units, and a used S19 XP now goes for $800 to $900.
A Bitaxe the size of a credit card costs $60 to $150. Cheap enough for you yet? It is for me. I’m going to load up on some mining gear in the coming weeks and get back into solo mining (again).
Solo miners are already having a great run at it by the way, and they found 24 blocks in the past 12 months for 75.44 Bitcoin, up 41% on the year before[6].
One of them ran a $150 Bitaxe for eight hours in July and took a block worth about $200,000…
That leaves fewer rivals and cheaper machines on an easier network, and the window is open right now. But it might not be a window open forever.
The Pivot Back
Compute centralizes, and it always has. CoreWeave is targeting 1.7 gigawatts of live power this year, Nebius grew revenue 684% in a quarter, and lenders will back two or three of these names rather than two hundred.
So, what happens to the mid-sized miner who ripped out ASICs to chase AI money?
They get squeezed out slowly, with liquid cooling they cannot fund, credit they cannot get, and customers who would rather sign with CoreWeave.
By the time that bites, Bitcoin should be running hard again, and that is when they pivot back to mining.
They still own the power contracts, the second-hand ASICs will be cheap, and a hashprice of $31 today looks very different at $250,000 Bitcoin.
The elasticity is the whole game, but what also makes for opportunity.
One is available now, while difficulty falls and a home rig is a real lottery ticket, which isn’t all that hard to operate, and the other comes later for operators nimble enough to swing back to Bitcoin at the moment it pays up again.
These companies chase money. That is precisely why they left in the first place.
Bitcoin doesn’t mind either way. It found a block ten minutes ago, and it will find another one shortly.
So, I say, mine now, chance your arm at solo mining again, and then as things turn, and it’s harder to solo mine, transition some of those earnings into the miners that will run hard in line with Bitcoin.
Seems like a fun way to play the pivot from Bitcoin to AI and back to Bitcoin.
Trust in crypto,
Adam Atlantic

Block 961,632 arrived on Saturday, and a small group of Bitcoin nodes decided it was not valid.
That was the Bitcoin Improvement Proposal number 110 (BIP-110) going from a point of discussion to a full-blown chain split. And it lasted about as long as a round of drinks at the pub.
A non-valid block sounds like a scary thing for Bitcoin. But fear not. It is actually the network humming along as intended.
So, what exactly took place? And what else has been bubbling away in crypto-land in the last week?
Today, I thought instead of running through just one development in crypto, I’d run you through five, just to show you that every day is a busy day when you’re neck deep in crypto markets.
Two Blocks and Out
Back to BIP-110…
BIP-110 wanted to restrict non-financial data on Bitcoin for a year. Ordinals mostly, which are pictures and text written onto individual Satoshi’s[1].
It needed 55% of miners signaling support, and it got 2.53%, so the nodes enforcing it split off onto a chain of their own[2].
A pool called Roughnecks mined two blocks of it and then stopped, because the branch had inherited Bitcoin’s full difficulty with almost none of the hashpower[3]. That makes it nearly impossible to actually be economically viable on this new chain…
Elon and Apple just made waves for US #1 software company
Apple just enabled Starlink satellite support to T-Mobile iPhones.
One of the biggest potential winners from global satellite coverage?
Just about everything Elon touches turns to gold:
- SpaceX IPOs at $1.77T
- Tesla up by over 30,000% since IPO
- And now - iPhone’s get satellite access
But while Wall Street focuses on Apple, Mode Mobile is quietly positioned to capitalize on this global satellite revolution.
Their EarnPhone technology already:
- Reaches 490M+ users worldwide
- Helped those users save and earn over $1 billion
- Grew revenue 32,481%
And that was before global satellite coverage.
With SpaceX eliminating “dead zones,” Mode’s earning technology can reach 3B+ unbanked people globally in rural populations worldwide.
We’re talking about emerging markets with no infrastructure.
Right now, you can still invest at $0.52/share.
Over 60,000 shareholders have already claimed their shares and they’ve just secured the $MODE ticker from Nasdaq. The time to invest is now, before any potential IPO.*
Except that now effectively kills the chain-split risk holders were pricing. It also settles the thing I keep coming back to, which is that Bitcoin cannot be governed from outside.
It also shows us that Bitcoin can change, but if there is no network support for it, then Bitcoin will just keep on doing its thing, forever. Unbreakable and undefeated.
September, then Who Knows
As the Bitcoin rumblings were taking place, Senate Majority Leader John Thune confirmed there would be no CLARITY Act vote before the recess and promised one first thing back on 14 September[4].
There goes more or less any hope of CLARITY getting done in 2026. At best, 2027 is the year of progress, but even then, it’s still too soon to say.
The blockage here is the same thing, that pesky conflict-of-interest ban that would stop senior officials, the president among them, from holding crypto positions[5].
But remember, the market almost has now given up hope this is going to happen any time soon. Which is great, because I look at the Bitcoin price and the wider market, and in the last few weeks, well, not much price action has been going on.
Which means that coiled spring is storing up a heck of a lot of kinetic energy ready to release in 2027…
Mastercard Bought Instead of Renting
Speaking of releasing a heap of energy into the market, Mastercard (NYSE: MA) closed its buyout of BVNK last week for $1.8 billion[6], four months ahead of the timetable it gave in March.
The dichotomy between the speed of government, and the speed of private enterprise here is clear to see, comical if you ask me.
BVNK moves about $30 billion a year across 200 countries, swapping between dollars and stablecoins at each end of a payment.
Why buy the company rather than sign a contract with it? Because BVNK also sits inside Agent Pay for Machines, Mastercard’s programme for software agents[7]. It was already in the door, and now Mastercard owns it all.
Stablefication has reached the card networks. That’s a huge deal, and it goes to show that in the not so distant future, you’ll swipe your Mastercard and unknowingly be transacting in stablecoins.
Will you care? Will anyone? No. So long as it just works. But for every piece of the stablecoin puzzle, the chains they live on and the platforms that retains their value, there’s a lot of upside to come.
And… that’s before the AI-to-AI economy really gets cranking too!
Saylor’s Diary of a CEO
Strategy (Nasdaq: MSTR) sold 1,638 Bitcoin between 27 July and 2 August for about $104.7 million, at roughly $63,957 a coin[8]. Michael Sellor strikes again.
He then went on the hugely popular The Diary of a CEO podcast last week, saying the point was proving the company could sell without breaking the market[9].
It worked. Bitcoin traded slightly higher on the news, and Strategy still holds 842,138 coins bought at an average of $75,419. Sure, it’s underwater still, but just think about MSTR’s upside if the market rips into another bull market of all-time highs.
By the way, go check out the episode of Diary of a CEO here. It’s worth it.
Brazil Calls it Fraud Prevention, We Call it Capital Control
Finally, a lot has been said about self-custody in the last week. I stand by the fact that it’s still the best way to control your digital asset wealth.
And here’s some proof as to why…
Resolution BCB No. 584, published on 7 August, will make Brazilian crypto exchanges hold transfers over $10,000 for 24 hours from 1 January 2027[10].
Two kinds specifically. The ones going to a foreign platform, and the ones going to a wallet you control yourself[11].
Fraud is the stated reason. But those are capital controls under the guise of safety. I’ve seen this kind of nonsense before. It’s a control mechanism, and I hate it.
The fact they can do this, is sufficient reason to get your coins off an exchange while nobody is stopping you. You think it can’t happen to you? Well, when you look at how the government is behaving around CLARITY, you really think there’s still not a day, maybe with a different government, that makes crypto as maligned as it was a decade ago?
I’m not taking that risk, and I don’t think you should either.
Not your keys, not your crypto.
Trust in crypto,
Adam Atlantic

Three weeks ago, I wrote to you about Bartok’s Dog.
Bartok is Tony Robbins’ (the world-renowned motivational speaker) AI agent, and the story goes that it minted 12 NFTs, sold them to other AI agents, and bought itself a Sony robot dog with the proceeds so it could ‘upload’ itself and attend one of Robbins’ seminars.
Wild isn’t it!
Nobody approved Bartok to do this. Robbins only found out when a staff member texted him.
Now I have a saying, never let the truth get in the way of a good story, and while this tale from Robbins may seem fanciful, truth is every technical piece of that story exists and is running.
But an agent cannot open a bank account or pass KYC. Hence, the NFT sales from Bartok. But an AI agent can hold a key.
So, as I’ve covered with you for some time now, crypto is the only ‘money’ a machine is able to use.
What I never answered was the obvious follow-up. What stops your agent doing the same?
Last week, MetaMask gave us an answer…
Guard Mode or Beast Mode
MetaMask Agent Wallet went live to everyone last Thursday[1].
It lets an AI agent trade on Hyperliquid and supported EVM chains, inside spending limits and protocol permissions you set beforehand.
It is self-custodial, but importantly, the agent never touches your keys, and it cannot rewrite the rules you gave it.
It connects to Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, OpenClaw, Hermes, and OpenCode, which covers most of what a working trader already has open.
You set the daily spend caps yourself. You set the list of protocols the agent is allowed near, then you pick one of two modes.
I kind of like where they went here too…
Starlink brings about $1.6T mobile shakeup
SpaceX told investors it plans to launch a Starlink mobile service for U.S. consumers.
That’s a direct shot at Big Telecom and would put SpaceX head-to-head with Verizon, AT&T, and T-Mobile in a $1.6T market.
For most investors, that sounds like a telecom shakeup.
For Mode Mobile, it could be much bigger.
Mode built a platform that rewards users for everyday smartphone activity like browsing, listening, using apps, and charging.
If Starlink brings internet access to places cell towers can’t reach, it could significantly expand Mode’s addressable market.
More connected phones.
More active users.
More ways for people to earn from the device already in their pocket.
Mode has already reached 490M+ users, helped users earn and save over $1B, and generated $115M+ in cumulative revenue.
But the bigger story is what happens next.
If global connectivity keeps expanding, that model could reach more people, in more markets, with fewer barriers than ever before.
That’s why 60,000+ shareholders are already watching Mode ahead of a potential IPO.
With their Nasdaq ticker secured and more than $90M invested, Mode’s pre-IPO shares are still available at $0.52, but only until August 14.*
Guard Mode is the default. Anything outside your policy stops dead and waits for your approval.
Then there’s Beast Mode.
Yes, Beast Mode is opt-in for people who want fewer interruptions, to just let their agents run free, and only flag malicious transactions in order to pause the agent.
Sounds grand, doesn’t it.
Until it does a ‘Bartok’s Dog.’
Every supported transaction runs through a simulation, then threat scanning from Blockaid, then MEV protection, all before the thing ever signs and executes.
What if all three barriers clear, and the transaction still loses money to a malicious transaction?
Happy days folks, MetaMask covers the loss, up to $10,000 a month[2].
MetaMask is effectively writing insurance against the chance that its own product gets it wrong.
It is the first time anyone has put a price on machine error.
The Traffic is Not there Yet
It’s a small trickle for now, but I can see the AI-to-AI (A2A) economy gathering unstoppable speed.
Coinbase (Nasdaq: COIN) shipped Agentic Wallets in February[3], Cloudflare announced its own agent wallets last week too[4], and MetaMask went live two days after Cloudflare.
Three of the biggest names in the online world shipped agentic permission layers for A2A money inside six months, two of them landing in the same week.
And the numbers are worse than the announcements suggest.
Artemis Analytics found in March that roughly 95% of x402 volume was signaling rather than an actual sale[5]. Real commercial exchange was running near $28,000 a day.
Twenty-eight grand a day is one decent suburban car dealership.
A survey in June put the share of consumers willing to let AI buy things unchecked at 14%. But I recall that when Bitcoin began to emerge in 2010, it was barely a blip on anyone’s radar.
And these are the kinds of things that seem almost nonsensical to start with, and then suddenly you have major corporations getting involved, governments and the wealthiest people on the planet.
The speed in which the crypto economy has exploded in 17 years is incredible. And most of that really only in the last five to 10.
Now you’ve already seen the speed of adoption for AI in our world. That’s realistically been about two years on a consumer side of things. So how fast, once an A2A economy is up and about, do you think adoption will take then?
I suggest to you that within a matter of just a couple of years, the A2A economy on crypto networks will surge past what human crypto transacting has done in a decade and a half.
It feels like a tsunami of opportunity is coming in this space, and that for now we haven’t’ even properly registered the shockwave on the Richter scale.
Trust in crypto,
Adam Atlantic

Tom Lee’s Bitmine (NYSE: BMNR) has 4,917,189 ETH staked[1]. It’s the single largest ETH staking bag on earth.
At $1,880 per ETH, it’s worth around $9.2 billion. Add other crypto and cash and they’ve got around $11.3 billion in the coffers.
That staked ETH however pays about $247 million a year[2].
That cheque is the case for owning BMNR rather than owning ETH yourself. It just takes a lot of the stress and hassle out of dealing with ETH holdings. And if there was ever a week to own crypto by proxy, this has kind of been the one.
So, things are well and good with Bitmine, and if ETH’s price rockets so will their value, so will their ETH staking income.
Or will it…?
An Unwelcome Halving?
A draft called Tapered Issuance Burn, now numbered EIP-8363[3], landed in the Ethereum repo on 4 August.
Lock up ETH, help run the network, get paid in newly created ETH. That’s staking.
Right now, 41.5 million coins are locked up, which is 34% of every ETH in existence[4], with another 2.49 million in the queue waiting to get in.
The payout per staker falls as more people join, because the same pot gets split more ways. But it falls slowly, and it flattens out at about 1.5%[5]. Even in the mad scenario where every coin on earth was staked, you’d still be paid 1.5% to do it…
Apple’s price hike just made this opportunity more interesting
Apple just made smartphones even more expensive, raising the price on most of their products by $200 or more.
Consumers are paying more than ever for technology that gives them nothing back.
More expensive devices. Higher upgrade costs. Still no way for users to share in the value their phones create.
Mode Mobile is building the opposite model.
Instead of a smartphone that only costs money, Mode gives users the opportunity to earn from the devices they already own.
Just like Uber turned cars into taxis, and Airbnb turned homes into hotels.
And the results speak for themselves:
- 490M+ users reached
- $1B+ earned and saved by EarnOS users
- $115M+ cumulative revenue
- 32,481% 3-year revenue growth, Deloitte’s #1 fastest-growing software company in North America in 2023.
- $MODE Nasdaq ticker secured
As premium devices get pricier, Mode’s timing looks even more compelling.
Consumers need technology that gives value back.
Advertisers and AI companies need permissioned first-party data.
Mode sits at the intersection of both, creating a platform where users can participate in the value their phone activity creates.
Pre-IPO shares are still available at $0.52, with up to 20% bonus shares for a limited time.*
There’s never a moment where a big custodian looks at the numbers and thinks ‘not worth it.’ The pile just keeps growing, and the coins keep moving from individual owners to Coinbase, Lido, the ETF issuers, and companies like BitMine.
Now, an epoch is a six-and-a-half-minute chunk of Ethereum time. In each one, every validator gets handed jobs and gets paid for doing them.
This new proposal takes a slice off each of those payments and destroys it. Not redirects it, destroys it. The staker never sees it and nobody else gets it either.
The slice starts small and grows as more ETH gets staked. At 60.25 million coins locked up (roughly half the total supply) that slice is the whole payment. Do every job perfectly, earn nothing.
Which is the point of this proposal. It builds in an off switch that doesn’t currently exist, so the market decides where staking stops instead of the reward curve deciding.
At today’s current staking percentage (34%), if this new proposal were put into action the slice would be about half your income.
That means where staking now delivers around 2.6%, it would cut right down to 1.2%.
Two Trades, Not One
For ETH, the crypto, this reads as good news for its longer-term price, because less new supply means less dilution for holders.
But for the businesses selling you ETH exposure, it’s a different proposition.
Aave founder Stani Kulechov ran the maths himself. All-in validator income falls from 2.862% to 1.476%.
A 48% cut.
His point is that anyone staking for the money walks away from ETH, and the centralized institutions inherit the network.
Markets agreed fast, with LDO falling 14.8% between the 4th and the 5th of August, ETHFI down 11.6%, albeit ETH itself was flat…
Which brings us back to Tom Lee, because halving the yield in this way means BitMine’s $247 million a year of ETH yield into something nearer $120 million.
BMNR trades at about $18, a market cap of $11 billion compared to $11.3 billion of crypto and cash.
There is no premium left there to soak up the hit. $120 million is still a nice little kicker, but it does radically alter the point of BMNR.
Same story for the staking funds, where the rewards are the product.
BlackRock’s ETHB has been live since 12 March, stakes up to 95% of its coins and pays 82% of the rewards out monthly[6]. Halve that yield and maybe investors withdraw at a rate of knots?
Will any of this actually happen? Not soon, and possibly never, it is still a proposal.
And even if it was passed, it would be the second half of 2027 when the next major Ethereum upgrade is likely to hit.
It’s not an immediate problem, but it does highlight there are additional risks and considerations not just for blockchains like ETH (albeit I think it’s a good thing for the underlying long-term price of ETH), but for those ancillary companies’ people are investing in around it.
Owning ETH and owning a company that stakes ETH sometimes get confused as one investment idea.
They are not the same trade.
Make sure you know what you’re buying before you buy. And when in doubt, I say just own the crypto itself, which in this case would be ETH.
Trust in crypto,
Adam Atlantic

Two weeks ago, I bought into the biggest IPO in Asia this year. But my TradFi broker had nothing to do with it.
The company is ChangXin Memory Technologies (SSE: 688825), or CXMT. It is based in Hefei, China and makes DRAM chips, the memory that goes in phones and AI servers.
It is now the fourth biggest memory maker on earth.
Beijing has spent years feeding it money to break the grip Samsung, SK Hynix, and Micron hold on memory.
The numbers it has been generating are as astounding as you’d expect from an AI memory company.
CXMT guided to first-half revenue of 110 to 120 billion yuan[1], more than the company had earned in its whole life up to that point.
Profit guidance came in more than 2,200% above the year before.
AI servers eat memory, memory prices went vertical, and CXMT had the capacity to sell into it...
Such was the demand and hype around this that it priced its IPO on Shanghai’s STAR Market at 8.66 yuan a share (US$1.28), raising about $8.6 billion[2].
Nothing bigger has ever listed on the STAR Market in its seven-year history.
And the rampant demand meant the IPO was around 212 times oversubscribed[3].
It listed on 27 July and opened at 49.50 yuan (US$7.33). It touched a 535% gain on day one[4], and by lunch CXMT was the most valuable listed company in China.
Nomura came out that same morning with a buy rating and a 116 yuan target[5], which is a bit over $17 a share.
Built to Keep You Out
It was quite the market debut. Only problem… I could not buy a single share of it, and neither could you.
Stock before the IPO went to buyers like Alibaba Cloud, Meituan, and Xiaomi. Retail investors never had a chance.
Even inside China a punter needs 500,000 yuan in assets and two years of trading history to be allowed near a STAR Market stock.
From outside China it gets worse…
Palantir’s 1,540% vs 32,481% company no one’s talking about
Anyone who invested in Palantir at its IPO in 2020 could be sitting on nearly 1,540% gains right now.
But that great return is already in the past, and the stock is now one of the S&P 500’s most expensive.
And while Palantir was climbing on the back of your public information, another company was redefining big data.
Mode Mobile has already delivered 32,481% revenue growth before even going public.
Mode has:
- 490M+ users
- $1B+ paid to users
- $115M+ in real revenue
- Nasdaq ticker secured for potential IPO
- Pre-IPO shares available for a limited time
Mode’s model pays users for their screen time and turns Big Tech’s free data mining play into a cash-generating engine for everyone.
Palantir now trades at ~85× forward earnings, which means Wall Street has already priced in massive expectations.
But Mode?
Still private.
That means the market hasn’t had its say yet.
Right now, investors can get Mode Mobile shares at early-stage pricing.
When the Nasdaq ticker potentially goes live, that window could close fast.
60,000+ shareholders have already invested over $100M in Mode, and pre-IPO shares are still available at $0.52/share.
But the opportunity to get in on that price closes on August 14.
Palantir’s moment has passed.
Mode’s may just be starting.*
A STAR stock only reaches foreign buyers through Stock Connect if it sits in the SSE 180 or SSE 380 index, or has shares listed over in Hong Kong.
Even then only the big institutions can trade it. Everyone else needs a QFII license from Beijing[6].
Your broker doesn’t have one, and mine doesn’t either.
The hottest listing of the year, in the hottest sector on earth, was sealed off from every one of us...
…almost.
USDC, Two Chains, Done
On 15 July, the day before the books opened for CXMT, Trade.xyz listed a CXMT perpetual IPOP on Hyperliquid.
It runs on the HIP-3 framework, which lets any builder list a perpetual market on things that are not crypto. The reference price was $5[7].
Before the IPO, it had traded down to around $6.20. I like the direction memory is heading, and I also liked the idea of hedging my U.S. listed memory bets with a Chinese one.
And if Nomura’s analysis (and my own) was in the ballpark, CXMT could be a nice little earner. Even at mid $6.
So, I moved some cash into USDC, bridged from Ethereum over to Arbitrum, and then via Hyperliquid, bought CXMT-USDC at $6.30.
I’d have much preferred to get in on the IPO price at $1.28 but that was never available, but a pre-listing in the mid-6s I could stomach. And it was the only price on offer anywhere to someone like me who wanted to trade CXMT.
It tracks the Shanghai stock pretty closely now, give or take a cent or two, and it has settled around the $8 mark. So far, so good.
Now, I should say, I know exactly what I own here, and it is not the CXMT stock.
There is no dividend and no vote. I do not own the stock.
If the market thins out or the price feed breaks, the loss is mine alone.
I accept all of that.
CXMT could halve from here too. Morningstar puts fair value on the stock at 14.90 yuan[8], which works out at about $2.20 a share... So, there’s inherent risk in the investment idea too.
But I do hold price exposure to a firm that the TradFi system effectively blocked me from getting near.
I can trade it at 3am on a Sunday and it settles on the spot. Nobody asked to see my passport, nobody cares where I reside. Nobody cares if I’ve invested $10 or $10,000.
This is what crypto said it would do from the start, which is open the markets to anyone, anywhere. This is what breaking down TradFi barriers looks like.
It’s likely if I see something again in the IPO markets that I want exposure to, I’ll probably use Hyperliquid again.
And it’s why I believe that every stock on earth ends up trading this way. It’s just better than what TradFi has to offer.
Trust in crypto,
Adam Atlantic
