One day in 2013, the FBI delivered an awkward piece of news to Senator Dianne Feinstein: She appeared to have a spy in her midst. Or something remarkably close to one. And for quite some time.
This was not just any senator.
Feinstein was one of the most powerful political figures in California.
And, at the time the FBI came calling, she was chairwoman of the Senate Select Committee on Intelligence—the committee charged with overseeing America’s spies.
Now America’s spies were telling her that Chinese intelligence had cultivated someone working for her.
One contemporary source described Feinstein’s reaction in a single word: “Mortified.”
One can understand why.
The employee was forced to retire. The matter went unreported by the media.
Even the rest of Feinstein’s staff wasn’t told what had happened.
No prosecution followed.
And for roughly five years almost nobody outside a small circle knew anything about it.
Until, in 2018, the story escaped.
And was promptly reduced to: Dianne Feinstein’s Chinese spy driver.
Trivial, right?
Wrong.
He Wasn’t Just “The Driver”
Driving Senator Feinstein was one of the man’s duties.
According to reporting at the time, he also worked as a gofer in her San Francisco office and, much more importantly, served as a liaison to the Asian-American community.
He attended functions involving the Chinese Consulate on Feinstein’s behalf.
In other words, he wasn’t merely the fellow waiting outside with the Lincoln.
He was inside Sen. Dianne Feinstein’s political machinery.
The individual was never officially named, although subsequent reporting identified longtime staffer Russell Lowe as the likely employee. Lowe had worked in Feinstein’s San Francisco operation for about 20 years and was listed on payroll records as an office director.
Feinstein never confirmed Lowe’s identity as the employee involved, and Lowe was never charged with espionage or any other crime arising from the matter.
The Friend
According to the San Francisco Chronicle’s reconstruction, the story began during a trip to Asia. The staffer was visiting relatives. He met someone. They became friendly. The new acquaintance stayed in touch during subsequent visits.
The friend, according to the Chronicle’s source, was connected to China’s Ministry of State Security (MSS)—the principal civilian intelligence service.
And apparently the American staffer did not initially understand what was happening.
“He just thought it was some friend,” the source said.
Intelligence recruitment rarely begins: Good afternoon. I’m from Chinese intelligence. Would you care to betray the United States?
It begins: Lovely to meet you.
Then: Let’s have dinner next time you’re in town.
Then: You work for Senator Feinstein? Fascinating.
Then: What does she really think about China?
Was He a Spy?
Feinstein emphatically rejected the word.
After the story broke, Feinstein said, “He was not a mole or a spy, but someone who a foreign intelligence service thought it could recruit.”
She added that the employee had no access to classified or sensitive information or legislative matters, that the FBI had found no compromise of national-security information, and that he left her office immediately after she was briefed.
But Politico reported that, according to four former intelligence officials, a staffer in Feinstein’s San Francisco office had been reporting back to the MSS.
Another former official said the suspected informant was being “run” by officials at China’s San Francisco Consulate.
And one former official offered the driest assessment of all: The handler in San Francisco had “probably got an award back in China.”
The staffer may genuinely not have considered himself a spy.
The Chinese service may have considered him a source.
This is one of the charming asymmetries of espionage.
You do not necessarily have to know you’ve been recruited to be useful.
What Did He Give the MSS?
Feinstein’s California employees did not hold security clearances, according to her office, and the FBI apparently concluded that nothing of substance involving classified information had been passed.
Case closed.
Except… classified information is only one species of intelligence.
Imagine you are the MSS officer responsible for understanding California politics.
Would you rather steal a classified memorandum that becomes obsolete next Tuesday? Or have someone inside the office of California’s senior senator telling you…
Who really has influence with her? Who gets returned telephone calls?
Which Chinese-American organizations matter? Which donors matter?
Which politicians are rising? Which ones dislike Beijing? Which ones merely pretend to?
When will Feinstein visit China? Who accompanies her? Who briefs her? What arguments persuade her?
What does she say privately that differs from what she says publicly?
Who is likely to become the next mayor? Governor? Congressman? Senator?
That is political intelligence. And unlike a classified report, it keeps paying dividends.
The Driver’s Seat
Which brings us back to the much-mocked job of driver.
Suppose he did drive Feinstein regularly.
People dismiss drivers because drivers do not appear on organizational charts beside the national-security adviser.
Intelligence officers do not dismiss drivers.
Drivers know where you go, when you go, whom you meet, who gets picked up, who gets dropped off, which meetings run long, which ones end badly.
Who telephones while you’re in the car. What you say immediately after leaving a meeting.
A driver is frequently present during the moment when public people stop performing for the public.
They get into the car. The door closes. And they talk.
No security clearance required.
The chauffeur merely needs ears.
San Francisco: Nirvana
To understand why Beijing might care so much about a California field office, forget Washington for a moment.
Look west.
Former American intelligence officials told Politico that California occupied an exceptional place in Chinese intelligence operations.
One said California was the only U.S. state for which the MSS maintained a dedicated unit, apart from its Washington operation.
And San Francisco?
One former official called it: “Nirvana.”
Why?
Technology. Money. Universities.
A vast Chinese and Chinese-American community.
Political influence. And perhaps more important: future politicians.
Mayors become congressmen. District attorneys become senators. City councilmen become governors.
Young politicians who appear insignificant today may be sitting on intelligence committees 15 years later.
You don’t wait until then to meet them. You meet them now.
Sound familiar? It should.
Fang Fang.
Before Fang Fang
Years later, another Chinese intelligence story emerged from precisely the same political ecosystem.
Christine Fang.
Fang Fang.
Student. Networker. Fundraiser. Political enthusiast.
Friend to ambitious young California politicians.
She cultivated Eric Swalwell while he was still climbing the ladder.
Helped with fundraising. Helped place an intern.
And disappeared back to China after the FBI became interested.
Again, the value was not necessarily classified information.
It was access.
Habits. Preferences. Networks. Personalities.
The politicians who might someday matter.
Same geography. Same patience. Same interest in California political networks.
Different asset. Different target.
Very similar philosophy: Plant early.
Dianne & China
If you were drawing up a list of California politicians worth understanding, Dianne Feinstein would have been near the top.
Her relationship with China went back decades.
As mayor of San Francisco, she championed the city’s sister-city relationship with Shanghai.
She developed an unusually close political relationship with Shanghai mayor Jiang Zemin, who subsequently became China’s paramount leader.
They visited one another. Dined together.
Feinstein became a prominent advocate of engagement with Beijing and of maintaining favorable U.S.-China trade relations.
Her husband, financier Richard Blum, meanwhile developed business interests in China.
A major Los Angeles Times investigation in 1997 reported that Blum’s investment activities in China had expanded substantially while Feinstein’s foreign-policy role concerning China was also expanding.
Blum accompanied his wife to meetings with senior Chinese leaders, including Jiang.
Both repeatedly maintained that there was a firewall between Feinstein’s public duties and Blum’s private business activities.
The Times found no evidence that Feinstein had acted improperly because of those investments.
That isn’t the point here.
The point is access.
Feinstein’s office dealt extensively with Chinese officials and Chinese-American political organizations.
Her California staff therefore occupied precisely the kind of intersection a foreign intelligence service would find interesting.
And Beijing had already demonstrated that interest.
The First Warning
Here is a detail often omitted from the driver story.
The 2013 FBI visit was not Feinstein’s first warning about Chinese political influence.
In 1996, the FBI privately warned six members of Congress—including Feinstein—that U.S. intelligence had information suggesting the Chinese government might try to funnel illegal campaign contributions to them through Asian donors or foreign corporations.
Officials described the intelligence behind those warnings as “specific and credible.”
Feinstein subsequently returned approximately $12,000 in donations connected to individuals associated with Indonesia’s Lippo Group amid the broader campaign-finance controversy.
The Consulate
The San Francisco Chinese Consulate sits on Laguna Street.
Consulates issue visas. Promote trade. Assist nationals. Host receptions.
And, throughout the history of diplomacy, provide extraordinarily convenient cover for intelligence officers.
According to Politico’s reporting, the Feinstein informant was “run” by officials based at the San Francisco Consulate.
Which makes his role as Asian-American community liaison particularly interesting.
A liaison liaises. He attends events. Meets community leaders. Maintains relationships. Represents the senator. And among the institutions with which such a liaison might naturally interact is… the Chinese Consulate.
No clandestine rendezvous required. No dead drop in Golden Gate Park.
The relationship itself provides the cover.
Official contact conceals unofficial collection.
Elegant.
Why No Prosecution?
The obvious question is why nobody was arrested.
If the FBI truly believed someone inside the office of the Senate Intelligence Committee chairwoman was reporting to Chinese intelligence, why simply escort him toward retirement?
The likely answer lies in what he reportedly provided.
Political information.
Not classified documents. Not national-defense information. Not missile plans.
One former intelligence official told Politico that this probably made prosecution considerably more difficult.
So the FBI did what counterintelligence services sometimes do when prosecution is impossible or undesirable.
Disrupt the operation.
Tell Feinstein. Remove the access. Burn the relationship.
Watch what happens next.
From a CI perspective, arrest is not always victory.
Sometimes merely making the other service close the file is enough.
And Then Everyone Kept Quiet
Perhaps the most Washington detail is what happened afterward.
Almost nothing.
The employee departed. Feinstein’s broader staff wasn’t informed why.
There was no public announcement. No congressional hearing. No great public investigation into Chinese intelligence operations targeting California politicians.
Then five years later reporters found it.
By which time the alleged operation was old news to the people who mattered.
And what was the public debate?
Mostly whether Donald Trump had exaggerated matters by calling the man a Chinese spy.
A wonderfully American solution.
Take a serious counterintelligence question—and turn it into an argument about terminology.
Spy or Source?
Let’s settle the terminology.
Was the man a trained MSS intelligence officer? There is no evidence of that.
Was he knowingly stealing classified intelligence? Apparently not.
Was he prosecuted as a foreign agent? No.
Did Feinstein say he was a spy? She specifically said he wasn’t.
But did former U.S. intelligence officials say someone in her office was reporting political information to the MSS and being run from the Chinese Consulate?
Yes.
At some point, semantic modesty becomes rather exhausting.
Call him an informant. A source. A contact. A cultivated asset. A dupe.
A recruit who did not fully appreciate his recruitment.
The Chinese probably had their own term. And theirs is the one that ultimately matters.
The Chinese Method
China’s political collection is patient.
Build relationships. Cultivate communities. Understand local politics. Spot rising figures.
Develop access. Make yourself useful.
Wait.
The target need not commit treason. He merely needs to talk.
The information need not be classified. It merely needs to be useful.
And the source need not even think of himself as a source.
That is the beauty of it.
Imagine the situation reversed.
Suppose CIA had cultivated someone working inside the office of a senior Chinese official. For years.
Not just any official. Someone responsible for overseeing Chinese intelligence.
Our source drove him and managed parts of his local office. Represented him in dealings with the American diplomatic community.
Knew political leaders. Knew schedules. Knew personalities.
And quietly reported political information back to us.
There would be champagne. Promotions. Perhaps an award.
The Man Behind the Wheel
The story of Feinstein’s staffer never became the national scandal it might have become.
There was no evidence Feinstein knowingly permitted anything improper. No evidence classified information was compromised.
But viewed beside Parlor Maid, Fang Fang, OPM and the other Chinese counterintelligence cases we’ve been examining, the episode looks less like an amusing historical footnote.
It looks like another piece of a pattern.
Katrina Leung cultivated FBI counterintelligence officers.
Fang Fang cultivated ambitious politicians.
The OPM hackers stole the biographies of millions of clearance holders.
And somewhere in San Francisco, Chinese intelligence apparently discovered that you could learn quite a lot about American politics from the man who answered the telephone, attended the consulate reception—and occasionally drove the senator home.
The lesson is almost embarrassingly simple.
We spend billions protecting classified information.
SCIFs. Clearances. Encryption. Polygraphs. Armed guards.
But intelligence is not merely what sits inside the safe.
Sometimes it is what gets said in the car on the way home.

Claude Palmero chose an interesting man with whom to proclaim his innocence.
Thierry Lacoste.
In July, the two former intimates of Prince Albert II appeared together at a press conference and portrayed themselves as victims of a judicial vendetta in Monaco.
Two months later, Lacoste was taken into police custody.
And now the former lawyer, childhood friend and longtime confidant of Prince Albert finds himself caught in a criminal investigation involving allegations of corruption and influence peddling surrounding one of Monaco’s most controversial property developments: the Esplanade des Pêcheurs.
Investigators believe Lacoste traded upon his extraordinary proximity to the prince for the benefit of private interests.
We have no doubt, having investigated Lacoste—and Palmero—and discovered a pattern of corruption.
The arrest creates an awkward problem for Palmero, who—of course—is under investigation himself.
His July press conference with Lacoste was supposed to be a counterattack.
They described themselves as targets of a judicial campaign and pointed toward a small group of people whom they blamed for their exclusion from the Palace.
Lacoste presented his campaign as a matter of principle.
Palmero complained about the manner in which Monaco’s justice system was treating him.
It was quite the performance.
Now one of them has been hauled into police custody and charged with serious crimes.
Which left me pondering the latest news about the other.
So I checked for an update.
CLAUDE PALMERO…
…wasn’t merely Prince Albert’s bean-counter.
He was administrator of the assets of the Sovereign and the princely family.
His father had performed a similar function for Prince Rainier (until a scandal got him ousted).
Claude Palmero consequently occupied a position of almost unparalleled financial intimacy with the Grimaldis.
He knew where the money was. He knew where it went. He knew the structures through which it moved.
He knew the property deals. He knew the players. And he played the players to his own personal advantage.
And he knew the secrets. For more than 20 years.
Then Albert fired him in June 2023. Escorted from his office by the Palace Guard—and told to not come back.
Read about it here…
And—just like that—Claude Palmero discovered transparency and shape-shifted into… a “reformer.”
PALMERO IS A CRIMINAL DEFENDANT
In January 2026, he was charged with violating the secrecy of an investigation after procedural documents relating to cases in which he was not a party were reportedly discovered during a search of his home.
Then, in March, following a complaint by the princely family, Palmero was charged again, this time over alleged violation of professional secrecy and invasion of privacy relating to confidential material that found its way into the press.
WE KNEW PALMERO
This is where our perspective differs somewhat from that of journalists who discovered Claude Palmero after his dismissal and trumpet his claims.
We knew about him two decades ago.
While operating an intelligence service for Prince Albert, we investigated and reported on precisely the networks of influence, questionable characters and entrenched interests surrounding the Palace that Palmero now professes to find so disturbing.
Back then, Claude Palmero wasn’t standing outside that establishment blowing a whistle.
He was inside it. Deep inside it.
He was one of the most entrenched insiders in Monaco.
And when our intelligence reporting began putting a spotlight on relationships around the Palace and various ministries, Palmero did not join us on the barricades demanding transparency.
Quite the opposite.
Which is why his subsequent reinvention is laughable.
The question therefore isn’t simply whether Palmero’s accusations against others are true.
There are more interesting questions.
What did Claude Palmero know? When did he know it? What did he do about it?
And perhaps most importantly:
What did Claude Palmero tolerate while Claude Palmero remained powerful?
Because for more than two decades he wasn’t some helpless functionary watching Monaco’s machinery from the pavement.
He was sitting inside the engine room—and directing a fair amount of it.
For years: Palace insider. Keeper of secrets. Participant in the very dirty system surrounding Prince Albert.
Then: June 2023. Abruptly fired.
After which came revelations, accusations, interviews, and the transformation of Claude Palmero into a supposed crusader against the very establishment in which he had spent decades flourishing.
BACK TO LACOSTE
Twenty years ago, Lacoste was one of the people who helped turn Prince Albert against his own intelligence service.
That intelligence service had been reporting uncomfortable information about people surrounding the prince.
Including Thierry Lacoste.
Now Lacoste himself is a criminal defendant in Monaco.
The war consuming Monaco is not a struggle between reformers and corrupt insiders.
It is a struggle among insiders—men who operated within the same small ecosystem for decades.
So forget Claude Palmero’s campaign to rehabilitate Claude Palmero.
Forget the victimhood.
Forget the carefully cultivated image of the “courageous” former insider finally telling Monaco how Monaco really works.
We already knew how Monaco worked.
We reported it to Prince Albert 20 years ago.
And people around him—notably, Palmero and Lacoste—persuaded Albert not to listen.
Thierry Lacoste’s predicament now makes Palmero’s protestations even harder to swallow.
Standing beside an accused man and declaring that both of you are victims of the system may have looked impressive in July.
It hasn’t aged well.

The door to Scheimer’s office is closed.
This is odd.
I knock. No answer.
I try the knob. Locked.
Is Scheimer hiding out from creditors? Had the clutter finally driven him crazy? Or maybe Vladimir from Chicago had paid a visit with Krutskov’s nephew and their goons?
Because I cannot imagine Scheimer anyplace else, except maybe upstairs in PJ’s.
I ascend and adjust my eyes to the dark and dingy bar.
No Scheimer.
The Darconti look-a-like is on stage, bending over. She stumps me long enough to fall prey to a beer, no hardship.
Three nude dancers and two Buds later, I return downstairs.
Scheimer’s door is open.
I peek inside.
No Scheimer.
“Scheimer?” I call.
He darts out of the fulfillment room.
“You had me worried, Scheimer.”
“Why?” Perspiration drips from Scheimer’s face.
“The door was locked earlier—never seen that before.”
“Denzel’s out sick and the copier’s busted. I had to go out for photocopies.”
“Why don’t you get the copier fixed?”
“I’m six months overdue with leasing payments and they won’t fix it till I settle up. Lou Gurliacci called three more times looking for you. You should call her.”
“Listen, Scheimer, I’ve got something more important going on. Have they started printing the book yet?”
Scheimer shrugs. “Dunno.”
“Find out. And if they’ve started, make them stop. I have to make a couple of changes.”
Scheimer rolls his eyes. As if his life wasn’t complicated enough with Denzel out and 22 creditors demanding payment. He picks up the phone, taps a number, connects to the job manager. He speaks, listens, grunts and returns the phone to its cradle.
“You’re in luck,” he says. “They were just about to start. They’ll wait, but no guarantees about a ship date since the delay is on us.”
I rump my rear on a swivel chair, tap out Gurliacci’s number.
“Where’ve you been?” the 60 Minutes producer practically bounces into my eardrum. “We need our film. Where is it?”
“I’m waiting for it to arrive.”
“You don’t have it?” Gurliacci’s voice oozes anguish. She seems inches away from a nervous breakdown.
“Don’t worry. It should arrive by tomorrow.”
“Tomorrow? But we’ve been slotted for this Sunday! I need that tape to edit or I’ll be looking for a new job!”
“You’ve got to get them to delay,” I say. “There’s a new dimension to the story you’ll want to include.”
“Mr. Safer likes the story just the way it is,” says Gurliacci. “I’ll shuttle down in the morning so I’m there when it arrives.”

A solemn-faced Pikestaff sits behind his desk.
“Bleiler,” he preempts any smartass remark from me. “You were right.”
“Moscow?”
Pikestaff nods. “We confirmed it through a source inside the Kremlin.”
“Where are they keeping him?”
“A safehouse,” said Pikestaff. “Outside Moscow.”
“Do we know exactly which dacha?”
“We could probably find out.” Pikestaff studies me.” No, uh-uh, you can’t...” he splutters. “It’s out of the question. It would compromise our spy.”
“I had tea with Ligichansky yesterday,” I toss in.
Pikestaff almost falls out of his chair. “Where?”
“Fortnum and Mason in London. Where else does one have tea?”
Pikestaff harrumphs. “You didn’t take Concorde again?”
“Just one way.”
Pikestaff scowls. “What did Ligichansky have to say?”
“He said he’s not a monster octopus.”
“He said that?”
“Of course not, Pikestaff. His eyes said it. Eyes are more credible than tongues.”
“I don’t get it.” Pikestaff shakes his head. “What’s going on?”
“I didn’t get it either. Until three hours ago.”
Pikestaff wipes his brow. “So, what the hell happened three hours ago?”
“Herbert Picklewart.”
“The Deputy Secretary of State?”
“Precisely.”
“You got it from Picklewart?”
“For chrissakes, Pikestaff. You make him sound like a disease. And maybe he is. But, to answer your question: yes and no.”
“What is that supposed to mean?”
“Warthead’s tongue went one way, his eyes went another.”
Pikestaff consults his wristwatch. “I have to leave here in exactly five minutes. Would you mind telling me what the hell is going on?”
“I’m getting there, Pikestaff. Bear with me a minute. How did Warthead get to be Deputy Secretary of State for the Near East? Do you happen to know?”
“Yes. He was a partner in President Prescott’s law firm. But what does...?”
“Exactly,” I say. “Don’t you think that’s odd?”
“Odd?”
“Of course. He’s not competent. I wouldn’t trust Warthead to write a will. Herb Picklewart is Deputy Secretary because he knows.”
“Knows what?”
“Warthead knows about President Prescott’s secret stake in Kazakh oil. He must have found out about it at the law firm. He’s been blackmailing the President.”
Pikestaff cups his hands around his mouth in mock secrecy. “Aren’t we doing that, too?”
“Yes.” I cup my hands around my mouth and whisper back. “But not for personal gain.” I put my hands down. “Here’s the deal as I see it. Warthead is going to end up Secretary of State. That’s the next step.”
“But how...?”
“It was very subtle, Pikestaff. Warthead didn’t come right out and confront the President with what he knows. He asked CIA to gather intelligence on Podex, knowing full well that the President would eventually hear about it and ask him to quash the investigation. In that scenario, Warthead is doing the President a favor—they both know why without saying a word—and Warthead needs to be repaid. To justify his request for us to target Podex, Warthead exaggerated their importance, calling it a monster octopus when it’s really they just a dirty little squid. He never figured that Krutskov would write a memoir and ignite a series of events that led me to Podex. He never figured that we would uncover the President’s secret deal. And he especially never figured that we would pinpoint his own duplicity.”
Pikestaff is harrumph-less. He sits, mouth agape. “What about Kobo?” he finally asks, an anguished tone that suggests maybe we terminated an innocent man with extreme prejudice.
“Kobo was a bad guy. The truly ugly side of Podex. He would have exposed the President to get his hands on the President’s shareholding. This country doesn’t need that kind of scandal. And the world doesn’t need Kobo.”
“So, assuming everything you’ve told me is true, what are you going to do about it?”

As the 25th anniversary of 9/11 approaches, let’s poke into an obscure file you’re probably not supposed to know about.
On February 1, 2000, Omar al-Bayoumi, a Saudi national living in San Diego, drove to Los Angeles and visited the Saudi consulate.
Afterward, he went to a restaurant.
There he happened to encounter two young Saudis who had recently arrived in America and were having difficulty adjusting to their new surroundings.
Their names were Nawaf al-Hazmi and Khalid al-Mihdhar.
Both men would later hijack American Airlines Flight 77 and fly it into the Pentagon.
Bayoumi said the meeting was accidental.
Stranger things have happened. Though not many.
A Helpful Fellow
Bayoumi did not merely recommend a decent motel.
He persuaded—or at least encouraged—the two men to move to San Diego.
He helped them find an apartment in his own complex. He assisted with the lease. He co-signed it. He helped them obtain the money needed for the security deposit.
He helped them open a bank account.
He introduced them around.
He threw them a welcoming party. And he videotaped it.
All this for two strangers he had supposedly encountered by chance over lunch.
Some people collect stray cats.
Omar al-Bayoumi collected future hijackers.
There was another curiosity.
The FBI already knew who Bayoumi was.
In 1998, two years before his encounter with Hazmi and Mihdhar, the Bureau opened a preliminary investigation into Bayoumi after receiving reports about suspicious behavior.
One FBI source reportedly concluded that Bayoumi “must be an agent of a foreign power or an agent of Saudi Arabia.”
The investigation was closed in 1999.
Nothing to see here. Move along.
The Student Who Didn’t Study Much
Bayoumi’s official biography was peculiar.
He was supposedly in the United States as a student and was being paid by Dallah/Avco, a Saudi contractor connected to the kingdom’s civil aviation establishment.
Except he did not appear to do much work for the company.
His academic pursuits were similarly relaxed.
Yet the money kept arriving.
Even more curiously, his allowances increased substantially in March 2000.
That was one month after he befriended Hazmi and Mihdhar.
Later FBI reporting would make the story considerably more interesting.
A declassified FBI report from 2017 recorded information identifying Bayoumi as a “cooptee” of Saudi Arabia’s General Intelligence Presidency.
Not necessarily a professional intelligence officer.
An asset.
Someone who will observe, report and perform occasional tasks.
The FBI determined that Bayoumi collected information within Saudi communities in California and passed intelligence through Saudi channels.
London Calling
Bayoumi left America in June 2001.
Three months later, the world changed.
On September 11, Hazmi and Mihdhar helped crash Flight 77 into the Pentagon.
Ten days later, British counterterrorism police arrested Bayoumi in Birmingham at the request of the FBI.
Scotland Yard searched his home.
This is where our story becomes very interesting indeed.
Because the British found things. Lots of things.
Among them were roughly 80 videotapes. One had been recorded during a trip Bayoumi made to Washington in the summer of 1999.
It showed the United States Capitol.
Bayoumi had filmed entrances. Exits. Security positions. The surrounding area.
He examined a model of the building. He discussed nearby landmarks.
At one point he referred to a “plan.”
A former FBI supervisor who later examined the recording considered it consistent with what intelligence professionals call pre-operational surveillance.
British police also seized a notebook belonging to Bayoumi.
Inside was a drawing involving an aircraft accompanied by a mathematical equation.
The calculation concerned altitude, distance and the horizon.
FBI aviation specialists subsequently concluded that the equation could be used by a pilot to calculate a descent toward a target on the horizon.
Bayoumi acknowledged that the writing was his. He later suggested that perhaps he had been remembering something from high school mathematics.
We have a man subsequently identified in FBI reporting as a Saudi intelligence asset.
He encounters two future 9/11 hijackers immediately after visiting the Saudi consulate in Los Angeles.
He helps establish them in California.
His Saudi-funded allowances increase shortly afterward.
He possesses unusual footage of the U.S. Capitol.
And British police find an aircraft-descent calculation among his papers.
You might imagine that ten days after September 11 the United States government would have regarded this material with some urgency.
You would be mistaken.
Federal Express
According to an internal FBI report, copies of material seized from Bayoumi’s British residence were shipped back to the United States.
By Federal Express.
It was October 2001.
Three thousand people had just been murdered.
The largest terrorist investigation in American history was underway.
British police had arrested a man closely connected to two of the hijackers and discovered potentially explosive evidence in his home.
And some of that evidence apparently went home like Christmas presents from Aunt Edna.
Where was the urgent classified cable from FBI London?
Where was the immediate secure notification to Washington?
Where was the message to San Diego saying, in essence: YOU NEED TO SEE WHAT WE JUST FOUND.
Secure communications existed. Diplomatic pouches existed.
Nobody needed to wait for the FedEx man.
Destination Unknown
There is evidence that some information concerning the British investigation was transmitted to San Diego.
Which makes what happened next even stranger.
The FBI agents in San Diego investigating Bayoumi say they never saw the Capitol tape.
One of the principal investigators, Danny Gonzalez, did not learn about some of the British evidence until years later.
In 2012, more than a decade after 9/11, an FBI evidence technician contacted Gonzalez.
Boxes marked OMAR AL-BAYOUMI had been sitting in a Washington warehouse.
They were apparently being prepared for relocation and disposal.
Inside was evidence from the British search.
Including the notebook. Including the aircraft calculation.
Evidence connected to the greatest terrorist attack in American history sitting unnoticed in a government warehouse for eleven years.
Nobody Saw It
Perhaps the 9/11 Commission examined the Capitol tape.
Nope.
Its executive director Philip Zelikow later said he had never seen it.
(Thomas Kean, former Governor of New Jersey, told a trusted source of mine, “If I’d known then what I know now, I never would have signed off on the 9/11 National Commission report.”)
Perhaps the CIA analyzed Bayoumi’s Capitol tape.
Apparently not.
Former senior CIA officials have said they were unaware of it.
Perhaps the FBI investigators pursuing Bayoumi in San Diego studied it carefully.
They say they didn’t know it existed.
This presents us with an intriguing question: Who did know?
And another: Why didn’t everybody who needed to know, know?
In 2025, Senators Richard Blumenthal and John Cornyn formally asked the FBI essentially the same thing.
They demanded an explanation for why the Bayoumi evidence had not been provided to the 9/11 Commission and CIA.
They also asked for the chain of custody.
Excellent questions. A quarter-century late.
And Bayoumi?
The British could initially hold him only briefly.
He was released.
Saudi diplomatic pressure reportedly accompanied the effort to secure his freedom.
The United States did not extradite him.
The man who had befriended two hijackers, helped establish them in America and possessed what would later look like potentially significant evidence simply walked away.
Which brings us to perhaps the most important aspect of the Bayoumi affair.
The problem may not merely be what investigators missed.
It may be what the American government decided very early that it did not want the evidence to mean.
The Answer Before the Investigation
Richard Lambert supervised the FBI’s San Diego investigation after 9/11.
He later recalled helping prepare FBI Director Robert Mueller for congressional testimony in 2002.
According to Lambert, a senior FBI official told him: “The bureau’s position is that there was no complicity.”
Think about those words.
Not: We have found no complicity.
Not: The investigation has ruled out complicity.
The Bureau’s position was that there was no complicity.
Jeez—sounds just like the FBI’s “position”on the assassination of JFK!
The Saudi Question
The old portrait of Omar al-Bayoumi as an innocent Saudi student who happened upon two countrymen in a restaurant and kindly helped them settle into San Diego has become increasingly difficult to swallow.
The FBI itself later developed information identifying him as connected to Saudi intelligence.
And Bayoumi was not operating in a vacuum.
Investigators examined his relationships with Saudi diplomatic and religious officials, including Fahad al-Thumairy at the Saudi consulate in Los Angeles and Musaed al-Jarrah at the Saudi embassy in Washington.
The FBI eventually created Operation Encore to examine whether Saudi officials or associates had knowingly provided assistance to the hijackers.
The question became sufficiently substantial that litigation brought by 9/11 families against Saudi Arabia survived another major attempt at dismissal in federal court in 2025.
Twenty-Five Years Later
And so we return to London.
British police arrested Omar al-Bayoumi ten days after 9/11.
They searched his home. They discovered material of obvious significance.
The FBI’s San Diego investigators say they never saw crucial parts of it.
The CIA also did not see it.
Neither the 9/11 Commission.
Some of the evidence subsequently spent more than a decade sitting in an FBI warehouse.
Perhaps the United States government was simply overwhelmed after September 11.
Agencies were drowning in leads. People made mistakes.
If so, the FBI should have little difficulty explaining it as such.
Who received the evidence from London? Who reviewed it? Who decided where it should go?
Why wasn’t the Capitol recording immediately sent to San Diego?
Why wasn’t it shown to the CIA?
Why wasn’t it provided to the 9/11 Commission?
Why did evidence seized from one of the most intriguing figures in the entire 9/11 investigation wind up gathering dust in a warehouse?
And why, while all this was happening, did Omar al-Bayoumi remain a free man?
These are chain-of-custody questions.
A former CIA case officer who spent much of his career in the Middle East recently reviewed the Bayoumi story and found the handling of the London evidence almost impossible to reconcile with normal intelligence practice.
He told me: “This smells like a dead camel.”
Twenty-five years after 9/11, the stench hasn’t gone away.
Just to be clear, CIA Director George Tenet and FBI Director Louis Freeh took an oath to keep this country and its citizens safe.
That was their most fundamental responsibility.
The intelligence system (foreign and domestic) over which both presided failed miserably.
Freeh left the FBI less than three months before September 11, was director while the attacks were being planned.
Tenet remained in place before and after.
And after the CIA, under his watch, failed to detect the conspiracy that killed nearly 3,000 people on American soil, Tenet went on to preside over another intelligence catastrophe: the assessment that Saddam Hussein possessed weapons of mass destruction.
Tenet famously assured President George W. Bush that making the case for invasion by finding the weapons would be a “slam dunk.”
There were no stockpiles of the weapons America went to war expecting to find.
A total of 7,074 Americans were killed in Iraq and Afghanistan during the wars Tenet instigated under a false pretense.
In less tolerant countries, such failures might have ended rather more unpleasantly for those presiding over them.
In ours, the men at the top write books, collect speaking fees and migrate into lucrative private-sector positions—marketable, apparently, because of the very government positions in which they failed the American people.
For more…

Thierry Lacoste—the man who helped turn Prince Albert II of Monaco against his own intelligence service—spent two days in police custody this past week before being charged with the very kinds of wrongdoing we warned the prince about 20 years ago.
Back then, Lacoste was deeply unhappy with information we had uncovered about him and about his cohort Claude Palmero, Albert’s longtime financial administrator.
They had reason to be.
The intelligence service was doing something Lacoste and Palmero apparently found inconvenient:
Finding things out.
First came the effort to remove Jean-Luc Allavena as Albert’s chief of staff, who was charged with implementing a crackdown on precisely the illegal activities in which Lacoste and Palmero were engaged.
Then came the effort—led by Lacoste and Palmero—to sever Albert’s access to the intelligence service that provided him with something he could not reliably obtain from courtiers, advisers and ministers:
The truth.
Twenty years later, Thierry Lacoste walked into Monaco’s Sûreté Publique.
He did not walk straight back out.
Lacoste presented himself to the Sûreté Publique on Wednesday, September 2.
He remained in police custody.
Then his detention was extended.
On Friday, Monaco’s judicial authorities charged the 66-year-old lawyer with criminal conspiracy, active corruption of a national public official as part of an organized group, passive influence peddling as part of an organized group, and money laundering.
He has since been placed under judicial supervision.
These are criminal charges brought by the Monegasque justice system against a man who for decades occupied one of the most privileged positions imaginable in the principality:
Friend of the Sovereign. Lawyer to the Sovereign. Keeper of the Sovereign’s confidences.
The Prince’s Friend
Thierry Lacoste grew up alongside Albert.
They attended school together, moved through the same social circles and remained close into adulthood. Lacoste eventually became Albert’s personal lawyer, a position he held for approximately two decades.
Le Parisien describes him as having been not simply Albert’s attorney but his ami intime—intimate friend—and guardian of his interests and secrets.
Now Monaco’s prosecutors allege that that Lacoste turned his closeness to the prince into a commodity.
(Not unlike many others around Albert.)
The French phrase used by Le Parisien is wonderfully precise:
Fait commerce de sa proximité avec le Prince.
Translation: Made a business of his proximity to the prince.
Access, for Lacoste, was merchandise.
Influence for sale.
We recognized the pattern 20 years ago.
We reported our concerns about Lacoste directly to Prince Albert 20 years ago.
The €136 Million Question
At the center of the investigation is one of Monaco’s great property sagas: the Esplanade des Pêcheurs, an ambitious construction venture near Port Hercule—the principality’s main port—that collapsed into litigation after the Monegasque government abandoned the project.
The developer, Caroli Group, went to court.
Monaco lost.
The resulting compensation was enormous: about €136 million, excluding interest.
Hovering around that litigation was Thierry Lacoste.
This part is not new.
As far back as 2022, Le Monde examined hundreds of leaked emails relating to Monaco’s property establishment and reported the existence of a Lacoste law-firm invoice for €589,200 connected with the Esplanade affair.
Lacoste did not deny receiving the money.
His explanation was that he had introduced the case to another lawyer and received a fee-sharing payment.
He even acknowledged the obvious ethical problem.
Given that he was the prince’s lawyer, Lacoste conceded to Le Monde that perhaps it would have been better not to accept anything.
In other words, caught with both hands in the cookie jar and expecting nothing more than a mild reprimand.
Enter Didier Linotte
Didier Linotte became president of Monaco’s Supreme Court—the very institution involved in the Esplanade litigation.
He was also part of the small circle surrounding Lacoste and others that became known through the leaked Dossiers du Rocher correspondence as the G4.
Linotte has himself been charged in connection with the broader affair.
The juxtaposition was always, well, quaintly Monaco.
Lacoste was Albert’s lawyer.
Lacoste had financial involvement with the developer’s litigation against Albert’s State.
And the institution deciding the case was headed by Lacoste’s associate Didier Linotte.
Le Monde spotted the overlap years ago.
Its reporting noted that the €589,200 payment arose from an affair in which the developer obtained an enormous judgment against Monaco while the Supreme Court was headed by Lacoste’s friend.
Now investigators have reached their own conclusion.
It is no longer about bad optics.
It is criminal.
The G4
In 2021 someone hacked an extraordinary quantity of private correspondence belonging to prominent members of Albert’s entourage.
The material appeared online under the title Les Dossiers du Rocher.
Four names kept appearing:
Thierry Lacoste.
Didier Linotte.
Claude Palmero.
Laurent Anselmi.
They became known as the G4.
The leaked correspondence suggested an extraordinary degree of interaction among men positioned throughout Monaco’s legal, financial and governmental machinery.
Le Monde, which examined hundreds of the emails, described interventions, arrangements and discussions concerning appointments among members of this highly connected circle.
At the time, the provenance of the documents was deemed toxic by some because they were hacked and disseminated anonymously. And the website publishing them was polemical.
Those targeted could therefore attack the messenger. And they did.
But something fundamental has changed.
No Longer Just the Dossiers du Rocher
Didier Linotte has been charged.
Now Thierry Lacoste has been charged.
And these charges did not come from a website.
They came from Monaco’s judicial authorities.
According to the prosecutor-general’s announcement, Lacoste faces accusations of: association de malfaiteurs—criminal conspiracy; corruption active sur un agent public national en bande organisée—active corruption of a national public official as part of an organized group; trafic d’influence passif en bande organisée—passive influence peddling as part of an organized group; and blanchiment—money laundering.
If convicted, Lacoste faces serious prison time.
Under Monaco's Penal Code, corruption and influence peddling ordinarily carry sentences of five to ten years. But when committed as part of an organized group—the aggravating circumstance specifically alleged against Lacoste—the potential punishment rises to 10 to 20 years. Aggravated money laundering can likewise carry 10 to 20 years.
At 66, Thierry Lacoste is facing charges that could put him behind bars well into old age.
This is seismic for Monaco.
The prince’s former close friend and personal lawyer is now a criminal defendant.
Lacoste—the confidant who helped persuade Albert to dismantle the intelligence service that had been keeping him informed about the questionable and potentially criminal behavior of those around him.
Including Thierry Lacoste.
We warned Prince Albert 20 years ago.
He chose not to listen.
Step inside the gilded world of Monaco—where breathtaking beauty masks a labyrinth of corruption, intrigue, and espionage.
In this electrifying true story, American Robert Eringer is summoned by Prince Albert II—son of Hollywood legend Grace Kelly—to create Monaco’s first-ever intelligence service.
Reporting directly to the prince, Eringer built an extraordinary operation: cultivating secret relationships with the CIA, MI6 and 18 other foreign intelligence services, and key figures on U.S. Senate and House intelligence committees.
He arranged meetings for Prince Albert with CIA Director Porter Goss and FBI Director Robert Mueller III.
He led operations targeting money-laundering networks, exposed mafia influence, and uncovered deep corruption at the highest levels of Monaco’s government.
But when the time came for action, Prince Albert’s courage faltered—and a promised “new ethic” for Monaco crumbled under the weight of old-world power plays.
Set against the dazzling backdrop of the French Riviera, Spymaster of Monte Carlo reveals how truth, loyalty, and power collide in the shadows behind a royal façade.

For nearly nine years we have called it a natural disaster.
Perhaps we should reconsider the adjective.
On January 9, 2018, Mother Nature unquestionably tried to smother Montecito, as it has before and will again.
She had help.
Twenty-three people died. Homes disappeared. Families were torn apart.
Boulders the size of automobiles came crashing out of the Santa Ynez Mountains in the middle of the night.
And in the years since, the story has hardened into something simple and almost biblical:
There was a terrible fire. Then there was terrible rain. Then the mountain came down.
An act of God.
Except the case was never quite that simple.
Because when you go back through the investigations, government records, lawsuits and contemporary reporting, another story emerges.
A utility was implicated in starting the fire that stripped the mountains.
Government officials had been warned for decades that Montecito’s debris basins were inadequate. Some of those basins were not restored to their designed capacity before the storm.
Officials possessed a remarkably prescient map showing where debris could go.
They removed it from the county website. And replaced it with a mandatory evacuation boundary along a road running sideways across Montecito that, in hindsight, made no sense whatsoever.
Nineteen people died south of that line.
And the cellphone warning telling residents to seek higher ground wasn’t sent until the debris flow was already underway.
So perhaps we should not blame everything on Mother Nature.
She had accomplices.
ACCOMPLICE NO. 1: SOUTHERN CALIFORNIA EDISON
Before there could be a catastrophic post-fire debris flow, there had to be a fire.
And there certainly was.
The Thomas Fire began on December 4, 2017, eventually scorching more than 280,000 acres across Ventura and Santa Barbara counties.
It burned the watersheds above Montecito.
Then came January 9.
The significance is not complicated.
Vegetation stabilizes mountain soil and slows runoff. Severe fire removes that protection and leaves soil dramatically less able to absorb water.
The mountains above Montecito had been stripped of their natural defense system.
But who lit the fire?
Investigators traced two ignitions associated with what became the Thomas Fire to Southern California Edison electrical equipment. Edison disputed aspects of investigators’ findings concerning one ignition, while litigation subsequently engulfed the company. The connection between the fires and the Montecito disaster became the subject of thousands of claims.
By July 2026, Edison reported that it had reached settlements with approximately 13,800 individual plaintiffs arising from the 2017/2018 wildfire and mudslide events. Insurance subrogation claims were also settled, including an initial $1.2 billion payment under one agreement. Public entities settled claims as well.
Settlements are not admissions of liability.
But billions of dollars have an eloquence all their own.
ACCOMPLICE NO. 2: THE DEBRIS BASINS
Here the part that becomes considerably harder to excuse.
Those who govern Montecito had been warned.
Warned by the United States Army Corps of Engineers.
The danger had been understood for decades.
After earlier fires and debris flows, catchment basins were constructed at canyon mouths to intercept rocks, trees, sediment and other material before it could roar into the neighborhoods below.
But they weren’t big enough.
According to an eight-month Los Angeles Times investigation, government officials had known for roughly half a century that there were too few debris basins and that existing ones were inadequate for the enormous flows the Santa Ynez Mountains were capable of producing.
As far back as 1969, an Army Corps district engineer warned Santa Barbara County:“The danger of loss of life … is great.”
And still the basins remained inadequate.
Worse, some had accumulated sediment and vegetation over the years, further reducing their capacity.
After the Thomas Fire, county officials understood the urgency. Crews worked frantically to remove material before the first major storm.
More than 1,200 truckloads were hauled away.
Then came an awkward discovery.
County surveys indicated that the basins still had substantially less capacity than their original designs called for. Six other basins in burned drainages had not received comparable emergency clearing.
Would perfectly cleaned, larger debris basins have stopped January 9?
Probably not.
But that’s the wrong question.
The question is: Could adequate infrastructure have reduced the destruction?
Southern California Edison apparently thought so.
Because after being sued over the disaster, Edison turned around and sued Santa Barbara County and other public agencies.
Its allegations were brutal.
Edison accused public entities of failing to adequately plan for known flood hazards, failing to build and maintain adequate debris basins, allowing inadequate bridges and channel crossings, and otherwise causing, contributing to or exacerbating the destruction.
Pot, meet kettle.
But the kettle had problems of its own.
Remarkably, the argument isn’t entirely ancient history. Edison’s July 2026 SEC filing says it still intends to preserve its ability to pursue certain cross-claims arising from those alleged failures.
Eight years later, the lawyers are still sorting out who helped Mother Nature.
ACCOMPLICE NO. 3: THE EVACUATION LINE
Before the storm, officials had to decide whom to evacuate.
Forecasting debris flows is extraordinarily difficult. Evacuating an entire community carries risks of its own. Officials were exhausted from the Thomas Fire. Residents were exhausted from evacuations.
These were not easy decisions.
But they were life-and-death decisions.
State scientists hurriedly produced a hazard map showing where floodwater and debris might leave creek channels and spread across Montecito’s alluvial fan.
Afterward, it proved disturbingly accurate.
The map identified danger extending south along the creeks into neighborhoods below Highway 192.
Then county emergency managers did something disturbingly unbelievable.
They drew the mandatory evacuation boundary largely along Highway 192.
Think about that.
The debris was coming north to south.
The creeks run north to south.
Gravity operates north to south.
Highway 192 runs east to west.
And here’s the detail that should still make every Montecito resident’s blood run cold.
The more topographically specific flood/debris-flow map was removed from the county website and replaced with the Highway 192 evacuation map.
Why?
Officials later said they were trying to avoid confusion.
Huh?
A county spokesperson later acknowledged that the emergency management director’s “biggest regret” was probably that the map showing the waterways had been pulled.
I should think so.
Seventeen of the 23 people who died were outside the mandatory evacuation zone.
Let that number sit for a moment.
Seventeen out of twenty-three.
ACCOMPLICE NO. 4: THE WARNING THAT ARRIVED WITH THE DISASTER
Surely, then, there was an emergency alert.
There was… a little too late.
Actually, a lot too late.
At approximately 3:50 a.m., Santa Barbara County sent an emergency cellphone warning to residents in evacuation areas.
There was just one problem.
The destructive flooding had already begun.
Mud, trees and boulders were already coming down the mountain. And coming swiftly.
An earlier county opt-in alert at 2:46 a.m. instructed recipients to “GO TO HIGH GROUND.” Officials later acknowledged that such wording could itself be confusing in a flash-flood situation: the safer interpretation could mean going to the highest part of a building rather than venturing outside into the path of a debris flow.
Afterward, officials changed the terminology.
Santa Barbara County stopped calling evacuation warnings “voluntary.”
Twenty-three people had just participated in the focus group.
ACCOMPLICE. NO. 5: MONTECITO WATER DISTRICT
One allegation deserves special care because it has circulated around Montecito ever since.
The Montecito Water District lost millions of gallons of water during the catastrophe.
Edison’s lawsuit subsequently accused the district of contributing to the deluge through ruptured infrastructure.
That sounds explosive.
The district says it isn’t.
According to the Montecito Water District, no storage reservoir ruptured.
Rather, seven tanks containing approximately 5.8 million gallons drained gradually over roughly 11 hours through more than 300 breaks in pipelines, hydrants and service connections caused by the disaster.
The district says its peak release was about 24,000 gallons per minute.
Estimated peak rainfall runoff?
More than 14 million gallons per minute.
By the time destruction was first being reported, the district estimates approximately 300,000 gallons had escaped its system compared with nearly 200 million gallons of accumulated rainfall.
LAWSUITS
Victims sued Edison.
Public entities pursued Edison.
Edison sued public entities.
Insurance companies pursued claims.
The Water District defended itself.
Billions changed hands.
Thousands of cases were settled.
And by 2026, some litigation stemming from the Thomas/Koenigstein fires and Montecito mudslides was still unresolved.
Which raises an uncomfortable question.
If January 9 was simply an unavoidable act of nature—why did everybody spend the next eight years arguing about human responsibility?
Because disasters have two histories.
There is the history we tell at memorials.
And there is the history contained in depositions.
The first speaks of courage, loss, community and recovery.
The second asks who knew what, when they knew it, what they did about it—and who should pay.
That history is considerably less comforting.
MOTHER NATURE’S RAP SHEET
None of this absolves nature.
As I wrote previously, Montecito sits on the evidence of its own geological past.
The boulders are everywhere.
Debris flows occurred long before Edison strung a wire, long before Santa Barbara County drew an evacuation map, long before anybody built a debris basin.
Another one will happen.
No bureaucracy can repeal gravity.
But that does not mean the scale of every natural disaster is itself entirely natural.
The Thomas Fire stripped the watershed.
Investigators linked electrical equipment to fire ignitions.
Government agencies had decades of warning that debris basins were inadequate.
Some basins had diminished capacity.
Officials possessed a hazard map showing danger extending into neighborhoods south of Highway 192.
That map was removed from the county website.
A mandatory evacuation line was drawn across the community.
Nineteen people died south of it.
Seventeen of the 23 victims were outside the mandatory evacuation zone.
And the broad emergency cellphone warning arrived after the catastrophe had begun.
Those are facts.
The conspiracy theory would be believing that 23 deaths, billions of dollars in litigation and eight years of finger-pointing can all be filed neatly under ACT OF GOD.
If we are serious about preparing Montecito for the next debris flow, we should stop asking only what the mountain might do.
We should ask what our high-paid public servants are doing to ensure they do not fail next time.
Speaking of which…
POTENTIAL ACCOMPLICE NO. 5 WHEN THE NEXT MUDSLIDE HAPPENS
There is one final chapter to this story.
After 23 people died, Montecito residents did something unusually sensible.
They acted.
A privately funded nonprofit called The Project for Resilient Communities (TPRC) raised millions of dollars and installed six massive Swiss-engineered steel ring nets across San Ysidro, Cold Spring and Buena Vista canyons.
The idea was wonderfully uncomplicated.
When the mountain comes down again, catch some of it.
The nets went up in 2019.
And in January 2023, nature provided a test.
After heavy storms, the upper San Ysidro net filled with an enormous mass of rock, mud and debris, creating an accumulation roughly 25 feet high.
In other words, the net caught debris.
You might imagine that would settle the question of whether Montecito should keep its debris nets.
This is California.
It settled nothing.
The five-year emergency permits were expiring.
Environmental groups opposed extending them, arguing that the watershed had revegetated, the nets interfered with sensitive riparian habitat, and newer debris basins downstream provided better protection.
TPRC countered that five years of environmental monitoring had produced no environmental violations.
Meanwhile, Santa Barbara County and TPRC attempted to negotiate a transfer of the system to public control.
They couldn’t agree who would pay.
And here we encounter that most immovable object in California:
Not a fifteen-foot sandstone boulder. A maintenance budget.
Cleaning the San Ysidro net after the 2023 storm cost approximately $1.2 million.
TPRC, a small private nonprofit, concluded that it could not responsibly leave six nets in place without guaranteed funding to empty them after another major storm.
The County wasn’t prepared to assume that financial exposure on the proposed terms.
So in November 2023, a helicopter flew into the canyons above Montecito.
And removed all six nets.
Think about that for a moment.
Twenty-three people had died.
Private citizens raised the money.
Engineers installed a second layer of protection.
One of the nets subsequently caught a substantial quantity of debris during a major storm.
And four years after installation, we took them all down.
The steel nets themselves now reside at a manufacturer’s facility in New Mexico.
Fortunately, somebody had the foresight to leave their anchors drilled into the mountainside.
Which means they could theoretically return.
Perhaps that’s worth remembering.
Because while Santa Barbara County, environmental organizations, regulators and nonprofit directors debated permits, habitat, maintenance obligations and who would pick up the bill—the mountain did not participate in the meeting.
Nor did it agree to wait.

China did not need to work hard to discover who worked for American intelligence.
The United States government kept a list.
Then somebody—probably china—stole it.
Millions of personnel records belonging to federal employees and contractors. Security-clearance investigations. Fingerprints. Employment histories. Financial problems. Foreign contacts. Family members. Drug use. Psychological information. Romantic complications.
The intimate biographies of people entrusted with the secrets of the United States.
In 2015, the U.S. government disclosed that hackers had penetrated the computer systems of the Office of Personnel Management—OPM—the federal government’s human-resources department.
At first it sounded like just another cyberattack.
It wasn’t.
Viewed through counterintelligence eyes, it was potentially one of the greatest intelligence hauls in modern history.
“Tell Us Everything”
Anyone who has held a security clearance knows the ritual.
You fill out forms. Lots of forms.
For access to classified information, that has traditionally meant the dreaded Standard Form 86.
SF-86.
Approximately 125 pages of intimacy.
Where have you lived? Where have you worked? Where have you traveled?
Who are your foreign friends? Have you used drugs? Been arrested? Had financial difficulties?
Received psychiatric treatment under circumstances the government considers relevant?
Do you have relatives overseas? Business interests abroad? Foreign property? Dual citizenship?
Unusual relationships? Anything someone might use to pressure you?
The government asks because counterintelligence officers need to know whether you are vulnerable to recruitment or coercion.
Perfectly sensible.
Unless somebody steals the answers.
Then you’ve conducted the enemy’s background investigation for him.
21.5 Million People
The scale was breathtaking.
OPM eventually determined that sensitive background-investigation information belonging to approximately 21.5 million people had been compromised.
A separate personnel-record breach affected millions more, with substantial overlap.
Among the stolen material were approximately 5.6 million sets of fingerprints.
Think about 21.5 million for a moment.
Federal employees. Former federal employees. Contractors. Security-clearance applicants.
And because background investigations necessarily ask about other people… spouses, children, friends, neighbors, references, foreign contacts… the intelligence value extended far beyond the individuals whose names appeared at the top of the forms.
America had inadvertently assembled an enormous social map of its own national-security establishment.
Then left the map where somebody could take it.
Beijing
The United States did not publicly name Chinese government hackers for the OPM breach, and Beijing denied involvement.
But American officials and subsequent government assessments overwhelmingly attributed the intrusion to actors connected with China.
James Clapper, then Director of National Intelligence, offered an unusually candid assessment. Asked about China’s presumed responsibility, Clapper observed that from an intelligence perspective, it was precisely the kind of target the United States itself would find attractive.
Translation: Of course they stole it. Look what we left lying around.
The Recruiter’s Dream
Imagine you are a foreign intelligence officer trying to recruit an American.
You need to know things.
Does he have money problems? Does he gamble? Is his marriage unhappy?
Does he have relatives in China? A mistress? A child with expensive needs?
A drinking problem? Career grievances?
In the old days, acquiring this information required work.
Surveillance. Sources. Interviews. Bugging hotel rooms. Following people. Opening mail. Recruiting secretaries.
Now imagine receiving the target’s security-clearance file.
He has already answered the questions, under penalty of law.
Dear Foreign Intelligence Service: Here are the things I would prefer nobody knew about me.
The Mosaic
Put millions of such records together and something extraordinary becomes possible.
You can begin mapping networks.
Who worked where. Who knew whom. Who served overseas. Who overlapped at particular embassies. Who suddenly appeared in an unusual posting.
Suppose someone possesses several databases.
OPM records.
Plus airline manifests. Hotel records. Health-insurance information. Financial information. Stolen corporate databases.
Now cross-reference them.
The question is no longer: Who has a security clearance?
The question becomes: Who among these people might actually be CIA?
Counterintelligence people call this the mosaic problem.
One piece of information may be meaningless.
Combine it with another. And another. And another. Eventually a picture appears.
For years China has been collecting enormous datasets precisely because the value lies not merely in each individual database but in combining them.
The OPM breach therefore becomes more interesting when placed beside other major intrusions attributed to Chinese actors.
Health insurer Anthem. Hotel giant Marriott.
Each breach generated headlines about cybersecurity.
But a counterintelligence officer sees something else.
A mosaic.
Connections. Overlaps.
So it’s no surprise that after the OPM breach, intelligence officials worried that American officers and sources could potentially be identified by comparing stolen personnel data with other information.
Computers—and especially AI—are very good at finding patterns humans miss.
The traditional counterintelligence officer needed intuition. The modern one has data analytics.
Twenty-one million background investigations provide quite a training set.
Then there were the fingerprints.
Initially OPM believed about 1.1 million fingerprint records had been compromised.
Later it revised the figure dramatically upward: 5.6 million.
At the time, government officials tried to reassure people that the immediate ability to misuse fingerprint data was limited.
Hold on a moment… passwords can be changed, credit-card numbers replaced, passports renewed.
Fingerprints are inconvenient in this regard.
You are issued ten. For life.
Biometric identification has become increasingly important.
The real scandal of OPM was not simply that hackers were clever. It was that the United States government had concentrated extraordinarily sensitive information in systems that were inadequately protected.
OPM’s inspector general had been warning about cybersecurity deficiencies.
Legacy systems. Weak controls. Security problems.
The information was extraordinarily valuable; the protection was not commensurate with its value.
Return to Parlor Maid. Return to Honeytrap.com. Return to Fang Fang.
All depend upon the same fundamental process.
Find the person. Understand the person. Discover what the person wants.
Create the approach. Develop the relationship. Be patient.
Traditionally this required a case officer.
The OPM breach industrialized the first half of the process.
Millions of Americans were already assessed, their histories collected, their vulnerabilities investigated, their relationships recorded, their fingerprints catalogued.
Not by China.
By us.
China merely had to steal the whole lot.
The Irony
The security-clearance system exists to protect America from espionage.
Its purpose is to identify people who might represent counterintelligence risks.
So the government assembled everything it needed to know about them.
Then, in one magnificent bureaucratic catastrophe, Chinese intelligence learn which Americans out of 21.5 million are worth trying to recruit—oh, and what it might use as leverage to cultivate them.
And we thoughtfully gave it to them on a silver platter.
Your tax dollars at work.

September-October 1999
Note: This is a flashback from before two previous segments in this serial.
So far as the Edward Lee Howard case was concerned, things looked bad.
Not for Howard.
For the United States of America:
FBI Special Agent John H opted for early retirement, effective the first week of September 1999.
He would not have folded ahead of schedule had he not been signaled by headquarters that the “related conflict” holding up a Howard rendition would never be lifted by the Justice Department. It had been John H’s intention to remain at his desk until the Howard case was resolved.
A couple years earlier, John H’s boss, Jim S, who provided enthusiastic support for capturing Howard, left Albuquerque for a U.S. embassy legat position in Athens, Greece. Not long after that, Jim S retired from the Bureau. Bob G, the gung-ho assistant U.S. Attorney, had also left public service and gone into private practice.
Once retired, John H would be out of the loop, exempt from learning anything more about the Howard case, which would be absorbed by another Albuquerque-based special agent for whom Howard would likely be a nuisance, not a priority.
Although I did not realize it yet, I had become the de facto advocate for keeping the Big Cheese Family aware that a) the Howard case still existed and b) the Howard case was important.
The day I could no longer phone John H with new developments evolving from the Howard case was terribly sad for me.
We had been a good team: he, an extraordinary special agent. I did not appreciate till I started working with others just how skilled John H was with what he called Bu biz.
In his low-key manner, John H knew how to work the system with finesse; how to walk the labyrinth of headquarters, take the hard knocks, and get back up for a return bout with never a sour word about anyone.
He was one of very few who knew how to operate within a bureaucracy that had become ridiculously disconnected. Everyone I worked with thereafter paled in comparison to the soft-spoken but very savvy John H.
But life goes on, and so did my Cuban operation, still administrated by FBI Albuquerque, yet managed by Washington Field Office.
At the request of Luis Fernandez, I organized a dinner party on October 1st to introduce him to new media people:
A British journalist of Indian descent and a producer from NBC News (both unwitting to my FBI role), and Rick K, who I’d taken to Moscow and now signed on as a witting asset in my Cuban coversion.
The venue, as usual, Saigon Gourmet, as stipulated by Fernandez, very much a creature of habit.
Luis Abierno had left Washington and returned to Havana.
So in his place Fernandez brought along the oddly-named Reuben de Wong Corchou, who had arrived one week earlier from Cuba.
Couchou was better dressed than Fernandez, who wore a paisley tie with striped shirt and (to quote the NBC producer) “looked like he just got off a boat from Bangladesh.”
A black tweed sportcoat made Couchou look more like a mortician than a diplomat. His pockmarked, funereal face glistened with grease and came adorned with thick, Soviet-era spectacles. He wore his dark hair slick-backed—with what looked like natural perspiration.
I almost asked if I could hire him out for Halloween to scare the kids.
Even worse than his countenance, Couchou possessed a grim and dour personality, totally devoid of humor. He did not smile, could not laugh.
Within two minutes it became clear this guy was the dinner guest from hell. Getting him to talk was harder than pulling teeth. More like drilling a root canal.
Under pressure from me to loosen his tongue, Couchou divulged that he had studied English and Cuban History at Havana University then taught these subjects for ten years before joining the foreign ministry through the 1990s.
As for foreign travel, Couchou had taken a grand tour of the Soviet Union in 1981 and spent much of 1998 in Tokyo, during which he visited China.
This tour in Washington was his first time in the United States.
Although he professed himself to be a staunch Marxist ideologue, Couchou wore a Rolex Submariner wristwatch, though I reckoned this extravagance was a counterfeit bought on the cheap in Asia.
I asked Couchou, and Fernandez, to speculate what Cuba would be like five years from now.
Both men seemed at a loss to respond.
The British journalist asked Fernandez what he thought of Castro.
Fernandez choked up, composed himself, and said, “He is my father.”
(In my report to the FBI, I wrote, “Does this mean we should add Luis’s name to the list of Fidel’s illegitimate children?”)
I sensed that Fernandez was showing off for Couchou, as if he thought the new guy was in town to audit his behavior and spy on him.
The British journalist, a loquacious chap, asked both Cubans, “So what’s your problem with the USA?”
Fernandez straightened himself and said, “Two words.”
This should be good, I thought. What two words could possibly sum it all up?
But, alackaday, Fernandez had mistaken this expression for meaning something else entirely, because what he actually spewed was a two-thousand word diatribe on how Cuban people are deprived of food and medicine because of U.S. policies.
“Why don’t you do what China does and hire Henry Kissinger to lobby in Washington?” posed the British journalist.
Fernandez did not understand the question.
The Brit rephrased it.
Fernandez still didn’t get it.
I rejigged the question myself.
“Ah,” said Fernandez, finally grasping it. “We have no money for this. We are effective in our own way.”
The British journalist asked about Che Guevara’s standing in contemporary Cuba.
Couchou, the historian, fielded this question by reciting Che’s birthday: “June 14th, 1928.”
Could this get any more comical?
For a mad moment, I thought Couchou might stand and sing Commandante Che Guevara. Mercifully, this did not happen.
I asked Fernandez if my package from Juan Hernandez had arrived. (Earlier, Hernandez confirmed by email from Havana that he had finally sent material by diplomatic pouch, as promised seven months earlier.)
Yes, he had phoned Hernandez, said Fernandez. The material, he was told, had been sent to someone named Pedro.
“Who’s Pedro?” I said.
Fernandez shook his head. He did not know. It remained unclear whether Pedro was supposed to contact me or what.
When the bill came, Fernandez did not remember that this dinner party had been his idea. Nor that it was his turn.
So the FBI took another hit.
I next met Fernandez, whom I codenamed Flakester, four weeks later, on October 30th, in the Pavilion, Chevy Chase—a coffee morning at Starbucks.
Luis trudged in bleary-eyed, clad in a Nike windbreaker, black polo shirt and freshly trimmed crew-cut.
He launched into another harangue about how a small minority of anti-Castro Cubans in Miami and three Congressmen can manipulate U.S. policy toward Cuba.
Again, he implied that they were funded by a mysterious source.
My earlier request for leads, said Fernandez, had been sent to Havana.
Their reply: Instruct Eringer to get started, show us results, we’ll help fill the holes.
“You go to Cuba,” he said. “We give you facilities.”
Fernandez added that he had to be careful because the Cuban Interests Section was not supposed to assist writers.
As we parted, I said, “Happy Halloween. Go spook a few people.” (And take Reuben de Wong Corchou with you.)
Almost six weeks later, I still hadn’t heard from Pedro.
I phoned Fernandez, who was sick with flu.
“Who’s Pedro?” he asked, preempting me.
“Exactly,” I said. “What have you heard?”
“Nothing, man. Who was that guy who was supposed to do this?” Fernandez was flakier than a dandruff attack in a blizzard.
“Juan Hernandez.”
“Right, Hernandez,” said Ferndandez. “I will phone Hernandez.”
“Excellent,” I said. “Phone Hernandez. Find out who the hell Pedro is.”

Hours before she died, Allison Guerriero went for a walk.
She turned on her phone.
And she left us all a message.
Not about Charles McGonigal. We already know that name.
McGonigal was the FBI’s former Special Agent in Charge of Counterintelligence in New York who accepted secret cash from an Albanian-connected associate and, after leaving the Bureau, went to work for sanctioned Russian oligarch Oleg Deripaska.
He is in prison.
Case closed?
Not according to Allison Guerriero.
She mentioned names everybody knows: James Comey. Christopher Wray—both former FBI directors.
And then:
“Why don’t you start looking for the names that you do not know?”
Hours later, Allison Guerriero was dead.
In my previous post, THE McGONIGAL WITNESS IS DEAD, I wrote that her final words deserved attention.
So let’s pay attention.
Let’s look for the names.
Because Allison Guerriero had already given us some of them.
William Sweeney
Start with William F. Sweeney Jr.
Sweeney was Assistant Director in Charge of the FBI’s New York Field Office.
While Charles McGonigal ran counterintelligence in New York, Sweeney occupied one of the most powerful positions above him.
According to Guerriero, after her relationship with McGonigal ended and she began piecing together what she had witnessed, she emailed Sweeney in 2019.
Her warning concerned McGonigal’s treasonous dealings with Albania.
She later said nothing came of it.
Albania alone should have set counterintelligence alarm bells ringing.
It was two years later, according to Guerriero, before FBI agents appeared at her home to talk about Albania and show her a photograph of McGonigal with Albanian Prime Minister Edi Rama and question her about the relationship.
Which leaves a very simple question:
What did William Sweeney do with Allison Guerriero’s warning in 2019?
Was it documented? Was it referred? Was it investigated?
Was it filed somewhere and forgotten until investigators came knocking on her door two years later?
Writing publicly in support of former NYPD detective Michael McMahon, Guerriero said she possessed documents containing familiar FBI names—including Sweeney’s—and called for a broad investigation into people at the Justice Department whom she believed had protected McGonigal.
Sweeney retired from the FBI in 2021. He subsequently joined Citi, where he serves as Managing Director and Chief Security Officer.
Douglas Leff
Another was Douglas Leff.
Leff served in senior FBI positions including Chief of the Inspection Division at FBI Headquarters.
The Inspection Division is responsible for inspecting the FBI itself—including internal investigations and special inquiries ordered by FBI leadership.
In other words, Guerriero says she sought help from a man who ultimately occupied one of the Bureau’s principal internal-oversight positions.
Guerriero said she knew him.
More importantly, she said he knew about her relationship with McGonigal.
According to Guerriero, when she began trying to alert the Bureau to what she believed McGonigal had been doing, she reached out to Leff for help.
She said he ignored her.
Again, that is Guerriero’s account.
As with William Sweeney, it does not establish misconduct.
But there is a pattern here that deserves scrutiny.
Guerriero repeatedly claimed she attempted to warn senior people inside the FBI about one of the most important counterintelligence officials in America.
