And repeatedly, according to her, nobody wanted to know.
Leff left the FBI in 2022 and is now an Assistant District Attorney in the Bronx.
Eventually the Justice Department proved that McGonigal had indeed been compromised.
Which raises a rather awkward question.
Why didn’t the FBI want to hear it earlier?
“One of Many”
Guerriero eventually became explicit about what she believed.
McGonigal, she wrote, was not simply one rogue FBI agent who had wandered off the reservation.
“He is one of many.”
That was Guerriero's allegation.
There is no evidence currently available to establish that McGonigal was literally “one of many” compromised FBI officials.
But coming from a woman who had lived with the head of FBI counterintelligence in New York, discovered his unexplained cash, watched his foreign relationships develop and subsequently spent years trying to persuade the Bureau to investigate him, it cannot simply be waved away as she wants revenge after a break-up (assuming that was what the officials believed).
Especially because her central suspicion was correct: McGonigal had turned rotten.
The unanswered question is whether Guerriero was also correct about the other three words.
One of many.
Others
This is where the story becomes more interesting.
Earlier this year Guerriero wrote: “There is more I want to say and reveal. A lot more! Right now, I simply can’t.”
Read that again.
Something she wanted to reveal.
And in another public statement she described herself as being in the middle of what she believed was an ongoing espionage and money-laundering investigation involving:
“Charles McGonigal and others.”
Those words again.
And others.
Who?
The Russian
One of the most intriguing names in the McGonigal story is Sergey Shestakov.
Shestakov was not an FBI official. He was something rather more exotic.
A former Soviet and Russian diplomat who had served at the United Nations before becoming an American citizen and working as an interpreter for federal courts.
Guerriero knew him.
According to Guerriero, she and McGonigal dined repeatedly with Shestakov and his wife. They attended hockey games together.
And Guerriero noticed something peculiar.
At dinner, Shestakov would sometimes hand McGonigal a sealed envelope.
Not once.
According to Guerriero, it happened three or four times between roughly mid-2017 and late 2018.
Always the same direction.
Shestakov to McGonigal.
Guerriero never saw what was inside.
At the time, she rationalized it. Perhaps Shestakov had translated something. Perhaps it involved legitimate FBI business.
After all, McGonigal was the head of FBI counterintelligence in New York.
Who questions the man whose job is to catch spies?
Then came the indictments.
And there, alongside Charles McGonigal, was Sergey Shestakov.
Federal prosecutors accused the two men of working on behalf of Russian oligarch Oleg Deripaska in violation of U.S. sanctions.
Shestakov, according to prosecutors, helped connect McGonigal to Deripaska’s world.
Which suddenly makes those envelopes across the dinner table considerably more interesting.
Enter Deripaska
Oleg Deripaska is not simply a wealthy Russian businessman.
He is one of the best-known oligarchs in Vladimir Putin’s orbit.
McGonigal had once participated, as an FBI official, in investigations involving Russian oligarchs—including Deripaska.
Then, after leaving the FBI, he went to work for Deripaska.
There is a sentence worth savoring.
The former head of counterintelligence for the FBI’s New York office wound up secretly working for a Russian oligarch whom the United States had sanctioned.
And Guerriero said McGonigal once invited her to accompany him to Vienna to meet Deripaska.
She declined.
The Man in the Middle
There may have been another Russian figure in the chain.
Court filings described an individual as Agent-1, a person associated with Deripaska.
Investigative reporting subsequently pointed toward Evgeny Fokin, an executive associated with Deripaska’s En+ Group and a former Russian diplomat, as the likely identity of Agent-1.
That identification has not, to my knowledge, been officially confirmed.
So we tread carefully.
But prosecutors alleged that while McGonigal was still working for the FBI, he was already developing a relationship with Deripaska’s circle.
He even arranged for Agent-1’s daughter to receive VIP treatment from the New York Police Department.
While running counterintelligence for the FBI.
Thus a possible chain begins to emerge:
DERIPASKA to people in his orbit, to SHESTAKOV, to McGONIGAL, and potentially into the most sensitive counterintelligence office in America.
And sitting at some of those dinners, watching envelopes change hands, was Allison Guerriero.
The Bag of Cash
Then there is the money.
Guerriero said that in October 2017 she found a bag containing roughly $80,000 in cash in McGonigal’s Brooklyn apartment.
She asked him about it.
Baseball winnings, he told her.
Lucky fellow, Charlie.
Except federal prosecutors subsequently established that on October 5, 2017, McGonigal received $80,000 in cash from an Albanian-connected associate sitting in a parked car outside a New York restaurant.
That payment was part of $225,000 McGonigal secretly received.
This matters because Guerriero wasn’t merely making allegations from afar.
She was inside the room.
She saw the bag of cash.
She saw the envelopes.
She saw the people involved.
Eventually, she began connecting the dots.
The Second Phone
Then there was McGonigal’s other telephone.
According to Guerriero, after the FBI prohibited employees from using WhatsApp on Bureau phones, McGonigal acquired a second iPhone.
He carried both phones everywhere.
The second phone, she said, was used almost exclusively for WhatsApp.
McGonigal told her he needed it to communicate with sources.
For the head of FBI counterintelligence, maintaining sensitive communications outside ordinary channels need not, by itself, be sinister.
But McGonigal was subsequently convicted of concealing foreign financial relationships and illegally working for a sanctioned Russian oligarch.
That context changes everything.
Somewhere inside the McGonigal investigation should therefore be the answer to a remarkably simple question:
Who was on the other end of that second phone?
Were its contents recovered?
Were its WhatsApp communications preserved?
Were the numbers identified?
Were foreign contacts among them?
And did investigators establish when McGonigal began communicating with the people who would eventually connect him to Oleg Deripaska?
Who Else Knew?
This is the question that has never received a satisfactory answer.
McGonigal was one of the FBI’s most senior counterintelligence executives.
People worked above him. People worked below him. People approved things. People saw things. People received reports. People reviewed expenses. People knew whom he met.
And at least one woman outside the Bureau says she began warning senior FBI officials that something was wrong.
And eventually the FBI came back to her.
According to Guerriero, in November 2021 two FBI agents arrived at her home and began asking questions about precisely the territory she said she had raised two years earlier.
Albania. McGonigal.
Think about that sequence.
2019: Guerriero says she warns senior FBI management about McGonigal and Albania.
2021: FBI investigators question Guerriero about McGonigal and Albania.
2023: McGonigal is arrested.
Perhaps Guerriero’s warning played no role whatsoever in what followed. She apparently did not believe it triggered the investigation.
But that makes the question more interesting, not less.
What caused the FBI finally to start looking?
How thoroughly were those warnings investigated? When? By whom?
And after McGonigal was finally exposed, did the FBI conduct the kind of ruthless counterintelligence damage assessment that would ordinarily follow the compromise of someone with his level of access?
If so, where is it?
If not, why not?
The Unfinished Book
There may be one repository of names we have overlooked.
Allison Guerriero was writing a book.
As far back as April 2023, shortly after McGonigal’s arrest, Guerriero publicly announced that she was writing a book about McGonigal—and, significantly, how the FBI treated her after she began raising alarms about him.
She even said she had spoken with literary agents and was shopping the rights.
We do not know how far she got.
We do not know whether there was a completed manuscript, a partial manuscript, chapter drafts, interview transcripts, recordings, emails, text messages or simply a collection of research notes.
But we know she continued writing publicly about McGonigal until shortly before her death.
On August 9—just 18 days before she died—Guerriero published another lengthy examination of the case.
And months earlier she had written:
“There is more I want to say and reveal. A lot more! Right now, I simply can’t.”
Which leaves this important question.
Where is Allison Guerriero’s unfinished book?
Because if a manuscript—or the research behind it—still exists, we may not have to speculate about what she meant when she told us to look for “the names that you do not know.”
Follow the Names
Before she died, Allison Guerriero was telling anyone who would listen that the Charles McGonigal scandal was larger than Charles McGonigal.
She said there were other people.
She said there were names.
She said she wanted to reveal more.
And on August 27, walking through the Florida sunshine with her telephone held in front of her, she issued what would become her final challenge:
Don’t look at the names everybody knows. Look for the names you don’t.
So we shall.
William Sweeney
Douglas Leff.
Sergey Shestakov.
Evgeny Fokin.
Those are some of them.
But I suspect Allison Guerriero was telling us something else.
There are more.
They may be in Allison’s manuscript.
Or they may already be sitting in somebody's FBI files.

There was a time when seduction required effort.
A good intelligence service needed an attractive operative.
Wardrobe. Training. Travel. A hotel suite.
Perhaps champagne.
Certainly patience.
The target had to be identified, approached, flattered, compromised and, with luck, recruited.
It was expensive. Labor-intensive.
The Internet has changed all that.
Now the beautiful stranger may not be beautiful.
She may not be a stranger. She may not even be a she.
And nobody has to leave home.
Welcome to Honeytrap.com.
Meet Dave
David Franklin Slater had the sort of résumé that should have made him extremely difficult to fool.
A retired Army lieutenant colonel. Civilian employee of the Air Force. Top Secret clearance.
And not just anywhere.
Slater worked at United States Strategic Command—USSTRATCOM—at Offutt Air Force Base in Nebraska.
STRATCOM is involved in nuclear deterrence and some of America’s most sensitive military planning.
Slater worked in a classified space and attended briefings concerning Russia’s invasion of Ukraine classified as high as TOP SECRET//SENSITIVE.
Then Dave went online.
You Have a Match
On a foreign dating website, Slater encountered someone claiming to be a woman living in Ukraine.
We still do not publicly know who this person actually was.
The Justice Department calls this individual Slater’s co-conspirator and says she claimed to be a Ukrainian woman.
Maybe she was. Maybe she wasn’t.
Maybe “she” was a 53-year-old intelligence officer sitting beneath fluorescent lights somewhere drinking instant coffee.
Which is rather the point.
Slater apparently believed. And his correspondent knew how to keep him believing.
She called him “My sweet Dave” and “Beloved Dave” and “My secret agent” and— surely destined for the Honey Trap Hall of Fame—“My secret informant love.”
One feels that final phrase might have prompted a moment’s reflection.
Secret informant. Hmm.
But love, as they say, is blind.
Darling, How Was Work?
The questions began arriving.
Not: What are you wearing?
But: “Beloved Dave, do NATO and Biden have a secret plan to help us?”
And Dave answered.
According to his eventual guilty plea, between February and April 2022, David transmitted classified national-defense information learned from military briefings through the dating platform.
Information concerning military targets. Russian military capabilities.
He ultimately pleaded guilty to conspiring to willfully communicate national-defense information to an unauthorized person.
So much for pillow talk.
There wasn’t even a pillow.
The Perfect Honey Trap
Whether or not an intelligence service was behind Slater’s correspondent, the method illustrates the modern honey trap almost perfectly.
For centuries, intelligence services have understood something governments occasionally forget.
The weakest point in any security system is usually a human being.
You can build a SCIF. Install biometric locks. Encrypt communications.
Polygraph employees. Conduct background investigations. Require annual security training.
Then somebody types:
Hello handsome.
And it all collapses.
The brilliance of the online honey trap is not merely that it is cheap.
It is scalable.
The traditional seductress could cultivate perhaps one target at a time.
An online persona can theoretically cultivate dozens. Hundreds. Thousands.
The same photograph. The same compliments. The same affectionate punctuation.
The same: You are so interesting. Tell me more about your work.
Mata Hari has been automated.
No Woman Required
And Slater's case points toward an even more unsettling possibility. Artificial intelligence makes the problem considerably worse.
Photographs can be created. Voices synthesized. Video manipulated. Biographies fabricated. Entire personalities constructed.
The target may spend months developing an emotional relationship with a person who has never existed.
Which represents a rather remarkable advance in espionage.
The intelligence service no longer needs to recruit a beautiful woman. It merely needs to render one.
The seduction has become software.
Why It Works
People tend to imagine honey traps as primarily sexual.
They aren’t. They are psychological.
Sex is merely one door.
The real target is need. Loneliness. Vanity. Recognition. Romance.
The desire to impress.
The sensation that somewhere in the world there is a person who finds everything about you fascinating.
Particularly dangerous for someone accustomed to importance.
A military officer spends decades being Colonel.
People listen when he speaks. His opinion matters. He enters rooms other people cannot enter.
Then retirement comes. The uniform goes into the closet. The telephone rings less frequently.
And suddenly… My sweet Dave.
Someone wants to know everything.
Including, unfortunately, what happened at this morning’s classified briefing.
The Truly Amazing Part
Slater wasn’t an inexperienced 19-year-old private.
He had spent decades in the military. He possessed a Top Secret clearance. He had received security training. He worked at one of the most sensitive commands in the United States.
And his correspondent was not exactly subtle.
She called him her secret agent.
Imagine receiving an email from someone saying: Please send your bank details. I am definitely not committing fraud.
One might become suspicious.
Yet therein lies another old intelligence truth.
People see what they want to see.
The successful confidence trick does not persuade the victim to believe something absurd. It discovers the absurd thing the victim already wants to believe.
Dave apparently believed someone adored him.
Who Was She?
And now we arrive at the most interesting unanswered question.
Who was on the other end?
The public record still does not identify the correspondent.
Nor does it establish publicly that she—or he—was working for Russia, Ukraine or any other intelligence service.
A person of unknown identity, communicating remotely through a dating website, persuaded a Top Secret-cleared employee at U.S. Strategic Command to disclose classified national-defense information.
No dead drop. No clandestine meeting. No suitcase full of cash.
Just messages. And pet names.
Five Years and Ten Months
Reality eventually intervened.
Slater pleaded guilty in July 2025 to conspiracy to disclose national-defense information.
In October, a federal judge sentenced him to 70 months in prison and imposed a $25,000 fine.
The romance, such as it was, proved expensive.
And presumably disappointing. Because we still don't know whether the person he risked everything for was anything like the person presented to him online.
Mata Hari 2.0
The traditional honey trap depended upon physical proximity.
That was also its weakness.
The operative could be photographed. Followed. Identified. Recognized entering a hotel.
Her passport could be examined. Her background investigated. Her connections traced.
Honeytrap.com eliminates much of that.
The seducer can be anywhere. Be anyone. Become whatever the target requires.
Young. Blonde. Brunette. French.
Interested in nuclear deterrence.
Very impressed by retired lieutenant colonels.
The perfect lover.
Because the perfect lover has always been the person who finds you endlessly fascinating.
The New Tradecraft
The dead drop has become encrypted messaging.
The false passport is now a fake profile.
The safe house, a chat room.
The surveillance photograph, a screenshot.
And the honey trap?
It no longer requires honey. Only a target with a secret—and the desire to be loved.
Somewhere tonight, a man with a security clearance may be staring at his telephone.
A photograph appears. A message follows.
Hello.
He smiles.
Perhaps she is beautiful. Perhaps she is lonely. Perhaps she lives in Ukraine.
Perhaps she doesn’t.
Perhaps she doesn’t exist.
Mata Hari aimed for your bedroom.
Now she aims for your inbox.

When we last encountered Karl-Magnus Carlsson, he was sitting in custody on the African island nation of São Tomé & Príncipe.
Things have moved along.
Carlsson has now been extradited to Sweden.
But before we get to that, there is a fun new twist.
The fugitive had become a presidential adviser.
On December 4, 2025, the President of São Tomé & Príncipe, Carlos Vila Nova, appointed Carlsson as a special adviser.
His purported areas of expertise?
Health projects and maritime security in the Gulf of Guinea.
Yeah, right—did Carlsson also offer the Brooklyn Bridge?
This, the Swedish conman I investigated more than two decades ago at the request of Prince Albert of Monaco,.
Carlsson—I warned the prince—lived lavishly on other people’s investment money and used his proximity to the prince as bait for new investors.
Years later, Carlsson found himself another head of state.
São Tomé & Príncipe even issued Carlsson a diplomatic passport.
You have to admire the chutzpah.
Most people fleeing trouble attempt to disappear.
The São Tomé presidency says Carlsson presented a clean criminal-record certificate when he was appointed.
Not so clean, it turned out, when Swedish police pinpointed his whereabouts and— through Interpol—requested his extradition on suspicions of aggravated rape, aggravated weapons offenses and aggravated assault in Bohuslän.
President Vila Nova dismissed Carlsson by decree on February 4, 2026.
He has since been extradited to Sweden and remanded in custody.
Another Trail
British corporate records show that Carlsson became a director of Evolved Aerospace Ltd in June 2025.
His directorship ended on February 23, 2026—around the time of his arrest.
His registered country of residence?
Cyprus.
Carlsson was also a director of MedPal AI PLC.
That appointment ended on March 30.
Thus the evolving Carlsson itinerary now looks something like this:
Monaco
Cyprus.
British companies.
São Tomé & Príncipe, presidential adviser, diplomatic passport.
Interpol.
Swedish custody.
The most interesting question about Karl-Magnus Carlsson has never been how he operates.
It is why powerful men keep letting him through the door.
Prince Albert asked me to investigate Carlsson because he was concerned about some of the people who had attached themselves to his entourage.
I reported what I found and recommended that Albert distance himself from Carlsson.
He didn’t.
Indeed, Albert subsequently invited Carlsson to his birthday celebration at a Moscow brothel.
Two decades pass.
In São Tomé & Príncipe, the doors somehow opened wide enough for Carlsson to walk through and emerge with a diplomatic passport.
Now he is back in Sweden, in custody, facing serious charges.
Conmen come and go.
The open doors are the real story—and the corruption that allows them entry.

This appeared in Santa Barbara Current.
There are certain things one comes to accept as permanent features of life in Montecito.
The Pacific Ocean. The mountains. Fine weather.
Oh, and quakes, fire—and a biblical mudslide every 20-30 years (not once a century, as realtors like to say).
And Highway 101 under construction.
It’s been going on for so long that the orange traffic cone should be California’s new state emblem.
Highway 101’s ancestor, El Camino Real—the King’s Highway—linked California’s Spanish missions and settlements.
People walked it. Horses walked it. Mules walked it.
Traffic moved slowly, but at least it moved.
Then came the automobile.
California created its Highway Commission in 1911 and began constructing a state highway system just as Californians discovered the pleasure of going somewhere without a horse.
The coastal road connecting Los Angeles with Santa Barbara became increasingly popular. And increasingly crowded.
Thus began a problem with which we remain intimately acquainted.
Montecito’s First Traffic Jam
By the 1920s, planners were already worrying about traffic through Montecito.
In 1926, California highway officials reported that traffic between Los Angeles and Santa Barbara was “heavy” and “steadily increasing.”
The existing Montecito road, parts of which dated to 1909, was no longer adequate.
There were dangerous curves. There wasn’t enough capacity.
Something had to be done.
So they widened it.
Remember this. It becomes something of a theme.
That same year, the federal government introduced its numbered highway system and the great coastal road became U.S. Highway 101.
It stretched from Southern California through Santa Barbara, San Francisco and the redwoods, eventually reaching Washington State.
Through Montecito, engineers widened and straightened 1.9 miles of roadway.
The result was hailed as one of the finest sections of the Coast Highway.
Traffic problem solved.
For approximately five minutes.
More Cars, More Road
California boomed. Automobile ownership exploded. The highway evolved.
Sections became divided highway and eventually freeway.
Then, in 1956, President Eisenhower created the Interstate Highway System.
But 101 did not become Interstate 101.
There is no Interstate 101.
Our road remained U.S. Route 101, a survivor of the older federal highway system, while Interstate 5 became California’s great north-south interstate artery.
101 nevertheless gradually acquired all the characteristics of an interstate: multiple lanes, controlled access, interchanges, concrete barriers—and the ability to bring enormous numbers of automobiles to a complete standstill simultaneously.
By the 1960s, officials were once again worrying about congestion through Santa Barbara and considering whether 101 should be widened from four lanes to six.
This means Santa Barbara has been discussing how to fix Highway 101 for roughly as long as the Rolling Stones have been performing.
Parts of 101 were widened. Parts weren’t.
Three lanes became two. Traffic compressed. A bottleneck was created.
And eventually government did what government does best when confronted with a problem everyone can see.
It commissioned a study.
101 in Motion
After many years of deliberation came 101 In Motion, the major transportation study completed in 2006.
Its finding was revolutionary: Highway 101 needed more capacity.
This discovery produced plans for transit improvements, passenger rail and, most importantly, a continuous third freeway lane in each direction between Carpinteria and Santa Barbara.
The additional lane would operate as a high-occupancy vehicle lane during peak periods.
Thus began the enormous Highway 101: Carpinteria to Santa Barbara project.
Twenty years after 101 In Motion, Highway 101 is certainly in motion.
Mostly sideways.
Welcome to the Cone Zone
To be fair, an enormous amount of work has been accomplished.
The project has crawled northward through Mussel Shoals, Carpinteria, Padaro Lane, Summerland and now Montecito and Santa Barbara.
Interchanges reconstructed. On-ramps moved. Off-ramps moved. Retaining walls erected. Roundabouts created.
Lanes disappeared. Lanes reappeared.
Concrete barriers migrated mysteriously during the night.
And everywhere: orange cones.
Hundreds of them.
The Coast Village Road Parking Lot
The official project descriptions are reassuring.
The lived experience is somewhat different.
Take Coast Village Road. Please. (As the old joke goes.)
Almost every day now it becomes gridlocked from one end to the other—from circle to circle. For hours.
Once upon a time, locals possessed secret knowledge.
When 101 backed up, we knew the escape routes.
And then, when Coast Village Road backed up, we could still find refuge in Hot Springs Road or Coast Village Circle.
Not anymore.
Now everyone else—thanks to GPS navigation—knows them too, transforming shortcuts into long-cuts converging into bottlenecks.
Then there is Hermosillo Road.
Someone decided in the midst of all this Coast Village Road desperately needed a traffic light. (To my knowledge, Coast Village Road has never had a traffic light.)
A temporary traffic light.
“Temporary” is one of government’s lovelier words.
Income tax was “temporary” too.
The light arrived in April at the western entrance to Coast Village Road and now interrupts what was once a free-flowing village street.
There are presumably traffic engineers who possess sophisticated computer models proving this makes perfect sense.
Those of us sitting motionless in our cars have developed a simpler analytical model.
It consists of one question: What are the roadway/traffic engineers smoking?
Especially when you consider the non-flowing circle…
No Way Out
The really clever part is that escaping Highway 101 does not necessarily free you from construction.
Santa Barbara appears to be conducting a citywide experiment to determine how many roads can be dug up simultaneously before the population cracks.
Roadworks. Utility works. Lane closures. Barricades. Detours. Heavy equipment.
Signs directing you away from one closed road and toward another sign directing you away from another closed road.
One detour turns into another detour and you realize you have become a lab mouse in a maze. Instead of trying to reach your destination you’re resigned to going wherever the city has decided to send you.
But There is a Plan
Beneath this apparent municipal nervous breakdown lies an actual objective.
When the cones finally disappear, Highway 101 through the corridor is supposed to have three lanes instead of two in each direction, with the new lane operating as a carpool lane during peak periods.
Montecito gets new carpool lanes.
There will be auxiliary lanes between San Ysidro and Olive Mill, intended to separate cars entering and leaving the freeway.
New bridges are being constructed over Romero, San Ysidro and Oak creeks.
Olive Mill, Hot Springs and San Ysidro already have their roundabouts.
Farther north, another carpool lane extends between Hermosillo Road and Salinas Street.
The Cabrillo Boulevard interchange is being rebuilt, with new freeway bridges and redesigned ramps.
The ultimate objective is a continuous six-lane corridor through what has historically been the great Carpinteria-Santa Barbara bottleneck.
Which sounds splendid.
There is just one minor matter.
When Do We Get It ?
The work is being completed in stages.
Some Montecito sections are said to be approaching completion—though you’d never know it by what you see with your own eyes.
Santa Barbara is another story.
The Cabrillo portion began construction in April 2026.
Its currently projected completion: December 8, 2028.
The northbound and southbound Cabrillo off-ramps are expected to remain closed until summer 2028.
So we have a while.
This assumes, of course, that December 8, 2028 means December 8, 2028.
Anyone who has lived through a home renovation knows better than to become emotionally attached to a completion date.
And this is a home renovation approximately sixteen miles long.
Progress
Perhaps we should take comfort from history.
In the 1920s, officials discovered that too many automobiles were using the road through Montecito.
They widened it.
More automobiles came.
By the 1960s there were too many automobiles again.
They planned to widen it.
More automobiles came.
Eventually they studied the problem.
Then they studied the study.
Then they devised a plan.
Then they funded the plan.
Then they began construction.
Now we are widening it again.
And when the magnificent new Highway 101 is finally finished, we shall have six beautiful lanes.
Of course, with many more automobiles coming our way, it will by then be obsolete—and, yes, in need of more widening.
On the brighter side…
A morning walk before sunrise.

There is a new and disturbing development in the strange case of Charles McGonigal.
Allison Guerriero is dead.
She was 52.
Guerriero was the former girlfriend of Charles McGonigal, once one of the most powerful counterintelligence officials in the FBI—and subsequently a convicted felon who admitted taking secret payments connected to Albania and illegally working for Russian oligarch Oleg Deripaska.
I have written about McGonigal.
I have also argued that the official story of his betrayal leaves far too many questions unanswered.
Now there is another.
What happened to Allison Guerriero?
According to the Daily Mail, Guerriero was found dead at her apartment in Boynton Beach, Florida, on Thursday evening, August 27.
Police were called at 8:03 p.m.
As of this writing, the cause of death has not been publicly established.
Boynton Beach police say there “do not appear to be any signs of foul play at this time.” The investigation remains open while police await information from the medical examiner.
Guerriero was not an ordinary 52-year-old woman who happened to die unexpectedly in Florida.
She was an important witness to one of the strangest counterintelligence scandals in FBI history.
And only hours before her death, she was talking about it.
The Woman Who Knew
Guerriero began a relationship with McGonigal in 2017.
McGonigal was then Special Agent in Charge of Counterintelligence for the FBI’s New York Field Office.
His job was to find spies.
Meanwhile, according to federal prosecutors, McGonigal was embarking upon precisely the kind of undisclosed foreign relationships and financial arrangements that counterintelligence officers are trained to detect.
Guerriero was there.
She lived with him in his Park Slope apartment.
She watched him operate.
And, most significantly, she saw the money.
In October 2017, according to Guerriero, she discovered a bag near the entrance to McGonigal’s apartment containing approximately $80,000 in cash, rolled in $100 bills.
When she questioned him, McGonigal supposedly explained that he had won it betting on baseball.
Federal prosecutors subsequently established something rather more interesting.
On October 5, 2017, McGonigal received $80,000 in cash from an Albanian-American associate in a parked car outside a New York restaurant.
Guerriero later wondered whether her birthday dinner with McGonigal around that same period had provided camouflage for the transaction.
She also said McGonigal invited her to accompany him to Vienna to meet Oleg Deripaska.
The Russian oligarch sanctioned by the United States.
The man McGonigal would eventually admit illegally working for.
At some point, Guerriero’s counterintelligence instincts began functioning better than those of the FBI.
She concluded that something was very wrong.
After their relationship ended, she began contacting senior FBI officials.
Her message, she later recalled, was essentially this: Your superstar is compromised.
She claimed they didn’t want to hear it.
McGonigal was finally arrested in January 2023.
He ultimately pleaded guilty in two federal cases and received prison sentences totaling six years and six months.
But Guerriero never believed the government had gotten to the bottom of the story.
Neither do I.
I Knew McGonigal Too
More than two decades ago, while working in Monaco, I encountered McGonigal in connection with an FBI counterintelligence matter.
This was long before Albania. Long before Deripaska. Long before Allison Guerriero.
And long before the United States government acknowledged that one of its senior counterintelligence officials had himself become compromised.
That experience has always left me with a rather obvious question:
When did Charles McGonigal really go bad?
The government’s prosecutions established crimes.
They did not establish the full extent of the damage.
McGonigal occupied extraordinarily sensitive positions during his FBI career. He possessed access to intelligence operations, sources, investigations, foreign liaison relationships and some of the most closely guarded counterintelligence information in the United States government.
Yet the public accounting of what happened has remained remarkably narrow.
Which brings us back to Allison Guerriero.
“Look For the Names You Do Not Know”
On the morning of August 27—the day she died—Guerriero went walking through Boynton Beach.
She filmed herself. She appeared energetic. She addressed “friends and enemies.”
And she returned to the subject that had consumed much of her life since McGonigal’s downfall.
The FBI.
She posted approximately 75 times on X that day, according to the Daily Mail.
In one video she said: “Here’s the problem with Charles McGonigal.”
Then came something much more interesting. “You know his name, but you never did before that.”
She mentioned former FBI directors James Comey and Christopher Wray.
And then she said: “Why don’t you start looking for the names that you do not know?”
Hours later, Allison Guerriero was dead.
At this writing, we do not know how Allison Guerriero died.
But her final words deserve attention because they encapsulate the unanswered question at the center of the entire McGonigal affair.
Was Charles McGonigal an isolated corrupt FBI official?
Or was he part of something larger?
The Last Witness
There is another intriguing detail.
According to Roger Stone, Guerriero texted him on the day she died.
Stone told the Daily Mail that the messages were work-related and that Guerriero was helping him with research.
He said she seemed to be in “excellent spirits.”
Her father similarly said that since moving to Florida she had been happier than he had seen her in years.
Counterintelligence begins with unanswered questions.
So let us ask them.
What was the cause of Allison Guerriero’s death?
What will the medical examiner find?
What was she researching in the days before she died?
Who was she communicating with?
What did she mean by “the names that you do not know”?
And what, if anything, did Allison Guerriero still know about Charles McGonigal that has never become public?
For now, we wait for the autopsy.
And we look for the names we do not know.

In my dreams, I keep searching for Kate Darconti—a frantic, fruitless search that produces only Ligichansky’s round Latvian face saying, “You look, you look, you look.”
I awake and stare at the ceiling.
Where had I first learned about Podex?
Not Krutskov. That chapter of his book was my own invention, based on hearing about it from... Skeeter Leland, the DDO.
Then corroborated—if unwittingly—by Darconti, chief of Central Asia.
And then the White House wanted to kill it.
Was that staged to egg me on?
No.
The simple truth is, I do not possess all the pieces.
⁂
An express elevator ups me to the seventh floor of CIA headquarters.
I aim myself at Skeeter LeLand’s office and plunk myself into a chair facing him.
“There’s something I need to know,” I say. “From whom did you first learn about Podex?”
Skeeter considers this. “I guess it would have come from Darconti. Her division, Central Asia.”
“Don’t guess. My question is very specific: Who asked Darconti’s division to look into Podex in the first place? The original request had to come from somewhere, right?”
Skeeter nods.
“CIA responds to requests for information from policy-makers,” I say. “So let me re-phrase my question: Did the White House originally request that we gather intelligence on Podex?”
“No,” says Skeeter, his memory jogged. “That request came from the State Department.”
“Now we’re getting somewhere. Who at State?”
“The Deputy Secretary of State,” says Skeeter. “Herbert Picklewart.”
“Warthead?”
“You know him?”
“Of him. Ask Warhead if he’d be kind enough to stop by for a chat.”
“When?”
“Right now. But if he’s busy, I’ll settle for this afternoon.”
Skeeter hits a button right in front of me, asks his secretary to find Herbert Picklewart, and she does.
“Skeeter?” says a voice over the speakerphone. “Herb Picklewart.” He says his name like it bewilders him.
“Herb, I need to talk to you,” says Skeeter. “Can you come out to Langley?”
“What is it about?”
“Podex.”
Silence.
“Herb?”
“Yes, uh yes. Uh, what, hmmm.” Warthead splutters like Pikestaff. “What about Podex?”
Skeeter looks at me.
I shake my head and put an index finger to my lips.
“Better to talk in person,” says Skeeter.
“I don’t understand,” says Warhead. “Podex is a non issue. Weren’t you told to stand down?”
“Something’s come up.”
“Uh, okay. Could you come to my office?” Warthead prefers his own turf. “Say, 2:45?”
Skeeter looks at me. I nod.
⁂
At 2:45 precisely, Skeeter and I sit in Herbert Picklewart’s waiting room in Foggy Bottom, waiting for the Deputy Secretary of State to return from lunch.
Eight minutes later, Warthead strides in.
Picklewart is a beanpole of a man in expensive pinstripe flannels cuffed over highly-polished black Allen Edmunds wingtips. His balding pate sports a huge wart—either his signature trademark or an unfortunate feature given his name.
“Please.” Warthead gestures that we enter his grand stateroom, then motions again, not toward the informal suite seating, but toward his imposing desk.
If we are going to impose, so will he.
In this way, Warthead plays his turf to the hilt, reclining in a leather-tooled swivel chair, facing us over his desk. At one point, he loses balance and almost spills off, a consequence of trying to disguise his discomfort.
“Long day.” Warthead fiddles with a pen. “What is it you’ve come to see me about?”
As if he doesn’t know.
“Podex,” I say.
Warthead studies me, like, who asked you? Or more likely, who are you?
“Jay is attached to us,” says Skeeter.
“I gather that, or he wouldn’t be here. I wondered beyond attached.” Warthead regards me with a long gaze, meant to intimidate, and when neither Skeeter nor I say anything more, he readdresses Skeeter. “What about Podex?”
“You asked CIA to find out about Podex,” says Skeeter.
“We’d like to know why?” I add.
Warthead fixes on Skeeter. “You must be mistaken.”
A bewildered expression crosses Skeeter’s face. “Am I?”
Warthead shakes his head. “I have no recollection of requesting anything like that.”
I do not expect Warthead’s vocal cords to produce what I need to know. Instead, I look into Warthead’s unyielding hawk-brown eyes, trying to unlock the secret within. That’s all I need: the opportunity to look at somebody face-to-face, study their eyes—an open the window to their brain.
Herbert Picklewart’s eyes deliver.
Warthead says nothing more; just sits there with his arms folded, body language that defies anyone to call him a liar.
I rise, wordless. Skeeter, too.
Warthead appears surprised. And relieved it is over so soon.
“Sorry,” he feels a need to say.
“Don’t apologize, Herb,” I say. “It’s been a real pleasure.”
Warthead blinks, unfolds his arms, and rises to see us out.
Skeeter shakes his head in quiet disgust as we descend from State’s seventh floor.
“Foggy Bottom, foggy brains,” he mutters, rolling his eyes.
“I like that,” I say. “The beginning of a nursery rhyme. About snakes.” I see Skeeter into a taxi. “I’ve got to run an errand. Catch you later.”

A curving stretch of road from the Monterey Peninsula through Big Sur to Morrow Bay is widely regarded as one of the most spectacularly scenic drives America.
But on this day, Pacific Coast Highway is layered in fog and haze.
Somewhat gloomy.
In other words, just the right setting and mood for the final leg of a road trip commemorating Lulu’s life and, with her ashes along for the ride, memorializing her transcendence to doggie heaven.
We launch from Carmel and cruise through the towering redwoods of Big Sur.
Thereafter, the Santa Lucia Mountains rise to our left while the land falls away in sheer drops to the Pacific on our right.
The music, alternately, is Yiruma’s melancholy piano and Autumn in Tuscany by Tim Janis.
Soothing.
Meditative.
Evoking memories of Lulu from our cross-country road-tripping days.
We stop in quaint Cambria to stretch our legs and, at Linn’s Restaurant, pick up their famed olallieberry pie (a blackberry-raspberry hybrid).
Lunch is twelve miles farther on in Cayucos, a summer vacation spot in full swing.
Duckies Chowder House is a few feet from the sand in this beachy burg.
Clam chowder and fish tacos.
A feast.
Dessert is a no-brainer: The Original Sea Salt shortbread from Brown Butter Cookie Co.
Lulu would have approved.
Rejoining the road, we soon pass Morro Bay and its famed subvolcanic plug, Morro Rock— “the Gibraltar of the Pacific.”
And then, farther south, I ramp onto 154 toward Los Olivos, where Lulu spent most of her final 15 months—and follow the route she traveled so many times between the Santa Ynez Valley and Montecito.
Only this time, for Lulu, it is the last.
