Images of a catastrophic mudslide in Nepal filling our screens bring to mind the Montecito mudslide of January 9, 2018.
In the aftermath, we heard a comforting phrase repeated again and again.
The storm of the century.
Sometimes the estimates became even more reassuring.
A 500-year event.
The implication was obvious.
Terrible. Tragic. But freakish.
Nature had dealt Montecito an almost unimaginably bad hand and, having done so, would presumably leave us alone for another century or two.
There is only one problem.
It isn’t true.
Not remotely.
The rain that triggered the catastrophe was indeed extraordinary. At one Montecito gauge, more than half an inch fell in five minutes—an intensity estimated at roughly a 200-year recurrence interval.
But the resulting debris flow? That’s another matter entirely.
Geologists who subsequently went digging through two centuries of records discovered something rather unsettling.
Montecito has done this before.
Again. And again. And again.
The Night the Mountain Came Down
Anyone who lived here in January 2018 needs no reminder.
The Thomas Fire had burned the mountains above us only weeks earlier, stripping vegetation from steep slopes and leaving enormous quantities of loose sediment behind.
Then came the rain.
At about 3:45 on the morning of January 9, an extraordinarily intense burst fell on the burned mountains.
Water rushed downhill. Soil moved. Then rocks. Then boulders. Then trees.
Then everything.
Within minutes, the creeks descending through Montecito became torrents of mud, rock and debris.
Some boulders measured more than 13 feet across.
The flows traveled at speeds approaching nine miles an hour—which doesn’t sound particularly impressive until you imagine several tons of rock coming through your in seconds.
About 680,000 cubic meters of material came down.
Homes were ripped from foundations. Cars were tossed about.
Olive Mill Road became a river.
Coast Village Road became No Man’s Land.
The flow crossed Highway 101 and continued to the Pacific.
Twenty-three people died. At least 167 were injured. More than 400 homes were damaged.
It was one of the worst disasters in Santa Barbara County history.
Surely something of this magnitude had never happened here before.
Except it had.
1825
In 1825, a wildfire burned the mountains behind Santa Barbara and Montecito.
Then came heavy rain. Then debris.
The historical record is imperfect—the population was tiny—but geological and documentary research identifies a major post-fire debris-flow event.
The pattern had already been established.
Fire. Rain. Mountain.
And Montecito sits below it.
1861–62
Then came something much bigger.
California’s legendary winter of 1861–62 produced flooding on a scale almost unimaginable today.
Weeks of storms transformed much of the Central Valley into an inland sea.
Santa Barbara County was hammered. And Montecito experienced another enormous debris-flow episode.
How enormous?
Researchers studying the history of our debris flows concluded that the 1861–62 event was larger than 2018.
Much larger.
1914
Then it happened again.
In January 1914, tremendous rainfall struck the region.
Floodwaters and debris descended from the mountains.
Montecito creeks overflowed. Roads and bridges were damaged. Boulders and sediment swept down from the canyons.
Contemporary newspaper accounts described the destruction.
And one eyewitness compared what he had just seen with the great events of 1825 and 1862.
In other words, people living here more than a century ago already understood something we somehow managed to forget: Montecito has a history of catastrophic debris flows.
1926
Only 12 years later: Again.
Following wildfire, major debris flows came down San Ysidro Creek in April 1926.
Not once. Several times.
Mountains again reminded everyone what they were made of.
We continued building beneath them.
1964
The Coyote Fire.
It burned tens of thousands of acres in the mountains above Santa Barbara and Montecito in September and October 1964.
Two months later came rain.
Debris flows descended through Hot Springs, Cold Springs, Montecito and San Ysidro watersheds.
Homes and infrastructure were damaged.
1969
Five years later, the burned watershed still had something to say.
Heavy storms struck again in January and February 1969.
Debris flows and debris-laden floods poured through Montecito and Carpinteria creeks.
Around 100 Montecito homes were damaged.
Highway 101 flooded.
Older Montecito residents remembered it.
Some who survived 2018 had survived 1969 too.
One resident, hearing that terrible roar coming down Olive Mill in 2018, recognized it.
He had heard the mountain before.
1971
Then came the Romero Fire.
On December 27, only about forty minutes of intense rainfall was sufficient to produce flooding and debris flows through Romero, Toro and neighboring watersheds.
Mud blocked Highway 101 near Carpinteria for hours.
Again: Fire. Rain. Mountain.
By now you may have noticed a pattern.
1995
And then, only 23 years before the catastrophe most of us remember:
January brought destructive debris-laden flooding through the Montecito, Santa Barbara, Carpinteria and Goleta watersheds.
Then it happened again in March.
People died.
And researchers now place 1995 among the five largest debris-flow or debris-laden-flood episodes affecting Montecito during the last two centuries.
Nine major events in roughly 200 years.
Suddenly “storm of the century” begins to sound rather less reassuring.
The Numbers We Should Have Known
After 2018, engineering geologist Larry Gurrola and geological engineer J. David Rogers undertook an extraordinary reconstruction of the region’s history.
They examined hundreds of documents: old maps, government reports, newspaper accounts, historical archives, surveys, fire records, flood records.
They reconstructed approximately two centuries of fire and flood history.
Their findings deserve far more attention in Montecito than they have received.
They identified 22 debris flows and debris-laden floods that damaged the downstream community of Montecito.
Nearly two-thirds were associated with recent wildfire.
Of the five greatest events identified over the last two centuries, 2018 was the smallest.
We Live On the Evidence
Look around Montecito.
Those enormous rounded sandstone boulders decorating estates and creek beds did not arrive courtesy of a landscape architect.
The mountains put them there.
Geologists have found ancient debris-flow deposits beneath Montecito extending back tens of thousands of years.
During excavation work around San Ysidro Creek, boulders up to 15 feet in diameter were found in ancient deposits.
Researchers have identified evidence of an enormous prehistoric debris flow along Montecito Creek extending roughly two and a quarter miles toward the ocean.
Estimated age: Between 1,000 and 2,000 years.
Go farther back and the geological record extends tens of thousands of years.
This changes the way one sees Montecito.
Our beautiful little community between mountain and sea isn’t merely threatened by debris flows.
Much of it was built by them.
The mountains erode. Canyons collect rock. Fire strips vegetation. Rain arrives.
Gravity takes over. Material comes down.
It spreads across the alluvial fan.
Then humans arrive and build houses on top of it.
The Good News
Debris basins have been enlarged and improved. Creeks have been cleared.
New debris-control systems have been installed. Ring nets now sit in several canyons above the community, designed to catch boulders and large woody debris before they reach homes below.
Emergency monitoring is vastly better.
Evacuation maps are better.
Warnings come earlier.
The Real Lesson of 1/9/2018
Nature doesn’t keep appointments.
An average recurrence interval isn’t a timetable.
Fifty years does not mean we have 42 years remaining on some geological warranty.
The next major debris flow could occur a century from now.
Or much sooner.
It depends upon fire. And rainfall.
Where the rain falls. How intensely it falls.
What condition the watershed is in when it arrives.
And chance.
But there is one thing we can discard: The notion that January 9, 2018 was some bizarre geological aberration unlikely ever to trouble Montecito again.
It wasn’t.
The historical record says so. The geological record says so. And the landscape itself says so.
Perhaps the strangest thing about Montecito is that the evidence has been sitting in front of us all along.
We admire it. We landscape around it. We illuminate it at night. We pay gardeners to make it look attractive.
The boulders are not decorations.
They are warnings.
The mountain has been sending them down for thousands of years.
And sooner or later, it will send more.
Which brings us to El Niño.
As I write this, El Niño is strengthening rapidly.
The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) now puts the odds of a very strong El Niño this fall and winter at more than 90 percent—and gives it a 69 percent chance of becoming stronger than any event in its modern record dating to 1950.
More to the point for those of us living beneath the Santa Ynez Mountains, NOAA has just shifted its winter outlook toward above-normal rainfall in California, with Southern California showing the greatest likelihood of a wet winter.
Couple that with the current heatwave and subsequent dry conditions—and the ingredients are assembling.
For now, catastrophe in Nepal is safely contained within our TV screens.
Many of us in Montecito have already witnessed a mudslide up close and personal.
Those paying attention know it will happen again.
Maybe sooner than we think.

Vladimir Putin does not merely read history.
He appears to keep appointments with it.
And something has Washington worried.
On Tuesday, CIA Director John Ratcliffe made a surprise, unannounced visit to Moscow aboard a U.S. military transport aircraft.
He stayed about eight and a half hours.
Ratcliffe did not meet Putin.
He met the men who whisper into Putin’s ear.
At least two of Russia’s most powerful intelligence chiefs were involved: Sergei Naryshkin, director of the SVR, Russia’s Foreign Intelligence Service, and Aleksandr Bortnikov, director of the FSB.
Naryshkin has publicly confirmed meeting Ratcliffe, describing their encounter as a “working-level meeting” involving sensitive intelligence matters.
The New York Times has since reported that Ratcliffe delivered a much more interesting message to Bortnikov.
According to the Times, the CIA director presented a bleak American assessment of Russia’s position in Ukraine: its battlefield advances have stalled, its casualties are enormous, its economic prospects are deteriorating and Ukraine shows no inclination to surrender.
The message, essentially: Make a deal before things get worse.
There was something else behind Ratcliffe’s mission.
American intelligence has reportedly questioned whether Putin’s own advisers are giving him an accurate picture of the war.
That may explain why the messenger mattered.
Putin is a former intelligence officer. If his political and military apparatus is feeding him what he wants to hear, perhaps Washington calculated that an assessment delivered directly from one intelligence chief to another might penetrate the bubble.
Putin was briefed immediately afterward.
President Trump called Ratcliffe’s visit “semi-routine.”
Naryshkin called it routine, too.
Yeah, right.
CIA directors do not routinely fly secretly to Moscow aboard military transport aircraft to tell Russian intelligence chiefs their war is going badly, warn them about escalation, discuss NATO and Iran, and attempt to correct what American intelligence apparently fears may be Vladimir Putin’s dangerously distorted understanding of reality.
Something is Stirring
The Wall Street Journal, citing people briefed on the mission, reported that Ratcliffe reaffirmed America’s commitment to NATO’s Article 5 and warned Moscow against provocations that might test the alliance.
The visit was so sensitive, according to the Journal, that some senior White House and military officials were unaware of it beforehand.
Then came another piece of the puzzle.
The Washington Post reported Thursday that fresh classified U.S. intelligence preceding Ratcliffe’s trip indicated that Putin believes America has been weakened by its six-month war with Iran.
In other words, Putin may see an opportunity.
American weapons stocks have been depleted. Patriot interceptors and other air-defense systems are under pressure. Washington is preoccupied in the Middle East. Ukraine’s own air-defense supplies are dwindling.
According to the Post, Ratcliffe warned Russian officials that significantly escalating the war in Ukraine would backfire—and could push Trump closer to Zelensky.
Put the pieces together:
Putin may believe America is weakened.
Washington believes Russia itself is weaker than Putin may appreciate.
That is how miscalculations begin.
And there is an uncomfortable historical echo.
The last publicly known CIA-director visit to Moscow came in November 2021.
His name was William Burns.
President Biden sent Burns to warn Putin that Washington knew Russia was preparing to invade Ukraine.
Burns later recalled returning home more troubled than when he arrived.
Three months later, Russia invaded.
So much for “semi-routine.”
The Nuclear Question
Bloomberg reported this week that Moscow believes peace efforts have reached a dead end and is considering substantially escalating its assault on Ukraine.
Among the possibilities: heavier conventional ballistic-missile attacks against Kyiv—including the city center—and infrastructure elsewhere in Ukraine.
More ominously, Bloomberg reported that a growing number of Russian officials have discussed whether Putin might ultimately resort to tactical nuclear weapons as a last resort.
Bloomberg reported no signs that Russia is actually preparing to use tactical nuclear weapons.
Russian nuclear threats have repeatedly been employed as instruments of intimidation.
But something else has changed.
According to Kremlin-connected sources, Moscow increasingly regards Ukrainian strikes on Russian territory as attacks by NATO countries because NATO members supply Ukraine with weapons and intelligence.
Russia has now gone further, threatening that British military targets could be struck in retaliation for Ukraine’s use of British-supplied weapons.
That brings us back to Ratcliffe.
Perhaps the question is no longer: What is Putin planning?
Perhaps it is: What did American intelligence see that made the director of the CIA get on that plane?
Watch the Calendar
Which brings us to something stranger.
Putin is fascinated by historical dates, anniversaries and symbolic occasions.
Foreign Policy examined this phenomenon in 2022, observing that Putin’s actions have repeatedly coincided with dates carrying personal or Russian historical significance.
Consider October 7.
Putin’s birthday.
Journalist and Kremlin critic Anna Politkovskaya was murdered on October 7, 2006.
Ten years later, on Putin’s birthday in 2016, WikiLeaks began releasing John Podesta’s hacked emails during the U.S. presidential campaign.
Then there is Putin’s great historical wound: the collapse of the Soviet Union.
He has famously described its dissolution as a geopolitical catastrophe.
Foreign Policy noted another coincidence.
The 25th anniversary of the Soviet collapse fell in 2016—the year Russia conducted an extensive campaign to interfere in the American presidential election.
The 30th anniversary arrived in December 2021.
Putin marked that winter by massing an invasion army around Ukraine.
And now we approach the 35th.
September 30
Russia’s official “Reunification Day,” commemorating Putin’s proclaimed 2022 annexation of Donetsk, Luhansk, Zaporizhzhia and Kherson—territories whose annexation is rejected by Ukraine and most of the international community.
October 7
Putin’s 74th birthday.
Keep an eye on it.
December
December 17 is Strategic Missile Forces Day—the professional holiday of the branch entrusted with Russia’s land-based nuclear arsenal.
December 20 is Security Services Day—the holiday of Putin’s old KGB/FSB fraternity.
And December 21–26 takes us into the anniversary week of the event that shaped Putin perhaps more profoundly than anything else in his political life.
The death of the Soviet Union.
On December 25, 1991, Mikhail Gorbachev resigned.
On December 26, the USSR formally disappeared.
The Mystical Putin
There is another aspect of the Kremlin mentality routinely misunderstood in the West.
We tend to imagine Vladimir Putin as a cold rationalist—a calculating former KGB officer moving pieces around a chessboard.
But modern Putinism contains another strand: Russian exceptionalism, destiny, Orthodoxy, Eurasian mythology and an almost mystical conception of Russia as a civilization with a historical mission.
Alexander Dugin—the philosopher routinely described in Western shorthand as “Putin’s brain”—occupies this intellectual universe, although his direct influence over Putin is often exaggerated.
The worldview is nevertheless unmistakable:
Russia as something more than a country.
Russia as civilization.
Russia surrounded by decadent enemies.
Russia fulfilling destiny.
History as recurrence.
Sacrifice as purification.
Moscow as the center of a world that must somehow be reordered.
Such people tend to like anniversaries.
Which brings us full circle.
Peace negotiations apparently going nowhere.
Kremlin talk of escalation.
Ukrainian attacks increasingly characterized by Moscow as NATO attacks.
Threats against British military targets.
Russian officials discussing tactical nuclear weapons, however remote the actual possibility may presently be.
American intelligence concluding that Putin believes the United States is weakened and distracted.
American intelligence apparently wondering whether Putin is receiving an accurate picture of Russia’s own predicament.
And suddenly… the Director of the CIA flies secretly to Moscow.
The most dangerous mistake one can make with Vladimir Putin is to assume that because something seems irrational to us, it must therefore seem irrational to him.
William Burns flew to Moscow in November 2021 carrying a warning.
Three months later, Russian tanks crossed into Ukraine.
John Ratcliffe flew to Moscow this week carrying another.
We do not yet know exactly what prompted it.
And if history tells us anything about the man in the Kremlin, it is this:
When Vladimir Putin looks at a calendar, he may be seeing something the rest of us do not.

March-September 2000
Soon after I returned to Washington, D.C. from London, Alexey Sokolov sent me an e-mail saying that British spy George Blake had agreed to translate everything: Sokolov’s existing book plus 180 pages of additional material (topics of interest to me and, by extension, the FBI) for $9,000.
(A few years later, Blake told me that he had actually declined this opportunity. Reason: He wanted nothing to do with Igor Prelin, whom he found sleazy.)
But then a hiccup my end.
The FBI’s Washington Field Office was experiencing a budget crunch.
And I was the one they wanted to crunch.
I learned about it from Special Agent Mike S over latte at our usual Starbucks in northwest DC, on March 10th, 2000.
I could scarcely believe my ears.
The problem: WFO was funding my operations but, aside from my Cuban coversion, their office did not benefit from my work product.
Word was, WFO National Security chief James “Tim” Caruso had grown weary of subsidizing data destined for headquarters (positive intelligence from Russia), Albuquerque (Edward Lee Howard), and Philadelphia (another sting operation, upcoming in this serial).
Said Mike, WFO considered me “too diverse.”
Caruso’s solution, without consulting headquarters, Philadelphia, or Albuquerque: terminate the arrangement.
“You’re expensive,” said Mike.
“I’m good,” I said. “And you guys knew the cost when you took me over from Albuquerque.”
Mike shrugged.
Was I supposed to just stand everything down? I asked.
“I’ve been instructed to tell you to stop billing hours effective immediately,” said Mike, “so that would be the obvious result.”
“That’s ridiculous,” I said. “Am I supposed to now just ignore everybody I’ve been rusing for the FBI?”
Mike agreed it was ridiculous, but WFO had to expect that a comprehensive stand-down would necessarily result from cutting off my funds.
I considered the situation.
“Here’s what we’ll do,” I said. “The Sokolov op is killed, because George Blake wants nine grand to translate, and you don’t have nine grand. The Batamirov lure is killed, too, because he’s expecting me to pay for his trip to Washington, once he decides to visit. The others, it’s just my time. I’ll keep everything running in passive mode. I’ll keep track of my hours. If your budget un-crunches, you take care of me. If it doesn’t un-crunch by October 1st (the new federal government fiscal year, six months off) I’m done and you’re under no obligation for my time between now and then.”
Mike said the arrangement was cool with him, but would be at my own discretion.
“Trust me,” I said, “everything I do is at my own discretion.”
Truth be known, that’s part of what irked WFO.
I plodded on, in passive mode.
But I got my own back come summer when I lunched with the House Intelligence Committee’s chief investigator, an old friend who, of course, had no idea I’d been working secretly for the Bureau.
“What would you say if we could have caught Edward Lee Howard and didn’t?” I asked him.
My friend was appalled.
“Do you mind if I go see FBI Director Louis Freeh and see what he has to say?” he asked.
“Do I mind?” I said. “It’s about time somebody came up with a straight answer.”
And why not take this to the Biggest Cheese?
After all, Director Freeh had experienced sting-undercover up close and personal. As a young FBI special agent in the mid-1970s he had infiltrated the Cosa Nostra in New York, had been nicknamed Mad Dog because he liked to buck bureaucracy.
And so at 4:30 p.m. on September 8th, my friend and the Intelligence Committee’s chief counsel buttonholed Louis Freeh.
The FBI director told them he’d heard that somebody from his shop had gotten close to Edward Howard, but no one ever told him Howard wanted to visit New Mexico, where a trouble-free apprehension could be arranged.
In principle, Director Freeh expressed great interest in capturing Howard, and surprise that his organization was not actively pursuing this.
Director Freeh, my friend later told me, said he knew how his Bureau treated those who went around the back door, not following the chain of command, however disconnected. And he was also appreciative that my friend had dealt with this matter in a positive, non-partisan manner. For that reason, the director promised to handle this situation with great discretion.
The opposite occurred.
Director Freeh flushed at the top and sent sewage scudding everywhere.
Neil Gallagher, Assistant Director for National Security, caught it full in the face (as deserved), before it cascaded downward, soiling James “Tim” Caruso (even more deserved), and mystifying middle managers, until Special Agent Mike S caught some of the crap and brought it to my attention at Starbucks.
Had I (horror of horrors) disclosed my relationship with the FBI to somebody on the House Intelligence Committee?
Yup, I replied. Sure did.
“This isn’t good,” said Mike. “Some of our middle-managers will take this to mean you’re not a trustworthy guy.”
I looked Mike square in the eye. “Tell your middle-managers to go fuck themselves. They should do their job and catch Ed Howard.”
The role of middle-managers at headquarters is to hammer down special agents.
First, make them travel to Washington and walk the labyrinth of corridors trying to find the right new person who had to sign off on some aspect of a new twist; then make them endure several rounds of cynical meetings designed to make any new initiative appear that it might somehow put the Bureau at risk of (egads!) embarrassing itself. And if the plan survives the first dozen hurdles, send the special agents back to the boonies and give it to a gaggle of Justice Department attorneys to quash, just so they have one less risk to worry about.
John H had walked this walk. With exceptional patience and savvy he had been the sole advocate for keeping the Howard case alive.
“You’re looking at the new advocate,” I told Mike.

If the Fang Fang affair seems familiar, it should.
We’ve seen this movie before.
Different woman. Different city. Different targets.
But the choreography is remarkably similar.
A socially adept Chinese woman enters the orbit of ambitious or strategically useful Americans.
She charms. She cultivates. She develops access.
Personal relationships blur into professional ones.
Sex enters the equation.
And somewhere pulling the strings is Chinese intelligence.
The point is not necessarily to steal a classified document.
That is the Hollywood version.
The more sophisticated objective is access.
Access to people. Access to offices. Access to conversations. Access to the people who will someday have access.
Fang Fang cultivated politicians.
Parlor Maid did something considerably more audacious. She cultivated the people whose job was to catch her.
Her name was Katrina Leung. And for 20 years she occupied one of the strangest positions in the history of the FBI.
The Bureau recruited her to penetrate Chinese intelligence.
Chinese intelligence recruited her to penetrate the Bureau.
And she was sleeping with her FBI handler.
Then she slept with another FBI agent.
Both G-men worked Chinese counterintelligence.
The FBI Gets a Maid
Katrina Leung was a wealthy, socially prominent Chinese-American businesswoman in Los Angeles.
Well connected. Charming. Politically active. Comfortable among diplomats and useful senior officials.
Precisely the quality Christine Fang would demonstrate a generation later.
Not the woman lurking outside the secure room. The woman everyone is delighted to invite inside.
In 1982, FBI Special Agent James J. “J.J.” Smith, a veteran China counterintelligence officer, recruited Leung as an FBI asset.
The Bureau gave her a cryptonym: PARLOR MAID.
The concept was rather clever.
Leung possessed access to Chinese officials.
The FBI wanted intelligence about Chinese operations in America. So it encouraged her relationships with Chinese intelligence.
Let them recruit her. Let them believe she belonged to them.
She would actually belong to us. Classic double-agent tradecraft.
What could possibly go wrong?
Quite a Lot
Over 18 years, the FBI paid Parlor Maid $1.7 million in fees and expenses.
Information attributed to her reached the highest levels of the American government.
And she became one of the Bureau’s premier sources on China.
There was only one slight complication. Her handler was sleeping with her.
Smith and Leung maintained an intermittent sexual relationship extending across much of their professional association.
This was not encouraged by the FBI employee handbook.
Smith sometimes debriefed Leung at her home. And because he was her handler—and felt rather comfortable there—he sometimes brought classified documents. Then left them unattended.
According to the government’s subsequent case, Leung secretly copied some of them.
This is generally considered suboptimal source handling.
Then There Were Three
If the story ended there, it would already deserve a miniseries.
It doesn’t.
Another FBI agent named William Cleveland had also worked Chinese counterintelligence.
Cleveland knew Leung. Very well, as it turned out. He too had a sexual relationship with her.
So let us diagram the operation.
The FBI recruited Katrina Leung.
The FBI encouraged Katrina Leung to develop relationships with Chinese intelligence.
Chinese intelligence cultivated Katrina Leung.
Katrina Leung slept with FBI Agent Number One.
Katrina Leung slept with FBI Agent Number Two.
Both agents were involved in Chinese counterintelligence.
And apparently neither initially knew the other was sleeping with her.
This is less Tinker Tailor Soldier Spy than Noises Off.
One imagines Beijing receiving the reports. Anything new from the FBI?
The Telephone Call
Then something happened that should have ended the comedy.
In the fall of 1990, U.S. intelligence intercepted a telephone conversation between a woman in Los Angeles and a Chinese intelligence contact in Beijing. The following spring, Cleveland heard the recording and recognized the woman’s voice.
Investigators tried to determine her identity. Cleveland recognized the voice.
It was Katrina. Parlor Maid. The FBI’s prized source.
This presented the Bureau with a rather serious counterintelligence question.
Had the FBI successfully recruited a woman who had penetrated Chinese intelligence?
Or had Chinese intelligence successfully recruited a woman who had penetrated the FBI?
There was also a more immediate problem. The agents confronting this question had neglected to mention something. They both had slept with her.
One of the great rules of intelligence work is: Tell headquarters anything the opposition could use against you.
An affair with the suspected double agent qualifies. Yet the relationships were concealed… and, unbelievably the operation continued.
Yes, the warning signs existed by 1990. Yet Leung remained an FBI source for years afterward.
Think about that.
An extraordinarily sensitive human source.
Suspected unauthorized contact with Chinese intelligence.
Handled by an FBI agent having a sexual relationship with her.
Also sexually involved with another FBI counterintelligence agent.
Potential access to classified material.
And the arrangement continued.
This is the moment when bureaucracies become fascinating.
Institutions are very good at discovering threats that originate outside themselves.
They are considerably less enthusiastic about threats that require admitting: We created this one.
Then Came Robert Hanssen
In February 2001—eleven years later!—the FBI suffered one of the most humiliating moments in its history when Robert Hanssen, a veteran FBI counterintelligence official, was arrested for spying for Moscow.
He had been spying—from inside the Bureau—for 22 years (intermittently).
Suddenly, FBI leadership developed a keen interest in the possibility that its own counterintelligence operations might have some problems. A novel concept.
Parlor Maid was given another look.
A new FBI agent assigned to the case, Steve Conley, began examining the relationship more skeptically.
By late 2001, Leung was under serious surveillance.
FISA coverage. Telephone monitoring. Emails. Faxes. Physical surveillance. Secret searches.
The results were not reassuring. Investigators searching Leung’s home discovered copies of classified documents.
The government alleged that she had taken material Smith brought into her residence and copied it without authorization. Some of the information could potentially reveal FBI investigations, personnel and operations.
Now consider the counterintelligence implications.
The FBI had deliberately placed a source close to Chinese intelligence.
That source had intimate access to her FBI handler.
Her handler brought classified material into her home.
She copied it.
And she maintained contacts with Chinese intelligence she had not reported to her FBI handlers.
The Perfect Penetration
Foreign intelligence services dream of penetrating the FBI.
It is designed to be difficult.
FBI employees undergo background investigations. Security clearances. Polygraphs.
Continuous scrutiny.
So perhaps the easiest way to penetrate the FBI is not to recruit an FBI agent. Perhaps you recruit the person the FBI agent has already recruited.
Better still, perhaps she sleeps with him. Better still again… two of them.
No burglar alarm protects against someone who has been given the key.
Who Was Running Whom?
This is where Parlor Maid becomes something larger than a sex scandal.
Suppose Leung was providing genuine intelligence about China to the FBI.
Fine.
Suppose she was simultaneously providing FBI information to China.
Not fine.
But there is a third possibility, far more disturbing.
What if some of the intelligence she supplied to Washington was information Beijing wanted Washington to believe?
That is the nightmare of every double-agent operation.
A penetration agent can steal your secrets.
A controlled source can do something potentially more damaging. She can corrupt your understanding of reality.
Chinese intentions. Chinese military capabilities. Chinese intelligence priorities. Chinese political maneuvering.
If Washington policymakers relied upon reporting from Parlor Maid, and if any of that reporting had been manipulated by Beijing, then China wasn’t merely learning what America knew. It may have been helping decide what America thought it knew.
Disinformation.
Counterintelligence at a considerably higher level.
And Then the Case Collapsed
In 2003, the FBI arrested Leung and Smith.
At last, one might imagine, the whole extraordinary business would be explained in court.
It wasn’t.
The prosecution against Leung largely collapsed after a federal judge found serious prosecutorial misconduct involving the handling of the case and dismissed the principal charges.
After further litigation, Leung eventually pleaded guilty to lesser offenses.
Smith also resolved his case through a plea to a reduced charge.
No great espionage trial. No definitive public accounting.
No final revelation explaining precisely what Parlor Maid had done for Beijing, what Beijing had done with her, and for how long.
The curtain came down with the central mystery intact.
Very Washington.
Honey Trap, Reconsidered
We’ve been looking recently at honey traps.
Fang Fang and the cultivation of politicians—particularly, Eric Swalwell.
But Parlor Maid is different.
She didn’t merely compromise someone possessing secrets.
She compromised the people responsible for protecting the secrets.
The Parlor Maid School
Parlor Maid did not end with Katrina Leung.
Successful intelligence services learn. They study what worked. What failed.
Which personalities responded. Which vulnerabilities opened doors. Which approaches frightened targets away. And which made them lean closer.
That is why the Katrina Leung affair becomes more interesting when viewed not as an historical curiosity but as a prototype.
Because two decades later, some of the same ingredients keep appearing.
Prominent Chinese woman.
American political or government target.
Social access. Flattery. Fundraising. Romance or sex. Professional opportunity.
The target believes he is cultivating the relationship.
The relationship may actually be cultivating him.
From Parlor Maid to Fang Fang
Consider Christine Fang.
She arrived as a student.
Then she began meeting politicians. Not powerful politicians. Promising politicians.
Foreign intelligence services are interested not only in who possesses power today. They are interested in who might possess power tomorrow.
Eric Swalwell was a young local politician when Fang Fang entered his orbit.
She helped with fundraising. She networked. She developed relationships. She helped place an intern in his congressional office. And according to the newly released FBI material, Swalwell later acknowledged having “physical relations” with her on a handful of occasions.
Years later, Swalwell would sit on the House Intelligence Committee.
Get there early.
Today’s useful acquaintance becomes tomorrow’s important official.
Not unlike compound interest from a bank, access compounds.
Chinese intelligence understands and appreciates this.
And Something Else
Intelligence collection often begins with information the target does not consider secret.
Who dislikes whom? Who is likely to be promoted? Which official drinks too much?
Whose marriage is failing? Who needs money? Who feels overlooked?
Who wants to become governor? Who wants to become president?
None of that is classified.
All of it is intelligence.
The Long Game
Western political culture operates on extraordinarily short horizons.
Election cycles. Cable-news segments. Tomorrow morning’s poll.
Chinese intelligence plays a longer game.
You do not necessarily cultivate someone because of what he can provide today. You cultivate him because of where he might be ten years from now.
This is why young politicians are attractive. So are junior diplomats. Military officers halfway through promising careers. Graduate students headed toward government. Scientists whose research is becoming important. Congressional staffers.
People on the escalator.
The secret is finding them before they become powerful.
Vanity
Money is useful in recruitment. Sex is useful. Ideology occasionally works.
Few people recognize flattery as payment.
You’re fascinating.
Your analysis is brilliant.
You should be in higher office.
My friends in Beijing would very much like to meet you.
You understand China better than anyone in Washington.
No envelope changes hands. No crime occurs. The highly-flattered target merely begins looking forward to the next dinner—and more flattery.
The most effective seduction is not necessarily sexual.
It is attention.
The successful intelligence cultivator remembers birthdays. Asks about children. Knows which wine you prefer. Laughs at stories your wife stopped finding amusing fifteen years ago.
And above all… wants to hear what you think.
This can be intoxicating to powerful men.
It can be even more intoxicating to men who expect to become powerful.
That technique predates China.
It predates the CIA.
Parlor Maid demonstrated how extraordinarily effective it could be against two FBI counterintelligence agents who should have known better.
Perhaps expertise creates its own vulnerability.
The counterintelligence officer knows what a recruitment operation looks like. Therefore, he assumes he will recognize one.
The politician knows people want things from him. Therefore, he assumes he can manage them.
Everyone believes himself to be the sophisticated party.
The Chinese Bamboo
There is a temptation to imagine espionage as theft.
Steal the document. Steal the technology. Steal the secret.
But the more sophisticated operation may resemble gardening.
Plant relationships. Water them. Wait.
Intelligence services are patient.
And the Chinese have always understood bamboo.
For years, the important growth is the part you cannot see.
Then suddenly… it’s everywhere.

This appeared in Santa Barbara Current.
Lately, stepping onto Butterfly Beach means returning home with something resembling roofing compound attached to the soles of your feet, sandals or running shoes.
Tar has always been a minor irritant.
This summer tar is a major one.
Not merely bits of tar here and there after a stroll on the sand along the surf.
At various points along the coast from Carpinteria to Santa Barbara, beach-goers are experiencing saturated globs of thick black oil. You can even see patches of fresh-looking crude washing ashore (it usually hides beneath the sand). And smell petroleum odors.
Some of it is natural.
Some, man-made, albeit from a century ago.
Long before anyone drilled for fossil fuel beneath Santa Barbara County, the Santa Barbara Channel was leaking it all by itself.
Off Coal Oil Point, near UC Santa Barbara, oil and natural gas escape continuously through cracks in the ocean floor. The seep field there is among the most prolific known marine petroleum seep areas in the world.
The Chumash knew about the tar long before Europeans arrived. They called the naturally occurring substance woqo and put it to practical use, including sealing their plank canoes.
Then the European-Americans arrived and thought: We should drill this.
In the 1890s, oil was discovered around Summerland, an enclave just east of Montecito settled originally as a spiritualist community. They must have been channeling dinosaurs.
Much of the fossil fuel was just offshore.
Oilmen built piers and put oil derricks on them.
By the turn of the century, the Summerland shoreline had become an extraordinary industrial forest: wooden piers shot into the Pacific, each crowded with derricks reaching down into the oil-bearing formations beneath the seabed.
In fact, Summerland is credited (or blamed) with pioneering offshore oil production in the United States.
Eventually the wells stopped producing.
The derricks disappeared. The beaches became beaches again.
But underneath the water: old wells.
Many were abandoned according to standards that would not impress a modern petroleum engineer. Some have subsequently leaked, and California has spent decades locating and sealing remnants of the first offshore-oil age.
When unusually large amounts of oily material began appearing this summer, authorities investigated.
The Coast Guard and California Department of Fish and Wildlife got involved.
The conclusion: natural seepage rather than a known industrial spill.
Add to the mix Santa Barbara Channel’s own delivery system.
Oil rises naturally from the seabed. Sun, waves and microorganisms weather it. The lighter components evaporate. What remains becomes increasingly thick and sticky.
Currents take over. And Wind. Tides participate.
Eventually black packages arrive on the beach, some barely concealed beneath sand, others (this summer) blatantly visible.
A change in currents, swell, wind or tides can concentrate material and deposit it along a particular section of coastline, explaining why one particular week can seem dramatically worse than another.
Butterfly appears to have drawn the short straw this season
The Great Equalizer
Tar does not recognize room rates at the Miramar. It has zero interest in ZIP codes.
It waits for everyone.
There are remedies.
Oil dissolves oil, which is why baby oil, mineral oil, olive oil and similar substances work better than attacking it with soap and water.
Even better, a solution from my favorite acupuncturist…
Tourists, caught unprepared, have been seen ferociously wiping their feet or footwear on cement surfaces, leaving a trail of dried tar in their wake between the beach and Coast Village Road.
Montecitans have quietly avoided the beach this summer.
Local realtors whisper, “Tell no one.”
I’m telling all—along with this silver-lining:
Day-trippers filling this town with traffic and noise pollution, visiting the beach and getting their feet covered in tar, well, with any luck… they won’t return.
(As TC Boyle wrote so eloquently in The New Yorker after the 2018 debris flow—a favored euphemism for mudslide— “I want my village back.”)
Drill, Baby, Drill?
There is one final twist to this tale.
The Trump administration is pushing to revive and expand offshore oil production along the California coast. One proposal would hydraulically fracture sixteen existing wells from Platform Gilda in the Santa Barbara Channel.
For those scraping tar from their feet this summer, the obvious question is:
Will more drilling mean more tar?
More offshore production unquestionably opens the possibility of wells failing, pipelines leaking. Santa Barbara requires no history lesson about what happens when large quantities of crude oil escape into the Channel.
But beneath these waters, something rather peculiar has already been observed: natural hydrocarbon seepage declined dramatically in an area where oil was extracted.
Why?
Drilling relieves pressure.
Think of a petroleum reservoir beneath the seabed as a pressurized container riddled with tiny escape routes. Left alone, oil and gas find cracks and faults and push their way upward into the ocean. But when you place a producing well into that reservoir and remove hydrocarbons, pressure subsides and natural leaks diminish.
That’s the good news.
The bad: If something goes catastrophically wrong with offshore drilling, spills would lead to vastly more oil on the beach.
Which leaves us with a wonderfully Californian paradox:
Drilling for oil will likely reduce the amount of oil washing ashore.
Unless, of course, Murphy’s Law cuts in… and something goes terribly wrong.

“They’re expecting you.” Pikestaff’s secretary waves me into the Director’s office.
I see Darconti first. “Welcome home, Kate.”
She smiles. “Thanks for figuring out where I was.”
“Did Al Stanko grovel?” I ask
“He was very formal,” says Darconti. “He explained that the Bureau had designed a new security policy, which he had believed, erroneously, already had presidential approval.”
“What a hippo.”
“The Bureau is very suspicious about what you are working on.” Darconti cracks a grin. “Their questions always come back to you. They seem to think you’re trouble.”
I wink. “I think I just proved to Al Stanko how much trouble I can be.”
“And Bleiler,” adds Darconti. “They’re convinced we know more about Bleiler then we’re saying.”
“Astute bastards. What did you say?”
“Only what we know. Bleiler appears to have drowned. And then they brought your name up again.”
“Do they think I drowned him?”
“They want to know what you think happened to Bleiler.”
I exchange glances with Pikestaff. “And…?”
“I told them I’m not clairvoyant, they’d have to ask you.”
⁂
Scheimer is neck-deep in clutter, scratching his scalp when I enter his hovel.
“You’re getting popular,” he says.
“Someone looking for me?”
“Two someones. First, Lou Gurliacci. She said she needs her film back as soon as possible. I assume you know what that means?”
“I do.”
“Second, Vladimir Ligichansky.”
“What did he say?”
“He said he wants to talk to you. He’s going to call back this afternoon.”
“Where are we with the book?” I ask.
“I expect to see some cover mock-ups later today. You want to see them?”
“Yeah. I might as well stick around.”
I look up. Somewhere, above Scheimer’s stained ceiling, women danced naked.
“I think I’ll grab a beer.”
“Good idea.” Scheimer starts to rise.
“Not you, Scheimer. Someone has to answer the phone when Ligichansky calls back.”
I’m into my second brew when Scheimer enters PJ’s, catches my eye. Bottle of Bud in hand, I follow him downstairs and grab his phone.
“This is Vladimir Ligichansky.” It is a soft, accented voice. “I need us to talk.”
“Start talking.”
“We can meet?” he asked.
“Sure. You coming to Washington?”
“No. You can visit Vienna?”
“No.”
We compromise. London. Tea at Fortnum and Mason.
⁂
British Airways plunks me at Heathrow in time for morning commuter traffic into town.
London is ragged around the edges, consumed by diesel fumes and too many people.
An hour before game time, I stroll Jermyn Street inspecting fine shirtings displayed at Turnbull & Asser, Hilditch & Key, and Bollocks & Buggers.
At five-past-four, I enter Fortnum & Mason’s grocery department and mosey a few steps down to the Fountain Restaurant. My eyes settle on Vladimir Ligichansky, by himself, cornered between colorful murals.
Fortnum’s is a good choice for a dubious rendezvous. In addition to three different ways in and out, the bustle inside blends into a bustle outside.
The Latvian looks up from the salmon-colored Financial Times as I slip into a chair facing him over the table.
A stern waitress interrupts our eyeball grasp and takes the Latvian’s order for a pot of Earl Grey.
“Why you target me?” says Ligichansky, like a little kid about to bawl.
“I’m a book publisher,” I say. “I’m not targeting anyone.”
“A book publisher. A book publisher in CIA.” He pauses. “Why you make me target? I am no angel. I make business best I know.”
“According to Krutskov, the best way you know is murdering and cheating. Your company is at the top of the mafia pyramid.”
Ligichansky shrugs. “You can no do business in Russia without mafia. Is impossible. I don’t like, but I do. I am not at top.”
“What about Podex being a front for KGB money?”
Ligichansky blows a gust of air from his lungs. “Nobody cares for KGB anymore. Everyone tries to make better life, make money. KGB? I hate KGB. I make business. Many are like me. So why you target me?”
“I’m not targeting you. I’m publishing Krutskov’s book. He identified Podex as a mafia octopus.”
Ligichansky shakes his head, and waits for the waitress to serve our tea before continuing. “No. Krutskov would not do. I show you my books. You see my transactions. You will see. I tell truth.”
I don’t have to inspect Ligichansky’s books for truth.
The truth is right there, in his eyes.
“What do you expect me to do?” I say.
“Look deeper. Something is not correct. If you look deeper, you will find.”
“Find what?”
“Whole picture. You must see whole picture.”
Ligichansky wipes his mouth with a linen serviette and plunks a ten-pound note on the table. “You look,” he says.
And with that, he gets up and ambles out to a waiting limo.

After three nights of Fog City, it’s time for Dot.Calm, my nickname for Carmel-by-the-Sea, an enchanting enclave tucked along the Monterey Peninsula.
Lulu loved Carmel—as all dogs do.
That’s because the most dog-friendly town in the USA is full of dog lovers and, more especially, full of scents left behind by the countless canines who reside here or come to enjoy its pleasures. For them, Carmel is one enormous message board.
This extends to dog owners, who begin chatting to strangers, exchanging restaurant recommendations, all due to their dogs sniffing around one another.
New friendships are forged, canine as catalyst.
Then, inside restaurants, the doggies are served water before humans—and are even offered a pooch menu from which to select a meal.
At Diggidy Dog, one of three shops in town devoted to dogs, Teo is given a choice:
Bow tie or tie-dye bandana?
Having just come from Haight-Ashbury, it’s a no-brainer…
The Cypress Inn is so full, not even Teo’s cute face can get us checked in.
However, it does work some magic at the Pine Inn, which bends its no-pet policy to accommodate us with a pair of rooms.
Spontaneity and freedom win another day.
Lunch at Mission Bistro.
A BurGerrr Patty for Teo…
Then we walk Ocean Avenue down to Carmel Beach.
The world’s dog-friendliest.
Doris Day and Dogs
Doris Day came to Carmel to disappear.
Hollywood had spent three decades making her impossible to miss.
She sang with the big bands, became one of America’s most popular recording artists, starred in 39 movies and, for four consecutive years, ranked as the country’s top female box-office attraction.
Hitchcock gave her The Man Who Knew Too Much.
Rock Hudson gave her Pillow Talk.
And somewhere along the way she gave the world Que Sera, Sera.
Whatever will be, will be.
Eventually, Doris decided what would be.
She left Hollywood. And chose Carmel.
More precisely, she settled into Carmel Valley, early 1980s, where she could finally devote herself to something she cared about more than movies or recording stardom.
Animals.
Day’s devotion to animals wasn’t a Hollywood affectation. It went back decades. She rescued strays, campaigned for animal welfare and established what became the Doris Day Animal Foundation.
Her Carmel Valley home reflected her priorities rather wonderfully.
There was a cattery.
There was a separate area for dogs—with its own kitchen.
There were gardens and pathways specifically designed for walking them.
The woman once billed as America’s Sweetheart built a retirement community for creatures with tails.
“When I moved to Carmel, I didn’t see dogs and cats around town,” Day later recalled.
This is where the Cypress Inn enters our story.
The site once housed Carmel’s first art gallery, established in 1906 by watercolorist Sidney J. Yard.
The present Spanish-style building opened in 1929 as Hotel La Ribera and quickly became one of the showplaces of the Monterey Peninsula.
In the mid-1980s, Doris Day went inside without being recognized, looked around and fell for its old-fashioned charm.
Day told her son, record producer Terry Melcher, that she wanted to become involved with a hotel—and turn it into a place where people could travel with their animals.
Melcher approached local hotelier Dennis LeVett and casually dropped his mother’s name, saying she would become his partner on one condition.
Animals are allowed.
It was a strange proposition four decades ago.
Today, hotels compete to describe themselves as pet-friendly. They provide dog bowls, monogrammed blankets, organic biscuits and occasionally amenities so elaborate that one suspects the canine has booked the room and brought the humans along to carry their luggage.
Back then, some thought Doris had lost her marbles.
The Cypress Inn became one of America’s pioneering pet-friendly boutique hotels.
Dogs stayed in guest rooms. They lounged with their owners in communal zones and became part of the landscape.
Don’t like dogs? Adios, amigo—and don’t come back.
Gradually, the idea escaped from the hotel.
Shopkeepers put out water bowls.
Carmel’s restaurants welcomed dogs.
Other hotels followed Doris Day’s example.
Hotels discovered that customers did not wish to leave a member of the family locked in a kennel.
Restaurants discovered patrons did not want to lock their dogs in a hotel room when they went out for breakfast, lunch and dinner.
Carmel Beach became canine heaven: white sand, crashing waves, cypress trees—and dogs running free and jumping for joy.
The dogs became part of Carmel’s identity.
Golden Retrievers. Labs. Terriers. Dachshunds. Poodles.
Designer mixtures of uncertain provenance.
And, today, a Teddy-poo named Teo.
The Cypress Inn remains their unofficial clubhouse.
Up to three pets may occupy one of its rooms, without breed or weight restrictions.
Doris Day died in 2019 at the age of 97.
But walk into the Cypress Inn and she isn’t entirely gone.
Her photographs remain. Her movie posters remain. Her Hollywood mementos remain.
And, most importantly, the dogs remain.
Lincoln Steffens—the granddaddy of investigative journalism—made it Bohemia.
Clint Eastwood, as mayor in the 1980s, changed a few rules, made his day)—and retained Carmel’s quaintness.
Robinson Jeffers made it poetry: “We must uncenter our minds from ourselves.” Carmel Point, 1954.
Doris Day made it a haven for dogs.
Que Sera, Sera.
