Something rather peculiar happened while I was writing this story.
Today—August 21, 2026—former FBI Counterintelligence agent Johnathan Buma published a 312-page book on Kindle.
No conventional publisher is identified in Amazon's product details. No familiar imprint. No apparent publishing fanfare. Just the book, released under the banner Truth's Last Stand.
This does not look like a man primarily trying to sell books.
It looks like a man trying to get something on the record.
And perhaps get it there while he still can.
Buma is awaiting federal trial in October. The government accuses him of improperly disclosing protected FBI information connected, among other things, to a manuscript he was attempting to publish.
And now, suddenly, here is a book.
Is this that manuscript? If so, what survived? What disappeared? What did lawyers remove?
What did Buma decide he could finally say?
And perhaps most interestingly: What does the FBI wish he hadn’t?
In advance of tackling this book, we need to understand how an FBI counterintelligence agent who spent 15 years looking for Russian penetration eventually found himself on the other side of an FBI investigation.
Counterintelligence is an unusual profession.
You spend your career looking for people who may have betrayed the institution.
Then one morning the institution begins looking at you.
Johnathan Buma knows the feeling.
He investigated foreign influence. He handled informants.
He pursued allegations involving some of the most politically radioactive people in America.
Then he accused the FBI of suppressing intelligence.
The FBI searched his house.
He resigned.
Federal agents later arrested him at JFK.
The Russians
Buma spoke Russian.
He worked cases involving Russian oligarchs, organized crime, money laundering, foreign influence and weapons proliferation.
And he developed sources.
One of them became particularly important.
The FBI gave the source a suitably dramatic cryptonym: DYNAMO.
Buma considered DYNAMO exceptional.
Productive. Connected. Able to get inside places the FBI otherwise couldn’t reach.
This is what every case officer dreams about.
It is also where trouble sometimes begins.
Hunter Biden Enters the Room
In January 2019, DYNAMO brought two Ukrainians to the U.S. Attorney’s Office in Los Angeles.
They came bearing information: Hunter Biden. Burisma. Money laundering. Ukraine.
One of the men presented himself as a former KGB and Ukrainian intelligence officer.
Buma immediately wondered whether something else was happening.
Could Russian intelligence be attempting to insert derogatory information about Biden into the American law-enforcement system?
Buma wasn’t trying to protect Hunter Biden.
He was doing precisely what a counterintelligence officer is supposed to do.
Where did the information come from?
Who benefits if we believe it?
And who wants it inside the FBI?
According to Buma, FBI personnel investigating Hunter Biden were nevertheless interested in what his sources had to say.
Then DYNAMO produced information concerning someone else.
Rudy Giuliani.
And suddenly, Buma says, the atmosphere changed.
Enter Rudy
Rudy Giuliani was not merely Donald Trump’s personal lawyer.
He had also developed an extraordinary network of relationships in Ukraine and the former Soviet world.
One of those relationships involved Pavel Fuks, a wealthy Ukrainian-Russian businessman who had made much of his fortune in Moscow.
Fuks hired Giuliani’s consulting firm for work involving Kharkiv.
Giuliani described the assignment as security and emergency-management consulting.
Fuks publicly called Giuliani a “lobbyist.”
A minor difference in job description.
But the FBI had another concern.
According to Buma’s whistleblower disclosure, the Bureau assessed Fuks as likely a “co-opted asset” of Russian intelligence.
That does not mean Fuks was established to be a Russian spy. He denied ties to Russian security services.
But co-opted asset is an interesting counterintelligence phrase.
It means someone a foreign service may be able to influence, exploit or use.
And now such a person had developed a paid relationship with the personal lawyer of the President of the United States.
One would imagine the FBI might be curious.
Buma certainly was.
Please Stop Talking
In October 2019, Buma briefed senior FBI officials in Los Angeles.
He began discussing DYNAMO’s reporting.
Then he reached the part about Giuliani.
According to Buma, his boss—Paul Delacourt, then the senior FBI official in Los Angeles—forcefully interrupted him and ended the presentation.
That is Buma’s account.
The FBI has not publicly established that the meeting was terminated in order to protect Giuliani.
But Buma noticed a pattern.
Information concerning Hunter Biden?
Interest.
Information concerning people around Donald Trump?
Resistance.
Eventually, Buma says, the restrictions became explicit.
He was instructed that he could no longer report certain information concerning public corruption, White House figures and current or former Trump associates.
Then The White House Came Looking
There was another episode.
In June 2019, according to Buma, the FBI received a White House-related name-check request seeking “any/all information” concerning DYNAMO’s real identity.
There may have been an entirely innocent explanation.
DYNAMO had apparently attended a White House-related event. Vetting happens.
But consider the view from Buma’s desk.
DYNAMO was a sensitive FBI source.
He was reporting on matters involving people connected to the White House.
And now a request connected to the White House wanted information identifying him.
The Los Angeles FBI office declined to provide it.
Then Rudy Recruited the Informant
Now the plot begins drinking.
Giuliani himself apparently approached DYNAMO.
He wanted DYNAMO involved in a documentary project examining Hunter Biden, Ukraine and alleged corruption.
Republican activists hoped such a film might prove useful during the 2020 election.
So consider where we are.
DYNAMO is an FBI confidential source.
Buma is handling DYNAMO.
Buma is concerned Russian intelligence may be injecting anti-Biden information into American channels.
Giuliani is gathering Ukrainian information concerning Biden.
And Giuliani approaches DYNAMO… who reports the approach back to Buma and, by extension, the FBI.
Enter “Russian Gangsters”
The documentary project reportedly sought foreign investment.
This interested the FBI.
Foreign money supporting something potentially intended to influence an American presidential election tends to do that.
So the FBI devised an operation.
It sent in undercover agents.
Posing as… Russian gangsters.
There are moments when the FBI displays an almost theatrical sense of humor.
Russian influence. Ukrainian intrigue. Rudy Giuliani. Donald Trump. Hunter Biden. An FBI informant.
And now two pretend Russian mobsters.
The undercover operation ultimately helped expose corruption elsewhere, including wrongdoing involving federal law-enforcement personnel.
But the Giuliani thread continued.
Briefly.
The Wire
In 2020, Buma’s operation intersected with the FBI investigation in New York involving Lev Parnas and Igor Fruman.
Buma arranged for a cooperating witness to secretly record conversations between Giuliani and Ukrainian officials.
Now we had reached serious territory.
A cooperating witness. A wire. The President’s personal lawyer. Ukrainian figures.
An effort to obtain damaging information concerning the President’s political opponent.
The recording operation began.
It lasted approximately one day.
Then Attorney General William Barr fired Geoffrey Berman, the U.S. Attorney for the Southern District of New York.
The Giuliani recording operation ended.
There is no publicly established evidence that Barr fired Berman in order to stop Buma’s operation.
Berman himself later accused Barr of political interference at SDNY, but did not establish that particular connection.
So we shall merely place the two events beside one another.
Wire begins. Berman fired. Wire ends.
But Wait
Up to this point, Buma sounds like the hero of the story.
Perhaps he was.
But the FBI had developed a rather serious concern of its own.
About DYNAMO.
The Bureau’s Foreign Influence Task Force suspected that Russian intelligence might be exploiting FBI confidential sources themselves to inject information into American investigations.
The technique: Don’t fool the FBI, let the FBI fool itself.
Feed information to someone you know is an FBI source. The source reports it to his handler. The handler writes an official intelligence report. The report enters FBI systems. Other agents read it. Perhaps prosecutors see it. Perhaps policymakers eventually hear it.
Russian disinformation has now been dry-cleaned, having arrived with an FBI file number.
DYNAMO Becomes the Problem
By 2022, the Foreign Influence Task Force wanted Dynamo shut down.
Buma resisted.
He believed Dynamo was one of the FBI’s most productive sources.
Then headquarters told him that highly classified intelligence—reportedly from NSA—raised sufficient concerns about DYNAMO that the relationship had to end.
Buma has spent years handling this man. He believes the source is producing extraordinary intelligence about Russian influence.
Now he’s told: Your source may be compromised.
Why?
We can’t tell you. Trust us.
Perhaps FBI management was uncomfortable with politically sensitive reporting and used counterintelligence concerns to shut him down.
But perhaps headquarters knew something Buma didn’t.
Perhaps NSA had intercepted intelligence demonstrating that Dynamo was being manipulated.
Perhaps Buma had become too close to his source.
Handlers are human. A productive source makes cases. Wins praise. Produces intelligence nobody else possesses.
Eventually the handler’s professional reputation becomes entwined with the source’s reliability.
If DYNAMO is compromised, Buma hasn’t merely lost an informant.
Years of Buma’s work become questionable.
That creates a powerful psychological incentive: My source isn’t the problem. Headquarters is.
Maybe headquarters really was the problem.
Welcome to counterintelligence.
Musk
And then there was Elon Musk.
In 2022, Buma became concerned that Russian intelligence was attempting to penetrate the billionaire’s inner circle.
Buma wanted to warn Musk.
Buma says the Russian effort was “intense” and “ongoing.”
Which makes sense from a counterintelligence perspective.
Musk controlled SpaceX. Starlink. Satellite technology. Launch capability. Defense contracts.
And increasingly, access to political power.
If you were sitting in Moscow drawing up a list of Americans worth cultivating, Elon Musk would presumably not appear on page twelve.
Buma wanted to give him a defensive briefing.
So Buma says he approached an FBI agent who served as liaison to SpaceX and attempted to get the warning passed along.
According to Buma: Nothing.
The agent was “not responsive.”
Musk never received the briefing.
And here the story acquires another of those irritating little counterintelligence coincidences.
Around Musk at the time was Igor Kurganov, a Russian-born former professional poker player who had become sufficiently close to Musk to become involved in his charitable foundation.
Musk’s own longtime adviser, Jared Birchall, reportedly became concerned about Kurganov’s foreign ties and access.
Birchall contacted the FBI. Kurganov eventually departed the foundation.
Then came another interesting date.
Buma says he was trying to warn Musk in 2022.
Subsequent reporting would reveal that Musk began having regular conversations with Vladimir Putin in late 2022.
There is no evidence connecting the two. But Buma presumably noticed the date.
Buma’s problem was becoming increasingly peculiar.
He believed he could see Russians approaching some of the most influential people in America.
Yet every time he tried to sound the alarm, somebody seemed remarkably uninterested in hearing it.
The Whistleblower
Buma increasingly believed the FBI was suppressing legitimate intelligence for political reasons.
He went through whistleblower channels. He approached Congress. In 2023 he testified about his concerns.
And he began writing a book.
The FBI Investigates Buma
In October 2023, according to prosecutors, Buma entered his FBI office and printed approximately 130 files from Bureau systems, along with additional documents containing material derived from confidential-human-source reporting and communications.
The government alleges some of this information had explicit restrictions upon its dissemination.
Days later, prosecutors say, protected information found its way into material provided to a publisher.
The proposed manuscript allegedly contained information involving confidential human sources and an FBI investigation concerning a foreign country’s weapons-of-mass-destruction program.
Now the story had completed its circle.
Buma had spent years worrying that the FBI wasn’t adequately protecting counterintelligence investigations.
The FBI was now accusing Buma of failing adequately to protect FBI information.
The Raid
In November 2023, the FBI searched Buma’s home.
This occurred during the Biden administration, an inconvenient fact for anyone wishing to reduce the story to Trump taking revenge upon an FBI whistleblower.
Buma’s representatives portrayed the investigation as retaliation.
The government saw things differently.
Buma eventually left the FBI.
Then, in March 2025, federal agents arrested him at JFK Airport as he prepared to travel internationally.
He has pleaded not guilty.
His trial is currently scheduled for October 2026.
Everybody Thinks Everybody Else is Compromised
Look at the board.
Buma believes Russian intelligence is trying to manipulate American politics.
Buma suspects anti-Biden information may be part of that effort.
Buma believes DYNAMO provided valuable intelligence about Russian influence surrounding Giuliani.
FBI headquarters begins suspecting DYNAMO may be contaminated by Russian influence.
Buma suspects headquarters is suppressing politically inconvenient intelligence.
Headquarters suspects Buma has become too attached to his source.
Buma becomes a whistleblower.
The FBI begins investigating Buma.
The government alleges that the counterintelligence agent who handled confidential sources improperly disclosed information concerning confidential sources.
Everyone thinks someone else has been compromised.
Which is precisely how Moscow likes it.
The McGonigal Shadow
And then, lurking at the edge of the story, is Charles McGonigal.
McGonigal once ran counterintelligence for the FBI’s New York office.
Buma raised questions about whether resistance to some of his work might somehow connect to McGonigal’s orbit, despite a chronology issue. McGonigal left the FBI in 2018, before much of Buma’s dispute unfolded.
But what happened to McGonigal afterward is difficult to ignore.
The former FBI counterintelligence chief was later convicted in cases arising from illicit dealings connected to Russian interests, including sanctioned oligarch Oleg Deripaska.
The man responsible for watching the Russians had become entangled with Russians.
The Perfect Russian Operation
Perhaps the most sophisticated Russian influence operation would not require recruiting anybody at all.
Simply introduce enough questionable information into the American political bloodstream.
Some true. Some false. Some impossible to verify.
Make Republicans believe the FBI is protecting Democrats.
Make Democrats believe Republicans are working with Moscow.
Make field agents distrust headquarters. Make headquarters distrust field agents.
Make Congress investigate the investigators.
Then sit back.
The brilliance of disinformation is not in persuading everyone to believe the same lie.
It is persuading everyone that nobody can be trusted.
Johnathan Buma spent fifteen years trying to determine whom the Russians had compromised.
Eventually the FBI wondered whether Buma himself had become a problem.
Buma wondered the same thing about the FBI.
And somewhere in Moscow, one suspects, nobody particularly cared which of them was right.
Because by then… the operation had succeeded.

There are certain stories that arrive in Washington with a tremendous bang and depart on tiptoe.
This is one of them.
In November 2023, the United States Department of Justice announced that federal agents had broken up a network of high-end brothels operating in Massachusetts and Northern Virginia.
Brothels are not exactly unknown to civilization.
Nor are politicians, military officers and government contractors unknown to brothels.
What made this particular arrangement interesting was geography.
The Virginia establishments were in Tysons and Fairfax—the well-upholstered suburbia inhabited by the Pentagon, CIA and defense contractors.
According to federal prosecutors, their clientele should have set every counterintelligence alarm in Washington ringing.
It included military officers, government contractors with security clearances and elected officials.
And then something curious happened.
We never learned who they were.
“Brown Eyes Girls”
This sophisticated operation was principally run by a woman named Han “Hana” Lee, along with Junmyung Lee and James Lee.
In Virginia, women were advertised through a website called Brown Eyes Girls VA, presented as Asian models available for nude photography.
Apparently, quite a number of Washingtonians suddenly developed an interest in portraiture.
Appointments cost between $350 and $600 an hour.
But here is where the story becomes considerably more interesting.
The customers were vetted. by management. Yes, a prospective client was required to provide identifying information in exchange for an appointment.
Real name. Telephone number. Email address. Employer. Sometimes even a reference.
Stop there for a moment and imagine you are a counterintelligence officer.
You discover a private organization operating discreet sexual services within easy reach of Washington that assembles a database containing the identities, telephone numbers, email addresses and employers of men who include military officers and others holding United States government security clearances.
What is your first question?
How about: Who else had access to the database?
And: Where did the women come from?
And: Did anyone ever attempt to exploit the information?
And: Why did we hear so little about any of this afterward?
The Oldest Trick in the Book
Espionage is largely about human weakness.
Money. Vanity. Ideology. Resentment.
And sex.
Intelligence services have understood this since intelligence services existed.
The Russians gave sexual entrapment its own vocabulary: the honey trap.
East Germany’s Stasi cultivated Romeo agents.
The Chinese services have been repeatedly used intimate relationships to gain proximity to useful targets.
Western services are hardly strangers to the possibilities. Former CIA official Miles Copeland once gave me an unpublished manual titled The Cupid Game about what he called “the CIA’s super-secret research into The Love Weapon.”
It’s very simple: A married man does not want his wife, employer, commanding officer or security-clearance investigator to discover where he spent Thursday afternoon.
The Curious Silence
Federal investigators possessed enough information to identify customers through surveillance, telephone records and interviews. And they publicly acknowledged that military officers and security-cleared contractors were among them.
Yet the names remained hidden.
The operators became the story. The customers became ghosts. Kind of like the Jeffrey Epstein operation.
Han Lee eventually pleaded guilty and, in March 2025, was sentenced to four years in federal prison. Prosecutors said the organization had generated more than $5.6 million from approximately 9,450 scheduled encounters.
That is not a few lonely fellows wandering in from the rain.
In Massachusetts, A Peek Behind the Curtain
Something revealing happened on the Massachusetts end.
Lawyers representing 28 alleged customers fought to keep court proceedings secret.
One can understand why. Public exposure can demolish a marriage, a career and a reputation before breakfast.
But the Massachusetts Supreme Judicial Court ultimately decided that the hearings should be public. The court recognized another consideration: The public has an interest in knowing what happens when influential people become entangled in a criminal investigation.
Yet the Virginia side—the side sitting in the shadow of the Pentagon and America’s enormous national-security establishment—remained remarkably indistinct.
Which leaves a question.
What Happened to the List?
Washington loves lists.
Donor lists. Christmas-card lists. Embassy reception lists. No-fly lists. Watch lists.
Somewhere in the evidentiary entrails of this investigation is another sort of list: men who submitted their identities and employment information to obtain sexual services.
Some, according to the Justice Department, occupied sensitive positions.
What happened to those names? Were the security-clearance holders reported to their agencies? Were their clearances reviewed?
Did FBI Counterintelligence examine whether any foreign intelligence service had created or penetrated the operation?
Was the customer information checked against intelligence databases?
Did anybody ask whether photographs or video existed?
Were any of the women interviewed from a counterintelligence perspective rather than just a prostitution investigation?
Perhaps all of this occurred quietly. Much of it appropriately would.
But if so, the public record offers precious little indication.
And that is what makes this story interesting.
Not what we know. What we don’t.
The Washington Way
There is a temptation to call this a cover-up.
But there is another phenomenon, subtler and far more common.
Institutional evaporation.
A story/court case appears. It contains uncomfortable facts. The uncomfortable facts point toward powerful institutions.
No one officially suppresses it.
No mysterious man from Langley telephones an editor.
The news cycle simply moves along. The prosecution narrows. The media narrative quickly shifts to the next scandal.
The uncomfortable facts are never answered. And the public forgets there was a question.
Even though the important part of the Northern Virginia brothel case is not prostitution, but access to military and intelligence officers, security-clearance holders and politicians.
The Russians have a word for this: Kompromat.
Compromising or incriminating information that can be used as leverage to induce a secret-keeper to share his secrets with a foreign intelligence service.
The brothel is now closed.
Its operator is in prison.
Case closed.
But somewhere, one imagines, there was once a rather interesting customer list.
And in Washington, the most interesting list is the one nobody wants you to see.

Britain, get ready—it’s time for Me-again!
Is this due to the tremendous amount of tar on Montecito beaches this summer?
Because six years after the great Sussex abdication—after Oprah, Netflix, Spare, lawsuits, documentaries, podcasts, grievances, revelations, accusations and enough dirty royal laundry to keep a Chinese industrial laundromat operating around the clock… Harry is going home!
And Meghan is going with him.
The kids—Archie and Lilibet—have been enrolled in British schools.
That is the detail to watch. Because school means roots. And roots are precisely what Harry chopped through when he departed Britain in 2020.
The Great Escape
Remember the premise of Megxit?
Britain was intolerable. The press was intolerable. Royal life was intolerable. The institution was intolerable.
And then later, after they left and Royal Protection was removed, “Britain was unsafe.”
The Sussexes initially escaped to Canada, then migrated south and landed among us in Montecito, a tiny coastal enclave known as “Hollywood North,” where privacy is guarded fiercely… until someone has a television series to promote.
It seemed perfect.
Sunshine. Palm trees. Security gates. Oprah nearby. Netflix down the road. And no requirement to open a municipal leisure centre in Wolverhampton on a wet Tuesday afternoon.
Harry had escaped The Firm.
There was only one small problem.
The Firm remained the most interesting thing about him. And her.
This is the inconvenient truth at the heart of the Sussex experiment.
In London, Harry is a prince.
In Montecito, Harry is a chap walking the dog on Butterfly Beach.
As he (and Megs) discovered: If you disappear from Hollywood for a few months, life moves on without you, almost as if you’ve been cancelled.
Which means Harry had exchanged an institution built to endure centuries for an industry built on vanity mirrors.
Something Happened
Looking back, the clues began appearing in June.
Harry wanted to bring Meghan and the children to Britain in July.
Security—in his mind—immediately became the obstacle.
The same issue has bedeviled him for years: Harry believes his family cannot safely visit Britain without adequate police protection.
Consequently, reports suggested Meghan and the children might not come.
Then they weren’t coming.
And then they went.
And on July 10th something extraordinary happened.
Harry, Meghan, Archie and Lilibet went to Highgrove and were greeted by King Charles and Queen Camilla.
For the first time in four years, the King was reunited with his California grandchildren.
That meeting now looks much more important than it did at the time. Because six weeks later, the Sussexes are packing.
Highgrove
Not Buckingham Palace. Not courtiers scurrying through gilded corridors.
Highgrove. Charles’s place. His gardens. His trees.
His grandchildren. Archie is seven. Lilibet is five.
Charles is 77 and has been undergoing treatment for cancer.
Suddenly the great Sussex War must have seemed rather small.
Whatever one thinks of Harry—and opinions on the matter tend to arrive fully armed—there is a brutal arithmetic to family estrangement.
You may spend years arguing about who said what to whom, who leaked what to which newspaper, who made whom cry, who failed to telephone, who failed to apologize and who failed to understand one’s truth.
Then Grandpa gets old. The grandchildren barely know him. And all those grievances that once seemed monumental begin to look somewhat trivial.
Highgrove changed something.
Not necessarily with a great reconciliation scene. No violins.
Perhaps simply the sight of Charles with Archie and Lilibet.
Sometimes the most important intelligence comes not from what somebody says but from what someone suddenly sees.
Harry saw his father. He saw his children. And perhaps he saw the clock.
Camilla
Harry did not exactly send his stepmother a bouquet in Spare. To say his portrayal of her was sufficiently unflattering would be a vast understatement.
Yet there she was.
The Queen. At Highgrove. With Meghan. With the children.
The Security Mystery
Then we come to the most intriguing part.
For years Harry maintained that Britain was simply too dangerous for his family without the security arrangements he considered necessary.
As recent as early July, this was apparently serious enough to keep Meghan and the children away.
Now they’re moving there.
What happened?
The official accounts are remarkably vague.
Perhaps private security arrangements have been strengthened.
Perhaps cooperation with the authorities has quietly improved.
Perhaps Harry’s assessment of the threat has changed.
Or perhaps some arrangement has been reached that nobody particularly wishes to advertise.
Whatever the explanation, something has changed. Because there is an enormous difference between:
My children cannot safely visit Britain and My children start school there next month.
Somewhere between those two sentences lies another story.
The Cali Experiment
And then there is the matter of California.
Megxit was not merely an escape. It was a business plan.
Harry and Meghan were going to prove that royalty was unnecessary—that the titles, palace connections and global recognition could be detached from the dreary business of actually being royal, and converted into something altogether more modern.
Content.
There would be Netflix.
And Spotify.
Podcasts. Documentaries. Production companies.
Lifestyle brands.
And… jam?
For a brief moment, the numbers were dazzling.
Then came reality.
Harry’s memoir, Spare, was an undeniable triumph. It sold spectacularly because Harry had something the public genuinely wanted: royal secrets.
But you can only reveal that your brother pushed you into a dog bowl once. After that, the cupboard is bare.
The rest of the Sussex media empire has not so much conquered Hollywood as wandered around it looking for the valet.
Spotify ended its relationship with them. That great podcasting adventure produced considerably more announcements than memorable broadcasting.
Netflix yielded the documentary some folks watched (and found quite dull) because it was about the Royal Family. This was followed by projects that generated, shall be say, rather less cultural merit.
And Meghan’s subsequent ventures have increasingly resembled the sort of business ideas conceived at lunch after the second glass of rosé.
A cookery show. Flower arranging. Entertaining. Preserves.
Jam, dispensed to friends in numbered jars like evidence exhibits.
This from a woman who once stood on the Buckingham Palace balcony.
There is something magnificently comic about renouncing the House of Windsor and attempting to replace it with raspberry spread.
The grand proposition behind Megxit was that Harry and Meghan themselves were the valuable commodity.
California has spent six years testing that hypothesis.
A C- grade would be overly generous.
Harry is famous. Meghan is famous.
But what made them famous was the enormous, ancient and formidable—if dysfunctional—institution standing behind them.
Remove Buckingham Palace and you are left with two wealthy people—ultimately seen by some in Hollywood as “grifters”—living in Montecito and discussing their feelings.
The Crown does not cancel you when ratings slip.
But Netflix does.
This was always the flaw in the Sussex business model. They wanted to retain the commercial electricity of royalty while disconnecting themselves from the generating station.
For a while there was residual charge. Until the lights began to dim.
And so the great California experiment has reached an awkward conclusion.
Harry’s most successful commercial product was a book about the family he left.
Their most successful television was about the family they left.
Which raises a rather devastating question: If your independence depends upon continually discussing the institution from which you declared independence… how independent were you?
Not Back in The Firm
Harry and Meghan are not returning as working royals.
They are not moving into Buckingham Palace.
They will apparently occupy a privately rented home outside London.
Instead they become a son, his wife and their children living within driving distance of Grandpa.
After six years of constitutional melodrama, the solution turns out to resemble something arranged by a family therapist.
Except for William
Nothing about recent events suggests the brothers have reconciled.
Oh contraire.
During Harry’s July visit they were both in London. They did not meet. And have not in several years.
Harry may have made peace with his father. He may have accepted Camilla.
But William is another matter.
And here lies the fascinating long game.
Charles will not always be King. Eventually, Harry’s relationship with the British monarchy will cease to be determined by his father.
It will be determined by his brother.
And with Harry in King William V’s backyard, the Netflix people may wish they had kept the cameras rolling.

Washington has always had difficulty distinguishing foreign affairs from dating.
Benjamin Franklin managed the problem rather elegantly in Paris.
John F. Kennedy internationalized it.
Bill Clinton preferred domestic sourcing.
And then came Eric Swalwell, the disgraced U.S. Congressman from California’s 14th District who resigned last April amid allegations of sexual assault.
For years, the story was simple enough.
A young Chinese woman named Christine Fang—universally known as Fang Fang—arrived in California, cultivated ambitious politicians, helped them raise money, placed an intern in Congressman Eric Swalwell’s office—and became sufficiently interesting to the FBI that agents tried to recruit her before warning Swalwell off.
Swalwell severed contact, so he said.
Nothing improper occurred, he insisted.
Now the file is finally open.
Enter Fang Fang
Christine Fang arrived in the United States in 2011 as a student at California State University, East Bay. But she possessed a talent not generally taught in school.
She knew how to meet politicians. Particularly, politicians on the way up.
Ambitious city councilmen. Mayors. Young congressmen.
This is good intelligence practice.
Espionage, like venture capital, is about getting in early.
Swalwell was an especially promising startup.
He was young. Photogenic. A former prosecutor rising through California politics.
Fang Fang noticed.
And FBI Counterintelligence noticed Fang Fang.
The FBI wanted to recruit her.
Standard procedure.
Agents believed she might have useful information about Chinese influence operations in the United States.
Particularly, herself.
Typical intelligence situation:
China cultivates Fang Fang (whose parents were both CCP intelligence officers) to cultivate politicians.
The FBI cultivates Fang Fang.
And Fang Fang cultivates Swalwell.
According to the newly released material, an FBI employee, operating undercover, met Fang Fang in Las Vegas in May 2013 as part of an effort to assess whether she could be turned into an asset.
Fang Fang discussed her political connections. She appeared to understand something else rather well.
Herself.
According to FBI memos, she acknowledged that her appearance alone could help her influence politicians.
Enter Eric
Swalwell and Fang met in 2012.
For years, one particular question hovered over their relationship.
Were they lovers?
Swalwell declined to answer publicly.
The FBI files now provide an answer attributed to Swalwell himself.
During an FBI interview in Oakland in 2015, Swalwell told agents that he’d had “physical relations” with Fang on a “handful of occasions.”
Physical relations.
Diplomacy has bilateral relations. Congress has foreign relations.
Eric had physical ones.
He emphasized that they never dated and did not have a romantic relationship.
Apparently one can repeatedly have sex with a suspected intelligence operative without the unpleasant complications of dinner.
The Fang Fang Bang
Then we arrive at the kind of detail Gore Vidal would have refused to invent on the grounds that it was insufficiently believable.
According to the FBI interview summary from the newly released records, Fang Fang once arrived at Swalwell’s apartment late at night banging on the door.
Swalwell says he’d taken Ambien.
They “hooked up.”
He remembered very little else, he said, because of the Ambien.
This was a future member of the House Intelligence Committee.
And a woman suspected of connections to Chinese intelligence.
A late-night visit.
Ambien. And partial amnesia.
Somewhere, John le Carré is demanding a rewrite.
Money
The newly released records show that investigators believed Fang Fang arranged campaign contributions through intermediaries, disguising money that originated from prohibited foreign sources.
The FBI’s investigation—codename: FRESHMAN FIFTEEN—looked into allegations involving illegal campaign contributions and congressional internships.
Fang Fang’s activities came under suspicion.
Swalwell was interviewed but not charged.
The Intern
Fang Fang also helped place at least one intern in Swalwell’s congressional office.
Again, this has been publicly known for years.
But viewed alongside the newly released investigative material, it becomes more interesting.
Because intelligence work is fundamentally about access.
Access to people. Access to offices. Access to information. Access to calendars. Access to conversations.
An intern doesn’t need to steal nuclear codes.
An intern learns who comes through the door, who telephones, who matters, who drinks. Who talks too much.
And perhaps most useful of all: Who is going somewhere.
Fang Fang had apparently developed an eye for that.
Then She Left
By 2015 the FBI had become sufficiently concerned about Fang Fang that it alerted Swalwell.
He says he immediately broke off contact.
Fang Fang departed the United States, returned to China.
Investigators considered charging her with criminal violations, but the case went no further due to her departure.
Question: Did the FBI screw up (again)—or was there political interference (again)?
For years, the public was left with a strangely sanitized version of events. Nancy Pelosi even refused to remove Swalwell from the very sensitive Intelligence Committee when urged to do so by Republican House Minority Leader Kevin McCarthy.
Chinese woman. Young politician. Fundraising. Intern.
FBI warning.
Then: “Nothing to see here.”
But the newly released files supply something the original story lacked.
Texture.
Breaking it Down
Wannabe congressman meets attractive Chinese political networker. They have “physical relations.” He accepts fundraising assistance from her and—by extension—funds arrive (illegally) from foreign entities. And said Chinese networker manages to install an intern inside his congressional office.
Politicians are ambitious.
Intelligence services are patient.
Rather like Chinese bamboo.

President Theodore Roosevelt was thinking of Lincoln Steffens when he coined the word muckraker. It was not intended as a compliment.
Steffens wore it as one anyway.
At the turn of the twentieth century, Steffens became America’s most feared investigative reporter.
Writing for McClure’smagazine alongside Ida Tarbell and Ray Stannard Baker, he exposed political machines, municipal corruption and the unholy alliances between elected officials and the moneyed interests that quietly owned them.
Wall Street loathed him. Readers adored him.
His reporting helped define a new kind of journalism: one that didn’t merely report events but followed the money, named names and aimed a spotlight in dark corners occupied by the powerful.
It is difficult to imagine such journalism flourishing in today’s corporate media landscape, where many of the institutions Steffens would have investigated now own the newspapers, television networks and digital platforms that shape public opinion.
Ironically, Steffens himself had been born into privilege.
His father prospered in Sacramento, where the family mansion would eventually become California’s Governor’s Mansion.
Lincoln could easily have joined respectable society. Instead, he spent much of his life investigating it.
Part of the explanation for this lay in childhood.
He was a dreadful classroom student—not because he lacked intelligence but because his curiosity refused to march in formation. Had he been born a century later, he would most certainly have been labelled ADHD and handed medication to improve his attention span.
But his attention span wasn’t broken.
It simply refused to focus on the narratives educators thought important.
Steffens wanted to know what was really happening. And that restless curiosity eventually became his profession, where he questioned the narrative provided by officialdom.
Late in life, he concluded that education often had to be undone before genuine understanding could begin. He wanted to call his memoir My Life of Un-learning. His publisher, however, insisted on a safer title: The Autobiography of Lincoln Steffens.
Published in 1931, it became an immediate bestseller.
Bohemia
By 1927, having just turned 60, Steffens had grown tired.
He’d spent decades chasing corruption through America’s biggest cities. He no longer wished to board another train in pursuit of another crooked mayor or another robber baron. He wanted somewhere quiet enough to make sense of the life he had lived.
He found it on California’s central coast.
Carmel-by-the-Sea was then proudly known as Bohemia.
It attracted painters, poets, novelists, iconoclasts and delightful misfits who valued conversation more than status. Here, amid cypress trees, sea mist and cottages that looked as though they’d wandered out of a Grimm fairy tale, Steffens discovered precisely what every exhausted truth-seeker eventually craves:
Perspective.
He bought a modest cottage on San Antonio Street near the ocean and christened it The Getaway.
It became far more than a house.
Its living room evolved into one of Carmel’s informal literary salons.
Ernest Hemingway dropped by. John Steinbeck came calling. Sinclair Lewis joined the conversation. Ideas flowed as readily as drinks. (Although publicly known as a teetotaler—with a disdain for alcohol-fueled backroom politics—Steffens discreetly indulged.)
Steffens spent his remaining years writing, reflecting and entertaining fellow curiosity seekers until his death in 1936.
His choice of Carmel was no accident.
After spending a lifetime exposing civilization’s machinery, he chose to retire somewhere that still valued imagination over ambition, creativity over material wealth.
There is an irony here.
Ninety miles north sits San Francisco’s famed Bohemian Club, founded by artists but eventually colonized by financiers, industrialists and presidents—the very establishment Steffens had spent his career investigating.
Carmel’s Bohemia moved in precisely the opposite direction.
Or at least it did back then.
Today, many of the painters and writers have been replaced by affluent retirees and second-home owners whose investment portfolios probably resemble those of the captains of commerce Steffens once pursued.
The cottages remain enchanting. The conversations (last week, anyway) revolve around high-value historic automobiles, and portfolios.
Lincoln Steffens believed that most people needed un-learning before they could begin learning.
A century after he settled in Carmel, that may be truer than ever.

Concorde from London and a shuttle to DC puts me in Langley by 4:30.
The seventh floor is a morgue.
Skeeter Leland looks up from his desk, surprised. “Back already?” He rises. “Let’s go see Pikestaff.”
Pikestaff is jabbering into a phone. As soon as he sees me he puts it down and starts talking in tongues—either that or an incoherent splutter. Something about me seeing what I started.
“They’ve kidnapped Darconti!” he finally spits out something intelligible.
“Who kidnapped Darconti?”
“The KGB.”
“How do you know this?”
“She called.”
“Darconti called here?”
“She managed a call in the wee hours this morning. The duty officer took it. She identified herself and said she was being held against her will, then she got cut off.”
“Where?”
“She didn’t have a chance to say. The Russians must be holding her.”
“Did she say Russians are holding her?”
“No. I’ve already told you everything she said. But it’s obvious.”
“Not to me it isn’t, Pikestaff. The KGB wouldn’t kidnap a CIA executive. You know it’s against the code. Sure, they’ll kidnap a Russian defector if he pisses them off enough. But not an American.” I shake my head. “They know we’d retaliate—and KGB executives wouldn’t want that.”
“Who else would kidnap her?” Pikestaff narrows his eyebrows.
“Hezbollah?” This is Skeeter’s offering.
“Not Hezbollah,” I say. “I’ll tell you who’s got her.”
Pikestaff and Skeeter look at me like an expectant couple.
“The feebs,” I say.
Pikestaff looks at Skeeter, then back at me. “Have you gone completely nuts?”
Pikestaff knew I was already halfway there; the downside of genius.
“I smell Al Stanko behind this,” I say. “That bastard is retaliating.”
“But, but,” Pikestaff splutters, “Stanko can’t kidnap one of our top people!”
“He won’t call it kidnapping, Pikestaff. He’ll call it a routine security check. They pick up a senior Agency officer, scare the hell out of her, see if she cracks. They’ll call it a new policy. Post-Ames. That’s the facade. In reality, Stanko’s trying to figure out what we’re up to. We wouldn’t tell him, so he has a few goons pick up Darconti.”
Skeeter watches, wide-eyed, neutral.
Pikestaff reaches for a phone. “Get me Al Stanko.” He turns to me. “Let’s put your overactive imagination to rest, shall we?” He returns to his phone. “Al? I have a question for you: Is your Bureau detaining one of our senior employees?”
Pikestaff listens.
His eyes visibly bulge from their sockets. His face reddens.
“WHAT?” he hollers. “WITHOUT EVEN TELLING ME...?”
He listens some more.
“POST-AMES SECURITY PROCEDURES?” He listens. “DON’T GIVE ME THAT CRAP, GODAMMIT!”
He listens.
“She said WHAT? I’ve heard just about enough.”
Pikestaff thumps the phone down and faces Skeeter and me. “The Bureau is holding Darconti—part of a post-Ames security procedure designed to ferret out moles. How did you...?”
“Just a hunch, Pikestaff.”
“He says Kate Darconti has requested immunity from prosecution.”
“Immunity from what?”
“Stanko’s calling it a rogue operation. And he had the gall to complain that it took us too long to inform the Bureau that Darconti was missing. He says he wants to give me the opportunity to come clean.”
“Bullshit,” I say. “He’s bluffing.”
“About what?”
“This immunity nonsense. Darconti hasn’t told them squat. If she had, Stanko wouldn’t be offering any opportunities. He’d be on the Hill this second, trying to make a trophy out of your head.”
“Where do you suppose they’re holding her?” says Skeeter.
“Quantico,” I say. “That’s where they pull all this shit. We could retrieve Darconti by force, but if one thumb got broken, there’d be investigations, hearings… hell, just call the President, Pikestaff. Aside from anything else, it wasn’t a rogue operation, the President approved it. But that’s none of Stanko’s business.”
“Yeah, that’s what I’ll do, by God.” Pikestaff is seething. “I’ll call the President.”
“Don’t tell him what’s eating us, just say we need to see him to deliver a progress report.”
Pikestaff pushes a few buttons and organizes a pre-dinner drink at the White House.
⁂
President Prescott is effusive in his welcome of Pikestaff and me. Hands everywhere. Big smile. It gets me thinking he has another three hundred million stashed away somewhere.
“Everything okay?” he asks with just a hint of angst.
“Everything will be better after you pour me a scotch,” I say.
This is probably the first and last president I’ll own, so I might as well make the most of the rare moments I spend on his turf.
We stand inside the President’s private den, adjacent to the Oval Office. He uncaps a fresh bottle of 1977 Macallan single malt scotch whiskey and pours three shots.
“Gentlemen.”
The President toasts nothing, not even my health.
I throw mine back in gulp and offer my glass for a refill.
President Prescott eyeballs me, pours another, recaps the bottle.
We sit in comfortable leather chairs.
The President lights a cigar.
“We have a problem,” says Pikestaff.
An intestinal gas pain crosses the President’s face, like, these spooks have returned for more and maybe they’ll never stop spooking me. He grits his teeth in anticipation.
Says Pikestaff, “The Director of the FBI is trying to find out what’s going on.”
“Al? Wh-what does he know?”
“That’s part of the problem,” says Pikestaff. “We’re not sure.”
The President raises both eyebrows.
“Under the guise of a security check,” says Pikestaff, “the Bureau is holding one of our senior officials, against her will, and subjecting her to interrogation.”
“A she?”
“Katherine Darconti. Central Asia Division Chief.”
“Does Ms. Darconti know about our, uh, little business?”
I shake my head. “No one knows except present company.”
President Prescott relaxes his shoulders.
“But,” adds Pikestaff, ominously, “Kate is intimately familiar with our Podex operation.”
“And,” I add, “she knows about our executive-ordered assassination of Kobo.”
The President’s shoulders re-tense. He drains his scotch and picks up a phone.
“Get me FBI Director Stanko.” He slams the phone into its cradle and puffs his cigar.
The phone rings less than a minute later—a testament to White House operators and the also the obedience of those running large federal agencies.
President Prescott picks up. “Al? Can you come over to the White House? Now.”
Prescott disconnects Stanko and returns to us for a more general update.
Pikestaff defers to me and I take President Prescott through Almaaty and Kobo (he grimaces), Vienna and Ligichansky (he grins)—and I tell him we believe our CoS Geneva had defected to Moscow.
Prescott closes his eyes. “Can we keep it from the media?”
“As long as the Russians do,” I say.
“What does that mean?”
“During the Cold War, they’d throw a huge party for the media if someone from our side joined them, because they’d get maybe one defector for every hundred who came to us. But it’s no longer in their best interests to do that.”
Prescott nods, picks up a ringing phone.
“Okay,” he says, “give me two minutes and send him in.” He cradles the phone, faces Pikestaff and me. “Stanko’s here. Let’s take this into the other room.”
Pikestaff and I re-rump our rears on comfortable armchairs in the Oval Office.
Prescott remains on his feet, buttons his suit-coat, greets the FBI Director.
Al Stanko flicks his eyes our way and stiffens. He’s been around DC long enough to know an ambush when he sees one.
“Sit down, Al,” says the President. “We have a small problem to resolve.”
A sheepish Stanko nods at us, and rumps his fat ass.
“The Bureau has some kind of new security procedure, eh, Al?”
“That’s correct, Mister President. You see, after the CIA’s Ames debacle...”
“Cut the crap, Al,” Prescott growls as he commences tearing Stanko a new asshole. “I don’t recall signing any new directives giving you special powers to arbitrarily pick a U.S. government employee off the street and hold them against their will. It’s a violation of their rights as Americans. And probably illegal. Are you prepared to be sued for false imprisonment, Al? Are you? Because I’m not.”
“Mr. President, the only way we can prevent another Ames...”
Prescott raises his right hand—and his voice. “You’re not hearing me, Al.”
Stanko recoils, his face tomato-red.
“This is what we’re going to do,” says President Prescott. “We’re going to consider this a temporary lapse of your good judgment.” Prescott pauses. “Right, Al?”
“Uh, right, Mr. President.”
“Where is Kathryn Darconti at this moment?”
Stanko gulps. “Quantico, Virginia.”
“Okay, Al, here’s what you’re going to do, and you’re going to do it the moment you leave my office. You are going to board a helicopter and fly directly to Quantico. When you arrive there you are going to apologize to Ms. Darconti—profusely— for the inconvenience you’ve caused her. And then you are personally going to escort her back to Washington, D.C. You are also going to seal all notes pertaining to your questioning of Ms. Darconti, without reading them, and deliver everything to the CIA for shredding. And you are going to discipline the official responsible for executing this new unauthorized policy. You got all that?”
Stanko gulps again. “Yes, Mister President.” His mind seems to be spinning as he rummages it for a scapegoat. “We at the Bureau,” he says, “are concerned about the disappearance of a CIA employee...”
“Don’t press your luck with me,” Prescott growls, rising. “Get moving. Now.”
Stanko rises on wobbly knees and slinks out, tail tucked between his fat cheeks.
We are next to leave.
Pikestaff pisses off to a social engagement at the Kennedy Center.
I aim for Archibald’s.
A Beefeater martini, three olives, an assortment of tits and ass.

After assessing various options—desert, mountains, etc.— it finally becomes obvious where to take Lulu (her ashes) on a final road trip—and Teo on his first.
Ultimately, the weather settled the matter.
It’s hot everywhere this summer.
Everywhere, that is, except the Monterey Peninsula, where mercury does not rise—and also a vibrant, picturesque city further north about which Mark Twain was believed to have said, “The coldest winter I ever spent was summer in San Francisco.”
I usually like to start road trips on a Monday.
That’s because I never make hotel reservations.
Road trips should be spontaneous. They’re about freedom.
About not having to be anywhere in particular on any particular day.
During the summer, hotels are packed at weekends—particularly along the California coastline.
So when I jump the gun and launch on a Sunday, it’s not altogether surprising that Carmel-by-the-Sea is sold out.
We discover this by phone somewhere beyond Atascadero.
Which is fine by me.
It simply means that we—Teo, a daughter, grandson and Spooky, their terrier mix…
…roll with 101 all the way to Frisco, stopping only once, in Pismo, for a pit stop and a quick snack…
The Argonaut at Fisherman’s Wharf has plenty of rooms—and a walk-in price better than anything offered online.
First stop after dumping our bags: Scoma’s.
Iconic.
Boat to table seafood. A bayside breeze.
A Vesper with a dash of orange bitters at sunset, followed in the afterglow by chowder and cioppino.
Pure magic after many hours on the road.
Then some fresh air—very fresh—strolling Jefferson Street to Pier 39 and all its color and amusements.
Vibrant.
Happy.
Not what I’ve been seeing on TV news.
Just as the Daily Mail has a propensity for turning every approaching rain cloud into the Apocalypse, Fox News seems to relish portraying San Francisco as a hellscape of homeless encampments, drugs and crime.
But block after block—in North Beach, the Financial District and around Union Square—all I see are tourists and locals having a good time.
And Teo is in his element.
Chasing leaves along the sidewalk. Picking up a new scent every few steps. Investigating a city as only a dog can: nose first.
As in Montecito, everyone we pass wants a minute or two of puppy love.
The two lines I hear over and over again:
“Oh. My. God!”
And:
“That is the cutest dog I’ve ever seen!”
Teo laps it up.
Literally.
He washes multiple faces with his tongue. The louder they squeal, the faster he dances.
⁂
Over the next couple of days, Teo enjoys his first experience with Waymo…
…a driverless taxi.
A restaurant in Chinatown…
A stroll (and modeling session) through Haight-Ashbury…
The Buena Vista for drinks…
Dinner at Joe’s Original…
And at Ghirardelli Square in a doggy store called Yap…
…Teo scores a new harness…
…and finishes the evening with a whirl on the SkyStar Wheel…
It’s a wonder he didn’t finish up in…

I turn my attention to the antique file cabinet on the right and pull out the top drawer. Inside, a diligently alphabetized set of manilla files starting with M.
The first batch labeled MKUltra.
This was a CIA mind control program from the 1950s and 1960s.
Seems to me these reports—typed in caps—were written by Warren Chester. They reference numbers, which I guess connect presumably to the boxes containing raw data—memo, notes, field reports—that corroborate Warren’s findings.
I sit in the wooden chair and swivel it toward the banker lamps, illuminating the pages.
And I begin reading…

Christopher Lathom was once a literary lion.
Then the years passed.
Decades after the book that made him famous, he finally produces another.
There is only one problem.
The world has moved on.
His name no longer opens doors.
His reputation no longer fills rooms.
The publishing business he remembers has vanished, replaced by a new machinery of social media platforms, sales rankings, and the deeply undignified expectation that an author should help sell his own book.
Lathom is appalled.
Sour, imperious, and still convinced that literary stature ought to exempt him from inconvenience, he resists the idea of a promotional road trip with every ounce of energy he possesses.
Naturally, he is compelled to take one.
That is where Book Drive begins.
What follows is not really a book tour.
It is the slow dismantling of a man’s assumptions about himself.
Lathom sets out believing the trip is beneath him.
He discovers, mile by mile, that obscurity may be less humiliating than irrelevance—and that irrelevance may not be the end of the story.
The publishing world has changed.
So has the reading public.
So, whether he likes it or not, must he.
That is the comedy of Book Drive.
Its deeper subject is what happens when a man who has spent years living off an old identity is forced into the present tense.
The road trip he dreads becomes the one thing capable of rescuing him.
Not his career, necessarily.
Something more important.
His life.
Looking back, I suppose Book Drive is about a truth every literary icon eventually confronts:
The world is under no obligation to remember you.
But it may still offer you another journey—one that opens your eyes.

Levi Strauss discovered that money during California’s Gold Rush was made not from gold but through what prospectors and miners needed. And wanted.
Enter Domenico Ghirardelli.
Born near Genoa in 1817, he apprenticed as a confectioner before wandering farther afield than most nineteenth-century Italians ever dreamed: Uruguay, Peru, and finally California after hearing feverish tales pouring out of the Sierra Nevada.
Like everyone else, he was seduced by gold.
Unlike most, he quickly came to his senses.
Prospecting was uncertain.
Providing provisions was truly golden.
It is one of history’s enduring lessons.
Gold Rush. Oil Rush. Dot-com Rush. Artificial Intelligence Rush.
Most prospectors fail. Merchants cash in.
He opened a store supplying miners with coffee, spices—and then something they desperately needed after months of beans and bad whiskey: chocolate.
He founded—in1852—what became the Ghirardelli Chocolate Company.
The next stroke of genius arrived by accident.
Around 1865, one of Ghirardelli’s employees noticed that hanging warm chocolate in cloth bags allowed cocoa butter to drip away naturally, leaving behind a richer cocoa mass. The discovery became known as the Broma Process, producing a smoother, deeper-flavored chocolate that helped establish Ghirardelli as one of America’s finest chocolatiers.
By the 1880s, Ghirardelli chocolate was traveling throughout the American West and across the Pacific.
While much of San Francisco was reduced to ashes by the earthquake and fire of 1906, the Ghirardelli factory survived. Within days, chocolate production resumed.
The old waterfront factory eventually ceased manufacturing, but rather than bulldozing it—as America has an unfortunate habit of doing—San Francisco reinvented it as Ghirardelli Square, one of the nation’s earliest and most successful examples of preserving industrial history by giving it a second act.
Today, tourists arrive not to watch cocoa beans being roasted but to order classic hot-fudge sundaes beneath the famous illuminated sign.
Did Domenico Ghirardelli and Levi Strauss know one another?
No historian has yet unearthed evidence of this. But they occupied the same compact city, walked many of the same streets, attended many of the same civic gatherings, and built two of San Francisco’s most enduring businesses.
It would have been harder not to cross paths.
Mark Twain arrived a decade later.
Again, no diary records the three men sharing cigars over coffee and chocolate.
Too bad. It would have been a gathering worth gate-crashing.
Every great city has its signature aroma.
Paris has freshly-baked croissants.
Rome has espresso.
London has rain-soaked leaves and grass.
San Francisco?
Salt air, sourdough, chocolate… and…
Cioppino: a bowl of fish stew that became as symbolic of the city as the Golden Gate Bridge.
Its origins lie not in an elegant restaurant but aboard fishing boats and along the old Meiggs Wharf in the late nineteenth century, when North Beach was filling with immigrants from Genoa and the Ligurian coast.
They brought with them a humble fishermen’s soup—a practical meal made from whatever from their catch had declined to sell that day.
The Mediterranean gave way to the Pacific.
Sea bream became rockfish. Tiny European crabs became Dungeness.
Mussels, clams, shrimp, squid and whatever else the fishermen had hauled aboard found their way into the pot.
Italian tradition meets Californian abundance.
The name derives from the Ligurian word ciuppìn.
Fishermen walking the wharf carrying an empty pot after a disappointing day’s catch, asking their mates to “chip in” whatever fish or shellfish they could spare. One contributed a crab. Another a cod. Someone else a handful of mussels.
At suppertime, everyone ate from the stockpot.
No single ingredient dominated. Every contribution mattered.
It also embodies an old maritime code that has disappeared from much of modern life.
Today, we compete.
Those fishermen cooperated.
Cioppino has no canonical recipe.
Ask ten San Francisco chefs and you’ll receive ten different answers. The constants are a tomato-and-wine broth, Pacific seafood—especially Dungeness crab when in season—and a loaf of San Francisco sourdough to ensure not a drop goes to waste.
Cioppino began as leftovers.
It became a legend.
Every spoonful carries the Pacific.
Every bite carries Italy.
Sometimes the richest meal begins when everyone simply chips in.

February 2000
John H would have seized upon Edward Lee Howard’s plan to steal into the USA for a surreptitious visit to his native New Mexico, the one state that had a warrant on file for his arrest.
But John H was gone from the FBI.
And no one at Washington Field Office (WFO) or headquarters desired to do anything more about Howard than pile paper—the bureaucrat’s cherished pastime.
In fact, the FBI’s Albuquerque field office had so little interest left in Howard, they breached protocol and transferred administration of me to WFO, which by now had a greater stake in my other operations.
Enter Mike S, a well-meaning, hard-working agent special agent charged with processing the product of my various sting ops.
Mike summed up the current thinking in WFO about Ed Howard when we met on January 8th at Chef Geoff’s, a restaurant in the leafy, affluent northwest Washington neighborhood of Wesley Heights:
“Nobody’s going to get into trouble for not doing anything on this, but somebody might [get into trouble] if they do something and it goes wrong.”
Think about that.
Because it describes how Washington D.C.’s bureaucracies operate most of the time.
Mike was simply conveying the bureaucratic sentiments of his Big Cheezer, James “Tim” Caruso, National Security chief at WFO.
But to me it stank like overripe Camembert.
“I thought the FBI always gets its man?” I said.
Mike shrugged.
Guess not.
“The Bureau should catch Ed Howard,” I said. “It sets the right example for any future would-be traitors: It may take 15 years but we never forget you and we’ll eventually nail your ass. So what if some U.S. Attorney can’t win in court? That’s their problem, which they’re trying to shirk. The Bureau’s job is to catch Howard, throw him in the clink. If he walks later—like O.J. did—at least we did our part.”
If WFO smelled cheesy, kGB Colonel Igor Prelin reeked even worse—and that was just by email.
Always on the make, cagey Prelin had harnessed a new book, and he asked me to meet him in London, to which he would travel with the book’s author, a former KGB colleague named Stalian “Alexey” Sokolov.
The FBI said, Sure, why not?
By this time, I managed a cluster of ever-evolving operations without geographic restraint, with enough clout to set my own agenda and travel in style. This was in contrast to special agents, who could do only what they told and, on their meagre per diem, were compelled to fly coach and overnight at a Holiday Inn or Motel 6.
And so off again, to London, just two months after my rendezvous in Switzerland with Edward Howard.
Prelin and his friend Sokolov awaited me near their inexpensive hotel off Bayswater Road.
I’d made dinner reservations nearby at Royal China.
We sat, studied menus, each other, ordered hot sake.
I congratulated Prelin on his foresight: He had predicted a Putin presidency two years before anyone could have known.
“Yes.” Prelin chuckled, brushing modesty aside. “I get your message from Edward [Howard]. You remember our conversation. I say it will be name nobody knows. We at KGB engineer Putin to power.”
“How?” I asked.
“Finally, deal with Yeltsin,” said Prelin. “Yeltsin receives immunity from corruption. But after he dies, we go after all Yeltsin relatives.”
(A Russian tradition.)
Said Prelin: “Putin’s power-base is from GRU and FSB. He will increase intelligence presence around him from 40 to 80 percent.”
(This came true.)
I asked about my old Uncle Vlad—Kryuchkov, the former KGB chairman.
Said Prelin: Kryuchkov had been in hospital for knee surgery. He had become an unofficial advisor to Putin, counseling the new Russian president to take strict control of government and build a strong Russia.
Alexey Sokolov nodded, displaying a perpetual expression of gloom that reminded me of Abe Vigoda in The Godfather.
At 69—eight years older than Prelin—this was Sokolov’s first visit to London.
Hot sake arrived.
I poured, we toasted.
Soon after, three bowls of wonton soup appeared before us, followed by prawns with honey and black bean sauce, scallops with asparagus, stir-fried Dover sole and two bowls of steamed rice.
Following my example, both KGB veterans attempted to use chopsticks. They fumbled their food and turned our table into a war zone. When they finally gave up, instead of asking for cutlery they switched to soup ladles—and made an even bigger mess.
(A competence of multicultural eating utensils should be a prerequisite for espionage work.)
In between swallows, Prelin raised the reason for their trip: Sokolov’s book.
They pitched it as a nonfiction expose of Oleg Kalugin, the former KGB First Directorate chief who had settled in the USA but never actually defected.
“Cool,” I said. “What’s the story on Kalugin? Why won’t he return to Moscow?”
“If he comes back to Moscow,” said Prelin, “he will be executed within 24 hours.”
Sokolov looked at his buddy with a quizzical expression. “But we no longer have death penalty, Igor.”
“No matter.” Prelin was vehement. “Execution within 24 hours.”
“So you’d like to kill Kalugin?” I said.
“Of course.” Prelin was matter-of-fact on this point.
“Do you know where he lives?” I asked.
“Washington,” said Prelin. “He lives with two daughters.”
“Would you ever try to kill him in the United States?” I asked.
Prelin shrugged. “Who knows?”
Back to Sokolov’s book, already written in Russian and published in Russia.
Its theme: Kalugin was personally responsible for every Russian spy case that ever went south on the KGB over a 40-year period, including Aldrich Ames.
“Oh, c’mon,” I said, just like Clair George would have.
“I tell you!” Prelin whined. “Kalugin gives Ames up! We know this!”
Sokolov nodded. This KGB veteran had done a four-year stint in Washington, in the late 1960s, and spent the rest of his career at headquarters in Moscow analyzing the U.S. intelligence services.
He did not tell me whatI already knew about why he’d never served overseas again: Sokolov’s superiors discovered he was gay and chose not to avail him to honey-trap blackmail scenarios.
Sokolov told me that he personally recruited John Walker, the NSA spy; that the English-language version of his book would detail this case.
“I once recruited American couple working for the State Department in one elevator ride,” Sokolov boasted. “Twelve floors. By the time we reach bottom—one minute—I recruit.”
As for the mechanics regarding Sokolov’s book, Prelin offered George Blake—the British traitor—as translator.
“Ah, we have MI5 behind us,” Prelin suddenly erupted, looking over his shoulder. “I know them!”
Sokolov, facing me (I’m seated next to Prelin), craned his neck. “Where, Igor, where you see?”
(This was like a Bullwinkle cartoon with a gay version of Boris and Natasha.)
I didn’t even turn around.
“I am kidding!” Prelin said with glee.
I settled the check. Prelin requested that we walk to their hotel to collect some gifts they’d brought for me.
As we walked Bayswater Road, Prelin occasionally slipped his elbow through mine. Soon we arrived at the Lancaster Court Hotel. Prelin suggested we go up to the room they shared “to drink vodka.”
I declined, suggesting I wait in the small lobby while they grabbed their gifts and we take the party to my hotel, The Lowndes, which had a cozy lounge and a decent bar.
Fifteen minutes later, a taxi deposited us on Lowndes Street. Inside, Prelin ordered a cocktail of his own creation: gin, Campari and tonic. He instructed Sokolov to drink the same.
I opted for armagnac and went to my room to find a Cuban cigar.
Upon my return, Sokolov reached into his plastic bag (from a duty free shop at Sheremtevo Airport) and handed me gifts:
- A copy of his Russian book, Spy Story, in which he had scribed: “To Robert Eringer, Who are going to know more about spies than I do, with the best regard of the author...” signed and dated
- A bottle of KCTOK vodka (good for cleaning ovens).
- A jar of caviar
“Gee, thanks, Alexey.”
I snipped the tip of a Monte Cristo No. 5, lit, puffed, and consulted my armagnac.
That’s when Prelin offered me $2 million for the CIA’s file on Aldrich Ames.
I laughed. “How could I possibly get the Ames file?”
Prelin shrugged. “Any way you can. If you get, two million dollars.”
I asked Prelin if he was still chief of the retired KGB officers association.
He whipped out a red faux leather, gold-embossed card. “This is my membership.”
I studied Prelin’s photograph (20 years younger). “Nice.”
“You want?” asked Prelin.
“What do you mean?” I asked.
“I make you honorary member of FIVA, retired KGB association. For services to the Motherland.”
“Really?”
“You will receive card exactly like card carried by Edward [Howard] and George [Blake].”
“And you get nice badge, too,” added Sokolov. “Five stars.”
“Is that,” I replied, “how many years of prison I’d get if the FBI finds out?”
“No more than 20 years,” cracked Prelin.
Sokolov suggested that I share with him the byline of his Kalugin book.
“But you’ve already written it,” I said. “You’ve done all the work.”
Prelin jumped in. “It would be better for the book to have an American author, no?”
Yes, it would. But no Western author is going to give your crap-book credibility on my watch.
I said I’d think about it.
Next day, I hosted a lunch for Prelin, Sokolov, and Nicholas Davies, a British nonfiction book author.
I’d known Davies since he was foreign editor of the UK Daily Mirror years earlier. I told him, as an invite to this lunch, I was developing book projects with a pair of Russians.
We met at The Lowndes and walked to Zaffarano, a high-end Italian restaurant two doors away.
Prelin deliberately sat with his back to the wall.
“Ah, this is good,” he exulted. “I can see the door!”
“Tell me if anyone from MI5 walks in,” I deadpanned, but my sarcasm deriving from his Royal China joke was lost on him.
We got off to a faltering start. Davies spoke too fast for the Russians, though they pretended to understand what clearly they did not.
It was clear we needed lubrication. I ordered a bottle of pinot grigio.
Conversation centered on Davies. The Russians had done their homework and knew he had authored a slew of books on British royalty—primarily about Princess Diana.
Sokolov, sitting across from me, said little. He steadied his eyes in my direction.
A propos of nothing, he finally said, “It is true you join Ku Klux Klan?”
“Yep,” I replied. “I still have my robe and hood. “Of course,” I added, “I did it to expose them in a British newspaper.”
A follow-up question from Sokolov: “What is meaning dream bed?”
Apparently, Sokolov had thought the term dream bed meant twin beds. Consequently, he and Prelin were doubling as bedmates in a standard double bed.
Such imagery was most unappetizing.
And then our meal arrived.
Digging into salmon over a bed of spinach, Prelin reported with glee that during his career he had never worked with a female KGB agent. He said women were no good to work with.
Sokolov nodded agreement.
(Jeez, if I had to double up in a cheap hotel and share a dream bed, I would certainly prefer working with a female agent.…)
Davies departed.
My two Russian guests and I reassembled in lounge of The Lowndes hotel so I could coach Sokolov on what to write to amend his book for American readers:
- Ames. You must address Ames.
- Analysis. If, as you say, your job was to analyze U.S. intelligence services, what were your assessments?
- SVR and FSB. No one, I pointed out, had yet written a book on Russian intelligence since the disintegration of the KGB.
- Putin. A strong chapter on how the intelligence apparatus engineered the ascension of Putin to the presidency.
Sokolov agreed. Prelin concurred.
All that remained was payment for George Blake to translate from Russian to English. They promised to check with Blake and let me know the cost.
“And I will send you KGB card,” said Prelin.
⁂
Six weeks later a large envelope arrived by Fed Ex.
(It had been opened and resealed with U.S. Customs tape.)
Inside was my red faux leather gold-embossed KGB card, membership number 4038.
And a five-star badge.
It was official: I’d been inducted into the KGB—a made man.

The diary was bad enough.
More than a thousand pages chronicling the great pandemic drama—and, with astonishing frequency, the glory—according to Anthony Fauci—of being Anthony Fauci.
The television appearances.
The famous people.
The adulation.
Julia Roberts declaring him her personal hero. And Fauci reveling in it.
Anthony Fauci had become a celebrity and, judging from his diary, found the experience sufficiently noteworthy to chronicle it for posterity.
America was locked down.
Businesses were dying.
Children were kept out of school.
Families were separated from dying relatives.
Weddings were cancelled. Funerals restricted. Faces masked. Lives suspended.
And Anthony Fauci was keeping notes on the greatness of Anthony Fauci.
A tragic pandemic had created something unprecedented in American public health: The celebrity scientist.
And Fauci occupied that role with gusto.
Ultimately, Fauci’s dream of fame was everyone else’s nightmare.
There is, however, an exquisite postscript to Fauci’s compulsive aggrandizement.
Fast-forward six years.
Anthony Fauci is summoned before Congress. And suddenly the most talkative doctor in America has absolutely nothing to say.
The Great Silence
On July 29, subpoenaed before the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee, Fauci finally discovered a subject upon which he was unwilling to elaborate:
Anthony Fauci.
He invoked the Fifth Amendment.
Then invoked it again.
And again.
And again.
More than one hundred times. In fact, 111 times.
This was quite the transformation.
During the pandemic it had sometimes seemed impossible to turn on a television without finding Fauci explaining something.
Cases. Masks. Vaccines. Variants. Social distancing.
Christmas. Thanksgiving. Schools. Restaurants.
What you should do. What you shouldn’t do.
And, occasionally, what you were permitted to do after doing what he had previously told you not to do.
Dr. Fauci was everywhere.
And now that Congress is asking questions—suddenly: No comment.
Or, more precisely: Fifth Amendment.
Dr. Fauci, did the pandemic begin in a laboratory?
Fifth Amendment.
Dr. Fauci, what did you know about government-funded coronavirus research?
Fifth Amendment.
Dr. Fauci, why did your public pronouncements sometimes differ from discussions taking place privately?
Fifth Amendment.
For a man whose diary reveals such enthusiasm for documenting his own pandemic adventures, this newfound devotion to brevity was almost touching.
The man who once seemed capable of explaining a viral particle down to its shoelaces had been reduced to three words: I plead the Fifth.
Perhaps we have finally discovered the most effective Fauci public-health intervention of all.
Silence.
There is something wonderfully absurd about America’s former Explainer-in-Chief—the face, voice and occasionally wagging finger of the pandemic—suddenly reinventing himself as Harpo Marx.
The Senate committee was less entertained.
It subsequently voted 8–5 to hold Fauci in contempt of Congress and referred the matter to the Justice Department.
In his diary, Fauci couldn’t stop talking.
Before Congress, Fauci couldn’t start.
And now we have the third act of Fauci.
The Fauci on his government-issued iPhone.
Most unfortunately for him, Senators Ron Johnson and Rand Paul have obtained more than 34,000 text messages and 522 voicemails from Fauci’s government phone.
They have begun releasing them.
Those texts take us back to January 2021.
To pregnant women.
And to a private conversation considerably more consequential than whoever celebrity had most recently congratulated Anthony Fauci on being Anthony Fauci.
On January 25–26, Fauci was discussing COVID vaccination and pregnancy with incoming CDC Director Rochelle Walensky and future Surgeon General Vivek Murthy.
Something concerned him.
The powerful immune response following the second vaccine dose—including fever—Fauci wrote, “theoretically could be associated with miscarriage in the 1st trimester.”
Pause there.
Because this is where the comedy ends.
Fauci was contemplating the possibility that the mRNA COVID vaccination increased miscarriage risk
Privately.
He did not tell the public we have discovered a danger.
Pregnant women were in an extraordinarily difficult position in early 2021.
The vaccines were new.
Pregnant women had largely been excluded from the original clinical trials.
There was uncertainty. Real uncertainty.
And pregnant women deserved to hear it.
Tell her what you know. Tell her what you don’t know. Tell her what worries you.
And then let her decide.
That is not anti-vaccine.
That is informed consent.
And this is where Fauci’s diary becomes relevant again.
While the private Fauci was concerned that a vaccine-induced inflammatory response might precipitate first-trimester miscarriage (and keeping it to himself), the diarist Fauci was busily recording the extraordinary experience of becoming a national celebrity.
The famous people. The interviews. The television appearances. The praise.
Julia Roberts.
It is a juxtaposition almost too perfect to invent.
On one side of the curtain: Fauci the celebrity.
On the other: Fauci the scientist and public official—\ not being honest with the public that paid his salary.
And while millions of Americans got shamed into taking a vaccine that Fauci knew could be harmful to their health—could, in fact, terminate pregnancies—he relished in… himself.
In front of the cameras: Loquacious confidence.
Years later: The Fifth Amendment.
And now: The phone.
More than 34,000 texts.
More than 500 voicemails.
Only a fraction has so far been released.
Perhaps the most revealing Fauci document will not be his diary after all.
The diary tells us what Anthony Fauci thought worth recording.
Congress showed us what Anthony Fauci no longer wishes to discuss.
But the iPhone may prove more interesting than either.
Because unlike the diary, the phone wasn’t written for posterity.
And unlike his reticence in front of Congress, the phone isn’t taking the Fifth.

This appeared inSanta Barbara Current.
For one extraordinary summer in 1967, a few square blocks in San Francisco became the unofficial capital of an international revolution.
A revolution of hair. Of music. Of clothing.
Of consciousness.
Most of all, of peace and love.
And an audacious notion that love might accomplish what governments never could.
The Summer of Love
