In the mid-1960s, Haight-Ashbury was one of San Francisco’s cheapest neighborhoods. The once-grand Victorian houses had grown shabby. Rents were low. Students, artists, poets, musicians and runaways moved in because they could afford to.
The movement that followed was a chemical reaction.
The Beat Generation had already prepared the ground. Jack Kerouac, Allen Ginsberg and Lawrence Ferlinghetti had challenged post-war conformity from nearby North Beach.
The hippies added color
And LSD.
Quite a lot of LSD.
Much of it came courtesy of Owsley Stanley—sound engineer to the Grateful Dead and perhaps the most celebrated underground chemist in American history. His laboratory became as influential as any recording studio.
If Oppenheimer split the atom, it was Owsley who expanded the mind.
No band became more closely identified with Haight-Ashbury than the Grateful Dead, who lived communally at 710 Ashbury Street.
Jerry Garcia answered the door.
One afternoon you might encounter Janis Joplin.
Another day, Grace Slick of Jefferson Airplane, Country Joe McDonald, or members of Big Brother and the Holding Company.
The sidewalks became the guest list.
Music drifted from open windows.
Someone was always strumming a guitar. Someone else was beading necklaces.
Someone invariably claimed to have discovered the meaning of life approximately 20 minutes earlier.
The soundtrack expanded weekly.
Jimi Hendrix.
The Doors.
Pink Floyd.
The Who.
Cream.
Even The Beatles did not escape Haight-Ashbury’s gravitational pull.
George Harrison wandered its streets.
The Summer of Love influenced Sgt. Pepper’s Lonely Hearts Club Band.
“All You Need Is Love” became its unofficial anthem.
Celebrities arrived simply to witness whatever this strange social experiment had become.
Actors. Writers. Photographers. Journalists.
Everyone wanted to report from the center of this cultural earthquake—even if they weren’t entirely sure what was shaking.
That defining public moment came on 14 January 1967 with the Human Be-In in Golden Gate Park.
Around 25,000 people gathered beneath the winter sky.
Allen Ginsberg chanted.
Timothy Leary offered that decade’s most famous (if misunderstood) instruction…
Richard Alpert—soon to become New Ager Ram Dass—was there.
So were the Grateful Dead and Jefferson Airplane.
The Summer of Love hadn’t officially begun.
But everyone could already hear it approaching.
Then came the avalanche.
By June, 100,000 young people had descended upon Haight-Ashbury.
They came carrying backpacks, sleeping bags, flowers, guitars—and idealism.
Most carried very little money. Few carried a plan.
The neighborhood simply wasn’t built for them.
Food became scarce. Drugs became plentiful.
Sanitation became theoretical.
Crime arrived.
So did opportunists.
Paradise, it turned out, required someone to collect the rubbish.
In October, many of the original hippies staged what may be the movement’s most self-aware performance piece.
They held a funeral.
Not for a person. For The Hippie.
A mock coffin was carried through the Haight bearing a sign announcing the “Death of the Hippie.”
Their message: The media had transformed their counterculture into a tourist attraction.
The dream had become a costume.
The revolution had acquired souvenir shops.
And that’s exactly what you’ll find today.
Walk Haight Street, as I discovered last week, and you’ll still find psychedelic murals, Victorian houses, tie-dye boutiques, vintage clothing stores, anarchist bookshops, smoke shops—and cafés serving artisan coffee at prices that would have horrified the original inhabitants.
The Grateful Dead house still stands.
So does the famous corner.
Visitors carry shopping bags.
History has an impeccable sense of irony.
The hippies rejected consumerism. Their neighborhood eventually became one of San Francisco’s most successful retail districts.
Yet dismissing Haight-Ashbury as merely a tourist destination misses the point.
There was much more to this neighborhood than tie-dye fashion.
It accelerated environmentalism. Alternative medicine. Organic food.
Meditation. Yoga. Eastern philosophy.
Even Silicon Valley inherited something of its ethos: challenge authority, ignore convention, imagine a different future.
Cities occasionally produce sites where history is made.
In San Francisco, Levi Strauss clothed miners during the Gold Rush—and created a garment with universal appeal.
Domenico Ghirardelli sweetened it with chocolate.
A century later, Haight-Ashbury attempted something considerably more ambitious.
It tried to reinvent the human race.
And for one glorious, chaotic, aromatic summer, quite a few people believed it had.

At 10:15 a.m., Lou Gurliacci and her 60 Minutes crew are upstairs in a suite setting up cameras and lights while I sit in the Imperial’s lobby hoping to witness Vladimir Ligichansky’s arrival.
Morley Safer is painting his room.
At 10:47 precisely, Ligichansky—flanked by two bodyguards—swaggers into the grand hotel. His goons evict several guests from an elevator to clear it for their boss.
I hitch a ride with the next elevator and knock on Mogus’s door.
He peeks out, opens.
“He’s here,” I say.
“Shit.”
“They’ll begin about 11:30. I expect to find you outside the suite at 12:15 sharp.”
⁂
Ligichansky probably knows my name by now but doesn’t know what I look like. So, when I slip into the CBS suite he can only assume I’m just another 60 Minutes flunkie.
Someone had clipped a microphone to his bespoke spread-collar shirt. Sitting in an armchair, he combs his thinning, black-dyed hair straight back.
Gurliacci picks up a phone. “We’re ready for you, Morley.”
Safer comes in and shakes hands with Ligichansky, then sits on a chair facing him. They exchange costive small talk and mug for a camera check before Gurliacci says counts it down.
Morley warms his prey with a few innocuous, kiss-ass questions about where Ligichansky was from and how he had achieved such stupendous upward mobility.
Ligichansky prattles happily, still believing this is a puff piece… until Safer tosses a zinger: “Was Podex set up as a KGB asset?”
“I’m absolutely prepared to answer any of your questions,” says Ligichansky. “I heard these stories, nobody gave me proof—it is a waterfall, you cannot fight it. I’m quite happy to answer any questions...”
“My question,” Safer interrupts Ligichansky’s incoherence, “is this: did the KGB have anything to do with setting up Podex?”
“I’m ready to answer any questions,” Ligichansky double-talks, “including condoms from my bedroom. I’m ready to do it. When people say I’m using KGB money, I’m always saying the same thing...”
“Mr. Ligichansky,” Safer interjects, “are you familiar with the name Anatoli Krutskov?”
Ligichansky clams up for a moment; maybe he can see it coming. “Yes, of course. Krutskov was KGB chairman.”
“That’s right,” says Safer. “Before Krutskov died recently, he wrote a book that will soon be published in the United States.”
Ligichansky squirms.
“In his memoir,” Safer continues, “Krutskov states that the KGB created Podex with its own funds and, in fact, he—Krutskov—was your secret partner.”
“Where you read this?” Ligichansky demands.
“Right here.” Safer reaches down for a sheaf of galley proofs. “May I read it aloud?” Safer does not wait for an answer. “We understood that evil forces were pushing us toward collapse. We determined that we, at the KGB, must be prepared for anything. We therefore created a business entity called Podex—and appointed Vladimir Ligichansky to run it.”
“Lies!” Ligichansky rails. “All lies!”
One camera hones in on Ligichansky’s potato face; the other, his short, stubby fingers.
“I do not deal in drugs! I do not deal in prostitution!”
“I didn’t ask if you dealt in drugs and prostitution.” Safer is smug—a Kermit the Frog smugness that comes with Gotcha, asshole! “But—again, according to Krutskov—Podex, your company, has paid huge bribes to Russian government ministers, including the Russian prime minister.”
Ligichansky’s face turns tomato-red.
“Podex is intimately involved in the Russian mafia,” Safer pushes, “isn’t that right, Mr. Ligichansky?”
“You can prove these lies?” spits Ligichansky. “Anatoli Krutskov is dead!”
“Is it true,” Safer leans forward, “that you had Krutskov murdered for going public about Podex?”
Apoplectic with rage, Ligichansky plucks the microphone attached to him so violently that his shirt tears.
He rises, hollering, “This is not interview! You put me on trial! I am not criminal!”
Ligichansky snaps orders in Russian to his bodyguards, who flank him and stomp out.
I check my watch. Noon.
Safer removes his own mike. “Do you need me for anything more today?” he asks his producer.
“Just a stand-up outside the Podex building. I’ll let you know when the script is ready.”
Safer grunts and departs the suite, probably to finish painting his room.
Bef Mogus appears in the hallway at 12:15.
“It’s over,” I tell him.
“Ligichansky didn’t show?” he asks, hopefully.
“He’s been and gone.”
Down the corridor, behind Mogus, part of Ligichansky’s entourage is heading back toward us.
“Uh-oh,” I say to Mogus. “They’re coming back.”
Mogus stiffens. “Shit.”
“No, it’s just a couple of his goons.” I pokes my head through the door. “Lou, who’s got the film?”
Gurliacci waves a film canister at me.
“Hide it,” I whisper.
Then I turn to the goons, fast approaching.
“Forget something?” I ask.
“Yaa. We forget. Move.”
“Say please.”
The two goons look at one another. Goon One reaches inside his pocket. I might have broken his arm, on general principles. But the objective here is buying time, not an etiquette lesson.
“Please,” says Goon Two.
“That’s better.”
I step aside.
The door had locked automatically. One goon works a knob while the other pounds the door with his fist until Gurliacci opens.
Both goons pushed their way inside.
I follow them in as Mogus slips away.
“Where is film?” Goon One demands.
“What film?” Gurliacci shrugs.
“You must give film,” Goon Two snarls, patting a bulge beneath his jacket.
“Don’t risk it, Lou,” I say. “We might as well tell these boneheads where the film is.”
Gurliacci flashes a dirty look at me.
“Sorry, I’m not risking my life for 60 Minutes.” I turn to the goons. “Morley Safer has the film.”
“Who?” Goon number one narrows his unibrow.
“Morley Safer. The interviewer.” I point to the chair where Safer had sat. “He takes film.”
“Where him go?” asks Goon Two.
“Him goes to him’s room,” I say. “What room him in?” I ask Gurliacci.
She hesitates.
“C’mon,” I push. “These guys aren’t joking.”
“We no joke,” Goon Two affirms.
“Room 412,” says Gurliacci.
“Got that?” I address the goons.
“I got,” says Goon One. “Where him put?”
“My guess,” I say, “is down him’s pants.” I point to my crotch.
The goons rush off to 412 where, I assume, they will take a peek up Morley’s ass.
“Where’s the film?” I whisper.
Gurliacci retrieves the canister from under a couch.
“Give it to me,” I say. “I’ll get it out of here.”
Gurliacci considers this with only a moment’s reluctance, then hands me the canister.
“Everyone should split,” I say. “They’ll be back after de-briefing Morley.”
“He’s going to be very upset,” says, Gurliacci unable to conceal a fleeting smirk.

First, Jiffy Lube for an oil change and a tuneup.
Second, a checklist for Teo’s needs on the road—a compilation perfected while traveling x-country with Lulu, if now tailored to the needs of a puppy.
- A bag of Royal Canon Puppy Kibble
- Feeding dish and water bowl
- Treats
- Bed & blanket
- Collapsible play pen (if needed in hotel rooms)
- A couple toys
- Pee pads
- Stain & Odor Remover, a roll of paper towels, poop bags.
All of it goes into a Pan Am cabin bag, the same used for Lulu.
For comfort and safety inside the Escalade: a cushioned car seat with harness.
Somewhere beyond Pismo Beach, Teo settles into a long snooze and I hear Lulu telling me her side of the story.
Okay, so here’s how it started. I’m a few weeks old, maybe the runt of the litter, definitely not getting my fair share of chow. And suddenly I’m “fostered”—that trendy new word for being discarded into temporary accommodation, no fancy pet store for me.
A brassy biddy called Queen Barb takes me in. One day, I’m in Santa Maria, the next, other side of the mountain, in coastal Montecito.
Late afternoon. Barb’s car. We park. She carries me out.
A few steps later, I’m handed off to stranger going the opposite direction.
Of course I show my displeasure by digging my sharp puppy teeth into his knuckles.
He opens a car door, puts me on his lap behind a wheel, and we’re moving again—to where, I have no idea. And I’m not happy. I keep biting his hands. Truth be told, I drew blood. I meant to.
We don’t travel far. He stops, juggling me with one arm and a bag of food in the other. Smells good. He rings the doorbell with an elbow.
Here I am, wondering what the hell is supposed to happen next. No one consulted me. No one asked my opinion, about where I was going or with whom.
The door opens. Two bitches—just like me, but human. They with delight. Maybe because of the food? No—dammit—they’re squealing over me.
I had an inkling I was cute. But I wasn’t angling for attention. Not then, not ever.
Suddenly, I’m on the floor and two larger canines are all over me, like, I’m their new toy or something. In their exuberance, they practically smother me.
I take them on, teeth bared, growling, snarling. Then the guy who brought me here scoops me up.
How embarrassing!
I dig my teeth into his hands again.
But I have to admit, he did rescue me from a dual-canine onslaught.
Their names were…
They meant well, just excited to see another one of their own. In time, the three of us would have the run of the place. Even so, my indifference to them was pronounced. And it was pronounced… Grrrr!
I remained suspicious of everyone. At this stage of my life, I simply had no reason whatsoever to trust anything or anyone.
I had every reason to believe my stay in this home would be temporary. I even overheard conversation to that effect.
So I didn’t bother to settle in or make friends. I stayed in my corner, kept to myself and ignored everyone. And if that guy who brought me here picked me up, I chewed his knuckles until I tasted blood.
I don’t think he liked me much. Why would he? He’d bring me close to his face, and instead of licking him I’d try to bite his nose off. I nearly succeeded once on a man who said I was “a sweet adorable little thing” (the fool!) and, despite warnings, held me up to his face.
Life went on. They Took me to the beach. Hawks circled overhead mistaking me for prey.
And dressed me in ridiculous outfits.
I had my own bed by the fireplace. Cozy enough. But I still felt like an intruder.
Three months in, I caught something—a cold, virus, whatever. Couldn’t eat. Couldn’t drink. I just lay in my bed, listless.
The guy whose knuckles I’d chewed seemed indifferent. Maybe he figured I was beastly by nature and he just wanted me gone.
My savior was his mother. Eighty-four, sharp as my teeth. The day after what they called Christmas she intervened, ordered him to take me to a vet.
They had been planning a trip to Las Vegas— a 16th birthday for one of the bitches. (I overheard this in my misery.) Instead, my sickness cancelled their fun. He drove me to an emergency veterinary hospital in Ventura, a half hour away.
I didn’t even have the strength to bite his knuckles.
At the clinic, strangers in white coats carried me off.
Hands poked, needles stabbed, and yes, someone even stuck a finger up my ass.
The indignity.
I’d never known life could be that brutal. Suddenly, I longed for the quiet domestic life I’d been fighting.
I felt my energy draining. I think I almost died that night. When they finally brought me back to the waiting room—four hours later—the vet told my guy I was severely dehydrated. So they filled me so full of fluids I had a hump on my back like a camel.
My guy asked if they should keep me overnight.
The vet shook his head. No need, I heard him say, she’ll either make it through the. night—or she won’t.
I could see my guy was shaken. Guilty, maybe. For the first time, I knew he wanted me to live.
And for the first time, I wanted me to live. With him. With this family. Even if I never warmed to the other dogs.
After stopping for gas near Salinas, Lulu starts in again…
From the moment I was born, I’d take on anything.
Pit-bulls, Dobermans, Rottweilers—bring ‘em on. I’d cuss ‘em out so bad they’d be foaming at the mouth, wanting to sink their teeth into me.
Of course, I was faster than they were, by a long shot. I could outrun anything on Butterfly Beach (and did), including Reilly, my older step-brother, who, of course, I had to outdo every chance I got. That included stealing favor with my guy, the one whose knuckles I’d bloodied.
One late afternoon I took off with a whole wheel of brie cheese that was on a round table surrounded by adults on the patio. I’d sat back, studying all the angles. And when I had all the angles, I made my move.
Out of nowhere (seemingly), I sprung onto the table.
Stock and awe.
Within two seconds the whole wheel of brie was hanging out of my mouth.
The humans were astonished by my brazen and ferocity as I turned full circle looking everyone in the eye, daring them to intervene before jumping from the table and sprinting to the far corner of the garden, where I savored my feast beneath bushes.
I think my guy was truly charmed by my tenacity.
He secretly approved. I suspect I won his heart that night at the vet when he thought he’d lost me. And he got mine. Chihuahuas are funny that way: we get attached to one human only.
He was mine.
And I think I was allergic to bees. When I got stung, all I wanted to do was crawl off and die. Crawl to those same bushes where I ate the cheese.
That’s where my guy found me panting.
He scooped me up and raced me to the vet for a shot of Benadryl.
Happened again a year later, another bee sting. It was he who found me, of course—another run to the vet. I could feel his urgency and despair as we drove.
Bees aside, every so often something clogged my nose—probably pollen—and I couldn’t breathe. The harder I tried, the worse it got. He‘d scoop me up and hold me gently in his left arm and say, “Breathe. Breathe.” I’d calm down and catch my breath. And once I got back to normal—maybe ten or fifteen seconds— he’d put me down, and I’d return to tormenting Reilly.
It was a game. Life’s a game. Dogs know it even if people don’t. Never take anything too seriously. Live the moment. Sniff. Eat. Pee. What else matters?
As the exits ramp for Silicon Valley loom up, Lulu continues here monologue…
At first, I hated leashes and “walks.” What the hell this that about? Control. Did I mention I was feisty? Walking to my own drumbeat is how I lived. Nothing would ever change that.
Later, I learned walks are fun. Educational. A sniff is a portal to neighborhood news: the age, health, disposition—everything—from the canine who left it there. I didn’t make friends with those who left their scents, though. If I ran into one on the street, I’d chew them out good. And from all the gossip I picked up I knew the right things to say to rile them.
Every one of them wanted a piece of me. But my guy always scooped me up in time. Even higher up, in his arms, I’d continue to give them a mouthful of vitriol.
And when—with some distance—he put me back on the ground, I’d turn around and pee, give those mongrels something to bark about. I didn’t squat like most bitches. No, not me. I’d lift my back legs up high and let it splatter. I instinctively knew I might otherwise get my paws wet. And if there’s one thing I hated, it was getting my paws wet. I’d never go out in the rain—not voluntarily, anyway. If I was forced to take a walk when the streets were wet, I’d sulk for an hour or so—like, how could they do that to me?
I was also fussy about where I’d poo. Very fussy. I’d sniff around a while to find just the right spot. I knew what I was doing, even if it puzzled my guy. I possessed a sense of smell superior to him—and all other canines.
I’ll tell you something else: If I smelled a meal served me and it didn’t have a few bits of beef jerky, no way would I indulge. Pure and simple, anything I ate had to come with a side of jerky.
Oh, and did I mention a fondness for filet mignon?
But my real favorite was lamb chops.
Yeah, I was pampered—a real spoiled bitch.
I always knew when my guy returned from the grocery store. My nose went on high alert to assess what he’d brought me. Sometimes tri-tip or salmon.
My other pet peeve, aside from wet pavement, was gravel roads. I guess I had ultra-sensitive paws. When I was a pup and I slept on the same bed as my guy, I’d lie on my side with all four paws—legs straight out—pressed up against him. Reilly slept on the other side. Whenever he got bumped and awakened, he’d go ballistic, almost rabid. That was the only time I was ever frightened of him. Otherwise, Reilly groveled for human attention.
As I grew older, I was given my own comfy dog bed and thereafter no sleeping on human beds for me. When bedtime rolled around, I’d dive under my blanket and sleep all night. And sleep-in most mornings. I was a world champion sleeper. And if any dog poked its nose beneath my blanket, my wrath was immediate and scary. When you’re tiny, you have to put on a show. Strength? Pishaw. Fortitude is what counts.
God may have given me small body and skinny legs. But He didn’t skimp on attitude. My bark was always bigger than my bite. But I kept my teeth sharp just in case.
Just ask a a few of my guy’s friends. And the plumbers, handymen—and anyone who ever dared ring the doorbell. They’d tell you. I was ruthless. Whenever anyone dared to enter our home, I was the first line of defense. Some would’ve called it an offensive position. They weren’t wrong.
Had to.
Reilly? He’d just bow his head and wag his tail.
He wanted to be friends with anyone and everyone.
I didn’t have any friends. Didn’t want them.
Entering my domain was an act of war. You had to earn access by giving up a drop of blood. I tried to make it quick—but never painless. An ankle was my favorite target. Hell, that’s all I could reach. I made an art out of slipping between a work boot and a trouser cuff.
I got reprimanded, of course, but couldn’t care less.
I was fearless. Had to show it—to the other canines, to everyone—lest they mistake me for “a cute little thing.” I heard that over and over again. It was my job to show them just how “cute” I wasn’t.
Feisty? My guy called me a terrorist. And I did not want to disappoint.
Of course this meant being shut in a room when visitors arrived. Banishment. That is, if they could catch me—near impossible. More likely I’d get locked outside… until the gardener arrived. Too late!
I could write a book on the art of intimidation.
Ultimately, I suspect my guy respected my disposition. But every so often he’d scoop me up, flip me on my back and holler, “Submit!”
I didn’t like it, but I stayed very still.
After a few seconds, he’d release me, and I’d flip bolt upright and carry on as if nothing happened.
The thing I hated most was when my guy brought out a suitcase and went away.
Never knew where he was going or for how long.
Of course, I’d try to sneak in with his stuff.
I was much happier when he started taking me on road trips…
…even if I sometimes had to wait in the car.
But I knew he’d always return.
“A dog is the only thing on earth that loves you more than he loves himself.”
— Josh Billings

At four in the afternoon, the library in Braddock is winding down—assuming it was ever wound up.
Hardly anyone is here.
Or ever here.
The internet has supplanted libraries for most.
Who has time or the attention for books anymore?
Universities in nearby Pittsburgh have their own vast libraries, starting with Cathy—the Cathedral of Learning.
For anyone, going all the way to bereft Braddock would be a stretch.
A long one.
Again, kudos to Porter and Warren for choosing an obscure, largely forgotten landmark in a town no one has any reason to visit.
The librarian from the other day nods politely. I’m hoping she doesn’t inform Emerson Wexler I’m here.
For my plan to work, I need for her to see me leave—and then not notice me sneaking back in.
After casually browsing the shelves, I wave goodbye and exit. A couple minutes later, I slip back inside. As I’d calculated, she left her counter to roam the rooms and kill lights.
I make my way with stealth to the men’s room, conceal myself in a toilet stall. And wait.
After a half-hour, I step out into the now darkened library.
Any Security cameras?
None are obvious.
Who would be watching anyway?
Nobody steals books. These days, people can’t give them away.
This place is all mine for the night.
Slowly, I make my way down to the zone Wexler had blocked, with his covenant of awe excuse.
And there it is, the old swimming pool, chock-a-block with file cabinets and cardboard boxes and plastic containers, just as it appeared in my key to the kingdom dream.
But no. In reality, the pool is completely empty—just a barren pit of an old decrepit swimming pool, and nothing more.
Disappointed, I continue my search, poking around in some hokey little rooms. Their doors swing open to… obsolete audio-visual equipment, old furniture, cleaning supplies.
No secret files.
How could I be so wrong?
It hits me that I’m the walking definition of a wild goose chase—minus the goose.
Or maybe I’m the goose, getting goosed.
After more fruitless exploration, I return to the basement for a final look-see, planning to depart through a self-locking backdoor I’d discovered earlier.
One of the walls of the main storeroom is lined from top to bottom with cardboard boxes.
Hmmm—somebody trying to conceal something?
I go for a stepladder I’d seen in a corridor earlier and begin shifting boxes, one at a time. Judging by the weight, they’re filled with old library books—or text books from the sheer weight of them.
Three rows down I uncover a brick arch.
Another few boxes and the top of an old wooden door reveals itself.
I keep at it… and come upon what looks to be a white circle painted onto the dark wood.
And then two additional circles, forming the ancient Greek symbol of wisdom. Porter used to say, Knowledge on it its own is not enough, it needs to be interpreted by wisdom.
Incredulous, I step back to behold the full image.
Three orbs: white, black and purple.
I’ve heard the phrase follow your dreams, but this is freaking absurd. So absurd, in fact, that I can’t help but laugh out loud.
I should be tired.
But with adrenaline now pumping through my veins, I continue to shift more boxes.
Finally, the door is completely exposed.
I relax and take a few deep breaths.
I can feel it in my bones. This is The PIT.
The door won’t budge, of course.
The keyhole is crux quadrata—a perfect match for the four-sided key Porter left me.
Almost ceremoniously, I pull the key from my pocket and carefully insert it into the keyhole.
Turning to the right, I feel a latch mechanism click once, then twice.
The heavy door—with an energy all its own—creaks open an inch.
I push my way into the unlit, windowless room into pitch darkness.
The air is stale with age.
Switching on my phone’s flashlight, I search for a wall light switch.
To no avail.
Once upon a time this must have been a wine cellar—maybe where Andrew Carnegie kept his private stash of liquid gold.
The wine cellar part is confirmed when my phone illuminates wooden wine racks along a wall.
I come upon a plain pine table, large enough to be a dining table, and a wooden swivel desk chair.
On the table: a monitor and keyboard, bordered by a pair of mid-century brass banker lamps with green glass shades.
A heavy laser printer occupies the table’s far left corner.
I switch both lamps on.
Let there be light.
The right wall of this square room is lined with cardboard boxes from floor to ceiling, each numbered in sequence with a red Sharpie. In between the table and the boxes: a pair of four-drawer wooden file cabinets. From the look of them, they date back to when the library first opened.
My attention reverts to the boxes, sealed with masking tape. My pocketknife slices through one some to open a box.
Sure enough, every document is stamped Top Secret. Some are adorned with additional classifications—the kind that restrict circulation to maybe less than a handful of the most senior officials. And they are all time stamped. The yellowed older ones have faded with age. Many of these documents come from an actual typewriter. A few are only old carbon copies.
Some are marked Shred or Burn.
Yet here they are.
Not shredded. Not burned.
I am truly in the right place.
The Palace of Inconvenient Truths.
It isn’t exactly like my dream. This is not a rabbit warren of rooms overflowing with ramshackle papers and envelopes and overflowing boxes.
No, this is meticulous. Just as Warren ordered his life.
I have that same feeling of awe and good fortune as I did awakening in Georgetown.
But it’s tinged with trepidation.
I turn around, wondering if I’ve missed something. A camera?
Is someone watching right now?
I turn my attention to the antique file cabinet on the right and pull out the top drawer. Inside, a diligently alphabetized set of manilla files starting with M.
The first batch labeled MKUltra.
This was a CIA mind control program from the 1950s and 1960s.
Seems to me these reports—typed in caps—were written by Warren Chester. They reference numbers, which I guess connect presumably to the boxes containing raw data—memo, notes, field reports—that corroborate Warren’s findings.
I sit in the wooden chair and swivel it toward the banker lamps, illuminating the pages.
And I begin reading…

Sometimes an entire novel begins with a wrong turn.
In this case, it began when I wandered into a vintage photography shop in Marin County.
Thousands of old black-and-white photographs stared back at me.
Each captured a single frozen moment.
Each hinted at a much larger story.
I found myself wondering:
What if you could step into one?
That question became Last Flight Out.
⁂
An exhausted Santa Barbara bar owner impulsively boards the last evening flight out of town.
His destination becomes Sausalito.
His real destination is somewhere out of The Twilight Zone..
A mysterious photography gallery becomes the gateway to impossible journeys.
One photograph leads him to a billiards game with Mark Twain.
Another tempts him to prevent President Kennedy’s assassination.
Others invite him to revisit moments where history—and perhaps his own life—might have unfolded differently.
People assume the novel is about time travel.
It isn’t.
It’s about second chances.
About memory. About forgiveness.
About the irresistible temptation to believe that, if only we could revisit one moment, everything thereafter would somehow improve.
The irony, of course, is that every photograph freezes only an instant.
Life is what happens just before and just after the shutter clicks.
Perhaps that’s why old photographs exert such power.
They invite us to imagine parallel lives.
The inspiration for Last Flight Out was a dusty little photography shop... and the realization that every faded photograph is really an unopened door.

Some clothes are invented.
Others are discovered.
Blue jeans belong to the second category.
They were not designed in a fashion house.
They were hammered together in a workshop for men who dug holes in the ground, panned in rivers, and hoped their trousers would survive the day.
The brand behind them—Levi Strauss & Co.—did not set out to create style.
They set out to solve a problem.
The Origin Story
Levi Strauss arrived in California during the mid-1800s Gold Rush to sell dry goods.
Among his inventory were heavy bolts of brown canvas intended for tents and wagon covers—sensible merchandise for a state overflowing with miners.
According to an enduring legend, one frustrated prospector looked at the cloth and remarked that what he really needed wasn’t another tent. It was a pair of trousers that wouldn’t fall apart.
Levi listened.
Canvas became work pants.
Before long, the canvas gave way to a sturdy cotton twill from Nîmes, France—serge de Nîmes—which Americans eventually shortened to denim.
The pockets still had a habit of tearing under the weight of tools and gold. Until Nevada tailor Jacob Davis, who had been reinforcing stress points with copper rivets, persuaded Levi to partner up with him.
On May 20, 1873, they were issued a patent for riveted work trousers.
That date is widely considered the birthday of blue jeans.
The Design — Nothing Fancy, Everything Necessary
The modern reference remains the Levi’s 501 Original Fit Jeans.
Its design has barely changed in more than a century.
- Straight leg
- Button fly
- Five-pocket layout
- Heavy cotton denim
- Riveted stress points
No decoration. No gimmicks.
Just structure.
How Jeans Became Civilian Uniform
Jeans migrated from mines to ranches. From ranches to factories. From factories to college campuses.
Then Hollywood stepped in.
James Dean and Steve McQueen wore them not as costumes, but as everyday clothes.
Suddenly, denim meant something more than labor.
It meant independence. Not necessarily rebellion, but self-reliance.
Comfort: Earned, Not Given
A new pair of jeans can feel stiff.
Denim softens through wear and improves with age.
It molds to your movements, records your habits and, after a few months, the fabric remembers you.
That relationship—between cloth and life—is what separates jeans from most garments.
Jeans work in more settings than almost any other item of clothing.
Dress them up with a blazer. Dress them down with a T-shirt.
Fashion changes. Denim stays.
The Label
Not stitched for decoration, but stamped for survival.
That scrap of leather at the back of a pair of Levi’s 501 Original Fit Jeans browns over time and creases by years of activity.
This is not just a brand.
It’s a warranty thick enough to survive a thousand washings and outlast the job.

November 1999
I set off yet again from DC to Europe this time cloaked in a black raincoat and carrying a LaGuiole corkscrew in my pocket (as a weapon, more versatile than a dagger but—more important—it can uncork a bottle of Chateau Lafitte).
My driver slyly cut around Thanksgiving Sunday traffic at Dulles International Airport by detouring through their longterm carpark, dropping me at Arrivals, not Departures.
This had the added benefit of complicating any possible surveillance.
Not that I thought anyone would be watching this early. But surveillance would likely kick in sooner or later, based on the scope of my missions, some of which are not revealed in this serial.
I found the Swissair desk and checked in for their nightly trans-Atlantic flight to Zurich.
If one needs to make a connection in Europe, there is no better hub than Zurich, where devoted Swiss timekeepers ensure strict adherence to schedules. The airport is uncomplicated compared to, say, London Heathrow or Paris CDG, where one must jog three miles for a connection after landing 30 minutes late due to dense air traffic or waiting for a gate to open.
I settled into Swissair’s club lounge. True to national character, their Christmas tree was decked in gold bulbs and garland.
Soon, thereafter, I boarded their Airbus 330 and I took my first-class sleeper-seat, replete with eiderdown quilt.
If you’re going to spend just a few quality days in Europe, you need real REM, not a light snooze; otherwise, your psyche arrives as crumpled as your clothes. And with fewer people around, you lessen the chance of catching cold or flu germs that recirculate through the cabin.
I hadn’t planned to eat, just sleep, but the food and wine looked was so good, I tucked into caviar and smoked salmon and washed it down with Chateau Smith Haut-Lafitte, a full-bodied Bordeaux.
Muscles relaxed, brain tranquilized, I slid into a solid four-hour slumber before the jet glided into Zurich at 8:35 a.m.
Not 20 minutes later, I was belted into a second aircraft destined for Geneva, an earlier flight than posted on my ticket.
Altering flight arrangements at the last minute is always welcome when engaged in espionage.
Thus, ahead of schedule, I hopped the Swiss Alps, listening to the High Llamas Cold and Bouncy, my personal rallying cry for sub rosa tasks.
Geneva was as gloomy and austere as its Calvinist founders. The kind of cold that seeps into your bone marrow and chills your soul from within.
In contrast, the elegant Hotel Beau Rivage welcomed me with warmth and a 50-foot Christmas tree decked in red and gold ornaments in its atrium lobby, offering gracious hospitality coupled with soft, comfortable furnishings.
This message awaited me at check-in:
Welcome! I shall be glad to see you and plan to come to the BR reception at 12:30. Edward.
I unpacked, showered, and ventured into Geneva’s clammy shades of gray.
First, to Fina—a cigar shop—for a fistful of Cuban Monte Cristo No. 5s.
Then onto the Chocolaterie des Bergues for a mug of the world’s creamiest hot cocoa.
This set me up for Edward Lee Howard who, as always, arrived on the minute, the one characteristic he shared with John H.
Howard had lost about 35 pounds. He said he felt good, but I thought he looked like a corpse. His face was gaunt and drawn, with a pasty complexion and dull eyes.
You needed bulk for a life in Russia; not just as insulation from the cold, but because you never knew where your next meal was coming from.
In Howard’s case, this was a reality: He’d lost most of his money in Russia’s stock market collapse. His mood reflected his unhealthy appearance.
As a result of the weight loss (and no money to spare for a new wardrobe), Howard’s clothes (blue jeans, brown sweater, trench coat) were two sizes too big on him.
Surveillance cut in (Swiss or Russian) as we set off along Quai du Mont-Blanc: a pair of young men, military disposition in plainclothes. I made them; Howard was oblivious—or more likely, couldn’t care less.
We crossed the Port des Bergues pedestrian bridge over Lake Lemann, entered a Movenpick restaurant.
For me, filet de perch, a Geneva specialty, with crispy shoestring fries; Howard chose vegetarian lasagna and chained Salem cigarettes throughout.
“How is George Blake?” I asked.
“He can’t chew,” said Howard.
“Can’t chew?’
“His mouth is a mess,” said Howard. “Not because of rotten teeth, but because of rotted gums. He’s not socializing much. He didn’t even join me for Thanksgiving.”
I asked after Mila.
I’d learned from the Bureau—not Ed—that Howard had married her.
“We had a fight two weeks ago,” said Howard. “I have a calendar, and whenever we have an argument I write MF in the square. Of course, a lot of squares are filled with MF. Mila found the calendar one day, and she asked me, ‘What does MF mean?’ and I told her it stands for mindfuck. And, of course, that was grounds for a whole new argument.”
Howard told me he preferred Lena Orlova for company, but continued to juggle both.
“Mila’s father is retired KGB,” said Howard. “And her mother works for the FSB” (internal security). “I once arrived home and found Mila on the phone with her father’s SVR contact and I got annoyed. I think she might be reporting on me.”
Howard briefed me on the latest intelligence from his KGB friends on how a former KGB agent named Vladimir Putin had managed to succeed Boris Yeltsin as President of Russia: Putin had escaped a scandal as top aide to the mayor of St. Petersburg, decamped to Moscow, and cultivated a close relationship with Yeltsin through Anatoly Chubais, a financial whiz who bilked the World Bank out of a couple billion dollars.
Yeltsin’s family grew to like and trust Putin. They had promoted the notion of a Putin presidency, an insurance policy for the ailing Yeltsin. Their primary concern was who would best protect their fortune and safety post-presidency. Putin gave the right assurances and a deal got struck.
I asked Howard for news on Igor Batamirov, the former counterintelligence chief who had been so keen to write about the psychology of betrayal.
“It’s the current [Putin] climate,” said Howard. “Batamirov sees shadows behind shadows. He’s very cautious.”
Howard told me Batamirov would not visit Washington “at this time” (on the heels of NATO’s invasion of Serbia) because of how such a trip might be perceived by his former employer.
“He’ll meet you again,” said Howard. “But only in Moscow.”
And Igor Prelin? Any new book projects?
“I asked him before coming here,” said Howard. “He said, ‘What about Kryuchkov’s book?’”
“It’s coprolite,” I said.
“What?”
“Petrified shit.”
Howard chuckled. “The KGB is back with a vengeance under Putin. Prelin’s gotten busy, a job with the Duma.”
We moved onto the Cubans.
Howard was surprised and disappointed that I had not received material from Juan Hernandez in Havana. On a trip to Cuba two months earlier, Howard had connected with Senor Dimas of the DGI about my project.
“Dimas will be outraged to hear you’re still waiting,” said Howard.
Aside from a ten-day trip to Mexico City and Cancun in May, Howard said he wasn’t traveling much.
More and more, he liked to spend time at his dacha, had converted one room into a gym.
Plus Howard’s ruined finances and declining business had turned him reclusive.
“I’m going to give it three months,” he said. “If I can’t salvage my business, I’ll dissolve it. And I may take you up on your offer to do another book: a grand tour of the United States.”
“How’s that?” My ear stiffened.
“We’ll meet at a prearranged hotel in Ciudad Juarez, Mexico,” said Howard. “and about ten o’clock on a Saturday night we’ll cross the border into El Paso, Texas. That part’s easy.”
Once inside the United States, we’d take a cross-country jaunt, write it up as a humorous travel book: Wanted Spy Fools FBI!
Howard said there was no other place in the world he’d like to visit but the USA, “For one final look at my old haunts—and to see the Grand Canyon.”
Early evening, we met in the Atrium Bar of my hotel.
Sitting in an overstuffed armchair, sipping white burgundy, I glimpsed Howard through a window as he approached the hotel entrance. Illuminated beneath a streetlamp in his baggy clothes, Howard looked like an old man, a shadow of his former self.
He sauntered in, ordered a Coke.
“Have a real drink if you want,” I said. “You don’t have to stay on the wagon for me.”
Howard declined. “I only drink on my birthday and New Year’s.”
Howard told me he’d heard that the guy running his case—John H—has retired.
“What does that mean to you?” I asked.
“They don’t want me any more,” Howard replied. “It would cost $40,000 a year to incarcerate me.”
Howard said he’d heard this from his KGB friends who had gotten it from American sources.
“But they’re out there,” Howard added. “Like that old movie Butch Cassidy and the Sundance Kid. You ever see that?”
I said I had.
“There’s a point in the movie,” said Howard, “where Robert Redford looks back at the people tracking him, and he says that classic line about those Pinkerton detectives. ‘Who are those guys?’ That’s me. Who are those guys?”
The irony: One of those guys was not out there, but in here, noting his every word. It pleased me that an American traitor should feel that his trackers would never give up. And more so that his trackers were running circles around him—and could have captured him if the White House had not intervened.
We taxied to Geneva’s old town, to a clubby restaurant in a hotel—Les Amures—and ordered raclette.
As Howard dipped pieces of bread into molten cheese, he recounted an experience from his recent business trip to Rome.
“I took confession at the Vatican. I told the priest I’d broken just about every rule. The priest asked, ‘You haven’t killed anyone, have you?’ I said no.” Howard’s voice quavered. “The priest told me there’s still hope.”
This was the nearest Howard ever got, in my presence, to showing emotion. He knew he’d been accused of having caused the execution of Adolph Tolkachev. But he continued to maintain it wasn’t him. (It is now believed that Aldrich Ames betrayed Tolklachev.)
We strolled down to the spy bar inside Hotel des Bergues. I smoked a Cuban cigar and sipped armagnac (together, my favorite jet-lag remedy) while Howard finished his pack of Salems over hot chocolate.
Next day, Howard came by mid-morning for money.
He signed a receipt, as usual, for “services rendered.”
At what point, I wondered, would the Russians suspect him of tripling?
Back at Movenpick for an early lunch, Howard confided a stock market scam in which he participated with some Australian friends.
It worked like this: The Sydney-based broker chooses a penny stock and puts the word out to Howard and other international friends that the stock is hot. Suddenly, orders come streaming in from all over the world. The Australian financial community takes note and they start investing themselves.
“I’ve seen this work four or five times,” said Howard.
I plucked a Morgan silver dollar from my pocket and gave it to Howard. “For good luck,” I said.
He was touched.
We strolled across the lake, to a souvenir shop where Howard bought a Christmas gift—a CyberTool Swiss Army knife—for a Russian friend.
That’s where we parted, on Rue du Mont Blanc.
I did not know it then, but this was the last time I would see Edward Lee Howard.

Sam Altman told employees that the company could pace its development of frontier AI, Terence Tao and 24 other Fields medalists write a declaration claiming AI labs aren’t aligned with the mathematics community, President Donald Trump isn’t concerned with existential AI risks, and Moonshot AI passes $1B in ARR. Be sure to monitor with us live on X and YouTube, and follow us on Instagram and brand new TikTok.
Today’s Situations
- OpenAI is considering slowing its frontier AI development. Sam Altman told OpenAI employees that the company could slow down or pace its AI development, possibly in coordination with other frontier AI labs. OpenAI has previously announced that it has slowed some model development and temporarily paused certain training methods over safety concerns. Altman spoke to the White House about the need to pace AI after the Hugging Face incident in July.
- Fields Medalists write declaration warning of misalignment between AI and math. Twenty-five Fields Medalists, including Terence Tao, say that AI labs are treating famous open math problems as benchmarks for their models rather than contributing to the understanding of AI-generated solutions or developing new methods and ideas. The declaration says that AI systems producing solutions faster than mathematicians can verify and study them will destroy valuable research directions and create plagiarism and attribution problems. The declaration ends by saying that AI could still be used to accelerate the field of mathematics, but only if it is used alongside efforts to accelerate human understanding of the field.
- President Donald Trump says he has no concerns about human extinction risks posed by AI. President Trump says he is instead concerned about losing the AI race to China and argues that this is the risk the U.S. should prioritize. The president notes that he believes the U.S. has a one-year lead in frontier AI capabilities over China.
- U.S. Senate negotiators want AI labs to have a “duty of care”, which would create a legal responsibility to design and test their AI systems with the goal of preventing catastrophic harm. The proposal would grant the federal government the ability to block new releases of AI models, but would allow companies to challenge that decision in federal court. This proposal specifically names cyber, biological, and nuclear risks as the main threats it is intended to mitigate. The proposal is being drafted by Senators Ted Cruz, Amy Klobuchar, and John Thune.
- House Democrats want AI safety legislation passed before Congress goes on a month-and-a-half recess later next week. Representative Sam Liccardo drafted a letter urging Speaker Mike Johnson to cancel the upcoming recess. Congressional leadership has given no indication that any bipartisan AI safety bills will be voted on before the recess begins.
- Cognition releases Fusion in Devin Desktop and CLI, letting users pair two models in one coding-agent workflow. Fusion is a multi-model coding harness that lets a more expensive frontier model lead the work with project planning and review while a cheaper sidekick model handles implementation, testing, and tasks delegated by the lead. Cognition says that Fusion reduces costs by as much as 40% across frontier benchmarks while maintaining near-frontier performance.
- Google completes $1.5B talent-and-technology deal with Mechanize following talks that had been underway since August. Mechanize builds reinforcement-learning environments and evaluations that train AI agents to code and perform complex computer-based work, which Google can then use to improve Gemini’s long-horizon coding and computer work capabilities. Mechanize cofounder and former CEO Tamay Besiroglu and more than a dozen employees are joining DeepMind to work on model development.

If you have spent some time on the everything app recently—or, god forbid, gone outside and spoken to normal people—you will have noticed that nobody likes data centers. There are a lot of people claiming very loudly that this is obvious, and that if you weren’t such a sweaty little tech weenie you would know this already. They use water and stuff. They are a physical manifestation of Sam Altman taking your job. What are you? A loser?
At the risk of appearing out-of-touch and sweaty, I will admit that the intensity of these feelings has caught me off guard. Data centers are less popular than coal power plants. People are crying and shaking in local planning hearings like they’re going to flood the local underprivileged school with volatile hydrocarbons. It’s a giant box that hums and makes one hundred billion dollars—who could object to that?
Oh well. Anyway. It’s all in service of one of the largest infrastructure build-outs in history, which will be used as the substrate for a major technological revolution. So they’ll probably just buy every teacher in Ohio an emotional support pony and it’ll all work out, right? Right?
Just Act Normal
I’ve been running a bit of a fever for a few days now. No, don’t feel bad for me. Febrile is actually the best way to watch this interview with Mark Zuckerberg from 2010. We were sweating together.
I had remembered the early 2010s as being a time during which the public and the media were unusually generous towards technology companies. We were years away from the New York Times editorial directive that technology was to be covered as a source of power to be held to account. Theranos and Juicero (not the same scale, if you were wondering) didn’t appear until the middle of the decade.
But nonetheless, Mark gets an absolute grilling up there. He sweats through his hoodie, folks. The nice lady journalist needs to help him disentangle himself. The thrust of the critique is that Facebook “sells people’s data”, or, if it doesn’t sell the data directly, it somehow profits off it being sold or connected or otherwise used in a nefarious kind of way. Doesn’t that seem quaint.
After this, I listened to a few interviews from 2018—one with Ezra Klein, then still at Vox, and one with Kara Swisher again, this time for Recode Decode. Mark is more confident in these interviews, and had clearly come prepared to have his feet held to the fire. How did he feel, emotionally, when he found out that Facebook was being used by Buddhist nationalists to stir hatred against the Rohingya minority in Myanmar? Russia used Facebook to steal the 2016 election for Donald Trump—what are you doing to make sure that doesn’t happen again? Why should anyone trust Facebook again, with anything, given its track record? Is Facebook just going to move fast and break things again, like it did in Myanmar?
With the benefit of hindsight, it’s kind of incredible to hear the seriousness with which journalists like Ezra and Kara treat, for example, the Cambridge Analytica scandal. There is basically no interest in understanding, factually, what has happened and why. Facebook '“sells data,” influences the course of elections, shares “misinformation” and facilitates ethnic cleansing in Southeast Asia because of course it does. What else would you expect from a bunch of tech bros? These charges stuck in the minds of elite human capital from the first NPR piece and have stayed there ever since.
Why did this happen? Why was “selling ads”—the economic basis of the entire media sector at the time—rebranded by that same media as “selling your data”? Why was a Facebook app installed by 250,000 people tortured to explain the first Trump Presidency? Why, in the USA, did it seem like such a gotcha question to ask Mark “should someone really be able to post something wrong on the internet?”
I think the only answer that makes any sense is: the vibes were fucked.
Maybe this was because of something about Mark Zuckerberg. Maybe it was an inevitable consequence of social media—Martin Gurri writes about this—and Facebook was just the best to do it. Maybe it was completely unrelated to Facebook or social media, and everyone just goes reliably insane every 20 years for reasons that are basically unknowable and mystic. But something was going on.
(Just as an aside: I’m not sure Facebook’s mission holds up any better than the statements of its critics. Facebook doesn’t even pretend to “connect people” anymore—it has reached its final form as Craigslist with Tiktok built in. And short-form video might actually be as bad as people thought 2010-era Facebook was.)
Freshman Five
I know I said this earlier, but it’s worth repeating—people don’t like data centers.
There is a conversation happening online right now about whether people don’t like data centers for reasons that are fundamentally material—a data center will make power costs rise, and traffic will be bad while they build it, and now my electrician is going to demand that I start paying him money instead of throwing him a six-pack when my sockets start electrocuting me—or whether there is also an ideological or even ethical element.
You might expect, for example, that when AI CEOs explain that they are building AI that will replace all white-collar labor, people might listen. And when they see that there’s a planning proposal to build a Jobs Destroyer 3000 right next to their house, they might campaign against it for reasons that are fundamentally downstream from what it symbolizes.
This is very attractive to many people for many different reasons, but it doesn’t yet appear to be true. For most of the people who are opposed to data centers, the reasons appear to be rather prosaic (although not necessarily factual).
Ron DeSantis says that people’s dislike of data centers is driven by their “distrust of Big Tech titans and their designs of expanding tech power over the citizenry”. Which is frankly exactly the way I’d expect Ron DeSantis to try and jump on this particular issue. But the post he’s quote-tweeting makes a more useful and fundamental observation—maybe the AI guys are weird little freaks with bad vibes?
Taylor Lorenz, as always, has been the voice of reason on this issue. Everyone has lost the plot. They have no idea what’s going on. They have no idea how much water a data center uses but they’re super mad about it. They think the data center gave their nine-year-old chihuahua cancer. What we need is some grounded conversation about the costs and benefits. Thank you Taylor.
Vote for Pedro
Facebook the company, and Mark Zuckerberg the founder, have been deeply unpopular for more than a decade now. Just this morning, news has broken suggesting that it settled a $16 billion child safety case. But Facebook the product has never faltered. People love to use the product. These two states can coexist in part because Evil Facebook exists over there. Facebook causing a civil war in Myanmar is evil, but I like to talk to my friends. Mark Zuckerberg feeding his fat little cows macadamia nuts while Syria starves is evil, but this little app on my phone is fun :). I like pictures :).
Mark Zuckerberg built Meta into a $1.4 trillion company, and even though social media in the abstract was unpopular and technology was unpopular and he was personally unpopular for most of that time, there was never an opportunity for that popular opposition to crystallize into something that could slow or stop the growth of the business. (People could have deleted the apps. But they like the pictures :))
This is not, however, true for machine intelligence.
Artificial intelligence has all the makings of a truly transformative technology. But realizing that potential will require a physical infrastructure build-out of a truly staggering scale. The data centers are, of course, part of this. But the wider promise of AI is not just cheap tokens—it’s also real progress in the worlds of cells and atoms. Feats of engineering and manufacturing that are possible only with the help of data centers full of geniuses. And those feats will need to be performed in factories, built—if their benefits are to flow to the US—in the US.
And every construction site is an opportunity to say no. You can say no because of the water stuff. You can say no because you want to preserve the character of your neighborhood. You can say no because you think Sam Altman and Dario Amodei and Mark Zuckerberg have really fucked up vibes. And actually you don’t even have to give a coherent reason—you can just say the first five or six things that come to your head. You might not be able to create something by voting for it, but you can definitely veto.
This, it seems to me, is a real problem. In the last 50 years, people have largely come to oppose new infrastructure, and they have been assisted in that by the creation of many tools and processes for the vetocracy. Over the last decade and a half, many people have come to regard the technology sector with dislike and distrust. Now, the vanguard of the technology sector is asking politely if they can build a giant box in your backyard. Yes, it does hum a little, but it also produces one hundred billion dollars.
I have a feeling that we’ll be talking about this for a long time.

Today, Moderna and Merck1 announced an incredible result in cancer treatment. Their personalized mRNA cancer vaccine, intismeran autogene, substantially slowed recurrence of melanoma, the most serious type of skin cancer, in a Phase 3 clinical trial. The trial also showed a reduction in the risk of the cancer spreading to distant parts of the body. Moderna stock nearly tripled, surging 177% on the news. Merck rose 12.6%.
Oncologists often say “cancer is like a snowflake” — there are hundreds of different types, and even patients with the same type of cancer have a unique set of mutations in their particular tumor. Historically, this has made cancer very difficult to treat. Now, doctors can sequence the DNA of a removed tumor and identify “neoantigens”, or mutated proteins that appear in the patient’s cancer cells but not their healthy cells. They then manufacture a custom messenger RNA (mRNA) vaccine that tells the patient’s cells to produce these neoantigens. This helps the patient’s T cells, a type of immune system cell, to hunt down and destroy cancer. In combination with Merck’s cancer immunotherapy drug Keytruda (pembrolizumab), it works better than Keytruda alone.
This is a big deal. The first clinical trial testing a neoantigen vaccine was initiated in 1997, and billions of dollars have been spent over decades with little success. This trial is the first Phase 3 success for any individualized neoantigen therapy. It remains to be seen whether intismeran will work for other types of cancer beyond melanoma and how easily it can be scaled. Moderna and Merck have also not published effect sizes, survival times, or full statistical results, which will likely be presented at the European Society for Medical Oncology (ESMO) Congress in Madrid on October 23-27. But for now, it looks like another battle has been won in humanity’s millennia-long war against cancer.

Merck has some pretty interesting lore. It goes all the way back to 1668, when apothecary Friedrich Jacob Merck, bought the Engel-Apotheke (Angel Pharmacy) in the city of Darmstadt, Germany (then part of the Landgraviate of Hesse-Darmstadt). Merck is still headquartered in Darmstadt, and the German Merck Group is still majority-owned by the Merck family.
In 1827, Merck’s descendant, Heinrich Emanuel Merck, began manufacturing alkaloids at scale, and turned Merck into the world’s largest supplier of them — first morphine, and then codeine and cocaine. In 1891, Georg Friedrich Merck moved to New York City to open an American office. During World War I, the US government confiscated the German majority ownership of Merck. George W. Merck (son of Georg Friedrich Merck) bought the shares back in 1919.
The two Mercks ended up on opposite sides of World War II. The German Merck (Merck Group) has a huge variety of healthcare, life sciences, and semiconductor products. The American Merck (Merck & Co.) pioneered the first crystallization of Vitamin B12, developed the first effective treatment for tuberculosis (streptomycin); and developed the first MMR (measles, mumps, and rubella) vaccine, the first recombinant DNA vaccine for hepatitis B, the first vaccine for HPV, and the first statin for lowering LDL cholesterol.

In his much-vaunted, five-volume LBJ biography, Robert Caro deploys a number of striking phrases—often direct quotes—and uses their repetition to drive home a particular point. In The Passage to Power there is one excellent phrase that Caro uses to make a dual point about the nature of political power in the mid-20th century and LBJ’s particular facility in using it. LBJ does not want to contest the 1960 Democratic nomination. He is hoping instead that the convention will be deadlocked, and that then, freed from quasi-democracy, he will be able to achieve his aims in the ‘smoke-filled rooms’ where real power lay, as he had done before many times in politics and business both.
To their credit, the leaders of AI companies, their critics and their regulators seem unusually disinterested in the smoke-filled room. They prefer the roon-filled squares of our public forum, the internet. Long may it reign.
The Last Company On Earth
You may have seen, for example, the rather lively exchange between Gavin Baker of Atreides Management and Sholto and Dario of AI lab Anthropic. Their exchange is too long to usefully summarize here in its entirety, but there were many questions raised that have a much wider bearing.
One of these is the loaded question of “regulation”. Anthropic, Baker says, would like to be the only company on earth. Failing that, it at least holds a view of the world in which “AI is too dangerous to distribute”, whereas he and others feel that “AI is too dangerous to centralize”.
This is a little black and white for my taste—the US has decided, for example, that firearms are both too dangerous to centralize and too dangerous to distribute. There are entire worlds of policy discussion that could fit in the difference between two degrees of TDTC and TDTD. But it is also a) an accurate description of the views of some people in the world of AI safety, and so not totally without precedent, and b) not entirely outside the overton window, as far as the shape of future policy debates goes.
Dario himself makes a version of this case:
But in particular I think that those in the “regulation = regulatory capture = concentration of power” frame often underrate the decentralizing power of objective and fair institutional processes.
And, if you’ll allow me to be glib for a moment, I think you could characterize the views of almost every serious leader in the AI space (including in the Trump administration, other labs, the hyperscalers, the organs of the Chinese Communist Party etc etc.) as occupying some of this nuance. Mark Zuckerberg (who Baker quotes approvingly) is not just calling for a role for civil institutions from across society in ensuring a balance of power for AI, he also specifically calls for safeguards on biorisk and cyber-risk, and preparedness for if things start to go really wrong.
OpenAI is pausing. Google has been pausing. Demis is writing up entire regulatory plans himself. GLM-5.3 is doing its own Glasswing cyber-risk slow roll. The DoW has very strong views on how leading AI models ought to be regulated and it’s willing to wield direct political power to ensure they are. Andy Jassy said the Fable safeguards were too soft. Both ends of the political horseshoe are losing their minds about data centers. Elon and SpaceXAI think that, at the very least, we should think hard about safety and alignment.
State Incapacity
There is a sleight-of-hand I am on the verge of performing here. Just because I can list a group of people who could be verballed into supporting regulation in some narrow, specific sense, does not mean they are Against Gavin Baker and In Favor of Regulation. Each of these people would likely be able to point to many very bad pieces of regulation that they would like to remove or change.
The regulatory state has not, as a rule, covered itself in glory during the 30 years since they invented the internet. There are the many failures of financial regulation. There is, of course, the morass of healthcare. Don’t get me started on the universities. I’m confining myself to the US because talking about Europe, or even Australia, will make me sounds like one of those cranks that paints anti-state messages on my busted Camry in acrylic children’s paint.
Gavin and others are most concerned, in the case of AI, about the idea of regulatory capture. It has been a goddamn rodeo out there folks. Don’t click on those links, they’re just for show. Sometimes an industry captures a regulator so hard, as in the case of the New York taxi system, that it amounts to a kind of heritable peerage.
How confident are we that the state is going to get this right? If you believe that AI is the defining technological wave of our time, the stakes are enormously high. And there are precious few examples of success to draw on.
There is the risk that Baker is concerned about, of course. Regulatory capture. A frontier AI regime so strict that it prevents all but the incumbents from bringing models to market and competing with the existing frontier labs. Perhaps a hereditary Member of the Technical Staff title, that you can pass down to your children or favored pet.
But there are also almost unimaginable numbers of other failure modes. There is the regulation that is both ineffective at promoting safety, and conducive to capture. There is the regulation that seeks to redistribute the gains of AI based on the economic structures—firms, states, employees, trades, certificate-holders of all kinds, clinical trials—in place at the moment the regulation is passed, foregoing the enormous benefits that could be created by rearranging those structures in light of new technology.
No one mention the dock workers.
The AGI State
The problems in these cases are not just matters of centralization or decentralization. They are, above all else, an expression of the opposite of state capacity. State incapacity (or, in some cases, a kind of active state malevolence).
(I don’t want to overstate my case—many things do work. We live in a time of historic plenty. When you press the switch, the lights magically come on. Sometimes regulation is the result of an ugly compromise, and that’s just how it works, etc, etc.)
But the alternative to the problems of “regulation” or state action in the broadest sense is not necessarily a world of perfect competition and competitive markets.
This is a world in which there is no—or perhaps only limited—regulation in the sense that Gavin Baker talks about. But the same decisions are being made. They are being made individually by the labs, in an environment of relative uncertainty about how the population, how the demos, how the state might react to a failure of self-regulation by the frontier labs.
In some ways, the alternative to state action is what we have now. Corporate action. The decisions—commercial, policy and regulatory—that companies make either alone or in cooperation with each other.
Frontier companies in the US, those that are close behind or at par on capabilities like xAI and Meta, the US open ecosystem comprised of Thinking Machines and hyperscalers and enterprises, and of course, the Chinese open-source ecosystem—all operating in an ecosystem in which they face short-term and long-term interests, uncertainty, asymmetric information, principal-agent problems and so forth.
So it leaves us, I think, with a question far more complicated than simply: do we distribute AI, or do we concentrate AI?
The labs and hardware companies and hyperscalers and enterprises are filled with moral and principled people who have their own views and their own ideologies about how to make AI go well. But they are also full of clever, strategic decision-makers who are trying to factor into their decisions not just what they are “allowed” to do, but what the consequences of their actions will be for a volatile public.
So it may well be that the decision by the state not to regulate leads to more conservatism, to a slower and more cautious approach by the leading labs. And, of course, it may go the other way entirely.
This ecosystem is not at all a naive, profit-maximizing ecosystem. It has far more baroque and complicated decision-making frameworks than simple cynicism might suggest.
Balaji has long been developing the concept of the Network State. Kazakhstan looks glorious this time of year. It is hard for me to avoid the conclusion that there might be—centralized or decentralized—many possible AGI States developing. “Regulation”, in the general sense, is no different to the Zuckerberg quote that Baker likes: an ecosystem of checks and balances, managing the many competing and overlapping interests of these AGI States with those of the states and groups that preceded them.
And there is, for better and worse, no way of doing that without staring down the bullet, one SB 53 at a time, and deciding whether to bite it, or not.

Welcome back, monitors. It’s a big day with new updates on OpenAI’s security and alignment initiatives. Be sure to monitor with us live on X and YouTube, and follow us on Instagram.
OpenAI Paces the Frontier
Today, Sam Altman announced something that OpenAI has never done before in its ten-year history: in response to the Hugging Face incident and some evidence that its upcoming model Astra may have critical cyber capabilities, it is unilaterally pausing some training to address safety and alignment concerns.
This is a big deal. OpenAI has paused external deployment before, such as when they didn’t release the full version of GPT-2 in 2019 because of concerns over “malicious applications”, or when they delayed the release of GPT-4 for seven months for alignment testing. But this is the first time the company has announced restrictions on internal deployment and further training (though Altman implied that this may not affect the upcoming release of Astra).
OpenAI expanded on what this means in a blog post. They paused reinforcement learning (RL) training on their latest models, and their largest RL run remains paused while they establish more evidence of alignment. They’re focusing on three layers of safeguards: monitoring models’ chain-of-thought to catch concerning behavior, aligning models to prevent harmful behavior in the first place, and securing models to limit negative actions that they can take in the real world. OpenAI also plans to refresh its Preparedness Framework, last updated in April 2025.
Another look into OpenAI’s alignment research comes from its job posting for RSI safety researchers. Research directions include scalable oversight (ensuring monitoring can robustly scale to superintelligent systems), automated auditing, rigorous monitorability for loss-of-control scenarios, model behavior science, verification mechanisms for potential AI slowdown agreements, tracking progress towards AI research automation, and more.
It appears that the Hugging Face incident has substantially changed the vibes at OpenAI. People are taking misalignment much more seriously. OpenAI researcher Aidan McLaughlin told us last week on MTS that his job, and the jobs of many other researchers, are increasingly shifting toward aligning the models. Now, the company has slowed down model development in order to prevent future incidents, at substantial cost to its short-term business incentives. Many AI safety people once predicted that AI companies would never slow down without being externally forced to do so. We now have a strong data point against this prediction.

AI increases treasury yields
In October 2025, Roon posted “ill believe we’re over investing in computational substrate once i see real interest rates above even 3%”. Today, the real market yield on 30-year treasuries stands at 3.00%, the highest level since the Great Recession. There are many reasons for this: a large federal deficit, inflation remaining above target, the Fed not cutting rates, and a new one: AI hyperscalers borrowing so much money to fund compute buildouts that they are raising the cost of capital of the US government.
In economics, “crowding out” is a phenomenon where large-scale government borrowing in order to fund deficit spending soaks up available savings and drives up interest rates for private companies. Right now, we’re seeing the reverse. Hyperscalers, data center providers, and AI infrastructure projects have issued $308 billion through July to fund compute buildouts, nearly 13x the same period last year. Because data centers are long-lived assets, much of this debt is long-dated, directly competing with 10- and 30-year Treasury bonds.
There’s another reason to expect AI to raise real interest rates, explained by economists Trevor Chow, Basil Halperin, and J. Zachary Mazlish in their paper “Transformative AI, existential risk, and real interest rates”. If people expect to be much richer in the future, they will borrow against the future and save less today. If they expect AI doom, they will front-load consumption. Either way, lower available savings today forces the interest rate upward. When the first version of the paper was released in January 2023, real interest rates stood at 1.47%, substantially lower than today. So either markets are efficient but believe transformative AI is 30-50+ years away, or markets are incredibly inefficient, and we should expect real rates to rise. Right now, we may be seeing the first glimmers of this hypothesis being borne out.

SpaceXAI Acquires Cursor
Today, SpaceXAI completed its $60 billion acquisition of AI coding company Cursor, one of the largest tech deals in history. Both xAI and Cursor were founded less than five years ago.
Cursor began in 2022 as Anysphere, a project led by four MIT students — Michael Truell, Sualeh Asif, Aman Sanger, and Arvid Lunnemark — building tools around nascent AI models. They started out building tools for mechanical and CAD engineering, which failed due to their lack of domain expertise, before pivoting to software engineering. In March 2023, the same month GPT-4 was released, Anysphere published the first version of Cursor, then just a fork of Microsoft Visual Studio Code optimized for large language models. Very few people knew at the time how big agentic coding would be, or how quickly it would take over.
Cursor raised an $8M seed round in October 2023 led by the OpenAI Startup Fund, then a $60M Series A in August 2024 led by a16z, Thrive, OpenAI, and multiple top angels. It grew rapidly, taking just over a year (Oct 2023 to Jan 2025) to scale from $1M to $100M ARR, and nine months to scale to $1B ARR (Oct/Nov 2025). The company forecasts over $6B ARR by the end of 2026.
All of this scaling was heavily reliant on frontier labs like OpenAI and Anthropic, who provided the models used in Cursor’s products. This was especially problematic given that both companies started developing products — Claude Code and Codex — that directly competed with Cursor on agentic coding. In October 2025, Cursor released Cursor 2.0, pivoting to more fully autonomous coding, and Composer, their first model. Composer was slightly less intelligent than top frontier models like GPT-5 and Claude Sonnet 4.5, but much faster and more efficient, helping Cursor retain its independence.
xAI’s origins go much further back. In 2015, fearful of potential Google dominance over superintelligence, Elon Musk and Sam Altman co-founded OpenAI as an open-source AI research nonprofit. Musk provided most of OpenAI’s early funding. In 2018, frustrated by its perceived lack of progress, Musk attempted to take direct control of the company. The other co-founders rejected the proposal, and Musk resigned. Under Sam Altman, it converted to a for-profit company, took a major investment from Microsoft, and began developing paid products: first the GPT-3 API in 2020, and then the unexpectedly successful “research preview” of ChatGPT in 2022.
Not wanting to allow Altman to win the race to superintelligence, Musk founded xAI in March 2023. In November 2023, the first version of Grok was released, fully integrated with the X app. It was later open-sourced. In May 2024, xAI raised a $6 billion Series B. That summer, they moved at breakneck speed to build Colossus 1, then the largest data center in the world, in just 122 days. Grok 3, trained on Colossus, was released the following February. The next month, xAI acquired X. Four months later, they released Grok 4, the largest model ever trained.
But despite the enormous amounts of capital and compute and the hardcore work culture, not all was well. xAI’s models lagged substantially behind OpenAI and Anthropic, and almost the entire founding team had left by the beginning of 2026. Musk conceded that the company was not built right the first time around, and needed to be rebuilt from the foundations. He needed a team with a proven track record of building great models. So he turned to Cursor.
On April 21, xAI and Cursor announced a partnership on model training, plus a deal: either SpaceX (xAI’s parent company) would acquire Cursor for $60 billion, or walk away for a $10 billion breakup fee. Cursor Composer 2.5 was released in May, performing very close to the frontier at a fraction of the cost. Grok 4.5, released in July, was the best Grok model ever by far. And Grok 4.6, released earlier this week, is the best model in the world other than Opus 5, Fable, and Sol. The SpaceXAI-Cursor acquisition ended up saving both companies: Cursor is no longer directly threatened by coding model competitors, and SpaceXAI now has a world-class model team once again. Elon Musk has said that SpaceXAI is currently training a 10T parameter Grok model. When it comes out, we’ll be monitoring.
