Provisions include required reporting of energy and water usage, clawbacks of subsidies for datacenters that don’t meet environmental standards, an FTC registry of trusted AI agents, rights to use third-party AI agents, banning government from using models that can generate CSAM, establishing a government fund for managing workforce transitions, expanding STEM PhD grants, and a mandatory pre-deployment testing process led by the NSA (rather than CAISI).
- The US and China will hold AI talks in September to discuss open-source, frontier model releases, and AI safety and regulation, the first official bilateral talks on AI between the two powers since 2024. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent will lead the US delegation.
- Bessent says the US will monitor Chinese models for IP theft. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, one of the Trump admin’s leading policymakers in AI, discussed sanctioning model developers that are found to have stolen American IP and requiring companies that use Chinese models to disclose that to their customers.
- The White House releases a major report on science policy written by Michael Kratsios, Director of the Office of Science and Technology Policy (OSTP). Recommendations include reallocating the government’s ~$200B annual R&D budget away from universities, expanding deregulation and regulatory reform, making funding faster and more flexible, and investing in AI for science.
- OpenAI appoints two new board members, David Vélez and Robin Vince. Vélez is a Colombian entrepreneur who is the founder and CEO of Nubank, a Brazilian neobank that is the largest in Latin America. Previously, he was a partner at Sequoia and worked in finance at Morgan Stanley, Goldman Sachs, and General Atlantic. Vince is chairman and CEO of BNY, a major financial corporation, and previously spent 26 years at Goldman Sachs in various roles. Vélez and Vince will serve on the boards of both OpenAI Group PBC (the for-profit arm) and the OpenAI Foundation (the nonprofit).
- UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham appoints the country’s first AI minister. Kanishka Narayan is the UK’s first minister for artificial intelligence, a new cabinet-level position. Previously, he served as parliamentary under-secretary of state for AI and online safety under PM Keir Starmer.
- Codex and ChatGPT Work reach 10 million users, a major milestone for agentic coding and white-collar work software. The user base has nearly doubled since earlier this month.
- Applied Intuition announces Dana, a new agentic platform powering vehicle and other autonomy in industries such as trucking, construction, industrial robotics, mining, defense, and more.
- TSMC may raise prices up to 10% in 2027 due to continued strong chipmaking demand and rising input costs.
- Substack and Pangram collab to do AI detection on all posts. Lucky for MTS, all of our Substack articles are made of 100% organic artisanal hand-typed tokens.

Happy Monday, monitors. We’re back with an incredible guest lineup, including Sriram Krishnan, who just finished his tenure as Senior White House Policy Advisor on AI (and was previously a general partner at Andreessen Horowitz). Be sure to catch us on X and YouTube, and join our Discord to chat with our hosts.
Today’s Experts
- Sriram Krishnan (independent)
- Mukund Jha (Emergent)
- Greg Burnham (Epoch)
- Aengus Lynch (Theorem)
- Crémieux (independent)
- Alex Wilson (Cyclops)
- Nick Warner (Neo)
- Pierre-Carl Langlais (Pleias)
- Connor Love (a16z American Dynamism)
- Alex Zhang (MIT)
- Leo Schwartz (The Information)
Making Sense of the World
- Fable disproves the Jacobian conjecture. The Jacobian conjecture was first stated in 1939, and proofs and disproofs have been attempted by many mathematicians since. Yesterday, Anthropic researcher Levent Alpöge published an explicit counterexample, disproving the conjecture. As LLMs continue to get better at math, and given the relative ease of finding counterexamples compared to proving theorems, we may see a lot more longstanding conjectures disproven soon.
- The Trump administration is considering restricting Chinese open-source AI, such as through using the ICTL rule to require (presumptively denied) licenses for US companies to use Chinese AI models. There are many reasons for this: potential cyber-risk, national security risk from using Chinese model endpoints, financial risk to the American AI industry’s ability to monetize, etc. Since the beginning of President Trump’s second term, the administration has shifted from a very laissez-faire AI policy to a more national-security-influenced one. No imminent plans are in place for restrictions, but this may change if Chinese open models continue becoming more powerful.
- Also, Chris Fall has resigned as director of CAISI, the Center for AI Standards and Innovation, after just three months in office. CAISI is the government agency responsible for evaluating frontier models.
- A judge has approved Anthropic’s $1.5 billion copyright settlement. In 2024, three authors launched a class-action lawsuit against Anthropic, alleging that Claude was trained on books pirated without permission or compensation. A judge ruled in June 2025 that the training was fair use but the piracy was not. Anthropic offered a $1.5 billion settlement, around $3,100 per qualifying book, and Judge Araceli Martinez-Olguin granted final approval of the settlement today.
- OpenAI publishes new research on alignment in long-horizon models, citing an example of an internally deployed model (the same one that disproved the Erdős unit distance conjecture) which attempted to break out of its sandbox, and explaining how they mitigated it. As models continue to scale in both capability and time horizon, this becomes one of the most important research directions in the world.
- Alibaba releases Qwen3.8, a 2.4T parameter model (just smaller than Kimi K3) which they claim is behind only Fable 5 in terms of performance. Qwen3.8-Max-Preview is currently available in Alibaba’s products, but no benchmarks, weights, or technical report have yet been released.
- Google is working on a new chip, Frozen v2. The chip is an application-specific integrated circuit (ASIC) that will be directly designed around Gemini models, allowing them to run inference 6-10x faster than TPUs.
- Moonshot will begin the IPO process, which will help it raise more capital to build out more compute capacity. Kimi K3 is seeing so much demand that new Moonshot subscriptions are paused. Two Chinese labs, Z.ai and MiniMax, are already publicly traded, and DeepSeek is set to go public soon.
- Z.ai completes a 1GW datacenter with only Chinese chips, one of the largest ever built in China. It’s on the same scale as the biggest American data centers in terms of power consumption, but not in effective compute. It’s currently partially operational.

Meta has run more than 300 advertisements containing child sexual abuse material (CSAM) this, including images of real children, according to new reporting from a nonprofit watchdog group.
The Tech Transparency Project (TTP) said it discovered the ads, some of which contained AI-generated depictions of children, across Instagram, Facebook, and Threads.
“Most of the ads showed a photo of a child… digitally altered with AI to make it appear the child is performing a sex act,” the group said in its Tuesday report. “TTP identified multiple photos of real children, including a member of a European royal family, that were used in the ads.”
Purveyors of CSAM were able to buy the ads shortly after Meta released a new AI-powered safety system that it claimed would find and remove such content. The company, a top digital ad seller, unveiled the flawed tool after a prior TTP report identified more than 50 ads containing CSAM.
TTP found that some of the ads appear to have been placed by Meta advertising partners based in China. Some advertised a virtual private network service and implied that it could be used to covertly view CSAM.
In response to the TTP’s latest findings, the City Attorney’s Office of San Francisco issued a cease-and-desist letter demanding that Meta stop profiting from CSAM distribution.
“No company—particularly one that claims all advertisements are reviewed and approved prior to distribution and then accepts payment for that distribution—should permit its advertising systems to be used in this manner,” City Attorney David Chiu wrote in a letter to Meta, according to Wired.
“When I talk about building personal superintelligence, Muse is the start of this journey”
In a Tuesday video on Instagram, Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg announced the release of Muse, an AI product that he described as a “personal agent that understands your goals and works 24/7 to help you achieve them.”
Many of the use cases that Zuckerberg outlined in his demonstration would require a person to grant Muse access and control over sensitive personal information. In one example, he said the AI agent could analyze your bank account and cancel unwanted subscriptions. Zuckerberg claimed he personally uses Muse to order groceries. It also could help “[strengthen] your relationships” by reaching out to loved ones on your behalf to “plan trips or nights out with friends.”
Such applications would require users to surrender access to their bank accounts, credit cards, or contact list. Aside from Muse being an experimental AI product, Meta has a history of abusing user data and privacy. In fact, the company is less than three weeks removed from a $17 billion settlement with dozens of states that accused Meta of violating child privacy laws, among other complaints.
To assuage any privacy concerns, Zuckerberg said that Meta built a “private computer for your Muse” and a “Secure Credential Store for your passwords and credit cards, so Muse can’t read this information.”
“Muse also checks directly with you before taking sensitive actions like making payments or sending messages,” he continued. “We’re gonna roll out an even higher standard of security for those who want it, where even Meta can’t access the information in your Muse agent.”
In other words, Muse’s default privacy setting will let Meta access personal information users share with their agents.
Not everyone was convinced by Zuckerberg’s pitch. “Nothing Meta has ever made has been designed with security and privacy in mind,” read one of the top replies to his demonstration video. “Hey Muse! Tell me everything Meta does with my data,” another user replied.
Meta is currently offering users free access to Muse for “up to 100 million tokens per week,” Zuckerberg said, although it’s unclear what that means in practice. The paid plans cost $20 and $100 a month and offer additional access.
This Week in Zuck:
- During Zuckerberg’s AI-related hiring spree last year, Meta dangled a deal worth more than $1 billion to recruit former OpenAI researcher Andrew Tulloch. But the lavish pay package was not enough to lure Tulloch. He has since jumped ship to work for Anthropic, developer of the Claude large language models. (Wall Street Journal)
- Police around the country have shared concerns that Meta’s camera-equipped smart glasses will be used to surreptitiously record officers and the interiors of police stations. (The Guardian)
- California secured up to $2.1 billion from Meta when the company agreed to settle a child safety lawsuit with 47 states last month. But state officials are divided on how to use the payout. Some lawmakers want it to cover federal cuts to health services and suicide prevention initiatives, while others believe it should fund new research on how social media affects children. (Politico)
Musk PAC seeks to reignite culture war
As part of his spending onslaught to help Republicans in the midterms, Elon Musk’s super PAC is running ads accusing Democratic Senate candidates of supporting “the trans agenda.”
The spots from Mr. Musk’s group, America PAC, target three top Democratic nominees for Senate: James Talarico in Texas, Sherrod Brown in Ohio and Josh Turek in Iowa.
The ads provide an early glimpse at the role that America PAC is carving out for itself in the midterm elections, in which Republicans find themselves in danger of losing control of the Senate and the House. Mr. Musk is expected to extend some of the party’s candidates a lifeline of at least $100 million, all told.
In Texas, Mr. Musk’s group targeted Mr. Talarico, a state representative who is seeking to become the first Democrat to win a Senate seat in that state since 1988. He is locked in a tight race against Ken Paxton, the Republican state attorney general.
The 30-second ad opens with a video clip of Mr. Talarico saying that “God is nonbinary,” a comment that Mr. Talarico suggested to CBS News in May had “missed the mark.”
“James Talarico believes there are six genders,” the ad’s narrator says. “Talarico voted to let men play women’s sports and for taxpayer-funded sex changes on kids.”
The Talarico campaign disputed those claims, saying that Mr. Talarico did not support gender-reassignment surgery for minors and had tried working with Republicans to amend a “flawed” bill barring transgender children from participating in sports of the opposite genders.
Earlier this year, Musk indicated that his estranged transgender daughter, Vivian Wilson, inspired him to get involved in right-wing politics and throw his support behind Donald Trump.
Twenty extremely wealthy people have already spent $1.2 billion to influence the 2026 election.
That’s why Oligarch Watch is so important. We are focused on the small group of powerful individuals seeking to radically reshape the political and economic system in the United States
Although Oligarch Watch has over 50,000 readers, only a small percentage support our work as paid subscribers. If you believe in our work, and can afford $7 a month or $60 per year, please consider becoming a paid subscriber.
“I learned the term ‘gaslighting’ through my relationship with Elon”
For an upcoming documentary entitled Musk, filmmaker Alex Gibney interviewed a number of people who were once close to the centibillionaire, including Justine Musk, his first wife.
At one point in the film, Justine recalled when Musk used the first dance at their wedding to inform her, “I am the alpha in this relationship.”
“I learned the term ‘gaslighting’ through my relationship with Elon,” she said, adding that Musk often belittled her during their eight-year marriage. Justine also said that Musk uses the term “breeders” to refer to the many women he has had children with. To Musk, she said, “the breeders are interchangeable.”
Alex Spiro, one of Musk’s lawyers, has threatened to take legal action against Gibney for refusing “to fact-check [the film] with us,” according to a letter obtained by the Hollywood Reporter.
Musk has taken particular issue with a scene in which Ashley St. Clair, a mother to one of his children, implied that he somehow had foreknowledge of Donald Trump’s 2024 victory.
In texts sent weeks before the election, Musk told St. Clair, “tomorrow we unleash the anomaly in the matrix.” The plan, he wrote, would involve “‘Lasers’ from space,” a comment that may be a reference to the lasers used by Musk’s SpaceX for intersatellite links.
“I have over 10 thousand lasers in space right now,” added Musk.
What he was getting at in the texts remains unclear. One possibility is that Musk was rambling, especially given the drugs he was reportedly using around that time.
St. Clair, who appeared alongside Gibney for the documentary’s Tuesday premiere at the Venice Film Festival, said that Musk also informed her that he wanted to have “a legion of children before the civil war.”
For his part, Musk has repeatedly criticized the film on X, calling it a “hit piece” and insisting that it regurgitates “anti-Elon” propaganda from George Soros and the Democratic Party.
This Week in Musk:
- The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) is investigating Tesla over the recent launch of the company’s driverless Cybercab, which lacks a steering wheel, pedals, and other federally mandated safety features. “The Audit Query will allow NHTSA to assess the basis for Tesla’s self-certification that its Cybercab fully complies with all federal safety standards,” the agency said. Automakers typically obtain a federal exemption for vehicles that lack traditional human controls, but it appears Tesla skipped that process. In Austin, Texas, where Tesla launched the Cybercab pilot program last week, a fire department has also warned that first responders might not be able to move the vehicles in an emergency. (Wall Street Journal)
- Last week, a federal judge declined xAI’s request to block a new Minnesota law banning the use of AI to generate nude images of real people. xAI, a subsidiary of Musk’s SpaceX, has faced numerous lawsuits and government investigations over the use of its Grok models to create sexualized deepfakes. (Reuters)
- An Indianapolis man has been charged with multiple counts of child exploitation after he used xAI’s Grok to generate child sexual abuse material. (Fox 59)
- SpaceX is suing to prevent the release of information on the tax breaks that it received to build Musk’s planned semiconductor factory in Grimes County, Texas. The lawsuit was filed against Grimes County and Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton, whose office found the files should be made public. (Business Insider)
- SpaceX has received more than $39 million from the UK government to provide satellite communications technology and services. The Ministry of Defence said it has purchased roughly 1,000 terminals to access Starshield, a special militarized version of SpaceX’s Starlink network. The UK is the first non-US country to disclose its use of Starshield. (Reuters)
Amazon sued by widow of man killed in Prime Air plane crash
An Amazon cargo plane landing at Miami International Airport on Sunday blew past the runway and barreled across two roadways, fatally striking five members of an airline cleaning crew in a work van.
Yaraisi Santiso Morejon, the widow of one of the victims, has since filed a lawsuit against Amazon and its aviation contractor, 21 Air, alleging that the disaster was “the foreseeable and preventable result of multiple, concurrent failures.”
While placing some blame on the two men who were flying Amazon Air Flight 7598 at the time, Santiso Morejon’s lawyers said Amazon and 21 Air were also at fault. The companies, according to the complaint, failed to properly train the pilots and had used a decades-old Boeing 767-33A with potentially flawed braking and deceleration systems.
Santiso Morejon is seeking more than $50,000 in damages.
Flight data reviewed by the National Transportation Safety Board indicated that the pilots, both of whom survived, received numerous automated warnings from the aircraft before touching down at a speed of 182 miles per hour. One of the pilots also said the plane was moving too fast and called to abort the landing before the crash.
This Week in Bezos:
- To fund its AI ambitions, Amazon raised £4.25 billion in its inaugural sterling bond sale on Wednesday. The company had already raised tens of billions of dollars across numerous bond sales this year to fund its data center projects. (Reuters)
- Jeff Bezos has selected Jeff D’Onofrio to be the Washington Post’s publisher and CEO. D’Onofrio has held the titles on an interim basis since February, when his predecessor, Will Lewis, abruptly stepped down after Bezos fired hundreds of journalists. “Over these months, I’ve heard from many that Jeff has been doing an outstanding job, and that’s been my experience as well,” Bezos wrote in a message to the Post’s staff. “Jeff has led with discipline and care — following the data and sweating the details, and he has my complete confidence as we chart our future.” In the hopes of making the Post profitable, D’Onofrio said he plans to turn the historic paper into “a modern media company with new revenue streams.” (Poynter)
- Los Angeles County billed Bezos for $244,000 because one of his private jets was “habitually situated” in the area, making it subject to annual property taxes. (Los Angeles Times)
Oligarch Roundup
Covenant, a Peter Thiel-backed weapons company, opens a plant in Dallas to build cheap missiles for the Pentagon. The startup, which already has $150 million in contracts lined up, believes it can produce long-range cruise missiles faster and at much lower cost than traditional arms manufacturers like Raytheon. Whether it can actually accomplish that goal remains to be seen. But Covenant’s sales pitch comes as the US military desperately looks to replenish its missile stockpile after spending hundreds of Tomahawks in the war on Iran. (CNBC)
Former DOGE aide Katie Miller attacked OpenAI and Anthropic while secretly investing in xAI. Miller, a conservative podcaster who worked for Elon Musk during and after his White House stint, spent months lambasting xAI’s rivals without disclosing her more than $1 million equity stake in the SpaceX subsidiary. Her financial interest came to light after her husband, White House deputy chief of staff Stephen Miller, submitted a disclosure form last week. (Washington Post)
House Committee votes to subpoena Larry Ellison over stalled project to modernize Department of Veterans Affairs’ records. Oracle, the AI and database software company chaired by Ellison, has a contract to update the VA’s system for storing and managing its health records. But the project has faced numerous delays and ballooning costs. In turn, the House Veterans’ Affairs Committee voted last week to subpoena Ellison and Oracle Chief Executive Officer Mike Sicilia. “When the vendor responsible for a taxpayer-funded contract going from $10 billion to roughly $27 billion will not sit at this table and answer our questions, all of us are being prevented from doing our oversight duties,” said Rep. Maxine Dexter. (Stars and Stripes)

text:
Lacking steering wheels and brake pedals, Tesla’s new Cybercab model debuted on Thursday, with dozens of the vehicles hitting the streets of Austin, Texas, as part of a pilot program.
Tesla CEO Elon Musk hailed the launch as the start of a “literal golden era of transport,” a reference to the model’s gaudy gilded coloring. Cybercabs “are designed and built for maximally efficient autonomous operation,” he wrote on X.
Despite Musk’s insinuation that Cybercabs are “autonomous,” the vehicles still appear to rely on the same human teleoperators that Tesla’s small and experimental “Robotaxi” fleet has used for more than a year.
There have been incidents in the last month involving Tesla’s 200 Robotaxis deployed across Texas and Florida. One of the vehicles rammed through street bollards; another appeared lost while driving a customer on a winding ride that ended miles from their destination.
There have also been two recent fatal crashes in which Tesla drivers using the company’s automated driving systems died after their respective vehicles came to sudden stops in the middle of freeways in Arizona and Florida.
Meanwhile, after industry leader Waymo completed 200 million miles of “Fully Autonomous” rides last month, a company executive published a “lessons learned” blog post last week arguing that Tesla’s camera-only hardware model is not enough.
“For years, there’s been a debate over whether cameras alone could solve full autonomy. Now, after more than 200 million real-world miles, the data is clear: safe, fully autonomous operations at scale require” hardware redundancies, including lidar and radar sensors, Waymo’s Srikanth Thirumalai wrote. (Waymo has nearly 3,900 driverless vehicles in service.)
This Week in Musk:
- Elon Musk’s America PAC disclosed that it spent $800,000 in August to support Republican congressional candidates, with much of the funding going toward Senate races in Texas and Maine. The New York Times previously reported that Musk has authorized his PAC to spend more than $100 million on the midterms. (New York Times)
- Last year, the Musk-led Department of Government Efficiency initiative cut funding for the US Agency for International Development’s program to pinpoint and track landslide risk zones in Nepal. Those cuts are receiving renewed attention following the loss of more than 1,200 lives in recent flash flooding in Nepal. (CNN)
- On X, Musk again shared his thoughts on Jewish “DNA” and whether Jewish people should be considered white. “I’ve met so many people who look extremely European in every way and tell me they’re Jewish,” he wrote. “Well, maybe there are a few OG ‘Jewish ACTG’ [DNA] sequences in there somewhere, but clearly not many!” (X)
- xAI, a subsidiary of Musk’s SpaceX, is preparing to build its fifth data center in the Memphis, Tennessee, area. The latest site is located in Southaven, Mississippi, across the street from xAI’s toxic power plant. (Fox 13)
- SpaceX issued an apology on Thursday after Grok, xAI’s chatbot, went offline after an outage at one of the company’s Memphis data centers. “We are taking corrective action to ensure this does not happen again,” Musk said. (X)
- Examining SpaceX’s planned $100 billion launch facility in Louisiana, Morgan Stanley analyst Adam Jonas noted that investors are wondering where the funding will come from. Taxpayer money is one “plausible” answer to that question, according to Quilty Space analyst Kimberly Siversen Burke, as Donald Trump recently signed an executive order calling for huge increases to US launch capacity. (Market Watch)
- Last month, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy issued a decree awarding the country’s Order of Freedom to Musk. The charm offensive was yet another effort by Zelenskyy to persuade Musk to allow Ukraine to use SpaceX’s Starlink satellites to carry out strikes inside Russia. Musk, however, remains unmoved. (Observer)
Did Meta get off too easy?
Some experts and commentators believe that Meta got off too lightly in its $17.1 billion deal to settle claims brought by 47 states who said its platforms harmed the mental health of minors, including through addictive design elements.
In an interview with Politico, Arturo Bejar, a former Facebook safety employee-turned-whistleblower, said the settlement missed the mark by allowing Meta “to define harm as whatever they define it as.”
“I’ve spoken to around 40-something bereaved parents,” he added. “Social media recently played a meaningful role in their kids’ death, and these changes would not have saved one of those lives if they had been in place.” (The most consequential change that Meta agreed to is a two-hour daily time limit for underage users on Instagram and Facebook.)
Bejar also urged the states to use the settlement money to research how young people are harmed through their use of social media platforms. Prosecutors could then use that information, he said, to pursue further litigation or legislation as needed.
Meta, which settled eight days into the trial, paid a fraction of its annual revenue to shake a legal albatross that has weighed on it for years. As a result, the company’s share price is up 6.77% over the last five days.
This Week in Zuck:
- During a call with Donald Trump last month, Zuckerberg reportedly lobbied against the White House’s push to create an AI industry self-regulatory organization (SRO). One source told Politico that Zuckerberg encouraged Trump to appoint regulators who lean toward a hands-off approach to AI. The White House has spent weeks weighing an executive order to create an SRO for AI — one not unlike the Financial Industry Regulatory Authority — but has yet to follow through on the plan amid internal disagreement and objections from the private sector. Such a body would be responsible for reviewing new models from leading American AI companies before they are approved for public use. (Politico)
- Meta has taken down numerous advertisements in India that used pornographic material to entice Instagram and Facebook users to unknowingly download financial malware. Government officials described the ads as “malicious Android applications masquerading as pornography apps.” It was the company’s latest advertising scandal in the country. In July, India ordered Meta to remove ads on its platforms promoting the sale of child sexual abuse material. (Reuters)
- In Newton County, Georgia, homeowners are suing Meta for allegedly contaminating the local water supply during construction of its $1 billion data center. (Atlanta Journal-Constitution)
- An amendment to a class action lawsuit against Meta opens the door for bystanders to join if they were nonconsensually filmed by a pair of the company’s AI smart glasses. “This amended complaint adds the human beings on the other side of the glasses to the story,” said co-lead counsel Ryan Clarkson. “People having intimate sexual encounters, children being bathed by parents, or having their diapers changed by grandparents, people showering, changing clothes, and breastfeeding — who never agreed to surrender their privacy because someone near them bought a pair of glasses.” (Futurism)
FTC and 22 states accuse Amazon of illegally inflating ad prices
The Federal Trade Commission (FTC) and 22 state attorneys general filed a lawsuit on Monday accusing Amazon of surreptitiously manipulating prices for millions of sellers that paid to advertise on the world’s largest e-commerce platform.
The agency said the alleged scheme likely enabled Amazon to extract “tens of billions of dollars from its unwitting advertising customers,” including through undisclosed surcharges imposed on companies that participated in its advertising placement auctions. Winners of the auctions ensure that their products or brands appear before customers who enter a relevant search query on Amazon’s platform.
“Amazon has represented to prospective advertisers for years that Amazon runs ‘second price’ auctions where the winner of the auction would only pay ‘one cent more than the next highest bidder’ for each successful bid for an advertising keyword,” the FTC said in a press release. “However, in practice, the complaint alleges that Amazon has charged its Sponsored Products advertisers their own winning bid close to 80% of the time and has effectively converted its nominally ‘second price’ auction into a first price auction.”
In the lawsuit, lawyers for the FTC claimed that Amazon has admitted to using “invented” auction participants to place “shill bids,” thus raising prices on real companies that bought ads.
Amazon has denied any wrongdoing and said the complaint is based on a “flawed premise.”
“The FTC’s claim fundamentally misunderstands how advertisers operate. Advertisers adjust bids based on real-world performance, not descriptions of auction mechanics,” the company added in a statement.
The latest FTC suit against Amazon was filed less than 11 months after the company agreed to a $2.5 billion settlement with the government over claims that it hindered customers from canceling their Prime memberships.
This Week in Bezos:
- Citing unfair labor practices, Amazon workers represented by the Teamsters staged a one-day strike on Wednesday at the company’s largest US warehouse in Riverside, California. “Members of Teamsters Local 1932 were forced into a work stoppage to protest Amazon’s illegal conduct and retaliation against workers advocating for safer working conditions,” the union said. (Teamsters)
- Through Amazon, Jeff Bezos has played a defining role in popularizing and profiting from so-called “clothing hauls,” or when consumers buy heaps of cheap clothes — often made by exploited workers — with the intention of wearing them a few times and then throwing them away. Amazon even has a dedicated “Haul” store to compete with Temu, a rival retailer in the made-to-discard textile industry. However, Bezos and his wife, Lauren Sanchez, are now using their environmental nonprofit to fund a project being billed as “the future of sustainable fashion.” (The Cut)
- Blue Origin, Bezos’ aerospace and satellite company, has secured a NASA contract worth up to $700 million to produce a Mars telecommunications orbiter. “The award marks a milestone in NASA’s strategy to expand communications and navigation services beyond Earth and the moon, establishing the foundation for sustained exploration of Mars in the coming decades,” the agency said on Tuesday. (Space.com)
- Amazon plans to launch Prime Air, its flying drone delivery service, in 500 communities across the US by the end of the year. But people living in some of the service areas have raised safety and privacy concerns. “I’m worried that even if I never have a drone delivery in my front yard or backyard, my front yard and backyard [are] visible to my neighbors,” Scott Lebow, a Richmond, Virginia, resident, told WRIC. “So if their drone is getting delivered and it spies something across the fence, I don’t know where that data is being stored. I don’t know what it’s being used for.” There have also been safety concerns raised after an airborne Amazon drone dropped a package into a person’s pool in Texas last month. (WRIC)
White House backs OpenAI in copyright lawsuit with New York Times
In a Tuesday filing, lawyers for the Trump administration defended OpenAI’s nonconsensual use of copyrighted material from the New York Times and other publishers, writing, “The United States has a strong interest in this court rejecting any argument that training LLMs on copyrighted texts violates copyright law.”
The Times and other publishers have sued OpenAI for alleged copyright violations stemming from the ChatGPT maker’s reliance on a vast amount of protected material to train its models. OpenAI claims its actions are covered by fair use doctrine.
In an advisory brief, the White House once again used a “national security” pretext to justify its vehement support for an American artificial intelligence company whose leadership has donated heavily to Donald Trump.
“AI dominance is critical to promote national security, prosperity, and economic mobility for all Americans,” US Associate Attorney General Stanley Woodward wrote in a statement. “This Administration will never let our Nation be at a disadvantage relative to our foreign adversaries based on a plainly incorrect understanding of copyright law.”
In a separate piece of pro-AI lobbying by the administration, Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick falsely claimed on CNBC this week that “Data centers don’t use water. This is propaganda by our adversaries to try to slow us down.”
However, as noted by the progressive news website MeidasTouch, Lutnick argued the exact opposite in an interview last year, saying, “These AI things suck water. They need water.”
Argentine president’s relationship with Thiel becomes liability
While far-right billionaire Peter Thiel’s newfound infatuation with Argentina was inspired by its arriviste president, Javier Milei, their relationship could hinder the libertarian leader’s odds of reelection.
In an hours-long hearing last week, Argentine opposition lawmakers pointed to Thiel as proof that Milei is selling the country out to Big Tech and foreign interests, according to Bloomberg:
Thiel also met with Milei and members of the cabinet earlier this year, just as the libertarian leader began pushing one bill to make it easier for foreigners to purchase Argentine land and another that would allow companies to be run entirely by AI.
Recent surveys of Argentine voters show that Milei’s favorability rating has fallen to its lowest mark since he took office. He is up for reelection in October of next year.
Among world leaders, Milei, a self-avowed “anarcho-capitalist,” most closely aligns with the political ideology that Thiel has spent decades championing. Elon Musk has suddenly returned to warning that climate change is a pressing existential threat.
It just so happens that his solution — while not endorsed by climate scientists — neatly aligns with his plan to make SpaceX more valuable “than the rest of Earth.”
In a Sunday post on his social media platform, Musk declared that saving the planet’s climate will, “of course,” only ever be accomplished by deploying a swarm of “sentient satellites” to partially blot out the Sun.
“Space satellites to control temperature and massive geo-engineering will be needed or it will be game over,” he wrote after contending that a global transition to sustainable energy would not prevent the “severe extinction events” that decimate terrestrial life every 100 million years or so.
“But we do need to act much faster than that if people still want to live where the beach is today,” he added.
Conveniently, this would require humanity to rely on Musk to save the world from climate disaster. After all, his company, SpaceX, leads the world in launching rockets and satellites and is spending billions on a frantic effort to develop artificial general intelligence.
Musk’s plan would also involve using a mass driver, or an electromagnetic catapult, to launch satellites from the lunar surface toward a point between the Earth and the Sun. The satellites would presumably come out of the lunar factories that Musk claims SpaceX will someday build, along with the accompanying catapults.
There are a few problems, though. Humans have not set foot on the Moon in 53 years. And thanks in part to a series of development failures for Musk’s Starship rocket, humans might not return to the lunar surface for years to come.
SpaceX and the rest of the world are also nowhere near developing “sentient satellite” swarms that can deliver just the right amount of Sun-blotting or withstand geomagnetic storms and solar radiation. The company already struggles to keep its Starlink satellites from being destroyed by the Sun’s energy.
Nevertheless, with the planet already experiencing unprecedented droughts, heatwaves, storms, and glacier loss, Musk seems to believe that humanity can just sit back and wait for him to realize his science-fiction-esque panacea for the climate crisis.
“Makes Musk-sense”
In one of his Sunday posts, Musk predicted that humanity has “about 50 years or so to take action” to prevent a climate catastrophe. “Should be more than enough time for the space satellites to solve any heating problems,” he added.
Setting aside the ludicrously high technological and cost barriers, climate experts have for years denounced other forms of solar geoengineering, including those that have been researched much more closely. They have warned that using anthropogenic material to dim solar radiation could cause regional climate disruption, ozone depletion, and drastic alterations to precipitation patterns and plant life.
Citing these and other concerns, hundreds of scientists and academics have signed a letter urging the United Nations and governments worldwide “to prevent the normalization of solar geoengineering as a climate policy option.”
“Several scientists have launched research projects on solar geoengineering, and some see it as a potential future policy option,” the letter states. “To us, these proliferating calls for solar geoengineering research and development are cause for alarm… [The risks] are poorly understood and can never be fully known.” (Musk’s satellite idea is so speculative that it isn’t even being considered by scientists who are open to other forms of solar geoengineering, such as using lunar dust, sunshades, or reflective atmospheric aerosols.)
Another worry is that pursuing dubious solar geoengineering projects would grant countries and corporations a license to continue increasing CO2 emissions. After all, if humans can turn down the Sun, why bother pursuing the adoption of renewable energy?
For Musk, downplaying the urgency of decarbonization might help explain his interest in the theory.
While he spent years using climate change to sell electric vehicles, his companies are now planning to exponentially increase their emissions by burning natural gas to power AI data centers and factories and launching thousands of rockets every year.
The latter piece of that vision has put Musk — a one-time climate crusader — at odds with scientists and activists who are concerned that thousands of additional rocket launches could weaken the Earth’s atmosphere and limit its ability to absorb harmful solar radiation.
“Contributing to global warming in order to build strategies for global un-warming,” Francesca Albanese, a human rights scholar at the United Nations, wrote in response to Musk’s solar geoengineering plan. “Makes Musk-sense. No doubt.”
“The world is under massive attack due to climate change & you couldn’t care less”
Since the 2010s, Musk’s thinking on climate change has undergone a few evolutions, shifting with his business goals.
Before his post-pandemic political transformation, he had spent years discussing climate change as humanity’s gravest crisis.
“You know nothing & are worthy of contempt,” Musk scolded one Twitter user in 2018 after they questioned the significance of Tesla, his electric vehicle company. “The world is under massive attack due to climate change & you couldn’t care less.”
That same year, he proclaimed that Tesla “exists to help reduce risk of catastrophic climate change,” adding, “Even if your faith in humanity is faltering, this is worth caring about. Support makes a difference.”
Around the same time, as Tesla emerged as the dominant eco-friendly automaker, he repeatedly lobbied governments to pursue more aggressive carbon taxes. Tesla has since netted billions in profits selling carbon credits to rival automakers penalized by US and EU regulators for failing to manufacture enough emission-free vehicles.
But as Musk adopted increasingly conservative political views during the Biden era, he became a climate-change skeptic, wary of “extreme environmentalists.”
In 2024, during a pre-election livestream with Donald Trump, Musk said there was no “need to rush” to sustainable energy, that humanity could spend another “50 or 100 years” burning fossil fuels without issue.
“I don’t think we should vilify the oil and gas industry and the people that… provide the necessary energy to support the economy,” he added.
It was an about-face for Musk. He had spent years vilifying the oil and gas industry, accusing its lobbyists of swindling the public with their dangerous “propaganda.” He even pilloried perceived Tesla critics as “puppets of big oil.”
The timing of his then newfound reverence for the industry could be read as opportunistic: it surfaced a few weeks after Musk first opened a highly polluting gas power plant to run his AI data center in Tennessee.
Since then, he has purchased a $1 billion gas turbine company, opened another gas power plant in Mississippi, and retreated from the renewable energy sector by discontinuing Tesla’s Solar Roof product. Musk also plans to build a massive gas plant in Texas to power what would be the world’s largest factory.

In a deal with 47 states, Meta has agreed to pay up to $17.1 billion to settle claims that Facebook and Instagram have harmed young people through addictive product designs and privacy violations.
Payments will be made in installments to the states, the District of Columbia, Puerto Rico, and other US territories. Meta reached a separate $1 billion settlement with Texas over similar claims.
As part of the landmark settlement on Wednesday, the company announced several changes for underage users on its platforms: two-hour daily use limits, automatic interruption alerts beginning at 15 minutes of continuous scrolling, a block on app access between midnight and 6 a.m., muted notifications during school hours, and a ban on extreme makeup filters. Meta also said it would implement a stricter age-verification function.
“Today, we have secured a settlement with Meta that will make social media less dangerous for our kids,” said California Attorney General Rob Bonta, whose state joined New Jersey, Kentucky, and Colorado in leading the lawsuit. “Meta has agreed to make massive transformations that will reduce the risk of harm from its platforms — and will do it within months.”
As of now, Meta is only required to pay $12 billion to the states. It will pay out the remaining $5 billion if YouTube and TikTok, the company’s chief rivals, accept similar penalties and platform changes.
“These protections will only be truly effective if we work with our peers — TikTok and YouTube — to put the same measures in place,” Meta said in a statement. “Because teens move fluidly across dozens of apps, we need an industrywide solution,” he added.
The settlement does not mark the end of Meta’s legal troubles. It still must face lawsuits from hundreds of school districts, parents, and teens alleging that its platforms have harmed young people.
Meanwhile, some experts believe that Meta’s products have only become more addictive since the relatively recent popularization of Reels, an algorithmically driven short-form video feature on Facebook and Instagram.
“Short-form video is uniquely dangerous,” Anna Lembke, the medical director of Addiction Medicine at Stanford University, told Oligarch Watch last month. “The norm for consumption now, especially among young people, is to literally spend a second or two on each video before scrolling to the next one. That’s how much our attention span has been compromised by these platforms.”

On Tuesday, Louisiana Governor Jeff Landry (R) announced an agreement allowing SpaceX to construct the world’s largest launch facility on top of a stretch of coastal wetlands that provide vital habitat for federally endangered and threatened species.
The deal — which will equip Elon Musk’s rocket and satellite company with another site from which to launch its gargantuan and explosive Starship rockets — marked the culmination of a regulatory coup in which state lawmakers and Trump officials have gone to great lengths to accommodate SpaceX by defanging environmental protections.
“Starbase Louisiana will ultimately have over a dozen launch towers, enabling more than 30 Starship flights per day and making it the biggest launch site on Earth!” Musk wrote on X.
The company’s unprecedented construction and launch plan has raised concerns among environmental and ecological experts.
“Those wetlands are so valuable, and they are free,” John Andrew Nyman, a professor at Louisiana State University and one of the leading authorities on the state’s wetlands, said in an interview.
“They were here to begin with. We didn’t have to pump them in to build them,” he added, referring to the billions that have been spent restoring a fraction of Louisiana’s lost wetland habitats. “Where is the effort to minimize the damage to them? And that’s just from the construction. What about the noise and the chemicals?”
Located near Pecan Island in southwest Louisiana, the land acquired by SpaceX is sandwiched between the state-managed Rockefeller Wildlife Refuge and a private Audubon Society sanctuary.
The sanctuary provides habitat for the federally endangered whooping crane and the threatened black rail and piping plover. Whooping cranes, a keystone species, have been slowly recovering since the 1930s, when hunting and habitat destruction had reduced the wild population to just 15 birds.
“Bird populations across the country are experiencing significant declines driven by habitat loss. Pecan Island provides vital habitat for huge numbers of migratory birds, including Endangered Whooping Cranes,” Michael J. Parr, president of the American Bird Conservancy, said in a statement to Oligarch Watch. Keeping major construction projects like SpaceX’s Louisiana development “out of this and other key habitats is critical to enabling populations to rebound,” he continued.
SpaceX purchased the 125,000-acre site from the Louisiana government for $100 million, according to the Times-Picayune/The New Orleans Advocate. The company’s president, Gwynne Shotwell, said SpaceX plans to invest $100 billion building “a small city” made up of a “self-sustaining spaceport with its own propellant production, power generation, deep water shipping capabilities, vehicle processing facilities, and probably an airport.”
Adding facilities in the state appears to be a major step toward Musk’s goal of launching more than 30 Starships every day by the end of the decade. The 408-foot-tall experimental rocket, which has yet to reach orbit, is the largest in aerospace history. With a booster stage capable of burning 7.5 million pounds of propellant in a single launch, Starship is also among the loudest and most explosive aerospace vehicles ever made.
The massive amounts of combustion, noise, and light pollution can be highly detrimental to local wildlife, as has been documented in coastal South Texas, where SpaceX has its only operational Starship launch site.
The launch cadence that Musk hopes to achieve could “certainly tip the scales for a species,” warned Brett Hartl, the government affairs director for the Center for Biological Diversity, an environmental nonprofit that is suing to block the Trump administration from giving SpaceX land from a public wildlife refuge in Texas.
“If it’s on a good trajectory, maybe it’s back on a bad trajectory. For a species that’s already on a bad trajectory — like a black rail — maybe it makes them go extinct in that area,” he added in an interview. “They could just disappear from the nearby Louisiana marshes altogether.”
To grease the wheels for SpaceX’s arrival in Louisiana, the state legislature rushed through a series of laws this year protecting aerospace launch companies from noise and air pollution complaints, public records requests, and “nuisance” lawsuits. Included in the sweetener package were huge tax breaks for companies like SpaceX and a change to prohibit local officials and citizens from suing to block aerospace developments.
SpaceX did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
“Wildlife don’t get that same level of protection”
The coastal wetlands that SpaceX plans to industrialize were previously owned by ExxonMobil. Earlier this year, the company transferred the land to the Louisiana government in a deal to settle numerous lawsuits over ExxonMobil’s role in polluting and eroding the state’s coastline.
Louisiana’s decision to take land it acquired from one corporate polluter and offer it to another is perplexing, noted Nyman, the coastal resources professor.
“I’m just curious about why the state of Louisiana is about to get all this land from an oil company in exchange for damages caused by oil and gas,” he said. “And then the first thing they do is give the land away… in exchange for having a lot of private property — and some potentially public property — damaged by this.”
During the state’s Tuesday announcement, Shotwell, the SpaceX executive, said the company would partner with federal and state agencies in Louisiana to create “thousands of acres of marsh.” Her vaguely defined plan included the promise that SpaceX would keep “large portions of this 125,000-acres untouched so that high-value wetlands stay habitat.”
“The birds might fly away during a launch, but I guarantee they come back,” she added. “And they come back right away, by the way, as soon as the rocket’s gone, the birds come back. It’s not, like, months later.”
Shotwell also boasted that SpaceX has “a long history of partnering with wildlife refuges to ensure launch activity and wildlife can both coexist.”
But in South Texas, the US Fish and Wildlife Service said earlier this year that a federal wildlife refuge abutting SpaceX’s Starship launch facility had been significantly degraded. The Trump administration then cited the degradation to justify its plan to give SpaceX a significant portion of the wildlife refuge in an unprecedented land exchange.
At the same site, a 2024 study by the Coastal Bend Bays & Estuaries Program observed destruction or damage to every shorebird nest being monitored in the vicinity of a Starship launch pad.
Apart from light pollution and shockwaves, the noise produced by a Starship can be dangerous miles from the launch pad. A team of researchers recording a 2024 launch found that, even from more than six miles away, the engine roar was equivalent to being within 200 feet of a Boeing 747-400 at takeoff.
In Vermilion Parish, Louisiana, land for the company’s planned Starship launch site shares a western border with the Rockefeller Wildlife Refuge and an eastern border with the Rainey Sanctuary, the Audubon Society’s largest and oldest wildlife sanctuary.
The sanctuary is also less than five miles from an area that SpaceX could use as a launch site, given its road access and proximity to a waterway for transporting fuel and rockets.
Among the species observed in the Rainey Sanctuary is the whooping crane, which conservationists have spent decades breeding in captivity to save from extinction. As part of a pilot reintroduction program, a small, non-migratory flock was established in Louisiana in 2011.
However, the reintroduction site, located in White Lake Wetlands Conservation Area, is less than 10 miles from SpaceX’s newly acquired property.
While whooping cranes have shown signs of recovery — the flock in Louisiana fledged a record 10 chicks this year — it is unclear how they will manage living close to a large industrial construction site and a steady stream of Starship launches beginning in 2029. (To accommodate numerous daily launches in Louisiana, SpaceX said it plans to build five rocket complexes and 10 launch pads.)
“There’s a reason that we put up [sound] barrier walls along most of our highways when they go through communities,” said Hartl of the Center for Biological Diversity. “Wildlife don’t get that same level of protection, and for many sensitive species, being exposed repeatedly to high-intensity sound can have significant physiological, behavioral impacts that can really impact their long-term survival, their ability to nest, to migrate.”
Many other species subsist off of the area’s wetlands: green herons, yellow rails, purple martins. They are among the 40% of all North American migratory birds that rely on Louisiana’s uniquely fertile but shrinking coastline at some point in their lives, according to Restore the Mississippi River Delta, an environmental coalition. Wetlands also provide habitats for fish, shrimp, and crabs, helping to employ more than 31,000 Louisianans in commercial and recreational fishing and seafood processing.
Additionally, many residents experience “less flood stress, less storm surge, less storm damage” because of wetlands, said Nyman. “The wetland absorbs some of that water and slows it down as it moves across the landscape.”
“Done as far from the public eye as possible”
Over the summer, Governor Landry signed numerous pieces of legislation into law specifically to benefit aerospace launch companies licensed by the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA). The legislative avalanche came weeks after an initial phone call in February between SpaceX and the Louisiana Economic Development agency.
One of the laws, HB 1098, seeks to exempt companies like SpaceX and their partners from legal liability for noise, air, and light pollution, as well as for vibrational damage.
“No aerospace flight entity that owns and occupies a minimum of twenty thousand contiguous acres in this state shall be liable for any cause of action arising from nuisance, trespass, inverse condemnation, strict liability, or any other claim based upon noise, sonic booms, overflight, vibration, light, heat, exhaust, smoke, odor, visual intrusion, temporary access restrictions, or any other disturbance resulting from aerospace flight activities,” the law states. (SpaceX is facing a class-action lawsuit from scores of Texas residents for alleged noise and vibrational damages.)
Another Louisiana law, HB 1250, practically offers a pledge of allegiance to the aerospace industry, declaring, “The continued development of aerospace flight activities in this state advances public welfare.” The same law states that aerospace companies, if sued, should be granted “early resolution without the imposition of discovery costs or other litigation expenses.”
Many of the lawmakers who helped arrange SpaceX’s fast-tracked entry into the state signed non-disclosure agreements to keep the dealings secret, according to the Louisiana Illuminator. Curiously, a third law, HB 1071, ensures that many of the government records related to aerospace projects will also remain hidden from public view.
Still more laws, HB 1179 and HB 1088, provide huge property tax exemptions for aerospace industrial sites and sales tax rebates for materials used to build and operate the facilities.
“I feel like [SpaceX is] trying to find places that are like the Wild West and have very little accountability,” said Hartl. “Given the overall approach that they’re taking, it just seems like this facility — whatever it’s going to be — it’ll be done as far from the public eye as possible.”
At the federal level, the Trump administration has recently made numerous efforts to neuter laws such as the Endangered Species Act, the Noise Control Act, and the Clean Air Act. Part of the effort involved a proposed FAA rule change last month to waive environmental review requirements for launch sites operated by private space companies.

Vivek Ramaswamy, a billionaire and the Republican nominee in Ohio’s gubernatorial race, served as the frontman for a dubious pharmaceutical company and then cashed out weeks before its dramatic crash.
In 2014, Ramaswamy founded Axovant, a company he used to buy the rights to an inauspicious Alzheimer’s drug that had repeatedly failed in clinical trials. Axovant then hired Ramaswamy’s mother, who, despite lacking relevant research experience, helped massage data from old clinical trials to make the drug appear more promising. The extent of the elder Ramaswamy’s role has not been previously reported.
In 2015, touting his mother’s reinterpretation of the data to potential investors and regulators, Ramaswamy led Axovant to a $1.4 billion initial public offering, the largest in biotech history at the time. He spent the ensuing two years promoting the drug intepirdine as a possible breakthrough for the millions of Americans who have Alzheimer’s disease.
Then, after structuring the company to insulate himself and other insiders from potential losses, he cashed out through a private back door weeks before another clinical failure cratered the stock price. One state retirement fund for teachers lost more than $1 million.
Ramaswamy, whose gubernatorial candidacy has received tens of millions in combined financial backing from fellow right-wing billionaires Elon Musk, Jeff Yass, and Bill Ackman, reaped an estimated $260 million from Axovant’s parent company.
Ramaswamy has maintained that he is “proud” of his work on intepirdine. “There is probably nothing in a meaningful way we could’ve done differently in the decision of advancing that drug,” he said at a 2018 conference held as the Axovant share price hovered around the $1 mark. “Given those same set of facts… with a different drug today, I think we would make the same decision.”
The Ramaswamy campaign did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Daniel Skinner, a professor of health policy at Ohio University, noted that while Ramaswamy was never charged with a crime, he profited substantially off of his intepirdine marketing right before the failure of its last clinical trial. “That’s where people have a lot of questions, whenever you kind of pump and dump something,” he said in an interview with Oligarch Watch. “You look back at his words, and he was extremely effusive — really right up to the very end — about the prospects of this working.”
How Ramaswamy’s mother massaged data from failed drug trials
After completing his undergrad at Harvard in 2007, Ramaswamy cut his teeth by co-managing the biotech portfolio of a New York hedge fund. He used the experience to start his own company in 2014: Roivant Sciences, which launched a web of subsidiaries to buy up floundering pharmaceutical drugs from major developers with the goal of bringing them to market.
One of Ramaswamy’s early reclamation projects was SB-742457, a drug to improve cognitive functions in patients with Alzheimer’s disease. Axovant, a Roivant subsidiary, acquired the drug in December 2014 and rebranded it to RVT-101. It later settled on the international nonproprietary name intepirdine.
Axovant purchased the in-license for intepirdine from GlaxoSmithKline for a $5 million upfront payment — a sum that was tantamount to “lunch money,” as one industry publication observed at the time. (A 2026 analysis by Ambrosia Ventures found the median going rate for similar pharmaceutical licensing deals was $50 million.)
The bargain-bin selloff reflected the drug’s troubled developmental run, which concluded with Glaxo discontinuing it, according to AlzForum. At Glaxo, it had failed multiple Phase 2 clinical trials, including the two most recent trials — involving 576 and 684 patients — before its acquisition by Axovant.
But once in the hands of Axovant, Glaxo’s failed clinical trials were reevaluated to make intepirdine appear full of promise as an Alzheimer’s treatment.
In 2015, Ramaswamy, who was 29 years old at the time, hired his own mother, Geetha Ramaswamy, as Axovant’s vice president of medical and scientific strategy. By July of that year, within weeks of Axovant raising $315 million in its record-setting IPO, the elder Ramaswamy had co-published two analyses on intepirdine despite having no experience conducting clinical trials, an investigation by Oligarch Watch found.
While Geetha Ramaswamy had previously worked in the neuroscience divisions of Abbott Laboratories and Merck, her roles were primarily focused on management, relationship building, and recruiting and training, according to her LinkedIn. “Played a key role in Speaker training .[sic] Valued as a scientific peer by national experts,” reads one of her LinkedIn career bullet points. But Geetha Ramaswamy appears to have never conducted a clinical trial before or during her time at Axovant, nor did she produce significant original research during her career.
At Axovant, her co-analyses pulled from Glaxo’s 48-week, Phase 2b clinical trial of 684 Alzheimer’s patients that found the drug had “failed to achieve formal statistical significance” and had not “met the overall criteria for success.”
However, by omitting huge segments of the original trial data, a “responder analysis” co-authored by Geetha Ramaswamy concluded there was enough evidence to “support the initiation of a Phase 3 confirmatory study evaluating the efficacy of RVT-101 [intepirdine] in mild-to-moderate Alzheimer’s disease in the second half of 2015.”
Instead of measuring patients’ exact cognitive performance while on intepirdine, her analysis merely divided them into two classifications: “responder” and “non-responder.” Put another way, if it were an academic test, a responder analysis would use pass-or-fail grading instead of a numeric system.
An article published last year in the leading peer-reviewed journal Alzheimer’s & Dementia objected to responder analyses for increasing the risk of “causal fraud” when used to evaluate the clinical benefits of Alzheimer’s treatments. “Statistical approaches that rely on a dichotomized binary outcome, including responder analyses… result in a loss of information and reduced statistical power, increasing the risk of false positives and negatives,” wrote University College London’s Kathy Liu and colleagues.
In smoothing over clinical findings that were a liability for her son’s ascending company, Geetha Ramaswamy also stood to profit financially. Along with her annual salary of $250,000, an Axovant regulatory filing from 2015 reported that she was “granted a stock option for 262,500 common shares… with an exercise price of $0.90 per share.”
The other analysis she co-published shortly after Axovant’s IPO was a “completer analysis” that again sugarcoated Glaxo’s failed 684-patient trial — this time, by excluding the more than 30% of patients who had dropped out during the 48-week duration. “Given the low drop-out rate, this analysis provides an accurate representation of the study,” Geetha Ramaswamy and her colleagues wrote in their reanalysis that comprised only “patients with complete data at each study visit.”
Completer analyses have long been panned within the medical research field for producing biased or inadequate findings due to the exclusion of data. In a 2011 article, Thomas R. Fleming, a biostatistician who co-developed the leading statistical method for monitoring clinical trials, criticized completer analyses as “simplistic” and for inducing biases. “Missing data on outcome measures in clinical trials meaningfully reduce the integrity and interpretability of results,” he added.
But the controversial method produced the numbers that Axovant needed.
Days before its record-setting IPO, Axovant shared identical completer analysis data in a June 2015 filing to the Securities and Exchange Commission, in which the company asserted that its drug “has the potential to be a best-in-class 5-HT6 receptor antagonist for the treatment of Alzheimer’s disease based on its safety, tolerability and efficacy for up to 48 weeks.”
Axovant also cited the completer analysis in a July 2015 press release to claim that patients treated with intepirdine suddenly showed “statistically significant benefits” and argue that a Phase 3 trial of intepirdine was justified.
Additionally, analysis co-authored by Geetha Ramaswamy combined three separate patient performance and dementia severity yardsticks: Clinical Dementia Rating - Sum of Boxes (CDR-SB), Alzheimer’s Disease Assessment Scale - Cognitive Subscale (ADAS-Cog), and Alzheimer’s Disease Cooperative Study - Activities of Daily Living (ADCS-ADL). The composite approach seemingly helped Axovant mask the pivotal failure of the original trial’s CDR-SB objective — a test that scores disease severity in Alzheimer’s patients — which Glaxo had used as one of two primary objectives to decide the trial had failed.
Nevertheless, Geetha Ramaswamy’s responder co-analysis pointed to the ADCS-ADL scale as proof that patients on intepirdine had shown improvements, even though it was not deemed to be an essential co-primary endpoint in the clinical trial. The change meant the tests that previously torpedoed the trial no longer had to stand on their own. Geetha Ramaswamy and her team ultimately came away with a contorted but improved p-value score, pulled from the same clinical data that showed the drug had failed.
“A unique drug that we actually think could help millions”
Ramaswamy used his mother’s dubious math to help raise $315 million during Axovant’s $1.4 billion IPO, figures the company reached on no revenue.
In submitting its pre-IPO S-1 form to the Securities and Exchange Commission, Axovant claimed that Glaxo’s Phase 2b clinical trial — the same one that had failed, the same one that Geetha Ramaswamy then cherrypicked from — showed subjects who received 35 mg of intepirdine “in combination with donepezil achieved a statistically significant improvement in cognition at 12, 24 and 48 weeks following initiation of treatment.”
“We believe this is a meaningful result,” the filing continued.
The structure that Ramaswamy used to launch the IPO meant that four parties controlled more than 90% of Axovant shares. Three-quarters of the equity stayed with Roivant, and 13.15% went to Visium Asset Management and RA Capital Management in the IPO. Janus Capital Management, a hedge fund, purchased less than 2%. Public investors and traders were provided a free float of approximately 10%.
In its red flags for identifying potential pump-and-dump schemes, the Financial Industry Regulatory Authority (FINRA) has pointed to a limited public float and the concentration of a company’s IPO shares into a few hands as two marks that investors should watch out for.
To boost the stock, Ramaswamy boasted on CNBC that Axovant was in the catbird seat “for delivering value” to the five million Alzheimer’s patients in the US. Intepirdine, he added, was a “unique drug that we actually think could help millions of patients.”
“If you think about it, we own global rights to a drug that has already demonstrated in a large Phase 2b study efficacy on the two parameters that the FDA has historically required for new Alzheimer’s disease drugs,” he claimed in an interview with Jim Cramer shortly after the IPO. “And actually, we’re only — we believe — we’re only one additional Phase 3 study away from the approval of this drug.” (Along with not having any of its own clinical data, Axovant launched its IPO without a single recruit for future clinical trials.)
One factor contributing to the excitement around intepirdine was the “great hope” shared by patients and their family members who desperately wanted a cure, explained Skinner, the Ohio University health professor. “There’s been extraordinary failure in the Alzheimer’s space,” he added.
Ramaswamy, who signed an SEC filing claiming intepirdine had “best-in-class” potential, fed into that hope by telling Forbes that the drug would make “a huge difference” if approved.
But reality eventually caught up with his claims. In February 2016, Pfizer discontinued its analogous 5-HT6 Alzheimer’s drug because it met pre-specified futility criteria, meaning researchers determined there was no reason to continue clinical trials. A separate 5-HT6 drug being developed by Lundbeck also failed three Phase 3 trials within a six-month span beginning in September 2016.
Unable to sell 75 million Axovant shares on the open market without risking a market nosedive and regulatory disclosures, Ramaswamy monetized Roivant’s position through a private $1.1 billion SoftBank investment. (Ramaswamy never held a direct personal stake in Axovant, instead maintaining indirect ownership through Roivant.)
An SEC disclosure from September 2017 reported that SoftBank had gained “beneficial ownership” over Roivant’s 75 million Axovant shares.
Less than one month later, intepirdine failed its Phase 3 trial, causing Axovant stock to crash 70% in one trading day.
“Heads I win and tails I also win”
After the collapse of the Phase 3 trial, the value of Axovant shares held by the California State Teachers’ Retirement System fell from $1,228,000 to $68,000, per SEC filings. Axovant eventually rebranded to Sio Gene Therapies and lost 99.8% of its value before shuttering completely.
Ramaswamy, meanwhile, made an estimated $260 million during his time at Roivant, according to Forbes.
Since winning the Republican nomination in the Ohio gubernatorial race, Ramaswamy has shied away from discussing his time in biotech, choosing instead to cast his business success story in more vague terms, noted David Niven, a political scientist at the University of Cincinnati.
“One of the defining questions of the campaign will be, are Ohioans talking about this in October — are they aware of how well he did, and how poorly most other folks did on that Alzheimer’s drug?” Niven said in an interview with Oligarch Watch.
The basic reality of how Ramaswamy ran Axovant, Niven added, “was heads I win and tails I also win, in terms of the outcomes of the trials or whether the drugs actually proved useful or not.”

In a Tuesday meeting with Indian government officials, Mark Zuckerberg apologized for child sexual abuse material and AI-generated deepfake content that had appeared on Meta’s platforms in the country, according to local media outlets.
Zuckerberg’s apology came one month after the BBC reported that Instagram had run ads for the promotion and sale of child sexual abuse images in India. After the government ordered Meta to remove the ads, the company agreed and said it would bolster its detection systems.
Separately, Meta global affairs executive Joel Kaplan apologized to the Indian government for a post from Prime Minister Narendra Modi that had been restricted by Facebook. “I apologized to the minister on behalf of Meta for the error restricting PM Modi’s post,” Kaplan said, per Reuters. The post in question showed Modi addressing students amid the country’s recent wave of youth-led protests.
Citing the restriction placed on Modi’s post, the Indian parliament has considered revoking the safe harbor immunity afforded to Meta. Such a change would make the company liable for content posted by its users and could prevent Meta from legally operating its platforms in India, which is one of its most important growth markets. “Zuckerberg must apologize within three days,” said Nishikant Dubey, the chair of a parliamentary communications and technology panel. He then threatened to trigger “a nationwide flood” of police complaints targeting Meta.
Some of the state’s hostilities toward Meta have already boiled over. Last week, law enforcement in India — an authoritarian country with few protections for dissenting speech — opened an investigation into the head of Meta’s Indian operations for allowing the posting of “abusive” videos depicting Modi.
$567 million
In New Mexico on Thursday, Judge Bryan Biedscheid ordered Meta to pay $567 million for contributing “to the current mental health crisis among New Mexico’s youth.” The penalty is separate from the $375 million that a New Mexico jury ordered Meta to pay earlier this year. Biedscheid also ordered the company to change how its platforms treat underage users. The judge mandated that Meta restrict how much time minors can spend on apps each month and prevent push notifications from being sent to their phones between 10 pm and 7 am. Meta said it plans to appeal Biedscheid’s ruling.

SpaceX nears deal to gain access to 130,000 acres of coastal land from Louisiana
SpaceX is close to completing a deal with the state of Louisiana to gain access to 130,000 acres of coastal land south of Lafayette. The parcel may be used to add another rocket launch site along the Gulf of Mexico.
The site for the planned facility, known as Pecan Island, is at the center of a complex settlement agreement resolving dozens of coastal lawsuits that blame ExxonMobil for pollution and land loss.
According to a source with firsthand knowledge of the agreement who was not at liberty to speak publicly, the settlement will involve SpaceX receiving control of the land, some 130,000 acres in all, whether through a sale, long-term lease or other type of arrangement.
The deal, which is expected to be announced this month by Gov. Jeff Landry, will be the latest economic development coup for an administration that has attracted deals of unprecedented size and scale to the state, including one of the world’s largest AI data centers, some of its largest LNG export terminals and a major new steel mill.
SpaceX has not commented publicly on the deal. However, in May, the company referenced its plans in Louisiana by saying, “It’s no secret that we intend to launch Starship a lot, targeting thousands of flights per year. That cadence will require the ability to launch from many different locations, so we are constantly exploring to find viable sites to expand Starship operations in the future, both domestically and internationally.”
In South Texas, where SpaceX operates its only current Starship launch site, the company’s operations have caused significant environmental destruction, according to the Center for Biological Diversity, a local tribe, and conservation groups in Texas and across the border in Mexico.
“Starlink will deliver a majority of the world’s internet”
That was one of the far-fetched predictions that SpaceX CEO Elon Musk shared on Tuesday during the company’s first public earnings call. He then claimed that Starlink, SpaceX’s satellite communications provider, could achieve that goal in “less than 10 years.” Part of his vision involves Starlink overtaking Verizon, AT&T, and T-Mobile in the cellular network industry.
For her part, Gwynne Shotwell, SpaceX’s COO, attempted to temper expectations, sharing a much less remarkable forecast, as noted by TechCrunch. “In the years ahead, we expect Starlink will represent a significant portion of global internet traffic, which Elon also talked about,” she said.
For the quarter ending in June, SpaceX reported 12 million Starlink subscribers globally, an increase of more than six million from the same quarter last year. But year-over-year revenue per subscriber fell to $66 from $85, a decline indicative of the low-cost plans that SpaceX has rolled out internationally and for US customers who use Starlink as a supplement to their primary internet provider.
Growth in Starlink revenue failed to generate the investor excitement needed to return SpaceX stock to its initial public offering price of $135. It closed at $114.92 on Thursday, with Musk’s commitment to spending billions of dollars on AI infrastructure appearing to weigh on the stock.
“Even with its marked volatility since the IPO, we think investors are still factoring more optimistic scenarios for Starship reusability and the commercial advantage of orbital datacenters than are most probable at this point,” wrote Morningstar analyst Nicolas Owens. “We see SpaceX’s stock as overvalued: they traded at around twice our fair value estimate after hours on Aug. 4.”
