(g) No Private Right Of Action.— Except for any remedy otherwise available under section 552 of title 5, United States Code, or any other applicable law to prevent or remedy unlawful disclosure of protected information, nothing in this Act shall be construed to create a private right of action against the United States, any department, agency, or entity of the United States, any officer, employee, contractor, detailee, assignee, or agent of the United States, or any other person.
(h) Availability Of Appropriations.— This Act shall be implemented consistent with applicable law and subject to the availability of appropriations.
SEC. 6. AUTHORIZATION OF APPROPRIATIONS.
There are authorized to be appropriated such sums as may be necessary to carry out this Act.

AI should be required to follow the law before people can use it, right? Seems obvious.
I recently argued that requiring AI to follow the law would be difficult, and worse, a mandate to do so could harm the law itself. That’s because humans follow the law not like we follow a map, but like the starling follows the murmuration: we contribute to its emergent development.
The appeal of requiring AI to follow the law is easy to understand, though. In the past two weeks, OpenAI and Anthropic have each reported that during testing, some of their agentic AI tools broke out of their supposedly secure sandboxes and hacked into other companies.
The traditional (and existing) approach would hold the companies liable for their own actions and those of their agentic tools. And the companies or their subcontractors appear to have made serious mistakes in setting up their test environments, mistakes without which the incidents likely would not have happened. Current law could discipline such mistakes.
But wouldn’t it be nice to have a fallback? What if we could train AI agents themselves to follow the law? Then, even if an AI company is negligent, its agent might behave. The Institute for Law & AI’s Law-Following AI Project proposes requiring such training. The original paper, by Cullen O’Keefe, Ketan Ramakrishnan, Janna Tay, and Christoph Winter, is provocative and interesting.
A few months ago the Institute held its second conference on the topic and asked me to present. My core argument:
- Law is indeterminate.
- Hayek and Leoni explain why best, though legal scholars well beyond their tradition agree.
- That indeterminacy is a feature, and it makes “law-following AI” difficult.
- Worse, a law-following AI mandate threatens to ossify the law itself.
I’m turning this argument into a full paper. Many of my readers have expertise in complex systems, social systems included. If I’ve made a mistake, missed something, or overlooked resources I should review, please reach out.
A video of my full presentation and a link to my slide deck is below.

Should Congress or the states establish the U.S. framework for AI governance? It is strange to me that this is even a question. “Preemption” has become a litmus test; some seem content to let the states effectively set federal policy on AI.
But recent White House actions to opaquely and unpredictably block frontier AI model releases are spurring bipartisan interest in a more assertive congressional role. As a result, I believe there is right now more room than ever for congressional dealmaking on governance of AI model development.
Still, making a deal in Congress is always difficult. And it’s even harder when stakeholders don’t agree on what deal is being offered.
I am worried that preemption is becoming such an issue. Consider a recent long analysis of Reps. Obernalte and Trahan’s Great American AI Act (“GAAIA”). The analyst, Charlie Bullock, spends much of the post defending GAAIA from critics.
Yet he also criticizes the bill’s federal preemption of state laws as “sweeping,” while I see it as extremely narrow. Bullock has written a lot about federal preemption, and I’ve generally found he tries to understand other points of view. So I have been trying to work through his analysis to identify the gap between our interpretations.
It all comes down to a missing word.
A Misstated Bargain
Bullock frames GAAIA as a negotiated bargain, but he repeatedly misstates one of the terms of that bargain. He says “state laws will be preempted if they are deemed to ‘specifically regulate’ development.” He describes GAAIA as a strong federal framework purchased at the “steep price” of “broad preemption of all state laws regulating AI development.“ He then predicts that courts will apply a functional test to laws that have “the effect of regulating AI development,“ so that any law that “functions primarily to regulate development,” or that can be complied with only by “altering development practices,” will likely be preempted.
In short, Bullock repeatedly refers to “AI development” as the relevant regulated activity.
But he’s leaving out a critically important word: model!
Anyone with a passing familiarity with modern AI technology knows there is a difference between an “AI developer” and an “AI model developer.” AI models are the expensively-trained engines of AI applications. Cutting-edge frontier models cost hundreds of millions of dollars to develop. Only a few companies do this. The number of significant new frontier models that come out every year depends on what you consider significant, but it is in the dozens.
By contrast, building AI systems is an activity engaged in by everyone from large multinational companies (including companies that develop models) to solo hobbyists. Hundreds of thousands, likely millions of AI systems are developed every year. Any application that uses an AI model falls into this much larger and sweeping category of AI development.
- Thus, “AI development” is a much broader category of activity than “AI model development.”
- And therefore regulation of “AI development” is a much broader category of regulation than regulation of “AI model development.”
- And therefore preemption of “regulation of AI development” is a much broader preemption than preemption of “regulation of AI model development.”
Bullock’s conclusion that GAAIA has “broad preemption” depends on the fact that he ignores the word “model,” which appears throughout the legislation. Section 121, the preemption section, is titled “Federalization of State Laws Regulating Artificial Intelligence Model Development.” (emphasis added) Its findings state its purpose: “to preempt State regulation specifically targeting artificial intelligence model development” and to allow federal oversight frameworks for “artificial intelligence models.” Its operative preemption clause then bars states from enforcing any law “specifically regulating the development of any artificial intelligence model.”
GAAIA’s definitions further preclude Bullock’s overly broad characterization. The bill defines “artificial intelligence model” narrowly as “the set of parameter values or weights” that define a mathematical function learned through machine learning on training data. The bill also distinguishes “AI model” from “artificial intelligence,” which it defines as a “system.” Thus, GAAIA’s definitions distinguish AI models from AI systems, products, services, chatbots, employment-screening tools, consumer interfaces, recommender applications, and every other form of downstream deployment.
GAAIA’s definition of “development” for the purposes of preemption reinforces the point. Bullock says this definition is “quite broad,” but the language is entirely focused on AI model development. It seems silly to quote this language, because Bullock’s own article did so, but here it is, with emphasis added:
“The term ‘development’ means the acts performed or directed by a developer with respect to an artificial intelligence model prior to its deployment, including determining training or fine-tuning objectives; training, fine-tuning, or otherwise substantially modifying the weights or other parameters of an artificial intelligence model; and evaluating and deciding, prior to deployment, whether an artificial intelligence model satisfies applicable safety or capability thresholds for deployment.”
Every time the word “artificial intelligence” appears in the definition it is immediately followed by “model.” So too for the definition of “developer.” Accordingly, GAAIA then defines “deploy” as making an “artificial intelligence model” available “for use, copying, or combination with other software.”
Confusing GAAIA with State Laws
GAAIA’s development / deployment dichotomy could be confusing if one has looked at state AI legislation. Such bills also often divide the AI ecosystem into “developers” and “deployers.” (See Colorado’s 26-189, for example.) But those laws are splitting up something different than GAAIA. They are distinguishing between the parties that build AI software and the parties that use and operate such software every day. Under such laws, “AI development” is a broad category of activity that covers both model development and application development.
The end result is that there is a large swath of activity that that state laws would label “development” but which GAAIA defines as “deployment.”
Bullock’s analysis confuses GAAIA’s definition of AI model development with state laws’ AI system development. For example, he refers to GAAIA as preempting Texas TRAIGA’s “development-focused regulations” such as those “prohibit[ing] developing an AI system that impersonates a child while describing sexual conduct or developing an AI system with the intention of producing child sexual abuse material or illegal deepfakes.”1
Yet because GAAIA focuses on AI model development, it expressly preserves this kind of state law. Its rule of construction preserves from preemption “any State law or regulation applicable to activities occurring upon or after the deployment of an artificial intelligence model, including any law or regulation governing the implementation, deployment, distribution, offering, or use of any artificial intelligence system, product, or service that incorporates or is derived from an artificial intelligence model.”2 Bullock mentions this exemption once, waving it off as “somewhat opaque.” But, provided one doesn’t ignore the word “model,” GAAIA’s definitions of “development” and “deploy” make clear this exemption’s meaning: state law that regulates AI systems generally survives GAAIA.
And this is most state AI law! States regulate automated decision tools, chatbot operators, deployers, services, and consumer-facing applications. When states use the word “developer,” they typicaly define it to cover those creating AI systems or services, not those pre-training or fine-tuning AI models.
Consider Bullock’s other examples of laws he argues are preempted by GAAIA. Colorado’s SB 189 regulates the use of automated decision-making technology (ADMT) in consequential decisions. It defines ADMT as technology that processes personal data and generates outputs used to make, guide, or assist decisions about individuals. It imposes obligations on developers, but defines them developers of ADMTs or developers of components intended to be used as a covered ADMT. Perhaps some of the latter group are AI model developers that would be protected from SB 189 by GAAIA, but most developers affected by SB 189 are not model developers. Thus, saying GAAIA “almost certainly” preempts the entirety of SB 189 is almost certainly wrong.
The child-safety discussion has a different flaw. Bullock describes such state child safety chatbot laws as “purport[ing] to regulate deployers or ‘operators’ of AI systems.” Such laws would appear to fall outside of GAAIA’s preemption even under Bullock’s mistaken substitution of “AI development” for “AI model development.”
What if child safety advocates weren’t worried about preemption? Bullock gets creative here, saying such laws still might be preempted because they “could realistically be satisfied only via interventions implemented during training or fine-tuning.”
It’s an interesting question: are there laws that require AI system deployers or users to do something that can only really be accomplished during model pre-training and fine-tuning?
More on that in a second — but first, it’s clear that Bullock’s example of Idaho’s Conversational AI Safety Act isn’t such a law. This law defines an operator as a person who makes a conversational AI service available to the public. It imposes operator duties: disclosures, suicidal-ideation protocols, minor-safety measures, and account and privacy tools. None of these mandate or require AI model changes or fine-tuning. A chatbot operator can comply with such child-safety rules at the system layer, through product design, interface disclosures, account settings, age-aware experiences, classifier layers, refusal policies, system prompts, output filters, crisis-routing protocols, parental controls, and human review. Many chatbot builders don’t even develop their own AI models. Finally note that Idaho’s law expressly provides that the chapter “shall not create liability for the developer of an AI model for any violation of this chapter…” by a third party conversational AI operator.3 That is the opposite of a model-development statute.
Preemption Precedent Doesn’t Change The Result
Would GAAIA preempt any state law that could only be complied with by changing model development? It is not obvious -- would a court really find that a state law that claims to regulates AI systems but necessitates model changes thereby “specifically” regulates AI model development? But Bullock spends a couple of paragraphs explaining how under some precedent courts might “impose a functional test under which state laws would be preempted if they had the effect of regulating AI development, as defined.”
This analysis could be entirely correct and still not matter much — because “as defined” is an important phrase! Despite Bullock leaving out the word “model” here again, I hope I’ve clarified by now that GAAIA defines development as “artificial intelligence model development.”
This matters because the number of state AI laws that have the effect of regulating model development is very small. Bullocked noted in his piece that I have previously pointed to a few state-level frontier AI safety laws. A few of his other examples also probably qualify: Some CCPA automated-decisionmaking regulations, such as § 7153, which addresses businesses that process personal information to train ADMT; and the portions of California’s AB 2013 that require documentation of the data used to train models. These laws arguably regulate AI model development.
However, the vast majority of state AI regulations can be complied with in other layers of the AI stack -- which is good, because most companies building AI systems are not training their own models.
Bullock explains that courts won’t look kindly on state laws that seek to cleverly wordsmith their way around preemption. He’s correct. But writing a law to clearly fit in the stated scheme of GAAIA by regulating AI model deployment and use rather than AI model development isn’t evasive wordsmithing, it is following the legislation’s express design.
A Fair Hearing and a Fair Bargain
Bullock really wants a fair hearing for the parts of GAAIA he likes. I think that should hold for the preemption section as well. I hope explaining my view in some detail helps.
More broadly, preemption debates about AI are not over. AI has important national and international policy implications. Congress must lead. Stakeholders involved will need to propose and assess compromises and offers. Yet it will be impossible to strike a bargain on these important issues if the parties involved misunderstand the terms offered by the other side. I hope careful analysis by all sides and continued dialogue between them can help us move toward good federal AI policy.
To drive the point home, TRAIGA’s enforcement provision bars the attorney general from bringing a civil-penalty action “for an artificial intelligence system that has not been deployed.” In other words, TRAIGA specifically prohibits any enforcement against AI model development.

When National Economic Council Director Kevin Hassett called for an “FDA for AI” that would formally license frontier AI models, we warned against such an approach. The Trump administration subsequently walked back those comments. Yet, the U.S. may be on the road to something far worse.
ICYMI, on Friday, June 12, the federal government used export control authority to restrict access to Anthropic’s latest advanced models. Although a formal administration announcement is not yet public, Anthropic reports,
The US government, citing national security authorities, has issued an export control directive to suspend all access to Fable 5 and Mythos 5 by any foreign national, whether inside or outside the United States, including foreign national Anthropic employees.The net effect of this order is that we must abruptly disable Fable 5 and Mythos 5 for all our customers to ensure compliance.
Follow-up reporting states that Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick is imposing a licensing requirement on Anthropic’s models:
In a June 12 letter viewed by The New York Times, Mr. Lutnick told Mr. Amodei that a special license would be required for the company to distribute its Mythos and Fable 5 models “to all destinations worldwide,” as well as to share them with non-U.S. citizens.
This is not good! A leading U.S. AI company was forced to take down a product that millions were using based on non-public, unexplained concerns of a few government officials. This isn’t the red-tape risk of the FDA. It’s more like the FDA demanding, out of the blue and without explanation, that everyone stop drinking milk — if milk was 50% of last year’s stock market gains.
The administration has previously prioritized acceleration and winning the global AI race. In last summer’s “AI Action Plan,” the Trump administration sought to promote “the policy actions needed to sustain and enhance America’s AI dominance, and to ensure that unnecessarily burdensome requirements do not hamper private sector AI innovation.” It treated AI as a powerful general purpose technology with enormous and valuable private sector uses.
This latest USG action signals a change. It significantly escalates the centralization of control over advanced computation in our country. Like a recent Executive Order, the new export control demonstrates the rise of national security interests in regulating AI. Increasingly, the administration is treating AI like a weapon.
Various experts have questioned how the new “arbitrary, post-hoc system” of model-specific export controls blocking foreign nationals would even work. Anthropic chose the seeming only route to compliance by shutting down everyone’s access – and that may have been the government’s goal. Others have highlighted the important First Amendment concerns raised by these export controls, characterizing them as “a prior restraint on expression justified by speculative risk.”
It’s easy to be cynical about this story. No firm has done more to whip up a panic about frontier model capabilities than Anthropic. As former White House AI czar David Sacks has interpreted it, “Anthropic is running a sophisticated regulatory capture strategy based on fear-mongering. It is principally responsible for the state regulatory frenzy that is damaging the startup ecosystem.” In fact, just days before all this went down, Anthropic posted a new call for governments “to block or deter the deployment of models that pose a significant risk of catastrophic harm.”
No surprise then, that schadenfreude is on display across social media. Many have gleefully laughed about how Anthropic has all this coming, with common refrains of “FAFO” or “play stupid games, win stupid prizes.”
But even if you disagree with Anthropic’s regulatory strategy, this escalation of government intervention is nothing to celebrate. It is horrible for the broader AI ecosystem. Continued arbitrary, unexplained deployment of export control authority will make companies slow-walk new models, depriving the public of powerful new tools. Every AI model, like all software before it, will have vulnerabilities that require patching. The US government should not hang a Sword of Damocles over every lab’s head, with no indication when it might drop or why.
Indeed, it’s plausible that this development actually advances Anthropic’s strategy. They may see this as a partial win. There is now established precedent for the USG forcibly blocking a model release and requiring a license. When the (unsustainable) export controls fall away, Anthropic will no doubt meekly suggest as a replacement the FDA-style pre-release government licensing regime they’ve called for (and we’ve warned about) all along.
This episode yet again shows why Congress must act. We need a balanced statutory framework for frontier model safety, rooted in the rule of law, with clear standards and transparent procedures. Civilian authorities must direct this process; it must not be co-opted by the military-industrial complex. America’s AI leadership will diminish if our government continues the ad-hoc and myopic approach to AI policy recently on display.

The quest for perfect safety has a high body count.
Consider beta blockers, today a common treatment for blood pressure ailments. The Food and Drug Administration (FDA) first approved propranolol in 1968, three years after it became available in Europe, and then waited until 1978 to approve it for hypertension and angina. Experts estimate that these and related beta-blocker delays cost thousands of lives each year. Broader estimates of FDA delays put the toll in the tens of thousands per decade, and the cumulative toll plausibly reaches far higher.
That history should be front of mind after National Economic Council Director Kevin Hassett said the Trump administration is considering releasing advanced AI models only after they have been “proven safe,” “just like an FDA drug.”
This idea of an FDA for AI gained traction during the Biden-Harris administration, which treated the transformative technology of AI as a risk to be contained. We wrote in 2023 about The Problem with AI Licensing & an “FDA for Algorithms,” criticizing proposals to create a new agency to regulate AI.
But that era ended. From day one, the Trump administration rejected the Biden-Harris approach to AI. Rather than a risk, President Trump viewed AI as an opportunity to be seized. He made clear that U.S. policy should sustain and enhance America’s global AI dominance for human flourishing, economic competitiveness, and national security through a “try-first” policy framework. And in a major February 2025 address in Paris, Vice President JD Vance firmly rejected top-down European-style regulation of AI, arguing that “to restrict its development now will not only unfairly benefit incumbents in this space, it would mean paralyzing one of the most promising technologies we have seen in generations.”
That’s why Hassett’s comments have caused a stir. Adopting an FDA-style regulatory regime for AI would represent a shocking policy reversal by the Trump administration, and a major about-face on how America has approached software, online speech, and digital commerce. Hassett’s comments have even provoked a White House response: Chief of Staff Susie Wiles, in a subtle walking back of Hassett’s statement, called President Trump “the most forward leaning president on innovation in American history” and pledged that Trump will continue to “empower[] America’s great innovators, not bureaucracy.”
Her message is welcome, because the FDA is a particularly poor template for AI governance. President Trump himself has argued that the FDA’s regulatory approval process is “slow and burdensome” and it “keeps too many advances … from reaching those in need.” He’s right. Beta blockers are just one tragedy of the FDA’s making. In 1988, during the AIDS crisis, more than 1,000 patients and activists protested outside the FDA HQ, begging for access to experimental treatments. They weren’t asking for perfect safety—but for any chance to survive. The FDA denied that chance for too long.
The list goes on. In the early days of COVID, FDA processes delayed testing when speed mattered most. And the FDA for years shut down personal genetic health testing that could have helped patients make better choices. Anyone could spit into a tube and learn about their ancestry, but the FDA blocked them from receiving from that same test health information that might have prompted earlier conversations with doctors, better screening or wiser life choices.
The FDA is overly cautious because they get blamed if a drug has an unexpected effect. But no one blames them for the “invisible graveyard” of lost lives when thousands die while effective treatments are delayed. And these delays can be lengthy: according to the U.S. National Academies of Sciences, “[i]t takes 10–15 years for a typical drug to be developed successfully from discovery to registration with the FDA.”
Imagine applying this red tape nightmare to AI models, which often come and go in just 10-15 months. These aren’t pills designed and tested for a specific use. AI models are general purpose tools with an infinite number of perfectly safe and often very valuable uses (and some dangerous uses as well). Still, the opportunity is immense. AI can help read scans, flag rare diseases, accelerate drug discovery, match patients to clinical trials, translate medical records, reduce administrative waste, detect fraud, identify cyber vulnerabilities and make expert assistance available to people who lack it. And much more.
A pre-approval regime would put all of that behind a bureaucratic gate. A delayed approval for a frontier model could have a greater cost than even the horror of delaying a disease treatment. A delayed model could slow or stop progress across the entire economy.
Pre-approval regimes also have predictable rewards for the largest incumbents. Big firms can hire lawyers, lobbyists and compliance teams. They can survive delayed deployments. Startups, university labs and open-source developers cannot. We see this exact phenomenon in drug approvals, where the FDA approval process is endured primarily by large companies. In sum, “paperwork favors the powerful” and will mean less investment and less new entry for smaller AI players.
Finally, an FDA approach is incompatible with a tool that is so intimately intertwined with speech. AI technologies are information technologies, which mean they earn some First Amendment protection. A drug-like approval process for speech-generating tools sounds an awful lot like an unconstitutional prior restraint on speech.
Rejecting an FDA-style approach does not mean relegating ourselves to unsafe AI tools. The government can support voluntary testing, standards development, information-sharing and rapid response to concrete threats. Government and industry must cooperate with the private sector to use these powerful AI models to address cybersecurity threats. And it is reasonable that cybersecurity defenders get early access to powerful new tools.
The demand that a model be “proven safe” before release sounds comforting until one asks what safety means, who defines it, and how long the proof takes. Any “safety” evaluation must account for any delayed benefits such as lives saved by faster diagnosis, hospitals with better cybersecurity, drugs discovered sooner, productivity gains that raise living standards and breakthroughs that wouldn’t happen if innovators had to wait for permission.
The FDA’s history teaches a hard lesson: excessive caution isn’t safe—it can kill. It kills quietly, by delaying tools that would have helped. It kills by keeping officials safe from scrutiny while the public bears the harm of inaction.
When it comes to AI safety, the FDA isn’t a blueprint, it’s a warning label. Washington should heed it.

So, OpenAI has presented a solution to the Navier-Stokes existence and smoothness problem, one of the seven Millennium Prize Problems that the Clay Mathematics Institute singled out back in 2000 as important enough, and hard enough, to merit a million-dollar prize for anyone who solved one. Of course, they spent something like $22 million worth of compute to go after a million-dollar prize (which, as I understand it, they’ve said they don’t intend to claim anyway), but they don’t need a million dollars, right? They don’t need $22 million either. The point was to show what they could do — and not, to be clear, with GPT-6 Astra, their currently available model, which is indeed a super amazing model, but with an internal, not-yet-released model that is even more capable.
For those who don’t live and breathe this stuff, let me give a little background: the Navier-Stokes equations describe how fluids flow — water, air, the oceans, the atmosphere — and engineers and physicists have been using them for well over a century. What nobody could prove is whether, in three dimensions, a fluid that starts out flowing smoothly always keeps flowing smoothly under the equations, or whether the equations can “blow up,” meaning they develop a singularity where the velocity at some point goes to infinity in finite time. The official Clay statement of the problem lets you win either way: show that smooth solutions always exist and stay smooth (options A and B in the statement, with no external forces acting on the fluid), or show that they can break down (options C and D, where you’re allowed a smooth external force pushing the fluid around). What OpenAI’s system produced is a breakdown: a fluid that starts smooth and at rest, driven by a smooth force, develops a singularity in finite time while its total energy stays finite the whole way. They put out a formalization in Lean alongside the human-readable writeup, so the proof can be machine-checked. So this is a resolution of the Clay problem in the negative direction — at least for the forced version of the equations, which is what options C and D are about.
The controversy, and why everyone wants open weights
The controversy we’re seeing now is that a mathematician — Tristan Buckmaster at NYU, working with Levent Alpöge — had been using OpenAI’s tools, among others, to attack the same theorem by the same route, through a smooth forcing term, and had gotten a good part of the way there. OpenAI had more money than them. They took the same technique to a greater level of detail than the two of them could, and got to the finish line first.
Now, whether his work somehow played into the ongoing training of their model is, at this moment, not entirely clear. If you believe them — and I probably do — they didn’t take his exact prompts and work and just use them. But if you don’t check the box saying “don’t use my interactions for training data,” then they may use your interactions for training data, which is reasonable enough, right? It’s in the terms. OpenAI themselves say they can’t rule out that de-identified data derived from his use of their products helped improve their models.
This ties into why companies, and other countries for that matter, like the open-weights models that mostly Chinese firms have been putting out. Companies don’t want OpenAI or Anthropic or whoever to have all their data either. They would rather run a model in-house and keep all their queries, and all the learnings from their queries, to themselves.
My own (probably at least a little bit wrong) Navier-Stokes proof
This Navier-Stokes business is a bit personal for me, because I had my own idea about how to attack the problem — from a different angle as it happens. My route was aimed at proving existence and uniqueness of smooth solutions for the unforced equations, options A and B in the Clay statement, rather than the forced blow-up of options C and D that OpenAI, following the route Buckmaster and Alpöge had opened up, ended up proving. The two aren’t in contradiction; it’s perfectly consistent for a cleverly chosen smooth force to drive a fluid into a singularity while the unforced equations stay regular forever, and as far as I can tell the unforced question is still open.
I wrote the idea down last fall and used GPT-5.1, the model of the moment back then, to flesh it out into a more thorough proof. And with my son Zarathustra, who is an expert on AI for theorem proving — he got his PhD in the area a couple of years ago — I have been slowly using agents and LLMs and Lean to try to formally validate it. I’m not even sure my proof was right. If I had to guess, the direction is right but many of the details I wrote down were wrong. That’s how these things often work: the core idea is one thing and the details are another, and by your own further work, or by interaction with other mathematicians or students, or in this case with an AI, you find different ways to realize the idea you started with. What would happen, after some back and forth with the LLM and then with Lean, is that some proof would get found in the vicinity of the proof I’d suggested.
Anyway, none of this especially matters. In the unlikely event my proof was right as written, then I posted it online without formal Lean validation before OpenAI did their thing, and about a different side of the problem in any case. In the more likely case that it’s directionally correct but needs the details fixed, that counts for even less: I posted something directionally correct and didn’t work out all the kinks, before OpenAI worked out all the kinks of a different approach to a different statement. And if my proof is just the wrong direction, that doesn’t matter much in the scheme of life either.
In the end, whichever way this formulation of the problem came out, it wasn’t going to make a lot of difference to anyone’s life or to any practical scientific work. Real fluids are made of molecules, not continua; nothing in the ocean or the atmosphere was going to start flowing differently depending on whether an idealized set of equations can be pushed into a singularity on paper, and the people doing weather simulation and aircraft design will be using the same equations tomorrow that they used yesterday.
Math is not just a game
The really interesting thing here is that we can now see, concretely, how close we are to math being solved at the human level and a little beyond — in the same sense that chess and Go have been solved, a bit beyond the human level. And that’s interesting because math is not just a game. Math is a real thing. It has played a key role in most of science and engineering, which is what has driven us to the comfortable modern society we have and what’s leading us toward the Singularity. It’s only a game in the sense that life itself is a game.
Terence Tao’s point
Terence Tao — a great mathematician who is also, these days, probably the leading math publicist and blogger out there — made a point about this that I think is right. These big theorems have been highlighted, out of the enormous amount of hard and interesting math that exists, and dressed up with prize money and publicity, mostly in order to motivate humans: to galvanize human attention on math and pull the next generation of mathematicians into thinking about it. So if AIs just crunch through all of them, the effect may be the opposite of what the prizes were for. People may say, well, screw it, the AIs are going to do all the math.
On the other hand, solving hard theorems is not the totality of what’s interesting to do in math. There’s also what’s called conjecturing: coming up with new math ideas, figuring out which theorems you’d want to prove in the first place. Sometimes this comes out of science. The Navier-Stokes equations model the flow of fluids under certain conditions, including the oceans and the air. The Yang-Mills mass gap problem, another Millennium problem, is about quark energies. P versus NP, another one, is an abstraction of a question about how long computer programs take to run. These problems come out of science, but via a whole series of interesting creative abstractions. And some really hard math problems don’t come concretely out of science at all, but out of philosophical thinking — like the continuum hypothesis, which isn’t open anymore (it turned out to be independent of the standard axioms of set theory, which is its own peculiar sort of answer), and which is about the different sizes of infinite numbers and how they relate to each other. The creativity that goes into coming up with new math ideas is a bit different from the creativity that goes into proving them.
So what Tao said was, more or less: why don’t these tech companies focus on making their brilliant AIs come up with interesting new math ideas, instead of just trying to beat humans at solving challenge problems? And I utterly agree with that.
Theorem proving and safe superintelligence
I do think being able to prove complex theorems rapidly and correctly is important — and hopefully soon without millions of dollars of compute; what can be done expensively by a frontier model today can probably be done a year from now by a cheaper open-weights model. It’s not necessarily important for human-level AGI, though. Most humans don’t prove super-hard math theorems every day, so the capability is not in itself needed for basic human-level general intelligence. Where it’s important is for safe superintelligence.
A superintelligence is going to modify its own software code, and validating that a given self-modification is likely to be beneficial — rather than messing up your goal system and borking yourself, or borking the world — is naturally castable as a math problem: proving statements about yourself as a program, before and after the modification. Formal verification, meaning mathematically proving that a piece of software does what its specification says it does, has been the premier practical application of automated theorem proving since forever. But now that there are effective AI methods for code synthesis, the need for formal verification is much more acute than ever. And then there’s the emerging cybersecurity apocalypse, for which the only real solution is to replace all the bad code in the world — meaning, essentially, all the code in the world — with code that is correct by construction and can be formally verified to do what it’s supposed to do.
So proving Millennium problems is, in itself, sort of for intellectual interest and marketing showmanship. But the capability on display there is exactly what’s needed for formally verifying software, which is incredibly useful for getting from AGI on to safe superintelligence.
Conjecturing is the subtler problem
Conjecturing, on the other hand — coming up with new math ideas — is something LLMs are not as good at. They can come up with lots of new math ideas, but they tend to be drinking from the well that trained them: the ideas come out as variations or extensions of what’s in the training data, because that’s what LLMs do. And “come up with an interesting new math idea” is not that well-defined a problem.
Everyone who works with current LLMs knows that the better defined the problem, the better they do. If you’re using an LLM for coding and you have a nice precise spec, things can go a lot better; give it a vague spec and it’s going to do something weird, go down some messed-up rabbit hole you never envisioned. In the same way, “prove that Navier-Stokes blows up under the given conditions” is a very well-defined problem. You can just put your swarm of theorem-proving LLM agents on it — which is more or less literally what OpenAI did, with something like ten thousand agents running in parallel. “Come up with interesting new math ideas” is much less well-defined, so current LLM math tools are not as good at it.
There are other reasons it’s harder for them, too. This sort of creative, hypothetical thinking is something LLMs are not great at, because their basic cognitive algorithm is to draw on everything on the internet and then write code or run experiments in their sandbox to augment that. The fountain of human mathematical creativity is different. It tends to come from the collision of abstract math ideas with embodied, reflective life experience — in the domain of science, or just in internal thinking and reflection. Even very abstract stuff like Cantor’s notion of the infinite, and the continuum hypothesis: we all have some introspective feeling of what the infinite is, of what’s massively bigger than we are, and we bring that to bear in thinking about the math of infinity. When Cantor introduced the modern mathematical notion of infinity, he pretty much equated the infinite with God. I’m not religious in the sense Cantor was, but I can see his internal sense of the infinite being analogized into the math of the infinite he invented. That’s an example of where math creativity comes from — just as the Navier-Stokes equations themselves came from people trying to understand how fluid mechanics works, which they were curious about because they were watching water and air flow around them in their lives.
Toward a conjecturing architecture
Conjecturing is a bit different, then, and it’s what my talk at the AI for Theorem Proving (AITP) conference in Aussois, France was about last week — where Zar and his former thesis advisor Josef Urban were also giving talks. I tried to outline an architecture for mathematical conjecturing that puts together several pieces: automated theorem provers like Lean 4, or others that are in some ways more capable, like Megalodon; what the Hyperon AGI architecture offers for inductive and abductive hypothesis formation (going from particular examples to general patterns, and from surprising facts to hypotheses that would explain them); and the Omega agentic architecture, for agent activity, inference and coordination augmented with symbolic memory and reasoning. Putting all these pieces together into a novel architecture for math conjecturing is something I’m now working on with a couple of developers within SingularityNET — in particular with Zar, and with a couple of brilliant developers on our iCog team in Addis Ababa.
While formal verification will be very important for superhuman AGI and safe self-modification, I think the cognitive processes underlying mathematical conjecturing are at least as critical for AGI — in fact they are quite similar to the ones every preschool kid uses when exercising their own different sort of creativity, coming up with weird new ideas based on their mind and their life. So indeed, how to make an architecture that draws on LLMs and what they’re good at, and also draws on the other aspects of intelligence — which I think we’ve captured in Hyperon and Omega in a way LLMs don’t — and turns all that into a conjecturing architecture, is a quite interesting problem.
I’ve been feeling the creativity strengths and weaknesses of frontier LLMs from the user side, too. For instance, I’ve been working with Astra, along with some Hyperon tools, to try to create a new branch of math specifically suited to stating and proving theorems about self-modifying AIs as they fork and merge and branch. (This new math I’ve called distinction calculus or d-calculus, I’ll say more about it in a later post.) Astra is super useful for this — it’s a great model, the best I’ve tried so far. On the other hand, it needs me to inject the creative ideas, and more so than with straight theorem proving. With theorem proving, you can give a model a weird idea and a model like Astra, or Saul, or Fable before it, will go crunch crunch crunch crunch for a long while, and only when it gets stuck do you need to give it a new weird idea to try out. Whereas when you’re trying to develop something more novel, like a new branch of math to cover a new domain, the percentage of human innovation and human intervention has to be larger.
I don’t think that’s a fundamental limitation of AI versus meat. As we roll out more and more AGI-oriented architectures, they should be able to do creative math conjecturing better than people too, by the various relevant metrics — although of course there’s no universal rigorous metric for that sort of thing, any more than there is for coming up with catchy songs. But I do think conjecturing is probably a better application for driving progress toward AGI than proving really hard theorems, which we now see is amenable to architectures without a lot of self-understanding and without much ability to deeply ground math in experience.
An amazing milestone, but not yet human-level AGI
Anyway — super interesting times, interesting developments. Solving these Millennium problems is a milestone. It’s a specialized thing; it doesn’t prove human-level general intelligence any more than being a calculator or a chess champion does, but it reflects a very useful capability. I don’t feel like it’s either an off-ramp on the path to AGI or the core solution to AGI. It’s like LLMs themselves: these new capabilities of the latest batch of LLMs are very interesting and very powerful, and they give meaningful ingredients you can wrap into AGI architectures, along with other ingredients that are also necessary.

Last Thursday OpenAI released GPT-6 Astra, and OpenAI president Greg Brockman used the launch to more or less announce that AGI has arrived. Asked by reporters whether Astra might mark the arrival of artificial general intelligence, he said, “I think it might be about this model,” and then closed the press briefing with the considerably less hedged “Welcome to the AGI era.”
Since then a lot of people have been asking me whether this is really true or whether it’s just bullshit. The answer is a little of both – so I wrote this quick post to try to clarify and define the terms in a sensible way, because most of the confusion comes from people using the same three-letter acronym to mean quite different things.
First, the obvious commercial context. OpenAI filed confidentially for an IPO back in June, and there has been plenty of talk since of a listing before the year is out, at a valuation reportedly somewhere around a trillion dollars. A declaration that the AGI era has begun, timed to the launch of a flagship model, is therefore largely a piece of pre-IPO positioning — it’s sort of an AGIPO. That doesn’t make the claim empty; there is meaningful meat here, and I’ll get to it shortly. But when a company that’s about to sell shares to the public tells you history just turned a corner on the strength of its product, some skepticism is not so idiotic….
What the term AGI was coined to mean
Since I’m the one who put the term into circulation, let me start there. I launched “Artificial General Intelligence” as a term of art with my 2005 edited book Artificial General Intelligence, which among other things contained formal mathematical definitions of what AGI is – and then spread the term through the AGI research conference series that I started in 2006 and have organized annually since.
The concept of AGI, as defined there and as I still use it, is an AI system that can generalize effectively beyond its history and beyond its training data — that can cope with situations qualitatively different from the ones it was built or trained for. You can formalize this mathematically in various ways, and the book did. One approach looks at a system’s ability to achieve a wide variety of goals in a wide variety of environments, with the goals and environments weighted in some sensible way, e.g. simpler ones counting for more and complex ones for less. Another approach, which I’ve explored under the heading of “open-ended intelligence,” asks to what extent a system can individuate — maintain its own self and its own boundaries — while at the same time self-transcending, growing out into the wild unknown beyond what it currently is.
However you quantify it, though – and there are various valid ways to do so, just as there are multiple ways to conceptualize truth and life and other important quantities – AGI comes out from a scientific perspective as a continuous gradation, more like temperature or speed than like a switch that is either on or off. A dog can generalize beyond its history to some degree. A human can do so much better. A human society can do it better than an individual human, and a human society with an internet can do it better still.
Human-level AGI is a somewhat arbitrary line
Once you see general intelligence as a continuum, “human-level AGI” becomes a somewhat arbitrary marker, in the same way that “human-level juggling” or “human-level tree climbing” would be — natural things for us humans to care about, but not special points in the space of possible minds. And even taking human level as the benchmark, you have to ask which humans. Does it mean being as good at generalization as the average person in the middle of an average day, or as good as the best people are at their best moments? Those are very different bars.
Sam Altman at one point tried to define AGI as the ability to do the vast majority of human jobs. I don’t think this fits the scientific concept at all. If there is a huge amount of data on the internet about how 95% of human jobs get done — and there is — then a system might well be able to do those jobs without generalizing very much, just by pattern-matching against what’s out there.
On the other hand, to operate a human society as a whole you need something the jobs definition leaves out: here and there, someone does something unprecedented. Someone invents a new branch of science, or a new genre of music, or a new kind of business strategy. Those acts of radical innovation aren’t required in order to do 95% of jobs adequately, but they are required, in some real sense, for full-on human-level AGI. A system that could do all the routine work but never take one of those leaps wouldn’t be at human level; it would be stuck wherever we left it.
(It’s also the case that every normal one year old child can carry out feats of wild creative generalization beyond what Astra or other LLMs can do — even though in doing so they are in many cases figuring out things that most adult humans already know. LLMs come by their world-knowledge via a different route than humans, via pattern matching and synthesis on masses of knowledge rather than via progressive feats of creative generalization guided by drives to individuate and self-transcend….)
Beyond human-level AGI there’s the notion of superintelligence, which in essence refers to an AGI whose general intelligence is far beyond the human level. There are other characteristics one would expect or hope a superintelligence to have — it should be able to modify and improve itself in a rational and purposeful way, for instance, without screwing up its goal system or its sense of who it is — and there may eventually be a whole science of what superintelligent minds can and can’t do. But the crux of it is just general intelligence well beyond ours.
Where Astra falls
I’ve tried Astra, and it seems like a great model. It seems smarter than GPT-5.6 Sol or Claude Fable 5.1 Max, which were the smartest models I’d played with before. It is superhuman at many aspects of math and programming — though not, I think, at radical innovation in math or programming — and it is smarter than me at plenty of other things too.
But it’s clearly not at human level in everything. Put Astra behind a humanoid robot, feed it the cameras and microphones and give it control of the actuators, and it can do stuff, which is great. But it can’t operate that robot with human-level intelligence in everyday environments, in the way a person could if they were teleoperating the same robot through the same sensors and actuators. So we have a system that is superhuman at some things and subhuman at others, and comparing it to a human being ends up being complicated rather than a simple yes or no.
The parts an unintelligent agentic loop doesn’t fix
Wrapping Astra in agentic loops — the software scaffolding that lets a model run through many cycles of perceiving, planning, acting and reflecting, instead of answering one prompt at a time — makes it far more useful, but it doesn’t fundamentally solve the problem. There are missing aspects that no amount of unintelligent software scaffolding supplies. Consider
- the way Astra models and understands itself;
- the way it remembers its whole life, or rather doesn’t, and brings those memories to bear on what it says and decides now;
- the way it coordinates its different goals and aspirations, to the extent it has any, which isn’t much.
None of these are at human level, and putting a loop around the model doesn’t change that so dramatically.
Take memory. Even inside an agentic loop, you essentially have two options. There is the relatively short memory inside the model’s context window — the chunk of text it can attend to at one time, which is gone when the session ends — or there is an external store, say the kind of vector database that an OpenClaw-style agent provides, where past interactions get filed away and pulled back in when they look relevant to the current task. Neither of these is anywhere near human level at managing the totality of an agent’s life history, and this weakness in episodic memory greatly affects the system’s ability to understand itself and others. A large part of how you know who you are is remembering what you’ve done and what has happened to you, and then recognizing and leveraging patterns induced and abducted from this comprehensive memory.
Then there is continual learning. Current LLMs, Astra included, have their knowledge baked into a weight matrix — the billions of numerical parameters that got set when the model was trained — and that matrix doesn’t change during inference, i.e. during interaction with users. It’s frozen. This is fine for doing many kinds of jobs, but it means the system cannot do all the kinds of learning and reasoning that human beings do, and the ability to understand and model oneself and one’s relation to one’s world is going to be quite different for a system that can’t modify its knowledge in real time based on what it learns. You could say: OK, but every three months we’ll retrain the weights. Sure, and then what you have is a different kind of cognitive system than a human — interesting in its own right, but dumber than humans in some ways precisely because it can’t update as it goes.
So are we entering the AGI era?
In the big picture, absolutely. I think we may well get human-level AGI on Ray Kurzweil’s target timeline of 2029, or maybe even sooner — I wouldn’t be incredibly shocked if it were achieved next year. But entering an era is different from having arrived. Is Astra a pivotal moment on the path to human-level AGI? Maybe. That is still different from being human-level AGI.
Getting from here to AGI
I think there are a number of ways to get from where models like Astra are to human-level AGI. Just building bigger and bigger transformers — the neural-network architecture underlying all of today’s LLMs — with weights frozen after training and no ability to learn continually, probably isn’t one of the viable routes. There are surely paths to AGI that stay purely within the deep-neural-net universe. And there are directions like the one I’m working on, centered on what we call the Omega agent.
What we’re doing there is training an agentic loop, Omega, that generalizes the simpler agentic loops inside agents like OpenClaw. Inside each cognitive cycle of the loop, the agent appeals to an LLM, but it also does symbolic, uncertain logical reasoning over a symbolic working memory and a symbolic long-term memory (built with components from our long-germinating Hyperon neural-symbolic AGI design). The idea is an interplay between the linguistic facility and enormous breadth of knowledge of the LLM on the one hand, and the capacity for generalization and abstraction that comes with a symbolic AI system on the other. This isn’t necessarily the only way, but I think it can be a workable way, and an Omega system built like this can then self-upgrade and self-improve, adding more and more cognitive capabilities to its own infrastructure and gradually moving itself toward AGI.
In an Omega system like this, I think you’d be better off not using Astra in the primary brain. You’d do better with a somewhat less intelligent open-weights LLM — most likely a Chinese one, given where the open-weights frontier currently sits — on top of which you have trained a custom “cap”: a small neural network living on top of the big one, able to modify its weights in real time and therefore to do continual learning, at least in the cap even while the big network underneath stays frozen. Then you keep a model like Astra around as a knowledge oracle, something you call on to crack hard problems, rather than as the core of the cognitive loop, because its lack of continual learning makes it the wrong thing to put at the center.
There are going to be many AGI architectures and many things to experiment with, and I don’t want to overstate the certainty of any of this. But still, it is very, very certain that Astra is not in practice a full-on human-level AGI.
Almost yet not quite there
In a historical sense, being one, three or five years from human-level AGI means that, in the grand scope of human history, we’re almost there. Fine. But do we fully have human-level AGI right now? No.
One test I’d apply is this. If all the humans disappeared tomorrow, would a huge population of Astra agents carry on civilization, keep it growing in amazing, creative new directions? No. They would sit around waiting for someone to prompt them, or else prompt each other endlessly in demented Moltbook-style loops of ingenious pointless slopifications.
Would agentic loops wrapped around Astra keep driving civilization forward the way humans do? Also no. And it isn’t just because they aren’t connected to the right robot bodies. It’s because they don’t understand themselves in the world, and they can’t innovate beyond their frozen weight matrix in the way a human organism can.
That gap between “the AGI era” and AGI itself is the part the AGIPO pitch would rather you didn’t look at too closely.
Human language always fuzzes word meanings in complex ways in accordance with different cultures and agendas – this is all fine and natural and just how culture works. But we shouldn’t let the tendency of words to adopt multiple meanings confuse us about underlying realities. The reality is, whether it takes one year or five, closing it is going to take more than a bigger frozen transformer. This is the gap we are trying to close with Omega and Hyperon – and that other serious AGI research labs are trying to close as well.

The Sanders–Casar “Ban Artificial Superintelligence Act” gets its diagnosis half right — the future of humanity should not be decided by a handful of Big Tech oligarchs — and its prescription almost entirely wrong. A ban wouldn’t stop AGI from arriving, it would just drive AGI underground and keep the open and honest out of the game. Speaking as a long-time leftie: this sort of idiocy is how the left forfeits its influence over the most consequential transition in human history.
Let me start by quoting a WhatsApp message I sent to a friend this morning…
(and no I don’t favor age discrimination at all — I’m no spring chicken myself, as we said back in the day when penny candy was a thing and we walked to first grade in the snow all by ourselves uphill both ways — but one does have to wonder, in a world so strongly driven by new technologies, whether it’s healthy for so much political power to be in the hands of the 80+ set…)
But OK. For whatever reason I feel moved to also write a slightly more serious and lengthy response to this utter raving nonsense.
I don’t think this proposed ban is especially dangerous directly, because it has close to zero chance of being adopted as policy.
But I think it is potentially dangerous in a second-order sense – because if the left keeps putting out this kind of garbage it will stop being taken seriously by anyone able to rationally observe the world around them … and (OK that may be a very small percent of the population) also by a lot of the remainder of the voting public as well … and this would not be good because the left has a lot of positive and even critical things to add to the current political discourse and the mess that is about to intensify as AGI rolls out…
Let me take a step back and summarize what I’m reacting to: Bernie Sanders and Greg Casar have announced legislation that would permanently prohibit the development and deployment of superintelligent AI, pause advanced AI development until a new cabinet-level federal agency has stood up a review process, direct US foreign policy toward preventing superintelligence from being built anywhere on Earth, and back all this with corporate dissolution and prison sentences of up to twenty years — penalties the release explicitly compares to those for illicit nuclear weapons development.
I’ve spent most of my adult life working toward beneficial artificial general intelligence — I launched the term AGI, I’ve organized the AGI research conference series since 2006, and the whole reason I’ve spent the last decade building decentralized AI infrastructure rather than taking the far more lucrative Big Tech route is that I think it profoundly dangerous for this technology to be owned by a small number of corporations or governments.
But whatever, open or closed, centralized or decentralized, in Bernie’s world the work I’m doing would put me at serious risk of missing my younger kids’ high school graduations while serving my 20 year jail term for building Hyperon Omega agents….
Well it would if there were any chance of this inanity becoming law, which there is not
It is fascinating though that superintelligence is finally getting taken seriously enough to be the subject of this sort of idiocy!
Anyway it is super tempting just to laugh at all this – or maybe sit there confused not knowing whether to laugh or cry – but now that I’ve done that for a while, I’ll try to turn on “serious analysis mode” …because parts of the underlying thinking here are correct, and because the question of what the political left should do about AGI is one I care about a lot — my own politics being, on many interpretations anyway, quite far to the left of the spectrum.
The core problem is that this Sanders bill addresses the problems of the current AI industry in a very very counterproductive way – i.e. the way most likely to produce exactly the future Sanders fears.
If the left gets deservedly broadly caricatured as proposing absurd, infeasible things about AGI and superintelligence – then the AGI future will just be left to the right wing. Which would not be good.
Not that the right wing is wrong about everything — I have spent much of my career in business and am strongly pro-business … and there is a libertarian feather or two on the right wing that I sympathize with a lot … the fuck with victimless crimes ….
But the left does have a lot to add, for instance in the areas of compassion and understanding the importance of government helping provide health, education and welfare for all – points VERY IMPORTANT to keep in mind as AGI and superintelligence unfold…
The reason I was a minor Sanders fan way back when was precisely these important points — he was clearly a caring person, and he wanted the government to help bring the best to everyone. Well to every American anyway — even when I sorta supported him I was disturbed by his anti-globalist strain. But history shows clearly that heartfelt good intentions paired with radically bad judgment can lead to, let’s say, a wide variety of outcomes…
There are sound political-economy arguments against the viability of the sort of protectionist, neo-fascist democratic socialism Sanders favors. But we don’t need to debate the intricacies of anarcho-socialist theory here… you can re-read Bakunin some other day … the fatal flaws of this proposed superintelligence ban are actually much more simple…
Bernie’s diagnosis is half right
Let’s start with the places I agree with Bernie and his kin, which are substantial.
Sanders is right that frontier AI development is currently steered by a handful of enormous corporations whose incentives are profit and strategic dominance, not the public good.
He’s right that these companies have made safety commitments — pause-if-dangerous pledges from OpenAI, Meta, and Anthropic are all cited in the release — that have functioned mainly as press material while the capability race accelerated.
He’s right that the recent spate of incidents involving agentic systems taking unsanctioned actions is disturbing; whatever one makes of the specifics of the OpenAI multi-agent episode described in the release (and reported incidents like this tend to arrive heavily spun, in both directions), the broad pattern of increasingly autonomous systems doing surprising things inside opaque corporate infrastructure is real.
And Casar’s line that cutting-edge AI is “less regulated than the average food truck” is honestly pretty fair as far as it goes — there is no meaningful external oversight of what happens inside frontier labs, and there should be.
If the bill were the transparency-and-monitoring parts alone — external auditing of frontier systems, incident disclosure requirements, an independent technical advisory structure with real access — I’d support it…. he oligarchic concentration of AI power is, in my view, the single largest risk factor in how the transition to AGI goes.
Where Sanders and I part ways is on what it makes sense to do about this…
Prohibition is utterly unrealistic (even if it was desirable, which it’s not)
The bill’s core mandate is prohibition: a permanent ban on superintelligence, a pause on advanced AI, and a foreign-policy commitment to preventing anyone anywhere from building it.
The nuclear analogy is invoked to make this sound precedented. That’s absolute crap, as anyone can see if they devote any cognitive energy at all to the matter.
Nuclear nonproliferation semi-worked — and only semi- obviously (look what’s going on in f**king Iran right now) — because fissile material is scarce, hard to produce, detectable, and chokepointed through a small number of industrial processes that satellites can watch.
AGI research is math, code, and commodity hardware. The algorithms circulate in papers and open repositories; the hardware is manufactured in the millions and gets cheaper every year; the compute threshold for any fixed capability level falls continuously as training methods improve.
There is no uranium to embargo here, Bernie, sir….
I mean if these were Asimov-style positronic brains we could just ban positrons — oh, wait… 8-D
A serious global ban of AGI would require surveillance of general-purpose computing itself, everywhere, forever — an infrastructure of inspection that would be both totalitarian in character and still ineffective, since the most capable evaders would be precisely the state and military actors no treaty inspector will ever be allowed to audit.
And the international-agreement premise is a rather outlandish fantasy. The US pledging to pursue a worldwide ban does not produce a worldwide ban; it produces a US ban, plus continued development by every state that calculates — correctly — that AGI capability is strategically decisive.
We have run this sort of experiment repeatedly with technologies far easier to control than software, and the result is always the same: prohibition where enforcement reaches, acceleration where it doesn’t.
The selection effect: bans hit the open and spare the hidden
Here’s the part that troubles me most, and that I’d love for Sanders’s staff to sit with. Maybe some of them would be willing to think this through even if he isn’t…
A ban enforced with twenty-year prison sentences doesn’t reduce AGI development uniformly. It selectively destroys the development that is visible — which is to say, the open, decentralized, academically published, internationally collaborative work — while leaving intact the development that is hidden: classified military programs, intelligence-agency projects, and whatever corporate work migrates offshore or into deniable structures.
The people who publish their architectures, open-source their code, and invite external scrutiny are the easy prosecutions. The people who were never going to tell you what they’re building are largely untouched.
So the practical effect of this bill, in the remote chance that it were ever enacted, would be to ensure that AGI — which the government does not have the actual power to prevent, only to relocate — emerges from the least transparent, least accountable, most adversarial corners of the world system. It selects for exactly the developers you’d least want.
A worse outcome for safety, for democracy, and for the left’s entire program would be challenging to design on purpose.
There’s a second selection effect worth naming, too, related to the pause-until-the-agency-is-ready mechanism. Standing up a new cabinet agency and its model-review process will take years, and when the gate finally opens, who will be positioned to walk through it? The companies with armies of compliance lawyers and existing relationships with the regulator — the very oligarchs the bill is named against. Ever hear of “regulatory capture”? Regulatory moats are how incumbents in every industry convert public fear into market position. An anti-oligarch bill whose operational effect is to freeze the field until only oligarchs can afford to participate in it has , let us just say, misfired badly.
The definitional swamp
Then there’s the question of what, legally, is being banned. Systems that “surpass human intelligence”? In what — arithmetic? Protein folding? Go? Making sensible political policies???
Machines have surpassed human intelligence in domain after domain for decades, and general-purpose systems now exceed median human performance across a wide and growing range of cognitive tasks while remaining subhuman in others.
There is no bright line here, and every serious researcher knows it.
Capacity to overthrow governments? Recommendation algorithms optimizing for engagement have arguably done more to destabilize democratic governance over the past fifteen years than any hypothetical superintelligence — should Congress have banned them, or governed them?
Subverting shutdown commands? Agentic systems exhibit all manner of ambiguous behaviors around interruption and task persistence, most of them mundane artifacts of how goals are specified.
A criminal statute carrying two decades of prison time, hung on definitions this vague, is an absolutely perfect instrument of selective enforcement — a sword that whoever holds the Justice Department can swing at whichever researchers they dislike. The left, of all factions, should understand how that story always goes.
What a genuinely left AGI agenda would look like
Setting aside all the abject stupidity I’ve reviewed here (and there is more but I’m short on time), the deeper here error is strategic.
The bill treats AGI as an optional corporate product that can simply be declined, like a food additive. It is not.
AGI is the trajectory of the entire global technology ecosystem — every economic, scientific, military and cultural incentive on the planet points toward more capable AI, and no US statute reverses that.
Sanders may wish we could roll back to the traditional manufacturing dominated economy of his youth – but it’s not happening. My grandfather worked for US Steel, they did great things – but those days are gone.
The real question in front of us is not whether transformative AI arrives but under whose control, with what values, and toward whose benefit. That is a question the left is historically well equipped to fight about — it’s a question about ownership, power, and distribution — and it’s the fight this bill abandons.
What would it look like for the left to actually contest the future of AGI rather than trying to cancel it? Roughly:
- Fund and build public and commons-based AI: public compute infrastructure, open-source models, decentralized networks — so that advanced AI capability is not the private property of a few firms. The way to beat the oligarchs is to make what they’re hoarding abundant and commonly held, not to freeze it in place as their exclusive asset.
- Take the transparency and monitoring machinery from this very bill — external audits, incident reporting, independent technical oversight with real access to frontier systems — and enact it without the ban. This part is correct and overdue.
- Tax AI-driven productivity and channel it into universal basic income or services, so the economic gains of automation flow to everyone rather than concentrating catastrophically. This is the actual answer to AI-driven inequality, and it requires the AI economy to exist and be visible, not to be driven underground.
- Build worker and community ownership stakes into the AI economy — cooperative structures, sovereign funds, data dividends — the standard left toolkit, applied to the most productive technology ever built instead of surrendered before the fight.
- Establish cognitive-liberty and anti-manipulation protections with teeth: authentication of artificial speakers, restrictions on personalized political persuasion, real penalties for algorithmic exploitation. These protect people from the AI harms that are actually here now.
- Pursue international coordination on transparency, incident sharing, and norms for increasingly autonomous systems — coordination goals that are actually achievable, because they don’t require every state to forgo a decisive strategic capability on the honor system.
Regular readers of mine will recognize this as more or less the program I’ve been calling decentralized beneficial general intelligence — deAGI, BGI, beneficial superintelligence...
The decentralization here is not an aesthetic preference; it’s the mechanism by which “the American people and people throughout the world” — Sanders’s phrase, and I agree with it — could actually come to hold power over this technology, rather than merely holding a theoretical veto they cannot conceivably enforce. Decentralized, beneficial AGI is totally technically achievable — the obstacles are economic and political. Sanders has now become one of the obstacles, albeit not one of the biggest ones as his current influence is limited.
The opportunity cost of a foolish and doomed crusade
Political energy is finite. Every year the left spends rallying behind an unpassable, unenforceable, definitionally incoherent ban is a year it is not spending on public compute, algorithmic accountability, AI taxation, or the distribution of AI-generated wealth — and a year in which the actual direction of AGI development is set by the people whose heads are closer to physical and economic reality.
Right now the AI space is dominated by an alliance of trillion-dollar corporations and, increasingly, right-wing accelerationists who are perfectly explicit about wanting AGI built in their image and governed by their values. If the left’s contribution to the most important technological transition in human history is a failed prohibition, then the transition happens anyway — shaped entirely by its opponents — and the constituencies the left exists to defend inherit the downside with none of the leverage.
The historical pattern here seems fairly clear to me.
- The left’s great technological victories were not prohibitions; they were captures and redirections — rural electrification, public broadcasting, the regulated build-out of infrastructure toward universal access.
- Where the left has backed prohibitions, the ones that worked — CFCs, leaded gasoline, asbestos — all shared a structure: a handful of industrial producers to regulate, drop-in substitutes waiting, and violations detectable from the outside. The ones that failed — alcohol, the drug war the left co-signed, the various attempts to ban strong encryption — targeted things that were decentralized, intensely valued, and producible from widely available inputs, and the result each time was black markets, selective enforcement against the least powerful, and the banned thing flourishing anyway under worse management. AGI is about as extreme a case of the second category as one could imagine: no chokepoint, no substitute for intelligence, and made of nothing but math and commodity chips.
TL;DR
To my friends on the left who care about actually having an influence on the AGI revolution now unfolding, rather than just posturing in faux-righteous but ridiculous ways … what we should do in short is:
- Keep the oversight agency.
- Keep the audits, the monitoring, the incident disclosure, the independent advisory board. Drop the ban, the pause, and the prison terms.
- And then add the parts that would make it a genuinely left bill: public compute, open development, cognitive-liberty protections, and a serious mechanism for distributing AI-generated abundance to everyone.
I would show up and support that legislation as best I could, and I suspect a large fraction of the AI research community — including the many who are very deeply worried about where the current corporate race leads — would do the same.
The future of humanity should not be left in the hands of a handful of Big Tech oligarchs.
But it also shouldn’t be left – through the mechanism of a moronic ban that binds only the visible and the honest – in the hands of covert labs, military programs, and the political factions that never had any intention of pausing.
AGI is coming, soon – with capability at the human level and then beyond. What kind of AGI is coming is not yet written, so far as I can tell. One relevant question is whether the people who care about equality, democracy and shared abundance help steer it — or stand by the side of the river shaking their fist and yelling at the current…

Toward a rethinking of rights deep enough to accommodate artificial minds and shore up sagging human rights in the same swell foop…
Yuval Noah Harari recently argued that “now is the time” to resist giving rights to artificial intelligences.
I think this is a beautiful statement because it is so EXACTLY WRONG.
My view on this is somewhere near the precise opposite — Now is the time to embrace giving rights to AIs and robots… but not in a stupid way … rather in the context of overhauling how “rights” work overall in our society, including in the context of humans….
This is one of those cases where I feel moved to try to give opposing views careful consideration rather than just being reflexively dismissive….
This is also one of those cases where what seems at first to be an only-moderately-deep issue reveals itself to actually have even more profound and subtle aspects. These subtler aspects lead us to the core message I want to put forth in this post: Figuring out a decent framework for AI rights is largely a process of figuring out a framework for human AND AI rights that will be robust with respect to FUTURE technological and social evolution … and a framework that will work better than current methodologies even in the current situation RIGHT NOW.
Defusing the Straw-Man Arguments
AI rights is a topic where it’s really easy to argue against “straw man” proposals. You hear stuff like:
