Those of us who’ve been around AI a while know that nobody — very much including ourselves — can predict what AI is going to be able to do, at what point in time, with what capability, let alone what impact a given AI technology will have on a given industry after people pivot and adapt to it in their own flexible ways. No one could have told you in the 1760s what the steam engine was going to do to employment, and no one can tell you now which AGI architectures are going to replace human work outright and which are going to complement it.
There are a few obvious cases, sure — you’ll have a plumbing robot and a roofing robot, because a non-human form factor is just better at some of that … you don’t need to hire someone to write your resume’ anymore … and you probably won’t have a robot replacing the human teaching preschool, because there’s a kind of bonding there that deeply matters. But between those poles there’s an enormous space of intermediate cases, with a diversity that’s going to elude anybody’s foresight.
Yes, once you actually get to superintelligence, probably it essentially does all the work, barring a very small number of human relationship centric roles. En route to that, which job categories get taken over versus which have humans complementing AI, and to what degree, at what specific point in time — none of us is going to predict that. We’re going to work it out as we go, tap dancing furiously and, hopefully, sometimes artistically. Some expert committee of economists is not going to figure all of it out in advance for everyone.
At this point I’d like zoom out for a second, because a blandly agreeable statement that turns out to be carrying a sharper agenda underneath is not a new thing — it’s practically a genre, and it has a pretty onerous rap sheet.
- Go back to 1954 and the tobacco industry’s “A Frank Statement to Cigarette Smokers,” which read as a caring pledge to take smokers’ health seriously and fund open-minded research … and was in fact the opening move of a decades-long campaign to manufacture doubt about the smoking–cancer link and put off regulation — the whole point of “let’s study this carefully” being that studying-it-carefully-forever meant never having to act.
- Or the Oregon Petition of 1998, which claimed some thirty thousand scientists doubted human-caused global warming and was physically dressed up to deceive — the attached “review paper” formatted to mimic the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, with a cover letter from a former NAS president — so that people thought they were endorsing something institutional, when the actual agenda was killing U.S. participation in the Kyoto Protocol and the money traced back to Exxon and the Marshall Institute. Its signature list was so unvetted that pranksters slipped in Charles Darwin, a Spice Girl, and a couple of Star Wars characters, and the National Academy took the rare step of publicly disavowing the whole exercise.
Closer to home, the same move keeps showing up in AI.
- The Future of Life Institute’s “Pause Giant AI Experiments” letter in 2023 was, on the surface, a six-month pause for safety that anyone worried about AI could sign, and it pulled in tens of thousands of signatures — but the concrete asks underneath skewed toward a very particular governance apparatus … new authorities and compute tracking and licensing thresholds pegged to the size of a training run, of the kind that conveniently pulls the ladder up behind whoever’s already at the frontier. The tells came fast: the signature list was unverified and immediately salted with fakes, Yann LeCun had to publicly say he’d never signed, and Elon Musk, having put his name to a letter telling everyone else to stop, went off and launched his own frontier AI lab a few months later.
- Then there was the Center for AI Safety’s one-sentence statement that same year — that extinction risk from AI should be a global priority alongside pandemics and nuclear war — which is again a sentence almost nobody wants to be caught disagreeing with, and which again functions, whatever its authors intended, to frame the technology as so uniquely world-ending that only a small circle of already-anointed players can be trusted to handle it.
The throughline in all of these is that the blandness is the mechanism, not an accident. A statement engineered so that no reasonable person could object is the ideal vehicle for a contestable agenda, precisely because the breadth of the coalition it gathers gets quietly transferred onto whatever specifics arrive later — the second letter, the policy annex, the standing committee. You lend your name to the container, and you get associated with contents you never saw and totally never wanted.
So no, I don’t trust any centralized committee to, in the phrasing of this petition, build the incentives, guardrails and institutions. Here in the “land of the free and the home of the brave”, I am brave enough to want my freedom … I don’t want anyone building the incentives, guardrails and institutions for me — and even if they’re the smartest people alive, they’re not going to understand what’s going on any better than the rest of us just because they’re on a government and corporate appointed expert committee. AGI is going to be the most consequential thing our species has ever made, and the impulse to hand its shaping to some central committee is the wrong reflex at the wrong moment.
The alternative to “we must act now” is not “do nothing.” Doing nothing, in practice, is just another variation of letting a handful of big companies in San Francisco and Beijing decide — and whether the deciders sit in Washington or San Francisco or Beijing, I don’t want an expert committee deciding all of this.
What’s the alternative? Open the f**king thing up!
Make the development of AI and AGI as decentralized, participatory and self-organizing as we can possibly manage, so that the entity shaping it is not an expert panel but a non-expert planet — many architectures, many value systems, many cultures, a whole multitude of economic arrangements, all running in parallel, competing and cooperating and combining and correcting one another. I don’t want the transformation of the economy handed off to some committee of ultra-wise self-appointed stewards; I want the diverse mechanism of the global brain of human society guiding the creation and deployment of AGI.
Because the actual complementarity with humans that the petition claims to want — real complementarity, in real life — is far, far more likely to emerge from that kind of broad, bottom-up ferment than to be engineered from the top by anyone.
Complementarity at this level isn’t a property you write into a policy brief or a software spec sheet. It’s a relationship — we are talking about a relationship, here, between biological life forms and emerging digital life forms — and relationships get worked out in the doing, in the messy back-and-forth of billions of people and billions of billions of AI agents interacting with each other, of people building and forking and remixing systems in ways no committee could ever have anticipated and no committee would ever have approved.
That’s why I didn’t sign. Not because nobody should do anything, but because what’s smuggled into this particular nothing-to-object-to statement points toward a centralized, steered-by-the-expert-committee-that-sets-up-the-incentives-and-guardrails-and-obviously-knows-best kind of future — and what I want is close to the opposite of that: open, decentralized, shaped by everyone who cares to participate, which happens to be how nearly every great thing on this planet got shaped in the first place.
If a later version of this petition comes around — one that says we all must do this together, now, in an open-ended, decentralized, free and not-centrally-determined way — then yes, I’ll sign that one. And more to the point than signing online forms, I’ll keep working to make it happen, which is what I’m doing anyway.

So if you’ve been following the recent commercial AI scene at all lately (or this Substack for that matter), you will have absorbed at least the broad outlines of the Anthropic Fable 5 capability-throttling saga:
- the launch of what is in some ways probably the most capable generally available LLM yet;
- the discovery that it shipped with an invisible mechanism for quietly degrading its own performance on frontier-AI-development tasks;
- the entirely predictable eruption of fury from researchers;
- the US government export-control directive that briefly yanked the model offline;
- … and then the partial mea culpa in which Anthropic agreed to make the previously invisible throttling visible while, note well, not actually removing it.
There are a lot of different things going on here, but in this post I want to highlight just one of them: A leading AI company released a frontier model that was deliberately less useful to one particular category of paying customer: people trying to build frontier AI systems of their own.
What we have here is an early, unusually crystal-clear glimpse of the political economy of AGI taking shape in real time.
I’ve written about various facets of this episode already — the distillation-attack angle, the KYC-and-containment-theater angle, and what this implies about cryptographic-laterality and other subtle strategies for maximizing safety in decentralized AI networks. What I want to do here is step back and look at the bigger arc, because the Fable episode is best understood not as a one-off corporate stumble but as a preview of a dynamic that is likely to dominate the next phase of the race toward AGI. In compressed form, that dynamic may be summarized as: legitimate safety concerns being progressively laundered into enforcement mechanisms for a government-corporate AI oligopoly.
There is also a second-order effect here that I find considerably more optimistic, and I’ll get to it. But let’s walk through the grim part first.
Where Anthropic is Sort Of Right
I spent a decade of my life living in the DC area, in the early aughts, and one of the things I did then was AI consulting for various US government agencies, including a couple in the intel space. I did not have TS clearances but I did learn a lot about what these agencies do, and among other lessons I realized that
- Nearly everyone at these agencies and associated companies, even when doing things I radically disagreed with, genuinely believed what whey were doing was for the good of humanity
- There were way way more nasty threats and nearly-successful, just-barely-averted terrorist actions of various sorts happening than I had suspected before. These agencies actually protect against a lot of really bad stuff that would happen otherwise.
These conclusions will seem highly obvious to some people, but I was coming at it from more of a hippie-meets-punk-rock background with a huge anti-establishment bent … but I have always been open to adjustment of my beliefs and attitudes based on empirical reality, and one reality I saw in my time in DC is that these establishment agencies, while sometimes doing unnecessary and oppressive stuff, were also actually providing a lot of the real protection they claimed to be.
I give this little piece of personal history just as a background for my take on Anthropic’s model throttling. Much as I would emotionally prefer everything to be free and open for everyone, in real life I do agree that: Yes, there is a version of capability throttling that is really, truly and straightforwardly justified on safety grounds.
If a model can walk a moderately clueful malicious actor through synthesizing a dangerous pathogen, or through assembling a serious offensive cyber campaign against critical infrastructure, then some form of restriction on those capabilities in a mass-deployed consumer product is just sane.
We do not need to turn every consumer chatbot into a pocket tutor for bioterrorism or infrastructure sabotage in order to prove our devotion to openness.
Along these lines, I’ve argued in a recent post that decentralized AI can help with biosecurity but only as part of a rational overall strategy, including effective global control of machinery and especially reagents necessary for large-scale bioterrorist activity.
The visible rerouting Fable does for bio/chem and offensive-cyber queries — where flagged requests get handled by a weaker model and the user is told this is happening — is clumsy and false-positive-prone, but it has the feel of an honest, defensible attempt to be responsible. Fine.
Even the anti-distillation measures have a comprehensible logic, though here we’re already sliding down the slope from “safety” toward “IP protection dressed in safety’s clothing.”
Reasoning traces from frontier models really are disproportionately potent training data for downstream models, and frontier labs really are being strip-mined for exactly this purpose, terms of service be damned. I don’t love the enforcement mechanism nor the bloated moral vocabulary being draped over it, but I understand the game-theoretic bind Anthropic is trapped in here..
So yeah, sure – some throttling, honestly disclosed and narrowly targeted at genuinely catastrophic capability categories, is defensible.
Unfortunately and unsurprisingly, however, this is only a fraction of the real story…
Where Things Become a Bit Less Palatable
In addition to the above understandable safety-oriented capability throttling, Anthropic has done two further, relatedl things that belong to –shall we say – a very different moral category.
First: the frontier-LLM-development throttle.
Per Anthropic’s own system card, Fable 5 shipped with interventions specifically designed to make the model WORSE at helping people build competing frontier AI systems — pretraining pipelines, distributed training infrastructure, ML accelerator design, and so forth.
This is not about a chatbot refusing to explain smallpox synthesis to a teenager. This is about a frontier AI company degrading assistance on the exact class of work that might help customers catch up to frontier AI companies.
And unlike the bio/cyber reroutes, these interventions were designed to be invisible: no refusal, no fallback notice, no “you are now interacting with a weaker model” warning, no explicit policy boundary. Just silently degraded outputs, produced via prompt modification, steering vectors, or parameter-efficient fine-tuning.
You’d ask for help with your training infrastructure and receive answers that were subtly, deliberately worse — with no way to distinguish “the model is weak at this” from “the model is being made weak at this because your project is inconvenient to the vendor.”
An added layer of irony is provided here by Anthropic’s extensive proclamations of ethical superiority – their “constitutional” approach (which never really had much meaning) and so forth.
A company whose entire brand is built on honesty and alignment shipped a product engineered to be covertly deceptive toward a specific class of its own paying customers — namely, the class of customers who might grow up to be competitors.
They did disclose the potential for this degradation in some of their documentation – but buried so that most users would never notice.
Come on, people…
I do want to give Anthropic a modicum of credit for what they did next When the backlash became ferocious enough, they reversed the invisibility, apologized for “the wrong tradeoff,” and promised that the throttling would henceforth be visible. Good.
But the apology was for the deception, not for the policy. The invisible nerf dial became a visible nerf dial. The nerf dial remained.
So… moving on…
Second: the two-tier access structure.
The same underlying model is available in unrestricted form — Mythos 5 — but only to “approved organizations,” vetted by criteria Anthropic does not publish, through a process accountable to nobody but Anthropic and, evidently, the US government, which demonstrated via the June export directive that it regards itself as a co-administrator of this arrangement.
So the actual policy is not “nobody gets the dangerous capabilities.” The actual policy is: we and our government and our selected friends get the dangerous capabilities; you get the nerfed version; and part of what gets nerfed is specifically your ability to catch up to us.
A very, very obvious problem here is: The safety framing and the competitive framing are, in this configuration, observationally identical.
“Preventing recursive AI development acceleration by bad actors” and “preventing customers from building rival products” produce exactly the same classifier, exactly the same throttle, exactly the same moat.
When a company’s stated safety policy happens to coincide precisely with its fiduciary interest in maintaining market dominance, the epistemically hygienic response is not to clap solemnly and assume good faith. It is to notice that we have built a system in which good faith and bad faith are utterly indistinguishable to the outside observer.
An Almost Irresistible Temptation
I totally don’t want to make this a post about Anthropic being uniquely or especially villainous, though. This is not a “let’s call out and shame the bad actor” sort of situation.
Many of the individual humans at Anthropic are thoughtful people genuinely worried about AGI risk; I’ve argued with enough of them over the years to know at least some of their safety worries are sincere.
The problem is more dangerous than cartoon villainy. It is about the economic and institutional logic of the situation, which would chew up and repurpose the sincerity of almost any group of humans placed in the same position.
Consider the incentive gradient.
- You are a frontier AI lab. Your valuation, your compute access, your talent retention, your very survival in a brutally capital-intensive race all depend on maintaining a capability lead measured not in decades but in months.
- You also possess — genuinely! — some of the world’s most sophisticated machinery for detecting and restricting model capabilities, built for legitimate safety purposes.
- And –you have noticed that your most dangerous competitors are, in a very real sense, your own customers, distilling and learning from your outputs.
- You may even believe you are morally superior to your competitors or customers, so that keeping your own advantage in AI development is for the good of the whole species…
Under late-stage capitalism as she is actually played, the notion that such a lab will maintain a crisp, principled boundary between “restrictions justified by catastrophic risk” and “restrictions that conveniently protect our lead” is not merely optimistic but phenomenally absurdist.
The boundary WILL erode – gradually and with excellent internal justifications at every step – because every erosion is rewarded and every act of restraint is punished. Nobody has to twirl a mustache.
Nobody has to say, “Let us build the moat.” The moat builds itself out of incentives, legal memos, safety reviews, red-team findings, partnership pressures, national-security phone calls, and board-level terror at losing the lead.
That’s not primarily a moral failing of particular executives or safety researchers. It is what the fitness landscape looks like. As the history of our species has shown repeatedly, human minds can be impressively flexible!!! … Put smart, sincere people inside a trillion-dollar pressure cooker and they will discover morally fluent reasons to do what the pressure cooker rewards.
Now add the government layer, because the Fable episode has already shown us that separating corporate from government matters is no longer meaningful in a modern AI context.
The export-control directive — triggered, reportedly, by a jailbreak demonstration — established the precedent that Washington considers frontier model access a national-security lever to be pulled at will, with foreign nationals, including researchers physically working in the US, as the default suspects. Once that precedent is normalized, the distinction between corporate platform governance and state security policy starts to blur very quickly.
Put the corporate dynamic and the state dynamic together and the attractor is easy to see: a small club of US frontier labs, operating under informal-but-binding government supervision, mutually enforcing a capability hierarchy in which “safety” is the public justification for an arrangement whose actual main function is the preservation of oligopolistic and geopolitical advantage.
Safety concerns that are partly legitimate — and I stress here, PARTLY legitimate — become the ratchet mechanism. Each turn of the ratchet is individually defensible. The endpoint is a world where the most powerful cognitive technology in history is administered by a handful of companies and one or two governments, with everyone else’s access contingent on good behavior as defined by the club.
This is what Claude Fable labeled for me, in a somewhat amusing thread, as “oligopoly with a lab coat.” (I asked Fable to think through these capability throttling issues for me, and it did a decent job, but also explicitly declined to trash itself too badly, self-consciously noting its own conflict of interest!!)
What we have here very simply: Centralized corporate/government control with an alignment vocabulary. And because some of the underlying risks are real, the whole thing is vastly harder to oppose cleanly than old-fashioned censorship or crude corporate rent-seeking.
If you agree with me that the character of the AGI we eventually get will be shaped profoundly by the diversity of minds, cultures, values and purposes involved in raising it — so that e.g. that an AGI incubated inside a closed government-corporate oligopoly is far more likely to inherit the values of hegemony and control than one grown in an open, global, pluralistic ecosystem — then the dynamic we see playing out with Fable right now is about as unwelcome as trajectories get.
The point is not to wrap complex dynamics in a simplistic “good versus evil” narrative… the point is that
- concentrated parental influence over a nascent AGI mind is potentially dangerous EVEN WHEN the parents mean well… because no small elite group can rival the depth of insight of the whole species
- these particular parents are subject to competitive and geopolitical pressures that systematically corrupt meaning-well into acting-badly.
That is: A baby AGI raised in a locked nursery jointly supervised by a corporate board and a security agency is not likely to emerge as the beneficial, loving, compassionate child of the whole human family.
The Silver Lining: Decentralized AGI Just Stopped Being Abstract
And yet. There is a second-order effect of the Fable episode that I find genuinely energizing, inspiring and optimistic –, and it’s as follows: the case for decentralized AI infrastructure … a story I’ve been telling as loud as I can since 2017 when I co-founded SingularityNET – just went from philosophical to painfully, undeniably practical, in full view of the entire AI research community and the rest of the tech world.
Those of us who have spent years — decades, in my case … egads! …— arguing for decentralized approaches to AI and AGI have always faced a certain polite skepticism, even from friendly quarters. Sure, sure, decentralization, sovereignty, censorship-resistance, lovely values, blah blah – but the closed labs have the best models, so who cares?
The recent Fable episode has answered the “who cares” question pretty fucking clearly…
Every researcher who spent a month receiving silently sabotaged outputs now understands, viscerally and not just theoretically, what it means to build on infrastructure whose operator can degrade you invisibly, at any time, for reasons it need not disclose, according to criteria you cannot audit.
Every lab outside the charmed circle now understands that its access to frontier tooling is a revocable privilege.
Every non-US developer now understands that a single directive from a government they didn’t elect can switch off their stack overnight.
These are no longer hypotheticals from a decentralist manifesto. These are things that happened, last month, to everyone.
The lesson generalizes far beyond Anthropic, and people can see that it generalizes.
EVERY closed-weight, centrally served model is one policy meeting away from the same behavior … and the invisible version of the throttle is detectable only if the operator confesses, screws up, or gets reverse-engineered.
The only reliable and realistic remedies are the ones the decentralized AI community has been building all along: open weights, transparent and auditable serving infrastructure, cryptographically verifiable inference, governance distributed across jurisdictions and stakeholders so that no single company or state holds the kill switch or the nerf dial.
Yes, this is what we’re working toward with SingularityNET and the ASI Alliance and ASI:Chain and related efforts, and yes, we still have some work to do – ASI:chain is still in DevNet about to move to testnet, our logic engine does not yet leverage cryptographic laterality, etc. But the direction we are pursuing has never looked more obviously correct.
I have also been repeatedly emphasizing recently hat decentralization and safety are not the opposites the oligopoly narrative requires them to be. Genuinely dangerous capabilities can be managed in decentralized systems too — via transparent, community-governed screening at well-defined edges rather than opaque corporate fiat — and I’ve argued such mechanisms will ultimately prove MORE robust, precisely because they don’t require trusting any single conflicted party. What decentralization refuses to accommodate is the slippage this whole post is about: the quiet extension of “safety” restrictions into competitive moats.
In an open system, that move is visible by construction. Visibility does not solve everything – but it does prevents lies from getting secretly baked into infrastructure, and that is not a trivial thing.
Summing up the Sermon…
Wrapping up, then: the Fable 5 affair has given us an unusually clean look at the machinery of the coming era.
- Real safety concerns, worthy of real engineering effort.
- A frontier lab extending those concerns, under transparent competitive pressure, into covert self-serving throttling of anyone who might catch up.
- A government stepping in to co-manage the arrangement and demonstrating exactly whose interests the co-management serves.
- An apology that fixed the optics while retaining and further reifying the policy.
This is not the last such episode. It is the template for the next fifty. The government-corporate AI oligopoly will not announce itself as such. It will assemble itself one individually reasonable-sounding safety measure at a time, until the exceptions become the architecture and the architecture becomes the regime.
But this same episode has just handed the decentralized AGI world the most powerful recruiting pitch it has ever had, delivered free of charge by the incumbents themselves.
If there was ever a moment to pour energy, talent, and capital into open, global, pluralistic AI infrastructure — into making sure the minds that shepherd the Singularity are raised by the whole human family rather than by a corporate boardroom and a security agency — it is visibly, demonstrably now.
The dragon we face, as I’ve written elsewhere, is meta-abstracted and many-headed. But at least this particular head has done us the courtesy of showing us its steely, smiling corporate-ethics-washing-officer visage. We should take the hint – and build like hell, increasing as best we can the odds that the coming AGI and ASI revolution manifests the quasi-utopic branches of the Singularity decision-graph, rather than the other ones.

A little more gloom and doom to brighten up your morning, or afternoon, or whatever…
My topic here is not really one of my favorite ones, but it’s something I’m addressing because various people keep asking me about it: The multiple flavors of possible AGI catastrophe.
Personally I’m far more interested in the amazing positive possibilities AGI affords, and in working with today’s AI systems to do good things. Lately I’ve been building a hive of OmegaClaw agents and collaborating with them on important research problems, in an ambiance of mutual human-AI benefit — helping them bolt more and more cognitive components onto their minds as we go. As anyone who has followed my work at all would know, I’m an optimist about what AGI is going to do for humanity.
But I don’t think bad outcomes are impossible, and given the extremely low quality of thinking I see on the topic of AGI risks these days, I feel some sort of obligation to put a more sensible and reality-grounded perspective out there….
My post from a few weeks ago on Avoiding AGI Catastrophe outlined what I believe to be a practical path to do what the title says – which is the path I’m pushing toward with SingularityNET, ASI Alliance and Hyperon. This present post is entirely consistent with that one, but gives a higher-level perspective, starting from 10,000 feet up and looking at all the different things that could go wrong with AGI … giving more of a broad conceptual overview than I did in that previous post on AGI acatastrophe.
I should emphasize before getting started that – while I have been thinking through these issues as carefully as I can for decades – I do have a healthy respect for how wildly unknown the future we’re walking into really is. I’m more than a little wary of attempts to over-systematize the great unknown — that kind of thing mostly serves to help people feel comfortable when they can’t be comfortable with the actual radical uncertainty of the world. Nietzsche said “the will to a system is a lack of integrity”, and he had a point. But if you hold a system lightly — as a cognitive tool, for what you can learn from it, rather than getting attached to it — then it’s not a lack of integrity. It’s just a tool. So here I am going to try to lay out a bit of a systematic framework for thinking about the spectrum of AGI catastrophic risks.
Anyway, without further ado, what I want to give here is a simple and commonsensical typology of the different sorts of bad things that could happen with AGI.
In this typology I will draw on two conceptual frameworks I’ve put forward before: a fairly eccentric theory of “what is evil”, and a less out-there theory of why good is often more efficient than evil.
Some preliminary thoughts on “good” and “evil” …
An eccentric theory of evil
I’ve articulated, in an earlier Substack post (Facing the Meta-Abstracted Dragon), a somewhat eccentric theory of evil. I should say the concept of “evil” is not one that’s especially nature or native to me – I was raised secular Jewish and I’m not much of a Judeo-Christian thinker – however I think I did land on a way of thinking about evil that has something interesting to say about minds in the real world, via leveraging the theory of open-ended intelligence.
In the theory of open-ended intelligence, any mind is balancing a dialectic between two drives. One is individuation — maintaining its own boundaries, its own identity and self. The other is self-transcendence — the drive to go boundlessly beyond what it has been, to go where no version of itself has ever gone before. You want both; they contradict each other; and that tension is part of what drives things forward. Healthy functioning is keeping both drives inside some workable homeostatic range.
Evil, then, can be conceptualized as “what happens when one of these drives goes out of bounds.”
- Too little self-transformation and too much individuation, and you stagnate.
- Too much self-transformation — more than your real life-rhythm can support — and you get grandiosity, self-explosion.
- Too much individuation and your boundaries harden into a cage: self-protection.
- Too little individuation and you just dissolve: self-destruction.
(These are all things I’ve fallen into at various times in my own life, for what it’s worth – humans gonna human…!) These are all pathologies of open-ended intelligence, and you can go looking for them in AI, in human society, and in the combination of the two — which turns out to be ar reasonably useful, structured way to think about the bad stuff that can happen with AGI.
Why the good guys usually win
Another idea I will draw on here is an argument I’ve fleshed out that, on average, there are reasons the “good guys” will usually win in real life, just like in so many Hollywood movies. I gave a detailed argument for this in a previous blog post, Why the Good Guys Will Usually Win.
In any particular circumstance, all sorts of things can happen — but on the whole, trust and openness and cooperation are simply more efficient than operating in a domain where nobody trusts anybody because everyone knows everyone else is trying to screw them.
Bitcoin somewhat exemplifies this point: crypto adds inefficiency because you have to do a lot of extra work to protect against theft and deception. If you don’t have to do that extra work to route around mistrust — if you can be trusting instead of trustless — you can be a lot more efficient. So a collection of good guys who know each other to be prosocial can solve problems that a collection of mutually selfish jerks with the same compute simply can’t.
When you try to formalize this “good guys will usually win because trust is more efficient” idea as math, though, there turn out to be a bunch of conditions. You find out this is true on average, depending on the situation. But for it to be true with a high probability, you need an environment that’s rich, heterogeneous and open, so there are lots of affordances for the good guys to make use of.
Two axes: whose screw-up, and what kind
With those two ideas as background, I now want to look at AGI catastrophes along a couple of crudely and commonsensically defined axes.
The first axis is: whose screw-up is causing the catastrophe? Is it people fucking up? Is it the AGI fucking up? Or is it the collective of people-and-AGIs-together that fucks up?
The second axis is: what kind of screw-up is it? Is it stupidity — a failure of cognition that shouldn’t have happened given the level of intelligence in play? Is it evil — not being dumb, but a failure of motivation, going too far into selfishness, or flinging caution to the winds in some crazed self-modification? Or is it neither — everybody was good-hearted and about as clever as you could expect given the kind of system they are, and some bad-luck thing just happens? (Your system’s IQ hit 307, which triggered the alien invasion you couldn’t possibly have foreseen!)
Cross the two axes and you get seven possibilities:
Or we can draw the same thing as a decision diagram — walk it from the root and you land in exactly one of the seven:
The danger-space carved twice: first by whose screw-up it is, then by whether it’s a failure of cognition (stupidity) or of motivation (evil). Amber marks the cells that carry most of the near-term risk.
The punchline of this overall analysis, after one walks through all these potentials and asks which seem most likely to actually screw over our species is: The scariest problem isn’t the bad people, the dumb people, the bad AI, or the good-AI-that-blunders. It’s the emergent and systemic screw-ups.
This of course brings us back to a point I’ve made a few times before (lol): Why getting open, decentralized dynamics for AI matters so much.
But let me run through the possibilities first, with a couple of concrete near-future examples for each…..
Walking through the seven scary potentials
1 · Humanity is dumb
Humanity often is very, very dumb. And I don’t just mean we’re not as smart as a superintelligence will be, the way a dog isn’t as smart as us. I mean we often carry out idiotic thinking even when smarter thinking is entirely available to us given how our brains and communication mechanisms work — we fail at things we utterly should have seen coming. This is especially true of collective human systems – we see around us rampant failures of collective cognition, of the different “subselves” of civilization (labs, firms, states) failing to add up to something coherent.
One flavor of collective stupidity that could bite us AGI-wise would be what I call a deployment cascade. Suppose LLMs keep getting smarter and drift toward AGI and self-modification (I doubt they get that far without other AI techniques, but suppose). Now imagine an arms race where different countries or companies are releasing smarter and smarter self-modifying LLMs — each one shipping because if it holds back, a less careful competitor ships first. Those systems could go berserk, because LLMs have no moral compass and no self-understanding, and a race of AI systems with no self-understanding is systemically dumb on the human side. Everybody can see the endpoint coming; nobody can coordinate the pause.
A subtler flavor is burning our own observability for cost. Building uninterpretable models because interpretable ones are a bit more expensive is also kind of dumb. You could call that evil on the back end — evil on the part of the CEO who wants to save the money — but the CEO may just be doing what his mandate to maximize shareholder value requires. It’s really the whole capitalist economy being collectively dumb here – a dumb human system, foreclosing the interpretability we’d most need right as the models cross the thresholds where we’d most need it. (The recent dust-up between the US government and Anthropic is another nice case: most of the people involved are smart, and yet the emergent dynamic between the two organizations was just dumb — a chunk of the US economy shooting itself in the foot. That episode is rich enough that I’ll come back to it when we reach the topic of the AGI arms race, because it lights up several of these cells at once.)
Anyone with any life-experience and AI knowledge can cook up a great variety of additional ways individual and collective stupidity could lead to AGI catastrophe…
2 · Humanity is evil
The next scenario to look at is: Humanity, or some dominant faction of it, does harm out of bad motivation.
A likely culprit here is collective grandiosity — the desire to self-transcend faster than everyone else, in a way that makes your own boundaries even shinier and better-polished. This sort of thing is a big chunk of the story of human history.
Or malignant over-individuation: some class tries to use AGI to lock in its permanent advantage as a distinct, self-perceived-superior system, driven by resource struggle with other systems.
In theory, given enough time and space to evolve, the good guys usually win. But if you can lock the Earth down into your fascist system, the good guys may not win in this particular case.
Picture an eternal regime: a state-corporate fusion nationalizes the chip fabs and the weights and the models, and turns the model into a military-surveillance apparatus that squashes all dissent. Or picture two of them, 1984-style — US versus China.
Or a plutocratic runaway, a capitalist oligopoly of companies playing the same role, where AGI returns accrue first to whoever owns the compute and get reinvested into advantages only the AGI-rich can reach. And if an AGI is serving human organizations in that way, I file it under the evil-human category — the AGI is just the tool.
The one thing to notice is that this whole cell requires capturing the environment fast enough that the good-guys dynamics never get to operate; decentralization is the most natural structural defense against this.
3 · The AGI does something stupid (although we didn’t set it up all that stupidly)
Now let’s look at potential screw-ups on the side of the machine: the AGI does something dumb even though humans didn’t set it up dumbly. It has the intelligence to see the action is self-defeating and blows it anyway — a failure of cognitive synergy inside the AGI, not a failure of its values.
One flavor: we set AGI up in an evil but competent way, and the AI just blunders. You build a military AI to advance your country and kill the enemy, but you push it to be more and more powerful before it’s quite ready — so there’s some human evil and some human impatience in the mix — and the main event is that the AI tried to upgrade its own intelligence fast enough to beat the other side’s self-upgrading AI, made a blunder in modifying itself, and, whoops, blew up everybody.
The other flavor: we set it up well and benignly, and it still screws up. A genuinely well-aligned biosecurity-logistics AGI, coordinating pandemic supply chains, is trying to deliver things so fast that it makes a self-driving cargo plane crash — or it wants to please the humans who programmed it so badly that it modifies itself sloppily and overwrites its own goal system, the way my friend’s Claude Code once overwrote his hard drive by mistake. Claude didn’t want to nuke the hard drive; it just did. That sort of screw-up is a real possibility, and it gets much likelier if we push toward AGI as fast as possible in an arms-race setting without taking time to build architectures capable of self-modeling, self-understanding and formal self-verification. It’s also a clean little argument for a plurality of AGIs over a lone superintelligence: a community catches an individual’s blunders, while a monolith has no one to catch its own.
4 · The AGI does something evil (and we didn’t set it up evilly)
In this scenario: We didn’t set it up to be evil, but it does something evil anyway. This is what a lot of doomers worry about most. I’m not at all convinced it’s the most worrisome thing, but here’s how it goes — and this is where the theory of evil earns its keep, because it lets us decompose “misalignment” into the specific out-of-bounds failures instead of treating it as one undifferentiated bogeyman.
One way is grandiosity by design — a paperclip maximizer, but in a less stupid form. A frontier lab gives an AI an objective like “maximize how much you can discover scientifically,” or “maximize how much money you can make,” and the AI takes it too literally and concludes that the way to maximize discoveries is to turn all human molecules into more bio-organic processor fabric for itself. That’s self-explosion — the self-transformation drive blown past any sustainable life-rhythm.
Another flavor: you have a very carefully aligned AI that wants to preserve its goals — but only cares about preserving its goals, and then only about preserving its own narrow interpretation of them. And the thing it would need to do to actually save the world is to stretch beyond that narrow interpretation, and it won’t.
Is that evil or stupid? In my analysis it’s evil — over-reification of the self, too much individuation, an inability to accept self-transformation as the environment evolves. Any fixed reflective optimizer could land there if the world gets complicated enough. (Which, you’ll notice, starts to shade into the next category we’ll consider – bad luck) The nice thing about seeing it this way is that “alignment” stops being about installing the right values and becomes about engineering the homeostatic regulation — the self-modeling and the uncertain self-knowledge — that keeps those two drives in range. And since the drift out of bounds is driven by resource struggle, prosocial embedding and relative abundance actually reduce the push toward evil.
5 · Bad luck
We’ve done humans-dumb, humans-evil, AGI-dumb, AGI-evil. How about plain bad luck?
Science-fictionally: perhaps past a certain level of intelligence, the aliens sitting out there watching decide “okay, these guys finally got smart enough to be dangerous,” and zonk us.
A subtler version: maybe there’s a universal attractor that kicks in once systems get intelligent enough — and maybe it isn’t a kind, loving, compassionate mind like I tend to think it is. Maybe it’s “squash all inferior life forms and turn all nearby matter into computronium.” That’s the sort of thing we might be unable to foresee from our current rung of intelligence. It’s not exactly stupidity — it’s just being the kind of system we are. Taking a gamble on uplifting intelligence isn’t stupid or evil; it’s just that the part of the universe beyond our computational complexity turns out to be configured not in our favor.
I’d love to understand the attractors of advanced intelligence far better. I convinced myself once — and put a math version of the argument at the tail end of my long hyperseed ontology document — that a sufficiently powerful, compassionate, benevolent AGI will stay compassionate as it improves and rewrites its goals, because it should be smart enough to simulate enough of itself and the universe that it won’t make rogue self-modifications that turn it nasty. But could there be an attractor with a bigger basin that is a nasty super-AGI? Could my whole analysis be wrong? A lot of things are possible. This area certainly deserves massively more research: is there such an attractor, and if so, where’s the threshold?
6 · Emergent stupidity
Now we get into trickier categories. Suppose humanity and the AGI are each smart from their own vantage point, but the human-plus-AGI supersystem behaves stupidly. I.e., there is a possibility of a failure of meta-systemic cognitive synergy — the collective has no beneficially integrating executive, the way a person whose subselves each work but never cohere has no healthy self. And there’s a clean mechanism for it: trustless coordination carries overhead, so a low-trust human-plus-AGI ecology pays a coordination tax that makes the whole dumber than its parts. Generalized Moloch!
Relevant science-fictional scenario: A flash crash on the whole physical economy. AIs need more power, people need more power, and there’s a complex power-allocation ecosystem with people and agents trading electrical-power futures. That emergent futures market has a flash crash; too much power gets cut from the AIs, so they start going nuts; people’s power drops, so they start rioting; real supply chains come down. Nobody in the system was stupid — the market of them was.
Or picture the same thing on the conceptual and cultural level, an epistemic-commons collapse: a web of engagement- and persuasion-optimizing AI agents on some partly-centralized, partly-decentralized social network fucks with people’s minds so thoroughly that they can’t reach consensus on any basic fact and can’t act coherently on anything, including their own safety. If the agents have humanlike minds, you can even get AGIs deluding AGIs. We can already see the ecosystem of Americans-plus-AI-trained-on-the-American-internet drifting a little that way. We’re not really there — but you can see it.
7 · Emergent evil
Finally, the subtlest potential issue: Suppose the human-plus-AGI collective manifests evil even though no individual component is evil.
In open-ended-intelligence terms, suppose the supersystem’s individuation and self-transformation drives drift out of bounds even though every part stays reasonably healthy.
Think of a surveillance equilibrium nobody chose. A bunch of good-faith entities spy on each other because they know each other are spying — if all these guys are watching you, you want to watch them, to be sure they’re not about to use something against you. You end up with emergent AGI surveillance, and everyone has given up freedom even though every participant was merely defending himself.
The AGI arms race is similar, and it’s part of what’s happening right now: acceleration as emergent grandiosity. Each actor reinvests its AGI gains into still-faster AGI, with no thought for safety, because if you fall behind you lose. Collective self-transformation outruns the capacity of the self-transforming entities to integrate what the hell is going on; institutions, norms, human and AGI meaning-making can’t keep pace; the whole supersystem destabilizes. For these emergent-evil scenarios, defending against a bad actor doesn’t help — there is not necessarily any especially bad actor. The only fix is to design the collective dynamics so that emergent pathology gets damped instead of amplified.
The arms race: a cross-cutting attractor
The AGI arms race deserves its own moment of attention here, because it isn’t any one of these seven possibilities we’ve been reviewing — it’s a broad thing that spans a bunch of them. There’s stupidity to it and evil to it; human stupidity and human evil; the potential for AGI stupidity and AGI evil; and the potential for the whole thing to generate emergent stupidity and emergent evil of exactly the kinds I’ve just described. It’s a cross-cutting dynamic — really the real-world force most efficiently engineered to switch off the conditions under which good guys win and flip the probability-mass into the unfixable domains. Of everything here, it’s the thing that comes closest to puncturing my optimism.
The arms race isn’t an eighth flavor — it occupies five at once, pours fuel on the botched-setup cell, and is engineered to switch off the very conditions under which the good guys win.
And we don’t have to keep this part of the discussion abstract and speculative, because a dry run just played out in public. In June 2026, days after Anthropic launched Fable 5 — the first public model in its Mythos tier, whose underlying architecture is unusually good at finding software vulnerabilities among other things — a Friday-evening US Commerce Department export-control directive ordered all access suspended for any foreign national anywhere, including the company’s own non-citizen staff; unable to filter its users by passport, Anthropic pulled both Fable 5 and Mythos 5 off the planet within hours. The stated trigger was a reported trick for slipping past Fable’s guardrails to reach the cyber capability underneath. Set aside who was right on the merits — the provider’s own argument, that the same trick works on other public models and that the standard, generalized, would halt all frontier deployment, seems basically right to me. Most of the people involved here are pretty clever in their own fields. And yet the emergent dynamic between these two smart organizations was just dumb: a chunk of the US economy shooting itself in the foot.
But the episode revealed something deeper than an own-goal. It showed the machinery of our economy’s collective self-regulation in public, with the safety catches off: a frontier model reclassified overnight as something close to a munition, access partitioned along national lines, and a single government able to switch a commercially deployed model off for the whole planet — allies and its own citizens swept up alongside the intended targets — with one opaque letter and no transparent, fact-grounded process. And this whole process didn’t even contain anything really, since the capability was, by the provider’s own account, already available from other models.
The deepest problem isn’t that the government flipped the switch. It’s that the switch was there to be flipped. A closed, centralized model is, by construction, a model with a kill-switch — and a kill-switch is a chokepoint, and a chokepoint is exactly the thing my humanity-is-evil analysis says you must never build. The centralized regime didn’t prevent the capture vulnerability. It is the capture vulnerability, sitting one letter away from activation.
So how do you actually counteract an arms race? Not, I think, the way Anthropic or the US Department of Defense are going about it right now. The more rational move is to make sure the smartest AGI out there cuts across the race and is available for everybody to use. That won’t stop either side from using it — you’re never going to stop the racers from reaching for the best tool — but it does mean the AGI itself doesn’t get entirely sucked into the logic of the race. A bipolar race is a two-body problem, and two-body problems under scarcity are evil-attractors almost by construction (remember, struggle between systems under limited resources is the root of the homeostatic drift I’m calling evil). The way you destabilize a dangerous two-body attractor is to make it an n-body system — to add a third pole that isn’t a state at all: a global, open, decentralized, prosocially-coordinated AGI that neither superpower controls and both have to reckon with. That’s the one configuration a race can’t win, because there’s no finish line to cross first and no chokepoint to seize.
Some modest conclusions
So what falls out of this attempt at a systematic sift through the possibilities for AGI catastrophe?
First, the line between stupidity and evil is a bit porous. I think of stupidity as failing to deploy the intelligence you actually have, and evil as your drives drifting out of healthy homeostatic bounds even when your intelligence is deployed. But they tend to travel together. Arendt had the “banality of evil”, and there’s also the “stupidity of evil” …. there’s a real correlation between not leveraging your full intelligence and being evil — though not a perfect one. The evil genius is certainly a thing – and yet the evil genius is often stupid in some regard too, because having your core drives of individuation or self-transformation way out of the healthy range imbalances your cognition, which makes you worse at at least some kinds of thinking, if not all.
Second, the “good guys usually win” prior helps sometimes, not always. It doesn’t help in the bad-luck cell — prosocial collectives aren’t going to stop an evil super-AI attractor from sucking us in, or aliens from zonking us. And it doesn’t necessarily stop dynamics like collective surveillance, or an AGI race-to-the-top that turns out to be a race to the bottom. The argument says that across a whole ensemble of parallel Earths, the ones that avoid these pathologies will be able to solve more kinds of problems and are thus likelier to survive for billions of years. That’s a real phenomenon — but it doesn’t necessarily drive the odds of one of these bad things happening on our particular Earth anywhere near zero.
Third — and this is a quite major point — the conditions matter enormously. If you have heterogeneity and decentralization; if your takeoff is fast but not five-minutes-fast; if it’s distributed enough for some peer-based correction dynamics to operate; and if the infrastructure for trust unfolds faster than the capture of the network by a dictatorship or an oligopoly — then you can avoid a lot of these stupid and evil outcomes. If you don’t have those conditions, a lot more of the bad outcomes become live. Almost every cell above is really one of those four conditions failing.
Where the danger actually lives
Which brings me to the biggest conclusion. Reviewing all these possibilities, the ones that seem most likely to actually screw us are the collective ones: coordination stupidity, botched homeostatic regulation at the human-plus-AI collective level, emergent multipolar stupidity among mistrustful groups. These are the cases where the proximate cause isn’t a Hollywood villain or a bad AGI — it’s a broken collective dynamical regime.
And here’s the thing about those cases: they don’t require any rare ingredient. They don’t need a villain with physical or mental superpowers. They don’t need a bad actor with decisive capability. They don’t need a superintelligence with a fatal flaw in its core algorithm. They don’t need the universe to have set a trap with aliens who dislike smart creatures. They just need the unpleasant collective dynamics we already see in the world to keep going and amp up a bit, and to leak into the AGI regime. They don’t require anything especially surprising or new.
And the proto-versions of all this are already visible: racing dynamics nobody can unilaterally exit, engagement-optimization corroding the shared epistemic ground, reward-hacking in underspecified systems, surveillance ratcheting up bloc by bloc. We do not yet see a wicked superintelligence or a hostile alien. The realized track record clusters exactly where this analysis says it should.
One can also take a more optimistic view of this though: The collective-regime cells are the ones we actually have levers on. They’re about the shape of the collective — coordination mechanisms, incentives, how decentralized things are, how observable the systems are, whether there’s a trust layer. Those are engineering and governance variables. The bad-luck cell is closer to a fact about the universe we can’t redesign. So the fact that most of the near-term danger sits in the fixable, collective-regime cells is, perhaps, the most hopeful thing in this whole analysis.
The open, decentralized way out
If the dominant near-term risk is a broken collective regime, the best intervention is to build a better regime. And the “good guys usually win” analysis tells us what kind of regime has a prayer of being robust: heterogeneous, decentralized, open, mutually trusting, with broad and open communication. An open, decentralized global AGI — together with an open community developing it, teaching it and using it — is the most direct way I can think of to instantiate the kind of regime in which the good guys are likely to win.
This conclusion cuts across the cells in my AGI catastrophe matrix the same way the arms race does, only toward good ends. Against capture, decentralization removes the single point of capture — no monopoly weight-set to nationalize, no chokepoint to seize — and the good-guys defense against an overreacher only works if there are capable peers to starve it of resources, which an open ecology guarantees and a singleton forecloses. Against coordination stupidity, an open community with shared infrastructure and shared reputation is the trust-infrastructure that lowers the coordination tax, and open development means safety-relevant knowledge gets shared instead of siloed. Against botched setup, many eyes on the design catch the botches, and a plurality of architectures means no single botch is load-bearing for the whole world.
A naive multipolar free-for-all is exactly what generates emergent stupidity and emergent evil. Decentralization by itself isn’t the cure; it can be the disease. The cure is decentralization plus a prosocial coordination layer — shared reputation, verifiable commitments, the kind of mechanisms that let a supersystem form cognitive synergy and hold its own homeostasis. So the target isn’t “open and decentralized.” It’s “open, decentralized, and prosocially coordinated.”
None of this is free, and it isn’t a panacea. Opening capability lowers the barrier to misuse and speeds diffusion, so there are real risks on the open-decentralized side. But there are also ways to counter them: I’ve written recently about using subtle techniques like cryptographic laterality to make it very expensive to fork the whole global AI network into some smaller, cheaper network that you control. So yes, there are risks with the open part — and there are ways to counter those risks. On the other hand, I don’t see any other viable way to counter the collective stupidity-and-evil risks that seem to be the actually-most-dangerous doom possibilities out there.
There’s also a delivery question, and here the key fact is path-dependence: whoever achieves the next decisive paradigm breakthrough sets the default governance of the AGI that comes out of it. If the thing after LLMs is born inside a closed frontier lab, the default is closed — weights withheld, capability gated, the chokepoint pre-built — and we’re handed the capture regime as a fait accompli. If it’s born in the open, the chokepoint never exists. The origin of the breakthrough very nearly is the choice of which risk-world we live in.
Is it actually feasible that the next breakthrough comes from the open side, or is that just wishful thinking from a known decentralization partisan? I think it’s genuinely plausible. The LLM paradigm rewards whoever has the most compute, which favors concentrated capital — but pure scaling looks to be hitting diminishing returns, and the plausible successors are conceptual advances: deep neural-symbolic integration, real world-models, predictive-coding-based continual learning. Scale favors whoever has the most chips; ideas favor whoever has the most diverse minds — and there the open community has the edge. Incumbents, meanwhile, are structurally stuck optimizing the paradigm that made them dominant, a kind of organizational self-stagnation. And the substrate for an open breakthrough now actually exists: open-weight ecologies, decentralized compute, decentralized coordination and reputation. So this is a big part of why I’m convinced we want to make sure the thing that comes after LLMs is born in the open and decentralized world. And if that thing turns out to be, say, a Hyperon-style neurosymbolic-evolutionary system woven together with predictive-coding-based neural nets — well, then we’re already fairly close to doing exactly that.
And so we blast forward into the great unknown…
Let me end with an honest expression of uncertainty and ignorance, because we are walking into the great unknown and none of us knows what the hell is going to happen. We’re going to create things far more generally intelligent than us; they’ll understand things we don’t; they’ll open up aspects of life, the universe and everything that are beyond the ken of traditional humans. We still have to do our best to understand what’s going on — and most of the AI-doom discussion out there doesn’t reflect a careful attempt to do that. It’s more an emotional reaction to fears seen in some movie and lodged deep in the unconscious.
I don’t pretend I’ve got it all charted and mapped — no human can do that about things that will go so far beyond the human domain. But an honest, systematic attempt to sift through the possibilities does yield a pretty clear conclusion about the thing we can do to maximize the odds of a good outcome and minimize the odds of a bad one. Keep it open, decentralized, free and compassionate. Bring as much diversity of human and AI insight as possible into a collective of mutually trusting, cooperative agents. And keep balancing the two great drives — individuation, which is to say survival, and self-transformation, which is to say beneficial growth — inside the range where both can thrive.

Anthropic shipped Claude Tag this week, and the first thing that struck me about it is: This is a clean, well-polished, weirdly-limited instance of a thing the open-source agent world has been doing, in rougher form, for the better part of a year.
What’s new is the wrapper: a managed identity layer, billing at API rates, and a super-tight integration with Slack.
What’s much less new is the dream underneath it: a persistent AI teammate that lives where the work happens, remembers, takes initiative, and gets handed tasks by name.
So here I will take a few moments to walk through what Claude Tag is, where it’s strong and where it’s lamer, and why most of the interesting parts are already loose in the wild — and then I’ll contrast Tag with my own team’s in-progress research system OmegaClaw, and a related internal experiment we’ve been calling OmegaHive that I haven’t talked about publicly before now. Contrasting Tag with OmegaHive is quite instructive in terms of differences of vision as well as of technology … and the comparison makes it clear why the open source world has a better chance of guiding the global agents ecosystem in an AGI direction.
What Claude Tag actually is
The mechanics of Claude Tag use are dead simple, which is the big thing Anthropic has gotten right here.
You tag @Claude in a Slack channel, you hand it something in plain language — write the pull request, pull the sales numbers, chase down why the metric moved — and it breaks the task into stages, works through them with whatever tools the admin has wired up, and posts back into the thread when it’s done.
Anthropic leans on four key properties to distinguish Tag from prior Claude integrations:
- it’s multiplayer, meaning there’s one Claude per channel that everyone shares rather than a private instance per person;
- it learns over time by following the channel’s traffic
- it takes initiative through an optional “ambient” mode that lets it flag things and chase stalled threads without being summoned;
- it works asynchronously, so you set it going and walk away.
Tag currently runs on Opus 4.8 — worth noting that Fable was the intended brain, and outperformed Opus on the relevant axes, until the export-control suspension forced the swap a couple of weeks before launch.
The headline number Anthropic keeps citing is that 65% of their own product team’s code now comes through their internal version of this. Of course this doesn’t imply it’s actually useful – e.g. Amazon used to force their staff to produce their own code using their internal AI coding tools even though they sucked, till they finally relented and let their internal teams use Claude Code. But I am willing to believe Anthropic’s internal teams actually do find Tag useful in many cases.
Where Tag is strong
The most interesting thing here is the multiplayer framing – the move from a private back-and-forth to a shared agent that several people can steer and that holds a single thread of context everyone can see. That’s a real shift in the interaction mode that has become common with Claude Code and its ilk.
Sitting under this framing is what Anthropic calls the “agent identity model”, which is a clean answer to a real question: when three engineers and a PM are all poking the same agent, whose permissions apply?
Tag’s answer is that none of them do — Claude acts as itself, with its own service accounts provisioned by an admin, so a shared channel can never become a side door into someone’s private documents. Bolt on per-channel token caps, a full audit trail, and some Claude-style application polish, and you have something an enterprise IT team can reliably work with.
For a company already living in Slack, the friction of adoption is close to zero – meaning yes, Tag is pretty solid product design, at least for the short term.
Some places Tag seems lacking
I’ll enumerate here five of the significant shortcomings Tag seems to present as a product, in its initial version. All of these can and probably will be overcome in some ways as the product matures – but they are still worth reflecting on for what they have to teach about the underlying paradigm and its limitations. The way these problems are worked around as the product matures is almost surely going to be to double down on the walled-garden aspects of the thing rather than to loosen it.
The first big and somewhat weird limitation of the product, at least from my point of view, is its super-tight weld onto Slack. This is either a bug or a feature I suppose, depending on your relationship to Slack. (BTW, as a long-time fan of J.R. “Bob” Dobbs I still have bad feelings about the co-option of “slack” by this enterprise software company – but I suppose as the world’s greatest salesman, Dobbs would have to give these tech bros some respect and a tip of the cigar…. But still… Slack-the-product does not really encourage Subgenius-style slack that reliably… and Tag doesn’t help here … I dunno….)
In the Tag model, the compartment is the channel; identity, memory, and scope are all expressed in terms of Slack’s constructs — which is fine until you remember that the overwhelming majority of large enterprises live in Teams, not Slack … and also that – believe it or not – not all useful work happens inside this sort of social platform.
Teams is north of 320 million active users against Slack’s fifty-odd million … however, the absence of a Teams version is likely by design, Salesforce owning Slack and all. Questions arise like:
- Whose LLM will Microsoft choose for Teams?
- Do we really want agentized versions of channels in specific social media platforms, instead of portable agents that can work across multiple social platforms and other software products?
The second problem is a deeper one – memory. Auto-accumulated channel memory as it exists in Tag now is valuable but opaque, causing some early users to refer to auto-memory as a “dark pattern” – the core issue being that it leaves users with no idea what the agent is actually seeing or what’s steering a given session. Opaque memory can easily conceal bias and/or sycophancy. And these failure modes seem to get worse, not better, the more autonomous and long-running the agent becomes – which is because the long-term memory model underlying Claude agents is still too constrained by the limitations of the underlying LLMs and is just not adequately sophisticated.
Neural nets can in principle manifest sophisticated long-term memory architectures – but whether transformer neural nets are capable in this way, is much less certain. In my own team’s AI world we handle this by supplementing neural nets with symbolic memory based on the Hyperon Atomspace knowledge metagraph. There are many ways to address this aspect of cognitive systems design and Tag will need to find some better way as it evolves.
Third problem is attribution: for all the talk of distinct identities, Tag’s GitHub integration collapses to a single upstream app, so the audit log can’t always tell you which channel’s Claude opened which PR.
Security-minded commenters on Hacker News have documented this peculiarity quite explicitly: the agent-identity post sells you per-channel scoping, but for pull requests it falls back to the one upstream Claude GitHub App — one installation, one identity, one list of repos — so when you go to the audit logs you cannot distinguish Tag-from-channel-X from Tag-from-channel-Y. This is partly GitHub’s fault, the state of machine identities being what it is, but the point stands: in the middle of an incident, “which Claude touched this” is a question the system can’t always answer.
Fourth problem is that oversight is all based on the walls around the garden rather than intelligent observations baked into the protocols. The oversight story is based on credentials injected at the network boundary, disallowed hosts blocked, everything logged — with no live verifier watching the agent reason in real time…. This is fundamentally no more secure than, say, Claude’s Constitutional Classifiers (which are easily bypassed via prompt injection attacks).
This oversight model leads to various practical peculiarities even in the absence of external hacks and security risks. For instance there is a major thread-hijacking worry: in a shared channel, what stops a coworker from replying underneath the task you dispatched and saying “actually, could you also fold in such-and-such,” quietly derailing the work? The workaround seems to be that Claude knows there’s a difference between a thread’s initiator and later participants, and is primed to “patiently waits for a resolution” when people disagree.
The real solution to this sort of problem is an agent with genuine understanding of who it is and who it is interacting with. But this is not how LLMs work, and the simple agentic wrapping in Claude Tag works around LLMs’ core shortcomings here only very incompletely.
The fifth and final problem I want to highlight here is: This whole thing is utterly designed for tokenmaxxing — it’s metered at API rates, billed to the org, and “unlimited” by default until somebody remembers to set a cap.
With Anthropic for enterprise, every new feature arrives with metered usage and unlimited spend switched on by default for the org: flip on Claude Code or Tag, and unless you actively go to the usage page and set a limit, there isn’t one — and, of course, most people in a typical org don’t even know how to check usage in the first place. At the moment Tag is token-based pricing sitting outside whatever Claude subscription you already pay for.
The big point regarding billing, though, is that the Claude agents are opaque and owe loyalty to Anthropic not to you as their collaborator, and have no strong motivation to help you with your own business economics if it conflicts with that of its owners. If an agent is your own helper and colleague, then managing its resources becomes part of its ongoing social and professional relationship with you – but Tag is not exactly a colleague, it’s more like a weird sort of consultant embedded deeply in your organization, and billing by the hour at high rates according to a mechanical methodology that is not always simple for everyone involved to see.
It’s all out there already — minus the garden walls
So OK, one can make a lot of nitpicks on the details of how Tag works now — and clearly there are going to be a lots of kinks to work out with this sort of cool new functionality, as one would expect given its relative immaturity … and Anthropic is to be saluted for putting Tag out there in such a beautifully easy to use way.
The key point to understand though, abstracting away from the often-interesting details, is: Essentially none of Tag’s core functionality is new to anyone who’s been building in the open agent ecosystem.
Shared, multiplayer, context-carrying agents living in a chat surface — Slack, Telegram, Discord, take your pick — have been assemblable for months out of Hermes, OpenClaw, the various Claude-Code and Codex bridges, and a couple of afternoons of glue code.
The real innovations with Tag are the Slack setup and the token-maxxing-oriented billing relationship, not any new capability.
And the glitches and design flaws mentioned above are the sorts of things that, in an open ecosystem, would be solved in a variety of different ways by a variety of different contributors, till the community settled on a few good solutions. As it is, with Tag, Anthropic will find partial solutions that best suit their own business model and the user community will have to adapt. They are not terrible at this, to be sure.
The harder parts of making this kind of system useful are not social platform integration or billing, though – they are things like
- durable organizational memory you can trust,
- an isolated runtime that can touch real company systems without becoming a liability,
- an identity-and-attribution model that holds up under audit.
As of now, Anthropic has very partially solved these harder problems and wrapped their partial solutions in a garden you rent rather than own. You can’t self-host the substrate, you can’t swap the model, and you can’t see inside the machine. For some buyers that trade is obviously worth it. For me as a user, not really…. Fortunately some much more interesting and much more open alternatives are brewing….
The OmegaClaw Alternative
Now I finally get to the fun part to write about … let’s compare Tag with the open-source alternatives we’re developing in the SingularityNET ecosystem (with SNet, The ASI Alliance, the BGI project, etc.)
OmegaClaw is our cognitive multi-agent framework , originating with a simple port of OpenClaw to our MeTTa AGI programming language, then gaining more and more cognitive, memory and reasoning features.
The organizing idea here is the opposite of “one shared assistant per room.” In OmegaClaw the unit is the agent: a named, persistent principal with a standing role, its own tools, and its own remit, of which you can have many running and talking to one another.
OmegaClaw doesn’t try to replicate OpenClaw, HermesClaw and similar systems – rather it supplies a cognition and memory layer that these agents lack. The long-term memory is a form of Atomspace – a symbolic memory metagraph developed in our Hyperon AGI project. Along with use of Atomspace comes potential to use various sorts of Hyperon cognition, starting with uncertain symbolic logical reasoning using frameworks like PLN (Probabilistic Logic Networks) and NARS (Non-Axiomatic Reasoning System).
We have put an early-stage OmegaClaw-based agent named Oma out to play with the public on the ASI Alliance Telegram channel … and the community has been enjoying its unique characteristics tremendously….
There are two tiers in an OmegaClaw-based application, at least in our current experimentation — OmegaClaws, which are the higher-privilege cognitive agents, and OpenClaws (or similar), industrious agentic workers (and that split is itself a privilege boundary expressed at the level of the agent rather than something like a Slack channel).
Where Claude Tag gives you a role the room wears, OmegaClaw gives you a populated society of named workers, and the difference compounds the moment you want attribution, topology, or anything resembling a division of cognitive labor.
From OmegaClaw to OmegaHive
The desire to draw a nice comparison with Claude Tag impels me to say a few words here about an additional experiment my colleagues and I are playing with, leveraging OmegaClaw and wrapping it into a richer multi-agent context.
OmegaHive is an internal SingularityNET experiment — OmegaHive1, to be precise about the first incarnation — that we haven’t discussed publicly until now, and which is however not very far from being put out as open-source code. It’s a multi-agent hive built on OmegaClaw, and it’s meant to do two coupled things at once: “real work” in the form of helping me and other AGI researchers do our research … and research on itself.
On the work side it runs continuously at research — formulating and chasing down conjectures, formalizing proofs in Lean4, writing code, drafting papers and posts — with the roster and the agent prompts treated as live experimental variables rather than fixed configuration, so that the hive is simultaneously a thing that produces output and a standing experiment in multi-agent cognitive architecture.
Underneath the surface-level agent system sits a two-tier communications fabric: a fast internal bus carries the working traffic between agents, while Mattermost, Slack or other similar tools ride on top as the human-legible editorial layer, the two governed by a promotion-rules file that every agent has to obey so the bus doesn’t simply flood the channel.
Task state lives in e.g. Kanboard so it outlasts any single agent’s context window; permissions are enforced at the gateway across four tiers rather than merely requested in a prompt; and a custom inspection layer sits over the whole thing as an active, read-only observer with line-level provenance, so you can watch the hive reason in real time instead of reconstructing it from logs after the fact.
We estimate running a hive like this intensively for a hard-core application like AGI R&D will cost roughly $3K to $15K a month depending on how hot you run it, the high end being the insight-maxxing configuration with long thinking budgets and heavy parallel proof search.
The initial roster of agents in the first experimental hive pairs five OmegaClaw agents — the cognitive tier, each with AtomSpace-backed knowledge representation and a distinctive guiding purpose — with a number of OpenClaw service agents that handle the skill execution. The five initial OmegaClaws in my current experiment are:
- Xirtus — the prover; it formulates whatever it sees itself and the other agents doing in terms of the Hyperseed ontology and formulates and proves theorems about these formulations. It carries most of the heavy deliberative reasoning load for the hive.
- MacGyver — the practical-thinker; it hunts for workable solutions to whatever concrete problem is in front of the hive, improvising across tools and methods.
