A journalist wrote me earlier today asking for a quick comment on the Zcash situation — by which he meant the Orchard pool bug that just lopped something on the order of forty percent off the price of ZEC over the span of a day or so — and whether other cryptocurrencies are exposed to the same sort of risk.
Indeed, I do suspect what we’re looking at here is a small early tremor of something considerably larger that’s coming for essentially all the software in the world — not just the crypto corner of it, and not even mostly the crypto corner of it, though crypto is one place it happens to be showing up first and most visibly.
The specific bug that bit Zcash is not going to bite anyone else, because it was a specific bug — a subtle under-constrained element buried in the Orchard circuit, down in the elliptic-curve arithmetic, where a constraint that was supposed to enforce a particular check on transaction inputs quietly failed to actually enforce it. The upshot, at least in principle, was that someone could have minted counterfeit ZEC inside the shielded pool without leaving any trace on the transparent ledger — a supply-inflation problem rather than the more familiar double-spend, and a particularly nasty one precisely because Orchard is private by design, which means there is no cryptographic way to go back and prove the thing was never exploited during the years it sat there. Strip away the zero-knowledge exotica and what you have is a plain old logic error: a place where the code did not in fact do the thing its designers were confident it was doing.
One striking thing here is the way this flaw lived undetected for roughly four years — it had been there since Orchard went live back in May of 2022 — and in that time it survived multiple rounds of review by some of the very best zero-knowledge cryptographers on the planet, people who do this for a living and are extremely good at it. And it was finally caught not by yet another careful human audit, but by a security researcher (Taylor Hornby, working under Shielded Labs) pointing a current-generation AI model at the Orchard circuit and, more or less in a single concentrated effort, watching it surface the gap. The model in question, as it happens, was Anthropic’s Opus 4.8. So the AI implications for crypto aren’t some speculative thing I have to gesture at hypothetically — the AI implication is sitting right there in the etiology of this very incident: an AI found, in a matter of days, what four years of world-class human scrutiny did not.
So, to answer the journo’s core question: Are other cryptocurrencies vulnerable to this? To this exact bug, no — it was an implementation error particular to the Zcash codebase. But are other cryptocurrencies, and other smart-contract platforms, and DeFi protocols, and bridges, and wallets, very likely to harbor analogous vulnerabilities of their own — subtle logic gaps that have likewise been sitting quietly through multiple audits? Almost certainly yes: I’d expect a meaningful fraction of them to be found over the coming weeks and months, and I’d expect AI tools to be doing most of the finding. The economics of bug-finding are simply too favorable now. A capability that previously required a scarce, expensive specialist and weeks of attention can increasingly be deployed at scale and at speed, and the same kind of targeted circuit review that turned up the Orchard flaw can be turned, more or less mechanically, on the next protocol, and the one after that.
And this is in no way a crypto-specific problem, even though crypto is one of the places the spotlight is right now. The software infrastructures of banks, payment networks, clearing systems, insurers, exchanges, government agencies — the whole sprawling, decades-deep accretion of centralized financial and institutional code — is every bit as likely to be riddled with serious, long-dormant bugs that the same class of AI tools will start to surface in the near future. If anything the crypto codebases, being newer, smaller, open-source, and written by people who are at least nominally paranoid about exactly this category of failure, are probably in better shape than the average sixty-million-line legacy core-banking system that nobody alive fully understands anymore. The reckoning that’s arriving for crypto is arriving for everyone else too.
The cure for this ailment is well understood, and we mostly haven’t bothered
Here’s the part that I find genuinely heartening, though, and it’s the part that tends to get lost when these stories get told as pure doom. The solution to this whole category of problem is not unknown, not exotic, and not waiting on some future research breakthrough. It is simple and well established and goes by the name of formal verification: you prove, using mathematics, that the software actually does what it was designed to do — not test it, not audit it, not eyeball it very hard, but prove it, with the same kind of deductive certainty you’d want behind a textbook math theorem.
A formally verified implementation of the Orchard circuit would not have shipped with that under-constrained element, because the proof obligation would simply have failed to discharge; the gap would have announced itself at build time rather than four years and several billion dollars of market cap later.
The reason we don’t do this everywhere already is not that we can’t — it’s that it takes extra work. Not at all surprisingly, the software industry, left to its own incentives, has consistently chosen to ship faster rather than ship provably-correct. Rust, which is the language the Zcash circuit code (the halo2 gadgets crate, as it happens) was written in, is perfectly amenable to formal verification — there’s a whole healthy ecosystem of tooling for exactly this — but it’s simply not commonly used, because verifying carries a real cost in effort and time that, until very recently, was hard to justify against the next deadline. What needs to happen — and what I think is going to be forced to happen, partly by exactly the sort of incident we just watched — is a broad shift in the norms of software practice, toward a world in which formal verification is the default expectation rather than a luxury reserved for avionics, nuclear control systems and academic researchers.
When Cardano formally verified its Ourobors consensus mechanisms years ago, it was a big deal to have such an academic technique used in the actual commercial blockchain world. This sort of practice and more now needs to become the norm.
Some languages make this harder than others. Solidity, the workhorse language for an enormous share of the world’s smart contracts, presents real challenges for tractable formal verification — enough so that a number of blockchain networks would need a moderate amount of re-implementation before they could be verified in any practical way. That’s not a counsel of despair, it’s just a cost that has to be reckoned with honestly: some of the existing crypto stack can be hardened more or less in place, and some of it is going to have to be partly rebuilt on foundations that are friendlier to proof.
What we’re doing with ASI:chain — and why “correct by construction” beats “verified after the fact”
All is very much on my mind beyond the latest news headlines, because it’s precisely the discipline we’re building into the ASI:chain layer-1 work my team is now doing at SingularityNET, in collaboration with Greg Meredith’s team at F1R3FLY.io. We’re using formalization-friendly methods throughout — but we’re also going a step further than the usual write-it-then-verify-it loop, which is itself a meaningful improvement over the prevailing write-it-then-hope approach. For key parts of the system, rather than programming the software in the conventional sense and then attempting to prove the resulting artifact correct, we’re deriving the software directly from its mathematical specification, so that it comes out correct by construction — the implementation and its proof of correctness are, in effect, two views of the same underlying mathematical object, and there’s no gap between “what we meant” and “what we built” for a bug like the Orchard one to hide in.
To make this concrete: I spent a fair chunk of last month working out a way to derive consensus mechanisms for ASI:chain in exactly this correct-by-construction fashion — in particular a variant of the Cordial Miners protocol that is reputation-based, centralized/replicated-ledger-free, and suited to deployment on mesh networks and on weak, heterogeneous processing infrastructure rather than assuming a fleet of beefy, homogeneous, always-on validators. Getting the consensus layer itself out of a mathematical spec, rather than hand-coding it and praying, is the sort of thing that sounded like over-engineering or academic self-indulgence right up until Anthropic started making noise about Mythos.
Of course, none of this is free, it’s all hard but very interesting work – and the hard work needed won’t be confined to fancy financial cryptography. Look at the Rust language itself: a great many of its core libraries are written using “unsafe” constructs, the very escape hatches that step outside the guarantees the language is otherwise so proud of, and those constructs are exactly the parts that are hardest to formally verify. They can, of course, be rewritten in safe, verifiable form — but doing so naively tends to make them slower, which is precisely why nobody’s rushed to do it. The interesting wrinkle is that this apparent tradeoff isn’t actually fundamental: with sufficiently advanced techniques — supercompilation being the oneof my old favorites. Using a Rust supercompiler, you could take the safe, verifiable rewrite and aggressively transform it into something that ends up faster than the original unsafe version, not slower. This way you could have the proof and the performance both. It just takes work, and the right tools, and someone willing to put in the effort.
Problem = Solution
TL;DR – yes, this kind of problem that just hit Zcash is likely to be pervasive — not just across cryptocurrencies but across the centralized institutions that are forever lecturing crypto about its riskiness, and across the unglamorous infrastructure underneath all of it. We are about to find out, in fairly short order and at least partly the hard way, just how much latent fragility has been quietly accumulating in the world’s software all these years. But — and this is the part I keep wanting to emphasize — we already know how to fix it. The mathematical methods are reasonably mature, the tooling exists, the theory is settled; this is advanced engineering and deployment, not blue-sky research. The whole of the challenge lies in actually applying these methods, rapidly and at enormous scale, across the staggering quantity of software that runs the world.
The lovely symmetry of the moment we’re in is that: The same AI capabilities that are about to expose all of these long-buried vulnerabilities — the very tools that found the Orchard bug — are also exactly the tools that can help us do the verification and the correct-by-construction derivation and the safe-and-supercompiled rewriting at a pace and scale that would have been simply unthinkable for human engineers working alone in the pre-coding-agents era. The threat and the remedy are, to a remarkable degree, the same technology pointed in two different directions. Which one wins out is going to depend on how quickly and how seriously we choose to take the current cybersecurity situation
Such interesting times… and bound to get more and more so… at an exponential pace!

I’m writing this sitting in the SeaTac airport lounge waiting for a flight, looking at Bernie Sanders’ latest op-ed about AI, where he proposes that the solution to America’s AI woes is for the government to take a 50% ownership stake in the big tech companies — half the shares, half the board seats, packaged as a “sovereign wealth fund” funded by a one-time tax paid in stock.
OMG … Noooooo !!!
One of the many ironies that’s hit me lately, as AGI moves toward realization and the world at large starts to grasp that AGI really is coming soon, is this: the left wing of US politics — which in many ways I’m deeply sympathetic with, and agree with on many important matters — is more or less diametrically opposed to what I think is right on the two technologies most central to my own work, AI and blockchain.
On social policy, I lean strongly toward the government helping out the poor and the disadvantaged. My mother ran social welfare programs for most of her career, and I came away from watching her triumphs and struggles with a solid understanding that it’s usually not someone’s fault that they’re in a bad economic spot — and that we do a lot of good by helping both adults and kids improve their circumstances with education , with counseling and coaching, and also with practical material assistance. I’m also pacifist by default, if not by dogma; most of America’s military adventures, I think, have made things worse rather than better.
But on blockchain, it seems right now most of the left wants to ban it outright or regulate it into dysfunction, and I think that would be very badly wrong, both morally and pragmatically. Yes, crypto can be abused. It also has amazing potential for good — for coordinating people and AI agents to do cool and useful things in genuinely novel ways.
And on AI, it also seems most of the left wants to regulate it into submission. The implicit logic seems to be: if advanced AI is going to take people’s jobs, then kill the AI, because people need jobs. That’s a terrifyingly short-sighted way of looking at things.
Over-regulating AI is going to be far worse than letting it self-organize and evolve. There could, in principle, be helpful AI regulations — rules that actually guide AI development in a positive direction — but essentially none of the regulations being proposed are of that nature. Almost all of them would make things worse. We’re far better off with minimal AI regulation than with foolish, paranoid or dogmatic AI regulation that holds back progress, or that simply hands ownership to the big companies best at capturing the regulators.
Sanders’ proposal, I think, sits squarely in the large family of well-meaning but wrong-headed ideas about AI and the government’s relationship to it — ideas from left-leaning thinkers whose heart is in the right place but whose mind is not.
White all this seems extremely obvious to me, I can see it isn’t obvious to everyone because I am reading quite a few online comments in support of Sanders’ unintentionally absurdist proposal.
So let’s roll through a few of the details…
What Sanders gets right
Sanders’ core suggestion is to give agency, control, and a share of the AI wealth to the general public, on the grounds that AI models are built on everybody’s data. And that is a noble thing to want, for sure. Modern AI has been built on the accumulated knowledge, creativity, labor, culture, language, science, code, art, and conversation of our entire species — the hate speech and the trolling very much included. So if AI becomes a central productive force on the planet, which indeed is in the midst of happening, its benefits should not accrue only to a handful of billionaires, VCs, and big companies.
The moral intuition here is fairly sound. Sanders is, at last, seeing AI as a civilization-shaping force. AI will change everything.
Where Sanders goes insanely wrong
But the remedy Bernie proposes — the government owning half the shares and appointing half the boards — goes in entirely the wrong direction.
One thing I find interesting is the assumption baked into his proposal: that big companies are going to dominate the future of AI. That doesn’t have to be the case.
AGI is powerful, fast-moving, and not something we fully understand yet. It’s a fragile assumption that AGI will be dominated by a few big firms.
Sanders has understood that AI is going to be big; he hasn’t understood that the moat around the big companies is neither that wide nor that deep. We have open-source AGI projects. We have decentralized AGI projects. There’s an enormous and growing amount of AGI innovation happening all over the place — including my own efforts with SingularityNET, the ASI Alliance, OmegaClaw, and so forth. There is also plenty of serious AGI work outside the US entirely.
Trying to nationalize today’s AI leaders, among its many other problems, builds a long-term policy around a short-term reality — around the assumption that those leaders won’t simply get innovator’s-dilemma’d out of the lead they currently hold.
But let’s grant Bernies “Big Tech Uber Alles” assumption for the sake of argument. Suppose today’s big tech companies do remain utterly central to pushing AGI forward. What are the risks of handing the government a 50% stake and board-level control?
The obvious one: it would slow these companies down and make them dysfunctional and incompetent at the very things they do best.
It’s not that I think government is always bad at fostering innovation — far from it. Public funding built the internet, GPS, modern computing, and a lot of space exploration (much of it military funding, which is another story). US military funding literally invented AI. The NIH has driven amazing medical progress — not perfect, too conservative in many ways, but epically valuable nonetheless. Government is genuinely good at certain kinds of powerful and critical invention.
However, AGI, at this stage, is not likely to fall into this category. AGI research right now is exploratory, uncertain, weird, and extremely fast-moving. It depends on rapid iteration, fierce technical disagreement, speculative architectures, and open-ended experimentation. A company half-governed by political appointees is going to optimize for optics, compliance, and political acceptability. It’s going to move very, very slowly. It’s going to turn into a utility, like the power company.
And then what happens? The center of AI progress moves elsewhere — to open-source networks, smaller companies, foreign companies. At which point the government faces a choice: accept that innovation has moved beyond its control, or try to extend the same control regime to the new innovators — nationalizing every startup the moment it shows promise, or simply outlawing them. Either way, it would be a huge mess which would slow down innovation and lead to all manner of complex new practical dilemmas.
The importance of asking suitably deep questions…
What Sanders’ proposal overlooks is that ownership is not really the crux of the matter. Who holds the stock, who has the board votes — those matter, but they’re surface. The deeper relevant question is: what species of governance and guidance system can actually do what AGI needs? What kind of system can make wise, adaptive, transparent, participatory decisions at the speed and complexity AGI demands?
Our current political system is not the one, that’s for sure. Legislatures move slowly. Regulatory agencies are routinely captured by the industries they’re meant to regulate. Public debate on the big social networks is fragmented, emotionally charged, and easily manipulated. (And nationalizing the social networks wouldn’t solve any of that; it would just create something even more dysfunctional. You have to get far more creative.)
I’ve been thinking about this sort of issue a fair bit lately. My father, Ted Goertzel, is a political sociologist, and he and I have been working on a book called AGI Nation, about what public policy in the US and other modern democracies should look like as AGI unfolds. One of the central notions we’re exploring is what we call creative decentralized governance.
We don’t want to replace human democracy with AI, and nor do we want to let corporations rule the future. What we want is for AI systems to help people enact democracy more intelligently. The question isn’t which federal appointees get to sit on OpenAI’s board. The questions are things like:
- How can citizens meaningfully participate in AI governance?
- How can expert knowledge be integrated without sliding into technocracy?
- How can local communities shape AI deployment in their own lives?
- How can AI systems make their reasoning transparent enough to be challenged?
- How can competing AI systems audit each other?
- How do we avoid both corporate monopoly and government monopoly?
- How can AGI help humanity deliberate better, rather than just shifting power from one institution to another?
These are the sorts of issues my dad and I are trying to address. They don’t seem to be things Bernie Sanders — wonderful, good-hearted human being though he is — is considering.
So what should we actually do?
It’s a long story (which is why we’re writing a book about it), but here are a few clues:
Support decentralized AI infrastructure. Don’t try to ban it. Credit where it’s due: the Trump administration’s openness to crypto is, at least, not standing in the way here….
If the government wants to invest, don’t just buy shares of big tech companies. Invest in open-source and open-science AI. Fund decentralized AI networks and open AGI architectures. Create public AI infrastructure that is genuinely open and decentralized — not monolithically owned and controlled.
Use the tools the government already has well. Antitrust law and interoperability policy are reasonably powerful instruments for preventing lock-in. The point isn’t for the government to own the monopolists; the point is to stop monopolies and oligopolies from forming in the first plac, and bust them up as needed. Foster decentralized tooling and open science, and use antitrust to keep the monopolies from dominating.
Build mechanisms for broad economic sharing that don’t freeze innovation. Maybe we do want a sovereign wealth fund that helps provide a basic income. But that can be done without the government owning shares of a few big companies — it could be done, say, through dividend flows from decentralized AI networks the government helped fund. Public stakes in publicly funded decentralized ventures. We don’t need to replace a corporate monopoly with a government-plus-corporate monopoly that’s just as oligopolistic and even less efficient.
Think globally. Focusing on the US makes sense for those of us here, but AI governance is global — it has to be species-wide. If we reform AI in a way that’s confined to the US, then whether we intend to or not, we’re feeding the AI-arms-race narrative, which is destructive and harmful at best and existentially catastrophic at worst. The right long-term frame isn’t US government ownership of US AI companies. It’s: how do we foster the emergence of open, cooperative, international, decentralized institutions capable of guiding AI for the benefit of all sentient beings?
Not rigidly-constrained nationalized quasi-AGI bureacracy — self-organizing global decentralized AGI for broad human benefit
Summing up…
- Bernie is right that it’s wrong for a handful of billionaires running a handful of tech companies to decide the future of AI — and thus, potentially, the future of our species and its successors. He’s right that the public deserves a share in the wealth generated from humanity’s collective knowledge. He’s right that AI governance must be democratized.
- But a mechanism as blunt as giving the government 50% control of the big tech companies would almost certainly cause more harm than good. Fortunately, it has essentially no chance of actually happening.
To say it differently:
We don’t want the government to nationalize big AI.
We want to make sure AGI never becomes “big AI” in the first place.
A fortunate fact is, we more or less do know how to achieve this. The AGI research community (including my team in the SingularityNET ecosystem) does actually know better ways of building AGI than what big tech is doing — including ways suited to running on open, decentralized networks — and we’re getting more and more people interested in building such things. We could use help, including from the government. But reifying today’s big-AI oligarchy into an oligarchic government bureaucracy is not actually going to be helpful.
It’s disappointing, as someone who’s been sympathetic to many aspects of the political left for a long time, to watch the left try to impose an archaic way of thinking onto something fundamentally new. The left often has its heart in the right place — but you have to have your mind in the right place too. My hope is that the book my dad and I are writing can add a little more depth of thinking across the whole political spectrum on these critical issues.
In the end, if we’re going to have a positive outcome, the best route is for humanity to build AGI together. This has to go beyond left versus right, and it has to go beyond US versus China versus Russia. It has to transcend ideological, national, and global divisions, and return to the source of what brings us together in the first place: our common human bodies, human minds, human species — our compassion, our ambition, our fears. We have to go back to that commonality, and from there work together to think up genuinely innovative, creative, powerful solutions for guiding AGI’s growth… solutions that match (and can adapt with) the power of the astonishing technologies we’re bringing into this world. We need an innovative energetic decentralized community to help turn rough proto-solutions like the ones I’ve sketched above — and my dad and I are fleshing out in more detail in our book — into impactful realities…

A new mathematical framework joining grammar theory, large-scale typological evidence, and the architecture of continual learning. This is part 2 of 3.
I described for you last time how the linguistic universals observed empirically across multiple human languages, display properties that map very neatly into causal-coding based neural architectures. Now I’ll take the next step and explain how this correspondence can be put into a much more general mathematical and conceptual form – a general morphic mapping between language patterns and cognitive patterns!
Making the bridge precise
The alignment of universal grammatical patterns with causal-coding-related cognitive patterns, when I first stumbled across it, smelled to me like an indication of some sort of deeper mathematical order. And this order wasn’t sooooo hard to find. In this paper I work out the mathematical machinery that makes the relationship between linguistic universals and cognitive architecture into a precise correspondence rather than a list of analogies. The framework is category-theoretic, but the conceptual content is straightforward and worth understanding even if you skip the formalism.
The picture has three layers, which are also three different kinds of mathematical object. On the left is the cognitive substrate — a continual learner whose internal state is causally factorized into modules and whose contexts induce update operators with bounded support. In the middle are semantic frames — argument-role frames, person and number frames, force-dynamic frames, possession frames, spatial frames, attention frames, and the other meaning-pattern schemas that frame semantics has been cataloguing for decades. On the right are linguistic TUG cores — the typological side, the actual cross-linguistic patterns that the data record. The two arrows in between are the operations that translate one layer to the next: extract the frame-level structure that a cognitive module supports, then externalize those frames into linguistic form.
The three-layer correspondence between cognition, semantic frames, and language. The forward direction is direct image; the reverse direction is weakest pullback.
The middle layer is essential. It would be too rigid to map directly from cognitive modules to surface linguistic features — a single causal module typically supports a cluster of related schemas, and a linguistic feature usually externalizes only a part of one such schema, often through an interface that mixes meaning, sound, and morphology. Semantic frames are where the action lives: they’re abstract enough to be shared across cognitive substrates but structured enough to determine recognizable linguistic patterns. A person hierarchy isn’t merely a syntactic pattern; it’s the externalized trace of a frame distinguishing speech-act participants from third parties. A case hierarchy isn’t merely a list of morphological markings; it’s the externalized trace of an argument-role frame.
Once the three-layer picture is in place, two precise statements drop out, and they package up the whole thesis.
Claim one: linguistic universals are direct images of cognitive invariants. A cognitive invariant is a pattern in the cognitive substrate that’s stable across contexts. “Direct image” is the mathematical version of pushing a pattern forward through a structure-preserving map. If a cognitive pattern is stable inside the mind, and if the language-production system preserves the relevant structure, then the image of that cognitive pattern shows up downstream as a linguistic regularity. The first arrow in the diagram is what does the pushing.
Claim two: cognitive universals are weakest pullback explanations of stable linguistic subobjects. This is the inverse direction. “Pullback” is the categorical version of asking what upstream structure must have existed to produce a given downstream pattern. Given a stable linguistic universal, you can pull it back through the diagram to ask what cognitive structure would have to be in place to produce it. “Weakest” is doing crucial work here: among all the cognitive structures that would suffice, you pick the one that introduces the least extra commitment, the fewest unnecessary distinctions, the smallest amount of double-counting.
Together these two statements say: cognition pushes forward into language, and language pulls back to cognition, and a quantitative Occam principle picks out the right answer when the inverse problem is underdetermined.
Why weakness is the right selection principle
The inverse direction, in its use of Occam’s Razor, hits right at the core of general-intelligence theory. When you start from a stable typological pattern and try to infer what cognitive structure produced it, the data don’t usually pick out a unique answer. Many cognitive architectures could in principle generate the same surface regularity. You need a selection principle, and the classic Occam’s Razor principle – “shortest description” — is awkward in this context. A short description can be wrong-headed. A long description can be the natural one. What you actually want is the explanation that commits to as little as necessary, that doesn’t multiply hidden distinctions, that doesn’t represent the same dependency through several overlapping mechanisms when one would do.
The framework I’ve been calling quantale weakness – building on Michael Timothy Bennett’s elegant set-theoretic “weakness” concept – gives this idea an algebraic form. It generalizes Occam’s razor from “shorter description = better” to “fewer unnecessary distinctions = better,” and it lets you compare explanations along several axes at once: how much admissible indistinction they preserve, how well they fit the data, how costly they are, how much cross-context confusion they introduce, and — crucially — how much they double-count the same dependency through redundant pathways. An explanation wins not because someone called it elegant, but because it dominates its competitors in this product order.
This is what makes causal explanations beat correlation-only explanations in the framework, in a precise sense rather than as an aesthetic preference. A causal explanation that posits a single genuine mediator typically represents one dependency once. A correlation-only explanation, in trying to capture the same regularity through pairwise links, typically represents the same dependency many times over. The first wins on the double-counting axis, and on the confusion axis, and usually on cost too. “Causal” isn’t a magic word here; it’s a structural property that the weakness order can detect.
The five correspondences, sharpened
With the categorical machinery in place, the five linguistic-cognitive correspondences sharpen into theorem-shaped statements. The strongest is an identity. The other four are conditional transport results: under explicit assumptions about how cognition externalizes into language, cognitive structure maps to specific linguistic structure.
The factorization correspondence is an identity theorem. Cognitive updates supported on disjoint causal modules commute, in the appropriate symmetric monoidal sense. Their linguistic images are then swap-equivalent in the TUG trace quotient — the linguistic theory has no way to keep them apart. If cognition factors and the externalization map preserves factorization, the linguistic core factors too. Nontrivial broad universals can only survive when the cognitive substrate fails to factor on the relevant modules, or when an explicit mediator couples them. This is the rigorous version of “broad cross-module universals are rare,” and it’s the rigorous version of “causal coding bounds catastrophic forgetting,” all at the same time. Two theorems become one.
Hierarchical universals arise by closure transport. A closure system on the cognitive side — a hard-kernel substrate organized by accessibility relations — pushes forward to a closure system on the linguistic side, under the right kind of map. The fixed points correspond. Person, number, case, and accessibility hierarchies are linguistic shadows of cognitive closure structure that’s protected by the kernel-shell architecture from being torn up by new learning.
Narrow word-order universals arise by sparse-energy pushforward. A sparse signed-energy controller on the cognitive side — many local routing pressures, few global parameters — produces, after marginalizing over the cognitive variables that don’t externalize, a sparse signed-energy network at the linguistic level. The pushforward preserves the sparsity structure provided the externalization map is local enough. Word-order coherence patterns are the result.
Graded universalhood arises by stability-rate transport. The stability coefficient proposed for linguistic universals is the linguistic image of an underlying cognitive stability coefficient. A hard-kernel cognitive invariant has very low forgetting rate; its linguistic image has very low diachronic transition rate away from satisfaction. As long as the cognition-to-language map doesn’t dramatically distort transition rates, the two stabilities are close.
Context-indexed laws arise by gluing. Local closure systems indexed by a context category glue, under the right compatibility conditions, into a global closure operator on compatible sections — but only the global operator, not a single global law. When local closure operators almost commute with restriction but not exactly, the failure of global closure is bounded by the cognitive confusion-pair costs from the approximate causal-coding theorem. This is the rigorous version of “forgetting context is a functor that may fail to preserve closure,” which is the rigorous version of “Simpson’s paradox can hide a real local law.”
This isn’t a complete derivation of grammar from cognitive architecture, and the framework doesn’t claim to be one. The four conditional results all rest on assumptions about the cognition-to-language map that have to be tested empirically. But it’s a substantively different kind of statement than “these five things kind of look alike.” Each of the five correspondences is now a precise claim that links a cognitive structure to a linguistic structure through a specific mathematical operation.
Beyond grammar: how meaning space itself grows
So far I’ve talked here about linguistic universals as constraints on grammatical form — what shapes a paradigm can take, what implications can hold across modules, what word orders cluster together. But there is a second, complementary question that the same framework turns out to handle pretty nicely as well: not which regions of grammar space are stable, but by what laws meaning space itself expands over historical time.
A team led by Steven Skiena at Stony Brook recently published a study in Proceedings of the Royal Society B that reports four robust statistical regularities in word-embedding spaces, drawn from English and 21 other languages. None of them is a fact about grammar. All of them are facts about the structure and growth of the semantic space that lexical items live in.
The four regularities are these. First, frequency assortativity: high-popularity words cluster near other high-popularity words in semantic space, and low-popularity words live in low-popularity neighborhoods. Second, characteristic clustering velocity profiles: as you change the resolution at which you draw cluster boundaries, the number of distinct clusters changes in a regular, scale-structured way that reveals nested hierarchical organization. Third, persistent local temporal dynamics: when a new word enters the language, it tends to appear in the same neighborhood where other recent words have been appearing, and that local activity persists for a while. Fourth, Taylor’s law: across regions of semantic space and across time windows, the variance in the number of newly created entities scales as a power of the mean — meaning innovation is bursty and regionally structured rather than uniformly random.
Guo et al. show that a fairly minimalist generative model — directed preferential placement, in which new entities are placed in semantic space under combined influence of popularity, history, and local context — reproduces all four regularities. Simpler models (uniform placement, plain preferential attachment without spatial context) miss at least one of them.
What makes this interesting for the present framework is that the same three-layer cognition–frames–language picture extends naturally from grammar to semantic growth. You just add a time index and a lexical-semantic layer. Cognitive frames don’t only constrain how meaning gets externalized as form; they also drive how meaning space itself fills in over time. When a frame is active in a culture — because of technology, social change, scientific discovery, whatever — distinctions get made nearby, and those distinctions show up in the lexicon as new words clustered in the corresponding semantic neighborhood. The growth of meaning space is, in this picture, the lexical shadow of cognitive-cultural attention dynamics.
Once you write down the dynamic version of the diagram, the four embedding-space regularities pull back to specific claims about cognitive architecture, and they line up almost exactly with the architectural features the rest of this post has been developing.
Frequency assortativity is the lexical signature of attention-weighted reusable substrate. Heavily reused cognitive modules — the conceptual analogue of HBCML hard kernels — accumulate many contextual uses, which externalize as dense high-frequency lexical neighborhoods. Words don’t get popular in isolation; they get popular because they live near other concepts that the cognitive-cultural system keeps coming back to.
Clustering velocity is the lexical signature of hierarchical frame organization. Where grammatical hierarchies generate implication closures (third-person agreement implies first- and second-person; dual implies plural), semantic hierarchies generate stable multiresolution cluster profiles. Same closure structure, different observational window. The mind organizes both the paradigms and the concept space hierarchically, and both hierarchies show up as stable empirical patterns.
Persistent temporal dynamics is the lexical signature of context-local cognitive update. When a context activates a cognitive support, the support keeps generating nearby distinctions until the context cools off. That’s the same context-gating mechanism that produces context-indexed grammatical laws like German verb-second in subordinate clauses; on the semantic-growth side, it shows up as bursts of lexical innovation localized in particular regions of meaning space.
Taylor’s law is the lexical signature of bursty allocation of cognitive-cultural effort. A modular attention system doesn’t distribute innovation uniformly across all regions. It concentrates effort on currently active supports, producing the scaling-law fluctuations Guo et al. measure. Uniform random innovation would produce a slope of 1.0; the empirical slopes (1.8 to 2.1 in the temporal direction) are exactly what you’d expect from a system that allocates resources to attentionally-prioritized regions.
This adds a sixth class to the taxonomy of linguistic universals. The original five — closure, factorization with mediators, low-frustration coherence, graded stability, context-indexed locality — are all about which patterns are stable in linguistic form. The sixth — semantic growth-scaling — is about how patterns get created in lexical-semantic space. Cognitive universals, the framework now suggests, don’t always have to appear as exceptionless symbolic laws. Some of them appear as scaling laws governing the rate and spatial distribution of new distinctions.
The weakness principle does the same work here that it did for grammar. Among models that explain the four regularities, directed preferential placement wins not because someone judged it elegant but because it dominates its competitors in the relevant Pareto order. It explains all four regularities with a single small set of generative commitments. A baroque model that stipulates frequency assortativity, clustering profiles, persistent dynamics, and Taylor’s law as four separate mechanisms would have worse weakness — more cost, more double-counting, less generality across languages and corpora. One causal mediator beats four overlapping correlations, in concept formation just as in grammar.
There are two things worth noting about this extension before moving on.
The first is empirical. Guo et al.’s evidence comes from a research line completely independent of the typological universals literature — different methods (word embeddings rather than implicational universals), different data (lexical innovation traced through historical dictionaries rather than feature databases), different models (directed preferential placement rather than spatiophylogenetic Bayesian filtering). The fact that the same architectural fingerprint shows up in both is a real form of triangulation. Two qualitatively different empirical anchors point at the same cognitive architecture, with no methodological overlap in how they were obtained.
The second is methodological, and it matters for what comes next. Static word embeddings collapse polysemy — they put each word at a single point even when it has many distinct senses — and historical timing data are much better for English than for most languages. So the cross-linguistic part of the result is necessarily partial. Semantic-growth universals should be treated as evidence about how cognitive-cultural dynamics project into available lexical data, not as direct measurements of cognitive dynamics themselves. This is a real limitation. It is also exactly the kind of limitation a category-guided causal-coding Transformer is in a position to do something useful about, which is one of the ideas we’ll get to below.
