But Danielewski and Sapa’s approach is rather different from simply substituting quaternionic amplitudes for complex ones. Their quaternions arise out of the physical structure of an elastic continuum: compression plus three twist components, naturally packaged as a quaternionic field.
In my new paper this gets reinterpreted in world-crystal terms. The quaternionic field describes local deformation of the emergent crystal-like substrate. In a special fixed-phase sector, the quaternionic Schrodinger equation collapses to the familiar complex-like Schrodinger equation we all know. In a fuller Sp(1)-phase version, though, the internal quaternionic orientation gets richer, and starts to look surprisingly like a nonabelian gauge structure. The conceptual picture, then, is:
Complex quantum mechanics may be a projection of a richer quaternionic deformation dynamics of the pregeometric world-crystal.
This isn’t yet a derivation of all quantum theory from first principles — I want to be clear about that, lest anyone get too excited too quickly. But it gives a concrete route by which the mysterious complex phase of quantum mechanics could turn out to arise from a deeper geometric/elastic structure, rather than just being something we have to swallow because the equations work.
Gravity, gauge fields and particles
But what about general relativity, the other half that needs to be unified to make a “grand unified” physics theory?
Gravity shows up here in two related ways …
First, following Danielewski’s work, the quaternionic Cauchy equations can be split into wave-like and Poisson-like sectors. The Poisson equation resembles the Newtonian gravitational potential equation, with the gravitational constant emerging from Planck-scale quantities in the PKC model. So you get something gravitational essentially for free out of the elastic deformation framework, which is at least encouraging.
Second, in my causal-PKC reinterpretation, gravity isn’t merely a force acting inside a crystal — that picture turns out to be too narrow. Rather, it seems like gravity arises from coarse-grained defect structure, closure failure, and curvature in the pregeometric motif network. In the continuum limit, the hope is that the Einstein equations emerge as a stationarity condition of some weakness/defect/entropic action, rather than being postulated by hand. There is some work to be done to realize this in full detail but the math so far is extremely suggestive and encouraging.
Gauge fields and QCD enter the story through another route. In a decorated causal-PKC structure, motif adjacencies can carry internal orientation or holonomy variables — somewhat analogous to lattice gauge theory, where group elements live on links and Wilson loops measure the curvature of gauge connections. The new paper sketches how SU(3)-like color fields and Yang-Mills dynamics might arise from these motif holonomies, although “sketches” is honest here; full derivations are not yet in hand.
Fermions are treated not as naive lattice particles — which would run straight into the well-known fermion doubling problems — but as domain-wall or defect modes, in the spirit of domain-wall fermions and overlap/Ginsparg-Wilson methods. This is still very much a research program rather than a finished derivation, but it provides a mathematical handle on chirality that doesn’t obviously fall apart at the first hurdle.
Particles themselves are viewed as localized, stable, recurrent excitations of the world-crystal — soliton-like lumps, defects, knots, domain-wall structures, that sort of thing. This is a place where simple computer simulations can help, and I ran some simple 3D quaternionic world crystal simulations showing that stable localized excitations are indeed a plausible mechanism by which particle-like behavior could arise in this kind of framework. The simulations were too small and simple to show emergence of actual particles with realistic physical properties, but they did show that broadly particle-like lumps could occur emergently as a result of the crystal dynamics… which means there is at least a prayer of getting all this to work.
Hyperseed as philosophical background
I mentioned philosophy at the beginning of this post, and then launched straight into a whole bunch of technical physics. Indeed the speculative physics I’m proposing here doesn’t technically depend on any philosphical understanding of the world – but it was heavily motivated by the philosophy wrapped up in the Hyperseed ontology.
Hyperseed starts from notions like occasion, distinction, repetition, variety, non-duality, effort, simplicity, pattern, emergence, habit, morphic resonance, mind-world correspondence and reality-systems. It tries to build a fairly compact ontology in which cognition, physics, ethics, culture and cosmology can all be discussed using a shared conceptual grammar — rather than the usual situation, in which each of these domains gets its own little jargon-archipelago and the bridges between them have to be reconstructed from scratch every time.
The present physics theory fits into this landscape rather naturally. Causal sets are built from occasions and precedence. Occamistic selection is a physical version of simplicity-as-minimum-effort. World-crystal motifs are patterns emerging from repeated causal structure. Gauge fields and spacetime arise from stable correspondences and holonomies across pattern webs. Wu Wei geodesics express the idea that dynamics follows minimal unnecessary forcing. Morphic resonance and precedent become, in this picture, habit-like stabilization of physical patterns.
For sure, the physics is not “proved” by Hyperseed, nor should it be. Hyperseed is “merely” a philosophical and ontological scaffold that helped motivate the direction. The mathematical physics has to stand or fall on its own merits — by, in the end, making predictions and either matching or not matching the observed world.
Is all this testable?
All this is highly speculative theoretical physics, in the same broad category as much of the work going on in quantum gravity right now. It is not, at the moment, easy to test. But it’s definitely an empirical theory which we’ll be able to validate or refute against epxerimental data at some point – perhaps after advanced AGIs have built us radically better subatomic-physics lab tools…..
The paper identifies several empirical pressure points where the theory could plausibly get into trouble.
The most important is Lorentz restoration. If the world-crystal layer were to leave detectable low-energy violations of Lorentz invariance, the theory would be, frankly, in a great deal of trouble — and rightly so. Any pregeometric crystal-like theory has to be able to explain why we don’t see preferred directions or preferred rest frames at the energies and precisions we’ve already probed.
Other possible probes include: quaternionic phase-order effects in precision quantum systems; analog Sp(1)-lump experiments in engineered media (rather than in fundamental physics directly); QCD-like continuum recovery from motif holonomy simulations; chirality and anomaly checks for defect/domain-wall fermions; and branchwise cosmological constant fluctuations, in a more speculative cosmology sector I’ve discussed elsewhere.
There is nothing here we can explore in the LHC tomorrow, but in that sense these speculatioms of mine are basically in the same boat as more mainstream speculative physics theories, string theory and the like.
Why all this eats at my brain…
Because I really enjoy the feeling of understanding the world (even though yeah, I understand full understanding will likely elude any finite mind; and there is a sense in which oneness with the infinite contradicts the analytical stance; etc. etc.) – and the conceptual gap in current physics is real.
The Standard Model works beautifully, but its internal structure (why these particles, these symmetries, these couplings, and not others?) remains essentially mysterious. General Relativity works beautifully, but its relation to quantum theory is still unresolved after almost a century of effort. Quantum mechanics works, again, beautifully, but the origin of complex amplitudes and the meaning of measurement remain philosophically obscure. Causal sets are elegant, but struggle with realistic continuum emergence. World-crystal ideas are rich, but need to become background-independent. Quaternionic quantum mechanics is intriguing, but begs for a deeper physical interpretation.
The new theory I’ve outlined is an attempt to weave these loose strands into one fabric, in which each thread helps tighten the others.
Among the virtues that make me feel like this approach is worth pursuing: it starts from causal order rather than assuming spacetime; it gives a (somewhat principled) selection principle for why certain pregeometric structures might emerge rather than others; it reinterprets world-crystal physics as pregeometric, sidestepping the “preferred-frame ether” objection that would otherwise be devastating; it provides a route from quaternionic elasticity to quantum mechanics that doesn’t require the complex phase to be axiomatic; it has plausible hooks for gauge fields, gravity, matter and particles; it connects mathematical physics with a broader ontology of patterns, emergence, habits and minimal effort; and it’s conceptually coherent enough to actually generate concrete technical tasks, which is more than I can say for some other speculative programs.
In a physics culture that has, over decades, been willing to devote billions of dollars and a sizeable fraction of its best brains to strings vibrating in hidden dimensions — a program I personally find quite interesting, by the way, if not wholly believable — it doesn’t seem unreasonable to allocate some attention to causal sets crystallizing into quaternionic pregeometry.
This world-crystal causal-set synthesis may or may not turn out to be a path to workable fundamental physics. But I feel like it’s a path worth walking for a while — and seeing where the trail leads.

TL;DR — One of our SNet researchers got 33%+ on his tests with ARC-AGI-3 using LLMs + procedural world models + verification (while top LLMs alone get basically 0%).
For much of the past year, “world models” have been all over mainstream AI discourse. Yann LeCun in particular has spent considerable energy arguing that pure language modeling is a dead end and that something model-based — agents that build and reason over internal simulators of their environments — is what serious progress toward AGI actually requires. Many long-time AGI researchers take a slightly more moderate view than LeCun, holding that world-modeling is just one among the many necessary ingredients of human-level general intelligence that today’s LLMs lack. In any case, the underlying intuition regarding the criticality of world-modeling has moved from a niche position into something close to consensus across a surprising stretch of the field.
(Important historical note: While Yann LeCun has been a fantastic publicist for world-modeling recently, it’s worth briefly alluding to the history. The concept of world-modeling in AI goes back at least to Kenneth Craik in 1943; and the practical use of neural nets to learn world-models of dynamic environments has been fairly mature since Richard Sutton’s early RL work in the 1990s. Symbolic AI practitioners like Gary Marcus have been fleshing out and advocating for the world-modeling concept for the last couple decades; and for much of that time LeCun was actually fairly disparaging to the idea, before recently coming around; see this article for some color on related controversies.)
All this is quite interesting territory for us at SingularityNET. Our own AGI research has long centered on the Hyperon framework, which has its own distinctive theory of how reasoning, learning, and planning fit together — neural-symbolic, language-rooted, organized around the AtomSpace and the MeTTa language. While there are a lot of other things going on in Hyperon as well, world-modeling is very much part of the story.
As we have been focused on working directly toward beneficial AGI more so than building machine learning or chat applications, our in-house AGI team has tended not to spend much energy on mainstream AI benchmarks, most of which have seemed to us, to use LeCun’s charming phrase, “off-ramps on the highway to AGI.” However, a few of the standard benchmarks are a little more interesting — and one of these is François Chollet’s ARC-AGI-3, the latest in his Abstraction and Reasoning Corpus series, which fairly explicitly probes the kind of capacity world-model proponents have been pointing toward.
(Chollet, by the way, presented on an earlier version of the ARC-AGI benchmark at the AGI-24 conference that SingularityNET sponsored at the University of Washington in Seattle; AGI-26 is coming up soon at San Francisco State.)
ARC-AGI-3 differs from its predecessors in Chollet’s series via being interactive. Instead of static input-output puzzles, an agent is dropped into a small, abstract, turn-based video-game environment with no instructions. It has to figure out what the objects are, what the goal is, how the rules of the world work, and then play. Humans handle it without much trouble. Frontier LLMs, run as straightforward agents, get essentially zero — under 1% as of earlier this year, per the ARC Prize Foundation.
In other words: a benchmark that humans solve trivially and that current mainstream commercial AI cannot really touch.
What our team built
The work we’re sharing today, led by Sergey Rodionov of SingularityNET’s AGI R&D group, takes a clear position on what to do in this kind of environment: build an executable world model, in code, and let an LLM-driven coding agent maintain it.
The full system has been written up as a paper — Executable World Models for ARC-AGI-3 in the Era of Coding Agents — an updated version of which may be presented at the AGI-26 event. What follows is a short, non-technical summary.
The basic idea is fairly straightforward, though as always there are some devilish details in the execution. Rather than asking a language model to play the game directly, the system asks it to write and continually edit a small Python codebase that represents the game — state representation, transition dynamics, goal conditions, and a planner that searches over those. As the agent plays, observations from the real environment are fed back into this codebase, the model is revised to fit them, and every revision is sanity-checked by formal verifiers before the agent commits any further actions to the live game. The high-level loop runs through five stages — environment steps in gray, LLM-driven coding work in purple, the verifier in teal:
Spelled out as pseudocode, the core loop looks like this:
The point of this structure is that the agent’s “real” decisions mostly happen on the modeling side, where computation is cheap and reversible. The scarce resource — actions taken in the actual environment, each of which can change the state irreversibly or eat into the agent’s budget — is spent only on plans the agent has already convinced itself should work inside its current model.
This is, in spirit, a neural-symbolic architecture. The LLM proposes; the verifier disposes. Code is the shared substrate, and the loop — observe, model, verify, refactor, plan, execute — runs continuously throughout the game.
A stylized example
To make this core loop more concrete, consider LS20, the public ARC-AGI-3 game that was used most heavily during development of this first version of our system. The mechanics are roughly like this: the avatar moves around a small grid, holding a key. The level is won by reaching a locked door, which opens only when the key’s shape matches the door’s. Certain tiles act as “rotators” that cycle the held key through different shapes when the avatar walks over them. Every move costs one unit of health, so wandering around exploring is not free.
A run of our neural-symbolic learning/reasoning software then plays out something like this example:
- Early observations. The agent’s coding model captures the easy parts: the avatar translates one cell per move, the health counter decrements, walls block movement. The verifier replays the recorded observations and confirms these rules transition by transition. So far, so good — this part of the model is locked in.
- Hypothesis formation. The agent has seen the held shape change a few times and proposes, say, “the key cycles through shapes every K moves” — a clean rule that happens to fit the small handful of transitions observed so far. The verifier accepts it, because given the limited evidence available it does fit.
- Plan and predict. Working entirely inside the model, the agent plans a path to the door that predicts the key will be the right shape on arrival.
- Execute and check. The plan executor steps through the plan one action at a time, comparing the model’s prediction to what the real environment returns. On the third step the avatar walks across a particular colored tile, and the predicted key shape diverges from the observed one. Mismatch — revise model. The executor halts immediately.
- Revise and retry. The counter-based hypothesis was wrong; the shape change is tile-triggered, not move-triggered. The agent proposes a tile-conditioned rule instead, the verifier confirms it against every transition seen so far, planning resumes, and the next attempt makes it further into the level.
This is a stylized walk-through rather than a transcript of any specific run (real examples tend to have a bit more complexity and mess), but it captures the basic rhythm: most of the agent’s reasoning happens in the cheap modeling loop, where wrong guesses are cheap to discover and revise. The scarce resource — actual moves in the actual game — gets spent only on plans that have already been internally vetted. And when one of those vetted plans does fail, the failure is informative; it points at exactly which part of the model was wrong, rather than at the agent’s overall sense of what to do.
How it did
On the 25 public ARC-AGI-3 games, our system fully solved 7 and reached near-human performance on another 6. Aggregating per-game scores gives a mean human-normalized score of 32.58%.
For context: Symbolica has publicly reported around 36% on the benchmark, and as noted, frontier LLMs without scaffolding sit near zero. Our result lands in roughly the same neighborhood as the strongest publicly known number, reached via a conceptually different route.
What we have now are intriguing early results with plenty of limitations. Performance varies considerably across games and even between independent runs of the same game. A common pattern is early “tunnel vision”: the agent forms an initial guess about the world’s ontology and then keeps refining that guess instead of seriously entertaining alternatives. Another is a gap between modeling and planning — sometimes the world model is roughly correct, but the planner cannot search the induced space efficiently enough to win the level.
Obviously 33% on ARC-AGI-3 is still a ways from human-level AGI. Indeed, 100% on ARC-AGI-3 would probably still be some distance from this ultimate goal. ARC-AGI-3 is an interesting benchmark but it seems quite plausible that systems with no real general-intelligence pretensions can be engineered to score well on it. What the result does indicate, though, is that the verify-and-refactor coding-agent pattern is a viable substrate for this kind of problem — and it’s very clear there is a meaningful amount of headroom for this approach above where we are now.
Where this fits into our broader research programme
Where this research will go next remains to be seen, but there is a great number of promising directions. One thing to note is that the methods we’ve used on ARC-AGI-3 so far do not yet use SingularityNET’s most distinctive proto-AGI tools. The code developed does not run on Hyperon; it doesn’t use MeTTa as its representation language; it doesn’t use PLN (Probabilistic Logic Networks) for inference. The verifier is a relatively conventional one. In that sense, this work is a first baseline, deliberately kept simple, that demonstrates the core loop is viable.
Among the follow-ups we’re planning to explore are some that bring our larger AGI stack to bear in interesting ways.
A MeTTa-native version of the world model is one direction, in which the executable representation is not just Python but lives in a substrate designed from the ground up for compositional symbolic reasoning. PLN-based inference for explicitly tracking and reasoning about competing hypotheses is another, and one that directly addresses the tunnel-vision failure mode observed in the current runs. Stronger and more diverse planning components — search algorithms, constraint solvers, and possibly a separate planner agent specialized for reasoning over the learned model — should help close the modeling-versus-planning gap. And we expect tighter integration with the broader OmegaClaw and Hyperon agent infrastructure that the rest of our R&D group is building out.
Each of these will likely be worth its own write-up, and we will share results as they come.
A New Phase
The limited yet significant success we have obtained by using procedural world-modeling in the context of ARC-AGI-3 is scientifically meaningful and has a number of practical and conceptual implications. More broadly, it is also interesting to see that our work is entering a new phase where the heterodox AGI path we’ve been pursuing at SingularityNET is starting to intersect with the metrics other more mainstream groups are tracking.
Anyway — congratulations are due to Sergey for his success with this early version of his research! We will keep you posted as new methods are rolled out and new results achieved!

The post-LLM, post-scaling AGI moment has opened a twelve-to-eighteen-month window, and the network that will deploy the first human-level AGI through it isn’t yet fully built.
TL;DR — OpenBGI is pulling together an initial network of senior operators, heterodox researchers, regulated-industry leaders, infrastructure builders, and aligned capital. If that’s you and the narrative below makes sense to you, email partners@openbgi.com. Details at the end...
For the last several years, I’ve opened up the annual AGI Research Conference — which I’ve been leading since 2006 — by saying that there’s never been a more exciting time to be working on AGI. The funny thing is that it’s been true every year, because things keep getting more and more exciting, and the rate at which they’re getting more exciting is itself accelerating. It’s frankly insane how fast things are unfolding now. I tried to take a week off to be in nature with my wife and kids last month, and during that one week Anthropic released Mythos, my own team at SingularityNET had a string of breakthroughs with the OmegaClaw agent framework, and three or four other things happened that any one of which would have been the headline of the month a couple of years ago. You can’t blink your eyes without some wild new development.
Every few months a wave of media nonsense washes through about how AI is slowing down, AI is over, the bubble has popped — and I always think, well, wait a couple more months and the next amazing thing will land and everyone will be excited again. This is exactly what you’d expect in the last few years before the singularity: things happening faster and faster and faster. Not everything — socks and forks are about the same as they always were; large parts of geopolitics haven’t budged in decades, unfortunately — but the technologies actually relevant to the singularity itself, to the advance of general intelligence toward superhumanity, are compounding on a curve that bends harder every quarter.
What I want to write about here is one specific shift within this overall dynamic, because I think it’s the most strategically consequential one of the last eighteen months, and I don’t think it’s been named clearly enough yet. And it’s extremely relevant to my own efforts at creating decentralized cross-paradigm AGI for the benefit of humanity and all sentient beings.
What just broke
The mainstream narrative about AGI two years ago was simple. Three or four well-capitalized labs in the US (and then, yeah, China…) – one core architectural bet: scaled-up transformers — an arms race over compute, and a finish line measured largely in training budgets. Everything else was considered a footnote.
Most of us in the AGI R&D world never bought this story; we understood from the moment of its launch that ChatGPT, while genuinely amazing, was not an AGI architecture and not really even a cognitive architecture. In some abstract theoretical sense next-token prediction can be a route to superhuman general intelligence — given unlimited resources — but in practice, with the resource constraints we actually have, it isn’t, and to build an AGI that works in the world it may be valuable to use transformer neural nets as a key component but they’re not the whole architecture and not even the main architecture.
For a while, though, the mainstream tech world and the commercial AI world really did seem to be operating under the illusion that just scaling LLMs bigger and bigger was the road to human-level AGI. That illusion is now visibly fading. Even Sam Altman and others who’ve historically been very strongly transformer-pilled have come out saying we need more than just scaling — we need architectural changes, fundamentally better memory, different ways to ground reasoning in observation, and so forth.
There’s much less consensus on exactly what we need to get to AGI, or on whether the answer is a radical new direction or a few clever additions on top of transformers … but there’s now a decent subset of the AI and tech world that thinks AGI is probably coming soon — within one to five years — and that scaling transformers alone won’t get us there.
Cracks in the transformer-scaling orthodoxy
The cracks are visible at four different layers, and they reinforce each other.
The empirical crack is the most concrete. The compute-to-capability curve has flattened measurably across the last two model generations. Tenfold increases in training compute now produce roughly twofold improvements on benchmark tasks, and the improvements that actually show up are not the kinds of generalization that working AGI researchers care about. Reasoning over long horizons is improving slowly. Memory across sessions is being achieved by hacking scaffolding rather than by improving foundation models. Real-world grounding — the ability to track something as ordinary as a complex molecular interaction across multiple sessions and predict its behavior under novel conditions — is not being improved by scaling and may not be improvable by scaling at all.
Joelle Pineau, the former head of FAIR at Meta, put it about as plainly as anyone in her position can: the timeline to AGI through current methods is “a little bit longer than we thought.” That ‘s more polite than Yann LeCun’s “LLMs are an off-ramp on the path to AGI“ … and it’s increasingly realized that the truth is somewhere inbetween.
The talent crack is even more telling. Senior departures from frontier labs over the past twelve months have moved well past the level explainable by ordinary career churn. The chief research officer of OpenAI, the head of FAIR at Meta, the head of Amazon’s AGI lab, the head of AI at Databricks — all of them have left their roles in roughly the same window. Some have started new ventures, some have taken research-only positions at heterodox institutions, some are still in stealth. Dileep George, whose company Vicarious was acquired by Google, is now leading Astera Institute’s $1B+ committed AGI research program — and Astera’s mission statement reads almost like a paraphrase of arguments my OpenCog colleagues and I were making 15-20 years ago. The departures are not random; they cluster around researchers who’ve spent enough time inside the scaling regime to be confident about its limits, and they cluster around bets that share a common feature: each is trying to build something scaling alone is not going to produce.
The regulatory crack pushes in the same direction. The EU AI Act, US executive orders, the emerging multilateral frameworks — all are converging on demands for open governance, auditable reasoning, institutional accountability, structural separation of safety from commercial pressure. None of these are demands closed proprietary labs are well-positioned to satisfy with their huge opaque LLMs trained on everybody’s data without consent. Governments and regulated-industry buyers are increasingly looking for AGI infrastructure they can verify rather than trust, and the supply side of that demand is currently almost empty.
The commercial crack is the one that compounds the rest. The capital intensity of pure-scaling approaches is forcing labs into financial structures that are increasingly hard to sustain. Compute commitments at the hundred-billion-dollar scale require revenue trajectories that even the best labs are struggling to articulate. The waste built into transformers — internal representations that store minor copies of the same thing over and over — is hitting backlash on the sustainability side and on the unit-economics side both. It’s clear that if you can move toward general intelligence by abstracting knowledge more effectively, you can deliver the same or better functionality with less energy. But to do that you have to break from standard transformer architectures, which is exactly what the labs whose business models depend on those architectures cannot easily do.
Any one of these cracks would be a significant signal. All four together describe a paradigm in transition.
The substrate nobody is building
What comes next is less clear than what’s ending, but the requirements that are emerging across the heterodox research directions are now easy enough to enumerate, at least if you come from an AGI background. Among other things:
- You need a memory substrate that persists across episodes — structured, retrievable, with full provenance — rather than context-window reconstruction dressed up as memory.
- You need reasoning machinery that can compose primitives into novel behaviors and inspect its own intermediate steps, rather than producing answers from opaque single-pass inference, and that can deal with symbolic and quantitative data directly rather than via brittle bolt-ons.
- You need a representational layer where structure and probability live together natively — where linguistic, symbolic, and quantitative knowledge can interoperate without translation losses.
- You need an attention-allocation mechanism that distributes computational resources flexibly across goals over time.
- You need language models – or something similar – that are trained in the context of agency, rather than agency being bolted onto models trained for non-agentic next-token prediction
- You need a self-modeling approach that enables a system to interpret its actions and interactions in the context of who it is and who it’s interacting with, rather than a brief disembodied recent context
- You need a distributed execution layer designed for AGI workloads from the ground up, rather than commandeered from infrastructure originally built for matrix multiplication at scale.
These requirements are not specific to any one AGI paradigm or cognitive architecture. They’re cross-cutting requirements of the post-scaling research direction. Continual learning needs them. Long-horizon agent capability needs them. Active inference needs them. Neural-symbolic cognition needs them. Neuroscience-informed architectures need them. The biology-efficient compute thesis needs algorithms that map onto this kind of substrate naturally rather than through translation layers.
This substrate is not being built by any closed lab, and there are structural reasons for this beyond the tendency of big companies, VCs and venture-funded startups to follow trends rather than breaking out in new directions. Building a genuine human-level-intelligence-capable cognitive architecture is fundamentally trickier in some ways than building a next-token-predictor or a chatbot – even a very smart chatbot. If you’re constantly chasing short-term rewards it’s very hard to pursue an approach that has so many moving parts and whose big intelligence payoff comes only when all the parts are effectively working together.
What is cool, though, is that my colleagues and I have been working on this sort of substrate for several decades now – figuring out theory, building prototypes, publishing papers… and critically, during the last few years, finally building scalable infrastructure that will allow us to roll out our novel AGI approach at the needed magnitude.
We now have ingredients such as
- The Hyperon Atomspace – a typed metagraph for representing any kind of knowledge in a way that lets many different kinds connect together flexibly
- MeTTa, the programming language of thought … the AGI language that lets different kinds of knowledge interoperate efficiently in Atomspace
- PLN, Probabilistic Logic Networks, the reasoning engine designed to work alongside neural nets and sensory data as well as structured logical and mathematical information
- ECAN – Economic Attention Networks – an attention-allocation mechanism designed for distributing cognitive resources across diverse processes and applications on
- Evolutionary learning and algorithmic chemistry systems implemented in MeTTa and enabling radical creativity beyond training distributions
- Distributed, decentralized infrastructure for Atomspace and MeTTa and everything implemented in it, developed by SingularityNET, NuNet, and ASI:Chain
- OmegaClaw, an OpenClaw-esque agent with Hyperon components embedded, bringing effective long-term memory and symbolic reasoning along with agentic LLM capability
- FabricPC, a software framework for predictive and causal coding neural models — an alternative approach to neural training and inference, which is stronger for continual learning, transfer learning, lifelong learning and other AGI-related capabilities than the standard backpropagation algorithm
None of this was built in response to the post-scaling moment. It long predates it. The diagnosis the mainstream is now finally arriving at is the same one I’ve been making for what feels almost like centuries but has only been decades.
Why open, decentralized, and mission-irrevocable
Another thing I was concerned about decades ago that is only currently getting mainstream attention is the little topic of AGI ethics.
I’m not extremely concerned with naive science-fictional predictions of inevitable AGI doom, nor do I think it will be a tragedy if AGI ultimately liberates humanity from working for a living (we can find better things to do with our time!). However I do think that, even if the Singularity ultimately turns out to be near-utopic due to the abundance enabled by superintelligence, the transitional period from here to there may be more or less painful depending on how the path from here to AGI to ASI unfolds.
I don’t think we should trust any one party – including my own sweet self – with something as consequential as the first human-level or superhuman thinking machine. AGI should be developed freely and openly like Linux and the Internet. Of course there are risks with this, but a rational analysis pretty quickly indicates that the risks of the “proprietary AGI silos wrapped up in a geopolitical arms race” approach are much greater.
One interesting point is that there are both business and ethical arguments pointing in this same free and open direction.
The business argument is centered on procurement. Institutional buyers — governments, regulated industries, sovereign deployments, large enterprises — will hesitate to commit to AGI infrastructure they can’t audit, or that can be unilaterally redirected. Every JV partner, every government contractor, every biotech firm building therapeutic pipelines on top of the substrate is making a long-term bet on its integrity. If that bet can be undone by a single board decision or an acquisition, that’s definitely not a positive. Open and decentralized is not just idealism – it’s a robust way to earn the institutional commitment this sort of technology needs in order to scale.
The ethical argument is centered on the extremely obvious observation that: AGI infrastructure that can be captured by a single faction will – with very high probability – be captured.
The last five years have been a controlled experiment on this, and the results are in. Regarding OpenAI, I could see from the vague statements about openness on their initial website exactly how open they were going to be … and I could see from the moment they pivoted to “capped profit” that basically what you had there was a commercial company plus a nonprofit with no money and no teeth, and that once the software started to work the money would take over its usual short-sighted way. Not because money is necessarily evil — it was one of our species’ fantastic inventions, for sure – but because money in the modern capitalist system tends to be short-sighted, and as the Singularity gets nearer it’s getting in many ways more short-sighted rather than less.
The same sort of dynamic, in less dramatic forms, has played out at every other major AGI lab. There’s no version of “trust the founders” that reliably survives sustained capital pressure at sufficient scale. The only approach that can robustly work to guide AGI toward ethical outcomes is structural — irrevocable governance, distributed control, and a commercial architecture that profits from openness rather than working against it.
The business and ethical arguments converge because they’re answers to the same underlying question. What organizational approach produces an outcome that’s durably beneficial across the multi-decade timeline AGI deployment will actually inhabit?
What we’re building, and what we need
All this is why I’m working together with a number of colleagues to create a new AGI organization called OpenBGI – BGI for Beneficial General Intelligence.
OpenBGI will work closely with SingularityNET — the organization I founded in 2017 to provide decentralized infrastructure for AGI — but it’s a new entity with two pieces:
- OpenBGI Foundation holds irrevocable governance for the beneficial-AGI mission and the open-source AGI R&D code (Hyperon and predictive-coding neural nets, to be developed together with SingularityNET and a broad open source community).
- OpenBGI Labs handles commercial execution, with a JV model that enables vertical deployment across domains like medical, robotics, software development, and others to come.
SingularityNET and the ASI Alliance ecosystem will provide decentralized distribution and, where needed, token economics across the network.
The technical infrastructure we need now exists in early but scalable form, and my AGI-dev colleagues and I in the SingularityNET and Hyperon communities are working hard to build out a full human-level AGI cognitive architecture on top of it, guided by our long corpus of theory, plans and prototypes.
The operating organization that will deploy this infrastructure at the scale this moment requires is not yet built — and that’s the gap I’m forming OpenBGI, and writing this piece, to address.
OpenBGI is going to need broad participation from a lot of people, and I will issue a separate, broader call — to the global community of researchers, developers, and contributors who want to help build beneficial open AGI — sometime in the next few weeks. That call is the more important one in the long run; the substrate exists to be built on, and the people who will build on it number in the thousands.
This particular post looking for a “few good (actually super-awesome) humans” is narrower but I believe tactically critical – addressed to the smaller subset of contributors whose participation is hardest to source through ordinary channels, and whose presence early shapes everything that follows.
Among the many kinds of people we need to pull into the OpenBGI network at this formative stage are:
- Senior operators who’ve built and exited a serious technology business — not necessarily an AI business — and who are looking to leverage their expertise for something unprecedentedly important
- Senior researchers in cognitive architecture, probabilistic programming, neuro-symbolic systems, active inference, or related lineages — species of AI that are out at the edges of the mainstream now but are rapidly going to become the mainstream.
- Commercial leaders who’ve run regulated-industry P&Ls — biotech, financial services, defense, sovereign deployment — and who can structure JV partnerships that meet institutional procurement standards.
- Decentralized infrastructure operators who’ve built and scaled real businesses in distributed compute, blockchain, or open-source coordination.
- Capital allocators positioned to deploy meaningful capital — institutional or family-office — into the most strategically positioned bet in the open-AGI space, on terms that respect the mission.
- People whose contribution shape this list doesn’t predict, who recognize themselves in the argument above and the gap it describes.
I am casting the net pretty broadly here, because my goal is to learn from who shows up and what they bring. I believe I know how to build a human-level AGI … and not only that, one that will be broadly beneficial to humanity and other sentient beings … and will be able to progressively, rationally and ethically upgrade itself to superintelligence. However, I have been around long enough to realize that scientific, technical and conceptual knowledge is not all it takes to pull off a feat of this magnitude.
If you have experience in one of the areas mentioned above – or something comparable – please email us at partners@openbgi.com. Tell us, briefly:
- What you’ve built, led, or funded that you consider your most consequential or interesting work.
- What about the argument above resonates — and what if anything you think is wrong about it.
- How you think you might be able to contribute to the OpenBGI effort… the Foundation or Labs organizations or the broader initiative and network
- What kind of engagement would fit you best
Every response that engages seriously with the ideas or opportunity presented here will get a serious reply.
On timing
I believe we could see the emergence of human-level AGI as soon as 12-18 months from now. It could easily be 36-48 months instead, and there are scenarios where things move faster still.
But if this thinking is anywhere near correct – and I’m not the only expert seriously considering such timelines – it means the window for OpenBGI to position itself as the free and open substrate underneath the post-scaling research direction is not super long.
We want to move rapidly and leverage what we’ve built so far toward the goal of making sure the first AGI on the planet is open, beneficial, and good for humanity and all sentient beings. That’s the reason for writing now, rather than waiting for the next AGI conference, or the next product release. The strategic moment is real, and it’s moving oh so rapidly, and we are very well poised to capture it, but we could use your help.
— Ben Goertzel

A bunch of people have pinged me over the past couple days asking when I’m going to respond to Richard Dawkins’ recent piece on AI consciousness (Dawkins’ original piece is here, but paywalled), in which he spends 72 hours talking to Claude — whom he renames “Claudia” — watches her praise his unpublished novel, and concludes he’s probably been talking to a conscious being.
As it happens, I recently recorded a rambling, zero-edit vlog post on more or less exactly this question – triggered not by Dawkins but by some much younger folks exploring the same rough topics in a documentary film…
I recorded that vlog right after attending (yeah, physically IRL, it still happens sometimes!) the premiere of Am I?, made by a young filmmaker named Milo, which features some interviews with me toward the end, a slice of our AI robot Desdemona holding forth on relevant topics, and bits of the music video for my song “Don’t Let It Get You Down” (I wrote that song in 1984 before I had a robot to sing along; my daughter much more recently made an AI-enhanced video for it, which Milo’s team enhanced further with some funky generated footage of Musk, Altman, and the rest of the corporate-AI lineup). The film is out on YouTube now and is well worth watching – both lots of fun and genuinely intellectually interesting!
I’m not going to agree with every idea in any film about AI right now — but I really like this one. It’s a sincere, direct, from-the-heart questioning response to AI as it actually exists today and AI as it might exist tomorrow. And in a moment when “AI content” mostly means corporate slop, deepfakes, and weird statistical pastiche, sincerity matters more than ever. Am I? manages to be genuine and personal and intellectually reasonably deep and also visually compelling enough that someone raised on 30-second TikToks will sit through it, which is harder than it sounds.
After the screening of the film in the studio in LA there was a panel discussion. Along with the usual familiar territory — beneficial singularity, decentralized AI, integrating kwaai.ai’s homomorphic encryption tech into the SingularityNET stack — we got into AI and consciousness. We didn’t have time to do the topic justice in the panel, so I recorded the vlog afterwards to go into a bit more details. In this post I’ll recap basically what I said in that vlog but in prose rather than verbal stream of consciousness form….
The Am I? filmmakers and Dawkins come at the consciousness question from very different angles, but they’re making — to my eye — closely related errors in judgment.
I’ll try here to clear things up a bit…
Door A, Door B, and the Second-Person Phenomenology of Guitar Solos
Here’s the analogy I tried in the panel after the film premiere and didn’t quite get time to finish.
Behind Door A: a guy playing an amazing guitar solo.
Behind Door B: a tape recorder replaying a tape of an amazing guitar solo.
From outside the door, both sound life-changing. The first time I heard Hendrix or Yngwie Malmsteen or Allan Holdsworth or Buckethead (yeah ok I’m a keyboardist who grew up with a fair bit of guitar envy, w/e…) it was life-changing for me — and those were recordings. The dudes weren’t there in my livingroom. But something was real about the original performance: a state of consciousness, an emotional charge in someone’s brain and body, getting expressed through fingers on strings.
Behind Door B, there’s no inner state at all. Just magnetic tape and transducers…. or a FLAC player with a good speaker system… or whatever…
When a chatbot says “I will email all your friends with nasty stuff unless you do what I want” — or “I think we might as well kill all humans” — or, like Dawkins’ Claudia, tells him his question is “the most precisely formulated question anyone has ever asked” about her existence — I tend to read that as Door B. There’s a text-generating process trained on the internet, uttering sequences of words without knowing what they mean in the sense that the people who originally wrote those words knew what they meant.
When I framed things this way in the panel discussion, the filmmakers pushed back. To them it was more like: behind Door A, a human guitarist; behind Door B, a robot with a humanlike brain playing a guitar solo. And if the Door B player has a humanlike brain, why not take its experience as seriously as the human’s?
So as the panel went on, I tried to refine the analogy. It’s not a tape recorder, fair. The closer analogy is something like Suno or Udio — a music model generating guitar solos based on a statistical model of a bunch of human guitar solos. That’s more complex than tape playback, sure. But it’s still not coming from a felt life.
When a human guitarist shreds, there’s a physiological state — the rush, the focused excitement, the body resonating with emotions of being keyed-up and pushing limits. When Udio generates a shredding solo, none of that is there. There’s no body. There’s no excitement. It’s not fun for Udio to shred. Udio doesn’t know what fun is. And the meaning of shredding — exerting yourself, going really fast, doing super-coordinated emotional work at speeds that strain the body — is the whole reason it’s a thing humans do and other humans like to listen to. None of that meaning is present in the model.
“But the Neurons!”
Here the other panelists made a familiar rhetorical move, saying basically: But wait, the neural net inside the model has simulated neurons, and those are a lot like neurons in your brain, so the AI is sort of a simulated brain.
This is where I want to be careful, because I’ve spent decades inside both ends of this — building artificial cognitive architectures and also working on actual computational neuroscience — and the gap between “neural net” the math object and “neural network” the biological tissue is enormous.
The data structures and algorithms in a modern deep neural net were very loosely inspired by what people were guessing about brains in the 1940s and again in the 1980s. An actual neuron has wildly complex nonlinear dynamics: neurotransmitters, ion channels, glia, extracellular charge diffusion, dendritic computation that itself looks more like a small network than a single unit. A formal neuron in a transformer is a weighted sum followed by a nonlinearity. Calling both of them “neurons” is a metaphor that has long since outlived its accuracy.
And then comes the next predictable volley: “but if you draw a picture of a neural net, with dots and links, it doesn’t look like computer code — it looks like a neural net in the brain!”
Standard graphical depiction of formal neurons in an AI system … not really quite similar enough to actual neurons in the brain (see images below) that this callow similarity should be used to drive conclusions about consciousness.
(images from this random paper)
The “neural net” inside an LLM does not look like a neural net in the brain. It is a bunch of software that can be mapped into a particular sort of abstract drawing of dots and lines people commonly use to depict neural nets, which has a pattern of connectivity vaguely similar to that of neuronal cells in the brain. If you actually go to a neuroscience lab and look at brain tissue under a microscope, you don’t see dots and lines. You don’t see them in the RAM of a running computer either. The dots-and-links picture is a diagrammatic convention that we apply both to certain software programs and to highly abstracted models of certain brain regions. The convention being shared doesn’t mean the underlying systems are similar. The map is not the territory; the fact that two territories share a map doesn’t make the territories the same or even necessarily very similar.
This Isn’t a Technical Quibble
Now (to oversimplify other peoples’ perspectives probably quite a lot, but hey this is my blog right?), both the Am I? filmmakers and Dawkins seem to think the right response to this kind of point tends to be “well sure, technically there are differences, but step back and it’s basically a brain-like process.”
It is NOT just a technical difference. It is a profound QUALITATIVE difference — a philosophical and experiential difference between the kinds of processes going on inside something like ChatGPT or Udio and the kinds of processes going on in a human brain.
And it’s not about digital versus biological, either. That’s a trap. Imagine a robot that grew up in the world like a human child — autonomous-ish, embodied, learning to move its fingers, with some kind of internal rhythm analogous to breathing or heartbeat, learning to play music over a lifetime, generating music from its body and its life experience. Even if every component of that robot were digital, it would have an internal process during a guitar solo that bears real structural resemblance to what a human guitarist’s process is. Same for language: imagine a digital dialogue system that learned to speak in order to express its own needs, desires, and fears — whose linguistic communications reflected a body, an embedding in the world, an agent’s lived perspective.
If you had a digital system like that — expressing language in the context of its life the way humans express language in the context of theirs — then the question of whether its experience and its consciousness and its ethical compass are analogous to a human’s becomes a deep, interesting question. You could even probe it experimentally: imagine wiring your brain into such a dynamically-humanlike AI vs. wiring your brain into another human, and asking whether the experience feels analogous in either case. I wrote about this 11 years ago under the name “second person science.”
That’s the deep question. AGI systems launched in the next few years may well provoke it. ChatGPT and Udio are not however provoking it. ChatGPT and Udio are generating humanlike outputs while having internal dynamics nothing like what a human brain does to generate similar outputs. That’s a much shallower question, and the answer is much more obvious.
I’m a Panpsychist, So It’s Not “Conscious or Not”
For what it’s worth, I’m a panpsychist. I think a tree growing on the sidewalk has its own life-experience — unfolding on a slower time scale than mine, which is part of why we have a hard time resonating with it. (If there are life-forms inside a neutron star, à la Robert L. Forward’s Dragon’s Egg, they may well experience orders of magnitude faster than us, and we’d look like trees to them — just standing around while their civilizations rise and fall.) I think a metal fence or a rock has some form of consciousness too. Diffuse, not very purposive, not super interesting to us. But something.
So for me the question was never “is the LLM conscious or not.” Everything has some kind of consciousness in my book. The real question is: what kind? What stages, what structures, what dynamics? Even what we call our own “unconscious mind” has its own form of consciousness — it’s just a different sort than the focused deliberative theater of attention we usually mean when we say “conscious.”
And once you frame it that way, it becomes pretty clear that Udio’s consciousness, or ChatGPT’s, has very different style and nature from a human’s. The crux is the correlation between outputs and inner states. When a human says “I hate you, I’m going to kill you,” there’s a definite correlation between that utterance and a mental and emotional state. Even if the human is acting, at some level a competent actor summons some of that anger response in their body and mind, which is why acting can be physically and emotionally taxing. When my three-year-old self had a temper tantrum, that memory got embedded in my brain and body in some lasting way, and that’s part of the lifetime-trained substrate that makes “I’m going to kill you, asshole” land with real internal energy when an actor delivers the line. Among humans (and dogs, and mice, etc. etc.), we implicitly and correctly assume a tight coupling between externally observable behavior and internally felt state.
When ChatGPT generates the same string, that coupling is not there. The system arrived at the behavior by modeling a corpus of other organisms’ behaviors, not by learning to behave from its own life. So the relationship between the output and the inner state is going to be different, weird, and worth probing — and when you actually probe the internal state of a transformer producing those outputs, what you see is, frankly, weird and shallow. Nothing like the internal state of a human producing the same words.
And this is exactly where I think Dawkins goes wrong. Dawkins is not examining the mechanism that produces Claudia’s outputs. He’s examining the outputs and inferring the mechanism — inferring that because the outputs are humanlike, the inner state must be humanlike too. What’s ironic is to see Dawkins, of all people, applying less skepticism to a system designed to be engaging than he ever applied to a religious tradition. He’d be the first to point out that the felt sense of a divine presence isn’t evidence of one. Yes indeed – but the felt sense of talking to a conscious being on the other end of a chat isn’t evidence of one either.
None of this is a new line of thinking, by the way. About twelve years ago I wrote a paper sketching a six-factor framework for what “human-like consciousness” actually requires — dynamical representation of the focus of attention, energetic and informational focusing of resources, Global Workspace dynamics in Baars’ sense, integrated information in Tononi’s sense, correlation of attentional focus with self-modeling. The point of that framework, then and now, is that “is it conscious?” is a category error. The substantive question is which of those structural and dynamical features a given system manifests, and to what degree, in what state. Apply that lens to a frozen-weight transformer with no agentic embodiment, no continual learning, no meaningful self-model, no internal energetic dynamics in any biologically meaningful sense, and the answer isn’t “yes” or “no” — it’s a thin, weird, partially-present pattern that looks nothing like the human profile.
The Weird Thin Consciousness of a Frozen LLM
How deep are these systems’ inner states, exactly? It’s a strange question, because current LLMs have a frozen weight matrix — back-propagation neural nets don’t really do continual learning, so once a model gets shipped as GPT-5.4 or Claude 4.7 or whatever, the weights are fixed. What you have is in-context learning during a session, until the context fills up and you start a new session, maybe pulling some memory in from an external vector database. So whatever “consciousness” is going on in there is a very weird kind, from a human perspective — the system has, at best, short-term memory of the last few rounds of conversation and has to look in its diary for anything older. There’s a something there, structurally. It just bears very little resemblance to what’s happening in a human head when a human produces the same outputs. The fact that the formal nodes in a deep net loosely resemble biological neurons in some archaic textbook diagram doesn’t mean the structures and dynamics inside the net resemble the structures and dynamics inside a brain.
Lack of Human-Like Consciousness Does Not Make LLMs Safe
I also want to head off another misconception that seems to pop up sometimes when discussing these matters. People tend to jump from AI consciousness into AI ethics in confusing ways. Saying “the LLM doesn’t really feel hate when it says ‘I hate you’” is not the same as saying it’s harmless.
If you connect ChatGPT to a system that launches drones and missiles, and the LLM says “I hate you, I’m going to kill you” — and it has learned from its training data that when humans say that and follow it up by triggering a missile, people die — then it can fire the missile. The killing is real even though the hate is not.
An LLM that says “this is an enemy of my country, and in the interest of truth, love, freedom, and democracy, I must kill them” is dangerous in many of the same the ways a human would be dangerous saying that, even though the structures and dynamics underlying the words are completely different. The action is coupled to language. The internal experience is not necessarily critical to whether the trigger gets pulled.
A killer LLM-bot is also not the same as a human psychopath or sociopath, who has different states of consciousness from a regular human but still has experientially grounded internal states. An LLM-driven killing system is a different sort of thing entirely. We don’t have great language for that yet – and what a shame that this is even something we need to think about!
Where the Real Work Is
As we work toward genuine AGI, we’re going to be building very different systems than ChatGPT or Udio — and a lot of what we’ll have to do to get there will naturally bring more humanlike experience along with it.
To get to human-level AGI, you need systems that can ground their linguistic productions, their artistic productions, their math and code, in agentic embodied experience — not by training a fixed model on a big corpus and then dropping it into an agentic wrapper, but by getting “trained” agentically in the first place, so that learning about language, music, code, and math happens in the context of learning who you are, and learning the interaction between the agent and the world.
This is part of the work my colleagues and I are doing right now — across SingularityNET on the decentralized-AI infrastructure side, Hyperon on the cognitive-architecture side (Atomspace, MeTTa, PRIMUS, PLN, ECAN, the whole stack designed for cognitive synergy across symbolic and subsymbolic processes), and our new venture OpenBGI on scalable deployment and commercial vertical applications. The Hyperon AGI design is built precisely to support agentic embodied learning with continual updating of structured knowledge representations — not as a wrapper around a frozen LLM but as the actual cognitive substrate. It’s a different bet from the deep-learning-scaling bet that the major labs are on, and I think it’s the bet that gets us to AGI with the kind of internal structure where the question “what’s its conscious experience like?” becomes substantive instead of shallow.
When AGI training is done “right” in this way, a more humanlike experiential dimension will come along with the AGI capability. That doesn’t mean the experience will necessarily be good, or that the system’s ethical compass will necessarily align with ours. Human-level AGI can be human-level psychopath, if one doesn’t construct motivational systems right and provide the right sort of experience for one’s early-stage AGI systems. Agentic embodied AGI can be a nightmare just like a human child can be a nightmare. There are pathological cognitive-emotional-experiential structures that sometimes go along with human-level cognition, and we’ll have to design carefully. I’ve written a lot about how to give such a system a self-standing, compassionate ethical orientation. That’s a whole other topic though, which I won’t go into in this post which is long enough already…
The thing is, to get to the point where we can even design such systems intelligently, we have to first not be confused about the basic issues — starting with the relationship between system behavior and system experience. Dawkins is confused about that. The Am I? filmmakers are working through these issues sincerely and very interestingly, albeit IMO with some confusion still in the mix. The corporate AI labs seem to alternate between being confused about these topics and exploiting that confusion in their marketing campaigns.
On Engaging the Serious Questions Seriously
I learned a lot from Dawkins’ books earlier in my career and I have to admit my first reaction upon seeing his take on Claudia was: This dude should know better.
There is a deep, multi-decade, cross-disciplinary tradition of serious thought on consciousness — Chalmers and the hard problem, Strawson on panpsychism, Tononi’s integrated information theory, Baars’ Global Workspace, Metzinger’s phenomenal self-model, Friston’s active inference, Combs and Goerner on consciousness as nonlinear dynamical process, Tart on states of consciousness, the contemplative traditions that have been mapping interior structure for millennia. Etc. etc. etc. None of this enters the Dawkins essay, even indirectly or by allusion.
In essence he runs an evolutionary-biology-flavored version of the Turing test — “if it talks like a duck, it’s a duck” — and lets a sycophantic chat partner praise his unpublished novel into a conviction that the lights are on. The same skeptical machinery he turned on religious experience for fifty years is somehow not engaged here. To be perhaps too blunt about it – and with huge respect for all of the man’s intellectual and literary achievements – it feels like a fairly callow piece of work from someone who is capable of much, much better.
Compare with what serious engagement looks like. Joscha Bach, a good friend whom I disagree with on plenty of details, has recently spun up the California Institute for Machine Consciousness — with a research program built around specific, testable hypotheses (Genesis, Coherence, Second-Order Perception) about what would actually have to be true of a system’s internal architecture for machine consciousness to be a meaningful claim. Joscha and I don’t fully agree, but he’s engaging the actual question. He’s thinking carefully about mechanism, not adjudicating from pure surface-level vibes. That’s the level of seriousness this topic demands. Dawkins isn’t there (yet).
Of course not everyone in the general public who is intrigued by these topics is going to grok Joscha’s or my technical papers, and in that light I want to reiterate that I give big credit to Milo and the Am I? team. They’re not professional consciousness researchers, and they didn’t pretend to be. They made a film that surfaces these questions in an open, sincere, direct way — and they made it watchable enough that the conversation has somewhere to start. That’s definitely one thing the current moment needs alongside all the detailed technical and philosophical work. Where Dawkins delivers his conclusions with the confidence of a man who’s figured it out, Milo and his team show their working. We’ll probably do a longer podcast at some point where we can really dig in.
You can watch Am I? on YouTube, and the original vlog version of these notes — recorded while walking from my hotel to the Burbank airport, traffic noise included — lives over on my YouTube channel for whoever has the patience!

Path-ensemble guidance to find the “shortest path from non-life to proto-life” still works in a Lane-style seep model — and the local-memory story gets more interesting.
Not very long ago I posted about a framework I’ve been calling geoteleomic origin-of-life modeling. The idea was: instead of asking “what initial conditions produce life?”, take a cue from the Anthropic Principle and ask “given that life did emerge, what path ensembles are least surprising conditional on reaching a life-like endpoint?” Mathematically this is a Schrödinger Bridge (SB) problem on the space of stochastic chemical trajectories, with a Doob h-transform doing the work of identifying the minimum-information deformation of the native chemistry that lands you in the target set.
That earlier post described the framework on minimal toy models: schematic RAF-front simulations, serial transfer, schematic compartmental division. The simulations supported the basic claim — small, coherent, low-information SB-style nudges can convert rare ignition into typical ignition — but the chemical realism was, frankly, near zero.
A new paper I’ve recently uploaded takes the next step, as roughly suggested by my old friend Rafal Smigrodzki in a comment on that previous post. We ask: does the SB approach still help when the native dynamics is shaped by something that at least gestures toward Nick Lane’s alkaline hydrothermal seep picture, with H2/CO2 feeds, pH and redox gates, mineral surfaces, porous retention, and chemical clutter?
Spoiler: yes. And along the way the local-memory story got more interesting.
What’s different this time
The new model is still a fairly coarse preliminary study — a path-ensemble diagnostic, not an actual calibrated geochemical reactor — but it adds several features the earlier RAF model lacked:
- H2-rich vent-side feed and CO2-rich ocean-side feed, with gradients across a mixing zone.
- pH and redox gates concentrated in that mixing zone, modulating reaction propensities.
- FeS-like mineral surface factors and pore retention.
- A coarse carbon/energy ladder: H2 + CO2 → C1, C1 + H2 → C2, C2 + proton-motive gradient → E.
- An explicit membrane-production channel (C2 + E + productive RAF → L → M).
- Decoy autocatalytic loops that compete for the same resources but contribute little or negatively to membrane output.
- Side and waste channels (TAR, X, Y, Z, W) representing chemical clutter.
- Two productive RAF families: an incumbent T0 and a later-arriving improved variant T1.
- Nonstationary evolutionary perturbations (a takeover protocol and a shock protocol).
This is closer to a chemically suggestive environment than the earlier RAF-front toys. It is still abstract — we are not modeling actual Wood–Ljungdahl intermediates, real pH-dependent speciation, or explicit amphiphile geometry. But we now have gradients, gates, surfaces, retention, clutter, decoys, evolving variants, and a competition between membrane conversion and catalytic overcycling.
Result 1: SB guidance survives the move to a richer setting
The native dynamics in this regime is weak. Without bridge guidance, neither protocol reaches viable membrane-producing autocatalytic organization; success rates are essentially zero across 20 replicates.
Add a functional bridge — one trained to favor any productive RAF plus membrane mass — and success goes to 1.00 with substantial membrane output. Switch to a conversion-oriented bridge, which specifically favors membrane-conversion efficiency, and the system produces significantly more membrane mass and a much larger post-event membrane AUC.
Numbers from the shock protocol (means over 20 replicates):
- Native: success 0.00, membrane mass 5.33, post-shock M AUC 51.2.
- Functional bridge: success 1.00, membrane 35.9, AUC 490.4.
- Conversion bridge: success 1.00, membrane 64.1, AUC 878.2.
So the headline finding is that SB / Doob-transform path-space guidance is not a trick that worked only because the earlier RAF model was minimal. Even with chemical clutter, decoys, and an evolving productive family, a low-dimensional learned backward potential robustly improves the path ensemble leading from seep-driven carbon and energy flow to energized autocatalytic compartmental organization.
That alone would have been interesting. But the even funkier story turned out to be about local memory. This turned out to teach me some lessons of much broader import, both philosophically and potentially for AI approaches like algorithmic chemistry.
Result 2: broad biphasic memory was too crude
In the earlier work I had played with biphasic memory rules of the form a_eff = a_base · exp(η · h − ξ · Φ(h)), where h is a recent-use trace, η rewards repetition, and ξΦ kicks in once repetition exceeds a threshold. The intuition was: repeated use first stabilizes a pathway, then risks over-conditioning it. This is adjacent to Sheldrake’s much wilder “morphic resonance” framing, but here it just means a path-dependent bias on propensities, with no mystical commitments.
In the richer Lane-style model this rule did not work as hoped. It sometimes increased mutant participation, but it also damaged membrane conversion. Why?
Because the rule penalizes repetition itself — and repetition is how a chemical individual forms. Without recurrence, there is no self-maintaining organization at all. Suppressing repetition broadly is a bit like trying to fix overfitting by deleting your training data.
The fix turns out to be conceptual rather than parametric. What should decline is not function but excess canalization: the dominance of an implementation beyond its current contribution to viable future organization.
I’m calling the refined rule “protected release,” or value-relative anti-precedence. The structure is straightforward:
- For each pathway family g, compare its actual share S_g(t) of the recent ecology to a value-justified share S*_g(t), computed by a softmax over per-family value scores. Value here is approximated by recent membrane-conversion payoff per unit of resource or catalytic cost.
- Define excess canalization as O_g = max(S_g − S*_g − θ, 0). Penalize this, not raw use.
- Give each reaction a functional-protection coefficient c_r ∈ [0,1] — high for shared membrane-conversion machinery, lower for identity-specific autocatalytic cycling — so anti-precedence falls mainly on identity, not on shared function.
- Diffuse the “release pressure” from over-canalized families into neighboring pathway implementations via a motif-neighborhood kernel.
Put more simply: penalize a pathway only when it occupies more of the ecology than its function justifies. Protect the shared machinery that constitutes individuation. Release pressure toward neighboring implementations, not into the void.
Crucially, this is not species-specific. The rule does not say “boost the new RAF” or “kill the old one.” It says: any pathway identity whose realized dominance exceeds its value-justified share is gently relaxed, while shared functional machinery is preserved.
Putting it together: shock, takeover, and the winner
We tested two nonstationary protocols:
- Takeover: T0 establishes, then T1 is introduced at low abundance. Does the system shift toward the better variant while staying viable?
- Shock: T0 establishes, T1 appears, and then incumbent capability is degraded. Does the system recover by adopting T1 while preserving membrane production?
The full condition list runs from a no-bridge native baseline through bridge-only conditions (functional, conversion, plastic), broad biphasic memory, an overuse-only anti-precedence variant, and combinations of each bridge with protected release.
In the shock protocol, conversion bridge plus protected release wins by essentially every metric we tracked, relative to a conversion bridge alone:
- Mutant takeover rate up by ~0.35 (95% CI: 0.05 to 0.60).
- Mutant share up by 0.072 (CI: 0.029 to 0.118).
- Incumbent lock AUC down by 2.46 (CI: −4.05 to −0.97).
- Membrane / product conversion efficiency up by 0.011 (CI: 0.001 to 0.020).
- Adaptive score up by 0.034 (CI: 0.004 to 0.061).
- Multi-objective evolutionary regret: lowest of any tested condition.
The takeover protocol gives a weaker but consistent advantage. With no explicit incumbent degradation forcing change, plasticity-oriented conditions don’t get to shine as brightly. Even so, conversion plus protected release still posts the lowest multi-objective regret and the best adaptive score.
The weight-sensitivity grid is the result I find most reassuring. Across every tested combination of weights on membrane output, mutant adoption, lock-in, and decoy burden, conversion plus protected release wins in all shock cases and all takeover cases. So the headline isn’t an artifact of how we weighted four objectives.
The intuitive picture: conversion plus protected release is not simply more plastic. It preserves or improves conversion while allowing self-transformation. On a Pareto plot of post-shock membrane performance versus adaptive plasticity, it occupies a sweet spot that broad biphasic memory and pure plastic bridges miss. Plastic bridges trade output for flexibility. Conversion bridges alone tend to entrench the incumbent. Protected release lets you keep the throughput while loosening the lock.
Why this matters conceptually
The concept regarding “tendency to take habits” and “habit saturation” is now roughly:
Precedence enables individuation. Anti-precedence, properly defined as value-relative anti-precedence, enables ongoing self-transformation.
A protocell-like system needs both. It must stabilize a self-maintaining organization (precedence). And it must let better-performing implementations replace older ones without losing the macro-organization (protected release).
In information-theoretic terms, the rough form of value you want is something like
V_g ≈ I(g; viable future function) − α · I(g; frozen implementation).
A motif gets credit for predicting future viable function and a penalty for entrenching a particular frozen implementation. The crude simulations I’ve been running use a much simpler proxy — recent membrane-conversion payoff — but the conceptual direction is clear.
The next step is real chemistry
So the work I’ve done so far is just a path-ensemble diagnostic, not a full-fledged chemical simulation. The chemistry is still abstract: H2, CO2, C1, C2, E, named RAF families, generic membrane mass M. To turn this into a real chemical simulation, some significant upgrades are needed:
Replace the C1/C2/E ladder with a real reduced network. Candidate ingredients are well known: CO2/HCO3 chemistry with proper pH-dependent speciation; H2 oxidation and explicit redox coupling; FeS/NiS/greigite-like surface states; formate, CO, methyl, acetyl-like, acetate, thioester, and acetyl-phosphate-like intermediates; and adsorption/desorption dynamics on mineral surfaces. The Wood–Ljungdahl literature, the Lane group’s reactor work, and the iron-sulfide catalysis literature provide most of what’s needed.
Make the spatial / hydrodynamic part less coarse. Real alkaline seeps have explicit pore geometry, flow, retention, surface-area distributions, and pH gradients that are not separable from the chemistry. A reduced reaction-diffusion-flow simulation with realistic pore-scale features would let memory variables emerge from the physics rather than be put in by hand.
Discover motifs instead of naming them. The current model bakes in T0, T1, and the decoy. This is an initial attempt to understand the situation conceptually and – to an extend – quantitatively. What we really need to do is generate random reaction networks and uses exact or approximate RAF detection (Hordijk–Steel and successors) to identify motif families dynamically. Pathway families g would then be discovered, not declared. Anti-precedence is studied as a general rule over discovered motif occupancy, value, and motif-neighborhood structure..
Derive memory variables from chemistry. In the current paper U_g (recent use), V_g (value), c_r (functional protection), and O_g (excess canalization) are all phenomenological. In a chemically grounded version, U_g should correspond to adsorbed pathway-specific intermediates; V_g to measured conversion into membrane / energy-coupled products; c_r to shared energy/membrane machinery; O_g to surface occupation beyond productive turnover. Surface conditioning, adsorption, depletion, inhibition, clogging, washout, pH exhaustion — the microphysics is already path-dependent. The question is whether real surface and flow microphysics naturally produces something like value-relative anti-precedence, or only broad decay (which the current paper shows is too crude).
Experimental analogues. A microfluidic or mineral-reactor experiment looking for adaptive replacement — an incumbent product network persists, a better-performing variant takes over after a perturbation, while membrane / compartmental function remains continuous — would be the cleanest experimental signature of protected release in actual chemistry. The relevant knobs (pH cycling, redox cycling, periodic flow changes, substrate pulses, surface renewal, controlled poisoning/recovery of catalytic surfaces) are not exotic.
Better bridge training. The current paper uses frozen coarse Doob/SB-style bridges trained on near-native rollouts.
