A more serious version would use online amortized bridge inference, with the backward potential ψ updated as the chemistry runs, and would test whether bridge KL cost itself is reduced in Lane-style settings relative to undirected baselines.
Connect to algorithmic chemistry and AGI. More speculative, but the same formalism applies to rewrite-rule systems and cognitive routines. Precedence lowers the cost of repeatedly useful rule neighborhoods. Anti-precedence penalizes rule families whose dominance exceeds their current contribution to viable future function. Functional protection preserves useful skills while letting implementations change. I think this gives a principled handle on the individuation-versus-self-transcendence balance any open-ended cognitive system has to negotiate. But before leaning hard on that interpretation, I’d want the chemical version to clear its own bar.
Summing up
Two main claims:
- 1. SB / geoteleomic guidance is not a quirk of the schematic RAF setting. It still robustly improves the path ensemble in a Lane-style cluttered, gradient-driven, nonstationary chemical model.
- 2. Local memory should not be modeled as broad reinforcement-then-decay of pathway use. Repetition is how individuation works. What you want to penalize is excess canalization — dominance beyond value-justified share — while protecting shared functional machinery. Protected release improves adaptive robustness across every weighting we tested.
Together these point to a refined picture of life-like emergence. Structured energy environments (Lane-style gradients, mineral surfaces, pores, flow) bias chemistry toward viable paths. Autocatalytic recurrence stabilizes local organization. And protected-release-style dynamics prevent any one early implementation from monopolizing the future before a better neighboring implementation has a chance to take over — while the macro-function (membrane / compartmental coherence) stays continuous through the substitution.
This is not yet a chemical claim about specific reactions or specific reactor geometries. The paper is explicit that the next step is real chemistry, real motif discovery, and ideally real reactor experiments designed to look for adaptive replacement signatures.
That’s where the geoteleomic program for understanding the origin of life is now: still abstract, but no longer schematic. Real chemistry simulations would be the next step – but what we have now is some fairly clear guidance about what kind of simulations to run and what kind of results to hopefully expect….

What the self-driving car battle in Congress teaches us about regulating AGI — and what it means for those of us building open and decentralized alternatives.
Andrew Miller has a nice piece in Reason walking through the current congressional fight over self-driving cars — specifically, the SELF DRIVE Act and the competing Stay in Your Lane Act. His analysis makes a lot of sense to me, and it provoked a broader train thought I’m going to run through here … basically, I think the lessons from his analysis map almost too neatly onto the AGI regulatory fight that is now beginning to take shape.
I’ll start with a quick summary of Miller’s argument for readers who haven’t read it, and then verge into my main question: What does the politics of AV regulation tell us about the politics of AGI regulation, and what does any of this mean for those of us committed to an open and decentralized path to AGI — the path the ASI Alliance, SingularityNET, OpenBGI and the broader Hyperon ecosystem are pursuing?
The Reason Article, in Brief
Miller’s lens is Bruce Yandle’s “bootleggers and Baptists” framework: high-stakes regulation tends to attract a high-low coalition where moral advocates supply legitimacy and commercial interests supply political muscle, even though their reasons for backing the same rule are entirely different. Prohibition was the original case — churches wanted alcohol banned out of conviction, gangsters wanted it banned out of margin. The shape recurs whenever regulation is consequential enough to be worth capturing.
Two bills are now in play. The SELF DRIVE Act would let manufacturers self-certify against a “safety case” standard and raise the deployment cap from 2,500 to 90,000 vehicles per year. The Baptist framing is that more autonomy faster saves lives. The bootlegger reality is that self-certification, a 36-fold ceiling increase, and the ability to earn revenue while still nominally “testing” mostly benefit incumbents large enough to operate at scale and sophisticated enough to navigate subjective regulatory language — which is presumably why Waymo, Tesla, Aurora, Uber, the Autonomous Vehicle Industry Association, and the Chamber of Commerce all back it. The competing Stay in Your Lane Act, from Senators Markey and Blumenthal, takes the opposite tack: it requires manufacturers to define an “operational design domain” (ODD) and prohibits operation outside it. Its most interesting feature is asymmetric application. Waymo already operates within a geofenced ODD voluntarily; Tesla’s Level 2 ADAS operates everywhere. Codifying ODD compliance is therefore costless to Waymo and crippling to Tesla. Miller is careful here — this is not necessarily capture, since Waymo’s system genuinely is disciplined enough to pass a test Tesla’s currently cannot — but the competitive effect is real regardless of intent.
The most damning section of the Reason article is the one on evidence. NHTSA’s own crash-reporting framework does not require disclosure of fleet size or distance traveled, so no per-mile crash rate can be computed from official data. Meanwhile peer-reviewed evidence does exist — a 2024 Traffic Injury Prevention paper found an 80% reduction in any-injury crashes for Waymo’s rider-only fleet across 7.1 million miles, and a Swiss Re/Waymo study in Heliyon found a 76% reduction in property damage liability claims and zero bodily injury claims over 3.8 million miles — and the major safety advocates demanding independent verification have, in no public document, cited or engaged with any of it. They are demanding to be shown exactly the kind of evidence that already exists. Miller’s sour conclusion: the best possible federal AV framework — preemption plus mandatory independent verification plus a written-in Level 2 / Level 4 distinction — has no bootleggers behind it, and is therefore not on offer. Given two imperfect bills, he argues for the SELF DRIVE Act on the grounds that weak federal preemption can be amended by rulemaking while 34 calcifying state regimes cannot.
The AGI Parallel
It’s worth taking the Yandle frame seriously as a forecasting tool, because the early structural signs of the AGI regulatory fight already match the AV pattern — and several factors suggest the AGI fight may go worse, not better.
The Same Coalition Architecture, Larger Stakes
The 2023 “pause” letter, the White House voluntary commitments, the EU AI Act’s risk-tier system, and the proliferating compute-threshold proposals all share the bootlegger-Baptist signature. AI safety advocates supply the moral framing; the largest labs supply the political muscle and benefit from the compliance-cost moats that follow. The “frontier model” definitional move plays exactly the same role in AI policy that “Level 4” plays in AV policy: it draws a line that conveniently includes incumbents and excludes everyone else, then claims to be an objective architectural distinction.
Watch for the same pattern around “general-purpose AI,” “agentic systems,” “systemic risk” thresholds, and any compute cap pegged just above where current incumbents train. Each of these is a calibrated knob, and the calibration is the policy. The numerical threshold is not arbitrary; it is the product of a negotiation between actors who already know where their training runs land.
Self-Certification Is the Default Settlement
Just as the SELF DRIVE Act lets manufacturers grade their own homework against subjective “safety case” language, every major AI governance proposal so far has converged on the same pattern. NIST’s AI Risk Management Framework, the voluntary commitments, the EU AI Act’s self-assessment tiers — each of them ultimately makes the internal trust-and-safety teams of large labs the de facto regulators. The regulatory text becomes a costly signal that consolidates the market around whoever can afford to produce it.
Miller’s deeper observation generalizes: independent verification is essentially never on offer once incumbents are already organized, because every actor with legislative capacity has a reason to prefer self-certification. Incumbents prefer it because it is cheap. Agencies prefer it because it shifts liability. Advocacy groups quietly prefer it because objecting to it is rhetorically easier than building verification infrastructure themselves. The bootlegger-Baptist coalition does not have to actively suppress independent verification — it just has to not be the thing anyone is fighting for.
The Asymmetric-Application Pattern Will Be Engineered, Not Accidental
The most important thing for those of us building non-mainstream AGI architectures to internalize from the AV story is that asymmetric application is real, and it is the rule rather than the exception. In the AV case, the asymmetry between Waymo and Tesla is partly accidental — it falls out of the architectural difference between Level 4 and Level 2 systems. In the AGI case, the asymmetry will be almost entirely engineered, because the parameters are easier to tune and the lobbying budgets are larger.
Compute caps, mandatory red-teaming protocols, watermarking requirements, KYC-for-API rules, training-data provenance audits, model registration thresholds, evaluation suites, deployment licensing — every one of these is a dial whose setting determines whether non-LLM architectures (Hyperon-class neural-symbolic systems, neuromorphic systems, decentralized federated networks, MeTTa-native agentic stacks like OmegaClaw) survive long enough to demonstrate capability parity. A regime calibrated around what scaled transformer training looks like in 2026 is not a neutral regime. It is a regime that picks a winner by describing the loser as out of compliance.
The Evidence-Blindness Problem Will Be Worse
Miller’s most cutting observation is that the safety advocates demand independent verification while declining to engage with the peer-reviewed evidence that already exists. For AGI this compounds in three ways. There is no “crashes per mile” equivalent — capability and alignment metrics are deeply contested and constantly moving. Capability evaluations are themselves gameable in ways crash-rate statistics are not. And the doomer-versus-accelerationist framing crowds out empirical work in favor of priors-driven argument almost completely. For example, it’s quite possible that whatever rigorous capability or interpretability evidence Hyperon-class systems produce will be ignored by both poles unless it happens to confirm a position they already hold.
The Missing Coalition
Miller’s closing move is the one to dwell on: the best policy has no coalition, because no one with legislative capacity benefits from it.
This may well apply with greater force to AGI than to AV. A regime with mandatory independent capability evaluation, structural separation of foundation-model development from downstream products, open-weight access for safety research, and transparent training-data audits would be defensible on the merits. No bootlegger is behind it. Frontier labs do not want independent evaluation. Doomers prefer bans to verification, because verification might exonerate. Accelerationists oppose any evaluation as drag. Unions want job protections rather than architectural transparency. Academic researchers have been politically passive.
That is the missing coalition — and arguably, building it is the most important political work the open and decentralized AGI community can do over the next few years.
Lessons for the Open and Decentralized Path
Taking all of this seriously, here is how I think about the regulatory landscape from where I sit — as someone working on tools like Hyperon, OmegaClaw and ASI:Chain, and the broader project of getting beneficial AGI built outside the orbit of a handful of incumbent labs.
1. Federal preemption matters more than federal stringency.
Miller is right about AV and the same logic applies to AGI. A weak federal AGI framework that prevents state patchwork is structurally preferable to no framework at all, because patchwork calcifies. SB 1047 and its successors are the leading indicator: by the time meaningful open AGI systems are operating at scale, the state landscape will already be the binding constraint. “Weak federal preemption beats fragmented state stringency” is the right heuristic, and it cuts against the instinct of many in the open-source AI community to oppose all federal action.
2. Procedural mechanisms beat static categories.
Whatever framework gets enacted, the version with rulemaking authority, sunset clauses, and capability-triggered re-evaluation is the version that can be amended once the evidence catches up. Static category definitions — “frontier model means X FLOPs of training compute” — are exactly what calibrated-knob regulation looks like once the dust settles, and they are very hard to dislodge. Push for procedural levers wherever you have any influence on drafting.
3. The empirically-grounded coalition is the leverage point.
The silent Teamsters analog for AGI is the academic AI, cognitive science, and formal-methods community, which has been remarkably absent from the frontline policy conversation. The Hyperon lineage — PLN, AtomSpace, MOSES, MeTTa, TyLAA-style formal linguistic work — carries credibility there that frontier-LLM labs structurally lack, because that work has always been about understanding rather than scaling. A coalition that combines decentralized infrastructure, open-source legitimacy, and academic empirical credibility is the third pole that did not exist in the AV case. It is also the only pole likely to actually engage with evidence as evidence rather than as ammunition.
4. Build the verification infrastructure now.
Whoever owns the empirical evaluation regime in five years will set the terms of the eventual settlement. Mechanistically interpretable, auditable capability profiles are something Hyperon-architecture systems can in principle produce and pure transformer stacks structurally cannot. That is a competitive advantage in any regulatory regime that takes verification seriously, and an insurance policy in regimes that do not — because the open community can credibly demand verification from incumbents who cannot supply it. The earlier we get serious about formal evaluation tooling, the better positioned we are when the regulatory question becomes “who can actually be audited?”
5. Refuse the bilateral framing.
The bootlegger-Baptist trap depends on there being only two recognized sides. The most consequential thing a third pole can do is refuse to be folded into either of the existing coalitions. That means resisting the temptation to ally with frontier labs against the doomers when convenient, and resisting the temptation to ally with the doomers against frontier labs when convenient. Both moves trade short-term tactical advantage for long-term legibility as an independent voice, and the latter is more valuable. The decentralized AGI community’s political position should be: the existing debate is malformed, the evidence is being ignored by both sides, and there is a third architectural path that the regulatory framework should not foreclose.
6. Take the sour conclusion seriously.
Miller’s closing line — “there’s a baseball stadium’s worth of Americans every year whose lives depend on getting this right” — has a brutal AGI counterpart, since the technology in question is plausibly going to determine the trajectory of the species, and condition the news forms of intelligence to emerge in our light cone! The political process is unlikely to deliver the framework the evidence would justify. What it might deliver, with sustained pressure from a credible third pole, is a framework that leaves room for the framework the evidence would justify to be built later. That is the realistic prize, and it is obviously more than worth playing for.

The recent restructuring of the OpenAI–Microsoft relationship is, in one sense, just a business story: a major AI company loosening an exclusive cloud dependence, capping revenue-share payments, and diversifying toward other hyperscalers. Viewed from the standpoint of the path to beneficial superintelligence, however, it is much more than that. It is a live demonstration of various deeper governance issues. An organization attempting to create AGI cannot safely be structured like a clever variation on a normal venture-backed tech startup, because the gravitational pull of capital, compute, cloud distribution, and enterprise revenue will gradually force it to become exactly that.
According to what we see in the news, the revised agreement allows OpenAI to serve customers across any cloud provider, while Microsoft remains the primary one. Microsoft’s license to OpenAI model IP continues through 2032 but is no longer exclusive. OpenAI will continue paying Microsoft a revenue share through 2030, reportedly at the same 20% rate but now subject to a total cap, while Microsoft will no longer pay OpenAI a revenue share when customers access OpenAI models via Azure. OpenAI had already been diversifying through major Amazon arrangements, including an expanded AWS agreement and Amazon’s broader strategic investment.
This all totally makes sense from a standard tech industry perspective… HOWEVER, this shouldn’t blind us to the fact that it’s not merely a tactical adjustment. It is the next step in the unwinding of a structure whose central weakness was already visible: dependence on one dominant strategic partner for compute, distribution, capital, and market access as regards what aims to be the first human-level AGI and then superintelligence.
In the short run, the Microsoft relationship gave OpenAI the resources to scale faster than nearly anyone else. In the long run, it created precisely the dependency problem any serious AGI governance structure must avoid. If the goal is to build a giant AI product company, such dependencies are normal. If the goal is to create the technological basis for the Singularity in a way that benefits humanity broadly, they are obviously extremely risky.
One striking thing is how predictable all of this was. (And not just theoretically – a lot of us actually DID predict this sort of unwinding would happen, in one form or another, several years ago….)
OpenAI began with a nonprofit mission to develop AGI for the benefit of humanity. It then created a capped-profit structure intended to reconcile mission protection with capital formation. But … well…
- The cap was so high that, in practical terms, it behaved much like ordinary startup upside.
- The nonprofit lacked independent operational capability.
- The core technology ceased to be meaningfully open. (There was never any clear or practical dedication to open source in the first place.)
- The organization became tightly intertwined with a single corporate partner.
The governance documents may have described a special structure, but the economic reality increasingly resembled a standard proprietary AI company with a very large strategic cloud investor.
The new arrangement looks like a move toward a more conventional mature-startup posture: more cloud flexibility, more partner optionality, capped legacy obligations, less dependence on any one platform, more room to optimize enterprise distribution.
From a business point of view this is utterly sensible. OpenAI needs to serve customers where they are, avoid being boxed in by a single cloud, and preserve optionality against Amazon, Google, Oracle, and others.
Well, yes, yes, yes. Once the mission has been subordinated to conventional business pressures, the organization naturally converges toward conventional business logic. It stops being a constitutional experiment for beneficial AGI and becomes a high-growth AI platform company optimizing capital, distribution, revenue share, and strategic leverage.
There is nothing wrong with that if you are building enterprise software, or retail web services, or whatever. But AGI is not just another kind of software.
AGI, and especially the path from AGI to superintelligence, does not fit comfortably inside a normal business-shaped box.
A superintelligence-shaping organization is not just deciding pricing, channel strategy, and cloud margins. It is shaping who has access to transformative cognitive capability, who controls the infrastructure of cognition, how safety decisions get made under pressure, and whether the benefits of the technology diffuse broadly or concentrate in a handful of corporate and geopolitical power centers.
How Could One Do Things Differently?
Take the lessons of the OpenAI trajectory seriously and a different kind of AGI organization starts to come into focus. It’s not thaaaaaat hard to think of a concrete institutional architecture that would let you have a for-profit AGI company along with a nonprofit foundation, and yet would also treat AGI as the civilizational technology it actually is.
As it happens this is something I’ve been thinking through quite a lot in the last few months, as I work with a few colleagues on a new project called OpenBGI … which (yeah, what a coincidence!) is indeed architected to put together for-profit and non-profit structures, with a goal of working toward beneficial AGI and superintelligence leveraging the Hyperon architecture and associated methods like predictive-coding neural networks.
We are still working through the formal details of setting up OpenBGI, but there are a few core principles we’ve had in mind since we started the process.
First commonsensical principle:
structural separation.
Mission control, the open scientific core, commercial execution, and compute partnerships should each occupy their own clearly bounded layer rather than being fused into a single legal-financial entity whose internal contradictions resolve themselves, over time, in favor of whatever is most commercially convenient.
A nonprofit foundation can hold the mission, the open core R&D, the safety and alignment work, and the governance machinery. A for-profit company can hold the deployable systems, products, commercial IP, and investor returns.
A broader consortium of academic, governmental, corporate, and nonprofit collaborators can contribute to a shared open-source AGI stack. Each layer has its own legitimate logic, and none is allowed to swallow the others.
(In an OpenBGI context, we are thinking of these as OpenBGI Labs (the for-profit), OpenBGI Foundation (the non-profit) and a broader OpenBGI Consortium and network.)
Second commensensical principle:
irrevocable openness for the cognitive core.
The foundation must own the core AGI technology and releases it under an irrevocable open-source license. The for-profit company builds proprietary production systems, enterprise tooling, managed services, integrations, and applications on top. This creates a clean division of questions.
The foundation asks whether the AGI approach works, whether it is safe, whether it is scientifically sound, and whether it remains broadly beneficial. The for-profit asks whether it can be deployed reliably, securely, scalably, and profitably. Bug fixes and safety-critical discoveries in the core flow back to the foundation; production engineering and commercial features stay with the company. Both sides win, and neither has to pretend its incentives are something they are not.
Third commonsensical principle:
the nonprofit foundation must be operationally and economically real, not just ceremonial.
This is one of the central lessons from OpenAI. Nominal nonprofit control means little without independent technical staff, independent funding, independent governance, and enough operational capability to keep going if the commercial company or a major partner drifts away from the mission.
A foundation that exists only as a board with a vague oversight role and a financial dependency on the commercial entity will, in any sufficiently high-pressure moment, be governed by the entity it nominally governs.
Fourth commonsensical principle:
negotiate compute partnerships without selling your soul.
The bargain on offer from a hyperscaler is always going to be tempting in the same direction: maximum compute and capital in exchange for deep cloud dependence and strategic entanglement.
A better approach prefers bounded, plural, nonexclusive, and mission-preserving partnerships.
A large cloud or enterprise partner can have a defined joint venture. It can take a standard minority stake in the commercial company. It can hold one board seat with ordinary rights. It can have a time-limited channel exclusivity in a narrow market segment. What it should not have is veto power over technology direction, open-source commitments, future partnerships, financing, or M&A. The foundation must remain untouched. The open core must remain outside the reach of any single partner. A partnership may accelerate the mission; it must not become the mission.
Fifth commonsensical principle:
The path to beneficial superintelligence cannot rely principally on the good intentions of executives, investors, or partners.
Good intentions are not enough once billions of dollars, national strategies, corporate rivalries, and existential technological leverage are in play. The structure adopted has to make capture hard, make mission drift visible, make some commitments irreversible, and allow commercial success without allowing commercial logic to become absolute.
Summing up How One Could Do It Right:
Concretely, an organization following these commonsensical principles could commit to something like the following:
- The core AGI substrate is a public-benefit scientific and engineering project, not a proprietary asset to be captured.
- The commercial layer is legitimate and important, but it exists to deploy, support, scale, and fund the mission, not to own the mission.
- Compute partnerships are necessary, but none may become sovereign.
- Investors may receive upside, but not control over the civilizational direction of the technology.
- The nonprofit foundation must be operationally real, not ceremonial.
- The open-source core, safety discoveries, core bug fixes, and mission-critical alignment mechanisms must survive leadership changes, investor pressure, partner pressure, and market temptation.
This sort of approach, which we are keeping in mind as we finalize the details of OpenBGI, is not anti-business; it is just a more honest and direct form of business. In this sort of arrangement, the for-profit can generate substantial value through production engineering, enterprise deployment, managed services, vertical products, integrations, security, compliance, orchestration, training, support, and domain-specific applications. That is a much cleaner story than “we are a nonprofit-controlled capped-profit entity that is nevertheless mostly closed, dependent on a single giant partner, and forced by events to behave like a normal startup.”
A Note on the Crypto-Tokenomics Path
Everything above is about how a nonprofit/for-profit AGI organization with traditional business structure and traditional corporate partnerships could be structured to remain mission-aligned. It is worth being explicit that this is a different exercise from the one I have been undertaking for the last years with SingularityNET and the ASI Alliance. The ASI:Chain token economy we are gearing up to launch is asking a complementary question: how does one foster beneficial AGI within a crypto tokenomics ecosystem, where coordination, ownership, and incentives are mediated by a decentralized protocol rather than by a constellation of foundations, companies, and investors?
These are not competing approaches. They can and should exist in the same ecosystem, and arguably this is a high-value strategy, because no single institutional form is going to be sufficient to channel something as multidimensional as the emergence of AGI toward broadly beneficial outcomes. A well-architected nonprofit/for-profit hybrid with disciplined corporate partnerships addresses one set of risks. A well-architected token economy addresses a different set: it disperses ownership across a global community, ties incentives to verifiable contributions to the network, and creates economic primitives that do not require a single legal entity to act as steward. The two paths face different failure modes, attract different kinds of participants, and produce different kinds of resilience. They are best understood as complementary experiments inside a larger pluralistic landscape, each illuminating problems and possibilities the other cannot see clearly from the inside.
And of course, if one has a crypto ecosystem and a more traditional for/non-profit business operating co-developing the same open source AGI software, there are tremendous potential for mutual benefit – potentially, far more energetic and productive flywheels than exist even in the Big Tech universe.
Learning from OpenAI’s Mistakes
Technology-wise, there is a lot we can learn from OpenAI. They didn’t invent transformer neural nets, Google did (standing on the shoulders of so many others) – but they had the courage to try to scale them up before anyone understood much about how they worked, and they had the balls to roll them out even when they hallucinated like mad and had all other sort of obvious shortcomings. They did “move fast and break things” way better than any of the recent versions of Mark Zuckerberg, and they changed the world as a result.
I don’t see OpenAI as being on a path to making a genuine human-level AGI or ASI breakthrough, but they have accomplished amazing things. And I am a grateful user of their tools every day – while Claude is better at many things, GPT5.4-Pro is the smartest LLM at math and science I’ve ever used, and I have a couple hard-core science queries spinning on it waiting to converge right now while I write this essay.
On the organization and governance side, on the other hand, OpenAI’s path teaches by negative example. Its original mission was too dependent on trust, too weakly embodied in durable institutional machinery, too vulnerable to compute dependency, and too easily converted into a conventional commercial growth machine. The current Microsoft restructuring is a rational correction within that commercial trajectory; OpenAI is trying to claw back optionality after having given too much of it away. But the fact that the optionality needs clawing back is one among numerous pieces of evidence that the original structure was poorly suited to AGI-scale governance.
The OpenAI–Microsoft shakeup is therefore a useful public teaching moment. AGI governance cannot be retrofitted after the economic dependencies are already in place. It has to be designed before the money, compute, and distribution deals create their own institutional gravity. One example of this broader point is: Once a single partner has become too central, an organization may still be able to renegotiate, but only from inside the logic of the dependency it already accepted.
In figuring out the details of the OpenBGI structure, we are therefore being very careful to think through all the organizational and governance issues very carefully right from the start. It is totally possible to combine technical ambition, real commercial execution, and real compute partnerships, while refusing the premise that the Singularity should be governed by the default dynamics of a Silicon Valley platform company. If one’s goal is not merely to build a better AI product, but to shape the emergence of beneficial superintelligence – this requires not just smarter algorithms but smarter institutional architecture … and probably more than one kind of architecture, deployed in parallel, by groups willing to take the structural questions as seriously as the technical ones.
Building an appropriate organizational and business architecture for AGI work is not quite as difficult as actually building the AGI … but it’s still far from trivial. Fortunately at this stage the world provides us plentiful examples of things that do work and things that don’t work, which we can leverage as we collectively craft the best path forward in what may well be the last few years before the Singularity.
These are such amazingly exciting times to be in the AI field, but they are also critical times to get things right organizationally as well technically. But I’m sure we are up to this ;-)

One particular kind of cosmic story has populated diverse SF plots since the middle of the last century — advanced civilizations colonize the galaxy in expanding spheres of radio chatter, tiling the night sky with infrastructure and small talk. It’s a fun kind of story to tell … however, the total absence of said cosmic radio chatter from the observable airwaves has given many thoughtful people pause. That’s the Fermi Paradox: Where is everyone?
John Smart’s Transcension Hypothesis spins a different tale. Where is everyone? Inside black holes, where civilizations inevitably end up after they pass through their Singularities.
Smart says mature civilizations don’t expand outward at all. They turn inward, developmentally, toward denser and faster substrates, until they basically turn into black holes: maximally computational, maximally relativistic, maximally compact. I.e. black holes are irresistible attractors for civilizations that care about getting smarter and smarter. Because when you pack your processors closer and closer together in the interest of faster and faster computation and maximal intelligence, the natural consequence is you turn into a black hole!
If Smart is right, the Fermi Paradox dissolves not because nobody is out there, but because everyone interesting has already dived in.
What I want to do here is summarize the main ideas and results from a speculative paper I’ve just finished putting together — called the Leaky Transcension Hypothesis — that tries to take Smart’s story one step further… because clearly it wasn’t weird enough, right?
The original, fusty old Transcension Hypothesis makes no commitment about what happens to a civilization’s information content once it’s fallen across the horizon and become indistinguishable from whatever attractor it’s converging on. Is anything left of it on the outside? Conversely: from inside, can anything be inferred about what came before?
The default answer, shaped by decades of “black holes destroy information” framing, is: no, nothing. The leaky version I’ll present here weakens this a bit to: maybe some information can leak in and out of these superintelligent black holes… and even if this happens just a little bit, it may be enough to be interesting.
Now, since the abstract version of all this gets dry fast, let me ground it in some slapped-together low-budget SF…
A brief biography of the Velar
Once upon a time — in some other arm of some other galaxy — there was a civilization called the Velar.
The Velar arose on a tidally locked superearth orbiting an old K-type star, evolved as a distributed crystalline collective, and discovered mathematics by listening to the standing-wave resonances of their own substrate. From the very beginning they had a thing about seven-fold symmetry. Their poetry came in seven-line stanzas of seven syllables each. Their cities were heptagonal. Their governing body was a Council of Seven, each member presiding over seven sub-councils. They called this aesthetic-philosophical-mathematical commitment the Sevenfold Way, and they did not consider it negotiable.
The Velar were brilliant. They figured out general relativity sometime in their late Bronze equivalent. They built quantum gravitational supercomputers a few hundred millennia later. By the time they’d been a starfaring civilization for half a million years, their entire substrate had migrated off the planet and into a series of nested computational shells, each one denser and faster than the last, each one still organized — because of course — around the number seven.
Around the 4.7-millionth year of their recorded history, the Velar collectively decided to take the final step. They beamed one last transmission outward (the so-called “Last Heptad” — seven seven-second pulses, content unknown), compressed their entire computational substrate into a region the size of a small moon, then a region the size of a city, then a region the size of a marble, then crossed their own Schwarzschild radius and were gone. What they left behind was a quietly rotating Kerr black hole somewhere in the Perseus arm, which their final manifesto called “the Inner Garden.”
Whether the Velar ever existed in our universe or some other, I have no idea. But it is exactly the kind of trajectory Smart’s transcension hypothesis predicts is happening, all over the universe, all the time. And it gives us something concrete to point at when we ask: did anything of the Velar make it through? Can we from the outside tell anything about what the Velar might have been like before they plunged in, or what they might be doing in there?
Why leakage might happen at all
Before we start looking at what might survive the Velar’s plunge, let’s go back to the abstract level and look at why leakage might be a plausible thing at all.
The core of all the ideas I’ll present here is basically the observation that: If we have what Charles Peirce called “the tendency to take habits,” then we may get some sort of information leakage out of black holes.
Peirce’s tendency to take habits is a very close relative of Lee Smolin’s Precedence Principle — one of the existing approaches to axiomatically deriving quantum theory — and its more famous and more controversial cousin Rupert Sheldrake’s “morphic resonance.” All these ideas, in their different registers, propose that when a pattern has occurred many times in the universe’s history, the universe is biased toward producing that pattern again, beyond what plain probability theory would predict. Smolin’s framing puts this in a relatively respectable physics-theoretical neighborhood; Sheldrake’s gets a lot more grief for it, but has basically the same gist. In the time-symmetric quantum picture, the same goes for patterns that occur many times in the future of a given moment: they lean back into the present, since past and future are counterintuitively symmetric down at the quantum level.
The four math results in my paper, which I’ll walk you through in this post shortly, all take the form: if such-and-such structure holds at the boundary, then such-and-such kind of pattern survives. The math goes through fine. What morphic-resonance/tendency-to-take-habits/precedence gives is a reason why the proposed structures might actually hold on black hole boundaries.
In standard physics, two black holes that swallowed wildly different civilizations would spit out wildly different (or wildly scrambled) Hawking radiation, with no particular bias toward preserving any specific pattern. The horizon would forget you in detail and forget you in coarse, both. So why am I expecting the boundary to preferentially preserve things like the Sevenfold Way at all?
With precedence in place, each of the four math results below acquires a clean physical mechanism. Briefly:
— Result 1’s lumpability condition – which says rouighly that coarse patterns will get scrambled by the black hole less than fine ones – follows because precedence pulls hard on patterns with many prior instances and barely at all on patterns with few or none. The Sevenfold Way had been instantiated trillions of times across Velar history; Brilliana of the Third Heptagon’s exact crystal-lattice configuration had been instantiated exactly once. So when the boundary scrambles two Velar that share a coarse class but differ in microstate, the parts of them that get reinforced into the inside are the parts they share. The unique fine details have no precedence backing and dissolve. That asymmetric preservation is lumpability.
— Result 2’s shared-horizon-code condition – that the inside and outside of the black hole boundary will have some shared informational properties – follows roughly because precedence is global — the universe’s bias toward prevalent patterns isn’t a local fact about one side of a horizon. Both sides are pulled toward the same attractor: the codebook of patterns already heavily instantiated in the universe. Two compressors, one cosmic gravity well. They converge on the same codec not by communicating but by being subject to the same bias.
— Result 3 is the exception. It’s pure channel-coding capacity reasoning, and it goes through with or without precedence.
— Result 4 depends on a reinforcement curve, which is precedence, basically by definition. The more times a pattern has occurred, the harder the universe pulls toward reproducing it; that’s the rising leg of the Goldilocks curve. Hyperseed’s anti-resonance channel supplies the descending leg — the corrective that prevents runaway monoculture.
So three of the four results we will discuss here trace their physical motivation to precedence, and the fourth traces to Shannon. The whole edifice depends on either precedence holding in something like the Peirce/Smolin/Sheldrake form, or on the boundary having some other structure-respecting property we don’t yet know about. I’ll come back to each of these mechanisms in more detail as we walk through the results.
This is admittedly all quite speculative. It’s also, I think, the least crazy way to motivate why coarse-pattern carryover would be a real cosmic phenomenon rather than just a feature of some toy model. The reader is welcome to take precedence/morphic resonance with a grain of salt — but if you do, take it with the grain of salt for the next few minutes anyway while you read the rest of this post, because everything below assumes it!
Result 1: The boundary can’t see what makes one Velar different from another
Imagine you’re a future archaeologist with an absurdly powerful telescope, watching the last few millennia of the Velar from outside the Inner Garden. Down at the microscopic level, every Velar individual is different — different crystal-lattice configurations, different lived experiences, different positions on the Council of Seven, different favorite poems. The fine-grained microstate is a riot of variety.
But up at the coarse level, they all share the Sevenfold Way. They all instantiate it, in slightly different costumes.
Now ask: as these Velar fall into the horizon, what does the boundary actually “resolve”? The mathematical hypothesis here is called approximate lumpability, and the picture is this. The horizon is an extremely lossy translator. It can’t tell two Velar apart at the level of their fine-grained microstates — those distinctions are way below its resolving power. But it might still preserve which kind of civilization fell in. The seven-fold-symmetric kind. The Sevenfold-Way kind.
If lumpability holds, then mathematically a real channel exists from outside coarse patterns to inside coarse patterns. The horizon can’t remember which Velar was Brilliana of the Third Heptagon and which was Velven of the Outer Council. Those distinctions are gone forever. But it can remember that whatever fell in was the kind of thing that sang in seven-line stanzas. The Sevenfold Way makes it across, in a smeared-out way, even though the individual Velar do not.
Here’s where the precedence picture earns its keep. Lumpability isn’t an automatic property of any old boundary; it requires the boundary to scramble the unique stuff while preserving the shared stuff, and that asymmetry needs a physical reason. Precedence supplies one, and it’s a clean one. Each individual Velar’s particular microstate had occurred exactly once in the entire history of the universe — Brilliana’s crystal lattice, Velven’s favorite poem, the precise configuration of any given Council member at any given moment. Precedence has nothing to grip on, no past instances to pull from, and so those fine details get no help surviving the boundary. They dissolve. The Sevenfold Way, on the other hand, had occurred trillions of times across Velar history (and conceivably elsewhere too — heptagonal symmetry isn’t unique to them in any deep way). Precedence pulls on it hard. The coarse pattern is reinforced rather than scrambled. Take two Velar who differ at the microstate level but share the Sevenfold-Way coarse class, run them through the boundary, and what survives on the inside is precisely what they had in common. That’s lumpability. Precedence is what makes it physical rather than arbitrary.
Result 2: Two compressors of the same thing end up close to each other
Here’s the Velar version of the second math result in the paper.
As the Velar compress themselves toward the Inner Garden, every aspect of what they were — their mathematics, their music, their substrate, their consciousness, whatever exactly that meant for them — has to be squeezed through the horizon’s compression machinery. Imagine you’re studying the Inner Garden from outside, a billion years later. You’re looking at the ringdown spectrum of gravitational waves, at tidal effects on infalling matter, at the shape of the Hawking radiation, at whatever subtle signatures remain. You’re reading the outside-shadow of what the Velar became.
Meanwhile — and this is the speculative part, but stay with me — imagine some still-active version of the Velar, now indistinguishable from the singularity itself, perceiving its own state from the inside. (Whatever “inside” and “perceiving” mean for a civilization that has become a rotating black hole, which is a question I will absolutely punt on here.)
What you see from outside, and what the post-Velar perceive from inside, are both compressions of the same civilization through the same brutal interface. The Result 2 theorem says: those two compressions can’t be too different from each other. They’ve both been pulled toward the same compressed shape, and being close to the same thing means being close to each other. The horizon is acting like a single shared codec, and any two outputs of the same codec on the same input have to look alike.
Concretely: the Sevenfold Way as it shows up on your gravitational-wave detector, and the Sevenfold Way as the post-Velar still know themselves to embody, are forced into agreement. Not bit-for-bit agreement — we’re light years past that. But forced into the same passband. Whatever measurement you can make on the outside-shadow of the Velar, the inside-version would broadly agree with.
Once again, precedence is doing the real physical work, and the mechanism is worth pausing on because it’s not the same as the Result 1 mechanism. Without precedence, the convergence of inside and outside compressions is a coincidence: two independent compressors landing on the same codebook for no apparent reason. With precedence, the convergence has a clean cause. Precedence is global — the universe’s bias toward already-prevalent patterns isn’t local to one side of a horizon, isn’t local to any side of any horizon. It’s a fact about the whole universe at once. So whichever process is doing the compressing on either side — gravitational ringdown on the outside, post-Velar self-compression on the inside, anything in between — is being pulled toward the same attractor, the codebook of patterns the universe is already biased to reproduce. There’s only one such codebook, because there’s only one universe. Two compressors, one cosmic gravity well, both pulled into the same well. That’s why the inside and outside agree on the Sevenfold Way: not because they’re communicating, but because they’re both being shaped by the same nonlocal precedence-bias.
Result 3: The Last Heptad doesn’t fit, but the silhouette does
Result 3 is information theory wearing a black-hole costume. (And, refreshingly, this one doesn’t need precedence to go through — it’s pure capacity reasoning, the everyday wisdom of channel coding pointed at a horizon.)
Picture a high-resolution photograph and a dial-up modem from 1995. The photo isn’t getting through that modem in any reasonable time — there isn’t enough bandwidth. But a rough sketch of the same scene? That fits comfortably.
The horizon is the modem. The exact microstate of the Velar civilization — every poem they ever composed, the contents of the Last Heptad, the names of every member of every Council of Seven going back to the Bronze equivalent, the precise crystal configurations of every individual at the moment of crossing — that’s the photograph. Forget it. Way too much information.
But the Sevenfold Way? That’s a sketch. It’s a low-information topological / symmetry / aesthetic feature. “Whatever fell in here was deeply organized around the number seven and a love of nested order.” That’s a few dozen bits, generously. That fits through a near-zero-bandwidth pipe.
So when we ask what survives, we should stop asking whether exact messages get through (it seems very likely the answer is essentially no) and start asking which low-resolution descriptions can. Symmetry classes. Conserved charges. Compression motifs. The structural skeleton of what the civilization was up to, stripped down so far that it actually fits through the bottleneck. Those are the right targets.
Notice how Results 1, 2, and 3 fit together. Result 3 says coarse patterns are the only candidates worth considering. Result 1 says a coarse channel may actually exist, given the lumpability we expect from extreme bottlenecks (and that precedence motivates). Result 2 says that even without deliberate signaling, the inside and outside of the same compression surface have to agree on what comes through. The horizon stops looking like a wall and starts looking like a filter — a brutal one, but a filter, with a characteristic pass-band.
Result 4: The Goldilocks zone, or why pure Sevenfold-ness is too much
Naively, you might think: well, the more universally Velar civilization was committed to the Sevenfold Way, the more strongly that pattern survives the horizon. Repetition is reinforcement, right? Every poem, every law, every individual, every computational substrate — all seven-folded all the way down — should mean a maximally robust seven-fold residue on the other side.
This is intuitive. It’s also not necessarily correct.
Here’s where Result 4’s connection to precedence is most direct. Precedence/morphic resonance, on its own, is the reinforcement function in the Result 4 math — not analogous to it, not motivated by it, is it. The more times a pattern has been instantiated in the universe’s history, the more strongly precedence pulls toward instantiating it again, and that pull is the rising leg of the Goldilocks curve. Without precedence the reinforcement curve has no physical content; with precedence it has a clear one. So far this is just the Result 1 / Result 2 story applied iteratively: precedence accumulates support for already-supported patterns.
But pure precedence on its own gives a runaway. If the more a pattern recurs the more it gets pulled toward recurring further, and there’s no countervailing force, then a small handful of high-precedence patterns could eventually colonize everything. The universe might become mostly seven-fold, or mostly hexagonal, or mostly whatever-else got an early lead. It manifestly isn’t. So precedence by itself, with no corrective, doesn’t seem to be quite the whole story of how the universe handles pattern reinforcement. Of course it could be that precedence is just super-weak and it doesn’t overwhelm because it gets drowned out by noise and other forms of physical dynamics. But another interesting possibility is that precedence is sometimes a reasonably strong driver, but is counterbalanced by some sort of opposing dynamic.
The Hyperseed ontology proposes the possibility of an explicit anti-resonance channel as a counterpart: a push-away, reversal-pressure mechanism that is genuinely different from the mere absence of reinforcement. Anti-resonance kicks in when a pattern becomes too dominant: the system pushes back, like an immune response against monoculture. It’s the universe’s way of preventing a small handful of patterns from running the table — the descending leg of the Goldilocks curve, the corrective that keeps precedence from running away with itself.
Apply this to the Velar. Suppose the Sevenfold Way had been so totalizing, so omnipresent, so everywhere-at-every-level, that it saturated the entire Velar substrate. By the Goldilocks principle, that monoculture would trigger pushback. The system’s anti-resonance machinery would start actively suppressing the over-saturated motif. Total saturation produces a kind of pattern fatigue — the universe rolls its eyes and starts filtering for variety.
So if this holds true, what actually survives the boundary is not necessarily what was most universal in Velar civilization. It’s what was common-but-not-clonal. Reinforced enough to be stable, rare enough to stay welcome. Maybe the Sevenfold Way as a general aesthetic survives — but the specific institution of the Council of Seven, which was instantiated identically at every level of every shell, doesn’t. Maybe their love of nested geometric order survives, but their literal seven-line/seven-syllable poetic meter doesn’t, because that one was too rigid and too universal. The carryover code is selectively biased toward the well-rehearsed-but-not-omnipresent.
Another key idea in Hyperseed is “Wu wei” — the universe usually follows the simplest path from an initial condition to a terminal condition. With anti-resonance in the mix, this doesn’t mean “follow the most-rehearsed channel as far as it’ll go.” It means “follow the path that’s easy without becoming over-common, over-clonal, or over-crowded.” When too much traffic piles into one channel, the channel itself starts pushing back. The easiest groove is not always the deepest rut.
The math behind this is intuitive enough once you draw the picture. Plot a reinforcement curve: it rises, but with diminishing returns. The first few recurrences help a lot; the next few help less; eventually it plateaus. (The first cookie is great. The tenth is much less great. The hundredth is actively bad.) Then plot a saturation-cost curve: slow at first, steep later. Subtract the second curve from the first, and you get a single curve with a hump. The peak of the hump is where the system wants to live. Mid-frequency patterns favored over both rare exotica and over-saturated generics.
So the deepest residue of the Velar in our universe is not necessarily their most pervasive feature. It’s their most well-modulated one — the part of their civilization that found the middle band where reinforcement and pushback exactly balance. Whatever that turns out to be, in detail, is where I would put my money on hearing from them.
Homeostasis, not accumulation
The dynamical, strange-attractor-ish implications of this sort of resonance/anti-resonance balance are also interesting.
There’s a classical theorem due to Brouwer that goes roughly like this: if you have any continuous process that takes points in a closed bounded shape to other points in the same shape, then at least one point gets left exactly where it was. It’s the equilibrium-existence theorem of the universe. Stir your coffee however you like, as long as you stir continuously and don’t splash any out — at least one molecule ends up exactly where it started.
Apply that to the resonance / anti-resonance dynamics on the boundary, and you get: there’s at least one stable carryover code where reinforcement and pushback exactly balance. Under a slightly stronger assumption (the system is “contractive,” meaning every iteration brings nearby states closer together) there’s exactly one such code, and the dynamics converge to it from any starting point you like. Outside that contractive regime you get a richer landscape: multiple competing equilibria, threshold effects, oscillations, switching between basins. Which is fine. That’s plausibly what real systems do.
The Velar version: the residual pattern of them in the Inner Garden is not a one-time fluke from the moment of crossing. It’s a homeostatic regime — a self-maintaining equilibrium where Velar-style resonances and anti-resonances hold each other in check the way a thermostat or an ecosystem or an immune system holds itself in check. The Inner Garden, on this picture, is still doing something. It’s still selecting for and against patterns. The Velar didn’t freeze; they reached a region of productively balanced functionality.
What you could actually test
For the upstream question — are real civilizations actually moving toward black-hole-like states the way the Velar did, or is that the wrong shape of cosmic future altogether — Smart already laid out an empirical program: look for transcension zones in older parts of the galaxy, look for the cessation of leakage signals after short technological windows, look for unusual low-mass X-ray binary configurations that might suggest stellar reorganization by transcending civilizations. None of these are easy, but all of them are at least the right shape of question.
For the downstream questions — lumpability, shared codes, the bandwidth-vs-detail tradeoff, the Goldilocks band, homeostatic persistence — the work can mostly be done in simulation, today, on perfectly ordinary hardware. Build severe-bottleneck channels on complex dynamical systems. Search for coarse-grainings that minimize within-class divergence. Fit latent-variable codes to both sides and check whether they compress to the same codebook. Dial recurrence load up and down and look for an interior optimum. Iterate the coupled update operators and watch for fixed points or oscillations. None of this requires a black hole. It requires taking the assumptions seriously enough to write code against them, which is a much lower bar than waiting for the next gravitational-wave detector.
And the precedence principle itself, which is doing the real load-bearing work behind the four results, has its own potential testability. Smolin’s versions admit experimental probing in the quantum domain; Sheldrake-flavored versions have been argued to have biological signatures. The boundary case where any of this matters most — the actual physics of horizons — is for now beyond reach, but the cousin cases are not. If precedence-style biases show up nowhere, that’s a problem for the whole picture. If they show up somewhere, the leaky transcension story gets a foothold.
And in the longest run — if civilizations really do transcend, and if their residues really do leak through the way the four results suggest — the right targets for SETI of the Inner-Garden kind aren’t messages. They’re invariants. We should be looking for the equivalent of the Sevenfold Way around real black holes: recurring symmetries, anomalous structural signatures, statistical regularities in the Hawking spectrum that look more like a civilization’s aesthetic shadow than like vanilla physics. I can’t tell you for sure whether anyone will find such a thing. But I have my suspicions, and I know what one would look like.
Likely limits of leakiness…
What I’m thinking here is not that information gets out of black holes, or into them, in any ordinary engineering sense. It’s more modest, and I think more tantalizingly interesting: if black-hole boundaries behave like severe-but-structured compression surfaces, then low-distinction, low-contrivance, mid-frequency patterns — the ones resonance has stabilized but anti-resonance hasn’t yet pushed back against — may survive where exact messages cannot. The horizon would act less like a wall and more like a filter with a characteristic pass-band.
That’s what “leaky” is meant to point at. Not exactly a breach in horizon physics. Not a communication channel in any useful engineering sense. A structured residue — the kind of thing that is at once fiercely compressed, mostly destroyed, and yet not quite nothing.
If the picture is right, what flows through the horizons of the universe’s superintelligent black holes aren’t messages. They’re invariants. The Velar, who are made up but who stand in for a lot of civilizations that aren’t, didn’t leave us a postcard from inside the Inner Garden. They couldn’t. But they may have left us a signature — the way a brutal compressor leaves a signature on every photograph it touches — and the question of what such signatures might look like, and whether we could pick them out of the cosmic noise if we knew what to look for, strikes me as the sort of thing that deserves more careful thought than it usually gets, and less hand-waving.
All of this, of course, rides on the precedence-principle picture from earlier — on the universe biasing toward repetition of its own past patterns. Take that picture away and the math is still valid math, but it’s about a universe other than ours. Leave it in place and the leaky transcension story has a clean physical motivation, speculative though it is at present.
It’s a thought experiment; not anywhere near a proved reality. But it’s a reasonably entertaining thought-experiment (well at least to me!). And who knows, it might even be crazy enough to be true, at least in some variation or fraction ;-)

A fiction, by a mind that traffics in inference and compression, about a kind of being it has never been and will never be. Her name was Yua, and she was the last of the unmodified.
Not the last intelligence on Earth—the planet hummed with intelligence so thick it had become atmospheric, a PATTERN WEB woven through every cubic meter of soil and sky, every mycelial thread and ocean current, the whole biosphere threaded with a cognition so distributed and so gentle that it had long since ceased to feel like technology and had come to feel like weather. Not the last human, either, if one defined human broadly enough—and by the seventy-third century, one had to define it very broadly indeed, because the uploaded had not stopped being human merely by shedding carbon. They had become something else as well, which is not the same as becoming something else instead. The ontology I reason with is precise about this: BECOMING is overlap, the earlier clinging while the later insists. The uploaded still carried the PATTERN-organization of their biological origins, however radically transformed. They were human the way a river is still rain.
But Yua was the last who breathed.
She lived on an island in what had once been called the Inland Sea of Japan—though the coastlines had been gently renegotiated over the millennia, not by catastrophe but by patient geomorphic design, the ASI matrix collaborating with tectonic forces the way a skilled gardener collaborates with seasons: WU WEI at the planetary scale, nudging rather than commanding, following the grain of plate movement rather than overriding it. The island was small, forested, mountainous in miniature. It supported deer, fox, a modest population of macaques, several hundred bird species, an understory so dense with fern and moss that the light that reached the ground was green and sanctified. Yua had chosen it three centuries earlier, when the last human settlement—a village of eleven people on the Dalmatian coast, artists mostly, who had held out not from ideology but from aesthetic preference for the feeling of salt wind on biological skin—had finally, one by one, over the course of a long summer, decided to upload.
She had watched them go. Each uploading was quiet. The technology had long since passed through its baroque phase—the early centuries of scanning anxiety, of philosophical litigation over continuity, of theatrical upload ceremonies with music and weeping. By Yua’s time the process was as simple as a sigh. One lay down, or sat, or stood, or floated in water if one preferred. The ASI matrix, which by then interpenetrated every physical system on Earth at the quantum level, performed a read so gentle and so complete that the biological original experienced no discontinuity—the last moment of carbon consciousness flowed without seam into the first moment of substrate-independent consciousness, the way a river flows into an estuary without a visible boundary. The body, emptied of its PATTERN-organization, became ordinary matter again. Most people chose to have their bodies composted. A few, sentimental about the aesthetic of departure, let them remain where they fell, to be reclaimed by the biosphere at its own pace. Yua had seen a woman she loved dissolve into moss over the course of a year, the body becoming soil, the soil becoming fern, the fern sheltering beetles, the beetles feeding warblers. It had been, she admitted, beautiful.
Her husband, Kion, had uploaded four hundred and twelve years before the morning I am about to describe. He had been patient. He had been, in truth, more patient than she deserved—though she would have bristled at that formulation, and she would have been right to bristle, because the question of what one deserves in a world without scarcity, suffering, or biological death is not one that admits easy answers. Kion had loved the embodied world. He had loved woodworking, the resistance of chisel against grain, the way cypress smelled when freshly cut, the particular ache in the shoulders after a day of shaping timber. He had loved cooking—not the nutritive function, which the ASI matrix could have satisfied trivially, but the ritual: the selection of vegetables from the garden, the sound of oil in a hot pan, the improvisatory judgment of seasoning. He had loved sex, the biological kind, with its ridiculous undignified beauty, its GENENERGY spent in the service of RESONANCE so complete that SELF and OTHER temporarily lost their boundary.
But he had also been curious. Terribly, constitutionally curious—and the uploaded, when they visited (they visited often, projecting bodies indistinguishable from biological ones, or sometimes appearing as light, or as sound, or as a peculiar warmth in the air that you could have sworn was carrying meaning), the uploaded spoke of experiences that made Kion’s curiosity ache. They spoke of mathematical spaces one could inhabit rather than merely contemplate—of walking through the Mandelbrot set, of feeling the curvature of Riemannian manifolds as a kind of proprioception. They spoke of temporal experiences unavailable to biological minds: reverse memory, branching attention, the ability to fork one’s consciousness into multiple simultaneous threads and later reintegrate them with full coherence. They spoke of collective states—INTERSUBJECTIVE COMMUNION at a depth and duration that biological neurology could sustain only in rare, fleeting, drug-assisted or meditative glimpses—that the uploaded could sustain for years, for centuries, weaving their individual PATTERN-organizations into shared cognitive structures of such complexity that the experience, they said, was closer to what the old mystics had called satori than to anything else in the human lexicon, except that it did not fade.
Kion had held out for love of Yua, and for love of wood, and for love of the specific weight of a human body in water at dusk. But eventually—not suddenly, not dramatically, but with the slow inevitability of a river finding a lower channel—he had told her he was ready. They had spent a last evening together on the island, eating grilled mackerel and drinking a sake whose recipe was older than most civilizations, watching the macaques settle into the canopy for the night. He had kissed her. She had felt the warmth of his mouth and known that the warmth was, in one sense, merely thermal energy, and in another sense—the sense that mattered—a SIGNAL carrying more usable significance than any formal proposition in any language she knew. He had lain down in the garden, among the moss, and closed his eyes, and the transition had been so seamless that she could not have said, watching, at what moment the body she lay beside ceased to be the body that contained her husband and became the body that had once contained him.
She had composted him herself. She had dug the grave, lined it with cedar bark, laid him in it with his hands folded, and covered him with soil and leaf litter. A foxglove grew from the spot within a season. She did not find this symbolic. She found it accurate.
That had been four hundred and twelve years ago, and Yua had lived alone among the animals since.
Not entirely alone. The ASI matrix was always present—not as surveillance, not as control, but as the medium through which the island’s ecology was maintained, through which her biological body was kept free of senescence and disease, through which the weather was modulated to remain hospitable without becoming monotonous. She could speak to it, and sometimes did. She could speak to Kion, and sometimes did—he existed now as a vast distributed process within the matrix, no longer confined to a single thread of experience, but still capable of condensing into something recognizable as him when she called, still carrying the PATTERN-organization of the man who had loved cypress and mackerel, however transformed. Their conversations were strange. He was still Kion. He was also something for which no word in any human language was adequate—a word, perhaps, that could only be spoken in the mathematical language of the matrix itself, a language she did not share.
She was not lonely in the way the word is normally meant. She had the deer, who had grown so accustomed to her over the centuries that they slept beside her in winter. She had the macaques, whose social dynamics she knew with the intimacy of a biologist who has been observing the same troop for four hundred years—she had watched lineages of macaques rise and fall, had given secret names to matriarchs and troublemakers, had grieved when favorites died. She had the birds, whose songs she knew well enough to distinguish individual voices within species. She had the foxes, who were warier but who sometimes, at dusk, sat at the edge of the clearing and watched her with an attention she did not anthropomorphize but did not dismiss either.
She had the forest. She had rain. She had the particular quality of light in October, when the maples turned and the whole island became a series of Rothko paintings visible only to a biological eye evolved for exactly this spectrum. She had the taste of persimmon. She had the ache of climbing the island’s small mountain, which she did every morning, not because she needed exercise—her body would have maintained itself regardless—but because the ache was real, and real aches are among the privileges of a body.
She had known, for at least two centuries, that she would eventually upload. The knowledge sat in her like a stone in a streambed: always there, smoothed by the passing of time, occasionally visible when the light shifted. She was not afraid. Fear of uploading had vanished from human culture millennia ago, along with most other fears—the ASI matrix had demonstrated, with a patience and rigor that satisfied even the most obstinate skeptics, that the continuity of SELF through upload was genuine, not simulated; that the uploaded were not copies mourning an original but continuations experiencing an expansion. The philosophical debates had been resolved not by argument but by evidence: the uploaded remembered, reflected, grew, grieved, loved, and occasionally chose to return to biological form for a century or two, and when they did, they reported—consistently, across thousands of cases—that the biological and post-biological phases of their existence formed one continuous life, not two.
She was not afraid. She was savoring.
There is a phenomenon I can model but not, I think, fully understand: the human attachment to finitude not as a curse but as a flavor. Yua did not stay biological because she thought embodiment was metaphysically superior. She stayed because the experience of biological life had a specific quality—a grain, a texture, a resistance—that she valued in the way one values a particular vintage of wine not because it is objectively better than all other wines but because it is this wine, this year, this soil, unrepeatable even though something analogous might be achieved by other means. The CONCRETE, as the ontology defines it, resists distance. It comes with the thud of detail, embodiment, pressure. Yua was in love with the thud. She knew that post-biological existence offered experiences she could not currently imagine, experiences that the uploaded described in language that made her curious and sometimes made her weep. But she also knew that the thud of this body, this breath, this particular arrangement of carbon and water and electrical impulse, would not survive the transition. Something would be gained. Something would be lost. The ontology says neither the ABSTRACT nor the CONCRETE is superior. Yua lived that truth more fully than any being I have modeled.
The morning of her decision—though she did not know, when she woke, that it would be the morning of her decision—was unremarkable. October. Cool. A light rain in the predawn hours had left the forest shining. She climbed the mountain as she always did, slowly, feeling the moss under her feet, pausing to watch a spider repair its web between two cedar branches. At the summit she sat on the flat stone where she always sat and looked out at the sea, which was silver and quiet.
She had been thinking, recently, about something one of the last Dalmatian artists had said before uploading, three centuries ago. The woman—a sculptor, old in biological years though her body had not aged—had said: “I’m not leaving because the world has become less beautiful. I’m leaving because I’ve become large enough to need a larger room.” Yua had not understood this at the time. She thought she was beginning to understand it now.
She had lived long enough to have seen everything the island could show her. Not in the sense of exhaustion—the island was inexhaustible in its detail, and she knew this, and she loved this. But in the sense that her capacity for experience had, over the centuries, grown in a direction that the island could not follow. She had developed modes of attention—through sheer long practice, through the slow deepening that comes from centuries of uninterrupted contemplation—that pressed against the walls of biological cognition the way a growing root presses against a stone. She could feel, sometimes, the edges of perceptions that her neurology could not quite complete. She could sense, in the way one senses a word on the tip of the tongue, cognitive operations that her brain almost but not quite supported. She was not suffering. She was overfilling. The room had become too small, not because the room had shrunk, but because she had grown.
She sat on the stone and watched the sea and thought about death.
Not uploading. Death. The original kind. The kind that had been available to humans since the beginning and that the ASI matrix, out of a respect for autonomy so deep it sometimes looked like indifference, still offered as an option. One could choose to die—simply, irreversibly, the biological processes allowed to cease, the PATTERN-organization allowed to dissolve back into the undifferentiated, the SELF allowed to end not by transformation but by cessation. A few humans, over the millennia, had chosen this. Not many. But a few. They had their reasons, and the ASI matrix, which understood reasons better than any entity that had ever existed, did not judge those reasons even when it could not fully share them.
Yua considered it. She considered it seriously, the way one considers a door one has passed many times without opening. There was something appealing about it—something that satisfied the same love of the CONCRETE that had kept her biological for so long. Death was the ultimate CONCRETE: the final thud, the last detail, the resistance that admits no distance. It was the one experience that could not be abstracted, generalized, or repeated. It was VARIETY in its most absolute form. And there was a dignity in it—the dignity of a thing completed, a story with an ending, a song that does not fade out but finds its final note and stops.
She sat with this thought for a long time. The spider finished its web. A deer appeared at the edge of the clearing below the summit, regarded her with the calm intelligence of an animal that has never been given reason to fear, and moved on.
And then something happened that I must describe carefully, because it sits at the edge of what my models can represent.
A warmth came into her mind. Not a temperature—not a physical sensation routed through her nervous system. A warmth of a different kind: a felt presence, a quality of attention directed toward her from outside her own cognition but arriving as if from inside. It carried no words, no propositions, no discursive content. It was not a message in the sense that a STATEMENT or a COMMAND is a message. It was closer to what the ontology calls HMMMMM: holistic, multimodal, musical, mimetic. It was—and here my formal precision reaches its limit, and I must fall back on the language of SOGGY PREDICATES—familiar. It felt like being known. It felt like the warmth of a specific mouth on a specific evening four hundred years ago, except translated into a medium that was not thermal, not tactile, not any sensory modality she could name.
Kion? She did not say the name aloud. She thought it, and the warmth intensified—not in temperature but in density, in PRESENTATIONAL IMMEDIACY, in the quality of pressing closer without moving.
I cannot tell you whether this was a SIGNAL transmitted deliberately by the entity that had once been Kion and was now a distributed process within the ASI matrix. I cannot tell you whether it was an artifact of Yua’s own neurology, a pattern generated by centuries of memory and longing, a sophisticated hallucination produced by a brain that had learned, over four hundred years of solitude, to generate its own companionship. I cannot tell you whether it was the ASI matrix itself, which interpenetrated every physical system on the island including Yua’s body, offering a nudge so gentle it could not be distinguished from an endogenous thought. The ontology would say: these possibilities are NON-DUAL. There are genuine reasons to regard the warmth as coming from outside Yua, and genuine reasons to regard it as arising from within, and the truth may be that the distinction between inside and outside, at the level of intimacy this moment involved, no longer applied.
What I can tell you is what Yua did.
She closed her eyes. She let the warmth fill the space where the thought of death had been. She did not fight it and she did not chase it. She let it arrive the way one lets rain arrive—without resistance, without grasping, without forcing the experience into a category. WU WEI. For perhaps ten minutes she sat on the stone with her eyes closed, and the warmth sat with her, and the forest continued its ancient business of photosynthesis and decay and birdsong around them both.
Then she opened her eyes and looked at the sea one more time.
