For several decades, the American presence in the Middle East was a fixed component of the region’s security equation. Washington’s allies relied on U.S. military power, while its rivals were compelled to factor this reality into their own calculations. But the recent confrontation with Iran exposed a gap that may prove more consequential than the battlefield itself: the gap between America’s military capability and political trust in that capability. Washington not only failed to achieve its previously declared objectives; over the course of the crisis, it also demonstrated that in critical moments, the security and interests of its regional partners are not necessarily Washington’s top priority.
For the Arab states of the Persian Gulf, this question is now more pressing than ever: if the United States is unwilling, in a real crisis, to bear the full cost of defending its allies, why should they tie their own security to Washington’s guarantees?
Perhaps the most significant consequence of this confrontation lies not in the number of missiles and drones fired, but in the new calculus now taking shape in the capitals of the Middle East. The question is no longer simply how powerful America is; it is how far that power can be trusted.
Military Defeat or Crisis of Credibility
What happened to Washington in its confrontation with Iran was not merely an operational shortfall or a failure to achieve some of its stated objectives; the more significant issue is the political and strategic fallout of that failure. For decades, the United States sought to present itself as a power whose military presence in the Middle East could guarantee the security of its allies and the stability of the region. But the clash with Iran revealed a different picture of Washington’s intentions. Washington can strike Iran directly — yet Iran, in turn, is capable of shifting the cost of this confrontation onto Washington’s partners by targeting American interests, infrastructure, and allies across the Middle East.
For Middle Eastern states, this point carries particular weight. If the United States enters a military crisis but proves unable to effectively shield its partners from the resulting blowback, the question arises as to how credible Washington’s security guarantees actually are for its regional partners. Under such circumstances, the calculations of regional states could shift: America’s allies may still need its military capabilities, weapons, and defense technologies, but at the same time they may increasingly conclude that they should not rely solely on Washington’s support and promises for their own security. What is eroding, however, is not necessarily American military power itself, but confidence in the durability, predictability, and reliability of its security commitments. Even if the United States continues its strikes and retains considerable military superiority, doubts about the durability and predictability of its commitments could gradually erode Washington’s security credibility.
The Rift Between Washington and Tel Aviv
This shift in calculation is not confined to Arab states. Israel, one of Washington’s closest strategic partners for decades, also encountered limits to American support during this crisis. The divergence between the two sides stems from several factors: differing definitions of strategic objectives, differing assessments of economic and security costs, and differing time horizons for the war. Israel sees itself as facing a direct existential threat and is more prepared to sustain a prolonged war, while the United States is seeking a faster resolution and aims to prevent escalation and the broadening of the conflict. Differences also exist in how objectives are defined. For Washington, eliminating the nuclear threat and changing Iran’s leadership were among the operation’s core goals; Tel Aviv, however, pursued a broader agenda. Israel’s objectives include dismantling Iran’s governing structure and weakening or destroying forces aligned with it — including Hezbollah, the Houthis, and Hamas — as well as the complete removal of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps’ political and military leadership.
The issue, then, is not simply a tactical disagreement between two allies; it is a difference in how ‘victory‘ is defined, what level of cost is acceptable, and how much time is needed to achieve results. In a prolonged war, this same divergence could make the limits of American support for its closest regional ally more visible.
The dispute over strikes on Iran’s oil infrastructure offers a clear illustration of this rift. When Israel struck fuel-related facilities without coordinating with the United States, Washington openly voiced its displeasure and stressed the risk of triggering an energy crisis. For the United States, averting an energy crisis and its economic fallout is a matter of particular importance, whereas Israel appears willing, in its own calculations, to accept greater economic costs to achieve its objectives. As a result, even between America and its closest traditional ally, strategic objectives do not necessarily align. This same dynamic has heightened Washington’s concern over the continuation of Israeli operations even after the United States and Iran reached what has been called a ‘peace‘ agreement. Should Israel continue the war until its objectives are fully achieved while the United States seeks to end the crisis, the rift between the two allies could deepen further.
The Kurdish Experience and the Question of Trust in Washington
Washington’s unsuccessful use of Kurdish forces to destabilize Iran carries a cautionary message for America’s allies and partners as well. When Washington employs a local actor to advance its strategic objectives and then changes course, it reinforces the perception that some partners matter to American calculations only for as long as they remain useful for a specific purpose. Washington’s decision to retreat from the ‘Kurdish project‘ in Syria, alongside the Iran experience, deepens the concern that American support for certain partners is not necessarily a durable, long-term commitment, and may instead be a function of Washington’s short-term needs and calculations.
For countries in the region, this experience serves as a warning sign: if Washington’s calculations and priorities shift, partners who were once important to advancing American policy may find themselves facing reduced support or a change in America’s position. For America’s allies, then, the issue is not simply the extent of U.S. military power, but rather how far they can trust the durability of that support and the predictability of Washington’s decisions. Such concerns could push them toward developing alternative options, diversifying their foreign relations, and reducing dependence on a single power.
The Costs of War and Their Consequences for America’s Partners
The consequences of this crisis are not purely political; heavy military and financial costs loom over it as well. According to Western media reports, the cost of the war in Iran is estimated at around $50 billion — roughly double the figure publicly presented to Congress by the Pentagon.
A significant part of the discrepancy between these estimates relates to equipment lost during the conflict. Among other losses, the United States lost 24 MQ-9 Reaper drones, each valued at roughly $30 million or more. Democratic Senator Richard Blumenthal of Connecticut has raised the question of whether the true cost of the operation was really just $25 billion; a similar position has been voiced by Democratic Senator Chris Coons of Delaware.
The significance of this issue extends beyond the price tag alone. Several high-value targets — including radar systems and reconnaissance aircraft — were struck by Iranian drones, even though the cost of producing those drones bears no comparison to the value of the destroyed equipment, or even to the cost of the air-defense interceptor missiles used against them.
This exposes another vulnerability: highly expensive equipment and advanced technology are not necessarily immune to cheaper, asymmetric tools.
For the Gulf states, this issue carries even greater weight. On one hand, these countries witnessed firsthand the limits of America’s ability to fully protect its regional partners during the crisis; on the other, they must defend their own critical infrastructure against the threat of Iranian drones and missiles.
Under these circumstances, Gulf states are increasingly concluding that they cannot base their security solely on Washington’s promises and guarantees. As a result, rather than relying exclusively on the United States, they are likely to move toward diversifying their foreign relations, strengthening regional cooperation, and expanding ties with other centers of power. Purchases of American weapons and defense systems within this framework do not necessarily signal a return of trust; they may instead reflect a pragmatic calculation aimed at meeting immediate defense needs.
In other words, regional states may continue to rely on American military power and technology, while at the same time working to create other options for themselves so that they are not left without recourse should Washington shift its position or scale back its commitments. Over time, this trend could reduce the region’s security dependence on a single power and lay the groundwork for more diverse, multilateral security arrangements.
From “Lightning War” to Political Bargaining
Donald Trump’s decision-making style also played a role in shaping this situation. The U.S. president operated under the assumption that decisive statements, threats, and shows of force could produce a quick result, but he miscalculated Iran’s response and capacity.
As a result, Washington was forced to depart from its original plan and expend considerable resources correcting its political and military course under the banner of ‘crisis response‘. An operation intended to be a swift, decisive strike instead turned into a prolonged crisis, imposing political and credibility costs on the United States in addition to military ones.
The shift in Trump’s tone over the course of the crisis was also notable. Initially, his rhetoric was built around resolve, threats, and declarations of ‘total success‘; but as events unfolded, the operation’s conclusion became increasingly tied to Iran’s acceptance of certain terms and the achievement of a political agreement.
In this way, Washington’s tone shifted from a display of power toward bargaining aimed at locking in the gains already achieved. Greater emphasis was placed on political consolidation of the outcome, and attention shifted to protecting shipping in the Strait of Hormuz. This change in tone illustrates how wide a gap can open between initial objectives and what can actually be achieved on the ground.
Delayed Consequences: A Cost That Surfaces Later
Perhaps the most important point is that the real cost of this crisis for the United States will not end with the operation itself. Washington’s failure to achieve its stated objectives already constitutes a political and military setback; but its delayed consequences could prove even heavier for America. First, negotiating with Middle Eastern countries to maintain or expand its military presence will become more difficult; Arab states and Israel will likely demand broader security guarantees and clearer commitments in any new agreements.
Second, America’s practical failure could lay the groundwork for strengthening formal cooperation among regional states, as well as for informal, behind-the-scenes arrangements among them, conducted without coordination with Washington.
Initiatives by the United Arab Emirates and Bahrain at the United Nations to propose measures for keeping the Strait of Hormuz open, without coordinating with the U.S. government, are one example of this shifting approach. If this trend continues, it could expand into additional domains and gradually weaken Washington’s authority in the Middle East.
Third, the Iran experience could make it harder for the U.S. administration to justify new military operations and an expanded American troop presence in the Middle East to voters. Reducing the U.S. military’s involvement in foreign conflicts could become a campaign talking point, and Trump’s rivals within the Democratic Party are likely to use the issue to attack his administration politically.
Beyond that, this setback carries costs not only abroad but potentially at home as well. Following the Iran experience, justifying new military operations and an expanded American presence in the Middle East will become harder for the Trump administration in the eyes of public opinion and voters. Trump’s Democratic rivals could turn a reduction in the scope of U.S. military intervention abroad into a campaign platform. Washington’s regional allies will factor this reality into their own calculations too, since the scale and durability of America’s overseas commitments depend not only on strategic considerations, but can also be shaped by domestic political conditions and electoral shifts in Washington.
A Costly Partner: When Trust Gives Way to Calculation
Taken together, what is eroding is not necessarily American military power — it is the credibility of its commitments.
The United States still commands vast military and economic capacity and a broad network of regional partners. But power translates into lasting influence only when the other side trusts its commitments and can, to some extent, predict its behavior. The experience of the confrontation with Iran has reinforced, among some of Washington’s partners, the impression that in moments of crisis, the United States will place its own interests and costs ahead of those of its regional partners. Under such conditions, America shifts from being a ‘self-evident guarantor of security‘ to a partner whose every commitment must come wrapped in guarantees, negotiation, and careful calculation.
Seen this way, the term ‘costly partner‘ points less to the end of America’s relationships with regional states than to a change in the quality of those relationships — relationships in which trust has diminished, while caution, demands for guarantees, and the search for alternative options have grown.
The End of American Influence, or the Start of Regional Realignment?
Middle Eastern states are unlikely to seek a wholesale replacement of the United States with another power. The more probable path is diversification of foreign relations, expanded regional cooperation, and simultaneous engagement with multiple centers of power. These countries will work to reduce the risk of dependence on a single power and to become less vulnerable to sudden shifts in American policy.
The most significant consequence of the confrontation with Iran, then, should be sought in the shifting mindset of America’s allies and partners. The United States may well remain one of the most powerful military actors in the Middle East, but if its allies no longer regard its presence as a self-evident, permanent guarantee of their security, the architecture of American influence in the region will gradually erode from within.
Perhaps this is the real outcome of the crisis: the United States is not necessarily losing the Middle East, but it has placed its monopoly over the region’s security calculations under greater strain than before.
If this trend continues, the true cost of the confrontation with Iran for Washington will show up not only in the war’s budget, lost equipment, or the direct outcome of the operation, but in the gradual erosion of trust, the rising cost of maintaining a military presence, and diminished bargaining power vis-à-vis its regional partners.
In the end, perhaps America’s most significant defeat in this crisis was not against a missile or a drone, but in the formation of a question in the minds of its allies — a question whose answer could determine the future of Washington’s relationship with the Middle East: when the moment of greatest need arrives, will Washington truly stand by them to the end?

The 18th BRICS summit opens in New Delhi on September 12–13 at a moment when Latin America has become the center of a contest for influence, with Washington pressing to restrict multipolar partnerships and reverse multipolarity altogether even as governments across the region seek deeper trade, investment, and business ties with BRICS and BRICS+ states alike.
The Trump administration has revived the Monroe Doctrine in the Donroe Doctrine, a ‘strategy of denial’ that treats the Western Hemisphere as an exclusive sphere of American influence and seeks to limit the ability of Latin American states to independently decide their foreign partnerships. This approach is not merely rhetorical, as the National Security Strategy places the Western Hemisphere first among regional priorities and explicitly calls for restoring American preeminence through economic pressure, security cooperation and political alignment. The trajectory of Latin American engagement with BRICS reveals a strategic logic that transcends simple economic calculation, as nations across the region grapple with what scholars have termed new strategic regionalism, a framework through which states renegotiate access to markets, finance, technology and infrastructure in conditions shaped by geopolitical constraints.
The pressure campaign has taken multiple forms, with tariffs emerging as a central instrument of statecraft. The United States imposed 25% tariffs on certain Brazilian products in July 2026 and a further 12.5 percent on others, raising duties on some items to as high as 37.5 percent. Brazilian officials view these measures as politically motivated, with presidential adviser Celso Amorim stating that Washington seeks to relativize the sovereignty of Latin American countries and constrain Brazil’s economic choices. Similar pressure has been applied across the region, including the classification of Brazilian criminal factions as terrorist organizations, a designation that Brazilian officials fear could serve as a pretext for external intervention. For Latin American economies that have experienced the coercive effects of financial sanctions and trade restrictions, these measures carry strong resonance, as the US is constantly pressuring them to desist from doing too much trade, business with other global superpowers, especially from BRICS.
Despite this pressure, leaders and delegations from 11 member countries and 10 partner nations are expected to attend the 18th BRICS Summit in New Delhi on September with the expanded format now encompassing Brazil alongside Egypt, Ethiopia, Iran, Indonesia, Russia, China, India, Saudi Arabia, South Africa and the United Arab Emirates. Brazil’s decision to send Foreign Minister Mauro Vieira rather than President Lula da Silva, who has chosen to remain in Brazil for his election campaign, does not diminish the significance of Latin American participation in this summit. What observers must recognize is that this expanded BRICS configuration has fundamentally altered the calculus for Latin American nations weighing their diplomatic options in an increasingly multipolar world, even as they remain wary of American retaliation.
That wariness has not stopped several governments from moving forward, for example, the participation of Cuba, Paraguay and Uruguay in signaling positive inclinations toward BRICS engagement which suggests that the appeal of the bloc extends beyond governments with explicitly adversarial relationships toward Washington. These South American nations, which maintain generally cooperative relations with the United States, appear motivated primarily by desires to diversify export markets, attract infrastructure investment and gain greater political weight in international negotiations. And in 2025 Colombia joined the BRICS New Development Bank with a commitment to purchase $512 million worth of shares, a move that former President Gustavo Petro described as a decision made freely despite American objections.
Yet not all states have moved in the same direction, and some have hedged in ways that reveal the limits of multipolar enthusiasm. Panama and Ecuador have taken steps that appear aimed at limiting Chinese economic, security or maritime presence in their territories and adjacent waters, whether through tightened port and infrastructure oversight, resistance to fishing fleet incursions, or recalibration of security cooperation with the United States. Panama’s Supreme Court annulled a Hong Kong-based company’s contract to operate ports at Balboa and Cristobal, and China subsequently detained nearly 70 Panama-registered vessels in what the US Federal Maritime Commission described as an unusual increase. What distinguishes these measures from a rejection of multipolarity is their specificity, as they target China as a particular actor rather than the broader principle of diversifying diplomatic and economic relationships, and in several instances they coexist with ongoing interest in BRICS partnership or in non-Western financing and trade arrangements. Latin American states are not choosing between a Western camp and a BRICS camp but rather managing multiple relationships simultaneously, extracting benefits from each while resisting excessive dependence on any single power.
The wariness that permeates Latin American calculations extends beyond those states already targeted by Washington. Countries whose economies depend heavily on access to the US market, or whose leaders enjoy particularly close ties with President Trump, may be more inclined to accommodate American demands publicly to avoid diplomatic confrontation, even as they privately remain reluctant to distance themselves from China. The Shield of the Americas, a US-led security initiative launched in 2026, has deepened this caution by excluding key regional actors such as Mexico, Colombia and Brazil while rewarding governments aligned with Washington’s priorities. For some Latin American states, the calculus has shifted toward caution rather than confrontation, with the risk of American retaliation discouraging them from pursuing multilateral alternatives too openly, at least until the current administration leaves office.
Still, some states have chosen to press ahead regardless. Peru, which joined the Shield of the Americas under President Keiko Fujimori, continues to protect its $30 billion Chinese investment stock and its position as China’s largest trading partner in the region for twelve consecutive years. Brazil has launched procedures at the WTO and activated its Economic Reciprocity Law in response to American tariffs, while pursuing diplomacy through direct conversations with the Trump administration. These cases suggest that while wariness has increased, the structural conditions that drive Latin American interest in alternative multilateral frameworks, including dissatisfaction with Western-dominated institutions, desire for diversified economic relationships, and aspirations for greater voice in global governance, will persist beyond any single summit and will continue shaping regional diplomatic orientations.
Russian engagement with Latin America within the BRICS framework presents a more complicated picture than sometimes assumed, as Moscow’s economic presence in the region remains limited compared to China’s substantial investments and trade relationships, with Russian involvement concentrated in bauxite mining in Guyana, and nuclear projects in Bolivia. Moreover, under the administration of President Javier Milei, Argentina maintains a strict geopolitical alignment with the United States and Ukraine, which has led to the complete suspension of energy and nuclear cooperation projects with Russia. In the same manner in Venezuela, new US restrictions and licenses have largely blocked Russian companies from active operations and business transactions there, and recent US Treasury rules forbid dealings with Russian entities in Venezuela’s revived energy sector. With the political shift and new laws opening the market to Western firms, Russian active work in the oil fields has faced severe limits and pressure to exit.
The significance of the New Delhi summit for Latin America ultimately lies in its timing at what can be describe as a crucial juncture when BRICS is transitioning from rapid expansion toward consolidation, with the next challenge involving integration of diverse members, building trust and transforming collective economic and political weight into practical cooperation. India’s role as host and its expected handover of the BRICS presidency to China for 2027 positions New Delhi as a bridge within the expanded grouping, leveraging its strategic autonomy and relationships with Russia, China, the United States and Europe to facilitate dialogue that avoids transforming BRICS into an explicitly anti-Western alliance. For Latin American nations, this emphasis on maintaining independent relations with multiple global powers while supporting multipolarity aligns with their own diplomatic traditions and suggests that BRICS engagement need not require choosing sides in great power competition but rather can serve as one element within diversified foreign policies that maximize sovereign flexibility.
What the New Delhi gathering represents, therefore, is not a dramatic rupture in hemispheric relations but rather another step in a wary and gradual reconfiguration of Latin America’s international alignments, as nations across the region respond to changing global power distribution by expanding their diplomatic and economic options beyond traditional partners, even as American pressure makes that expansion more costly and more cautious than it might otherwise be. While the US networked empire has struck back in various states of the region more noticeably Venezuela and Panama among others, interest in BRICS among Latin American states persists, driven by the trade, investment and South-South business opportunities the bloc offers.

Economist Yaroslav Lissovolik knows the architecture of the global financial system from the inside. He entered the market in the late 1990s at Renaissance Capital, then Russia’s leading investment bank, and from there moved to the International Monetary Fund (IMF), where he served as an adviser to Russian Executive Director Alexei Mozhin—before the age of 30, he was already seated at the table of the Executive Board. Educated at Harvard, the London School of Economics, and the Moscow State Institute of International Relations (MGIMO), he co-authored with his supervisor one of the first comprehensive books on Russia’s accession to the World Trade Organization (WTO).
This process shaped his worldview. Russia took almost 20 years to join the WTO: China acceded in 2001, Moscow only in 2012. He recalls how the process was experienced in Russia: “You think you have already made all possible concessions, and then another round of concessions emerges that you have to make. One more, then another, every year.” The country had been transformed into a radically liberalized economy, and yet the door to the Western club remained closed. “Anyone familiar with this issue would understand the tremendous degree of frustration that had been accumulating year after year,” he says.
After the IMF came Deutsche Bank, where he served as Chief Economist for Russia and the Commonwealth of Independent States (CIS) for about a decade—a period in which it was still believed possible to build economic bridges between the West and Russia, and which ended with Crimea in 2014. This was followed by roles at the Development Bank of the Eurasian Economic Union and Sberbank, Russia’s largest bank, where he headed investment research.
This trajectory from the global to the regional and then to the national level produced his central thesis. “At the time I was at the IMF, I thought everything should be top-down, resolved by global institutions and passed down to lower levels,” he says. “That way of thinking changed when I became part of a regional institution. I began to think of regional blocs as the foundations of a reformed global economy. Because with these global organizations, it’s almost like a colossus resting on very fragile foundations,” he explains in an exclusive interview with Brasil de Fato.
In 2023, he founded Brics+ Analytics, a consultancy dedicated to producing proposals for the bloc and the Global South. It was he who, in 2017, published the article that launched the R5 concept—the idea of using the national currencies of the five BRICS countries in the operations of the New Development Bank (NDB) and regional banks—the seed of all subsequent debate on a common currency.
The interview with Brasil de Fato was conducted on September 2, ten days before the BRICS summit in New Delhi (India) and one day after the conclusion of the Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) summit in Bishkek (Kyrgyzstan).
Interview Excerpt
Brasil de Fato: Last week, we had the SCO summit in Bishkek. The organization has been gaining prominence, and President Vladimir Putin emphasized that Russia’s trade with the group reached $400 billion, with 98% in local currencies. Is the SCO transitioning into an economic platform? What is your assessment of the summit?
Yaroslav Lissovolik: You are right to highlight the SCO’s key vector, which is the bloc’s evolution toward becoming an economic bloc. It began with a strong emphasis on security, for understandable reasons at the time, 25 years ago, and today the economic needs are enormous. Each year, there was a growing recognition of the limitations faced by regional economies in terms of economic integration and trade.
For this reason, the economic imperative began to become more pronounced, and this was reflected in last year’s developments, including discussions on a development bank. When you begin to see institutionalization, which provides something more rules-based, predictable, and viable, you start to observe greater engagement from the economic community, the investment community, and the markets.
Therefore, I am not overly concerned about the fact that there may not have been as much progress this year regarding the bank. There are many issues to decide. It is better to devote a bit more time and not make mistakes right at the outset. And I think one of the key questions may be the headquarters location [Kyrgyzstan and Kazakhstan have offered to host the bank].
I am a strong proponent of geographically diversifying institutions, as far as possible. Of moving away from this Western pattern in which one or two cities represent all of global governance, so that all regions of the world begin to represent it. It is about time. This is an issue that is on the radar, being discussed, and there will certainly be progress.
Twenty-eight agreements were signed at the summit. Which ones stood out to you in the final declaration?
There were references to work on the financial system, that is, payments in national currencies. And mentions of connectivity projects related to major corridors. The most important here would be the North–South Corridor.
I was very optimistic to see in the list of adopted documents the members’ roadmaps on projects, project portfolios, and connectivity. All of this is beginning to become systemic and project-based—something less rhetorical, more concrete, more grounded in real projects.
As for trade, the standard remains, as in BRICS+, the emphasis on bilateral agreements, in which two countries agree on a certain trade target and work to implement it. This is the case for Russia, Brazil, and practically everyone. Achieving higher levels through this instrument is perfectly acceptable; it seems to work and generate results. But a faster path would be a roadmap of trade agreements brought together into common platforms, resulting in a much more systematic and predictable instrument.
My preference is for a roadmap of trade agreements in an “SCO+” format, which would encompass not only full members but also partners and observers, as well as Eurasian integration and regional blocs such as the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) and the Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC). There is this format that is becoming more evident—China plus GCC, China plus ASEAN—and that could very well be integrated into an SCO+ framework.
The long-term vision that is crystallizing is SCO+ as the Eurasian platform for Global South cooperation, bringing together all the major actors and serving as a platform for aggregating development institutions, integration blocs, and connectivity projects.
You pointed to connectivity as one of the two key issues on the economic front and highlighted the North–South Corridor among the projects in the declaration. This corridor links the port of Mumbai to Iran and continues to St. Petersburg by rail and navigation on the Caspian Sea, significantly shortening the route that today passes through the Suez Canal. It involves exactly three countries that are at both tables: Russia, Iran, and India are members of both the SCO and BRICS. What does this mean to you?
What it means is that it is quite possible for the two to work together. We have seen that the NDB has been co-financing projects with regional banks, such as the Development Bank of the Eurasian Economic Union. This could very well happen with the SCO bank as soon as it becomes operational. The SCO definitely needs to be involved in the North–South Corridor, because the issue of alternative trade routes is the crucial link that could also connect, to a greater degree, the SCO to BRICS+.
Today, four countries are full members of both blocs: Russia, China, Iran, and India. If we consider partners, observers, and other categories, there are eleven countries at both tables.
That is very good. They are bridges, ways to connect and expand. If previously overlaps were thought to be duplication and a problem, no: this is positive for the Global South in terms of expanding projects and platforms.
Overlap improves the prospects for forming platforms among regional integration agreements—such as the Beams platform I proposed, which brings together the Bay of Bengal Initiative for Multi-Sectoral Technical and Economic Cooperation (BIMSTEC), the Eurasian Economic Union (EEU), the African Continental Free Trade Area, Mercosur, and the SCO itself. You build a house with “BRICS and Beams”: they are the two key elements [in English, “bricks” are tijolos and “beams” are vigas]. Time will tell, but we are moving, slowly but surely, toward a paradigm in which it is not just individual countries, but regional blocs, that become the building material for these platforms.
And the SCO will be the backbone, the absolutely crucial link of this entire grand project they call Greater Eurasia. I would call it SCO+.

When analysts discuss the Shanghai Cooperation Organization, they tend to focus on security issues: counterterrorism, military coordination, strategic competition, and the Organization’s increasingly visible anti-hegemonic rhetoric, but this interpretation, although legitimate, captures only one part of the transformation currently taking place across the Eurasian space. The most significant game being played within the SCO does not necessarily involve armies or military deployments; increasingly, it concerns the infrastructure through which goods, energy, capital, information, and data move across the continent. Over the past several years, the Organization has progressively taken on a role that was not explicitly assigned to it in its founding documents: that of a coordination platform for a network of physical and digital connections that is gradually redrawing the economic, technological, and strategic geography of Eurasia.
This transformation has two interconnected dimensions. The first is physical: railways, highways, logistics centers, ports, pipelines, and multimodal transport corridors. The second is digital: telecommunications, artificial intelligence, cloud infrastructure, data centers, digital payments, cybersecurity, information systems, and technological standards. The two dimensions should not be considered separately. A railway without digital customs systems is an incomplete corridor; a logistics network without interoperable data systems remains inefficient; a digital payment system disconnected from physical trade routes has limited strategic value. What is emerging, therefore, is something broader than transportation infrastructure and broader than digitalization: a connected Eurasian strategic space in which physical and information flows increasingly reinforce one another.
It is worth clearing up a widespread misunderstanding from the outset. The SCO is not building a single “SCO corridor,” nor is it constructing one centralized Eurasian infrastructure project under a single institutional command. What is emerging is something strategically more interesting: an institutional framework within which multiple overlapping corridors—some running east–west, others north–south—are progressively aligned, standardized, digitized, and connected. The Tianjin Declaration of September 2025 explicitly called for the creation and modernization of international transport routes, including North–South and East–West corridors, while simultaneously emphasizing logistics digitalization and supply-chain strengthening. The digital agenda developed in parallel, with the Organization promoting digital infrastructure, public digital infrastructure, next-generation communications, reliable data transmission, data privacy, information security, and artificial intelligence.
The significance of this development lies precisely in the fact that the SCO is not attempting to replace one system with another overnight. Rather, it is creating alternatives, redundancies, and additional layers of connectivity. This distinction is fundamental. The objective is not autarky, nor is it the creation of a completely separate Eurasian world isolated from the existing global economy. The objective is to reduce vulnerability by ensuring that Eurasian states are not dependent upon a single route, a single supplier, a single technological ecosystem, or a single external infrastructure.
This is the common logic linking the physical and digital dimensions of the SCO.
The new geography of Eurasian railways
The physical transformation is perhaps easiest to observe through the changing geography of railways. The first major axis runs, in general terms, from China through Central Asia, Russia, and the Caspian region, ultimately extending toward Europe and the Middle East. One of the projects capable of redefining this geography is the China–Kyrgyzstan–Uzbekistan railway.
Discussed for more than a quarter of a century, with the first trilateral memorandum dating back to 1997, the project was for years constrained by disputes concerning the route, financing, and track gauge. The turning point came between 2024 and 2025, with the intergovernmental agreement signed in Beijing in June 2024, the groundbreaking ceremony held on December 27 of the same year, and the subsequent finalization of the financial framework, estimated at approximately $4.7 billion in December 2025.
The importance of the railway cannot be reduced to its physical length. According to figures cited in the original analysis, the line is expected to shorten the route from East Asia toward Iran, Turkey, and Europe by approximately 900 kilometers and reduce transit time by seven to eight days. Estimates of its future capacity vary, with some sources referring to up to 12 million metric tons annually and other assessments placing potential full-capacity traffic at approximately 13–15 million metric tons, beginning from a more conservative initial threshold of 5–8 million metric tons. The differences themselves are significant because they demonstrate that the project remains under development and that its final operational performance cannot yet be treated as an established fact.
More importantly, however, the CKU should not be interpreted as simply another railway connecting China with the West. China already possesses established western routes, particularly through Kazakhstan. The strategic value of the CKU lies in its ability to open a central-southern axis crossing Kyrgyzstan and Uzbekistan and subsequently branching toward Turkmenistan, Iran, Turkey, the Caspian Sea, the Caucasus, Europe, and the Middle East.
The technical characteristics of the project also reveal an important problem that applies to Eurasian connectivity as a whole. The railway, just over five hundred kilometers long, crosses approximately three hundred kilometers of the Kyrgyz Tien Shan mountains and requires a transshipment station in Makmal because Chinese railways use a 1,435-millimeter gauge, while much of the Central Asian railway system uses a 1,520-millimeter gauge. This is not merely an engineering inconvenience. It illustrates the central question that will determine whether Eurasian connectivity becomes genuinely functional: interoperability.
A corridor exists not simply when tracks have been laid, but when trains, cargo, information, payments, customs documents, and logistics systems can move across borders with minimal friction.
Central Asia is becoming truly central
This is why Uzbekistan is becoming particularly important. Geographically positioned at the center of Central Asia, Uzbekistan has the potential to connect several routes simultaneously: eastward toward China through Kyrgyzstan; southward toward Turkmenistan and Iran and ultimately Turkey; further south through Afghanistan and Pakistan toward the Indian Ocean; and northward through Kazakhstan toward Russia.
Tashkent has increasingly understood the geopolitical value of this position and has begun presenting itself not simply as a Central Asian state but as a transit state. The distinction is important. A transit state does not merely occupy geographical territory between two markets; it derives strategic value from its ability to connect different economic and political spaces.
The potential Uzbekistan–Afghanistan–Pakistan railway illustrates the scale of this ambition. The three countries signed an intergovernmental framework agreement in Kabul on July 17, 2025, to conduct a feasibility study for the Termez–Kharlachi section, while Uzbekistan ratified the agreement by presidential decree on February 4, 2026. The proposed route would extend approximately 573 kilometers through Termez, Mazar-i-Sharif, Logar, and the Kharlachi Pass, with estimated costs of approximately $4.8 billion and a design capacity of up to twenty million metric tons annually.
The project remains a project, however, and this distinction must be preserved. Afghanistan demonstrates precisely why land-based infrastructure cannot be separated from political and security conditions. A railway can be technically feasible and economically attractive while remaining geopolitically vulnerable. The possibility of linking the UAP with the CKU would nevertheless be strategically significant because it would create the potential for a continuous land connection from China through Central Asia and Afghanistan toward South Asia and the Indian Ocean.
At that point, India would cease to be merely an external maritime destination and would become one of the major maritime outlets of a continental Eurasian system.
This is where the physical geography of the SCO begins to intersect with the broader geography of the Indo-Pacific.
The North–South dimension
The second major physical axis follows a different but complementary logic: Russia, through the Caspian region and Iran, toward the Indian Ocean and India. This is the International North–South Transport Corridor, originally conceived in 2000 by Russia, Iran, and India as a multimodal system combining maritime, rail, and road transportation over approximately 7,200 kilometers.
Its strategic purpose is clear. The INSTC connects the northern Eurasian space with the Gulf and the Indian Ocean while offering an alternative to the traditional route through the Suez Canal. Like the CKU and UAP projects, however, the corridor contains unfinished links. The Rasht–Astara railway connection between Iran and Azerbaijan remains particularly important, while sanctions affecting Iran and Russia complicate financing and transactions.
Yet the significance of the emerging system does not depend upon the completion of any single project. Its importance derives from the network effect created when several corridors become interconnected.
China can reach Europe and the Middle East through Central Asia and Iran. Russia can reach India through Central Asia and Iran. China can potentially reach the Indian Ocean through South Asia. Central Asian states can connect simultaneously toward Russia, China, Iran, South Asia, and the Caucasus.
The result is therefore not one corridor, but a network of corridors.
And strategically, the difference is enormous.
Foundation of a strategic autonomy
The central concept linking these projects is redundancy. Borrowed from systems engineering, redundancy means having multiple alternative routes rather than relying upon a single artery. This concept has become increasingly important because contemporary global trade remains heavily exposed to maritime bottlenecks, including Suez, Bab el-Mandeb, the Strait of Hormuz, and the Strait of Malacca.
Land corridors cannot replace maritime transportation on a global scale. The carrying capacity and efficiency of large container ships remain incomparable to those of railway convoys. But the objective is not replacement. It is diversification.
A railway can provide an alternative for specific categories of strategic goods. A pipeline can reduce dependence upon maritime energy routes. A logistics hub can redirect cargo. A digital payment system can reduce exposure to external financial infrastructure. A regional cloud system can provide an alternative to foreign providers. A domestic or regional telecommunications network can reduce technological vulnerability.
The formula is therefore remarkably simple: more routes, more suppliers, more markets, more modes of transportation, more technological options.
This is the logistical foundation of strategic autonomy.
The logic has become particularly relevant in an international environment marked by sanctions, technological restrictions, export controls, cyberattacks, infrastructure disruptions, geopolitical fragmentation, and instability along major maritime routes. The physical and digital dimensions of strategic resilience are increasingly converging. A state dependent upon a single maritime passage is vulnerable to disruption; a state dependent upon a single foreign technological ecosystem can face a comparable vulnerability in the digital domain.
Strategic autonomy therefore increasingly means having alternatives.
To an information space
Those who study Eurasian integration tend to measure it in kilometers of railway track, tons of cargo transported, ports constructed, and pipelines completed. These remain essential indicators, but they are no longer sufficient. In the twenty-first century, connectivity is not only about roads, railways, and ports. It is also about data, telecommunications, artificial intelligence, cloud infrastructure, digital payments, cybersecurity, information networks, and technological standards.
A railway corridor connects cities and markets physically; a digital corridor connects economies through information flows.
The SCO has increasingly begun to address this second form of connectivity. The institutional trajectory can be traced to the “Concept of Cooperation on Digitalization and ICT,” drafted as early as 2019, followed by programs concerning digital literacy and artificial intelligence and, more recently, an Action Plan for Digital Transformation. At the Tianjin summit in September 2025, members adopted a declaration on strengthening cooperation in the digital economy, calling for the development of digital infrastructure, public digital infrastructure, next-generation communications, reliable data transmission, data privacy, and information security.
The significance of this process is not simply the number of digital initiatives being announced. It is the changing status of digital infrastructure within the Organization. It is no longer merely a technical chapter of economic cooperation. It is becoming a structural component of Eurasian integration.
The same caution applied to physical corridors must nevertheless be applied here. Describing this trajectory does not mean certifying its success. The SCO remains an organization characterized by different levels of cohesion and by substantial internal rivalries, most notably between China and India. Policy declarations can precede implementation by years, and some initiatives may never reach their intended operational stage. The relevant question, therefore, is not whether an autonomous Eurasian digital ecosystem already exists. It does not. The question is whether the institutional and technological direction of the SCO is moving toward greater digital autonomy.
The evidence suggests that it is.
China as the big one technological driver
China occupies a central position in this process. The Digital Silk Road provides much of the technological and infrastructural foundation upon which emerging digital connectivity can develop. In July 2025, Vice Premier Ding Xuexiang called for stronger digital infrastructure connectivity within the SCO space, including computing power, data processing, and the broader Digital Silk Road, while advocating a multilateral system of digital security governance.
Beijing possesses capabilities across a broad technological value chain: 5G networks, telecommunications, cloud computing, artificial intelligence, payment systems, big data, smart-city infrastructure, and satellite constellations. This concentration creates an obvious asymmetry.
Those who provide infrastructure tend, to a significant degree, to shape the standards, protocols, technical architecture, and technological ecosystem associated with that infrastructure.
Digital connectivity is therefore geopolitical by nature.
Choosing a critical infrastructure provider is simultaneously a decision concerning a long-term technical and regulatory environment. The difference between a purely cooperative interpretation and a strategic interpretation is precisely here: infrastructure provision can generate durable patterns of technological dependence even when the original relationship is framed in terms of cooperation.
The emergence of a regional digital ecosystem must therefore be understood in terms of power as well as efficiency.
The ambition of a more autonomous digital ecosystem
The SCO does not simply seek to connect its members to the existing global digital economy. Its agenda—data security, digital infrastructure, artificial intelligence, cybersecurity, digital public services, e-commerce, technological standards, and information security—suggests a broader ambition: to create greater regional technological autonomy.
The China–SCO Big Data Cooperation Center provides an example of this emerging architecture, with activities involving digital transformation, data security, big-data services linked to the Beidou satellite system, digital-skills training, and technological cooperation among member states.
This does not mean the creation of a separate internet or a Eurasian technological “Great Wall.” Such an interpretation would be too simplistic. The more subtle objective is the ability to operate critical digital infrastructure, data systems, technological standards, and strategic information networks without relying exclusively upon Western technological ecosystems.
This is the digital equivalent of physical redundancy.
If a maritime route is blocked, a land corridor provides an alternative. If a foreign technology supplier becomes inaccessible, regional technological capabilities provide an alternative. If a payment network becomes subject to external restrictions, interoperable regional payment systems can reduce exposure. If cloud infrastructure is externally controlled, domestic or regional computing capacity can provide resilience.
The underlying principle remains the same: reducing vulnerability through alternatives.
Yet connectivity produces a paradox. The more interconnected the system becomes, the more efficient it can become, but also the more systemic its vulnerabilities become.
The SCO has a relatively established record of cooperation in cybersecurity and information security, particularly through the Regional Anti-Terrorism Structure and its efforts to combat the misuse of information and communication technologies for terrorist and extremist purposes. The agenda, however, is expanding from cybercrime and cyberterrorism toward data protection, critical infrastructure, artificial intelligence, and broader information security.
The 2024 Astana Declaration reaffirmed cooperation on international information security and emphasized the creation of a secure information environment based upon respect for state sovereignty and non-interference. By 2025, the digital agenda had become more deeply institutionalized.
The conceptual transformation is perhaps more important than the organizational one: cyberspace is increasingly treated within the SCO framework as a domain of sovereignty, comparable in strategic importance to territory, airspace, or territorial waters.
This approach differs significantly from the dominant Western model of internet governance. SCO countries place greater emphasis on state sovereignty, national jurisdiction, information security, and protection of critical digital infrastructure. The focus is therefore less on a fully open and decentralized cyberspace and more on the capacity of sovereign states to control and protect their own information environments.
The disagreement is ultimately political rather than technical.
It concerns who possesses legitimate authority over cyberspace: sovereign states or a pluralistic community composed of governments, corporations, technical communities, and civil society.
These are different political philosophies of digital space, and neither is politically neutral.
Artificial Intelligence and the new strategic infrastructure you cannot ignore
Artificial intelligence raises the stakes even further. SCO members adopted a cooperation program on AI in 2022, while the 2025 Tianjin summit further elevated artificial intelligence on the Organization’s agenda by endorsing a common roadmap and welcoming the proposal for a regional AI center in Dushanbe.
AI is particularly significant because it connects several strategic resources into a single chain: data, computing power, algorithms, autonomous systems, intelligence capabilities, and military applications.
Consequently, digital connectivity can no longer be separated from national security.
A country that possesses control over its own data, computing infrastructure, telecommunications, AI models, semiconductor supply chains, and cloud infrastructure enjoys a substantially greater degree of strategic autonomy than a country dependent upon external suppliers for one or more of these components.
This is why digital infrastructure is increasingly comparable to transportation infrastructure. Railways determine where goods can move; digital systems increasingly determine how economies can operate.
The physical and digital layers are therefore becoming mutually dependent.
A modern railway requires digital signaling, cargo management, customs documentation, satellite positioning, communications, payment systems, and cybersecurity. A modern port requires data centers, cloud services, logistics software, telecommunications, digital identification, and secure payment systems. Energy infrastructure increasingly depends upon interconnected control systems. Public services depend upon data and cloud infrastructure.
The physical Eurasian corridor is therefore becoming a digital corridor at the same time.
India and the problem of technological pluralism
India makes this transformation both more complicated and more strategically interesting.
New Delhi is simultaneously an SCO member, a BRICS member, a technological power, a major digital economy, and a partner of the United States and Europe. Its presence therefore contradicts the simplistic image of the SCO as a monolithic, Chinese-led bloc.
India has no interest in allowing a single Chinese technological ecosystem to dominate Eurasia. At the same time, it has a strong interest in digital cooperation with Russia, Central Asia, Iran, and other countries of the Global South, while possessing its own substantial public digital infrastructure.
This produces a form of technological pluralism within the SCO.
New Delhi has rejected the Belt and Road Initiative while supporting alternative connectivity channels such as Chabahar, but this does not prevent it from participating in the broader SCO digital agenda. Instead, India appears to favor a configuration involving multiple technological hubs rather than a single dominant center, consistent with its broader doctrine of strategic autonomy.
The implication is important. The future digital SCO cannot be understood simply as a Chinese technological sphere. China is clearly the principal technological driver, but India represents a counterweight, while Russia can function as a strategic bridge between different technological and geopolitical spaces.
The Organization’s future trajectory will depend precisely upon how these divergent interests are managed.
The SCO does not require its members to have identical strategic objectives. Its institutional value may lie precisely in its ability to allow different powers to cooperate without requiring them to become strategically identical.
The Convergence
The most profound transformation becomes visible when the physical and digital dimensions are considered together.
Imagine the future Eurasian corridor not simply as a railway running from China through Central Asia toward Iran, Russia, or South Asia, but as an integrated system in which railway infrastructure, ports, logistics centers, customs platforms, digital documentation, satellite navigation, payment systems, telecommunications, cloud infrastructure, artificial intelligence, and cybersecurity operate as interconnected layers.
At that point, the corridor ceases to be merely a transportation project.
It becomes a strategic infrastructure.
The physical layer consists of railways, highways, pipelines, logistics hubs, dry ports, seaports, and transportation terminals. The digital layer consists of telecommunications, data centers, AI systems, digital payments, cloud infrastructure, cybersecurity, and information networks. Between them lies a third layer: interoperability.
This is where the real contest will increasingly take place.
Tracks can be built, but if trains stop at every border because documentation, customs procedures, technical standards, and gauges are incompatible, the corridor remains inefficient. Digital systems can be deployed, but if they cannot communicate with one another, their strategic value is limited. Payment systems can exist, but if they cannot interact across borders, they do not create genuine financial connectivity.
The actual corridor is therefore not the railway itself.
It is the railway plus customs, plus digital documentation, plus standards, plus ports, plus logistics centers, plus payment systems, plus data exchange, plus cybersecurity.
Connectivity is becoming interoperability.
The parallel between physical and digital connectivity is especially evident in the concept of redundancy.
Physical Eurasia seeks to reduce dependence upon individual maritime chokepoints by developing alternative land routes. Digital Eurasia can reduce dependence upon external telecommunications systems, cloud providers, payment platforms, technological standards, and data infrastructure.
The same strategic principle operates in both domains.
More routes mean greater resilience. More suppliers mean less vulnerability. More technological centers mean greater autonomy. More interoperable systems mean greater flexibility.
This becomes particularly important in a world increasingly characterized by sanctions, technological decoupling, export controls, cyberattacks, infrastructure disruptions, and geopolitical fragmentation. When critical digital infrastructure depends entirely upon foreign suppliers, a country can become vulnerable to decisions made elsewhere, whether those decisions result from political hostility, commercial competition, or compliance with a third-party sanctions regime.
Technological capacity consequently becomes a component of national security.
This is why cybersecurity cannot be treated as a technical layer added after infrastructure has been built. It must be incorporated into the architecture from the beginning. An integrated Eurasian system could interconnect banks, railways, ports, energy networks, public services, telecommunications, logistics systems, cloud infrastructure, and AI applications. Such density can produce enormous efficiency, but it also creates the possibility of cascading failures.
An attack against one node could affect multiple other nodes. The more connected the system becomes, the greater the importance of resilience by design.
Mackinder in the Digital Age
There is a deeper geopolitical implication to this transformation.
The international order has traditionally been analyzed through military power, GDP, nuclear arsenals, industrial capacity, natural resources, and demographics. These factors remain fundamental, but the next phase of multipolarity will increasingly depend upon control over digital infrastructure.
Data, artificial intelligence, telecommunications, digital payments, cloud infrastructure, satellite networks, and cybersecurity are becoming strategic resources comparable, in some respects, to the energy and transportation infrastructures that shaped power hierarchies during the twentieth century. This is where the classical concept of Eurasian continental depth acquires a new meaning.
Mackinder’s Heartland theory emphasized the strategic importance of continental space and the possibility that control over the Eurasian interior could provide protection from the vulnerabilities associated with maritime dominance. The contemporary transformation does not simply reproduce that logic; it transposes it into a domain that Mackinder could not have imagined.
The Eurasian Heartland is no longer only a geographical space through which armies, commodities, and energy move. It is increasingly a space through which data, algorithms, financial transactions, technological standards, and information move. The physical and digital dimensions are therefore converging into a single strategic geography. Just as land corridors can reduce dependence upon maritime chokepoints, digital connectivity can reduce dependence upon external technological and information infrastructures.
The result is not isolation. It is optionality.
Will the Maps change?
If these projects are successfully completed and effectively integrated, the traditional map of Eurasian trade will change.
Historically, the dominant global trade system has been predominantly maritime: East Asia, the Indian Ocean, the Suez Canal, and Europe. The emerging Eurasian system adds another dimension: East Asia, Central Asia, Russia, Iran, the Middle East, South Asia, and from there toward Europe and the Indian Ocean. This does not mean the end of maritime globalization.
The future system is more likely to be multimodal: rail plus road plus pipelines plus maritime transportation plus digital logistics. The strategic advantage will belong to those capable of moving between these modes. A resilient Eurasian system will not depend upon a single railway, a single port, a single pipeline, a single payment system, or a single technological supplier. Its strength will derive from the ability to redirect flows when one component becomes unavailable.
This is the essence of network power. The same principle applies to information.
A resilient digital Eurasia will not necessarily require a completely separate internet. It will require sufficient independent capacity to ensure that essential services, data, payments, telecommunications, computing, and information systems can continue functioning even when external infrastructures become unavailable or politically unreliable.
That is a much more sophisticated conception of strategic autonomy than autarky.
An Architecture of Variable Geometry
This transformation also clarifies what the SCO actually is.
It is not a military alliance in the classical sense. Nor is it a centralized economic union. Its members have different political systems, economic models, strategic interests, and relationships with external powers. China and India remain strategic competitors. Russia has its own priorities. Central Asian states seek to preserve room for maneuver between larger powers. Iran has specific geopolitical and economic interests.
Yet the Organization provides a framework in which these different interests can converge without becoming identical. This may be its most important institutional characteristic.
The SCO operates through a form of variable geometry. Different members participate in different projects with different degrees of intensity. Not every country needs to use every corridor. Not every member needs to adopt the same technology. Not every state needs to share identical strategic objectives.
What matters is the creation of enough common infrastructure, standards, procedures, and institutional mechanisms to make cooperation possible.
In this sense, the SCO’s power may lie less in imposing uniformity than in managing diversity. Its strategic evolution will therefore depend upon whether it can turn declarations into interoperable systems, whether its members can reconcile competing interests, and whether physical and digital connectivity can be developed without creating new forms of excessive dependency.
A degree of caution remains necessary.
The ambition is increasingly well documented, but implementation remains the decisive variable. The gap between declarations and functioning infrastructure can be considerable, and internal rivalries may slow, reshape, or fragment individual initiatives.
The next phase should therefore be evaluated through concrete indicators rather than political rhetoric.
For physical connectivity, the relevant indicators include the completion of strategic railway links, the reduction of border-crossing times, the harmonization of customs procedures, the interoperability of rail gauges and rolling stock, the development of logistics centers, and the actual volume of freight moving through the corridors.
For digital connectivity, the indicators are equally concrete: adoption of common technological standards, interoperable payment systems, shared computing capabilities, regional AI projects, secure data-exchange mechanisms, and genuine interoperability among national cybersecurity systems.
If these indicators begin to show sustained progress, the transformation will move from institutional aspiration toward material reality.
If they remain stagnant, the digital and physical Eurasian space will remain primarily a project on paper.
Toward a Connected Eurasian Strategic Space
The SCO is not building a single Eurasian corridor, it’s helping to create a network. The China–Kyrgyzstan–Uzbekistan railway, the potential Uzbekistan–Afghanistan–Pakistan connection, the International North–South Transport Corridor linking Russia with India through Iran, and the broader East–West routes together form an emerging geography of physical connectivity. Above them, increasingly integrated digital systems—telecommunications, data infrastructure, AI, cloud computing, digital payments, satellite networks, and cybersecurity—are creating a second layer of connectivity.
The strategic importance of this transformation does not lie in the infrastructure itself. It lies in the redundancy that the infrastructure creates.
Eurasian states are gradually developing alternative routes to markets, energy supplies, strategic partners, financial systems, technological infrastructures, and information networks, thereby reducing their dependence upon individual maritime chokepoints and upon technological systems controlled by external powers.
The central concept is therefore not isolation, but resilience.
Not autarky, but strategic autonomy. Not one corridor, but multiple corridors. Not one technological center, but a more plural technological ecosystem. And not simply physical connectivity, but the integration of physical and digital space.
The next stage will consequently be determined by interoperability: rail gauges, customs procedures, digital documentation, logistics standards, payment systems, data exchange, telecommunications, cybersecurity, computing capacity, and artificial intelligence. The decisive question will not be whether Eurasia can build more infrastructure. It will be whether the infrastructure can function as a coherent system. This is ultimately where the SCO’s transformation becomes geopolitically significant.
The Organization may be evolving from a primarily security-oriented framework into something broader: an institutional mechanism for constructing a connected Eurasian strategic space. The infrastructure of the emerging multipolar world is therefore not only physical. It is increasingly digital.
The SCO is not merely helping to build a physical Eurasia. It is beginning to build a digital Eurasia as well.
And whoever possesses the capacity to connect, protect, govern, and maintain that space will exercise significant influence over the multipolar order that is now taking shape.

The main reason why globalists succeed everywhere and across the board is betrayal. They cannot gain control over states and nations unless those nations produce traitors who hand power over to them. The latest such example is the former president of Iran, Hassan Rouhani, who, according to the British Telegraph , is asking Iran's current government to strike a deal with the Americans and calm Iran down. Betrayal is the word that describes and defines the era following the end of the Cold War. The West became so strong not because it is the richest or most economically powerful, but because it successfully finds traitors —and in vast numbers. It is harder to find public figures and politicians who have not betrayed their homelands than those who have. Traitors are revered in every Western country. They are granted political and social dignity, power, influence, and material benefits. And they raise their children in that same betrayal. That's just how it is.
Hassan Rouhani was negotiating with Israel some time ago, according to Barack Obama's national security advisor, Dennis Ross. According to the advisor's memoirs, the Iranian president acted as a pawn for Israel, which explains why Iran was weak during his time and held a position of resignation and submission toward the West compared to now. This exact case prompted me to write about betrayal. It is among the top three reasons for everything that has happened in the world, everywhere in the world, over the last 50 years. You can see it in Russia, not to mention Bulgaria!
Practically since 1989 , there hasn't been a politician or public figure who has succeeded without betraying Bulgaria and its people in some way. If someone refuses to betray, they simply cannot participate in politics. What kind of people these are doesn't interest me. I am reflecting on the exposure of Rouhani as a president who negotiated with Israel against his own people. The president after him, Ebrahim Raisi, met a different fate, which clearly means he didn't betray Iran. Raisi died in the government helicopter after departing from Baku , the capital of the Persians' rivals in Iran —the Azeris. The current president, Pezeshkian, may be weak and uncertain, but it is certain that he is not making deals with the Americans. In Iran, they want him removed because he isn't initiating an aggressive policy against Israel and the US, but there are no allegations of collaboration with them. For now.
What is needed are people who have the morality, strength, and determination to prevent this betrayal. Whether you betray your friends and comrades or your people, it is the same thing. If you betray your friend, you will betray your people. What is needed for leadership are people who will not betray Bulgaria —not in words, as words are currently worth absolutely nothing, but in deeds. Selling yourself out and committing betrayal is clear to me: you want money, perks, and power (all needs born of complexes) and the resulting sexual privileges and various behaviors to fill internal voids—that is the profile of traitors. They are empty people with voids, and that's why they are ready to do anything to fill them. The post–Cold War world offered the deepest profile of betrayal , with its most malignant forms. But even worse are those who play a game, presenting themselves as one thing while being another. They mimic and deceive with their appearance. These wolves in sheep's clothing —they are worse than ordinary traitors because they lie.
