New Delhi spent the first week of September executing two parallel realities.
On the surface, the city prepared for a spectacle. Five-star hotels pushed premium suites to ₹20 lakh a night. The municipal corporation deployed specialized squads to sweep stray monkeys and dogs out of Central Delhi. Traffic police rehearsed motorcade protocols across 22 corridors. On September 11, the central government declared a public holiday to clear the roads for arriving heads of state.
Beneath the theater, something far more consequential was already finished.
Over the preceding twelve months, across 30 Indian cities, more than 400 working-level meetings quietly executed the most extensive preparatory campaign in BRICS history. Finance deputies standardized customs documentation. Technical committees mapped cross-border payment interoperability. Trade officials designed invoice discounting mechanisms for small businesses locked out of Western credit markets.
None of this made the front page. That is precisely the point.
The Wrong Question
The dominant narrative surrounding the 18th BRICS Summit asks whether the Leaders’ Declaration will hold together. Will Iran and the UAE agree on West Asia? Will China and India manage a functional photo opportunity? Will the final document survive the same geopolitical fractures that killed the joint statement at the Jaipur Trade Ministers’ Meeting in August?
These are legitimate questions. They are also the wrong ones.
They assume the summit’s value lives or dies by a single political communiqué. That assumption reflects a specific, outdated way of reading international politics—one that treats diplomatic statements as the primary measure of institutional relevance. It makes sense if you believe the purpose of multilateral forums is to produce aligned political slogans.
BRICS stopped functioning as that kind of forum a long time ago. The real work has migrated downward, into technical committees, deputy-level working groups, and financial infrastructure projects that operate regardless of whether the leaders can agree on a paragraph about the Strait of Hormuz.
The Administrative Machine
India assumed the rotating BRICS chairmanship on January 1, 2026. The theme—”Building for Resilience, Innovation, Cooperation and Sustainability”—sounds like standard diplomatic boilerplate. The execution behind it has been anything but.
The Indian chairship ran 35 distinct working-group tracks covering trade, health, energy, digital infrastructure, agriculture, and logistics. These groups did not convene once for a photo. They met repeatedly, from Jaipur to Chandigarh to Lucknow, producing technical frameworks that will outlast any single leaders’ declaration.
The output is dense. A BRICS Global Value Chains Action Plan running through 2030. Voluntary principles for climate-resilient urban infrastructure. A digital agriculture network coordinating AI and geospatial tools. A logistics supply-chain cooperation framework designed to protect trade corridors from tariff disruptions. Guiding principles for smart grids, anchored by a new centre of excellence in Gurugram.
None of these require unanimous political agreement on West Asia. They require technical consensus among specialists who share a practical problem: how to keep goods, capital, and data moving across borders that Western institutions were never configured to serve efficiently.
The Jaipur Trade Ministers’ Meeting in August illustrated this dynamic with unusual clarity. The meeting ended without a joint statement. West Asia tensions made consensus impossible on the political language. But the ministers still agreed on an invoice discounting mechanism for cross-border SME trade and guiding principles for assessing export-oriented small businesses. The political headline read as failure. The technical output was functional.
That distinction carries more weight than the headline.
The Financial Railroads
The most important number at this summit will not appear in any leaders’ statement. It is $4.2 trillion.
That is the estimated financing gap for small and medium enterprises across eight BRICS+ economies, representing nearly 20% of their combined GDP. These businesses form the backbone of employment and production in the Global South. They are also systematically starved of capital by a global financial architecture that routes credit through Western-dominated rating agencies, dollar-denominated lending windows, and IMF conditionality frameworks.
The New Development Bank, established in 2015, has approved roughly $45 billion in cumulative project funding without the political conditions attached to Bretton Woods lending. That is a meaningful track record, but it barely touches the surface of the $4.2 trillion gap.
The response being constructed in New Delhi targets that gap directly. A BRICS+ SME Financing Facility, backed by India’s SIDBI and EXIM Bank, aims to provide credit guarantees and digital lending infrastructure across member states. The iBRICS sovereign-capital summit, running parallel to the leaders’ meeting at The Oberoi, gathered more than 500 institutional investors to map non-dollar settlement routes for a $1 trillion pool of sovereign capital.
Alongside this, the payment infrastructure is being physically rewired. India’s UPI system is being linked to Brazil’s Pix. Central bank digital currency corridors are under development. Local-currency settlement frameworks are expanding bilateral trade clearing without routing transactions through dollar intermediaries.
Analytical honesty requires acknowledging the friction. India itself illustrates the tension. New Delhi promotes rupee-denominated trade and UPI integration as tools for lowering transaction costs. At the same time, India pays for Russian crude oil in Chinese yuan because the rupee lacks sufficient liquidity in Moscow. The aspiration toward local-currency sovereignty and the practical reality of yuan dependency coexist in the same policy framework. That contradiction does not invalidate the project. It reveals the early, messy stage of a structural shift that will take years to mature.
Saudi Arabia’s status adds another layer of uncertainty. Riyadh is treated as a member by India and the BRICS Secretariat, but has never publicly confirmed formal accession, maintaining a strategic pause that functions as a bargaining chip in parallel negotiations with Washington. Whether Saudi financial commitments materialize for NDB capitalization remains an open question.
These are real constraints. They do not erase the direction of travel.
Two Ways of Reading the Same Room
Western policy circles tend to read BRICS through a single frame: an anti-Western cartel led by authoritarian states, designed to dismantle the rules-based international order and weaponize de-dollarization. This frame treats Western financial hegemony as neutral and universally beneficial. It treats any alternative payment system as inherently aggressive. It assumes that India, Brazil, and Indonesia are either unwitting participants in a revisionist project or insufficiently committed to the cause.
This reading gets the motivation backwards.
From the Global South, the construction of parallel payment systems, development banks, and supply-chain frameworks is a matter of economic survival. The Trump administration imposed tariffs of up to 50% on Indian goods in 2025. Western sanctions regimes routinely freeze sovereign assets and cut entire economies off from dollar clearing. IMF quota formulas continue to underrepresent the economic weight of emerging markets decades after the balance of global GDP shifted. The Bretton Woods institutions attach political conditions to development lending that no Western government would accept for itself.
In that context, building alternative financial infrastructure is a defensive response to a system that was never designed to treat the Global South as an equal. The Global South is constructing a fallback because the existing architecture treats its members as leverage points rather than stakeholders.
The distinction changes what you look for. If you expect a unified anti-Western manifesto, the Jaipur fracture looks like failure. If you understand that the purpose is defensive insulation rather than offensive confrontation, the fact that technical cooperation continued despite the political breakdown looks like exactly the kind of resilience the architecture was designed to produce.
Why This Changes the Calculus
The strategic significance of what is happening in New Delhi extends well beyond the immediate summit.
Payment system interoperability reduces the leverage of unilateral sanctions. Every time a UPI-Pix corridor successfully clears a transaction outside SWIFT, the cost of financial coercion rises for the country wielding it. South-South supply chain frameworks reduce dependence on routing trade through Western-controlled logistics hubs and insurance markets. Development lending without political conditions gives borrowing governments policy space that Bretton Woods institutions have historically denied them.
None of this happens overnight. The $1 trillion sovereign capital pool mapped at the iBRICS summit is a framework, not a fund. The SME financing facility still needs capitalization commitments. The CBDC corridors are pilots, not operational networks. The Sino-Indian border agreement from October 2024 is fragile, with fresh patrol friction reported in Arunachal Pradesh as recently as July.
These are not minor caveats. They are the real constraints that will determine whether the parallel architecture scales or stalls.
But the direction is structural, not cyclical. Western tariff shocks and sanctions episodes are accelerating the demand for alternatives. Every new protectionist measure strengthens the case for parallel infrastructure. The Global South does not need to agree on a unified geopolitical vision to agree that it needs more options. That shared practical need is a more durable foundation than any shared ideology.
The Sum of the Parts
The 18th BRICS Summit will produce a Leaders’ Declaration. Whether that document contains consensus language on West Asia or fractures along the same lines as Jaipur will dominate the news cycle for 48 hours.
The more durable outcome is the administrative and financial architecture that was built before the leaders ever arrived. Thirty-five working groups. Four hundred meetings. A $45 billion development bank. A $4.2 trillion financing gap being targeted with new instruments. Payment systems being physically linked across continents. Supply chain frameworks designed to withstand tariff shocks.
This is what multipolarity looks like in practice. It does not arrive as a single dramatic announcement. It accumulates, meeting by meeting, corridor by corridor, in the unglamorous work of deputies and technical committees solving problems that no one else is solving for them.
Back to the Motorcades
New Delhi will spend September 12 and 13 hosting heads of state at the Bharat Mandapam. The motorcades will roll through the 22 rehearsed corridors. The cameras will capture the family photo. Hotel rates will remain at ₹20 lakh. The stray monkey squads will have completed their work.
All of that is real, and all of it is secondary to what was already finished before the first motorcade arrived.
While the cameras were pointed at the arrivals gate, the financial plumbing of the Global South was being quietly rewired in conference rooms that no journalist bothered to enter. The motorcades will leave on September 14. The payment corridors, the SME credit frameworks, and the digital agriculture networks will remain.
That is the difference between a summit that makes headlines and a summit that changes the operating system. You are watching the second kind.

Originally published on Brasil de Fato as part of “Columna Valdai”, a biweekly column by Marco Fernandes, who serves as its curator. Republished with permission. Article written by Radhika Desai.
United States Treasury Secretary, Scott Beasant, portrayed the recent US-Japanese intervention in world currency markets, the largest markets in the world, to shore up the declining Japanese yen as act of solidarity for an ally. In an interview with Nikkei, he claimed that the Treasury purchased yen to prevent a broader Asian currency crisis, saying that “many Asian currencies follow the Japanese yen”. President Trump portrayed it as a ‘signal of friendship’ and ‘beneficial for the world economy’. He further observed, with the usual Trumpian sting in the tail: “We’re very strong -- very very strong financially. They are, you know, they have a weakening yen, and they wanted a little bit of help. And we’re always there for Japan. Japan’s been very good to us, with the exception, of course, of Pearl Harbor”.
However, much more is going on in this currency market intervention than US benevolence. Surprising though that might be, even more so is that this is being openly admitted and discussed in the mainstream financial press. Truths about the dollar system rarely are.
For decades, discussion of the dollar system, dominated as it is by a small group of mostly United States based scholars, has been all about the strength and endurance of the dollar system, usually attributed to the United States’s economic and military strength and, ultimately, to its ‘wide and deep financial markets’, as the phrase goes. Since President Trump won election for a second time nearly two years ago and since he took office, jarring notes have been appearing in this otherwise consensual discourse. Thanks, in particular, to Trump’s brazen and unrestrained, and one might add, erratic pursuit of his MAGA agenda, Trump’s detractors, both outside and in his own party, have begun discussing the problems of the dollar system increasingly openly and volubly, chiefly to blame them on Trump. The world has been finding out the truth about the dollar system as increasingly rancorous opposition to Trump has been washing very dirty political laundry in public.
There are, of course, the inevitable complaints about the recent weaponization of the dollar system which, rather than being effective, is exposing the system’s own weaknesses. As a commentator noted, “As the US ratchets up pressure, other countries will look to escape dollar power, likely provoking the US to double down in response”. The result is not effective weaponization, but revelation that the dollar system is more water pistol than AK-47. Meanwhile, the Financial Times’s prestigious Lex column pointed out that the ECB now holds more gold than dollars in its reserves. If the US’s most loyal allies are choosing another reserve asset, that’s saying something. And yet another columnist noted the simple truth that the dollar system is reliant on massive capital inflows and that these are now endangered in many ways: by US stock markets’ dominance by a handful of companies investing in AI (and that dominance is already faltering); by the difficulty investors in dollar-denominated assets, whose circle has narrowed in recent years to other western countries, Japan and the countries of the Persian Gulf, may find sparing money for investment into the dollar system when they need it for so much else, including their own expanding economic and military needs; and by the declining tolerance of other countries for the currency weakness which is often the flip side of dollar strength. This declining tolerance must, in turn, put pressure on the dollar.
This last possibility became real with the recent weakness of the yen, prompted by many factors including rises in US interest rates in the wake of the post-pandemic inflationary tide, the requirements of the carry trade – borrowing cheaply in yen to engage in leveraged speculation on US markets, which requires yen to remain cheap even after Japan transitioned to positive interest rates – and by rising inflation making critical Japanese imports more expensive, a problem sharply exacerbated by the US-Israeli war on Iran.
Japan is particularly badly placed to tolerate yen weakness. With inflation already biting Japanese families and businesses used to stable or even declining prices for decades, a weak yen can only worsen things further. If the situation is to be addressed, there are two options. Both have monumentally adverse implications for the dollar.
One is intervention in currency markets. The Bank of Japan could use its dollar reserves usually held in US treasuries – and remember, today, Japan is the world’s largest single foreign holder of US treasuries – to buy yen and thus support the currency. However, this is precisely what the US would wish to avoid. Such an action would only throw more dollar assets onto a market that seems to have had its fill of them and, on top of that, is facing a torrent of new assets being offered it. They include higher borrowing and higher US deficits that Trump is piling up with his penchant for tax cuts and his half a trillion dollar increase in the military budget, which will result in higher issuance of US treasuries which the market must find the will to buy. They will also include the additional issuance that will be necessitated by higher interest costs as the US has been forced to increase interest rates to combat inflation, so far unsuccessfully. Finally, the torrent of assets on its way to find buyers on markets also includes new equity and debt issuance spurred by the bubble of US AI investment. All this would put too much strain on markets for US dollar-denominated assets, the foundation of the dollar system.
The second way the Japanese could deal with the problem of a lower yen is by raising Japanese interest rates. It is true that Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi does not favour this option and nor does the considerable political and business lobby behind her reflationary agenda. However, difficult though this choice may be, they may yet have to make it. What is more important from our point of view is that it is worse for the dollar system than for Japan on at least two counts. First, higher Japanese interest rates would set back the carry trade through which low-cost borrowing in Japan has facilitated the leveraged trading that has been so important in keeping up prices of dollar denominated assets on which the influx of money into the dollar system ultimately depends. Secondly, higher interest rates in Japan will also set back demand for US dollar-denominated assets more directly, as money pours into higher yielding Japanese bonds.
This is why the US government intervened in currency markets to ‘save the yen’. It is noteworthy that the US did not buy yen and sell dollars but bought yen and sold euros, that too without informing the European Central Bank first. Another demonstration that the US’s allies are now required to be vassals.
In addition to these long-standing problems maturing, the credibility of the Federal Reserve has been thrown into question by many recent developments. There is, first, the Federal Reserve’s support for asset markets through Quantitative Easing after 2008 as well as, more recently, former Federal Reserve Chair Jay Powell’s tardy response to inflation. And in office, Trump has unusually and dangerously interfered in the policies of the ‘independent’ Federal Reserve, demanding lower interest rates. His Treasury Secretary, Scott Bessent has openly accepted, indeed boasted about, the political nature of Federal Reserve decisions. And now new questions about the strategy and competence of the new Federal Reserve Chair, Kevin Warsh, just appointed by the Trump administration, are already being aired.
It is therefore not a surprise that even a scholar as Barry Eichengreen, who has long talked up the dollar believes that the most important lesson of the yen intervention is that it is pushing the dollar system to the brink: ‘The bottom line is that Washington, fearing the consequences for US financial markets, is reluctant to see foreign central banks use their dollar reserves. This is telling us that the dollar is not the attractive reserve currency it once was. When this message sinks in, other countries will redouble their search for more attractive, readily usable alternatives. Reserve diversification is apt to gather steam.’
Well, there you have it, from the horses’ mouth. And the worst of it is that the intervention has not been particularly successful: the yen lost half its gains a couple of days later. It’s going to be a rocky ride for the dollar and the dollar system from here on.

In the five previous articles in this series, we examined the shifting coalition, the accusation of a “terrorist state,” Zelenskyy’s power structure, widespread corruption, and the Crimea case. In this final installment, we turn to two other dimensions of the war that have received comparatively little attention from the international media: first, the human and social costs of the war inside Ukraine, from the situation of the Hungarian minority to the crisis of confidence in the mobilization system; and second, the financial and security burden that the war has placed on Europe.
The Hungarian Minority: Tensions Between Kyiv and Budapest
The Zakarpattia region in western Ukraine is home to one of the country’s oldest ethnic minorities, the Hungarians, a minority that has affected relations between Kyiv and Budapest for years.
Fedir Shandor, Ukraine’s current ambassador to Hungary, is himself a member of this minority. Before entering the diplomatic sphere, he fought in the 101st Zakarpattia Territorial Defense Brigade.
This fact itself shows that the issue of the Hungarians of Zakarpattia cannot simply be explained in terms of a confrontation between the Ukrainian government and its ethnic minorities.
With the outbreak of the war in 2022, however, this longstanding divide took on new dimensions. One of the most important points of contention has been the mobilization of Hungarian men and allegations concerning the way Ukrainian forces have treated them.
Two deaths among mobilized Hungarians, in particular, have become focal points of tension between Kyiv and Budapest.
The first case concerns József Sebestyén. According to Hungarian officials, he was forcibly mobilized in Berehove on June 14, 2025, and was beaten with iron rods during the process. He eventually died in hospital on July 6.
Ukraine rejects this account.
According to the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine, Sebestyén had been legally mobilized after passing a medical examination, but four days later left his unit without authorization. He was subsequently hospitalized in a psychiatric ward after being diagnosed with an “acute stress reaction,” and the cause of his death was reported as a “pulmonary embolism.”
An official autopsy, according to Ukrainian officials, also recorded no evidence of beating.
By contrast, the Hungarian newspaper Index has alleged that a forensic medical examiner distorted the report under pressure from Ukraine’s Security Service (SBU).
The second case concerns Zsolt Reban. According to Hungarian officials, despite a history of heart disease and having received medical exemptions, he was transferred to a training center near Lviv on January 6, 2026, and died 12 days later.
The official document states the cause of death as “cardiorespiratory failure accompanied by mild pneumonia.”
Ukraine has also denied any mistreatment in this case.
The significance of these two cases is not limited merely to the fate of the two individuals. Behind them lies a more sensitive issue: the relationship between the central Ukrainian government and a minority that has deep historical, linguistic, and cultural ties to another country.
In wartime, when the government turns to large-scale mobilization to provide the necessary manpower, the way it treats such minorities can quickly turn from a domestic issue into a diplomatic crisis.
This is precisely what has happened between Kyiv and Budapest.
Hungary regards these cases as evidence of mistreatment of the Hungarian minority in Ukraine, while Kyiv has rejected the allegations and regards Budapest’s actions as part of that country’s political pressure against Ukraine.
As tensions continued, Hungary summoned Ukraine’s ambassador, called for European Union sanctions against the officials responsible, and the government of Viktor Orbán, who was then in office, also prevented several Ukrainian military officials from entering the Schengen Area.
The issue of the Hungarians of Zakarpattia, therefore, cannot be viewed merely as a bilateral dispute between Kyiv and Budapest.
The war has intensified longstanding ethnic and political divisions, and an issue that before the war largely revolved around minority rights and Ukrainian-Hungarian relations is now intertwined with mobilization, security, and the deaths of citizens.
For this reason, Zakarpattia is one of the places that demonstrates that the costs of the Ukraine war are not determined solely on the front lines. Part of these costs is reflected in relations between the state and ethnic minorities, as well as in the tense relations between Ukraine and its neighbors.
The Crisis of Confidence in Ukraine’s Mobilization System
The story of these two Hungarian citizens is not merely a matter of two controversial cases; rather, it provides a window into the broader crisis of Ukraine’s mobilization system.
Fedir Venislavskyi, a member of the National Security Committee of the Ukrainian Parliament, has said that up to 90 percent of personnel entering the army are recruited through compulsory mobilization at TCC centers, rather than voluntarily.
At the same time, research by the Rating Sociological Group shows that public trust in these centers fell from 67 percent in 2024 to 61 percent in 2025.
Even “busification”—a term used to describe violent and coercive methods of recruiting personnel—was selected as Ukraine’s Word of the Year in 2024.
The significance of these figures lies in the change that has taken place in the relationship between the state and its citizens: the army that was formed at the beginning of the war amid a wave of volunteers has, as the war has continued, become increasingly dependent on coercion to provide manpower.
When mobilization is accompanied, for part of society, by fear of detention, forced transfer, or violent treatment, it is natural for trust in this system to erode as well.
This crisis has even reached the level of the political leadership. In January 2026, Zelenskyy appointed Mykhailo Fedorov as Minister of Defense and made “resolving the issue of busification” his second priority, after air defense.
When presenting his program to parliament, Fedorov said that nearly two million draft-eligible men had refused mobilization, while approximately 200,000 soldiers had left their units without authorization.
Alongside these figures, according to an explanatory memorandum to a parliamentary bill, more than six million draft-eligible men had failed in 2024 to update their information through the Reserv+ system or in person.
These figures cannot be explained simply as “draft evasion.” When hundreds of thousands of people are unwilling to continue serving and millions of others refuse even to register or update their information, one can speak of a gap between the policy of continuing the war and the willingness of part of society to bear its human costs.
Corruption has also intensified this distrust. According to a member of parliament from the ruling party, the average bribe for securing one’s release from a TCC center after detention is between $10,000 and $15,000. This allegation suggests that, alongside the formal mobilization system, an informal network for evading it has also emerged.
Under such circumstances, the cost of war can effectively be distributed unequally: someone with money and connections has a greater opportunity to evade mobilization, while the main pressure falls on those who do not have such opportunities.
Nevertheless, published polls indicate that around 65 percent of the population wants serious reform of the mobilization system. At the same time, public anger toward figures who, despite having exemptions themselves, encourage others to fight is significant.
This issue shows that opposition to compulsory mobilization does not necessarily mean opposition to defending the country; for many, the main issue is fairness in the distribution of the costs of war.
The question is whether someone who did not have a choice about going to war can be asked to risk his life for a decision that others have made.
Ultimately, the Ukrainian government still has the ability to compulsorily mobilize citizens, but the longer the war continues, the more difficult it will become to persuade them to accept this cost.
This is where the mobilization crisis becomes a crisis of trust: people may be sent to war through coercion, but trust and motivation cannot be built through force.
The Fate of the “Reparations Loan”: A Plan Abandoned at the Last Minute
One of the most controversial financial cases of the Ukraine war was the so-called “Reparations Loan,” an idea proposed by the European Commission and the German Chancellor to use approximately €140 billion to €210 billion in frozen assets of the Russian Central Bank. most of which are held by the Belgian institution Euroclear, to finance Ukraine.
For months, Bart De Wever, the Prime Minister of Belgium, opposed the plan, citing three concerns: the possibility of legal action by Russia against Belgium and Euroclear; the risk of reciprocal seizure of the assets of European companies in Russia; and the absence of a legally binding guarantee from other EU members to compensate for potential losses.
This case has now reached an outcome different from what was anticipated at the beginning of the negotiations. At the European Union leaders’ summit on December 18–19, 2025, due to Belgium’s continued opposition, the “Reparations Loan” was effectively abandoned. Instead, EU leaders agreed on a €90 billion ($106 billion) interest-free joint loan, financed through borrowing in the capital markets. Hungary, the Czech Republic, and Slovakia did not participate in the arrangement.
The frozen Russian assets remained untouched, although European leaders, including German Chancellor Friedrich Merz, emphasized that if Russia refused to pay war reparations, they reserved the right to use these assets to repay the loan.
Thus, Belgium’s concerns about the stability of Europe’s financial system, which had been raised in the earlier versions of the proposal, effectively influenced the European Union’s final decision.
Ultimately, this decision shows that freezing Russian assets does not mean having unrestricted control over them. These resources remain Russian assets, and converting them into a financing instrument for Ukraine, unlike merely freezing them, carries much more serious legal and financial consequences.
Therefore, even Merz’s warning and the emphasis by other European leaders on the possibility of using these assets in the future cannot, on their own, resolve this issue in a unilateral and straightforward manner.
The Financial Burden of War: Questions About Europe’s Responsibility
After Belgium opposed the direct use of frozen Russian assets, the European Union ultimately turned to financing through joint borrowing instead of using these assets and approved a €90 billion loan to support Ukraine.
As a result, part of the cost of continuing the war will be financed not from Russian assets, but from the financial resources and commitments of European countries—a commitment that, if the war continues, will naturally not be limited to a short period.
However, the cost of the war for Europe is not reflected solely in the budgetary line for aid to Ukraine.
A study by the Kiel Institute, titled “The Price of War,” examining the economic consequences of more than 150 wars since 1870, has estimated that the Ukraine war could reduce the economic output of third countries by approximately $250 billion, of which nearly $70 billion would be attributable to EU countries.
This cost comes alongside disruptions to trade and supply chains, higher energy costs, and inflationary pressures.
In addition to these indirect costs, Europe continues to allocate billions of euros in financial, military, and humanitarian assistance to Ukraine, while also facing other costs, such as hosting millions of Ukrainian refugees and increasing defense spending.
Therefore, the longer the war continues, the issue is no longer simply the amount of assistance to Ukraine; rather, the economic and political sustainability of this level of support is also becoming a serious question.
This question becomes more important when we consider the rising costs of the war alongside governance problems inside Ukraine.
The extensive corruption cases exposed during the war, which we also addressed in previous articles in this series, show that the issue is not merely the provision of resources; how these resources are managed, monitored, and spent is also important.
The greater the share of the cost of the war that Europe assumes, the greater the expectation for transparency and accountability regarding how these resources are spent.
Europe now faces a difficult dilemma: on the one hand, it regards continued support for Ukraine as part of its own security; on the other hand, the prolongation of the war means the gradual transfer of its costs to public budgets and the economies of European countries.
By the end of 2026, the main question will no longer be simply how much Europe can afford to pay; rather, it will be how long it is willing to finance the cost of the war, and what guarantees exist in return for these growing costs regarding an end to the war, financial transparency, and accountability in Ukraine.
Ukraine and Concerns Over Arms Trafficking in Post-War Europe
Concerns over the trafficking of weapons leaving Ukraine, unlike some other claims made in this series of reports, are an issue that has also been taken seriously by independent Western media and institutions, rather than solely by Russian officials.
The Organized Crime and Corruption Reporting Project (OCCRP), citing Reuters, has reported that some weapons outside the control of Ukraine’s official institutions, including weapons passing through the Port of Odesa, reach organized criminal groups, which sell them to the Middle East.
A senior Finnish police investigator has also independently stated that arms-trafficking routes from Ukraine to Sweden, Denmark, and the Netherlands have emerged.
The Harvard International Review has also recalled that during the Crimea conflict (2013-2015, approximately 300,000 small arms were lost or stolen from Ukraine, a precedent that reinforces current concerns.
At the operational level, Ukraine’s own Security Service (SBU) has also acknowledged the discovery of several major arms-trafficking shipments.
In one operation, on January 12, an organized group in the Kyiv and Dnipropetrovsk regions that intended to sell a shipment of “trophy” weapons was identified, and authorities seized 75 small arms, 38 hand grenades, more than 20 explosive detonators, two grenade launchers, and 13,000 rounds of ammunition.
In another operation, on February 25, an arms-trafficking network in the Kyiv region was dismantled in cooperation with the National Police, in which the sale of more than 90 grenades with their corresponding fuses had been documented.
These two cases, unlike the overall and unverified figure cited by Polyansky, were reported by an official Ukrainian institution and therefore have a more substantial documentary basis.
This concern may be reminiscent of the experience of the Balkans after the 1990s, when the wars in the former Yugoslavia left millions of illegal firearms behind, which, even today—three decades later—continue to circulate on Europe’s black market.
Conclusion
The Ukraine war cannot be understood solely through maps of the front lines and the advances of military forces. Behind this war, a network of power, corruption, minorities, a crisis of legitimacy, geopolitical interests, and financial costs has taken shape; from the power structure in Kyiv and the Crimea case to the compulsory mobilization of citizens, the fate of the Hungarian minority, and the billions of euros that Europe is spending to sustain the war.
The six articles in this series ultimately arrive at a common point: when a war becomes prolonged, it crosses beyond the front lines. It enters state institutions, family life, the economies of supporting countries, and even the calculations of major powers, and its cost can no longer be measured solely by the kilometers of advance or retreat on the battlefield.
Perhaps the most important lesson of this war is precisely this: to understand the Ukraine crisis, one should not ask only who will win on the battlefield. One must ask what remains behind the front lines; how much trust, how much stability, and how much cost will remain for a generation that is expected to live with the consequences after the war.

Western athletes have taken part in nomadic competitions in large numbers for the first time this year. Dr. Alireza Abbasi, an international figure in sports science, suggested many did so simply to test their nerve.
The sixth World Nomad Games are unfolding on the shores of Lake Issyk-Kul, the vast alpine lake in northern Kyrgyzstan. Athletes are competing in dozens of disciplines that range from traditional board games to arm wrestling and mas-wrestling. Although most of these sports remain little known outside Central Asia, they have drawn a growing number of first-time foreign participants.
Afton Caldwell, competing for the United States, called it an honour to share the field with his opponents. His team lost 16–7 to Kyrgyzstan, the tournament favourites, in kok boru. “To be honest, this was the first game I’ve ever played,” the 38-year-old said.
The Games began in Kyrgyzstan in 2014 and are held every two years. The next edition is scheduled for Tatarstan in Russia in 2028. This year’s event is the largest yet: more than 100 national teams from every continent are contesting 43 disciplines rooted in the ancient cultures of Asian nomads.
The opening coincided with Kyrgyzstan’s Independence Day and with a Shanghai Cooperation Organization summit in Bishkek that brought together Chinese President Xi Jinping, Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi, Russian President Vladimir Putin and other heads of state. The gathering gave the Games an unusually prominent international audience.
Often called the “Nomad Olympics”, the event has been recognised by the United Nations as a platform for intercultural dialogue and sustainable development. This edition includes ancient sports and traditional intellectual contests that originated on the Central Asian steppes, where they served both as military training and as social occasions in which young men displayed strength, skill and endurance.
The comparison with other multi-sport gatherings is instructive. The Commonwealth Games bring together countries once linked to the British Empire. The Francophonie Games combine sport and culture for states where French is spoken or institutionally recognised. Nearby, the CIS Games serve countries that belong to the post-Soviet intergovernmental bloc.
The World Nomad Games stand apart. Participation is not based on political membership, linguistic affiliation or post-imperial networks, but on a shared civilizational and historical idea of nomadic heritage. While the CIS and Francophone events recast older imperial structures as soft-power communities, and the CIS Games ritualise a post-Soviet space under a low-key political banner, the Nomad Games assemble a coalition around an ancestral cultural complex that is neither overtly geopolitical nor legally institutionalised. Their legitimacy is symbolic rather than treaty-based.
The Games themselves have been built. The real task now is to make them matter: to turn spectacle into substance and to turn a living legacy into a shared regional story.

Academic research is rarely known for its timing. But a recent study in Argumenta Oeconomica, analysing labour income determinants across ten BRICS countries from 2004 to 2022, arrives as labour policy takes centre stage in the bloc’s agenda.
The study is straightforward. Using panel data from the IMF, ILO, UNDP, and the World Justice Project, researchers found that the Human Development Index (HDI) , Rule of Law Index, Financial Institution Depth Index, and Internet access all correlate positively with labour income share as a percentage of GDP. The conclusion: invest in education, health, legal institutions, financial inclusion, and digital infrastructure, and labour income improves.
It is a finding that aligns with decades of development economics. It is also incomplete.
The Missing Frame
The study measures what is measurable: institutions, financial depth, technology access. It does not measure what is structural: the global economic order that constrains all BRICS members, regardless of their domestic reform efforts.
Consider China. The study notes that China’s labour income share has remained stagnant despite rising HDI. It attributes this to polarised wage growth and automation shifting workers from manufacturing to informal services. But the deeper reality is that China’s export-led growth within a dollar-dominated trading system has structurally privileged capital accumulation over labour income growth. This is not a governance failure. It is a structural feature of the development pathway available to countries that must compete globally on cost.
South Africa offers another contradiction. The country scores relatively high on both the Rule of Law Index and the Financial Market Depth Index. Yet it has among the highest inequality in the world. The study treats these indicators as unambiguously positive. It does not ask: whose rights do these laws protect, and whose interests do these financial markets serve?
The UAE presents perhaps the starkest case. Its HDI is the highest among BRICS members, and its Internet penetration approaches 100%. Yet its labour income share remains comparatively low. This is not a puzzle for the study’s framework—it is a fundamental challenge to it. High HDI does not automatically produce high labour income when the economy is structured around capital-intensive sectors and migrant labour with limited rights.
What the Data Actually Reveals
The study’s own findings contain clues the authors do not pursue.
The Financial Market Depth Index coefficient is significant only at the 10% level—statistical noise by conventional standards—yet the study treats it as a confirmed finding. This overreach suggests an assumption that financial deepening must be beneficial, even when the data equivocates.
Meanwhile, the Financial Institution Depth Index shows a stronger and more consistent relationship with labour income. This distinction matters. Credit access for small enterprises and workers is not the same as stock market capitalisation. The study collapses these into a single narrative of financial development, but the data suggests a more nuanced picture: institutions that serve the real economy matter more than capital markets that serve investors.
The Rule of Law Index shows the strongest coefficient—a 1-unit increase corresponds to a 24.8 percentage point increase in labour income share. This is striking. But again, the study does not interrogate what “rule of law” means in practice. In South Africa, strong rule of law has not translated into equitable labour outcomes. In China, legal reforms have often served state economic priorities rather than worker bargaining power. The index measures form, not substance.
BRICS Ministers and the Missing Variable
The study’s timing is significant. In July 2026, under India’s presidency, BRICS Labour and Employment Ministers met to discuss “Building for Resilience, Innovation, Cooperation and Sustainability.” The ILO praised the agenda. Trade unions issued the Hyderabad Declaration calling for universal social protection and worker-centric digital transformation.
These are important steps. But they operate within the same framework as the study: domestic policy reform as the path to labour income improvement.
Civil society organisations have noted the limits of this approach. A coalition including INFID, TNI, and Publish What You Pay Indonesia assessed the BRICS Labour Ministers’ Declaration as insufficiently committed to workers’ rights, collective bargaining, and living wages. They argued that
BRICS must be “an alternative force that demonstrates that development can advance alongside respect for workers’ rights.”
The coalition also highlighted green transition risks. TNI researcher Rachmi Hertanti warned that BRICS cooperation on energy transition “must be accompanied by technology transfer and value creation in developing countries so that it does not merely reinforce extractive economic patterns.”
This is the missing variable: global structural constraints. The study treats BRICS countries as autonomous actors who can improve labour incomes by improving institutions. But sanctions on Iran and Russia, dollar dominance over global finance, debt service obligations, and the terms of technology transfer all shape labour outcomes in ways that domestic governance cannot fully address.
The Institutional Reform Trap
The study’s policy recommendations—strengthen the rule of law, expand financial inclusion, invest in digital infrastructure—are not wrong. They are simply insufficient.
Consider the rule of law. Yes, stronger legal protections correlate with higher labour income. But legal reforms require policy space. Countries under IMF programmes or carrying heavy external debt have reduced capacity to legislate and enforce labour protections. Their legal reforms must accommodate creditor interests.
Consider financial inclusion. Deeper financial institutions can expand credit access. But in economies where labour is structurally weak relative to capital—where global competition pressures wages downward, where automation displaces workers faster than new jobs are created—credit does not automatically translate into higher labour income.
Consider technology. Internet access has clear benefits. But digital platforms have also created gig economies with precarious employment and minimal protections. The study treats technology as neutral infrastructure. It is not. It is shaped by power relations. Without governance frameworks that actively shape technology’s labour outcomes, digitisation can reduce labour income share even as it raises productivity.
What BRICS Collective Action Could Change
The study implicitly assumes that labour income is a national policy problem. The strategic insight is that it is also a collective action problem.
BRICS has already started building alternatives to the Western-dominated order: the New Development Bank, the Contingent Reserve Arrangement, the push for alternative payment systems, the expansion of the bloc itself. These institutions could, if oriented correctly, create the policy space for member states to pursue labour-centred development strategies.
The ILO has acknowledged this potential. Director-General Gilbert Houngbo noted that India’s progress on social protection “offers lessons that can be shared through South-South cooperation.” BRICS CONNECT—the Cooperation Network for Capacity Building, Employability, New Skills and Technology—aims to institutionalise such knowledge sharing.
But the scale of the challenge is larger. As researchers have argued, economic catch-up requires investment in the productivity of ordinary citizens, policies that increase wages and labour bargaining power, and strategic use of exchange rates to encourage export-led growth. These require not just domestic reform but coordination to manage competitive pressures within the bloc.
The study’s finding that stronger institutions correlate with labour income is useful evidence. But the conclusion that BRICS should pursue more of the same governance reforms—more rule of law, more financial depth, more digital access—misses the strategic opportunity. The bloc exists because existing global institutions have not served its members’ interests. Labour income policy should be no exception.
The Larger Question
The study is a useful addition to the literature. It provides empirical support for investments in human capital, legal institutions, and financial access. But it does not ask the question that matters most:
why do some societies with strong institutions still fail to deliver labour income growth, and what does that tell us about the limits of institutional reform?
The answer is structural. Labour income share is not just a function of domestic governance. It is shaped by global power relations, by the position of economies in global value chains, by the terms of technology transfer, by the structure of the financial system, by the reality of sanctions and debt.
BRICS was formed to address these structural constraints. The bloc’s labour agenda should do the same. Domestic reforms are necessary. But they are not sufficient. The real agenda is the one the bloc itself exists to advance: a more just, multipolar international system that creates genuine policy space for member states to pursue labour-centred development.
The study’s data confirms the value of institutional reform. Its interpretation obscures the political economy that makes such reform necessary in the first place. Once you see that, the rest makes more sense.

A Global South policy brief published in Washington this June states the institutional problem without euphemism. The Security Council still runs on a 1945 membership list. The IMF and World Bank still weight influence by a mid-century map of wealth. African conflicts occupy a large share of the Council’s agenda; Africa has no permanent seat. Emerging economies have taken modest IMF quota adjustments and a G20 that now includes the African Union. The gap between who lives under the rules and who writes them has not closed.
The same brief then tells the United States how to handle what comes next. Congress should support “discussions” on representativeness. The administration should stop treating Southern demands as an attack on the order. Established institutions should coordinate with the New Development Bank and the Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank so diversification does not harden into fragmentation. The United Nations should remain the center.
That sequence is the political fact worth sitting with. The diagnosis is Southern. The recommended remedy is still addressed to Washington.
What the reform argument is actually selling
The question is not whether outdated boards look illegitimate. They do. The question is whether more flags on those boards restore legitimacy to institutions that can still freeze reserves, bury agendas, and keep vetoes in the same hands—or whether parts of the Global South have already answered by building capacity that does not wait on a Charter amendment.
Marta Fernández of the BRICS Policy Center wrote the brief for the Global South Policy Hub. It is useful because it is disciplined. This is the version of the Southern case now packaged for North Atlantic rooms: widen participation, treat alternative institutions as complements, and multilateralism can be renewed. Most of the institutional history it uses is accurate. The strategy it draws from that history is the part that will not travel.
The map is not in dispute
Post-1945 institutions encoded a distribution of power. Eighty years on, that distribution fails ordinary tests of output, population, the geography of war, and the geography of debt. Calling the result a legitimacy crisis is description, not performance. Governments that preach democracy at home and defend oligarchy in the Council make the contradiction visible from Brasília or Pretoria without a theory seminar.
The older claim—that more voices destroy effectiveness—has done political work for incumbents. 2008 remains the clean historical example: the G7 could not coordinate a shock running through emerging and advanced economies alike. Elevating the G20 conceded that the guest list had to change if the meeting was going to matter. The African Union’s permanent G20 seat in 2023 was another concession of the same type.
Alternative institutions did not arrive as decoration. The New Development Bank followed years of argument over voice and votes in the Bretton Woods system. BRICS expansion is, among other things, a demand for participation existing clubs would not grant on acceptable terms. Debates on local-currency settlement and payment mechanisms track a material vulnerability: a single reserve currency and payment networks that can be switched into instruments of dispute. The brief notes that last point with care. It belongs in the center of the argument. The plumbing of the world economy is part of the legitimacy problem.
None of this rehabilitates nostalgia for the unreconstructed postwar order. None of it proves the operational claim the brief needs: that wider representation inside the same architecture, plus courteous coordination with the newcomers, will restore the capacity to act.
What the openings actually changed
Take the record the brief cites and stop where the evidence stops.
IMF quota reform shifted some voting power toward emerging economies. Governance in the Fund and the Bank still follows older hierarchies. Agenda-setting, surveillance, and conditionality did not migrate with a few percentage points. Permanent membership and the veto on the Security Council are essentially untouched. An African seat is still a demand. The G20 is broader than the G7. It is a forum, not a legislature, and it does not rewrite the Council or the Fund.
Inclusion can be real and still leave control where it was. That distinction is what the reform genre keeps sanding down. A government can sit in the room, sign the communiqué, and watch a veto or a payments cutoff decide the outcome.
The brief holds that broader participation can deepen compliance and political ownership. Plausible. Not shown here in outcomes—speed, enforcement, or crisis performance after each incremental opening. Treating the claim as settled would be generosity, not reading.
How Southern agency gets translated
Fernández writes that alternative institutions should not be read mainly as a project to dismantle the existing order. They often reflect frustration with the pace of reform. Western efforts to discourage Southern agency, she adds, deepen exclusion.
Both statements can be true and still miss what states are doing with the frustration. Building a development bank after failing to rewrite another bank is a complaint. It is also insurance. Discussing settlement systems after finance has been used as a weapon is a debate about representation. It is also a debate about whether the pipes of trade settlement should remain a privilege that can be revoked.
The brief wants those projects filed as complementary so the UN can stay the coordinating roof and the United States can be talked out of punishment. The filing serves a venue. A Washington platform whose job is to insert Southern expertise into Northern policy circles has a reason to turn Southern agency into a request the host city can accept: engage, reform, do not punish. That is not a charge against the author. It is the ceiling of the room.
Incumbents keep the core institutions, offer process, and describe Southern institution-building as a coordination problem. Southern elites who want access without the cost of building parallel systems get a language of democratic consistency that sounds principled in New York and workable on the Hill. What drops out is the harder line: legitimacy does not return while the same capitals write exceptions for themselves and enforce discipline on others.
Two readings of the same facts
The dominant frame, including in this Southern-authored Washington edition, runs as follows. The system is strained. Representation lagged. Effectiveness now depends on legitimacy. Therefore expand participation, keep alternatives inside a UN-centered whole, and persuade the United States that reform is burden-sharing.
The multipolar reading starts from the same institutional facts and refuses the last instruction. A crisis produced by selective rules and a frozen hierarchy will not be cured by a more diverse photograph of the board. If voting weights, vetoes, and payment rails stay put, extra seats are a method of absorption. Alternative institutions then look like a hedge, not a mood. Fragmentation is not only a failure of coordination. It is what states do when the timetable of reform is known and so is the result.
One frame preserves the presumption that the postwar core is the only serious place to solve collective problems, provided it is updated. The other treats that presumption as a preference already qualified by practice—NDB, AIIB, regional organizations, BRICS expansion, payment experiments—whether or not every experiment matures.
That last clause matters. Local-currency proposals can be visible and still stall. New banks can lend and remain small beside the older ones. Coordination among alternatives can fail. Failure of this or that instrument does not restore authority to a model that asks the South to wait for permission to matter.
Where the leverage actually sits
Power in this file is institutional design plus financial leverage: who can halt a resolution, attach conditions to liquidity, and disconnect a country from the pipes through which trade is settled. Development finance follows those pipes. Security debates follow the Council’s map of who may block action. The narrative fight is over whether Southern institution-building is “reform energy” or “revisionism,” a label that tracks threat to incumbents more closely than it tracks legal form.
For a multipolar order the live issue is not a slogan about UN centrality. The UN may remain central on some files for a long time. The issue is whether Global South strategy is organized around making that centrality more inclusive or around lowering the cost of exclusion from it. Those are different budgets. One funds another cycle of membership working groups. The other funds balance sheets, payment options, and clubs that do not need a P5 conversion experience to move money or set a development priority.
Intra-South hierarchy belongs in the same frame without becoming an alibi for the old one. A larger BRICS does not automatically speak for every African or Latin American state. China and India are not interchangeable with smaller members. Reform that only promotes a handful of large emerging powers can reproduce exclusion at a new scale. That is an argument against romance. It is not an argument for a Council that still has no permanent African member.
The offer on the table
Order the pieces without inflating them. The institutional map is outdated. Incremental inclusion has occurred and has not transferred control. Alternative institutions grew where reform inside the old houses was too slow. Influential Southern commentary aimed at Washington still asks the United States to bless that process and keep a familiar roof overhead. The evidence that “more representation restores effectiveness” is thinner than the evidence that unmet demands produce new venues. The coercive use of finance is admitted and then folded back into a plea for engagement.
The conclusion that holds is limited and sharp. Representation is a real deficit. It is not a sufficient theory of how legitimacy returns. A strategy that ends with better access to unreformed boards will keep mistaking presence for power. The work already underway in new banks and payment debates is the part of the record that does not wait for New York to finish the conversation.
Some facts should stay marked as open. The precise legal reach of the 2026 U.S. withdrawals belongs to the underlying executive action, not to adjectives. Quota tables and the operational scale of NDB and AIIB should be checked before anyone treats size as settled. Whether any coalition can amend the Charter is politics, not atmosphere. Those uncertainties do not rescue process-plus-seats as the Southern interest.
A serious Global South scholar can itemize an eighty-year lag in voice and still close by instructing Congress and “whatever administration is in power” to support discussions, avoid punishment, and keep coordination under the old roof. As diplomacy, the closing is intelligible. As strategy, it describes the offer: more chairs, same plumbing.
That is what the reform genre can concede without conceding control. A seat is not worthless. It is also what is for sale. Parts of the Global South have already started building the pieces that do not require a better invitation.

In mid-2026, the rupiah did something it hadn’t done in years: it broke past 18,000 per dollar. Foreign-exchange reserves fell by more than US$11 billion. Bank Indonesia executed a surprise, off-cycle rate hike to steady the currency.
At almost the same time, official data showed the economy still growing above 5 percent a year, inflation anchored within target, and reserves remaining substantial by regional standards.
That combination should stop anyone from accepting the headline that Indonesia is collapsing. The real question is sharper: can Jakarta’s new model of state-led economic sovereignty be institutionalized without creating the very financial vulnerabilities it’s meant to overcome?
The Surface Story and the Real Problem
On the surface, this looks familiar: a sharp currency move, reserve drawdowns, equity-market losses, a credit-rating outlook revision to negative. Investors point to policy inconsistency, a more centralized executive, and new rules that force commodity exporters to keep all their foreign-currency earnings onshore for a year.
The deeper problem is structural. Indonesia is attempting to change the terms on which it integrates into the global economy: who controls its resources, who captures the value added, and who holds the foreign exchange those resources generate.
That ambition is being tested through two concrete mechanisms:
- Danantara, a state super-holding company tasked with managing roughly US$900 billion in assets across around 1,000 entities, including major state banks and strategic SOEs.
- Export-proceeds regulations that require non-oil and gas exporters to retain 100 percent of their foreign-currency earnings domestically for 12 months, increasingly in state-owned banks, with limits on how much can be used for ordinary operations.
These tools are presented as ways to ensure that Indonesia’s resource wealth stays in Indonesia. They are also the immediate source of market anxiety.
Growth, Stress, and the Dual Reality
Any honest account has to start with the dual reality that the data show.
On one side:
- Real GDP growth remained above 5 percent in the first half of 2026.
- Inflation stayed within the central bank’s target band.
- Foreign-exchange reserves, though lower, still stood at around US$145 billion — enough for more than five months of imports.
On the other:
- The rupiah depreciated sharply, touching roughly 18,190 per dollar before a partial rebound.
- Reserves fell by more than US$11 billion from end-2025 to mid-2026.
- The main equity index lost about a third of its value before a sharp one-day rebound after the surprise rate hike.
- A major rating agency shifted Indonesia’s outlook to negative, citing policy uncertainty and growing centralization.
This is not a picture of straightforward collapse. It is a picture of an economy whose real activity remains relatively resilient while its financial layer is under significant stress.
The crucial question is what is driving that stress.
The Sovereignty Project in Concrete Terms
Indonesia’s post-1998 reputation was built on macroeconomic prudence: an independent central bank, conservative fiscal rules, and openness to foreign capital. The current administration is not abandoning growth or stability as goals. It is changing the means.
The stated objective is to move beyond exporting raw materials and low-value intermediates toward capturing more of the value chain domestically — the logic that underpinned the nickel downstreaming push and is now being extended to other commodities.
Danantara is the institutional vehicle for this shift. It is described as a sovereign wealth fund and super-holding in one, with a mandate to:
- Consolidate state assets.
- Direct investment into strategic sectors.
- Raise domestic financing through instruments such as “Patriot Bonds.”
- Support national priorities ranging from energy and infrastructure to social programs.
At the same time, the export-proceeds regime is designed to:
- Keep foreign exchange generated from natural resources inside the Indonesian banking system.
- Increase the state’s ability to manage liquidity and fund development.
- Reduce reliance on external borrowing and dollar funding for domestic priorities.
From Jakarta’s perspective, this is not reckless experimentation. It is an attempt to correct a long-standing pattern: resources extracted in Indonesia, value added abroad, foreign exchange intermediated by external actors, and policy space constrained by external financial conditions.
Where the Financial Risk Enters
The market’s reaction is not simply ideological resistance to state intervention. It reflects specific, tangible concerns.
First, liquidity and corporate cash flow. Forcing exporters to park all their foreign-currency earnings onshore for 12 months, with limits on how much of the converted rupiah can be used for operations, directly affects working capital. Companies that rely on foreign-currency revenue to service foreign loans, pay imported inputs, or hedge commodity cycles now face tighter constraints.
If those constraints are severe enough, they can:
- Compress investment and production.
- Increase the risk of defaults in mining, plantations, and related sectors.
- Reduce the very foreign-exchange inflows the rules are meant to capture.
Second, governance and transparency. Danantara’s reported asset base is enormous — on the order of 60 percent of Indonesia’s GDP. Yet, as of mid-2026, it had not published its first consolidated financial statements on time. That opacity makes it difficult for investors, rating agencies, and even domestic analysts to assess:
- How much of the US$900 billion is genuinely liquid or mobilizable.
- What liabilities sit underneath those assets.
- How much risk is being transferred onto state-owned banks.
- Whether Danantara is operating as a commercial investor or as a financing vehicle for political priorities.
Third, monetary credibility. The central bank’s mandate is to maintain price and exchange-rate stability. But when fiscal and monetary policy become more tightly intertwined — through burden-sharing arrangements, transfers of fiscal cash to public banks, and administrative capital-flow measures — the perception of independence erodes. That perception matters because it affects how markets price risk.
None of this means Indonesia is on the brink of systemic crisis. It does mean that the state is concentrating more risk in its own institutions at the same time that those institutions are least transparent.
Two Frames, One Reality
Here the story splits into two competing interpretations.
The dominant investor frame reads these developments as a slide away from orthodoxy: policy inconsistency, weakened central-bank autonomy, opaque state vehicles, and coercive capital controls. In this reading, the rupiah’s depreciation and the negative rating outlook are market verdicts on a government that is prioritizing political objectives over financial prudence.
There is truth in that frame. The concerns about liquidity, transparency, and quasi-fiscal risk are not imaginary. Rating agencies and investors are responding to real changes in Indonesia’s policy mix.
But that frame is incomplete. It treats “market confidence” as an end in itself and assumes that the pre-existing model was neutral rather than structured around specific interests. It does not ask:
- Who benefited from the old arrangement of raw-material exports and external intermediation?
- How much of Indonesia’s resource wealth was captured domestically versus abroad?
- Whether “confidence” primarily reflects productive investment or short-term portfolio positioning?
- What strategic options a large Global South economy has when global financial conditions tighten and dollar liquidity becomes a weapon?
The Global South frame starts from a different baseline: Indonesia is trying to renegotiate the terms of its integration into the global economy. It is using state power to:
- Retain more foreign exchange from its own resources.
- Build domestic processing capacity.
- Reduce vulnerability to external interest-rate shocks and dollar cycles.
- Create institutional levers that can be used to pursue national development goals rather than only external approval.
In this view, the stress in financial markets is not simply evidence of policy error. It is also the friction that arises when a major resource exporter tries to shift value and control inward.
Both frames capture part of the reality. The investor frame correctly identifies financial risks. The sovereignty frame correctly identifies the strategic intent. The analytical task is to hold both at once.
The Real Pressure Point: Institutions, Not Slogans
Once you see that, the core issue becomes clearer.
Indonesia’s experiment is not primarily about whether resource nationalism is good or bad in principle. It is about whether the institutions built to enact that nationalism can:
- Operate with sufficient transparency to be credible.
- Distinguish between developmental projects and political spending.
- Manage risk without loading it silently onto state banks and the sovereign balance sheet.
- Ensure that the gains from downstreaming and retained foreign exchange flow beyond a narrow set of connected actors.
Danantara could, in principle, function as a serious investment vehicle that channels resource rents into productive capacity. It could also become a black box that accumulates hidden liabilities and directs credit to politically favored projects with low returns.
The export-proceeds regime could, in principle, strengthen Indonesia’s external position by ensuring that resource earnings are available for domestic use. It could also cripple exporters’ ability to operate, pushing activity into informal channels or prompting disinvestment.
The difference between those outcomes will not be decided by rhetoric about sovereignty. It will be decided by:
- Whether Danantara publishes audited, consolidated accounts and submits to real oversight.
- Whether state-owned banks are allowed to build large, unhedged exposures to political projects.
- Whether the export rules are calibrated to avoid widespread corporate distress.
- Whether the gains from downstreaming show up in jobs, regional development, and fiscal capacity, not just in balance-sheet consolidation.
Why This Matters Beyond Indonesia
This is not just an Indonesian story. It is a test case for a broader question in the multipolar order: how can resource-rich Global South states increase strategic autonomy without reproducing dependency in a new form?
If Indonesia succeeds in building transparent, capable institutions that convert resource wealth into domestic capacity, it will offer a model for other states seeking to:
- Reduce dollar dependence.
- Use local-currency settlement and bilateral swap lines more effectively.
- Capture more value from critical minerals, energy, and agricultural commodities.
- Navigate between Western and non-Western partners without being locked into either bloc.
If it fails — not because sovereignty is inherently wrong, but because the institutional design is opaque, politicized, or financially unsustainable — it will reinforce the orthodox view that any deviation from market orthodoxy leads inevitably to crisis.
The stakes are therefore not only financial. They are also about narrative control over what development paths are considered legitimate for the Global South.
The Defensible Conclusion
What can be said with reasonable confidence?
- Indonesia is not experiencing a simple economic collapse. Growth remains positive, inflation is controlled, and reserves, though lower, are still substantial.
- The country is undergoing a deliberate shift toward a more centralized, state-directed model that seeks greater control over resources, foreign exchange, and development finance.
- That shift has introduced new financial risks: corporate liquidity constraints, opaque state vehicles, and potential quasi-fiscal exposures in the banking system.
- The market’s negative reaction reflects real concerns, but it also reflects a particular set of interests and assumptions about how emerging economies should be governed.
- The long-term outcome will depend less on the idea of sovereignty and more on the quality of the institutions built to implement it.
The most defensible conclusion is not that Indonesia is “falling” or “rising.” It is that Indonesia is in a high-stakes transition where the balance between autonomy and vulnerability is being recalibrated.
Returning to the Currency Shock
Look again at the opening image: a currency under pressure, reserves down, a surprise rate hike, and at the same time an economy still growing at more than 5 percent.
Seen through the investor frame, that looks like a warning sign: fundamentals are being undermined by policy. Seen through the sovereignty frame, it looks like a temporary cost of restructuring a dependent economy.
Seen through a Global South strategic lens, it looks like something more precise: a stress test of whether a major resource exporter can convert political sovereignty into institutional capacity without creating new forms of financial fragility.
That is the story that matters. Not whether Indonesia is collapsing, but whether it can build institutions that make sovereignty sustainable.
For the informed observer, the lesson is clear. The next indicators to watch are not only exchange rates and rating actions. They are Danantara’s financial disclosures, the health of exporters under the new rules, and the distribution of gains from downstreaming across the real economy.
Those will tell you whether Indonesia is simply shifting risk from external markets to internal structures, or whether it is doing something more difficult: constructing a form of sovereignty that can endure.
