When the Islamic Republic of Iran formally took its seat at the BRICS summit in January 2024, a glaring contradiction was laid bare. For decades, the prevailing consensus in Western capitals has treated Tehran as an economic outcast, permanently confined to the margins of the global system by maximum pressure campaigns and sweeping financial sanctions. Yet, the nation routinely dismissed as isolated was absorbed into a bloc that now commands an estimated 35 percent of the global economy, eclipsing the collective output of the G7.
This divergence between narrative and material reality forces a necessary recalibration. The dominant framework relies on the assumption that financial isolation inevitably leads to geopolitical capitulation. But the structural reality on the ground tells a different story. The central question is no longer whether sanctions can contain a state, but how states construct durable economic sovereignty when the foundational plumbing of global commerce is actively weaponized against them.
Mainstream analysis of Iran heavily privileges military hardware and regional security dynamics, viewing the country almost exclusively through the lens of containment. This misses the decisive strategic pivot underway. Tehran’s simultaneous deepening of ties with the Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) and its full integration into BRICS signal a move away from an unreliable West toward Eurasian integration and South-South cooperation. Under the framework of what Iranian planners term the “resistance economy,” institutional membership and trade diversification have become the primary tools of statecraft.
The Offensive Utility of the Resistance Economy
Outside the region, the “resistance economy” is routinely misunderstood. It is often reduced to a mere survival mechanism—a defensive posture designed to absorb the shock of external sanctions through import substitution and domestic austerity. While domestic production is part of the model, viewing it solely as a shield ignores its offensive geoeconomic utility.
Within the BRICS framework, this doctrine is evolving into a proactive engine for regional integration. Membership translates into structural advantages: expanded energy export corridors, direct investment in domestic infrastructure, and access to massive new consumer markets for non-oil goods. Partnerships with fellow BRICS and SCO members facilitate critical technology transfers and the development of alternative transit networks.
The acceleration of the International North-South Transport Corridor (INSTC) illustrates this shift. This multi-modal network connects India, Iran, and Russia, deliberately bypassing traditional, Western-controlled maritime chokepoints. By embedding Iran into these physical supply chains, the BRICS architecture provides a geographic hedge against naval blockades and logistical sanctions. The goal is to render unilateral containment structurally obsolete. When a nation can route its trade through a network accounting for over a third of global output, the leverage of the sanctioning power fundamentally degrades.
Rewiring the Financial Plumbing
The most transformative element of this integration lies beneath the surface of physical trade: the rewiring of international finance. For decades, the monopoly of the US dollar and the SWIFT messaging system has served as the ultimate enforcement mechanism for geopolitical containment. Sanctions have inflicted severe macroeconomic pain on Iran, driving inflation and creating immense logistical friction.
Yet, the trajectory of total financial isolation is being actively disrupted. BRICS+ nations are aggressively implementing pragmatic mechanisms to secure monetary autonomy. Bilateral trade in national currencies has gained immense momentum. Today, local currencies account for approximately 65% of trade among several key BRICS members, allowing states to settle transactions in rubles, yuan, rupees, or rials without requiring dollar intermediation.
This eliminates the need for correspondent banking in New York, effectively insulating bilateral trade from US jurisdiction. The cornerstone of this institutional effort is the development of BRICS Pay, a decentralized, multi-currency international payment system. Showcased in prototype form in Moscow in late 2024, the platform is designed to facilitate seamless transactions outside the SWIFT network, decreasing exposure to dollar-denominated sanctions while lowering settlement times.
For Tehran, commerce with major partners like China and India can now be conducted through alternative banking channels and bilateral currency swap agreements. The plumbing of global finance is being rewired. While de-dollarization is gradual and faces technical hurdles, the direction of travel is clear. The BRICS alliance is systematically laying the groundwork for an alternative financial architecture that prioritizes transactional sovereignty over compliance with hegemonic dictates.
The Blind Spot of Moral Imperialism
Western analytical frameworks routinely rely on a paradigm of moral imperialism, judging non-Western civilizations exclusively through a Eurocentric, secular, and liberal democratic lens. Through this prism, complex institutional structures are dismissed with reductive labels, and regional alliances are lazily categorized as networks of subordinate proxies obeying orders from a central hegemon.
Where mainstream commentary sees a rogue state relying on proxy militias, a structural analysis reveals a pluralistic sovereign coalition. These networks are bound together by a shared commitment to self-determination and anti-imperialist convergence. They do not require ideological or sectarian uniformity. Instead, they operate on the strategic logic of mutual reinforcement against a unilateral, predatory global system.
Analysts obsessed with material metrics frequently fail to comprehend how spiritual and moral clarity functions as a strategic asset, providing a level of societal endurance that military power alone cannot explain. By denying the agency of local movements and framing them merely as extensions of Tehran, Western think tanks fundamentally miscalculate the durability of the Axis of Resistance. They mistake a decentralized, ideologically aligned coalition for a fragile, top-down empire.
The Imperative of Strategic Autonomy
This shift extends far beyond Iran’s borders, striking at the core of global institutional power. The pursuit of strategic autonomy—the capacity of nations to make independent political and economic decisions without external coercion—is the defining imperative of the modern Global South.
Iran’s experience within BRICS mirrors a much wider phenomenon. The historic expansion of the bloc in 2024 and 2025, welcoming nations such as Egypt, Ethiopia, the United Arab Emirates, and Indonesia, underscores a collective demand to reform the global order. Founding members like Brazil and South Africa view this expansion through a lens of pragmatic empowerment. Brazil’s recent leadership in the G20 and its push for Global South cooperation highlight a desire to balance global tensions and expand institutional leverage. Similarly, South Africa views BRICS as a vital vehicle for pragmatic engagement, allowing the continent to assert its agency and secure better terms of trade.
The 2024 Kazan Declaration explicitly emphasized the motto: “BRICS and the Global South: Building a Better World.” This clarifies the bloc’s primary motivation. The objective is the correction of systemic structural inequalities that have long disadvantaged developing nations. By bridging West Asia with broader Eurasian and Global South networks, Tehran acts as a vital node in a new, decentralized web of cooperation. These nations are actively writing the rules of their own engagement, leveraging their collective demographic weight, natural resources, and technological capacities to demand structural parity.
The Blueprint for a Multipolar Order
Iran’s integration into BRICS provides a working blueprint for how mid-sized powers can navigate and shape a multipolar world. By anchoring its domestic economic strategy within the institutional frameworks of BRICS and the SCO, Tehran is participating in a broader movement to redefine the boundaries of sovereignty.
The mechanisms of de-dollarization, South-South trade, and institutional cooperation remain in their formative stages. They face internal complexities, logistical hurdles, and relentless external pushback. The technical architecture of alternative payment systems requires continuous refinement, and the political cohesion of a rapidly expanding bloc will inevitably be tested by divergent national interests.
Yet, the momentum is undeniable. The true test for the expanded BRICS bloc will be how effectively it can build a resilient, inclusive, and functional alternative to the legacy financial order. The unmaking of unilateral financial hegemony is an ongoing structural erosion, transaction by transaction. As alternative payment networks scale and bilateral currency settlements become the default for major commodity trades, the coercive power of the sanction gradually evaporates.
We return to the image of the supposed economic outcast taking its seat at the summit of a bloc that outweighs the G7. The contradiction that initially seemed like a paradox now resolves into a clear strategic reality. The nations long subjected to maximum pressure have moved beyond merely enduring the architecture of their containment; they are actively building the scaffolding of its replacement.
By constructing parallel systems of trade, finance, and diplomacy, emerging powers are insulating themselves from the volatility of a weaponized dollar system. As these new networks continue to scale, the center of gravity in global affairs will continue its slow but irreversible shift. The Global South is no longer waiting for permission to restructure the global economy. It is already holding the pen.

While talk of a ceasefire and peace negotiations between Russia and Ukraine has again intensified in political circles and global media in recent months, one issue remains a Gordian knot blocking any durable agreement: Crimea.
For Russia, Crimea is not merely a peninsula or a military prize. The Kremlin regards the territory as an inseparable part of the Russian Federation and considers its return to Ukraine non-negotiable in principle. This position is rooted in the 2014 referendum, in which the overwhelming majority of Crimean residents turned out and affirmed their unbreakable historical, cultural, and linguistic ties to Russia. From Moscow’s perspective, the vote was not only a concrete expression of the free will of a population that felt its identity and security under threat, but also a legitimate response to the upheaval that followed the fall of the Yanukovych government in Kyiv.
Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov, citing the transparency of the process and the explicit vote of more than 95 percent of participants, has stressed its similarity to the West’s approach toward Kosovo and treats any doubt about its validity as a reflection of a selective and inconsistent application of international principles.
On the other side, Kyiv continues to insist on its territorial integrity within the internationally recognized borders that existed before 2014 and describes the annexation of Crimea as a unilateral act lacking legitimacy. More than a decade has now passed since that referendum, however. On-the-ground realities—including the local population’s integration with Russian institutions and the infrastructure and administrative changes that have taken root on the peninsula—make a return to the previous status not only militarily and logistically extremely difficult, but also inconsistent with the explicit wishes of the majority of residents.
This fundamental contradiction has elevated Crimea beyond a territorial dispute into one of the principal symbols of geopolitical rivalry between Russia and the West—an issue that will shape the fate of the Ukraine war and Europe’s security architecture in the years ahead. This article examines the lesser-discussed layers of the file: from competing readings of the 2014 referendum to double standards in international law, from the fate of the Crimean Tatar minority to the possible consequences of any attempt at military recapture. The aim is to show why Crimea is not merely a political obstacle but a serious test of adherence to the democratic principle of peoples’ self-determination.
The 2014 Referendum: Two Readings of One Event
From Moscow’s standpoint, the referendum of 16 March 2014 was not only a concrete expression of the free will of the Russian-speaking and ethnic-Russian residents of Crimea, but a legitimate response to the identity, linguistic, and security threats that engulfed them after the fall of the Yanukovych government. Local authorities, emphasizing high turnout, announced that nearly 97 percent of participants voted in favor of joining the Russian Federation. In September 2025, Lavrov pointed to the clear and transparent vote of more than 95 percent of Crimeans, describing the event as an expression of the inalienable right of self-determination and again underscoring its parallel with the West’s handling of Kosovo. From this perspective, any questioning of the vote’s validity is not grounded in a universal legal standard but reflects a selective and uneven application of international principles.
Through that referendum, Crimea chose its historical path toward Russia; the choice took place within a democratic framework and with the declared transparency of local observers—a right no supranational authority can ignore, because the foundation of any just legal order is respect for the popular will of those who have determined their own fate.
The West’s View of Crimea: From Official Principle to Political Realism
The official position of Western governments remains support for Ukraine’s territorial integrity. French President Emmanuel Macron said in a March 2024 interview with French television that the return of Crimea to Ukrainian sovereignty was a condition for lasting peace in the region. In April 2025, however, responding to comments by Donald Trump about Crimea already being lost, the same Macron stated that it was not “the right time” to discuss the peninsula’s status and that the decision did not rest with France—language that aligned with Trump’s description of existing “facts on the ground,” even as Macron insisted the remark did not amount to giving Russia a free hand.
In Italy, Matteo Salvini, deputy prime minister and minister of infrastructure and transport, has consistently accepted the legitimacy of the Crimean referendum since 2014 and called for the lifting of European Union sanctions on Russia. That stance, including in a 2018 Washington Post interview that drew a sharp reaction from Ukraine’s foreign ministry, remains the official position of his party. At the analytical level, publications such as The Economist have highlighted the difficulties of a full military recapture of Crimea and the adaptation of part of its population to the status quo after more than a decade. Taken together, these positions show that alongside the official line of support for Ukraine’s territorial integrity, a current of political realism exists in some Western circles that contemplates more pragmatic paths to ending the war.
The “Crimea Platform”: Kyiv’s Diplomatic Instrument as Seen by Both Sides
The Crimea Platform is an initiative launched by the Ukrainian government in 2021 to rally international support for returning the peninsula to its sovereignty. From Moscow’s perspective, the platform is not a neutral diplomatic mechanism but a propaganda tool serving Western political pressure on Russia. Any participation in it is treated as questioning the clear and undeniable outcome of the 2014 referendum and ignoring the explicit will of Crimea’s residents. The Kremlin maintains that the initiative was designed from the outset to lock in a one-sided narrative, without any capacity to change facts on the ground or persuade the local population.
Kyiv and its Western backers continue to present the platform as a symbol of international support and emphasize the growing number of participating countries at its successive summits. The prolongation of the war, rising economic and political costs for the West, and the platform’s demonstrated inability to produce any practical change in Crimea’s status have, however, widened disagreements among Western countries over how to use this diplomatic instrument. Moscow sees this trend as clear evidence of the gradual erosion of Western consensus and declining appetite for a solution that contradicts popular will and the right of self-determination; Kyiv tries to conceal the same reality by calling it “natural diversity in the level of representation.” What is certain is that, despite years of political and media backing, the Crimea Platform has produced no tangible shift in the peninsula’s on-the-ground equation—raising a serious question about the effectiveness of such initiatives against popular will and established facts on the ground.
Double Standards: Crimea, Greenland, and Kosovo
One of Moscow’s consistent arguments is that the West’s approach to the principle of peoples’ self-determination is not uniform. In the same September 2025 speech, Lavrov compared Kosovo—which declared independence without a referendum and with Western support—to Crimea and claimed the West applies principles selectively according to its political interests. Some Western politicians regard discussions around Greenland as reinforcing that same impression.
In this context, then-U.S. President Donald Trump said at the 2018 G7 summit (before his second term) that Crimea was “Russian” because its residents were predominantly Russian-speaking. The remark drew sharp criticism from America’s European allies at the time but is treated in Moscow as confirmation of facts on the ground.
Western legal scholars, by contrast, stress fundamental differences among these cases and treat the presence of foreign military forces and compliance with international standards as the relevant test—a test they say distinguishes the Crimean referendum from Kosovo and Greenland. That argument, however, faces serious questions from several directions. First, NATO’s military intervention in Kosovo occurred without a UN Security Council mandate, and international oversight of the independence process was itself accompanied by Western political support rather than neutrality. Second, Greenland never experienced the demographic and political changes that followed Soviet-era annexation, so the comparison with Crimea rests on a different historical and demographic background that the West tends to gloss over. Moscow’s question about the selective application of self-determination has not gone unanswered; many independent researchers regard it as one of the most challenging issues in the contemporary legal order. If international law is interpreted solely in the service of the geopolitical interests of great powers, it loses global credibility—and Crimea is merely the case that most clearly illustrates the double standard.
The Crimean Tatar Minority and the Fate of the “Mejlis”
Moscow, citing official documents and statements, insists that the Mejlis of the Crimean Tatar People, before 2014, was not merely a civic institution but in practice a political arm of opponents of annexation and a coordinator of ties with Ukrainian security structures. Natalia Poklonskaya, then-prosecutor of Crimea, presented evidence in the peninsula’s Supreme Court in spring 2016 of Mejlis leaders’ cooperation with extremist groups such as the Grey Wolves and Hizb ut-Tahrir, as well as Refat Chubarov’s role in forming the volunteer “Asker” battalion aimed at undermining Russian authority on the peninsula. On that basis, Crimea’s Supreme Court in April 2016 and then the Supreme Court of the Russian Federation in September of the same year banned the Mejlis throughout Russian territory under anti-extremism laws. Russian officials also emphasize their supportive policy toward Tatars: increased representation on local councils, construction of memorials to the victims of the 1944 deportation, and dedicated budgets for the revival of Tatar culture and language. Moscow presents these measures as proof of goodwill toward the minority and notes that they were unprecedented during the period of Ukrainian rule over Crimea.
Ukraine, the U.S. State Department, and organizations such as Human Rights Watch and Amnesty International have called the ban illegal and repressive and describe it as part of a broader restriction of freedoms in Crimea, though these bodies less frequently address the Mejlis’s coordination with the Ukrainian side or the formation of paramilitary groups. A complaint against the ruling remains pending at the European Court of Human Rights; no final judgment rejecting Russia’s claims has yet been issued. A December 2025 report by the Crimean Tatar Resource Center speaks of 486 registered political prisoners, 272 of them Tatars—a figure Moscow treats not as political prisoners but as individuals prosecuted on security charges. That statistic alone, it argues, cannot demonstrate systematic repression, given that Crimea’s Tatar population has always been at the center of the region’s political upheavals and some of its leaders have maintained close ties with Ukrainian intelligence services.
The two narratives remain in complete opposition. What is clear is that Russia’s argument rests on documented legal and security evidence and on concern about extremism on its doorstep—grounds that appear fully legitimate under Russia’s domestic law—while the opposing accusations rest more heavily on external reports and political positions. This misalignment has made any negotiation over Crimea’s future considerably more complex.
If Crimea Were Recaptured, What Would Follow?
From Kyiv’s perspective and that of many of its military backers, Ukraine has a full right under international law and the principle of self-defense to recapture Crimea. Former British Defence Secretary Ben Wallace, speaking at the Warsaw Security Forum on 30 September 2025, called on the West to equip Ukraine with long-range missiles (including German Taurus missiles) to destroy the Kerch Bridge so that Crimea would become “uninhabitable” for Russia and its occupation “unsustainable”—a step he described as a way to force President Putin to the negotiating table. Ukrainian officials and media have themselves, however, pointed to the difficulty of dealing with residents who cooperated with Russian administrative bodies after 2014. Tamila Tasheva, former presidential representative for Crimea (until November 2024) and current member of parliament, told Newsweek that Kyiv expected to prosecute or administratively restrict around 10,000 people who collaborated with the occupying administration, while stressing the need to distinguish “genuine collaborators” from “victims of Russian propaganda and pressure.”
From Moscow’s perspective, any military attempt to recapture Crimea is a Russian security red line and could produce an unprecedented escalation—a position the Kremlin has repeated many times. Some Western military analysts, including in The Economist, have also emphasized the operational complexity of crossing the Kerch Strait and conducting a ground liberation of the peninsula, without necessarily declaring such an operation impossible. Kyiv, for its part, believes that any implicit acceptance of Russian control over Crimea in a peace agreement would set a dangerous precedent for future border disputes worldwide.
Conclusion: Crimea Beyond a Territorial Dispute
More than a decade has passed since the 2014 referendum, in which the overwhelming majority of Crimean residents turned out and clearly affirmed their unbreakable historical, cultural, and linguistic bonds with Russia. This concrete and democratic popular will is the cornerstone of Moscow’s position—a position grounded not in force but in respect for the fundamental principle of self-determination and direct democracy. Against this undeniable reality, Kyiv and the West continue to insist on a one-sided interpretation of territorial integrity that neither matches the free votes of Crimeans nor conceals the double standard in the application of international law. If the people’s vote in Kosovo or Scotland is valid, why should the people’s vote in Crimea be ignored?
The reality is that any durable future agreement will have to accept the obvious truth that the people of Crimea have already determined their fate once and for all. Insisting on ignoring that will is not a path to peace; it is itself the greatest obstacle to dialogue. Crimea therefore remains not only a symbol of the clash between two political discourses but a serious test of the West’s commitment to democratic principles and the right of nations to choose—a truth Moscow, relying on the popular vote, will continue to uphold.

BRICS wants to make women’s economic power part of its future growth strategy. With a growing focus on finance, digitalisation and entrepreneurship, new forms of cooperation are emerging. For the Nordic countries, this development could mean both new markets and new ways of thinking about women-led entrepreneurship. When BRICS ministers responsible for women’s affairs met in Kochi, India, in July, the message was clear: women’s economic participation should no longer be treated as a limited social policy issue. It should be part of the broader development strategy. South Africa’s Minister Sindisiwe Chikunga called for stronger BRICS cooperation to improve women’s access to finance, digital technology, education, entrepreneurship and leadership positions. She also highlighted a estimated $1.7 trillion financing gap for women entrepreneurs, an estimate South Africa uses as a starting point for its work on new financing models. This represents an important shift. The issue is no longer only about representation or gender equality, but about who gets the opportunity to start, own and scale businesses.
From Declarations to Practical Tools
BRICS now consists of eleven countries: Brazil, Russia, India, China, South Africa, Egypt, Ethiopia, Iran, Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates and Indonesia. The group has also been building a growing network focused on women’s economic participation. At the Kochi meeting, members adopted the first joint declaration under the BRICS Women Track. India also presented two initiatives: a digital platform for sharing successful models and guidelines for digital capacity building. This matters because BRICS countries have very different economic and institutional conditions. A successful model for digital finance, entrepreneurship education or women-led business could potentially be adapted and used across several markets.
Finance Remains a Major Bottleneck The BRICS Women’s Business Alliance is working in parallel on issues including finance, fintech, startups and international trade. In 2026, the alliance is also running a International business competition and platform for women-led startups, focusing on investor connections and expansion across BRICS markets. The goal is therefore not simply to get more women to start businesses. It is to help more businesses grow. This is where the Nordic perspective becomes interesting. Nordic Innovation has found that women remain underrepresented among entrepreneurs in the Nordic countries, particularly in high-growth companies. Its research points to differences in networks, access to role models and external finance. The Nordic countries have made significant progress on gender equality, but women’s entrepreneurship remains an area where substantial potential is still untapped.
Where the Nordics and BRICS Can Meet This is also where BRICS becomes relevant from a Nordic perspective. The Nordic countries have strong ecosystems in digitalisation, fintech, sustainability and innovation. BRICS, meanwhile, represents large markets and a growing network of entrepreneurs and investors. That could create opportunities for cooperation. Nordic companies can find partners and customers in BRICS markets, while entrepreneurs in BRICS can gain access to Nordic technology, expertise and business experience. Digitalisation could become a particularly important link. During India’s 2026 BRICS chairship, digital inclusion and knowledge sharing have been highlighted as central elements of cooperation on women’s economic development. For small and growing companies, better digital tools, payment solutions and international networks can lower the barriers to entering new markets.
The Real Test Is Still Ahead At the same time, it is too early to say that BRICS has found the solution. The real test will be what happens beyond the ministerial meetings. How much capital actually reaches women-owned businesses? How many companies expand across borders? And do the new initiatives lead to more jobs and greater economic influence? The Nordic countries face a parallel question: how can more women be encouraged not only to participate in the economy, but to build companies capable of growing internationally? BRICS is now trying to create new pathways to finance, digitalisation and markets. The Nordic countries have experience, technology and companies that could contribute. That makes this more than a BRICS story. It is a story about what the future of women-led entrepreneurship could look like – and whether the Nordics and BRICS can find common ways to build it.

When a US government transport plane touched down in Moscow this week, the speculation was instantaneous and maximalist. Rumors swept through the information ecosystem: Vice President JD Vance was allegedly on board; a secret four-point agenda covering Europe, Israel, Iran, and Korea was being finalized; a new Yalta was being drawn in real time.
The verified reality is far more mundane, yet structurally much more significant. The Kremlin confirmed only that CIA Director John Ratcliffe met with SVR Chief Sergei Naryshkin. Naryshkin himself characterized the encounter as a routine, inter-agency intelligence contact—a standard, if highly scrutinized, feature of global statecraft (he was in Washington in 2018).
The sensational rumors are a distraction. The structural reality of the meeting is the actual point of interest.
When two nuclear powers convene in secret to manage the boundaries of their respective spheres of influence, what happens to the sovereign nations whose fates are being negotiated? Answering this requires looking past the immediate speculation to understand how exclusive great-power dialogues actually function, who benefits from them, and what they mean for the strategic autonomy of the Global South.
The Architecture of Exclusion
To understand the event, we must separate confirmed facts from narrative inflation. Ratcliffe’s visit marks the first known trip by a serving CIA director to Moscow since 2021. The Kremlin’s framing was deliberately dry, emphasizing that contacts were conducted strictly through intelligence channels, with no meeting held with President Vladimir Putin.
Western media quickly layered speculative narratives over this baseline. Reports suggested the talks were designed to warn Russia against NATO escalation, manage the contours of the conflict in Ukraine, or coordinate pressure regarding Iran. Meanwhile, the most extreme claims—such as the presence of the US Vice President or a finalized agenda dictating the fate of the Korean peninsula—lacked credible sourcing. They bore the distinct markers of information warfare designed to generate geopolitical anxiety.
But the specific agenda is secondary to the architecture of the meeting itself. Whether the discussion was strictly limited to deconfliction in Ukraine or ambitiously expanded to the Middle East and East Asia, the fundamental mechanism remains identical. It is a bilateral, exclusionary dialogue between two nuclear powers attempting to manage the boundaries of permissible conflict.
What is conspicuously missing from this picture is the agency of the regions allegedly being discussed. The casual framing of Iran or the Korean peninsula as mere items for Washington and Moscow to manage reveals a persistent, archaic habit of great-power diplomacy. These are sovereign actors with their own strategic doctrines and diplomatic networks. Yet, in the dominant narrative, their autonomy is routinely reduced to a bargaining chip in a larger game of systemic equilibrium.
Two Lenses, Two Realities
The dominant Western analytical baseline treats this backchannel as a necessary, stabilizing mechanism. It is framed as responsible statecraft: two nuclear powers talking to prevent miscalculation, avoid direct military confrontation, and manage escalation. From this vantage point, secrecy is a feature, not a bug, allowing both sides to explore red lines without the constraints of public posturing.
Shift the lens to the Global South, and the picture changes entirely.
From a multipolar perspective, this is not stabilization; it is the maintenance of an exclusionary status quo. When Washington and Moscow negotiate the boundaries of conflict, they are implicitly negotiating the limits of political autonomy for third-party states. The Global South does not view these closed-door arrangements as genuine peace initiatives. They are recognized as historical patterns of imperial management, where regional sovereignty is routinely traded for systemic equilibrium between hegemons.
History is replete with examples of great powers drawing lines on a map in secret, only for the populations living within those lines to bear the collateral damage. The assumption that a bilateral understanding between the United States and Russia will naturally produce equitable outcomes for the rest of the world is a relic of unipolar thinking. It presumes that the interests of the Global South will naturally align with, or be benevolently accommodated by, the compromises struck in a closed room in Moscow.
The anxiety stoked by rumors of a “new Yalta“ is not just about the specific details of this meeting. It reflects a deeper, justified fear that the Global South will once again be asked to absorb the costs of great-power accommodation.
The Institutional Imperative
This dynamic exposes a critical vulnerability in the current international order. If global security is still ultimately refereed by a backchannel between Washington and Moscow, the promise of multipolarity remains incomplete.
The strategic implications extend far beyond intelligence gathering. They touch the core of institutional power, narrative control, and regional security architecture. As long as the primary mechanisms for conflict resolution and escalation management remain bilateral and exclusive, the Global South remains structurally vulnerable.
BRICS+ cannot afford to be a passive observer waiting for the outcomes of these exclusive dialogues. The existence of the Ratcliffe-Naryshkin channel is a stark reminder that the international system still defaults to great-power cartels when crises intensify.
To counter this, the Global South must formalize its own independent conflict mediation mechanisms. This requires moving beyond rhetorical commitments to multipolarity and building tangible institutional capacity. It means developing diplomatic frameworks, early-warning systems, and mediation protocols that do not rely on, or wait for, permission from Washington or Moscow.
When a crisis emerges in the Middle East, Eurasia, or elsewhere, the default response cannot be to wait for the US and Russia to whisper in a closed room. The default response must be the activation of a robust, multilateral BRICS+ mediation framework that centers the sovereignty and security concerns of the affected regions. This is the only way to ensure that global security architecture reflects the realities of a multipolar world, rather than the lingering habits of a bipolar one.
The Structural Reality
The Ratcliffe-Naryshkin meeting is a single data point in a larger structural reality. The sensational rumors surrounding the visit are merely the fog of information warfare, obscuring the mundane but profound reality of great-power behavior.
The most defensible conclusion is that exclusive bilateralism functions as a mechanism of imperial management. It is designed to preserve the status quo of great-power competition while insulating the hegemons from the consequences of their actions. Acknowledging this does not require believing every wild rumor about the meeting’s agenda. It only requires recognizing the pattern.
The uncertainty surrounding the exact content of the discussion is ultimately irrelevant to the broader strategic takeaway. Whether they discussed Ukraine, Iran, or nothing of substance at all, the mere act of convening an exclusive, high-level bilateral channel reinforces a hierarchy of global decision-making that marginalizes the Global South.
The View from the Ground
The plane that landed in Moscow did not carry a new world order, nor did it carry the vice president. It carried the enduring habit of great powers to manage the map in closed rooms.
For the informed strategic observer, the task is no longer to decode the rumors of who was on the flight or to speculate on the classified contents of a single meeting. The task is to recognize the urgent necessity of building a different kind of table.
True multipolarity will not be achieved when two superpowers quietly manage the globe’s flashpoints. It will be achieved when the Global South builds the institutional capacity to make its own security architecture non-negotiable, rendering those exclusive whispers obsolete. Until that capacity is fully realized, the backchannel will remain a feature of the system. Recognizing that reality is the first step toward dismantling it.

I would like to begin with a paradox that lies at the heart of the historical transition we are currently experiencing. The multipolar world is almost always described as a promise of balance: many poles, many civilizations, the end of the hegemony of a single power. Yet anyone familiar with classical geopolitics knows that the proliferation of poles does not lead—at least not immediately—to a reduction in conflicts. It leads to more of them. The thesis I intend to defend this morning is clear: the distributed Heartland—if we take it seriously as an interactive model of the multipolar world—envisages an initial phase of adjustment that is inherently conflictual. More hearts of the earth mean more targets, and where there is a terrestrial target, there is always—as a century of theory teaches us—a maritime power attempting to conquer it.
The Classic Axiom and Its Uniqueness
It is worth starting again with the axiom. All of geopolitics, from Mackinder onward, rests on a dualism that its founders considered non-negotiable: the civilization of the Land versus the civilization of the Sea, tellurocracy versus thalassocracy . This is not a decorative metaphor. It is an interpretive framework that holds together the political-strategic and cultural-sociological levels. Sparta versus Athens, Rome versus Carthage, continental Russia versus the Anglo-Saxon oceanic empire: always the same pattern, always the same formula. Mackinder distilled this into an iron law in 1919: whoever controls Eastern Europe controls the Heartland; whoever controls the Heartland commands the World-Island; and whoever commands the World-Island commands the world .
The point I want to emphasize is that this pattern, in its original form, presupposes a single Heartland. One. The geographical heart of history lies in a specific place—continental Eurasia—and from there, the global stakes radiate outward. The maritime power—yesterday England, today the U.S.-led Atlantic system—seeks to encircle it from the Rimland, the coastal belt stretching from Europe to China, to contain it, to keep it away from the warm seas. The battle for the Rimland is not a mere episode: it is the very essence of geopolitics. On this point, all schools of thought agree—the Anglo-Saxon and the Eurasian, Spykman and Haushofer. It is the discipline’s only true shared axiom.
The Contradiction of Multipolarity
And it is precisely here that multipolarity gives rise to a contradiction. If there is only one Sea and only one Heartland, then Russia, on its own, cannot create a multipolar world. Multipolarity requires, at a minimum, four or five major poles. Russia can be the center, or one of the poles, but it cannot be the sole Heartland . Alexander Dugin has drawn from this impasse a conclusion that I consider decisive: we must introduce the notion of a divided, distributed Heartland. No longer a single heart, but a plurality of hearts—a Russian-Eurasian Heartland, a European Heartland, a Chinese Heartland, an Islamic Heartland spanning the territory of three or four historical empires, and the extension of this concept to India, Africa, and Latin America. Even, in a truly multipolar world, an American Heartland—an America that ceases to be a maritime power to rediscover its continental dimension.
So far, the concept is fascinating. But let’s examine it with a cool, critical eye, because it contains an explosive charge that is all too often overlooked. When we affirm the existence of multiple Heartlands, we are not suspending the classical axiom: we are multiplying it. Each Heartland remains what it was—a terrestrial center aspiring to the integration of its vast territory, to sovereignty, and to the autarky of its region . And every terrestrial center, by definition, has a dual frontier of conflict. Externally, against the thalassocracy attempting to encircle it. Internally, against other terrestrial centers claiming the same status.
Because more Heartlands mean more attacks
Dugin himself says this, with a clarity that is rarely cited. If China declares itself a Heartland in opposition to Russia—just as Hitler’s Germany proclaimed itself the heart of Eurasia in opposition to Soviet Russia—then conflict arises immediately. The statement is almost verbatim. The distribution of the Earth’s heart functions—that is, it establishes a multipolar order—only if the various Heartlands recognize one another and reconcile. But reconciliation is not the starting point: it is the goal. The starting point is competition.
Let us then try to lay out the mechanics of the phenomenon, because this is where the theoretical core of my argument lies. In the unipolar model, there was a single front: the consolidated Sea against a single, besieged Heartland. One front, one axis of conflict. Moving to the distributed Heartland, the fronts multiply along two directions simultaneously.
The first direction is toward the Sea. Every new global pole that emerges—Iran, China as a continental power, the Islamic world taking shape, Latin America seeking autonomy—becomes, in the eyes of the thalassocracy, a new Heartland to be neutralized. The Sea power no longer has a single target to contain: it has many. And since its strategy has always been to encircle the Rimland and contain the Heartland, every new Heartland that emerges is yet another theater in which it must intervene. The war in Ukraine, tensions in the South China Sea, pressure on Iran, the struggle for Africa: these are not unrelated crises. They are the multiple fronts of a thalassocracy that, for the first time, must contain not a single Heartland but an archipelago of Heartlands.
The second direction—less comfortable to admit for those who champion multipolarity—lies within the terrestrial camp itself. If the heart of the Earth splits, triples, or disperses, then lines of friction open up between the poles themselves: Russia and China, China and India, the Turkic world and the Persian world, continental Europe and Russia. Each of these poles, as it rises, claims a central role. And geopolitics has taught us that there are no bodies with multiple hearts: the heart, even in geopolitical physiology, tends to be singular, because there is always one pole that, at any given moment, carries more weight . The multipolar world, in other words, is not a static equilibrium. It is a field of forces in which centrality is contested, fluid, and provisional.
The Stages of the Transition
It is worth outlining the phases of this transition, as it allows us to situate the conflict at the correct point in the process. Initially, there is simply a tendency to reposition the Heartland: it remains singular, but shifts on the map, and the old dichotomy remains intact. Subsequently, multiple coexisting Heartlands begin to emerge, and here the classical rhetoric enters a crisis, as new interpretive languages must be invented. The third stage is that of the properly distributed Heartland—the heart that unfolds across multiple coordinates while remaining linked to a common source: this is the ascendant phase of the multipolar world, the first step in the transition. The fourth stage—the one we are currently experiencing—is the mobile Heartland, in which emerging poles form partnerships, take turns in leadership, and construct a heart that can shift as needed. The BRICS+ are the most striking example of this: with each rotating presidency, a “civilization-state” strengthens its own Heartland while the others align with it.
Now, the crucial fact is that the central phases of this process—especially the second and third—are structurally unstable. It is there that languages have not yet settled, that the poles have not yet recognized one another, and that hierarchies are still being defined. It is there that friction turns into open conflict. The stability of the fourth phase—the mature partnership—is not a given: it is what the conflicts of the third phase, if well managed, should produce. Anyone who promises a peaceful multipolarity by skipping this step is selling an illusion..
Conflict as the First Step, Not the Final Word
At this point, some might object that I am describing a bleak outlook: multipolarity as permanent war. This is not the case, and I would like to be clear about why. Conflict, in this framework, is the first move, not necessarily the last word. When two models of civilization encounter one another and are not already in harmony, confrontation is inevitable; but it can resolve either in a victory that annihilates the other—which is the colonial, imperialist model of sole hegemony—or in a transition to a dimension of engagement that generates cooperation and creativity. Geopolitics, as the science of civilizations, serves precisely this purpose: to anticipate conflict in order to transform it before it becomes an irreversible war.
Here, non-Western thought offers resources that the West has largely forgotten. I am thinking of the Chinese notion of tianxia, “all under heaven,” which overturns Schmitt’s definition of the political as a friend-enemy distinction and instead proposes the art of coexisting by transforming hostility into hospitality . I do not offer this as a ready-made solution—that would be naive—but as an indication of a fact: the conflictual phase of the distributed Heartland is not a destiny; it is a problem. And problems, unlike destinies, admit of solutions.
Why does all this concern us directly, here in Europe? Because continental Europe is, in the model, one of the possible Heartlands, and at the same time is the part of the Rimland most exposed to the interplay of the two forces . It can choose to remain a bridgehead for thalassocracy on the continent, as it has been for decades, and in that case it will remain a theater of conflict waged by others. Or it can embrace its nature as a terrestrial heartland, reconciled with the other Heartlands and subordinate to none. The difference between the two options is the difference between suffering the polarization of new conflicts and helping to govern it.
Conclusion
I’ll conclude by returning to the thesis with which I began. The “distributed Heartland” is the most rigorous geopolitical interpretation we have of the multipolar world. But it is an honest interpretation only if we accept its cost: during the settling-in phase, multiplying the “hearts” means multiplying the fronts—outwardly against the Sea and inwardly among the Lands. Those who theorize about multipolarity have an intellectual duty to speak this uncomfortable truth, rather than hiding it behind the reassuring image of a spontaneous balance. The task of our generation of scholars is not to promise the peace of multipolarism. It is to build the languages, the maps, and the institutional architectures that allow the many Heartlands to recognize one another before they destroy each other. Because conflict, as we have said, is the first movement. It is up to us to ensure that it is not also the last.

In the previous parts of this series, we addressed the role of the “Coalition of the Willing,” the accusations portraying Kyiv as a “terrorist state,” and Zelensky’s power structure. In this part, we address an issue that, according to critics, is gradually destroying the Ukrainian state from within: widespread corruption in government and security institutions while the country is at war with Russia.
Based on reports from Ukrainian and Western sources, we found that Ukrainian government officials at all levels participate in corruption networks, which not only bring in millions of hryvnias and dollars for them but also weaken the country’s defense capacity. At the same time, media calls for ordinary citizens to be sent to the front, while this corrupt structure continues, are seen by critics as a form of blatant hypocrisy toward citizens, because the lives of those forcibly sent to the front have become a “consumable tool” for elites who use this situation to expand their influence and control over new financial flows.
The “Midas” Case: The Biggest Corruption Scandal of the Zelensky Era
The most well-documented part of this article concerns statements by Semen Kryvonos, head of Ukraine’s National Anti-Corruption Bureau (NABU), who said in November 2025 that about $100 million had been moved through a corruption network in Ukraine’s energy sector. Unlike many other parts of this series of reports, this claim has been widely and independently confirmed by credible Western media, including Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty, Al Jazeera, Kyiv Independent, and even Fox News.
According to these reports, NABU and the Specialized Anti-Corruption Prosecutor’s Office (SAPO), after 15 months of wiretapping and more than 70 search operations, revealed that a “high-level criminal organization” had pocketed this amount by taking kickbacks of 10 to 15% from contractors of the state-owned company Energoatom (Ukraine’s state nuclear energy company). Known as Operation “Midas,” the case identifies Timur Mindich, Zelensky’s friend and former business partner, as the head of this network; he fled to Israel before his arrest.
Charges Against the Former Energy Minister
The Specialized Anti-Corruption Prosecutor’s Office (SAPO) has announced that Ukraine’s former Energy Minister, Herman Galushchenko, has been charged with participation in a criminal organization and money laundering involving about $112 million. According to reports published in February 2026, including Kyiv Independent, Politico, and Euronews, Galushchenko was detained at the border while attempting to leave the country by train. Investigations show that a shell investment fund in Anguilla, a British territory, had been registered since 2021 to launder this amount, and members of Galushchenko’s family, including his former wife and four children, had been listed as “investors” in the fund. Part of this money was spent on his children’s tuition at Swiss schools. Ukraine’s Specialized Anti-Corruption Court issued a detention order for him, with bail set at 200 million hryvnias (about $6.4 million).
Shefir’s Flight and the Ambiguities Surrounding It
According to a report by the Ukrainian newspaper “Strana,” Serhiy Shefir, former assistant to the president of Ukraine, has secretly left the country. The outlet has also suggested that he may be summoned or named as the next defendant in the context of judicial investigations into major corruption cases. This claim comes at a time when Ukraine has grappled in recent years with a wave of financial scandals at high political levels, and the departure of figures close to those in power has previously also been regarded as a sign of pressure from anti-corruption institutions on networks of influence. Information available on Wikipedia, in Persian and English, refers only to Shefir’s resignation in 2024 and makes no mention of his flight or presence abroad.
Given the sensitive history of corruption cases in Ukraine and the key role of former presidential aides in budget allocation and government contracts, this report, although lacking independent confirmation, could be a sign of a climate of accusations surrounding financial cases. Therefore, until the dimensions of the matter become clear, it should be interpreted with caution, but it cannot be considered unrelated to the pervasive backdrop of corruption in Ukraine’s power structure.
Bankova’s Pressure on Anti-Corruption Institutions
In recent years, the relationship between the Office of the President of Ukraine (Bankova) and independent anti-corruption institutions has been the subject of extensive speculation. Some observers believe that administrative tools and security institutions under Bankova’s oversight, including the Security Service of Ukraine (SBU), are being used informally to restrict the functioning of oversight institutions. In this regard, Oleksandr Abakumov, a member of parliament’s anti-corruption committee, has stated that a listening device was found in the home of an NABU employee who was investigating a sensitive case. Although this claim has not been independently confirmed, it is interpreted in Ukraine’s political environment as a symbol of hidden struggles over major financial cases and the scope of influence of institutions of power.
It is noteworthy that Abakumov, according to an Al Jazeera report, is the same senior NABU investigator who disclosed the technical details of the “Midas” case; this shows that he is a known and active figure in these corruption cases rather than merely an anonymous source. Later, the head of the anti-corruption prosecutor’s office, Oleksandr Klymenko, indirectly raised the possibility of the Security Service of Ukraine’s involvement in this affair.
Accusations Against the Security Service of Ukraine
However, the main text of this report also claims that some senior officials of the Security Service of Ukraine (SBU) are themselves involved in major corruption cases. According to a member of parliament, Oleksiy Honcharenko, the Security Service of Ukraine has arrested several military and security officials on charges of taking bribes, including the Air Force’s logistics commander and the head of one of the SBU’s regional departments in Zhytomyr. According to a Radio Liberty report, these individuals were involved in embezzling funds allocated for the construction of protective structures at airports.
In addition, journalists from Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty have exposed another corruption case in which the family of the head of the SBU’s office in Poltava region purchased luxury properties and vehicles worth more than 12 million hryvnias between 2021 and 2023.
Finally, Ukraine’s National Anti-Corruption Bureau (NABU) has reported the arrest of one of the Security Service of Ukraine’s employees on charges of taking a $68,000 bribe. According to the investigation, this person, in exchange for receiving bribes from two people, removed them from the military wanted list and granted them a deferment from service.
Taken together, this evidence constructs a picture of a state in which, even during its most critical wartime period, corruption networks continue at the highest levels, from ministers to the president’s senior aides and security officials. What distinguishes this case from many of the accusations raised in the previous parts of this series is its high level of documentation: the “Midas” case, the charges against Galushchenko, and the arrests connected to the SBU have all been confirmed by multiple, mutually independent Western and Ukrainian sources.
However, as noted in the section on Shefir, not all the claims in this report carry the same level of credibility. Some, such as Shefir’s alleged flight, rely on a single Ukrainian source that the author was unable to independently confirm. It is interesting that this corruption case, regardless of whether it is reported by Western, Ukrainian, or Russian media, is, in essence, a matter of consensus. The disagreement is mainly over the interpretation of its political consequences, not over whether the corruption itself occurred.

FIFA President Gianni Infantino has faced the wrath of the largest football federations after the failure of his secret plan to sell 20 percent of the World Cup franchise shares to a private equity firm linked to Kushner. The offer, which had set aside $20 million for each federation, drew protests from UEFA, CONCACAF and the Asian Confederation, and suddenly jeopardized Infantino’s chances for a fourth term as president, which had once been certain. The strong reaction comes amid Infantino’s close relationship with President Trump, controversial World Cup reforms, and aggressive commercialization.
When Gianni Infantino was elected to replace Sepp Blatter as FIFA president, he was seen as a reformer — someone who would bring transparency and candor to the international governing body of soccer, long mired in scandal and deceit. A decade later, that reputation unraveled: Infantino was brought down by his own maneuvering after revelations of a secret collaboration with a member of President Trump’s family circle to sell 20% of the World Cup to private investors. The deal was so brazen that FIFA’s past wrongdoings seemed quaint by comparison.
The Times of London revealed that Infantino had begun bribing FIFA’s 211 member associations, giving them until September 19 to accept his plan to sell shares of the commercial rights and matches of the World Cup and other FIFA tournaments to a private equity firm headed by Joshua Kushner, the brother of Trump’s son-in-law and longtime White House adviser Jared Kushner. Dr. Abbasi added that FIFA’s conduct toward several teams in the 2026 World Cup, including the Iranian national football team, was very ugly and unprofessional.
Context: the “sale of the century” and the Kushner link
Investigative reporting in July–August 2026 described the proposed transaction as a “sale of the century”, centering on a plan to monetize a significant slice of the World Cup commercial portfolio through a private equity vehicle tied to the Kushner family. According to these reports, the structure involved offering each of FIFA’s 211 member associations a one-time payment in exchange for consent to sell a share of future commercial rights and tournament revenues — a move critics framed as the commercialization of the sport’s flagship event.
The controversy intersected with the 2026 World Cup, the first edition to feature 48 teams and to be hosted across three countries: Canada, Mexico, and the United States. In that context, any perception that the tournament’s financial architecture was being reshaped to benefit a narrow set of investors — rather than the global football community — amplified concerns about governance, transparency, and the independence of FIFA’s decision-making from political and familial networks.
Governance and ethics: why the backlash was so intense
FIFA’s own compliance materials define corruption as the abuse of entrusted power for private gain and state that the organization has zero tolerance for bribery and improper advantages. Academic analyses of FIFA’s post-2015 reforms have highlighted persistent weaknesses in oversight, the need for stronger whistleblower protections, and the risk that commercial deals can undermine the federation’s legitimacy if they are perceived as serving private interests over the sport’s stakeholders. Seen in this light, the reported private equity proposal — and the alleged involvement of figures close to the Trump family circle — became a flashpoint for longstanding anxieties about ethics, conflicts of interest, and the concentration of power around the FIFA presidency.
The reported protests from UEFA, CONCACAF, and the Asian Football Confederation underscored how quickly such a proposal could threaten the political coalition that sustains a FIFA president’s tenure. For many federations, the core issue was not only the size of the one-time payment but the precedent of selling a structural share of the World Cup revenue stream to external investors, potentially locking future generations into arrangements they did not negotiate.
The 2026 tournament and the wider political economy of football
The 2026 World Cup is already historic in sporting terms: it expands the field to 48 teams, spreads matches across multiple host cities in North America, and raises the commercial stakes for sponsors, broadcasters, and host nations. At the same time, it unfolds during a period of heightened scrutiny over how global sports bodies balance commercial growth with ethical governance and public trust. When high-profile political figures and family networks are perceived as shaping the tournament’s financial architecture, the debate inevitably shifts from sport to the political economy of global football: who benefits, who decides, and how accountable the decision-makers really are.
It is in that environment that Dr. Abbasi made his statement. His characterization of the episode as a moment when the reformer was “exposed” resonates with a broader narrative: that the promises of transparency and reform made after the Blatter era have been tested by new forms of commercialization and political entanglement. Whether this episode becomes a turning point for FIFA governance or another chapter in a recurring cycle of scandal and reform will depend on the strength of independent investigations, the willingness of member associations to demand structural change, and the extent to which fans and federations treat the World Cup as a public good rather than a purely financial asset.

“The U.S. military lost to Iran because of a shortage of weapons, didn’t they?”
“The U.S. will bounce back eventually.”
“Ukraine is fighting a battle it can’t win. They’re bound to lose.”
“No, I think it’s a stalemate—a quagmire.”
The other day, I had dinner with a Moscow correspondent for a TV network who was temporarily back in Japan.
“In May 2025, Russia overtook Japan to become the world’s fourth-largest economy. Not on a nominal basis, but on a real basis…”
“Really? Wasn’t Russia’s economic power supposed to be on par with South Korea’s?” was the reply.
The Japanese mass media only reports information originating from the West. Their sources include Reuters, the BBC, and the U.S. Institute for the Study of War. Many Japanese people trust the Japanese mass media and are satisfied with the information they receive from it.
Although the Japanese media is not subject to government censorship, it practices self-censorship. In Japan, this is called “SONTAKU” (anticipating the authorities’ wishes).
The Japanese, who are sensitive to authority, have a culture of “SONTAKU” toward those in power. They even practice “SONTAKU” toward the United States, a superpower.
As a result of this “SONTAKU” the Japanese media does not report information that is unfavorable to the U.S. or Europe. The mainstream media reports only what aligns with government policy.
Because Japan is an “America First” country, even if journalists or experts believe that the U.S.’s “rule by force” is wrong, they do not voice this openly.
Even when ICC (International Criminal Court) Director Akane was subjected to economic sanctions, journalists and experts remained silent. In other words, even if they feel anger, they do not speak their “true feelings.”
The Japanese take action only when they are on the verge of being colonized by Western nations, as was the case during the Meiji Restoration.
In other words, the Japanese do not take action until they are on the brink of being pushed off a cliff. However, once they do start moving, they act swiftly and in unison, like a massive school of sardines.
I have written an essay in English about this Japanese trait, so I recommend giving it a read.
“CIVIL WARISM AND HARMONISM: Keys to understanding the Japanese” [link]
Japan currently stands at a crossroads.
It wishes to break away from the U.S. policy of “might makes right.”
However, it is being ignored by China and Russia and is currently unable to form partnerships with them.
While the United States is reverting to 19th-century imperialism, China is making the independence and prosperity that the Japanese dream of a reality.
Last December, I visited China for the first time in a long while. I traveled to Shanghai, Nanjing, and Chengdu. Chinese companies were engaged in fierce domestic competition, and society was brimming with vitality. It was exactly like Japan during the 1970s, when the country was experiencing rapid economic growth.
Japan’s automotive industry is struggling under the pressure of rising Chinese companies, but it is now partnering with them to strengthen its competitiveness.
The Toyota electric vehicle launched in China this August incorporates Huawei’s OS and AI technology. Honda is also adopting DEEPSEEK’s AI technology. Other automakers are partnering with companies such as Alibaba.
During this trip, I sensed that the Chinese people are pro-Japanese and friendly. I also realized once again just how important ties with China are for Japan, a nation that relies heavily on trade. Japan is a country that cannot wage war. With few natural resources, trade is vital for Japan, and it must push forward with “diplomacy for peace.”
Although Japan stands at a crossroads, one of the major events that will determine its future is expected to occur by the end of this year. The Takaichi administration reportedly plans to entrust the storage of top-secret national information—including military data—to the cloud services of Amazon and Google.
Although Japan is often referred to as a “digital loser,” it possesses the technological capabilities and financial resources to develop its own AI, operating systems, and data centers. All it takes is the determination to develop our own AI, OS, and data centers. By the end of this year, it will become clear whether Japan has lost its spirit as an independent nation.

A Chinese industrial company blacklisted by Washington has quietly opened operations on Spain’s eastern coast. It isn’t alone. According to the Spanish outlet Libertad Digital, several U.S.-restricted Chinese firms have been re-establishing themselves in the country, even as Spanish imports from China have climbed by an estimated 89% since Pedro Sánchez took office. Around the same time, Spain’s national statistics agency, the INE, has been quietly publishing a very different kind of number: the country’s population is growing, and almost entirely because more people are arriving than leaving.
Two data points, one contradiction. For years now, Western governments have talked about “de-risking” and “decoupling” from China — shorthand for reducing economic dependence, partly on competitiveness grounds and partly over security concerns tied to firms with alleged links to the Chinese state. In at least one major European economy, the underlying numbers appear to be moving the other way. That gap between what governments say and what their economies actually do is worth sitting with, because it raises a question that matters well beyond Spain: how much power does any single country, however large, really have to isolate another economy in a world this interconnected — and what does that tell BRICS nations and the broader Global South about the sanctions and pressure campaigns many of them have faced themselves?
The trade story decoupling rhetoric doesn’t explain
Start with the number that’s hardest to ignore: Spanish imports from China reportedly up 89% under the current government. That figure comes from a single outlet with a well-known conservative editorial line, and it hasn’t been checked here against Spain’s own trade ministry data — a gap worth stating plainly rather than papering over. Still, the broader trend it points to isn’t far-fetched. European supply chains, especially in batteries, electronics and green technology, have leaned harder on Chinese manufacturing even as Brussels debates tariffs on Chinese electric vehicles and solar equipment.
Then there’s the more unusual piece: Chinese companies under U.S. sanction or export restriction reportedly setting up new European operations in Spain rather than folding. Trade analysts have a name for this pattern — sanctions rerouting, where a restricted firm doesn’t disappear so much as relocate to a jurisdiction the sanctioning country can’t reach directly. It’s a dynamic that will look familiar to anyone who has watched Russian commodities find new buyers, Iranian trade move through intermediaries, or now, apparently, Chinese firms find a foothold on the Iberian Peninsula.
For BRICS governments and their partners, this isn’t an academic case study. It goes to a question that sits near the center of the bloc’s own economic diplomacy: can unilateral sanctions from one power durably isolate a targeted economy when the rest of the world keeps trading with it? Spain’s experience suggests, at minimum, that the answer isn’t simple.
The “return queue” claim, and what the data actually shows
A separate, more politically loaded story has been circulating: that Chinese immigrants in Europe are “queuing to return home,” pulled back by patriotic sentiment and by Beijing’s own talent-recruitment push. It’s a narrative that shows up in Chinese state-aligned media, but it’s difficult to verify against the migration data currently available. Eurostat’s emigration figures, broken down by citizenship, don’t offer a clear picture of Chinese nationals leaving Europe in significant numbers. Spain’s own data points the other way for the country as a whole: a net migration surplus of 258,547 people in the first half of 2022 alone, more than offsetting a negative natural population balance and driving total population growth of 182,141 in that period. Spain’s population stood at roughly 49.8 million as of 2026.
None of this proves Chinese nationals aren’t returning home in meaningful numbers — only that clear, citizenship-specific evidence for a large “return queue” doesn’t appear in the available data. That gap matters. Claims about mass migration, in either direction, are easy to make and hard to check, and both the exodus narrative and any confident dismissal of it deserve the same scrutiny until someone actually examines national exit records alongside Chinese entry statistics.
What is on the public record is that China has been investing heavily, and openly, in a long-term human capital strategy. The Education Strong Nation Construction Planning Outline, running through 2035, sets out a multi-decade push to strengthen domestic universities, research institutions and talent pipelines. Alongside it sits a long-standing institutional network connecting Beijing’s Overseas Chinese Affairs Office to provincial and municipal branches tasked with maintaining ties to Chinese communities abroad.
How to read that network is itself contested, and probably shouldn’t be settled from the outside. Chinese officials describe it as an effort to deepen ties with the diaspora and invite participation in national development — language that isn’t so different from the diaspora ministries run by India, the Philippines or Nigeria, all of which actively court remittances, investment and returning talent from citizens overseas. Some Western security officials view China’s version with more suspicion, framing it as political influence rather than ordinary outreach. Both readings deserve real scrutiny rather than automatic acceptance, and the honest answer is that the public evidence here is thinner than either side’s confidence suggests.
A talent race with more than one runner
China isn’t the only government treating skilled migration as a strategic asset. In Germany, the BAMF Research Centre and the Institute for Employment Research launched a large-scale survey in March 2026 to evaluate migrants who arrived under a skilled-labor framework known as FEG 2.0, aimed at a labor market facing demographic decline. Set next to China’s education push, a picture emerges of a genuinely global contest for skilled workers, with European governments, Chinese planners and Global South economies all playing, in different ways, the same game.
That’s where this becomes especially relevant to BRICS readers. Brazil, South Africa, India and other Global South economies have spent decades watching doctors, engineers and scientists leave for wealthier countries — the dynamic usually called brain drain. China’s approach, whatever its ultimate success, represents one model for how a large developing economy might try to reverse that flow through sustained state investment rather than relying on migration restrictions abroad. Whether it actually works, and whether countries with far smaller budgets and less centralized administration could replicate it, is an open question rather than a settled one.
Reading the contradictions
What makes this story worth telling is how many contradictions it holds at once. Western governments talk about reducing reliance on China even as a major European economy’s imports from China climb sharply. Sanctioned companies, instead of shrinking, relocate. Migration debates in Europe fixate on border pressure — visible in the recurring crossings recorded at Ceuta — even as the same governments try to ease pathways for skilled foreign labor. And a narrative of Chinese nationals streaming home sits uneasily next to statistics showing broad immigration growth into one of Europe’s largest economies.
None of this resolves neatly, and it shouldn’t be forced into a single verdict. What it does suggest is that the language governments use — decoupling, de-risking, return migration — may be running ahead of, or simply diverging from, the actual flows of goods, capital and people underneath it. That gap isn’t unique to Europe or to China. It echoes debates familiar to BRICS members themselves: how far de-dollarization can really proceed while so much trade stays dollar-denominated, or how much sovereignty any state retains over its own economic decisions once its industries and labor markets are this tightly woven into global supply chains.
What it means from here
For Global South observers, Spain offers a useful, if incomplete, window into how economic gravity can pull in a different direction than political intention. Sanctions announced in Washington don’t automatically translate into isolation on the ground. Capital and personnel find new channels, and host economies hungry for investment often have real reasons to welcome them, whatever diplomatic friction follows. For BRICS countries that have themselves faced sanctions or pressure to pick sides in great-power competition, that pattern is worth watching closely — not as proof that any particular government’s strategy has worked, but as evidence that the tools of economic statecraft, however powerful the country wielding them, run into real limits when the rest of the world keeps trading.
At the same time, how thin the underlying data still is — on migration flows, on the real scale and intent of corporate relocations, on how far diaspora institutions actually reach — is itself worth flagging. Sweeping claims, whether about mass returns, hidden influence networks, or the outright failure of Western policy, are easier to assert than to prove. What the available material actually supports is more modest: trade ties between China and at least one Southern European economy appear to be deepening, migration into Spain remains strongly positive, and multiple governments — Chinese, German and others — are investing seriously in the race for skilled talent.
What’s still unresolved is how these threads play out from here, as European institutions weigh further tariffs on Chinese goods, as Germany’s labor survey produces results, and as China’s education strategy moves toward its 2035 target. Does economic interdependence keep outpacing political attempts to unwind it, as this case suggests it might? And if it does, what does that mean for how BRICS nations — many of them navigating relationships with Washington, Brussels and Beijing all at once — define economic sovereignty in the years ahead?
This piece draws on Spanish, German and EU statistical sources (INE, BAMF/IAB, Eurostat), Spanish press reporting (Libertad Digital), and Chinese government publications on education and diaspora policy. Claims about the scale of Chinese return migration and the motives behind specific corporate relocations could not be independently confirmed and are presented with that caveat.
