In the previous two articles, we addressed two components: the Coalition of the Willing and the “terrorist state” label. Now we arrive at the core of the puzzle: the structure of power in Kyiv.
The question is this: are Zelensky and his inner circle the true rulers, or merely visible figures in a stage-managed scene?
Critics of the Zelensky government believe that the decision-making structure in Kyiv, rather than being in the hands of official institutions, is under the influence of a network of domestic and foreign actors. In this article, the most important evidence and arguments put forward in support of this view are examined.
Yermak’s Apparent Resignation and His Continuing Influence
One of the most well-documented claims concerns Andriy Yermak, the former head of the Office of the President of Ukraine.
On November 28, 2025, following searches by Ukraine’s National Anti-Corruption Bureau (NABU) at his office in connection with the major “Energoatom” corruption case, Yermak resigned. However, according to a report by the Ukrainian newspaper “Ukrainska Pravda”, this resignation did not prevent him from continuing to influence the country’s most important political processes.
According to this newspaper’s field investigation, published in the form of a documentary titled “The Godfather from Afar,” Yermak, after a brief pause, continued meeting with government officials. Among other things, on January 30, 2026, he met with Rustem Umerov, Secretary of Ukraine’s National Security and Defense Council; a meeting that lasted about three hours. He also met with Oleksandr Kamyshin, Zelensky’s strategic advisor, on January 27.
According to sources cited by the newspaper in political circles, “Yermak is not here, but he is here”—meaning that despite his formal departure, his influence over political decision-making and appointments remains intact.
Two months after Yermak’s resignation, one senior member of Zelensky’s team reportedly told Ukrainian journalist Mykhailo Tkach of Pravda, off the record:
“We thought Yermak was the problem, so we fought Yermak. But the problem was the president.”
The 2022 Istanbul Talks and Boris Johnson
Another case that highlights the debate over the influence of foreign powers on Ukraine’s sovereignty concerns the events of 2022 and the role of Boris Johnson, then British Prime Minister, in Kyiv’s withdrawal from the Istanbul peace talks.
According to this account, Johnson was instrumental in halting the negotiations and in Kyiv’s abandonment of the preliminary agreements reached with Moscow.
This point, unlike many other parts of this series, is a subject that has also been seriously discussed in Western media. David Arakhamia, head of the ruling party’s faction in Ukraine’s parliament and one of the key members of Kyiv’s negotiating delegation in Istanbul, said in an interview with the Ukrainian television channel “1+1” that Russia, in those negotiations, was prepared to end the war in exchange for Ukraine’s declaration of neutrality.
However, Arakhamia said that after the Ukrainian delegation returned from Istanbul, Boris Johnson travelled to Kyiv and told them, “Do not sign anything—just fight.” Foreign Affairs also addressed this account in a detailed report published in April 2024, citing Arakhamia and other negotiators.
The claim is nevertheless disputed. The European Union-affiliated platform EUvsDisinfo classified it among disinformation narratives, arguing that Arakhamia had emphasized in the same interview that Kyiv had already decided not to sign an agreement before receiving Johnson’s advice. According to this interpretation, Western partners were informed about the negotiations but were not the decision-makers.
In other words, the account presented in the report should not be treated as an established fact. It remains a contested issue among Western analysts, with evidence supporting both sides: Arakhamia’s direct statement on the one hand, and Zelensky’s denial and alternative interpretations of Arakhamia’s remarks on the other.
Sunak’s Appointment and Freeland’s Role
In this same context, this piece refers to the appointment of Rishi Sunak, former British Prime Minister, as an advisor to Ukraine’s head of government on matters of Ukraine’s economic reconstruction; this appointment, unlike many other items in this series of reports, is fully documented and verifiable from official British sources: according to documents published in February 2026 by the UK’s Independent Adviser on Ministerial Interests, Sunak has joined, voluntarily and without pay, the “International Advisory Council for the Reconstruction of Ukraine.”
The council is intended to advise both Zelensky and his economic adviser on reconstruction policy.
Zelensky’s economic adviser in this area is Chrystia Freeland, Canada’s former finance minister. The President of the World Bank Group and the President of the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development are also members of the council. Companies including Siemens, BlackRock, and Citigroup attended its inaugural meeting.
Why Is Zelensky Reluctant to Hold Elections?
The final section of this piece addresses an issue that has repeatedly been raised at the international level in recent years: the postponement of Ukraine’s presidential election.
Zelensky’s presidential term, which began in 2019, formally ended in May 2024, but no election has been held, citing martial law. Zelensky, in numerous interviews with Western media, including the BBC and ITV News, has repeated the position that suspending martial law to hold an election would mean the loss of the army’s combat capacity and an opportunity for Russia.
Alfred Kokh, a former deputy prime minister of Russia who is now regarded as a Kremlin opponent and lives in Germany, has also expressed a sharply critical view of the election postponement. In one statement, he said:
“The fear of holding elections is visible on Zelensky’s face.”
Kokh argued that it would be easier for Zelensky to lose the war completely and establish himself in Europe as a president in exile than to accept a ceasefire, hold elections, lose them, and face prosecution.
Kokh described Zelensky as an “ineffective and self-satisfied individual” and stressed the need for a compromise with Russia over Donbas.
He also insisted that Zelensky does not legally have the authority to schedule elections. Under Article 85, Paragraph 7 of the Constitution of Ukraine, he argued, determining the timing of elections is the legal responsibility of the Verkhovna Rada, Ukraine’s parliament—not the president.
Another example cited as evidence that Zelensky fears elections is his reaction to an interview given by Valerii Zaluzhnyi, the former commander-in-chief of Ukraine’s armed forces and the country’s current ambassador to the United Kingdom.
Some Western and Ukrainian analysts interpreted the interview as the beginning of a possible Zaluzhnyi election campaign. Zelensky responded by saying that Zaluzhnyi’s decision to raise such issues was “hasty” and “inappropriate.”
This reaction is consistent with other reports suggesting that Zelensky’s team regards Zaluzhnyi as its principal potential rival in any future election. Some Ukrainian media outlets have recently reported that Zelensky’s campaign team is concerned about Zaluzhnyi’s high popularity in opinion polls and therefore has little interest in holding elections before the war ends.
Conclusion
Taken together, these claims present a picture of a leadership that, according to its critics, is influenced both from within—through figures such as Yermak—and from outside—through advisers such as Freeland and Sunak. At the same time, the leadership is portrayed as avoiding elections for both political and legal reasons.
It is important, however, to distinguish between the varying levels of credibility attached to these claims.
- The allegation that Yermak continued to wield influence after his resignation is supported by the independent field reporting of Ukrainska Pravda.
- The appointments and advisory roles involving Sunak and Freeland are described as corroborated by official British sources.
- Johnson’s alleged role in the collapse of the Istanbul negotiations remains contested, with evidence both supporting and challenging the claim.
What is clear is that the war in Ukraine is not being fought solely on the battlefield. It is also continuing in the arenas of politics, diplomacy, media, and competing narratives.

The geopolitical paradox of a European Union leading the Green Deal, yet dependent on highly polluting road transport. Conversely, the Russian Federation preserves and promotes a freight logistics system dominated by railways, which is far more environmentally sustainable.
The European Green Deal
In 2019, Brussels established the Green Deal as «the EU’s growth strategy». The green transition has thus become one of the main pillars of the Old Continent’s policy, aiming to «legally binding the 2050 neutrality goal». This means reducing emissions, but above all promoting «a clean transition that protects people and planet, is economically sound and socially fair».
Among the main sectors disrupting climate neutrality, alongside the industrial sector, energy production, and construction, transport plays a fundamental role. This sector contributes «around 5% to EU GDP and employing more than 10 million people in Europe», but above all, it is central to «European businesses and global supply chains».
Transport still accounts for «around 25% of the EU’s total greenhouse gas emissions, and these emissions have increased over recent years», even though the Green Deal’s objective is to reduce these emissions by «90% […] by 2050».
The difficulty of reducing pollution in the European domestic transport sector must be contextualized within the modalities through which it is carried out: in 2024, 78.2% of freight travelled by road, 16.6% by rail, and the remaining 5.2% on inland waterways (excluding maritime, pipeline, and air transport).
Europe therefore relies on a logistics system still heavily dominated by road transport, generally considered more flexible, faster, well-structured, and better suited to logistics and market demands. However, it is precisely here that one of the major contradictions of European climate policies emerges.
According to a report by the European Environment Agency, road freight transport produces an average of 137 grams of CO₂ equivalent per tonne-kilometre, compared to 33 grams for inland waterway navigation and 24 grams for rail transport. Therefore, road freight transport presents an emission intensity over 4 times higher than river barges and almost six times higher than rail transport.
In a Europe dominated by nearly 80% road transport, the sector’s climate neutrality is destined to remain a mirage, not due to a lack of technology, but rather because of governance choices and the use of modal infrastructures. The EU does not ignore the problem and aims to double rail traffic, but the technical fragmentation of national systems, limited cross-border interoperability, fixed infrastructure costs, the scarcity of available train paths, and the priority often granted to passenger trains are severely limiting factors.
The European Court of Auditors itself has acknowledged this. In a 2023 report, it certified that the goal of doubling rail freight transport is «off the road», recognizing that the rail sector does not yet compete on a level playing field with road transport and that European support has not been sufficiently effective in removing existing obstacles.
In this sector, private interests and lobbies carry more weight than political objectives. It is no coincidence that the European Union Agency for Railways has noted that in past decades «about 53,000 km of motorways have been constructed whereas approximately 55,500 km of rail lines have been removed». A picture from which the European political priorities for transport infrastructures clearly emerge.
The Russian modal model
Russia, too, presents an internal logistics system that is seemingly unbalanced at first glance. The enormous geographical distances, the climate, the historical context, and the forms of infrastructure governance have bequeathed a vast and highly prosperous railway network, which even today represents the backbone of transport within the territory of the Federation.
According to Rosstat, in 2024, approximately 86.3% of freight in Russia traveled on tracks, 11.8% on roads, and the remaining 1.9% on inland waterways (excluding maritime, pipeline, and air transport). A situation that is the exact opposite and a mirror image of what occurs in Europe.
The Russian railway system is dominated by the operator Russian Railways (RZD), a joint-stock company fully owned by the Russian Federation, which controls almost the entirety of the public network, traffic management, and most of the traction. However, it is not the sole operator, as, following specific liberalization policies, there are other entities operating in the sector.
In any case, the economic and political weight of this giant, the largest employer in the entire country, acts as a further catalyst for the promotion of the rail transport sector, even at the expense of road transport, which is nevertheless growing, particularly in European Russia. This does not detract from the fact that the vertically integrated structure and the dominant role of the State have allowed Russia to preserve a network designed to move massive quantities of goods – including coal, minerals, timber, petroleum products, fertilizers, and grain – across continental distances.
The environmental advantage of rail transport in Russia is further reinforced by the electrification of the lines and the composition of the electrical system. According to the U.S. Energy Information Administration, in 2023, nuclear, hydroelectric, and other renewables together provided about 38% of Russian electricity generation: a low-emission baseline that further reduces the ecological footprint of railway convoys, albeit within an energy system still heavily dependent on fossil fuels.
When «green» becomes the positive externality of other policies
Moscow has not set the Green Deal and the green transition as the primary goal of its policies and remains, also from a strategic point of view, a major producer and consumer of hydrocarbons. Yet, looking at the structure of its internal logistics, the Federation manages to be far more environmentally sustainable than Brussels.
The geopolitical paradox is evident: the European Union possesses the most ambitious climate goals on the entire planet, but continues to depend on highly polluting road transport. Russia, on the other hand, has built a logistics system for strategic, market, and territorial control purposes, including military ones. It did not set its sights on an ecological horizon. And yet, it is endowed with a less carbon-intensive transport system.
This context demonstrates that environmental sustainability depends not only on declared objectives, regulations, available technologies, and technological innovation. Environmental protection also depends on the State’s capacity to plan, finance, govern, and preserve consistent infrastructures across space and time. Sometimes, green externalities stem from far-sighted policies that were not conceived with a strictly environmental purpose.

He teaches at the University of Udine and contributes to Krisis.info on agriculture and geopolitics. He is the author of La città rurale (The Rural City). His contributions are professional, not institutional.

There are headlines that make you raise an eyebrow. “Dirty Business: Why Millions of Russians Watch Trash Content and How to Control It” is certainly one of them.
On August 12, the Russian news agency National News Service held a press conference about what is described in Russia as “trash content” online. This includes shock, provocation, explicit scenes and deliberately antisocial behaviour that can be turned into both fame and money. Among the participants were State Duma deputies Vitaly Milonov and Andrey Svintsov. The discussion focused on why such content has become popular, how bloggers should be held accountable and whether internet regulations need to be tightened.
At first glance, it is easy to dismiss this as Russian moral panic and yet another attempt to control the internet. But behind the sensational headline lies a question that is not only about Russia:
What happens to a society when algorithms reward the most provocative, emotional and extreme content?
A real problem
We do not have to defend “trash content” to recognise the problem. Social media has transformed the entire media landscape. What once might have remained within a small circle of friends can now reach hundreds of thousands or even millions of people.
And it does not have to be good content that gets the greatest reach. Someone who provokes, creates conflict or does something shocking can attract far more attention than someone trying to explain something complicated and nuanced.
This is also connected to how the platforms work. The longer we stay, the more money can be made. There is therefore a strong economic incentive to capture our attention. Content that triggers anger, fear or curiosity can simply be more profitable than content that is factual and balanced.
The problem is therefore not exclusively Russian.
It is an internet problem.
Europe and Sweden
This is where developments in Europe become interesting. Through the Digital Services Act, or DSA, the EU has introduced extensive rules for major digital platforms. Among other things, they are required to address systemic risks that can affect users and society. At the same time, the EU is dealing with issues such as disinformation, foreign interference and the influence of algorithms on public debate.
Sweden is, of course, part of this development. We are covered by the DSA, and the Swedish government has supported measures aimed at protecting children and young people from harmful online content. The discussion includes issues such as age verification and platform responsibility.
The basic idea is easy to understand. Children should be protected and illegal content should be fought. But at the same time, we need to be careful about where the line between protection and control is drawn.
Because who decides what is harmful?
Today, the discussion may concern pornography, violence, extreme influencers or trash content. But what happens if the definition changes? What happens when the fight against disinformation begins to include political opinions that someone considers dangerous?
These are questions we should be able to ask both Moscow and Brussels – and Stockholm as well.
Propaganda has changed
When we hear the word propaganda, many people still think of state television, newspapers and political posters. But information influence works differently today.
An influencer, a troll account, a politician, a company or an algorithm can all contribute to the same information chaos. And sometimes nobody even needs to lie. It is enough that certain things receive enormous exposure while others never reach the public.
We have more information than any generation before us, but that does not automatically mean that we are better informed. Algorithms do not care about what is true. They care about what works – and what works is often what triggers the strongest emotions.
That may be one of the greatest challenges of our time.
Who controls the controllers?
I can understand the argument that governments must protect people from exploitation, illegal content and manipulation. But at the same time, we must defend another principle:
The power over information must also be subject to scrutiny.
That applies in Russia. It applies in the EU. It applies in Sweden. And it applies to the major technology companies.
Because whoever controls the flow of information has enormous power over society.
That is why I do not think we should simply laugh off the Russian discussion about trash content. The problem exists. But the solution cannot automatically be more government control. Otherwise, we risk fighting one problem by creating another.
And where does BRICS fit in?
This should also be an issue for BRICS. The flow of information is no longer something that can be viewed solely from a European or Western perspective.
The BRICS countries consist of societies with very different political systems and views on media and freedom of expression. But they have one thing in common: they exist in a digital world where a large part of the information flow still passes through global platforms and technological systems developed outside BRICS.
If BRICS wants greater independence in economics, trade, payment systems and technology, should information also become part of that discussion?
But digital independence must not automatically mean government control over information. It would be unfortunate if the world simply moved from one information monopoly to another.
Perhaps BRICS could instead contribute to a more pluralistic digital landscape where people have access to different perspectives, where the power of algorithms is scrutinised and where no single government or technology company gets to decide what the entire world sees.
Because if the world becomes more multipolar economically and politically, but remains dependent on a handful of actors for its information flow – is it really multipolar?
So where should the line be drawn?
Is it right for governments and platforms to have greater power to remove trash content and disinformation – or are we at the same time opening the door to a form of information control that could eventually be used against completely different opinions?
And if BRICS wants to be part of a genuinely multipolar world, shouldn’t the right to a diverse and open flow of information also be part of that struggle?

Few borders in Asia carry as much history, strategic weight and political sensitivity as the one India shares with China. Nowhere is that more evident than in Arunachal Pradesh, the eastern frontier that Beijing claims as “South Tibet” and New Delhi regar ds as an integral part of India.
The latest reports of a possible Chinese incursion near Pukar La have once again brought this difficult frontier into focus. Reports have alleged that Chinese troops crossed the Line of Actual Control (LAC) near Taksing. Arunachal Pradesh Chief Minister Pema Khandu, however, has denied reports of an ongoing incursion and said the matter would be verified with the Army and local organisations.
But whether this particular episode proves to be an incursion, a patrol face-off or a misreading of competing LAC perceptions, it comes at a consequential moment. India and China have spent the past two years trying to stabilise ties after the military crisis that began in Ladakh in 2020.
In October 2024, the two sides reached an agreement on patrolling arrangements in Depsang and Demchok, followed by disengagement and the resumption of coordinated patrolling. It was an important step towards repairing a relationship that had suffered its worst rupture in decades.
Yet the boundary remains unresolved, the LAC remains contested and distrust has not disappeared.
That is why New Delhi’s latest response is important. External Affairs Ministry spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal has reiterated that peace along the border are essential to the wider relationship, adding that the state of the border will reflect on the state of bilateral ties. The message is clear: India no longer sees the border as an isolated security problem that can be compartmentalised from the rest of the relationship.
The timing is also important because the dispute has moved beyond patrols and military positions. India has recently identified 27 places and geographical features in Arunachal Pradesh by their official Indian names. China objected, calling India’s move illegal and reiterating its claim over what it calls Zangnan, or South Tibet. India has rejected the Chinese position as an attempt to manufacture territorial claims and has repeatedly said that no renaming exercise can alter the status of Arunachal Pradesh.
To understand why Arunachal has become so central to India-China relations, one has to go back to the beginning of the modern boundary dispute.
The roots of the conflict lie in the 1914 Simla Convention, where British India and Tibet negotiated a boundary that came to be known as the McMahon Line. The line runs through the eastern Himalayas and places present-day Arunachal Pradesh on the Indian side.
China did not accept the agreement, arguing that Tibet did not have the authority to conclude such an arrangement independently. India, inheriting the British Indian position after independence, has treated the McMahon Line as the legitimate boundary.
This is the fundamental disagreement. India sees the eastern boundary as an established frontier. China sees the McMahon Line as a colonial-era imposition and claims large parts of Arunachal Pradesh as southern Tibet. The dispute is rooted in competing interpretations of Tibet’s historical status and of the legal validity of the 1914 agreement.
For decades, however, the remoteness of the eastern Himalayas kept the dispute from becoming a constant military confrontation. The region was administered as the North-East Frontier Agency, or NEFA, rather than as a full-fledged state. That changed after the 1962 war.
The war remains the defining moment in India’s understanding of Arunachal. Chinese forces attacked across the disputed frontier in October 1962, overwhelmed Indian positions in the eastern sector and captured Tawang before advancing further into NEFA.
For India, the military defeat was devastating. But its longer-term consequence was equally important: Arunachal could no longer be treated as a distant frontier. New Delhi accelerated political integration, administration and infrastructure.
NEFA became the present day Indian state Arunachal Pradesh, meaning “Land of the Dawn-Lit Mountains’ in 1972. The Indian state increasingly understood that sovereignty in the Himalayas could not be secured by declaring a border from Delhi. It had to be demonstrated through roads, administration, civilian settlement and a permanent security presence.
The Chinese claim did not disappear. In 1975, four Assam Rifles personnel were killed at Tulung La; the last fatal India-China border incident until Galwan in 2020. A decade later, the Sumdorong Chu standoff brought the two sides close to war, with India launching Operation Falcon after Chinese troops established a presence in the area. Arunachal was soon tested again. In December 2022, Indian and Chinese troops clashed at Yangtse near Tawang after India said Chinese troops attempted to cross the LAC.
Arunachal is tied to China’s broader Tibet policy and its effort to control the narrative over Tibetan history and political identity. India’s position is equally firm: whatever Beijing’s interpretation of Tibet’s history, it cannot be used to question India’s sovereignty over Arunachal Pradesh.
The result is a dispute in which neither side is likely to abandon its basic position. Today, the two countries are fighting an infrastructure war. Roads, bridges, forward posts, airstrips, surveillance systems and border villages matter; so do maps and names. A road can alter military mobility, a permanent settlement can strengthen administrative presence. A new place name can establish a narrative. All these collectively alter the strategic balance.
The India-China relationship is larger than the border. The two countries are major Asian economies, important members of BRICS and influential actors in the Global South. These countries drive 44% of global economic growth as dominant manufacturing and technology hubs. Their rivalry affects regional security, trade, supply chains and the wider balance of power in Asia. A prolonged military confrontation between the world’s two most populous countries would have consequences well beyond the Himalayas.
As of now, Arunachal Pradesh will remain one of the hardest questions in India-China relations as neither country has yet found a way to live permanently with the other’s version of the map.

On August 14, 2026, Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov sat down with the state broadcaster VGTRK in Moscow for an interview that laid bare the increasingly volatile mechanics of global trade and diplomacy. While Western media often filters such statements through the lens of immediate conflict, a closer reading of the transcript reveals a profound structural crisis that extends far beyond the borders of the nations directly involved.
For the Global South, the most alarming takeaway from the interview was not the rhetoric of the battlefield, but the escalating weaponization of international maritime law and the systematic erosion of neutral diplomatic spaces. As regional blocs increasingly assert the right to intercept commercial shipping and coerce neutral states, the foundational principles of global commerce are being rewritten in real-time.
At the heart of these developments lies a fundamental question about who controls the world’s most vital trade routes—and what economic sovereignty means for developing nations in an era of unilateral enforcement.
The Weaponization of the Seas
The most immediate threat to global supply chains detailed in the interview centers on the European Union’s aggressive posture toward commercial shipping. Brussels has increasingly targeted vessels it accuses of transporting sanctioned energy commodities, labeling them a “shadow fleet.” However, as Lavrov pointed out, this terminology does not exist in any foundational document of international maritime law.
Instead, the EU has effectively unilaterally authorized itself to halt ships sailing under various national flags, confiscate their cargo, sell the commodities on global markets, and redirect the revenues to fund foreign military efforts. From the perspective of international law, this represents a radical departure from the established norms of the freedom of navigation.
For a commodities trader in São Paulo, a shipping magnate in Mumbai, or an energy importer in Johannesburg, this precedent is deeply unsettling. The vessels Western capitals label as “shadowy” are often the very lifelines that have allowed developing economies to secure discounted energy, manage domestic inflation, and sustain industrial growth amid global market disruptions. If a regional bloc can seize a commercial asset on the high seas based on its own domestic decrees, the oceans cease to be a shared global commons. They become contested zones where the strongest naval powers dictate the flow of goods.
In response to these seizures, Moscow has signaled a hardline pivot. Lavrov noted that Russian President Vladimir Putin has authorized a “mirror response,” warning that vessels operating in the interests of nations engaging in what the Kremlin terms “maritime piracy” will now be targeted in kind.
This escalation transforms commercial shipping from a neutral enterprise into a geopolitical battleground. For the Think BRICS community, this reality underscores an urgent strategic vulnerability. The Global South can no longer assume that its supply chains are protected by universal maritime conventions. Securing the physical movement of goods now requires the accelerated development of alternative maritime insurance consortiums, independent shipping registries, and secure logistical corridors insulated from Western legal jurisdiction.
Diplomatic Whiplash and the Sabotage of Peace
The instability on the high seas is mirrored by a profound fracturing within Western diplomatic circles, a dynamic that complicates the Global South’s ability to engage in predictable statecraft. The VGTRK interview provided rare, detailed insights into recent backchannel negotiations involving the United States, revealing a stark disconnect between American executive initiatives and transatlantic alliances.
According to Lavrov, US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner recently engaged in high-stakes diplomacy that culminated in a summit in Alaska. During this meeting, Moscow reportedly accepted a peace framework proposed by the Trump administration, signaling a potential off-ramp to the ongoing conflict.
Yet, this diplomatic breakthrough was swiftly undermined. Lavrov detailed how leaders from the European Union and NATO immediately traveled to Washington to pressure the US into abandoning the initiative. The result was not a peace agreement, but a fresh wave of sweeping sanctions targeting major energy corporations like Lukoil and Rosneft. Even senior US officials like Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Vice President J.D. Vance have been caught in this policy tug-of-war, reflecting deep institutional fractures.
For emerging economies, this diplomatic whiplash is highly disruptive. When the US executive branch negotiates a framework that is immediately torpedoes by its own allies, it signals a severe lack of policy cohesion. How can the Global South negotiate long-term trade or security agreements with Western powers when those powers cannot maintain a unified diplomatic front?
Furthermore, the decision to target giants like Lukoil and Rosneft is not a victimless bureaucratic exercise. These corporations are deeply integrated into global energy markets. Disrupting their operations inevitably triggers volatility in global oil prices, which translates directly into increased domestic costs for transport, food production, and manufacturing across the developing world. The rush by European leaders to impose further energy sanctions demonstrates a willingness to inflict collateral economic damage on the Global South to maintain geopolitical leverage.
The Caspian Flashpoint and the Limits of Security Guarantees
Amidst this Western dysfunction, Middle Powers are actively asserting their agency to protect their regional interests, though they face severe constraints. Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan recently traveled to the Russian city of Kazan for high-level meetings, highlighting Turkey’s complex balancing act. Ankara maintains its NATO membership while deeply integrating its economy and energy infrastructure with Eurasia.
Lavrov highlighted a critical and dangerous incident that exposes the limits of current security architectures. Civilian tankers associated with the Caspian Pipeline Consortium—some of which are linked to American energy giants like Chevron and ExxonMobil—were recently targeted by drone strikes in the Caspian Sea.
The public silence from Washington and Ankara regarding these strikes is highly revealing. Despite private diplomatic “signals” reportedly being sent to the perpetrators, there has been no robust public condemnation or mobilization of naval assets to protect these commercial corridors. For BRICS nations, this demonstrates that relying on Western-led security frameworks for the protection of vital energy infrastructure is a profound strategic risk. If Western security guarantees fail to protect Western corporate assets in the Caspian, they will certainly not protect the shared infrastructure of the Global South.
This reality demands that emerging economies forge their own security dialogues and joint naval patrols to protect shared maritime and overland corridors from becoming collateral damage in great-power conflicts.
The Shrinking Space for Neutrality
The pressure to conform to a unipolar worldview is intensifying globally, leaving little room for the independent foreign policies that have historically defined the Non-Aligned Movement. Lavrov’s comments shed light on the intense coercion faced by nations attempting to balance their international relationships, offering a stark warning to the Global South about the cost of strategic autonomy.
Consider the situation in Serbia. President Aleksandar Vučić has faced what Lavrov described as relentless pressure from Brussels. The EU has explicitly tied Serbia’s progress toward European integration to two non-negotiable demands: recognizing the independence of Kosovo and fully aligning with anti-Russia sanctions. Vučić’s dilemma is a microcosm of the pressure faced by all non-aligned states. Serbia relies on Russian gas, which Moscow provides at highly favorable, stable prices without attaching political conditions. Yet, the EU demands that Belgrade sever these ties and adopt hostile postures. This dynamic forces leaders in the Global South to constantly weigh the immediate economic benefits of Western market access against the long-term erosion of their sovereignty.
Similarly, in Asia, the geopolitical landscape is shifting dangerously. Japan has pivoted sharply away from the pragmatic, balanced foreign policy championed by the late Shinzo Abe. Current Japanese leadership has embraced rapid militarization, designated Russia as a primary threat, and aligned its security apparatus entirely with Washington. Lavrov recounted a jarring anecdote from a recent multilateral gathering in the Philippines, likely on the sidelines of ASEAN meetings. During a crowded, formal banquet, the Japanese foreign minister reportedly tapped Lavrov on the shoulder merely to exchange brief pleasantries, only to later tell the press that they had engaged in deep “bilateral and regional discussions.” This performative diplomacy highlights the lengths to which some nations will go to project an illusion of alignment with Western narratives, even when substantive engagement is nonexistent.
Even within Europe, the political rhetoric is darkening. Lavrov pointed to the political ascent of figures like Friedrich Merz in Germany, warning of a desire to rebuild Germany as the dominant military force on the continent. When a German journalist recently asked a Serbian leader how Berlin could actively help “kill Russians,” it underscored a profound and alarming departure from the diplomatic norms that once governed international relations.
For BRICS, these developments validate the absolute necessity of a multipolar world order. While Western media frequently frames the Global South’s refusal to join sanctions regimes as tacit support for aggression, these nations view their stance as a steadfast defense of the principle that international relations should be based on mutual respect, equitable trade, and the pursuit of sovereign national interests.
Building Parallel Architectures
The events of August 2026 serve as a stark reminder that the architecture of the post-Cold War world is actively fracturing under the weight of unilateralism. As Brussels seizes cargo on the high seas and Washington oscillates between peace proposals and crippling sanctions, the Global South is left to navigate a highly volatile and unpredictable landscape.
The path forward for BRICS and its expanding network of partners requires more than just rhetorical solidarity; it demands the construction of resilient, independent institutions. This means accelerating the development of alternative financial messaging systems and digital currencies through platforms like the New Development Bank (NDB) to bypass Western-controlled chokepoints. It requires the establishment of joint maritime insurance pools that can underwrite Global South trade without the threat of secondary sanctions.
Furthermore, it demands a robust, coordinated diplomatic front within the United Nations and other international forums to formally challenge the unilateral seizure of commercial assets on the high seas as a violation of the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS). The Global South must leverage its collective voting power and economic weight to ensure that the oceans remain a shared commons, rather than a theater for unilateral enforcement.
When the fundamental freedom of the seas is held hostage by regional decrees, and when the diplomatic channels of the world’s leading powers are routinely sabotaged by their own allies, the traditional rules of engagement no longer apply. The question facing the Think BRICS community is no longer whether the global order is changing, but how quickly emerging economies can build the parallel architectures required to secure their own economic survival and strategic autonomy in the years ahead.

What happened with Radev’s attempt to be convenient to both the West and the East, as well as the incident in Plovdiv, once again showed how wide the gulf is between Bulgarians and the truth about Russia and our shared past. Until Bulgaria overcomes this bipolar hatred and amnesia, nothing will change.
I read such incredible fictions about Russophilia—invented in the mainstream media, on social media, and in all circles of our public space—that it makes my hair stand on end. Not because of what is happening, but because of the information war on the subject, deliberately stoked by the Russophobic stratum that is still in power in Bulgaria. Very little time in power remains for them—37 years have passed, 8 years remain, and then it is gone.
It is very difficult to speak of genuine Russophilia in our country, but it does exist and on a particularly large scale—much more than in any other country from the former Eastern Bloc. But that is not what matters. What matters to me are the attempts to rewrite history; as unbelievable as it may seem, the West deliberately erases facts, alters facts, and changes the significance of facts. And this practice is quite well established here.
I do not know what Rumen Radev will do in politics, nor do I know what vision he has for Bulgaria and its place among the world’s cardinal directions, but I want to point out two extremely severe problems.
Beyond the extreme, malignant Russophobia that poisons Bulgaria, there is another problem. People who are not actually Russophiles claim to be such (I wrote a post about this regarding a reception at the Russian embassy)—people who engage in no public activity for the benefit of shared relations, but merely profit personally from their Russophilia. An example of this is the chairman of the “Russophiles” Association.
This is one of the two reasons why Russia neglects the selection of people in our country to act as contacts with Russia itself. In fact, Russia is relying on long-standing momentum regarding its influence here, but very soon the tires of this bus will blow out. Natural Russophilia in our country has been abandoned to fate, neglected both by our official Russophile figures or organizations and by the Russians themselves. That is why Western propaganda flies its flag completely unhindered, rewriting history however it pleases and harassing society at all levels. Meanwhile, people like me are left to fend for themselves as best they can.
I am in contact with people from other Eastern European countries who, like me, are trying to change the public climate toward normalizing the insane attitude toward and with Russia, and I know they face the exact same problems. It was then that I realized the main reason for the rabid Russophobia in Europe (and in Bulgaria) is the severely neglected—if not entirely abandoned—Russian propaganda toward Europe. The truth—and it is shocking, because talking heads appear on European TV all day long finding Russian spies everywhere and in everything—is that Russia has completely neglected its work with its supporters on the continent. It is not just here; it is the same in other Eastern European countries. This is a failure of their foreign policy and a weakness in every respect on the information front.
You cannot rely on oligarchs and lumpens to represent you and expect results. The Russian leadership must keep in mind that, despite them, Bulgaria manages to breathe through these poisonous Russophobic miasmas thanks to the deep spiritual strength we carry. And one day we will demand accountability for this oversight!
That is why all kinds of nonsense about Russia and Russophilia are possible here.

There are few figures in modern history who can claim to have quite literally built the economic engine of the 21st century. If you’ve tuned into the DeCoding China Podcast on our Think BRICS YouTube Channel, you already know his name. While our work explores the many dimensions of China’s transformation, few figures have shaped our conversations as profoundly as Zhu Rongji. A driving force behind our outreach has been to ensure international audiences recognize just how fundamental his legacy is to the China we see today.
But time passes for everyone, and on August 12, at the age of 98, former Prime Minister Zhu Rongji passed away.
When a titan of this magnitude leaves the stage, the Chinese state doesn’t merely issue a press release; it drafts a historical monument in text. To truly understand the man who shaped the modern Chinese economy, you must read how the system he fundamentally transformed chooses to remember him. Below, we present the complete, translated official obituary released by Beijing’s central leadership today.
Obituary from the CPC Central Committee, the NPC Standing Committee, the State Council, and the CPPCC National Committee: Passing of Comrade Zhu Rongji
Chang’an Avenue Zhishi - August 12, 2026 06:08
Xinhua News Agency, Beijing, August 12 – The Central Committee of the Communist Party of China, the Standing Committee of the National People’s Congress of the People’s Republic of China, the State Council of the People’s Republic of China, and the National Committee of the Chinese People’s Political Consultative Conference deeply mourn to announce: An outstanding member of the Communist Party of China, a time-tested and loyal communist fighter, an outstanding proletarian revolutionary and politician, and an exceptional leader of the Party and the State, Comrade Zhu Rongji, member of the Standing Committee of the Political Bureau of the 14th and 15th CPC Central Committees and former Premier of the State Council, passed away in Beijing at 11:06 on August 12, 2026, at the age of 98, after medical treatment proved ineffective.
Comrade Zhu Rongji was born in October 1928 in Changsha, Hunan Province. He participated in revolutionary work in December 1948 and joined the Communist Party of China in October 1949. During his youth, he deeply loved his motherland, studied diligently, pursued progress, and was determined to serve his country. From 1947 to 1951, he studied electrical machinery manufacturing in the Department of Electrical Engineering at Tsinghua University and participated in the “New Democratic Youth League“. From 1951 to 1952, he served as Deputy Director of the Production Planning Office in the Planning Division of the Ministry of Industry of the Northeast. From 1952 to 1958, he successively served as Group Leader in the Fuel and Power Bureau and the Comprehensive Bureau of the State Planning Commission, Deputy Division Chief of the Director’s Office of the State Planning Commission, and Deputy Division Chief of the Comprehensive Division of the Machinery Bureau of the State Planning Commission. From 1958 to 1969, he successively served as an instructor at the Spare-time Cadre School of the State Planning Commission and an engineer at the Comprehensive Bureau of the National Economy. From 1970 to 1975, he was sent down to do manual labor at the “May Seventh Cadre School“ of the State Planning Commission. From 1975 to 1979, he successively served as Deputy Director of the Office and Deputy Chief Engineer of the Electric Power and Telecommunications Engineering Company under the Pipeline Bureau of the Ministry of Petroleum Industry, and as Director of the Office at the Institute of Industrial Economics of the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences. From 1979 to 1983, he successively served as Division Chief of the Fuel and Power Bureau, Deputy Director of the Comprehensive Bureau, Director of the Technological Transformation Bureau, and a member of the State Economic Commission. From 1983 to 1987, he successively served as Deputy Director and member of the Leading Party Members’ Group of the State Economic Commission, and as Deputy Director and Deputy Secretary of the Leading Party Members’ Group of the State Economic Commission. From 1987 to 1991, he successively served as Deputy Secretary of the CPC Shanghai Municipal Committee, Mayor, and Secretary of the CPC Shanghai Municipal Committee. He proposed that Shanghai should adjust its industrial structure, reorganize new development advantages, enhance its international competitiveness, pursue a path of developing an outward-oriented economy, and push the development and opening-up of Pudong into a substantive startup phase, laying a solid foundation for Shanghai‘s further reform, opening-up, and development. In 1991, Comrade Zhu Rongji was appointed Vice Premier of the State Council and concurrently Director and Secretary of the Leading Party Members’ Group of the State Council Production Office, as well as Director and Secretary of the Leading Party Members’ Group of the State Council Economic and Trade Office, taking charge of electromechanical energy, railway transportation, metallurgy and chemicals, and light industry and textiles.
In October 1992, Comrade Zhu Rongji was elected as a member and Standing Committee member of the Political Bureau of the Central Committee at the First Plenary Session of the 14th CPC Central Committee, taking charge of the routine work of the State Council. In June 1993, he concurrently served as Governor of the People’s Bank of China. He actively publicized and implemented the spirit of Comrade Deng Xiaoping‘s Southern Tour Talks, thoroughly implemented the spirit of the 14th CPC National Congress, and focused on advancing reform, opening-up, and modernization. He organized and carried out the cleanup of “triangular debts,” focusing on addressing root causes to enhance the vitality of enterprise operations. He studied and formulated ideas and measures to strengthen and improve macroeconomic regulation, further unifying understanding, and did a massive amount of highly effective work to reverse economic overheating, curb inflation, and achieve a “soft landing.” He focused on rectifying the financial and tax order, enforcing financial and economic discipline, strengthening tax collection and administration, accelerating fiscal and tax reform, and perfecting the financial regulation system. He promoted the reform of the grain price and purchase and sales system, establishing a grain purchase and sales system adapted to the requirements of the socialist market economy, implementing contracting by large grain-producing households on a voluntary basis for farmers, and developing moderate-scale operations. In September 1997, Comrade Zhu Rongji was re-elected as a member and Standing Committee member of the Political Bureau of the Central Committee at the First Plenary Session of the 15th CPC Central Committee. In March 1998, at the First Session of the 9th National People’s Congress, he was appointed Premier of the State Council, and later served as Secretary of the Leading Party Members’ Group of the State Council. Facing the impact of the Asian Financial Crisis and severe domestic floods, in accordance with the deployment of the CPC Central Committee, he shifted from implementing a moderately tight fiscal and monetary policy to implementing a proactive fiscal policy and a prudent monetary policy, focusing on expanding domestic demand and deepening reforms in key areas, thereby maintaining stable and rapid economic growth. He comprehensively adjusted the industrial structure, regional structure, and urban-rural structure, vigorously developed high-tech industries, especially the information industry, actively supported the accelerated development of the modern service industry, and focused on improving the quality and efficiency of economic growth. He placed the resolution of the “Three Rural Issues“ (agriculture, rural areas, and farmers) in a prominent position, promoted agricultural structural adjustment tailored to local conditions, strengthened rural poverty alleviation and development, and promoted coordinated urban-rural development. He adopted a series of policy measures to expand opening-up and encourage exports, adhered to the non-devaluation of the RMB, implemented a market diversification strategy and a quality-winning strategy, actively attracted foreign investment, made better use of both domestic and international markets and resources, and resolutely safeguarded the prosperity and stability of Hong Kong as an international financial center. He intensified efforts in ecological environment protection and construction, strengthened the management of resources such as land and minerals, and concentrated efforts to tackle pollution in key river basins and regions. He established the basic living guarantee system for laid-off workers of state-owned enterprises, unemployment insurance, and the minimum living guarantee system for urban residents, making great efforts to solve issues such as arrears in workers’ wages and the re-employment of laid-off workers. He continuously transformed government functions, promoted government institutional reform, and focused on strengthening the government’s own construction. After assuming the role of Premier of the State Council, Comrade Zhu Rongji also successively concurrently served as Director of the Central Special Commission, Director of the State Commission for Economic Restructuring, Head of the State Science, Technology and Education Leading Group, Director of the State Council Three Gorges Project Construction Committee, Director of the National Defense Mobilization Commission, and Head of the State Council Western Region Development Leading Group, dedicating tremendous effort to the fields of economic restructuring, science and technology, education, Western Development, and national defense industry.
During Comrade Zhu Rongji‘s tenure as Vice Premier of the State Council and Premier of the State Council, our country was in a critical period of transition from a planned economic system to a socialist market economic system. Under the strong leadership of the CPC Central Committee with Comrade Jiang Zemin at its core, he presided over the fiscal and tax structural reform, comprehensively implemented a major tax system reform centered on fair tax burdens and tax simplification, implemented a tax-sharing fiscal system based on a rational division of administrative powers between the central and local governments, and carried out pilot reforms of rural taxes and fees. He actively promoted financial structural reform, further standardized the functions of the central bank, deepened the reforms of commercial banks, the foreign exchange system, and the securities and futures markets, and promoted the establishment of a national unified, open, orderly competitive, and strictly managed financial market system. He regarded the reform of state-owned enterprises (SOEs) as the central link of economic structural reform. In accordance with the requirements of “clear property rights, well-defined rights and responsibilities, separation of government functions from enterprise functions, and scientific management,” he accelerated the establishment of a modern enterprise system, strategically adjusted the layout of the state-owned economy, and reorganized state-owned enterprises. He emphasized that every possible means must be used to promote the re-employment of laid-off and unemployed workers and strengthen the construction of the social security system. He promoted housing system reform, gradually implemented the monetization of housing distribution, and established and improved a multi-tier urban housing supply system dominated by economically affordable housing. He continuously deepened the reform of the grain circulation system, implemented the open purchase of farmers’ surplus grain at protective prices, the sale of grain at reasonable prices by state-owned grain purchase and sales enterprises, and the closed operation of grain acquisition funds, gradually liberalizing the grain acquisition market and prices in major sales areas. He also presided over the implementation of a series of major reforms in the social security system, medical and health system, and investment and financing system, promoted the establishment of the basic framework of the socialist market economic system, presided over the completion of the arduous negotiations for China’s accession to the World Trade Organization (WTO), and promoted the expansion of opening-up in breadth and depth. Comrade Zhu Rongji was deeply affectionate towards the people, emphasizing that government staff must bear in mind that they are public servants of the people, dare to speak the truth, are not afraid of offending others, do not engage in privilege, and with a strong sense of responsibility, take the initiative to shoulder heavy burdens and tackle the toughest challenges, going all out to do practical things for the people.
In March 2003, Comrade Zhu Rongji stepped down from the post of Premier of the State Council. After retiring from his leadership post, he resolutely supported and backed the CPC Central Committee with Comrade Hu Jintao as General Secretary, and resolutely supported and backed the CPC Central Committee with Comrade Xi Jinping at its core. He continuously cared about the great cause of socialism with Chinese characteristics and firmly supported the construction of Party conduct and clean government and the anti-corruption struggle.
The life of Comrade Zhu Rongji was a life of revolution, struggle, and glory, a life of wholeheartedly serving the people and dedicating himself to the communist cause. His passing is a major loss to the Party and the State. We must turn our grief into strength, learn from his revolutionary spirit, noble character, and fine work style, unite more closely around the CPC Central Committee with Comrade Xi Jinping at its core, hold high the great banner of socialism with Chinese characteristics, comprehensively implement Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era, profoundly grasp the decisive significance of the “Two Establishments”, strengthen the “Four Consciousnesses,” firm up the “Four Confidences,” and achieve the “Two Upholds.” With firm confidence and united as one, we must strive in unity to comprehensively advance the building of a strong country and the great cause of national rejuvenation through Chinese modernization.
Comrade Zhu Rongji is immortal!

Not very long ago, China resumed exports of fertilizers, rare earth minerals, and other industrial goods such as magnets and tunnel boring machines that had been restricted against India. The direct flights between India and China, which had been suspended for some time, have also resumed since 2023. Both countries are key members of the increasingly solid BRICS framework. There is enormous potential for their bilateral relationship to grow and prosper. That doesn’t, however, mean everything is smooth sailing. There are still many problems to resolve. Yet if we look at the trajectory of history, we can see where human society is heading, driven by technological progress. In this short article, we will examine this historical development from Myanmar’s perspective, and from this point of view, I believe the reader can grasp, at least in part, just how significant Myanmar is in shaping the history of the future, and that an able governance is necessary to build up its significance.
Throughout history, the influence of these two great civilizations on the region has been considerable — and in many ways, similar. Particularly in Southeast Asia, we can see the deep and extensive influence from both China and India. The current improvement in China-India relations is nothing less than an inevitable historical development. These two nations have been trying to establish connections since ancient times. The Indian subcontinent, on the other side of the Himalayas, was once legendary and mysterious to the ancient Chinese. Some Chinese monks, traveling around the western side of the Himalayan range, journeyed to India during the 5th, 6th, and 7th centuries, bringing back Buddhist scriptures to China. The stories of Our beloved Wu Kong and Tang Sanzang are based precisely on those journeys. There is also a historical record of an Indian-born Buddhist monk named Bodhidharma who traveled to China around the 5th century. It was Bodhidharma who gave rise to the Chan school of Buddhism — known as Zen in Japan. Scholars from both countries traveled back and forth. The Chinese believed there must be a land route connecting to India somewhere in the south, but they never managed to traverse it. In those days, traveling through the territory that is now Myanmar to reach India was near unimaginable. Rugged terrains, dense and unforgiving forests, and tropical diseases scared away anyone who dared to venture. Today, no country is geographically better positioned than Myanmar to connect these two very ancient civilizations who have been trying to find each other.
China is India’s largest trading partner. In 2023–2024, bilateral trade exceeded $130 billion. For China, India is its sixth-largest trading partner. Both countries recognize how important they are to each other. One issue, however, is the trade deficit: China exports more to India than India exports to China. This is largely a reflection of India’s manufacturing challenges, but Myanmar holds the key to solving this trade imbalance between the two. China’s recent decision to resume exports of fertilizers, rare earth minerals, and industrial machinery to India could significantly boost India’s manufacturing sector, given these resources and materials reach India efficiently. Technological and infrastructure advancements will also serve as drivers that bring these two nations closer together. Both countries have enormous populations, so any increase in economic activity between them will undoubtedly have a profound impact not just on the regional economy, but on the global economy as well. Looking at current developments, it is clear that both nations desire stronger relations and increased trade. Their participation in BRICS reveals their ambition to build a multipolar world, not to mention India’s growing ties with Russia. The productive forces are creating objective pressure that demands greater economic integration — a necessity for survival and growth in the coming decades. Hence, it is not an unreasonable assessment to say that BRICS is likely to become more cohesive in the future.
China’s most densely populated regions lie in the east and southeast. India’s population is more concentrated along the north and northeast. Between these two densely populated regions lies Myanmar, a strategically crucial country. Are you seeing just how vital Myanmar is for this unstoppable development? The country holds influence not only over these two countries, but over the historical process itself. The history of the Second World War offers us a glimpse of the significance of the country to these two nations. During the war, the India-China roads known as the Burma Road and the Ledo Road that passed through Myanmar were absolutely critical for the Allied forces in their fight against imperial Japan. Myanmar’s role in the history of the anti-fascist struggle was no small one
International politics is not a playground where children dance and play happily, nor is it a matter of throwing tantrums and saying, “I won’t play with you anymore.” Every country is simply maneuvering on the grand stage of world history to secure its own national interests. On that stage, there are conflicts of interest as well as shared gains. There are also those who, out of fear of the changes taking place and self-imposed insecurity, close their eyes and ears and resist. But if one has the desire to participate in this development — and the will to figure out how — there is nothing to fear. When shared economic prosperity becomes a common goal, the obstacles become problems to solve, not to run away from. Whether some countries are left behind or move forward will be determined by how they position themselves in relation to these changes. Let me reiterate that Myanmar is the country that can connect over 40% of the world’s population. No other country on Earth has such an opportunity.
On the other hand, the problems between China and India cannot be ignored. India is particularly concerned about the deepening China-Pakistan relationship, which it views as a threat to its national security. There is also the issue of Hindu nationalist extremism that jeopardizes the social harmony within India. Territorial disputes in the north remain unresolved. Both nations also carry the weight of ancient, rivalrous civilizations. For China, while the China-Pakistan Economic Corridor is important for energy trade, it primarily connects to China’s western regions — home to less than 10% of China’s population. Over 90% of China’s population along with major industrial zones are in the east and southeast. The China-Myanmar-India Economic Corridor is far more strategic and valuable than the China-Pakistan Economic Corridor.
How can Myanmar then facilitate trade growth between India and China? Let us look at the tropical fruit trade as an example. India is currently one of the world’s largest producers of mangoes, bananas, pomegranates, papayas, and other tropical fruits. At present, Thailand, Vietnam, and the Philippines are the largest exporters of mangoes and bananas to China. But China’s market still has plenty of room, and the demands are growing day by day. Tropical fruits are in popular demand in China, which is also the world’s largest importer. India’s geography makes it an ideal producer of tropical fruits. Mind you that India is a country larger than the entire Southeast Asian mainland combined! Currently, shipping Indian food products to China by sea takes anywhere from two to four weeks through the congested Malacca Strait and subsequently Singapore Strait. By transiting through Myanmar, travel time can be drastically reduced, opening many doors for economic opportunities. This doesn’t even include India’s vast production of spices or freshwater and marine products yet. For our neighbor Bangladesh who has a large seafood sector and a sizable population, this is also an opportunity to expand their economic outreach to the north and the east. It should be clear by now what potential Myanmar holds to open economic doors in the regio
Now let’s turn towards the political climate of Myanmar. If the resistance forces were to prioritize national economic development, they would recognize the importance of these opportunities. If they continue to view these regional developments through the naive lens of “everyone is self-serving” rhetoric, they are not going to become an actor in these transformations themselves. At the present, the military government is actively carving out its own place amidst these changes. That is precisely why the international community is still engaging with the military government because no matter what, they are trying to position themselves on the global stage. This is not about favoritism. It is about engaging with the government that represents the country regardless of internal dissatisfaction. The junta recognizes that their existence lies in recognition of the New World Order. Meanwhile, the elitist media that largely dominates the resistance circle uses the general mass to campaign against and denounce any development happening in the region, which only strengthens the role of the military government in this new era. The wheels of history continue to turn, nevertheless. As these elites sell Myanmar using Western-friendly buzzwords to fill their own moral pockets, the resistance gradually drifts away from the current development, alienating themselves from the world. The junta, on the other hand, simply does what needs to be done, quietly and steadily. The resistance forces are perpetually one step behind. Alas!
The changes happening in the world today are accelerating rapidly. Looking at the current global political landscape, with the exception of a few Western nations still tied to the US, most countries are showing keen interest in the new economic terrain. The Western powers, who entered the global stage through colonialism, are still clinging to their fading “glory” as much as they can. But the world has reached a point where it will not look back. In the coming decades, we will witness enormous transformations driven by technology and sheer will of humanity to grow and thrive.
So how do we, on our side, capitalize on these changes? For instance, what opportunities does improving India-China relationship present for Myanmar? What role will Myanmar play in the regional transformation process? How can the people of Myanmar contribute to and be a part of the grand historical process? These should be the central theme of discussions while talking about Myanmar’s affairs. What Myanmar needs most right now is economic development which fundamentally affects the livelihoods of our people, and a revolutionary leadership driven by a strong determination to transform the country into what it rightfully ought to be: a Htarni of people and the land they call home. Regardless of the circumstances, the importance of building and improving the nation’s economy through better means than the current power structure must be brought to the light. But as long as the elites — who have no stake in the country’s economic well-being — continue to act as though they represent the nation, we will not see genuine discussions regarding economic development that benefit the people. Their conversation will continue to revolve around ressentiment and upholding a moral stance that never was.
So, what is to be done? To seize the economic potential before us, there must be a revolutionary will. Looking at how generations have suffered the consequences of economic stagnation, it is evident why a movement centered around economic progress and material development is needed more than ever. At present, the elites in the resistance circles — who do not directly bear the burden of economic hardship — are not speaking about economic development. Instead, they speak at length about identity politics and instigate confrontations. While the country is suffering economically, they posture abroad with grand political rhetoric. Just as the junta is carving out its place in the multipolar world, they too are carving out a role for themselves in the geopolitical theater staged by the West. When the worst comes, they still have their little studios abroad from where they continue to preach human rights and democracy. They pursue their own agendas, and it goes without saying that those agendas are often disconnected from the grassroots.
In conclusion, I encourage the readers to take a moment and consider the potential Myanmar holds and what it takes to grasp it. The answer is not far away. This is a perspective for organizing and mobilization. If we speak with the priority of what we can do for Myanmar and the people, and what opportunities lie before them, the public can gradually develop confidence in Myanmar’s strategically vital location. Not only can it position itself as a bridge between China and India but also serve as a hub connecting all 3 giants in the region: China, the Indian subcontinent, and Southeast Asia. For that to happen, the resistance needs to be made aware of economic development as the epitome of human progress. No amount of moral signaling nor virtue signaling can bring about the change and development they are aspiring to build, for the world is shaped by a universal praxis — the collective, material action of people transforming their reality.
“Everything that is possible has the inherent drive to come into existence,” as the German philosopher Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz once said. If Myanmar cannot become a bridge between the elephant and the dragon, then who else could ever conceive of such a role?
