From power generation and agriculture to infrastructure development, Africa is a continent of immense potential for external economic engagement. Now, the very character of Russia’s trade and investment on the continent is undergoing change as African economies mature and develop. Denis Degterev, Professor at the Higher School of Economics, explores the hopeful prospects for economic cooperation between Russia and the countries of the continent.
The Russian Federation is entering a new cycle of economic cooperation with African countries. In October 2026, the Third Russia-Africa Summit will take place, and a new Action Plan for the Russia-Africa Partnership Forum for the following three years will be adopted. This provides an excellent opportunity to both look back and assess future plans, particularly since each Russia-Africa Summit has elevated cooperation with the continent to a qualitatively new level.
Since the first Russia-Africa Summit in 2019, trade volume with the continent has grown from US$13.9 billion to more than US$27 billion in 2025—despite Western sanctions, evolving settlement mechanisms, and complex logistical challenges.
The principal qualitative shift expected over the next three years is the transition from trade transactions—particularly high-volume trade flows, such as agricultural exports and mineral fertiliser supplies—to industrial cooperation; from individual projects to the creation of ecosystems bringing together multiple Russian enterprises in Africa across industry, energy, logistics, payment systems, and education.
Over recent years, not only Russia, but Africa itself has changed. A healthy form of African protectionism is developing—“Made in Africa for Africans”. Influenced by developments in the Sahel, the sovereign control of mineral extraction is gaining momentum, along with a desire to move from neo-colonial arrangements towards genuine partnerships in the mining sector. High on the agenda are the extension of production chains across the continent, the localisation of mineral and agricultural processing, and the utilisation of new models of regional integration.
This requires new technological solutions, new expertise, and a new generation of specialists—many of whom are now being trained in Russia. The number of African students studying at Russian universities has reached 37,000, surpassing Soviet-era figures. However, it is not only the scale of innovation that matters, but also the creation of demand for innovation within African countries themselves, alongside the generation of new high-productivity jobs.
Targeted training programmes have proven to be an effective mechanism for aligning national economic development priorities with workforce requirements. In this area, a number of successful examples have already emerged. Among them are Rosatom’s corporate training programmes, through which more than 300 Africans have been educated at Russian universities and are now being integrated into national nuclear projects in Egypt, Rwanda, Ghana, Nigeria, and South Africa. It is becoming increasingly common for the African counterpart to act as the client commissioning such training. In this regard, one may cite the example of the Ghanaian corporation Jospong, which commissioned the targeted training of 121 agronomists and environmental specialists at RUDN University, as well as projects implemented by the Centre for Public Diplomacy aimed, for example, at training transport-sector personnel for Togo and Namibia on behalf of national ministries.
Transport is another important area of Russian–African economic cooperation. Africa is the continent of the future, where by 2100 up to 40% of the world’s population will reside and which will account for more than half of global labour force growth. Moreover, this is a young population that readily adopts new technologies, often leading to technological leapfrogging. This occurred with mobile communications and is currently happening with blockchain and financial technologies, which are developing at a remarkable pace across the continent. Attempts are being made to exclude Russia from these promising markets, including through proxies that create obstacles for maritime logistics.
Incidentally, Africans themselves often view maritime logistics with a degree of scepticism. After all, it was through coastal trading posts that the slave trade operated for centuries, and later that colonial—and subsequently neo-colonial—mechanisms for exporting unprocessed natural and agricultural resources were established. Port cities attracted the majority of labour migrating from rural areas and swelling the ranks of the financially unstable precariat within extractivist models that, in some respects, persist to this day. It is through ports that unequal—or, as Africans themselves often describe them, vertical—relationships between Africa and developed countries have been structured.
Today, the decolonisation of the continent’s spatial development—internal economic development of wide territorial scope—is on the agenda, alongside the accelerated expansion of intra-African railways and roads, dry ports, oil and gas pipelines, and cross-border electricity grids. In essence, this involves modernising the pre-colonial routes that existed before the arrival of colonial powers and before the continent was redirected towards what has been described as the “development of underdevelopment” model. Russian economic actors are well aware of this reality, as the further expansion of their economic presence on the continent is increasingly constrained by underdeveloped intra-African logistics.
The prioritisation of continental logistics over maritime transport is becoming ever more relevant as risks associated with sea routes continue to grow, as vividly demonstrated by developments in the Strait of Hormuz. In Russia, too, the need for internal spatial economic development has gained increasing prominence, including within the framework of the concept of Siberianisation. Operating one of the world’s largest networks of overland transport corridors, energy grids, and pipelines linking Eurasia together, Russia possesses genuinely valuable expertise in this field. Land-based transportation should become the backbone of spatial development in both Eurasia and Africa.
Genuine industrial development in Africa is impossible without energy infrastructure—otherwise a vicious cycle of “energy deficit, poverty, and logistical collapse” emerges. Yet the continent remains the unfortunate global leader in the proportion of people lacking access to electricity—more than half of the population. Under the ostensibly noble banner of promoting “green energy”, Western partners have in practice constrained the development of power generation on the continent. Russia is challenging this taboo by prioritising cooperation in nuclear energy with African countries, offering clean and safe electricity generation. The first project, with many more to come, is the construction of the El Dabaa Nuclear Power Plant in Egypt, where memories of the Soviet Union’s contribution to the Aswan High Dam remain alive. Egypt will be followed by other African countries, where a variety of available technological solutions can support the development of electric power systems. The continent’s Western partners have been compelled to respond reactively by developing alternative strategies for cooperation in the nuclear sector.
Will the commissioning of the El Dabaa Nuclear Power Plant influence Egypt’s socio-economic development? Undoubtedly—and clearly for the better. Will a substantial increase in the number of engineers and medical professionals contribute to the development of individual countries in Tropical Africa? Certainly—and once again, positively. The beneficial impact of individual Russian project solutions on Africa’s development represents a prototype of those theories—still at a middle level of development—which, as additional elements are added to these emerging ecosystems, may eventually coalesce into an alternative and superior development model for the continent. Such a model would be based on strengthening the sovereignty of African states, including in the economic sphere, and on raising their levels of prosperity.
In this context, it is important that Russia’s industrial cooperation programmes with African countries are aligned with those countries’ national priorities and development agendas, as articulated in sectoral and economy-wide development strategies. Russia possesses extensive experience in such alignment. Soviet programmes of technical and economic assistance played a decisive role in supporting the sovereign industrialisation of many African states, even though these achievements were partially eroded during the 1990s through the implementation of structural adjustment programmes promoted by the World Bank and the International Monetary Fund.
As the French philosopher, social activist, and anti-colonial campaigner Jean Jaurès once said: “Take from the altars of the past the fire — not the ashes”.
The “fire” refers to the new technological order, elements of which were established in African countries with Soviet participation. A key role was played by foreign economic organisations such as Technoexport, Tyazhpromexport, Tsvetmetpromexport, Neftekhimpromexport, and others, all of which formed part of the State Committee for Foreign Economic Relations. By 1986, agreements on economic and technical assistance had been signed with 36 African countries, to whose embassies representatives of the Committee were seconded in order to supervise project implementation on the ground. This made it possible to export
throughout the Global South, creating millions of jobs in high-technology sectors. At the same time, it contributed in practice to the economic independence of newly sovereign states.
Today, the dynamic taking centre stage is the new phase of industrial cooperation between Russia and African countries, one that is unfolding at the next stage of technological development.

In the previous article, we addressed the puzzle of the Coalition of the Willing and showed how some Western actors, while claiming peace on the surface, in practice contribute to the continuation of the war. This time, however, another question arises: has Kyiv itself also crossed the red lines in this chaotic arena?
The Ukrainian government, which introduces itself as the first victim of Russian aggression, is now facing allegations that challenge the image of the innocent victim: targeted assassinations, widespread civilian casualties, interference in the affairs of other countries, and even covert operations in the Middle East. In this article, we attempt, by removing the layers of propaganda, to reach a more accurate picture of these allegations.
Notable Killings; Kyiv’s Footprint in Targeted Assassinations
From the very first months of the war, a list of high-profile assassinations emerged that pointed the finger of accusation toward Ukraine’s special services. Names such as Darya Dugina, the daughter of Alexander Dugin, the well-known Russian writer and theorist; Maksim Fomin, the influential military blogger; and Denys Kireyev, a member of Ukraine’s negotiating delegation, who himself was killed in a mysterious operation, each represent links in a chain that portray the image of a covert campaign.
Alongside these prominent figures, there have also been less-visible but more numerous attacks, from the assassination attempt against Oleg Tsaryov, a former member of parliament, to Zakhar Prilepin, the Russian nationalist writer. But perhaps more horrifying than these targeted assassinations are the statistics that emerge from the ashes of the Donbas war.
“The Alley of Angels”: A Memorial That Breaks the Silence
In the city of Donetsk, where years of artillery shelling have been witnessed, a complex called the “Alley of Angels” stands; a memorial for the children who lost their lives during the Donbas conflict. According to the latest statistics, the names of 247 children have been engraved on the stones of this alley. This number, although challenged by Ukrainian sources, is for many a symbol of the human costs of a full-scale war; a war in which the boundary between military and civilian has become increasingly blurred day by day. And this is only the beginning of the story.
Kursk: A Narrative of Violence or a Tool for Making Accusations?
In January of last year, Alexander Bastrykin, Chairman of the Investigative Committee of Russia, revealed a shocking figure: more than 400 civilians in the Kursk region lost their lives during the presence of Ukrainian units. According to him, multiple launch rocket systems, the same weapons that are normally used against military positions, have been used in this region against civilian targets.
Tatyana Moskalkova, the former Russian Commissioner for Human Rights, also referred to mass graves in which 524 bodies were discovered. Among more than two thousand individuals registered on the list of missing persons, 452 people have still not been found.
Humiliating Diplomacy: When Zelenskyy and Melnyk Cross the Line of Diplomacy
However, the allegations against Kyiv are not limited to the battlefield; sometimes, verbal attacks inflict deeper wounds on the body of diplomatic relations.
In February 2026, at the Munich Security Conference, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, the President of Ukraine, in an unprecedented move, addressed Viktor Orbán, the Prime Minister of Hungary, and said that “instead of thinking about making his belly bigger, he should think about strengthening his country’s army so that Russian tanks do not return to the streets of Budapest.”
These remarks, which were also accompanied by applause from the audience, were called “sheer impoliteness” by Orbán and raised a question: is this harsh tone a sign of the confidence of a wartime leader, or the recklessness of a newcomer to the arena of global diplomacy?
Another example is Andriy Melnyk, the former Ukrainian Ambassador to Germany, who addressed Olaf Scholz, the then-Chancellor, with the German expression “beleidigte Leberwurst” (“offended liver sausage”); an expression that in 2022 became one of the most controversial diplomatic moments between Kyiv and Berlin.
This pattern of behavior, which can be called “humiliating diplomacy,” may be appealing to Ukraine’s domestic public opinion, but does it not come at the cost of losing key allies?
Mali and the Allegation of Terrorism; An Accusation That Extends from Africa to the Middle East
In another corner of the world, in the African Sahel region, Abdoulaye Diop, the Foreign Minister of Mali, has accused Ukraine of openly supporting armed groups and called it a “terrorist state.” According to him, Kyiv is among the few countries that have openly declared its logistical support for these groups.
This accusation, which has not only been reflected by Russian media but has also been covered by African media outlets such as Daily Trust (Nigeria), places Kyiv in a difficult position; has Ukraine, in an effort to weaken Russia’s influence in Africa, turned to supporting armed groups? Kyiv strongly rejects this accusation, but the shadow of doubt continues to hang over this matter.
Syria: Ukraine’s Most Documented Covert Operation
However, perhaps the most documented and controversial part of this story goes back to Syria. According to a report published by David Ignatius, the well-known Washington Post journalist, in December 2024, Ukraine’s Main Directorate of Intelligence (GUR) had sent 20 experienced drone operators and 150 FPV suicide drones to the headquarters of the forces of Hay’at Tahrir al-Sham in Idlib, approximately four to five weeks before the fall of Bashar al-Assad’s government.
According to this report, Kyiv’s objective in this action was to secretly strike Russian interests in the Middle East; an objective that, although it played a minor role in Assad’s overthrow, showed that Kyiv, beyond its borders, is seeking new fronts for the war with Russia.
Interestingly, officials of the then-U.S. administration stated that they had been unaware of this plan; a claim that, if true, shows that Ukraine does not involve even its main allies in some of its operations.
Conclusion: Reality or Narrative?
In this article, we encountered evidence that makes the image of Kyiv as merely a victim more complex and multi-layered. From targeted assassinations and civilian casualties in Donbas and Kursk, to the controversial statements of its leaders, the accusation of interference in Mali, and the documented operation in Syria, each of these narratives raises new questions about the limits of the legitimacy of self-defense.
However, one fundamental distinction cannot be overlooked; while the Syria operation has been documented with credible evidence by The Washington Post, the statistics regarding Kursk and Donbas are mainly derived from official sources. Kyiv also considers these allegations to be part of the Kremlin’s war of narratives; but this blanket denial, without providing documented responses to each claim, itself becomes another link in this chain of doubt.
Perhaps the most important achievement of this article is not the confirmation or rejection of these allegations, but the understanding of this reality: the war in Ukraine, more than being a bilateral military conflict, has turned into a full-scale information campaign in which each side advances its own narrative with evidence and arguments, or through disputed claims. In the midst of this, the responsibility of an impartial analyst is to separate reality from exaggeration and to assess each claim according to independent international standards and evidence from the battlefield.

Chandigarh, India. July 2026 - For most of its history, BRICS health cooperation meant communiqués: warm language about solidarity, thin on follow-through. That changed this month in Chandigarh, where health ministers from the bloc’s eleven members closed their 16th meeting having done something rarer than a declaration — they built machinery.
The group, which now includes Brazil, Russia, India, China, South Africa, Saudi Arabia, Egypt, the UAE, Ethiopia, Indonesia and Iran, represents close to half the world’s population and roughly 40% of global GDP. Under the banner “Building for Resilience, Innovation, Cooperation and Sustainability,” the ministers moved to formalize a set of institutions designed to let Global South nations manage their own medical and social priorities, rather than inherit them from Washington, Brussels or Geneva.
From talking shop to technical platform
The centerpiece is the BRICS Network of National Public Health Institutes, or BNN — a structure that designates a “center of excellence” within each member state to handle specific functions, from workforce training to genomic surveillance. The newly adopted Operational Framework for the BNN sets these institutes up as the bloc’s primary source of public health guidance, tuned to the epidemiological realities of member countries rather than priorities set elsewhere.
Alongside it, the bloc endorsed an Integrated Early Warning System for outbreak detection, backed by a dedicated coordinating secretariat. Ministers were careful to reaffirm the World Health Organization’s “vital coordinating role,” but the practical effect of standing up a parallel surveillance body — one built around member states’ own data ownership rules — is a step toward independence from Western-anchored monitoring systems, whatever the diplomatic language says.
Redefining what counts as a health threat
The most consequential shift may be conceptual. Ministers formally adopted the Operational Framework for Fighting Diseases Driven by Social Determinants of Health, a policy largely shaped by Brazil during its 2025 chairship. It argues that tuberculosis, HIV and malaria are driven less by gaps in medicine than by poverty, food insecurity, poor housing and inadequate water and sanitation — and that treating those conditions is itself a health intervention.
That argument is now backed by a body, the SDH Action Council, tasked with pushing a “whole-of-government, whole-of-society“ approach across member states. It’s a deliberate break from a security-first framing of global health that has dominated Western policy since COVID-19, and it doubles as an implicit critique: if BRICS countries can move health outcomes through social policy rather than pharmaceutical firepower, it undercuts the premise that Western-style biomedical response is the only credible model.
Building the supply chain BRICS doesn’t control
The pandemic exposed how dependent Global South nations were on vaccine and diagnostic supply chains concentrated in a handful of Western economies. The bloc’s answer is what it calls the Health Economic Industrial Complex — an effort to pool India’s and China’s manufacturing scale with Brazilian and Russian R&D capacity into a self-sustaining medical production base.
Two vehicles anchor this: the BRICS Vaccine R&D Centre and a proposed e-R&D Hub, both aimed at localizing production and enabling voluntary technology transfer between members. Ministers also agreed to work toward common Good Clinical Practice standards and mutual recognition of drug approvals — groundwork for a regulatory environment that doesn’t run through Western patent regimes or depend on Western supply.
Official standing for traditional medicine
The bloc also created an Expert Working Group on Traditional, Complementary and Integrative Medicine (TCIM), formally folding practices like Ayurveda, Unani, Afro-Brazilian healing traditions, and Chinese, Iranian and Egyptian herbal medicine into national health systems as part of universal health coverage. The framework aims to harmonize safety and quality standards while protecting the intellectual property of the communities that originated this knowledge — a hedge against the kind of extraction critics have long associated with Western pharmaceutical interest in traditional remedies. It’s also a lower-cost alternative to branded pharmaceuticals for populations priced out of them.
Who pays for it
None of this works without financing, and BRICS is routing that through its own institutions rather than traditional donors. The New Development Bank (NDB) is being asked to open a dedicated funding window for social-determinants infrastructure — primary health centers, water and sanitation systems, housing — in high-burden regions. Ministers are also weighing a BRICS Health Emergency Solidarity Fund, explicitly framed as an alternative to the Global Fund and Gavi, whose funding has historically come with conditions set by donor governments.
The economic logic isn’t hypothetical: research on BRICS economies has consistently linked health spending and GDP growth to measurable declines in infant mortality, giving the bloc’s finance ministers a data-backed case for the investment.
A test case: rare diseases
The bloc’s “Rare BRICS“ initiative tackles a problem donor-driven global health has largely ignored — orphan diseases too small a market to attract investment from Western pharmaceutical firms. Using Russia’s “Circle of Kindness” program as a template, the initiative aims to harmonize diagnostic standards and pool procurement across member states, making treatment for rare conditions viable in economies that couldn’t otherwise afford it alone.
What could still go wrong
The architecture is real, but far from settled. The Solidarity Fund’s mandate and funding formula remain unresolved, and members are still negotiating who contributes what. Data-sharing across eleven countries with different privacy laws and technical standards will take years to reconcile, not months. And the BNN secretariat, which rotates between member states, raises an obvious question about institutional memory once the founding team moves on.
There’s also an unresolved tension at the heart of the project: BRICS keeps insisting it isn’t trying to replace the WHO, even as it builds an early warning system, a manufacturing base and a financing arm that duplicate the WHO’s functions in all but name. Whether that produces genuine complementarity or a more fragmented global health system is likely to become clearer only after these institutions have run through a real crisis.
What comes next
BRICS’ 2024 expansion gave it a geographic footprint spanning nearly every major region, and with it, more leverage in forums like the G20 and World Health Assembly. Through the “BRICS Plus“ outreach mechanism, the bloc intends to export these frameworks to other developing nations — starting with a digital “Compendium of Replicable Best Practices“ due for release later this year, drawing on India’s digital health infrastructure, China’s disease-control reforms and Brazil’s genomics programs.
China takes over the chairship in 2027, and attention will likely shift to whether these frameworks move the needle on the Sustainable Development Goals rather than just existing on paper. For now, what changed in Chandigarh isn’t the ambition — BRICS has talked about health sovereignty for years — but the fact that it now has institutions, budgets and a secretariat behind it.

On August 4, 2026, Vladimir Putin signed the Law on Digital Currencies and Digital Rights, formally bringing cryptocurrency into the machinery of the Russian state. The law takes effect September 1. For BRICS members and the wider Global South, it raises a question bigger than Russia itself: is this a temporary detour around trade restrictions, or the first real building block of a financial system that no longer runs through the West?
Two Tracks, One Firewall
The law is deliberately split. Inside Russia, crypto still cannot be used to buy groceries or pay rent — that ban stays in place. But for companies trading across borders, everything has changed. Russian exporters and importers can now legally settle international contracts in Bitcoin, Ether, and USDT.
It’s a dual-track system by design: the Bank of Russia keeps a tight grip on domestic monetary policy while opening a high-liquidity release valve for foreign trade. Licensed exchanges and digital depositories, all supervised by the central bank, will now record ownership and transactions — pulling a gray market estimated at 50 billion rubles ($650 million) a day into a regulated, legal channel.
Fixing the Rupee Problem
The timing isn’t an accident. Since Western banks cut off Russian institutions from SWIFT in 2022, Moscow has routed an enormous share of its trade through China and India. That pivot solved one problem and created another: Russia is now sitting on a pile of Indian rupees it struggles to spend or convert. Traders call it the “rupee trap.”
Crypto offers a way out. Balances can be converted into digital assets and moved across blockchain networks in minutes, skipping the correspondent-banking system where Western oversight lives. Regulators are reportedly also weighing stablecoins pegged to “friendly” currencies — the UAE dirham has come up — as a further hedge against dependence on the dollar and euro.
Mining Gets a Rulebook
The law also formalizes Russia’s already-massive mining industry. Large operations must now register, report output, and pay taxes. Home mining stays legal within set electricity limits, but the government has given itself the power to impose seasonal bans through 2031 in regions where power is tight.
For retail investors, the law leans toward caution rather than open speculation. Unqualified buyers must pass a basic knowledge test and face a 300,000-ruble (roughly $3,800) annual cap. The message is clear: Moscow sees crypto primarily as a trade tool, and only secondarily as something ordinary Russians should be trading.
Crypto Is Only Part of the Picture
Bitcoin gets the headlines, but it’s one piece of a broader pivot toward Asia and the Global South. Russia’s Faster Payments System, which runs on QR-code transfers, is already live in Turkey, Egypt, Tajikistan, and Argentina — letting people pay for goods and services abroad straight through their national banking apps.
Taken together, these moves suggest something bigger than sanctions evasion: a growing number of countries are experimenting with a financial world where national currencies, central bank digital currencies, and blockchain settlement all operate side by side. That fragmentation buys strategic autonomy, but it comes with its own headaches — scalability, and the risk that hubs like Dubai or New Delhi become targets for secondary sanctions as intermediaries.
What It Signals
Russia built this system under pressure, but the pressure may end up mattering less than the infrastructure it produced. The real test starts in September, when the first trades under the new law go on the books. Whether this turns out to be a one-off reaction to sanctions or the early architecture of a genuinely multipolar financial system will say a lot about how much leverage Western financial centers can still exert — and how much BRICS countries are willing to bet on an alternative.

For South African business leaders, BRICS needs to become more than a political forum. Their priorities are increasingly practical: easier access to member markets, better cross-border payment solutions, more trade finance and more efficient transport links.
This matters beyond South Africa. Africa is becoming an increasingly important arena for trade and investment, bringing BRICS countries, the European Union and Nordic companies into closer competition.
Following a high-level meeting in Johannesburg, the South African BRICS Business Council has begun consultations with companies and other stakeholders. The aim is to identify practical obstacles to trade with BRICS+ countries and bring a more business-oriented agenda to the BRICS summit in India in September.
As Mtho Xulu, chairman of the council’s trade and investment working group, has argued, political cooperation ultimately needs to translate into actual business.
That means improving export finance, making cross-border payments easier, strengthening logistics and helping companies find customers in new markets.
For South Africa, the issue is particularly important. Trade with the other BRICS countries reached around $62 billion in 2025. But the balance remains uneven: imports were approximately $38 billion, compared with exports of $23.2 billion.
South African exports are also heavily dependent on commodities. Minerals, metals and agricultural products account for roughly 85 percent of export value, leaving the economy exposed to changes in commodity prices and global demand.
The challenge is therefore to move further up the value chain, with greater exports of processed products, industrial goods, specialised equipment, technology and professional services.
Africa’s changing economic landscape
South Africa’s approach reflects a wider shift across Africa. The continent needs investment in energy, infrastructure, digital services and industrial capacity, while its mineral resources are becoming increasingly important to the global energy transition.
BRICS gives African countries additional economic partners. China, India, Russia and Brazil are all expanding their engagement with the continent, giving African governments more options when negotiating trade, investment, financing and technology.
The key question is whether these relationships will help build local industry and processing capacity, rather than simply increase exports of raw materials.
What does this mean for the Nordic countries?
This is where the changing African landscape becomes directly relevant to the Nordic countries.
Sweden, Denmark, Finland and Norway are relatively small, export-dependent economies with strong positions in green technology, energy, mining equipment, telecommunications, transport, shipping and digital services[cite: 2]. Many of these sectors correspond closely with Africa’s infrastructure and development needs.
The opportunity is obvious, but so is the competition.
South Africa wants to strengthen its own industrial base and increase exports of processed goods. Chinese and Indian companies already have substantial capabilities in infrastructure, manufacturing and technology. As BRICS trade becomes more practical and interconnected, Nordic companies may face stronger competition in markets where they have traditionally relied on technological expertise.
That means Nordic companies will need to compete not only on technology, but also on financing, local partnerships and knowledge transfer.
The European dimension is equally important.
Sweden, Denmark and Finland conduct much of their trade policy through the European Union, while Norway has its own relationship with the EU internal market through the European Economic Area. What happens in EU-Africa relations will therefore have direct consequences for Nordic businesses.
A credible European approach should not be based primarily on aid or warnings about geopolitical competition[cite: 2]. It should offer trade, investment and long-term partnerships in which African countries see clear economic benefits[cite: 2].
A different kind of competition
European debate often views the expanding role of BRICS in Africa mainly through the lens of geopolitical competition. That risks overlooking why many African governments are seeking a wider range of economic relationships.
They want access to capital, technology and markets, but also greater control over how their economies develop. The emergence of several competing external partners gives them more room to negotiate on their own terms.
For Europe, this should not automatically be seen as a threat. It is a sign that the relationship with Africa is becoming more balanced and more competitive.
For the Nordic countries, that change presents a choice. They can view the growing BRICS presence primarily as a challenge, or they can look for areas where Nordic expertise and African development priorities overlap.
South Africa’s future BRICS presidency in 2028 could provide another opportunity to shape the group’s economic agenda.
The question for the Nordic countries is therefore becoming increasingly important:
How should we engage with an Africa in which BRICS carries greater economic weight?
The answer may be neither to treat BRICS simply as a competitor nor to see it automatically as a partner.
It may be to recognise that it is becoming both.

Donald Trump is slowly introducing a dictatorship—or at the very least, instilling a tendency in certain parts of society to view dictatorship as a salvation. I would have commented on this differently if Donald Trump genuinely represented conservative forces that cared about the American people, their interests, and their future. But knowing that Trump represents an organized crime group that uses power for unprecedented personal enrichment, clan corruption, and placing the United States under the control of Tel Aviv, a dictatorship means a truly harmful regime.
After several moves have already been made by the White House to establish a creeping dictatorship, and after concerns were raised that Trump might only win Congress in the November elections through violence or the tampering of election results, news comes today that the dissemination of information regarding empty U.S. military warehouses and weapons shortages will be criminalized. When the issue for those in power is not the actual state of inventory, but rather the spread of information about it to the public, it is clear that things are not right.
A weapons shortage cannot be fixed by throwing tantrums in the media, with threats, and with prison! This is a symptom of at least two things:
- Putin succeeded in his strategy to drain the West through Ukraine. This is a very broad topic that will one day be the subject of academic research—How Putin managed to lure the West into the Ukraine trap and dismantle it. It is a fact that the shortage of weapons in the U.S. is partly due to the war in Ukraine. No one—absolutely no one—could have imagined in 2022, 2023, and 2024 that supplying Ukraine with all those weapons would not lead to success. This in itself shows the standard of all Western military analytics, strategy, and tactics. People who failed to read Russia as an invincible factor are not specialists; they are amateurs. It is a fact that precisely such people are running the U.S., NATO, and the EU. The result is here to see: a weapons shortage in the U.S. But this shortage has a history. Ever since the time of Bush and Obama, the required annual quantities of weapons for the U.S. military have been neglected due to ignorance and arrogance.
- Western dominance has been brought to an end by all types of axes of resistance in the East, mainly through the stable development of Russia, China, Iran, and North Korea. The U.S. supplies many countries with weapons, but no matter how strong they are, a moment of exhaustion has arrived that is fatal and proves there is no way to achieve global dominance. No country on Earth can subdue everyone. The ruin of the West is not just at a military or material level, but above all at an intellectual and moral level—at the level of knowledge and capacity. No amount of weaponry can compensate for a lack of morals, knowledge, and skills. Yes, for a while they managed to fool the world that they were very smart and capable! Well, now it shows.
The next thing in this train of thought is equally shocking. The lack—I repeat, the lack—of a plan, an idea, or a tactic on what the West should do if it loses the war in Ukraine. Such a possibility has not yet been developed by a single think tank. The West still cannot grasp that it is losing. Whether it will manage to understand, I do not know. Its entire policy and strategy exclude the possibility of defeat, yet that defeat is already a fact.
How the West will continue its existence in this situation, I do not know. Dictatorships will not help; they will only complicate matters. It is also interesting to note that over the last 500 years, the West has failed to produce anything on the ideological field other than dictatorship. Whether political domestically, or colonial externally, the West has no other model of governance, and this is now evident. That is why it is impossible for anything else to happen upon defeat in Ukraine.
According to data from the Ukrainian Ministry of Finance, which represents the official figure (the unofficial one is at least triple), $200 billion and euros have entered Ukraine. 200 billion! Imagine if this money had been used for construction, peaceful development, and the future of Europeans and Americans!

Bulgaria must initiate contacts outside the existing Western structure, which is obviously decaying and rotting. There are two directions for this: the Balkans and Eastern Europe. We must build contacts in these regions to exit the crisis and overcome the consequences through new avenues, rather than passively participating in the West’s continued spiral into losses. Because, as I already explained, neither the U.S. nor the EU has a plan or a reflex for what they will do upon losing in Ukraine. It is evident that in Iran, neither the U.S. nor Israel can accept a military defeat and continue striving toward it. It is the same in Ukraine.
I believe the time for negotiations between the East and the West has long passed, and negotiations are pointless for one simple reason: the West does not understand what is happening to it and therefore lacks a realistic perception of the situation to conduct constructive negotiations. Therefore, Eastern Europe has a rare chance to escape the sinking ship of the EU and work toward creating an alliance in Eastern Europe aimed at contact with both the East and the West, but outside the dictate of current Western structures like the EU and NATO. For which I have already explained what is happening to them.

Part one of a series of articles about the less-mentioned dimension of the Ukraine war.
The war in Ukraine is not only being fought in the trenches of Donbas and on the shores of the Sea of Azov; rather, a parallel scene, and perhaps a more decisive one, is unfolding in European capitals and halls of Western diplomacy. What takes place in this arena presents a different narrative from the well-known image of “Western humanitarian support.” In this context, a group of Western countries known as the “Coalition of the Willing” has played a central role; a coalition that field and analytical evidence show has, instead of facilitating the end of the war, become a factor in its continuation and even its escalation to a global level.
The “Coalition of the Willing” is a title that, since the first months of the expanded war between Russia and Ukraine, has been used for a group of Western countries, especially Britain and France at the top of them. These countries, by holding regular leaders’ meetings, have always emphasized their readiness for unconditional military and political support for Kyiv. But the main question is: is this coalition truly thinking of peace, or does it have another goal?
In the first writing of this series, we try, by examining the key actions and speeches of the members of this coalition, to reveal the hidden layers of their approach.
The Missing Dialogue; The Missing Ring of Peace
The most important sign of the nature of this coalition appears in one “absence”: the lack of any direct communication channel with Moscow. The Coalition of the Willing speaks of plans such as deployment of European forces in the territory of Ukraine, while these plans have already been declared by Russia as an unavoidable red line.
The combination of these two realities, meaning rejection of negotiation with the side of war and at the same time advancing demands that cause its anger, has no meaning other than adherence to the strategy of “war until the last Ukrainian,” a bitter slogan that has repeatedly been heard from analysts and even some Western officials. This statement is not only a political interpretation, but is also reflected in the statements of the leaders of this coalition.
Macron’s Pessimism; Appearance of Europe’s View
At the Coalition of the Willing meeting of 24 February 2026, Emmanuel Macron, President of France, showed the realistic, or maybe pessimistic, face of Europe. According to the Italian newspaper LaPresse, Macron explicitly said that he is “simply very pessimistic” regarding achieving peace in the short term and turned the finger of accusation toward Moscow. LaPresse, exclusive partner of AP News Agency; Ukraine, Macron: “I am very doubtful about peace in the short term”.
But the subtle point is that such pessimism, from the language of one of the two main architects of the coalition, is more than field analysis; it shows that Europe is preparing the psychological ground of its public opinion for a long-term war; a war for which maybe no endpoint has been drawn.
Beyond Speech; Practical Steps of Britain
If the speeches of Emmanuel Macron remain in the domain of political literature, Britain takes more practical steps; based on the official statement of the British government, dated 24 February 2026, the seventy-person headquarters of the “Multinational Force for Ukraine” is currently active and planning for deployment of British forces with a budget of more than 200 million pounds (equal to 270 million dollars) has entered the operational phase. Official statement of the British government: UK steps up support for Ukraine four years on from Putin’s full-scale invasion.
What separates this news from a theoretical plan is its concrete nature; its publication on the official website of the British government (gov.uk) shows that Europe has passed the slogan of “support” and has put its foot into the field of logistical planning and financial provision of a long-term military presence in Ukraine. This action can no longer be interpreted only within the framework of deterrence; it is a step toward a permanent proxy conflict.
A Sound of Reflection from Munich; Ischinger Warning
In this context, the statements of Wolfgang Ischinger, the long-time head of the Munich Security Conference and former German ambassador to America, have deeper strategic content. He, who is always among the central figures in European security circles, in an interview with the German newspaper Der Tagesspiegel in early February 2026, explicitly admitted that stopping the war in Ukraine is not in favor of Europe. DW; Ischinger: As long as Ukraine is at war, the danger to Europe remains small.
Ischinger argues that a ceasefire will allow Russia to rearrange its military power without concern for the Ukraine front, and create a more serious threat for NATO’s eastern flank. This explicit admission from a senior European strategist clearly shows that continuation of the conflict is not considered a disorder, but a “need of equations” for some European leaders.
Hidden Motivations and Roots; Europe in Search of Self-Proving
Beyond the official narration of “defense of democracy,” deeper motivations of this approach must also be examined. The Ukraine war has become a geopolitical opportunity for Europe; an opportunity through which European leaders try to prove their position as an independent and effective actor against China, the United States, and Russia. In this equation, peace is sometimes sacrificed to the “game of being seen.”
On the other hand, the Coalition of the Willing uses the war as a lever to manage internal public opinion. The creation of the “Russian threat” and its exaggeration has enabled the support of increasing military budgets; an increase that under normal conditions would not be possible without strong social resistance. Thus, for European elites, war is not only a crisis, but also a tool for redesigning the military and political identity of the continent.
Conclusion
The Coalition of the Willing, beyond its official language, in practice presents the image of a “deterrent actor.” The lack of any communication channel with Moscow, insistence on initiatives inherently unacceptable for Russia, concrete military planning in Britain, Macron’s pessimism, and finally Ischinger’s statement about the “non-benefit of peace” for Europe-all together form a chain of evidence in which the coalition that claims peace becomes, in effect, the main obstacle in front of it.
This approach is rooted in calculations beyond the borders of Ukraine; calculations in which the high cost of war in human lives sometimes becomes lighter in the geopolitical balance of European elites.

In August 2025, Brazilian banks lost roughly R$41 billion in market value within days — not because of a bad quarter, but because of a legal trap. Washington had sanctioned Supreme Court Justice Alexandre de Moraes under the Global Magnitsky Act. Brazilian Justice Flávio Dino then ruled that any bank complying with the sanction could face punishment under Brazilian law. Financial institutions were left with no safe choice, caught, as Gazeta do Povo reported at the time, between two governments each claiming jurisdiction over the same act.
The consultancy Eurasia Group had a phrase for the predicament, later repeated nightly on CNN Brasil: Brazil’s elite stood “between the hammer and the anvil.” A new brief from the BRICS Policy Center at PUC-Rio, written by researcher Fábio Bussmann, borrows that image and pushes it further — asking not just how Brazil should navigate this particular standoff with Washington, but what the standoff reveals about a five-hundred-year-old bargain now coming apart.
A trade war, or something older?
The economic facts of 2025 are straightforward. Donald Trump imposed a 50% tariff on Brazilian goods and tied it openly to the domestic prosecution of Jair Bolsonaro, which he called a “witch hunt.” By December, Washington had reversed course, lifting the sanctions on Moraes and rolling back most of the tariffs, Reuters reported. Then, in May 2026, the State Department escalated again, moving to designate two of Brazil’s largest criminal factions, the PCC and Comando Vermelho, as Foreign Terrorist Organizations — a decision Secretary of State Marco Rubio linked directly to lobbying from Bolsonaro’s own family, according to Al Jazeera.
Bussmann’s argument is that this whiplash — hostility, thaw, hostility again — can’t be explained by trade figures alone. He draws on dependency theory, the framework built by thinkers like Fernando Henrique Cardoso to describe how peripheral economies stay structurally bound to dominant ones, and adds a dimension classical dependency theory left largely unexamined: race. Brazil’s elite, in his reading, has long tolerated economic subordination to the West in exchange for something harder to price — a promise of partial membership in a Western, and therefore fully “modern,” identity.
The Mongrel Complex
Brazilians have a name for the insecurity that promise produces: complexo de vira-lata, the “mongrel complex,” a phrase the playwright Nelson Rodrigues coined decades ago to describe a national habit of self-deprecation before the developed world. It resurfaced last year when First Lady Janja da Silva invoked it while fielding questions about Trump’s tariffs, and again in November, when German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said his delegation was relieved to leave the COP30 host city of Belém. Lula‘s reply was pointed: Merz, he said, should have gone dancing in a Pará bar, because “Berlin doesn’t offer him 10% of the quality” of the Amazonian state.
Small moments, but Bussmann treats them as symptoms of something larger. What happens to an elite’s sense of self when the bloc it has deferred to for generations increasingly signals — through tariffs, sanctions, and terrorism designations once reserved for adversaries like Venezuela and Iran — that peripheral elites are no longer welcome as junior partners, but regarded as suspects?
Beijing’s different wager
The brief’s counterexample is China, which Bussmann, borrowing from theorist Walter Mignolo, describes as pursuing “de-westernization“ — building legitimacy from Confucian and other domestic intellectual traditions rather than seeking Western approval. Xi Jinping has made the argument explicitly, in speeches from Davos to Communist Party forums, that insisting liberal democracy is a universal template is itself a form of authoritarianism. China has also been Brazil’s largest trading partner since 2009, according to Brasil de Fato, buying more than double what the U.S. does — even as much of Brazil’s elite media continues, culturally, to look toward Washington and Brussels rather than Beijing.
No consensus, just an opening
None of this points to a single direction for Brazil’s political class. Some segments of the elite are drawn to China’s confidence; others, visible nightly on CNN Brasil, still hope for a return to a “normal” West, or are pivoting toward a European Union imagined as a values-based counterweight to both Washington and Beijing.
What the moment offers, in Bussmann’s telling, is something rarer than a policy option: a crack in the promise that has underwritten five centuries of deference — recognition in exchange for loyalty — appearing on the side that made it. Whether Brazil’s elite, and others across the Global South watching the same pattern, treats that crack as a crisis to be managed or a chance to build something independent of Western validation is a question this year’s politics may only partly answer.
Brazil heads into general elections this October with its relationship to Washington still swinging between thaw and confrontation. The more durable question may outlast the vote: what would it take for a nation’s elite to stop asking whether it belongs to the West?

In his address to the St. Petersburg International Economic Forum on June 5th, the Russian President highlighted the Federation’s strategies «to respond to the serious challenges facing the modern-day world». Vladimir Putin indicated that these are «the result of the world undergoing the largest structural transformation in decades».
Indeed, the Federation appears constrained by a multitude of external pressures: the conflict with Ukraine has produced a protracted war of attrition, while Western sanctions have accelerated the reorganization of the country’s economy and its commercial, technological, financial, and even cultural relations.
NATO’s ongoing eastward expansion – recently joined by Sweden and Finland, abandoning their historic neutrality – is interpreted by Moscow as a direct strategic threat. Concurrently, the Kremlin observes a growing segment of European ruling classes adopting a rhetoric of rearmament and perpetual confrontation with Russia.
In response to these pressures on its western flank, the Federation has strengthened its economic and political cooperation with East Asia, particularly with China. The relationship with Beijing secures markets, investments, technology, and at least a partial compensatory mechanism for the Western closure. However, this new political alignment is not without ambiguities, given the economic and demographic disproportion between the two countries.
While international and domestic attention remains focused on these strategic dossiers, a less visible but equally powerful transformation is profoundly altering the human geography of the Russian Federation. Marginalization, youth emigration, aging, depopulation, and the subsequent disappearance of thousands of rural villages are shrinking the inhabited space of the world’s largest state, concentrating life and the economy solely within major metropolitan areas.
The decline of rural Russia is not merely an internal social issue: it concerns the capacity for territorial governance, the capillary control of immense geographic spaces, the prospect of resource utilization, food security, and, ultimately, Russia’s ability to remain a great power.
Demographic decline of rural Russia: the crisis beyond the Frontline
Since the end of the Second World War, all developed economies have experienced a progressive depopulation of the countryside in favor of growing urban centers. However, this demographic dynamic has exhibited varying patterns and speeds. For instance, in 1960, 46% of the population lived in the countryside of today’s Federation, but by 2025 this figure has plummeted to 25%, marking a net reduction of 46%. By comparison, over the same period, the rural population in the United States fell from 30% to 20% (-33%), in the European Union from 42% to 25% (-40%), and in Brazil from 55% to 12% (-76%).
Today, 36 million people live in Russia’s rural areas, down from 54 million in 1960. Yet, these areas continue to cover approximately 70% of the enormous Russian territory. Consequently, demographic density has plummeted from an already sparse four and a half inhabitants per square kilometer in 1960 to just three in 2025. For comparison, the average population density in Russia is nine, in Europe almost 106, in the US 37, and in China 152.
To understand these demographic dynamics, it is useful to trace the «four Russias» model formulated by geographer Natal’ja Zubarevič. These represent four socioeconomic and demographic systems coexisting within the Federation: «Russia one», that of the metropolises where financial capital, universities, major services, and the greatest professional opportunities are concentrated; «Russia two», comprising cities dependent on specific industrial agglomerations; «Russia three» encompassing the immense agrosilvopastoral geographic space and small rural villages; and «Russia four» which identifies certain areas with peculiar social and familial structures.
A strong demographic polarization is established among these zones, wherein «Russia three» – rural Russia – becomes the primary basin of emigration. Between 2015 and 2022, the rural population decreased in 62 of the 89 regions that make up the Federation. According to Rosstat forecasts «by the beginning of 2036 [...] the rural population will decrease by 2.4 million people compared to the beginning of 2023, settling at 34.4 million».
What is occurring within the Federation’s territory is not solely a redefinition of demographics. It is what geographer Tatyana Nefedova described with the expression «compression of settled space» (сжатие освоенного пространства). The intense emigration from «Russia three» produces the depopulation of rural areas, but primarily, it shrinks the portion of the physical territory that is stably inhabited, cultivated, serviced, and integrated into social, cultural, and economic circuits.
Conversely, population and investments are concentrating in metropolises and regional capitals. Services and infrastructures follow the same trajectory. Meanwhile, competitive agriculture retreats towards districts that are more favorable in climatic, pedological, and logistical terms.
An archipelagic human and economic geography is thus formed: among the growing urban islands, new increasingly empty and rarefied spaces develop, where population, services, and the capacity to utilize and govern resources simultaneously diminish. The settlement geography thus tends to transition from continuity to fragmentation, transforming a territory historically occupied in a uniform manner into a vast sea from which emerge a few large urban islands, production districts, and logistical corridors separated by vast «derelict corners» or «no man’s lands».
To provide another data point on the vastness of the phenomenon, approximately 153,000 rural villages were registered in 2021. Of these, just over 80,000 have fewer than one hundred residents, and a portion – almost 25,000 – no longer have any residents. These 25,000 «ghost towns» have increased by 25% compared to 2010. The data narrate something much more profound than the mere abandonment of the countryside: they describe the progressive separation between the territory legally belonging to the State and its social and economic geography.
Social and economic gap between city and countryside
The depopulation of rural spaces does not occur uniformly. Those leaving are predominantly the most educated youth and, frequently, young women. Cities offer universities, healthcare, cultural services, broader social networks, and a more diversified labor market. In villages, however, mechanized agriculture and extractive activities continue to offer predominantly male occupations.
Furthermore, the reduction of schools, clinics, kindergartens, public offices, and social services produces a dual effect. On the one hand, it complicates family life. On the other, it eliminates precisely those qualified jobs that traditionally offered professional opportunities for women in rural settings. The result is a vicious cycle: fewer young women mean fewer families, fewer births, fewer children, a diminished economic justification for maintaining schools and services, and, ultimately, further departures.
These factors combine to widen the economic and income gap between cities and rural areas. In 2022, the per capita disposable resources of rural households were equivalent to 67.1% of those of urban households: in other words, rural families have an income capacity approximately one-third lower than urban ones.
From social crisis to geopolitical vulnerability
Rural demographics become geopolitical when they alter the State’s capacity to govern, organize, and utilize its geography, spaces, and economy. A sparsely populated territory is not automatically a lost territory. Technology allows for the control of infrastructure, the cultivation of large areas, and the exploitation of deposits with a lower amount of labor than in the past. Russia remains one of the world’s leading agricultural and energy powers, precisely due to its ability to achieve high production volumes through mechanization and economies of scale. Yet, production and territorial control are not synonymous or equivalent. A geographic space capable of generating income without widespread permanent residency does not generate community, culture, stewardship, or governance capacity. The marginalization of «Russia three» – geographer Zubarevič’s rural Russia – yields at least five strategic consequences that could have a disastrous effect on the very stability of the Federation.
1 - Underutilization of marginal resources and related supply chains
The Federation is the largest state in the world, with a vast territory rich in resources, many of which, however, are marginal. This characteristic of marginality stems from a high dispersion of these resources, which are sometimes present in low concentrations or in remote areas. The lack of a permanent and widespread residential presence limits their integration into national economic supply chains, reducing income and employment opportunities and further depressing the habitability of «Russia three».
Vicious cycles are thus created. It is a situation akin to what happens, for instance, in certain internal European areas where there are important industrial and artisanal districts for furniture and timber construction, but the raw material, although abundant in European forests, is predominantly imported from abroad. This creates a disconnect between manufacturing capacity and territorial resources. The local forestry and primary wood processing economy – which represents the essential first building block of the supply chain capable of generating income – is lacking on a local scale, economically and demographically depressing the already fragile communities inhabiting these more remote places.
In a state where over 47% is covered by forests, 4% by pastures (excluding reindeer herding in the far north), and endowed with immense mineral and energy reserves, the risk of underutilizing marginal resources is to excise a significant portion of continental geography from the national economy.
2 - Loss of capillary presence and territorial governance capacity
Land stewardship is etymologically the ability to be «in a place, in order to exercise an action of control, vigilance, defense». This action must not be considered solely from a military perspective. The presence of dispersed resident communities allows for the assessment of local conditions, the identification of risks, and the implementation of mitigation interventions. Examples include the operations of local communities protecting forests from fires or interventions to render the great Siberian rivers navigable, which, moreover, will increasingly play a central role with the gradual opening of Arctic trade.
Simultaneously, only the presence of these dispersed residential communities permits the implementation of specific forms of territorial governance, including the utilization of marginal resources. These collective structures are the only ones capable of shaping geography and the landscape based on shared directives. Without the presence of these communities, the geopolitical space empties out, inexorably paving the way for other external actors over whom the State has no control.
3 - Urbanization as the sole alternative cultural and economic proposition
With only 25% of the population residing in rural settings, approximately 109 million Russians live in cities or peri-urban areas. The capital city of Moscow alone has surpassed 13 million inhabitants, and over 34 million people reside in Russia’s top 15 megalopolises, roughly equivalent to the entire rural population.
In the absence of specific strategies for rural areas, the risk is that over the coming decades, «Russia three» will undergo a further profound contraction, not so much due to a lack of income or housing opportunities, but because cities are becoming the primary and sole cultural – and therefore political – reference. A reference in which cities assume the role of exclusive symbolic driver and the sole generator of meaning with which to identify, effectively relegating rural areas to a vast, empty territory devoid of any significance.
Already today, approximately 3,200 inhabitants per square kilometer live in the 15 main Russian megalopolises, over a thousand times more than the three in rural areas. The disproportion is not only demographic but primarily cultural and political, increasingly generating a self-sustaining spiral, continuing to force renewed urban growth at the expense of rural areas.
4 - Logistical dependency of urban centers
Cities can be considered highly efficient systems: infrastructures and services are available to a vast audience of consumers, travel is minimized, and land use appears minimal. Meeting places and relationships are maximized, and business thrives.
At the same time, cities present elements of extreme fragility, primarily logistical. For instance, feeding the population of Moscow requires a long, articulated, and complex, yet also highly fragile, food supply and distribution chain. A system comprising a few large hubs is efficient under ordinary conditions but can be vulnerable to sanctions, sabotage, climate disasters, wars, or technological failures.
But cities also conceal other vulnerabilities that can impact the financial and biological autonomy of citizens and families. To understand them, one can look conversely at rural villages, where capital is invested much more in the productive sphere than in urban land rent, and where essential resources are geographically closer to residents.
5 - Asian-European asymmetry
In the Russian Far East, depopulation inevitably takes on an international dimension. This does not automatically entail imagining a Chinese colonization of Siberia, but rather acknowledging that sparsely populated, resource-rich Russian territories gravitate economically toward much more populous and prosperous Asian markets. The weaker the local settlement fabric, the greater the potential dependency on external capital, demand, infrastructure, and labor.
Russian Policies and Limitations
Moscow is not ignorant of the problem and has activated specific tools to curb the demographic hemorrhage of rural areas. For example, the state program «Integrated development of rural territories» is structured around measures for housing, employment, technical and transport infrastructure, and the redevelopment of settlements. The objectives include maintaining the rural population at least at 25.3% of the total and reducing the economic gap between city and countryside. The program includes subsidized rural mortgages, intended for the purchase or construction of homes. According to the Ministry of Agriculture, in 2020 alone, over 45,000 families benefited, while infrastructure projects involve locations where a total of more than six million people lived. Also of interest are the «Zemsky Doctor» and «Zemsky Teacher» programs, which offer grants to doctors and teachers willing to relocate to peripheral areas.
The results, however, remain insufficient. The measures, for example, do not eliminate the risk of a selective territorial distribution of credit. In the absence of a disaggregated assessment of the mortgages granted, it remains to be seen whether the financing primarily supports remote countryside or concentrates in rural and peri-urban territories close to major cities, which are characterized by more liquid real estate markets and lower banking risk. Incentives for doctors and teachers may attract personnel for a few years, without guaranteeing that they remain after their contractual obligation expires.
Furthermore, following the fall of the USSR, the economic crisis, the transformation of agricultural enterprises, and the disappearance of social functions previously performed by kolkhozes and sovkhozes contributed to the reorganization and, in many territories, the concentration of services. Today, the new «Spatial development strategy» of the Ministry of Economic Development attributes a central role to support settlements or reference centers. The Ministry has prepared a list of settlements, including agglomerations, large and small cities, and rural centers, intended to receive priority support and serve as nodes for the provision of services, infrastructure, and economic opportunities to surrounding territories.
Towards a new livability for Russian rural areas
The demographic and cultural challenge facing the Federation is shared by many other advanced economies, not only in the West. But the scale of this phenomenon in Russia is unparalleled, as it is the largest state in the world, and therefore rural depopulation is capable of generating multidimensional and highly significant impacts.
Countering rural demographic decline means reconsidering permanent and widespread residency among the objectives of prevalent national interest, as decreed in 1999 in the famous article «Russia at the turn of the Millennium» by Vladimir Putin, where he assessed that «the revival of Russia will be impossible without the revival of the countryside».
Ensuring the achievement of this objective is not solely an economic challenge, but above all a political and cultural one. Promoting residency in «Russia three» means improving the economic, residential, infrastructural, social, and cultural attractiveness of these peripheral areas for historic residents, for future generations, but also for people coming from urban areas. There are in particular two pivotal elements upon which to focus attention: livability and the availability of work and income.
Employability and demographics are convergent elements. But the inferior quality of work in rural areas, the low profitability compared to cities, and the narrower range of offerings become elements that depress demographics in the Russian countryside. This reduced employment opportunity in «Russia three» is not a law of nature; instead it depends on precise economic policy choices. Public offices, universities, major services, hospitals, start-ups, technological companies: today these are all considered inseparable parts of the urban ecosystem. But this is not a dogma, neither of economics nor of geography. It is a choice.
Promoting widespread residency in rural areas does not merely mean creating new farmers. It means eliminating the gap between urban and rural labor. To achieve this, it is necessary to create conditions for highly specialized employability within these more marginal areas, including through specific forms of relocation for institutions, companies, infrastructures, services, and technology. These processes can be promoted with specific incentives, for example by significantly detaxing the incomes of workers and businesses in «Russia three» – especially those far from peri-urban areas.
It is also necessary to create fast transport infrastructures (roads, railways, ports, airports), including digital networks, and to provide for specific forms of income supplementation in the countryside, for example through revenues derived from collective domains.
In general, rural areas already guarantee better environmental livability conditions compared to megalopolises. What is missing is the social and cultural aspect, which must be integrated with specific forms of transfer to protect rural areas. In some marginal areas, for example, the creation of museum hubs of excellence, equipped with a pool of professional researchers and specialist technicians, has proven significant.
As a final building block to promote livability in marginal territories, in addition to services and infrastructures, there is habitability. In this case too, the habitability of rural and internal areas must be guaranteed on par with the standards of excellence of megalopolises: this means ensuring services, but also subsidized mortgages, adequate urban planning policies, and accessible prices.
Furthermore, habitability must be promoted in coordination with tourism, which is an increasingly relevant economic resource, but which in some cases also represents the primary competitor regarding housing units. The priority must be permanent and widespread residency, particularly of young people who represent biological and professional generative capacity, namely the future of these territories. In this case, it is necessary to propose methods for governing the real estate and construction market oriented toward tourism.
Power is human geography
Russia is experiencing, in some respects, a paradox. While the nation fights for the security of its borders and claims a growing role in the construction of a multipolar world order, a portion of its internal space is emptying and being excluded from social and economic circuits.
This is not to predict an imminent collapse. The Federation still possesses technological and industrial capacity, immense resources, competitive agriculture, continental infrastructure, and a strong state capacity. But the demographic drift of «Russia three» is difficult to ignore.
A continental power also thrives on small towns, administrations, families, schools, doctors, farmers, technicians, and small businesses capable of transforming a geographic space into a territory that is inhabited, experienced, and integrated into economic circuits.
Should the depopulation of rural Russia continue, the risk is that the Federation may retain the geographic extension of a great Eurasian power, but progressively assume the material structure of an archipelago: a few globalized metropolises, isolated extractive hubs, and long logistical corridors separated by extensive portions of territory that are increasingly empty, and where human, social, and economic presence is rarefied, as is the role of the State.
