The Italian media coverage of the Palestinian struggle from October 7, 2023, to the Freedom Flotilla:
There is a long-standing and well-established friendship between the Italian and Palestinian peoples, rooted in religious ties through the Catholic Church — particularly with reference to the Holy City of Jerusalem — as well as in political affinities: both during the fascist regime of Benito Mussolini and, subsequently, in the partisan resistance and the legacy of the political left throughout the 1960s, 1970s, and 1980s.
A significant change occurred with the events of October 7, 2023, when Hamas launched a large-scale attack against Israel from the Gaza Strip, leading 1to the capture of 240 hostages and the death of about 900 Israeli civilians. As is well known, the Israeli government reacted quickly with aerial bombardments of Gaza, ushering in a new phase of the conflict with the stated goal of destroying Hamas and freeing the hostages. Since then, the conflict has escalated dramatically, mainly due to Israeli air raids and military operations that have resulted in a very high number of Palestinian civilian casualties. This represented a repeated crime against humanity and a tragedy perceived on an international scale, so much so that it has sparked a popular reaction in many countries. This situation has generated a political, humanitarian, and health crisis, which – since 2024 and particularly in 2025 – has spread beyond the borders of the Gaza Strip, involving more political forces.
Israel’s response, deemed disproportionate, has deeply shaken global civil society. For the first time, war crimes of this magnitude, documented through videos and photographs, are being brought directly to the attention of world public opinion. Demonstrations of solidarity with the Palestinian people have multiplied and gradually intensified around the world. According to data from the Institute for National Security Studies (INSS) at Tel Aviv University, while in the first six days of the war 69% of protests were against Israel and 31% in its favor, the percentage of demonstrations against Israeli policy has now risen to 95% of total demonstrations in 92 countries. The map of the conflict highlights how the United States and Europe represent the main epicenter of this mobilization, despite the opposition of their respective governments.
The Italian case also fits into this picture. Despite weak calls for moderation, the government has adhered to the US line of unconditional support for Israel, even when military operations have mainly targeted civilian infrastructure and defenseless populations. Reflecting, at least in part, a society that is increasingly critical of automatic alignment with US foreign policy strategies and uncertain about the offensive on Gaza, it is mainly young people, particularly students, who have mobilized in support of Palestine.
This study aims to analyze the narrative strategies of the affair and to understand its instrumental political use. First, it analyzes the general situation of the Italian society’s involvement, with a focus on youth and political forces; then it delves into an analysis of communication strategies through social media; as an exemplary case study, the article uses the now iconic story of the Freedom Flotilla; finally, it analyzes the discrepancy between the underlying political elements, between state, military, and popular actors.
Academic literature on youth political participation considers multiple forms of involvement, from electoral behavior to membership in associations and social movements. Youth voting has long been a central theme in political science studies, which have highlighted a lower propensity for electoral participation compared to older generations, especially in consolidated democracies. This gap is attributed to factors such as a reduced perception of political effectiveness, weak connections with political parties, and dissatisfaction with the available alternatives. In Italy, too, young people seem to have followed this European trend (Andretta and della Porta, 2020).
Despite the electoral growth of protest parties over the past decade, which temporarily reactivated previously disillusioned young people thanks to anti-establishment rhetoric, the subsequent ebb has restored centrality to the process of erosion of traditional political structures and cultures. This trend is confirmed by the recent ISTAT survey on political participation, which reports very low levels of trust in politics and a decline of almost 10% in participation among young people aged 14 to 35 in the period 2011-2023.
At the same time, associations continue to represent an important area of political engagement for young people, acting as a veritable ‘school of democracy’ through which young people develop civic skills, social capital, and a sense of political efficacy. Some studies indicate that, faced with a decline in involvement in formal political institutions, young people tend to turn to local community development activities or the defense of human, social, and environmental rights on a global scale. Although there has been a slight decline in association participation, volunteering is still more widespread among young people than among adults.
However, the sector that has attracted the most youth participation in recent decades remains that of social movements. From the Arab Spring to the climate strikes promoted by Greta Thunberg, young people have shown a strong willingness to take collective action. Social media has amplified this phenomenon, facilitating forms of transnational mobilization and coordination, enabling rapid organization, the dissemination of information, and the visibility of issues ignored by institutional politics.
Italy has a long tradition of youth activism, from the student movements of the 1960s and 1970s to the protests against globalization and the No TAV movement in the early 2000s, to the recent environmentalism. Recent studies confirm that young Italians are more inclined to protest than adults and that exposure to new media encourages participation rather than isolating them in virtual spaces. Mobilizations have also gone through recent critical phases: against job insecurity, university reforms, and austerity policies following the economic crisis; subsequently for the climate issue; and, finally, during the pandemic, with the creation of solidarity networks and forms of self-organization to make up for institutional shortcomings.
However, the mobilizations in solidarity with Palestine are developing in a very peculiar context. Unlike previous experiences, they are emerging in a scenario marked by a “moral panic” fueled by the media and political actors, who tend to equate critical positions towards the massacre of Palestinians with anti-Semitic sentiments. While data show that anti-Semitic violence can be traced back to reactionary and extremist individuals, the most significant reaction to the Gaza conflict appears to be the repression of public demonstrations of solidarity with the Palestinian people, justified by the instrumental attribution of anti-Semitic danger to pro-Palestinian movements and translated into particularly restrictive control strategies.
Precisely for this reason, given the highly hostile nature of the context in which these mobilizations are taking place, it is all the more important to analyze the mechanisms that have allowed the emergence of a coordinated protest according to the classic model of social movements, based on the sharing of resources, values, and common goals by groups and individuals connected through informal networks.
Media Coverage of Palestine in Italy: University Protests
Over the past year, civil society organizations committed to supporting the Palestinian cause have intensified their activities in parallel with the deterioration of the political and humanitarian situation. Protests have spread throughout the country, from north to south, with varying intensity, but with a persistence in media coverage that has intrigued scholars due to its atypical nature. What characterized this cycle of mobilization has been its marked youthful imprint, with about 90% of protests originating in schools and universities. In the fall of 2023, the first promoters of the mobilization were left-wing student collectives and university organizations, whose actions were rooted in political visions developed within activist spaces and based on principles such as self-determination of peoples, internationalism, transfeminism, and the rejection of war and colonial policies. Students began to mobilize through sit-ins, marches, and public assemblies, giving rise to the first occupations within universities or in symbolic locations (Dalton 2020). In Pisa, for example, the removal and replacement of the flag produced an image that was destined to circulate globally, fueling the imagination of a nascent transnational youth movement for Palestine.
Several factors explain the widespread youth participation. First, the central role of social media, described as tools that have allowed access to information perceived as distorted by traditional media. The media coverage was significant, with an overabundance of multimedia material constantly inserted into the global information flow, representing, in fact, the first situation of genocide documented directly by the victims on social media. It can be said that this media pervasiveness, indiscriminate in its distribution on conventional and alternative platforms, has at least transformed the younger generations into direct spectators of the conflict (Chironi et al. 2024). A further element is represented by the legacy of previous cycles of youth mobilization, particularly those related to climate justice, which have contributed to the formation of new political sensibilities and a greater propensity for solidarity with Palestine. In Padua, for example, a significant role was also played by the mobilization against gender-based violence, which exploded after the murder of Giulia Cecchettin, an event that generated a wave of indignation and widespread participation, to the extent that it became an iconic national case, requiring strong political involvement on the part of parliamentary forces.
Parallel to the expansion of the protest, there was a political attempt to reduce the movement's room for maneuver by resorting to a dynamic of “moral panic” (della Porta 2024). This was evident, for example, in February 2024, when, on the one hand, critical positions expressed in the cultural sphere were excluded and, on the other, repressive strategies were adopted by the police during student demonstrations. In particular, police repression was repeated until the acute phase of the conflict ended, which we identify for convenience of study with the achievement of the Trump peace agreement.
According to PEA data available at the end of 2024, coercive police interventions occurred in 17% of recorded cases, a percentage that drops to 8% when students were not present. Although such interventions were sometimes justified by fears of a supposed resurgence of anti-Semitism, this narrative was strongly contested by students, who reiterated the distinction between criticism of Zionism and hostility towards the Jewish community. At the same time, the solidarity generated around the students helped to broaden the scope of the mobilization and contain the intensity of state repression, especially with the emergence of camps and the spread of protests.
In a context characterized by strong constraints and hostility, the pro-Palestinian student mobilization has emerged as a phenomenon of particular analytical relevance, as it demonstrates the ability of young people to build coordinated forms of collective action through informal networks, the sharing of common values and objectives, and the strategic use of available resources. It is emblematic and significant that the Italian mainstream media have begun to use a dedicated linguistic category, recognized by the term “Pro-Pal,” a contraction of “in favor of Palestine.” This label will be fundamental in analyzing the instrumental contrast with anti-Semitism.
Since its inception, the pro-Palestine movement has been characterized by the use of a heterogeneous and pluralistic repertoire of action, where alongside traditional and conventional forms of protest—such as assemblies, signature collections, leafleting, and information stands—more demonstrative methods have emerged over time, including marches, large-scale national strikes, and symbolic initiatives. Subsequently, especially during the most intense phases of mobilization, direct action practices were added, such as sit-ins, roadblocks, event disruptions, occupations, and university camps. These actions were explicitly aimed at disrupting daily life and drawing attention to what United Nations reports have defined as genocide. However, it was the tents set up on university campuses that became the most evocative symbol of the movement.
In April 2024, a wave of university occupations spread from the United States to quickly reach Europe (Paris, Lausanne, Amsterdam, Madrid, Geneva, Grenoble, Lyon, Lisbon, Barcelona, Brussels, Berlin, Krakow, Ljubljana, among others), but also Australia, Argentina, Brazil, Canada, and Japan. The week of the 76th anniversary of the Nakba, commemorated on May 15, was an opportunity to launch the so-called “student intifada” in Italy as well. On May 8, in Bologna, students set up a camp for Palestine, which quickly spread to numerous universities in large and small cities, from Palermo to Turin, from Naples to Bari, passing through Rome, Milan, Pavia, Parma, Siena, Cosenza, and many others. This widespread symbolic action had a boomerang effect in Italy, where, following the example of their foreign counterparts, students at many universities began residential protests and occupations of university buildings (Mendelsohn et al. 2024).
It is curious how even in the world of state schools there has been a strong awareness of the Palestinian struggle, with particular reference to the ongoing genocide, which has been identified as a serious issue deserving of moral condemnation.
This phenomenon of widespread involvement of young people through coordinated action networks deserves to be examined through the lens of social movement theory, which emphasizes that collective identity formation occurs when individuals recognize shared claims and mobilize through communication channels. The role of informal networks in facilitating this coordination is particularly significant in the Italian context, where university students have exploited both physical assemblies and digital platforms to build what scholars call “networked publics,” spaces where information circulates and collective contexts develop independently of institutional control. The transition from individual awareness of the Palestinian crisis to organized collective action thus reflects a broader pattern observable in contemporary youth activism, in which social media platforms function not only as disseminators of information, but also as crucial infrastructures for building solidarity and sustaining momentum among geographically dispersed groups. This infrastructure proved essential in Italy, where decentralized student collectives were able to coordinate simultaneous actions across multiple universities while maintaining ideological coherence around the fundamental principles of anti-imperialism and the defense of human rights.
The coordination of student mobilizations across geographical boundaries and institutional contexts reveals sophisticated narrative-building mechanisms that go far beyond spontaneous digital expression, including deliberate strategies of information dissemination and counter-framing that deserve detailed examination. To understand these mechanisms, it is essential to recognize how narrative strategies function in contemporary media environments as tools for both mobilization and contestation (Zhai et al. 2025). In the Italian context, pro-Palestinian student movements have employed strategic framing routines that have transformed individual grievances into frames for collective action, using what scholars identify as diagnostic framing—articulating the problem of Palestinian suffering as a humanitarian crisis requiring an immediate moral response—along with prognostic framing that proposes specific solutions such as university divestment campaigns and changes in institutional policies (Mendelsohn et al. 2024). These schemes were not developed organically, but rather constructed strategically through deliberate narrative choices disseminated across multiple media platforms, from university assemblies to social media posts, creating what communication scholars call “cross-media storytelling” strategies that maintain thematic consistency while adapting content to the possibilities offered by individual platforms.
The effectiveness of these strategies depended crucially on emotional resonance, with narrative formats emphasizing human suffering and testimonials generating significantly higher engagement and comments in favor of the movement than expository presentations of political arguments. At the same time, however, counter-narratives emerged through the official communication channels of institutions and the government, which used what has been termed “strategic framing” toward delegitimization, in which pro-Palestinian activism was systematically recategorized through linguistic categories such as “Pro-Pal,” which framed such movements as potential vectors of anti-Semitism rather than as legitimate political expression (Mosca and Quaranta 2017).
This discursive contestation operated through multiple channels: traditional media selectively emphasized incidents of disruption while downplaying substantial engagement with the movement's demands; political actors issued statements equating criticism of Israeli military operations with hostility toward Jewish communities; and police interventions were justified through narratives that portrayed student protesters as security threats. The instrumental use of “moral panic”—a sociological phenomenon in which media, political actors, and law enforcement collectively construct exaggerated narratives of threat around particular groups—functioned as a form of information warfare designed to fragment the movement’s coalition potential and reduce public sympathy.
However, the students’ counterstrategy involved narrative construction work: explicitly distinguishing between anti-Zionism (criticism of state policies) and anti-Semitism (hostility toward Jewish people), repeatedly articulating this distinction in assemblies, on social media, and in direct engagement with skeptical observers. Such a distinction reflected a sophisticated understanding of framing effects, namely the recognition that the way issues are presented linguistically and visually shapes public interpretation and political attitudes. The proliferation of visual images—photographs and videos of student encampments, police interventions, and Palestinian suffering circulating across multiple platforms—constituted a form of visual narrative strategy that conveyed meaning independent of textual explanation, transforming abstract political claims about genocide into concrete and emotionally engaging experiences.
The encampment phase marked a turning point in the nature of the protest: from a widespread but intermittent phenomenon, it transformed into a more structured and continuous movement; its composition changed, its repertoire of action expanded and radicalized, its internal organizational forms were redefined, and the pace of the struggle intensified and accelerated. On the one hand, there was active involvement from the student base, which began to mobilize, with self-managed assemblies, even on a daily basis, and the inclusion of universities traditionally less inclined to protest, such as the European University Institute in Florence, the IUAV in Venice, and UniDolomiti in Belluno. On the other hand, a form of national coordination was established, with university camps linked together through weekly online meetings.
The mobilization also went beyond the student body, involving other members of the university community—researchers, teachers, administrative staff—giving rise to an unprecedented alliance between different roles, which fostered broader and more sustained pressure and prompted demands for universities to take responsibility for their “complicity with war.” One of the most obvious manifestations of this politicization was the national opposition to the MAECI call for scientific and technological cooperation between Italy and Israel, which became a focal point of the protest and led numerous universities to withdraw their participation.
The expansion of the movement inevitably also affected the role of political organizations: while on the one hand more identity-based dynamics emerged, on the other the plurality of the movement encouraged an attempt at unity, accompanied by an awareness of the need to provide tools without representative pretensions, rethinking established organizational methods. In fact, consideration was given to the presence of young people who had never participated in political activities, emphasizing the need to collectively build new forms of occupation of public space.
Political demands and instrumental use
At the same time, the camp was interpreted not only as a form of protest, but also as an expression of prefigurative politics, a space in which the rhythms of everyday life and forms of collective organization were reworked, offering students the opportunity to reclaim university spaces and create an alternative to the alienating environment experienced in the departments. The daily management of the camp posed logistical and relational challenges, requiring a progressive redistribution of responsibilities. “Fuchsia” spaces were also created, dedicated to the prevention of harassment and emotional support, promoting community building and mutual care, partly attributable to the previous work of transfeminist movements. LGBT+ activism played an active role in the battle.
In Sicily, student mobilization merged with the campaign against the Strait Bridge, a project defined by the government as strategic infrastructure for military logistics but interpreted by activists as emblematic of war-oriented capitalist development. The project was also linked to protests against repression. In Veneto, the links between the liberation of Palestine, pacifist activism, and climate protection appeared even more immediate, thanks to the multiple affiliations of many activists with social centers in the Northeast and with the Venice Climate Camp. Overall, through a strategy of convergence, the youth movement for Palestine has managed to bring together different demands and engage the city, intersecting with existing struggles and movements.
This represented a new element in the dialectic of the struggle for Palestine: if in past years participation was characterized by the political banners of opposing parliamentary factions and militant movements, now the opposition has found a sort of common ground, which, however, appears unclear or, probably, open to broad interpretation. This is where the purely political element comes in. In previous years, support for Palestine had been driven primarily by left-wing parliamentary and extra-parliamentary parties, where the battle for Palestine and against Zionism was seen as part of the anti-fascist struggle and in the context of war, recognized as one of the main divisions in the contemporary world. The characterization was that of “Red Palestine,” as a partisan struggle against the occupying oppressor. On the right-wing political side, the division was more marked, between an openly Zionist faction and a minority anti-Zionist faction, which supported Palestine because it was opposed to Zionism as a movement and to Israel as a state, claiming the Palestinian struggle as a nationalist struggle. The current configuration that we want to highlight, on the other hand, has a less political connotation in the ideological sense and a more political one in the pragmatic sense. In fact, there is no official statement on what unites the two distinct factions, which are probably united by anti-Zionism, which is reiterated as distinct from anti-Semitism, and by the struggle against what represents the interests of Western powers with regard to the self-determination of the Palestinian people.
This last passage clearly highlights the intersectional approach adopted by the university movement for Palestine: an intersectionality that serves both as an interpretative lens and a relational method, and which draws on other struggles, such as feminist, anti-militarist, environmentalist, and decolonial struggles. This is why, in demonstrations in the streets, strikes, and universities, the Palestinian flag has often been flown alongside the flags of the progressive movements mentioned above.
One of the tools of colonialism, according to activists, is to exploit the prejudices of Western ideology, according to which the rich world embodies freedom of thought, rights, and civilization, while the Global South—and in this case the Arab community—represents its opposite. This colonial imagery finds its maximum expression in Israel, through narratives such as “Israel is the only democracy in the Middle East” or “the only place where rights exist.” According to activists, this colonial thinking leads to the representation of Palestinians and Muslims in general as inherently misogynistic and homophobic, justifying their domination in the name of Western liberal values. While recognizing that in the Middle East, as elsewhere, there are groups committed to the feminist cause, they point out that feminism is often exploited to legitimize Israel. Furthermore, they emphasize that there can be no salvation for women and queer people under bombardment, stressing the priority of ending the conflict in order to create real conditions for discussion about rights.
How the Pro-Pal movement worked in a communicative war strategy
This curious mixture does not seem to have been examined through a careful and detailed analysis of the cultural, religious, and political values that belong to Palestine, the Arab world in general, and Islam. In a certain sense—and this is the most interesting point—the Palestinian struggle has been ‘Westernized’, becoming integrated into the Western mindset through its languages, symbols, and values. A useful first reference is Giacomo Buoncompagni’s study, published in 2024, which analyzes how the Italian media represented Israel in the period leading up to the escalation of 2023. The author observes that even before the conflict, the narratives present in public discourse tended to favor an imaginary centered on security and the terrorist threat (Buoncompagni 2024). This is important because it shows that many of the discursive structures that were reinforced in the following months did not arise out of nowhere. A framework already existed that made the subsequent polarization more natural and prepared the public to view events through the lens of emergency and defense.
From the point of view of information warfare, the mixture seen ‘on the ground’ in the protests was reflected in the narrative constructed by the Western media. With the outbreak of hostilities, the circulation of manipulated or misleading content increased throughout Europe. In this vein, Hameleers shows that visual disinformation was a central tool of information warfare. According to the author, most of the images or videos circulated during the conflict were not completely false, but decontextualized in time or space, and he observes that visual disinformation consists mainly of existing footage that is decontextualized in a misleading way (Hameleers 2025). In Italy, this dynamic had a significant impact because emotionally powerful content circulates rapidly on platforms such as WhatsApp, X, and TikTok. The power of images, presented as immediate and irrefutable evidence, often prevented critical analysis by the public.
In addition to visual manipulation, the construction of the narrative in Italy was based on selective use of language. A 2025 study found that many European media outlets employed rhetoric aimed at implicitly supporting Israeli military actions. The authors write that some of the media coverage used manipulative rhetoric and misleading facts to present Palestinian groups under the exclusive category of terrorism (Wafi and Zaini 2025). In Italy, this dynamic was visible in the systematic choice of labels such as “militants,” “terrorists,” or “jihadists” to refer to Palestinian fighters, while Palestinian civilian victims often appeared only as anonymous numbers. The way in which those involved are named influences moral perception. If one side of the conflict is defined through a lexicon that evokes fear and aggression, the other side automatically appears to be engaged in a form of defense.
Alongside linguistic selection, another relevant element is the management of empathy in narratives. In most Western media, Israeli victims are often presented with a name, a story, and a recognizable face, while Palestinian victims are represented by abstract figures. According to the authors, this asymmetry produces a form of “emotional distance” that makes it more difficult to perceive Palestinian suffering in its concreteness (Schepens et al. 2025). In Italy, this phenomenon manifested itself in the different treatment given by television news and newspapers in their descriptions of the victims on both sides. Personal stories, especially in the early days of the conflict, came almost exclusively from the Israeli side. The dominant narrative thus offered an implicitly unbalanced picture that pushed the public toward a one-sided moral interpretation.
However, disinformation about the conflict has not been linear over time. Reports from the Italian Digital Media Observatory (IDMO) show a fluctuating trend. In 2025, for example, the Israeli-Palestinian conflict accounted for almost a quarter of all cases of disinformation verified in October of that year (IDMO 2025). In 2024, the percentage was lower but still significant, especially in the months immediately following the start of military operations, when the topic accounted for over 12 percent of fact-checking cases (IDMO 2024). These data suggest that the information war depends heavily on peaks in media attention and developments in the conflict. When events become more dramatic, the production and circulation of manipulated content automatically increases.
It should also be noted that the Italian narrative is not isolated but part of a global network. Hameleers states that the construction of partisan truths through images and emotional content is now a transnational phenomenon affecting various international conflicts (Hameleers 2025). The study by Wafi and Zaini confirms that many European media outlets have adopted similar strategies, despite political and cultural differences between countries (Wafi and Zaini 2025). Consequently, dynamics that respond to broader trends in the Western information system can also be observed in Italy. The narrative is not only constructed within the country but is fed by the same sources, the same images, and the same interpretative frames that circulate in other contexts.
While sharing a common matrix with other European countries, Italy also has its own specific characteristics. The issue of immigration, the presence of communities of Middle Eastern origin, and a strong political sensitivity linked to internal security have contributed to amplifying certain narratives. In many cases, the conflict in the Middle East has been interpreted through codes that recall the debate on the management of migration flows, alleged cultural incompatibility, and the risk of radicalization. The war has thus been used as a metaphor for internal Italian issues and as a tool to fuel fears or political identities.
The consequences of these strategies are significant. The polarization of public debate has become more intense. Digital communities have quickly divided into opposing camps, often unable to engage in dialogue with each other. The dehumanization of Palestinian victims has reduced awareness of civilian suffering (Al Shebli et al. 2025). Furthermore, the frequent use of selective doubt about Palestinian sources has undermined confidence in information documenting war crimes or violations of international law. All this has made it more difficult to form an informed and aware public opinion. Nevertheless, the often-confusing mix of information and the resulting construction of an ambiguous narrative framework confirms that the information war remains a structural problem for the collective West and an equally significant problem for the Palestinian struggle itself, which is exploited according to the narrative utility of political forces in order to neutralize its ideological identity.
The case of the Freedom Flotilla and the disarticulation between Islamic countries, the Resistance, and Palestine
The Freedom Flotilla incident, which emerged as a central symbol of this broader movement, exemplifies how particular events become focal points of the narrative; the flotilla’s journey to Gaza, its interception, and the subsequent student mobilization around its symbolism created what narrative theorists identify as a main narrative, a general story that integrates multiple subordinate narratives into coherent frameworks of meaning-making that explain past events, justify present actions, and orient future possibilities. It is here that we can accurately observe the above.
The dimension of the information war, as mentioned, intensified when state and institutional actors sought to neutralize the narrative power of the movement through censorship, police surveillance, and restrictive administrative policies—tactics that paradoxically amplified the movement’s visibility by generating further events (police interventions, administrative repression) that confirmed the movement’s counter-narrative about institutional hostility toward dissent. This dynamic reflects broader patterns in digital media environments, where attempts at narrative suppression often generate boomerang effects, in which efforts to contain information instead accelerate its circulation and amplify its perceived significance (Zhao et al. 2024).
The information war was therefore not unidirectional, but rather constituted a contested terrain in which multiple actors deployed competing narrative strategies, each attempting to establish definitional authority over the meaning of events and the legitimacy of political actors, with the outcome determined not only by the accuracy of information, but also by the relative ability of different actors to reach audiences, mobilize resources, and construct emotionally engaging narratives in line with the public’s existing worldviews and political commitments. It is therefore useful to retrace the historical process of the narrative construction of the Freedom Flotilla. In its recent version—quite distinct from the 2010 attempt—the Flotilla began as an officially popular initiative to support the Palestinian population with humanitarian aid. Unlike previous missions, this new Flotilla was organized by a broader coalition of NGOs, doctors, activists, and parliamentary delegations, with the stated goal of delivering essential aid and denouncing the impact of the blockade on the healthcare system and the living conditions of civilians.
Between spring 2024 and summer 2025, several attempts to set sail were delayed or thwarted by diplomatic pressure. The ships, coming from Mediterranean ports and supported by international networks, carried medical supplies, food, water purifiers, and emergency equipment. The Flotilla was primarily symbolic in nature. The organizers called it a “civilian bridge” to highlight the suffering in Gaza and openly challenge the restrictions imposed by Israel.
In 2024, one of the main ships, then named Sumud Flotilla, carrying medical personnel and international observers, was stopped in international waters by Israeli naval units, which prevented it from advancing towards Gaza. Despite the lack of armed clashes, the operation generated diplomatic tensions and protests in various European countries. In 2025, the coalition attempted a new mission, this time with a modified route and a broader composition of organizations. This voyage also ended in interception, but it attracted more media attention because it was documented live by journalists on board. The Freedom Flotilla 2024-2025 did not achieve its goal of breaking the blockade, but it had a significant symbolic impact. The missions brought the humanitarian crisis back to the forefront of public opinion, fueled the debate on international maritime law and the proportionality of security measures, and showed how civil societies and non-governmental actors are still trying to intervene where traditional diplomacy fails.
The way in which the Flotilla was reported by the Italian media followed an irregular pattern. We can distinguish a first phase, relating to the first attempt in 2024 with the Sumud Flotilla, in which the initiative was demonized by the mainstream media as a non-institutional initiative, not attributable to a single international actor and not easily framed within a political context. Subsequently, the media narrative changed as a result of widespread popular support and intensifying protests by citizens. The Flotilla, now in its second attempt under the name Freedom, became a symbol of a humanitarian effort that transcended political and religious ideologies, while for Israel it meant increased criticism on a global scale, as military intervention against a humanitarian convoy represents a serious violation of international law.
At this point, the mainstream media, which tended to be against the Pro-Pal movement, began an operation to appropriate the cognitive and informational domain of the struggle for Palestine. The Freedom Flotilla, being a significant international case, was absorbed by the media system, and the narrative of the Palestinian struggle became subject to manipulation by the institutional media system. It was at this stage that many Italian politicians expressed their support for the Palestinian cause, abandoning their support for Israel only temporarily in order to exploit the wave of indignation for their own political gain.
What happened in parallel was the defusing of the protest and the gradual dissolution of the so-called Pro Pal movement. This happened gradually, until it was completely neutralized around October 2025, when the peace agreement proposed by US President Donald Trump was reached. At that point, the mainstream media narrative changed again and the Pro Pal demands were abandoned, offering an interpretation of events aimed at rehabilitating Israel and its role in the region and on the world stage. It should be noted that the dissolution of the Pro Pal movement was also made possible by its heterogeneous constitution. At least as far as the Italian case is concerned, which we have discussed in this analysis, there is a marked discrepancy between three main elements: what the Islamic countries that support this battle are; the Axis of Resistance as a military instrument of some of those countries; Palestine as a political, cultural, and religious entity (Henarni and Surwandono 2024).
In this case, the Italian public does not believe that the three elements constitute a continuity, either formal or ideal. With regard to the Muslim-majority countries that support the Palestinian cause, the Italian Pro Pal movement has been characterized by a strong opposition to the principles of Islam, the lifestyle, symbols, and customs of the Islamic tradition. In particular, the demonization of the Islamic Republic of Iran has never ceased, except during the brief period of the twelve-day war in 2025, when a minority of the Italian media supported Iran against Israel’s military aggression, but with the reservation that this support was only in reference to the military aggression, not because of Palestinian support.
As for the Axis of Resistance, it has been continuously demonized and deliberately dissociated from the Palestinian struggle. In particular, the media have continued to portray the Axis as one of the causes of the outbreak of the conflict, not as a solution, nor as an element in favor of Palestine and its liberation. This has been evident since October 7, 2023, and even more so as the conflict has continued, with Western media supporting Palestine, but only in a defensive logic against Israeli aggression, while consistently condemning Hamas and all other armed resistance movements, including Hezbollah, even during the period when Israel attacked Lebanon to counter the activities of the Axis of Resistance (Majid et al. 2025; Al Shebli et al. 2025).
In a sense, the Italian narrative deliberately excluded elements representing the Palestinian struggle. In this way, the struggle was partly distorted and transformed into an ideological battle, just like many other Western ideological battles. This is why some ideological movements that are distant from the values of Islam, but also of Arab Christianity, such as LGBT+ movements, were able to join the Pro-Pal movements. By distorting the real reasons and aims of the Palestinian struggle, it has become, in the eyes of Italians and Westerners in general, a battle of an oppressed minority that needed a voice in the media arena. The entire ideological and religious apparatus of the Palestinian struggle has been excluded from the Italian public’s narrative and understanding.
In conclusion to this analysis, we can say that the communicative frame of the Palestinian struggle in Italy, from October 7, 2023, to the present, has been characterized by three historical phases:
- contrast: the presence of Hamas and the Zionist tendency of the Italian media refused to observe the situation of the Palestinian struggle from the point of view of law and international relations, favoring criticism of Palestine and limited events;
- due to the exponential increase in protests and popular support for Palestine, with the escalation of genocide and other divisive events such as the attack on Lebanon and the attack on Iran, the Italian media adopted a strategy of acquisition and contamination of the cognitive and informational domain, saturating the construction of the narrative framework;
- gradual decrease in media coverage, until the peace agreement brokered by Donald Trump, returning to a politically correct narrative towards Israel and Zionism.
On the ideological and identity level embodied by the population, in parallel, we have had equally evident phases:
- growing participation in the name of opposition to war and ethnic discrimination, including the case of the Flotilla humanitarian expedition;
- exploitation of the political opportunity to integrate other types of social struggles;
- dissolution of the movement at the end of the hostilities, abandoning the Palestinian cause as something limited to specific events and not as something ideological and existential.
The lack of awareness of the existential and ideological dimension of the Palestinian struggle, together with the artificially maintained dissociation between Islamic countries in conflict—the Axis of Resistance—Palestine, as well as careful media management, meant that the struggle for Palestine ultimately became just another social struggle, motivated by the Western model of human rights and, therefore, adaptable to the mentality and political utility of the West.

Between May and June, a series of drone attacks carried out by Ukrainian forces against Russian territory and cities in the Donbas region occupied by the Russian Army achieved notable success, prompting speculation across international media about whether Kyiv might be altering the balance of a conflict that, since its outbreak in February 2022, has largely favored Moscow.
One of the most significant attacks in this series took place on June 18, when a Russian oil refinery near the capital was struck, along with several civilian targets. The incident followed a pattern seen in Ukrainian operations, which have alternated between attacks on civilian localities and facilities belonging to Russia’s energy infrastructure.
According to Marco Fernandes, a geopolitical analyst and member of the BRICS People’s Council, “over the past two or three months, Ukraine has clearly increased the effectiveness of its drone strikes against Russia, hitting numerous oil refineries. This has affected the country’s refining capacity, which is already facing fuel shortages in some regions and export suspensions.”
The scholar also notes that Kyiv recently carried out “more daring attacks against Moscow and St. Petersburg, as well as actions that can clearly be described as terrorist attacks, such as the strike on a college dormitory in Starobilsk (Luhansk), which killed 21 young people, most of them female pedagogy students.”
“One hypothesis advanced by some analysts is that this increased effectiveness may be linked to the growing use of artificial intelligence tools. The role of Palantir, a company that today operates almost as an extension of the Pentagon, on the Ukrainian side is well known. The fact that some factories have been relocated to European countries, making them more protected from Russian attacks, is also an advantage. In addition, more European manufacturers are now producing drones for Kyiv,” he argues.
International affairs analyst Rose Martins, however, contends that “Ukraine has intensified attacks on Russian territory and has struck the country’s energy infrastructure, but it is necessary to assess whether this has resulted in a shift on the battlefield or a weakening of Russian military power. The answer is no.”
“Russia still enjoys battlefield superiority and is not facing serious problems in the supply of military equipment. Another aspect of this development is its possible political consequences for Putin, since it disrupts the daily lives of the population. However, there is still no indication that the Ukrainian attacks have translated into political problems for him,” Martins assesses.
Fernandes, in turn, points out that “while it is true that the new wave of Ukrainian drone attacks has opened a new chapter in the war and caused unprecedented damage inside Russian territory, it is equally clear that Russia continues to advance, albeit slowly, in its conquest of territory in the Donbas. Likewise, its recent large-scale attacks on Kyiv and other Ukrainian cities have certainly inflicted significant losses on both urban and military infrastructure.”
Ukraine’s Domestic Challenges
Another counterpoint to the increase in Ukrainian operations is the country’s “loss of financial support from the United States, even if this has been partially offset by increased European backing,” which Fernandes describes as “a blow to Kyiv’s ambitions.”
“At this stage of the game,” he says, “the country has accumulated debts that may take decades to repay, if they are ever repaid at all. It has lost hundreds of thousands of soldiers (perhaps even millions), and millions of citizens have left the country. The economy has already been devastated, and whatever remains of the country will be carved up by BlackRock and conglomerates of American and European companies.”
In the analyst’s view, “the numerous corruption scandals involving the government’s inner circle, which continue to emerge, only further complicate Zelensky’s situation, which could end very badly once all of this is over.”
“Finally, no image better illustrates the country’s tragic condition than the frequent videos showing members of the Ukrainian Armed Forces literally abducting citizens from the streets, or even from the doorsteps of their homes in front of their families, and forcibly sending them to the front lines. You cannot win a war when your soldiers have been kidnapped into fighting it. Ukraine long ago ceased to be a sovereign actor and has become merely an instrument of the West in its crusade to weaken Russia,” he adds.
Changes in the Political Leadership
Martins also highlights recent changes within the Ukrainian government as an indication that, despite the positive optics created by recent attacks, the problems inside President Volodymyr Zelensky’s administration remain a challenge.
Among these developments, the most significant was the crisis in the Ministry of Defense, marked by the departure of Mykhailo Fedorov after only seven months in office. As one of Ukraine’s most popular politicians, his dismissal sparked protests not only in Kyiv but also in several other cities across the country.
“A reshuffle is underway in Ukraine, including the replacement of the defense minister, who was responsible for devising and implementing this strategy of medium- and long-range drone attacks. It remains to be seen who will replace him and what implications that will have for the country’s war strategy,” the analyst emphasizes.
The Russian Economy
The assaults launched by Kyiv in recent weeks have not gone unanswered by Moscow, although the response has not always been immediate, unlike in previous stages of the four-and-a-half-year conflict between the two countries.
According to Fernandes, “the increase in Russian losses caused by Ukrainian attacks in recent months has virtually compelled Russia to escalate its attacks against Ukraine.”
“In fact, over recent months there appears to have been growing pressure within certain sectors of Russian society for more forceful strikes against Ukraine, and even against some European countries. The Kremlin has signaled that it does not dismiss such a possibility,” he observes.
Another factor to consider is the growing distrust within Vladimir Putin’s government regarding the role of the United States as a mediator in any potential settlement, as well as the promise made by U.S. President Donald Trump to pursue a definitive end to the war.
“It is in the interests of Washington and Brussels to keep Moscow trapped in an endless war, with limited financial and human resources available. That leaves Russia with less capacity to invest in more strategic objectives, such as reindustrialization and a foreign policy aimed at strengthening the BRICS bloc and other initiatives,” Fernandes argues.
In that context, the analyst underscores what he sees as warning signs in the current state of the Russian economy.
“After three consecutive years of reasonably strong growth, with GDP expanding by 4.1% in 2025, the economy is struggling this year. GDP contracted by 0.2% in the first quarter, and Russian forecasts for the full year are far from optimistic. Growth may end up below 1%,” he notes.
According to Fernandes, “this situation is increasing tensions within the country, further exacerbated by the growing number of Ukrainian attacks. It could result in greater pressure on the Kremlin to adopt more decisive military measures against Kyiv, with the aim either of resolving the conflict militarily or finally compelling Ukraine to sit down and negotiate an end to the war.”

China has been expanding its financial infrastructure in Africa to reduce its dependence on the U.S. dollar, enabling the trade of goods and services through African currencies and the Chinese yuan.
Despite these developments, the use of the yuan (renminbi) remains limited across the continent, and so-called de-dollarization is still not a realistic prospect, even from the perspective of authorities in Beijing.
At the end of June, the People’s Bank of China (PBOC) authorized direct yuan-denominated payments through Standard Bank, Africa’s largest banking group, headquartered in South Africa, under a partnership with the Industrial and Commercial Bank of China (ICBC).
“The partnership places us in a unique position to handle Chinese renminbi (RMB), enabling businesses to make and receive RMB payments for trade settlement and facilitating commerce between Africa and China,” Standard Bank said in a statement. The bank operates in 21 African countries.
China is currently Africa’s largest trading partner. Between 2000 and 2024, trade between China and the continent grew at an average annual rate of 14%, according to China’s General Administration of Customs (GAC).
On May 1, China decided to eliminate import tariffs on African products, a measure expected to further strengthen trade ties between the Asian giant and African nations.
Yuan Still Plays a Minor Role
Geopolitical analyst Marco Fernandes, of the BRICS People’s Council, stated that the yuan’s advance in Africa remains modest. However, he emphasized that China has been steadily building the infrastructure needed to conduct trade without relying on the dollar.
“This is a beginning. China has launched a series of initiatives like this around the world to enable trade without the dollar. Yet the volume transacted in yuan is still insignificant relative to the size of the global economy. It’s as if they are laying the tracks for a future Chinese high-speed train,” he said.
The analyst, who also writes for the news outlet Brasil de Fato, added that most energy and agricultural commodities continue to be traded in U.S. dollars worldwide.
“Today, the yuan is the world’s fifth most-used trade currency, accounting for roughly 8.5% of global transactions, which is still very little. But it is growing when compared with three, five, or ten years ago,” Fernandes noted.
The Dollar’s Hegemony
One of the core agendas of the BRICS group, which includes Brazil, China, India, South Africa, and other countries of the Global South, has been the de-dollarization of the world economy, given that the dollar’s dominant role in international markets provides significant economic and political advantages to the United States.
This de-dollarization agenda has in turn been criticized by President Donald Trump, who has pledged to defend the global predominance of the U.S. currency.
China Is Reluctant to Accelerate Yuan Internationalization
Fernandes, who is also an editor of Wenhua Zongheng International, argues that China itself has little interest in rapid de-dollarization. One reason is that the country still holds substantial reserves denominated in U.S. dollars. In addition, Beijing seeks to maintain the value of its currency in a way that preserves the competitiveness of Chinese exports.
Another challenge is China’s reluctance to fully liberalize its capital account, a step often considered necessary for the internationalization of the yuan. Beijing avoids doing so because it does not want the Chinese financial system to become vulnerable to the turbulence and volatility of global speculative capital flows. The capital account refers to the movement of financial resources into and out of a country.
“A rapid depreciation of the dollar would result in major losses for both the Chinese state and Chinese companies. This de-dollarization process must therefore be slow, gradual, and secure,” Fernandes said.
An Alternative to the Dollar
Brazilian economist Paulo Nogueira Batista Jr., former Vice President of the New Development Bank (NDB), the BRICS bank, published an article in June proposing the creation of a new reserve currency for international trade.
Nogueira acknowledges that the payment network operated by the People’s Bank of China (PBOC), which involves more than 40 central banks, has expanded the role of the Chinese currency in the settlement of international trade transactions.
However, he argues that replacing the dollar with the yuan is not currently in China’s economic interest. Instead, he proposes a new currency for global trade based on a basket of currencies from BRICS members and other Global South countries.
“The initiative would involve creating a new unit of account by a group of BRICS countries, though not necessarily all of them, together with other Global South nations. At a later stage, this unit of account would be converted into a new currency while preserving the same weighting structure,” Nogueira wrote in an article for the Valdai Discussion Club, a Moscow-based think tank.
For geopolitical analyst Marco Fernandes, de-dollarization is important both for promoting greater fairness in the global economy and for reducing the political and economic leverage that the United States derives from its monetary dominance. Through financial sanctions and economic embargoes, Washington is often able to pressure other nations to align with its interests.
“Because of the dollar’s hegemony, every time the U.S. Federal Reserve raises interest rates, currencies in poorer countries tend to depreciate. As a result, imports become more expensive. Wheat, rice, corn, and other food products become costlier. Even a small change can mean hunger, or even death, for thousands of people,” he concluded.

The barricades are coming down at Jantar Mantar. The crowds are leaving, the microphones are being packed away, but the political message from the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) protest will not disappear as quickly.
The trigger was the crisis over competitive examinations and allegations of paper leaks and irregularities, but the protest grew into something larger: a test of whether a government that has built much of its political identity around strong leadership can still be forced to answer to citizens on the street. The answer, at least this time, is yes.
The resignation of Union Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan and the government’s subsequent assurances on the protesters’ other demands brought the 49-day agitation to an end. The government has also faced demands over compensation, withdrawal of cases against protesters and reforms to the examination system.
That matters because the CJP protest was not led by a traditional political party with an organisational network, a large parliamentary presence or the machinery of a national election campaign. It was driven largely by young people, amplified through Instagram and sustained through physical protest. That is why the movement deserves attention beyond the resignation of one minister.
India is a young country. More than half its population is under 30, and the median age is around 28. Every year, millions of young Indians enter an education system and job market that are increasingly competitive and unforgiving. For them, a compromised examination is not an administrative inconvenience. It can mean losing a year, spending more money, missing an opportunity or watching a planned career collapse.
This is where the paper-leak crisis becomes a political issue. The NEET-UG controversy, involving over 22 lakh medical aspirants, brought the scale of the problem into focus.
Competitive examinations have become one of the main gateways to social mobility in India. At least 152 major exam leaks have been reported over the past decade, affecting an estimated 7.5 crore (75 million) students and job aspirants through cancelled, postponed or compromised exams; an average of more than one leak every month.
For millions of young Indians, the issue is no longer just about one exam going wrong; it is about whether the system itself can be trusted.
The CJP movement also shows how India’s political language is changing. The name itself is a product of the internet age: irreverent, mocking and deliberately provocative. Young Indians who may have little interest in traditional party politics are increasingly comfortable using memes, satire and social media to organise themselves and challenge authority.
The CJP protest also exposed something else: the changing relationship between young Indians and political power.
For years, the dominant political narrative around Prime Minister Narendra Modi has rested heavily on the idea of decisive leadership. The BJP‘s electoral success since 2014 has been closely associated with Modi’s personal political appeal and his ability to project authority, stability and control. His political brand remains central to the party’s electoral strategy. The CJP protest does not, by itself, threaten that brand. It would be an exaggeration to say so but it does challenge the idea that political authority is beyond public pressure.
There is also a lesson here for India’s opposition. Traditional political parties were not at the centre of this movement, that should worry them. When young citizens choose to organise outside the established political system, it is often because they do not believe those institutions are capable of representing their concerns effectively.
The Opposition cannot simply arrive at a protest after the momentum has already built and claim ownership of it, nor can it treat youth anger as another electoral resource. It needs to understand why young Indians are increasingly sceptical of political institutions in the first place.
The government, too, should not mistake the end of a protest for the end of the problem. The CJP protest has also offered a reminder that India’s democratic system is more complicated than the electoral arithmetic of ruling party versus Opposition. There is another constituency that matters: citizens who may not identify with any political party but who are willing to mobilise when an issue directly affects their lives.
The immediate political test could come in next year’s assembly elections in Uttar-Pradesh, Punjab and Gujarat. Whether the protests translate into votes, however, remains to be seen. The bigger question is 2029. If the CJP decides to enter electoral politics, it could become a new vehicle for youth discontent.
That constituency is young, digitally connected and increasingly impatient with institutions that appear slow to accept responsibility. The real test will come after Jantar Mantar falls silent.
Will India’s examination system become more transparent? Will officials and institutions be held accountable when systems fail? Will young Indians once again believe that the system is worth trusting? Those are the questions the CJP protest leaves behind. The barricades may be gone, the problem that brought the young people there is not.

In June 2025, President Trump played a serious card in the decades-long dispute between the United States and International Criminal Court. He imposed the full weight of U.S. economic sanctions on several judges of the court.
The disagreement is over jurisdiction. Does the ICC have jurisdiction over non-member states, particularly the U.S. and Israel? The U.S. thinks no. The ICC argues it has jurisdiction if the alleged crimes occurred in territories that did sign the treaty, Afghanistan and Palestine.
Setting aside their actual dispute, the sanctions give us a unique opportunity to see American economic power in action. Typically when we think of sanctions we think of shadowy oligarchs and hidden terror groups. With these particular sanctions, we get to see what happens when a professionally established person living in a developed city is suddenly cut off from the U.S. financial/tech system.
The stories from those sanctioned paint a scary picture.
The effects were immediate yet remarkably mundane. Credit cards stopped working, including cards issued by banks outside the United States. European bank transfers were rejected or blocked. Peruvian judge Luz del Carmen Ibáñez Carranza had a card cancelled by her Dutch bank. “Why? It’s a European bank, not an American bank,” she told The Guardian. She blamed “a kind of over-compliance,” with foreign banks terrified of jeopardizing their relationships with U.S. institutions.
Then things got stranger. Canadian judge Kimberly Prost lost her Amazon account and came home to discover that Alexa would no longer respond to her. While traveling in New Zealand, her debit card failed when she tried to buy breakfast: “I wasn’t having breakfast that morning.” French judge Nicolas Guillou lost access to Amazon, Airbnb and PayPal, and even had a hotel reservation in France cancelled because he had booked it through Expedia. Slovenian judge Beti Hohler says a friend sent her a Christmas present through Amazon and subsequently had THEIR Amazon accounts suspended.
The effects could also spread to family members and other people who dealt with those sanctioned. A transfer from ICC prosecutor Karim Khan to his former wife for their children reportedly resulted in her bank account being frozen. Some officials lost access to email and other online services. Italian lawyer and UN Special Rapporteur Francesca Albanese says she has been unable to obtain ordinary banking services even in Europe and has resorted to cash and borrowing from friends and family. Her description of the experience gives this piece its title: “It equates to a civil death.”
The online world is intermediated. Those intermediaries are overwhelmingly dominated by U.S. companies, and most of the world follows our lead. The financial system is extremely risk averse. Both finance and tech are completely deferential in the name of compliance. Put those things together and sanctions are a magic order that can strike a person from the internet and banking completely.
No matter where you live in the world, even if you never touch dollars, if you do not take sovereignty into your own hands you are subject to the control of the current U.S. administration.
Seeing sanctions, a tool typically reserved for terrorists and rogue states, used in what would ordinarily be a wonkish international political debate must be striking to the rest of the world. It’s surely accelerating the European push for ‘digital sovereignty’ and the digital euro (which we analyzed from a privacy perspective last week). And perhaps is another talking point for Xi Jinping on his global tour promoting China as a stable partner amid US-led geopolitical uncertainty.
The recently sanctioned far-left hacker collective Autistici/Inventati (A/I) learned this. We covered those sanctions last week as well. Since then the story has developed. A/I was betting on its Italian bank defending Italian sovereignty by keeping their account open. Instead, their account was closed and funds seized.
When the sanctions were announced, I of course ran to their donation page to see they took crypto. They did not and have strong feelings as to why.
All this is to say, if you are doing anything that challenges the United States in any way, even if it’s just political activism or through the established processes of international law, you should consider reducing your reliance on compliance driven intermediaries. - Neeraj

Piero Cipollone, a member of the European Central Bank’s (ECB) Executive Board, recently claimed that the digital euro—Europe’s central bank digital currency (CBDC)—“guarantees the maximum level of privacy that current technology can offer.”
The surveillance capabilities of CBDCs have long been a concern, especially in Western Democracies that have increasingly taken an interest in techno-authoritarianism (whether they believe it or not). Cipollone, however, assured the interviewer that Europeans should not be concerned about financial surveillance with the digital euro since offline transaction details “will only be available to the payer and the payee.”
For online transactions, however, the Eurosystem (the monetary authority consisting of the ECB and the national central banks that have adopted the euro) would not be able to identify the parties involved, but “the banks involved in the transaction would be able to do so, including for anti-money laundering purposes.” Stated differently, the EU governments won’t be keeping a close eye on Europeans themselves, they’ll just have the banks do it for them and report back. So, not too different from the current more-or-less fully surveilled financial system.
These are two very different statements for the two modes of transactions that can occur with the digital euro (i.e., offline and online), so it would be good to better understand what’s actually going on, according to the ECB’s draft rulebook for a digital euro.
Cipollone states that transactions occurring offline are private and peer-to-peer (he doesn’t use that exact term but I’m contractually required to use it in our newsletter); whereas, online transactions would work the same as traditional digital payments, where an intermediary is involved but settlement would occur on one central infrastructure and not with various banks.
Online transactions go something like this:
- Alice wants to send money to Bob;
- Alice initiates the transaction through a payment service provider’s (PSP) application;
- The PSP authenticates her and validates/screens the transaction;
- Alice’s PSP sends the payment instruction to the Eurosystem’s Digital Euro Service Platform (DESP);
- DESP forwards it to Bob’s PSP for validation;
- After each PSP validates the transaction, DESP settles it and confirms settlement to both PSPs, which then notify Alice and Bob.
That last point is where Cipollone states that banks (i.e., PSPs) would identify parties involved in a transaction—that is, identify their respective customers. This is how the world currently works, so this is no surprise.
Offline transactions are more representative of peer-to-peer transactions (I get paid by the amount of times I say it), where a payer is able to send money to a payee between their devices without an intermediary, where transaction authentication happens locally on each participant’s device.
Here is how offline transactions work:
- Alice enters the transaction details into her application and the software in her device authenticates the details locally;
- The payer and payee tap their phones using near field communication (NFC), which allows two devices to exchange communications when they are near each other;
- The two applications authenticate each other; both devices validate the transaction (meaning the payer’s device ensures they have enough money and the payee’s device ensures that receiving the money would not exceed its offline holding limit or transaction-number limit);
- The balances then update locally;
- The payee confirms the settlement by sending confirmation back to the payer’s application. (Look to Annex B2, pages 222-224, for more details.)
But while the transaction itself is designed to be peer-to-peer when done offline (there’s my annual bonus), onboarding and device registration still requires user verification and identification with a PSP. The DESP is also informed of when euros are issued to a device and when they are redeemed. For example, Alice would go through the DESP to move €100 to her offline wallet; the DESP processes the transaction; and Alice’s device now has an offline balance of €100. The operation is processed through Alice’s PSP and DESP. And when Alice sends €80 to Bob, there is no involvement of a PSP nor DESP. However, if Bob then redeems the €80, he would have to do so online through a PSP and DESP.
Here is where things get tricky. These offline transactions are not entirely similar to cash transactions, because while the transaction can be done in a peer-to-peer manner, the registered devices are still subject to limits and periodically required to complete integrity checks with the DESP. Furthermore, as previously mentioned, there are offline holding limits that dictate how much a device can hold offline, meaning that a user’s device could reject a transaction if the user hits their limit. The device would also reject transactions if the user reaches a certain number of consecutive offline transactions.
All this in mind, the digital euro and its associated software would be best described as having mechanisms in place for peer-to-peer transactions, but also having mechanisms in place for centralized controls on transactions and checkpoints for user identification. Is this the kind of technology that would maximize privacy for users? Not quite. It allows for some privacy, but information leakage is very much prevalent. Nor is this the kind of technology that empowers Europeans with greater autonomy the way cash does. There are very strict limitations that exist at the discretion of EU authorities.
The digital euro remains in negotiations between the EU Commission, Parliament, and Council. Meanwhile, the ECB is currently developing a pilot and, as of mid-August, has requested participants for developing offline digital euro standards. The draftbook (that has acted as our point of reference) will continue evolving consistent with negotiations and technical developments.
This timeline has always seemed inevitable. Monetary policy and fiat currency have historically been useful instruments in domestic and foreign influence—nation states were not going to simply lie down while financial technology evolved towards peer-to-peer networks and (actual) user-controlled wallets. But we knew this, and so our fight continues towards privacy-preserving electronic cash that operates on open, decentralized blockchain networks.
-Laz

Yesterday, the State Department and Treasury designated an Italian collective, Autistici/Inventati or A/I, as a Specially Designated Global Terrorist and subjected it to sanctions. The designation warrants close scrutiny because much of what the government alleges as its basis is, effectively, the provision of communications and privacy infrastructure.
That doesn’t mean the sanctions are inappropriate. But it means the designation sits somewhere close to both the constitutional and statutory limits of sanctions authority. Our First Amendment limits the government’s ability to punish speech. Similarly, the Berman Amendments to the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (IEEPA) deny the President authority to sanction transactions involving information and informational materials. But the A/I designation also alleges activities that may go beyond speech and information, and it is difficult to evaluate the legal significance of those facts until more details emerge.
We did some quick digging to see what we could find about Autistici/Inventati on the internet from before the designation was announced.
By all accounts, it is not a politically neutral hosting company. Since 2001, A/I has openly described itself as a radical-left collective providing email, web hosting, mailing lists, blogs, anonymity tools, and other communications infrastructure to groups broadly aligned with its anti-capitalist, antifascist, and anarchist politics. Nor does A/I appear to operate like a typical commercial hosting provider. A/I claimed to manually review requests for service based on the ideological aims of prospective users. After repeated encounters with European law enforcement, A/I also openly said they engineered their infrastructure to resist surveillance and minimize the identifying information they retain.
Still, choosing who you do business with on ideological grounds is not itself unlawful, and minimizing your exposure to customers’ data is not only legal, it is good technical and security practice.
The government’s August 26 fact sheet alleges that violent groups “relied on” A/I services to publish communiqués, claim responsibility for attacks, distribute manifestos, circulate maps, and share sabotage manuals. Much of that kind of activity is typically treated as speech in our constitutional tradition even when it is despicable. Much of those transactions sound, without further details, like transactions in “information or informational materials,” which the Berman Amendments to IEEPA remove from presidential sanctions authority.
You can see why the facts matter here. If A/I really was merely transacting in information and offered no particularized assistance to bad actors with an intent to further their bad schemes, then this designation would be questionable.
If, on the other hand, A/I administrators actively helped attackers choose targets, specifically configured systems for a known planned attack, provided bespoke assistance designed to evade law enforcement in connection with an attack, or otherwise participated in violent operations, the government has a substantially stronger case for sanctions and other enforcement.
It’s important to stay level headed. Some of the apparent users were not merely distasteful political radicals. The government identifies groups responsible for firebombings, rail sabotage, attacks on energy infrastructure, and other acts of political violence. But if, in our zeal to stop these people from committing further violent acts, we support a rule that effectively allows the President to censor and sanction mere speech and communications infrastructure, then we will have further cut down the precious protections our laws and Constitution provide.
There are some parallels to Tornado Cash, of course. Roman Storm’s prosecution is back in the news because the SDNY has now set an April 26, 2027 retrial on the two conspiracy charges, money laundering and sanctions violations, on which the jury deadlocked the first time around.
Additionally, Roman took to Twitter this week describing how he never ran a relayer for private transactions, while Chainalysis, as emerged in the court record, apparently did.
Unlike the Tornado Cash developers, and even the Tornado Cash token holders, relayers interacted directly with Tornado Cash users and charged a fee for doing so. That puts relayers much closer to the conduct side of a speech (protected) versus conduct (unprotected) distinction for First Amendment and Berman Amendment purposes. We argued this point extensively during the first trial in our amicus brief to the court. - Peter
