China’s trade machine has reached a new scale. In the 12 months through July 2026, its goods trade hit a record $7.2 trillion, with exports exceeding $4.2 trillion and the trade surplus approaching $1.2 trillion.
But the most important story is no longer simply the size of China’s surplus. It is where that surplus is going—and how the rest of the world is becoming connected to China’s trade.
The geography of China’s trade imbalance has changed markedly in recent years. The U.S. once accounted for a large share of China’s trade surplus, but that role has diminished sharply. Meanwhile, Europe’s deficit with China has expanded, making the EU an increasingly important counterpart to China’s enormous export surplus.
At the same time, China remains deeply embedded in global trade. For many emerging and developing economies, China is a major trading partner, a critical source of manufactured imports, and an important destination for commodities and energy exports. Yet the degree of dependence varies significantly: a large share of trade with China does not necessarily translate into a large economic dependence when measured against the size of an economy.
The seven charts below trace this transformation—from the scale of China’s trade, to the geographic shift in its surplus, and finally to China’s expanding but uneven economic footprint across the world.
PART I — China’s Trade Surplus
1. China’s Goods Exports Top $4.2 Trillion as Trade Hits Record $7.2 Trillion
China’s total goods trade reached a record $7.2 trillion in the 12 months ending July 2026, with exports topping $4.2 trillion and imports reaching a record $3.0 trillion. The resulting trade surplus widened to $1.2 trillion, underscoring China’s continued dominance in global manufacturing and merchandise trade.
2. China’s Trade Surplus Plateaus Near $1.19 Trillion
China’s trade surplus surged 3.3× from $360 billion in 2018 to $1.18 trillion in 2025. The increase was uneven, with the surplus falling sharply after 2018 and again during the 2020 pandemic before resuming its climb and accelerating from 2022 onward. Since around August 2025, however, the surplus has largely plateaued near $1.17 trillion, reaching $1.19 trillion in the 12 months through July 2026.
After years of rapid expansion, China’s export surplus now appears to have settled at a historically exceptional level, even as the latest U.S.-China tariff period continues.
PART II — Where China’s Surplus Is Going
3. EU Trade Deficit with China Surpasses U.S. Deficit by 2.5×
The EU-U.S. divergence in trade deficits with China has widened sharply. The EU’s goods trade deficit with China was equivalent to about 50% of the U.S. deficit in 2005, rising above 70% in 2008 before declining to around 40% during 2013–2019. The ratio then climbed above 100% in 2023 and 2024, before surging above 250% in 2026.
In the 12 months ending June 2026, the EU’s goods trade deficit with China reached $453 billion, compared with $183 billion for the United States. Since June 2018, the U.S. deficit has fallen 56%, from $411 billion to $183 billion, while the EU deficit has surged 162%, from $173 billion to $453 billion.
The divergence has accelerated since 2025, as U.S. tariffs and trade restrictions coincided with a decline in imports from China, while EU imports from China continued to expand. China’s goods trade surplus with the EU is now more than twice its surplus with the United States, highlighting a growing transatlantic shift in China’s trade imbalance.
4. U.S. Share of China’s Trade Surplus Shrinks, While EU Holds Steady
The U.S. share of China’s total trade surplus has collapsed from 60% in 2021 to just 16% in the 12 months through June 2026. By contrast, the EU’s share has remained relatively stable, rising from around 40% in 2021 to nearly 50% in 2022 before settling at roughly 39% in 2026.
The divergence reflects a major shift in the geography of China’s trade surplus. U.S. tariffs and trade restrictions, supply-chain rerouting, and China’s export diversification have coincided with a sharp decline in the U.S. share, while Europe has remained a more consistent destination for China’s net exports.
PART III — China’s Global Trade Footprint
5. Global Trade Dependence on China
Who Depends Most on Trade with China?
Resource-rich economies across South America, the Middle East, Africa, and Central Asia conduct more than a quarter of their total trade with China, reflecting China’s role as a major market for raw materials, energy, and agricultural commodities. Russia’s trade dependence has also increased as trade has been reoriented following Western sanctions.
Across East and Southeast Asia, many economies likewise maintain strong trade ties with China, reflecting extensive flows of intermediate and capital goods that underpin regional manufacturing supply chains.
In contrast, the United States, Canada, and much of Western Europe have lower overall trade exposure to China, supported by diversified trading relationships and deep regional integration. The map reveals a divided global trading landscape: commodity exporters rely heavily on Chinese demand, while advanced economies tend to maintain more diversified trade relationships.
6. Global Import Dependence on China
China Remains the World’s Manufacturing Hub
China remains a major source of imports for economies across the developing world. Outside North America and Western Europe, many countries source a substantial share of their imports from China, reflecting its central role in global supply chains for electronics, machinery, vehicles, textiles, and consumer goods.
Import dependence is particularly high across Africa, Southeast Asia, Central Asia, the Middle East, and Latin America, where China has become a key supplier of manufactured goods. The United States has a lower share of imports sourced from China following years of tariff-driven diversification and supply-chain shifts, while Canada and much of Europe remain moderately exposed.
The map highlights China’s enduring position as the world’s manufacturing hub and a dominant supplier of goods to much of the global economy.
7. Global Economic Dependence on Trade with China
How Much Does Trade with China Matter to Each Economy?
This map measures trade with China as a share of each country’s GDP, highlighting its economic significance rather than its share of total trade.
Commodity exporters and smaller economies—including the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Kazakhstan, Turkmenistan, and several Southeast Asian economies—show the greatest exposure, with trade with China accounting for a significant share of economic output.
By contrast, large and diversified economies such as the United States, Brazil, and India appear less economically dependent because their economies are much larger relative to trade with any single partner.
The map underscores an important distinction: trade dependence is not determined solely by how much a country trades with China, but by the size of that trade relative to the overall economy.

Global broad money supply climbed above $150 trillion in June 2026, up from $26 trillion in 2000—equivalent to a 6.9% compound annual growth rate (CAGR) over the past 26 years.
Growth accelerated from April 2025, with broad money rising 11.9% year over year in February 2026. The increase in money supply in U.S. dollar terms was partly amplified by the depreciation of the dollar against major currencies, with the U.S. Dollar Index (DXY) averaging 9.2% lower year over year in February 2026.
Data covers 169 countries and territories, representing 99% of global GDP. All currencies are converted to U.S. dollars.
1. Global Broad Money Supply: 2000–H1 2026
Global Broad Money Supply Surpasses $150 Trillion in H1 2026
Global broad money supply climbed above $150 trillion in June 2026, up from $26 trillion in 2000—an average annual growth rate of 6.9%.
China accounted for the largest share at $52.6 trillion (35.0%), followed by the U.S. ($23.2 trillion, 15.4%), the EU ($22.8 trillion, 15.2%), Japan ($10.2 trillion, 6.8%), and the UK ($5.2 trillion, 3.4%). Together, these five economies accounted for three-quarters of global broad money.
Following a 25% surge between February 2020 and February 2022, global broad money largely stabilized, averaging around $124 trillion in 2022 and 2023. Growth then slowed sharply, averaging just 1.5% annually from 2021 to 2024, while the 2019–2024 average fell to 5.3%, below the long-term trend.
Growth accelerated from April 2025, with global broad money rising 11.9% year over year in February 2026. The increase in U.S. dollar terms was partly amplified by the depreciation of the dollar against major currencies, with the U.S. Dollar Index (DXY) averaging 9.2% lower year over year in February 2026.
Data covers 169 countries and territories, representing 99% of global GDP. All currencies are converted to U.S. dollars.
2. The Recent Acceleration
Global Broad Money Growth Accelerates Amid U.S. Dollar Depreciation
Global broad money supply climbed above $150 trillion in June 2026, up from $26 trillion in 2000—equivalent to a 6.9% compound annual growth rate (CAGR) over the past 26 years.
Growth accelerated from April 2025, with global broad money rising 11.9% year over year in February 2026. Since March 2026, growth has slowed, reaching 7.7% year over year in June 2026. The increase in U.S. dollar terms was partly amplified by the depreciation of the dollar against major currencies, with the U.S. Dollar Index (DXY) averaging 9.2% lower year over year in February 2026.
Data covers 169 countries and territories, representing 99% of global GDP. All currencies are converted to U.S. dollars.
The $150 trillion money stock is increasingly divided between two very different economic blocs. Advanced economies still hold enormous monetary balances, but their share of the global total has fallen dramatically since 2000.
3. Advanced Economies
Advanced Economies’ Broad Money Supply Reaches $75 Trillion
Broad money supply (M2) in advanced economies reached $75 trillion in June 2026, up from roughly $23 trillion in 2000—equivalent to a 4.7% compound annual growth rate (CAGR).
Following an exceptional 25% surge between February 2020 and February 2022, money supply growth moderated and largely returned to its long-term trend. After several years of relative stability, broad money accelerated in 2025, rising 9.1% year over year in February 2026. The increase in U.S. dollar terms was partly amplified by the depreciation of the dollar against major currencies.
EMDE broad money has expanded more than 19-fold since 2000, reaching the same $75 trillion level as advanced economies.
4. EMDEs
EMDE Broad Money Supply Surges to $75 Trillion
Broad money supply in emerging markets and developing economies (EMDEs) surged from $3.8 trillion in 2000 to $75 trillion in June 2026, equivalent to a 12.1% compound annual growth rate (CAGR). This far outpaced growth in global broad money (6.9%) and advanced economies (4.7%) over the same period.
EMDE broad money growth remained remarkably consistent with its long-term trend for most of the past 26 years. Even the 2008 global financial crisis caused only a brief pause rather than a sustained setback. Growth accelerated significantly after 2020 as the COVID-19 pandemic triggered a sharp expansion in money supply, and accelerated again in 2025 amid the depreciation of the U.S. dollar.
5. The Great Convergence
Emerging Markets Reach Parity With Advanced Economies in Global Money Supply
Advanced economies’ share of global broad money fell from 86% in 2000 to 50% in June 2026, bringing advanced economies and emerging markets and developing economies (EMDEs) to an equal share of global money supply.
The convergence has been driven largely by China. China’s share steadily increased, overtaking all other EMDEs combined in 2009, and reached 35% of global broad money in June 2026—more than twice the 15% share of all other EMDEs combined.
The decline in advanced economies’ share was not uniform. It accelerated around the 2008–09 global financial crisis, again following the COVID-19 pandemic, and more recently amid the depreciation of the U.S. dollar in 2025. Because all money supplies are measured in U.S. dollars, exchange-rate movements can significantly affect the relative shares.
With advanced economies and EMDEs now accounting for roughly equal shares of global broad money, the balance of global monetary weight has shifted dramatically since 2000.
6. China Reshapes the Global Money Supply Landscape
In June 2026, China’s broad money supply reached $52.6 trillion, compared with $22.4 trillion for the rest of EMDEs and $75 trillion for advanced economies. China overtook the rest of the EMDE bloc in 2009, when both stood at around $7 trillion. Since then, China’s money supply has increased more than sevenfold, while the rest of EMDEs has grown to $22.4 trillion.
China’s steady expansion contrasts with the more pronounced cycles in advanced economies, including sharp increases during the global financial crisis and COVID-19 pandemic. The result is a dramatic shift in the global distribution of broad money: China alone now accounts for 35% of the global total, while advanced economies and EMDEs each account for roughly half.

Persian Gulf oil flows are recovering, but the recovery is far from complete or uniform. Production and trade flows have improved sharply from their spring lows, led by Saudi Arabia, the UAE, and other Gulf producers, while Iran and Iraq remain significantly constrained. The uneven recovery means that regional output is still below normal levels, keeping global oil markets sensitive to further disruptions.
- Production partially recovers: Persian Gulf crude output rose from 14.4 Mb/d in May to 19.0 Mb/d in July, but remained 18% below the 2025 average.
- Shut-ins fall sharply: Production shut-ins declined 52%, from 8.9 Mb/d in May to 4.3 Mb/d in July.
- Saudi Arabia & UAE lead the recovery: Their combined shut-ins fell 57% from the May peak.
- Iran & Iraq lag: Their combined shut-ins fell only 37%, leaving 2.2 Mb/d still offline in July.
- China’s Gulf imports recover: Imports from the Persian Gulf rose from 2.1 Mb/d in June to 3.7 Mb/d in July, but remained well below earlier levels.
- Recovery remains uneven: July’s Gulf import recovery was driven mainly by Saudi Arabia, the UAE, and other Gulf suppliers, while Iran and Iraq contributed just 1.1 Mb/d.
- Global impact is easing—but significant: Persian Gulf shut-ins fell to 9.6% of global crude oil exports and 5.7% of global production in July, roughly half their May peak shares.
The Persian Gulf oil shock is beginning to ease, but the recovery is far from uniform. Regional crude production collapsed from 24.4 million barrels per day in February to 14.4 million in May, before recovering to 19.0 million in July. Production shut-ins also fell by more than half from their May peak.
But beneath that regional recovery lies a striking divergence among producers. Saudi Arabia, the UAE, Kuwait, Oman and Bahrain have restored production much faster, while Iran and Iraq remain significantly below earlier levels. The difference is particularly visible in China’s imports: July’s recovery in Persian Gulf supplies was driven almost entirely by Saudi Arabia, the UAE and other Gulf producers, while imports from Iran and Iraq remained subdued.
This suggests that the Persian Gulf is experiencing a partial recovery rather than a full normalization of oil flows. The region’s aggregate numbers are improving, but the underlying supply picture has become increasingly polarized between producers that are restoring output and those whose exports remain constrained.
I. The Persian Gulf Shock
1. Persian Gulf Crude Oil Production Collapses, Then Partially Recovers
Combined crude oil production across the six Persian Gulf producers fell from a peak of 24.4 million barrels per day in February 2026 to just 14.4 million barrels per day in May, a 41% decline in three months, before gradually recovering to 19.0 million barrels per day in July. Despite the recovery, output remained 18% below the 2025 average.
The decline affected all six producers relative to their 2025 averages, but its magnitude varied considerably. Iraq recorded the steepest decline at 35%, followed by Kuwait (-25%), Iran (-24%), and Saudi Arabia (-22%). By contrast, the UAE and Oman were the only two producers with output above their 2025 averages, at 20% and 19% higher, respectively.
The divergence shows that the production shock was unevenly distributed across the Persian Gulf, with the UAE and Oman maintaining or gaining relative output share while production in the region’s other major producers contracted sharply. Even after the partial recovery, regional output remained well below both its early-2026 peak and the 2025 baseline.
2. Persian Gulf Crude Oil Shut-Ins Are Winding Down
Persian Gulf crude oil production shut-ins relative to the 2025 average peaked at 8.9 million barrels per day in May 2026 and have since fallen sharply, reaching 4.3 million barrels per day in July—a 52% decline in just two months. The unwinding, however, has varied significantly across producers.
Kuwait, Oman, and Bahrain recorded the fastest reductions, with shut-ins falling 68% from their May peak, followed by Saudi Arabia and the UAE, where shut-ins declined 57%. Iran and Iraq saw a more modest 37% decline and remained the largest combined contributor to the remaining shut-ins, at 2.2 million barrels per day in July.
The pattern mirrors the broader recovery in Persian Gulf oil production: Saudi Arabia, the UAE, Kuwait, Oman, and Bahrain are restoring output faster than Iran and Iraq, whose supply disruptions remain more persistent.
3. Persian Gulf Oil Shut-Ins Lose Global Market Impact in July
At their peak in May 2026, Persian Gulf production shut-ins were equivalent to 19.9% of global crude oil exports and 11.9% of world production—an extraordinary share for disruptions concentrated in a single region. Both measures remained near peak levels through April and May before declining steadily. By July, shut-ins had fallen to 9.6% of global exports and 5.7% of global production, roughly half their May levels.
Throughout the period, shut-ins represented a larger share of global exports than of production, reflecting the Persian Gulf’s outsized role as a global oil-export hub relative to its share of world output. As a result, disruptions in the region can have a disproportionately large impact on international oil markets. The sharp decline by July points to partial normalization of regional oil flows, although remaining shut-ins still represented a significant share of global trade and production.
II. China Feels the Shock
4. China’s Crude Oil Imports Fall Sharply, Partially Recover in July
China’s crude oil imports fell sharply after reaching 13.1 million barrels per day in December 2025, the highest level in the 18-month period. Imports then declined for five consecutive months, bottoming at 7.1 million barrels per day in June 2026, a 46% drop, before partially recovering to 8.6 million barrels per day in July—up 22% from June but still 30% below February’s level.
The decline was concentrated overwhelmingly in the Persian Gulf. Imports from the region fell from 6.4 million barrels per day in March to just 2.1 million in June, while flows from the rest of the world remained comparatively stable at roughly 4.6–5.4 million barrels per day.
The divergence suggests that the spring collapse was driven more by Gulf supply and sourcing disruptions—potentially involving sanctions, pricing, or contract timing—than by a broad-based decline in China’s oil demand. July’s partial recovery provides an early indication that Gulf supplies may be beginning to normalize.
5. China’s Persian Gulf Oil Imports Partially Recover, but Iran and Iraq Lag
The composition of China’s Persian Gulf oil imports reveals where the mid-2026 collapse—and subsequent partial recovery—occurred. Total imports from the region reached 6.4 million barrels per day in February 2026, with Saudi Arabia, the UAE, and other Gulf suppliers accounting for 3.5 million barrels per day and Iran and Iraq contributing 2.9 million.
Both groups declined sharply through the spring, with total Gulf imports falling to just 2.1 million barrels per day in June. By July, imports had partially recovered to 3.7 million barrels per day, but the recovery was driven almost entirely by the rest-of-Gulf group, which rose to 2.6 million barrels per day. Imports from Iran and Iraq reached only 1.1 million barrels per day, remaining well below earlier levels.
The divergence suggests that Iran and Iraq have borne the brunt of the disruption, with their oil flows to China recovering much more slowly amid heightened regional tensions and disruptions to shipping through the Strait of Hormuz.
III. The Global Spillover
6. Fuel Import Growth Diverges Sharply Across Economies Following the Iran War
Fuel import values across the 20 countries tracked increased 23% year over year in Q2 2026, but growth varied sharply across economies. Australia led by a wide margin, with import values surging 109%, followed by Indonesia (83%) and Cambodia (69%). Several European and Asian economies also recorded above-average growth, including Greece (61%), Portugal (56%), the UK and Taiwan (53% each), and Spain (51%).
At the other end of the spectrum, South Korea matched the 20-country average at 23%, while India rose just 21% and Hungary 13%. China’s fuel import value increased only 4%, while Japan’s declined 5%, the only contraction among the countries tracked.
The wide dispersion suggests that fuel import growth in Q2 2026 was driven less by a uniform global trend than by country-specific changes in demand, energy prices, and import requirements.

From the decline of manufacturing in advanced economies to Asia’s dominance of global manufacturing exports, eight charts reveal one of the biggest structural shifts in the global economy.
Part II — From Manufacturing Output to Manufacturing Trade
Manufacturing is not only about what countries produce. It is also about what they sell to the world.
The shift becomes even more striking when viewed through international trade.
5. Asia Overtakes the West
Asia’s Top 10 Manufacturing Exporters Have Overtaken the West’s Top 10
The combined share of global manufacturing exports held by the 10 leading Western exporters—the U.S., Germany, the UK, France, Italy, Canada, Switzerland, the Netherlands, Belgium, and Spain—fell from more than 60% in 1980 to below 40% in 2025. Over the same period, China alone rose from a negligible share to more than 20% of global manufacturing exports. Together with Japan, South Korea, Taiwan, Hong Kong, Singapore, Vietnam, Malaysia, Thailand, and Indonesia, the 10 leading Asian exporters surpassed the Western group around 2015 and have since widened their lead. The shift reflects not only China’s extraordinary rise but also the broader expansion of Asian manufacturing, as Southeast Asian economies have gained export share amid supply-chain diversification and the reorganization of global production.
6. Seven Economies Supply More Than Half of Global Manufacturing Exports
China accounts for 20.5% of global manufacturing exports—more than the United States (7.8%) and Germany (9.1%) combined—highlighting its transformation into the world’s leading manufacturing exporter since joining the WTO. Four of the seven economies on this list are in East Asia (China, Japan, South Korea, and Hong Kong), together supplying over 31% of global manufacturing exports and reflecting the region’s deep integration into electronics, machinery, and industrial supply chains. Meanwhile, the Netherlands and Hong Kong derive much of their export share from their roles as major logistics and re-export hubs. Together, these seven economies account for more than half of world manufacturing exports, underscoring the continued concentration of global industrial production despite efforts to diversify supply chains.
7. The New Manufacturing Geography
EMDE Manufacturing Output Has Surpassed Advanced Economies
Manufacturing value added in emerging markets and developing economies (EMDEs) nearly quadrupled from $2.4 trillion in 2005 to $9.6 trillion in 2025, surpassing advanced economies, whose output grew more modestly from $5.4 trillion to $8.0 trillion. China accounts for $4.8 trillion—more than half of total EMDE manufacturing output—and alone produces more manufacturing value added than many advanced-economy blocs. Meanwhile, the rest of the developing world has expanded steadily to $4.8 trillion, reflecting the rise of manufacturing hubs such as India, Vietnam, and Mexico. The shift marks one of the defining structural transformations of the past two decades: global manufacturing has increasingly migrated toward the developing world, even as advanced economies continue to lead in high-value services and technology.
8. Manufacturing Trade Reveals a Sharp East–West Divide
China’s $1.93T Manufacturing Surplus Matches the Combined Deficit of Four Western Economies
In 2024, China recorded a $1.93 trillion manufacturing trade surplus—almost equal to the combined $1.92 trillion deficit of four major Western economies: the United States ($1.38T), Australia ($190B), the UK ($175B), and Canada ($171B). The U.S. alone accounted for nearly three-quarters of the combined shortfall. The near one-to-one match highlights the extraordinary scale of China’s manufacturing trade surplus and the concentration of manufacturing deficits among a handful of advanced economies—an increasingly important feature of global trade imbalances and ongoing tariff disputes.

The U.S. has normalized its pandemic-era monetary distortion, but liquidity has not disappeared. It has moved through the financial system—into deposits, money-market funds, and increasingly leveraged investment positions.
Part I — The Money Supply
1. U.S. M2 Hits a New Record
U.S. M2 Money Supply Hits Record $23.2 Trillion
U.S. M2 money supply reached a record $23.2 trillion in June 2026, up 5.6% year over year, an increase of roughly $1.2 trillion. Although M2 growth has rebounded, it remains below its 6.3% average annual growth rate since 2000. M2 has now surpassed its previous peak of $21.9 trillion reached in March 2022.
2. The Pandemic Surge Has Been Largely Reversed
From Pandemic Shock to Monetary Normalization
The ratio of U.S. broad money supply (M2) to GDP surged from roughly 70% to nearly 90% during the COVID-19 pandemic as extraordinary monetary and fiscal support expanded the money supply far faster than economic output. By Q2 2026, the ratio had fallen to 71%, almost exactly back on the long-term trend established between 2000 and 2019. The normalization reflects the unwinding of the pandemic-era surge and years of GDP growth outpacing money supply growth, largely erasing the pandemic anomaly without reversing the longer-term rise in M2 relative to GDP.
Part II — The Federal Reserve’s Balance Sheet
3. The Fed Has Turned the Corner
Fed Balance Sheet Ends 43-Month Contraction With First Increase Since 2022
After 43 consecutive months of contraction, the Federal Reserve’s balance sheet turned higher. Total assets increased by $186 billion, or 2.8%, from November 2025 to July 2026, reaching $6.7 trillion, after falling by roughly one-fifth from their 2022 peak. The increase marks a notable reversal from the prolonged post-pandemic tightening cycle. By comparison, the Fed’s balance sheet expanded dramatically during the 2008 financial crisis and the COVID-19 pandemic, when year-over-year asset growth exceeded 140% and 80%, respectively. The latest increase is far more modest, but it may signal a transition from balance-sheet contraction toward a more stable or expanding stance.
4. But the Fed Is Not Simply Returning to QE
Fed Treasury Holdings Reverse 42 Months of Runoff, Rising to $4.5 Trillion
After 42 consecutive months of decline, the Federal Reserve’s Treasury securities holdings increased by $328 billion, or 7.8%, from November 2025 to July 2026, reaching $4.5 trillion. Treasuries were the primary driver of the increase in the Fed’s total assets, while mortgage-backed securities (MBS) continued to decline, falling by $123 billion, or 6.0%. The divergence points to a changing composition of the Fed’s balance sheet, with Treasury holdings beginning to rise even as the MBS portfolio continues to run off.
5. The Fed’s Balance Sheet Has Normalized Relative to the Economy
Fed Balance Sheet-to-GDP Ratio Returns to Pre-Pandemic Levels
Following the Federal Reserve’s quantitative tightening, its balance sheet relative to U.S. GDP fell from a record 35% in Q2 2022 to 21% in Q2 2026, returning to levels last seen in 2018. The decline reflects both the reduction in the Fed’s asset holdings and continued growth in nominal GDP.
Part III — Where the Money Is
6. Bank Deposits Have Shifted Dramatically
U.S. Demand Deposits Surge 26% to $7.1 Trillion
U.S. demand deposits rose 26% year over year to $7.1 trillion in June 2026, extending their post-pandemic uptrend. Their share of M2 has increased dramatically, from 10.5% in December 2019 to 30.5% in June 2026, highlighting a major shift in the composition of U.S. money toward highly liquid bank deposits.
Demand deposits are bank account funds—primarily checking-account balances—that can be withdrawn on demand. They are highly liquid and form an important component of the money supply tracked by the Federal Reserve.
7. Households Are Holding More Cash-Like Assets
U.S. Retail Money Market Funds Surpass $3 Trillion
U.S. retail money market fund assets reached a record $3.05 trillion in June 2026, up 7.1% year over year. Since 2017, retail money market balances have more than tripled, highlighting a long-term shift toward cash and cash-equivalent instruments within household portfolios. Persistent inflows reflect the appeal of liquidity and relatively attractive yields, while suggesting that households continue to maintain substantial defensive cash positions despite strong equity-market performance.
Part IV — Liquidity Meets Risk
8. Money-Market Assets Have Become Highly Concentrated
U.S. Money Market Funds Stabilize Above $8 Trillion as Industry Concentration Rises
U.S. money market fund assets surged 67% from $5.0 trillion in June 2022 to $8.3 trillion in December 2025, before edging up to $8.4 trillion by June 2026. Growth has slowed sharply, with the latest six-month increase the smallest since 2022. Meanwhile, the five largest managers—Fidelity, Charles Schwab, JPMorgan Chase, Vanguard, and BlackRock—accounted for 71% of total industry growth between June 2022 and June 2026, adding a combined $2.7 trillion. Their combined market share rose from an average of 44% in 2011–2015 to 58% in 2026, highlighting the growing concentration of U.S. money-market assets.
Part V — The Other Side of Liquidity
9. Leverage Is Rising Too
U.S. Margin Debt Hits Record $1.42 Trillion
U.S. margin debt reached a record $1.42 trillion in May 2026, up 54% from a year earlier, as investors increased leverage amid rising equity valuations and strong stock-market performance. Margin debt climbed to 6.2% of M2, approaching the 6.3% record reached during the 2000 dot-com bubble. The combination of abundant liquidity and rising leverage points to increasing investor risk-taking, even as large pools of cash remain parked in money-market funds.

From the decline of manufacturing in advanced economies to Asia’s dominance of global manufacturing exports, eight charts reveal one of the biggest structural shifts in the global economy.
Part I — The Great Manufacturing Shift
1. Global Manufacturing’s Great Rebalancing
EMDEs Overtook Advanced Economies in Global Manufacturing
The global manufacturing landscape has undergone a historic rebalancing. In 2005, advanced economies accounted for nearly 70% of global manufacturing value added; two decades later, their share has fallen to 46%, while EMDEs’ share has risen from 31% to 54%. The crossover occurred in the mid-2010s, when emerging and developing economies collectively surpassed advanced economies in manufacturing output share for the first time in the modern data era.
China has been the central force behind this shift, accounting for 27% of global manufacturing value added — roughly equal to the combined share of all other EMDEs. In other words, a single economy now generates as much manufacturing value as the rest of the emerging world combined. The decline of advanced economies reflects not falling output, but a slower pace of growth relative to the rapid industrialization of EMDEs, which has reshaped the global manufacturing map away from its postwar concentration in North America, Western Europe, and Japan.
2. Emerging Markets Drove the Growth
Emerging Markets Drove 76% of Global Manufacturing Growth Since 2005 — China Alone 42%
Emerging market and developing economies (EMDEs) accounted for 76% of global manufacturing value-added growth between 2005 and 2025, compared with just 24% from advanced economies—a dramatic reversal of the industrial hierarchy that dominated much of the 20th century. China alone captured 42% of global manufacturing growth, more than three times the 12.3% contributed by the United States, the next-largest contributor. India, Russia, and Mexico formed the next tier of EMDE contributors, while Germany, South Korea, and Ireland led gains among advanced economies outside the U.S. The figures underscore how decisively the center of global manufacturing has shifted toward emerging economies.
3. China Became the World’s Manufacturing Powerhouse
Just Four Countries Account for Over Half of Global Manufacturing
China, the United States, Germany, and Japan together accounted for 53.5% of global manufacturing value added in 2025, leaving the remaining roughly 190 countries to share the other 46.5%. China alone contributed 27.4%—more than the United States, Germany, and Japan combined—cementing its position as the world’s manufacturing powerhouse. The U.S. ranked a distant second at 16.5%, followed by Germany at 5.1% and Japan at 4.5%. The concentration highlights how dominant a small group of economies remains in global manufacturing despite decades of globalization and supply-chain diversification.
4. Manufacturing Remains Much More Important in EMDEs
Manufacturing’s Share of GDP Fell in Advanced Economies but Held Steady in EMDEs
Manufacturing’s share of GDP in advanced economies fell from 17% in 2000 to 12% in 2025—a decline of nearly one-third—as these economies continued to shift toward services. In emerging market and developing economies (EMDEs), manufacturing remained far more prominent, with its share edging down only from 21% in 2005 to 20% in 2025. A temporary spike in 2021 reflected pandemic-related supply disruptions and a surge in industrial demand. As a result, the manufacturing gap between EMDEs and advanced economies widened from 6 percentage points in 2005 to 8 points in 2025, underscoring the increasingly divergent role of manufacturing across the two groups.

The Strait of Hormuz is one of the most strategically important waterways in the world. A narrow passage connecting the Persian Gulf to global markets, it normally carries around one-fifth of global seaborne oil trade and a large share of liquefied natural gas (LNG) shipments. Yet its importance extends beyond energy: the strait is also a vital artery for broader trade flows linking the Middle East with Asia, Europe, and the world.
That vulnerability became starkly visible in 2026.
Following U.S. and Israeli airstrikes on Iran on February 28, tanker traffic through Hormuz collapsed, triggering one of the largest disruptions to global energy trade in decades. Temporary ceasefires allowed partial recoveries, but renewed attacks on commercial shipping in July once again reduced traffic, highlighting how geopolitical conflict can rapidly reshape trade patterns, commodity markets, and energy security.
This article uses eight charts to examine how the Hormuz crisis disrupted global energy flows, exposed differences in national dependence, and revealed the broader economic significance of one of the world’s most critical chokepoints.
Tanker Traffic Collapsed After the Outbreak of War
The first chart tracks vessel movements through the Strait of Hormuz during 2026.
Before the conflict, around 1,500 vessels transited the strait each month. Following the outbreak of hostilities in late February, tanker traffic plunged as insurers raised premiums, shipping companies rerouted vessels, and military risks intensified.
A brief ceasefire in April produced only a modest recovery. A broader truce on June 8 and the U.S.–Iran Memorandum of Understanding signed on June 17 led to a stronger rebound, but the recovery proved short-lived. Renewed attacks on commercial shipping after July 8 triggered fresh military action and sanctions, causing tanker traffic to decline once again.
The episode demonstrated a fundamental reality of global trade: even temporary disruptions in key maritime chokepoints can have outsized effects on commodity markets and supply chains.
Asia Depends Far More on Hormuz Energy Flows Than the West
The second chart illustrates how dependence on Hormuz varies widely across countries.
Around 22% of the global value of fuel and refined petroleum exports transited the strait in 2025. But exposure is highly uneven.
Asian economies are the most vulnerable. Nearly half of fuel imports in South Korea, Japan, India, Taiwan, and China are linked to Hormuz transit. A second group—including Singapore, Vietnam, Malaysia, Bangladesh, and the Philippines—also relies heavily on Gulf energy supplies.
Western economies face much lower risks. Hormuz-linked fuel imports account for only single-digit shares in Germany, Sweden, the United States, and the United Kingdom, while France and Italy maintain somewhat higher exposure.
The geography of energy trade means that a disruption in Hormuz is primarily an Asian energy security issue, with Northeast and South Asia particularly exposed.
China’s Oil Imports Fell to Near-Decade Lows
China provides one of the clearest examples of this dependence.
As Persian Gulf supplies were disrupted, China’s crude oil imports fell from 12.4 million barrels per day (mb/d) in February 2026 to just 7.1 mb/d in June—a decline of 43% in four months.
Imports from the Persian Gulf collapsed by 67%, while imports from the rest of the world declined much less. The contrast highlights an important lesson: diversification can reduce risk, but it cannot fully replace large volumes of low-cost Gulf crude in the short term.
For China—the world’s largest crude oil importer—the crisis exposed the continuing strategic importance of the Persian Gulf despite years of efforts to broaden supply sources.
Nearly Half of China’s Oil Imports Depend on Hormuz
The next chart explains why the disruption had such a large impact.
In 2025, China imported approximately 5.55 mb/d of crude oil through the Strait of Hormuz, equivalent to about 49% of total imports.
Saudi Arabia, Iraq, the UAE, and Kuwait accounted for most officially recorded flows, while substantial imports from Iran—often reported under alternative origins—further increased dependence.
Even after years of diversification toward Russia, West Africa, and Latin America, nearly half of China’s oil imports remained tied to Hormuz-linked supplies.
This dependence helps explain why disruptions in the Persian Gulf can quickly affect China’s economy, industrial production, and energy security.
The United States Has Limited Exposure
The U.S. picture is very different.
In 2025, the United States imported about 490 thousand barrels per day (kb/d) through Hormuz—equivalent to only 7.9% of total crude imports and roughly 2.5% of combined domestic production and imports.
The shale revolution has fundamentally altered America’s energy position. Rising domestic production has reduced dependence on Middle Eastern crude, limiting direct exposure to disruptions in the Persian Gulf.
While Hormuz closures can still influence global oil prices—and therefore U.S. consumers—the country’s physical dependence on Gulf oil is relatively low.
Europe Faces Moderate Risks
The European Union occupies a middle position.
The EU imported around 1.12 mb/d of crude oil through Hormuz in 2025, equivalent to 12.8% of total imports. Saudi Arabia and Iraq accounted for most of these flows.
Although Europe remains connected to global oil markets, its dependence on Gulf crude is significantly lower than that of Asia.
This means that Hormuz disruptions affect Europe primarily through higher global energy prices rather than through direct supply shortages.
Hormuz Matters More for Energy Than for Total Trade
The final two charts broaden the perspective beyond oil.
Despite its critical role in energy markets, only 3.8% of total world trade passed through the Strait of Hormuz in 2025. In GDP terms, goods trade transiting the strait amounted to approximately 1.7% of global output.
Exposure again varies considerably across countries.
India is the most dependent major economy, with Hormuz-linked trade equal to 18.1% of total trade and 5.3% of GDP. South Korea, Malaysia, Japan, and China also show relatively high exposure.
By contrast, the United States, Germany, France, and the United Kingdom depend much less on Hormuz for overall trade flows.
Iran stands apart. Approximately 81% of its total trade and around 40% of its GDP are linked to goods passing through the strait, making Hormuz not only a global chokepoint, but also a critical lifeline for Iran’s own economy.
A Chokepoint That Shapes the Global Economy
The 2026 Hormuz crisis revealed a central feature of the modern global economy: strategic vulnerabilities are highly uneven.
For the world as a whole, only a small share of trade passes through the Strait of Hormuz. But for energy markets—and particularly for Asia—the strait remains indispensable.
China, Japan, South Korea, India, and many Southeast Asian economies continue to rely heavily on Gulf energy flows. The United States and Europe are less exposed than in previous decades, but no major economy is completely insulated from disruptions in global oil markets.
The crisis also underscored a broader lesson. Globalization has diversified supply chains, but it has not eliminated geographic chokepoints. A narrow waterway only a few kilometers wide continues to influence energy security, inflation, trade flows, and economic stability across the world.

Part II
Where Do Migrants Come From?
Destination tells only half the story.
To understand modern migration, we also need to examine where migrants originate and how emigration differs across countries.
The next four charts reveal that today’s migration increasingly originates in developing economies—but not equally across them.
5. Most Migrants Now Come from Developing Economies
By 2024, 222 million international migrants originated from low- and middle-income countries, compared with only 51 million from high-income economies.
This means nearly three-quarters of the world’s migrants now come from developing economies—a share that has continued to rise over time.
6. Emigration Rates Are Now Higher in Developing Economies
Measured relative to population, emigration from low- and middle-income countries has gradually overtaken that of high-income economies.
At the same time, high-income countries continue to absorb migrants at an increasingly rapid pace, reinforcing their role as net migration destinations.
7. Migrants from High-Income Countries Mostly Stay Within the High-Income World
People leaving high-income countries overwhelmingly move to other high-income countries.
Nearly 87% of emigrants from wealthy economies relocate within the high-income world, while only a small share move to lower-income economies.
8. Most Migrants from Developing Economies Head to High-Income Countries
The dominant migration corridor today runs from low- and middle-income countries to high-income economies.
Between 2000 and 2024, this corridor expanded from 60 million to 137 million migrants—an increase of 130%—far exceeding the growth of any other major migration pathway.
Bringing the Eight Charts Together
The four migration corridors shown throughout this series tell one consistent story.
One corridor stands apart. Migration from low- and middle-income countries to high-income economies has grown two to ten times faster than every other major migration pathway. This single structural shift explains much of the transformation in global migration over the past quarter century.
Rather than becoming more evenly connected, the world’s migration system has become increasingly centered on high-income economies as the primary destination for people seeking greater economic opportunity.
Conclusion
A More Concentrated Migration World
Taken together, the nine charts point to one overarching conclusion.
Global migration is becoming increasingly concentrated—not only geographically, but economically.
High-income economies have emerged as the world’s dominant migration destinations, while most migrants now originate in developing economies. Four regional hubs account for nearly 70% of all international migrants, and one migration corridor—from low- and middle-income to high-income countries—has become the principal engine of global migration growth.
Understanding this structural shift is essential for interpreting many of today’s economic and political debates, from labor shortages and demographic change to industrial competitiveness, border policy, refugee protection, and long-term economic development.
Migration will undoubtedly continue to evolve, but the evidence suggests that its geography is becoming increasingly defined by a simple reality: the movement of people is increasingly a movement toward opportunity.
Data & Methodology
This analysis is based primarily on the United Nations Department of Economic and Social Affairs (UN DESA), International Migrant Stock 2024.
Migration refers to the stock of international migrants—people living outside their country of birth—rather than annual migration flows. Countries are grouped according to the World Bank income classification. Unless otherwise noted, all figures refer to 2024.

The Geography of Global Migration
Four Regional Hubs Host Nearly 70% of the World’s Migrants
Introduction
International migration has become one of the defining features of the global economy. In 2024, 304 million people—roughly one in every 27 people worldwide—lived outside their country of birth. Yet global migration is far less evenly distributed than many assume.
Migration is not only concentrated by income—it is also concentrated geographically. Migration is increasingly concentrated in a relatively small number of destination countries and regions. Four regional hubs—Europe, North America, the Middle East, and the Commonwealth of Independent States (CIS)—together host nearly 70% of the world’s international migrants, despite accounting for a much smaller share of the global population.
Each reflects a distinct migration model:
- Europe combines labor mobility, asylum, and family migration.
- North America is dominated by permanent immigration.
- The Middle East relies heavily on temporary migrant workers.
- The CIS reflects both labor migration and the legacy of the Soviet Union.
Even more striking is the direction of migration. Most international migrants today originate in low- and middle-income countries but settle in high-income economies. This is not simply because migration has increased worldwide. Rather, migration has become increasingly organized around one dominant corridor—from developing to high-income economies.
This article explores that transformation through nine charts, examining migration from both the destination and origin perspectives. Together, they reveal how the geography of migration has evolved over the past quarter century and why high-income countries have become the world’s primary migration hubs.
Part I
Where Do the World’s Migrants Live?
Understanding migration begins with destination rather than origin.
Although migrants live in almost every country, their distribution is highly concentrated. High-income economies have steadily increased their share of the global migrant population, while migration within lower-income countries has grown much more slowly.
The first four charts examine where migrants live today—from the global picture to regional concentration.
1. Where the World’s Migrants Live
Nearly Two-Thirds of Migrants Now Live in High-Income Countries
Of the 304 million international migrants in 2024, 199 million (66%) lived in high-income economies, compared with 104 million in low- and middle-income countries.
Since 2000, the migrant population in high-income economies has grown by 91%, almost twice the pace observed elsewhere. As a result, their share of global migrants has increased from just over half to nearly two-thirds.
This reflects the growing economic pull of wealthier economies, where aging populations, labor shortages, and higher wages continue to attract workers from around the world.
2. Migration Is Far More Concentrated in High-Income Countries
Migrants Account for 14% of the Population in High-Income Economies
Looking at migrants relative to population reveals an even sharper contrast.
By 2024, international migrants accounted for 14.0% of the population in high-income countries, compared with only 1.6% in low- and middle-income economies. In other words, migrants are nearly nine times more concentrated in high-income countries.
The global average masks this widening divergence between destination and origin regions.
3. High-Income Countries Attract More Migrants from Developing Economies
Migration from Lower-Income Countries Drives Growth
The expansion of migration into high-income countries has been overwhelmingly driven by migrants from low- and middle-income economies.
Since 2000, this group has grown by 130%, from 60 million to 137 million, while migration between high-income countries has increased much more modestly.
Nearly seven out of every ten migrants living in high-income countries now originate from developing economies.
4. South–South Migration Remains Large—but Grows More Slowly
Migration within low- and middle-income countries remains substantial, reaching 84 million people in 2024.
However, its growth has been much slower than migration toward high-income economies. Today, most migrants leaving developing economies ultimately settle in high-income countries rather than elsewhere in the developing world.
Data & Methodology
This analysis is based primarily on the United Nations Department of Economic and Social Affairs (UN DESA), International Migrant Stock 2024.
Migration refers to the stock of international migrants—people living outside their country of birth—rather than annual migration flows. Countries are grouped according to the World Bank income classification. Unless otherwise noted, all figures refer to 2024.

Something major just happened for the XRP Ledger.
The Bank for International Settlements—the institution often described as the “central bank of central banks”—published a new working paper titled “Verifiable Official Statistics: A Blockchain-Based Approach.”
The researchers did not merely mention XRPL as a theoretical possibility.
They built and tested their proof of concept directly on the XRP Ledger.
What Did the BIS Researchers Build?
Governments, central banks and international institutions constantly publish economic and financial statistics.
However, once this information is redistributed across websites, databases or AI systems, users need a reliable way to confirm two things:
- Did the information genuinely come from the official institution?
- Has anyone altered the data since it was published?
The researchers created a system that generates a unique cryptographic fingerprint for each dataset and records a summary of that information on XRPL.
The original data remains private and off-chain. Only its cryptographic fingerprint is placed on the ledger.
Anyone receiving the file can then verify its authenticity with a single XRPL lookup.
In simple words, the XRP Ledger acts like a public, tamper-resistant notary for official information.
The Results Were Impressive
According to the official BIS working paper, the prototype achieved:
- Publication latency: 3–5 seconds
- Verification latency: 1–2 seconds
- One XRPL entry capable of securing thousands of datasets
- Negligible blockchain fees when datasets are processed in batches
- No sensitive underlying information stored on-chain
The researchers also released an open-source XRPL-based reference implementation.
This means we are not looking at an empty mention inside a theoretical report. A functioning prototype was actually developed and tested.
Why Did They Choose XRPL?
The paper explains that XRPL was selected because of its:
- Low transaction fees
- Fast consensus finality
- Available developer resources
- Existing technical analysis of its consensus protocol
These are precisely the characteristics the XRP community has discussed for years.
Institutions do not simply need a blockchain that works. They need infrastructure that is fast, inexpensive, predictable and sufficiently documented to survive serious technical evaluation.
XRPL checked those boxes.
The AI Connection Is Even Bigger
The paper specifically identifies automated verification by AI agents as a possible future extension.
This deserves attention.
As AI systems increasingly consume and redistribute financial information, verifying whether a dataset is authentic will become critically important. An AI agent could automatically check the XRP Ledger before using official economic data, confirming both the identity of the publisher and whether the figures were modified.
That potentially positions XRPL at the intersection of:
- Blockchain
- Artificial intelligence
- Government statistics
- Regulatory reporting
- Central-bank infrastructure
- Institutional data verification
The experiment initially focuses on official statistics, but the researchers state that the same approach could extend to other structured statistical and regulatory formats.
What This Does—and Does Not—Mean
Let’s remain accurate.
This is a BIS working paper and proof of concept, not an announcement that the BIS or the world’s central banks have officially adopted XRPL.
The tests were not a production rollout, and the paper clearly states that the authors’ views do not necessarily represent the BIS or its member central banks.
It is also important to understand that this particular experiment concerns data authentication, not XRP being used as a global bridge currency.
But that does not make it insignificant.
Researchers connected to one of the most influential institutions in global finance evaluated multiple technical requirements, selected XRPL and built a functioning system on it.
That is real.
The Bigger Picture for XRP
For years, critics dismissed the XRP Ledger as outdated or claimed institutions would never seriously consider public blockchain infrastructure.
Yet XRPL continues appearing in conversations involving payments, tokenization, stablecoins, digital identity—and now the cryptographic verification of official statistics.
This paper does not prove that XRP will become the world reserve currency tomorrow.
It demonstrates something more tangible:
When institutional researchers needed a fast and inexpensive public ledger for a real-world prototype, they selected XRPL—and it worked.
The transformation of global financial infrastructure will not happen through one announcement. It will happen through research papers, prototypes, regulatory approvals, institutional integrations and production systems that gradually connect.
This BIS paper represents another piece of that infrastructure quietly taking shape.
The crowd may see a technical experiment.
The XRP community should recognize what is actually happening: XRPL is continuing to prove that it was built for a world far larger than retail speculation.

BlackRock is pushing toward tokenized markets, Ripple is building institutional prime-brokerage infrastructure, and XRP could become a critical bridge connecting this new financial system.
XRP has reclaimed the $1.40 level as I write this, but the chart is not the most important development taking place right now.
What matters far more is what some of the largest institutions in the world are building behind the scenes.
BlackRock has made its position on tokenization increasingly clear. Ripple has expanded far beyond cross-border payments and entered institutional prime brokerage. Real-world assets are moving on-chain, markets are gradually becoming available 24 hours a day, and the infrastructure required to connect all of this is being assembled in real time.
This is where XRP becomes extremely interesting.
A Former BlackRock Executive Speaks About XRP
A former BlackRock managing director recently discussed the prospects of XRP and Ripple, arguing that institutional adoption could ultimately make the ecosystem successful.
His point was simple but important: Ripple does not need to capture the entire financial market—or even the majority of it—to become an enormously successful company.
The market Ripple is targeting is so vast that securing even a relatively small share could represent tremendous value. International payments, foreign exchange, tokenized securities, institutional liquidity and settlement are all multitrillion-dollar markets.
Retail investors frequently struggle to comprehend the scale involved. They debate whether XRP must replace SWIFT completely or dominate every financial institution on Earth. That is not necessary.
If major banks, asset managers, payment companies and trading institutions adopt Ripple’s infrastructure in any meaningful capacity, the addressable market is already enormous.
We should also be precise: the comments of a former BlackRock executive are not an official BlackRock endorsement of XRP. Nevertheless, it is significant to hear someone with experience inside the world’s largest asset manager openly recognize the potential institutional case for Ripple and XRP.
BlackRock’s Tokenization Ambition
BlackRock is the world’s largest asset-management company, investing trillions of dollars on behalf of individuals, institutions and governments.
That is why its increasingly public support for tokenization matters.
Commentary circulating in the market has attributed to BlackRock CFO Martin Small an aggressive timeline for tokenizing the firm’s ETF products. Whether every ETF ultimately moves on-chain within that precise window remains to be independently confirmed by BlackRock, but the broader direction is undeniable.
BlackRock CEO Larry Fink has repeatedly described tokenization as the next evolution of financial markets. BlackRock’s own research explains that tokenization can allow ownership or economic exposure to assets to be programmed, traded, settled and recorded on blockchain infrastructure. Fink has also discussed the tokenization of assets ranging from equities and bonds to real estate.
This is no longer a theoretical conversation restricted to cryptocurrency enthusiasts. The largest asset manager in the world is openly discussing blockchain as new infrastructure for traditional finance.
If BlackRock eventually tokenizes a meaningful portion of its ETF business, it would represent a monumental shift. Traditional investment products would begin operating through blockchain-based rails, potentially improving their programmability, accessibility and settlement.
That does not mean trillions of dollars would instantly flow into XRP. It means something more fundamental: blockchain would move from being treated primarily as a speculative market to becoming part of the plumbing of global finance.
Tokenized Markets Need More Than Tokens
It is easy to become distracted by the word “tokenization.” Creating a digital representation of an ETF, bond, treasury instrument or property is only the first step.
The more important question is how all these assets will move, trade and settle across different institutions and networks.
Tokenized markets will require:
- Fast and reliable settlement
- Extremely low transaction costs
- Deep institutional liquidity
- Interoperability between different networks
- Secure custody and risk management
- Efficient movement between tokenized assets and fiat currencies
- Infrastructure capable of operating continuously
This is not a market designed for slow, expensive or unpredictable transactions. Institutions cannot afford to wait hours for settlement whenever a network becomes congested. They require infrastructure that is dependable at scale.
The XRP Ledger was designed around many of these requirements. It offers rapid settlement, low transaction costs, a built-in decentralized exchange and the ability to issue and transfer tokenized assets.
Most importantly, XRP was designed to function as a neutral bridge asset.
As more assets and financial networks move on-chain, fragmentation may become one of the industry’s greatest problems. There will not necessarily be one blockchain, one stablecoin or one tokenized marketplace. There may be thousands of separate pools of value that need to communicate and exchange liquidity.
XRP could become one of the bridges connecting them.
Ripple Prime Changes the XRP Conversation
For years, the market treated Ripple almost exclusively as a cross-border payments company.
That description is now outdated.
Following its acquisition of Hidden Road, Ripple launched Ripple Prime, a global multi-asset prime-brokerage platform for institutional clients. Its services extend across digital assets, foreign exchange, derivatives, swaps and fixed income.
Prime brokers form part of the core infrastructure of traditional markets. They provide institutions with access to multiple products, trading venues, liquidity sources and balance sheets while consolidating execution, margin and risk management.
As real-world assets and financial products move on-chain, prime brokers will have to connect traditional markets with digital venues. Treasury management, collateral, liquidity and risk systems will need to function in an environment that never closes.
Ripple Prime is being built directly for that transition.
This places Ripple in a far larger position than many XRP holders realize. The company is no longer attempting merely to improve a cross-border payment. It is building an institutional layer through which professional investors can access and manage activity across traditional and digital markets.
Through Ripple Prime, XRP could potentially serve as a liquidity and settlement asset connecting institutional trading with the growing tokenized economy. RLUSD may also play an important role as stable collateral and settlement liquidity inside Ripple’s expanding financial ecosystem.
The exact level of XRP usage will depend on product design, regulation and institutional demand; Ripple Prime’s success alone does not guarantee that every transaction will use XRP. But the strategic alignment is clear: Ripple now controls infrastructure positioned at the point where traditional finance, crypto liquidity and on-chain markets converge.
XRP Is Becoming Financial Infrastructure
One of the greatest misconceptions in cryptocurrency is that XRP remains only a cross-border payments token.
The opportunity is becoming considerably larger.
If ETFs, bonds, equities, currencies and real-world assets move on-chain, institutions will need unified access to custody, credit, liquidity, collateral, execution and near-instant settlement.
Ripple is assembling these components:
- Ripple Payments for international value transfer
- Ripple Custody for institutional asset management
- RLUSD for stablecoin liquidity
- The XRP Ledger for tokenization and settlement
- Ripple Prime for institutional trading and capital efficiency
- XRP as a potential neutral bridge between fragmented assets and markets
This is not proof that BlackRock will select the XRP Ledger or use XRP directly. No such partnership has been officially announced.
However, BlackRock’s tokenization agenda validates the direction Ripple has pursued for more than a decade. The financial system is moving toward digital ownership, continuous markets and blockchain-based settlement—the exact environment in which Ripple’s infrastructure was designed to operate.
Why I Am Watching Institutions, Not Just the Chart
Short-term price action can easily distract investors from structural change.
XRP may rise, retrace or remain volatile. None of that changes the fact that institutional finance is moving steadily toward tokenized assets and blockchain-based infrastructure.
BlackRock is publicly championing tokenization. Ripple has built a global prime broker. Institutional liquidity is entering digital markets. Real-world assets are being issued on-chain. The boundaries separating traditional finance from cryptocurrency are beginning to disappear.
This could therefore be one of the worst possible moments to evaluate XRP exclusively through a short-term chart.
I am watching where institutional capital is moving, what infrastructure is being built and which assets are positioned to connect the new system.
The tokenization race is accelerating.
XRP does not need to control the entire financial system to succeed. It only needs to become useful infrastructure within a market measured in trillions of dollars.
And that possibility is becoming increasingly difficult to ignore.

For the past several years, I considered establishing my tax residency in Dubai. I travelled there frequently, enjoyed the lifestyle and understood why so many entrepreneurs and crypto investors had chosen the UAE.
But eventually, I made a different decision.
I have now officially chosen Cyprus as the base for my tax residency.
My primary home has traditionally been in Greece, and I still spend a significant amount of time there. But Cyprus gives me something increasingly difficult to find: a competitive tax framework, access to the European Union, a Mediterranean lifestyle and the flexibility to continue travelling around the world.
This is not simply a decision about paying less tax. If taxes were the only consideration, there would be several jurisdictions worth examining.
The real question is whether you actually want to live there.
And in Cyprus, the answer for me was yes.
A bridge between Europe and the Middle East
Location was one of the most important factors behind my decision.
Cyprus sits between Europe and the Middle East. From Larnaca, I can reach Athens in approximately one hour, while Dubai is only a few hours away. There are also affordable direct connections to numerous destinations across Europe and the surrounding region.
For someone who travels constantly for conferences, investments and business, Cyprus functions as an extremely practical base.
I can spend time in Limassol, return to Greece, attend an event in another European country or fly to the Middle East without feeling geographically isolated.
Cyprus is a member of the European Union, although it is not currently part of the Schengen Area. This provides an important level of institutional and political stability while preserving its strategic position at the crossroads of three continents.
Why I reconsidered Dubai
I still like Dubai, particularly during the European winter. It offers sunshine, luxury, exceptional service and an enormous international business community.
However, living somewhere is different from visiting it.
Residency requirements, extreme summer temperatures, regional uncertainty and the prospect of spending a substantial portion of every year in the desert made me reconsider whether it was the correct long-term base for me.
Cyprus offers many of the characteristics that originally attracted me to Dubai—but in a more European and Mediterranean environment.
Limassol has modern residential towers, luxury restaurants, international companies, marinas and an increasingly wealthy foreign population. At the same time, it still feels like an island.
Life moves more slowly. The sea is always nearby. You can walk along the coast at sunset, rent a boat, go fishing or drive into the mountains.
It feels less artificial and more connected to nature.
The Mediterranean lifestyle matters
Cyprus reportedly receives more than 300 days of sunshine per year. The island is surrounded by remarkably clean water, with everything from rocky swimming areas to long sandy beaches.
You can spend the morning working, walk beside the sea in the afternoon and have dinner overlooking the Mediterranean.
During winter, you can travel into the Troodos Mountains for hiking and even skiing. During summer, you have beaches, boats, diving and almost every water activity imaginable.
Limassol is also far more developed than many people expect. It offers food delivery, luxury properties, modern gyms, international restaurants and most of the conveniences found in a major city.
As an Italian, I take food seriously. Cyprus is naturally influenced by Greek and Mediterranean cuisine, but Limassol also has excellent Italian restaurants and pizzerias using imported ingredients and experienced chefs.
You receive the slower rhythm of island life without sacrificing the conveniences of a modern international city.
For me, that balance is extremely valuable.
Crypto markets never sleep. Trading and managing an online business can create enormous amounts of stress. Living near the sea, walking at sunset, fishing and swimming have helped me maintain a healthier balance.
And yes, during the filming of this video, a sea turtle unexpectedly appeared while I was swimming. Perhaps Cyprus already has its own XRP whales.
The tax framework attracting entrepreneurs
Now we arrive at the reason many entrepreneurs and crypto investors are beginning to pay attention.
Cyprus offers a competitive tax system for qualifying residents and businesses. The exact treatment of cryptocurrency depends on the nature and frequency of the activity, the taxpayer’s status, the source of income and the structure being used.
The framework discussed in my video includes a flat tax treatment for qualifying digital-asset gains, alongside a competitive corporate-tax environment. Qualifying non-domiciled residents may also benefit from exemptions relating to certain dividend and interest income.
These rules can make Cyprus particularly interesting for entrepreneurs who operate companies internationally or investors who may eventually realise gains from Bitcoin, XRP or other digital assets.
However, there is no universal “zero-tax” answer that applies to everyone.
Someone occasionally selling a long-term investment may be treated differently from a professional trader, a company or someone receiving crypto as business income. Your previous country of residence may also continue to have claims depending on its domestic rules and whether you have properly broken tax residency there.
This is why professional structuring is essential.
The 60-day tax-residency rule
One of Cyprus’s most significant advantages is its 60-day tax-residency route.
Simply spending 60 days on the island is not enough by itself. Applicants must satisfy all applicable legal conditions, including limits on time spent in other countries, maintaining the required connection to Cyprus and not being considered tax-resident elsewhere.
For internationally mobile entrepreneurs, however, the framework can provide considerably more flexibility than systems requiring someone to remain in one country for most of the year.
Evidence also matters.
Bank statements, airline tickets, accommodation records, local spending, utility bills and other documentation may be used to demonstrate your physical presence and connection to Cyprus. Opening a local bank account and obtaining a Cypriot telephone number can also become part of establishing a genuine presence.
The structure must exist in reality—not merely on paper.
Is Cyprus becoming the new Dubai?
I do not believe Cyprus will replace Dubai completely. They serve different markets and offer very different experiences.
But Cyprus is beginning to attract the same category of person: internationally mobile entrepreneurs, investors, executives and wealthy individuals looking for security, connectivity and a favourable environment in which to live and operate.
Limassol already has a significant international community. New developments are transforming its skyline, capital continues to enter the property market and networking opportunities are expanding.
The difference is that Cyprus combines this international capital with European institutions and Mediterranean culture.
You can live beside the sea, conduct business within the EU, reach Athens in approximately one hour and remain only a short flight from the Middle East.
For Bitcoin and XRP investors who want a European base, that combination is difficult to ignore.
Professional assistance with relocating to Cyprus
I am working with specialist lawyers who assist with Cyprus tax residency, relocation and company formation.
If you are seriously considering moving to Cyprus or establishing a business here, you can contact M.M. Global directly:
Website:
[link]
Email: mm@mmlaw.global
Mention that you discovered them through my video so they understand where your enquiry originated.
Every situation is different. Before changing your tax residency, selling digital assets or establishing a company, obtain advice based on your citizenship, current residence, income sources and business activities.
Cyprus is not a magic loophole. It is a legitimate jurisdiction with specific requirements that must be respected.
But when structured correctly—and when combined with the lifestyle available here—it may be one of the most compelling options in Europe for the new generation of globally mobile investors.
For me, Cyprus offers something rare: the ability to protect my time, preserve more of what I earn and enjoy the life I have worked to build.
And sometimes, after a stressful day in the crypto market, you may even find yourself swimming beside a sea turtle.

Tax treatment depends on individual circumstances and may change. Always consult a qualified professional before making decisions involving residency, corporate structures or digital assets.

However, the underlying data is clear: large XRP wallets are increasing their exposure while smaller holders are surrendering their positions. The question is whether retail investors are once again transferring their assets to patient capital immediately before the market enters its next phase.
