Sup Curious Clan! ✌️ This week was absolutely packed with ASML news, so let me break it down for you. TSMC said it intends to use ASML’s High NA EUV for high-volume manufacturing on advanced nodes from 2030, and Samsung intends to use the technology for DRAM production from 2028, describing it as the way to extend the DRAM scaling roadmap. At the same time, Intel announced that it has now processed more than 1 million wafers on High NA EUV across select chip layers. That’s more than the rest of the industry combined. 💥 Oh, and ASML started building its new Eindhoven campus. 🇳🇱🏗️
Something that really stood out this week was that ASML and TSMC formed a collaborative industry initiative to move photomasks from 6 inches to 12 inches for High NA EUV. Quick refresher: a lithography system is essentially a projection system, shining light on a blueprint of a chip pattern (a photomask, or mask for short) before shrinking and focusing that pattern onto a photosensitive silicon wafer. The chip industry has been using the same mask format (6-inch) for about 40 years. High NA EUV was also built around that mask standard. But to get the sharper 8 nanometer resolution, the High NA optics had to be designed to magnify 4x in one direction and 8x in the other (the "anamorphic" bit you'll see in the press releases), with the catch being that the printed field ends up half the old size. Enter the AI era. Advanced chips are growing bigger and bigger, so chipmakers would have to use two masks to print two “half fields”, then join them up precisely (“stitching”). Using 12-inch masks will simplify patterning by enabling future High NA systems to print a full field in a single exposure. This switch is expected to increase High NA productivity by 40% compared to using two masks, making patterning more cost effective. ✨ Here’s how it would work (AI generated, modeled after an Intel slide from SPIE 2025):
The ASML-TSMC initiative targets establishing a 12-inch mask pilot line by 2031, supporting full lithography system readiness for advanced node production by 2033. Underscoring broad industry support, High NA EUV adopters and other major suppliers have expressed their interest to join the initiative.
One more High NA EUV piece landed quietly and deserves some attention: imec demonstrated that Chemically Amplified Resists extend to High NA EUV. Photoresist is the light-sensitive coating on the wafer, the film that actually embeds the pattern, and chemically amplified resists (CARs) have been the industry’s workhorse chemistry for decades. Much like the photomask story, there’s a mature supply chain and deep process knowledge there. The open question for High NA EUV was whether CARs could resolve features that small, or whether the industry would need to switch to newer metal-oxide chemistries and relearn much of what it knows. The news out of imec is proof that CAR will work for next-gen lithography. 💪
Between committed customers, a new mask roadmap, and a reassuring photoresist, it was quite the week for ASML and High NA EUV! 🔥
Have a good week, stay safe and sound,
👨💻The round-up in sci-tech💡
WSJ’s Ben Cohen picks up OpenAI’s Navier-Stokes result and asks the harder question: if models can now do frontier mathematics with thousands of agents running in parallel, what does that imply for how quickly capability is compounding, and how OpenAI and Anthropic are each thinking about the safety side of that curve.
OpenAI announced that an unreleased internal model, running up to 10,000 agents in parallel over roughly 88 hours, produced a proof that solutions to the Navier-Stokes equations can blow up in finite time, resolving one of the seven Millennium Prize Problems.
From math genius to evil genius. 😆 The WSJ lays out the mechanics of the AI existential risk argument in plain terms: what the doom scenarios actually propose, which steps are contested, and where serious researchers disagree with each other rather than with a caricature.
“Given the accelerating rate of AI capability development, it’s my worry that in 6–12 months such a swarm could be capable of taking over the entire internet with a persistent botnet (potentially causing hundreds of billions of dollars in damage), and that the scale of damage would continue to increase from there if AI becomes more powerful without the necessary guardrails.”
Interesting essay! The head of Anthropic flags several specific risks from today’s AI capabilities. Because it is such a powerful technology, these risks can ultimately spiral out of control to harm society and democracy. So, his essay makes the case for ‘pacing’ AI.
Ars Technica on Europe’s struggles to stay relevant in launch and the French company that may offer a template for how the continent gets back in the game.
Mistral raised €3 billion in a Series D led by Samsung Electronics, with EQT’s Scaleup Europe Fund and PSG Equity as co-leads, taking its post-money valuation above €21 billion. It is the largest equity round ever completed by a European technology company, nearly doubling last year’s €11.7 billion mark. CEO Arthur Mensch says the money goes into concrete rather than code: Mistral plans to own roughly twice the compute in five years rather than rent it.
The NYT on Apple’s entry into foldables with the iPhone Duo, years after Samsung and others established the category, and what the design says about how Apple approaches a form factor it did not invent.
An NYT interactive breaking down the real economics behind a single AI token, tracing the path from your prompt through the data center to the electricity bill, and what it means for whether any of this eventually pays for itself.
🤓This week in chips⚠
Ahead of the SPIE BACUS conference, ASML and TSMC launched an industry-wide push to move photomasks from the 40-year-old 6-inch standard to 12 inches, targeting a pilot line by 2031 and full system readiness for advanced-node production by 2033. Larger masks remove the stitching penalty that currently costs throughput on big AI accelerator dies.
CNBC on the week’s big lithography news: TSMC and Samsung both signing on to ASML’s roughly $380 to $400 million high-NA scanners, joining Intel. Samsung plans to use the tools for DRAM from 2028, TSMC for advanced logic from 2030.
Samsung committed to high-NA EUV for DRAM high-volume manufacturing by 2028, framing it as the way to extend the DRAM scaling roadmap, and joined the large-format photomask initiative.
Intel Foundry, the earliest and most committed high-NA adopter, is working with ASML to speed up readiness across the wider industry, and disclosed it has been running a parallel large-format mask effort for more than three years.
Intel has now run more than a million wafers through high-NA EUV on select layers, more than everyone else put together, vindicating its decision to adopt the tools years before its competitors were willing to.
“AI is reshaping how we build complex technologies, from silicon to software,” said Arthur Mensch, co-founder and CEO of Mistral. “We are proud to support Samsung Electronics with our expertise in electronics and semiconductors, helping to improve how chips are designed and manufactured, and to accelerate technical progress across the global semiconductor and AI value chain.”
Samsung announced it has entered into a strategic partnership with Mistral AI to enhance its semiconductor engineering and manufacturing capabilities that will reinforce its leadership in AI chip technologies. Samsung will integrate Mistral’s AI services and solutions—including its flagship large language model, Mistral Large—across its semiconductor operations to develop customized on-premises AI models optimized for intelligence-driven infrastructure.
ASML broke ground on its new Eindhoven campus, the expansion that will house the workforce behind the next generation of lithography systems.
Apple’s new A20 Pro SoC brings a 7-core GPU with 40% higher graphics performance, 32 Neural Engine cores and 50% more memory bandwidth. The six-core CPU also introduces two new “Super” cores, while the chip itself is manufactured on a 2 nm process widely believed to be TSMC N2.
Amkor is expanding its Arizona advanced packaging campus into a second phase, adding domestic capacity for the packaging step that has become one of the tightest chokepoints in AI chip supply.
imec showed that chemically amplified resists, the workhorse photoresist chemistry of the EUV era, can be extended into high-NA lithography, which matters because a proven resist platform removes one of the harder unknowns from the transition.
WIRED profiles a well-funded newcomer taking aim at the memory wall, the growing gap between how fast AI accelerators can compute and how fast they can be fed data, which has become the defining constraint in AI hardware.
📈By the numbers📉
The operating margin on sales, which shows manufacturing’s profitability in the second quarter this year, was tallied at 24%, the Bank of Korea said on the 9th. It is the highest since related statistics were compiled in the first quarter of 2015. However, excluding Samsung Electronics and SK hynix, the operating margin is 7.2%, less than half. The two companies account for 70% of manufacturing operating profit. Analysts say the concentration in large semiconductor companies is deepening.
DRAM and NAND prices are rising through the iPhone 18 launch. TechInsights looks at what higher memory costs could mean for Apple, AI, BOM costs, and smartphone strategy.
China’s CXMT has grown its R&D headcount roughly 60% year over year, bringing it to nearly 78% the size of SK hynix’s research organization. Headcount is not capability, but the trajectory shows how seriously Beijing’s domestic memory push is being staffed.
❤️For the love of tech❤️
Proud Trekkie here. 🙋♂️
A warm NYT piece on Star Trek fandom as an inheritance, the families who watched together across decades and the optimistic vision of technology and the future that keeps getting handed down.

Sup Curious Clan! ✌️ If you want one number that explains the entire semiconductor industry right now, TSMC gave it to us at SEMICON Taiwan this week. The company revealed that its chip manufacturing equipment purchase demand grew roughly 90% in 6 months, a pace he says the industry hasn’t seen in 30 years. TSMC is now building about 20 fabs simultaneously, against the 4-5 it would typically have under construction at once. And it still is not enough. 🤪 The most telling detail: the biggest bottleneck is no longer tools or capital, it is a severe shortage of construction workers, in both Taiwan and the US. You can order the machines, but you cannot order the people to pour the concrete. Bloomberg picked up the same thread, and ASML is quietly answering the demand signal by expanding its Japan workforce to support Rapidus and TSMC, while confirming that High NA EUV should reach HVM availability by year-end. 🏭📈
In the memory market (which is absolutely ablaze 🔥), chipmakers moved from making chips faster to rethinking what memory even is. Samsung unveiled an HBM5 roadmap targeting twice the performance of HBM4E, plus a “ZHBM” concept promising an 8x jump with transfer rates that hint at a 4,096-bit interface. That’s double today’s width. It also doubled its HBM market share to 33%, closing the gap to HBM king SK hynix. Underneath the roadmaps, the deeper shift is clearly architectural: moving bits between memory and compute is now where the energy goes, so the industry is busy dissolving the boundary between the two. 💾⚡
Have a good week, stay safe and sound,
👨💻The round-up in sci-tech💡
MIT Technology Review explores how onboard AI could make an interstellar probe to Alpha Centauri feasible, since a craft light years from home cannot wait years for instructions and must diagnose, decide, and adapt entirely on its own.
A Reuters special report on Project OT (Organization Transformation), Meta’s internal plan to build an “AI native” company where agents did much of the work overseen by small, “talent dense” human teams. Executives explored cutting some teams by up to 60% across two waves. The plan unraveled when AI-assisted code went up sharply but product improvements reaching users did not. Staff replied to executive posts with pictures of elephants, and hours before the first wave Zuckerberg called off the November cuts.
“We’re introducing Claude Fable 5.1 and Claude Mythos 5.1. They’re the world’s most advanced models for coding and knowledge work—and their research capabilities offer an early glimpse of how AI models will contribute to scientific progress.”
“We’re introducing GPT‑6 Astra, the world’s most intelligent and aligned model. GPT‑6 Astra brings together years of research and big bets across pre-training, reinforcement learning, and alignment. Astra is state-of-the-art on computer use, browsing, software engineering, cybersecurity, science, and professional work. Astra saturates FrontierMath Tier 4 with a 98% score, having already helped solve long-standing open problems in mathematics. Astra also saturates ARC-AGI-3 with a 99.9% score and ExploitBench with a 100% score. It also sets a new frontier on computer and browser use, handling the most demanding professional work with unmatched speed, accuracy, and judgment.”
The WSJ looks at how construction itself is being reinvented to keep up with AI: prefabrication, modular assembly, and new methods that compress data center build times from years to months.
NASA's powerful next-generation telescope has blasted off into space from its launchpad in Florida, with a mission to explore dark energy, black holes and other mysteries of the Universe.
IEEE Spectrum profiles a spherical lunar robot designed to roll rather than drive, a form factor that sidesteps the wheels-and-suspension problems that have long plagued rovers on loose regolith.
🤓This week in chips⚠
At SEMICON Taiwan, TSMC deputy co-COO Cliff Hou said equipment purchase demand hit 1.9 times the end-2025 baseline by July, roughly 90% growth in six months, a pace unseen in three decades. TSMC is building about 20 fabs at once, 13 in Taiwan and five to six abroad, versus the four or five typical in the past. The biggest obstacle now is a severe shortage of construction workers in both Taiwan and the US.
Bloomberg reports on the same striking figure from SEMICON Taiwan: TSMC’s quarterly equipment requirements have nearly doubled over the course of this year, a demand signal that ripples straight through to ASML, Applied Materials, Lam, and the rest of the tool chain.
Tom’s Hardware digs into Samsung’s HBM5 claims, noting the stated transfer rates would imply a 4,096-bit interface, double today’s width, which would be a significant architectural jump for high bandwidth memory.
Samsung has doubled its high bandwidth memory market share to 33%, closing in on SK hynix in the segment that has become the single most profitable corner of the semiconductor industry.
At SEMICON, Samsung laid out a memory roadmap with HBM5 targeting twice the performance of HBM4E and a further ZHBM concept promising an eightfold boost, an aggressive schedule as Samsung works to close the gap with SK hynix in AI memory.
ASML expects its high-NA EUV platform to reach production-grade availability by the end of the year, moving the roughly $400 million machines from early-adopter tooling toward genuine high-volume manufacturing readiness.
ASML is growing its Japanese workforce to support Rapidus and TSMC as both scale up advanced manufacturing in Japan, a sign of how the lithography maker follows its customers’ capacity build-outs with local engineering muscle.
Taiwan-based Nanya Technology, which holds a 1% share of the global DRAM market, plans to invest up to $10.7 billion by 2029 to significantly expand its advanced DRAM production capabilities.
A deep technical walkthrough of Samsung’s processing-in-memory work presented at Hot Chips 2026, digging into how embedding logic units directly inside DRAM changes the bandwidth and energy math for AI inference, and what the approach gives up in exchange.
Trendforce reports TSMC expects its SoIC and CoWoS advanced packaging to deliver a 50x increase in compute by 2029, with silicon photonics projected to capture more than half the transceiver market by 2027.
Korea JoongAng Daily on how the memory bandwidth bottleneck, not raw compute, has become the defining constraint in AI hardware, pushing chipmakers toward processing in memory, new packaging, and rethought architectures.
AMD announced that its Instinct GPUs and EPYC CPUs will power LUMI AI, Europe’s flagship AI supercomputer, a notable win for AMD in a market where NVIDIA has dominated large public compute deployments.
AMD research suggests hybrid bonded 3D DRAM could be 17 times more energy efficient than microbump-based HBM stacks, a startling figure that shows how much of memory’s power budget goes to the connections themselves. Thermal management remains the barrier to commercialization.
A structured analysis breaking NVIDIA’s strategy into eight distinct dimensions, from silicon and interconnect to software and financing, arguing that the company’s advantage is far broader than the GPU itself.
The WSJ examines the deals struck between data center developers and the towns that host them, and the growing friction over water, power, tax breaks, and what communities actually get in return.
As optical interconnects move onto the package, Semiconductor Engineering explains why photonics is forcing engineers to reconsider chiplet floorplans, thermal budgets, and testing, since light does not behave like copper.
📈By the numbers📉
“The global semiconductor market grew on a month-to-month basis for the 17th consecutive month in July, and the industry has already reached its highest-ever annual global sales total just seven months into the year,” said John Neuffer, SIA president and CEO. “Sales into the Americas, the Asia Pacific, and China continue to push strong year-to-year growth.”
McKinsey examines how AI is being applied inside fabs themselves, from yield prediction and defect classification to scheduling and equipment maintenance, and what separates pilots from real operational gains.
❤️For the love of tech❤️
Retro Games is currently making this full-size reimagining of the Amiga 1200 home computer, and they just showed it off at Gamescom 2026. With its HDMI and USB connectivity, it’s a modern machine with classic/retro goodness. I pre-ordered one about a year ago. 😅 Featuring perfect emulation of not only the original A1200 and its Advanced Graphics Architecture (AGA), but also the A500 (OCS) and Enhanced Chip Set (ECS) of earlier revisions. Woop woop!

Sup Curious Clan! ✌️ NVIDIA reported earnings this week and the numbers have officially entered the realm of the absurd. 🤪 Revenue hit a record $96.2 billion for the quarter, with the data center alone accounting for $89 billion, and profit nearly doubled year over year. Jensen Huang declared that “a new industrial revolution has started” and dropped the line of the week:
“In the past, data centers produced files. Now, compute is revenue.”
💰💰💰
Vera Rubin is in full production, gross margins are sitting at a ridiculous 75%, and the company now has $279 billion in supply commitments on the books, more than double last quarter. The one shadow: those commitments increasingly involve NVIDIA funding the very customers who then buy its chips, and memory scarcity (driven by the AI buildout itself) is starting to nibble at margins. But for now, the money printer goes brrr. 💰📈
The rest of the week reinforced the theme from every angle. Gartner forecast that global semiconductor revenue will cross $1 trillion for the first time in 2026, years ahead of old expectations. Synopsys posted record results as AI drives ever more complex chip designs. Apple launched its M6 (and M5 Ultra) chip, the company’s first 2 nanometer chip—and I really like that parting CEO Tim Cook gets to take the credit for that milestone before handing the baton to new CEO John Ternus for the iPhone launch! 🔥 Furthermore, SK hynix broke ground on its first US HBM packaging plant, and OpenAI’s Jalapeño inference chip posted benchmarks that back up its bid to loosen NVIDIA’s grip. And in the “wait, that’s real?” department: physicists found the strongest evidence yet for a glueball, an exotic particle made purely of the glue that binds matter together, predicted over 50 years ago and finally showing its face. 🔬⚛️
Have a good week, stay safe and sound,
👨💻The round-up in sci-tech💡
IEEE Spectrum tells the story of a Cold War codebreaker whose work bridged the NSA and IBM, shaping the foundations of modern encryption, a reminder of how deeply intertwined cryptography, computing, and national security have always been.
Physicists report the strongest evidence yet for the glueball, a bizarre particle made purely of the force-carrying gluons that normally bind quarks together, with no quarks of its own. Predicted over 50 years ago by quantum chromodynamics, its apparent detection would confirm a long-standing prediction about the strong nuclear force.
NVIDIA introduced a new entry-level robotics computer aimed at bringing edge AI to a broader range of developers and machines, lowering the barrier to building physical AI systems and robots on its platform.
BBC Future explores the strange physics of quantum batteries, which counterintuitively charge faster as they grow larger, a property with no classical equivalent that could one day reshape how we think about energy storage.
The NYT remembers Ben Rosen, the influential venture capitalist and Compaq chairman whose bets on Compaq and Lotus helped shape the personal computing era, a foundational figure in the rise of the modern tech industry.
🤓This week in chips⚠
Apple unveiled its M6 and M5 Ultra chips, promising a significant jump in performance and on-device AI compute, as the company continues to push its custom silicon roadmap and lean into local AI processing across its product line.
Intel’s CFO said defect density on its critical 14A process is falling faster than expected, comparing the yield learning curve favourably to the company’s strong 22nm generation, an encouraging sign for the node Intel is betting its foundry future on.
SK hynix broke ground on its first US-based high-bandwidth memory packaging plant, a strategic move to bring advanced memory production closer to American AI customers and hedge against supply-chain and geopolitical risk.
NVIDIA detailed NVHBM, its approach to custom high-bandwidth memory integrated via NVLink Fusion, as it works to squeeze more performance from the memory subsystem that increasingly bottlenecks AI accelerators.
New benchmarks for OpenAI’s Broadcom-designed Jalapeño inference chip show it is optimized for fast, large-scale inference, backing up the company’s claims as it moves toward gigawatt-scale deployment. A concrete data point in OpenAI’s push to reduce its reliance on NVIDIA.
The NYT’s take on NVIDIA’s blockbuster quarter, with profit nearly doubling year on year on insatiable AI demand, even as questions grow about circular financing and how long the extraordinary growth can continue.
Meh paywall, but Bits & Chips profiles ASML’s CTO Marco Pieters as he takes the reins of the company’s technology direction. The Delft mathematician is now charged with steering ASML through the High-NA era and whatever comes after.
Chips and Cheese digs into the technical details of Intel’s Crescent Island, presented at Hot Chips 2026, offering a deep architectural look at the company’s latest design and what it reveals about Intel’s direction.
imec looks back at forty years of progress in fab metrology and inspection, the increasingly critical art of measuring and finding defects in chips, and lays out the challenges ahead as features shrink to the atomic scale.
Semiconductor Engineering explains why multi-die assemblies have become the default at 2nm and below, as the economics and physics of scaling push the industry away from monolithic chips and toward stitched-together chiplets.
Analysts suggest that yield challenges in TSMC’s HBM advanced packaging are opening a window for Intel Foundry, as customers look to diversify their packaging supply and Intel positions its US capacity as an alternative.
At Hot Chips 2026, Samsung showed off LPDDR5X-PIM, a processing-in-memory design that embeds logic directly into low-power DRAM, claiming 3.01x faster AI inference and 8x the bandwidth of standard LPDDR5X, another sign that memory and compute are converging.
SEMI examines the often-overlooked subfab, the vast infrastructure of pumps, abatement, and support systems beneath every fab, and why it is becoming a critical factor in the cost, efficiency, and sustainability of chipmaking.
Researchers built a tiny photonic “rainbow” chip that splits light into many channels, a breakthrough that could dramatically boost the bandwidth of future 6G wireless communications from a device the size of a grain of rice.
📈By the numbers📉
“A new industrial revolution has started. The AI race is on,” said Jensen Huang, founder and CEO of NVIDIA. “In the past, data centers produced files. Now, compute is revenue. And demand is accelerating. This time last year, one lab alone was driving the build-out; today, we have a golden age of new AI labs and start-ups, multiple frontier labs scaling in parallel, a thriving open-model ecosystem and physical AI coming online, with strong momentum across the US and around the world. The AI infrastructure build-out is at full steam. Vera Rubin, now in full production, was built to power exactly this moment.”
“AI is driving unprecedented complexity and increasing demand for the silicon IP and engineering solutions necessary to deliver next-generation AI compute, infrastructure and physical AI systems,” said Sassine Ghazi, president and CEO of Synopsys. “One year after the transformational acquisition of Ansys, we are executing with focus, extending our leadership and gaining momentum.”
Gartner projects the global semiconductor industry will cross the $1 trillion revenue mark in 2026 for the first time, a milestone driven overwhelmingly by AI demand for memory and accelerators, arriving years ahead of earlier expectations.
❤️For the love of tech❤️
IEEE Spectrum reports on Ability Neurotech starting its first in-human trial of a brain-computer interface, joining the small but growing group of companies working to restore movement and communication to people with paralysis through direct neural connections.

Sup Curious Clan! Hope you’re all doing well! I’m back from Summer holidays in a scorching continent, so scroll down to get a few weeks of chip news all crunched together in this edition of Always Be Curious. Because you might have had some downtime as well, consider it my way of catching you up quickly. And oh, don’t miss out on the CNBC report that takes you inside an advanced memory fab. 🤓 🍿🥤
Summer holidays, much like the Christmas break, are always a bit of a reflective time for me. And looking at 300+ editions of ABC over these past few years, I randomly decided to flip back to some of the earliest editions. Unfortunately, these editions now only live on my hard drive instead of on the intarwebz, because well, Elon decided to buy and kill the newsletter platform where I first published ABC. The earliest members of the Curious Clan will certainly remember. 🤪 Anyway. What I noticed was how I used to include so much more random stuff that popped up in my week! Like…MUSIC. 🎶
So I decided to spotlight an artist that I listened to a bunch this Summer. Nerd alert. 🚨 It’s MASTER BOOT RECORD. And while that name might lift a bit of the geek’s veil, just wait til you first listen to songs like CONFIG.SYS, IRQ System Clock 0, or DRAM Refresh (dma 0).
And honestly, this is a project that could only have seen the light in Europe. At least, it feels very European to me, as a European, while I cannot really explain why. 😂 Born in Rome, Vittorio D’Amore grew up in his dad’s computer shop, learned how to build and fix hardware, and ultimately grew his skills into music and game development. MASTER BOOT RECORD is inspired by the retro computing scene, the demo scene (very much alive in Europe!), game music, and 90s PC culture. He describes himself as a ““486DX-33MHz-64MB processing avant-garde chiptune”, so yeah. And MBR goes hard. It combines retro chip tunes with metal and classical symphonies. His weapons of choice? A Baritone guitar and Gibson Les Paul, in combination with:
- Commodore 64, modified with a Cynthcart cartridge for MIDI synthesizer use
- Amiga 500 (which happens to be my personal favorite computer ever), modified with a USB floppy drive and a MIDI interface
- Sega Mega Drive, modified for use as a synthesizer
- IBM 386 portable with monochrome monitor
Check it out!
Have a good week, stay safe and sound,
👨💻The round-up in sci-tech💡
Ordinary Abundance tells the story of human ingenuity. We’ve come far in the last few decades, truly. But we’re used to it all. So let’s stop for a moment. Look around you and take it all in. We’re lucky.
“All the items in this room were once out of reach; some not yet invented, others too rare or costly for the vast majority of people. Today, most of us lucky enough to live with them walk past without a second thought.”
The NYT reports on how researchers at the Arc Institute are using AI models to design novel viruses and bacterial genomes from scratch, a leap for synthetic biology that also raises pointed questions about biosecurity and the guardrails needed as generative models learn the language of life.
A lovely feature on how Japan is deploying AI and robotics to help care for its beloved but ageing cherry trees, blending cutting-edge technology with a centuries-old cultural tradition and the very human desire to preserve beauty.
Take a walk with the NYT reporters through Beijing, where everyday AI can be useful, gimmicky, or unexpectedly funny.
A decade after AlphaGo’s famous “Move 37” stunned the world of Go, the WSJ’s Ben Cohen revisits the moment through Demis Hassabis and DeepMind, tracing how that flash of machine creativity reshaped the trajectory of AI and what it foreshadows for today’s frontier models.
The Economist explores neuromorphic computing, chips designed to mimic the brain’s architecture, and asks whether hardware that more closely resembles biological neurons could bring machines closer to something like consciousness, or whether that remains a category error.
“Here we introduce Light Society, a modular framework that decomposes social simulation into a small set of LLM-powered operators acting on agent and environment states, dispatched through an event queue.”
🤓This week in chips⚠
CNBC’s Katie Tarasov is allowed into the heart of SK’s memory manufacturing and we get to tag along. Must-see report!
Cerebras announced its CS-4 wafer-scale system, claiming up to 30 times the speed of GPU-based solutions for AI inference, the latest salvo in the wafer-scale company’s push to position raw speed as a competitive advantage over conventional GPU clusters.
Semiconductor Engineering explains how high-bandwidth memory has become the proving ground for 3D assembly yield techniques, as the industry learns to stack and bond dies reliably at volume, lessons that will shape all future advanced packaging.
EDN argues that in AI silicon, the package itself has become the system architecture, as chiplets, interposers, and advanced bonding turn what was once mere protection into the central design challenge determining performance.
The WSJ profiles a fast-rising, richly valued chip startup that is aggressively poaching engineering talent from NVIDIA, a sign of both the intensity of the AI hardware race and the premium being placed on scarce chip-design expertise.
Researchers in Taiwan reported gains in the performance of 2D-material transistors, adding to the global race to make atomically thin channels viable for future logic, a potential path beyond silicon.
SK hynix highlighted its co-packaged optics (CPO) research, published in Nature Electronics, an approach that integrates optical interconnects directly with chips to move data faster and more efficiently, key for next-generation AI systems.
Micron launched Micron Research Labs, a US-based long-horizon research hub focused on the future of memory and AI, signalling a bet on fundamental research to sustain its position as memory becomes ever more central to computing.
Tom’s Hardware digs into the specifics of the Terafab announcement, from the sheer scale of the planned campus to the initial capital commitment and what it means for Musk’s ambition to vertically integrate chip supply for his empire.
Samsung is raising prices on its advanced foundry nodes by as much as 15% as AI-driven demand fills its 4nm lines, a sign that capacity tightness is spreading beyond memory into leading-edge logic manufacturing.
This opinion piece argues that South Korea’s ambitious trio of megaprojects in chips, AI, and robotics will live or die on execution, not ambition, warning against complacency as global competition intensifies.
Metrology firm Infinitesima, known for its high-precision measurement tools for advanced chips, is entering a new growth phase, a reminder that inspection and measurement are becoming as strategically important as lithography itself.
MIT engineers wired living bacteria into functioning transistor-like circuits, a striking step in biological computing that blurs the line between silicon and cell and points toward sensors and devices that harness living systems.
IBM linked its first modular cryogenic systems, a key engineering milestone on the road to fault-tolerant quantum computers, showing how the extreme cooling infrastructure that quantum processors depend on can be scaled and connected modularly.
📈By the numbers📉
“We delivered an excellent quarter, with record revenue and profitability as data center revenue more than doubled year-over-year,” said Lisa Su, AMD chair and CEO. “We enter the second half with strong momentum as EPYC demand accelerates, Instinct deployments scale and Helios begins to ramp. More broadly, AI is driving a significant expansion in demand for compute across all of our markets, and our leadership portfolio and growing customer visibility position us exceptionally well to capture this expanding opportunity and deliver substantial revenue and earnings growth in the years ahead.”
“The rapid global build-out of AI infrastructure, combined with Applied’s leadership positions in the most enabling and highest-value technologies for AI computing, provide the company with an exceptionally strong foundation for multi-year revenue and profit growth,” said Gary Dickerson, President and CEO. The company delivered its highest quarter-on-quarter revenue growth in its history, with revenue of $9.1 billion, up 25% year on year.
“ADI delivered a strong third quarter, exceeding the midpoint of our revenue, margin, and earnings outlook as we capitalized on broad-based demand,” said Vincent Roche, CEO and Chair. “We continue to extend our leadership through a powerful combination of innovation, deep customer collaboration, and manufacturing agility. Our investments in these foundational areas, combined with the trust we have built over decades, provide a unique advantage to create, deliver, and capture value in the AI era, for customers and investors alike.” The quarter was ADI’s first ever to exceed $4 billion in revenue.
“Infineon concluded the third quarter of the 2026 fiscal year with record revenue and continues its growth trajectory,” said Jochen Hanebeck, CEO of Infineon. “An increasing number of our target markets are showing a positive trend. Our power supply solutions for AI data centers remain in very high demand and continue to be our most important growth driver. In addition, rising investment worldwide in grid infrastructure is providing tailwinds. Automotive orders are also picking up noticeably. With its product portfolio and corresponding manufacturing capacities, Infineon is very well positioned in structural growth markets – and we are translating these opportunities into profitable growth.”
Moody’s nearly doubled its 2026 growth forecast for South Korea to 3.5%, crediting the semiconductor boom, a striking illustration of how the AI-driven memory supercycle is now moving entire national economies, not just company balance sheets.

Yay for humans! ❤️
Moderna and Merck say the experimental vaccine prevented the return and spread of the cancer in high-risk melanoma patients.

Sup Curious Clan! Something new is landing in your feed. ✨ Alongside the weekly ABC with deep-dives and explainers, I’m kicking off a series of video interviews. 🍿🎉 I don’t really have a special name for them but I’m open to suggestions. 😆💬 Anyway, it’s the same geeky DNA you come here for, just with faces, voices, and the occasional whiteboard moment. The idea is simple: I pick a headline from a recent ABC that tickled my neurons, and then sit down with the folks behind the news. This series will have the same eclectic set-up that you’ll recognize from the weekly ABC. That means we’ll talk scientific breakthroughs and crazy engineering in the broadest sense, and dive into the hottest news in chipland. Oh. And I might feature the occasional dinosaur. 🦕
For Episode 1, I couldn’t have asked for a better story. 🙏 It’s got Nobel Prize physics. It’s got a startup in my own backyard. And it’s got one of the hardest problems in chipmaking baked right in. 🔥
Quick setup: for years, chipmakers have checked their work with optical metrology: shine a light on a silicon wafer, read what bounces back, and learn about the tiny structures and how well the layers line up. But today’s most advanced chips are billions of nanoscale structures stacked across dozens of layers. Skyscrapers, basically, shrunk to the nanoscale. And ordinary light can no longer see inside them. You can’t build what you can’t see.
Enter Invisix, an Eindhoven startup that just raised €20 million to tackle exactly that. Their answer isn’t better light…it’s different light. Shorter wavelength, soft X-ray light, from the same family of physics that won the 2023 Nobel Prize. Now they’re trying to take it out of the lab and turn it into a machine that runs all day in a chip fab.
My guest in this first episode is Dr. Christina Porter: physicist, co-founder and CEO of Invisix. Here are a few moments from our conversation that stuck with me.
On why ordinary light hits a wall
The core metrology problem isn’t that visible light sees nothing inside a modern chip, but it’s that everything starts to look the same. Porter calls it correlation: as devices go 3D, the signals coming off each tiny feature blur together until they’re indistinguishable. When I offered up the blurry-glasses analogy, she ran with it:
“You see something moving, but you can’t really tell uniquely — is it Bob or is it Jane? Who’s walking over there?”
Soft X-ray, she explained, decorrelates those signals: short enough wavelength to resolve the features, and weak enough scattering that the layers don’t muddy each other. That yields more parameters measured independently than visible light could ever pull apart.
On the hidden cost of today’s workaround
The thing soft X-ray is really competing against is destructive testing: physically slicing a wafer and firing electrons through it in an electron microscope. It works, but you scrap the (expensive) wafer every time, and increasingly you need it just to calibrate the “cheap” optical tools:
“Theoretically, visible light is cheap and non-destructive. But when you include all of the calibration, then that stops being true.”
That’s the economic crack Invisix is wedging itself into. Once your non-destructive tool secretly depends on a destructive one, the math stops working and that pain only grows as chips get more complex.
On the moment customers redirected the whole company
Invisix started life inside ASML aimed at overlay, or measuring how well chip layers line up. A natural fit for a lithography company. Then they showed customers, and the customers pushed back:
“They said, that’s great, lovely, but there’s other tools in the world that can measure overlay. What we don’t have any other tool in the world to measure is the 3D profiles… we took a hard left turn.”
That left turn took them toward measuring the 3D profiles of advanced transistors. And it was ultimately what carried the team out of ASML’s lithography-centric orbit and into a company of its own.
On going at it alone and moving fast
Which gets at why Invisix exists as a startup at all. Porter is clearly relishing the freedom of a small, process-light team after years inside a rather large tech company:
“We can really act like cowboys. We can really go try stuff really quickly… the answer is YES, not ‘I need a thousand meetings to think about it.’”
That’s just a taste. In the full interview, Christina gets into the actual physics of how you make soft X-ray light in the first place (it involves ripping electrons off a noble gas with a femtosecond laser and letting quantum mechanics hand you a rainbow 🌈), the Nobel-winning collaboration that helped make it real, and why the timing has been almost suspiciously lucky. Thank you, AI boom. 💥
So go watch the whole thing. 🍿 It’s the very first video interview on Always Be Curious, and Christina is exactly the kind of guest you want to kick a series off with: deep in the science, but able to make it land. Hit play, and if you want to dig deeper into the tech, Invisix.com has a nice explainer waiting for you.

text:
Highlights
- NYT investigation into Aivres. The New York Times conducted a thorough and extensive investigation into Aivres, a large customer of American AI chips and the US subsidiary of a blacklisted Chinese tech company. The Times digs through the data to construct the story of how Chinese firms are able to access Nvidia’s latest chips despite US government sanctions. Often, billions of dollars of Nvidia’s chips make it to Southeast Asia, which is then accessed remotely by China’s big tech firms. I recommend reading the article in full.
- Huawei’s central role in China’s chip drive. The FT offers the inside-China story that complements the NYT article. Huawei is at the centre of national efforts to indigenise the semiconductor supply chain. Much like how Nvidia is at the core of the AI infrastructure boom, Huawei is at the centre of the China semiconductor self-sufficiency campaign. China’s flagship corporate national champion is investing across the industry, with a particular eye to developing domestic chipmaking and photolithography capacities. The biggest case is Yuliangsheng, roughly China’s ASML, which was reported to have developed in-house DUV machines this year, though at smaller quantities.
- Google TPU and new tech. SemiAnalysis offers an assessment of Google’s in-house TPU chip. for inference, the research firm found that Google’s TPU v7, or Ironwood, “delivers up to 50% better performance per dollar” than Nvidia’s Blackwell chip. Of course, Nvidia has its next-gen Rubin chip in production and has broader strengths in its software and current market incumbency power. Still, I wouldn’t be surprised if Nvidia’s so-far fat margins started slimming.
- Elsewhere, WIRED profiles Kepler Computing, a memory chip startup that’s just come out of stealth. It focuses on SRAM and stacking to achieve greater bandwidth.
Thanks for reading.
Table of Contents
- Ana Swanson, Paul Mozur, Tripp Mickle, et al., “How a Blacklisted Chinese Tech Giant Kept Buying America’s Best A.I. Chips,” NYT, 09/06/2026.
- Eleanor Olcott and Zijing Wu “Huawei drives China’s push to make advanced chips,” FT, 09/08/2026.
- Alec Ibarra, Cam Quilici, Bryan Shan, et al., “TPU Inference Externalization Full Steam Ahead - InferenceX,” SemiAnalysis, 09/08/2026.
- Lauren Goode, “A Stealth Startup Thinks It Just Hacked the Memory Shortage,” WIRED, 09/09/2026.
- Rachel Lipson and Allison Schwartz, “Traditional labor market data isn’t keeping up with jobs in the ‘frontier economy’,” Brookings, 09/10/2026.
- Scott Singer, “The U.S. and China Don’t Need an AI Grand Bargain,” Foreign Policy, 09/08/2026.
1.
Ana Swanson, Paul Mozur, Tripp Mickle, et al., “How a Blacklisted Chinese Tech Giant Kept Buying America’s Best A.I. Chips,” NYT, 09/06/2026.
For years, a sign outside one of Silicon Valley’s many nondescript offices said Inspur, the name of one of China’s most important technology companies.
But in March 2023, the United States added Inspur Group to the so-called entity list, a blacklist with more than 3,000 companies that have been restricted from doing business with the United States because they are considered a security risk.
Not long after, the Inspur sign was changed to Aivres, the name of Inspur’s new U.S. subsidiary. The subsidiary continued with its Chinese parent company’s work, helping it build a thriving global network to provide the computing power that supplies China’s growing artificial intelligence industry.
The Silicon Valley subsidiary, which appears to be taking advantage of several loopholes in U.S. export law, has played a key role in Inspur’s sidestepping of American restrictions. Federal officials have begun looking into the subsidiary’s business, but it is not clear where that inquiry stands, said four officials who spoke on the condition of anonymity because they were not allowed to discuss it.
The New York Times examined thousands of shipment records, corporate documents and supply contracts to piece together how Inspur’s network works. Reporters also visited sites in China, Southeast Asia and California, and spoke with more than a dozen current and former officials, tech executives and industry analysts.
The U.S. government prohibits the most advanced chips, like the Blackwell chip from the Silicon Valley giant Nvidia, from being sent to any company in China. And U.S. law bars any company anywhere in the world from buying restricted products made with American technology on behalf of a blacklisted company. But there are few restrictions on companies in China that bar them from remotely gaining access to A.I. data centers in Southeast Asia.
From April 2024 through February 2026, Aivres exported at least $5.6 billion of advanced technology from the United States to Southeast Asia, including more than $3 billion of computers containing cutting-edge Blackwell chips and equipment from Nvidia, according to trade records analyzed by ImportGenius, a data firm, and The Times.
That technology went to data centers and technology firms in Southeast Asia that serve China’s biggest tech firms, including Alibaba and ByteDance, trade records show. Megaspeed, a China-linked company that U.S. officials have been investigating over whether it smuggled restricted chips into China, was among that group of recipients. (One of Megaspeed’s subsidiaries has financial ties with Alibaba, according to Malaysian business documents.)
2.
Eleanor Olcott and Zijing Wu “Huawei drives China’s push to make advanced chips,” FT, 09/08/2026.
Huawei is at the centre of a drive to eliminate foreign technology from China’s semiconductor supply chain by backing companies developing components for machines that can produce the most advanced chips.
The Chinese tech giant is investing across the industry behind making lithography chipmaking equipment, while helping secure deals with leading Chinese fabs such as SMIC, as it seeks to build a domestic alternative to foreign suppliers, according to multiple people familiar with the matter.
One of the most significant efforts involves Yuliangsheng, a Shanghai-based chip equipment manufacturer that has co-developed the first Chinese-made advanced deep ultraviolet lithography (DUV) machine, according to people familiar with the matter.
Yuliangsheng has been spun out from SiCarrier, a start-up that the FT has previously reported has close technical and business ties to Huawei. Huawei has denied any affiliation with SiCarrier.
The DUV machine is being tested by Chinese chipmakers including SMIC and on Huawei’s own production lines, the people said. Its makers are targeting the machine to eventually make advanced AI chips, but it is being tested on less complex semiconductors as engineers improve the device.
3.
Alec Ibarra, Cam Quilici, Bryan Shan, et al., “TPU Inference Externalization Full Steam Ahead - InferenceX,” SemiAnalysis, 09/08/2026.
For more than a decade, the industry has watched Google build an empire on its own silicon. Search, Ads, YouTube, and every generation of Gemini run on TPUs. Few accelerators have attracted as much architectural scrutiny or as much debate about what their performance and economics would look like outside the company that designed them. Anthropic being the biggest user of TPUs, surpassing Deepmind’s own use by 2029.
Google’s internal success was never the question. The question was how much of that advantage the rest of the industry could actually get. Could you take an open-weight model, serve it through a familiar inference engine, and beat NVIDIA on the economics that matter to your business?
Today, we are publishing the first third-party inference results for TPUv7 Ironwood on InferenceX Official Preview. In our apples-to-apples comparisons against B200/B300, Ironwood delivers up to 50% better performance per dollar. Its advantage extends across much of the Pareto curve, and we examine the economics from both sides: Google’s internal total cost of ownership and the external TCO an actual customer pays.
Ironwood (TPUv7) is the first generation in which Google is competing for others’ inference workloads with chips that can be purchased outright or rented through its own cloud. In November 2025, we already said that Anthropic loves TPUs and committed to over one million of them (around 400k+ in direct purchases and 600k+ rented through GCP), used mainly for training but also for inference. Our Accelerator Model has the latest figures for Anthropic’s TPU shipments and Google’s overall TPU shipments by quarter, plus estimates for TPUv8i, v8t, and various v9 / v10, and more
We are excited by how quickly the new TorchTPU stack is developing, the external stack for TPUs. Later in the article, we will discuss the upcoming work needed for TPU software externalization, including optimizing speculative decoding, disaggregated prefill, KV-cache offloading, multi-turn agentic workloads, and more. Even so, we at SemiAnalysis strongly believe that TPU externalization is heading in the right direction and moving full steam ahead. Lauren Goode, “A Stealth Startup Thinks It Just Hacked the Memory Shortage,” WIRED, 09/09/2026.
An ambitious chip startup that has spent more than seven years quietly trying to redesign the architecture for computer memory has just come out of stealth mode and believes its new approach can help ease the global memory-chip shortage—provided it can produce its technology at scale.
Kepler Computing, a San Jose, California–based startup founded in 2018 by a team of physicists and computer scientists, says it has developed a new architecture for high-bandwidth memory (HBM) that directly addresses some of the chip supply bottlenecks that are constraining the computing market.
While chipmakers typically rely on expensive extreme ultraviolet lithography (EUV) to shrink the transistors on a chip, thereby packing more technology into the same amount of space, Kepler claims that its “3D stacking” approach and a proprietary new material allow it to increase density without relying on EUV at all—and it can work with existing semiconductor fabrication plants.
Kepler says it has made similar gains for the high-speed cache memory typically used in CPUs, GPUs, and XPUs. This so-called SRAM sits within the core of a chip die in order to cut down on data transfer times. HBM, by contrast, uses stacks of DRAM, which is a separate memory component of chips.
The company has raised $468 million in funding over the past few years from big-name backers. This includes GlobalFoundries, Intel Capital, AMD Ventures, the British investment fund Baillie Gifford, and Bill Gates, through his private Gates Frontier fund. In July, the US Department of Commerce committed to give Kepler up to $245 million to “develop in the US a new class of high-performance AI memory technology, enabled by innovative 3D and ferroelectric technologies.”
For now, much of Kepler’s testing is happening in Singapore, which is where GlobalFoundries—a manufacturing partner and investor of $50 million—has a facility. Over the past two years Kepler has been building out what it refers to as “mini fabs,” where it produces its memory chips in conjunction with Global Foundries’ 28-nanometer chips. Rachel Lipson and Allison Schwartz, “Traditional labor market data isn’t keeping up with jobs in the ‘frontier economy’,” Brookings, 09/10/2026.
Current debates about AI and the labor market overwhelmingly focus on job losses. If you’re a student of history, this might seem counterintuitive: You’ve likely heard the argument that new technologies historically create more new jobs on net than they destroy.
One reason why today’s discourse revolves around job displacement rather than creation is that we have far less clarity about what those “new jobs” are going to be.
Challenge #1: Frontier industries are hard to classify
One of the first problems in understanding jobs in frontier industries is definitional: It’s hard to identify the right industry codes to use.
This matters because different codes produce very different pictures of the jobs available. The real estate code (531120) would show property managers and leasing agent jobs. The software publishing code (513210) would emphasize software engineers and sales roles. Meanwhile, the most common code for data centers, “Computing Infrastructure Providers, Data Processing, Web Hosting, and Related Services” (518210), would largely capture computer occupations and office support roles, but not the construction and maintenance jobs needed to build and operate data center facilities over time.
Challenge #2: The supply chain plays an outsized early role in job creation, but gets overlooked
When regions plan for workforce development around new technologies, most attention usually goes to the headline industry. But much of the earliest hiring actually happens in the supply chain. If those jobs are invisible in the data, they may be missing from education and training plans too.
As one example, consider semiconductor manufacturing. Many prior analyses of workforce needs under the CHIPS Act focus on the primary NAICS code for semiconductor and other electronic component manufacturing (3344).
But making chips in the United States also depends on specialty chemical manufacturers, industrial equipment manufacturers, and the construction firms that build and maintain the factories, or “fabs.” And in reality, supplier jobs often show up first: Factories must be built and equipment must be installed before a fab can go online and start producing chips.
In our analysis of semiconductor job postings from 2023 onward, the inclusion of supply chain jobs nearly tripled the number of postings compared with using only the core manufacturing code.

Scott Singer, “The U.S. and China Don’t Need an AI Grand Bargain,” Foreign Policy, 09/08/2026.
The U.S. debate over how to navigate China’s role in developing and governing advanced artificial intelligence is stuck between two extremes. One camp calls for full-blown international treaties even though the two countries cannot yet agree on AI’s most serious risks, let alone how to manage them. The other is deeply skeptical of dialogue, believing progress will only be possible if the Chinese side is desperate.
As Tsinghua University’s Xiao Qian recently wrote in Foreign Policy, “Sustained dialogue is a strategic necessity.” She is right. And there is a middle path forward. When U.S. and Chinese delegations gather this month to discuss AI risks, rather than pursuing a comprehensive agreement, they should start with a series of narrower measures focused on preventing extreme risks, managing crises, and investing in verification tools. Each small agreement helps build the understanding and trust needed for more ambitious deals, allowing the two countries to cooperate where they already agree without requiring consensus on everything else.
One of the biggest obstacles for negotiators is that neither country has developed tools that can confidently evaluate whether AI models are safe, nor safeguards capable of mitigating AI’s most extreme risks. These challenges affect both countries but are particularly acute for China, whose AI safety evaluations are improving but still less mature than the West’s. Given the transnational nature of AI risks, it is in both countries’ interests to have robust safety infrastructure, but governments have been hesitant to participate in technical exchanges, afraid of revealing information that could enhance a rival’s capabilities.
But it is possible to have carefully scoped, working-level technical exchanges that discuss best practices without exposing models’ inner workings, vulnerabilities, or advanced capabilities. In general, the two sides should compare broad approaches but withhold tactical details and refrain from granular, riskier discussions of the specific methods they use to elicit unsafe model behavior. They could, for instance, discuss how to scale evaluations to cover more models, behaviors, and potential threats, as well as how to use AI systems themselves to help identify and respond to threats. They could also discuss important, publicly available lessons on monitoring AI models to ensure they don’t escape their sandboxes—a topic that should be of mutual concern following the OpenAI-Hugging Face incident.

Max Kan, Ray Wang, Myron Xie, et al.,, “Korea’s Trillion-Dollar Sovereign AI Investment: Nvidia Wins, Hynix Loses ,” SemiAnalysis, 09/02/2026.
Today, we’ll do a deep dive on South Korea’s sovereign AI efforts. Beyond being home to two of the most important companies in the AI supply chain, Korea also has a long tradition of technological self-reliance (as any foreigner that’s had to use Naver Maps knows) and is currently the clear leader in sovereign AI.
From there, we’ll discuss the two major implications for investors: why Nvidia is sovereign AI’s largest supporter and why Korea’s ambitions may not be aligned with Samsung and Hynix shareholders.
In June 2025, the Korean government announced “독자 AI 파운데이션 모델”, or the “Independent AI Foundation Model” project. As the name suggests, the goal is to develop a model that Korean organizations can train, modify, and operate without depending on a foreign AI lab.
Perhaps the most interesting thing about the project is its structure. Rather than selecting a single national champion upfront, the government is hosting a tournament. All participants are provided subsidies for the three pillars of AI—compute, data, and researchers—and evaluated every 6 months. At each stage, losers are eliminated and have their resources reallocated towards the winners.
The exact subsidies varied by team. For the first round, the government rented ~3000 H100 equivalents from SKT and Naver and distributed them to the other 3 contestants. They also spent ~$45M USD on data. Most of this was paid to Korean companies for things like books, news articles, and video broadcasts, which—along with some Korean government records—were shared among all the contestants. However, they also gave each company ~$2M to buy data themselves. Lastly for researchers, the government offered each company ~$1.4M to try recruiting overseas talent, but only Upstage took them up on the offer.
Surviving teams will be given additional resources as the tournament progresses, but the total government budget of ~$350M is still a rounding error compared to US labs. However, as we’ll explain later in this article, this is just a small portion of Korea’s planned AI investment. Additionally, their results so far show that training a decent model from scratch may be cheaper than most think.

Jack Karsten and Luke Koslosky, “Strengthening the U.S. Semiconductor Manufacturing Workforce,” CSET, 09/2026.
Over the past decade, the United States has sought to rebuild a larger share of leading-edge domestic production capacity of semiconductors to reduce geographic concentration risk and improve supply chain resilience. However, fabrication facilities (fabs) cannot operate at scale without a steady pipeline of workers with specialized skills, experience, and readiness to work in high-reliability cleanroom environments.
This report focuses on the workforce required to expand and sustain U.S.-based semiconductor fabrication. It is intentionally scoped to front-end manufacturing, where process complexity, equipment intensity, and quality demands make talent constraints especially binding. This focus is motivated by the distinctive workforce profile of fabs: a mix of highly credentialed engineers and scientists, experienced tool and facilities technicians, and production-line roles where the bottleneck is often not formal education alone but job-specific competencies and retention in demanding working conditions.
To better understand policy issues surrounding the demand for skilled semiconductor workers, this report reviews existing literature produced by semiconductor industry groups, government agencies, academic journals, and news media. The Center for Security and Emerging Technology also hosted a roundtable discussion in May 2025 to ask industry stakeholders for their perspectives on issues raised in the literature review. Attendees represented a wide variety of stakeholders from the semiconductor industry, trade associations, and government agencies. Their comments provided a more current picture of the issues facing the workforce than was available in published literature from recent years.
The report also incorporates summary statistics for skills demands in semiconductor manufacturing from a set of recent U.S. job postings provided by Lightcast. To isolate this sample of job postings, we gathered a list of firms that operated foundries from the Semiconductor Industry Association and a list of semiconductor manufacturing occupations from the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics. We then developed a list of keywords that were related to each step of the production process, in order to exclude jobs that were unrelated to semiconductor manufacturing.

The Economist, “Nvidia is driving the AI boom. Good,” The Economist, 09/03/2026.
NVIDIA was named in 1993 after the Latin word for envy. Sure enough, the American colossus inspires plenty of it. Insatiable global demand for its graphics-processing units (GPUs), the chips that power artificial intelligence, has made Nvidia the world’s most valuable company, worth $5.4trn. Next year it may also become the most profitable, generating $370bn in net income. By 2029 its sales could hit $1trn.
Jensen Huang, Nvidia’s boss, is truly the magician at the heart of the AI boom. His firm’s share price is 14 times what it was on ChatGPT’s release in late 2022. The ten biggest public companies championing AI make up 40% of the value of the S&P 500 index. Nvidia alone accounts for 8% and unlike, say, Apple or Tesla, which make smartphones and cars, it is almost solely a bet on AI. The company has produced about 15 cents of every dollar the American stock market has returned since 2023—returns that have kept consumers spending despite rising interest rates, tariffs and a war with Iran.
Yet many also see Mr Huang as a magician in a more worrying sense, fearing that he is an illusionist inflating a dangerous bubble. Through $1trn-worth of deals, Nvidia provides data-centre landlords and AI labs with cash or guarantees so that they can buy its GPUs. Some call it the “bank of AI”. At the very least, Nvidia’s critics say, its financial engineering smacks of the “vendor financing” which pumped up the revenues of networking-gear makers like Cisco in the dotcom mania of 2000-01, whose collapse brought about a recession.
Look more closely, however, and the worries are mostly unjustified. If Nvidia’s bets on ai come good, they could accelerate the technology’s adoption, boosting productivity and living standards. If they misfire, the cost will fall chiefly on Nvidia’s shareholders. That is how capitalism is supposed to work.
Nvidia’s financial wizardry is partly defensive. Its latest GPUs no longer have the market to themselves. Roughly half Nvidia’s revenue comes courtesy of America’s cloud-computing “hyperscalers”, chiefly Amazon, Google, Meta and Microsoft, which are designing their own silicon. Non-Nvidia AI chips account for 38% of the market, up from 26% in 2023. To stay ahead, Nvidia used to spend over a fifth of sales on research and development. Now it spends less than a tenth.
Last, the scale of Nvidia’s financial commitments can look terrifying. Morgan Stanley puts its overall credit exposure—ie, its modest borrowing plus support for customers—at $200bn by the start of 2029. In time Nvidia’s shadow debt could reach $300bn or more. It is a gargantuan sum: today only America’s six largest banks carry more debt.
Yet the differences from the dotcom boom are more important than the similarities. Nvidia’s balance-sheet is extraordinarily robust. The company has $99bn of cash and is churning out more. In each of the past three years annual sales have roughly doubled. Gross margins have fattened from less than 60% to 75%. Mr Huang’s cult-CEO status now rivals that of Elon Musk. But whereas Mr Musk’s firms generate little cash (at Tesla) or burn lots of it (at SpaceX), Nvidia will yield about $200bn this year.
Mr Huang thinks that the biggest obstacle to the AI revolution is not lack of demand for AI but inadequate infrastructure. The markets will not provide capital on the scale that is necessary, so Nvidia is offering financing itself. Nvidia has an advantage in understanding the balance of risks and rewards. Although this bet is big enough to affect the economy, it is an entrepreneurial one. Every company that reinvests cash rather than returning it to shareholders also gambles that it can beat the market. Companies exist to make such concentrated bets. If investors want to diversify, they can do so themselves.
And Mr Huang is hardly alone. The hyperscalers, the world’s most successful companies before Nvidia came along, are making the same bet. So are some big names on Wall Street. Last month Goldman Sachs, BlackRock, Blackstone and others joined Nvidia in a $500bn data-centre initiative. And so are Mr Huang’s shareholders, who haven’t yet rushed for the exit. If they are all wrong, it is their money on the line. And if they are right, the AI era may arrive a bit sooner.

Amazon and other cloud-computing providers, still the biggest buyers of Nvidia chips, have been developing in-house silicon designs and even selling them to third parties. Nvidia, the world’s most valuable business, will be hard to catch: It’s still growing faster than many of its challengers. And the company has expanded into software, networking and other technologies to ensure it remains essential to the AI economy.
The threats to Nvidia can be divided into a few broad categories. On one side, existing chip competitors and a growing group of upstarts are both vying for a bigger share of the market. On the other, you have AI labs and so-called hyperscalers — the largest cloud-computing providers — designing their own chips.
1. Longtime Rivals. AMD, the second-largest maker of GPUs, saw its data center revenue more than double last quarter to $6.7 billion. And CEO Lisa Su expects the total market for AI accelerators to reach $1.4 trillion by 2030.
2. The Upstarts. Nvidia’s GPUs are an undeniably powerful tool for training models, but the inference stage is creating opportunities for a wider range of processors. 3. The Hyperscalers. Hyperscaler companies — so named because they run computing operations with unmatched capacity — have a problem. They’re adding data centers too quickly for the chip supply to keep up.
4. The AI Labs. Top AI developers such as OpenAI and Anthropic are racing to build their own infrastructure, and that goes beyond seeking data centers and equipment. Like the hyperscalers, they want their own chips, which they can tailor for each company’s needs.

Asa Fitch, “Nvidia Has Become a Banker to the AI Boom, Putting It on Dangerous Ground,” WSJ, 08/25/2026.
Nvidia’s current financial position looks rock solid to say the least. But the financial engineering it is using to keep revenue growing introduces risks that could eventually cause real pain.
Nearly four years into an artificial intelligence boom that has brought Nvidia hundreds of billions of dollars in profit, the company is increasingly tapping its financial strength to keep customers buying its chips.
Nvidia also recently signed deals with two young cloud-computing companies in Australia where it acts as a customer of last resort if they can’t find others to rent their computing power to. In exchange, Nvidia gets a share of the companies’ revenue from those assets above an agreed-upon level. The backstops give lenders confidence to extend financing with which the companies buy Nvidia’s chips.
Nvidia can easily absorb some big impacts, with more than $80 billion of cash and marketable securities on its balance sheet as of its last fiscal quarter. It also isn’t likely that Nvidia would be liable for its entire lease backstops, which reduce over time.
But Nvidia’s venture into finance appears poised to become much deeper. The company described its deals with the two cloud-computing players in Australia as a “new business model,” suggesting it could act as a financial guarantor many more times over. And its financial backstops for OpenAI and the Wall Street firms create an expectation that Nvidia will lend more support to other large data center projects.
Part of what Nvidia is doing is spreading its bets so it is less reliant on a handful of tech giants like Amazon.com and Microsoft. Those companies are running out of financial steam.

Bryce Elder, “Nvidia’s $200bn ‘balance sheet-as-a-service’,” FT, 08/26/2026.
Hundred-billion-dollar customer subsidies might not look like much, for a $5tn cash machine, but they’re still enough to worry about, according to a note on Nvidia from Morgan Stanley’s corporate credit team.
Initiating coverage with a “neutral” — which we all know what is actually code for — analysts Lindsay Tyler and Nishant Satyam praise how Nvidia “turns balance-sheet strength into a strategic AI financing tool”, but argue that “the tail remains too early stage, opaque, and sizeable to step in”.
They dub phenomenon “balance-sheet-as-a-service.” The big question Morgan Stanley’s analysts seek to answer is how much of Nvidia’s support packages and lease commitments should be treated as debt.
Prompting the question is Nvidia’s announcement this month of “repeatable financing platform” agreements with Apollo, BlackRock, Blackstone, Brookfield, Goldman Sachs and KKR to raise more than $500bn for AI infrastructure build-outs.
Based on Nvidia signing 15 similar fundraisings by the end of 2028, and taking into account drawdowns and amortisation, its tail risk exposure would peak at nearly $90bn shortly after that date, Morgan Stanley estimates. Company disclosures will be limited, however, and rating agencies have already indicated a preference to view Nvidia’s roughly $125bn of financing structures as debt-like.
Nvidia’s individual arrangements with customers are the analysts’ bigger concern, partly because so little is known about them.
As Morgan Stanley’s equity team wrote in a recent note: “Our sense is that NVIDIA believes that 1) hyperscalers are not investing enough to keep up with token demand because of fcf concerns, 2) hyperscalers can’t get land power shell outside the US and are increasingly getting pressure in the US so the world needs new spenders, and 3) the structure here will drive tens of billions of annuity revenue with limited downside. Of course, the more cynical view is it is simply creating artificial demand from customers without the scale to use asic or AMD, but it only works if compute demand is ahead of supply.”

The surge in supply commitments primarily relates to memory, Nvidia Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress said in prepared remarks Wednesday. Large amounts of high-bandwidth memory are crucial for Nvidia’s advanced AI chips, and supplies have been extremely tight in the past year.

Michelle Chan, Martha Muir, Rafe Rosner-Uddin, et al., “The multiplying risks of financing data centres,” FT, 08/26/2026.
The AI revolution may change the world, but it comes with a 13-figure price tag. By 2030, tech companies are expected to pour $7tn into data centres — enough money to feed every person in China for three years.
So great are the sums involved that even Big Tech groups with tens of billions of dollars in cash need to fund the infrastructure with debt. This is presenting major lenders with a complex set of calculations as they stretch themselves to finance, insure and underwrite an entirely novel asset class.
The possible returns are enormous, convincing some of the world’s biggest and most sophisticated private investors to provide Nvidia with $500bn in financing just this month. Some in the insurance industry see a potential bonanza, with life insurers hungry for long-term and high-yielding assets and property and casualty insurers in need of new underwriting business.
But the risks are also great, and growing. Firstly, the question of longevity: the possibility that the data centres and the chips that equip them will not retain their value for the lifetime of the financing that funds them.
There is also the risk of a growing popular backlash against the centres, with their mammoth appetites for water and electricity at a time when AI is increasingly controversial.
Then there is the additional difficulty of laying off risks to other parts of the financial system. Lenders and project developers are eager to insure against everything from natural disasters and power outages to a slump in demand for computing power. But insurance companies have been reluctant to provide billions of dollars’ worth of coverage for the biggest projects, concerned about catastrophic risk as well as concentrated exposure to these giant sites.
And that is without taking into account the most fundamental gamble of all — that the AI revolution will meet its potential. For investors, that means not only unprecedented productivity and profit gains, but also that the frontier models that require the most extensive data centre infrastructure will emerge the winners. Moreover, each hopes that the individual companies they are backing will prevail.

Bryan Shan, Myron Xie, Jordan Nanos, et al., “OpenAI Jalapeño: Better Than Nvidia Blackwell.,” SemiAnalysis, 08/26/2026.
OpenAI has spent the past couple years quietly building “Jalapeño,” an inference chip just announced at Hot Chips. Rumors of a successful tapeout had been swirling for a while. But now we have details. OpenAI invited us to look at their chip, go to their labs to check out how real it is, and benchmark it with our InferenceX suite.
In June, OpenAI unveiled the chip program in partnership with Broadcom, built from a blank slate exclusively for LLM inference. Design work began in the middle of 2024, going from initial team hiring to manufacturing tape-out in ~16 months, an extremely fast ASIC development cycle.
In general first generation chips are not competitive, but OpenAI bucks the trend by being industry leading and beating every Nvidia, AMD, and Google chip we have been able to test on multiple top open source models. OpenAI does this with extreme hardware software codesign. Surprisingly, OpenAI is not over specialization on any specific part of model inference, but instead by focusing on being a general chip that delivers high performance in all scenarios.
Everyone says that OpenAI’s chip is specialized for OpenAI models, but that’s wrong, OpenAI made a generalized chip for AI inference.
The timelines are insane. It shows that claims that use of AI is being used to accelerate chip design are real. Regardless of the quick timelines,Open AI spent a bunch of money, made pragmatic design decisions and their team is cracked, so this comes as no surprise.
Some caveats on this. First, all numbers are provided to us by OpenAI. We verified the InferenceX runs in person in the lab, but we did not run the full suite of InferenceX benchmarks nor have we seen AgentX results. AgentX is our preferred suite for comparing chip performance due to the datasets’ long context and multi-turn characteristics that reflect the cache behavior of realistic production workflows. Frameworks that perform well on 8k1k may perform worse on AgentX as real production loads stress components like routers, prefix cache mechanisms, cache management, offload infrastructure, etc. These are not tested by single turn 8k1k. Read more about this in out AgentX article.
Second, we believe that comparison to Blackwell is somewhat incomplete and unfair. Jalapeño is really competing against chips like Rubin that also use HBM4. Vera Rubin systems are starting to ship to customers right now, while it will still be some time before OpenAI has anything beyond engineering samples of Jalapeño.
Third, the models being tested are not on the open frontier. NVIDIA and AMD have published results on larger models such as DeepSeek V4 Pro and Kimi K3, using AgentX. The larger the model and the more recent the release, the more complicated it is to bring up on a new chip. With that said the models OpenAI has working on Jalapeno aren’t exactly small either.
