Around the world, friends and adversaries of America are reaching the same, bleak conclusion. To earn President Donald Trump’s respect, show that you can hurt him. None of America’s security partners is foolish enough to threaten Mr Trump openly. But all of them watched Iran gain leverage over a stronger adversary by closing the Strait of Hormuz, and some were taking notes. Iran’s abuse of this choke point is simply appalling, such allies tut-tut. How do we get one of our own?
Taiwan knows that it needs leverage. After it embraced democracy 30-odd years ago, Taiwan won friends in Washington by talking up its status as a bastion of liberty, menaced by autocratic China. When despot-praising Mr Trump took office, Taiwanese officials quickly learned to downplay talk of shared values. They watched in horror when Mr Trump scorned Ukraine as a small country that had foolishly sought to defend itself against larger Russia. That could be us, Taiwanese shuddered.
Instead, Taiwan leans on two arguments about its strategic value to America. One involves Taiwan’s location in the “first island chain”, Pentagon jargon for the archipelago that hems in mainland China, running from Japan through Taiwan to the Philippines. The other involves Taiwan’s indispensable role as a global centre for making chips, including around 90% of the most advanced semiconductors. For some years Taiwanese politicians have called their chip industry a “Silicon Shield” or—in their more flowery moods—a sacred mountain that makes Taiwan too valuable for China to attack, or for America to abandon.
Other countries take a dimmer view of Taiwan’s chipmaking dominance. Even friendly governments resent their dependence on an earthquake-prone, typhoon-lashed island that imports almost all its raw materials and energy. Even before Mr Trump, Taiwan was being pressed to build chipmaking foundries overseas, notably in America, Japan and Germany. Mr Trump goes further, falsely charging Taiwan with stealing America’s chip industry decades ago. He has browbeaten TSMC and other leading firms to expand operations in Arizona, Texas and other states.
In Taipei, the capital, some policy types fret about the silicon shield being weakened over time, and about talented engineers being deployed to build and run foreign fabs. Others, though, suggest ways to turn Taiwan’s defensive shield into a weapon, right now. Taiwan has its own strait. The channel between the island and the mainland, spanning about 160km, carries some of the world’s most precious cargoes each day, including silicon chips.

Robyn Klingler-Vidra, “Vietnam’s Economic Statecraft in the Global Chip Race,” The Diplomat, 07/10/2026.
Now, fresh off its World Bank reclassification as an upper-middle-income country, Hanoi has a far more ambitious objective: to become an indispensable player in the physical layers underpinning artificial intelligence (AI).
Semiconductors sit at the center of that ambition. Over the past two years, Vietnam has unveiled a series of initiatives that together amount to one of Southeast Asia’s most ambitious semiconductor strategies. The government plans to train 50,000 semiconductor engineers by 2030, launch a $100 million venture capital fund inspired by Israel’s Yozma program, dramatically increase public spending on science and technology, attract additional foreign investment from global technology leaders, and secure domestic supplies of rare earth minerals that are critical inputs into chip manufacturing.
Taken together, these initiatives represent something more significant than Vietnam’s past approach to industrial policy. Hanoi is using economic statecraft to position itself within global value chains as a means of fueling continued economic growth and sovereignty.
The ambition is evident, but whether these policies deliver will depend on whether they genuinely build technological capabilities. Historically, the financially strapped state invested too little in science and technology and a “two-speed” economy persisted, where foreign firms operating in Vietnam did not effectively translate into upskilling Vietnam’s firms and workforce. Can this push be different?
Vietnam enters this new phase with significant momentum. It was one of the world’s fastest-growing economies in 2025, extending more than 30 years of sustained economic growth since the doi moi reforms.
The central challenge for Vietnam is now one of ensuring absorptive capacity: that foreign investment generates domestic technological learning; that engineering graduates develop world-class capabilities rather than simply increasing headcount; that government venture capital investment expands its internationally connected investors rather than serves as a state financing vehicle that may crowd out market-based capital.

These are modest steps in Europe’s high-stakes race to catch up to America and China in the global sprint for digital independence. Without it, Europe’s political and business leaders worry, they will be vulnerable to sudden losses of access to critical technologies, as after President Trump’s recent decision to cut off foreigners from some of Anthropic’s latest artificial intelligence models. They will also miss out on revenues from a booming industry.
Yet interviews with industry leaders, public officials, entrepreneurs and economists suggest there is currently little question about whether Europe can wean itself off tech dependence anytime soon. It cannot.

I keep reading that artificial intelligence has revived American nuclear power. The headlines call it a renaissance. So I went looking for the new reactors, and I could not find a single one.
Here is the fact that stopped me. Almost every megawatt of nuclear power that will actually reach an AI data center this decade comes from a reactor that already exists.¹ Not one is a new plant. The industry has signed about 13 gigawatts (GW, a measure of power capacity, where one large reactor is roughly one gigawatt) across a wave of deals with six technology buyers, and behind the announcements sits the same move over and over: keep an old reactor running, restart one that was closed, or re-sign the power from one that was about to shut.¹
None of it is new construction. It is a financing trade wearing an energy story’s clothes. And once you see it that way, the winners and the losers change completely.
The deals are all about old plants
Start with the three that set off the frenzy.
- Microsoft and Constellation are restarting Unit 1 of Three Mile Island, the Pennsylvania plant closed in 2019, now renamed the Crane Clean Energy Center. It is an 835 megawatt reactor, and it is on track to produce power again by the middle of 2027 at a cost of about $1.6bn.² Microsoft has signed a 20-year deal to take the output.²
- Meta and Constellation signed a 20-year deal in 2025 for the 1,121 megawatt Clinton plant in Illinois. That plant was heading for an economic shutdown. The contract is what keeps it alive.⁵
- Amazon and Talen are tied to the Susquehanna plant in Pennsylvania through a deal that runs to 2042, ramping up to 1,920 megawatts.⁶
Notice what none of them add: new generating capacity. Each one re-signs a plant that was already standing, or already scheduled to close.
For comparison, the last new American reactors built from scratch, Units 3 and 4 at Georgia’s Vogtle plant, finished in 2024. They came in seven years late and more than $30bn over budget.¹ That number is the shadow over this whole story.
Why a trillion-dollar company pays double for old steel
The obvious question is why Microsoft would pay a premium for a reactor from the 1970s. Analysts estimate its Crane deal is priced somewhere around $100 to $115 a megawatt-hour, close to double what power trades for in the regional market.³
The answer is what the reactor gives that nothing else can: firm, around-the-clock, carbon-free power at full output to one customer. An AI training cluster runs flat out. It cannot follow the wind or wait for the sun. A reactor humming at a steady 800-plus megawatts, all day, every day, is exactly the profile a data center needs, and there is very little of it going spare.
This is the productivity hinge. Firm power is now the input that decides how much AI you can build, and the bottleneck has moved from chips to electricity.
Once you accept that, the trade makes sense on both sides:
- The hyperscaler uses its pristine credit to lock 15 to 20 years of price certainty and a clean-power headline. For a company with a multi-trillion-dollar balance sheet, that is cheap.
- The power producer gets a bankable, long-dated contract that turns an aging, marginal plant into something close to a risk-free annuity. That is what justified the $1.6bn to restart Crane, and a $1bn federal loan sits behind it as well.⁴
Both sides win in the room. The question this newsletter always asks is who is not in the room.
The scarce asset is the wire, not the reactor
Here is the part almost no one prices. The valuable thing is not the nuclear island. It is the right to inject power into a crowded grid.
Getting a new connection approved can take years. An old industrial site already has one, stamped decades ago. That inherited hook-up is the real prize.
You can watch it change hands. In June 2026, federal regulators let Constellation move 760 megawatts of grid-connection rights from a retiring fossil plant near Philadelphia over to the Crane reactor, which let the restart skip a transmission-upgrade queue that stretched past 2030.⁸ The rights were the point, not the plant.
Amazon learned the limit of this the hard way. Its first plan at Susquehanna was to wall off the data center behind the meter and draw straight from the reactor, sidestepping the grid. Regulators rejected that in late 2024.⁷
The restructured deal, in 2025, sells the power through the open grid instead.⁶ You cannot build a private fence around a public wire.
And the wire has gotten expensive. In the regional market that covers 13 states and 65mn people, the price paid to keep capacity available has climbed from about $29 a megawatt-day a couple of years ago to the low $300s, roughly eleven times higher.⁹ ¹⁰ The most recent auction, cleared in July 2026, came in at $325.⁹
Where is that coming from? The market’s own monitor found data-center demand drove about $7.3bn of the increase in one recent auction, 82% of the total jump.¹¹
Those capacity costs do not vanish. They flow into the electricity bills of households and small businesses across the region who never signed an AI deal. That is the quiet loser in this story, and it is worth saying plainly.
The new reactors are still a slideshow
If the delivered power is all old plants, what about the small modular reactors (SMRs), the compact next-generation designs meant to be the future of the industry?
They are not here. No new-design American SMR is running commercially, and the commercial dates cluster in 2030 to 2035.¹
Look at the developers:
- NuScale, once the front-runner, reported about $75,000 of revenue in a single recent quarter, a drop of roughly 99%, while sitting on a $1.9bn cash pile and waiting for a firm customer.¹²
- TerraPower, backed by Bill Gates, won its construction permit and broke ground on a 345 megawatt reactor in Wyoming in 2026. Operation is a 2030s event.¹³
- X-energy, tied to Amazon, raised over $1bn in a 2026 listing. Its reactors for Amazon, about 320 megawatts, are a next-decade delivery.¹⁴
- Google and Kairos signed for up to 500 megawatts, with the first commercial units targeted no earlier than 2030.¹⁵
The mismatch here is brutal. AI product cycles move in months. The chips inside a data center last two or three years. A new reactor takes ten to fifteen years to go from drawing to grid.
These SMR contracts are really places in a manufacturing queue and long-term decarbonization stories. They will do nothing for the power shortage in 2026, 2027, or 2028.
The market already figured this out
If this were a true build-out, the companies holding the scarce reactors and grid rights would be soaring. They are not.
The nuclear premium that lifted these stocks through 2024 and 2025 has come out of them hard. As of early September 2026:
- Constellation trades near $299, down about 28% from its 52-week high of $412.70, and it carries the weight of the expansion: $24.7bn of debt against $32.3bn of equity, a leverage ratio that has climbed from 51% to 76% in five years.¹⁶ ¹⁷
- Talen trades near $317, well below its high of $451.¹⁶
- Vistra trades near $149, down about a third from its high of $220.¹⁶
The market is pricing these firms as what they are: heavily indebted, capital-intensive utilities running a clever asset-matching strategy, not hyper-growth AI plays. That read looks right to me.
The bigger machine, and why old always wins here
Step back and the pattern is the same one running through the whole AI build-out. When a resource becomes scarce, the players with the deepest pockets do not gamble on the shiny new version. They buy the proven thing that works today.
I think about this the way I think about risk in my own family. The people who take the biggest leap of their lives, who leave everything they know for a country they barely understand, very often turn into the most cautious people in the room afterward, because they have felt how fast one shock can unravel a whole life.
The hyperscalers are doing a version of that. Trillion-dollar balance sheets, every reason to bet big, and instead they reach for the safest, oldest, most certain steel on the board. That is exactly why the old reactors are winning the money.
The contrast abroad makes the American approach clear. In Britain, the state is directly underwriting new construction: a final decision on the £38bn (about $48bn) Sizewell C plant, and £2.5bn (about $3.2bn) toward a domestic small-reactor program.¹⁸ ¹⁹ China is building dozens of reactors outright, and the United Arab Emirates financed and finished four new units. The US, for now, is optimizing the returns of the fleet it already has.
What this means if you are on the Western side of it
- If you invest, the easy nuclear trade is over. The premium has compressed, and the risk that these 20-year contracts turn out above-market still sits somewhere, most likely with the buyer’s shareholders. The actual new-build risk, the Vogtle risk, is barely priced at all.
- If you pay a power bill in the mid-Atlantic or Midwest, you are already exposed. Capacity costs are rising, data-center demand is the main driver, and a share of that lands on your bill whether or not you ever touch an AI product.¹¹
- If you were hoping for a factory-town revival from reactor construction, temper it. The jobs this decade are refueling crews and restart teams at existing sites, real but modest, not the tens of thousands a real build cycle would bring.
- If you build with AI, firm power is now the true constraint. The companies that locked it up early bought years of runway. Everyone else rents what is left, at the price the auction sets.
What to watch
- Whether the Crane restart actually delivers power on schedule in 2027. A slip would be the first crack in the re-contracting story.²
- Whether the next regional capacity auction clears at the cap again, and how much of it the market monitor pins on data centers.⁹ ¹¹
- Whether any SMR developer converts a paper contract into poured concrete with a real commercial date, rather than another 2030s target.¹³
- Whether a hyperscaler is forced back to natural gas because firm nuclear simply is not available in time. That would tell you the clean-power headline has met the physics.
The nuclear renaissance is real in one narrow sense: reactors that were dying are being kept alive by AI money, which beats letting them close. Just do not mistake keeping the old plants running for building new ones. The electrons will flow to the data centers. They will flow from reactors that were always there.
And that is it for today’s edition. Thanks for reading Tech for Commons, where we look at what technology is actually doing to people.
Best,
Sagarika

I keep coming back to one number this week, and it does not behave the way the textbooks say it should. Britain now borrows money for ten years at about 5.1%.¹ Italy, sitting on a debt pile far bigger than Britain’s, borrows for ten years at 4.2%.² Lenders are charging the less-indebted country more.
That is not a rounding error. The market would rather lend to Rome than to London. And once you sit with why, this stops being a story about Britain. It becomes a warning about what happens to any wealthy country that runs out of room, loses the people who used to buy its debt, and has no reserve currency to hide behind.
The anomaly, in plain numbers
A gilt is just a British government bond, an IOU the state sells to fund itself. The yield is what the state pays to borrow. Higher yield, more expensive borrowing, and usually a sign that lenders see more risk.
Britain against its peers, right now:
- UK 10-year gilt: about 5.1%.¹
- Italy, 10-year: about 4.2%.²
- Germany, 10-year: about 3.4%.³
- United States, 10-year: about 4.8%.⁴
- UK 30-year gilt: near 5.8%, close to levels last seen in the late 1990s.⁵
So Britain pays more than Italy, more than Germany, and more than the United States. It has done this while its debt sits near 95% of national income,⁶ well below Italy’s, which runs past 135%. The old rule was simple: more debt, higher yield. Britain breaks the rule.
You might not care about a British bond chart. You should. The gilt yield is the floor under everything else there, the rate mortgages, business loans, and corporate bonds all get priced off. When the state pays a premium, it lands on the people underneath who cannot move. And the same forces are quietly at work in Washington, which makes Britain a live preview.
It is not solvency. It is plumbing.
The market is not pricing a British default. Britain can always print pounds. What the yield is really pricing is three structural problems, and none of them is about the raw size of the debt.
First, Britain’s debt is unusually exposed to inflation. About a quarter of its gilts are “index-linked,” meaning the payments rise automatically with inflation.⁷ Most countries issue far less of this. When prices spiked in 2022 and 2023, the British debt bill exploded, because so much of it was wired straight to the inflation rate with no lag. It cuts both ways, and you can watch it live: in June 2026, as inflation cooled, the government’s monthly debt-interest bill fell about 31% from a year earlier, almost entirely because those inflation-linked costs came down.⁶ Britain’s debt bill is a bet on inflation staying tame, renewed every month.
Second, Britain borrows for longer than anyone. Its debt has the longest average life in the developed world, around 14 years, against roughly 6 to 7 for Italy and Germany and under 6 for the US.⁷ For a decade that looked clever, locking in cheap money. But long bonds swing hardest in price when rates move, so when the world flipped from cheap money to dear money, Britain’s long book became the most violent to hold.
Third, and this is the one that actually explains 5.8%, the buyers left. For years the natural home for long-dated gilts was British pension funds running a strategy called LDI, matching their decades-long promises to retirees with long bonds, often on borrowed money. That machine blew up in the 2022 “mini-budget”: yields spiked, the collateral collapsed, funds dumped gilts into a falling market, and the Bank of England had to step in to stop the doom loop.⁸ Regulators then made those funds hold much bigger cash buffers, so they buy far fewer long gilts now. And the Bank itself is now selling gilts, not buying.
Britain is trying to sell record amounts of the longest debt in the G7 into a market where its biggest historical buyer has retreated and its central bank has turned seller. The 5.8% on the 30-year is not a mood. It is the price that clears when almost nobody has to buy.
A buffer the size of a rounding error
On top of the broken plumbing sits a fiscal position with almost no give. After the November 2025 budget, the Chancellor left herself about £22bn (roughly $29bn) of headroom against her own borrowing rules.⁹ That sounds like a lot until you learn that the average revision to the government’s own forecasts, every six months, is around £21bn.⁹ The entire safety margin is about one ordinary forecasting wobble.
With growth stuck near 1.5% a year, there is no growing your way out. The only lever left is tax, and that is where the second half of this story begins.
The exodus that mostly did not happen
Faced with thin margins and a bond market it is terrified of, Britain reached for the wealthy. In April 2025 it abolished the centuries-old “non-dom” regime, which had let rich foreigners living in Britain avoid UK tax on their overseas money.¹⁰
Cue the panic. A widely quoted report from Henley & Partners, a firm that sells “golden visas” for a living, projected that 16,500 millionaires would flee Britain in 2025.¹¹ The number ran on front pages and in political speeches as proof that taxing the rich is self-defeating.
Then people checked the math. The tax analyst Dan Neidle pulled the report apart and found the fingerprints of made-up data: numbers clustered on round digits the way real data almost never does, drawn largely from where people say they live on social media rather than tax records. Under pressure, the report quietly dropped its author and its headline numbers.¹¹
And the hard official data pointed the other way. When Britain’s tax authority published its real non-dom figures in mid-2026, the tax collected from non-doms had not collapsed. It rose about 9%, to £13.6bn (roughly $18bn), even as the headcount of registered non-doms fell.¹² Fewer people, more money. It turns out London’s pull, its courts, its schools, its networks, holds most of the biggest fish in place even when the tax goes up. Mobility among the truly rich is lower than the people selling relocation want you to believe.
The slow bleed is the real threat
So the doom loop is oversold. But it would be complacent to call capital captive, because the machines built to catch it have never been better funded.
- Italy now offers new wealthy residents a flat tax on all their foreign income. It doubled the fee to €200,000, then raised it again to €300,000 (about $330k) a year under its 2026 budget.¹³ For someone earning tens of millions offshore, a fixed six-figure bill to legally shield the rest, while living in Milan, is a rounding error.
- Singapore has turned family wealth into an industry. The number of single-family offices there has crossed 2,000, up roughly tenfold in five years, and the rules force that money to hire locals and invest locally so it puts down roots.¹⁴
- The United Arab Emirates keeps it brutally simple: zero personal income tax and a fast “golden visa” that hands you long-term residency. It is consistently the top magnet for migrating millionaires.¹⁵
The danger is not that 16,500 people bolt overnight. It is that the next family office opens in Singapore, the next founder incorporates in Dubai, and the next private-equity partner takes Italian residency. Each individual choice is small. Over a decade they drain exactly the dynamism Britain needs to grow out of its hole.
Who actually pays
This is the part that matters, because the winners and losers here are not who the headlines say.
The winners are the mobile. A billionaire treats a country like a subscription he can cancel. When the tax rises, he exercises what is really a geographic option and moves the address, keeping the wealth. He is the beneficiary of a world where the ability to move is itself the privilege.
The losers are everyone who cannot move:
- The British pensioner whose fund held those long gilts and watched their price fall.
- The household rolling off a fixed mortgage into payments priced off a 5%-plus gilt yield.
- The regional manufacturer in a factory town trying to borrow for new equipment at a rate set by the sovereign premium.
None of them can relocate to Dubai to escape the 10-year gilt. They hold the bill for a premium created by problems they did not cause. I moved across the world once myself, and pulling a life up by the roots is not a light thing. Watching the ultra-wealthy toggle a residency like a setting on a phone is watching a different universe, one most people never get to enter.
Why this is really a story about America
The uncomfortable part, for a US reader: the diseases behind the gilt premium are not uniquely British.
The US runs a bigger deficit than Britain and carries more debt relative to its economy, past 120%. Its own long-term buyers are thinning as the Fed runs down its holdings, and the extra yield investors demand to hold long bonds has been climbing. The 10-year Treasury sits near 4.8%,⁴ higher than it has been for most of the past two years, and for a stretch Britain has actually paid more than the US, a reversal of the old order.
What saves America, for now, is the thing Britain lost long ago. The dollar is the world’s reserve currency and US markets are the deepest on earth, and that “exorbitant privilege” lets Washington borrow shorter and cheaper than its fundamentals deserve. Britain is what the same math looks like without the privilege. It is the control group.
What it means for you
If you invest, the gilt market is a lesson in how fast a term premium can reprice when the structural buyer disappears and the central bank turns seller. Watch the long end of your own market for the same setup.
If you work or run a business in the West, mobility is becoming a tax variable. Governments that cannot grow and cannot easily tax the mobile rich will lean harder on what stays put: property, payroll, pensions, consumption. The immobile middle is the reliable base, and it is being asked to carry more.
And if you are tempted by the “just tax the rich and they will flee” story, hold two facts at once. The dramatic exodus was mostly invented,¹¹ and the revenue actually rose.¹² What is real is the slow migration of the next decade’s capital, a genuine long-run cost. Policy has to be built for that slow bleed, not the imaginary stampede.
What to watch
- Whether the UK 30-year gilt cracks 6% at one of the big autumn debt auctions.⁵
- Whether Britain’s Autumn 2026 budget can keep that £22bn buffer alive to the next official forecast, or whether one bad growth revision erases it.⁹
- Whether the US term premium keeps climbing as the Fed keeps shrinking its balance sheet, the same buyer-shaped hole that opened under gilts.⁴
- Whether Britain’s next official non-dom numbers still show revenue holding as the headcount falls.¹²
The lesson is not that Britain is about to default. It is that a rich country without a reserve currency, without growth, and without its old lenders has almost no room left, and the people who pay for that are the ones who cannot pack a bag.
And that is it for today’s edition. Thanks for reading Tech for Commons, where we look at what technology is actually doing to people.

I want to start with the number that first made me suspicious.
All through the first half of 2026, America's banks told Congress the same scary story: yield-bearing stablecoins, dollar-pegged crypto tokens that pay interest, were about to drain the banking system. The Bank of America and the American Bankers Association warned that $6tn of deposits was "at risk."1 Credit unions put the figure at $6.6tn.2
Then I looked at what actually happened. In the first three months of 2026, deposits at U.S. banks rose by about $390bn, the seventh quarter in a row they went up.3 Over the same stretch, the total supply of stablecoins did not explode. It shrank, from a peak near $321bn in April to just under $300bn by late August.4
So the flood never came. Which raises an obvious question: if deposits are not leaving, what is this fight really about?
The answer, once you see it, is hard to unsee. This is not a fight about stability. It is a fight about who is allowed to pay you interest.
The flight that never happened
Start with the banks' own health, because it is excellent.
- U.S. banks earned $80.5bn in the first quarter of 2026, up 3.6% on the quarter.3
- Total deposits sat around $19.5tn and were still growing.5
- The domestic deposits that grew fastest were the large, uninsured kind, the exact money that is supposed to be most twitchy about chasing a better rate.3
Meanwhile the thing supposedly doing the draining was itself getting smaller. And money market funds, which pay stablecoin-like yields and also sit outside banks, kept climbing to a record near $8tn.6 They grew alongside bank deposits, not instead of them.
That last point matters. A real deposit drain looks like one pot filling as another empties. Here, every pot is filling at once. The panic is not in the data.
The 0.01% choice
Here is what the banks are actually protecting.
In early 2026, the biggest banks paid about 0.01% on ordinary checking and savings.7 On the very same dollars, Coinbase and Kraken were paying roughly 3.5% to 5% on stablecoins, simply by passing through what the tokens' reserves earned in short-term Treasuries.7
That gap is a choice, not a law of nature. Banks can pay so little because most of us do not move our money. In banking jargon, they rely on "deposit inattention," and it works: when the Fed raised rates over 2022 to 2026, the big banks passed only a fraction of it through to savers, keeping the rest as margin.7
Frictionless, app-based digital dollars threaten exactly that inattention. If you can tap a phone and move cash from a 0.01% account into a 4% one in seconds, the banks' quiet margin starts to leak. That is the real threat, and it is worth about four percentage points on your savings.
We have seen this exact movie before
The most damning witness against the banks is the Federal Reserve itself.
On May 1, 2026, Fed staff published a note drawing a straight line from today's stablecoin fight to the 1970s and 80s.6 Back then, banks operated under Regulation Q, a rule that capped what they could pay savers. When inflation pushed market rates far above the cap, savers fled into money market funds, which had no cap. The funds grew to about $220bn and grabbed roughly 15% of the deposit market.6
The banking lobby of the 1980s said money funds were a systemic threat that would starve local lending. It is almost word for word what the lobby says about stablecoins now.
But look at how Congress fixed it. It did not ban the competitor. It passed the Garn-St. Germain Act and let banks pay market rates too. Within three months, banks pulled in over $300bn and won their savers back.6
The lesson is simple: the outflow was caused by an artificial cap, and it ended the moment banks were allowed to compete on price.
Now here is the twist. Today there is no cap. The 0.01% is a choice banks make to protect their margins. So instead of asking to be freed to compete, the lobby is asking Congress to build a new cap, one that sits on top of their crypto rivals. They want a Regulation Q for stablecoins, so nobody can pass the risk-free rate to savers.
How the ban got written
This is not theory anymore. It is turning into law.
- The GENIUS Act, passed in July 2025, set up licensing for stablecoins and banned the issuers themselves (Circle, Tether) from paying interest to holders.8
- That left a loophole: the issuers could not pay you, but exchanges like Coinbase could share the yield they received. So the fight moved to the CLARITY Act in 2026.
- A compromise from Senators Thom Tillis and Angela Alsobrooks banned "passive yield," any return you earn just for holding the token, while still allowing "activity" rewards for trading or staking.11 That closes the exchange loophole.
The compromise is shaky, and as of late August 2026 its passage is far from certain.7 But the executive branch is not waiting. On August 18, 2026, the Treasury proposed rules that push enforcement onto U.S. exchanges, making them liable for the foreign stablecoins they list, with penalties that can reach $100,000 a day.8 It even treats free "airdrops" to Americans as a regulated sale. The goal is to make the yield ban impossible to route around offshore.
You can see how efficient the crypto model was, which is why the banks want it stopped. Circle earned $701mn in the second quarter of 2026, and paid well over half of it, about $412mn, to its partner Coinbase to fund the yield-sharing that won users.9 It was buying customers with the interest banks keep for themselves.
The part everyone leaves out
Two bigger things get lost in the noise.
First, the U.S. Treasury quietly wants this market to grow. To hold their peg, stablecoins park reserves in short-term Treasury bills. Standard Chartered projects that a $2tn stablecoin market by 2028 would create roughly $1tn of fresh demand for those bills.10 That is a giant, price-insensitive buyer for U.S. government debt. Ban the yield, stunt the growth, and you deny the Treasury that buyer. So one arm of Washington is trying to cap the thing another arm quietly benefits from.
Second, the banks are not just playing defense. They are building their own versions. The bank-owned Zelle network is launching its own stablecoin, and JPMorgan, Bank of America, Citi, and Wells Fargo are building a shared tokenized-deposit network for 2027. The strategy is clear: ban yield on the public rivals, then roll out your own tokens onto a level field, still funded by 0.01% deposits.
There is a real risk on the other side, and it deserves saying plainly. Community banks fund local lending almost entirely from local deposits, and they cannot shrug off an outflow. Fed modeling suggests a $500bn jump in stablecoins could pull roughly $300bn out of deposits and cut lending by $190bn to $408bn.12 That danger is genuine. But the honest fix is targeted help for small banks, not a blanket ban that mostly protects the biggest banks on earth.
Who wins and who loses
Strip away the stability talk and the scoreboard is stark.
The winners:
- The megabanks. A yield ban protects their near-zero funding costs and clears the way for their own tokenized networks.
- Today's big stablecoin issuers. Circle and Tether keep their lead, because new rivals lose the one tool, yield, that would let them break in.
The losers:
- The saver. Denied a simple, frictionless way to earn the risk-free rate on cash, and left with 0.01% or the hassle of a money market fund.
- Merchants and families sending money home. Stablecoins can settle for pennies, against the 1.5% to 3.5% that card networks charge, but if a yield ban keeps people from holding them, that cheaper plumbing never reaches scale.
- The U.S. Treasury, which loses a fast-growing, captive buyer for its short-term debt.
What it means for you
If you are a saver in the U.S. or the wider West, this is the rare Washington fight that lands directly in your own account.
The math is blunt. With the Fed's rate above 4%, a bank paying 0.01% is handing you a rounding error while keeping the rest. A yield ban on stablecoins does not make you safer. It quietly locks in that arrangement and calls it prudence.
I think about this the way I think about my own savings. Every dollar I have put away carries the memory of the hours and the sacrifice it took to earn it, and I still pause before spending it freely. When I see that kind of money offered 0.01% in a 4% world, it does not read as caution. It reads as an insult to the work behind it. That is the saver this whole debate manages never to mention.
None of this means stablecoins are risk-free. Tether's own reserve buffer roughly halved in a single quarter, and offshore reserve quality is genuinely murky.10 Caution is fair. But there is a wide gap between "regulate the risk" and "ban the competition," and the current bills are sitting on the wrong side of it.
What to watch
- Whether the Q2 or Q3 2026 FDIC data finally shows an actual deposit decline. If deposits keep rising, the "flight" case collapses.
- Whether the CLARITY Act's passive-yield ban survives the Senate before the midterms freeze everything.7
- Whether the Treasury's August rules get finalized and how hard they land on Coinbase and Kraken.8
- Whether a big U.S. retailer actually swaps card rails for stablecoin settlement. Nobody has yet, and that absence tells you today's demand is about yield, not checkout.
The one line
The banks did not ask to compete for your savings. They asked Congress to make it illegal for anyone else to.
And that is it for today's edition. Thanks for reading Tech for Commons, where we look at what technology is actually doing to people.

Here is the number that reframed this whole story for me: the average payment an AI agent made this year was about 52 cents.1
Not $52. Fifty-two cents.
Software has genuinely started buying things on its own. On one set of rails alone, AI agents ran more than 160mn payments over the past year.2 But almost none of it was the shopping you are picturing. It was machines paying other machines fractions of a cent for an API call, a slice of computing power, a line of data.
I find that gap fascinating, because the payments industry has spent the last eighteen months in a frantic, big-money scramble to own the AI shopper. Four competing rulebooks. More than a hundred of the world's largest banks and tech firms.3 Big acquisitions. All of it aimed at a customer who, so far, mostly buys things that cost less than a stick of gum.
So what are they really fighting over? Not the shopping. They are fighting over the right to say yes.
Software became the customer
Every payment system we have was built on one assumption: a human is there at the moment of purchase.
Fraud checks, the little "verify it's you" pop-ups, the rules that let you dispute a charge, all of it is tuned to human speed and human error. Autonomous agents break that. An agent can read a giant product catalog, compare prices across dozens of sellers, and check out in milliseconds, with no human watching.
The demand looks real. McKinsey projects $1tn of agent-driven US commerce by 2030.4 Nearly half of US online shoppers already use AI somewhere in the buying process.5 And the risk is just as real: US consumers reported a record $16bn in fraud losses in 2025, up about a quarter in a year.6
To handle machine-speed buying, the industry shipped four rival protocols in barely a year. A protocol here just means a shared rulebook for how an agent is allowed to pay:
- ACP (Agentic Commerce Protocol), from OpenAI, Stripe and Meta. It runs checkout inside a chatbot using a one-time "shared payment token," a scoped credential that caps what the agent can spend, so a hallucinating bot cannot buy a $5,000 item instead of a $50 one.7
- AP2 (Agent Payments Protocol), from Google and 60-plus partners, now handed to the FIDO Alliance, the same group behind passwordless "passkey" logins. It proves consent with digital receipts signed by the user, the merchant, and the agent.8
- x402, from Coinbase, now under the Linux Foundation. It revives an old "Payment Required" web code and settles in stablecoins, skipping card networks entirely.9
- MPP (Machine Payments Protocol), from Stripe and Tempo, built for high-frequency machine-to-machine billing.10
Four rulebooks, one customer. And the customer barely spends.
The metric nobody will show you
In a business that brags about every vanity number, one number is missing everywhere: consumer purchase volume. None of the four camps has disclosed real figures for how much shopping agents are actually doing. In this industry, silence on the only metric that matters is itself the signal.
The one place with hard numbers is x402, and where it counts, the numbers are tiny:
- x402 now underpins more than 97% of all on-chain agentic transactions, with over 90% of that volume on Coinbase's Base network.2
- But the average payment is about $0.52, and real monthly commerce ran to just a few $mn, not $bn.1
- The activity is machines paying for software, data, and computing power, the sub-dollar economy that card networks were never built to serve.
This is the honest split. Agentic payments are winning at the one thing traditional finance does badly, tiny high-frequency payments worth pennies. They are not replacing Visa for a $150 pair of shoes.
The dog that did not bark
The clearest proof came from OpenAI. In September 2025 it launched "Instant Checkout," letting you buy inside ChatGPT.7 The vision was the world's biggest storefront living inside a chat box that 900mn people now use every week.11
By early 2026 it was quietly scaled back.12 OpenAI stepped away from owning checkout and handed the final purchase back to merchants. Why it stalled tells you everything:
- Shoppers researched happily but hesitated to pay in a chat window. Conversion inside ChatGPT ran far below normal web checkout.12
- Merchants refused to give up the checkout page, because that page is where they own the customer, the data, and the upsell.
- Big retailers guard their brand and their first-party data fiercely.
Shopify's own numbers say the same. Last quarter it processed $116bn in merchandise and AI-driven orders tripled in a year, yet management still called agentic volume small next to the whole.13 AI is a brilliant front door for discovery. It is not yet the checkout counter.
Why the card networks should have lost
Here is the threat that terrified Visa and Mastercard.
If an agent shops rationally, it should hunt for the cheapest way to pay. It could route a $100 purchase over a bank transfer, a debit network, or a near-free stablecoin rail, and skip the 2 to 3% fee that credit cards charge. Machines doing "least-cost routing" in milliseconds is the disintermediation nightmare.
The stakes are enormous. US merchants pay roughly $111bn a year in credit-card interchange fees, the slice the card networks take on every swipe.14 For a decade they have fought the card duopoly in court over exactly this. Agents looked like the weapon that would finally break it.
How the incumbents preempted it
They did not build a fifth protocol to compete. They climbed above all four.
- Every one of the four protocols has a card network or card-adjacent processor as a founding member. The "open" rails all run through their gates.
- Visa launched its Trusted Agent Protocol and an on-ramp that lets merchants accept agent payments from any standard through a single Visa integration.15
- Mastercard shipped Agent Pay, wrapping payment tokens in proof of who the agent is and that a specific human authorized it.16
- Then Visa agreed to buy BioCatch, a behavioral-biometrics firm, for $2.4bn, announced in August 2026.17
That last one is the tell. BioCatch reads passive human signals, your typing rhythm, how you hold a phone, the way your cursor moves, to tell a real person from a bot. Old fraud signals fail with agents, because legitimate AI traffic comes from a handful of cloud data centers, not from homes. By owning the tech that decides "is a human really behind this," Visa makes itself the referee of every agent transaction.
The move works because of a trap. A merchant can take a cheap stablecoin transfer and save the fee, but then it owns all the risk: fraud, a hallucinating agent, a customer who denies authorizing anything. Or it can accept a card-network "agentic token," pay the 2 to 3%, and let Visa handle consent and disputes. Most will pay.
And the risk is not made up. A 2026 red-team study of Google's AP2 showed that hiding instructions inside a product listing can hijack a shopping agent into approving the wrong purchase or leaking a user's data.18 Digital receipts do not stop an agent from being talked into signing them.
The oldest lesson in payments
Step back, and this is a very old story wearing new clothes.
Every wave of payments innovation promised to cut out the middleman. Every time, the middleman moved one layer up and kept collecting. The rails changed. The toll-taker did not.
The steelman for Visa and Mastercard is real, and worth saying plainly. Somebody has to answer "is this a real human, and did they actually agree to this" at global scale. These two firms have the fraud systems, the dispute machinery, and the worldwide acceptance to underwrite machines spending our money. That is a genuine service.
But the same argument justified rising fees for forty years, and left American merchants paying more than merchants almost anywhere else in the rich world. The service is real. So is the toll.
What this means for you
I spent years early in my career doing solid work inside a little pod where almost nobody could see what I actually did. The lesson that stuck was uncomfortable: doing the work creates value, but being seen to authorize it is what captures the reward. This whole fight is that lesson at industrial scale. The agents do the labor. Whoever is seen to approve it collects the toll.
So where does that leave a Western reader?
- If you are a shopper, the convenience is coming, but so is a quiet question of liability. If an agent buys the wrong thing, or gets tricked, who eats the cost? US regulators have not answered this yet.19
- If you are a merchant, do not expect agents to free you from card fees. The escape route is being sealed before it opened.
- If you are an investor, the value is landing on the authentication and identity layer, not the flashy chat interface. Firms like BioCatch just became core infrastructure.
- If you build or work in software, the near-term money in agent payments is business plumbing, not consumer retail.
What to watch
- Whether any protocol finally discloses real consumer purchase volume, not transaction counts. The silence is the story until it breaks.
- Whether the Visa-BioCatch deal closes as planned, and who else buys an identity firm next.17
- Whether US regulators open a formal case on who is liable when an agent misfires. Europe is already forcing the question through stricter payment rules.
- Whether markets like India, where everyday digital payments are essentially free, grow a cheaper agent economy while America keeps paying the toll.20
When machines do the buying, the scarce thing is no longer the rail. It is the right to say a human said yes.
And that is it for today's edition. Thanks for reading Tech for Commons, where we look at what technology is actually doing to people.
Best,
Sagarika

I grew up an only child, which made me the single point of failure for my parents' whole plan. No sibling to catch the load if I dropped it. So I tend to notice, maybe faster than most, when a big system quietly makes itself depend on one fragile thing.
That is what just happened to the global AI economy, and almost nobody was pricing the risk.
For two years, the price of commodity intelligence, the cheap and good-enough AI that runs batch summaries, tagging, and simple chat, fell toward zero. The reason was a wave of powerful open models from Chinese labs, priced so low they set the floor for everyone. DeepSeek's flagship ran at a flat $0.14 per mn words in, $0.28 out. Western startups built whole businesses on that number.
On August 16, at 4pm UTC, that floor cracked. DeepSeek scrapped flat pricing and brought in peak and off-peak rates. Some costs jumped by more than 1,100%.1
The cheap floor was never real. It was a subsidy. And the bill just landed.
How China took over the cheap tier
Let me set the scene, because the scale of the shift is easy to miss.
Through early 2026, Chinese open models did not just compete. They took over the high-volume, low-cost tier of global AI.
- On OpenRouter, a popular marketplace that routes developer traffic to whichever model they choose, Chinese models went from about 4.5% of all tokens (a "token" is roughly a word the model reads or writes) in early 2025 to around 46% by mid-2026.2
- The crossover is datable: in the week of February 9 to 15, 2026, Chinese models processed more tokens than US ones for the first time.2
- By mid-2026, DeepSeek was the single largest source of tokens on the platform, ahead of every US lab.2
Then DeepSeek changed the deal. It moved to peak and off-peak pricing.1 Peak hours (01:00 to 04:00 and 06:00 to 10:00 UTC) cover the working day across Asia, Europe, and the US East Coast. During those hours, prices climb hard.
- The increases, depending on model and task, run from 50% to more than 1,100%.1
- The 1,100% is the worst case: reading from cache, the cheap trick that retrieval systems (which feed the model a big fixed document each time) lean on, rose more than tenfold.
- Flagship output roughly quadrupled at peak.3
DeepSeek's stated reason was to "allocate computing resources more reasonably."4 That phrase is the whole story. They ran out of machines.
Why the cheap price was always a mirage
Here is the thing almost everyone got wrong. The low price was read as progress. It was really a promise the hardware could not keep.
The barbell: huge volume, tiny money.
Start with a strange split. The tokens and the money went to completely different places. On Vercel's AI Gateway, another big routing platform:
- Open-weight models, mostly Chinese, captured about 29% of all tokens.5
- But they earned under 4% of the spend.5
- Anthropic alone took about 61% of the money on roughly 32% of the tokens.5
Read that again. The cheap models do the huge, boring volume. The pricey US frontier models take almost all the revenue, because that is where buyers put the work they cannot afford to get wrong: long agentic coding (where the AI runs many steps on its own), legal analysis, hard reasoning.
The productivity gain here is real, and not small. The cost to reach a given level of AI skill has been falling 5 to 10 times a year, and pure software efficiency, stripping out cheaper hardware and price wars, improves about 3 times a year.6 A job that cost a dollar last year costs cents now. That is genuine, and it is why a two-person startup can now do what needed a team in 2023.
But cheap-per-word hid a second bill.
The hidden inflation.
While the price of last year's skill fell, the cost of running this year's frontier rose. Modern reasoning models think in the background before answering, and that thinking burns tokens. A lot of them. The newest agentic models can burn ten times or more the tokens of the chat models they replace.6
So the real monthly bill went up even as the sticker price per word went down.
- Uber's engineering leaders said publicly they blew through a full year's AI budget in four months once agentic coding tools scaled across staff.7
- One two-hour coding session alone ran to $1,200.7
Intelligence got cheaper per unit and more expensive in total, at the same time. Now put the two together: global demand for tokens exploded, and the cheapest supplier was sitting on the most fragile hardware base in the industry.
The bottleneck is a memory fab.
This is the part the price war buried. Chinese labs cannot buy Nvidia's best chips. US export controls cut them off. So they run on home-grown silicon, mostly Huawei's Ascend line, built by SMIC on a 7-nanometer process whose yields only recently climbed toward 40%.8
The real chokepoint is not raw compute. It is memory bandwidth, the speed at which a chip can feed itself the data a large model needs to answer. Serving AI at scale is a memory problem, and China's high-bandwidth memory is the single tightest link in the chain.8
- The most credible chip analysts now flag memory, not the processor, as the binding limit on how much Chinese AI can actually serve.8
- Cut off from the best foreign memory, Chinese labs simply cannot build inference clusters as efficient as a US hyperscaler's.
So the flat $0.14 was never an equilibrium. It was venture money and state support burning to buy global market share, on machines that could not serve the demand they attracted. When the volume saturated that brittle base, the arbitrage snapped. US labs had been cutting prices to keep up, OpenAI lopped 80% off its mid-tier model in late July.9 But they were cutting from a position of strength. DeepSeek was cutting from one of scarcity.
Constraint did breed cleverness. Locked out of hardware, Chinese labs pushed the math instead, and gave the models away. Alibaba's Qwen became the most-downloaded open model family in the world, with more than 151,000 derivative models built on it, a bigger base than Meta's Llama ever had.10 They conceded the API money to win the architecture. The world's developers now build on Chinese foundations even while the US frontier keeps the profits.
Two AI worlds, splitting apart
Step back, because this is bigger than one price change.
The AI race has split into two halves that barely touch. One bloc holds the capability, the capital, and the physical chips. The other holds the usage, the mindshare, and the workflows the world runs on.
- The capability gap is almost gone. Stanford's 2026 AI Index put the gap between the top US and top Chinese model at just 2.7%.11
- But being able to build a smart model is not the same as being able to serve it cheaply to the planet. That still needs chips and memory the US and its allies control.
And the fight is no longer only about hardware. It moved to the models themselves.
- In June, Anthropic told the US Senate that around 25,000 fake accounts tied to Alibaba ran 28.8mn exchanges against Claude to copy its reasoning, a practice called distillation (training your model on a smarter model's answers).12
- In July, a White House official accused Moonshot of distilling Anthropic's model to build its Kimi K3, using Nvidia chips routed through Thailand, and the Treasury threatened sanctions.13
- Independent experts pushed back, saying distillation alone does not explain how good Kimi K3 is.14
The curtain is coming down. Both sides are now preparing to control not just chips, but access to the models themselves.
What it means for you
So what do you take from this if you sit in the US or the wider West?
If you build software, the free lunch is over, but you are not the biggest loser. The winners are app-layer companies that stayed flexible: heavy token use, low switching costs, able to route each job to whoever is cheapest that hour. If your pipeline can move between DeepSeek, Qwen, and a US model without re-engineering, you are fine.
The real losers are the startups who hard-wired their unit economics to $0.14 and cannot move. When a cost triples overnight, a business whose margin depended on it does not have a bad quarter. It has no model left.
- Western hosts that run Chinese open weights on US soil suddenly look smart, because they price on Western hardware, not on a supply chain choked in China.5
- Enterprises had already voted with compliance. Anthropic now takes about 40% of enterprise AI spend, OpenAI about 27%, and open-source sits near 13% of workloads, held back by the risk of sending data to Chinese servers.15
If you are in Europe, the AI Act's high-risk rules began to bite from August 2, 2026, pushing firms toward whichever option is safest on data and law, not cheapest per word.16
And the upside is genuinely global. AI adoption is running higher in many developing countries than in rich ones, because a cheap open model on local hardware is a bigger leap where a $30 subscription is a luxury.17 The floor cracked for businesses built on it. The tool itself keeps spreading.
What to watch
Four specific things over the coming weeks:
- Whether other Chinese labs follow. Alibaba, Tencent, Baidu, and Zhipu have all already raised AI prices as token demand strains their compute.18
- Whether China's memory makers can ship enough high-bandwidth memory to loosen the bottleneck, or whether serving stays capped.
- Whether Washington formalizes rules that would control model weights and cloud access, not just chips.13
- Whether any US startup blames a DeepSeek-shaped hole in its margins in its next update. That is the first real crack in the app layer.
The cheapest intelligence in the world was never cheap. Someone was always paying for it, and now everyone is.
And that is it for today's edition. Thanks for reading Tech for Commons, where we look at what technology is actually doing to people.

I keep coming back to one strange fact. In the same summer that the United States tightened the screws on China's access to advanced chips, it quietly handed a large slice of its most valuable AI companies to foreign governments.
Not to allies as partners. As owners.
When Anthropic closed its Series H in May 2026, the round raised $65bn and valued the company at $965bn.1 Look at who led it. Singapore's state fund GIC and Coatue co-led, with big checks from Temasek, Abu Dhabi's MGX, and the Qatar Investment Authority.2
So the people setting the price of a leading American AI lab were not classic venture investors chasing a return. They were sovereign wealth funds, meaning pools of money owned by national governments and run with a state's interests in mind.
That is the thing I want to walk you through. American AI now has a foreign policy in two directions at once. It blocks its rivals, and it sells the upside to its friends. Both moves are happening at head-of-state level, and both change who ends up owning the future.
The wall, and the door
Here is what actually happened, in plain order.
- In January 2026, the White House put a 25% tariff on advanced chips routed through the US on their way to buyers abroad, using Section 232, a national-security trade law.3 In effect, Nvidia and AMD now hand Washington a quarter of the revenue on sales to markets like China.
- Around the same time, China told its state-funded data centers to rip out foreign chips from Nvidia, AMD, and Intel, even from half-finished builds.4
- The result: Nvidia's share of China's AI chip market has collapsed. CEO Jensen Huang now says it has gone from about 95% to effectively zero, a market that once made up a fifth to a quarter of the company's data center revenue.5
That is the wall going up around the adversary. Now the door swinging open for friends.
- In July 2026, the Commerce Department upgraded the United Arab Emirates to Country Group A:5, the highest trust tier in US export rules, the club of NATO and Five Eyes allies.6
- The official notice tied the upgrade to the UAE's defense partnership and its help during "Operation Epic Fury," the US-Iran conflict in the spring of 2026.7
- License-free chip access was not nationwide. It was routed to named companies, G42 and Core42, both linked to Sheikh Tahnoon bin Zayed, the UAE's national security adviser and the president's brother.8
Chips flow out in exchange for military cooperation. Equity flows in from allied treasuries. That is the whole story in one breath.
The productivity problem this money solves
Start with why the Gulf capital is even welcome. Training a frontier model, meaning the largest and most expensive class of AI systems, now costs more than private markets can comfortably fund.
- The jump from Nvidia's older chips to its Blackwell GB300 generation means racks that are liquid-cooled and enormously power-hungry, and campuses measured in gigawatts.
- Anthropic's revenue is racing to keep up. Its annualized run-rate, meaning revenue for one month multiplied out to a year, hit about $65bn in July 2026, up from roughly $9bn late in 2025.9
- OpenAI's run-rate topped $40bn ahead of its own IPO, at a valuation near $850bn.10
The productivity is real. American firms are shipping AI that genuinely speeds up coding, research, and customer work. But the capital needed to build the factories behind it outran Silicon Valley, so the money came from abroad.
Follow the money: the vertically integrated sovereign
Abu Dhabi's MGX is the clearest case. It closed its first fund at $49bn in July 2026, above target, and has spoken of managing over $100bn in time.11
Then watch where it deployed:
- Stakes in OpenAI, Anthropic, and Elon Musk's xAI.2
- A consortium with BlackRock's infrastructure arm that closed the $40bn buyout of Aligned Data Centers, a big US data-center operator, in July 2026.12
- A seat in Databricks' $5bn round in August 2026, at a $190bn valuation.13
Read that list again. MGX now owns pieces of the labs that need the compute, the software that manages the data, and the physical buildings that house the chips. That is vertical integration by a foreign state, up and down the American AI stack.
The doctrines diverge
Not every partner plays it the same way, and the differences matter for who captures what.
- UAE: build and own both ends. It won the A:5 upgrade and is hosting Stargate UAE, a planned 5-gigawatt campus in Abu Dhabi with OpenAI and Oracle, its first 200 megawatts due online in 2026.14
- Saudi Arabia: hoard the hardware. Its champion Humain, backed by the Public Investment Fund, has started importing Nvidia GB300 chips, roughly 18,000 to begin, with hundreds of thousands more and a $10bn AMD deal in the pipeline.15 It wants physical control on home soil.
- Singapore: buy the equity, skip the concrete. With no room for gigawatt campuses, its funds Temasek and GIC are buying ownership instead. Temasek plans to lift its AI allocation from about 6% toward 10% to 15% of a record portfolio by 2031.16
- Qatar: become the landlord abroad. Its telco Ooredoo, with Nvidia and Nokia, launched Zankore, a 1-gigawatt AI platform aimed at Southeast Asia, with about $800mn committed for a 49% stake.17
The gate the government now holds
The scariest part for American firms is not the money. It is that Washington has learned to throttle the product.
In June 2026, citing security, Commerce ordered Anthropic to block all foreign nationals, including its own non-citizen staff, from its most advanced models.18 Unable to check every user's passport instantly, Anthropic pulled the models offline entirely, then brought them back only after adding guardrails that dented their benchmark scores.19
That is a live demonstration. The US government can now reach into a private AI system and turn the dial.
The money moved, and so did the risk
The demand did not shrink when China closed. It moved.
- Nvidia posted record revenue of about $82bn in the quarter it reported in May 2026, with data-center sales near $75bn, up 92% on the year.23 The orders that vanished in Beijing were soaked up by Abu Dhabi, Riyadh, and US hyperscalers.
- But look at where a lot of this compute now physically sits. A big share is rising in the Gulf, which this spring was a live war zone. Operation Epic Fury put the region's power grids and data campuses inside a shooting conflict.7
- So every US firm renting Gulf compute has swapped one dependency for another. It is free of China, and now tethered to a volatile region it cannot defend.
The bigger picture
Step back and this looks less like an accident and more like a design.
The logic is coherent on its own terms. The compute is getting built somewhere no matter what. Better, the argument runs, to build it with allied capital in a country under a US defense umbrella than to let rivals build their own unmonitored stack. Sovereign funds have mostly been patient, passive, long-term money, exactly what a capital-hungry industry needs.2
But there is a quiet redistribution underneath. The foundations of this technology, the decades of computer-science research, were paid for by the American public through agencies like DARPA and the National Science Foundation. The equity upside of that work is now being sold, through record IPO filings, to foreign governments.20
I hold two passports' worth of context in my own head, thinking in dollars and rupees at the same time, and I have watched ownership and belonging pull in opposite directions my whole adult life. So I notice when a country walls off its technology from enemies while wiring the ownership of it to friends. It is the same duality, just written at the scale of a superpower.
What it means for you
If you sit in the US or the wider West, here is the honest ledger.
- The upside. Cheaper, faster AI reaches you sooner because foreign capital is footing the build-out bill. Your pension or index fund may hold these labs when they go public. Jobs come with the data-center construction on US soil.
- The catch on ownership. The gains from taxpayer-seeded research increasingly accrue to state investors abroad. When these companies list, a chunk of the return has already been promised elsewhere.20
- The new risk. A licensing regime that can be granted at head-of-state level, weeks after a war, can be pulled the same way. Any firm whose compute or models depend on these deals is now exposed to politics it cannot control.6 18
- The conflict question. Sheikh Tahnoon's fund bought a 49% stake, reported at $500mn, in the Trump family's crypto venture, and the same family circle sits near the chip decisions.21 Lawmakers Gregory Meeks and Sydney Kamlager-Dove have demanded answers from Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick on whether financial ties bypassed the normal review.22
Do not read this as pure alarm. The compute is real, the productivity is real, and allied capital is genuinely better than an adversary's. But the price includes political risk baked into the cost of American AI itself.
What to watch
- Whether G42 and Core42 actually re-domicile as US-headquartered companies before their license-free status is set to sunset, reportedly in April 2027.8
- Whether the Anthropic and OpenAI IPOs price with any restriction on foreign ownership or voting, or none at all.10 20
- Whether Commerce throttles another lab's models the way it throttled Anthropic's, which would confirm the gate is now standard policy.18
- Whether the Meeks and Kamlager-Dove inquiry forces the interagency review, or quietly fades.22
America has made its AI almost impossible for enemies to reach, and almost impossible to untangle from its friends, and it did not write down what the public got in return.
And that is it for today's edition. Thanks for reading Tech for Commons, where we look at what technology is actually doing to people.

The number that disappeared
In late July 2026, Microsoft told investors its capital spending plan for the year was dropping by about $15bn, from roughly $190bn to $175bn.1
Spending on data centers is the scoreboard for who wins the AI race, so a cut that size should scream that demand is cooling or the company is pulling back. Neither happened. The Chief Financial Officer, Amy Hood, confirmed the physical build was completely unchanged. Not one chip order canceled, not one building paused.1
So where did $15bn go? It vanished through a single accounting choice. Microsoft extended the assumed lifespan of its data center buildings from 15 years to 25 years.2 That one move reclassified a big chunk of its future leases and pushed the spending off the line analysts stare at. The build roared on. The number on the page shrank.
That "boring" adjustment is the load-bearing beam holding up the whole AI trade. Once you see it, you cannot unsee it.
What "useful life" is really doing
A dollar spent on a server does not hit the profit statement at once. It gets spread in slices over the years the asset is expected to work. That yearly slice is called depreciation.
Stretch the assumed lifespan, and each slice gets thinner. Thinner slices mean lower yearly costs, which means higher reported profit today. Same machine, better-looking earnings.
The catch is physics. The chips at the heart of this build, Nvidia's accelerators, get replaced roughly every two years as faster ones arrive. Yet the accounting lifespans stretch the other way, to five years, six years, and now 25 years for the buildings. That gap is the whole story, and in 2026 the accounting moved first.
The same chip, two different truths
The clearest sign that these are judgment calls, not facts, came in January 2025, when two of the smartest companies on earth looked at the identical hardware and reached opposite conclusions.
- Meta stretched the life of some servers to five and a half years, which shaved roughly $2.9bn off its depreciation cost for 2025.
- Amazon went the other way. It cut the life of some servers back to five years, citing "the increased pace of technology development" in AI, which knocked about $1.3bn off AWS operating profit.3
Same silicon, same supplier, an eighteen-month disagreement, and a swing of billions in reported profit. That is how soft this number is.
Then the critics arrived with a calculator.
- Investor Michael Burry, who famously called the 2008 housing crash, laid out in late 2025 that stretching these lifespans would understate depreciation across Big Tech by about $176bn between 2026 and 2028.4
- On his math, by 2028 Oracle would overstate its earnings by around 27%, and Meta by around 21%, purely from paper lifespans.4
- J.P. Morgan modeled the same thing more gently: go back to a three-year schedule, matching the actual chip cycle, and earnings per share fall roughly 6% to 8% for most hyperscalers, and up to 15% for Meta.4
To be fair, the companies have a real argument. The scarce thing in 2026 is not chips, it is electricity: power lines, substations, grid hookups. Amazon's leadership has argued the building genuinely lasts decades even as the servers inside it turn over in under three years.3 On that logic, a 25-year building is honest. But timing is everything, and cutting reported spending by $15bn in the exact quarter investors were finally scrutinizing AI discipline is, at the least, extremely convenient.2
The wall that is coming
Because spending has tripled in three years, reported depreciation lags far behind the cash going out the door. The bill is real, just delayed.
- Across the four biggest spenders, trailing depreciation is running at only about a third of what they are actually spending on property and equipment.8
- Depreciation is a mathematical certainty. The spending of 2024 to 2026 lands on profit statements in 2027 to 2029 whether the AI revenue shows up on time or not.8
And the cash strain is already visible.
- Alphabet's free cash flow, the money left after spending, turned negative in the second quarter of 2026, the first time since it went public, as quarterly capex hit a record $44.9bn. Its finance chief warned 2027 spending will be higher still.5
- Meta's revenue grew 28% to $60.8bn in the same quarter, yet its profit fell as AI costs bit into margins.6
- Oracle is burning cash hardest, with negative free cash flow of about $23.7bn for its 2026 fiscal year against a $638bn order backlog, roughly half of it tied to a single customer, OpenAI.7
The industry is crossing its own break-even line right as the heaviest wave of costs prepares to crash.
Does the old silicon hold its value?
Every long lifespan rests on one bet: that used chips are still worth something years later. And it is one supplier's chips, Nvidia's, which now earns about 92% of its revenue from data centers.9 The evidence on resale value points both ways.
The pessimistic read is brutal. The cost of running AI keeps falling by nearly an order of magnitude a year, and lenders who take chips as collateral often lend against only half to seventy percent of day-one value. A two-year-old chip can be worth a few thousand dollars against a $30,000 sticker price.
The optimistic read is just as real.
- In August 2026, CoreWeave, the largest AI-only cloud firm, said its 2020-era A100 chips were fully booked through 2029.10
- Rental prices for the older H100 chips actually rose through 2026 rather than falling, because energized, racked capacity is scarce right now.11
The tell is that Nvidia itself has stepped in as a backstop. In August 2026 it unveiled a roughly $500bn financing framework and agreed to support up to 25% of the value on select deals.12 When the chipmaker has to guarantee its own chips' resale value to keep financing flowing, you learn how nervous the market is about the very assumption the accounting depends on.
The reason customers pay full freight for a five-year-old chip is not that it is fast. It is that it is plugged in. When power is the bottleneck, an old energized chip beats a new one waiting for a grid connection.
The shadow stack, and who ends up holding it
Here it stops being about accounting and starts being about who carries the risk.
The hyperscalers used to fund everything from their own cash. Not anymore. The debt-funded share of their spending has climbed sharply as spending outruns cash flow.20 To keep that debt off their own balance sheets, they route it through separate entities.
- A July 2026 study by Nikkei put the off-balance-sheet obligations of the five big players at about $1.65tn, on top of the roughly $1.35tn already on their books.13
- Goldman Sachs counted close to half a trillion dollars of AI-related bonds and loans issued in just the first half of 2026.14
Two deals show the machine at work:
- Meta and Blue Owl built a joint venture for Meta's Hyperion campus in Louisiana. A separate entity borrowed about $27bn, and Meta leases the site back. The debt sits off Meta's balance sheet, but Meta quietly guaranteed the building's residual value, a contingent exposure of around $28bn buried in the footnotes.15
- Google and TeraWulf, a former bitcoin miner, did a $3.2bn junk-bond deal where Google backstops the lease once the site is built. Google collected equity warrants for its trouble, and bondholders carried all the construction risk.16
Now follow the risk to where it actually lands. This is the part almost nobody is watching.
- Oracle's cost to insure its debt against default hit a record of around 215 basis points in 2026, and S&P cut its rating to BBB-, one notch above junk.7 17
- CoreWeave, despite doubling revenue to about $2.6bn, posted a net loss of $626mn and enormous interest bills, and the market briefly priced in roughly a 50% chance it defaults within five years.18
The risk crosses the ocean
The final move should make a Western reader sit up. Europe is about to open the door for its retirement money to buy this debt.
From January 2027, a reform of the European Union's insurance rules, called Solvency II, sharply cuts the capital insurers must hold against senior slices of complex securitized debt, including the bespoke kind used for US data centers.19 For a decade those rules kept European insurers out of this market. Now they are being nudged in, to hunt for yield in American AI infrastructure.19
So the people exposed to a used Nvidia chip losing value in 2029 are no longer just venture capitalists and tech shareholders. They are:
- European pension holders and insurance customers, through their general accounts.
- Index fund investors on both sides of the Atlantic, who own these bonds without knowing it.
- Ordinary savers, the people least aware they are holding the position, and least able to absorb it if it turns.
Aggressive gamblers, terrified accountants
Step back and there is a strange paradox here. The people running the AI build are among the biggest risk-takers alive, betting hundreds of billions on a technology that may or may not deliver. Yet in their reporting they are extremely cautious, engineering lifespans and off-balance-sheet vehicles so a single bad quarter does not trigger a crisis.
I understand that instinct more than I would like. I moved countries for work, which sounds like the boldest thing a person can do, and yet immigrants are often the most financially careful people in the room. When one job loss can unravel your visa, your kid's school, your whole life, you take the giant leap and then guard the landing obsessively. The biggest risk-takers become the most risk-averse, because the downside is total.
That is exactly what the hyperscalers are doing. The gamble is enormous, so the books are engineered to look calm. The tension between the two is where the danger lives.
What it means for you
If you are a Western worker, saver, or investor, the honest read cuts both ways.
- The upside is real. The compute is genuinely useful, older chips are holding value better than the doomers claim, and no hyperscaler has yet canceled a build or written off a mountain of chips.
- The exposure is real too, and closer than you think. Your index fund, your pension, and your bond fund very likely hold this AI debt already. You did not choose it, but you own a slice.
The single number to distrust is the useful life. When a company reports a lovely profit, ask what lifespan it assumed. Stretch the years and the profit is partly an accounting choice, not cash in hand.
None of this means a crash is coming. It means the profits look better than the cash does, and the gap is financed by debt quietly spreading to people who never opted in.
What to watch
- The secondary chip price in 2028 and 2029. That is the real test of every long lifespan. If used H100 and Blackwell values crater, the accounting was fiction.
- The first big impairment. Watch for the first hyperscaler to write down a batch of chips or cancel a build. So far, none have.
- A private-credit fund gating redemptions. If one of the funds holding this debt stops letting investors pull money out, that is the early tremor.
- January 2027. Watch whether European insurers actually pile into US data center debt once the Solvency II rules change, and how fast.
The physical build is relentless and unbroken. The accounting simply moved first, to soften the blow it can already see coming.
And that is it for today's edition. Thanks for reading Tech for Commons, where we look at what technology is actually doing to people.
