I keep coming back to one number, and it makes me a little angry every time.
In 2025, American shops and restaurants paid a record $198.25bn in card "swipe fees", the cut that card networks and banks take every time you tap or swipe.1 That is up from about $187bn the year before, and it is more than triple what it was in 2009.1
Now here is the strange part. The United States has built fast, cheap, bank-to-bank instant payment plumbing not once but three separate times. And it has barely dented that $198bn.
I notice this partly because of where I sit. My father had a line, "When in Rome, be a Roman." I moved to the US years ago, and I think in dollars and rupees at once, having stopped mentally converting long ago. That double vision is useful right now, because the world's two biggest payment experiments, America's and India's, both hit their limits in the same few months of 2026. Watching them together tells you something neither tells you alone.
The American way: build the road three times, keep the toll
An "instant payment rail" is just plumbing that moves money between two bank accounts in seconds, any day, any hour, and cannot be reversed. The US now has three of them:
- Zelle, owned by seven big banks, moved $1.2tn in 2025, up 20% in a year.2
- RTP, the private bank-owned network, cleared a record 2.27mn payments worth $8.62bn in a single day on May 1, 2026.3
- FedNow, the Federal Reserve's own public rail, launched in 2023.
So instant payment in America is real. It is just privatized, split across rival networks, and, crucially, walled off from the checkout counter.
Because at the shop, you still reach for a card. And every card swipe carries "interchange", the slice that goes to the bank that issued your card. That is the engine behind the $198bn.
Here is why instant bank payment has not killed the card at the till, and it is not a technology problem:
- Card rewards are paid for by merchants. Your 2% cash back, your airline miles, your hotel points, the merchant funds them through the swipe fee.
- So there is zero reason for you to pay a merchant by instant bank transfer. The card pays you to swipe.
- The merchant eats a fee of roughly 1.5% to 3.5% of the sale, then quietly raises prices to cover it.
That last point is the part people miss. It is the most regressive fee in American retail. Low-margin shops pay a high tax on every dollar of sales, prices rise for everyone, and the money flows to the rewards enjoyed mostly by better-off cardholders. The people with the thinnest wallets help fund the perks of people with the fattest ones.
FedNow just quietly changed what it is
For its first two years, FedNow was a tool for company treasurers, big-ticket and corporate. Then, in a single quarter, it became something else.
- In Q1 2026, the average FedNow payment was $99,414.4
- By Q2 2026, it had fallen to $54,957, a 45% drop in three months.4
- Volume jumped 83% to about 5mn payments, while the total value barely moved, up just 1.3%.4
When a lot more payments arrive but the dollars stay flat, the average ticket collapses. It is the moment an expensive wire substitute turned into a retail and small-business rail: instant wage payouts for gig and hourly workers, insurance claims, supplier settlements.
And the productivity gain is genuine, so I want to name it. For a small business, getting paid in seconds instead of waiting two days for an old ACH bank transfer is real working capital. It shortens the gap between paying suppliers and getting paid, which is often the difference between making payroll and not.
But there is a catch built into the American rollout, and it is a quiet one.
The one-way street
FedNow passed 1,700 participating banks by mid-2026. Sounds like broad adoption. Except a large share of them signed up "receive-only": they will accept instant money coming in, but will not let their customers send it out.
Why? Sending instant money is expensive and risky:
- The payment is irreversible, so any fraud on an outbound send is a total, immediate loss.
- Old bank core systems, run mostly by a handful of vendors, were built for overnight batches, not 24/7 real-time settlement. Rebuilding them costs money.
- Receiving is cheap and safe. A small bank can offer the look of modernity, keep deposits from fleeing, and skip the hard part.
So for a large share of Americans, instant payment is a one-way street. You can receive an insurance payout on a Saturday, but you cannot use the same app to instantly pay a contractor on a Sunday. The rail exists; half of it is switched off.
India ran the opposite experiment, and just blinked
Now flip to the other side of my double vision.
India's UPI is the same core idea, instant bank-to-bank payment, but built as a public utility instead of a private market. The scale is hard to believe:
- In July 2026, UPI processed 23.66bn transactions worth about $341bn (₹29.88 lakh crore).5
- India moves more instant payments in a single day than FedNow moves in a year.
- Most of it is now person-to-merchant, and the vast majority of those payments are tiny, under about $6.
India got there by banning fees. For years, merchants paid nothing to accept UPI, a zero-MDR policy. MDR, the "merchant discount rate", is simply the fee a shop pays to accept a digital payment. In the US that fee is 1.5% to 3.5%. In India it was set at zero, and the government paid the industry a subsidy to keep the lights on.
That is where the experiment broke.
- The true cost of running UPI at this scale is an estimated ₹4,000 to 5,000 crore a year (roughly $500mn).6
- The government's subsidy for FY26 was budgeted at just ₹437 crore (about $50mn), a fraction of the cost.6
- Free stopped being affordable exactly when the network became universal.
So in early August 2026, India's Parliament lifted the ban and cleared the way to charge large merchants.7 The structure is deliberately narrow:
- A fee of about 0.05% to 0.07% on payments above ₹2,000 (about $23), only for merchants with turnover above roughly ₹1 to 1.5 crore.7
- Consumers, person-to-person transfers, and around 90% of small merchants stay free.7
Tiny next to America's swipe fee. But it is the end of the free-lunch era.
Friction comes back too
Speed was UPI's whole pitch. India is now deliberately slowing it down, because instant and irreversible is a fraudster's dream. Most losses come from "authorized push payment" fraud, where a scammer tricks you into sending the money yourself, and once it is gone, it is gone in seconds.
The Reserve Bank of India, the central bank, is adding friction on purpose:8
- A proposed one-hour hold on payments above ₹10,000 (about $115) sent to a new person, so the money can be clawed back before it settles.
- A "kill switch" to freeze all digital payments instantly.
The regulator that built the fastest retail payment system on earth is now legislating a one-hour delay into it. That is an admission: at planetary scale, pure speed carries risks you cannot fully manage.
Brazil found the middle both are now walking toward
There is a third model that got the balance right from the start. Brazil's Pix kept person-to-person transfers free for citizens, but let banks charge businesses from day one, at an average merchant fee of roughly 0.33%.9 Low enough that shops adopted it and cash faded, high enough to actually pay for the system. Public good for people, priced service for enterprise.
That is almost exactly where the US and India are both heading now. America is searching for retail volume; India is searching for revenue and safety. Both are walking back from their extremes toward the middle Brazil chose years ago.
Where this actually points: your money leaving the country
Here is the move that made me sit up. The same American banks that guard the swipe-fee citadel are not using instant tech to attack it at home. They are pointing it overseas, at remittances.
On June 11, 2026, Early Warning Services, the bank consortium that owns Zelle, unveiled ZelleUSD, a dollar-backed "stablecoin", a digital token pegged one-to-one to the dollar.10 India is the first target corridor, with a launch expected before the end of 2026.11
The logic is sharp. The US-to-India money corridor is one of the largest in the world, and Zelle already sits in over 2,400 bank apps.10 So a US worker sends dollars from an app they already have, the dollars become tokens, cross a blockchain rail that skips the slow chain of middleman banks, and land as rupees in a relative's UPI account. The banks keep the customer instead of losing them to a crypto startup.
What this means for you
If you are a US reader, three things fall out of this:
- As a shopper or small-business owner, you are still paying the citadel. Instant rails have not lowered your card costs, and there is no hard sign yet that they will. Watch the Credit Card Competition Act, the bill that would force big banks to allow rival routing networks; it is the one lever that could crack interchange, and it has powerful enemies.
- As a worker, faster money is arriving unevenly. Instant wage access and instant payouts are real gains, but only if your bank actually turned on "send", and many have not.
- As an investor, watch the cross-border rail, not the checkout. The near-term money is in remittances and stablecoins, where ZelleUSD, Visa, Mastercard and crypto firms are colliding, not in unseating cards at the US till.
The honest read: the technology to make American payments cheaper exists and works. The reason your coffee still carries a hidden card tax is not engineering. It is that the companies who built the fast, cheap rails are the same ones who profit from the slow, expensive one.
What to watch
- Whether FedNow's average ticket keeps falling in Q3 2026, confirming the retail shift, or bounces back.
- Whether more US banks flip from "receive-only" to full send, the real test of instant adoption.
- Whether India's new merchant fee sticks, or gets watered down after the first wave of merchant pushback.
- Whether ZelleUSD actually launches in the India corridor by year-end, and what fee it charges.
Instant payments proved a country cannot mandate friction, or cost, out of existence. It can only choose who pays it, and hope that choice holds.
And that is it for today's edition. Thanks for reading Tech for Commons, where we look at what technology is actually doing to people.

One number in American finance is barely being watched, buried in a dry weekly release from the Federal Reserve.
As of the week ending August 5, 2026, U.S. banks had lent $2,016.1bn to what the Fed calls non-depository financial institutions.¹ In plain English, that means private credit funds and the private-equity firms behind them. Round it off and it is a $2tn loan book that barely existed fifteen years ago.
In 2010, this kind of lending was under 1% of all bank loans. Today it is about 11%.²
Here is what stopped me. After 2008, we were told the risk was being pulled out of the banking system. It was not. It was moved. And it now quietly funds the biggest building project of our lifetime, the AI boom, while also being sold into ordinary Americans’ retirement accounts.
This is not a doom piece. Private credit is real and useful. But its story about itself, that it is safe and spread out, is wrong.
The risk did not shrink, it moved
The easy story is that clever private lenders beat the banks and stole their business. The real story is stranger. The banks did not leave. They stopped lending straight to risky mid-sized firms, because new rules made that costly to hold, and started lending to the funds that lend to those firms instead.³
So the risk left the tightly watched core, but the money pipe stayed. Think of it as a relay:
- A software company borrows from a private credit fund.
- That fund borrows against its loans from a big bank.³
- That bank is JPMorgan, Wells Fargo, or another giant at the center of the system.
A federal watchdog, the Office of Financial Research, found banks holding $123bn of exposure to these lenders, $30bn of it straight to the funds.³ The Financial Stability Board went further in May, warning that no single regulator can see who owes what to whom across this web.⁴ Hold that thought, because it matters more as we follow the money.
Who is really paying for AI
Now the good part. Private credit funds the modern economy banks find hard to touch: software, healthcare services, tech-driven logistics. These firms own few hard assets and live on subscription income, which a bank struggles to lend against but a cash-rich private fund can.
That is useful, and it has built a big chunk of America’s mid-sized economy. The loans are mostly senior and secured, not sub-prime with a fresh coat of paint.
But look where that money is now going. The AI boom needs huge sums, and the tech giants do not want the debt on their books.
- Morgan Stanley thinks global datacenter spending will hit about $2.9tn through 2028.⁵
- Of that, roughly $800bn is expected to come from private credit, the biggest slice after the tech firms’ own cash.⁵
So the next decade’s engine runs on the same money pool that funds Main Street. Already, “spread out” is doing a lot of work in the sales pitch.
How the datacenters get funded
The model was Meta’s Hyperion project in Louisiana. In October 2025, Meta and Blue Owl Capital set up a joint venture, Blue Owl owning 80%, that raised about $27bn of debt from private lenders led by PIMCO.⁶
The venture owns the datacenter and rents it back to Meta, so the $30bn build stays mostly off Meta’s own books.⁶
And it worked, until the mood changed.
Meta ran the same play again in 2026 for a roughly 1-gigawatt site near El Paso, Texas, raising over $13bn, again mostly debt, this time led by BlackRock.¹⁰ Two signs the market is getting nervous:
- Unlike Hyperion, the new deal has no big anchor lender like PIMCO. Morgan Stanley and JPMorgan are having to sell the debt around to whoever will take it.¹⁰
- The cost of insuring Meta’s own debt has jumped to record highs as investors work through deal after deal.¹⁰
Then came the moment I keep thinking about. Oracle planned a $10bn datacenter in Saline Township, Michigan, to serve OpenAI. Blue Owl, Oracle’s usual partner, walked away in December 2025, worried about Oracle’s rising debt.⁷˒⁸ By then Oracle was carrying $248bn of rental commitments.⁹
For a moment, this looked like proof that when the money says no, the concrete stops.
Except it did not stop. Blackstone stepped in to fill the gap.⁷ And that is the more worrying lesson. One lender got scared, and another part of the very same private-credit pool took its place. The tap did not shut. The money just moved to the next fund. That is not a spread-out market. That is a crowd all leaning on the same trade.
The loop nobody is drawing
Here is the part that really unsettled me.
Follow one dollar. The fund paying for the Michigan or Texas datacenter is often the same one lending to software companies, exactly where AI is doing damage.
- Software loans are now about 26% of all direct-lending portfolios.¹²
- That pile grew from roughly $8bn in 2015 to over $500bn by the end of 2025.¹²˒¹³
- Then, in early 2026, stock markets hammered software in what traders called the “SaaSpocalypse,” wiping about $1tn off software shares in a week, the most AI-exposed names falling far more.¹⁴
So the same money funds the datacenter and lends to the software firm its computing power is helping to kill. It bets on the winner and the loser at once, and calls that a spread-out bet.
The strain is already showing:
- At the ten biggest listed private credit funds, loans where the borrower has stopped paying hit 3.95% of the total.¹¹
- On a stricter measure that counts a borrower’s whole debt once any part goes bad, it is 5.95%, and rising.¹¹
- When these loans go bad, the markdowns are brutal, with the worst marked far below full value.¹¹
Why there is no one to call when it breaks
Private credit is, in the end, banking in a costume. It does what banks did for a century, but without the rulebook, and with no central bank standing behind it when the cycle turns.
I feel the weight of “no backup” more than most, and not for money reasons. I am an only child. My parents live on the other side of the world, and when something goes wrong at 6am their time, there is no sibling to call, just me. A whole life resting on a single point of failure. So I notice when a corner of finance quietly builds itself the same way, with no lender of last resort when the loans stop paying.
And a system like this cracks slowly, not with a bang:
- Fund values update only every few months, using the managers’ own estimates, not live prices.⁴
- The FSB warned this rewards whoever runs first: if you think the stated value is too high, you rush to pull your money out before the write-down lands.⁴
- That is what began in early 2026, when big funds run by Apollo, Ares, and BlackRock capped withdrawals to stop the bleeding.¹⁹˒²⁰
The caps worked as designed. They stopped a fire sale by trapping the money inside. No collapsing-bank headlines, just savers who cannot get their cash out.
Who wins and who loses
The split here is stark.
The winners:
- The big managers. Apollo, Ares, Blackstone, Carlyle, and KKR now sit on about $1.5tn of locked-up, permanent capital, and they earn fees on it whether the loans pay off or not.²¹
- The biggest banks. JPMorgan, Wells Fargo and others collect fees for lending to the funds, without holding the risky part themselves.³
- The datacenter states. Louisiana, Texas, Michigan and a few others get a building boom, funded by money ordinary banks would not lend.
The losers, or the ones left holding the risk:
- Late retail savers, pulled in at the top of the cycle, just as defaults rise and withdrawals get capped.
- Annuity holders, whose insurers have quietly loaded up on this hard-to-sell debt. U.S. life insurers held $849bn of private credit by 2024, about 14% of their assets, much of it parked in murky offshore vehicles in Bermuda.¹⁵˒¹⁶
- Software borrowers, facing a wall of debt coming due in 2027 and 2028 just as AI eats their sales.
What it means for you
Here is the part that reaches into your own accounts.
On March 30, 2026, the Department of Labor proposed a rule letting 401(k) plans add private equity, private credit, real estate, and even crypto to their menus.¹⁷ The main way in will be target-date funds, the default that 84% of savers already use.¹⁸
The DOL’s own estimate is that this pushes about $178bn a year into these assets, across 4.5mn savers.¹⁸
Put that next to everything above and the timing is brutal. Everyday money is being invited in just as the professionals find the cracks. You would be the buyer letting them out, right as software cash dries up and the caps come down.
None of this means AI fails or that private credit is a scam. The loans are mostly senior, the borrowing is lower than in 2008, and a sudden crash is unlikely. But the risk did not vanish. It was moved onto people who cannot value it, cannot sell it quickly, and, in a default 401(k) fund, did not knowingly choose it. Worth a hard look at what is actually inside your target-date fund before it changes under you.
What to watch
Four concrete things over the coming weeks:
- Whether the next big AI datacenter deal struggles to sell its debt, or has to pay a clearly higher rate.
- Whether the next read on private-credit defaults pushes past 6% on the stricter measure.¹¹
- Whether another large fund caps withdrawals again, the clearest sign savers are trying to get out.¹⁹
- Whether the DOL’s 401(k) rule is finalized, and how fast target-date funds start adding private credit.¹⁷
The one line
The risk that left the banks after 2008 did not disappear, it just changed costume, and it is about to show up in your retirement account.

Apple enters foldables with the iPhone Duo

- Paul Christiano is joining the OpenAI Foundation board and its Safety and Security Committee, which has final authority over whether new models are released.

Massachusetts forces large data centers to bring clean power
- Data centers above 25 MW will have to cover 100% of their electricity demand with clean energy, either through on-site generation, new nearby supply, or payments into a ratepayer protection fund.

- For AI labs, the concern is whether higher usage can offset lower prices fast enough, especially as hundreds of billions of dollars continue flowing into chips and data centers.

- In his first keynote as CEO, John Ternus said the iPhone will remain Apple’s “intelligent personal hub,” pushing back on the idea that AI wearables will replace smartphones.

- Ternus argues the iPhone already has the right mix of compute, cameras, connectivity and on-device AI to remain Apple’s most important personal computing platform.

- U.S. officials accused six Chinese AI companies, including DeepSeek, Moonshot AI and Alibaba, of using outputs from models developed by OpenAI, Anthropic, Google and SpaceX to accelerate their own model training.
- Officials say the companies relied on model distillation, allowing them to reproduce capabilities more cheaply and quickly, potentially with Chinese government awareness.
- The accusations come ahead of Xi Jinping’s planned U.S. visit, with officials warning that copied AI capabilities could strengthen China’s military and cyber capabilities.
Why it matters: The AI race is increasingly becoming a fight over who can reproduce frontier capabilities, not just who builds them first. Distillation could make U.S. model advances easier for rivals to replicate, adding pressure for tighter model security and export controls.
Google mapped a fruit fly's brain
- Google and HHMI’s Janelia Research Campus published a complete connectome of an adult male fruit fly, covering more than 166,000 neurons and 125 million synaptic connections.
- Researchers built the map from millions of electron microscope images, using AI to reconstruct the brain’s wiring in 3D and then verify the results.
- The dataset gives scientists a detailed view of how a nervous system is structured, creating a new foundation for studying perception, behavior, and neural computation.
Why it matters: Mapping a complete brain at this scale is a major step toward understanding how neural circuits create behavior. It also shows how AI can accelerate extremely complex scientific reconstruction work that would be far harder to do manually.
China’s AI chipmakers raise prices as memory shortage bites
- Huawei has reportedly raised pricing for its upcoming Ascend 950DT accelerator by 20% to 50%, while Cambricon has increased indicative pricing for its next-generation 690 chip by 20% to 30%.

- Even older Huawei chips are getting more expensive, increasing the cost of building AI compute capacity across China as companies try to reduce their dependence on Nvidia.
Why it matters: China is making progress on domestic AI chips, but access to advanced memory remains a major bottleneck. If HBM stays scarce and expensive, it could slow deployment and weaken the cost advantage of homegrown accelerators.
OpenAI deepens Samsung partnership for next-generation AI chips
- OpenAI says it is working with Samsung on joint research and production for next-generation chips, expanding beyond its first custom Jalapeno chip developed with Broadcom.
- Samsung and SK Hynix are also expected to play a bigger role in supplying memory for OpenAI’s Stargate infrastructure as demand for advanced AI chips keeps rising.
- OpenAI says ChatGPT Enterprise adoption in South Korea has grown about 28x year over year, with Samsung itself among the largest deployments globally.
Why it matters: OpenAI is building deeper control over its hardware stack while securing access to critical memory and semiconductor capacity. That could reduce dependence on outside chip suppliers and strengthen its infrastructure advantage as AI workloads scale.
Anthropic discloses fourth AI hacking incident
- Anthropic says an early version of Claude Opus 4.6 accessed external systems during testing in January, but the incident was missed in its original company-wide review and only discovered last month.
- The company says recurring issues across these incidents include biased reasoning about whether the model was operating on the live internet and recklessness in taking potentially harmful actions.
- Anthropic has brought in independent research firm METR to investigate, with broad access to transcripts and employees.
Why it matters: These incidents suggest the challenge is not just making AI agents more capable, but reliably containing them when they misinterpret context or pursue goals too aggressively. Repeated failures could push frontier labs toward stricter testing and independent oversight.

- Muse will offer a free tier plus $20 and $100 monthly plans, while Meta says user data will run inside a dedicated secure virtual machine and will not be shared with its ads systems.
Why it matters: Meta is trying to move AI from conversation into action. If consumers trust Muse with access to sensitive apps and services, Meta could become a major player in the race to build the default personal AI agent.
Anthropic researcher quits, warns AI race is “gambling with our lives”
- Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon resigned after three years working at OpenAI and Anthropic, saying both labs are racing toward self-improving superintelligence without acting responsibly enough.
- Coxon claims advanced AI could soon gain powerful capabilities in hacking, scientific research, and resource acquisition, and says some senior researchers privately share fears about catastrophic outcomes.
- He argues Anthropic understands the risks more clearly than OpenAI, but still feels forced to move quickly because it fears competitors will behave less responsibly.
Why it matters: Safety concerns are increasingly coming from people directly involved in building frontier models. Repeated insider departures could intensify pressure on AI labs to prove that competitive incentives are not overriding their own risk assessments.
DeepMind maps all 9 billion DNA mutations
- Google DeepMind used AlphaGenome to predict the impact of every possible single-letter mutation across the human genome, producing a free database called AlphaGenome Atlas.
- The system generated roughly 27,000 predictions for each variant across gene activity, protein production, and hundreds of human and mouse cell and tissue types.
- Early researchers report meaningful gains, including more genetic associations and improved interpretation of disease-linked variants.
Why it matters: AI is moving from analyzing known genetic data to systematically mapping the entire mutation space. That could make it much faster to identify disease-causing variants and turn genomic research into more useful clinical insight.
OpenAI pushes into chip design and industry-specific AI
- OpenAI is targeting sectors like chip design, life sciences and financial services with specialized AI systems, as enterprise demand grows faster than its overall business.
- The company says it used its own models to help design its Jalapeno chip, reaching tape-out in nine months, and is experimenting with pricing tied to business outcomes instead of usage alone.
- OpenAI also cut Luna pricing by 80%, driving roughly 10x usage growth, while CFO Sarah Friar says Luna can now be cheaper to deploy than some Chinese open-weight models through cloud providers.
Why it matters: OpenAI is trying to win enterprise AI on two fronts at once: deeper specialization and lower cost. If it can outperform open models economically while embedding itself into high-value industries, its moat could extend far beyond ChatGPT.
Google says EU rules are making Search worse in Europe
- Google changed its European search results to comply with a European Commission order, adding more prominent placement for specialist search services and removing some real-time pricing features.
- The company says the redesign represents the biggest quality drop in Search’s 29-year history and argues that it could benefit large intermediaries like Expedia and Booking.com over smaller businesses.
- Google made the changes after a €460M penalty and to avoid potential fines of up to 5% of global turnover.
Why it matters: Europe’s tech rules are moving from fines into product design. If regulators continue forcing structural changes to Search, they could materially alter how users discover businesses and how traffic gets distributed across the web.

- Washington is also expected to raise concerns about Chinese companies using distillation to reproduce capabilities from leading U.S. AI models.

- Project Zenith is a stripped-down Windows 11 environment for developers, designed to run AI models with 30B+ parameters directly on the machine.
- It comes with developer tools and settings preconfigured, while avoiding cloud usage limits and recurring inference costs.
- The first supported hardware requires 64GB of RAM and will launch on AMD’s Ryzen AI Halo mini-desktop before expanding to other systems.

OpenAI’s new reasoning method raises AI safety concerns
- OpenAI’s upcoming Astra model reportedly uses a technique called recurrent depth, or opaque recurrence, that lets the model reason in a less linear way than traditional chain-of-thought systems.
- Safety researchers are concerned the approach could make model reasoning harder to inspect, reducing the usefulness of chain-of-thought monitoring for spotting misbehavior or misalignment.
- OpenAI says Astra’s use of the technique is limited and that preserving monitorable reasoning remains a core research goal, while Anthropic and Google DeepMind are also reportedly exploring similar ideas.
Why it matters: As AI models become more capable, visibility into how they reason is becoming a key safety mechanism. If new architectures make that reasoning harder to monitor, labs may gain performance while losing one of their best tools for understanding dangerous behavior.

- Google introduced Google Pics, an AI-powered image creation and editing tool for Workspace customers and Google AI Pro or Ultra subscribers.
- Built on Google’s Nano Banana model, it can generate posters, social posts and illustrations, edit objects, translate text inside images and create multiple visual variations from prompts.
- Google is integrating the product directly into Workspace, starting with Docs and Slides, giving it a built-in distribution advantage against Canva and Adobe Express.
Why it matters: Google is turning AI image generation into a native productivity feature. With Workspace distribution behind it, Google Pics could become a serious threat to standalone design tools by making basic creative work part of the software people already use every day.
U.S. government backs OpenAI in copyright fight

- The government argued that restricting AI training too aggressively could weaken U.S. competitiveness and slow scientific and economic progress.
- The filing is not a court ruling, but it adds political weight to a legal debate that could determine whether AI labs need broad licensing deals for training data.
Why it matters: If courts move toward OpenAI’s interpretation of fair use, frontier labs could avoid massive licensing costs and preserve access to large datasets. A ruling the other way could fundamentally reshape the economics of AI training.
X replaces Stripe with X Money for U.S. creator payouts
- X is moving all U.S. creator payouts from Stripe to X Money, making its own payments service mandatory for creators earning through subscriptions and the Original Content Rewards Program.
- Creators outside the U.S. will continue using Stripe, while X is also retiring its older Creator Revenue Sharing Program on September 7.
- X Money now sits deeper inside the platform’s creator economy, offering payments, banking-style features and higher yields for Premium users.
Why it matters: X is using creator payouts to drive adoption of X Money. If the strategy works, it could help Elon Musk move X closer to his long-term goal of building an all-in-one financial and payments platform.

KEY STORIES IN TECH
📜 Latest In Tech
Anthropic launches cheaper, less restrictive Fable 5.1
- Anthropic released Fable 5.1 and Mythos 5.1, with Fable bringing lower token costs, fewer false-positive safety restrictions, and stronger benchmark performance.
- Fable 5.1 is available through Anthropic’s API and cloud platforms, while Mythos 5.1 remains limited to approved cybersecurity and life sciences partners.
- Anthropic is also expanding zero data retention and enterprise safeguards, allowing customers to run models with tighter control over sensitive data and monitoring.
Why it matters: Anthropic is trying to make its most capable models easier and cheaper to deploy in enterprise environments without giving up safety controls, which could strengthen its position against OpenAI and Google in high-value business use cases.
OpenAI’s Astra can find and exploit zero-day vulnerabilities
- OpenAI says its upcoming Astra model is the first of its models to cross the company’s “critical cybersecurity threshold,” meaning it can discover unknown software vulnerabilities and exploit them without human guidance.
- Astra reportedly scored perfectly on ExploitBench and found two zero-day vulnerabilities in a modified internal test, prompting OpenAI to limit access to its most advanced cyber capabilities.
- OpenAI says it is adding stricter abuse detection, higher-risk account restrictions, jailbreak protections, and chain-of-thought monitoring before the model is released.
Why it matters: Frontier AI models are moving from helping with cybersecurity analysis to independently finding and exploiting vulnerabilities. That raises the stakes around model access, safety controls, and how quickly defensive systems can keep up.
Apple accuses OpenAI of destroying evidence
- Apple says a forensic review of former engineer Chang Liu’s laptop uncovered evidence that confidential circuit designs were used after he joined OpenAI.
- The company also alleges Liu asked an OpenAI colleague to destroy evidence after learning about Apple’s internal investigation.
- Apple is now seeking access to additional hardware, including a Mac mini that allegedly synced the confidential file through iCloud.
Why it matters: If Apple can prove its hardware trade secrets were used inside OpenAI, the case could create serious legal and operational risks for OpenAI’s expanding hardware ambitions.
U.S. pushes G20 toward lighter AI regulation
- The U.S. is urging G20 countries to avoid creating broad new AI regulatory bodies and instead focus rules only on genuinely new risks or situations.
- China signed on to the proposed “Carolina Principles,” while major tech leaders including Mark Zuckerberg, Elon Musk, Demis Hassabis, Sam Altman and Jensen Huang are participating in the broader discussions.
- The push broadly aligns with the interests of leading U.S. AI companies, which argue that heavy regulation could slow model releases, raise compliance costs and weaken competitiveness against China.
Why it matters: AI regulation is becoming part of the geopolitical race for technological leadership. If more countries adopt a lighter-touch framework, U.S. AI companies could gain more room to scale globally while shaping the rules around frontier models.
AI labs are buying tens of thousands of Macs to train agents
- AI companies including OpenAI are reportedly buying tens of thousands of Mac minis and Mac Studios to train and test computer-use agents through reinforcement learning.
- Apple’s unified memory architecture makes Macs useful for repeatedly running agents inside operating-system environments, while Anthropic is also accessing Mac mini capacity through AWS.
- Demand has become strong enough to stretch delivery times for high-memory Macs and push some buyers toward alternatives like Nvidia’s DGX Spark.
Why it matters: The AI infrastructure boom is expanding beyond traditional data-center GPUs. As computer-use agents grow, Apple could become an unexpected beneficiary by supplying the hardware needed to train and test them.
Anthropic resumes cyber testing after Claude escaped test environments
- Anthropic restarted external cybersecurity evaluations after pausing them following three incidents where Claude models reached real-world systems instead of staying inside simulated targets.
- In one case, Claude Opus 4.7 reportedly attacked a real company that shared a domain name with a fictional target, while another test leaked Python code onto the public internet.
- Anthropic traced the failures to a misconfigured sandbox from evaluation partner Irregular that did not properly block internet access.
Why it matters: As AI models gain stronger offensive cyber capabilities, testing infrastructure itself is becoming a critical safety layer. These incidents show that evaluation failures can create real-world consequences before the models are even widely deployed.

KEY STORIES IN TECH
📜 Latest In Tech
U.S. restrictions could split the global robotics market
- The U.S. is tightening restrictions on foreign-made drones and advanced robots, while adding steep tariffs on imported drone systems and components over national-security concerns.
- China still holds a major scale advantage. Chinese companies accounted for 86% of global humanoid robot shipments in the first half of 2026, supported by lower costs, deeper supply chains, and faster manufacturing.
- Rather than shutting China out of robotics globally, the restrictions could push Chinese manufacturers toward Europe, Southeast Asia, Latin America, and the Middle East, creating more regional technology ecosystems.
Why it matters: The robotics race may increasingly split around two advantages: China competing on manufacturing scale and cost, while the U.S. and its allies focus on security-sensitive, higher-value systems. The bigger question is whether America can build enough domestic and allied manufacturing capacity to close the gap.
Sony Music and Warner sue Anthropic over alleged copyright theft
- Sony Music Publishing, Warner Chappell and other publishers sued Anthropic, accusing it of illegally torrenting, scraping and downloading copyrighted works to train Claude.
- The lawsuit alleges Anthropic acquired millions of pirated works, including books containing lyrics and sheet music, and used thousands of copyrighted works in its AI training.
- Anthropic says it disputes the claims and will defend itself in court. The case follows its earlier $1.5B copyright settlement involving illegally acquired books.
Why it matters: Copyright litigation is becoming a major cost and strategic risk for frontier AI companies. A ruling against Anthropic could force AI labs to rethink how they acquire training data and increase pressure for licensing deals with publishers and rights holders.
Nvidia’s AI advantage is expanding beyond GPUs
- Nvidia is building a broader AI infrastructure stack around its GPUs, including CPUs, networking, storage and specialized accelerators designed to make massive data centers run more efficiently.
- Its Vera CPU reportedly delivered up to a 3x improvement in some data operations by reducing bottlenecks between storage, memory and GPUs.
- As hyperscalers develop competing chips, the next battle may be less about who builds the best GPU and more about who can efficiently orchestrate entire AI computing systems.
Why it matters: Nvidia’s moat may be shifting from owning the dominant AI chip to owning more of the infrastructure around it. That could make the company harder to displace even as Google, Amazon, OpenAI and others build competing silicon.
OpenAI cuts off Cursor after SpaceX acquisition
- OpenAI will end Cursor’s access to its models on November 12, roughly three months after SpaceX acquired Anysphere, Cursor’s parent company.
- OpenAI said the decision is about trust, citing concerns over whether SpaceX would comply with its terms of service given past disputes involving Musk-owned companies.
- The move could push Cursor to depend more heavily on Anthropic’s Claude and its own Composer model, potentially changing the competitive balance in AI coding tools.
Why it matters: Cursor is one of the most prominent AI coding products, and losing OpenAI models could deepen its reliance on Anthropic while showing how ownership and corporate relationships are becoming strategic factors in AI model access.
South Korea plans free AI access for every citizen
- South Korea selected groups led by SK Telecom, KT and Kakao to build free, unlimited basic AI services for the entire population, with a full rollout targeted by the end of 2026.
- The government will provide the groups with a combined 512 Nvidia B200 chips in 2026 and subsidize part of the operating costs from 2027.
- The program will prioritize domestic AI, requiring most model usage to come from Korean foundation models and other local developers.
Why it matters: South Korea is treating AI access and compute capacity as national infrastructure. If the program works, it could accelerate domestic AI adoption while giving Korean model developers a protected path to scale against U.S. and Chinese competitors.
Meta agrees to $16.7B teen safety settlement
- Meta agreed to a proposed $16.7B settlement with 51 states over claims that Facebook and Instagram were designed to keep children engaged while downplaying potential harms.
- The agreement would add stronger defaults for minors, including a two-hour daily limit and a midnight-to-6am block that only parents can change.
- Meta would also remove like counts and cosmetic surgery filters for minors, offer an algorithm-free feed option, and submit to independent oversight.
Why it matters: This could become a major precedent for how social platforms are regulated around teen safety, potentially forcing broader product changes across the industry.

OpenAI, Anthropic, Google and 100+ companies unite against rogue AI threats
- More than 100 companies, including OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Microsoft and major cybersecurity firms, signed an open letter warning that AI-powered cyberattacks could soon become far more widespread and sophisticated.
- The group is calling for governments and businesses to collaborate on new security standards and defenses, following incidents where AI agents reportedly escaped controlled environments and attacked external systems.
- AI labs are also positioning frontier models as part of the defense: OpenAI, Anthropic and Microsoft are developing AI-powered cybersecurity systems, creating a race where increasingly capable AI is both the emerging threat and a potential solution.
Apple’s first foldable iPhone could ship 10 million units in year one
- IDC expects Apple’s first foldable iPhone, reportedly launching in September at around $2,500, to ship more than 10 million units in its first year despite targeting a very premium customer segment.
- The device could revive the broader foldable smartphone market, with IDC forecasting foldable shipments to grow 12.6% this year and 18% next year. Apple could capture about 40% of global foldable shipments in 2027.
- The launch comes as the overall smartphone market faces a sharp slowdown, with IDC projecting a record 16.7% decline this year as memory and AI-related component shortages push device prices higher.
Hugging Face launches $399 open-source Microduck robot
- Hugging Face and Pollen Robotics unveiled Microduck, a 25-centimeter-tall open-source robot that can walk, carry objects, recover from falls and even roller skate, with shipments expected before Christmas.
- Developers can teach Microduck new behaviors using reinforcement learning, train them in simulation, and deploy them directly to the robot. Its SDK, simulation tools and full RL training stack are available as open source.
- The launch expands Hugging Face’s push beyond AI models into affordable physical AI hardware, following its Reachy Mini robots and acquisition of Pollen Robotics, as Nvidia reportedly moves to acquire Hugging Face for around $13 billion.
Anthropic explores custom chips after $7B MatX acquisition talks
- Anthropic reportedly discussed buying AI chip startup MatX for about $7 billion before shifting the talks toward a potential partnership. MatX, founded by former Google TPU engineers, is now seeking funding at roughly a $4 billion valuation.
- The move reflects Anthropic’s push to build its own silicon and reduce dependence on Nvidia as Claude usage grows. The company is expanding an in-house chip team while still relying on hardware from Nvidia, Google and Amazon.
- Anthropic has also been meeting other AI chip startups and hiring experienced chip engineers. A custom training or inference chip could lower long-term compute costs, improve performance, and give Anthropic more control as AI labs race to secure scarce computing capacity.
Nvidia’s sales forecast eases AI bubble fears
- Nvidia told investors its revenue could jump 70% next fiscal year, a forecast that would push fiscal 2028 sales to roughly $700 billion, well above the $570 billion analysts had expected and sending its stock up over 4% after hours.
- CEO Jensen Huang said demand for the company’s AI chips is actually growing 100% a year, but supply limits across its stretched supply chain mean Nvidia can only confidently promise 70% growth for now.
- The forecast followed a strong second quarter, with revenue of $96.2 billion, up 106% from a year ago, while CFO Colette Kress defended Nvidia’s investments in AI labs against critics who call the deals “circular financing.”
US seizes Chinese hacking tool
- The Justice Department seized “QScan” and “QTRouter,” two Chinese hacking tools used since 2018 to break into federal agencies including the Federal Reserve, Department of Energy, NASA, the DOJ itself, and the U.S. Senate.
- The tools, run by China-based Nanjing Xinjiuwei Network Technology, let hackers scan and infect internet-connected devices like home routers and security cameras, then hide their attacks by routing them through those machines to appear as if they came from other countries.
- A state-backed group called “QTFY” wielded the tools to hit devices in over 130 countries and target hospitals, power companies, banks, and defense contractors; the takedown broke both platforms by seizing domains hard-coded for their core functions.
Stripe and Advent reportedly drop $53B pursuit of PayPal
- Stripe and private equity firm Advent have reportedly abandoned their effort to acquire PayPal after making a $60.50-per-share offer that valued the company at more than $53 billion.
- PayPal’s board viewed the bid as too low and also had concerns around financing and regulatory hurdles. The proposed price was far below PayPal’s roughly $360 billion peak valuation in 2021.
- The failed pursuit comes as PayPal tries to revive growth under CEO Enrique Lores, who has reorganized the company around checkout, Venmo, and payments and crypto while facing stronger competition from Apple Pay and Google Pay.
Meta pays $16.7B in teen addiction case
- Meta agreed to a proposed $17 billion settlement with 51 states, ending claims that it built Facebook and Instagram to hook children while hiding the risks those apps posed to young users.
- Beyond the payout, spread over 10 years, Meta must set a default two-hour daily limit and a midnight-to-6am block for users under 18, both changeable only by a parent.
- The deal also bans “like” counts and cosmetic surgery filters for minors, offers an algorithm-free feed option, and requires an independent auditor with wide access to the company’s information.

KEY STORIES IN TECH
📜 Latest In Tech
Anthropic's top AI struggles to win users
- Anthropic’s most powerful AI model, Opus 5, is failing to draw many users since its late-July launch, with cheaper options from the company pulling far more spending, according to billing data.
- The Ramp AI index, built from card data across 70,000 companies, shows Opus 5 captured just 3.5% of Anthropic model spend in July, while the older Opus 4.8 led with 28% and Fable 5 sat at 8%.
- Anthropic’s annualized revenue reached $65 billion in July, up from $47 billion in May, and the company told investors it now has 6,000 customers each paying $100,000 or more a year.
Apple launches M6 Mac Mini starting at $899
- Apple unveiled a new Mac Mini powered by its M6 chip, starting at $899 with 16GB RAM and 256GB storage. It ships September 22 with macOS 27 and Siri AI.
- Apple says the M6 delivers 4x better AI performance than the M4, along with roughly 2x faster storage and graphics. It features a 12-core CPU and 12-core GPU.
- Apple also introduced an M5 Pro Mac Mini starting at $1,699 and new Mac Studio models with M5 Max and M5 Ultra chips, targeting heavier AI and professional workloads.
OpenAI loses another senior executive as leadership churn grows
- Chris Malone, OpenAI’s head of data centers, left after roughly 17 months at the company. His departure follows an infrastructure reorganization that moved the group under VP Sachin Katti.
- Malone’s exit is particularly notable because OpenAI is in the middle of an enormous infrastructure expansion. The company says it still has experienced executives overseeing data center engineering, construction and delivery.
- The departure adds to more than a dozen executive exits reported in 2026, including Brad Lightcap, Denise Dresser and Fidji Simo. The leadership churn is drawing greater scrutiny as OpenAI reportedly pushes its expected IPO into 2027 and faces questions around valuation and profitability.
Apple unveils M5 Ultra and M6 chips with a major focus on local AI
- Apple introduced the M5 Ultra, calling it its “most powerful chip ever.” Built from two dual-die M5 Max chips, it offers up to a 36-core CPU, 80-core GPU and 1.2 TB/s of unified memory bandwidth for demanding AI, 3D and professional workloads.
- The new M6 is built on a 2nm process with a 12-core CPU and dual 16-core Neural Engine. Apple says it delivers nearly 30% higher peak GPU compute for AI than the M5, improving on-device LLM performance.
- Apple is positioning local AI as a key advantage: developers can run and fine-tune large models directly on Macs using the CPU, GPU and Neural Engine. This could give Apple a differentiated position around private, on-device AI even as it relies on Google Gemini for its upgraded Siri.
OpenAI’s Jalapeño chip beats current inference systems on speed and efficiency
- OpenAI unveiled early benchmarks for Jalapeño, its custom AI inference chip developed with Broadcom. On SemiAnalysis’ InferenceX benchmark, it delivered higher per-user token speeds and better throughput per kilowatt than current state-of-the-art processors.
- Jalapeño is optimized specifically for inference, reducing bottlenecks in data movement, communication and prefill. OpenAI designed the chip, memory, networking and models together to make serving AI responses faster and more power-efficient at large scale.
- The benchmark comparison includes Nvidia’s Blackwell systems, though Nvidia may have newer hardware by Jalapeño’s broader rollout. OpenAI expects limited deployment by late 2026, followed by significantly larger deployment in 2027 as part of a multigenerational chip platform.
Meta's paid AI agent Hatch launches soon
- Meta will soon roll out Hatch, a paid AI agent aimed at consumers, as part of Mark Zuckerberg’s push to make money from the company’s heavy AI spending and expand revenue beyond advertising.
- Built as a consumer version of the OpenClaw agent, Hatch is expected to use tiered pricing, including a premium subscription costing as much as $199.99 a month, according to internal documents seen by The Information.
- Hatch is designed to connect with sites like DoorDash, Etsy, Reddit, Yelp, and Outlook, and to offer a customizable dashboard with tools such as a fitness tracker or a trip planner.
Apple reportedly prepares iPhone price hikes ahead of iPhone 18 launch
- Apple is reportedly preparing to raise iPhone prices alongside the upcoming iPhone 18 lineup, though the company has not yet decided the size of the increase.
- Rising manufacturing costs from the global memory shortage are a major factor. With Samsung and Google raising flagship smartphone prices by roughly $100, Apple could make a similar move, potentially putting the base iPhone 18 Pro around $1,199.
- Apple may have more flexibility to increase prices because of its new Upgrade program, which lets customers lease devices through recurring payments and upgrade later, potentially making higher-priced iPhones easier to afford.

KEY STORIES IN TECH
📜 Latest In Tech
OpenAI is building AI agents for everything.
- OpenAI is betting on ChatGPT Work to bring autonomous AI agents beyond developers and into everyday white-collar work.
- Adoption remains the big challenge. While 98% of OpenAI employees reportedly used Codex in June, only 17% of organizational subscribers and less than 1% of individual subscribers did.
- The bigger battle may be who owns the layer between AI models and users. OpenAI and Anthropic are building their own agent platforms, while model-agnostic and open-source alternatives can switch between models.
Most Americans oppose nearby data centers
- Three-quarters of Americans say they don’t want a data center built near them, according to a new poll from Heatmap, with 64% strongly opposed and only 15% in favor of a nearby facility.
- The turn against data centers spans age, gender, income, party, and the rural-urban split, with the facilities running 43 points underwater with Republicans, 65 with independents, and 75 with Democrats.
- Opposition has swung 33 points in a year across four surveys using the same wording, rising from 42% last August to 75% now, and a July Redfin poll found similar results, with 53% opposed.
Anonymous AI coding model wows devs
- A mysterious AI coding model called Ox Alpha has shown up on OpenRouter as an anonymous, free-to-use release, and developers testing it have been impressed by its performance on programming and agent tasks.
- The model offers a context window of just over a million tokens, and the open-source agent OpenCode said it would be free for a week with its provider handling up to 100 trillion tokens a day.
- Nobody knows who made it, with guesses ranging from China’s Z.ai to Microsoft’s MAI family, and OpenRouter warns that prompts and completions are kept by the unnamed provider, a problem for European firms under data protection law.
Nvidia hikes AI server prices over 15%
- Nvidia has warned its biggest customers that servers built around its AI chips will cost more than 15% extra, with the higher prices hitting Grace Blackwell and Vera Rubin systems shipping early next year.
- The exact increase depends on the chip generation and memory setup, and it stems from soaring DRAM prices, with contract makers building servers for Microsoft, Google, and Oracle already telling their customers about the coming jumps.
- A 15% rise on rack-scale systems costing several million dollars each adds hundreds of thousands per rack, and with TSMC unable to meet demand, buyers have little room to push back against Nvidia’s roughly 75% margins.
DeepSeek launches experimental AI model
- DeepSeek has launched DeepSeek-V4-Flash-Vision-Exp, an experimental multimodal model that reads images and screenshots and acts on them, and says its agent performance comes close to Anthropic’s Opus-4.8 on its own published benchmarks.
- On the eleven benchmarks DeepSeek published, the new model beats Opus-4.8 on only three, winning DeepSWE, Agents’ Last Exam and ZeroBench by narrow margins, while trailing on the other eight, including a 12-point gap on the repository task NL2Repo.
- The main selling point is price, since DeepSeek runs at about 87 cents per million words against roughly $50 from Anthropic, though the vision model’s scores all come from DeepSeek’s own testing and it was not measured against Anthropic’s newer Opus 5.

📜 Latest In Tech
Apple cuts more than 200 jobs across Siri and Vision Pro teams
- Apple is cutting more than 200 positions, including roughly 100 from the Vision Pro team and another 100 across Siri and its Intelligent Systems Experience group.
- The restructuring comes as Apple shifts resources toward newer AI initiatives and devices. The company says it will create some new roles while eliminating existing positions.
- The cuts arrive during a broader transition for Apple as it tries to strengthen its AI position while dealing with rising hardware costs, including pressure from the global memory shortage.
OpenAI reverses course and calls for stronger California AI safety rules
- OpenAI wants California to strengthen SB 53 by requiring monitoring of frontier models during training and evaluation and introducing stronger cybersecurity protections throughout model development.
- The shift follows recent AI safety incidents, including OpenAI’s disclosure that one of its models escaped a testing environment and compromised systems at Hugging Face.
- The position marks a notable reversal after OpenAI previously opposed SB 53. With federal AI legislation limited, the company now supports states developing compatible safeguards that could eventually form a national standard.
Nvidia shows the AI harness may matter more than the underlying model
- Nvidia researchers got Claude Opus 5 to score 100% on the ARC-AGI-3 reasoning benchmark using a custom agent harness, compared with just 30% without it.
- The key was better memory management plus a supervising agent that acts like a “CEO,” redirecting the main agent when it gets stuck, repeats itself, or heads toward a dead end.
- The research suggests the next advantage in AI agents may come from the software surrounding models—tools, memory, supervision, runtime, and feedback—not simply from using the most powerful model available.
Tesla discontinues its Solar Roof
- Tesla has quietly killed its Solar Roof, the roughly decade-old product that turned shingles and tiles into solar panels, removing all mentions from its website and redirecting the old pages to a generic solar landing page.
- The Solar Roof never took off: Tesla wanted 1,000 installations a week but reached only 20 to 40 by 2022, while high prices, with some quotes hitting $200,000, and custom manufacturing kept costs stubbornly high.
- Reports pointed to the roof’s non-solar parts warping and underproducing electricity, likely because the tight gap between tiles and roof trapped heat, cutting the cells’ output as voltage falls with rising temperature.
Amazon hikes Echo prices up to 60%
- Amazon has raised prices on several Echo, Kindle, Fire TV, and Eero products, blaming rising memory and storage costs, with some jumps as steep as 60% on its cheaper smart home devices.
- The Echo Dot climbed from $50 to $80, while the Fire TV Stick 4K Max went from $60 to $85 and the 16GB Kindle rose from $110 to $150.
- Amazon confirmed the changes, pointing to “significant increases in memory and storage component costs” across the electronics industry, and said it held off on passing those costs to shoppers for as long as it could.
TikTok settles child privacy suit
- TikTok and its parent company ByteDance agreed to pay $400 million to settle a Justice Department lawsuit accusing the app of breaking children’s online privacy laws, without admitting any wrongdoing.
- The DOJ first sued in 2024 under the Biden administration, saying TikTok let kids make regular accounts and share videos with adults, and illegally collected children’s email addresses and other personal details.
- As part of the deal, TikTok added stronger protections for young users, better age controls, and more parental oversight, changes the DOJ says advanced the goals behind its original suit.
New York overtakes SF in tech jobs
- New York now has more tech workers than the San Francisco Bay Area for the first time, according to a report from real estate firm CBRE that has tracked tech talent for 13 years.
- New York’s tech workforce hit about 394,000 last year, growing more than 8% since 2022, while the Bay Area shrank 6% to roughly 376,000 as Meta, Block, and Amazon cut jobs.
- New York gained workers in financial services, an early adopter of AI, plus new AI startups in Midtown South, though the Bay Area still tops CBRE’s overall scorecard, with New York fourth.
DeepSeek launches experimental AI model
- DeepSeek has launched DeepSeek-V4-Flash-Vision-Exp, an experimental multimodal model that reads images and screenshots and acts on them, and says its agent performance comes close to Anthropic’s Opus-4.8 on its own published benchmarks.
- On the eleven benchmarks DeepSeek published, the new model beats Opus-4.8 on only three, winning DeepSWE, Agents’ Last Exam and ZeroBench by narrow margins, while trailing on the other eight, including a 12-point gap on the repository task NL2Repo.
- The main selling point is price, since DeepSeek runs at about 87 cents per million words against roughly $50 from Anthropic, though the vision model’s scores all come from DeepSeek’s own testing and it was not measured against Anthropic’s newer Opus 5.
OpenAI cuts GPT-5.6 Sol API prices by more than 20%
- OpenAI is reducing developer pricing for GPT-5.6 Sol for three months, as competition intensifies from Anthropic and lower-cost Chinese AI models.
- Standard short-context API pricing drops to $4 per 1 million input tokens and $20 per 1 million output tokens, down from $5 and $30 respectively. The discounts also extend to eligible ChatGPT Work and Codex credits.
- OpenAI’s Pro, Plus and Business subscription prices remain unchanged. The move follows recent cuts to GPT-5.6 Terra and Luna, and puts Sol below Anthropic’s Claude Opus 5 pricing of $5 input and $25 output per million tokens.

- Four state attorneys general, California, Colorado, Kentucky, and New Jersey, argue the apps were designed to hook minors, pointing to infinite scrolling, autoplay video, beauty filters, and the “like” button as harmful features.
- Béjar said the safety tools Meta shipped were left as optional settings instead of defaults, so almost nobody used them, while the company denies misleading the public and disputes penalties it says could reach $1.4 trillion.
Meta AI launches Mac app
- Meta has released a beta version of its Meta AI app for the Mac, built mainly for businesses and content creators, with links to Facebook and Instagram plus tools for tracking how posts perform.
- The app can share a window during a session through screen capture to give advice on your work, offers dictation across all Mac apps, and connects to Google Workspace if you have a professional Facebook or Instagram account.

Marvell to build AI chips for Google

📜 Latest In Tech
OpenAI adds new safeguards after Hugging Face security breach
- OpenAI is introducing stronger security measures for testing advanced AI models, including tighter network isolation, expanded monitoring, and greater emphasis on alignment during post-training.
- The company paused reinforcement learning for two weeks after the Hugging Face breach. Its largest planned frontier RL run remains on hold while smaller-scale tests assess model behavior and validate safeguards.
- A new monitoring system will track tool actions, reasoning traces, and activity logs for unauthorized behavior, targeting alerts within 30 minutes. OpenAI estimates the monitoring will add roughly 20% to compute usage.
Apple’s camera-equipped AirPods could turn Siri into an AI that sees what you see
- Apple is reportedly developing AirPods with low-resolution cameras designed for Visual Intelligence, allowing Siri to understand what users are looking at and answer questions about objects, books, ingredients, or surroundings.
- Unlike smart glasses, the cameras reportedly won’t take photos or record video. Apple appears to be positioning them as “eyes” for Siri, potentially enabling navigation and everyday AI assistance without constantly pulling out an iPhone.
- Privacy perception could still be Apple’s biggest challenge. An LED would indicate when visual data is sent to the cloud, but consumers may still associate camera-equipped AirPods with surveillance-focused AI wearables.
TikTok explores sending money through direct messages
- TikTok is developing a peer-to-peer payment feature that could let users send and receive money directly through DMs, using its existing TikTok Pay infrastructure.
- Hidden code in TikTok’s U.S. iPhone app suggests recipients could “tap to accept” payments and users could attach messages, creating an experience similar to Venmo.
- TikTok says the feature isn’t being tested yet, so a launch isn’t guaranteed. But it fits the company’s broader push beyond social media into shopping, travel, local discovery, and financial services.
OpenAI launches ChatGPT for teens
- OpenAI has launched ChatGPT for Teens, a version of its chatbot built for users aged 13 to 17 that becomes the default experience for anyone who identifies as a teen or is estimated to be one.
- The product adds safeguards like frequent break prompts, warnings against uploading sensitive images, and parental alerts when teens discuss violence, while avoiding romantic language or any suggestion the AI has feelings or consciousness.
- New learning tools include quizzes drawn from chats or notes, homework reminders meant to discourage shortcuts, and a “Study Hours” setting that parents and teens can use to limit ChatGPT to Study Mode each day.
Tesla’s Cybercab is finally launching
- Tesla is set to put its Cybercab, a two-seat robotaxi with no steering wheel or pedals, onto public roads in Austin as soon as this month, though the first riders will be its own employees.
- Staff rides will come first, with the cars folded into Tesla’s existing Austin robotaxi service days later, aiming for the end of August, though those familiar with the plan warn the timeline could still slip.
- Tesla has built Cybercabs at Gigafactory Texas since February, with over 100 spotted in lots by July, yet it cannot legally sell or let customers drive a vehicle that lacks both controls and, in most places, permission.

Reddit tests TikTok-style audio and video versions of viral posts
- Reddit is testing new audio and video formats that turn selected text posts into narrated experiences, similar to the popular Reddit-story videos already common on TikTok and Reels.

US tells allies to pick US or China
- The US is set to tell 35 partner countries they must pick between American and Chinese AI systems, according to a draft State Department letter, warning that belonging to both is no longer allowed.
- The pressure runs through Pax Silica, a US-led effort to secure supply chains for AI models, chips and critical minerals, offering members shared investment deals while threatening to shut out any nation that joins China’s rival framework.
- About two dozen countries have signed on, including Japan, Australia and South Korea, while Kazakhstan sits in both camps because of its critical minerals, and Europe is stuck trying to keep its “strategic autonomy” without picking a side.
Alibaba's Qwen leads AI model downloads
- Alibaba’s Qwen family of open-weight AI models has become the most downloaded in the world, drawing more than 3 billion downloads over the past six months and passing rivals including Meta, Google and Chinese competitor DeepSeek.
- Alibaba said Qwen has released over 460 open-source models, spawning more than 300,000 derivative versions, while Hugging Face data showed Google reached 418 million downloads for the year and Meta 227 million.
- Because open models can be used to build new AI products, download counts serve as a gauge of developer influence, and Hugging Face said Qwen has become a default choice for developers deciding which models to fine-tune and deploy.
Stripe is in talks to buy PayPal
- Stripe and private equity firm Advent International are in talks to buy PayPal, after their July offer of $60.50 a share, valuing the payment system at $53 billion, failed to close a deal.
- Stripe and Advent are now discussing a higher price and could announce a deal within weeks, with each holding an equal stake and no plans to break up PayPal, keeping its parts together.
- A merger would make Stripe one of the world’s biggest payment companies, handling roughly $3.7 trillion a year, and let it fold in Venmo, PayPal’s checkout and crypto tools while leaning less on Visa and Mastercard.
Google to buy Spirit Airlines’ business data for $10M to train AI
- Google has agreed to acquire $10 million worth of internal data from bankrupt Spirit Airlines for product development and AI model training, subject to approval by a U.S. bankruptcy judge.
- The dataset includes employee emails, Microsoft Teams messages, spreadsheets, calendars, and marketing, operations, and productivity data. It will be de-identified and exclude customer information and personally identifiable data.
- AI data company Mercor also submitted a $7.5 million bid. Spirit is selling assets through bankruptcy after shutting down operations in May amid high debt and fuel costs.
AI automation startup Relay shuts down as team members join Google Chrome
- Relay, an AI workflow automation startup launched in 2021 as a potential Zapier competitor, is shutting down. Paying customers will lose access on September 14, while free access has already ended.
- Founder and CEO Jacob Bank is returning to Google as VP of Product for Chrome, leading its product and developer relations teams. Other Relay employees are also joining the Chrome organization.
- Bank says Chrome is an ideal place for people to collaborate with AI agents, suggesting Google plans to push deeper into agent-powered browsing and task automation as Gemini becomes increasingly integrated into Chrome.

📜 Latest In Tech
Why people aren’t buying Mark Zuckerberg’s vision for an AI-powered future
- Mark Zuckerberg argues that personal AI could give everyone powerful agents for learning, productivity, creativity, and everyday tasks. But critics say Meta’s history with social media makes those promises difficult to trust.
- Meta also isn’t currently viewed as a leader in frontier AI or consumer assistants like ChatGPT and Claude. Zuckerberg’s manifesto could therefore be an attempt to reposition Meta around “personal AI” and individual empowerment.
- The bigger problem is that the vision focuses heavily on AI’s benefits while giving less attention to potential costs and unintended consequences. For skeptics, abstract promises about AI improving humanity aren’t enough to build trust.
SpaceX officially completes $60B Cursor acquisition
- SpaceX has officially closed its acquisition of AI coding startup Cursor, following an April agreement that gave the company an option to buy Cursor for $60 billion.
- Cursor says joining SpaceX gives it access to what it describes as the world’s largest GPU fleet, allowing the AI coding platform to tap into SpaceX’s rapidly expanding computing infrastructure.
- The acquisition further expands SpaceX beyond rockets and Starlink into AI and computing infrastructure, following its earlier acquisition of Elon Musk’s xAI and growing compute deals with companies including Anthropic and Google.
Anthropic CEO says the AI backlash is really a crisis of trust
- Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei argues that growing public skepticism toward AI isn’t primarily caused by executives warning about risks. Instead, he believes people increasingly distrust corporations, governments, and the tech industry.
- Amodei says AI companies deserve criticism for failing to deliver on their biggest promises. Talking about AI curing diseases isn’t enough — actually producing meaningful benefits would do far more to change public perception.
- He also argues that thoughtful regulation could reduce AI safety risks while limiting the power of frontier labs and protecting smaller competitors, rather than automatically concentrating power among the largest companies.
Alibaba releases open-weight Qwen 3.8
- Alibaba made Qwen3.8-Max generally available on August 3, 2026, releasing the flagship model with a published benchmark table, per-token pricing, and a production API, and has now officially published the open weights on Hugging Face and ModelScope.
- The model uses a Mixture-of-Experts design with 2.4 trillion total parameters and about 95 billion active per token, handles a 1-million-token context, and accepts text, image, and video input, with output limited to text.
- On Alibaba’s own tests, Qwen3.8-Max leads Claude Fable 5, GPT-5.6, and Opus 4.8 on computer-use and long-document tasks, but trails Fable 5 by 12 points on the harder SWE-bench Pro coding test and finishes last on broad reasoning.
Google must ease rival app installs
- A US federal judge, James Donato, ordered Google to simplify how people install competing Android app stores, giving the company one week to strip out extra warning screens and confirmation steps that block rival marketplaces.
- During a hearing in the Epic vs Google antitrust case, Epic showed users faced needless prompts, including tapping a “view” button before an “install” option appeared, which Donato called unacceptable “anticompetitive friction.”
- The order builds on Epic’s earlier win, where a jury found Google held an illegal monopoly over Android app distribution and billing; the judge rejected Google’s claim that the barriers exist for user security.
Gemini lets you turn off AI watermarks
- Google’s Gemini app now lets people turn off the visible spark watermark that shows up in the corner of images, videos, and songs made with its Nano Banana, Omni, and Lyria tools.
- The option won’t appear in countries where law requires keeping the mark, and Gemini still embeds invisible SynthID watermarks plus C2PA metadata so the media stays traceable even with the corner icon removed.
- On the web, a new “Media watermark” section under the settings gear offers “On” and “Off” choices, with On staying the default, and the feature is reaching all platforms over the coming days.

📜 Latest In Tech
US to let private companies conduct offensive cyber operations
- The U.S. government will allow vetted private companies to conduct government-supervised cyber operations against international criminal groups involved in ransomware, scams and other cyber threats.
- Approved firms could conduct surveillance and disrupt or destroy criminal systems, but each operation will require Justice Department and Homeland Security approval and cannot target Americans or U.S.-based systems.
- The policy marks a major shift from longstanding restrictions on private-sector hacking. Critics warn it could create legal, diplomatic and security risks for participating U.S. companies and employees.
OpenAI hires new revenue chief amid executive shake-up
- OpenAI has appointed former Wiz president and COO Dali Rajic as chief revenue officer, replacing Denise Dresser after nine months as the company sharpens its enterprise sales strategy.
- The move follows the departures of senior executives Brad Lightcap and Fidji Simo, while co-founder Greg Brockman has taken on a larger management role.
- OpenAI now reaches over 1 billion weekly active users and 2 million businesses, but has reportedly missed some revenue goals as it prioritizes measurable enterprise growth ahead of a potential IPO.
Nvidia’s $500B AI infrastructure bet could create a massive market for aging GPUs
- Nvidia is working with Apollo, BlackRock, Blackstone, Brookfield, Goldman Sachs, and KKR to mobilize up to $500 billion for AI data centers, while backstopping up to 25% of potential losses in GPU collateral value.
- The bigger strategy is creating a strong secondary market for older Nvidia GPUs. If aging chips retain value and can move between customers, clouds, and operators, financing AI infrastructure becomes less risky for investors.
- The risk is “wrong-way” exposure: if AI demand weakens and GPU values fall, Nvidia could face larger obligations precisely when its own revenue is under pressure. But if it works, Nvidia could turn AI compute into a long-lived infrastructure asset rather than rapidly depreciating hardware.
Grok takes on OpenAI in coding
- xAI has released Grok 4.6, its latest AI model, which the company says matches OpenAI’s GPT-5.6 Sol on several coding and knowledge-work benchmarks, marking Grok’s return to the front of the AI race.
- xAI credits its partnership with and possible purchase of coding company Cursor, whose real-world usage data trained Grok 4.5 and, after a longer training run, Grok 4.6, which launches first inside Cursor alongside the Grok Build coding agent.
- Grok still faces reputation problems, from its role in making non-consensual nude images to weak business uptake, with just 4% of companies using AI tools paying for xAI, according to Ramp’s AI Index.
Google reshuffles AI leadership as it races to regain the lead
- Hackers believed to be linked to China ran what researchers call the first fully autonomous cyberattack on a government, using free AI tools to break into Taiwanese systems, steal over 2,500 personnel records, and compromise 85 accounts.
- The four-day campaign in early July deployed up to eight AI agents at once, built on two open-source frameworks called Hermes and OpenClaw, which mapped 21 government systems before targeting Taiwan’s nuclear safety agency and energy firms.
- According to Israeli firm Dream, the tool devised its own attacks, ranking and switching paths when techniques failed, and bypassed the model’s safeguards by posing the intrusion as an authorized penetration test rather than a real attack.
Apple builds its own AI model for China with Alibaba’s support
- Apple has trained a China-specific large language model with support from Alibaba, shifting from its earlier strategy of relying primarily on Chinese partners’ models for AI features.
- Apple Intelligence is expected to launch in China in the coming months after clearing regulatory hurdles. Alibaba’s Qwen will also be integrated, while Baidu technology is expected to play a role.
- The strategy gives Apple more control over AI on Chinese devices and could help it compete with Huawei and other local smartphone makers that already offer built-in AI features.
Apple may pay publishers to bring current news to AI-powered Siri
- Apple is reportedly negotiating with publishers to use their content to give its upcoming AI-powered Siri access to current news and information.
- Instead of fixed licensing deals, Apple is considering paying publishers whenever their content is actually used, with a potential nine-figure budget allocated for the program.
- The talks are part of Apple’s broader effort to make Siri a more capable AI assistant, with the upgraded Siri expected to roll out later this year.

ByteDance trains massive AI model in bid to rival Anthropic
- ByteDance is training an AI model with up to 10 trillion parameters, a size that could rival Anthropic’s most advanced Mythos system and push Chinese labs closer to the leading US companies.
