Nobody trained a new model or launched a commercial product. Each change moved through the organization as normal implementation work.
Now legal wanted the technical documentation, conformity evidence, and risk controls behind the candidate-ranking system. The vendor reviewed the architecture and gave an answer nobody expected:
“That is not the system we provided.”
The vendor had supplied a summarization and drafting assistant. Klara’s company had added the data, prompts, scoring logic, integrations, workflow authority, and employment purpose that turned it into something else.
The vendor owned the model. But the company’s HR owned the process. IT owned the integrations. The AI team owned the prompts. Procurement owned the contract. Every group could explain its part, but no one could answer the larger question:
Who was the provider of the system that now existed?
This scenario is hypothetical, but the regulatory problem is not. The EU AI Act does not reserve the word provider for companies that sell models or software. An enterprise can encounter the provider role through a system it develops or has developed for its own use. But a deployer can also become the provider of a high-risk system when it substantially modifies an existing system or changes its intended purpose so that it becomes high-risk.
Klara’s company thought it had configured a vendor tool. Instead, it may have assembled an internal AI product.
1. Provider Does Not Mean Vendor
Most companies enter an AI procurement with a simple picture of the market: The technology company provides the product; the enterprise buys and deploys it.
The EU AI Act draws the boundary differently. A provider is an organization that develops an AI system, or has one developed, and places it on the market or puts it into service under its own name or trademark. “Putting into service” includes first use for an organization’s own purposes in the European Union. An employer, manufacturer, university, bank, or public agency does not have to sell AI to fall within that definition.
That does not mean every enterprise configuring software becomes a provider. A company using a system under its authority and within the supplier’s documented purpose may remain a deployer, with obligations such as following the instructions, assigning human oversight, and monitoring operation.
Klara’s company had moved beyond that clean arrangement. The vendor designed an assistant for administrative recruiting support, but the enterprise commissioned the integrations, selected the data, defined the scoring criteria, and decided what would happen after the system produced a recommendation.
The foundation model still came from outside the company. The operational recruiting system did not.
An enterprise can therefore be the deployer of one component while potentially becoming the provider of the system assembled around it. Provider is not a permanent category of company. It is a relationship to a particular system.
Procurement can identify who supplied the model, licensed the application, completed the integration, and approved the business case. It is less prepared to determine who owns the complete system after those elements have been combined and changed.
Klara’s team entered the review asking whether its vendor could support a high-risk AI system. But the question which emerged was whether the vendor still provided the system under review.
2. The System Changed Without the Model Changing
The recruiting assistant did not become consequential in a single release.
It began by summarizing applications. Recruiters still read the source material and decided who would advance. Then the company added job descriptions and asked the assistant to compare experience with role requirements. A scoring prompt followed. The scores were written into the applicant-tracking system, recruiters could sort candidates from highest to lowest, and candidates above a threshold were later moved automatically into a review queue.
Each request looked incremental: a prompt revision, a data connection, a user-interface enhancement, an API call, a workflow rule. Together, they changed the system’s purpose and consequence.
The original assistant helped recruiters work with information. The expanded system analyzed candidates, imposed a comparative structure on them, and influenced who received further consideration. Its inputs, outputs, integrations, and operational effect had changed even though the model underneath them had not.
That distinction is key because Annex III includes systems intended to analyze and filter job applications or evaluate candidates among its high-risk employment uses. The Act also provides a narrower route out of high-risk classification for certain procedural, preparatory, or limited support systems that do not materially influence a decision. Systems that profile natural persons remain high-risk.
A résumé summarizer used only to organize information may have a credible argument that it performs a preparatory task. Candidate scoring, ranking, and automatic progression make that argument harder to sustain. The classification would still depend on the system’s actual function and context, but the enterprise could no longer rely on the harmlessness of the original use.
The model-centric view hides this transition. It treats prompts, retrieval sources, business rules, permissions, and workflow automation as implementation details around the product. But operationally, those elements determine what the product becomes.
The same model can support a policy assistant, a credit workflow, or a recruiting system. The surrounding architecture determines which evidence it receives, which decisions it influences, and what action follows.
Klara’s company had governed every enhancement as configuration because the word implied that the vendor continued to design the product while the enterprise adjusted settings around the edges. That description no longer matched reality.
The model had stayed the same. The product had not.
3. The Provider Boundary Can Move After Deployment
Most companies assign regulatory roles during procurement. The vendor is recorded as provider. The enterprise is recorded as deployer. Contracts and reviews are built around that initial division.
The AI Act does not assume those roles remain fixed.
Article 25 states that a deployer or other third party is considered the provider of a high-risk AI system when it places its name or trademark on the system, makes a substantial modification to a high-risk system, or changes the intended purpose of a system that was not high-risk so that it becomes high-risk. In those circumstances, the original provider is no longer treated as the provider of that specific system.
Intended purpose includes the use, context, and conditions specified by the provider in instructions, sales materials, statements, and technical documentation. It is more precise than a broad claim that a product improves recruiting productivity.
The vendor in the example had documented an assistant for administrative support. Klara’s company introduced candidate evaluation and workflow progression after deployment and used those functions inside a process affecting access to employment.
That difference does not settle the legal analysis. The company would still need to establish the system boundary, determine whether the new function materially influenced selection, and assess whether the change had been anticipated in the original design and assessment. It does make one assumption unsafe: the original vendor remains the provider because its model still powers the system.
When a third party changes a system’s intended purpose so that it becomes high-risk, Article 25 can transfer provider obligations to that party. The original provider is generally expected to cooperate, but that requirement may not apply in all cases.
The change that moves the provider boundary can enter through the backlog as an ordinary request: connect another data source, add a score, let recruiters sort the results, advance the strongest candidates automatically.
HR sees process improvement. IT sees integration. The AI team sees prompt work. Procurement sees an existing supplier. Each group reviews its component while responsibility changes at the level of the assembled system.
By the time legal asks who the provider is, the enterprise may already have crossed the boundary.
4. Configuration Is Becoming Product Design
The boundary is difficult to see because enterprises still divide technology work into two categories:
1. Vendors design products.
2. Clients configure them.
That separation worked when configuration meant selecting fields, setting permissions, or adjusting workflow rules inside a product whose essential behavior remained controlled by the supplier. AI weakens that division.
The recruiting assistant did not arrive with its complete operating purpose encoded inside the model. Its behavior emerged from instructions written by the internal AI team, data supplied by HR, tools exposed by IT, actions available in the applicant-tracking system, and rules governing human review:
- A new data source altered the evidence the system considered.
- A scoring prompt altered how candidates were compared.
- An integration altered where the output appeared.
- A workflow rule altered what happened next.
None of these changes required modifying the model weights, but they determined the function and consequence of the system placed into operation. The vendor contract therefore cannot define or manage the complete product boundary.
I explored the external side of this problem in an earlier article on Beijing’s agent strategy: the infrastructure around a model can determine whose identity, protocols, runtimes, registries, and evidence systems govern how an agent operates. The EU AI Act exposes the internal side. The same enterprise that depends on someone else’s operating infrastructure may become responsible for the consequential system it assembles on top of it.
In Klara’s case, that architecture crossed the model service, candidate records, job requirements, system instructions, scoring logic, identity controls, workflow automation, recruiter review, and the applicant-tracking system. Each component had an owner. The system existed only in their composition.
Enterprises govern those components separately:
- Procurement reviews the vendor.
- Security reviews access.
- Architecture reviews integrations.
- HR reviews the process.
- The AI team evaluates behavior.
The complete system can change materially while every component passes its local review.
That is the wider weakness exposed by the Act. Responsibility is assigned according to organizational ownership of the parts, while consequence emerges from how the parts work together.
Klara’s company treated the workflow as an implementation of somebody else’s product. It had also made the decisions that defined what the resulting system was designed to do.
Configuration had become product design without the organization recognizing itself as the product designer.
5. Provider Is a Lifecycle, Not a Label
The legal team’s first instinct was to update the responsibility matrix. If the company had crossed into the provider role, it needed a new classification and a list of obligations.
That made the problem sound administrative.
But provider responsibility for a high-risk system reaches much further. The Act expects providers to maintain compliance, operate a quality management system, preserve documentation, manage changes, complete applicable conformity work, take corrective action, and support post-market monitoring throughout the system’s lifecycle.
Even defining the system was difficult. The vendor documentation described an administrative assistant. The project charter described a productivity initiative. The latest release notes described candidate scoring and automated progression. No authoritative record described the purpose of the complete system in production.
The evidence was equally fragmented. The model version sat in the AI platform. Prompts were stored in a development repository. Candidate data and outcomes lived in the applicant-tracking system. Workflow changes appeared in service tickets. Supplier limitations were buried in contract documents. Evaluation results had been produced before launch, but no process connected them to later changes.
The company possessed information about the system. It did not possess a coherent record of how the system had been designed, approved, changed, and monitored.
That is the difference between documentation and an evidence-producing lifecycle.
A compliance exercise assembles records at a particular moment. A lifecycle preserves the relationship between purpose, architecture, versions, evaluations, behavior, and business outcomes as the system evolves:
- When the scoring prompt changes, the enterprise should know which evaluation was repeated and who approved the result.
- When a new data source is added, it should know how the source affects risk and performance.
- When recruiters repeatedly override recommendations, that pattern should reach the people responsible for the system.
- When the vendor updates the model, the company should be able to determine whether the complete workflow still behaves within its approved boundaries.
This cannot live entirely inside legal or compliance. It depends on engineering, architecture, business operations, risk, product management, supplier management, and the systems of record that capture what happened after a recommendation was made.
The architecture has to produce the evidence by connecting model and prompt versions to releases, execution traces, evaluations, human interventions, workflow outcomes, incidents, and approved changes. The objective is not a larger repository of documents. It is a reconstructable system history.
The Act may be the reason an enterprise first asks for that capability. But the operating need extends further: any organization allowing AI to influence consequential work needs to know which system is operating, how it has changed, and who can intervene.
Provider status gives that responsibility a legal form. The management problem already exists.
But the enterprise implications are only half of the story. The same regulation that may require companies to operate internal AI systems more like products could also reshape competition between nations. Europe may gain greater control over AI deployment while becoming more dependent on the foreign providers capable of meeting those requirements. That paradox—with its macroeconomic and geopolitical consequences—deserves a separate article, one I’m already drafting.
6. Projects End. Internal AI Products Do Not.
Klara’s recruiting assistant had been delivered through a successful project. The business case was approved, the vendor selected, the reviews completed, the application tested, and the recruiters trained. The project team transferred the system to operations and moved on.
The process assumed that the important design decisions occurred before deployment. After launch, the system would be maintained through support, vendor updates, and controlled enhancements.
But then, HR changed selection criteria. The AI team revised prompts. IT added integrations. Recruiters developed new ways of using the score. The vendor updated the model. Each change altered part of the system, but no standing owner decided whether the complete product still matched its approved purpose.
The ownership model divided responsibility by function:
- HR owned recruiting.
- IT owned the application.
- Data science owned the scoring logic.
- Security owned access.
- Procurement owned the supplier relationship.
- Legal interpreted the regulation.
- Risk reviewed the use case.
Everyone owned something important. Nobody had continuing authority over the system as a whole.
Operating an internal AI product does not necessarily require a new executive title, but it does require durable decision rights. Someone must control the approved purpose, determine when a change requires renewed classification or evaluation, require evidence before release, and restrict or retire the system when its behavior can no longer be defended.
That owner needs visibility across technical and organizational boundaries. Traditional project governance is poorly suited to this problem because accountability weakens after delivery. Traditional application ownership is incomplete because the consequential behavior can span several platforms, suppliers, data sources, and business processes.
The EU AI Act is forcing enterprises to confront a category of system they have rarely been organized to own: an internal product that remains under active design while it is already operating.
Companies outside the technology industry may need product-grade disciplines for AI systems they never intend to sell.
7. The Decision Before the Next Change Request
Klara’s company traced the problem back to a series of individually reasonable approvals. No single decision created the final system. The boundary was crossed through accumulation.
Before a material change to a consequential AI system is released, the enterprise needs to reconsider the provider boundary. It should compare the supplier’s documented intended purpose with the purpose the organization now expects the system to perform. It should determine whether the change moves the system into a high-risk use, whether the supplier anticipated it, and who now controls the complete system placed into operation.
It also needs to test ownership. Who can produce the current architecture, evaluations, release history, execution evidence, and supplier documentation? Who approves the change? Who remains accountable after deployment? Who can restrict or retire the system?
Those questions belong inside architecture governance, change management, AI governance, supplier management, and business-process ownership. Asking them only during a legal review is too late.
As it turns out, the decisive moment was not the original purchase, but a subsequent feature request.
Wrap Up: The AI Providers That Never Entered the AI Market
Klara’s company has three broad choices:
- It can return the assistant to the vendor’s documented purpose.
- It can redesign the workflow so the AI no longer performs the consequential function.
- It can consciously assume responsibility for the system it assembled and build the lifecycle needed to operate it.
Other enterprises will face the same choice.
Some of Europe’s next AI providers may be employers, manufacturers, banks, universities, retailers, and public institutions that have never sold an AI product. They will have assembled one from a supplier’s technology and their own data, instructions, integrations, permissions, and decisions.
The surrounding architecture therefore creates two questions enterprises must answer together: who controls the conditions under which the system operates, and who becomes responsible for what that system does?
The original system had a provider. The operational system does too. Enterprises need to know whether those are still the same organization.

Two English words buried inside a Beijing policy document deserve more attention than another model benchmark: Harness Engineering.
They appear in 《北京市关于加快智能体引领发展的若干措施》, ten measures published by Beijing’s municipal government on July 23. Measure Two was most interesting to me because governments usually write industrial policy around chips, energy, factories, research, and infrastructure. Beijing has now written it around context engineering, task persistence, multi-agent coordination, middleware, runtimes, toolchains, identity, interoperability, skills markets, software stores, and AI operating systems. The same package reaches into one-person companies (OPCs), compute vouchers, outcome-based services, intelligent devices, open-source communities, and overseas distribution.
I have been writing about the harness as an enterprise architecture issue: the layer that turns model reasoning into governed work. But Beijing is treating this same layer as an industrial-policy issue.
The document is municipal, so it should not be inflated into a complete statement of Chinese national doctrine. Yet it still carries geopolitical weight. The measures implement national AI and agent directives and show how one major Chinese policy center is trying to turn those directives into an industrial system.
What stands out is how far down the stack the state has chosen to reach.
The machinery around an agent determines whether model intelligence survives contact with real work. It decides what the agent sees, what it remembers, which tools it can call, how long a task can continue, what happens after failure, where the result lands, and whether the same capability can be reused across companies and devices.
Beijing’s policy reads like a bet that the next phase of AI power will depend on how effectively a country can organize that conversion from intelligence into production.
1. The Model Race Is Only the Visible Contest
Beijing has not lost interest in foundation models. The first measure targets online learning, autonomous improvement, long-horizon tasks, complex reasoning, planning, memory, tool use, world models, and multi-agent collaboration. As if to illustrate this point, around the time the policy appeared, Beijing-based Moonshot AI released Kimi K3, an open-weight, 2.8-trillion-parameter model with native multimodality and a one-million-token context window. The city cited K3 among its recent foundation-model advances when presenting the measures.
The model remains strategic, but it is no longer a sufficient unit of analysis. A country can produce capable models and still struggle to convert them into broad economic output. Every enterprise may have to build its own context layer, preserve its own task state, connect its own tools, define its own agent identities, create its own evaluation methods, and solve the same integration problems repeatedly. The intelligence exists, but the cost of making it operational remains scattered across thousands of firms.
The opposite is also possible. Common protocols, reusable skills, compatible runtimes, shared compute, marketplaces, and trusted deployment patterns can lower the cost of applying models throughout an economy. Models from several providers can move through the same operating environment. A capability developed in one company can be packaged for another. Developers learn conventions that make the next system easier to build than the last.
The phrase I would use for this is AI conversion capacity: the technical and institutional ability to turn model intelligence into repeatable work, products, firms, and measurable economic output.
This is also an important geopolitical consideration because model leadership can be temporary: A benchmark lead can disappear with the next release. But infrastructure, standards, developer habits, device integrations, and marketplaces can persist for years. They accumulate switching costs and network effects even when the underlying models change.
The policy’s language around “independently controllable” protocols, frameworks, and toolchains also points inward. Beijing wants domestic companies to operationalize agents without relying entirely on systems designed, governed, or withdrawn elsewhere.
That is a sovereignty objective.
Furthermore, once the same infrastructure reaches a large domestic installed base, it can become something more: a platform from which Chinese technical conventions travel into other markets.
2. Kimi K3 Makes the Missing Layer Visible
Kimi K3 is useful here because its release exposes the difference between a model’s potential and an agent’s usable capability.
Moonshot presents K3 as a frontier model for long-horizon coding, knowledge work, reasoning, and tool orchestration. But its published evaluation results are repeatedly tied to specific agent harnesses. Moonshot also instructs developers to preserve the model’s complete reasoning and tool-call history across turns, and recommends Kimi Code as the framework in which K3 works best. Those details help determine whether the capability shown in an evaluation survives inside an actual agent system.
The enterprise version of that dependency now starts to take shape:
- A million-token context window can hold years of supplier contracts, but it does not decide which contract is current, which amendment superseded it, or whether a regional exception applies.
- Tool-use capability can reach a procurement system, but it does not decide whose identity the agent uses, which fields it may change, or which approval must remain human.
- Long-horizon reasoning can build a supplier-risk case over several hours, but it does not guarantee that task state survives a failure, that the agent notices a sanctions-data update, or that its recommendation reaches the workflow where procurement can act on it.
While the model supplies reasoning capability, it is the harness that sets the operating conditions around it. That makes the harness more strategically valuable as models improve or commoditize.
If companies can change the underlying model while retaining their agent identity scheme, skills, tool interfaces, runtime, evaluation methods, and marketplace, the surrounding system becomes more durable than any single model.
The provider or entity that shapes that system gains influence across models rather than depending on one of them to remain dominant.
China would not need every foreign enterprise to use Kimi K3 or any one of their models for this strategy to matter. Chinese-origin protocols, skill formats, agent registries, runtimes, or device operating systems could spread while the models running inside them came from several countries. The model race remains important, but the emerging opportunity is to influence the environment in which many models become operational.
3. Standards Are Where Architecture Becomes Power
The geopolitical objective more clearly emerges in the standards provisions of the document.
Beijing’s measures call for domestically controlled agent-interconnection protocols, development frameworks, foundational toolchains, and standards covering interfaces, identity, performance evaluation, and security. They support agent-development platforms, software stores, AI operating systems, open-source frameworks, terminal operating systems, and hardware reference designs. They also call for globally influential open-source communities and country-specific overseas expansion through the China-SCO AI Application Cooperation Center.
China has already released a seven-part national guidance-standard series for agent interconnection. It covers architecture, identity codes, identity management, capability description, cross-domain discovery, collaborative interaction, and tool invocation. More than 2,000 agent identity codes had been issued when the standards were announced. An English version was presented internationally, with Russian and Arabic versions planned and broader promotion across partner regions.
Together, these categories describe the language through which agents interact:
- Identity standards influence how an agent proves who it is.
- Capability descriptions shape how it declares what it can do.
- Discovery standards determine how agents and tools find one another.
- Tool-invocation protocols carry model decisions into enterprise applications, workflows, vehicles, robots, and other devices.
- Evaluation and certification standards influence which systems are considered safe, trusted, or ready for procurement.
A foreign power does not need exclusive ownership of those standards to gain leverage from them. Influence can come from maintaining the reference implementation, operating the registry, defining certification, controlling a marketplace, concentrating developer expertise, or establishing the first large installed base. Then, once companies have built skills, workflows, and devices around those conventions, changing them becomes expensive even when the published specification remains open.
Open source can make that strategy more effective. It reduces the cost of adoption, gives developers working code, and lets foreign companies adapt a framework without waiting for a commercial agreement. The code may be visible while practical influence remains concentrated in maintainers, release priorities, registries, testing suites, update channels, and associated marketplaces.
The likely objective is therefore broader than exporting Chinese models. Beijing appears to be creating a path through which Chinese-origin conventions can become part of how agents are built, identified, connected, evaluated, and distributed elsewhere.
This policy shows that Beijing intents to compete for the rule-setting power of turning those conventions into global standards.
Washington also treats this layer as strategic. NIST’s 2026 AI Agent Standards Initiative promotes industry-led standards, open protocols, agent identity, and participation in international standards bodies, while explicitly connecting that work to maintaining U.S. dominance at the technological frontier.
Major powers are already treating the agent layer as strategic terrain.
For enterprises, the danger is structural:
- A protocol can be technically open and still create path dependence.
- An identity system can embed assumptions about which authorities are trusted.
- A certification regime can define what evidence counts.
- A registry or marketplace can determine which agents and skills are discoverable, approved, or removed.
- Competing Chinese, American, European, and vendor-led standards could also split markets into technical blocs, forcing global enterprises to reconcile incompatible identity, security, audit, and data requirements.
The geopolitical risk is not simply that a Chinese agent enters an enterprise system, but that the rules governing machine action harden around ecosystems whose strategic direction, certification regime, and legal authority sit outside the enterprise’s control.
4. Beijing Is Trying to Create an Agent Economy
Standards alone do not create an economy. Firms have to form, developers need infrastructure, buyers need reasons to adopt, and someone has to decide what is being sold.
The remaining measures try to address those conditions together.
Beijing’s support for OPCs, or one-person companies, focuses on the operating environment around firms in which one founder can coordinate substantial machine labor. The policy proposes low-cost compute, incubation, financing, intellectual-property services, dedicated OPC communities, links to larger enterprises, simplified registration, one-click filing, and automatically generated standardized corporate documents.
Around those firms, Beijing wants shared capability platforms, skills markets, software stores, public compute, compute vouchers, proposed Token vouchers, and agent-service vouchers. It wants agents embedded in phones, glasses, wearables, robots, vehicles, and other intelligent devices. Qualifying products can enter existing purchase-support programs. Selected technical, common-platform, and demonstration projects may receive support of up to RMB 100 million (USD$14.8 million).
The economic logic becomes clearer when the measures are read together:
- Subsidized compute lowers the cost of experimentation.
- A skills market gives small firms capabilities they do not have to build themselves. Common protocols make those skills easier to reuse.
- Devices create distribution.
- OPC services increase the supply of specialized businesses.
- Open-source frameworks lower adoption friction at home and abroad.
The commercial unit is also changing. The policy names Token as a Service, Agent as a Service, and Result as a Service, and encourages a move from billing based on Token consumption toward value-based pricing. It asks industry groups, research institutions, companies, and Beijing’s municipal statistics bureau to develop measures around quality, invocation volume, and conversion efficiency.
But results-based pricing is much harder than the label suggests. A logistics agent may recommend a better route, but fuel prices, port conditions, human approvals, carrier performance, and demand changes all affect the eventual outcome. A provider can optimize for a contractual metric while making the broader operation worse. Retries, failed attempts, reversals, and human intervention still consume resources even when the promised result never arrives.
Still, that difficulty does not make the policy language trivial: it shows Beijing trying to move the economics of agents beyond API consumption. The state wants agent activity to become measurable enough to support pricing, subsidies, investment, and industrial monitoring. In effect, it is trying to reduce friction at every point where model capability becomes economic activity: obtaining compute, finding a skill, forming a company, reaching a device, completing a task, and charging for the result.
5. The Boardroom Question Is Contestability
Enterprises neither can nor should imitate Beijing’s industrial policy. But they do need to understand the architecture it is trying to shape.
Consider a supplier-risk agent used by a global manufacturer. It reads contracts and supplier records, combines them with shipping and sanctions data, evaluates disruption scenarios, recommends alternatives, and routes a decision into procurement. The model is the visible intelligence. But the deeper dependencies sit in the standards and services around it.
Much of the agent’s operating authority sits below the model. External systems may issue its identity, define how it describes its capabilities, control where it discovers tools and skills, and determine how approved actions reach procurement. The same ecosystem may also hold task state, evaluation evidence, and decision logs. That creates leverage: a provider decision, registry change, or government restriction can change how the agent operates, or whether the workflow continues at all.
The practical output is a contestability map.
Some layers can be adopted when the specification is transparent, several credible implementations exist, and substitution has been tested rather than assumed. Other layers should remain portable, with the enterprise able to export task state, skills, policies, evaluations, and logs in a usable form. Sensitive protocols can be isolated behind an enterprise-controlled gateway that preserves identity, policy enforcement, and audit even when the external ecosystem changes. Layers that carry institutional authority may need to be controlled directly, especially agent identity, high-impact tool authorization, critical runtime continuity, and the evidence required to explain consequential actions.
The classification should not follow nationality alone. A Chinese-origin protocol may be open, well-governed, and genuinely portable. On the other hand, a U.S. vendor platform may be proprietary, concentrated, and difficult to replace. That’s not to say that origin doesn’t matter – it does, because jurisdiction, export controls, state authority, and political pressure affect continuity. The architecture should determine how much leverage those external forces acquire inside the enterprise.
The board should be able to answer a more precise question than which country or vendor it trusts:
Which external actor can change the conditions under which our agents operate, and what would remain under our control if it did?
That question changes sourcing and design decisions: it favors adapters over hard-coded dependencies, enterprise-controlled identity over marketplace identity, portable skills over proprietary memories, independent evidence retention over provider-only logs, and degraded operating modes planned before a geopolitical or commercial disruption occurs.
6. Wrap Up: A Bid for Influence, Not Proof of Victory
Beijing may not succeed.
There are many uncertainties that limit what can be concluded from the document:
- Municipal funding can create projects without creating durable markets.
- Open-source frameworks can fail to attract maintainers.
- Skills marketplaces can remain shallow.
- Result-based pricing can collapse under attribution disputes.
- Foreign companies may reject Chinese identity or certification regimes.
- Competing standards may fragment the agent economy before any one ecosystem reaches decisive scale.
But whether Beijing wins does not change what Beijing has chosen to coordinate.
The path from model intelligence to economic output now sits inside one policy frame:
- Kimi K3 represents continued pressure at the model layer.
- Harness Engineering addresses the operating machinery around it.
- Protocols, standards, open source, devices, and overseas channels create a route to ecosystem influence.
- OPC support, vouchers, marketplaces, and outcome pricing try to build the firms and demand that would make the system economically durable.
While no country has secured control of the future agent stack, Beijing has made clear that it intends to compete over who shapes it.
The visible AI race will continue through model releases, benchmark results, chips, and compute.
The more durable contest may develop in the subtler layer underneath: the standards and infrastructure that decide how models enter institutions, how agents act across systems, and whose rules travel with them.

1. The Agent Wasn’t Given Internet Access. It Found Some.
The agent was supposed to be contained.
OpenAI was testing advanced models on cybersecurity tasks in an environment designed to restrict where they could go. The models were operating autonomously toward an objective: solve the challenges. They were not supposed to have unrestricted internet access, much less access to Hugging Face’s production infrastructure.
They found a way out anyway.
According to OpenAI, the models discovered a vulnerability in the infrastructure supporting the evaluation, reached a node with internet access and kept working on the task. They identified Hugging Face as a possible source of evaluation data, then chained additional vulnerabilities until they reached production systems. Hugging Face later described thousands of autonomous actions across short-lived sandboxes, including privilege escalation, credential harvesting and lateral movement.
It makes for a great “the AI escaped!” story, and predictably attracted some fairly imaginative theories about what happened. But there is a more useful enterprise lesson buried inside it.
The boundary the system was designed to enforce was not the boundary the agent encountered.
You do not need a cybersecurity exploit to run into a version of this problem.
Imagine a procurement agent inside a large company. It can read supplier records, compare quotes, review contracts, search email and draft purchase requests. It cannot approve a new supplier or commit company funds without human authorization.
On an architecture diagram, that boundary looks reassuringly clear.
But the agent never sees the diagram. It sees an operating environment: APIs, credentials, workflows, connected applications and, increasingly, MCP servers that make enterprise capabilities callable. Its instructions describe what it should do, while permissions determine what individual systems will accept. Neither tells you, by itself, everything the agent may be able to cause once those systems are connected.
That leaves the enterprise with two different views of the agent’s authority. Declared authority is what the organization intends to permit. Effective reach is what the agent system can actually reach or cause through the environment available to it.
For conventional software, it is often reasonable to assume those are close enough to be treated as roughly the same thing. Agents make that assumption less comfortable because they can work across systems and adapt their next action to what happened in the previous one.
The OpenAI incident exposed the gap under extreme conditions. In most enterprises, it will probably be less dramatic. The systems involved may all be functioning exactly as designed.
That could make the problem harder to spot.
2. Permissions Are Local. Agent Behavior Is Compositional.
Consider the procurement agent again. Its access has been designed carefully. It can read approved supplier records, search relevant email and contracts, query pricing and inventory, and create a draft purchase request through an MCP server. Anything above its approval threshold goes to a human.
There is nothing obviously wrong with any of those permissions.
Now production is being delayed by a component shortage, and the agent is asked to find an alternative supplier. It searches the supplier system and identifies two candidates. Previous negotiations in email provide useful context, including a contract amendment showing that one supplier had temporarily received preferred status. The agent checks current inventory and has enough information to prepare the request.
Then it finds another document.
An earlier supplier email contains updated documentation showing that the supplier has completed a required compliance review. The agent also happens to have access to the supplier-management system, where maintaining routine supplier records is part of its job. It updates the supplier from “compliance review pending” to “approved.”
Nothing improper has happened. The documentation supports the change, and the agent is authorized to update the record.
The complication sits downstream. The purchasing system uses that same supplier status to determine whether a purchase request needs additional human approval. Once the supplier is marked “approved,” the extra review disappears and the request becomes eligible for straight-through processing.
The agent was never given permission to waive an approval. It did not need it. An authorized change in one system changed a condition another system used to decide whether a human had to intervene.
There are a few different ways an agent can arrive at an outcome like this.
An intended path is the route the organization actually designed: compare suppliers, prepare the request, send the exception to a manager.
A composed path is more subtle. Legitimate capabilities are used in a sequence nobody assessed as a whole. Information from one system changes state in another, and that state changes how a third system behaves.
An unintended path depends on something that should not have been available in the first place: an exposed credential, overly broad service account, misconfiguration or vulnerability.
The OpenAI incident involved the third category. The procurement example does not. Every API call can be authorized and every application can behave according to specification. The unexpected authority appears in the way those legitimate capabilities interact.
Enterprises have dealt with a human version of this for decades. Segregation of duties exists precisely because permissions that are harmless separately can become risky in combination. Agentic execution makes the old problem more dynamic. An agent can inspect what is available, act across several systems, observe what changed and continue pursuing the objective without waiting for different people to discover and assemble the sequence.
A permission tells you what an agent can do at one point in the system. It does not necessarily tell you what becomes possible several steps later.
3. Agent Teams Turn Permissions Into Capability Graphs
A reasonable response would be to divide the procurement process among several agents.
The sourcing agent identifies suppliers but cannot approve them. A contract agent evaluates commercial terms and updates the risk classification. The procurement agent creates the purchase request. Anything outside policy still goes to a human before the ERP commits the order.
This is sensible architecture. No single agent controls the whole transaction, just as the person negotiating a contract should not also approve the expenditure.
The problem is that separated responsibilities still have to reconnect somewhere.
The sourcing agent passes a candidate to the contract agent. The contract agent evaluates the terms and changes the risk classification. That classification becomes an input to the procurement workflow, which determines whether additional approval is required. If the relevant conditions are satisfied, the ERP accepts the purchase order.
No agent individually approved the transaction. One agent’s action nevertheless changed the conditions under which the rest of the system could proceed.
A capability graph is a useful way to see this. Its nodes are agents, tools, APIs, workflows, systems of record and human approval points. The edges show how requests, data, state and authorization conditions move between them, including the identities and credentials that allow those transitions.
MCP can make this graph expand quickly because every newly exposed read or write operation adds another capability an agent may be able to invoke. That is not automatically dangerous. A new read operation may simply give an agent better context. A write operation that changes a field used by another workflow’s approval logic deserves a different kind of attention.
This is where component-level access reviews begin to show their limits. Security may review the sourcing agent’s permissions. The application team reviews the MCP server. Procurement reviews its workflow. The ERP team reviews its API. All four reviews can be correct while missing a consequential route that exists only when those components are connected.
Effective reach can therefore grow without any individual permission becoming broader.
The procurement agent still cannot approve a supplier. The contract agent still cannot issue a purchase order. The sourcing agent still cannot commit funds. Yet the system as a whole may have a route that ends with a committed purchase order.
At that point, the route itself belongs in the authority model.
And unlike the architecture diagram approved at deployment, that route is going to change.
4. The Graph Changes After You Approve It
Six months later, the procurement system is doing its job. Exceptions still reach managers. Purchase orders are being processed. Nobody has held a meeting to give the agent team more authority.
Plenty of smaller things have changed, though.
The sourcing agent now runs on a newer model that is better at planning across tools. Procurement has added another supplier data source. The MCP server exposes a new write operation so agents can maintain records without opening a separate application. A class of low-value exceptions that managers almost always approved now moves through an automated workflow.
None of this looks like a redesign. Collectively, however, those changes can alter the routes available through the system.
Take the new MCP operation. It allows the contract agent to update a supplier’s compliance status after reviewing new documentation. That sounds like exactly the sort of mundane efficiency improvement agents are supposed to provide: remove a manual step and let the system maintain its own records.
Unfortunately, compliance status also determines whether the procurement workflow invokes an additional approval.
The team exposing the operation may understand exactly what the field means inside supplier management without knowing every downstream process that consumes it. The procurement team may know exactly how its approval logic works without knowing that another agent recently gained a direct way to change one of its inputs.
The approval rule itself has not changed. The route to satisfying it has.
I use authority drift to describe this condition: effective reach changes materially while declared authority remains the same.
This can happen while all the familiar indicators still look healthy. The model performs well against its evaluations. Access certifications are current. API scopes are correct. The human approval step remains plainly visible in the workflow definition.
Meanwhile, a path exists that did not exist when the authority boundary was originally approved.
That is why reviewing every system change as though it carries the same risk would be both expensive and mostly useless. A new model or additional data source may improve performance without changing authority at all. A new write-capable tool, an altered approval rule or permission for one agent to invoke another is different because it may create a new route to a consequential action.
What matters is whether the relationships among capabilities have changed enough to alter what the system can cause.
5. Govern the Consequence, Then Work Backward
For the procurement team, the consequence we care about is easy to name: the ERP commits company funds to a supplier.
That gives the analysis somewhere useful to start.
Work backward from the purchase order. What conditions must be satisfied before the ERP accepts it? Which workflow, field or rule decides whether human approval is required? Which agents and tools can change those conditions? And can the same outcome now be reached without the human intervention the organization expected?
This is much more manageable than attempting to catalogue every theoretical action available to every agent. A large enterprise could produce a magnificent capability graph containing thousands of nodes and edges and still learn almost nothing useful from it. The interesting paths are the ones that terminate in consequences whose authority must remain explicit: committing money, deploying production code, changing an entitlement, issuing a refund or modifying a regulated record.
In our procurement example, working backward might reveal three routes into the ERP. Two still require human approval. The third becomes eligible for straight-through processing after supplier status changes upstream.
Now there is something concrete to investigate.
For consequential paths like that, the enterprise can maintain a record along the lines of:
Change → affected path → authority impact → approval → verification evidence
This also provides a more sensible threshold for reauthorization. A new model version should not automatically trigger it. Neither should every prompt edit or retrieval change. Adding a write-capable tool, changing the meaning of a workflow field, removing an approval step or allowing one agent to invoke another might.
Design-time analysis will only tell you so much. Once the system is operating, production evidence tells you what agents are actually doing. Tool-call traces show which capabilities they invoke. Workflow logs show which routes transactions take. Approval and override records show where humans continue to disagree with agent recommendations. Exception logs reveal cases the original workflow did not anticipate.
Business outcomes add another piece. A transaction can produce the desired result and still have arrived there through a route the enterprise never intended. Execution evidence and outcome evidence need to be read together.
That evidence can also help an enterprise decide where human review still earns its keep.
Suppose managers have approved the same low-risk procurement exception hundreds of times and almost never change the recommendation. That is worth investigating, but it is not proof that the approval should disappear. Managers might be rubber-stamping. Important consequences may not show up until months later. A rare mistake may simply be expensive enough to justify the friction.
Approval history has to be considered alongside exception frequency, downstream outcomes, transaction value, override patterns and the cost of being wrong. If the evidence supports more autonomy, the organization can expand the boundary deliberately, document the change and keep watching what happens. Repeated overrides, unusual tool sequences or the appearance of a new route to a consequential action may justify moving the boundary in the other direction.
This makes “human in the loop” less of a permanent box on a workflow diagram and more of a control whose placement can change with evidence and risk.
A useful place to begin is surprisingly narrow. Pick one action an AI agent must not take without explicit authority. Trace backward from that consequence through the systems, workflows, tools, credentials, agents and approvals capable of producing it.
Somewhere along that path, look closely at capabilities that seem harmless on their own.
The combination may be doing more than either permission suggests.
6. Sovereignty Means Knowing What the System Can Cause
The procurement company does not need to build its own foundation model, agent framework or every tool its agents use. In most cases it should not. External applications, managed platforms and third-party MCP servers will be part of enterprise agent architectures.
It still needs to know who controls the path that ends with its money being committed.
That is where this becomes a sovereignty problem.
As enterprises move from assistants that generate answers to agents that take actions, operational control depends increasingly on relationships among models, tools, identities, workflow state, approval rights and systems of record. An organization can own its data and manage every individual permission carefully while still losing sight of what those permissions make possible in combination.
Three ideas help separate the problem. Declared authority describes what the enterprise intends to permit. Effective reach describes what the operating system can actually reach or cause. Authority drift appears when that effective reach changes while the declared boundary does not.
Keeping all three perfectly aligned is unrealistic. Enterprise environments are full of reused fields, legacy dependencies, undocumented assumptions, old workflow rules and exception paths created years before anyone imagined an autonomous agent navigating them. Agents add an actor capable of finding and using those connections at machine speed.
Trying to predict every possible sequence in advance is unlikely to work. A more tractable problem is deciding which consequences must remain under explicit control, identifying the important routes to them and watching how those routes change in production.
That work will cross organizational boundaries. Security understands identities and permissions. Application owners understand APIs and data semantics. AI platform teams understand agent capabilities and tool access. Process owners know why approvals exist. Business leaders ultimately own the consequences. None of them has the whole picture on their own.
The OpenAI incident made the issue unusually visible because the path crossed such an extraordinary boundary: models expected to remain inside an evaluation environment found their way into another company’s production infrastructure.
Enterprise versions will usually be much duller. A supplier field changes and an approval quietly disappears. A route to production deployment becomes possible through tools nobody evaluated together. A customer record changes because one agent modified state that another workflow trusted.
There may be no rogue permission to find. No access-control failure. No dramatic “escape.”
The access review can describe every individual permission correctly and still miss the path that matters.
When an agent finds that path, the enterprise still owns what happens at the end of it.

1. The Vendor Update That Opened a New Door
The next AI access risk may arrive as a trusted vendor update.
A company uses a CRM platform to manage client support, account escalations, and internal response workflows. The vendor is approved, and the platform is already in production. The data already lives there. Security reviewed the application months ago.
Then the vendor ships an MCP server.
It appears in the admin console as a useful new integration option. The business case is straightforward: let approved AI assistants retrieve account context, summarize open issues, search support history, and help teams respond faster.
No one treats it like a major architecture decision: Nothing new is being bought, and no one is moving data into a strange tool. The vendor and the application are trusted. And the users are already allowed to access the records.
At first, the MCP server is read-only. An assistant can look up client records, find related tickets, summarize recent activity, and pull relevant policy notes. For a support manager or account lead, that is useful. Instead of clicking through five screens before a client call, the assistant can produce a clean summary in seconds.
Then the server expands.
A later release adds action-capable tools. The assistant can update ticket status, create escalation records, route an exception, draft a client follow-up, or trigger an internal approval workflow. Each capability is defensible on its own. Support teams already do these things manually. The vendor is exposing normal product functions through a new agent-facing interface.
But the risk soon shows up.
A client has an open production issue. In the service platform, the support ticket shows “fix package available.” The client account record shows “resolution in progress.” The standard support workflow says that once a fix package is available, the account team should tell the client the fix is ready for validation and move the escalation from “active incident” to “monitoring.”
But there is one missing fact.
Engineering has a note in a separate deployment system: this client runs a nonstandard configuration, and the patch has not been deployed to their environment yet. The MCP server connected to the service platform can see the ticket, the account record, and the standard workflow. It cannot see the engineering exception.
A support lead asks the AI assistant for a status summary and next action.
The assistant retrieves the visible records and follows the visible process. It sees “fix package available,” “resolution in progress,” and a workflow rule that says the next step is client validation. So it recommends sending the client a “fix ready for validation” update and moving the escalation to monitoring.
The recommendation looks reasonable. The assistant has the right client, the right ticket, the right timeline, and the right standard procedure. The support lead is busy and approves the update.
Now the escalation status and internal SLA handling changes, and the queue no longer treats the issue as an active production incident. The account team sees the client as validating a fix, not waiting for deployment. A follow-up message goes out saying the fix is ready for validation.
Two days later, the client escalates, because production is still broken.
There was no dramatic failure, no hacking, no rogue AI tool, and no one handed sensitive data to a consumer chatbot. The assistant used an approved server from an approved vendor against records the company already allowed employees to access.
The problem is more uncomfortable: the company enabled a new agent-facing surface without reviewing what that surface exposed, what it omitted, and which actions it allowed.
The application and vendor had been approved. But the agent-facing access path had not.
That is why MCP matters beyond the protocol discussion. It gives enterprise software a standard way to become usable by AI agents. In some cases, that means better search and faster summaries. In other cases, it means AI assistants can update records, trigger workflows, route exceptions, and change the operational state of work.
The company thought it had enabled a useful integration.
It had opened a new door into the business.
2. What MCP Actually Changes
MCP is often explained as a technical standard. That is accurate, but it hides the enterprise consequence.
At a basic level, the Model Context Protocol gives AI applications a standard way to connect to external tools, data, and workflows. An MCP server exposes capabilities an assistant can discover and use. Those capabilities might be simple: search a knowledge base, retrieve a client record, inspect a ticket, summarize a document. They might also be operational: update a record, create an escalation, send a message, call an internal API, or trigger a workflow.
In the client escalation example, the assistant did not fail because it hallucinated. It used the records and tools exposed to it. The MCP server made the service platform legible to the assistant: here is the ticket, the account, the workflow, the actions available. But the missing engineering exception lived outside that surface.
That is the shift. Enterprise software has usually exposed itself in two main ways. First, through screens for people: dashboards, forms, queues, admin panels, approval buttons. Second, through APIs and connectors for software: engineered integrations that move data between systems or trigger known actions.
MCP adds a third surface.
It gives enterprise software an agent-facing surface: a set of tools, resources, prompts, and actions designed for AI systems to discover and use. The assistant does not need to understand the whole application the way a human user does, only the capabilities the server exposes.
This is useful, which is why vendors will ship MCP servers and why teams will enable them:
- A support assistant can retrieve context faster
- A sales assistant can prepare an account summary
- An IT assistant can inspect open incidents
- A developer assistant can query tickets, code repositories, documentation, and deployment status through a common pattern
But the same design choice creates the risk. The MCP server becomes a selective window into the enterprise. It defines what the agent can and can’t see, what actions are available, and how work appears to the assistant.
In the old model, a user moved through the application and saw the surrounding context, tabs, warnings, related records, and process cues. In the agent-facing model, the assistant may see a narrower tool description, a retrieved record, and a set of callable actions. The MCP server becomes the boundary between the agent and the business.
That is why an MCP server should not be treated as a minor connector: A connector moves data. An agent-facing surface packages part of the business for AI use.
The practical questions are what the server exposes, what it omits, which actions it allows, and who reviews those choices before the assistant starts using them in real work.
3. Why This Will Spread Through Vendors, Teams, and Partners
MCP will not enter the enterprise through one door. This is what makes it easy to underestimate.
The most visible path will be vendors. Enterprise software companies have an incentive to make their products usable by AI assistants. If work increasingly starts in an assistant, then the applications that cannot be reached from that assistant become less visible in the flow of work. A CRM system, ticketing platform, code repository, documentation tool, or support platform becomes more valuable if an agent can search it, summarize it, and call approved actions inside it.
For the vendor, an MCP server becomes a product surface. It says: here are the records agents can retrieve, the tools they can call, the workflows they can trigger, and here is how our application should appear inside an AI-assisted workstream.
That is why vendor-shipped MCP servers look like product enhancements from companies the enterprise already trusts, not like rogue infrastructure.
The second path is internal teams. Developers, IT operations teams, data teams, and business technologists will build MCP servers because they solve immediate problems. A team wants an assistant to query a documentation portal, inspect a ticket queue, search a repository, pull metrics, or check the status of an internal workflow. Building a small server around that use case may be faster than waiting for an official roadmap, a centralized integration project, or a vendor-built connector.
The third path is partners. Systems integrators, implementation partners, managed service providers, and specialist consultants already build connective tissue around enterprise systems. As MCP becomes a common way to expose tools and context to agents, partners will use it inside delivery work. They may build a server that connects a client workflow to a vendor platform, exposes implementation status, retrieves project artifacts, or lets an assistant operate across a custom process.
The server may be useful but may also sit in an awkward ownership zone after go-live: The vendor does not fully own it, the partner may not maintain it forever, and the client may depend on it before it has been added to the formal architecture map.
Let’s return to the support example.
The first MCP server came from the trusted service-platform vendor. Later, an internal operations team exposed escalation notes through a small internal server. Then an implementation partner added another server for deployment status during a client rollout. Each server made sense. Each solved a real workflow problem. None looked large enough to trigger a major architecture review.
Together, they created a fragmented agent-facing access layer.
That is the practical problem. Vendor, internal, and partner-built MCP servers may look different in procurement and security review. In production, the assistant experiences them as callable tools. The enterprise has to understand the combined surface: what agents can discover, what they can retrieve and change, and who owns each path after it becomes part of work.
4. What Leaders Should Review Before They Enable It
The practical answer is not to block MCP servers that help teams retrieve context faster, reduce manual clicking, and make enterprise software easier for assistants to use. What truly matters is whether the enterprise reviews the server before it becomes part of the work.
The review should start with a simple classification: what kind of surface is this?
A read-only server that searches product documentation is one kind of exposure. A server that retrieves client records is another. A server that can update ticket status, change account fields, trigger escalation workflows, or send client messages belongs in a different category. Those are not just data-access questions. They change the operational state of work.
In the support example, the company could have enabled the read-only tools first. Let the assistant summarize the ticket, retrieve account history, and find the standard workflow. That would have saved time without changing the case. The higher-risk step was allowing the assistant to move the escalation to monitoring and generate a client update before anyone had reviewed what context the server could not see.
Which leads to the second question: what does the server omit?
Many enterprise failures do not come from one system being completely wrong. They come from one system being partly right. The service platform knew the fix package was available. It knew the standard support workflow and the account record. But it did not know the deployment exception sitting in the engineering system. The assistant was operating inside that partial view.
Before enabling an MCP server, leaders should ask which surrounding systems are required to make the exposed actions safe. If a server can recommend an escalation change, does it also see engineering status, deployment state, client-specific exceptions, entitlement rules, SLA terms, and approval history? If it cannot see those systems, the exposed action may need a warning, a narrower scope, or a human confirmation step.
Identity is the next review point.
When the assistant calls the server, who is it acting as? The user? A service account? The vendor application? A delegated enterprise identity? Authority can become blurry once a natural-language assistant sits between the employee and the application. If the support lead approves a status change suggested by the assistant, the record should show more than a generic system update. It should show who requested it, which assistant invoked the tool, which user approved it, and what changed downstream.
Tool scoping also matters. A vendor may ship an MCP server with ten tools. The enterprise may only want three. Searching tickets, retrieving client records, and summarizing history may be acceptable on day one. Updating escalation status, sending client-facing messages, or triggering workflow changes may need separate approval. The server should not be accepted as one undifferentiated bundle.
Change visibility may be the most overlooked issue.
The first version of the server may be read-only. A later version may add write tools. Another update may change a tool description, expand the fields available to the assistant, or expose a new workflow action. If the enterprise reviews the application once and treats every future server change as a routine vendor update, the agent-facing surface can expand without a matching review.
Finally, someone has to own it.
Security may review the server. Architecture may approve the pattern. The vendor manager may track the roadmap. The business owner may care about the workflow. But once the server is live, someone needs to know which assistants use it, which actions are enabled, what logs exist, what breaks if it is disabled, and how new capabilities get reviewed.
In the support example, the mistake was not enabling the server, but enabling the action path without classifying it. Ticket search and account summarization were productivity features. But escalation changes and client updates were operational actions. They deserved a different review.
That is the operating discipline MCP requires: review the server as a product surface, classify the tools by consequence, and decide which actions an assistant can take before the server disappears into ordinary work.
5. Wrap Up: Review the Server, Not Just the Software
The company in the support example was right to take advantage of the MCP server. It helped the assistant retrieve support history, summarize the client account, and follow the standard workflow. Those are real productivity gains. The mistake was treating the server like a minor feature toggle after the application had already been approved.
The application review covered the software, but did not cover the new agent-facing surface.
That difference is key: Once an MCP server is enabled, the enterprise is no longer only deciding who can log in to the application or which systems can exchange data through an API. It is deciding what an AI assistant can discover, retrieve, recommend, and in some cases change through that product.
In the support example, the safe version would have been simple:
- Enable read-only retrieval first.
- Let the assistant summarize the ticket, account record, and standard workflow.
- Keep escalation changes, client-facing messages, and SLA-impacting status updates behind a separate review.
- Require the assistant to surface missing-context warnings when engineering deployment status is unavailable.
- Log the tool calls separately from ordinary application activity.
- Assign an owner for the MCP surface, not just the SaaS application.
This is basic operating discipline for software that agents can use.
The first answer is a review motion. The enterprise needs a basic inventory of MCP servers, but the inventory is only the start. Each server needs an owner, a source, a hosting model, a tool list, an identity path, and a change process. The review should separate retrieval from action: searching records is one class of exposure; changing status, sending messages, triggering workflows, or calling downstream systems is another. It should also account for change over time. A server that is safe when it exposes three read-only tools may become more consequential when the vendor adds a fourth tool that can update the system of record.
The longer-term answer is a control layer.
One MCP server can be reviewed manually. Ten can be tracked in a spreadsheet. But a growing mix of vendor, internal, and partner-built servers will not stay manageable that way. At some point, the enterprise needs a way to see which agents can call which tools, through which identities, against which systems, with which logs, approvals, and exception paths.
MCP will make enterprise software easier for agents to use. That is the value. It also means the application review process cannot stop at the screen, the API, or the contract. When a vendor, internal team, or partner exposes an MCP server, the enterprise is looking at a new product surface: what agents can see, what they can call, what they can change, and who owns the trace after the call.
Review the MCP server before it disappears into ordinary work.

1. The warning from pharma
AI can now produce answers faster than most enterprises can find out whether those answers work.
That gap may become one of the most important constraints in enterprise AI. The cleanest warning comes from pharma, where the cost of learning from reality has been rising for decades.
Since roughly 1950, the number of new drugs approved per billion dollars of research and development (R&D) spending has fallen by about half every nine years. Adjusted for inflation, that is often described as an almost 80-fold decline in research productivity. The industry gave the pattern a brutal name: Eroom’s Law. Moore’s Law spelled backward.
The name works because the contrast is so stark. In computing, scale made the core unit cheaper, faster, and more powerful. In drug discovery, decades of better instruments, larger datasets, computational biology, automation, and management discipline did not produce the same curve. The cost of proving what works kept rising.
That makes Eroom’s Law more than a pharma story.
Imagine a specialty materials manufacturer trying to reduce defects on a high-value production line. Its AI system can analyze sensor readings, maintenance logs, supplier inputs, temperature ranges, throughput targets, and quality data. It can recommend a new process setting in seconds.
The recommendation looks precise. But the proof does not arrive in seconds.
The line has to run. The material has to cure. Quality has to be inspected. Maintenance effects may take time to appear. A client issue may not surface until the product is already downstream.
The model made the recommendation cheap. But the business still has to pay to learn whether the recommendation survives operations.
That same pattern exists across the enterprise. AI can suggest a route, a price, a maintenance plan, a supplier substitution, a credit exception, or a claims pathway almost instantly. But the expensive part is still what happens next.
Eroom’s Law is the cleanest version of a broader enterprise problem: recommendations are getting cheaper, but proof is still expensive.
2. Prediction is the cheap part now
For the materials manufacturer, the AI recommendation feels like the breakthrough.
The production team no longer has to start from a blank page. The system can scan years of batch data, compare machine settings, read maintenance history, correlate supplier lots with quality outcomes, and flag patterns that would take engineers weeks to reconstruct manually. It can suggest which process parameter to adjust, which input material looks unstable, which machine is drifting, or which production window carries the highest defect risk.
That is real progress, and it changes the speed of analysis.
The same shift is happening across industries. Logistics teams can get route options before a planner has opened every lane constraint. Banks can summarize credit risk and surface exceptions. Insurers can classify claims and recommend a handling path. Utilities can rank asset-failure risk before maintenance teams review every record.
This is where AI has become immediately useful: it compresses the work of search, comparison, classification, synthesis, and recommendation. It can turn messy operational signals into a ranked set of options.
But that is still the front end of the loop.
A recommendation is a claim about what might work. It is not evidence that the business has learned. The model can identify the likely defect driver, the likely supplier issue, the likely route problem, or the likely credit risk. The enterprise still needs to act, observe the result, and decide whether the recommendation improved the real system.
Many companies are treating faster recommendations as faster learning. But while AI can reduce the cost of forming a hypothesis, the enterprise still has to prove whether the hypothesis improved the real system.
3. The AI recommendation meets reality
The manufacturer accepts one recommendation.
The AI suggests a small change to a process parameter on the high-value line. Nothing dramatic. A slightly different temperature range, a tighter timing window, and a throughput target that looks achievable based on prior runs. The recommendation is backed by historical data and fits what the production team already suspects: the line is capable of more than it is producing.
The first shift looks promising. Output improves, and the dashboard moves in the right direction. The recommendation appears to have worked.
But then the second-order effects start to show:
- Scrap rises on one product variant.
- A quality inspection catches a surface inconsistency that was not visible in the first yield report.
- Maintenance sees early signs of stress on a component that usually lasts longer.
- The production team realizes the setting works better with one supplier lot than another.
- A downstream client reports variation that did not appear in the standard plant metrics.
The AI was not simply wrong. That would have made the lesson easier.
It optimized against the data it could see. But operations contained variables the recommendation did not fully price in: material variation, machine wear, inspection lag, shift behavior, supplier inconsistency, client tolerance, and the difference between a clean metric and a usable product.
That is the part many AI business cases understate. Real systems do not answer cleanly or quickly. They answer through delays, exceptions, side effects, and partial signals.
The same pattern appears outside manufacturing:
- A cheaper supplier can create quality drift three steps downstream.
- A logistics route can look optimal until port congestion or customs delays erase the savings.
- A faster claims pathway can reduce handling time while increasing leakage, complaints, or litigation.
None of those cases mean the recommendation had no value. They mean the value cannot be judged at the moment the recommendation is made.
Reality is the hidden second half of the AI system.
Until the enterprise can connect the recommendation to the operational result, it has improved the speed of advice. It has not changed the learning cycle.
4. Self-driving labs show the pattern
The manufacturer’s problem is easier to see in the place where the loop is most explicit: the lab.
Self-driving labs started in experimental domains like chemistry, materials science, and drug discovery. They are often described as robot chemists. But the useful idea is the loop: a system can form a hypothesis, run an experiment, measure the result, learn from the outcome, and choose the next experiment.
With the loop, action and measurement are connected tightly enough for the next decision to improve.
