That is what makes the pattern different from ordinary automation: A conventional automated system runs a predefined process faster. But a self-driving lab changes the next experiment based on what the last one revealed. It reduces the time between idea, evidence, and adjustment.
That is the lesson for the materials manufacturer.
The plant does not need to become a lab in the literal sense. It needs to copy the useful part: treat the AI recommendation as the start of a controlled test, measure what happens, and use the result to improve the next decision.
The company can take one process setting and test it on a defined product variant, shift, machine, or batch window. It can watch not only throughput, but scrap, rework, machine stress, quality variation, and downstream client issues. It can compare the result against the prior setting, record which conditions made the recommendation work and which conditions made it fail. Then the next recommendation has a better picture of the line.
That is the practical value of the self-driving lab idea outside science: It gives leaders a pattern for turning AI from a recommendation engine into a learning system.
Every industry has its own version of the lab. In another business, the “lab” may be a factory floor, a logistics network, a claims operation, or an IT estate.
The lab is just the visible version of what every operating business wants: a shorter path from idea to evidence.
5. Most enterprises waste their failures
After the production issue, the manufacturer looks back at previous attempts to improve the same line.
The useful evidence is everywhere and nowhere:
- One engineer remembers that a similar temperature change caused problems last year.
- A maintenance ticket mentions unusual wear after a prior throughput push.
- A quality report shows a defect pattern that appeared for only one product variant.
- Procurement has notes on a supplier lot that behaved differently from the others.
- A shift supervisor remembers that the setting worked better at night, when the line ran with a different crew and fewer changeovers.
All of this is valuable. And most of it is exactly the kind of evidence the next recommendation needs.
But the business did not preserve it as learning data. It preserved it as fragments: ticket comments, meeting notes, dashboard anomalies, email threads, local memory, and after-action explanations.
Successful changes made their way into the process. But failed attempts stayed behind as ticket comments, meeting notes, and things experienced operators remembered.
Most companies are better at recording transactions than experiments. They know what was ordered, approved, shipped, paid, closed, repaired, or escalated. They are less disciplined about preserving what was tried, what was rejected, what almost worked, what failed under specific conditions, and what an experienced operator overrode before it became visible in the metrics. And sometimes organizational politics get in the way of understanding why something failed.
If AI only learns from completed transactions and approved decisions, it sees a cleaned-up version of the business. It sees what survived the process, not the rough terrain around it:
- It may know the final supplier, but not the rejected substitute that failed quality review.
- It may know the approved maintenance plan, but not the workaround that prevented a larger outage.
- It may know the successful production setting, but not the boundary conditions that made nearby settings fail.
Failure data is not operational debris. It is the map of the terrain.
The practical question for leaders is simple:
Where does the business already pay for failed attempts, but fail to keep the learning?
That is where AI’s value is capped. A company that cannot remember its failed experiments will keep asking AI to make recommendations inside a partial picture of reality.
6. The practical question: where is your learning loop slow?
Eventually, the manufacturer’s attention shifts from the model to the loop.
The company has to stop treating AI adoption as the question. It already added AI: the system can analyze data, surface patterns, and recommend changes faster than the production team could do manually.
The subsequent question is: where does the business learn too slowly?
On the high-value line, the problem is easy to see. The team changes process settings constantly. When the setting is wrong, the cost shows up in scrap, rework, downtime, warranty exposure, and dissatisfied clients.
But the evidence arrives in pieces. Yield shows up quickly. Machine stress takes longer. Supplier variation may take several batches. Client impact may come later still.
That is a learning loop worth improving.
The same test applies across the enterprise. The best candidates are repeated decisions with measurable consequences: pricing changes, maintenance deferrals, supplier substitutions, logistics reroutes, credit exceptions, claims pathways, and production settings.
The practical inspection starts with five questions.
- Where do we make repeated decisions under uncertainty?
- Where does the outcome arrive late, indirectly, or in another system?
- Where do failed attempts, operator overrides, and near misses disappear?
- Where can we test a recommendation on a smaller slice before scaling it?
- Where would faster learning improve margin, uptime, quality, safety, capital efficiency, or client experience?
That last question is key because not every loop deserves the same attention. Some decisions are too rare or too hard to measure. Some changes take too long to evaluate. And some use cases are interesting but operationally trivial.
The best candidates usually have four traits:
- The decision happens repeatedly
- Mistakes are expensive
- Outcomes can be measured
- The business can compare alternatives without redesigning the whole operating model
That is where AI has something concrete to improve. The use case is the company’s ability to turn each recommendation into better evidence for the next decision.
The best AI use case may be the loop where the company is already paying too much to learn too slowly.
7. What leaders should build first
The manufacturer does not need to redesign the whole plant.
It starts with one repeated decision on one production line: which process setting to use for a specific product family. The scope is small enough to manage and important enough to matter. The line runs often, the cost of mistakes is visible, and the company already has the data. The problem is that the data is organized around production, quality, and maintenance, not around learning from each recommendation.
The first build is a simple learning loop:
1. Define the decision. In this case, the decision is the process setting the AI recommends before the run.
2. Define the action. The action is the controlled change made on the line: machine, shift, batch window, product variant, supplier lot, and operating conditions.
3. Define the outcome. The outcome is not one metric. It includes yield, scrap, rework, inspection results, machine stress, maintenance notes, and downstream quality signals.
4. Capture the exceptions. Record when operators override the recommendation, when the setting is rejected, when the result is mixed, and when the apparent win creates a later problem.
5. Compare alternatives. Don’t just ask whether the AI recommendation worked, but where it worked, under which conditions, compared with what previous setting, and at what downstream cost.
6. Feed the result forward. The next recommendation should be shaped by the prior result, including the failed attempts and boundary conditions.
Implementation starts with a shared record of the loop. Each recommendation needs a trace: what the system recommended, what evidence it used, who approved the test, where the change was applied, which conditions were present, what outcome followed, which exceptions appeared, and what changed for the next decision. The evidence will usually sit across production systems, quality reports, maintenance tickets, supplier records, operator notes, and downstream client issues. The work is to connect those signals around the decision. Without that record, the company is only running faster recommendations, not building memory.
That same pattern applies outside manufacturing. Pick one decision that repeats, costs money when wrong, and produces observable outcomes. Do not start with a portfolio of AI pilots. Start with one loop where better feedback can change the next decision.
The useful metric is learning cycle time: how long it takes to move from recommendation, to action, to observed result, to a better next decision.
That is where leaders should begin. Make one loop learn faster.
8. Wrap Up: The advantage is learning speed
The manufacturer does not win because the model generates more recommendations.
It wins when each recommendation makes the next one better:
- The process setting is tested
- The result is measured
- The exception is captured
- The failed condition is preserved
- The next decision carries more evidence than the last one
That is the practical lesson behind Eroom’s Law. Pharma gave the pattern a name because its productivity crisis was impossible to ignore. Other industries may not call it Eroom’s Law, but many live with their own version: rising cost, slow experimentation, fragmented feedback, and wasted failure data.
AI will keep making prediction cheaper. That’s important, but prediction is only the start of the operating cycle.
The larger advantage belongs to companies that reduce the cost of learning from the real world.
AI will make answers cheaper. The companies that win will make learning cheaper too.

1. The code is done. The work is still stuck.
The pull request is ready before lunch.
A developer opened an issue in the morning, pointed a coding agent at the repo, and asked for the change. The agent read the surrounding code, proposed an approach, wrote the first version, generated tests, explained the diff, and opened the PR. Work that might have taken a day now took an hour.
That is real progress. It changes the developer’s day. It reduces the blank-page problem, makes unfamiliar code easier to approach, and helps teams clear routine work that used to sit in the backlog for weeks.
Then the pull request waits.
It waits for an environment that has not been provisioned. It waits for access to a service account. It waits for dependency review, security findings, test data, network configuration, architecture approval, compliance evidence, or a release window. The code moved quickly. The delivery system did not.
Software does not reach production because code exists. It reaches production through controls, handoffs, and evidence. Some of those controls are technical: CI/CD pipelines, secrets management, vulnerability scans, infrastructure templates, deployment policies, rollback plans, observability hooks, and integration tests. Others are organizational: ownership, approval rights, change records, operational readiness, funding, and accountability.
In large enterprises, those controls are slow for a reason. Production software touches clients, employees, regulated data, critical infrastructure, revenue, and operational continuity. A bank cannot treat a credit-risk change like a personal script. A healthcare platform cannot ship a dependency upgrade without knowing what patient workflow it touches. An airline cannot modernize a scheduling service without understanding downstream systems, batch windows, and operational fallbacks.
AI coding agents make implementation faster. They do not automatically make the enterprise delivery system faster.
In some cases, they create more pressure downstream. More pull requests arrive. More fixes are proposed. More modernization candidates appear. Security, platform, compliance, architecture, and operations teams still have to decide what is safe to release, what needs more evidence, and who accepts the risk.
The code may be ready in an hour.
The software is not shipped until the enterprise can trust the path it took.
2. Coding assistants and agentic SDLC are different categories
The market still talks about AI software tools as if the main contest is code generation.
Most AI software tools are evaluated at the coding surface: Which tool writes the better function? Which one understands the repository faster? Which one produces cleaner tests? Which one fits best inside the IDE? Those questions are important, but they measure the part of software delivery closest to implementation.
That is the coding-assistant category.
A coding assistant lives inside the developer’s loop. It helps a developer understand the task, inspect the codebase, modify files, generate tests, explain the diff, and prepare the pull request. Its useful context is local: the repo, the issue, the surrounding code, the developer’s instructions, and the immediate build or test result.
The next category is larger.
Call it agentic SDLC: AI systems that help software work move across planning, coding, review, testing, security, release, modernization, and operations. In that category, the agent is judged by more than its ability to generate code. It is judged by whether it can understand the path a change has to travel before the enterprise can release it.
That changes the design problem.
An agent working across the SDLC needs to understand more than the repository. It needs enough delivery context to know what kind of change this is, where risk enters, and which controls shape the path forward.
It also needs to know when to slow down.
A routine internal fix may move through a lightweight path. A change touching regulated data, identity, payments, client-facing workflows, brittle integrations, or critical infrastructure requires a different chain of checks. The agent has to recognize that difference before the work reaches the final review queue.
In practice, that means the agent should do more than open a pull request. It should classify the change, surface affected services, attach relevant security findings, identify the approval path, check release readiness, and capture the evidence the next reviewer will need.
A well-written patch can still be blocked. It can pass unit tests and still miss a dependency. It can modernize a local component and still break a downstream workflow. It can close the issue and still fail the release process.
That is why the enterprise evaluation cannot stop at code quality.
The stronger system is the one that understands the route from change to production, not only the code inside the pull request.
For individual developers, the coding loop is the natural starting point.
For enterprises, the larger contest is the SDLC itself.
3. The harness is the missing layer between model and delivery
The model gets most of the attention because the model is the visible intelligence. It writes the function, explains the error, drafts the test, and proposes the fix.
But enterprise software delivery is not shaped by model capability alone.
The agent needs a surrounding system that determines what it can see, what it can touch, what it must check, and what record it leaves behind. That surrounding system is the harness.
In this context, the harness is the operating layer around the agent: context retrieval, tool permissions, workflow state, policy checks, CI/CD integration, evidence capture, evaluation, logging, and audit. It connects the model to the delivery system without letting the model become an unmanaged actor inside it.
A personal coding setup can run with a light harness. The agent sees the repo, follows a few local instructions, calls a command-line tool, and depends on the developer to catch what is missing. The developer supplies the institutional memory: which shortcut is safe, which test is meaningful, which service is fragile, which reviewer will care, which deployment pattern has caused trouble before.
Enterprise SDLC cannot depend on that much personal interpretation.
The harness has to carry enough of the delivery system to make the agent useful beyond code generation. It should know the work item, the approved engineering patterns, the relevant policies, the pipeline state, the release process, and the evidence expected by reviewers, auditors, and operations teams.
This is where many coding-agent deployments will hit their limit.
A stronger model may produce a cleaner patch. It may explain the diff more clearly. It may generate better tests. But if the harness cannot connect the work to dependency posture, security review, release readiness, change records, rollback planning, and operational handoff, the agent is still producing output at the edge of the delivery system.
The harness determines whether the agent is merely writing code or participating in controlled work.
For a routine fix, the harness may only need to confirm ownership, run tests, attach evidence, and prepare the pull request. For a sensitive change, it may need to check data classification, affected services, approved patterns, vulnerability findings, policy exceptions, release windows, and required approvers before the work can move.
That is why model improvement does not remove the need for the harness. It increases it.
As agents become more capable, they need richer context, clearer permissions, stronger evaluation, and a better record of what happened. The enterprise has to know which systems shaped the recommendation, which tools were called, which checks passed, which exceptions were raised, and where human judgment entered the path.
The model may write the code.
The harness determines whether the work can move through the enterprise.
4. Modernization proves code generation is insufficient
The waiting pull request becomes even more revealing when the work is modernization.
A coding agent can translate a function, update a syntax pattern, explain an unfamiliar class, or draft the first pass of a migration. In an old codebase, that is useful. Many enterprise systems contain logic that survived multiple owners, expired documentation, uneven naming conventions, and years of urgent fixes. Even basic comprehension can save time.
But modernization rarely fails because one function could not be rewritten.
It fails when the rewritten code changes behavior the enterprise did not understand.
A Java upgrade can change a serialization pattern that a downstream service quietly depends on. A framework migration can alter an authentication flow that behaves differently under production traffic. A dependency replacement may pass unit tests and still break the month-end batch job. Mainframe modernization can produce cleaner code while stripping out the operating assumptions that made the old system safe to run.
That is why the opening pull request waits.
The enterprise has to know what the change connects to, which systems depend on the current behavior, which data formats and integration contracts are exposed, which performance assumptions are buried in the old implementation, and which tests prove equivalence. It also has to know who owns the cutover, what rollback path exists, which operations team needs to prepare, and what evidence will satisfy audit, resilience, and risk.
The coding work may be the most visible part of modernization. It is rarely the whole job.
A coding assistant can help the developer move faster through the codebase. But agentic SDLC has a harder assignment: help the organization move safely through the change. That requires dependency awareness, approved migration patterns, security checks, test strategy, release planning, rollback paths, and evidence captured as the work progresses.
This is where the harness becomes practical. The agent needs enough context to see modernization as a delivery change, not a code rewrite: architecture, dependencies, deployment history, operational constraints, and the policies that determine whether the work can move forward.
Without that layer, modernization becomes a faster way to produce uncertain software.
The code may be cleaner. The syntax may be current. The tests may pass. But the enterprise still has to answer the more difficult question: whether the new implementation preserves the behavior, obligations, and operating assumptions that made the old system safe to run.
Modernization is controlled change, not translated syntax.
5. Runtime governance is too narrow for SDLC
A coding agent can be governed at the moment it acts.
The enterprise can control who invokes it, which repository it can reach, what tools it can call, which logs are captured, and which actions require approval. Those controls are important. Without identity, permissions, logging, and auditability, the agent becomes another unmanaged actor inside the software estate.
But SDLC risk does not end with the agent action.
The agent may have permission to write code and still produce a change that is unsafe to release. The pull request may be legitimate. The developer may be authorized. The repository access may be approved. The logs may show exactly what happened. None of that proves the change moved through the right delivery path.
The risk lives in the change itself.
A small UI fix, a dependency upgrade, and a modification to an identity workflow may all begin as code changes. They should not move through the same controls. One may need only tests and review. Another may require vulnerability evidence, architecture review, operational signoff, or a release window. A third may need stronger scrutiny because it changes how access is granted, logged, or revoked.
Runtime governance can tell the enterprise what the agent did.
SDLC governance has to tell the enterprise whether the change received the right level of scrutiny for the risk it introduced.
That requires governance to move with the work across planning, coding, review, testing, release, and operations. The enterprise needs to know whether the requirement was understood, whether the architecture was respected, whether dependencies were checked, whether security findings were resolved, whether test evidence is sufficient, whether the release path is valid, and whether operations can support the change after it ships.
Faster code generation pushes more unfinished decisions into the same review queues.
When coding agents generate more pull requests, more fixes, and more modernization candidates, they increase the volume of work entering the delivery system. If governance remains concentrated at execution time, the enterprise may see the agent’s actions clearly while still lacking confidence that the software is ready to ship.
That means risk classification, policy checks, approval paths, test evidence, release readiness, exception handling, and operational ownership should be attached to the work itself. The change record should not become a reconstruction exercise after the useful context has already scattered across tickets, pull request comments, chat threads, and meetings.
The point is not to add another review queue, but to make the path visible enough that the enterprise can distinguish routine work from sensitive work, lightweight review from required escalation, and a clean release from an unexamined shortcut.
Runtime governance records the agent’s action.
SDLC governance records whether the change passed the controls required for its risk.
6. The governed path has to become faster than the workaround
The goal is not to help agents route around enterprise controls. That would create a faster version of shadow IT: more code, more undocumented exceptions, more release pressure, and more risk pushed downstream.
The goal is to make the governed path easier to use than the workaround.
Return to the pull request from the opening. The code is ready before lunch, but the work is waiting on an environment, service account, dependency review, security findings, test data, architecture approval, compliance evidence, or a release window.
An agentic SDLC system should make those blockers visible while the work is still moving. It should recognize that the change touches a payment service, identify affected downstream systems, attach relevant vulnerability findings, prepare the change record, generate the test evidence request, find the right approver, and explain why the release path is blocked.
Governance shows up before the pull request reaches the final queue.
The developer does not have to chase five systems to understand why the work is stuck. The security reviewer does not have to reconstruct context from a diff and a vague ticket. The compliance team does not have to assemble evidence after release, when the useful details have already scattered across chat threads, pull request comments, and meeting notes.
The agent should capture the evidence while the work is happening.
For routine changes, the path can be lighter: confirm ownership, run tests, attach evidence, and move the pull request forward. For sensitive changes, the path can require more evidence, clearer escalation, and explicit risk acceptance. The value is that the path becomes visible, risk-adjusted, and harder to bypass.
The agent can help generate test evidence, draft the rollback plan, prepare release notes, surface affected services, route exceptions, and explain what still prevents the change from moving forward. Done well, the governed path becomes the easiest path because it is the clearest path.
If the workaround is faster, people will use the workaround.
Enterprise software delivery will not get meaningfully faster until the controlled path becomes easier to follow than the shortcut.
7. Wrap Up: Once embedded in SDLC, the agent becomes infrastructure
A coding assistant can remain a tool at the edge of the developer’s day.
An agent embedded in the SDLC becomes something else. It starts to learn how the enterprise builds software: which systems are fragile, which reviews matter, which exceptions recur, which teams own the risk, which release paths are trusted, and which evidence has to exist before a change can go live.
That knowledge is more strategic than code suggestions.
Once delivery memory lives inside the agent, vendor choice becomes harder. The enterprise is no longer moving only a model, an IDE plugin, or a chat surface. It is moving release logic, approval patterns, policy interpretation, modernization history, and operational memory.
Those are sovereignty questions inside the SDLC.
Delivery memory has to live somewhere. If it disappears into one agent surface, the enterprise loses more than prompts or chat history. It loses release logic, approval patterns, policy interpretation, modernization history, and the record of how risk was accepted.
That becomes a hard question after the fact: can leaders reconstruct how the agent shaped a release, why the work moved forward, why it stopped, and who accepted the risk?
This is where my previous article’s shared-agent problem becomes concrete:
Once agents become shared, personal behavior can become institutional behavior. In software delivery, that institutional behavior can shape how code is reviewed, how modernization happens, how exceptions are handled, how releases move, and how risk is accepted.
The coding agent may start as a productivity tool.
But the moment it becomes part of the governed path to production, it becomes part of the enterprise’s delivery infrastructure. It should be treated that way: with clear ownership, portable context, observable behavior, lifecycle controls, and an audit trail that survives the tool surface where the work began.
The code can be ready before lunch.
The release still waits for something harder: trust in the path from change to production.
That is where the next software contest moves: from who can generate the most code to who controls the path from change to production.

1. The personal agent worked because it was personal
The first version felt almost harmless.
A product lead built a small agent around her own work. It read her backlog notes, scanned customer calls, checked the roadmap, looked at open engineering issues, and drafted a product review before every planning meeting. Over time, she tuned it to her taste. It learned that she cared about adoption signals more than internal excitement. It knew she wanted engineering risk called out early. It knew vague customer demand should be treated differently from a signed expansion opportunity. It knew which executives needed a crisp summary and which architects wanted the underlying tradeoff.
It was useful because it was personal.
The agent acted inside one person’s working style. It used her access, her context, her habits, and her judgment. When it was too optimistic, she corrected it. When it missed a dependency, she added the note. When it drafted something clumsy, she rewrote it. The feedback loop was informal, but it worked because the person closest to the work was also the person closest to the agent.
Then the team wanted to use it.
The request sounded reasonable. Put the agent in Slack. Let anyone ask it to review a feature plan. Connect it to Linear, GitHub, and the shared customer folder. Let it prepare the same kind of review for every product pod.
That is where the agent changed categories.
The agent was no longer reflecting one person’s judgment. It was starting to shape the team’s judgment. The same review pattern that had been a private shortcut could now influence how features were prioritized, how risks were described, which customer signals were treated as strong evidence, and which engineering concerns were escalated before release.
Helpfulness was no longer the only operating issue. The harder issue was whose standards the agent was applying.
A personal agent can be governed by proximity. The user invokes it, watches it, corrects it, rejects the weak parts, and owns the consequence when it gets something wrong. That does not make personal agents safe. But it keeps the failure surface closer to one person’s access, attention, and judgment.
Once the agent moves into the places where teams coordinate work, it becomes part of the operating environment.
The first enterprise agent problem begins before full autonomy.
It begins when the agent becomes shared.
2. The model is not the system
The first governance mistake is to look only at the model.
The model may be impressive. It can reason through a product brief, summarize a customer call, inspect a pull request, find contradictions in requirements, and draft a cleaner plan. But inside an enterprise, the model is only one part of the working system.
The more important question is what surrounds it.
What context does the agent receive before it starts? Which documents does it trust? Which tickets, repositories, dashboards, and meeting notes can it reach? What tools can it call? What systems can it write to? What memory does it keep? What evidence does it preserve before its work becomes visible, actionable, or reusable?
That surrounding system is the harness.
The model reasons, but the harness determines how reasoning becomes work. It supplies context, limits tools, controls write access, manages memory, routes output, captures evidence, and enforces when a human has to review the result.
This is why two teams can use the same model and get very different outcomes.
One team has a fragile personal setup. A user opens a chat window, pastes context, asks for a review, copies the answer into Slack, updates the ticket manually, and tries to remember which corrections should be reused next time. The model may be strong, but the workflow depends on individual discipline.
Another team has the same model inside a governed workflow. The agent pulls from approved sources, checks the right tickets and documents, records which evidence it used, drafts the review in the right workspace, flags uncertainty, asks for approval when the risk crosses a threshold, and preserves the correction for future use.
Same model. Different system.
For a personal agent, the harness can be loose because the user fills the gaps. The user remembers the context, filters the answer, applies judgment, and catches many of the mistakes. In shared work, those gaps become institutional risk. The agent is no longer just helping one person think. It is helping the team move work through a repeatable path.
That is why the enterprise cannot govern only the model. It has to govern the system that makes model reasoning operational.
Once the harness becomes shared, private working style can become organizational machinery.
3. Preferences become policy
The risk shows up in the reusable skill.
A product lead creates a command for herself: /plan-pm-review.
The command reviews a feature plan before the weekly product meeting. It checks whether the client evidence is strong enough, whether the engineering dependency is real or speculative, whether the release risk is being softened, whether the success metric is meaningful, and whether the plan needs executive attention before the team spends another sprint on it.
Over time, the command gets sharper. The product lead corrects it. She tells it which customer signals count. She teaches it that three enthusiastic comments from sales are not the same as demand from a committed buyer. She reinforces that architectural debt should be named plainly. She pushes it to separate urgency from importance.
The command becomes useful because it carries her judgment.
Inside her own workflow, that is fine. It is a private review habit encoded into a personal agent. She still reads the output, makes the call, and owns the consequences.
Then the command becomes shared.
Someone adds it to the team agent in Slack. Now anyone can drop in a feature plan and ask for a product review. The agent responds with the same structure, the same weighting, the same escalation logic, and the same language for describing risk.
At first, this feels like leverage. The team gets more consistent reviews. Junior product managers learn what a strong plan looks like. Engineering gets clearer signals. Leadership sees a cleaner summary.
But the organization has also changed something important.
One person’s review style has become a reusable pattern for the team. Her preferences about evidence, risk, urgency, architecture, and escalation are now embedded in a shared workflow. They may be good preferences. They may even be better than the old process. That does not make them neutral.
A shared agent can make a judgment pattern feel procedural. It can make one way of seeing the work feel like the standard way. Over time, people may stop asking where the pattern came from. They may treat the output as the team’s review logic rather than one person’s encoded judgment.
The enterprise does not need to turn every prompt into a policy artifact. Most personal shortcuts should stay lightweight. But reusable skills that shape shared work need a different standard. If a skill affects prioritization, risk classification, release readiness, escalation, customer impact, security review, or financial analysis, it needs ownership.
Someone should know who created it, what judgment it encodes, when it was last reviewed, what evidence it uses, and when it should be revised or retired.
In a personal agent, a preference is a preference.
In a shared agent, a preference can become policy.
4. Memory becomes governance
If a shared skill can turn preference into policy, shared memory can make that policy durable.
A personal agent remembers for one person. It may remember how that person likes a briefing structured, which accounts matter this quarter, which risks should be called out, or which product assumptions have already been challenged. The memory is useful because it saves the user from restating the same context every time.
A shared agent remembers differently.
It may preserve a correction from one review and apply it to the next team’s work. It may learn that certain customer signals are strong, that certain security risks deserve escalation, that a particular architecture pattern is preferred, or that a class of objections should be treated as low priority. Some of that memory will improve the system. Some of it may quietly distort it.
The risk is not only that the agent gets something wrong once. The risk is that the wrong pattern becomes reusable.
A weak assumption can become part of the next recommendation. An outdated compliance interpretation can appear in future reviews. A shortcut used under deadline pressure can become normal. A product leader’s preference can be remembered as if it were a team standard. A temporary exception can survive long after the reason for it disappeared.
At that point, memory becomes part of the governance surface.
Enterprises should not treat shared agent memory as a bottomless notes field. They need to know what kind of memory is being created and who it is allowed to influence. A private correction should not automatically become team memory. A team pattern should not automatically become enterprise memory. A project-specific exception should not become a general rule.
At minimum, shared memory needs provenance. Who contributed it? What evidence supported it? Was it inferred by the agent or approved by a person? When was it last validated? Where has it been reused? How can it be corrected, rejected, superseded, or retired?
These questions are practical. Without them, the enterprise has no reliable way to tell whether the agent is improving with use or accumulating institutional noise.
The appeal of shared memory is obvious. A team agent that learns from repeated work can reduce friction, preserve judgment, and make good practices easier to reuse. But the same mechanism can preserve bad judgment with equal confidence.
In a personal agent, memory is convenience.
In a shared agent, memory is governance.
5. Seven checks before a shared agent scales
The practical test is simple: before a personal agent becomes a shared agent, the enterprise should know what kind of institutional behavior it is about to create.
That does not require a large governance ceremony for every experiment. It does require a sharper review before the agent becomes part of shared work.
Start with seven questions.
Who does the agent act as?
A personal agent usually acts with one person’s access. A shared agent may act for a requester, a team, a service account, or a bounded agent identity. That choice changes everything downstream. It determines what the agent can see, what it can touch, and who is accountable when it acts.
What authority does it have?
The enterprise should know whether the agent can only summarize, whether it can recommend, write to systems, open tickets, trigger workflows, and whether it can make changes that affect clients, employees, infrastructure, money, or compliance.
What can it remember?
Memory should have scope. Private memory should stay private. Team memory should not automatically become enterprise memory. A project exception should not become a general rule. The enterprise needs a way to correct, reject, supersede, or retire memory when it is wrong, outdated, or too narrow for broader reuse.
Who owns the skills?
Reusable skills should have owners when they affect shared work. A skill that drafts a meeting summary may not need much oversight. A skill that shapes release readiness, risk classification, escalation, financial analysis, client prioritization, or security review needs more discipline. Someone should know who created it, what it encodes, when it was last reviewed, and how it is changed.
How is behavior evaluated?
A shared agent needs more than user satisfaction. It needs tests for quality, drift, regression, policy adherence, cost, and recurring failure patterns. The enterprise should be able to tell whether the agent is improving with use or simply becoming more confident in its own habits.
When does it stop or escalate?
A shared agent should have clear limits. It should know when to ask for approval, when to route work to a human, when to flag uncertainty, and when to stop because the action is outside its authority. Escalation is not a weakness. It is how the enterprise keeps judgment attached to accountable people.
Who owns it over time?
Shared agents need stewardship. Without ownership, memory bloats, skills drift, access exceptions accumulate, costs rise, and shortcuts become hidden operating rules. An agent steward does not babysit every task. The steward owns the health of the shared agent as an institutional system.
This is the line enterprises should watch. A shared agent can begin as a helpful assistant and slowly become shadow infrastructure. It may sit in the channels where work is assigned, the tools where decisions are recorded, and the systems where actions are triggered. If no one owns its identity, authority, memory, skills, evaluation, escalation, and lifecycle, the organization may not notice when the agent stops reflecting an approved way of working.
The question is not whether the agent works once.
The question is whether the enterprise can govern how it keeps working.
6. The control plane becomes the consequence
The seven questions point to the same conclusion: once agents become shared, governance cannot live only inside prompts, skill files, or team habits.
A personal prompt can be messy because one person absorbs the mess. A shared agent needs a more durable layer around it. The enterprise has to know who the agent is acting for, what it is allowed to do, which memories it can reuse, which skills are approved, what evidence it must leave behind, and when it has to stop.
That is the role of the control plane.
The control plane is not another agent. It is the layer that governs the conditions under which agents can act. It should make identity explicit, bind authority to role and context, preserve traces, enforce policy, route exceptions, monitor behavior, and support shutdown when an agent no longer meets the standard.
This becomes more important as models improve.
A smarter model may need fewer brittle chains and less hand-holding. It may plan better, recover from failure, summarize more accurately, and carry longer tasks across more context. That does not remove the enterprise’s need for control. Identity, authority, auditability, escalation, rollback, and ownership are responsibility problems. Better reasoning does not make them disappear.
In fact, better reasoning can make the control problem sharper. A weak agent fails close to the user. A capable shared agent can move farther before anyone notices the pattern it is applying. It can touch more systems, reuse more memory, route more work, and make its output feel more procedural because it is coherent.
That is why shared agents need controls outside the agent’s own judgment.
Some controls can be flexible. Others have to be deterministic. A product review agent may be allowed to summarize evidence, identify risks, and propose next steps. It should not be able to rewrite the team’s release criteria, change a client commitment, approve an exception, or commit a new reusable rule without review.
The control plane exists to make those boundaries enforceable.
It also protects the future. Shared agents will change. Models will change. Skills will change. Teams will change. Regulations, costs, vendors, and operating requirements will change. If institutional memory, authority, and workflow logic are buried inside local prompts or one vendor’s agent surface, the enterprise loses leverage.
Once the agent becomes shared, governance has to move out of the prompt and into the control plane.
7. Wrap Up
This is the part of enterprise AI that can look ordinary while it is still small.
A useful personal agent becomes a shared team agent. A shortcut becomes a skill. A correction becomes memory. A preference becomes a pattern. The agent starts showing up in the places where work already happens, and the organization gets the benefit before it fully understands the dependency.
That is why the first governance threshold is not full autonomy.
It is sharing.
Once an agent becomes shared, it can shape how teams review work, classify risk, preserve judgment, escalate issues, and reuse prior decisions. Some of that will make the enterprise better. It will reduce repeated work, spread good practices, and help teams move with more consistency.
But shared agents also create a new kind of institutional machinery. They can carry old assumptions forward. They can make one person’s judgment look procedural. They can preserve a temporary exception as if it were a rule. They can quietly normalize patterns no one formally approved.
The point is not to slow every agent down with process. The point is to know when an agent has crossed from personal productivity into shared infrastructure.
That is the line enterprises need to see clearly.
The next version of this problem shows up in software delivery. Coding agents can help developers move faster, but production still runs through provisioning, security, compliance, network configuration, testing, deployment automation, rollback, and operational ownership.
The next article will look at that gap.
Coding agents can write the code.
They still cannot ship the enterprise.

1. The Enterprise Buys Software. The State Sees Infrastructure.
Enterprise procurement has long been built around vendor risk. Frontier AI adds a deeper exposure: dependence on capabilities shaped by compute, infrastructure, regulation, and state interest.
Procurement becomes harder when the dependency is shaped by power outside the contract.
Imagine a global bank evaluating a frontier AI security system. On paper, the purchase looks familiar. Procurement sees a vendor review. The CISO sees faster vulnerability detection. The board sees a cleaner cyber-risk story: fewer blind spots, faster remediation, better evidence, stronger resilience.
Everyone around the table thinks they are evaluating software.
But the same capability may look very different from outside the enterprise.
A model that can map dependencies across critical systems, reason through access paths, identify brittle infrastructure, and accelerate remediation belongs in a different category from dashboards and scanners. In the right hands, it can help defend critical infrastructure. In the wrong hands, it can expose it.
At that point, the product stops looking purely commercial.
The more difficult procurement consideration begins after purchase: what happens when the capability becomes part of how the enterprise defends itself? Once vulnerability discovery, exposure mapping, remediation planning, and incident response begin moving at machine speed, the system becomes part of the enterprise’s defensive posture rather than an occasional tool.
The enterprise may want to consume the capability commercially. The vendor may want to sell it at scale. But a government may see something else: a strategic cyber capability sitting inside the private market.
That tension is easy to miss because enterprise AI still arrives wearing familiar clothes. It comes through sales decks, pilots, procurement workflows, security reviews, integration plans, and subscription terms. It looks like the next generation of enterprise software.
But frontier AI does not behave like ordinary software.
It depends on scarce chips, energy, data centers, cloud capacity, model access, security restrictions, jurisdiction, and national-security pressure. The deeper it moves into security, finance, industrial operations, and critical infrastructure, the less credible it becomes to treat it as just another product category.
The risk is not only vendor lock-in. It is strategic dependency: the point where an enterprise can buy, integrate, and depend on a capability, but still not control the forces that determine whether it remains available, unrestricted, affordable, commercially usable, or governed only by contract.
That is the end of innocent AI procurement.
2. The SaaS Mental Model Is Breaking
Enterprise software used to hide its machinery.
That was part of the appeal. A vendor delivered the application. The enterprise evaluated the features, negotiated the contract, reviewed the security posture, checked the integrations, and monitored the service level. If the product worked, the machinery behind it mostly stayed out of view.
That mental model shaped a generation of technology procurement:
- Could the vendor deliver?
- Would the system integrate?
- Was the data protected?
- Could the contract manage uptime, liability, support, renewal, and exit?
Frontier AI adds questions that traditional SaaS procurement was not built to answer. It brings the hidden machinery back into the open because the capability depends on things enterprise buyers cannot treat as background assumptions: advanced chips, concentrated data centers, electrical capacity, cloud regions, model access, inference economics, cybersecurity controls, data residency, export restrictions, and government scrutiny.
It also breaks a basic assumption of enterprise control: that change can be isolated. Traditional procurement assumes the enterprise can evaluate a product, test the integration, monitor the vendor, and manage changes through release cycles. Frontier AI makes that harder because the model, policy layer, training data, inference environment, cloud region, pricing, safety restrictions, and regulatory posture may all change while the enterprise is changing how it uses the capability.
That makes frontier AI different from most SaaS products the enterprise has purchased before.
Most enterprise buyers encounter AI through the application layer: a chatbot, a copiloted workflow, a security assistant, a planning tool, a search interface, a code assistant. That visible layer makes frontier AI feel like software.
But the capability underneath is industrial. The application may arrive through a procurement workflow, but the capability depends on infrastructure the enterprise does not directly control.
CRM, productivity suites, and many cloud platforms could usually be evaluated through application fit, service reliability, integration, security, and commercial terms.
Frontier AI is harder to contain inside that frame because the product is only the visible surface. Beneath it sits a supply chain of compute, energy, jurisdiction, policy, and strategic pressure.
This is critical when an enterprise starts depending on AI for work that can’t be paused: fraud detection, vulnerability management, supply chain planning, claims routing, customer operations, industrial scheduling, or incident response. In those domains, degraded access is more than a convenience problem.
So in addition to considering whether the vendor has the right feature set, procurement now has to also ask what has to remain true for that capability to keep working:
Does the vendor have reliable access to compute? Can the workload run in the jurisdictions where the enterprise operates? Can logs, prompts, model outputs, and evidence be retained under the right controls? Can capability be throttled, restricted, or tiered? Can the enterprise continue operating if the frontier model becomes unavailable or politically constrained?
This is the part the SaaS playbook trained enterprises not to see. For years, the infrastructure layer disappeared from the application buyer’s view. Frontier AI reverses that. The visible product may be a security assistant, a fraud model, or an operations planner, but the real dependency may be electrical capacity, chip allocation, data-center geography, model access, and the government policies shaping all of them.
SaaS allowed many buyers to treat infrastructure as background. Frontier AI makes infrastructure part of the procurement risk.
3. Mythos Was the Warning Shot
Mythos showed how quickly a security tool can become a strategic capability.
A normal cybersecurity product helps an enterprise see more of its environment. It scans assets, flags vulnerabilities, ranks findings, and gives security teams another queue to manage. That is familiar: the enterprise understands the product as software operating inside a security workflow.
A frontier AI security model points to something different.
If a model can reason across software dependencies, access paths, misconfigurations, exploit chains, aging libraries, exposed services, and brittle infrastructure, it compresses expertise that used to be scarce, fragmented, and human-intensive.
This capability is valuable for defense precisely because it is sensitive: the same model that helps a bank identify the weak path into a payments system could help an attacker understand where to look. The same capability that helps an insurer prioritize claims-platform remediation could expose how older systems are stitched together. The same capability that helps a manufacturer find risk inside plant operations could reveal where digital fragility meets physical infrastructure.
There is another lesson inside Mythos: even the frontier AI company itself can lose control of its own warning label.
For months, the vendor (in this case, Anthropic) may describe the capability in the language of safety research, threat modeling, red teaming, and responsible disclosure. That language is meant to show seriousness. It tells clients the vendor understands the risk.
But the same language can also become evidence for regulators, national-security officials, and foreign governments. If a company spends months explaining that a model can accelerate cyber discovery across critical systems, the state may eventually treat that claim as operationally real.
That is what makes Mythos more than a product controversy. It shows that frontier AI risk is not only technical. It is interpretive. The same model can be described by the vendor as responsibly constrained, by clients as commercially useful, and by the state as strategically sensitive.
That is also where ordinary model risk becomes capability risk. A hallucinated vulnerability or noisy recommendation can usually be handled as model risk through testing, monitoring, tuning, and governance. But a capability that accelerates discovery across critical systems creates a different exposure: capability risk.
This changes the testing considerations. The enterprise cannot only check whether the model finds the right vulnerability or ranks the right exposure. It has to consider whether the capability can be misused, overextended, redirected, or induced to reveal more than the enterprise intended. In a frontier security system, regression testing is not only about proving that old controls still work. It is about proving that the new capability has not created a faster path to misuse, misclassification, data exposure, or operational overreach.
Correct model behavior is only one part of the question. Access, terms of use, sector restrictions, country restrictions, monitoring, and obligations to regulators or governments also matter.
That is why Mythos should not be understood only as a cybersecurity story, but rather as an early signal that frontier AI may create capabilities enterprises want to buy, vendors want to monetize, and governments may not want treated as normal software.
My previous article, Mythos Didn’t Create the Crisis. It Exposed the Ungoverned Enterprise, was about what happens when AI exposes enterprise risk faster than institutions can respond.
This article is about what happens when the capability that exposes the risk becomes strategic in its own right.
4. When Automation Becomes Mandatory
The most uncomfortable part of this shift is that some automation may stop being optional.
In ordinary procurement, automation is treated as an efficiency choice. The enterprise decides where it wants speed, where it wants human review, and where it wants manual fallback. But in cybersecurity, fraud detection, infrastructure remediation, and incident response, that assumption weakens. If adversaries, vulnerabilities, and operational failures move at machine speed, the enterprise may not be able to preserve human review as the primary control.
Human accountability remains, but governance has to move into the operating design: bounded autonomy, approved action classes, policy enforcement, observability, rollback, and degraded-mode plans.
Procurement has to consider whether the enterprise can rely on the capability when response time collapses, and whether it can constrain the system when autonomy becomes necessary.
That is where the procurement relationship stops being purely commercial, which leads us to “The New Triangle.”
5. The New Triangle: Enterprise, Vendor, State
For most of the SaaS era, the enterprise-vendor relationship was commercially legible.
The enterprise bought a product. The vendor delivered a service. The contract defined the operating boundaries: uptime, security, privacy, support, liability, data handling, renewal, and termination. Regulators could intervene, but they usually sat outside the core transaction.
Frontier AI changes these relationships.
The enterprise still wants a product it can use. The vendor still wants a market it can sell into. But the state, meaning government, regulators, national-security agencies, and industrial-policy actors, is no longer just a distant rulemaker. In the most sensitive AI categories, the state becomes a live actor in the system.
The transaction now has three centers of gravity.
The enterprise wants capability, reliability, auditability, continuity, and commercial leverage. It wants the model to work, the service to remain available, the data to stay protected, the outputs to be explainable enough for its risk posture, and the cost to be predictable enough for planning.
The vendor wants scale: clients, revenue, infrastructure access, market defensibility, regulatory permission, government credibility, and freedom to keep improving the model. It may present itself as a commercial supplier, but in frontier AI its most important assets may depend on scarce compute, privileged infrastructure partnerships, government contracts, and permission to commercialize sensitive capabilities.
The state wants national advantage, cyber defense, industrial capacity, energy security, domestic infrastructure, restricted adversary access, and influence over capabilities that may affect critical systems. It may want rapid commercialization for competitiveness and tighter control over the most sensitive versions.
Those interests can align for a while. A bank wants stronger cyber defense. The vendor wants to sell an advanced model. The government wants the financial system better protected.
The alignment becomes fragile when the capability moves from experimental to operationally necessary.
Export rules change. A model is judged too sensitive for broad access. A regulator asks where inference happens and whether evidence can be retained. A government directive targets one class of users, and the vendor’s practical response can affect clients beyond the original target.
Suddenly the enterprise has to consider whether it can still rely on a capability whose operating conditions are being shaped outside the contract.
That is the point where ordinary procurement language starts to fail, because the vendor is no longer just a supplier.
The Anthropic Mythos/Fable access dispute made the triangle visible.
A client may believe it is buying access from a vendor. Operationally, that is true. Commercially, that is true. But strategically, access may still depend on the jurisdiction that governs the vendor, the infrastructure, the model weights, the employees, the cloud region, or the export regime around the capability.
That is a different kind of dependency.
For a non-U.S. enterprise, the lesson is blunt: a frontier model supplied by an American vendor may remain subject to American national-security judgment even when the customer, workload, regulator, and business process sit somewhere else.
The same logic applies in reverse for any country trying to build sovereign AI capacity. Local control is not only about data residency. It is about who can interrupt access, who can narrow the capability, who can inspect the evidence, and who has authority over the infrastructure that keeps the model running.
Most AI products will remain ordinary commercial tools, not national-security issues. But the closer AI moves to cybersecurity, finance, industrial operations, critical infrastructure, intelligence, defense, or large-scale automation, the more this triangle matters.
The enterprise may still sign a commercial contract. But the real operating environment may be shaped by conditions beyond the contract: power, policy, infrastructure, and strategic priority.
6. Strategic Dependency Is Not Vendor Lock-In
Enterprises understand vendor lock-in.
Data becomes hard to move. Integrations become expensive to rebuild. Workflows become customized around one platform. Pricing power shifts to the supplier. The exit path exists mostly in theory.
That can be frustrating and strategically dangerous, but it is still a market problem.
Strategic dependency is a power problem. It begins when the capability itself becomes so important that normal vendor-risk controls no longer describe the exposure.
This dependency is complex because the enterprise may not be the actor changing the system. A model update, safety restriction, cloud-region change, API policy, government rule, compute constraint, or vendor roadmap shift can alter the capability from outside the enterprise’s own change-control process. The enterprise may not have changed its workflow, but the capability underneath the workflow may have changed anyway.
Switching vendors is only one part of the exposure. The deeper issue is whether the capability remains available, unrestricted, affordable, legally usable, operationally stable, and governed by commercial terms when larger forces act on it.
A company may be able to negotiate better support terms. It may be able to demand data portability. It may even maintain a credible second vendor. But those controls may still not fully answer the deeper issue: what happens when the more capable versions of the system depend on scarce compute, sensitive model access, export restrictions, energy availability, government scrutiny, or national-security priorities?
That is not traditional lock-in, but dependency on a capability shaped by power.
Consider cybersecurity. An enterprise may want the most advanced AI model available to reason across vulnerabilities, access paths, misconfigurations, legacy systems, and exploit chains. But if that capability becomes sensitive enough, it may not be distributed like an ordinary product feature. Access could be tiered. Usage could be monitored. Certain sectors could receive priority. Certain countries could face restrictions. The most capable version may be available only under special conditions, while the commercially available version becomes safer, narrower, or delayed.
Consider finance. A bank may rely on AI to detect fraud patterns, stress liquidity signals, monitor transaction anomalies, or accelerate investigations. But once that system becomes embedded in risk operations, the enterprise is no longer only dependent on a vendor. It is dependent on the continuity of model access, the jurisdiction where inference happens, the auditability of outputs, the availability of logs, the regulator’s acceptance of the system, and the vendor’s ability to keep serving that capability under pressure.
Consider industrial operations. A manufacturer may use AI to optimize production schedules, supplier substitutions, energy consumption, and maintenance decisions. The system may look like software, but its performance depends on compute capacity, real-time data flows, industrial connectivity, local regulations, and the availability of models trained or tuned for operational complexity. If those constraints change, the business may lose part of its operating rhythm, not just a feature.
This is the change:
- Vendor lock-in asks whether the enterprise can leave.
- Strategic dependency asks whether the enterprise can continue to operate when the capability it depends on is constrained by forces outside the contract.
While commercial contracts are good at defining obligations between parties, they are inherently weak at neutralizing scarcity, jurisdiction, geopolitical pressure, infrastructure limits, or national-security intervention.
The enterprise still owns the use case, including the data, workflow, and even the governance model around the deployment.
But if the underlying capability sits inside a larger system of compute, energy, data-center capacity, policy, jurisdiction, and state interest, ownership and control become partial.
Vendor lock-in is a market problem.
Strategic dependency is a power problem.
7. Wrap Up: What Enterprise Leaders Should Ask Now
The practical response is to separate ordinary AI procurement from critical capability procurement.
An assistant that summarizes internal documents is one kind of risk. A model embedded in fraud detection, vulnerability management, trading surveillance, claims routing, engineering workflows, industrial scheduling, or incident response is another. Once AI enters the operating rhythm of the enterprise, access is no longer a convenience. It is continuity.
In this environment, there are five questions enterprise leaders should be asking.
1. Criticality: is the capability becoming operationally critical?
That requires a more precise view of where AI sits in the business. Is it assisting a user, or is it becoming part of how work gets routed, investigated, approved, optimized, defended, or recovered? Is it a productivity layer, or is it becoming part of the operating rhythm?
2. Dependency: what does the capability depend on?
That dependency may include frontier model access, scarce compute, a specific cloud region, cross-border inference, security logs, real-time operational data, specialized cyber reasoning, vendor-managed logs, regulatory acceptance, or government tolerance for where and how the system is used. Those dependencies define the real operating boundary of the deployment.
Procurement should ask who can interrupt access besides the vendor. That includes the vendor’s government, the workload’s jurisdiction, the cloud provider’s jurisdiction, regulators, export-control authorities, and any contractual or legal regime that can alter who may use the model. It is not just about whether the vendor promises uptime, but about who has authority to make the service unavailable, narrower, slower, more expensive, or legally unusable.
3. Change: what can change outside the enterprise’s control?
Traditional procurement assumes change can be managed through release notes, service reviews, testing cycles, contract terms, and change windows. Frontier AI weakens that assumption. The enterprise may not change its workflow, but the capability underneath the workflow may change anyway.
The model may change. Access may narrow. Logging may shift. A cloud region may become unavailable. A regulator may alter where the system can operate or which clients can receive the most capable version.
The shifting consideration is this: what parts of this capability can change without our approval, how will we know they changed, and what proves the system still behaves within our risk tolerance?
For critical AI deployments, change control cannot stop at the enterprise boundary. It has to include model updates, access policy, inference location, logging, data retention, safety restrictions, pricing tiers, throttling, and regulatory constraints.
4. Degradation: what happens when access changes?
Leaders should treat human review as one fallback option, not the universal answer. In some domains, the environment may move too quickly for humans to review every decision before action. The relevant question is whether the enterprise has defined which actions require human approval, which can be automated within bounded limits, which require sampling or audit, and which must fall back to slower deterministic or manual paths.
Every critical AI deployment needs a degraded-mode plan. If the best model becomes unavailable, access is throttled, jurisdictions diverge, or the vendor narrows the capability, the enterprise should already know the fallback.
That fallback might be a smaller model, another provider, a deterministic workflow, or a slower human process.
The point is simple: do not design the fallback during the outage.
5. Ownership: who owns the risk?
Strategic dependency has to be owned across procurement, CIO, CISO, risk, legal, compliance, operations, finance, and the board. Procurement can negotiate terms. Security can review controls. Architecture can design fallback paths. Compliance can define evidence requirements. But none of those functions alone can answer the larger question: when does an AI capability become important enough that the enterprise must manage it as infrastructure, not software?
For the most critical capabilities, that question belongs at board level.
The board does not need to manage model architecture, vendor architecture, or technical fallback design. That belongs with the CIO, CISO, CRO, legal, compliance, procurement, and operations.
But when an AI capability becomes material to resilience, cybersecurity, regulated operations, or business continuity, it becomes an oversight issue. Directors should know which capabilities are becoming operationally critical, what external dependencies sustain them, and what happens if access is degraded, restricted, delayed, repriced, or politically constrained.
[Downloadable field checklist: I turned these five questions into a short PDF for enterprise leaders evaluating critical AI capabilities.]
SaaS made software feel commercially contained. The product lived inside the contract. The vendor relationship could be managed through service levels, data terms, security reviews, pricing, and exit provisions.
That is no longer sufficient for the most consequential AI systems.
Enterprises that miss this shift will think they are managing vendor risk while they are accumulating strategic dependency.
When a capability becomes operationally necessary, externally shaped, and strategically sensitive, procurement is no longer just buying software. It is choosing a dependency structure.
That is the end of innocent AI procurement.

1. Your Next AI Dependency May Arrive Through a Partner
The next AI risk may come from an agent your company didn’t build.
This article is about a part of the current AI cycle gets less attention than it deserves. Enterprises are talking about internal copilots, model selection, productivity gains, and agent pilots. But much of enterprise AI will arrive less cleanly, through the delivery ecosystem around the enterprise. It will enter through the delivery ecosystem around the enterprise: consulting firms, systems integrators, ISVs, managed service providers, marketplaces, implementation accelerators, and partner-built workflows.
Recent Big Four announcements are an early signal.
On May 19, 2026, KPMG and Anthropic announced a global alliance that embeds Claude into KPMG Digital Gateway, the firm’s client delivery platform, beginning with new capabilities for Tax & Legal clients. The announcement also gives KPMG’s 276,000+ global workforce access to Claude and names KPMG as a preferred consultant for Private Equity. Deloitte had already announced that Claude would be made available to 470,000 people across its global network, supported by a Claude Center of Excellence designed to move pilots into production. PwC followed with its own expanded Anthropic alliance, including Claude Code and Cowork rollout plans and a program to train and certify 30,000 professionals.
These announcements point beyond consulting productivity. They show AI moving into the platforms, workflows, and advisory channels through which enterprise work already reaches clients. Moving into the systems through which enterprise work already reaches clients: tax platforms, legal workflows, due diligence processes, modernization programs, managed services, implementation patterns, industry templates, and partner-built solutions.
The enterprise will not experience AI only through internal tools, but also through the ecosystem that helps design, deliver, operate, and advise on its work.
Agent adoption is already moving faster than agent control. According to OutSystems, 94% of enterprises report that AI sprawl is increasing complexity and security risk, while only 12% have implemented a centralized platform to manage that sprawl. At the same time, 38% of organizations are mixing custom and pre-built agents. Microsoft’s Cyber Pulse AI Security Report separately found that 29% of employees have used unsanctioned AI agents for work tasks. Combine all these and what emerges is that enterprises are creating harder-to-govern stacks.
Now add the partner ecosystem to that picture.
The control problem no longer stops at the enterprise boundary. Agents will arrive through the systems integrators, ISVs, consulting firms, managed service providers and cloud marketplaces that already help design, deliver, and operate enterprise work. Some will summarize or route, but others will shape recommendations that enter tax, legal, procurement, claims, credit, compliance, finance, or operational decisions.
That is where the governance problem changes. The enterprise won’t build every agent it depends on, but it will still own the workflows those agents enter, the decisions those workflows support, and the evidence required when something has to be explained later.
The deeper issue is context. A partner-built agent does not only perform a task; it shapes what the enterprise sees before a decision is made. It may decide which supplier record matters, which contract clause is relevant, which exception category applies, and which recommendation reaches the human reviewer. It is not just moving work, but helping construct the evidence boundary around the work.
While a partner may deliver the agent, the enterprise needs to explain which facts, tools, records, and recommendations shaped the work.
2. Build Versus Buy Is Breaking Down
Agentic AI creates a delivery model where capability is assembled across organizational boundaries.
In the agentic enterprise, many of the most important capabilities will be assembled across organizational boundaries. A systems integrator might build the agent, an ISV provide the workflow, a consulting firm package the methodology, a managed service provider run the process, and a platform vendor supply the runtime. Meanwhile, the client team may tune the policy, approve the integrations, and remain accountable for the business result.
The result is shared execution across partner logic, client data, platform runtime, integration credentials, and enterprise approval paths. The challenge is knowing whose assumptions, data relationships, prompts, retrieval sources, tool permissions, and exception logic now shape the work.
Consider a procurement agent delivered by an implementation partner. The agent classifies intake requests, checks supplier records, reads contract terms, drafts recommendations, and routes exceptions to category managers. The enterprise did not build the whole thing. The partner brought templates, integration patterns, and domain logic. The agent may use third-party tools or models behind the scenes. But once it touches supplier workflows, procurement policy, approval paths, or ERP data, it is no longer just a partner asset. It has entered the operating environment.
Or take a customer-care agent embedded by an ISV into a regulated service workflow. It summarizes cases, retrieves knowledge, recommends next steps, and hands off to a human when the request crosses a policy boundary. The agent may be vendor-provided, but the customer experience belongs to the enterprise. So does the complaint history, the escalation record, the data exposure risk, and the regulatory explanation if the interaction is challenged.
This is the practical problem hiding underneath partner-led AI adoption. The enterprise can outsource development, integration, and managed operation. It cannot fully outsource accountability for the work those systems affect.
That is why partner-delivered AI needs a different standard than ordinary software implementation. A traditional application can be tested against requirements and handed over. An agent is different. It reasons across context, calls tools, routes work, retrieves knowledge, uses credentials, responds to users, and may change behavior as prompts, policies, models, data, and workflows evolve.
The result is not just vendor dependency, but operational dependency: externally delivered agents acting inside workflows the enterprise must still govern. Partner-delivered agents should enter the enterprise with defined scope, controls, evidence expectations, and lifecycle ownership rather than relying on trust in the delivery relationship.
3. Partner Readiness Now Includes Governance Discipline
Partner readiness has to expand beyond product fluency and implementation skill.
For a long time, partner readiness was mostly about capability transfer: understand the product, pass the certification, learn the sales play, know the implementation pattern, build the demo, handle objections, and deliver the project. But when partners deliver agents into client workflows, readiness cannot stop at product fluency or implementation skill.
It has to include proof that the agent can enter a governed operating model.
A partner who can build an agent is useful. But a partner who can explain what the agent is allowed to do, how it was tested, what systems it can touch, what policies constrain it, what evidence it leaves behind, and how it will be monitored after deployment is more valuable. The first partner helps a client start. The second helps a client scale without losing control.
The difference shows up quickly in real work.
A consulting partner may build a finance operations agent that summarizes invoice exceptions and recommends whether they should be approved, rejected, or escalated. In a demo, the agent looks impressive: it reads the invoice, checks the purchase order, compares contract terms, and drafts a clean recommendation. But in production, the client needs harder answers. Can the agent approve anything, or only recommend? What happens when the vendor record is incomplete? Can it access banking details? Does it treat a policy exception differently from a data-quality exception? Are all tool calls logged? Can finance see whether a human accepted, changed, or rejected the recommendation? These are governance questions.
A consulting partner may build a finance operations agent that reviews invoice exceptions and recommends whether they should be approved, rejected, or escalated. In a demo, the value is easy to see: the agent reads the invoice, checks the purchase order, compares the relevant contract terms, and produces a clear recommendation. Production raises a different set of questions. Is the agent authorized to approve a transaction, or only to recommend an action? What should it do when vendor data is incomplete, a policy exception conflicts with the underlying record, or the workflow exposes sensitive banking information? Can finance reconstruct every tool call and determine whether a human accepted, modified, or rejected the recommendation? At that point, the problem is no longer just whether the agent works. It is whether the organization can govern how it works.
The burden does not sit with the partner alone. The client still owns the business process, risk appetite, approval thresholds, and regulatory explanation.
