Hey folks,
This is Pavel, welcome to a new edition of our Fireside Chats with Emerging Fund Managers where we ask recently-closed fund managers 10 rapid-fire questions about their fundraising journey.
Today’s guest: Jordan Wan, Founder and General Partner of CoFound.
About The Firm
CoFound is an early-stage VC firm founded in 2019 by Jordan Wan, an MIT engineer and former Founder/CEO of Formative and longtime NYC startup operator. Based in Denver, Wan focuses on leading/co-leading pre-seed investments in vertical AI across the US and Canada – with one differentiator: helping founders build repeatable go-to-market motions from day one.
Results validated the approach: early wins like Grow Therapy, Garner Health, and QA Wolf, lead to oversubscription and a backlog of LPs waiting for Fund II. Several LPs verbally committed before Jordan even officially kicked off the fundraise – a result of treating fundraising as continuous relationship-building, not episodic campaigning.
The active raise took ~6 months from first to final close, but Jordan learned something counterintuitive: “Performance and DPI is not enough in this market. It’s just as important to have strong GP legibility. It has to be easy for an LP to backchannel you and get a positive impression of your personal brand and reputation.”
Jordan found that in-person meetings were critical after reflecting on his early naivete to try and pitch IC’s over Zoom. Portfolio strength gets attention, but LPs commit after spending time with you and entrusting you’d be a good steward of capital.
Fund II writes $500k-$1.5M checks at pre-seed and seed, co-investing with boutiques, large seed and multi-stage funds. The LP base includes ~50 investors – institutions making up 2/3 of the fund (Cendana, Level, Fourbridge, FirstLook, Moses, and Slipstream), with the remaining third coming from private institutions, founders, and executives in Jordan’s network. The fund doesn’t reserve for follow on and optimizes for upfront ownership and high conviction alignment with founders.
Here is our fireside chat:
What is your fund’s superpower in one sentence?
Helping founders build a repeatable GTM motion.
How long did the active fundraising process take?
~6 months.
Did anybody help you during fundraising: existing LPs, fellow GPs, placement agents?
Existing LPs and other GPs are helpful. We also had a backlog of LPs from prior oversubscribed fund that also referred folks.
How many LPs are in the final cap table, and what’s their breakdown?
~50 in total, a group of institutions accounted for over 2/3 of the total fund. We allocated the remaining to helpful founders & industry executives in our network.
What was the fastest check – time from first call to signed subscription?
We had several verbal commitments before we even kicked off the fundraise, but took about a month to finalize our LPA before accepting signatures.
What were the top 3 reasons LPs said “NO”?
For Fund II, the size of the fund was still the main reason LPs passed. For most institutions, it was still prohibitively too small. Otherwise, it was just about getting LPs comfortable with a solo GP / generalist fund model.
What were the top 3 signals that an LP was truly interested in your fund?
Warm intros through other GP/LPs was a very high indicator. Also a good sign if they've backed other founder-centric fund strategies like CoFound.
What did LPs actually pay close attention to during fundraising?
Have found that performance and DPI is not enough in this market. It's just as important to have strong GP legibility. It has to be easy for an LP to backchannel you and get a positive impression of your personal brand and reputation.
What’s the biggest mistake fund managers make when fundraising?
Fundraising is a continuous, core responsibility. It's not an episodic thing you do at the end of a fund lifecycle. Most LPs have a backlog of great managers they've gotten to know. GPs have a scarcity of LP intros they can make. So you have to really spend time investing in relationships well in advance of fundraising. It's very easy for folks to tell when you're approaching things transactionally.
What advice would you give to your future self and to other emerging managers about fundraising?
Be patient and do more in-person meetings. Don't just rely on your portfolio strength. Venture investing has so much nuance and LPs have so many options, you have to give people a chance to get to know you through time.

The Prediction Cycle
Starting in December 2025 and continuing into early 2026, I began to notice how deeply the market had slipped into what I’d call “prediction mode” – a state where almost everyone felt compelled to publicly articulate their version of the future, even when that future was still highly uncertain.
Investors, founders, operators, journalists – nearly everyone I follow started publishing their own outlooks:
- where capital would flow
- which domains would overheat
- whether liquidity would return
- whether the window for mega-IPOs would reopen
- and much more
In isolation, none of this was new. The industry has always tried to look ahead. But what felt different this time was how many parallel storylines appeared at once and how poorly they spoke to each other. You could read ten different “2026 outlooks,” nod along to each of them – and still have no real sense of how those views interacted, overlapped, or contradicted one another.
There was no common frame, no shared coordinate system, not even a rough map of which convictions were widely shared and which were held by one or two loud voices. Everything lived in its own micro-context, optimized for distribution rather than synthesis.
This sense of fragmentation is what ultimately led to this Market Map.
I’m not trying to predict the future here. I’m trying to document how the market is thinking about the future right now – with all the contradictions, overlaps, and blind spots that come with that.
How This Map Was Built
Before turning to the insights, it’s important to explain the methodology. This project is primarily about capturing how investors talk about uncertainty and where they are willing to place actual capital behind those stories, rather than validating whether specific forecasts will turn out to be “right.”
Sources
Most of the data was collected from public sources:
- Analytical articles and industry roundups
- Substack newsletters
- LinkedIn
- X
- Personal blogs
- Fund websites
- Public interviews
In total, we initially identified close to 300 public sources, including journalists, researchers, venture investors, founders, and operators.
Given the volume and heterogeneity of perspectives, we deliberately narrowed the scope to VC investors, as they are most directly responsible for capital allocation.
Even within this group, many views were fragmented, incomplete, or insufficiently grounded to support reliable interpretation. Some predictions were little more than slogans or marketing copy. Others lacked any link to how a fund actually invests. As a result, we excluded a number of cases that did not meet our internal consistency thresholds.
The final dataset includes 132 venture investors.
Domains
We structured the map around 9 core clusters. Each could be further subdivided, but for this version we intentionally stayed at a higher level of abstraction, because once you slice the world too finely, it starts to look precise on paper while becoming less useful for real decisions.
Agentic Systems
This cluster covers autonomous and semi-autonomous AI systems capable of executing multi-step tasks with minimal human supervision. It includes agent frameworks, orchestration layers, multi-agent collaboration, AI-native workflows, and emerging agent-to-agent commerce and coordination models.
AI Infrastructure
This domain includes the technical backbone of AI development and deployment: compute, chips, cloud optimization, model serving, inference stacks, MLOps, developer tooling, and platforms that reduce the cost and complexity of building and scaling AI systems.
World Models & Planning
We use this category for systems focused on long-horizon reasoning, simulation, and environment modeling. This includes foundation models for planning, reasoning engines, digital twins, reinforcement learning at scale, and architectures designed to build internal representations of the world.
Physical AI & Energy
This cluster spans the intersection of AI with the physical world: robotics, autonomous systems, industrial automation, embodied AI, energy optimization, grid intelligence, and infrastructure required to support compute-intensive workloads.
AI Economics & Pricing
This domain captures business-model innovation around AI: usage-based pricing, outcome-based contracts, agent marketplaces, compute monetization, cost-passing mechanisms, and the emerging economics of deploying AI at scale.
Data & Memory Moats
We group here companies building defensible advantages through proprietary data, long-term memory systems, feedback loops, retrieval architectures, and domain-specific datasets that compound in value over time.
Talent & Distribution
This cluster reflects the human and go-to-market layer of AI: platforms for hiring and managing technical talent, developer communities, AI-native sales and marketing systems, workflow distribution, and mechanisms for acquiring and retaining users in increasingly crowded markets.
Fintech & Financial Rails
This domain includes payment infrastructure, embedded finance, compliance tooling, agent-native wallets, settlement systems, cross-border rails, and financial primitives designed to support AI-driven commerce and automation.
Liquidity & IPOs (Market)
Unlike the other clusters, this category captures market-level dynamics rather than technology. It includes expectations around exit environments, public market receptivity, M&A activity, secondary liquidity, and structural shifts in how venture-backed companies achieve liquidity.
Marker System
Each cell includes markers designed to clarify what an individual meant – especially in cases where their original statements were compressed, implicit, or spread across multiple posts and interviews:
- ● Full circle – strong conviction
- ◐ Half-filled – tentative hypothesis
- Empty – topic not addressed or deprioritized
Whenever possible, we added short contextual notes. Not to reinterpret statements, but to preserve their original intent while making them legible inside a larger system.
AI Support and Manual Verification
For analysis and clustering, we used:
- Perplexity Pro Research
- ChatGPT Pro
- Grok
- Claude
- Other research engines
These tools helped us scale the process and detect recurring patterns across large volumes of text that would have been impractical to read line by line.
At the same time, interpretation remained human. We manually reviewed every participant, every source, and every extracted prediction, because I’ve learned that without this layer of friction, it’s very easy to mistake surface-level similarity for genuine alignment.
Top-5 Bets
Based on aggregated signals, we identified 5 themes that appeared most frequently across predictions. These are not “best ideas.” They reflect collective market attention.
#1: Autonomous AI as the Next Platform Layer
Agentic systems are the most frequently cited theme across the dataset.
Investors are increasingly focused on AI systems that can operate autonomously, coordinate with other agents, execute multi-step workflows, and interact directly with digital and financial infrastructure.
This goes far beyond chatbots or copilots. What many investors are underwriting is the emergence of:
- multi-agent workflows
- agent-native products
- agent-to-agent commerce
- automated business processes
Underneath this, there is a simple belief: that productivity gains from AI will move from “human + AI” to “AI + AI,” with humans supervising rather than operating. In other words, most of the work will happen between systems in the background, not in a visible UI between a person and a chatbot.
I’m not sure this is the future everyone wants, but it is the one I see most often between the lines of these predictions. In 2026, early signs of this shift are likely to show up in:
- early agent marketplaces
- primitive autonomous companies
- vertical-specific agents
- growing tension around reliability and governance
This is the closest thing in the dataset to a “new platform shift.”
#2: AI Infrastructure
The second strongest theme is infrastructure.
This includes compute, inference optimization, deployment stacks, model serving, developer tooling, and cost-efficiency platforms. After two years of foundation-model hype, many investors now see infrastructure as the real bottleneck.
Capital is flowing into companies that help:
- reduce inference costs
- optimize GPU utilization
- manage AI workflows
- make AI systems production-grade
This looks less like a new hype cycle and more like a clean-up phase. After two years of foundation-model excitement, investors are trying to fund the “picks and shovels” that make AI cheaper, more reliable, and easier to operate at scale. Over the next year, I expect to see:
- consolidation in tooling
- pressure on margins
- verticalized infrastructure stacks
- and fewer “general-purpose” platforms
#3: AI Meets the Real World
This cluster reflects growing conviction that the next wave of AI value creation will happen outside pure software.
Robotics, automation, manufacturing, logistics, energy optimization, and embodied AI appear consistently across predictions.
Two forces are converging here:
- AI models are becoming capable enough to control physical systems
- energy and compute constraints are becoming strategic issues
Investors are positioning around:
- warehouse robotics
- autonomous systems
- industrial AI
- energy management
- grid intelligence
This also reads like a hedge. If consumer AI saturates, physical systems offer a longer runway and deeper moats. It is much harder to copy a robotics stack deployed across dozens of factories than a new interface on top of a public API. In 2026, expect:
- slower adoption cycles
- capital-intensive scaling
- but potentially more defensible businesses
#4: Rebuilding Payments for an AI-Native Economy
Fintech reappears in this dataset, but in a very different form than in 2020–2021. The focus is not on neobanks or consumer apps, but instead on infrastructure for AI-driven commerce. This includes:
- agent-native wallets
- automated payments
- compliance tooling
- settlement rails
- cross-border systems
Many investors are betting that if agents transact with each other, someone must own the rails. I think this is one of the most underappreciated themes. Every time software rewires a workflow, someone quietly rebuilds the payment layer underneath it – and those rails compound for years. AI agents will not be an exception. Key 2026 bets:
- early agent payment protocols
- regulatory friction
- fragmentation before consolidation
#5: AI Economics & Pricing
The fifth major theme is AI monetization. After years of subsidized usage, investors are increasingly focused on how AI businesses will actually make money. Recurring topics include:
- usage-based pricing
- outcome-based contracts
- cost pass-through
- compute-indexed fees
- margin compression
Many investors explicitly question whether current AI pricing models are sustainable. I think this reflects a shift from “growth at all costs” to “unit economics matter again.” In 2026, expect:
- pricing experimentation
- customer pushback
- consolidation of weaker models
- clearer segmentation between premium and commodity AI
Top-5 Selected Quotes
In parallel with mapping dominant themes, we also looked for statements that reflect deeper structural thinking about where the industry is heading. Out of hundreds of public predictions, we selected 5 quotes that we subjectively consider the most fundamental.
#1: David Cahn from Sequoia Capital
Why this matters: This is a quiet but important reframing. When AI becomes infrastructure rather than a product category, the category "AI company" disappears. Only companies that embedded AI into their operational DNA survive. This is the maturation moment where AI stops being a differentiator and becomes table stakes.
#2: Tomasz Tunguz from Theory Ventures
Why this matters: This is an inflection point in economics: when a company pays more for an agent than a human, it means humans no longer compete on price. They must compete on creativity, judgment, and strategic thinking. This fundamentally reshapes the labor market and creates new skill hierarchies.
#3: Macy Mills from A16Z Speedrun
Why this matters: This inverts the entire SaaS pricing model. Instead of paying for access to software, you pay for outcomes. This means AI vendors must be confident their agents will deliver results – and it eliminates the inefficiency of buyers paying for tools they don't fully utilize. This is the shift from seat-based to performance-based economics.
#4: Jeff Morris Jr. from Chapter One
Why this matters: Memory is the missing ingredient that will unlock the next wave of AI products. Just as location-awareness created entirely new categories that didn't exist before, persistent memory will enable products impossible today. The first companies to crack memory-driven products will have defensible moats that last for decades.
#5: Olivia Moore from A16Z
Why this matters: Voice agents are currently tactical tools, but in 2026 they become strategic infrastructure. The shift from "voice for scheduling" to "voice managing the entire customer lifecycle" captures massive value. Companies that expand voice from wedge to platform will generate revenue while saving costs simultaneously.
Conclusion
This is the first iteration of the 2026 VC Predictions Market Map.
It is incomplete by design, and we expect to keep editing and refining it as the year unfolds and today’s narratives either compound into real companies, rounds, and liquidity events (or quietly fade).
Toward the end of 2026, we perhaps plan to revisit this map, review which bets played out and which didn’t, and layer a second pass of analysis on top.
If this work is useful to you, follow Murph Capital and stay tuned. We are preparing the launch of our open-source “new media“ and community, along with a growing set of tools and resources designed to help emerging managers build better funds and LPs make better long-term investment decisions.

For the last 9 months, we’ve been quietly building this newsletter - a monthly snapshot of what’s happening across the VC/LP world. But the more we worked on it, the more obvious it became that just the news is only a trailer - the real movie is in the weeds.
So now we want to go a little deeper. We want essays, research, benchmarks, maybe even some market maps if we’re feeling particularly nerdy on a Sunday afternoon. Basically, the kind of things we ourselves would want to read.
Snapshot of the present
Currently, we’re all living in a very unusual moment, with AI representing a paradigm shift that is larger than just a new “tech wave.”
And venture capital is adding fuel to the fire at a record pace: over $200B has already been deployed into AI companies in 2025 alone. Fun times.
The check sizes, though, aren’t the most fascinating part of this cycle, with some deals that can be deemed unconventional, to name a few:
- A16Z led a $15M Series A into Cluely, a “cheat on everything” startup.
- An AI pre-product startup called Friend publicly raised $2.5M, then promptly spent $1.8M on a domain name and $1M on outdoor ads.
- AI hardware startup Rabbit raised more than $30M to develop a personal assistance device.
To the outside world, some of these bets look reckless, maybe even comical. When a new platform shift hits, missing one winner hurts more than backing nine weird experiments. And somewhere in that weirdness, VCs hope, they have their fund returner.
While VCs get the attention (and occasionally get meme’d on), none of these bets would even exist without the side of the industry that rarely gets talked about - LPs, the invisible capital behind every unicorn, every hype cycle, every “what were they thinking?” round.
They’re usually less public, more risk-averse. And yet… even they are leaning into the AI frenzy. How do we know? Money talks:
- Lightspeed quietly assembled a $9B AI war chest across 6 new funds, doubling down on Anthropic‑scale winners.
- AI‑focused VC funds already account for 31% of all VC capital raised in 2025.
- By mid‑2025, 75% of US AI deal value involved corporate balance sheets, as the most conservative capital on earth rushed to bolt AI exposure onto existing mandates.
When the most risk-aware capital providers start behaving like optimists, that’s when you know something big is going on.
If we really want to understand where AI is taking venture capital - and who will actually benefit from this shift - we need to zoom out. The real story isn’t about what startups or VCs are doing today. It’s more about how this entire capital “pyramid” was built: “LPs → VCs → Startups”.
This structure didn’t just magically appear one day. It came up to be through dozens of cycles, where different people in different eras tried something new, there were accidents, incentives, power struggles, and some outright delusional bets that somehow worked.
Until we get AGI and get replaced by robots, one of the better ways to read the future is to understand the past…
The first VCs, kind of…
Venture capital, as a formal term, appeared only in the 20th century, but it doesn’t mean that the premise of high-risk and high returns wasn’t a thing; heck, carried interest as a term came to be in the 16th century.
So, it’s only logical that we take a step back to review things that preceded us:
Sea Voyages
No, not the cozy ones we have today, but the ones people had in the medieval ages - those were nothing like the vacations we have now.
Trade was one of the main purposes of such voyages, and they were extremely dangerous:
- Pirates were a thing, and a very dangerous one
- Ships didn’t have GPS, were made of wood, but storms were as nasty
- And let’s not get into the state of medicine back then, and the diseases one could get
Lots of risk, and lots of potential profit – sounds like a venture, right?
There were also people back then who had the money and wanted to invest. Even though the term limited partner didn’t exist yet, the equivalent for the time did.
Medieval LPs were usually wealthy monarchs, merchant guilds, and aristocratic families. And their “due diligence” was simpler by today’s standards, but core principles seem similar - reputation of the captain, past voyage results, and intuition. The logic was the same as today - high risk, but potentially high upside.
And, with voyages covered, let’s dive into a few historical highlights (involving not only them):
Christopher Columbus, the contrarian (1490-1506)
LP: The Spanish Crown
VC: Queen Isabella and King Ferdinand of Spain
Portfolio Assets: Ocean‑voyage ships, trade routes
The theme of that time was about exploration, resources, and, well, building empires. Travel routes were really important, as the biggest money of the time was in things you couldn’t produce using your laptop at home.
Existing travel routes were controlled by other countries, which didn’t benefit Europe and the Spanish Crown in particular, and the experts didn’t see alternatives…
But a guy you might have heard of, with a last name of Columbus, believed that you could actually sail to East Asia by going West, and that the experts were wrong!
The idea Christopher Columbus had would seem pretty good (to him), so much that he actually wanted to pursue it, but he didn’t have any funding, and cold DMing VCs haven’t yet emerged…
- It took Christopher close to 5 years to get to just pitch the Queen
- It took almost 10 years to get the funding, and it’s worth a story alone!
- All while overcoming the fact that 2 separate commissions deemed Columbus’s plan nonsensical
Even then, Queen and Spain weren’t that excited about the idea, but they viewed it as a low-cost opportunity that could bring in a substantial upside.
To lower the risk, she asked the town of Palos to produce ships for Columbus, since the city owed a hefty fine.
Further, she even helped Columbus with hiring, as he struggled to recruit anyone into his risky venture. She pardoned criminals who were willing to go on the voyage…
6 months later, he got some traction, closed the next investment round that now got him 17 ships, 1200-1500 employees, and a fancy title!
As it happens with startups, Columbus’s calculations were off, but luckily for him, between Asia and Europe, he’d find America, and the Crown would make a great return on her risky investments.
Oh, and by the way, thanks to Columbus’s discoveries, we got to have a term called carried interest. Back then, the captain of the ship would take a 20% share of the profit from the carried goods to pay for the transport and the risk of sailing over oceans.
Charles W. Morgan, who might well be the first venture capitalist (1814-1861)
LP: Also Charles W. Morgan (some solo-GP energy here), New England merchants and banks
VC: Charles Wahn Morgan
Portfolio Assets: Whaling ships, barrels of high-margin whale oil
Let’s fast forward to the 19th century, when whale oil was the theme.
Oil was primarily used for illumination and lubrication, powering lamps and the machinery of the Industrial Revolution. Initially pioneered in Europe in the 1500s, later dominated by Americans after the American Revolution.
Whale oil meant you had, well, to get it from whales, creatures weighing more than 100 tons, and living in oceans and seas. So, at the time, the only way to get to them was by boat and organised voyages.
By some accounts, 34% of whaling voyages had a 0 or even negative returns, which loosely resembles VC industry numbers.
Charles W. Morgan was in the business of financing and organizing whaling ventures. He was an investor-first, not an operator. He was looking for the teams and ships that were succeeding and was looking to fund them.
Before launching his own firm, he worked in a whaling firm, where he became a partner in his late teens, with his father-in-law being one of the founding operators.
He eventually owned 15 ships; he had shares in 18 others, his portfolio ships, one might call them!
Charles didn’t have any LPs in the current sense; he was a mainly self-funded businessman. Apart from candleworks and whaling vessels, his investments included textile mills, railroads, banks, and a paper mill.
Here are a few things that Charles used then that are now a vital part of the VC:
- Power Law - he applied the logic before the term came to be, by investing in multiple expeditions and diversifying across different captains, ships, and destinations
- Exclusively not being an operator - he didn’t sail, hunt whales, and wasn’t a captain, he focused on evaluating talent, selecting promising teams, and getting them the money needed
- Carried interest-like compensation (lay system) - crew members received a fractional share of the voyage’s net profits, not a fixed wage
Electricity and the war of the currents (1880s-1890s)
LP: HNWIs (industrial tycoons), institutional capital (private banks)
VC: J.P. Morgan, Henry Villard
Portfolio Assets: Power stations, electrical grids, lighting systems, dynamos, transformers
Whaling oil’s demise came with the new theme of kerosene, electricity, and thus, more efficient solutions.
With a better solution, there was an opportunity to win the newly created market, which prompted a new “war”. The name that we have for it now is “the war of the currents”, as it was a fierce competition for the electrical energy markets.
This was the war, mainly, between Edison General Electric and Westinghouse; there were other prominent competitors, of course, but this framing fits for a better story.
The former resembled a VC-funded startup, backed by J.P. Morgan and the Vanderbilt family, and the latter was more like a self-funded company, but not exactly.
And whereas there are parallels with the current funding schemes, the even more resembling part is the ruthless market competition aspect of it.
The product part of the war was between the Alternating Current (AC) approach and the Direct Current (DC), both coming to replace the gas lightning system.
This competition looked a lot like how startups are currently battling for market share, Tesla FSD vs Google’s Waymo, iOS vs Android, Mac vs Windows, you get the idea.
Edison leaned on AC not being safe, similar to how companies today may use safety narratives to define regulations and barriers to their industries. But Edison went even further, funding very aggressive negative PR campaigns to win that war. As a matter of fact, the electric chair was invented at that time, as a by-product of the new technology, following the criticism of a series of botched hangings.
Long story short - Edison’s direct current approach lost, with the alternating current approach coming on top.
In 1891, the market was in a downturn, and investors behind Edison’s company saw an opportunity to merge with another competitor who had an AC approach called Thomson-Houston.
As a result of this merger, they’ve got a company that controlled 75% of the US electrical business and got the name of General Electric, which you might’ve seen listed on NYSE as $GE.
At that time, “VCs” sourced their funds from wealthy families, like the Vanderbilt family, and also banks like Deutsche Bank, the landscape, yet, wasn’t as robust as it is now.
With these honourable mentions, we are getting closer to the most industry-defining time periods and our days:
Arthur Rock, and the first VCs (1940s-1990s)
LP: HNWIs (Phipps family), small syndicates (Arthur Rock’s early backers), first institutional investors (John Hancock, Prudential)
VC: Arthur Rock, Georges Doriot, Laurance Rockefeller, Don Valentine
Portfolio Assets: Semiconductor companies, integrated circuit designs, fabrication plants, patents, silicon-based computing infrastructure
The days when the actual Venture Capital industry was born!
The first “hit” was the American Research and Development Corporation (ARDC), formed in 1946.
The firm has pioneered raising funds from institutions, rather than wealthy families. The firm raised $3.5M supported by MIT, University of Pennsylvania, University of Rochester, Rice University, and others.
Their first major success was Digital Equipment Corporation (DEC) in 1968. Following DEC’s initial public offering, ARDC shares were worth $355 million, 500 times their original investment.
ARDC had a couple of unicorns in its portfolio:
- Teradyne Inc. It was not making money when the company came to ARDC for an investment in the 1960s. Today, it is worth $28B.
- Ionics Inc., one of the early ARDC investments, was purchased by GE in 2004 for $1.1B
Importantly, ARDC became an “incubator” for the next generation of LPs and VCs.
Its alumni soon created firms like Greylock Partners and Morgan, Holland Ventures (predecessor to Flagship Ventures). These new firms attracted not only wealthy individuals, but also a growing base of institutional LPs - endowments, foundations, and later corporate investors. Thus marking the beginning of diversified LP capital entering the VC ecosystem.
The second “hit” was Arthur Rock (student of Georges Doriot, not to be confused with Arfur Rock), and the first-ever VC firm of his making.
Arthur has helped 8 founders to secure funding for their semiconductor firm. And those 8 founders had a name of Traitorous Eight.
Further, once the firm became successful, the 8 founders also started investing and helped Rock to found the first VC firm – Davis & Rock (they’ve later helped found Apple, Intel, and other companies).
Arthur is often credited with the introduction of the term “venture capitalist” that we are still using nowadays.
And that’s how the venture capital flywheel got started, one thing leading to another, and more importantly, accelerating one another.
Sand Hill Road and the rise of modern LP Capital (1970s-1990s)
LP: Post-ERISA pensions (IBM Pension Fund, AT&T Pension Fund), endowments (Yale, Stanford), corporate venture arms (XTV), family offices (Hillman family), fund-of-funds (Horsley Bridge, Adams Street Partners)
VC: Kleiner Perkins, Sequoia, Accel, Benchmark, early corporate VC groups
Portfolio Assets: Semiconductors, personal computing, software, biotech
Around that time, new categories of LPs emerged: pension funds entered venture capital after the ERISA Act of 1974 loosened fiduciary restrictions, unlocking billions in long-term institutional capital.
Family offices such as the Rockefellers and Pritzkers also didn’t want to miss out on new opportunities and were becoming consistent LPs in early VC funds. These shifts massively expanded the pool of LP capital available to emerging venture firms.
Further, that paved the way for the formation of the iconic Sand Hill Road, the home of many VCs (but do they have much sand there?). Nowadays, Sand Hill Road has some of the most expensive office spaces in the United States.
The first VC firm to be opened there was no other than Kleiner Perkins, with Eugene Kleiner being one of the 8 co-founders of Fairchild Semiconductors, which Arthur Rock helped get funding for, and we’ve talked about a few paragraphs before.
By the 1980s and 1990s, a new LP “archetype” appeared - fund of funds, such as Horsley Bridge and Adams Street Partners. They played a big role in defining which VC firms scaled and which didn’t, acting as backers of emerging managers.
Also around that time, David Swensen became Yale’s endowment manager and grew it from $1B in 1985 to more than $30B by the time of his death in 2021. So Yale was, more than just a university with an endowment fund, which alone would already be impressive enough.
Swensen’s model helped Yale’s endowment grow from ~$1B in 1985 to tens of billions of dollars by the 2010s and beyond, with roughly 55–60% allocated to alternatives by 2019.
By backing firms like Sequoia and Kleiner Perkins early, amongst other things, Yale proved that LP’s capital could outperform traditional asset classes.
Dot Com (1995-2001)
LP: HNWIs (Paul Allen, Michael Dell), pensions (CalPERS, OPERF), endowments (Yale, Harvard), corporate venture arms (Intel Capital), fund-of-funds (HarbourVest Partners)
VC: Softbank Capital, Index Ventures, Redpoint, Insights, and others
Portfolio Assets: Consumer internet startups, e-commerce platforms, online marketplaces, web portals, search engines, banner-ad networks, hosting providers
The Dot Com era happened almost 30 years ago, but many companies formed then are still defining our lives today.
Often we hear Dot Com and Bubble together, and that is reminiscing with the current AI era, and it’s important to remember that this “Dot Com Bubble” has brought us at least 2 trillion dollar companies:
Amazon
Now a household name, but then it was just getting started by Jeff Bezos.
Luckily for Kleiner Perkins, they were introduced to Amazon in 1996 when Coach Bill Campbell connected John Doerr to Leslie Koch, who at the time was vice president of marketing at Amazon.
This further led to an $8M Series A investment, which then became a return in excess of $1B. If we were to take the current Amazon’s market cap, the number would get even more impressive!
Now listed as Alphabet, and powering ~90% of the global internet search, Google wouldn’t be the same without Kleiner Perkins and Sequoia, who both invested in the 1999th $25M round.
Sequoia Capital invested about $12.5 million in Google in 1999, which had grown to a value of $4.3 billion by the time of Google’s 2004 IPO.
With Kleiner Perkins having similar numbers.
Both firms managed to get into the one and only financing round Google did.
Also, in 1999, the famous SoftBank raised $1.2 billion for SoftBank Capital Partners, trying to ride the Dot Com era, having raised money from the state of Michigan and the French media company Vivendi, among others.
But the times were brutal, with Nasdaq falling 80% from March 2000 to October 2002, and the funds returning pennies on the dollar to the LPs.
Speaking of LPs, during this era, pension funds became the dominant LP class for the first time.
Large systems like CalPERS, CalSTRS, and Oregon PERS poured unprecedented amounts of capital into venture funds, inflating fund sizes and accelerating the flywheel that pushed firms like Sequoia and Benchmark to the top.
There were also new corporate LPs - Intel, Cisco, Microsoft, and GE Capital all built venture programs or LP commitments, adding another wave of capital.
Yale’s Model got popularized, and more endowments started increasing their “alternative” investments as well, with examples of Ford and Getty Foundations seeing more than half of their assets in this category by the 2010s.
2000s-2020s and Our Days
LP: HNWIs (Jeff Bezos, Peter Thiel), sovereign wealth funds (GIC, PIF, ADIA), institutions (Allianz, Swiss Re), fund-of-funds (Cendana, TrueBridge), family offices (Pritzker), endowments (Michigan, Yale), pensions (CalPERS)
VC: Andreessen Horowitz, Insight Partners, Lightspeed Venture Partners, Founders Fund, Y Combinator and others
Portfolio Assets: Large language models, AI infrastructure, defence tech, biotech, SaaS, marketplaces, mobile apps, cloud infra, crypto
Now we are approaching AI, after many waves we’ve already passed.
The LP side, just like VCs, is also ever-changing:
- VC-specialised Funds of Funds have appeared, like True Bridge Capital Partners, Cendana Capital. These FoFs have become institutional “kingmakers”, professionalizing the discovery of new Fund I–III managers and shaping which emerging GPs scale.
- Sovereign wealth funds are becoming more prominent players, fueling 31% of global AI deal value. SWFs such as Mubadala, ADIA, QIA, and GIC are now writing $200M–$1B checks into late-stage AI rounds (Anthropic, OpenAI, CoreWeave), reshaping the balance of power in venture capital.
- European pension funds are catching up and increasing their investments into VC, from the 0.12% of capital previously allocated to that category. Nordic and Dutch systems (APG, PGGM, ATP) have started shifting into US-style private market allocations.
But that mid-2000 - 2022 period was rich in unicorns, and companies that have now become household names: AirBnB, Coinbase, Atlassian, Zoom, Slack, Solana, to name a few.
Amongst the notable VC winners of those days would arguably be:
- Bessemer – with just a $5M investment into Shopify in 2010 at $20M valuation, with Shopify now being at $200B. This single deal became one of the most iconic examples of early-stage ownership discipline paying off at a generational scale.
- Sequoia – the firm had a $9B week where their portcos (Unity, Snowflake and Sumo Logic) IPO’d in the same week. This moment reinforced how multi-decade platform funds compound value across multiple cycles.
- A16Z – having invested $25M at a Series B Coinbase in 2013, that turned into $11B by the time of Coinbase’s IPO in 2021. It remains one of the strongest single-check venture returns of the 2010s.
- Lightspeed – got into Snap at the seed stage in 2012, and turned $8.1M into $1.5B at 2017’s IPO. A textbook example of early-stage asymmetric upside.
- Lowercase Capital — their Fund I is rumoured to be “best-performing fund of all time from a return multiple perspectives”. With $8.4M fund size, it achieved 204X DPI.
So what about the LP side going forward?
The trends are already clear: more LPs, more specialization, more data, and a growing wave of emerging GPs. But this time, the change goes deeper. Funds will change. Startups will change. And the way venture firms operate will change as well.
AI will definitely play a central role here - not just in what funds invest in, but how they invest.
The ZIRP era accelerated capital deployment, while the 2020-2022 cycle stress-tested both VCs and LPs. Together, they created one of the most intense learning environments venture has ever seen.
But this period is simply too dense to unpack properly in a few paragraphs. One thing we do believe strongly: as the venture itself evolves, new types of LPs will emerge.
LPs whose behavior, decision-making, and engagement model will look very different from the past – more hands-on, more analytical, more operational, and more aligned with fund managers.
Possibly, something like Murph Capital.
But that’s a story for the next essay.

Hey folks,
This is Pavel, welcome to a new edition of our Fireside Chats with Emerging Fund Managers where we ask recently-closed fund managers 10 rapid-fire questions about their fundraising journey.
Today’s guest: Dr. Nadav Shimoni, co-founder of A-Squared Ventures.
About The Firm
A-Squared Ventures is a Seed-stage digital health fund founded by Dr. Nadav Shimoni (MD) and Sam Cronin, backed by Arkin Capital. After Nir Arkin identified that digital health founders were missing dedicated early-stage capital, they launched in 2020 with one obsession: “Who will buy the product and why?” This focus led Nadav to relocate from Israel to New York, establishing dual operations to maximize market friction and build bridges for founders across the ocean.
The model worked. Their first fund ($20M, 2020) already returned capital to LPs through follow-on rounds despite launching during one of the toughest periods for early-stage digital health startups. Fund I backed 11 companies including Eleos, Rhino, Laguna, Siftwell, Nest Genomics, and Revisto.
Now they’re scaling with A-Squared Ventures Fund II, cutting $1M-$2M checks at Seed to Series A with notable LPs such as Shira Eting (Vintage Investment Partners), Tomer Goldberg (Harel Insurance), and continued backing from Nir Arkin and the Arkin family.
The fund leverages Arkin Capital’s $2B+ infrastructure for follow-on rounds, focusing on B2B/B2B2C healthcare IT, tech-enabled care delivery, pharma-tech, and AI-driven solutions for US healthcare.
No hardware. No bio. Only software for unmet business needs.
Here is our fireside chat:
What is your fund’s superpower in one sentence?
Dedicated initiation capital for digital health founders.
How long did the active fundraising process take?
Several months.
Did anybody help you during fundraising: existing LPs, fellow GPs, placement agents?
We had terrific support from our anchor LP - Arkin Capital.
How many LPs are in the final cap table, and what’s their breakdown?
We have a few strategic institutional LPs (including Israel's largest health insurance) and on top of it, prominent individuals from the healthcare industry.
What was the fastest check – time from first call to signed subscription?
One month.
What were the top 3 reasons LPs said “NO”?
Fund size (targeting larger funds as they want to deploy more into each fund).
Sector (prioritizing other sectors).
Stage (interested in exposure to later stages).
What were the top 3 signals that an LP was truly interested in your fund?
They shared a specific number they want to invest, asked for the legal documents and reverted afterwards with comments.
What did LPs actually pay close attention to during fundraising?
I think - honesty, integrality and performance.
What’s the biggest mistake fund managers make when fundraising?
Who am I to say...
What advice would you give to your future self and to other emerging managers about fundraising?
At the end, it is worth it!

Buy 10,000 shares of Coca-Cola this morning and you have made a set of assumptions so basic that you will never consciously notice them. You know the price to the cent. You can sell 1,000 shares tomorrow and keep the rest. You own a rounding error of the company, so nobody at Coca-Cola will ever learn your name. You will never speak to the CEO, and you would not expect to. If you change your mind in an hour, you are out.
Now write a $10 million check into a Series A round of an up-and-coming startup.
Every single one of those assumptions is gone. You will wait the better part of a decade. You will find it difficult to impossible to sell a piece of your position. You will own a large enough share that the founders certainly do know your name. You may even take a board seat, and you will probably talk to the CEO every other week. There is no daily price to tell you the value fluctuations of what you hold, because no market exists to produce one.
Hi, I’m Ilya. I teach Venture Capital and Private Equity at Stanford GSB, and this is where I publish my research — including the investor rankings— along with materials straight from my Stanford classes.
In this VC 101 post, I take the investor’s side and ask how different the VC asset class from traditional financial markets, such as buying stocks or bonds. The answer is: more different than almost anyone assumes. Founders and startup employees: you should also know this, because all of this will determine your ability to fundraise and be successful.
I will concentrate on five major differences. These five differences don’t exist by themselves, they are all part of the same system, in which each feature influences the next.
1. Horizon: you are committing for the better part of a decade
Let’s start with time, because it is the difference people often underestimate most.
Average years from first Series A to exit, U.S. companies, 1990-2025. IPO N = 1,774; M&A N = 9,142. Source: PitchBook.
In the 1990s, a VC-backed company that made it to an exit did so around three to five years after its Series A. Today it is closer to six or seven, for both IPOs and acquisitions. The horizon has roughly doubled in a generation and continues rising.
And this chart, if anything, flatters the industry, because it is conditional on exiting at all. It can only measure companies that reached an exit. One of the most consequential changes in venture capital over the past decade is that many of the best companies stay private for much longer, sometimes for fifteen years or more. SpaceX is an example I always give to my Stanford students, but there are so many more. A large fraction of US-based unicorns is still privately owned after ten and even fifteen years. In the World Economic Forum report that I co-authored earlier in 2026 we showed that globally, 59% of unicorns were private after being founded more than 10 years ago and 20% after being founded more than 15 years ago as of the end of March 2026! Even though SpaceX and several other unicorns have gone public since then, the overall picture has not changed.
So the true expected holding period for investors, unconditional on outcome, is longer than what you see on this chart.
Which is why perhaps the single most underrated attribute in this business is patience. The plain need to hold something for a decade separates the VC asset class from traditional financial markets.
Why is this so important? First, I met lots of investors new to the VC industry for whom that was a big surprise. That included some large and sophisticated capital allocators globally who assumed they could get return on their VC portfolio within two or three years. That also included leaders of large companies that established corporate VC funds and expected a positive return quickly. And that also included government regulators who believed venture capital offers them a quick turnaround.
Second, because the VC industry is very illiquid as the next section makes abundantly clear.
2. Liquidity: it is (almost) all or nothing, and the timing is not yours
A long horizon would be tolerable if you could change your mind. You cannot.
In public markets, position sizing is continuous and reversible. You can sell a tenth of your holding, trim on the way up, average down, or exit entirely, and you can do any of it in the next thirty seconds. Even for very large positions investors can change their position directionally by trading in blocks. The stock market is known as liquid. It gives investors an important advantage: they act upon information that arrives about the company or the overall economy. They also can act when they need cash for other projects. It is true that some publicly traded companies are more liquid than many others. Yet, the whole idea behind the public market is the ability to trade on information and your liquidity needs.
Startup investing does not allow you any of these luxuries. More often than not, investors wait until the exit known as a liquidity event: failure, acquisition, public listing. If the exit is an acquisition, your entire stake is sold in one transaction, at a price and on a date negotiated between the company and the acquirer. If the company goes public, you have marginally more discretion, but in practice many investors distribute or sell their holdings over a short window rather than trickling out over years.
The way I like to put it to my Stanford students: it is a pie you cannot slice, and you have to wait a very long time before anyone will let you eat it. Let us hope it has not gone cold.
Of course, as with anything in the VC world, there are lots of subtleties. Very early investors, especially angels, could sometimes sell their stakes to investors in later rounds. But most VCs could not sell even if they wished to because of information asymmetry and corporate governance constraints. Over the past fifteen years or so, there has been a noticeable increase in secondary markets activity, in which investors could trade their shares. However, most of this activity was really concentrated in common shares, owned by employees not by investors.
Going back to the WEF report, at the end of 2025, $3.2 trillion was “trapped” as unrealized net asset value in VC funds globally. That’s what VC funds have on the books as the values of their investments in portfolio companies. If you add to this the unrealized value of all the founders and employees of these startups, that will increase substantially, of course.
There is another important point I need to emphasize. As there is no active market, there is no readily established price. A public portfolio is marked to market more or less continuously. A venture portfolio is often marked at the last round, which is a number produced by a negotiation that may be eighteen months stale and is not equal to fair value in the first place.
3. Uncertainty: the power law, and why strikeouts do not matter
Let’s now turn to another critical difference between the VC asset class and traditional financial markets.
Public equity returns are roughly lognormal. Most stocks do something unremarkable, a few do very well, a few do badly, and the average is a meaningful description of the distribution.
Venture returns on individual portfolio companies tend to follow what is known as a power law, in which the outcome is dominated by the extreme right tail.
The classic evidence for this comes from William Kerr of Harvard Business School, Ramana Nanda now at Imperial College, and Matthew Rhodes-Kropf now with MIT Sloan, who in 2014 opened up the portfolio of one large and successful VC firm. They found that deals returning more than 10x were about 7% of the firm’s portfolio and produced roughly 60% of its returns. Meanwhile the deals that returned less than the money invested consumed the majority of the capital and produced almost nothing.
Seven percent of the deals. Sixty percent of the outcome. From a single firm, more than a decade ago — but the shape has held up, and it drives the entire strategic logic of the business.
The shape of a typical venture portfolio: twenty bets, most worth nothing, a few worth a little, one worth everything.
In The Venture Mindset, we called this principle “Homeruns matter, strike outs don’t.” The chart nicely visualizes the finding of Kerr and colleagues on a much larger dataset. Out of 20 early-stage bets one on average becomes a home run and a fund returner. Most other deals return nothing and a few return two to four times. One very successful investment determines whether the entire fund was worth the candle. Which means the losses, individually, do not matter. You cannot lose more than 1x on any single position, and the aggregate of your failures is capped. Your winners are not capped.
This inverts an asymmetry that public-market investors take for granted. As Bill Gurley of Benchmark put it: invest in something that does not work and you lose 1x your money; miss Google and you lose ten thousand times your money. Or, in Alex Rampell’s formulation, errors of omission are much bigger than errors of commission.
Public-market investors don’t think this way.
Here is a related insight that comes from my research with Blake Jackson on the careers of individual venture capitalists.
The power law operates across venture capitalists inside the industry. We can now see the power law applied across the whole profession: more than 16,000 U.S. venture professionals and 130,000 investments over three decades.
Cumulative share of successful investment outcomes by cumulative share of individual VCs. 134,166 investments in 68,010 startups by 16,427 VCs.
Start with the flat stretch on the left. About 60% of VCs who made at least one investment contributed exactly zero successful outcomes over their entire careers. The curve does not lift off the floor until you are past that point. At the other end, the top 1% of individual VCs account for 16.7% of all successful outcomes, and the top 5% account for 45.6%.
That is counting deals. Now count dollars, and it becomes far more extreme.
Cumulative share of estimated net profits by cumulative share of individual VCs. 99,243 investments by 12,151 VCs; $1.2 trillion in net profits, 2024 dollars.
The top 1% of individual venture capitalists, roughly 120 people, generated 56.7% of all net profit in our sample. The top 5%, around 600 people, generated 90.2%. The remaining 95% of the profession divided up what was left of $1.2 trillion, which is to say about a tenth of it.
This is one of the reasons venture capital resists some standard tools of traditional finance. In a normal asset class you typically discuss the average manager. In VC, average is also important but be careful because the difference between the average and the median is much larger, and the average tends to be driven by top performers.
4. Ownership: concentration is the strategy, not a failure of diversification
In traditional portfolio theory the answer to the question, what a rational investor should own, is: a small slice of many things. Diversify, hold the market, own a fraction of a percent of thousands of companies, and let the law of large numbers do its work.
The challenge with the VC industry is that you can’t diversify as it is not easy to hold a small slice of all VC-backed companies and all VC funds. Moreover, there is an adverse selection: the funds that are very easy to get into are typically not run by the managers that delivered the best returns in the past.
Too often, for capital allocators returns from the VC industry come from a few positions. Similarly, for VC funds, returns come from just a few (or one) investments in each fund.
Distribution of cumulative VC ownership stake at the end of each round. 28,000 Series A deals, 22,000 Series B and C deals, 8,900 Series D+ deals. Source: PitchBook, Stanford GSB VCI.
This is one reason for concentrated ownership in the VC industry. By the end of a Series A, venture investors often collectively hold about 40% of the company on average. By the end of Series B and C, that rises to about 57%. By Series D and beyond, about 60%. These are cumulative stakes across all VC investors rather than any single fund, but the contrast with public markets is instructive. A large mutual fund holding 5% of a public company is a major shareholder who files disclosures. In venture, the investor side of the table routinely owns the majority of the equity.
Notice that this follows directly from the previous section. It is not that VCs are undisciplined about concentration risk. It is that under the conditions they operate in, concentration is the strategy that tends to work better. A 1% stake in the company that returns 100x does very little for your fund if other bets fail. A 20% stake in the same company returns the fund several times over. (As always, there are lots of subtleties: if you thought about “spray and pray” strategy while reading this paragraph, I will have a separate post about it!)
5. Governance: VCs are an active bunch
How often VCs interact with their portfolio companies. Source: Gompers, Gornall, Kaplan, and Strebulaev (2020).
VCs also get actively involved in their portfolio companies. In our survey of venture capitalists, 61% said they interact with their portfolio companies at least once a week. Another 26% do so two or three times a month. Fewer than one in eight are in touch less often than that. Compare this to the lack of contact even a large public equity investor has with a company they own: often an earnings call four times a year and infrequent road trip meetings with the C-suite.
The involvement is not merely advisory. It comes with real control, exercised through board seats, protective provisions, and voting rights. This is one of the main reasons why the founder’s position looks so different from what most people assume.
What this means if you are on the other side of the table
If you are a founder, the five differences translate into five things you are actually agreeing to when you take the check. A partner who will be around for eight to ten years. An investor who cannot exit if things go badly, which makes them both unusually committed and unusually motivated to intervene. An economic model in which your investor needs you to attempt something enormous, because a solid, profitable, modest outcome does nothing for a fund that needs a hundred-bagger. A cap table on which investors collectively own the majority before you reach Series D. And a governance structure under which you are, statistically, more likely than not to be replaced as CEO before an IPO.
None of this is a warning. Venture capital has financed a remarkable share of the most valuable companies in the world, and for the right kind of company it is the only instrument that works. But it is a specific instrument with a specific shape, and the founders who do best with it are the ones who understood the shape before they signed.
Key takeaways
— The horizon has roughly doubled in a generation, from three to five years to six or seven, and published figures understate it because they only count companies that actually exited.
— There is no partial exit and no continuous price revelation. You sell the whole stake, at an exit you do not control, and everything in between is an estimate.
— Returns follow a power law. Errors of omission cost far more than errors of commission.
— The power law repeats one level up. Across the industry, about 60% of individual VCs never produce a single successful outcome, and 5% of VCs generated 90% of all profits.
— Concentration and control are critical for VCs. VCs collectively own about 40% after Series A and 60% by Series D. 61% talk to their companies weekly. Contractual terms reflect their corporate governance preferences.

Recently I wrote about how (not) to become a VC partner. It struck a nerve. But only some partners become truly successful at what they do. What about actually being good at the job and can we predict and explain it?
In this post, I will be diving not into what you are called, but what you actually backed. I will be answering the following questions: Over an entire career, how many genuinely successful investments does a venture capitalist make? Who makes many of them? And can we tell in advance who will?
Hi, I’m Ilya. I teach Venture Capital and Private Equity at Stanford GSB, and this is where I publish my research — including the investor rankings — along with materials straight from my Stanford classes.
Blake Jackson and I have assembled what we believe is the largest and most comprehensive dataset of individual U.S. venture capitalists ever built: over 100,000 professionals affiliated with U.S. VC firms between 1996 and 2025, roughly 37,000 of them investment professionals. Critically, we do not just observe the famous partners. We observe people as they enter the industry, and we track their firm affiliations, deals, their outcomes, and their backgrounds through their entire careers. The firms in our data raised and deployed 96% of all institutional U.S. venture capital over the sample period.
What we find is, I think, the single most sobering set of numbers I have published about this industry. It is also, in a fundamental way, encouraging. Let me explain both halves.
First, what counts as a hit
Let me be precise about what we call a “successful investment.” We count an investment as “successful” if the startup subsequently did at least one of three things:
— went public;
— reached a unicorn valuation, meaning a post-money valuation of at least $1 billion; or
— was acquired for at least five times the total capital the company had raised.
Each of these three does work the others cannot. IPOs are the standard measure in the academic literature, but U.S. IPO rates have fallen sharply over the past two decades, so an IPO-only measure would badly understate recent success. Unicorn valuations let us capture companies that are still private, which matters enormously for investments made after 2015. And the 5x acquisition threshold catches the large category of good outcomes that never make headlines. Our results largely hold if we use a 2x or a 10x threshold instead (with lots of interesting subtleties, though).
A caveat is in order: this is not a perfect definition. There are unicorns that subsequently failed. There are companies that failed within the first six months of their IPO (before most lock-up provisions that VCs are often subject to expire). But this definition is simple and cleanly measured and I believe quite robust to various changes, especially because our analysis here is not about one successful investment but many.
Another important point about the definition: the “subsequently” condition is critical. We include only investments that VCs made before at least one of these three outcomes took place.
A VC gets credit for an investment if we can attribute the deal to them individually, from PitchBook, VentureSource, the archived firm websites and biographies we parse ourselves, and from very helpful data providers such as StepStone Group (to whom we are very grateful!). Roughly half of the data points we assemble are not available in commercial datasets alone. About 49% of the deal attributions come from board seats; the rest come from lead-investor records and self-reported deal lists.
Two caveats on attribution are in order as well. First, attribution in venture capital is genuinely messy. Deals get claimed by more than one person. A famous saying in the VC industry is that success has many fathers and mothers, but failures are orphans. We see this in our data and have tried to unbias as much as possible. Credit inside a partnership is also not always given where it is due. And some VC partnerships do not attribute deals to individual VCs as a matter of principle or internal culture.
Second, this is a count of successful deals, not a return. A VC who wrote a $200,000 check into a company that later became a unicorn gets the same credit here as the partner who led the Series A. Later in this piece I will show what happens when we weight by dollars instead, and the picture gets overall more extreme, not less.
Throughout, I will show two samples. The wider one is all VC investment professionals with at least one attributed investment that comes up to 16,427 people. This sample includes junior professionals, such as associates. The narrower one is the 11,087 middle- and senior-level VCs, whom I will call the decision-makers, since they are the ones that typically lead and sit on boards.
One hit is not rare
Here is the first result, and it is the encouraging half.
All VC professionals with at least one investment, 1996-2025. N = 16,427.
38% of all VC investment professionals who ever made an investment have been credited with at least one successful one. Broken down by type: 29% have at least one 5x-plus acquisition, 19% have at least one IPO, and 17% have at least one unicorn. This is an interesting observation with the following insight: one-time success is not rare.
Among the decision-makers, the number is higher still.
Middle- and senior-level VCs with at least one investment, 1996-2025. N = 11,087.
45% of middle- and senior-level VCs have at least one successful investment. 36% have a 5x acquisition, 24% an IPO, 21% a unicorn.
This result tells us that close to half of everyone who reaches a decision-making seat in a U.S. venture firm has backed at least one company that went public, crossed a billion dollars, or returned five times the capital raised. Roughly a coin flip.
If your ambition is to be able to say, at the end of your career, that you backed one real winner, the odds are far better than the folklore suggests. And of course the flip side is just as true: a single hit is not evidence of skill. It is close to the base rate.
Am I surprised by this result? Not really. First, I see it elsewhere in our VC data. For example, investing in one unicorn is not rare at all. Second, VCs invest in a portfolio of companies. A typical VC may invest in dozens of companies in their career (even if it is a relatively short one). My research shows that a “homerun” happens in about one out of every twenty deals. My definition of “successful investments” is more encompassing (about one out of nine companies is “successful.”)
Two is harder. Ten is very rare.
Now the sobering half. Everything changes when you ask not whether a VC ever hit, but how often.
All VC professionals with at least one investment. N = 16,427.
Among all VC professionals, 38% reach one successful investment, 22% reach two, 8% reach five, and just 3% reach ten.
Middle- and senior-level VCs with at least one investment. N = 11,087.
Among the decision-makers, 45% reach one, 28% reach two, 11% reach five, and 3% reach ten.
Look at what happens between the first bar and the last. Getting to one is a coin flip. Getting to ten is a 3% event. Fewer than one out of nine VCs make five or more successful investments and fewer than one in 30 make ten or more.
I also plotted the same data showing the number of VCs in our data that made between one and 15 successful investments.
Middle- and senior-level VCs, 1996-2025. Bars show the share with at least k successful investments; the line and labels show the number of professionals. N = 11,087.
Just over 5,000 decision-makers in thirty years of U.S. venture capital have one successful investment. About 3,100 have two. Around 1,200 have five. Fewer than 400 have ten. Roughly 150 have fifteen.
Fewer than four hundred people is the entire population of U.S. venture capitalists over three decades credited with ten or more successful investments. It is smaller than the combined partner rosters of a handful of large firms, and it is the group most people are implicitly picturing when they say “venture capitalist.”
Note also that the curve does not fall off a cliff at any particular point. It decays smoothly, roughly geometrically, with each additional hit costing you something like a third of the surviving population. There is no number of wins after which the next one becomes easy. Being a successful VC is a tough job, indeed.
It is not surprising then that hitting so many successful investments is not a matter of luck. When we randomly reassign VCs across deals, the number of VCs with ten or more successful investments declines substantially. This lends further support to the thesis that skill plays a critical role in long-term VC success.
Where the wins actually pile up
One more way to see this. Instead of counting people, we can count outcomes and ask how they are distributed across the profession.
Cumulative share of successful investment outcomes by cumulative share of VCs. 134,166 investments in 68,010 startups by 16,427 VCs.
The flat stretch on the left tells the story. About 60% of VCs with at least one investment contribute exactly zero successful outcomes. The curve does not lift off the floor until you are past that point. At the other end, the top 1% of VCs account for 16.7% of all successful outcomes, and the top 5% account for 45.6%.
And when we move from counting wins to counting dollars, the concentration goes dramatically up. We estimate the net profits generated by every VC investment in our data, adjusting for the cost of the investment and for dilution across subsequent rounds. Across the whole sample, that comes to just over $1.2 trillion in 2024 dollars.
Cumulative share of estimated net profits by cumulative share of VCs. 99,243 investments in 52,709 startups by 12,151 VCs. Sample net profits are $1.2 trillion in 2024 dollars.
The top 1% of venture capitalists, about 120 people, account for 56.7% of all net profits in our data, roughly $680 billion. The top 5%, about 600 people, account for 90.2%, roughly $1.08 trillion. The remaining 95% of the profession splits the last $120 billion. These few hundred investors are the population our Strebulaev-Jackson Venture Ranking is built to identify, drawn from this same dataset; the full top 100 is here:
The conclusion from all of this analysis: the economics of venture capital are produced by a few hundred people, and the distance between “hit once” and “generated a billion dollars of net profit” is enormous.
Which raises the obvious question. If a few hundred people produce almost all the value in this industry, is there anything about them we could have seen coming?
There is, and a surprising amount of it is visible before a person makes their first investment. In the companion post I will show you which characteristics predict lifetime success and the single cleanest piece of evidence I have that any of this is skill rather than sorting.
In the meantime: does the shape of that curve match what you see from inside the industry? Please comment and ask questions in the comments!
